entry.title: Counting solutions faster than the Exponential Time Hypothesis allows
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 378 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-27

1. The question

Suppose a system has a million yes-or-no choices and a list of conditions involving small groups of those choices. Can we determine whether all the conditions can hold simultaneously? Can we count every successful choice without examining every possibility?

Boolean satisfiability turns this question into a precise mathematical problem. Trying all assignments to nnn variables takes roughly 2n2^n2n steps. Decades of algorithms have reduced the base of that exponential for important versions of the problem. The Exponential Time Hypothesis, or ETH, predicts that a genuinely subexponential algorithm for three-literal satisfiability is impossible.

Family 378 claims such an algorithm, and more: it counts all satisfying assignments exactly, deterministically, using polynomial memory. Its exponent grows more slowly than nnn. The claimed advance would therefore cross the boundary that ETH was introduced to describe.

2. Background and essential definitions

Formulas and their solutions

A Boolean variable takes the value zero or one. A literal is a variable or its negation; a clause is an OR of literals. A formula in conjunctive normal form, abbreviated CNF, is an AND of clauses. A kkk-CNF has at most kkk literals in each clause.

For example,

F(x,y)=(x∨y)∧(¬x∨y)F(x,y)=(x\lor y)\land(\neg x\lor y)F(x,y)=(x∨y)∧(¬x∨y)

has exactly two satisfying assignments: (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) and (1,1)(1,1)(1,1). Both clauses hold precisely when y=1y=1y=1, while xxx is free. The symbols ∨\lor∨, ∧\land∧, and ¬\neg¬ mean OR, AND, and NOT.

The decision problem asks whether a satisfying assignment exists. The counting problem asks for

#F=∣{x∈{0,1}n:F(x)=1}∣.\#F=\bigl|\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:F(x)=1\}\bigr|.#F=​{x∈{0,1}n:F(x)=1}​.

Knowing the count solves the decision problem by testing whether it is positive. The reverse direction is substantially less direct: even 2-SAT, whose decision version has a polynomial-time algorithm, has a difficult exact-counting version.

What “subexponential” means

Here nnn is the number of declared variables, mmm the number of clauses, and kkk a fixed constant. Polynomial factors in the input size are allowed. A bound 2o(n)2^{o(n)}2o(n) means that its base-two logarithm, divided by nnn, tends to zero.

For example, 1.1n1.1^n1.1n remains exponential: its exponent is a fixed positive multiple of nnn. In contrast, 2n/log⁡n2^{n/\sqrt{\log n}}2n/logn​ is subexponential. It can still be enormous. A subexponential upper bound alone does not give a polynomial-time algorithm.

ETH asserts a positive exponential barrier for worst-case 3-SAT. Its stronger relative, SETH, predicts that as the fixed clause width increases, the best exponential rate approaches exhaustive search. These are quantitative assumptions about running time, beyond the usual question of whether polynomial time is possible.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The class NP consists of decision problems whose positive answers have certificates checkable in polynomial time. The theory of NP-completeness established satisfiability as a universal encoding of these problems. It compares them through polynomial-size transformations. ETH arose from asking a finer question: which transformations preserve a linear scale in the exponent?

Impagliazzo and Paturi’s 2001 paper studied the dependence of satisfiability complexity on clause width. Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane developed reductions suited to exponential complexity, including the sparsification lemma. Roughly, sparsification expresses a formula through a controlled collection of formulas with few clause occurrences per variable. Its counting version arranges that different branches have disjoint solution sets, so their counts can be added.

Earlier algorithms had already beaten brute force. Schöning’s 1999 randomized algorithm repeatedly repairs an unsatisfied clause by randomly flipping one of its variables. For 3-SAT its guarantee has exponential factor (4/3)n(4/3)^n(4/3)n. The PPSZ approach instead processes variables in a random order, using logical deductions when possible and guesses otherwise. Later analyses improved its exponential rate; Scheder’s 2024 work obtained further gains without changing the algorithm itself. These improvements leave a fixed positive coefficient multiplying nnn in the exponent.

Exact counting developed alongside decision algorithms. Branching, inclusion–exclusion, and algebraic methods improved its running times, but the counting analogue of ETH still predicted an unavoidable exponential cost. Practical SAT solvers supplied another kind of progress: they could handle many structured instances without providing subexponential worst-case guarantees.

ETH and SETH consequently became foundations for conditional lower bounds in parameterized and fine-grained complexity. Such results explain why a particular dependence on a parameter, or a quadratic running time, may be difficult to improve. Family 378 addresses the fixed-width SAT assumption underlying many of those explanations.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Exact counting with polynomial memory

Theorem 1.1 of the October 25 manuscript states that, for every fixed k≥2k\ge2k≥2, a deterministic algorithm computes #F\#F#F in

(n+m)Ok(1)2Ok ⁣(nlog⁡log⁡n/log⁡n)(n+m)^{O_k(1)}2^{O_k\!\left(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n}\right)}(n+m)Ok​(1)2Ok​(nloglogn/logn​)

bit operations, using (n+m)Ok(1)(n+m)^{O_k(1)}(n+m)Ok​(1) bits of memory. The subscript kkk permits constants to depend on the fixed width. Logarithms are natural here; changing their base only affects constants. The statement is formulated for n≥20n\ge20n≥20, with smaller inputs handled directly.

When the clause density is bounded, meaning m≤Dnm\le Dnm≤Dn for a fixed constant D>0D>0D>0, the claimed running time improves to

(n+m)Ok,D(1)2Ok,D ⁣(n/log⁡n).(n+m)^{O_{k,D}(1)}2^{O_{k,D}\!\left(n/\sqrt{\log n}\right)}.(n+m)Ok,D​(1)2Ok,D​(n/logn​).

These are bit-complexity bounds: operations on large integers are charged for their bit lengths. Polynomial space means the procedure avoids storing an exponentially large table, even though it performs a very large number of steps.

Consequences stated in the paper

Testing the count refutes ETH and its counting version. Since the theorem covers every fixed width, the manuscript also derives refutations of SETH and related gap and nondeterministic variants. A positive count can be converted into an actual satisfying assignment by fixing variables successively and checking which partial choice leaves solutions.

Other consequences have distinct guarantees. Conditional counts yield exactly uniform random satisfying assignments with polynomial expected overhead. A randomized approximation algorithm finds an assignment satisfying at least OPT⁡(F)−εm\operatorname{OPT}(F)-\varepsilon mOPT(F)−εm clauses, for any fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, in subexponential time. Here OPT⁡(F)\operatorname{OPT}(F)OPT(F) is the largest satisfiable number of clauses; the approximation has exponentially small failure probability.

For a graph with vvv vertices and eee edges, the paper gives deterministic algorithms counting independent sets and proper colorings with a fixed number of colors in 2o(v)2^{o(v)}2o(v) time. Its perfect-matching bound is 2o(v+e)2^{o(v+e)}2o(v+e), a different size parameter. An independent set contains no adjacent pair, a proper coloring gives adjacent vertices different colors, and a perfect matching pairs every vertex along selected edges.

The algorithm also gives a lower bound elsewhere. Corollary 1.4 states that some language LLL in ENP\mathsf E^{\mathsf{NP}}ENP has

CL(n)>c nlog⁡nC_L(n)>c\,n\sqrt{\log n}CL​(n)>cnlogn​

for a constant c>0c>0c>0 and infinitely many input lengths. The class ENP\mathsf E^{\mathsf{NP}}ENP allows deterministic 2O(n)2^{O(n)}2O(n) time with access to an oracle answering NP decision questions. The quantity CL(n)C_L(n)CL​(n) counts noninput gates in the smallest Boolean circuit for length-nnn inputs, allowing gates with at most two inputs. This is a specific superlinear lower bound with explicit quantifiers.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this result overturns one of the central quantitative assumptions in computational complexity. Improving an exponential base would strengthen an existing algorithmic tradition; making the exponent sublinear changes the type of running time that is possible.

Exact counting adds significance because it preserves much more information than a yes-or-no answer. Counts support sampling, optimization reductions, and combinatorial enumeration. Polynomial memory also avoids a common tradeoff in which faster search requires storing a huge collection of partial solutions.

The circuit consequence illustrates a productive connection established by Williams’s work on algorithms and lower bounds: an unexpectedly efficient search algorithm can imply that some other functions require large circuits. Thus an algorithmic upper bound can produce a complexity lower bound.

The consequences for conditional hardness need careful interpretation. A theorem saying “a faster algorithm would contradict ETH” remains a valid implication. If ETH is false, that implication no longer supplies the same reason to expect hardness. It does not itself construct the faster algorithm for the target problem.

6. The main idea

Turn logical conditions into algebra

For the clause xa∨¬xb∨xcx_a\lor\neg x_b\lor x_cxa​∨¬xb​∨xc​, the polynomial

Φ(xa,xb,xc)=1−(1−xa)xb(1−xc)\Phi(x_a,x_b,x_c)=1-(1-x_a)x_b(1-x_c)Φ(xa​,xb​,xc​)=1−(1−xa​)xb​(1−xc​)

equals one exactly when the clause holds, on Boolean inputs. Multiplying these indicators over clauses and summing over all assignments gives the exact count. This identity is easy; evaluating the resulting sum efficiently is the challenge.

If clauses connected variables only within small independent groups, one could count each group separately and multiply. General formulas have clauses crossing groups. The manuscript introduces algebraic replacements that make those interactions depend on a small collection of shared linear measurements, such as weighted sums of bits in a group.

Once the measurements are fixed, each group can be summed independently. The algorithm enumerates possible measurement values and small-group assignments, then combines their contributions. The construction must keep both enumerations small enough to save time.

Recover a difficult value from easier evaluations

The replacements depend polynomially on a parameter TTT. At T=0T=0T=0 they restore the original variables, giving a polynomial HHH with H(0)=#FH(0)=\#FH(0)=#F. At selected nonzero values of TTT, they admit the group decomposition.

The transformed expressions need not represent Boolean clauses at those other points. They are algebraic evaluations used to recover the original integer count. The paper constructs replacement forms of low degree through a matrix decomposition with few independent shared measurements and restricted nonzero entries.

Ordinary interpolation recovers a bounded-degree polynomial from enough values. Here the procedure also computes Taylor coefficients at its evaluation points. Hermite interpolation reconstructs a polynomial from this richer data. For instance, a quadratic is determined by its value and derivative at one point together with its value at a second point. The manuscript uses a much larger, carefully balanced version of this principle.

For arbitrary formulas, disjoint sparsification controls clause occurrences. Parity tests then encode whether an assignment violates selected clauses. The tests are constructed so that passing all of them is equivalent to satisfying the formula. Their deterministic construction uses exact counting for sparse polynomial systems, which is developed before it is used to solve SAT.

Sharpen the bound through tensor contraction

Appendix D obtains the stronger stated running times. A tensor here is a table with one Boolean index for each incident connection. Clause tables record satisfaction, and equality tables require different occurrences of a variable to agree. Multiplying table entries and summing over internal Boolean indices—contracting the network—counts satisfying assignments.

The proposed contraction algorithm recursively deforms connections to separate groups. It works with exact arithmetic modulo powers of two. Terms carrying sufficiently many factors of two vanish at the required precision, allowing the expansion to be truncated. Carefully chosen interpolation data and recursive group sizes control the work across all levels.

The arithmetic remains exact for the desired answer: since 0≤#F≤2n0\le\#F\le2^n0≤#F≤2n, its residue modulo 2n+12^{n+1}2n+1 uniquely determines it. Processing branches and intermediate sums sequentially supplies the polynomial-space guarantee. The general-density case combines this contraction method with the sparse polynomial encoding.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The width kkk is fixed. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on it; the theorem gives no comparable uniform guarantee when clause width grows with nnn. It is also an asymptotic result, with no practical crossover point established by the displayed bounds.

The claimed subexponential algorithm does not settle P versus NP. Nor do ordinary polynomial reductions transfer its running time unchanged: replacing an input of size NNN by a formula with N3N^3N3 variables can consume a subexponential saving. Faster algorithms for other problems require reductions controlling the relevant size parameter.

Some hardness conjectures weaker than SETH, including the Orthogonal Vectors Conjecture discussed in the manuscript, might still hold. Refuting a sufficient assumption for them does not refute those conjectures themselves. Finding useful replacement assumptions and extracting further algorithms are separate research questions.

The repository’s formalization description reports deterministic exact counting and polynomial space with the weaker exponent

Ok ⁣(n(log⁡log⁡n)2/log⁡n).O_k\!\left(n(\log\log n)^2/\sqrt{\log n}\right).Ok​(n(loglogn)2/logn​).

It distinguishes that bound from the sharper manuscript bounds above. The release announcement also describes a planned independent examination led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi and Ryan Williams; it does not report a completed assessment.

8. Sources and further reading

The principal statements are Theorem 1.1 and Corollaries 1.2–1.4. Section 2 explains the interpolation method; Sections 3–6 develop exact counting and its SAT reduction; Appendix D gives the sharper bounds through tensor contraction. Section 1.1 discusses earlier algorithms and implications for fine-grained complexity.

The linked papers by Impagliazzo–Paturi and Impagliazzo–Paturi–Zane supply the historical formulation and sparsification framework. Schöning and Scheder illustrate the earlier progress on exponential rates; Williams explains the algorithms-to-lower-bounds connection.

Optional background: Boolean satisfiability, the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and Hermite interpolation.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False (October 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 27 October 2026 at repository revision 7ef5c0c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A smooth surface metric that cannot fit locally in three-space
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 334 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A small piece of a smooth surface seems like something that ought to fit into three-dimensional space. But suppose the starting object is an abstract rule for measuring lengths, rather than a surface already sitting in space. Must some sufficiently small neighborhood have a smooth realization with exactly those measurements?

Family 334 claims that the answer is no. It constructs a smooth positive-definite metric on a square for which no neighborhood of the origin admits a smooth isometric immersion into R3\mathbb R^3R3.

The proposed example has a further surprise: at the origin, the metric agrees with the ordinary Euclidean metric to every derivative order. No finite Taylor expansion there detects a difference, and even the full formal Taylor series is the same. The obstruction is encoded in increasingly small surrounding regions.

This is a local statement. It does not rely on holes, global topology, completeness, or the difficulty of closing a surface up. It concerns whether a single neighborhood can be realized smoothly at all.

2. Background and essential definitions

A Riemannian metric on a planar domain is a smooth positive-definite symmetric matrix field g=(gij)g=(g_{ij})g=(gij​). A tangent vector vvv has squared length vTgvv^{\mathsf T}gvvTgv. Positive definiteness ensures that every nonzero vector has positive length. It says nothing about the sign of the metric’s Gaussian curvature.

A map F=(F1,F2,F3)F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)F=(F1​,F2​,F3​) is an isometric immersion if

⟨∂iF,∂jF⟩=gij(i,j∈{1,2}).\langle\partial_iF,\partial_jF\rangle=g_{ij}\qquad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).⟨∂i​F,∂j​F⟩=gij​(i,j∈{1,2}).

The derivative must have rank two. An immersion is locally an embedding after shrinking around a point, so the local existence questions for smooth immersions and smooth embeddings have the same content here. This differs from global problems, where self-intersections matter.

The Gaussian curvature KKK is determined by the metric and its derivatives. Positive curvature resembles a sphere locally, negative curvature a saddle, and zero curvature marks a potentially degenerate transition. These descriptions are geometric intuition, not complete local classifications.

Smooth means C∞C^\inftyC∞. Analytic means that a function equals a convergent power series near every point. Analytic functions are smooth, but smooth functions can be invisible to their Taylor series at one point. For example,

ψ(r)={e−1/r2,r≠0,0,r=0\psi(r)=\begin{cases}e^{-1/r^2},&r\ne0,\\0,&r=0\end{cases}ψ(r)={e−1/r2,0,​r=0,r=0​

has every derivative zero at zero but is positive elsewhere. This illustrates the kind of distinction that makes agreement of all Taylor coefficients compatible with different nearby geometry.

The full Taylor jet of a metric at a point is the collection of all derivatives of its coefficients there. Equality with the Euclidean jet means that the difference from du2+dv2du^2+dv^2du2+dv2 has every partial derivative zero at the origin. It does not mean that the metric equals the Euclidean metric on a neighborhood.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The analytic local problem was settled by the Janet–Cartan theorem: analytic surface metrics have local isometric realizations in three-space. Smooth metrics with nonzero Gaussian curvature also admit local smooth realizations through equations of elliptic or hyperbolic type. The difficult cases arise where curvature vanishes and the equation degenerates or changes type.

Lin established foundational results for nonnegative curvature and for clean changes of sign, with finite-differentiability estimates. A clean sign change means that K=0K=0K=0 but its differential is nonzero at the point. Nakamura and Maeda obtained smooth local existence under that condition. Later work treated more complicated zero sets, including transverse curves and cusps, under additional finite-order and geometric assumptions.

Regularity must be tracked on both sides of these results. A theorem producing a CmC^mCm immersion for each finite mmm, on neighborhoods that may shrink with mmm, does not automatically supply one C∞C^\inftyC∞ immersion on one fixed neighborhood. At lower regularity, Nash–Kuiper flexibility gives C1C^1C1 realizations, but these do not carry the second-order bending information used in a smooth obstruction.

Pogorelov constructed a C2,1C^{2,1}C2,1 metric with no local C2C^2C2 realization. The notation means that second derivatives are Lipschitz continuous. Nadirashvili and Yuan’s published refinement achieved such a counterexample with nonnegative curvature. These input metrics are less regular than the smooth metric claimed in M1.

There is a historical discrepancy that M1 explicitly leaves unresolved. A 2002 Nadirashvili–Yuan preprint states a smooth nonpositively curved counterexample with no local C3C^3C3 embedding. Their later published paper, and later literature cited by M1, describe the unrestricted smooth question as still open. The present digest reports those different statements without deciding between them. M1 does not use the earlier nonsolvability claim; it offers its own analytical obstruction.

4. What the new manuscript claims

M1 states that there is a smooth positive-definite metric ggg on (−1,1)2(-1,1)^2(−1,1)2 for which no open neighborhood UUU of the origin admits a smooth isometric immersion

F:(U,g)⟶R3.F:(U,g)\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3.F:(U,g)⟶R3.

The metric can additionally be chosen so that

∂α(gij−δij)(0)=0\partial^\alpha(g_{ij}-\delta_{ij})(0)=0∂α(gij​−δij​)(0)=0

for every multi-index α\alphaα and every i,ji,ji,j. A multi-index records how many derivatives are taken in each coordinate, and δij\delta_{ij}δij​ are the coefficients of the Euclidean metric.

The construction uses both positive and negative Gaussian curvature. It therefore does not settle the corresponding smooth local-existence question under either global sign restriction K≥0K\geq0K≥0 or K≤0K\leq0K≤0.

An intermediate statement obstructs certain scalar height functions on an entire fixed square. These heights must satisfy the Darboux equation, have gradient norm below one, have a nonzero selected diagonal Hessian entry, and have a sufficiently small mixed-to-diagonal Hessian ratio. The manuscript finds obstructing metrics densely, in the stronger sense of a residual set, within a specified space of perturbations.

This intermediate claim does not exclude every locally defined height on every tiny neighborhood of that square. In fact, its curvature zeros are clean sign changes, compatible with known pointwise local-existence theorems. The final construction is needed to ensure that any hypothetical immersion near the origin would induce one of the prohibited heights on a full selected square.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family claims a negative resolution of the unrestricted smooth local realization problem in three-space, a central boundary case in the geometry of isometric immersions.

Its force comes from combining maximum regularity of the metric with a genuinely local obstruction. There is no rough corner in the metric, no global topological obstruction, and no prescribed boundary behavior making the problem artificially restrictive.

Agreement with the entire Euclidean Taylor jet gives a particularly clear lesson about smooth geometry. Formal information at one point can fail to determine whether a neighborhood admits a smooth geometric realization. The arrangement of nearby regions matters even when every derivative measured exactly at the distinguished point looks flat.

The family complements the four-dimensional claim in family 333. An additional ambient direction changes the realization problem substantially. This comparison concerns the stated theorems; the digest does not independently establish their validity or settle the conflicting historical accounts.

6. The main idea

Reduce an immersion to a scalar equation

Choose a fixed unit vector eee in ambient three-space. Any hypothetical immersion gives a height function z=⟨F,e⟩z=\langle F,e\ranglez=⟨F,e⟩. Its covariant Hessian is the surface-corrected second derivative: in coordinates,

Hij=∂i∂jz−Γijr∂rz,H_{ij}=\partial_i\partial_jz-\Gamma^r_{ij}\partial_rz,Hij​=∂i​∂j​z−Γijr​∂r​z,

where the Christoffel coefficients Γijr\Gamma^r_{ij}Γijr​ are determined by the metric, and the repeated index rrr is summed. These corrections make the Hessian independent of the chosen coordinate description.

The Gauss equation, relating intrinsic curvature to extrinsic bending, implies the necessary Darboux equation

H11H22−H122=Kdet⁡(g)(1−∣dz∣g2).H_{11}H_{22}-H_{12}^2=K\det(g)\bigl(1-|dz|_g^2\bigr).H11​H22​−H122​=Kdet(g)(1−∣dz∣g2​).

The source uses only necessity: excluding an appropriate height excludes the corresponding immersion. It does not need to reconstruct an immersion from every solution of this scalar equation.

Obstruct a height across a whole patch

The model patch has a negative-curvature center and a positive-curvature exterior. Two cap regions provide estimates on opposite sides of a thin central slab. M1 claims that fixed low-order control of an admissible height, together with all-order control of the metric, yields all-order interior control on the caps. No high-order boundary data are imposed on the artificial edges facing the central region.

The manuscript then perturbs the metric itself in a thin oscillating strip. This is important: constructing an arbitrary unsolvable second-order equation would not suffice, because the Darboux coefficients must come from one actual Riemannian metric.

An integral test isolates the high-frequency effect forced by the strip. The strip width is chosen proportional to a small parameter divided by its oscillation frequency. The desired forcing is linear in that parameter, while leading competing terms are quadratic; smooth endpoint data have a small high-frequency contribution. M1 uses this separation of scales to exclude heights in each fixed bounded class.

A Baire-category argument then removes the a priori bounds. In this setting, a residual set is a countable intersection of open dense sets. One can organize candidate heights into countably many bounded classes and avoid all of them simultaneously. This is an existence argument about a complete function-space topology, not a probability distribution over metrics.

Make every hypothetical immersion encounter an obstruction

The geometric assembly places smaller obstructed patches around the boundary of a negatively curved disk. A boundary-saddle argument forces any hypothetical graph realization to have a boundary point where its second fundamental form is nonzero and rank one.

Taking the height in the normal direction at that point gives zero first derivative and a Hessian equal to the second fundamental form. In coordinates aligned with its kernel, the mixed Hessian entry vanishes while a transverse diagonal entry remains nonzero. A nearby orientation from a fixed finite collection retains the strict inequalities required by the patch obstruction.

This is why the argument uses patches approaching boundary points in several orientations. The immersion gets to choose its bending directions, so the metric construction must ensure that at least one whole patch detects whichever direction occurs.

Finally, disks with their surrounding patches accumulate at the origin. Their amplitudes are chosen sufficiently small that the total metric remains positive definite and smooth, with the Euclidean Taylor jet at the origin. Any neighborhood of the origin contains one of these complete configurations. A hypothetical smooth immersion there would produce a forbidden height on one of its patches, giving the claimed contradiction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The asserted obstruction is to smooth immersions for a smooth metric. It should not be silently strengthened to nonexistence at a specified finite differentiability class. Conversely, it does not obstruct the low-regularity realizations furnished by C1C^1C1 flexibility.

The metric has mixed-sign curvature. Smooth local realization under either one-sided curvature restriction remains outside this theorem’s conclusion. Positive definiteness of the metric must not be confused with positive curvature.

The whole-square analytical obstruction and the final local obstruction have different roles. The former concerns a restricted class of heights on a fixed domain; the latter follows only after the geometric construction forces any immersion to produce such a height somewhere. Retaining that distinction prevents an apparent conflict with known local existence at clean curvature zeros.

The source does not claim uniform estimates as the curvature amplitude of its shrinking patches tends to zero. Nor does it offer a simple finite formula from which a practical obstruction test for arbitrary smooth metrics follows. Classification of realizable smooth metrics, finite-regularity thresholds, and sign-restricted problems remain separate directions.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Ghomi, Open problems in geometry of curves and surfaces, for the local realization question.
  • Nadirashvili and Yuan, Improving Pogorelov’s isometric embedding counterexample, for the published finite-regularity result and historical discussion.
  • Nadirashvili and Yuan, Counterexamples for local isometric embedding, version 1, for the earlier claim whose status M1 leaves unresolved.
  • Optional background: isometric immersions and the second fundamental form.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Smooth Metric with No Local Isometric Immersion into Three-Space (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Every closed surface metric in four-dimensional Euclidean space
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 333 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Imagine a surface equipped with a complete set of instructions for measuring lengths and angles. Can that geometry be realized as a surface sitting in ordinary Euclidean space, without stretching any tangent direction?

A round sphere has an obvious realization in three dimensions. A general metric on a general surface need not resemble that familiar example. Its curvature may change sign, its topology may be complicated, and the lengths prescribed in neighboring coordinate patches must fit together globally.

Family 333 claims that four ambient dimensions always suffice for a smooth isometric immersion of a closed surface. Here “closed” means compact and without boundary. “Immersion” allows self-intersections: different points of the abstract surface may occupy the same location, although each small patch remains a regular surface. The manuscript includes nonorientable and disconnected surfaces, with no restriction on Gaussian curvature.

The question is about preserving the geometry measured along the surface. It does not ask for the ambient straight-line distance between every pair of image points to equal their intrinsic surface distance. Even a round sphere would fail that stronger requirement: its chords are shorter than its surface arcs.

2. Background and essential definitions

A smooth surface MMM is a space locally described by two real coordinates with smooth changes of coordinates. A Riemannian metric assigns an inner product gpg_pgp​ to the tangent plane at each point ppp, varying smoothly with ppp.

In local coordinates (u,v)(u,v)(u,v), write

g=g11 du2+2g12 du dv+g22 dv2.g=g_{11}\,du^2+2g_{12}\,du\,dv+g_{22}\,dv^2.g=g11​du2+2g12​dudv+g22​dv2.

The symmetric matrix (gij)(g_{ij})(gij​) is positive definite. It determines lengths of tangent vectors, angles, areas, and lengths of curves. Gaussian curvature is an intrinsic quantity derived from this metric; it describes how the local geometry differs from the flat plane.

A smooth map F:M→R4F:M\to\mathbb R^4F:M→R4 is an isometric immersion when its derivative preserves every tangent inner product:

⟨dFp(a),dFp(b)⟩=gp(a,b).\langle dF_p(a),dF_p(b)\rangle=g_p(a,b).⟨dFp​(a),dFp​(b)⟩=gp​(a,b).

In coordinates, this becomes the three equations

⟨Fu,Fu⟩=g11,⟨Fu,Fv⟩=g12,⟨Fv,Fv⟩=g22.\langle F_u,F_u\rangle=g_{11},\qquad\langle F_u,F_v\rangle=g_{12},\qquad\langle F_v,F_v\rangle=g_{22}.⟨Fu​,Fu​⟩=g11​,⟨Fu​,Fv​⟩=g12​,⟨Fv​,Fv​⟩=g22​.

Positive definiteness ensures that the two derivative vectors are linearly independent. An embedding adds a global requirement: the surface must be realized without identifying distinct points. The theorem here only asserts immersion.

An elementary four-dimensional example is a product of circles:

F(u,v)=(acos⁡u,asin⁡u,bcos⁡v,bsin⁡v).F(u,v)=(a\cos u,a\sin u,b\cos v,b\sin v).F(u,v)=(acosu,asinu,bcosv,bsinv).

For positive a,ba,ba,b and periodic coordinates, this realizes a flat torus with metric a2du2+b2dv2a^2du^2+b^2dv^2a2du2+b2dv2. It illustrates how an extra ambient direction can accommodate geometry that is not represented by the familiar curved doughnut in three-space. It does not by itself address arbitrary surface metrics.

Finally, C∞C^\inftyC∞, or smooth, means that derivatives of every order exist and are continuous. This is much stronger than C1C^1C1, which controls only the map and its first derivatives. The difference is central because the metric uses first derivatives, while classical curvature and bending involve second derivatives.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The local analytic theory is an early landmark. Janet and Cartan showed that an analytic two-dimensional Riemannian metric has a local isometric realization in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Analytic means locally representable by convergent power series. Both the regularity hypothesis and the local conclusion matter: neither can simply be replaced by an arbitrary smooth closed-surface statement.

Nash’s smooth embedding theorem established a far-reaching global existence principle in higher dimension. His original compact-manifold bound is n(3n+11)/2n(3n+11)/2n(3n+11)/2, which gives seventeen ambient dimensions for surfaces. This provides an embedding, a stronger global conclusion, but in substantially more room than the present four-dimensional immersion problem.

Gromov obtained smooth isometric immersions of closed surfaces into five-space. He also recorded the four-space question and later attributed it to Chern around 1950, while noting uncertainty about the original compactness qualification. M1 specifically addresses closed surfaces, so its scope should not be enlarged to every possible noncompact formulation of that historical question.

There was already a smooth four-dimensional theory for suitable planar domains. Poznyak’s work gives isometric immersions on compact portions of simply connected domains, with corresponding finite-regularity statements. Lewicka’s modern account explains the smooth version and develops finer flexibility results for metrics of low Hölder regularity. These theorems do not automatically assemble into a realization of an arbitrary closed surface: corrections in one patch must preserve the geometric conditions needed in later patches.

A different line of progress comes from Nash and Kuiper. Their oscillatory constructions produce C1C^1C1 isometric immersions approximating strictly short immersions. A map is strictly short when its induced metric is strictly smaller than the desired metric in every tangent direction. The flexibility available at C1C^1C1 regularity is striking, but it does not settle a C∞C^\inftyC∞ problem.

Family 334 supplies a complementary claimed obstruction in three-space: a smooth metric with no local smooth isometric immersion near one point. Together, the two families concern a sharp contrast between the smooth local three-dimensional problem and the smooth global closed-surface four-dimensional problem.

4. What the new manuscript claims

M1 states that every closed smooth Riemannian surface (M,g)(M,g)(M,g) admits a smooth map F:M→R4F:M\to\mathbb R^4F:M→R4 satisfying

F∗δ4=g,δ4=dx12+dx22+dx32+dx42.F^*\delta_4=g,\qquad\delta_4=dx_1^2+dx_2^2+dx_3^2+dx_4^2.F∗δ4​=g,δ4​=dx12​+dx22​+dx32​+dx42​.

The notation F∗δ4F^*\delta_4F∗δ4​ means the Euclidean metric pulled back by FFF: evaluate Euclidean inner products after applying its derivative. Thus the equality is exact, not an approximation or a limiting assertion about separate maps without a smooth limit.

There are no orientability, connectedness, or Gaussian-curvature restrictions. In particular, the statement covers smooth metrics on nonorientable closed surfaces. The resulting map can have self-intersections, and M1 does not claim that every such surface metric admits an isometric embedding into four-space.

The construction uses a finite list of positive local metric additions. Each addition includes an infinite smoothing iteration that converges in every smooth norm. Calling the global assembly finite therefore does not mean that an exact immersion is obtained after finitely many elementary numerical operations.

A central analytical ingredient is an exact correction theorem under a condition on the second fundamental form, which records how tangent planes bend into the normal directions. The manuscript requires this vector-valued tensor to be nonzero at every point in the relevant correction step. It does not assume the stronger rank conditions that would supply a simple global inverse for the linearized metric equation.

That intermediate condition is arranged and preserved by the construction. It is not an additional hypothesis on the surface metric in the main theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claim reaches a central low-dimensional target in the theory of smooth isometric immersions, lowering the known closed-surface immersion dimension from five to four without curvature or orientability assumptions.

The ambient dimension is not a superficial parameter. A two-dimensional surface in four-space has only two normal directions in which to bend. Metric correction must use that limited freedom while controlling the compatibility equations and all derivative orders. A general high-dimensional existence theorem does not explain how to accomplish this in codimension two.

The result would also clarify the division between local flexibility and global geometry. Having an immersion on each coordinate disk does not ensure that those disks can be joined isometrically. The manuscript’s claimed advance is a construction that keeps later corrections possible while modifying earlier regions.

The importance score concerns the theorem’s stated significance if correct. It does not certify the analytical argument or compare its reliability with independently checked results.

6. The main idea

Start with a smaller metric

The construction begins with an ordinary smooth immersion into a small round three-sphere inside R4\mathbb R^4R4. After scaling, its induced metric g0g_0g0​ is strictly below ggg. The inward radial direction provides a globally defined normal vector field, even when the surface itself is nonorientable.

The positive deficit is decomposed into finitely many local rank-one pieces:

g−g0=∑j=1Jaj2 dxj2.g-g_0=\sum_{j=1}^{J}a_j^2\,dx_j^2.g−g0​=j=1∑J​aj2​dxj2​.

Each coordinate function xjx_jxj​ belongs to a disk, and the smooth amplitude aja_jaj​ vanishes outside that disk. A rank-one piece adds length in one selected direction. The decomposition is prepared with conditions on the intermediate metrics, because the order of the additions affects what the next step can do.

Add one direction of length by oscillation

For one piece a2dx2a^2dx^2a2dx2, choose a complementary coordinate yyy. The manuscript places a periodic velocity loop in a plane perpendicular to both FyF_yFy​ and FyyF_{yy}Fyy​. Its mean is prescribed, while its circular motion supplies the desired extra contribution to the metric.

The idea resembles adding a fine corrugation to increase length along one direction, but the argument must preserve far more than a picture of corrugations suggests. Orthogonality to the second derivative FyyF_{yy}Fyy​ removes a leading transverse error. Further finite corrections cancel oscillatory errors to a chosen high order; separate slower-scale corrections handle the remaining mean terms.

Make the metric exact while retaining smoothness

High-frequency oscillation can make a map small in position while making its higher derivatives large. This is why an approximation in the visible shape is not enough. The source develops small oscillatory corrections with controlled second derivatives and solves the linearized metric equations mode by mode to high finite accuracy.

Smoothing between successive corrections controls the loss of derivatives. Increasing the required accuracy in successive blocks yields convergence in every CmC^mCm norm, for every fixed derivative order mmm. The endpoint is one smooth map with the exact metric, not merely a C1C^1C1 realization.

Preserve the geometry for later disks

A large oscillation can rotate or degenerate normal directions that a later patch needs. M1 therefore keeps track of specified boundary curves, crossings, preferred normals, and transverse derivatives. It chooses the velocity loop at its turns so that the necessary directions remain usable. The subsequent small exact correction preserves those conditions.

This last stage is the global compatibility mechanism. It allows the finite sequence of primitive additions to continue until their sum fills the entire metric deficit. The paper separates the large operation that adds length from the small operation that removes error, assigning each a different role in controlling second-order geometry.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns compact boundaryless surfaces with smooth positive-definite metrics and smooth immersions. It does not assert a general embedding theorem in four-space, a boundary-value theorem with prescribed boundary data, or a corresponding result for every complete noncompact surface.

Nor does it claim that every metric can be realized smoothly in three-space. Analytic local results and low-regularity flexibility theorems have different hypotheses and conclusions; the companion smooth local obstruction is part of that distinction.

The construction is existential and analytical. Its finite global decomposition still relies on limiting corrections. The statement does not provide a practical algorithm with effective complexity bounds or a way to visualize arbitrary exact realizations without self-intersections.

Questions about global injectivity, additional geometric constraints on the immersion, effective estimates, and other domain classes remain separate from the claim discussed here. This digest reports the manuscript’s theorem and mechanism without independently verifying the proof.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Nash, The imbedding problem for Riemannian manifolds, for the smooth high-dimensional existence theorem.
  • Gromov, Geometric, algebraic and analytic descendants of Nash isometric embedding theorems, for historical context and the five-dimensional surface result.
  • Lewicka, Full flexibility of isometric immersions in Poznyak’s dimension, version 3, for planar-domain results and the regularity distinction.
  • Family 334 discusses the claimed smooth local obstruction in three dimensions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Smooth isometric immersions of closed surfaces into Euclidean four-space (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How negative scalar curvature pays for topological complexity
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 335 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A metric describes the local shape of a manifold; topology describes features that survive continuous deformation. How strongly can a coarse local curvature measurement constrain global topology?

Scalar curvature is the most averaged of the standard curvature quantities. It combines curvature in all tangent two-dimensional directions into one number at each point. Positive contributions can compensate for negative ones, so a scalar lower bound contains much less information than a lower bound in every direction.

Family 335 claims two powerful connections. One manuscript states that a manifold’s simplicial volume, a topological measure of the cost of representing its fundamental class, is bounded by the integrated negative part of scalar curvature. The other states that strictly positive scalar curvature forces the fundamental class to disappear when mapped to the topology of the fundamental group.

The second claim implies the Gromov–Lawson obstruction for closed aspherical manifolds and supplies a vanishing theorem used by the first manuscript. The family therefore has a qualitative foundation and a further quantitative assertion, rather than two independent formulations of exactly the same result.

2. Background and essential definitions

A smooth nnn-manifold is locally modeled on Rn\mathbb R^nRn. A Riemannian metric ggg supplies lengths, angles, and a volume element dVgdV_gdVg​. Here “closed” means compact without boundary, and an orientation makes signed top-dimensional volume and a fundamental class available.

At a point, sectional curvature measures curvature in a chosen tangent two-plane. Ricci curvature sums suitable sectional curvatures while retaining a direction. Scalar curvature Scalg\mathrm{Scal}_gScalg​ takes a further trace, producing a single function. In dimension two it is twice Gaussian curvature; in higher dimensions its averaging leaves substantially more freedom.

Write the negative part as

Scalg−=max⁡{0,−Scalg}.\mathrm{Scal}_g^- =\max\{0,-\mathrm{Scal}_g\}.Scalg−​=max{0,−Scalg​}.

This is zero where scalar curvature is nonnegative and records its magnitude where it is negative.

To define simplicial volume, represent the manifold’s real fundamental class by a finite singular cycle

c=∑jajσj.c=\sum_j a_j\sigma_j.c=j∑​aj​σj​.

Each σj\sigma_jσj​ is a continuous map of an abstract nnn-simplex into the manifold, and the real coefficients aja_jaj​ are chosen so that boundaries cancel and the cycle represents the manifold once, with orientation. The real simplicial volume is

∥M∥=inf⁡c∑j∣aj∣.\|M\|=\inf_c\sum_j|a_j|.∥M∥=cinf​j∑​∣aj​∣.

This is not simply the minimum number of simplices in a triangulation. Arbitrary singular simplices and real coefficients are allowed, and the infimum may be zero even for topologically complicated manifolds.

The fundamental group Γ=π1(M)\Gamma=\pi_1(M)Γ=π1​(M) records loops up to deformation. Its classifying space BΓB\GammaBΓ has fundamental group Γ\GammaΓ and contractible universal cover. A classifying map cM:M→BΓc_M:M\to B\GammacM​:M→BΓ records the universal-cover data of MMM. The manifold is rationally essential if

(cM)∗[M]≠0in Hn(BΓ;Q).(c_M)_*[M]\ne0\quad\text{in }H_n(B\Gamma;\mathbb Q).(cM​)∗​[M]=0in Hn​(BΓ;Q).

In words, its fundamental class remains detectable in rational homology after retaining the topology associated with its fundamental group. Otherwise it is rationally inessential.

A manifold is aspherical when its universal cover is contractible. For a closed oriented aspherical manifold, the classifying map preserves the fundamental class nontrivially. Tori are familiar examples, but aspherical manifolds form a much broader class.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gromov introduced simplicial volume and connected it to bounded cohomology, a theory of topological measurements whose values on singular simplices stay uniformly bounded. Classical comparisons bound simplicial volume using Riemannian volume under lower Ricci-curvature assumptions.

In 1986 Gromov proposed the integral scalar-curvature inequality addressed by M1. Moving from Ricci curvature to its scalar trace is a major weakening of the hypothesis. The conjecture asks whether this much less directional information still controls the same topological invariant.

Two traditions shaped positive-scalar-curvature obstructions. Schoen and Yau used stable minimal hypersurfaces and conformal changes to pass information to lower dimensions. Their original methods faced the regularity threshold for minimizing hypersurfaces in high dimensions. Gromov and Lawson used Dirac operators and index theory, obtaining dimension-independent obstructions under geometric and spin assumptions. A spin structure is additional topological data enabling the relevant spinor-operator constructions; it is not available on every manifold.

More recent work broadened both approaches. Chodosh and Li proved the closed aspherical obstruction in dimensions four and five using generalized soap bubbles. Other results remove spin assumptions for particular classes characterized by maps of nonzero degree or geometric largeness. The general rational-essentiality statement is stronger than simply assuming one of those largeness properties.

For simplicial volume, Ma, Wang, Xie, Yu, and Zhu’s cited version proves nonnegative-scalar-curvature vanishing when the universal cover is spin. Braun and Sauer obtained a macroscopic comparison involving a uniform bound on volumes of unit balls in the universal cover. Min, Zheng, and Zhu established the integral conjecture for all metrics on closed Kähler surfaces and treated additional symplectic examples. These are substantial positive cases, with hypotheses absent from M1’s general claim.

M2, dated September 23, states the qualitative topological results. M1, in its October 5 edition, explicitly uses M2’s nonnegative-scalar-curvature vanishing theorem and adds the uniform integral estimate.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The quantitative integral estimate

M1 states that for every integer n≥3n\geq3n≥3, there is a constant an>0a_n>0an​>0, depending only on dimension, such that every closed connected oriented smooth nnn-manifold and every smooth metric satisfy

∫M(Scalg−)n/2 dVg≥an∥M∥.\int_M(\mathrm{Scal}_g^-)^{n/2}\,dV_g\geq a_n\|M\|.∫M​(Scalg−​)n/2dVg​≥an​∥M∥.

The same constant works across all topologies and metrics in that dimension. Negative curvature may be concentrated in a small region; the integral records both its magnitude and its concentration.

The exponent is forced by scaling. Replacing ggg by λ2g\lambda^2gλ2g multiplies scalar curvature by λ−2\lambda^{-2}λ−2 and volume by λn\lambda^nλn, so the integral remains unchanged. Its scale invariance matches that of the topological quantity on the right.

For example, if Scalg≥−κ2\mathrm{Scal}_g\geq-\kappa^2Scalg​≥−κ2, then

∥M∥≤an−1κnVol⁡g(M).\|M\|\leq a_n^{-1}\kappa^n\operatorname{Vol}_g(M).∥M∥≤an−1​κnVolg​(M).

Thus a scalar lower bound and positive simplicial volume prevent the total volume from becoming arbitrarily small at the fixed curvature scale. M1 does not claim an optimal value of ana_nan​.

Rational inessentiality and aspherical rigidity

M2 states that a closed connected oriented smooth manifold of dimension n≥2n\geq2n≥2 admitting strictly positive scalar curvature is rationally inessential:

(cM)∗[M]=0in Hn(Bπ1(M);Q).(c_M)_*[M]=0\quad\text{in }H_n(B\pi_1(M);\mathbb Q).(cM​)∗​[M]=0in Hn​(Bπ1​(M);Q).

There is no spin assumption, no upper dimension bound, and no restriction on the fundamental group. The group may have torsion, and its classifying space need not admit a finite-dimensional model.

M2 derives that no closed smooth aspherical manifold admits strictly positive scalar curvature. It further claims that every nonnegative-scalar-curvature metric on a closed aspherical manifold is flat, meaning that its full curvature tensor vanishes. These conclusions include nonorientable manifolds through the orientation double cover.

For closed connected oriented manifolds of the same dimension, a nonzero-degree map to an aspherical target also obstructs strictly positive scalar curvature on the source. Degree is the signed number of times the map covers the target at the level of fundamental classes. No injectivity or surjectivity requirement on the induced fundamental-group map is imposed.

Finally, M2 states that every closed oriented smooth manifold of positive dimension with nonnegative scalar curvature has zero real simplicial volume. This is the precise companion input used by M1.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family claims resolutions of central scalar-curvature conjectures, linking an averaged local quantity to topology in every dimension and without spin assumptions.

The integral estimate is stronger than a prohibition of everywhere nonnegative scalar curvature on a manifold with positive simplicial volume. It requires a definite total amount of negative curvature, measured at the scale-invariant exponent. Geometry cannot evade the bound simply by squeezing all the negative contribution into a smaller region.

Rational inessentiality detects more than simplicial volume alone. A positive-dimensional torus has zero simplicial volume but remains rationally essential. M2’s strict-positive-curvature obstruction therefore applies even when the quantitative right-hand side in M1 is zero.

The torus also explains why strict positivity cannot be replaced by nonnegativity in the rational-inessentiality theorem: a flat torus has nonnegative scalar curvature and a nonzero classifying image. The separate nonnegative conclusion is simplicial-volume vanishing, with flatness available under the additional aspherical hypothesis.

6. The main idea

Detect topology, then shorten comparison maps

M2 assumes that a rational fundamental class survives and uses a cohomology class to detect it. This produces a nonzero pairing: a topological quantity that cannot be removed by a small controlled deformation.

Rational essentiality does not automatically give arbitrarily contracting maps from covers to spheres. The manuscript therefore introduces an auxiliary parameter manifold and converts the cohomology pairing into a nonzero local degree. Distance profiles provide finitely many comparison coordinates on a suitable cover.

A graph deformation enlarges the metric in a selected direction, making the corresponding coordinate vary more slowly when measured in the new metric. A reciprocal warped circle supplies favorable terms in the scalar-curvature calculation. Repeating this for all comparison coordinates could be prohibitively expensive if each coordinate incurred an independent worst-case cost.

M2 instead tracks how the inverse metric decreases. These decreases telescope within the original nnn-dimensional tangent geometry, so the cost depends only logarithmically on the number of comparison coordinates. Successive finite passes shorten the map while keeping accumulated scalar-curvature loss small and preserving its nonzero degree.

The terminal input is a local torical obstruction of Cecchini and Schick. The manuscript arranges the scalar and differential bounds where that theorem requires them. A crucial point is that its resulting threshold does not deteriorate with the number of added circle factors. This allows a sufficiently long but finite shortening procedure to yield the claimed contradiction.

Turn qualitative vanishing into a quantitative bound

M1 first changes the metric conformally, meaning by a positive scalar factor that may vary with position. If simplicial volume is positive, M2 rules out a nonnegative-scalar-curvature representative. The Yamabe minimizer in the conformal class can therefore be normalized to scalar curvature minus one.

The Yamabe problem supplies a constant-scalar-curvature representative minimizing an appropriate normalized curvature functional. Combined with Hölder’s inequality, this reduces the desired integral estimate to bounding simplicial volume by the volume of a metric with scalar curvature minus one.

Bounded cohomology now provides a bounded detector whose pairing is comparable to simplicial volume. M1 represents it using probability-valued maps from the universal cover. It deforms these maps and the metric together, keeping a weighted density controlled while gaining energy that pays for derivatives of comparison coordinates.

A second construction estimates degrees through families of hypersurfaces minimizing perimeter minus a forcing term, often called μ\muμ-bubbles. Their normal speeds enter both the scalar-curvature identity and the formula for integrating over level sets. The manuscript uses this interaction to control the total cost through a dimension-reducing procedure, including a treatment of singular regions in high dimensions.

Finally, it converts the bounded cocycle into controlled comparison cycles with integer multiplicities by rounding and resolving them in an averaged construction. The choices are organized so that gains from added comparison directions cancel their volume costs. The remaining estimate depends on the original dimension, producing the claimed universal constant rather than a constant tied to the particular topology or auxiliary construction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 concerns real simplicial volume, not integral simplicial volume or a count of simplices in a fixed triangulation. Its theorem is stated for closed connected oriented manifolds of dimension at least three. It does not assert an analogous bound for arbitrary noncompact spaces or manifolds with boundary without additional conditions.

The quantitative theorem depends on the qualitative vanishing result in M2. The two statements are presented together here, but that dependency remains part of their mathematical scope.

Strict positivity, nonnegativity, and flatness have different roles. Rational inessentiality is asserted under strict positive scalar curvature. General nonnegative scalar curvature gives zero simplicial volume; it does not make every such manifold rationally inessential or every such metric flat. Flatness is the additional aspherical conclusion.

The dimension-dependent constant is existential and is not presented as sharp. Optimal constants, equality cases for the integral inequality, and effective geometric bounds remain separate questions. Both manuscripts’ claims and cited inputs are reported without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Chodosh and Li, Generalized soap bubbles and the topology of manifolds with positive scalar curvature.
  • Ma, Wang, Xie, Yu, and Zhu, the spin-universal-cover vanishing result, version 4.
  • Min, Zheng, and Zhu, Simplicial volume and scalar curvature on closed Kähler surfaces.
  • Optional background: simplicial volume and aspherical spaces.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An integral scalar curvature bound for real simplicial volume (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Positive scalar curvature forces rational inessentiality (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Positive spectral curvature and a controlled loss of two dimensions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 336 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Positive scalar curvature need not make a manifold small. A round two-sphere multiplied by a line has positive scalar curvature but extends indefinitely along the line. Its two spherical directions remain bounded while one direction stays large.

Gromov’s width question asks whether a general manifold with a uniformly positive scalar-curvature lower bound has a comparable description at a controlled scale: can it be mapped to a space with two fewer dimensions so that every fiber stays uniformly small?

Family 336 claims a quantitative answer and then weakens the curvature assumption from pointwise positivity to spectral positivity. The latter combines curvature with the gradient energy of test functions, allowing scalar curvature to be negative in some regions.

The three manuscripts have complementary roles. M3 develops the higher-dimensional pointwise theorem and a partition construction. M1 uses that construction to obtain the spectral theorem in dimensions at least four. M2 gives a separate weighted argument in dimension three, with an explicit convenient constant. Throughout, the final fiber diameters are measured in the original metric.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a metric space XXX, its Urysohn ddd-width is

UW⁡d(X)=inf⁡f:X→Ksup⁡y∈Kdiam⁡Xf−1(y),\operatorname{UW}_d(X)=\inf_{f:X\to K}\sup_{y\in K}\operatorname{diam}_X f^{-1}(y),UWd​(X)=f:X→Kinf​y∈Ksup​diamX​f−1(y),

where fff is continuous and KKK is a simplicial complex of dimension at most ddd. A simplicial complex is built from vertices, edges, triangles, and higher-dimensional simplices glued along faces. For d=1d=1d=1, it is a graph.

A fiber f−1(y)f^{-1}(y)f−1(y) consists of all points sent to the same target point. Its diameter is the supremum of distances between any two of its points, including points in different connected components. Bounding each component separately is weaker: many small components could be arbitrarily far apart while sharing one target value.

The width measures how much uncertainty remains after replacing XXX by a lower-dimensional description. Small fibers do not imply that the map preserves distances between different fibers, is injective, or is a homotopy equivalence.

A Riemannian manifold is complete when its metric has no missing finite-distance limit points. Let Δg=div⁡g∇g\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_gΔg​=divg​∇g​ be the Laplacian, with this sign convention. The spectral condition in the family is

∫M(4∣∇φ∣g2+Scalgφ2) dVg≥λ∫Mφ2 dVg\int_M\bigl(4|\nabla\varphi|_g^2+\mathrm{Scal}_g\varphi^2\bigr)\,dV_g\geq\lambda\int_M\varphi^2\,dV_g∫M​(4∣∇φ∣g2​+Scalg​φ2)dVg​≥λ∫M​φ2dVg​

for every smooth compactly supported real test function φ\varphiφ, where λ>0\lambda>0λ>0. It is abbreviated

−4Δg+Scalg≥λ.-4\Delta_g+\mathrm{Scal}_g\geq\lambda.−4Δg​+Scalg​≥λ.

This is a quadratic-form inequality, not a pointwise inequality between functions. A pointwise bound Scalg≥λ\mathrm{Scal}_g\geq\lambdaScalg​≥λ implies it, since gradient energy is nonnegative. The converse need not hold. On a noncompact manifold the definition does not require a lowest eigenvalue to be attained by an eigenfunction.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gromov’s macroscopic-dimension program relates positive scalar curvature to a loss of large-scale dimensions. Its quantitative form asks for one fiber bound depending only on dimension after normalizing the curvature scale. This is stronger than asking for some finite bound that can depend on each manifold and metric.

Three-dimensional geometry supplied important precedents. Stable minimal-surface arguments of Schoen and Yau, and distance-level estimates of Gromov and Lawson, connect curvature to the size of separating surfaces. Some distance-level arguments require additional control of first homology; they are not diameter bounds for every distance sphere in every manifold.

Liokumovich and Maximo constructed singular foliations of closed three-manifolds with bounds on the area, diameter, and genus of connected level components under pointwise positive scalar curvature. Liokumovich and Wang extended area and diameter control to complete noncompact three-manifolds. Passing from levels to a Reeb graph separates their connected components, explaining how such results yield a graph-valued description.

In higher dimensions, several macroscopic-dimension theorems concerned universal covers of closed manifolds and used spin, fundamental-group, homotopy, or related assumptions. These results gave important topological cases, but differed from a dimension-only quantitative bound for arbitrary complete manifolds.

The spectral viewpoint also has established origins. Perelman’s scalar-curvature functional naturally involves −4Δ+Scal-4\Delta+\mathrm{Scal}−4Δ+Scal. Gromov’s torus stabilization studies warped products with circles while keeping the base metric as the reference for width. His three-dimensional theorem in that framework is a close predecessor to M2. The new manuscript describes its contribution as a direct weighted proof covering nonorientable and noncompact cases without global control of the auxiliary weight.

A terminology warning matters here. “Macroscopic scalar curvature” can also mean a fixed-radius ball-volume comparison. Kumar and Sen give counterexamples to the analogous uniform width implication under that different condition. Neither ordinary scalar curvature nor the spectral condition should be replaced by it.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The spectral theorem in dimensions at least three

Combining M1 and M2, the family states that every connected complete smooth boundaryless Riemannian nnn-manifold, n≥3n\geq3n≥3, satisfying the spectral inequality admits a continuous map

f:M⟶K,dim⁡K≤n−2,f:M\longrightarrow K,\qquad \dim K\leq n-2,f:M⟶K,dimK≤n−2,

whose entire fibers satisfy

diam⁡gf−1(y)≤Cnλ.\operatorname{diam}_g f^{-1}(y)\leq\frac{C_n}{\sqrt\lambda}.diamg​f−1(y)≤λ​Cn​​.

The constant depends only on nnn. M2 gives C3=500C_3=500C3​=500, explicitly without claiming optimality. For higher dimensions, M1 asserts a finite dimension-dependent constant.

There is no orientability, spin, compactness, or bounded-geometry assumption. Bounded geometry would impose additional uniform local controls, such as curvature and injectivity-radius bounds; those are not part of these statements. The target complex has its ordinary polyhedral topology.

The pointwise theorem and closed-cover consequences

M3 states the corresponding theorem under Scalg≥1\mathrm{Scal}_g\geq1Scalg​≥1 in dimensions n≥4n\geq4n≥4. Its stabilized partition theorem is an imported geometric input in M1’s spectral extension, so these two proofs should not be described as independent alternatives for the full spectral conclusion.

M3 also obtains the continuous macroscopic-dimension statement for universal covers of closed positive-scalar-curvature manifolds in every dimension n≥2n\geq2n≥2:

dim⁡mcM~≤n−2.\dim_{\mathrm{mc}}\widetilde M\leq n-2.dimmc​M≤n−2.

Here the target has the uniform simplex metric, in which simplices have standard Euclidean shape and edge length, and the map is continuous with uniformly bounded entire fibers. This is not automatically the stronger variant requiring a Lipschitz map. The two- and three-dimensional cases use established low-dimensional inputs; M1’s general spectral theorem itself begins in dimension four, with M2 supplying dimension three.

For closed manifolds of dimension at least four, M3 derives a filling-radius bound from its width theorem. Filling radius measures how large a neighborhood of the manifold is needed before its fundamental cycle becomes a boundary in a canonical ambient function space. Under Scalg≥σ2>0\mathrm{Scal}_g\geq\sigma^2>0Scalg​≥σ2>0, the claimed bound is

FillRad⁡(M,g)≤Cn2σ.\operatorname{FillRad}(M,g)\leq\frac{C_n}{2\sigma}.FillRad(M,g)≤2σCn​​.

The fundamental class uses integer coefficients for orientable manifolds and mod-two coefficients otherwise. M3 further derives the closed aspherical positive-scalar-curvature obstruction in dimensions at least four, while pointing to the stronger independent rational-inessentiality claim in family 335.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family claims a central quantitative dimension-drop theorem under very weak global hypotheses, and extends it to a spectral condition permitting local negative scalar curvature.

Uniformity is the key. A compact manifold can always map to a point with fiber diameter equal to its own diameter, but that says nothing useful across a class of metrics. Here one constant is supposed to work for every manifold of the same dimension once the curvature scale is fixed.

The original metric is equally important. A conformal change might improve scalar curvature while stretching some distances uncontrollably. A width bound in the changed metric would not necessarily answer the original question. These manuscripts explicitly maintain the original metric for the final estimate.

The result would also distinguish geometric dimension at a curvature scale from topological dimension. A smooth nnn-manifold remains locally nnn-dimensional. The theorem only compresses it into an (n−2)(n-2)(n−2)-dimensional description with bounded ambiguity, as the sphere-times-line example illustrates.

6. The main idea

Convert spectral information into a weight

The spectral inequality supplies a positive smooth supersolution vvv of

(−4Δg+Scalg)v≥v(-4\Delta_g+\mathrm{Scal}_g)v\geq v(−4Δg​+Scalg​)v≥v

after scaling to λ=1\lambda=1λ=1. With t=−2log⁡vt=-2\log vt=−2logv, it yields a weighted curvature quantity

D(g,t)=Scalg+2Δgt−∣dt∣g2≥1.D(g,t)=\mathrm{Scal}_g+2\Delta_gt-|dt|_g^2\geq1.D(g,t)=Scalg​+2Δg​t−∣dt∣g2​≥1.

The weight can be unbounded and can oscillate substantially. The argument therefore cannot assume that replacing the metric by a weighted or conformal version preserves all distances up to a controlled factor.

In dimension three, cut into pieces controlled by surfaces

M2 uses the positive density associated with ttt in a weighted area-minus-volume minimization problem. Its critical surfaces have prescribed weighted mean curvature. Stability, together with the ambient weighted curvature inequality, gives diameter control on the resulting two-dimensional surfaces in their original induced metric.

The construction first cuts along a locally finite family of stable weighted minimal surfaces to simplify separation. It then doubles pieces, smooths the metric and weight compatibly, and inserts further separating surfaces. Distance slabs acquire controlled diameter, producing a cover in which at most two sets meet at a point. A partition of unity turns such a cover into a graph-valued map.

Gluing the pieces back together needs more than componentwise estimates. M2 keeps collar homotopies inside graph regions tied to a common cover set. This is what controls the distance between disconnected pieces of the same final fiber.

In higher dimensions, stretch first and partition compatibly

M1 first constructs a larger graph metric and a new signed weight with an additional quadratic reserve. This reserve absorbs the cost of later local stretching even when the starting weight has no global bound.

Choose a separated collection of centers in the original metric. Their inner balls cover the manifold, and the corresponding larger balls form a locally finite family. Local graph deformations make each inner ball far from the exterior of its outer ball in an auxiliary metric. A telescoping inverse-metric estimate controls the cost without requiring a uniform bound on how many balls overlap.

Each location is changed only finitely often. This local stabilization allows the construction to remain smooth on a noncompact manifold with uncontrolled geometry at infinity. Locally finite circle warps convert the weighted inequality into the stabilized curvature condition required by M3’s partition theorem.

M3 supplies the geometric dimension drop through compatible cuts and walls. A wall lowers the dimension of one part of the construction, but both adjacent bulk pieces must also be retained. In high dimensions, singular minimizing regions require shielding and regularization while preserving the curvature information where later cuts need it.

The resulting walls have a controlled intersection pattern: n−1n-1n−1 distinct walls cannot meet. Continuous sign coordinates associated with the walls therefore have at most n−2n-2n−2 simultaneously varying entries. They define a map to a complex of that dimension. Equality of all coordinates places two original points near the same original covering ball, yielding a bound on the entire fiber.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The spectral assertion is for dimensions at least three and a strictly positive lower spectral bound. It is not a theorem under mere pointwise positivity without a uniform lower bound on a noncompact manifold. Compact positive-scalar-curvature manifolds do have a positive minimum, which is why their universal covers enter the stated corollary.

The map is continuous. No global Lipschitz constant, equivariance under covering transformations, smooth fibration structure, or homotopy equivalence is claimed. The target may be an infinite complex.

The constants are not optimized, including the explicit three-dimensional value 500. Optimal width constants and stronger control on the maps or fibers remain separate questions. Fixed-scale macroscopic scalar curvature is a different hypothesis and cannot be substituted.

Finally, M1 depends on M3’s stabilized partition theorem, while M2 uses its own weighted surface construction. The digest preserves these dependencies and explains the statements without checking their proofs.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Gromov, Four lectures on scalar curvature, for width, stabilization, and macroscopic dimension.
  • Liokumovich and Maximo, Waist inequality for three-manifolds with positive scalar curvature.
  • Liokumovich and Wang, width and waist inequalities in complete three-manifolds.
  • Kumar and Sen, Urysohn width and macroscopic scalar curvature, for the distinction from fixed-scale macroscopic curvature.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Spectral scalar curvature and uniform Urysohn width (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Spectral scalar curvature and Urysohn width in dimension three (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Positive scalar curvature and uniform codimension-two width (September 23, 2026).

entry.title: Sharp isoperimetry and fillings in nonpositive curvature
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 337 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Among planar regions with a fixed area, a disk has the shortest boundary. In Euclidean space of any dimension, the analogous statement says that balls enclose the most volume for a given boundary area.

What happens when the ambient space is curved? Nonpositive curvature tends to spread geodesics apart. The Cartan–Hadamard isoperimetric conjecture predicts that this geometry cannot make enclosing volume cheaper than in Euclidean space. If curvature is bounded above by a negative constant, the proposed comparison is stronger: the benchmark becomes a ball in the corresponding hyperbolic space.

Family 337 claims the full smooth-manifold comparison in every dimension, including nonsmooth regions with finite perimeter. It also classifies bounded equality regions in the Euclidean comparison.

A companion manuscript asks a broader filling question. Given a closed, oriented geometric boundary, possibly singular and carrying integer multiplicities, can it be filled with no more volume than the Euclidean sharp formula allows? It claims this for proper CAT(0) spaces, which can have singularities and need not be manifolds at all.

2. Background and essential definitions

A Cartan–Hadamard manifold is a complete simply connected Riemannian manifold with nonpositive sectional curvature. Completeness rules out missing finite-distance endpoints. Simple connectedness means every loop can be contracted. Sectional curvature measures curvature in individual tangent two-planes; it is a stronger directional condition than a scalar-curvature bound.

Let ωn\omega_nωn​ be the volume of the unit ball in Rn\mathbb R^nRn. A Euclidean ball of radius rrr has volume ωnrn\omega_nr^nωn​rn and boundary area nωnrn−1n\omega_nr^{n-1}nωn​rn−1. Eliminating rrr gives the sharp benchmark

P≥nωn1/nV(n−1)/n.P\geq n\omega_n^{1/n}V^{(n-1)/n}.P≥nωn1/n​V(n−1)/n.

For a smooth bounded region, PPP is boundary area and VVV is enclosed volume. For a rough measurable region, perimeter is defined through the total variation of its indicator function. This extends boundary area to sets with corners or less regular boundaries. Sets differing on a volume-zero subset are identified.

The perimeter in M1 is full ambient perimeter. If an auxiliary ball confines a region during the proof, boundary lying on that ball still counts. It is not a relative perimeter that ignores contact with the confining boundary.

A CAT(0) space is a geodesic metric space whose triangles are no thicker than Euclidean comparison triangles: corresponding points on their sides are no farther apart. This is a metric version of nonpositive curvature. A space is proper if closed bounded balls are compact.

An integral current is a generalized oriented geometric object with integer multiplicities, an area or volume called its mass, and a boundary operation. It allows singular supports and cancellation between oppositely oriented pieces. A kkk-cycle TTT has zero boundary, ∂T=0\partial T=0∂T=0. A filling is a (k+1)(k+1)(k+1)-current SSS with ∂S=T\partial S=T∂S=T. This describes a geometric boundary equation, not necessarily a parametrized disk or ball.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The surface isoperimetric comparison goes back to Weil and to Beckenbach and Radó; Bol developed nonzero-curvature model comparisons. Kleiner proved the generalized comparison in dimension three. Croke proved the sharp Euclidean comparison in dimension four.

Further work developed different ways to compare domains. Kloeckner and Kuperberg used optical and chord-based methods. Ghomi and Spruck showed that an appropriate total-curvature inequality for convex hypersurfaces implies the Euclidean isoperimetric inequality and equality rigidity. Their analysis of confined minimizers also supplies a regularity input used by M1.

The manuscripts describe several recent overlapping advances. Chen, Ghomi, and Wang’s cited September 2026 preprint proves Euclidean comparison and rigidity in dimensions three through nine, with additional announced or computationally supported extensions. Other cited work gives small-volume comparisons, reductions to rigidity in certain Alexandrov spaces, or all-dimensional conclusions under extra control of negative curvature. M1 claims to remove those remaining dimensional and curvature restrictions in the smooth Cartan–Hadamard setting.

The current-filling problem has a parallel history. Almgren proved the sharp inequality for integral currents in Euclidean space in arbitrary dimension and codimension. Ambrosio and Kirchheim developed integral currents in metric spaces, making it possible to formulate the question without smooth ambient coordinates.

Wenger proved Euclidean-exponent filling inequalities in broad metric settings including CAT(0) spaces, with a dimension-dependent constant. Schulze obtained the sharp constant-curvature comparison for two-dimensional cycles in smooth Cartan–Hadamard manifolds, in any codimension. For Lipschitz loops, Reshetnyak’s majorization theorem already gives the sharp Euclidean disk-area bound.

M2’s claimed contribution is the universal sharp coefficient for every cycle dimension at least two in arbitrary proper CAT(0) spaces. It does not replace the earlier loop theorem, and it does not convert a current filling into every possible prescribed-topology extension problem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Generalized isoperimetry and equality

M1 assumes a complete simply connected smooth nnn-manifold, n≥2n\geq2n≥2, with sectional curvature at most κ≤0\kappa\leq0κ≤0. Every measurable set EEE of finite volume and finite ambient perimeter is claimed to have perimeter at least that of the equal-volume ball in the simply connected constant-curvature κ\kappaκ model.

For κ=0\kappa=0κ=0, this is

Pg(E)≥nωn1/nVol⁡g(E)(n−1)/n.P_g(E)\geq n\omega_n^{1/n}\operatorname{Vol}_g(E)^{(n-1)/n}.Pg​(E)≥nωn1/n​Volg​(E)(n−1)/n.

For κ=−b2<0\kappa=-b^2<0κ=−b2<0, define
