Vb(r)=nωn∫0r(sinh⁡(bt)b)n−1dt,V_b(r)=n\omega_n\int_0^r\left(\frac{\sinh(bt)}b\right)^{n-1}dt,Vb​(r)=nωn​∫0r​(bsinh(bt)​)n−1dt,
Ab(r)=nωn(sinh⁡(br)b)n−1.A_b(r)=n\omega_n\left(\frac{\sinh(br)}b\right)^{n-1}.Ab​(r)=nωn​(bsinh(br)​)n−1.

If Vb(r)=Vol⁡g(E)V_b(r)=\operatorname{Vol}_g(E)Vb​(r)=Volg​(E), the conclusion is Pg(E)≥Ab(r)P_g(E)\geq A_b(r)Pg​(E)≥Ab​(r). Both bounded regions and unbounded sets of finite volume are included in the inequality.

The equality theorem has narrower scope. For a bounded positive-volume set in a Cartan–Hadamard manifold, equality in the Euclidean formula holds precisely when the set agrees up to volume zero with an open region isometric, with its induced metric, to a round Euclidean ball. The conclusion determines the entire equality region, not just its boundary. It does not require the ambient manifold outside that region to be flat.

Sharp integral fillings

M2 uses cycle dimension rather than ambient dimension. To keep the distinction clear, denote it by kkk. For every compactly supported integral kkk-cycle in a proper CAT(0) space, with k≥2k\geq2k≥2, it claims a compactly supported integral filling satisfying

∂S=T,M(S)≤M(T)(k+1)/k(k+1)(k+1)/kωk+11/k.\partial S=T,\qquad\mathbf M(S)\leq\frac{\mathbf M(T)^{(k+1)/k}}{(k+1)^{(k+1)/k}\omega_{k+1}^{1/k}}.∂S=T,M(S)≤(k+1)(k+1)/kωk+11/k​M(T)(k+1)/k​.

Here M\mathbf MM denotes mass. The coefficient is sharp, as Euclidean spheres and their ball fillings show. There is no restriction on integer multiplicities or ambient dimension. For a two-dimensional cycle, the coefficient is 1/(6π)1/(6\sqrt\pi)1/(6π​).

Applying this theorem to the boundary of a region yields the Euclidean Cartan–Hadamard inequality in ambient dimensions at least three. Classical surface results supply ambient dimension two. This companion route gives the Euclidean comparison, while M1 also treats negative constant-curvature benchmarks and its stated equality classification.

Spectral and torsional consequences

M1 additionally derives model-ball comparisons for smooth relatively compact domains and every 1<p<∞1<p<\infty1<p<∞. Radial rearrangement preserves the relevant integrals and decreases the ppp-Dirichlet energy ∫∣∇u∣p\int|\nabla u|^p∫∣∇u∣p.

Consequently, the first variational Dirichlet ppp-eigenvalue is at least that of the equal-volume model ball, while the corresponding quotient-normalized ppp-torsional rigidity is at most the ball’s value. At p=2p=2p=2, these are the familiar lowest-frequency and torsional-response comparisons. They are consequences of the isoperimetric theorem through an established rearrangement principle.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family claims sharp all-dimensional resolutions of central isoperimetric and filling problems, retaining the Euclidean optimal constant rather than only the correct power law.

The exponent alone expresses how area and volume scale. A nonoptimal constant already gives useful control, but the optimal coefficient identifies the ball as the universal benchmark. Equality rigidity adds a structural statement: achieving that efficiency forces a Euclidean region throughout the enclosed interior.

The two manuscripts also broaden the admissible objects in different directions. M1 permits rough and unbounded finite-volume regions in smooth negatively curved geometry. M2 permits singular ambient spaces, arbitrary codimension, and integer multiplicities. These are related strengths, not interchangeable formulations.

The comparison has analytical consequences because level sets connect a function’s gradient energy to their boundary areas. Thus a geometric inequality becomes a source of spectral and variational estimates, explaining why the result reaches beyond the geometry of individual domains.

6. The main idea

Compare boundaries through an isoperimetric profile

M1 first claims a sharp critical Sobolev inequality on immersed hypersurfaces. A Sobolev inequality controls an integral norm of a function by its gradient energy and curvature terms. “Critical” refers to the exponent compatible with the dimension and scaling.

The source builds radial comparison maps into a sphere, with weights satisfying compatible curvature inequalities. Their center and scale can be balanced against a chosen measure. If the sharp threshold failed, a variational minimizer and these balanced coordinate variations would yield an incompatible first-order identity. This is the analytical engine of the smooth-manifold argument.

An arbitrary region’s boundary has uncontrolled mean curvature, so the manuscript does not apply that engine directly to every boundary. It first minimizes full perimeter among sets of fixed volume confined in a large geodesic ball. The resulting confined isoperimetric profile records the least perimeter as volume varies.

For a minimizer, first variation relates boundary mean curvature to the derivative of the profile. Contact with the confining sphere requires separate one-sided control. Cutoffs near singular sets make the constant function an admissible limiting test in the hypersurface inequality. The result is a differential inequality for the profile whose integrated form is the model-ball comparison.

Approximation and cutoffs then pass from confined minimizers to general finite-volume finite-perimeter sets. For equality, the manuscript combines boundary regularity, spectral or low-dimensional substitutes, radial flux identities, and equality in metric comparison. These steps recover a round boundary and then the flat metric throughout the occupied region.

Fill cycles without an ambient normal bundle

M2 begins inside a compact convex ball containing the cycle. Properness makes the ball compact, while CAT(0) geometry makes it convex. Compactness and filling continuity supply an extremizing cycle if the sharp inequality fails.

Radial deformation toward a fixed center produces a curvature-like inequality directly from triangle comparison. The calculation retains the exact transverse factor in the swept mass. This is important because a singular metric space need not have an ambient tangent bundle or normal vectors available for a classical hypersurface proof.

For two-dimensional cycles, the radial inequality and Euclidean lower density provide the base case. Higher cycle dimensions use induction: fill boundaries of small restrictions using the lower-dimensional sharp theorem. This gives an almost sharp local perimeter estimate, then a critical Sobolev inequality on the extremizing current.

A variational minimizer supplies a weighted measure and weighted chord lengths. The manuscript obtains an upper bound for their averaged squared size from radial variation and the minimizer equation. CAT(0) variance gives an incompatible lower bound for the same quantity. This closes the induction and yields an attained compactly supported filling with the sharp coefficient.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The curvature assumption is sectional, not merely Ricci or scalar curvature. Simple connectedness and completeness are part of M1’s hypothesis. Its inequality has the full finite-volume scope, but the Euclidean equality theorem requires boundedness and positive volume. No corresponding general negative-curvature equality classification is asserted in its headline theorem.

M2 requires proper CAT(0) spaces and compact support of the input cycle. It does not state the same result for every nonproper CAT(0) space. Ambient dimension is unrestricted, but the cycle has a finite integer dimension at least two.

A current filling need not be a disk, preserve a prescribed topology, or extend a specified parametrization. Those requirements belong to stronger map-extension formulations. Likewise, the sharp universal estimate does not rule out smaller large-mass growth rates for special spaces under additional rank or dimension hypotheses.

The two proof routes and their claimed consequences are reported as stated. Questions about broader equality classifications, prescribed-topology fillings, and removing properness remain distinct from the results presented here.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Chen, Ghomi, and Wang, The isoperimetric inequality and CMC hypersurfaces in Cartan–Hadamard manifolds.
  • Ghomi and Spruck, Total curvature and the isoperimetric inequality in Cartan–Hadamard manifolds.
  • Wenger, Isoperimetric inequalities of Euclidean type in metric spaces.
  • Schulze, Optimal isoperimetric inequalities for surfaces in any codimension.
  • Optional background: CAT(0) spaces.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Generalized Cartan–Hadamard isoperimetry and Euclidean equality rigidity (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Sharp integral fillings in CAT(0) spaces (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Positive bisectional curvature and global complex coordinates
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 338 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Local complex coordinates describe a complex manifold near each point. They need not combine into one coordinate system covering the entire space. Different global topologies and different complex structures can share the same local model.

Yau’s uniformization conjecture asks whether a strong positivity condition on a complete Kähler metric forces a connected noncompact complex manifold to be globally identical, in the holomorphic sense, to Cn\mathbb C^nCn.

Family 338 claims an affirmative answer under strictly positive holomorphic bisectional curvature, with no further assumptions at infinity. Curvature may be unbounded above, the manifold may have regions with very small volume relative to their scale, and no topological simplification is assumed in advance.

The conclusion concerns the complex structure. It does not say that the given metric becomes the ordinary Euclidean metric. In fact, Euclidean space with its usual metric has zero curvature, whereas the hypothesis requires positivity. The claim is that the manifold admits global holomorphic coordinates in which a possibly complicated curved metric can be expressed.

2. Background and essential definitions

A complex nnn-manifold is locally described by nnn complex coordinates, with holomorphic changes of coordinates. Its underlying real dimension is 2n2n2n. A map is biholomorphic if it is a bijection, holomorphic, and has a holomorphic inverse. This preserves complex analysis, a much stronger conclusion than merely preserving topology.

The complex structure acts on tangent vectors by an operator JJJ satisfying J2=−IJ^2=-IJ2=−I, analogous to multiplication by iii. A compatible Riemannian metric satisfies g(Ju,Jv)=g(u,v)g(Ju,Jv)=g(u,v)g(Ju,Jv)=g(u,v). Its associated two-form is

ω(u,v)=g(Ju,v).\omega(u,v)=g(Ju,v).ω(u,v)=g(Ju,v).

The metric is Kähler when this form is closed, dω=0d\omega=0dω=0. This compatibility tightly links Riemannian curvature with holomorphic analysis. Equivalently, the complex structure is parallel for the metric’s natural connection.

Holomorphic bisectional curvature measures the interaction between two complex tangent directions. In complex notation, its positivity can be expressed as

R(u,u‾,v,v‾)>0R(u,\overline u,v,\overline v)>0R(u,u,v,v)>0

for every pair of nonzero complex tangent vectors of type (1,0)(1,0)(1,0), using the convention in which the standard positively curved models have positive curvature. Dividing by the squared lengths gives the normalized value; its sign is what matters here.

This condition is weaker than positive real sectional curvature, which tests every real tangent two-plane. In complex dimension one, it reduces to positivity of Gaussian curvature.

Completeness means that the Riemannian distance has no missing finite-distance limit points. Noncompactness means that the whole manifold cannot be covered by one compact region. The theorem assumes pointwise strict positivity: each tested curvature value is positive, but there need not be a single positive constant bounding all values from below throughout the manifold.

A further condition appearing in earlier results is maximal volume growth. For a fixed basepoint, it requires the volume of large radius-rrr balls to grow at least as a positive constant times r2nr^{2n}r2n, the Euclidean order. Family 338 does not impose this condition.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The one-dimensional case belongs to classical uniformization and the relation between curvature and conformal type. Complete noncompact Riemann surfaces of positive Gaussian curvature are conformally the complex plane, through the topology and parabolicity results cited by M1.

The compact counterpart is the Frankel conjecture, resolved by Mori and by Siu and Yau: positive holomorphic bisectional curvature characterizes complex projective space in the compact setting. Yau’s 1982 question seeks the corresponding noncompact conclusion, where uncontrolled behavior at infinity becomes a central obstacle.

One line of work studies global holomorphic functions. Greene and Wu obtained strictly convex exhaustion functions under positive real sectional curvature, yielding Steinness. An exhaustion function has compact sublevel sets, so it organizes the manifold into increasingly large compact pieces. Mok proved an affine-algebraic embedding under positive bisectional curvature, maximal volume growth, and quadratic scalar-curvature decay. Such results linked curvature with global complex analysis while retaining substantial geometric hypotheses.

Chen and Zhu developed growth and averaged-curvature estimates under positive bisectional curvature, including estimates not requiring an upper curvature bound. Ni and Tam studied heat smoothing of plurisubharmonic functions under nonnegative bisectional curvature, with explicit growth conditions. A plurisubharmonic function is one whose restriction to every complex curve is subharmonic; it is a complex-analytic analogue of a convex function.

A second route evolves the metric by Kähler–Ricci flow, constructs shrinking holomorphic charts, and assembles them through complex dynamics. Cao’s differential Harnack estimates are a major analytical ingredient in this tradition. Chau and Tam proved uniformization under bounded nonnegative bisectional curvature and maximal volume growth, and developed related covering and domain results under other assumptions.

Liu later obtained uniformization under nonnegative bisectional curvature and maximal volume growth without an upper curvature bound. Lee and Tam gave another route using smoothing. The volume-growth assumption remained essential to the scope of those theorems.

Recent surface results remove further assumptions. Datar, Pingali, and Seshadri proved uniformization of complete noncompact Kähler surfaces with positive real sectional curvature. Their bisectional-curvature result retained extra function-theoretic and topological hypotheses, subsequently weakened by Wu. These are important precedents, but positive real sectional curvature is stronger than the bisectional hypothesis, and surface results do not cover every complex dimension.

4. What the new manuscript claims

M1 states that if a connected noncompact complex manifold MMM of complex dimension n≥1n\geq1n≥1 admits a smooth complete Kähler metric with strictly positive holomorphic bisectional curvature, then there is a biholomorphism

F:M⟶Cn.F:M\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n.F:M⟶Cn.

There is no upper curvature bound, no uniform positive lower bound, no maximal-volume-growth or noncollapse assumption, and no Ricci-pinching hypothesis. Pinching would compare curvature in different directions by fixed ratios. Nor is simple connectedness, contractibility, or a condition on topology at infinity assumed beforehand.

The map is onto all of Cn\mathbb C^nCn. A holomorphic injection into a proper domain, or a locally biholomorphic covering map, would be weaker. M1 explicitly treats the passage from local shrinking charts to global surjectivity as a separate part of the argument.

Consequently, the manifold is contractible and has the same global holomorphic function theory as complex affine space. In particular, it is Stein, meaning that global holomorphic functions separate points and provide the appropriate holomorphic convexity and local coordinates. These properties follow from the claimed biholomorphism rather than being additional hypotheses.

The original metric can remain highly nonuniform in the global coordinates. The theorem classifies the underlying complex manifold, not every metric satisfying the curvature condition.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family claims a full resolution of Yau’s noncompact uniformization conjecture in every complex dimension, removing the geometric and topological assumptions that characterized major earlier positive cases.

The statement says that curvature positivity determines a global complex structure despite potentially complicated geometry at infinity. This is stronger than a topological classification: even a manifold with simple underlying topology can carry a nontrivial complex structure.

The removal of an upper curvature bound matters analytically. Standard flow estimates and global maximum principles often require uniform geometric control. If the initial curvature can grow without bound, one must first build a setting in which those tools can legitimately be applied.

Surjectivity is another substantive part of the result. Local charts can become compatible and still produce only a proper domain in Cn\mathbb C^nCn. Identifying the whole affine space requires additional control on how the charts exhaust the manifold and how their images grow after correction.

The rating reflects the significance of these claimed conclusions, without treating the manuscript as independently verified.

6. The main idea

Build a flow without assuming bounded geometry

Kähler–Ricci flow deforms a Kähler metric according to its Ricci curvature. It changes the metric while keeping the complex structure fixed, making it a natural tool for discovering global holomorphic coordinates.

M1 constructs the flow through complete Hermitian approximations on exhausting domains. A Hermitian metric respects the complex structure but need not initially satisfy the full Kähler closedness condition. Local estimates on the metric and on logarithmic volume loss allow the approximations to pass to a limit without a global curvature bound.

The order of the argument is deliberate. The source proves a scalar comparison using weights adapted to the evolving metric before claiming completeness of that evolving metric. Completeness is then recovered later from stronger Harnack inequalities. This avoids assuming at the start a property that the unrestricted initial geometry does not automatically supply through standard flow theorems.

Obtain coupled spatial and temporal control

The main curvature argument takes place on the holomorphic cotangent bundle, whose fibers consist of complex-linear covectors. The evolving metric gives each covector a squared dual norm.

The manuscript compares this norm with an envelope formed by minimizing boundary costs over holomorphic disks. A holomorphic disk is a complex-analytic map from the unit disk into the bundle. Compact boundary restrictions and a small area penalty keep the minimization under control.

A deformation estimate gives a differential inequality for the envelope in a weak, viscosity sense: smooth functions touching it from above or below obey the appropriate inequality. Optimizing a Hermitian ellipsoid in each fiber connects this bundle-level inequality to the previously established scalar comparison. M1 then identifies the envelope with the squared dual norm itself.

The resulting positivity jointly in space and logarithmic time yields matrix and scalar Harnack estimates. Such estimates relate curvature or metric behavior at different points and times, supplying the control needed for complete shrinking charts.

Measure contraction with the right clock

Physical flow time need not measure chart contraction uniformly. M1 therefore introduces a volume clock at a basepoint ooo:

s(t)=log⁡det⁡g(o)det⁡ht(o),s(t)=\log\frac{\det g(o)}{\det h_t(o)},s(t)=logdetht​(o)detg(o)​,

where ggg is the initial metric and hth_tht​ the evolving one. The determinants are taken in fixed complex coordinates; their ratio is intrinsic.

For a transition map between normalized charts at volume-clock times s≤us\leq us≤u, the derivative determinant has the controlled loss

∣det⁡Fs,u′(0)∣=e−(u−s)/2.|\det F'_{s,u}(0)|=e^{-(u-s)/2}.∣detFs,u′​(0)∣=e−(u−s)/2.

Volume contraction alone would allow one direction to shrink while another grows. The manuscript combines it with a comparison between the largest and smallest directional scales, giving contraction in every direction. Selected intervals with favorable Ricci ratios also allow loops to be contracted, leading to simple connectedness and coherent continuation of inverse charts.

Correct coordinate changes and prove onto-ness

The final stage models transitions by polynomial automorphisms: globally invertible polynomial changes of coordinates. Their finite Taylor data are matched coherently, with determinant-one nonlinear shears handling corrections and the linear part retaining its prescribed contraction.

Contraction rates are allowed to vary. The source tracks the additional polynomial degree needed during unfavorable intervals using growth of the volume-clock speed, rather than requiring one uniform contraction pattern from the outset.

Corrected inverse charts converge to an injective holomorphic map into Cn\mathbb C^nCn. To prove that its image is the whole space, M1 uses a bound along selected stages on the degree of forward compositions, small errors on compact subsets, and an inverse-ball inclusion. These rule out a finite limiting radius for centered balls inside the image. Surjectivity is thus an additional conclusion of the coordinate construction, not an automatic consequence of local convergence.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem requires a complete Kähler metric with strictly positive holomorphic bisectional curvature. It does not classify all complete manifolds with merely nonnegative bisectional curvature, where splitting and quotient phenomena can occur. Positive Ricci curvature or positive holomorphic sectional curvature is also not a substitute for the stated hypothesis.

No Euclidean isometry is asserted. The complex coordinates identify the complex manifold, while the original metric may remain curved, unbounded in curvature, and geometrically nonuniform.

The theorem is existential. It does not provide an explicit coordinate formula, sharp bounds for the biholomorphism relative to the original metric, or an effective numerical construction for an arbitrary input metric. Quantitative coordinate control and classifications under weaker curvature assumptions are separate questions.

The local flow, bundle-envelope, chart-contraction, and surjectivity stages are reported as the manuscript’s proposed mechanism. Their estimates and proof are not independently checked in this digest.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Liu, On Yau’s uniformization conjecture, for the maximal-volume-growth theorem without an upper curvature bound.
  • Lee and Tam, Kähler–Ricci flow and the uniformization problem, for the smoothing approach cited by M1.
  • Datar, Pingali, and Seshadri, Uniformisation of complete Kähler surfaces with positive sectional curvature.
  • Wu, Conditional uniformization of Kähler surfaces.
  • Optional background: Kähler manifolds and biholomorphisms.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniformization of complete Kähler manifolds with positive bisectional curvature (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When geodesic entropy forces local symmetry
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 339 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Release a particle from a point of a curved space, choose its direction, and let it travel at unit speed without external forces. Its path is a geodesic, the curved-space analogue of a straight line. In negative curvature, nearby trajectories generally separate exponentially. Long observations therefore reveal increasingly many distinguishable motions.

There are two ways to measure this complexity. One counts all possible orbit patterns. The other asks how much information is produced by a typical particle, when initial positions and directions are sampled using the metric itself. The second cannot exceed the first. But when do they agree?

Katok’s entropy rigidity conjecture predicts that equality is exceptionally restrictive: the geometry must be locally symmetric. The manuscript in family 339 claims this characterization for every closed, strictly negatively curved smooth manifold of dimension at least three. Together with Katok’s earlier surface theorem, it addresses the full dimensional range of the conjecture.

The surprising feature is the distance between input and conclusion. The input is equality of two real numbers describing long-term motion. The output is an exact differential condition on the curvature tensor everywhere.

2. Background and essential definitions

The space of moving particles

A Riemannian metric ggg assigns an inner product to each tangent space of a manifold MMM. It determines lengths, angles, volume, and geodesics. Here closed means compact without boundary. Strictly negative sectional curvature means that every two-dimensional tangent plane has negative curvature.

The unit tangent bundle is

SM={(x,v):x∈M, v∈TxM, gx(v,v)=1}.SM=\{(x,v):x\in M,\ v\in T_xM,\ g_x(v,v)=1\}.SM={(x,v):x∈M, v∈Tx​M, gx​(v,v)=1}.

It records both position and velocity. The geodesic flow φt\varphi^tφt advances each particle by time ttt. If MMM has dimension nnn, its phase space SMSMSM has dimension 2n−12n-12n−1.

Normalized Liouville measure, denoted mLm_LmL​, samples position according to Riemannian volume divided by total volume, then samples a unit direction uniformly in that tangent sphere. It is a probability measure preserved by the flow.

Two notions of entropy

Topological entropy htop(φ1)h_{\mathrm{top}}(\varphi^1)htop​(φ1) measures the exponential growth rate of distinguishable orbit segments. Roughly, at a fixed small observational resolution, the number of distinguishable trajectories of duration TTT grows like ehTe^{hT}ehT. One then refines the resolution to obtain the entropy.

Measure entropy hmL(φ1)h_{m_L}(\varphi^1)hmL​​(φ1) measures the average information rate for trajectories sampled from mLm_LmL​. The time-one notation fixes the time convention; the paper uses unit-speed geodesics and natural logarithms. The variational principle gives

hmL(φ1)≤htop(φ1).h_{m_L}(\varphi^1)\leq h_{\mathrm{top}}(\varphi^1).hmL​​(φ1)≤htop​(φ1).

Equality says that the smooth geometric probability already captures all the available entropy. It does not say that every individual trajectory has maximal complexity: periodic orbits still exist.

What local symmetry means

Let RgR_gRg​ be the curvature tensor and ∇g\nabla_g∇g​ the covariant derivative, which differentiates tensor fields while accounting for the metric. Local symmetry is expressed by

∇gRg=0.\nabla_gR_g=0.∇g​Rg​=0.

Curvature is unchanged by parallel transport. In the present setting, the simply connected covering space is one of the negatively curved rank-one symmetric spaces: real, complex, quaternionic, or Cayley hyperbolic space, in the dimensions where these exist.

Real hyperbolic space has constant sectional curvature. The other types have different sectional curvatures in different tangent planes, despite being locally symmetric. Thus replacing “locally symmetric” by “constant curvature” would make the claimed theorem false in its stated generality.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Katok’s 1982 paper established the surface case. On a closed surface of negative Euler characteristic, the constant-curvature metric of the same area provides a reference entropy. Liouville entropy lies on one side of this reference value and topological entropy on the other, with rigidity in equality. Katok also proved a higher-dimensional statement within the conformal class of a locally symmetric metric. These results connected a dynamical comparison to a geometric extremum. Katok, Entropy and closed geodesics.

The direct surface argument does not extend unchanged. Flaminio studied variations near real hyperbolic metrics and obtained positivity of the second variation of the entropy gap in suitable directions. But his work also exhibited a hyperbolic three-manifold where the fixed-volume Liouville-entropy Hessian is indefinite. In higher dimensions, the symmetric metric need not be a local maximum of Liouville entropy. Flaminio, 1995.

More recently, Humbert established the conjecture throughout sufficiently small smooth neighborhoods of real and complex hyperbolic metrics. This is a genuine neighborhood theorem, beyond a calculation along individual infinitesimal variations, but it still starts near a known symmetric metric. Humbert, version 3.

Related rigidity results for three-dimensional Anosov flows also supplied important context. Their phase-space dimension is three, however, corresponding to a two-dimensional geodesic base. They do not directly settle the higher-dimensional base problem here.

Another major development was Besson–Courtois–Gallot’s minimal volume-entropy rigidity. That theorem compares a metric to a locally symmetric target in a fixed topological setting. Katok’s question begins without such a target: it asks whether symmetry can be recovered merely from entropy equality. The new manuscript uses classical rigidity at its final stage, after claiming to obtain the missing smooth invariant geometry. It also explicitly uses Ruan’s correction for the Cayley case. Besson–Courtois–Gallot, Ruan.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For every closed, connected, smooth Riemannian manifold (Mn,g)(M^n,g)(Mn,g) with n≥3n\geq3n≥3 and strictly negative sectional curvature, the manuscript asserts

hmL(φ1)=htop(φ1)⟺∇gRg=0.h_{m_L}(\varphi^1)=h_{\mathrm{top}}(\varphi^1)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_gR_g=0.hmL​​(φ1)=htop​(φ1)⟺∇g​Rg​=0.

There is no requirement that the metric be near a symmetric one, belong to a particular conformal class, or satisfy a specified curvature-pinching ratio. Compactness gives negative upper and lower curvature bounds for each given metric, but the ratio of their magnitudes is unrestricted.

All overall scales are allowed. Multiplying lengths by a positive factor changes the rate at which unit-speed particles explore the same geometric paths, and therefore rescales both entropies together. Equality remains meaningful without a chosen volume normalization.

The paper also states a consequence for invariant probabilities. In this setting there is a unique probability measure of maximal entropy. If the metric is not locally symmetric, this measure is distinct from Liouville measure and is, in fact, mutually singular with it. That means the two measures can give full mass to disjoint measurable sets. It is stronger than simply having different density functions, and it follows here from their distinctness and ergodicity.

The implication from local symmetry to equality is the familiar direction. The claimed advance is the global converse, including metrics far from the symmetric models.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the result resolves a central rigidity conjecture connecting Riemannian geometry, smooth dynamics, and entropy. Its strength lies in recovering an exact local geometric structure from one global statistical equality without starting near a symmetric example.

It would also clarify the special role of the metric’s natural volume. Smooth sampling usually favors orbit patterns differently from entropy-maximizing sampling. The theorem says that these viewpoints agree precisely for a very restricted geometric class.

The method’s proposed bridge from entropy to smoothness is significant in its own right. In hyperbolic dynamics, invariant structures can be smooth along individual leaves while varying irregularly from leaf to leaf. Turning a statistical identity into full transverse regularity would address an obstacle that appears well beyond this single conjecture.

The score measures the significance of the stated conclusion, not a mathematical verification of the manuscript.

6. The main idea

Exponential motion creates two transverse geometries

Negative curvature gives a stable direction, in which infinitesimal perturbations contract under forward motion, and an unstable direction, which contracts under backward motion. Together with the flow direction, they split the tangent bundle of phase space:

T(SM)=Es⊕RX⊕Eu.T(SM)=E^s\oplus\mathbb RX\oplus E^u.T(SM)=Es⊕RX⊕Eu.

Here XXX generates the geodesic flow. Stable and unstable directions integrate into leaves. Each leaf is smooth, but the collection need not vary smoothly in transverse directions. This distinction is the main difficulty: smoothness inside every page of a book does not by itself ensure smooth dependence on the page label.

Entropy equality fixes expansion up to a transported correction

Let JJJ denote the instantaneous rate at which unstable volume expands, and let hhh be the common entropy. The paper uses thermodynamic formalism and dynamical cohomology to obtain a function FFF satisfying

J=h+XF.J=h+XF.J=h+XF.

The term XFXFXF is the derivative of FFF along the flow. Its integral around a closed orbit is zero, so every closed orbit sees the same average unstable-volume expansion hhh. This does not make JJJ pointwise constant; it identifies the precise correction to constancy.

The manuscript converts that correction into stable and unstable volume data with exact exponential transport laws. These forms are initially continuous in the ambient space, with better regularity along appropriate leaves. Full smoothness is still a conclusion to be reached.

Finite Taylor data expose an algebraic choice

A finite jet is a finite list of Taylor coefficients. The construction studies jets of actual leaf pieces and the transported volume data. Contraction lets it organize these finite records into polynomial normal forms at each chosen order.

The resulting formal structures admit symmetries: formal vector fields preserving the contact geometry and certain families of covectors. A contact structure here encodes the relation between position and direction in unit-speed mechanics. The entropy transport laws impose a trace constraint on the symmetry algebra.

Using Lie-algebra structure theory, the paper obtains two alternatives. A finite-dimensional algebra provides formal stable and unstable geometric fields. An infinite-dimensional alternative produces particular flat relations between stable and unstable directions. The manuscript then uses the geometry of endpoints at infinity in negative curvature to rule out that second possibility.

This is not an argument that an arbitrary formal power series converges. The paper stresses finite-order truncations, estimates, and dynamical transport at each stage.

Recovering smooth geometry and the metric

In the remaining alternative, quantitative estimates turn the formal data into actual smooth functions labeling leaves. Bounds on volume distortion ensure that these labels have the required nondegeneracy, so their kernels recover globally smooth stable and unstable distributions.

Classical rigidity for smooth Anosov distributions then supplies a symmetric flow model. The final step also tracks orbit periods, contact volume, and the relation between topological and volume entropy. Minimal entropy rigidity converts this flow information into local symmetry of the original Riemannian metric, up to the overall scale already allowed by the theorem.

Thus the proposed chain is: entropy equality controls transported volume; transported volume constrains finite-order symmetries; those constraints force smooth invariant geometry; classical rigidity identifies the metric.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns closed manifolds with strictly negative sectional curvature. It does not assert the same equivalence for noncompact finite-volume spaces, metrics merely of nonpositive curvature, or arbitrary Anosov flows. Each change alters the available compactness or geometry.

The conclusion is local symmetry, not a classification of the manifold’s fundamental group or a claim that all such manifolds share the same topology. Different compact quotients of the symmetric universal covers remain possible.

The statement is exact. It does not provide a quantitative estimate saying that a small entropy gap forces a specified distance to a symmetric metric. Such a stability result would need choices of normalization, geometric bounds, and a topology on the space of metrics.

Finally, the manuscript’s main new work is the passage from leafwise information to ambient smoothness. This digest explains the claimed mechanism and its classical dependencies; it does not assess the validity of the formal-to-smooth argument or independently establish the claimed resolution.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical sources linked above explain the surface theorem, deformation results, local neighborhood theorem, and final minimal-entropy rigidity input. For optional terminology, see geodesic flow, topological entropy, and symmetric space.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Entropy equality and local symmetry in negative curvature (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: An exact Lagrangian that cannot be untied by Hamiltonian motion
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 340 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Classical mechanics describes a system by positions and momenta. If positions form a manifold QQQ, its phase space is the cotangent bundle T∗QT^*QT∗Q. The simplest distinguished submanifold consists of all positions with zero momentum: the zero section.

Many other submanifolds can look locally like the zero section from the viewpoint of symplectic geometry. Arnold’s nearby Lagrangian conjecture asks whether every closed exact Lagrangian in this phase space can be obtained from the zero section by a Hamiltonian motion.

The manuscript in family 340 claims a counterexample. Its Lagrangian has exactly the same abstract smooth manifold as the base, yet cannot be moved to the zero section by a Hamiltonian isotopy. The proposed obstruction lives in how the manifold is placed in phase space, beyond its ordinary topology.

The word “nearby” is historical terminology. The unrestricted conjecture concerns every closed exact embedded Lagrangian in a cotangent bundle; it does not assume that the submanifold is a small graph or lies close to the zero section in a specified norm.

2. Background and essential definitions

Positions, momenta, and symplectic area

A point of T∗QT^*QT∗Q is a pair (q,p)(q,p)(q,p), where qqq is a position and ppp is a linear functional on tangent vectors at qqq. In local coordinates, the canonical one-form and the paper’s symplectic form are

λ=∑ipi dqi,ω=dλ=∑idpi∧dqi.\lambda=\sum_i p_i\,dq_i,\qquad\omega=d\lambda=\sum_i dp_i\wedge dq_i.λ=i∑​pi​dqi​,ω=dλ=i∑​dpi​∧dqi​.

A symplectic form is a closed, nondegenerate differential two-form. It measures oriented area in position–momentum directions. The sign convention for ω\omegaω varies between texts; the manuscript uses the one displayed here.

If QQQ has dimension nnn, a Lagrangian submanifold L⊂T∗QL\subset T^*QL⊂T∗Q has dimension nnn and satisfies ω∣L=0\omega|_L=0ω∣L​=0. It is exact when there is a globally defined function f:L→Rf:L\to\mathbb Rf:L→R such that

λ∣L=df.\lambda|_L=df.λ∣L​=df.

Exactness is a global restriction, stronger than the Lagrangian condition. Equivalently, the integral of λ\lambdaλ around every closed curve in LLL vanishes. “Closed” here means compact without boundary, and “embedded” excludes self-intersections.

The allowed way to move a Lagrangian

A time-dependent Hamiltonian HtH_tHt​ determines a vector field through

ιXHtω=−dHt.\iota_{X_{H_t}}\omega=-dH_t.ιXHt​​​ω=−dHt​.

Its flow is a Hamiltonian isotopy. These motions preserve symplectic structure and form the natural class of deformations in the conjecture. The paper takes the Hamiltonians to have support in one fixed compact subset. For a compact isotopy trace, a cutoff makes this convention harmless.

There are easy positive examples. If u:Q→Ru:Q\to\mathbb Ru:Q→R is smooth, its differential defines the graph

Lu={(q,du(q)):q∈Q}.L_u=\{(q,du(q)):q\in Q\}.Lu​={(q,du(q)):q∈Q}.

It is exact Lagrangian and Hamiltonian isotopic to the zero section. The difficulty is that a general embedded exact Lagrangian need not project one-to-one onto QQQ. Its projection can fold, although the full submanifold in phase space remains embedded.

Being diffeomorphic means being the same abstract smooth manifold. Being Hamiltonian isotopic is much stronger: it specifies an allowed ambient motion of the embedding. Confusing these two notions would erase the point of the claimed counterexample.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Early intersection theorems by Hofer and Laudenbach–Sikorav constrained Hamiltonian deformations of the zero section. Generating functions made these constraints accessible through finite-dimensional critical-point theory: intersections become critical points of auxiliary functions. Chaperon, Sikorav, and others developed methods for transporting generating functions under Hamiltonian motion. Hofer, 1985, Laudenbach–Sikorav, 1985.

There are positive low-dimensional isotopy results. Hind’s work treats Lagrangian spheres in T∗S2T^*S^2T∗S2, and work of Dimitroglou Rizell, Goodman, and Ivrii gives the cotangent-torus theorem. These illustrate real rigidity in specific bases, rather than evidence that can simply be extrapolated to arbitrary dimension. Hind, Dimitroglou Rizell–Goodman–Ivrii.

Meanwhile, the topology of the projection L→QL\to QL→Q became increasingly constrained. Work of Fukaya–Seidel–Smith and Nadler established cohomological and categorical restrictions under additional hypotheses. Abouzaid proved a homotopy-equivalence theorem under a Maslov-class assumption, and Kragh’s work with Abouzaid’s appendix removed that assumption. Abouzaid–Kragh then proved that the projection is a simple homotopy equivalence, a refinement controlling an algebraic obstruction to elementary topological simplification. Abouzaid–Kragh, 2018.

These results concern the projection’s topology, not the full Hamiltonian isotopy class of the embedding. More recent work on twisted generating functions, normal invariants, and Floer homotopy theory imposed still finer necessary conditions. None of those conditions alone identifies the allowed ambient motion.

A particularly direct predecessor is Álvarez-Gavela–Igusa–Sullivan’s work on higher torsion. They constructed Legendrian submanifolds in the one-jet space J1Q=T∗Q×RJ^1Q=T^*Q\times\mathbb RJ1Q=T∗Q×R with nontrivial tube data even when their projections to the base are homotopic to diffeomorphisms. However, forgetting the extra real coordinate can introduce self-intersections in T∗QT^*QT∗Q. The new manuscript’s essential additional claim is an embedded exact Lagrangian construction that keeps a stable tube obstruction. Version 2 of that predecessor.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For some sufficiently large even integer NNN, set

Q=S9×SN−1.Q=S^9\times S^{N-1}.Q=S9×SN−1.

The manuscript asserts the existence of a closed exact smoothly embedded Lagrangian L⊂T∗QL\subset T^*QL⊂T∗Q such that

L≅Q,L\cong Q,L≅Q,

where ≅\cong≅ denotes diffeomorphism, but no compactly supported Hamiltonian isotopy carries the zero section to LLL.

Both QQQ and LLL are connected and simply connected. Thus the obstruction is not an exotic fundamental group or a mismatch of abstract smooth manifolds. The result is an existential high-dimensional example: the theorem does not specify a minimal numerical dimension or assert the construction in every dimension.

If correct, one such example disproves the unrestricted nearby Lagrangian conjecture. It leaves positive theorems for particular bases intact and does not automatically settle variants with additional restrictions.

The construction also distinguishes two roles of a parameter space. Here S9S^9S9 parametrizes the behavior at infinity of functions within one generating family. It is not a parameter indexing a collection of whole Lagrangians in one fixed cotangent bundle. The paper emphasizes this distinction when comparing its obstruction with vanishing theorems for parametrized Whitehead torsion of families of nearby Lagrangians.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The nearby Lagrangian conjecture is a central question about rigidity in cotangent bundles. A counterexample satisfying exactness, embeddedness, and equality of smooth type would change the expected relationship between topological classification and Hamiltonian classification.

The result would show that increasingly strong information about the projection can coexist with a remaining symplectic obstruction. Knowing that the Lagrangian has the right homotopy type—or even the right diffeomorphism type—would still not determine how it can move in phase space.

Its proposed mechanism also links generating functions to algebraic K-theory of spaces and smooth families of cobordisms. These tools detect information that simpler invariants discard. The significance of the claim therefore includes both the negative answer and the kind of invariant used to obtain it.

This rating concerns the stated mathematical consequences if the construction works as claimed.

6. The main idea

Encode a Lagrangian by critical points

Introduce auxiliary variables w∈Rrw\in\mathbb R^rw∈Rr and a smooth function F(q,w)F(q,w)F(q,w). Its fiber-critical set is defined by

dwF(q,w)=0.d_wF(q,w)=0.dw​F(q,w)=0.

A critical point is sent to the phase-space point

(q,w)⟼(q,dqF(q,w)).(q,w)\longmapsto(q,d_qF(q,w)).(q,w)⟼(q,dq​F(q,w)).

With the required regularity of the full critical equation, this gives an exact Lagrangian immersion. The value of FFF on the critical set supplies its primitive. Regularity involves derivatives in both qqq and www; it does not require every fiber Hessian to be invertible. Embeddedness requires a separate global argument.

Put a nontrivial family at infinity

Far out in the auxiliary variables, the generating functions agree with functions homogeneous of degree two:

gb(rw)=r2gb(w),b∈S9.g_b(rw)=r^2g_b(w),\qquad b\in S^9.gb​(rw)=r2gb​(w),b∈S9.

On the unit sphere, each negative domain resembles the negative domain of a nondegenerate quadratic form. The paper calls such a domain a smooth tube. Adding positive and negative quadratic variables gives a stabilization operation, allowing tube families of different dimensions to be compared.

Let T\mathcal TT denote the resulting stable space of tubes. Its elements retain smooth family information. There is also a forgetful map γ:T→BG\gamma:\mathcal T\to BGγ:T→BG recording only an associated stable spherical fibration; BGBGBG is the classifying space for these fibrations.

Using Waldhausen’s tube description and Rognes’s calculations, the paper selects a homotopy class

0≠a∈π9(T),γ∗a=0.0\ne a\in\pi_9(\mathcal T),\qquad \gamma_*a=0.0=a∈π9​(T),γ∗​a=0.

Here π9\pi_9π9​ records families parametrized by a nine-sphere up to deformation. The family remains nontrivial as smooth tube data even though its coarser spherical-fibration data become trivial.

Separate branches in phase space

The extra sphere factor SN−1S^{N-1}SN−1 provides a variable vvv. A suitable coupling arranges that the critical locus obeys

∇gb(w)=R(b)v,\nabla g_b(w)=R(b)v,∇gb​(w)=R(b)v,

where R(b)>0R(b)>0R(b)>0 is a chosen scale. Homogeneity parametrizes this locus by the product of spheres, giving the desired abstract smooth type.

The hard geometric issue is whether two critical points can produce the same covector. Equality of the momenta in the sphere directions forces their remaining difference into a specific line. The variation of RRR over S9S^9S9 is then used to distinguish them through their base-direction momenta. Near critical points of that variation, the tube family is chosen quadratic, where the relevant critical equation has a unique solution.

Thus the manuscript separately addresses both requirements: a regular critical locus produces an immersion, and the momentum-separation argument upgrades it to an embedding.

Why a Hamiltonian untangling would contradict the tube class

Suppose a Hamiltonian isotopy carried the constructed Lagrangian to the zero section. The paper transports its generating family through finitely many small Hamiltonian steps. Each step adds standard split quadratic variables while preserving the stable tube class at infinity.

At the zero section, the critical locus projects diffeomorphically to the base. Consequently, each fiber would have exactly one nondegenerate critical point. Restricting to a fixed sphere-coordinate slice leaves a family over S9S^9S9 with the original nontrivial class at infinity.

The manuscript establishes that this situation is impossible. Morse theory relates the negative directions at the sole critical point to the negative domain at infinity. Between a small inner sphere and a large outer sphere, regular level sets form a family of cobordisms. Stabilization and smooth-family classification then force the tube family to be trivial, contradicting the choice of aaa.

The obstruction therefore survives Hamiltonian motion but is incompatible with the simplest possible critical-point structure at the zero section.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result is a high-dimensional existence statement. It does not identify the lowest dimension permitting a counterexample, classify all exact Lagrangians in the example’s cotangent bundle, or settle the conjecture for every other base.

It also does not claim that LLL fails to be smoothly isotopic to the zero section under unrestricted ambient deformations. The stated obstruction is to Hamiltonian isotopy. Smooth, symplectic, and Hamiltonian equivalence are different questions and should not be interchanged.

Exactness and embeddedness are crucial. An immersed example with double points, or a nonexact Lagrangian, would not disprove the conjecture under discussion. The manuscript explicitly supplies separate steps for the critical equation, branch separation, and preservation of the obstruction under Hamiltonian transport.

Natural further questions concern which bases retain the conjectured rigidity, which stable tube classes can be realized by embeddings, and whether the construction can be made effective in a smaller dimension. This digest reports the claimed construction and its dependencies without checking the proof or independently assessing novelty.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary predecessors linked above explain intersection theory, positive low-dimensional cases, projection rigidity, and higher tube torsion. Optional background is available under cotangent bundle, Lagrangian submanifold, and Morse theory.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A counterexample to the nearby Lagrangian conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Deforming positive triples into hyperkähler geometry
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 341 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A differential two-form measures oriented area on tangent planes. On a four-dimensional manifold, three such forms can cooperate particularly well: every nonzero linear combination may define a symplectic structure with the same orientation. This is called a positive, or hypersymplectic, triple.

A hyperkähler triple is much more rigid. Its three forms come from one Riemannian metric and three interlocking complex structures, and all three are parallel. The geometric question is whether every positive closed triple can be continuously improved into this special form without changing its global integrals over surfaces.

Family 341 claims an affirmative answer on every closed connected smooth four-manifold carrying such a triple. The deformation keeps each of the three cohomology classes fixed. This is stronger than merely finding some hyperkähler metric on the underlying manifold.

The claim also has a striking topological consequence: the manifold itself must be diffeomorphic to the standard K3 manifold or the four-dimensional torus. The initial forms need not arise from an already chosen complex surface, and no symmetry of the initial triple is assumed.

2. Background and essential definitions

Positivity of three area forms

A two-form ω\omegaω is closed if dω=0d\omega=0dω=0. It is symplectic if it is also nondegenerate. In dimension four, nondegeneracy is equivalent to ω∧ω\omega\wedge\omegaω∧ω being nowhere zero.

Fix an orientation and a positive volume form μ\muμ. For three real two-forms, define a symmetric matrix Q(x)Q(x)Q(x) at each point by

ωi∧ωj=2Qijμ.\omega_i\wedge\omega_j=2Q_{ij}\mu.ωi​∧ωj​=2Qij​μ.

The triple is positive when Q(x)Q(x)Q(x) is positive definite everywhere. Equivalently, every nonzero combination ∑iciωi\sum_i c_i\omega_i∑i​ci​ωi​ has positive square. When the forms are closed, all these combinations are symplectic.

The word hypersymplectic here refers to this positive-triple convention in four dimensions. The positivity is pointwise: it is stronger than asking only that the integrated matrix be positive.

What is preserved during deformation?

Closed forms determine de Rham cohomology classes [ωi]∈H2(X;R)[\omega_i]\in H^2(X;\mathbb R)[ωi​]∈H2(X;R). Two closed forms represent the same class if their difference is exact, meaning it is dηd\etadη for a one-form η\etaη. They then have the same integrals over all closed oriented surfaces.

The integrated matrix

Gij=∫Xωi∧ωjG_{ij}=\int_X\omega_i\wedge\omega_jGij​=∫X​ωi​∧ωj​

is positive definite. A constant invertible linear change of the three forms can normalize it to the identity matrix. This is a global linear-algebra normalization; it does not make their pointwise matrix Q(x)Q(x)Q(x) equal to the identity.

The hyperkähler endpoint

An almost-complex structure is a tangent-bundle map JJJ satisfying J2=−IJ^2=-IJ2=−I. It is integrable if it comes from complex coordinates. A Kähler structure consists of an integrable JJJ, a compatible metric ggg, and a closed form ω(u,v)=g(Ju,v)\omega(u,v)=g(Ju,v)ω(u,v)=g(Ju,v).

A hyperkähler metric has three parallel complex structures satisfying the quaternion relations. Its associated two-forms can be normalized to satisfy

ωi∧ωj=2δijμ,\omega_i\wedge\omega_j=2\delta_{ij}\mu,ωi​∧ωj​=2δij​μ,

where δij\delta_{ij}δij​ is one for i=ji=ji=j and zero otherwise. Thus the forms are pointwise orthogonal and have equal square. In the setting of the paper, closedness together with these identities gives the desired parallel hyperkähler triple.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Donaldson’s 2006 study of closed two-forms connected their pointwise wedge geometry with nonlinear elliptic equations. He asked whether a compact four-manifold admitting a positive closed triple must admit a hyperkähler structure and discussed a continuity approach under additional analytic and geometric inputs. Fine and Yao subsequently formulated the normalized deformation problem with all three classes fixed. Donaldson’s paper, Fine–Yao’s account.

The principal analytic approach has been the hypersymplectic flow, obtained from the seven-dimensional G2G_2G2​-Laplacian flow on the product of the four-manifold with a three-torus. Fine–Yao proved extension results under scalar-curvature or torsion bounds and obtained global results near pointwise orthogonality. Such theorems identify what must be controlled; they do not automatically guarantee that every initial triple flows forever and converges.

Complete convergence was established in restricted situations. Huang–Wang–Yao treated a simple one-variable class on the four-torus. Picard–Suan treated flows arising from Kähler Calabi–Yau data. Fine–He–Yao extended convergence to appropriate triples invariant under a three-torus action and proved a cohomologous deformation result for triples preserved by an effective circle action. Three-torus symmetry, circle symmetry.

The topological background is also substantial. Existing constraints on symplectic four-manifolds with torsion first Chern class severely restrict the intersection form of a manifold carrying a positive triple. But an intersection lattice does not by itself identify a smooth four-manifold. The new manuscript uses those restrictions as input to its construction and derives the smooth classification only after obtaining a global hyperkähler structure.

Its other ingredients come from several established theories: positive currents and separation of cones, Seiberg–Witten invariants and pseudoholomorphic curves, elliptic fibrations with nodal fibers, and Yau’s prescribed-volume theorem. The manuscript’s claimed contribution is to connect them into a deformation for an arbitrary initial triple, without imposing the earlier symmetry or integrability hypotheses.

4. What the new manuscript claims

Let XXX be a closed connected oriented smooth four-manifold, and let ω=(ω1,ω2,ω3)\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)ω=(ω1​,ω2​,ω3​) be a smooth positive closed triple normalized by

∫Xωi∧ωj=δij.\int_X\omega_i\wedge\omega_j=\delta_{ij}.∫X​ωi​∧ωj​=δij​.

The manuscript asserts a smooth family ω(t)\omega(t)ω(t), for 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq10≤t≤1, of positive closed triples such that

ω(0)=ω,[ωi(t)]=[ωi],\omega(0)=\omega,\qquad[\omega_i(t)]=[\omega_i],ω(0)=ω,[ωi​(t)]=[ωi​],

and the endpoint is a hyperkähler triple. Positivity and all three individual cohomology classes are retained throughout, not just at the endpoints.

An unnormalized triple is covered by first applying a constant matrix that normalizes GGG, then undoing that matrix after the deformation. The resulting endpoint forms are still parallel and self-dual for a hyperkähler metric, with their original Gram matrix. They need not be the standard orthonormal basis of a hyperkähler triple in those original coordinates.

Two consequences are stated. First, XXX is diffeomorphic to standard K3 or T4T^4T4. Second, every fixed nonzero linear combination

αc=∑i=13ciωi\alpha_c=\sum_{i=1}^3c_i\omega_iαc​=i=1∑3​ci​ωi​

of the original forms is itself a Kähler form for some hyperkähler metric and a parallel integrable complex structure. That metric and complex structure are chosen separately for each ccc. The corollary does not assert a single common metric or a single diffeomorphism simultaneously realizing the entire original triple as hyperkähler.

The source used here is the October 7, 2026 manuscript. Its prescribed-class argument has specific hypotheses explained below; it does not require a general equality of tame and compatible symplectic cones.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the result settles a major deformation question in four-dimensional geometry and converts a flexible-looking positivity condition into a rigid smooth classification.

The fixed-class conclusion is especially strong. Cohomology records the forms’ global periods, so the theorem does not obtain a special metric by discarding the initial global data. It connects the actual triple to special geometry carrying the same three classes.

The individual Kähler realization consequence also illustrates the strength and precision of the claim. Each symplectic form in the three-dimensional span can be interpreted through complex geometry, but the interpretation is allowed to depend on which form is chosen.

The score reflects these consequences and the reach of the proposed construction. It does not imply that the manuscript’s arguments have been verified.

6. The main idea

Keep two forms in view and preserve room for the third

Write the triple as (A,C,B)(A,C,B)(A,C,B). The positive plane spanned by AAA and CCC determines an almost-complex structure, up to sign; BBB selects the sign by taming it. A form β\betaβ tames JJJ when β(v,Jv)>0\beta(v,Jv)>0β(v,Jv)>0 for every nonzero tangent vector. Compatibility additionally requires invariance under JJJ.

The strategy changes the pair while ensuring that the original class [B][B][B] continues to contain a closed tamer. This is a prescribed-class question, more demanding than finding a compatible form in some unspecified class.

The paper develops a cone-separation criterion under the closed definite-pair hypotheses and the condition b+=3b^+=3b+=3. Here b+b^+b+ is the number of positive directions of the intersection pairing on second cohomology. In the orthogonal complement of the two pair classes, a candidate class must lie in the appropriate positive component and pair positively with every relevant irreducible pseudoholomorphic curve.

Positive currents act as potential obstructions. A current generalizes integration over a surface and may also have diffuse mass. The manuscript uses mass and directional estimates to split these obstructions by density. The positive-density part yields curves; the diffuse part is handled using the intersection form. This is how positivity against curves enters the class criterion.

Build a torus fibration from the coefficient sphere

The triple determines a sphere of almost-complex structures by varying its coefficients. The paper combines this family with parametrized Seiberg–Witten theory and Taubes’s correspondence to obtain curves through points in a suitable square-zero integral class.

A lattice argument chooses the class so that curve configurations cannot split in unwanted ways. Perturbations of the closed forms then produce a fibration over a surface: regular fibers are tori, and singular fibers are rational curves with ordinary nodes. The construction begins on the original smooth manifold; it does not assume in advance that it is a complex K3 surface.

Construct an auxiliary equal-square pair

The torus fibration makes it possible to build an auxiliary closed form DDD satisfying

A∧D=C∧D=0,D∧D=A∧A.A\wedge D=C\wedge D=0,\qquadD\wedge D=A\wedge A.A∧D=C∧D=0,D∧D=A∧A.

Local models near nodal fibers come from the Gibbons–Hawking and Ooguri–Vafa constructions. They are glued to regular-fiber data with exponentially small errors as a fiber-area parameter ϵ\epsilonϵ tends to zero. The remaining elliptic estimates lose powers of ϵ−1\epsilon^{-1}ϵ−1, which the proposed construction absorbs into that smaller error.

The auxiliary form is a tool; its class need not be one of the original three. The actual deformation must still return to an endpoint in precisely the original classes.

Use two Kähler steps, then select the whole path

The equal-square closed pair A,DA,DA,D defines an integrable complex structure. Classical Kähler criteria and Yau’s volume theorem provide a representative C1∈[C]C_1\in[C]C1​∈[C] with the needed square and orthogonality properties.

Interpolating from CCC to C1C_1C1​ changes the almost-complex structure associated with (A,C)(A,C)(A,C). A uniform class inequality, obtained before this interpolation, and the prescribed-class taming criterion keep [B][B][B] available all along the path.

The final pair A,C1A,C_1A,C1​ is itself integrable and equal-square. A second Kähler step now produces B1∈[B]B_1\in[B]B1​∈[B]. Smoothly choosing the intervening tamers with both endpoints prescribed gives the actual family of triples. The preparatory paths and this final path are joined smoothly.

For the individual Kähler corollary, one takes a fixed combination along the resulting path. It stays symplectic in a fixed class, so Moser’s theorem supplies an isotopy identifying it with its hyperkähler endpoint. That isotopy depends on the chosen combination, explaining why the corollary is individual rather than simultaneous.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is about existence of a smooth deformation. It does not assert that the hypersymplectic flow exists for all time from arbitrary data, converges uniquely, or realizes the particular constructed path. Those remain distinct analytic questions.

The assumptions are global and specific: dimension four, compactness without boundary, and a positive triple of closed forms. A single symplectic form or three classes with positive intersection matrix do not supply the required pointwise triple.

Nor does the statement identify a unique endpoint metric or classify all paths between triples. Preserving periods gives strong control but is not a uniqueness theorem for the full geometric construction.

The relationship to family 342 is precise. That companion claims existence of a compatible form for a tamed almost-complex structure in an unrestricted class. Here the stronger prescribed-class step is proved under additional definite-pair and intersection-form assumptions. A general cone-comparison conclusion should not be substituted for that specialized argument.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked Donaldson and Fine–Yao works introduce the problem and flow approach; the symmetry papers describe earlier complete cases. For optional background see hyperkähler manifold, de Rham cohomology, and K3 surface.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Deforming hypersymplectic four-manifolds to hyperkähler triples (October 7, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Two inequalities for packing symplectic balls
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 343 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Packing round balls into a larger round ball sounds like elementary geometry. But symplectic packing permits the balls to deform through maps that preserve the position–momentum structure of classical mechanics. The images need not remain round, and Euclidean distances are not preserved.

This flexibility makes ordinary sphere-packing intuition unreliable. Volume is still preserved, but volume alone does not decide what fits. Gromov discovered an additional obstruction: the symplectic capacities of any two packed balls cannot exceed the target capacity when added together.

Family 343 claims that, in every real dimension at least six, these are the only obstructions for any finite collection of balls. The conclusion covers unequal sizes and arbitrarily many components. It gives a complete numerical criterion, rather than an asymptotic statement for sufficiently small or sufficiently numerous equal balls.

Dimension matters sharply. Four-dimensional symplectic ball packing has additional obstructions, and the manuscript does not claim its criterion there.

2. Background and essential definitions

What a symplectic embedding preserves

Write a point of Cn\mathbb C^nCn as zj=xj+iyjz_j=x_j+iy_jzj​=xj​+iyj​. The standard symplectic form is

ω0=∑j=1ndxj∧dyj.\omega_0=\sum_{j=1}^n dx_j\wedge dy_j.ω0​=j=1∑n​dxj​∧dyj​.

A smooth embedding fff is symplectic if f∗ω0=ω0f^*\omega_0=\omega_0f∗ω0​=ω0​. It preserves the two-form, and therefore the volume form ω0n/n!\omega_0^n/n!ω0n​/n!. This is a stronger condition than volume preservation but weaker than preserving lengths or the metric.

For instance, stretching one coordinate xjx_jxj​ by a factor and shrinking its paired coordinate yjy_jyj​ by the reciprocal factor preserves dxj∧dyjdx_j\wedge dy_jdxj​∧dyj​. Symplectic images can therefore be highly distorted.

Capacity is an area, not a radius

The manuscript uses the closed ball

B2n(R)={z∈Cn:π∑j=1n∣zj∣2≤R}.B^{2n}(R)=\left\{z\in\mathbb C^n:\pi\sum_{j=1}^n|z_j|^2\leq R\right\}.B2n(R)={z∈Cn:πj=1∑n​∣zj​∣2≤R}.

Its capacity is RRR, its Euclidean radius is R/π\sqrt{R/\pi}R/π​, and its volume is

Vol⁡(B2n(R))=Rnn!.\operatorname{Vol}(B^{2n}(R))=\frac{R^n}{n!}.Vol(B2n(R))=n!Rn​.

Thus adding capacities is not the same as adding radii. In real dimension six, for example, volume scales as the cube of capacity.

An embedding of a closed ball means a symplectic map defined on an open neighborhood of the entire closed source. The compact images must be pairwise disjoint and lie in the interior of the target ball. These conventions leave a positive amount of room and explain why the theorem uses strict inequalities.

Two necessary restrictions

For source capacities R1,…,RkR_1,\ldots,R_kR1​,…,Rk​, volume preservation requires

∑i=1kRin<Rn.\sum_{i=1}^kR_i^n<R^n.i=1∑k​Rin​<Rn.

Gromov’s two-ball obstruction gives another condition:

Ri+Rj<R(i≠j).R_i+R_j<R\qquad(i\ne j).Ri​+Rj​<R(i=j).

The latter can prohibit a packing even when there is ample unused volume. It reflects symplectic geometry, not the elementary measure of occupied space.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gromov’s 1985 pseudoholomorphic-curve methods transformed symplectic embedding theory. Alongside nonsqueezing phenomena, they produced the two-ball obstruction in all dimensions and additional restrictions in dimension four. McDuff–Polterovich subsequently connected packing to algebraic geometry and blowups. Gromov’s paper, McDuff–Polterovich.

Constructive methods developed in parallel. Traynor built explicit packings, while Schlenk developed planar and higher-dimensional folding techniques. Such constructions demonstrate how much more flexible symplectic images can be than rigid round balls, but a complete criterion for arbitrary collections remained a separate challenge.

Another line of progress established packing stability. Biran proved that sufficiently many equal balls can occupy arbitrarily nearly all the volume of a closed rational symplectic four-manifold. Buse–Hind extended equal-ball stability to higher-dimensional balls, projective spaces, and closed rational symplectic manifolds. Buse–Hind–Opshtein established strong packing stability for closed symplectic four-manifolds when all capacities are sufficiently small. These are regimes in which volume is effectively the only obstruction; they do not handle every arbitrary finite size list. Buse–Hind’s higher-dimensional stability paper.

Siegel–Yao formulated the conjecture settled by the new manuscript: for balls in dimensions at least six, volume and the two-ball inequalities should suffice. Their work also studied stabilized problems, where a four-dimensional domain is multiplied by a fixed symplectic surface. Four-dimensional obstructions can survive in those products. A higher-dimensional ball is a different target, so the two conclusions are compatible. Siegel–Yao.

The new paper combines explicit geometric models with a rearrangement mechanism. Its stated advance is sufficiency for every finite list of positive real capacities, including configurations with one large ball and many smaller ones.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For all integers n≥3n\geq3n≥3, all finite k≥1k\geq1k≥1, and all positive real capacities, a symplectic embedding

⨆i=1kB2n(Ri)↪int⁡B2n(R)\bigsqcup_{i=1}^kB^{2n}(R_i)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{int}B^{2n}(R)i=1⨆k​B2n(Ri​)↪intB2n(R)

exists if and only if both inequalities above hold. The disjoint-union symbol means that every source ball is embedded and their images do not meet.

For one ball, the pairwise condition is empty and the volume condition reduces to R1<RR_1<RR1​<R. For multiple balls, neither numerical test can generally be omitted.

Normalize the target capacity to one and consider real dimension six, so n=3n=3n=3:

Source capacitiesSum of cubed capacitiesLargest pair sumConclusion under the claim
Two balls of capacity 0.60.4321.2Impossible: pairwise obstruction
Eight balls of capacity 0.490.9411920.98A packing exists
Nine balls of capacity 0.491.0588410.98Impossible: volume obstruction

These examples also emphasize that the shapes of the images may be complicated. The theorem does not say that eight ordinary round balls of those radii fit by translations and rotations.

For k≥2k\geq2k≥2 equal balls of capacity rrr, the criterion becomes

rR<min⁡{k−1/n,12}.\frac rR<\min\left\{k^{-1/n},\frac12\right\}.Rr​<min{k−1/n,21​}.

The threshold is a supremum under the closed-source, open-target convention. The displayed equality case is not included. Arbitrary real capacities are allowed; rational parameters used inside the construction do not restrict the final theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the result gives a complete solution to a fundamental symplectic embedding problem throughout all higher dimensions. A geometric existence problem involving potentially complicated deformations becomes decidable from two elementary numerical tests.

The contrast with dimension four is part of its importance. Higher dimension brings flexibility, but not unlimited flexibility: the two-ball obstruction survives after other packing restrictions disappear.

The claimed construction also explains how an average resource constraint can be converted into a geometric arrangement. Total available volume is an integral condition. Actual embedding demands adequate room at each local position in a model. Bridging that difference is the main methodological contribution.

The score refers to the scope of the stated theorem, not independent verification of its construction.

6. The main idea

Express a ball as a varying area requirement

Normalize the target capacity to one. The construction uses a surface of positive genus as a base and a toric domain in Cn−1\mathbb C^{n-1}Cn−1 as a fiber. Positive genus means that the surface has at least one handle.

For the fiber, introduce moment coordinates

pj=π∣zj∣2,j=1,…,n−1.p_j=\pi|z_j|^2,\qquad j=1,\ldots,n-1.pj​=π∣zj​∣2,j=1,…,n−1.

A toric domain is described by allowed values of these coordinates. The remaining complex coordinate contributes an area in the base. A ball of capacity rir_iri​ requires the profile

(ri−∑jpj)+,x+=max⁡{x,0}.\left(r_i-\sum_jp_j\right)_+,\qquad x_+=\max\{x,0\}.(ri​−j∑​pj​)+​,x+​=max{x,0}.

Thus it needs much base area near small fiber moments and none after the fiber has consumed its capacity budget.

Let H(p)H(p)H(p) be the available base-area profile. After allocating the proposed balls, the unused profile is

P(p)=H(p)−∑i(ri−∑jpj)+.P(p)=H(p)-\sum_i\left(r_i-\sum_jp_j\right)_+.P(p)=H(p)−i∑​(ri​−j∑​pj​)+​.

The volume inequality gives positivity of its integral. But PPP can still be negative at individual points, so simply stacking the desired layers does not work.

Redistribute before constructing the layers

The manuscript proves a Hamiltonian comparison principle for the relevant concave profiles. Coordinate rearrangements preserve integrals and lead to a fixed-point construction with a uniform positive gap. Smooth area-preserving maps then realize the rearrangements, with errors kept below that gap.

The handle on the base surface provides two transverse annuli and a closed one-form with a nonzero period. These allow the fiber rearrangement to be inserted into an exact symplectic deformation. The uniform gap supplies disjoint layers large enough to contain the requested balls.

A relative version of Moser’s method transfers the resulting packing back to the original symplectic model while controlling its boundary. The construction deliberately begins with slightly larger auxiliary source capacities, so the final requested closed balls retain a neighborhood of definition.

Build models covering the relevant target region

The remaining issue is to find suitable surface–fiber models with nearly all the target’s available volume. The paper uses projective degenerations, normal-bundle models, and symplectic cuts. These replace a region by a more structured model while retaining the compact subsets needed for a packing.

There are three cases. If every requested capacity is below one half, a complete intersection of quadrics in projective space supplies a positive-genus curve and the required model.

If one capacity is at least one half, the pairwise inequalities make it the unique such capacity. The construction reserves a slightly larger central ball and packs the smaller balls into its exterior shell. In real dimensions at least eight, successive degenerations provide an appropriate curve model of that shell.

Real dimension six needs a separate construction. The analogous simple curve would be a conic, which has genus zero and lacks the handle used by the packing mechanism. The paper instead uses a plane cubic with two marked points. Their contributions modify the integrated area profile, and a carefully preserved circle moment permits the necessary lower cut.

Finally, the relative transfer maps move the compact packings from these models into the original target ball. Preserving the relevant moments and neighborhoods during transfer is essential: an area computation by itself would not supply the asserted embeddings.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is specifically about finite collections of standard balls embedded into a standard ball in real dimension at least six. It does not classify embeddings of ellipsoids, polydisks, arbitrary symplectic domains, or products with a fixed surface.

The strict inequalities matter. The paper does not establish boundary-touching packings or embeddings at exact volume equality under the stated convention. Packings can approach a limiting threshold without attaining it as compact subsets of an open target.

The result establishes existence, not uniqueness up to isotopy, a classification of the space of packings, or a computationally efficient recipe for producing explicit coordinate formulas. The proof’s auxiliary degenerations and Hamiltonian rearrangements are more elaborate than the final criterion suggests.

Finally, this digest treats the claimed sufficiency argument as stated. It does not check the Hamiltonian comparison, the six-dimensional model, or the symplectic transfer arguments independently.

8. Sources and further reading

Siegel–Yao’s paper is the closest source for the conjecture and the distinction from stabilized packing. Gromov and the subsequent packing literature explain the rigidity and stability background. Optional terminology appears under symplectic embedding and symplectic capacity.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Symplectic Ball Packings in Higher Dimensions (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: From taming to compatibility in four dimensions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 342 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Complex geometry begins with an operation on tangent vectors that behaves like multiplication by iii. Symplectic geometry begins with a closed, nondegenerate two-form that measures oriented area. These structures can cooperate in two different ways: the area form may be positive on complex lines, or it may also respect the complex structure exactly.
