The first relation is called taming; the stronger relation is compatibility. Donaldson asked whether, on a closed four-manifold, the existence of a taming symplectic form guarantees the existence of a compatible one.

Family 342 claims an affirmative answer. The almost-complex structure is held fixed. The compatible form is allowed to change its cohomology class, an essential qualification: the manuscript explicitly gives an example where some taming classes have no compatible representative.

The difficulty is easy to state. Averaging a taming form with its complex transform makes it compatible pointwise, but generally destroys the differential equation saying that the form is closed. The problem is to achieve both conditions simultaneously across the entire manifold.

2. Background and essential definitions

Two structures on a four-manifold

Let XXX be a smooth real four-manifold. An almost-complex structure is a smooth linear map JJJ on each tangent space satisfying

J2=−I.J^2=-I.J2=−I.

This is the algebra of a quarter-turn. It need not arise from complex coordinates; when it does, JJJ is called integrable. No integrability is assumed in the main theorem.

A real two-form ω\omegaω is symplectic if it is nondegenerate and closed, with dω=0d\omega=0dω=0. It tames JJJ if

ω(v,Jv)>0(v≠0).\omega(v,Jv)>0\qquad(v\ne0).ω(v,Jv)>0(v=0).

Thus every complex line has positive oriented area. Compatibility additionally requires

ω(Ju,Jv)=ω(u,v).\omega(Ju,Jv)=\omega(u,v).ω(Ju,Jv)=ω(u,v).

A compatible pair defines a Riemannian metric by g(u,v)=ω(u,Jv)g(u,v)=\omega(u,Jv)g(u,v)=ω(u,Jv). Together they form an almost-Kähler structure. It becomes Kähler only if JJJ is integrable.

Why projection is insufficient

For any two-form, its invariant part is

ωinv(u,v)=12(ω(u,v)+ω(Ju,Jv)).\omega^{\mathrm{inv}}(u,v)=\tfrac12\bigl(\omega(u,v)+\omega(Ju,Jv)\bigr).ωinv(u,v)=21​(ω(u,v)+ω(Ju,Jv)).

If ω\omegaω tames JJJ, this projection remains positive on complex lines and is invariant. But JJJ varies with position, and differentiation of the projected form introduces derivatives of JJJ. Therefore dω=0d\omega=0dω=0 does not generally imply dωinv=0d\omega^{\mathrm{inv}}=0dωinv=0.

The missing condition is global and differential, not a failure of pointwise linear algebra.

Classes and cones

A closed form determines a cohomology class [ω]∈H2(X;R)[\omega]\in H^2(X;\mathbb R)[ω]∈H2(X;R). The class records its integrals over closed surfaces. Write KJt\mathcal K_J^tKJt​ for the set of taming classes and KJc\mathcal K_J^cKJc​ for the compatible classes. They are cones: positive scaling and addition preserve the corresponding positivity conditions.

A two-form α\alphaα is anti-invariant when α(Ju,Jv)=−α(u,v)\alpha(Ju,Jv)=-\alpha(u,v)α(Ju,Jv)=−α(u,v). Such a form vanishes on every complex line. Let HJ−H_J^-HJ−​ be the subspace of cohomology represented by closed anti-invariant forms. Adding one of these to a compatible form preserves taming, though not compatibility.

The intersection pairing of two classes is

a⋅b=∫Xα∧β,a\cdot b=\int_X\alpha\wedge\beta,a⋅b=∫X​α∧β,

where α,β\alpha,\betaα,β are closed representatives and XXX has the orientation determined by JJJ. It depends only on the classes.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Donaldson formulated the existence question in his 2006 paper on two-forms and elliptic equations. He also proposed a related a priori estimate problem for prescribed volume. These are distinct problems: existence of some compatible form does not solve every prescribed-volume equation. Donaldson.

For integrable structures, the question belongs to the theory of compact complex surfaces. Buchdahl and Lamari established Kähler criteria without relying on the classification of surfaces. Positive currents supplied both existence tools and obstructions. Li–Zhang proved the equivalence between the existence of taming and compatible symplectic forms on complex surfaces and developed a cohomological framework for comparing the two cones. Li–Zhang, 2009.

Pseudoholomorphic curves offered another route. Gromov constructed compatible forms for almost-complex structures on the complex projective plane tamed by its standard symplectic form, using averages of currents associated with pseudoholomorphic lines. Taubes developed integration over curve moduli spaces to establish compatibility for a residual set of structures in the case b2+=1b_2^+=1b2+​=1, with prescribed-class conclusions under stated additional assumptions. Here residual means a countable intersection of open dense sets; it does not mean every structure. His later correction addresses the relevant first-Betti-number case. Taubes’s original paper, the correction.

Li–Zhang extended curve-based methods to all tamed structures on certain rational surfaces and to further cases under hypotheses involving embedded spheres. Other approaches used restrictions on the anti-invariant cohomology dimension. Li–Zhang, rational four-manifolds.

The new manuscript claims to remove these integrability, genericity, and cohomological-dimension restrictions for the existence question. It uses positive-current duality rather than assuming that a suitable family of pseudoholomorphic curves is already available.

4. What the new manuscript claims

The main theorem states: if a smooth almost-complex structure JJJ on a closed connected smooth real four-manifold is tamed by a symplectic form, then a smooth symplectic form compatible with that same JJJ exists.

The source is the October 6, 2026 manuscript. Its conclusion places no restriction on the compatible form’s cohomology class.

The second theorem describes the compatible cone more precisely. Define

V=(HJ−)⊥,C=KJt∩V.V=(H_J^-)^\perp,\qquad C=\mathcal K_J^t\cap V.V=(HJ−​)⊥,C=KJt​∩V.

Orthogonality is with respect to the intersection pairing. The manuscript asserts

KJt=C+HJ−,\mathcal K_J^t=C+H_J^-,KJt​=C+HJ−​,

and

KJc={a∈C:a⋅y>0 for all 0≠y∈C‾}.\mathcal K_J^c=\{a\in C:a\cdot y>0\text{ for all }0\ne y\in\overline C\}.KJc​={a∈C:a⋅y>0 for all 0=y∈C}.

The closure C‾\overline CC is taken inside VVV. The sum denotes all sums of one element from each set. Crucially, the strict positivity test includes every nonzero boundary point of the closed cone, not just its interior.

Write hJ−=dim⁡HJ−h_J^-=\dim H_J^-hJ−​=dimHJ−​, and let b2+b_2^+b2+​ be the positive index of the intersection form. Under the additional condition

hJ−=b2+−1,h_J^-=b_2^+-1,hJ−​=b2+​−1,

the paper obtains KJt=KJc+HJ−\mathcal K_J^t=\mathcal K_J^c+H_J^-KJt​=KJc​+HJ−​. In particular, if b2+=1b_2^+=1b2+​=1, every taming class has a compatible representative.

Without that dimension condition, the manuscript explicitly asserts that the inclusion can be strict, even when HJ−=0H_J^-=0HJ−​=0. Its four-torus example has two taming classes whose intersection is zero. A compatible class must pair strictly positively with every taming class, so neither of those two classes can be compatible. Nevertheless, the example has another compatible form. This makes the distinction between existence and prescribed class concrete.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the result settles a central existence question at the interface of symplectic and almost-complex geometry in dimension four. It says that positivity on complex lines can always be upgraded to a closed compatible geometry, even though the obvious pointwise projection fails.

Keeping JJJ fixed is important. Choosing a new almost-complex structure compatible with a given symplectic form is standard; finding a compatible form for a prescribed tamed structure is the difficult direction.

The cone theorem adds information about which global periods can occur. It would replace a bare existence statement with an intersection-theoretic test, while explaining why arbitrary taming classes need not survive the upgrade.

The manuscript’s current estimates also feed into the hypersymplectic deformation construction in family 341. That application adds its own prescribed-class hypotheses and deformation arguments. The rating concerns the significance of these stated claims, not their verification.

6. The main idea

Translate failure of existence into an obstruction

The proof begins by supposing that no compatible form exists. Positive invariant forms make an open convex cone, while closed invariant forms make a linear space. A separation theorem then provides a nonzero positive functional separating them.

This functional is a current PPP. One can think of a current as generalized integration over oriented surfaces, allowing both concentrated and diffuse mass. Positivity means that it evaluates nonnegatively on forms positive on complex lines. By construction, PPP vanishes on all closed invariant forms.

An elliptic correction supplies an anti-invariant distribution QQQ such that

T=P+QT=P+QT=P+Q

annihilates every closed two-form. If one could prove Q=0Q=0Q=0, the contradiction would be immediate: a nonzero positive current must evaluate positively on a taming form, but TTT is required to vanish on that closed form.

The analytic task is therefore to remove the anti-invariant correction without losing control of the positive current.

Control mass and changing directions

Represent PPP as a weighted average of oriented complex-line elements. Let μ\muμ be the resulting measure on XXX. Corrected radial tests produce a quadratic local mass bound

μ(Br(x))≤Cr2.\mu(B_r(x))\leq Cr^2.μ(Br​(x))≤Cr2.

This is the scaling expected for something surface-like inside a four-dimensional ambient space. It does not by itself say that PPP is integration over a smooth surface.

Regularization using the Hodge operator gives an L2L^2L2 bound for QQQ, meaning that its squared magnitude is integrable, and an estimate on how the complex-line directions vary between nearby points. The first regularized pairing gives boundedness, but a remaining negative error prevents it from directly proving Q=0Q=0Q=0.

Separate the part with positive density

The manuscript establishes existence of the two-dimensional density

θ(x)=lim⁡r↓0r−2μ(Br(x))\theta(x)=\lim_{r\downarrow0}r^{-2}\mu(B_r(x))θ(x)=r↓0lim​r−2μ(Br​(x))

and considers the set EEE where this density is positive. Its central step claims that the restriction PEP_EPE​ is closed. This is subtle: restricting a closed object to an arbitrary measurable set can create a boundary.

The argument uses smooth cutoffs of density and combines two kinds of error. An angular estimate controls variation of the tangent directions; a transverse estimate controls how nearby base points depart from the approximate tangent plane. After the appropriate normalization, their product tends to zero. The L2L^2L2 control of QQQ handles its contribution to the cutoff boundary.

This produces closedness of the positive-density part without requiring a specified rate of convergence of tangent measures. The remaining positive part is concentrated at zero-density centers, precisely where the troublesome error in the regularized pairing can be made to vanish.

Finish the contradiction and refine it by class

Pairing the residual current with TTT, using the closedness just obtained, forces Q=0Q=0Q=0. The resulting positive current cannot annihilate the original closed taming form. This contradicts the assumed absence of a compatible form.

For the cone theorem, the manuscript repeats separation with a cohomology class prescribed. The resulting obstruction is expressed through the intersection pairing and the closure of the invariant part of the taming cone. This yields the strict positivity condition in the theorem rather than a universal equality of taming and compatible classes.

A specifically four-dimensional identity supports the estimates: anti-invariant two-forms are self-dual for a compatible auxiliary metric. The proof therefore has a structural dependence on dimension, not merely a convenient choice of notation.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem assumes compactness without boundary and real dimension four. It does not assert an analogous implication in arbitrary dimension, where the two-form decompositions and available obstructions differ.

Compatibility does not make the prescribed JJJ integrable. The output is almost-Kähler geometry, with Kähler geometry only in the integrable case.

The result also does not preserve the original taming form, its class in general, or a prescribed volume density. It gives existence for fixed JJJ, plus the stated cone criterion. Donaldson’s stronger analytic estimate questions require separate treatment.

The cone statement is particularly sensitive to quantifiers: positivity against all nonzero elements of C‾\overline CC is stronger than positivity against a selected collection of classes. The special dimension condition gives a simpler equality, but the paper does not claim that equality without it.

These are the manuscript’s stated conclusions and mechanisms. The digest does not verify the density-splitting argument, the example, or the claimed resolution independently.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary sources linked above cover Donaldson’s question, cone comparisons, and curve-based partial results. Optional background appears under almost complex manifold, symplectic manifold, and current in mathematics.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Taming implies compatibility on four-manifolds (October 6, 2026).

entry.title: Infinitely many distinct closed geodesics on every sphere
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 345 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A geodesic is the path followed by a freely moving particle on a curved space. A closed geodesic returns to its starting point with its velocity aligned so that the motion repeats forever. On a round sphere, great circles provide infinitely many examples.

Now deform the metric arbitrarily. The sphere may no longer be round, have positive curvature, or possess any visible symmetry. Must infinitely many different closed geodesics survive?

Family 345 claims that they do for every smooth Riemannian metric on the standard sphere SnS^nSn, in every dimension n≥2n\geq2n≥2. The two-dimensional case is classical; the claimed advance includes all higher-dimensional metrics, even those with degeneracies that obstruct generic Morse-theoretic arguments.

The counting convention is essential. Running around the same path twice, starting at another point, or reversing direction does not create a new geometric image. The claim supplies infinitely many genuinely different paths in the manifold, rather than infinitely many parametrizations of a finite list.

2. Background and essential definitions

Prime geodesics and geometric distinction

A closed geodesic is prime if its period is the least positive period of the trajectory. Its iterates traverse that same trajectory repeatedly. A prime closed geodesic can have self-intersections; prime does not mean a simple embedded circle.

Two geodesics are geometrically distinct here if their images as subsets of the manifold differ. The theorem identifies changes of starting point and orientation, as well as repeated traversal.

The metric is arbitrary but smooth and Riemannian. Riemannian lengths come from a positive-definite quadratic form on each tangent space. More general Finsler metrics need not have this quadratic structure, and some are not symmetric under reversing velocity. The main theorem does not cover all Finsler metrics.

Geodesics as critical points on a space of loops

Let ΛM\Lambda MΛM be the space of loops γ:R/Z→M\gamma:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to Mγ:R/Z→M with square-integrable first derivative. This is the Sobolev space usually denoted H1H^1H1. It supports the energy functional

E(γ)=∫01∣γ˙(t)∣g2 dt.E(\gamma)=\int_0^1|\dot\gamma(t)|_g^2\,dt.E(γ)=∫01​∣γ˙​(t)∣g2​dt.

Its nonconstant critical points are closed geodesics parametrized at constant speed. Constant loops are also critical and must be distinguished from the desired trajectories.

The paper filters loop space using square-root energy

F(γ)=E(γ).F(\gamma)=\sqrt{E(\gamma)}.F(γ)=E(γ)​.

The usual length satisfies ℓ(γ)≤F(γ)\ell(\gamma)\leq F(\gamma)ℓ(γ)≤F(γ), with equality at constant speed. An energy threshold therefore gives a way to organize the topology of loops by their geometric cost.

Topology that persists, and topology that disappears

Homology measures cycles and holes in a space. A cycle in a low-energy part of loop space may remain nontrivial globally, or it may become the boundary of a higher-dimensional family after a larger energy threshold is allowed.

These temporary features matter. Simply counting local critical points or the final homology of loop space can miss information about when classes appear and disappear. The manuscript’s argument is designed to control that filtered behavior.

A geodesic is degenerate when its second variation has additional zero directions beyond the inevitable symmetry of changing the starting time. Such degeneracies can make families of critical loops interact. The theorem does not assume they are absent.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Birkhoff developed minimax methods for finding closed geodesics on surfaces of genus zero. Lyusternik–Fet later proved that every positive-dimensional closed Riemannian manifold has a nonconstant closed geodesic. Existence of one is much weaker than infinitude of distinct images.

Bott’s iteration theory and Gromoll–Meyer’s local Morse theory explain how the topology contributed by repeated traversals is constrained. For a simply connected closed manifold, unbounded Betti numbers of its free loop space over a field force infinitely many geometrically distinct geodesics. Vigué-Poirrier–Sullivan showed that sufficiently rich rational cohomology of the manifold supplies that growth. Spheres are a central exception: their cohomology has one algebra generator, and their degreewise loop Betti numbers are bounded. Gromoll–Meyer, Vigué-Poirrier–Sullivan.

For the two-sphere, Bangert’s work together with Franks’s or Hingston’s established infinitude. Later work extended this to reversible Finsler two-spheres, and Albach obtained a quantitative growth result in that setting. These powerful surface theorems do not automatically extend to higher-dimensional spheres. De Philippis–Marini–Mazzucchelli–Suhr, Albach.

In higher dimensions, Rademacher proved infinitude for strongly bumpy metrics on compact simply connected manifolds and showed that these metrics are generic. Finite multiplicity results also hold without genericity, including at least two geometrically distinct closed geodesics on every Riemannian three-sphere. Passing to a limit of generic metrics is insufficient for infinitude: different geodesics can merge or lose the distinctions used in the counting argument.

The new manuscript builds on string topology, particularly loop cutting and joining, and on Hingston–Rademacher’s resonance theorem for spheres. Block–Manin–Weinberger’s work provides a direct predecessor for its fixed-degree filling estimates. Resonance theorem, persistent homology of function spaces.

The source also discusses earlier unrestricted infinitude claims and reports objections to their proofs. Those objections are the manuscript’s assessment, not conclusions independently reached here. The present digest explains its claimed new argument without treating those earlier claims as established solutions.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For every integer n≥2n\geq2n≥2 and every smooth Riemannian metric on the standard smooth sphere SnS^nSn, there are infinitely many prime closed geodesics with pairwise distinct images.

No curvature bound, nondegeneracy, genericity, or symmetry hypothesis is imposed. “Standard smooth sphere” specifies the smooth manifold; the theorem does not automatically include every exotic smooth sphere in high dimension.

The manuscript gives a finite-cover corollary. If a closed manifold admits a finite smooth cover diffeomorphic to a standard SnS^nSn, every smooth Riemannian metric on that manifold also has infinitely many geodesic images. This includes real projective spaces and smooth spherical space forms. The metric downstairs need not be the standard quotient metric.

It then obtains the same conclusion for every nonempty closed smooth three-manifold, whether orientable or not. For infinite fundamental group, this uses Rademacher–Taimanov’s existing theorem. For finite fundamental group, Perelman’s geometrization gives a finite spherical cover, and the new sphere theorem applies. Disconnected manifolds are covered by working on one component. Rademacher–Taimanov.

These are statements about the number of images, not the number of distinct lengths. On a round sphere, infinitely many prime geodesics all have the same length. The manuscript does not claim a quantitative length-counting rate for its new finite-fundamental-group cases.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem resolves a central outstanding class in the closed-geodesic infinitude problem and completes the problem for closed three-manifolds.

Spheres are especially important because ordinary loop-space Betti-number growth does not supply the standard infinitude argument. They require finer use of topology and iteration, even though they are among the most familiar manifolds.

The inclusion of degenerate metrics is equally significant. Generic theorems describe a large and well-behaved collection of metrics, but the universal statement must also handle exceptional metrics where critical trajectories interact in more complicated ways.

The proposed degree-independent filling bound and filtered comparison of loop operations could also be useful beyond the final infinitude theorem. The rating concerns these stated advances, not proof verification.

6. The main idea

Assume there are only finitely many prime images

The argument proceeds by contradiction. If only finitely many prime images exist, every nonconstant critical loop is an iterate of one of finitely many oriented trajectories. Iteration theory constrains its Morse index, which counts independent directions in which energy decreases.

The local homology ranks of these iterates are uniformly bounded and occur near finitely many index-versus-length lines. Degenerate trajectories require additional local analysis, but the manuscript constructs the relevant comparison maps using one common flow, so it keeps track of the actual maps rather than only abstract group dimensions.

This restricts what can happen at each energy crossing. It does not yet control temporary topology accumulated between crossings.

Bound the lifetime of ordinary temporary cycles

The manuscript proves a uniform filling statement: there is a constant DDD, depending on the metric, such that any cycle below square-root energy aaa which bounds in the full loop space already bounds below

a+D.a+D.a+D.

The same DDD works in every homological degree. The statement concerns cycles that are globally boundaries; it does not say that all loop-space topology vanishes after a fixed threshold.

First, shortening and replacement of loop families give an estimate depending on degree. Then a filtered cut operation lowers a high-degree class into a bounded range of degrees. A loop product joins loops to restore the removed degree. Hingston–Rademacher resonance controls the difference between the lengths removed and added, yielding a bounded total increment.

The paper supplies a cut–join identity with explicit filtration bounds. Its unit is the fundamental class of constant loops in the loop product, so keeping the distinction between absolute and relative constructions is part of the argument.

Add reflection and half-period translation

Loop space has natural symmetries. Reflection reverses the parameter, while translation by half a period identifies loops that repeat a half-length root. The paper uses equivariant cohomology, which records topology together with these group actions, with coefficients in the two-element field F2\mathbb F_2F2​.

Let BaB_aBa​ be the reflection-equivariant cohomology below threshold aaa, relative to constant loops, and let B∞B_\inftyB∞​ be its full-loop-space counterpart. Define

T(a)=dim⁡coker⁡(B∞⟶Ba),T(a)=\dim\operatorname{coker}(B_\infty\longrightarrow B_a),T(a)=dimcoker(B∞​⟶Ba​),

summing over degrees. This measures extra sublevel classes that are not restrictions of global ones.

Under the finite-prime-image assumption, the manuscript proves that T(a)T(a)T(a) is uniformly bounded. It compares the actual equivariant degree on the half-translation fixed locus with the degree of the half-length root. The total discrepancy at a finite cutoff is at most linear in aaa. A long chain of extra classes would instead force a quadratic discrepancy. The ordinary filling estimate handles the remaining degree ranges.

Doubling forces an impossible first appearance

The full symmetry of loops gives

T(2a)≥T(a).T(2a)\geq T(a).T(2a)≥T(a).

This is monotonicity under doubling, not a claim that TTT is monotone between arbitrary thresholds. Since TTT is a bounded integer, an interval where it reaches its maximum propagates to arbitrarily large doubled intervals.

The equality case of the doubling comparison requires certain global classes, computed using the round-metric filtration, to appear with independent partners obtained by cup product with an evaluation class. On a sufficiently large maximal interval, one of these classes must become visible for the first time at a critical crossing.

But the local crossing calculation makes the relevant cup action vanish there. The new class has appeared while its required partner has not. This contradicts the equality condition and rules out the finite-prime assumption.

Finally, the finite-cover argument controls multiplicity: a covering of degree rrr has at most rrr upstairs prime images projecting to a given downstairs image. Infinitely many upstairs images therefore cannot collapse to finitely many downstairs ones, including when geodesics self-intersect.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The main theorem concerns standard spheres with smooth Riemannian metrics. The three-manifold conclusion uses additional established theorems, and the finite-cover conclusion requires an actual finite smooth spherical cover.

The general infinitude problem for every closed manifold in every dimension is not claimed here. Nor does the result imply that the geodesics are embedded, mutually disjoint, or have unbounded distinct lengths.

Quantitative questions remain separate: how many images occur below a length threshold, how their lengths are distributed, and what uniform estimates depend only on geometric bounds. The proof’s qualitative contradiction does not supply those conclusions automatically.

This digest reports the manuscript’s filtered-topology mechanism and its stated dependencies. It does not audit the cut–join identity, the equivariant calculations, or the treatment of degenerate local crossings.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked primary sources describe loop-space growth, surface results, resonance, quantitative fillings, and the three-manifold input. Optional definitions appear under closed geodesic, Morse theory, and equivariant cohomology.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Infinitely many closed geodesic images on every Riemannian sphere (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How large can the singular set of a stationary surface be?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 346 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A smooth minimal surface has zero first-order change of area under every small deformation supported away from its boundary. But limits of minimal surfaces need not stay smooth: sheets can merge, cross, or accumulate. Geometric measure theory uses varifolds to retain area and tangent-plane information through such limits.

The basic question is how much of a stationary varifold must still have a genuinely smooth neighborhood. A tangent plane almost everywhere is not enough. Several sheets could be nearly coincident, and singular points could accumulate near a point that looks planar under magnification.

Family 346 contains two related claims. The September manuscript says that the singular set has zero measure in the dimension of the varifold. The October manuscript strengthens this in Euclidean space to a sharp Hausdorff-dimension bound: an mmm-dimensional stationary integral varifold has singular set of dimension at most m−1m-1m−1.

No area-minimizing or stability assumption is imposed. The family therefore concerns the weakest usual variational notion of a minimal surface, in every positive dimension and codimension.

2. Background and essential definitions

A surface with multiplicity and tangent information

An integral mmm-varifold in an open set U⊂Rm+nU\subset\mathbb R^{m+n}U⊂Rm+n is built from a countably rectifiable set EEE, with a positive integer multiplicity θ\thetaθ. Rectifiability means that, outside a set of zero mmm-dimensional measure, the set can be covered by countably many Lipschitz images of subsets of Rm\mathbb R^mRm.

Its weight measure is

μ(A)=∫E∩Aθ dHm,\mu(A)=\int_{E\cap A}\theta\,d\mathcal H^m,μ(A)=∫E∩A​θdHm,

where Hm\mathcal H^mHm is mmm-dimensional Hausdorff measure, the extension of length, area, and volume to irregular sets. The varifold also records the approximate tangent mmm-plane at almost every point. It does not require a choice of orientation.

Multiplicity allows, for example, a plane counted twice. Local finiteness of the measure is required, but the theorems impose no fixed upper bound on multiplicity.

Stationary is weaker than minimizing

Stationarity means that the first derivative of area vanishes under every compactly supported ambient deformation. If PxP_xPx​ is orthogonal projection onto the approximate tangent plane and XXX is a compactly supported vector field, this is

∫tr⁡(PxDX(x)) dμ(x)=0.\int\operatorname{tr}(P_xDX(x))\,d\mu(x)=0.∫tr(Px​DX(x))dμ(x)=0.

The trace is tangential divergence: the infinitesimal rate of area change along the surface. On a smooth submanifold, stationarity is equivalent to zero mean curvature.

A stationary surface may still have deformations that decrease area to second order. Stability excludes those negative second variations, and area minimization is stronger still. Neither stronger condition is assumed here.

What counts as a singular point?

A support point is regular if an entire neighborhood contains exactly one smooth embedded minimal submanifold, counted with a constant positive integer multiplicity. Every other support point is singular.

A double plane is regular under this definition. Two distinct crossing planes are singular along their intersection, because their union is not one embedded submanifold there. Smooth parametrization of most of the mass is insufficient if extra pieces remain in every neighborhood.

Hausdorff dimension dim⁡H\dim_HdimH​ distinguishes the size of thin sets more finely than measure alone. A set can have zero mmm-dimensional measure while having dimension strictly greater than m−1m-1m−1, so the dimension theorem is stronger than almost-everywhere regularity.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Allard’s compactness and regularity theory established the foundational connection between weak convergence and smooth geometry. It gives regularity near appropriate multiplicity-one planar behavior and a relatively open dense regular set. At higher planar multiplicity, simply dividing by that multiplicity can destroy the neighborhood density hypotheses needed by the theorem. Allard, 1972.

Classical dimension reduction controls points at which no tangent cone is a plane. Naber–Valtorta strengthened understanding of these strata through rectifiability results. The remaining difficulty is singular points with higher-multiplicity planar tangents. Their blowups look flat even though their actual support may fail to be smooth nearby. Naber–Valtorta.

For area-minimizing integral currents, Almgren’s theory gives the stronger arbitrary-codimension bound m−2m-2m−2. De Lellis–Spadaro developed a new proof using multiple-valued functions, center manifolds, and frequency methods. Those results depend on minimizing hypotheses and cannot simply be applied to arbitrary stationary varifolds. Crossing planes already rule out an m−2m-2m−2 bound in the present setting. De Lellis–Spadaro, center manifolds.

Progress also came from special multiplicity and graphical classes. Hirsch–Spolaor proved the m−1m-1m−1 estimate for two-valued stationary Lipschitz graphs and almost-everywhere regularity for stationary codimension-one integral currents with density at most two. These are important predecessors but retain assumptions absent from the family’s general claims. Two-valued graphs, stationary hypercurrents.

A separate line concerns how smoothly one can cover almost all of the measure. Menne proved second-order rectifiability, and Brena–De Lellis–Franceschini proved smooth rectifiability and infinite-order approximation. Kolasiński later supplied an alternative approach. A countable smooth covering does not say that the whole support in a neighborhood equals one smooth piece; that stronger local conclusion is the issue here. Brena–De Lellis–Franceschini, Kolasiński.

Brena–Decio–De Lellis explicitly separated the measure-zero and dimension-bound conjectures. The two manuscripts in this family address those two levels. Their conjectures and background.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let m,n≥1m,n\geq1m,n≥1, let U⊂Rm+nU\subset\mathbb R^{m+n}U⊂Rm+n be open, and let VVV be a stationary integral mmm-varifold in UUU.

M2, September 23:

Hm(Sing⁡V)=0.\mathcal H^m(\operatorname{Sing}V)=0.Hm(SingV)=0.

Thus almost every support point has a neighborhood on which the varifold is a constant positive integer multiple of a smooth embedded minimal submanifold. M2 also states this almost-everywhere conclusion for integral varifolds stationary within a full round sphere of any positive radius, in arbitrary positive dimension and codimension.

M1, October 5:

dim⁡HSing⁡V≤m−1.\dim_H\operatorname{Sing}V\leq m-1.dimH​SingV≤m−1.

This Euclidean estimate is sharp. Take two distinct mmm-planes intersecting along an (m−1)(m-1)(m−1)-plane and add their varifolds. Each plane is stationary, so their sum is stationary. Its singular set is precisely the intersection, attaining the bound.

Both manuscripts omit stability, minimization, orientability, a prescribed density upper bound, and any codimension-one restriction. The conclusions are local inside UUU; boundary behavior outside that open set is not included.

M1 imports M2’s signed-excess theorem and local fitting and frequency estimates. It does not merely apply M2’s measure-zero conclusion, which by itself would not imply the dimension bound. These are connected stages of a program, not two independent proofs of the same theorem.

The round-sphere statement explicitly supplied by M2 is almost-everywhere regularity. The main sharp dimension theorem is stated in Euclidean open sets.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the family resolves fundamental regularity questions for a very general class of stationary geometric objects. It identifies the largest possible singular-set dimension without assuming the stronger variational properties used in much of minimal-surface regularity theory.

The result would close the gap between looking smooth in a measure-theoretic covering and having an actual smooth support neighborhood. Higher-multiplicity planar tangents are precisely where that gap is hardest to bridge.

The sharpness example also clarifies what can reasonably be expected. Crossings are allowed by stationarity, so universal complete smoothness is impossible. The claimed theorem gives the optimal dimension ceiling consistent with those unavoidable examples.

The methods combine signed estimates, curved reference surfaces, and measure-valued blowups. Their significance lies in adapting tools inspired by minimizing-current theory to a setting where minimization is unavailable. This rating concerns the stated claims, not a verification of those adaptations.

6. The main idea

Preserve a cancellation between excess mass and tilt

Near a planar tangent, choose horizontal and vertical coordinates. Project the weight measure to the horizontal plane. Relative to a multiplicity-QQQ plane, let MMM denote the signed projected-mass discrepancy, and let DDD measure how much the tangent planes tilt vertically.

The key quantity is

2M−D.2M-D.2M−D.

Both terms have leading contributions from a small graphical slope, so preserving their signs permits cancellation. Replacing everything by absolute values would discard the improvement the argument needs.

M2 claims a very small upper error for suitable weighted integrals of this signed quantity. Its proof proceeds by induction on integer multiplicity. When groups of sheets separate in height, lower-multiplicity estimates become available. Heat-potential contacts select centers and scales where a hypothetical violation can be measured, and a packing argument charges those contacts to an insufficient amount of excess mass.

Fit a curved center and force the support onto it

A flat plane is often too crude a reference. The manuscript fits smooth minimal graphs at successive scales, stopping when the support-height error is too large. Nearby successful fits agree sufficiently well to be glued into a single curved center.

A centered first-moment estimate controls average height, while second and higher moments measure spread. A frequency function compares height with derivative energy and records the order of vanishing. The signed estimate supplies an inward comparison and height doubling, rather than assuming doubling in advance.

At points where other multiplicities occupy vanishing relative mass, the failed-fit regions become too small to carry nonzero height. The support must therefore lie on the center in a neighborhood. Stationarity then makes the multiplicity constant and the center smooth and minimal. This yields M2’s almost-everywhere conclusion.

For the sphere consequence, M2 separately forms a Euclidean cone over the spherical varifold and relates stationarity and regularity away from the cone vertex. It is a geometric reduction specific to the round metric.

Retain a large set of singular centers through magnification

M1 assumes for contradiction that the singular set has dimension greater than m−1m-1m−1. Choose

m−1<s<dim⁡HSing⁡V.m-1<s<\dim_H\operatorname{Sing}V.m−1<s<dimH​SingV.

Dimension reduction supplies scales converging to a multiplicity-QQQ plane and measures σi\sigma_iσi​ on nearby singular centers satisfying

σi(Br(x))≤Crs,\sigma_i(B_r(x))\leq Cr^s,σi​(Br​(x))≤Crs,

with nonvanishing total mass. These estimates express that the centers are too numerous to concentrate on an (m−1)(m-1)(m−1)-dimensional plane.

The reference graphs must be constructed at these prescribed scales, not merely along another convenient sequence. After subtracting the reference and normalizing the height, the limit must retain a nonzero second moment while its first moment tends to zero. Otherwise the normalization could erase all the geometry or leave an irrelevant translation.

The limit is described by measures of height, tilt, mixed height–tilt, and signed mass. This avoids assuming that all sheets can be globally labeled as ordinary functions.

The exponent appears in a radial error integral

Curved reference graphs introduce errors into the comparison at each singular center. The paper corrects radial test fields by the inverse reference-volume density and averages their errors against the center measures. The decisive integral has the form

∫0ℓts−m dt<∞,\int_0^\ell t^{s-m}\,dt<\infty,∫0ℓ​ts−mdt<∞,

which holds exactly when s>m−1s>m-1s>m−1. This is where the claimed dimension threshold enters quantitatively.

A further blowup gives constant frequency at enough independent retained centers. Equality in a positive-semidefinite height–tilt inequality then forces the limiting height measure to vanish. That contradicts its nonzero normalization and yields the dimension bound.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The sharp estimate uses the Euclidean ambient metric. Smooth non-Euclidean metrics admit examples with planar tangents and accumulating topology; one should not silently extend the theorem to every Riemannian ambient manifold. De Lellis–Hirsch–Lihn–Spolaor.

A Hausdorff-dimension bound does not automatically give a locally finite (m−1)(m-1)(m−1)-dimensional measure, rectifiability of the entire singular set, or uniqueness of every tangent cone. The theorem states none of these stronger conclusions. For m=1m=1m=1, a zero-dimensional bound also does not by itself mean a discrete or finite singular set.

The result permits crossing singularities and arbitrary positive integer multiplicity. It does not upgrade stationarity to minimizing behavior or improve the universal bound below the sharp crossing example.

This digest explains the claims and the dependency between the manuscripts. It does not check their signed-excess estimates, fitting constructions, or final dimension-reduction argument.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary sources linked above give the classical regularity theory, recent partial results, and the precise conjectures. Optional background appears under varifold, Hausdorff dimension, and minimal surface.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Codimension-One Bound for the Singular Set of a Stationary Integral Varifold (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Almost-everywhere regularity of stationary integral varifolds (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When every geodesic minimizes for the same distance
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 344 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

On a round sphere, a traveler following a great circle takes a shortest route until reaching the antipode. Every starting point and every direction have the same cutoff distance: half a great circle, equal to the sphere’s diameter.

Could a different Riemannian geometry have this same property? The metric Blaschke conjecture says that the possibilities are exactly the standard compact rank-one symmetric spaces: round spheres, real, complex, and quaternionic projective spaces, and the Cayley plane, with arbitrary overall scale.

Family 344 claims the full metric classification. Its hypothesis compares two numbers: the global injectivity radius and the diameter. Their equality forces not merely the topology of a model but its exact Riemannian metric up to scale.

This is a strong distinction. Many geometries can share a topological space, and periodic geodesics alone do not determine a round metric. The crucial extra requirement is that every geodesic remain minimizing all the way to the common diameter.

2. Background and essential definitions

Diameter and the loss of shortest paths

For a Riemannian manifold (M,g)(M,g)(M,g), let dg(p,q)d_g(p,q)dg​(p,q) be the shortest-path distance. Its diameter is

diam⁡(M,g)=sup⁡p,q∈Mdg(p,q).\operatorname{diam}(M,g)=\sup_{p,q\in M}d_g(p,q).diam(M,g)=p,q∈Msup​dg​(p,q).

At a point ppp, the exponential map exp⁡p\exp_pexpp​ sends a tangent vector vvv to the point reached after following the geodesic with that initial velocity for time one. The pointwise injectivity radius inj⁡p\operatorname{inj}_pinjp​ is the largest radius on whose open tangent ball this map is a diffeomorphism onto its image.

Inside that radius, radial geodesics give unique shortest paths from ppp. At the cut locus, uniqueness or the local regularity of this description fails. The global injectivity radius is

inj⁡(M,g)=inf⁡p∈Minj⁡p(M,g).\operatorname{inj}(M,g)=\inf_{p\in M}\operatorname{inj}_p(M,g).inj(M,g)=p∈Minf​injp​(M,g).

The manuscript calls a connected closed positive-dimensional manifold Blaschke if

inj⁡(M,g)=diam⁡(M,g)=D.\operatorname{inj}(M,g)=\operatorname{diam}(M,g)=D.inj(M,g)=diam(M,g)=D.

Closed means compact without boundary. The equality implies that every unit-speed geodesic minimizes through length DDD, is uniquely minimizing for lengths less than DDD, and cannot minimize beyond DDD. At exactly DDD, uniqueness is not asserted.

The model spaces

Real projective space parametrizes real lines through the origin; complex and quaternionic projective spaces use lines over the corresponding number systems. Their standard metrics are highly symmetric. The Cayley plane is an exceptional sixteen-dimensional analogue associated with the octonions.

Together with spheres, these form the compact rank-one symmetric spaces. “Symmetric” means that geodesic reflection at each point is a local isometry. The projective metrics need not have constant sectional curvature: in the usual normalization, complex and quaternionic projective spaces have tangent-plane curvatures ranging between two values.

An isometry preserves all distances and the metric. A diffeomorphism preserves only the smooth manifold structure. The claimed theorem provides the stronger conclusion. Multiplying the metric by a positive constant is allowed because it rescales both injectivity radius and diameter by the same factor.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Blaschke’s original question arose from surfaces whose geodesics reconverge in a uniform way. Green settled the surface problem in 1963. The subsequent theory, developed in Besse’s book and summarized in McKay’s corrected survey, related the minimizing condition to smooth cut loci, closed geodesics, and fibrations of tangent spheres by great spheres. Bott and Samelson’s topological restrictions explain why the familiar symmetric models appear. Green, McKay’s corrected survey.

The metric sphere and real-projective cases were established through work of Berger, Kazdan, Weinstein, and Yang. Volume comparisons played a central role. Berger also proved a sharp lower bound for volume in terms of injectivity radius, using weighted estimates for Jacobi fields and a scalar inequality of Kazdan. Berger’s isoembolic inequality.

For the projective models, different partial conclusions needed careful separation. Knowing the cohomology ring, knowing the total volume at a fixed geodesic period, and knowing the metric are three different achievements. Yang established the model-volume statement for Blaschke manifolds of complex-projective homotopy type. Smooth incidence geometry and classification results identified the smooth type in projective-plane cases. Other equal-volume results required additional topological hypotheses. Yang.

There were also metric rigidity results under extra curvature assumptions or agreement with a model on part of the manifold. A September 2026 preprint by Song proves rigidity assuming an adapted complex structure on the entire tangent bundle. That entire-extension condition is additional to being Blaschke. Song.

The new manuscript claims to remove such extra geometric hypotheses. It combines a sharp lower volume bound with a matching upper bound, developing an intrinsic argument for all higher quaternionic dimensions rather than assuming the topology needed by a pre-existing equal-volume theorem.

4. What the new manuscript claims

Every connected closed smooth Riemannian manifold of positive dimension satisfying inj⁡=diam⁡\operatorname{inj}=\operatorname{diam}inj=diam is, up to multiplying its metric by a positive constant, isometric to one of the standard models:

  • A round sphere, including the circle.
  • Real, complex, or quaternionic projective space.
  • The Cayley plane.

All quaternionic projective dimensions are included. There is no assumed sectional-curvature bound, no hypothesis that the manifold is already diffeomorphic to the model, and no adapted-complex-structure assumption.

The paper states an intermediate comparison. Classical Blaschke structure assigns a symmetric model (M0,g0)(M_0,g_0)(M0​,g0​) of the appropriate type. Scale it to have the same diameter as (M,g)(M,g)(M,g). Then

Vol⁡(M,g)≥Vol⁡(M0,g0),\operatorname{Vol}(M,g)\geq\operatorname{Vol}(M_0,g_0),Vol(M,g)≥Vol(M0​,g0​),

with equality if and only if the two metrics are isometric.

The remaining argument supplies the opposite inequality in each model type, using classical inputs where their hypotheses apply and a new quaternionic calculation where needed. Equality then triggers metric rigidity.

Under the classical structure theory used in the paper, every unit geodesic is simple and closed with prime period 2D2D2D. “Prime” means the first return period, not a repeated traversal. The volume comparisons therefore use an equivalent normalization whether they fix the diameter or the prime period.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem resolves a classical global rigidity problem by characterizing a short list of exact metrics through a common minimizing-distance condition.

The claim is stronger than a topological classification. It rules out every nonstandard deformation of the metric that might preserve the global equality. It also covers the quaternionic families uniformly, where topology, characteristic classes, and geodesic geometry interact in a particularly intricate way.

The proposed lower-bound argument is notable because it extracts the necessary comparison from the cut-time structure without assuming the model’s parallel curvature eigenspaces. A proof that simply imposed that geometric splitting would have assumed much of the desired rigidity.

The rating concerns these stated consequences and methods. It does not constitute an independent assessment of the proof.

6. The main idea

Read the geometry of shortest-path failure

For each point ppp, send a unit tangent direction vvv to exp⁡p(Dv)\exp_p(Dv)expp​(Dv), its cut point. Classical Blaschke theory gives a smooth sphere fibration: several directions may reach the same cut point, and each fiber is a great sphere in the tangent sphere.

The fiber dimension identifies the model type. In the intermediate projective cases, the normal directions along a geodesic split numerically into two groups: those associated with Jacobi fields vanishing again at the cut time, and the remaining directions. This is information about vanishing and dimensions, not yet a parallel splitting of curvature.

A Jacobi field describes the infinitesimal separation of neighboring geodesics. Determinants built from such fields measure how volume expands in polar coordinates. They are the analytic bridge from geodesic behavior to total volume.

Obtain a sharp lower volume bound

Normalize D=π/2D=\pi/2D=π/2, so the prime period is π\piπ. In a standard projective model, the radial volume density has the form

w(t)=(sin⁡t)m(sin⁡2t2)k,0<t<D.w(t)=(\sin t)^m\left(\frac{\sin 2t}{2}\right)^k,\qquad 0<t<D.w(t)=(sint)m(2sin2t​)k,0<t<D.

Here kkk is the dimension of the great-sphere fiber at the cut locus, and m=n−1−km=n-1-km=n−1−k for real dimension nnn. For complex projective space k=1k=1k=1, for quaternionic projective space k=3k=3k=3, and for the Cayley plane k=7k=7k=7.

The new comparison represents vanishing Jacobi fields as Lagrangian planes in a symplectic vector space. A fixed matrix chart separates an endpoint determinant into a regular block and a Schur-complement block. A Schur complement is the matrix remaining after one block has been algebraically eliminated; it isolates the part sensitive to the cut-time intersection.

Both blocks are estimated by scalar interval integrals. A logarithmic version of Kazdan’s weighted cancellation combines them over the closed geodesic. Reflection symmetry cancels boundary contributions, while carefully matched half-period weights retain the right multiplicities.

A nonnegative strict-convexity remainder keeps track of equality. Integrating over all unit tangent directions gives the model lower bound. If equality holds, the radial volume densities agree with the model everywhere. The paper then invokes Szabó’s classification of compact simply connected harmonic manifolds to identify the metric. Harmonicity here means that polar volume density depends only on radius, not direction.

Obtain the quaternionic upper bound from integral topology

The opposite bound has a different source. For quaternionic type in dimension 4r4r4r, consider the incidence space of pairs of points separated by the cut distance. Its normal four-plane bundle records the great-three-sphere families of directions.

The nonintersection pattern of distinct direction planes constrains a Pontryagin class of the tangent bundle. Pontryagin classes are cohomological invariants of real vector bundles. The signature theorem relates their combinations to the signed intersection form, and the manuscript uses this relation to determine a coefficient in every quaternionic rank.

Next pass to the space of oriented geodesics, forgetting their marked starting points. The unit tangent bundle becomes a circle bundle over this space. Its Euler class records how those circles twist, and the contact volume expresses the manifold’s volume through a top intersection power of that class.

Integral Gysin sequences and closed-geodesic Morse theory connect this intersection number to the earlier incidence coefficient. The calculation retains primitive integral information, including checks over prime fields. Rational cohomology alone would lose the lattice normalization needed for the sharp numerical bound.

Finally, an algebraic intersection calculation gives volume at most that of quaternionic projective space. Combined with the lower bound, this forces equality. The other model types are completed using the appropriate classical volume and topological inputs, with their assumptions checked in the manuscript.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The hypothesis is the exact global equality of injectivity radius and diameter. The theorem does not classify manifolds where those quantities are merely close, where the equality holds at only one point, or where all geodesics are closed without the minimizing condition.

No claim is made about a quantitative stability estimate. To conclude that near-equality forces closeness to a model, one would need to specify the notion of closeness and probably additional compactness assumptions.

The conclusion includes projective spaces with nonconstant sectional curvature, so “every Blaschke manifold is round” would be misleading. Round spheres are one part of the classification, not its entirety.

The manuscript relies on established Blaschke structure theory and harmonic-manifold rigidity, then supplies its claimed determinant comparison and quaternionic upper bound. This digest reports those dependencies and conclusions without auditing the arguments or independently establishing the claimed resolution.

8. Sources and further reading

McKay’s corrected survey provides an accessible map of the historical distinctions between topology, volume, and metric rigidity. The primary papers linked above give representative milestones. Optional background appears under cut locus, Jacobi field, and symmetric space.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The metric Blaschke theorem (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Einstein four-manifolds from positive curvature to a topological gap
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 348 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Curvature can be measured in different ways. Sectional curvature describes a two-dimensional tangent plane. Ricci curvature averages these plane curvatures through a given direction. An Einstein metric makes that average the same in every unit direction, but it need not make all individual plane curvatures equal.

In dimension four, does adding positive sectional curvature force one of the familiar symmetric metrics? What happens at the boundary, when sectional curvature is merely nonnegative and one plane has zero curvature? And if the Einstein equation holds only approximately in an integral sense, does the underlying smooth manifold still come from a short list?

Family 348 addresses these three questions with three related manuscripts. The first classifies the zero-plane boundary case, the second derives an integral topological gap using that classification as an explicit premise, and the third treats strictly positive sectional curvature.

Their conclusions have different strengths. The exact Einstein results identify metrics up to isometry and scale. The small-error result identifies only the smooth manifold, not the original metric.

2. Background and essential definitions

Einstein curvature and its error

A Riemannian metric ggg is Einstein if

Ric⁡g=λg\operatorname{Ric}_g=\lambda gRicg​=λg

for a constant λ\lambdaλ. In real dimension four, scalar curvature is the trace of Ricci curvature, so it equals 4λ4\lambda4λ. Positive Einstein constant can be normalized by scaling to Ric⁡=3g\operatorname{Ric}=3gRic=3g, hence scalar curvature twelve.

For an arbitrary four-dimensional metric, the trace-free Ricci tensor is

Eg=Ric⁡g−Scal⁡g4g.E_g=\operatorname{Ric}_g-\frac{\operatorname{Scal}_g}{4}g.Eg​=Ricg​−4Scalg​​g.

On a connected manifold, its vanishing is equivalent to the Einstein condition. The manuscript measures the error by

D(g)=∫M∣Eg∣g2 dμg.D(g)=\int_M|E_g|_g^2\,d\mu_g.D(g)=∫M​∣Eg​∣g2​dμg​.

This integral is unchanged by constant rescaling in dimension four: squared curvature contributes the inverse square of the metric scale, while volume contributes its square. Small D(g)D(g)D(g) is therefore not achieved simply by enlarging the manifold.

Nonnegative sectional curvature is a separate assumption

For every tangent two-plane σ\sigmaσ, let Kg(σ)K_g(\sigma)Kg​(σ) be its sectional curvature. Strict positivity requires Kg(σ)>0K_g(\sigma)>0Kg​(σ)>0; nonnegativity permits zero. Neither condition should be replaced by a statement only about scalar or Ricci curvature.

A product of two round spheres illustrates the boundary. Planes tangent to one factor have positive curvature, while planes using one direction from each factor have zero curvature. With equal radii, the product metric is Einstein.

Metrics, covers, and smooth types

A universal Riemannian cover is the simply connected covering manifold equipped with the lifted metric. Identifying this cover does not necessarily identify the original quotient globally.

An isometry preserves the metric. A diffeomorphism identifies only the smooth manifold. Thus a theorem saying that MMM is diffeomorphic to S4S^4S4 does not say that its given metric is round.

The standard models here are the round four-sphere, the complex projective plane CP2\mathbb{CP}^2CP2 with its Fubini–Study metric, and the product S2×S2S^2\times S^2S2×S2 with equal round factors. Real projective four-space RP4\mathbb{RP}^4RP4 appears as a nonorientable quotient in the strictly positive case.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Einstein classification problem in positive sectional curvature has long been studied through additional pinching conditions. Berger’s early quarter-pinching rigidity was followed by quantitative curvature criteria of Yang, Costa, and Cao–Tran. Those conditions control how far sectional curvatures can vary relative to one another or to the Einstein constant.

Gursky–LeBrun obtained the Fubini–Study conclusion under nonnegative sectional curvature together with a nonzero positive-definite intersection form. Their analysis of the two Weyl curvature components supplies an important predecessor for this family. Results under nonnegative isotropic curvature, due to Micallef–Wang and later Brendle in higher dimensions, use a different curvature condition and should not be treated as the same theorem. Gursky–LeBrun.

Further classifications retained topology or symmetry. Liu treated torus-invariant Einstein metrics in the nonnegative case. Cheng’s September 2026 preprint treated oriented positive-sectional metrics with Euler characteristic at most three. Gursky–Malchiodi obtained classification under a condition involving Euler characteristic χ\chiχ and signature τ\tauτ, namely 2χ−3∣τ∣≤42\chi-3|\tau|\leq42χ−3∣τ∣≤4. Cheng, Gursky–Malchiodi.

The exact classification claimed here removes those additional restrictions. The boundary paper emphasizes that estimates proved with strict positivity do not automatically extend when curvature reaches zero; their equality cases need separate treatment.

The approximate Einstein question has a different history. De Lellis–Topping’s almost-Schur inequality relates scalar-curvature variation to trace-free Ricci error. Ricci-flow smoothing, entropy and Sobolev estimates, and compactness theory provide tools for extracting regular limits from metrics without initial pointwise curvature bounds. M2 combines these ideas to turn small integral Einstein error into a smooth classification, once the exact classification is supplied. Almost-Schur lemma.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Strictly positive sectional curvature: M3

Every connected smooth closed Einstein four-manifold with strictly positive sectional curvature is, up to positive scaling and isometry, one of

S4,CP2,RP4S^4,\qquad\mathbb{CP}^2,\qquad\mathbb{RP}^4S4,CP2,RP4

with the standard metrics specified above. No orientability assumption is imposed, and there is no further curvature-pinching or topological condition.

A single zero plane: M1

Suppose a connected smooth closed four-manifold satisfies

Ric⁡=3g,Kg≥0,\operatorname{Ric}=3g,\qquad K_g\geq0,Ric=3g,Kg​≥0,

and at least one tangent two-plane at one point has zero curvature. M1 claims that its universal Riemannian cover is isometric to

S2(1/3)×S2(1/3).S^2(1/\sqrt3)\times S^2(1/\sqrt3).S2(1/3​)×S2(1/3​).

Here S2(r)S^2(r)S2(r) is a round sphere of radius rrr. Under the general normalization Ric⁡=λg\operatorname{Ric}=\lambda gRic=λg, with λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, both radii become 1/λ1/\sqrt\lambda1/λ​.

Combining M1 with M3 gives the full universal-cover list under positive Einstein constant and nonnegative sectional curvature: round S4S^4S4, Fubini–Study CP2\mathbb{CP}^2CP2, or the equal-factor product. A zero plane at one point is enough to force the product alternative globally on the cover.

Small integral Einstein error: M2

M2 explicitly assumes the exact positive-Einstein classification supplied by M1’s corollary. Under that premise, it asserts a universal constant ϵ0>0\epsilon_0>0ϵ0​>0 such that every connected, simply connected, smooth closed four-manifold with Kg≥0K_g\geq0Kg​≥0 and

D(g)<ϵ0D(g)<\epsilon_0D(g)<ϵ0​

is diffeomorphic to the standard S4S^4S4, CP2\mathbb{CP}^2CP2, or S2×S2S^2\times S^2S2×S2, without a prescribed orientation.

There are no additional bounds on volume, diameter, curvature maximum, injectivity radius, Sobolev constants, or curvature derivatives. The conclusion is not an isometry statement and does not say that the original metric is Einstein.

The manuscripts are therefore connected by a dependency: M3 treats the positive interior, M1 treats its zero-curvature boundary and states the combined classification, and M2 uses that classification only after producing an exactly Einstein limit.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the family settles a central four-dimensional Einstein classification problem and extends its topological consequences to metrics with small scale-invariant error.

The zero-plane theorem is particularly rigid. A single vanishing sectional curvature, combined with the global assumptions, determines a parallel product splitting on the universal cover. It is much stronger than requiring a curvature equality at every point.

The gap theorem is significant because its hypothesis supplies no pointwise curvature control. It claims that concentration and possible geometric collapse can be handled well enough to recover a smooth topological classification. At the same time, its modest conclusion about the original metric is essential to understanding what has actually been asserted.

The rating reflects these stated consequences, not mathematical verification of the analytic estimates or classification arguments.

6. The main idea

In four dimensions, curvature has two Weyl blocks

Choose an orientation. The Hodge star splits two-forms into self-dual and anti-self-dual three-dimensional spaces. For an Einstein metric normalized by Ric⁡=3g\operatorname{Ric}=3gRic=3g, the curvature operator has two diagonal blocks

I+T,I+U,I+T,\qquad I+U,I+T,I+U,

where TTT and UUU are symmetric trace-free operators, the two Weyl components. The Einstein equation removes the off-diagonal Ricci contribution but does not force either Weyl block to vanish.

Set x=−λmin⁡(T)x=-\lambda_{\min}(T)x=−λmin​(T) and y=−λmin⁡(U)y=-\lambda_{\min}(U)y=−λmin​(U). The smallest sectional curvature is

Kmin⁡=1−x+y2.K_{\min}=1-\frac{x+y}{2}.Kmin​=1−2x+y​.

Thus strict positivity gives x+y<2x+y<2x+y<2, while nonnegativity gives x+y≤2x+y\leq2x+y≤2. The exact spectral condition is stronger than a rough estimate using only the norms of the blocks.

Balance the blocks, then analyze equality

M3 combines separate lower bounds for the averaged squared Weyl norms with a scalar variance inequality and an upper volume deficit. If both blocks are nonzero, these estimates force their second moments to balance.

A weighted Hessian identity then couples the blocks more strongly. The Bianchi identity constrains their derivatives, and curvature commutators control parts of their second derivatives. Completing weighted squares and using explicit polynomial inequalities gives an integral expression that must be both nonnegative and nonpositive, with strictness whenever a Weyl norm varies.

The norms must therefore be constant. In the strictly positive case, the separate norm gaps contradict the possibility that both blocks remain nonzero. One block vanishes, and the remaining equality analysis identifies a parallel curvature tensor with a standard model. An orientation-cover argument gives the nonorientable RP4\mathbb{RP}^4RP4 case.

M1 develops the boundary version. The relevant quadratic form may now have a kernel, and Weyl blocks may vanish at individual points. The manuscript retains nonstrict inequalities and treats these zero sets explicitly. If both blocks are present, their normalized norms become one, each block has spectrum (2,−1,−1)(2,-1,-1)(2,−1,−1), and both are parallel. Their distinguished eigenlines yield two parallel rank-two tangent subbundles, producing the sphere product.

The finite polynomial certificates are part of the manuscripts’ stated argument. This digest does not run their arithmetic checkers or assess their proof coverage.

Obtain geometry from a small integral defect

For M2, suppose there were a sequence outside the three claimed smooth types with D(gj)→0D(g_j)\to0D(gj​)→0. Normalize average scalar curvature to twelve. Almost-Schur estimates make scalar curvature close to twelve in L2L^2L2, so Ricci curvature becomes close to 3gj3g_j3gj​ in the same norm.

Nonnegative sectional curvature bounds the full curvature tensor by a dimensional multiple of scalar curvature. The Chern–Gauss–Bonnet formula, together with simple connectivity, gives a volume lower bound. Segment averaging and the second variation of geodesic length then produce a diameter bound and initial Sobolev control.

This step prevents collapse before smoothing. It does not assume that small integral defect automatically gives a bound on the maximum curvature.

Smooth first, classify the limit afterward

Run Ricci flow, ∂tg=−2Ric⁡\partial_tg=-2\operatorname{Ric}∂t​g=−2Ric. The paper controls the high-curvature tail above a fixed threshold in L2L^2L2, propagates that control, and derives a common positive lifespan. At positive times, derivative estimates and compactness provide smooth convergence to an exactly Einstein flow.

Nonnegative sectional curvature is not assumed to be preserved along these flows. Instead, the manuscript estimates the integral of its negative part by a multiple of time. The limiting Einstein flow is a simple rescaling,

h(t)=(1−6t)h,Ric⁡h=3h.h(t)=(1-6t)h,\qquad\operatorname{Ric}_h=3h.h(t)=(1−6t)h,Rich​=3h.

Its explicit scaling lets the negative-part estimate tend to zero as time decreases, recovering nonnegative sectional curvature for hhh. The exact classification premise now applies.

Smooth convergence at positive time identifies the manifolds diffeomorphically with the classified limit, contradicting the chosen sequence. The convergence asserted in this argument is after regularization, not smooth convergence of the original metrics at time zero.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The exact nonnegative-curvature classification assumes a positive Einstein constant. It should not be restated as covering every Einstein metric with nonnegative sectional curvature without accounting for the zero-constant case.

M1 classifies the universal cover; M3 gives the explicit global list under strict positivity. The gap theorem additionally assumes simple connectivity and concludes a smooth type rather than an exact metric.

The constant ϵ0\epsilon_0ϵ0​ is existential. The statement does not provide a numerical threshold, a quantitative distance from the original metric to a model, or a uniqueness theorem for a nearby Einstein metric.

Finally, M2’s exact classification premise is explicit, not an independent reproof of M1 and M3. The digest reports the three claims together while preserving that logical dependence and without checking their proofs.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary sources linked above describe the earlier curvature, topological, and integral-error results. Optional background appears under Einstein manifold, Weyl tensor, and Ricci flow.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Zero-Plane Rigidity for Einstein Four-Manifolds (October 4, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An L² Einstein Gap for Nonnegatively Curved Four-Manifolds (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Positively curved Einstein four-manifolds (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Which topological counts constrain Hamiltonian fixed points?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 347 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A Hamiltonian system evolves positions and momenta according to an energy function. For a sufficiently small time-independent Hamiltonian on a compact symplectic manifold, points returning after one unit of time are exactly its critical points. Topology forces a minimum number of critical points, so it is natural to ask whether arbitrary Hamiltonian motions must retain the same minimum number of fixed points.

This idea leads to several versions of the Arnold fixed-point conjecture, with different hypotheses and different topological counts. They are not interchangeable. Counting homology generators is weaker than minimizing the critical points of actual smooth functions, and allowing degenerate fixed points changes the problem again.

Family 347 contains five manuscripts claiming counterexamples to several stronger formulations. Three concern the stable Morse number with all fixed points nondegenerate. One concerns the ordinary Morse number in dimension twelve. The last constructs a smooth map with only three fixed points on a six-dimensional quadric, where the unrestricted critical-number benchmark is four.

The family’s message is a separation of precise bounds, not a claim that all established Arnold-type lower bounds fail.

2. Background and essential definitions

Hamiltonian fixed points

A symplectic manifold (M,ω)(M,\omega)(M,ω) has a closed nondegenerate two-form. A smooth time-dependent Hamiltonian HtH_tHt​ determines a flow φHt\varphi_H^tφHt​. A point xxx is fixed by the time-one map if φH1(x)=x\varphi_H^1(x)=xφH1​(x)=x; its trajectory over that time is a periodic loop.

The point is nondegenerate when the linear map DφH1(x)D\varphi_H^1(x)DφH1​(x) has no eigenvalue one. This is a condition on the return map, not a statement that its trajectory is constant. Some formulations count only fixed points whose trajectory loops can be contracted to a point. Choices of contracting disks do not create additional fixed points.

Three minima for smooth functions

A Morse function has only nondegenerate critical points: its Hessian is invertible at each critical point. Write Morse⁡(M)\operatorname{Morse}(M)Morse(M) for the least number of critical points of such a function on MMM.

The stable Morse number SM⁡(M)\operatorname{SM}(M)SM(M) permits auxiliary variables. One minimizes over Morse functions

F:M×Rk⟶RF:M\times\mathbb R^k\longrightarrow\mathbb RF:M×Rk⟶R

that agree with a nondegenerate quadratic form in the auxiliary variables outside a sufficiently large ball. The integer k≥0k\geq0k≥0 and the quadratic signature may vary. Thus

SM⁡(M)≤Morse⁡(M).\operatorname{SM}(M)\leq\operatorname{Morse}(M).SM(M)≤Morse(M).

This is a minimum over actual smooth functions, not merely algebraic chain complexes.

The critical number Crit⁡(M)\operatorname{Crit}(M)Crit(M) instead minimizes critical points of arbitrary smooth functions on MMM, allowing degeneracy. It is the benchmark relevant to one unrestricted formulation without a nondegeneracy assumption.

Homology counts can be smaller

Homology groups record topological cycles. Their free ranks are Betti numbers, while finite-order elements form the torsion subgroup. Let b(M)b(M)b(M) be the total free rank, and let d(T)d(T)d(T) be the least number of generators of a finite abelian group TTT. The degreewise quantity

λ(M)=b(M)+2∑id(Tor⁡Hi(M;Z))\lambda(M)=b(M)+2\sum_i d(\operatorname{Tor}H_i(M;\mathbb Z))λ(M)=b(M)+2i∑​d(TorHi​(M;Z))

is a lower bound for the geometric stable Morse number used in the manuscripts. In their simply connected high-dimensional examples, they invoke Smale’s handle theorem to attain it with an ordinary Morse function, so both geometric Morse minima equal λ(M)\lambda(M)λ(M).

A cyclically graded Floer bound may combine different integer degrees. For minimal Chern number one, it retains only even and odd degrees. The minimal Chern number is the positive generator of the first Chern class evaluated on spherical homotopy classes. Grouping degrees can reduce the number of generators required by mixed-prime torsion.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Conley–Zehnder established fixed-point bounds for standard symplectic tori through variational methods. Floer then built homology from Hamiltonian trajectories and pseudoholomorphic curves, creating a systematic bridge between dynamics and topology. Later work of Hofer–Salamon, Ono, Fukaya–Ono, Liu–Tian, and Ruan extended the theory and the rational homological lower bound. Conley–Zehnder, Floer.

These results do not automatically identify fixed-point counts with the minimum for a Morse function. Damian showed that ordinary and stable Morse numbers can differ. Positive stable-Morse theorems hold under extra conditions: Dimitroglou Rizell–Golovko proved the bound for generic Hamiltonians when both symplectic area and the first Chern class vanish on spherical homotopy classes, with an independent approach due to Pöder Balkeståhl. The sphere and blowup factors in the new examples lie outside those assumptions. Dimitroglou Rizell–Golovko.

Recent refinements retain more homological information. Abouzaid–Blumberg obtained bounds over fields of positive characteristic. Bai–Xu developed an integral bound incorporating torsion at every prime, with degrees reduced modulo twice the minimal Chern number. The family explicitly compares its examples with this cyclic bound rather than treating integral torsion as an automatic stable-Morse obstruction. Bai–Xu.

For possibly degenerate maps, cup-length and critical-number bounds have important positive cases, including tori, projective spaces, and suitable symplectically aspherical manifolds. Cup length, in the convention used here, is one plus the largest number of positive-degree cohomology classes with nonzero product. The added one includes the unit. Golovko’s survey of the different formulations.

Regularity also separates problems. Earlier Hamiltonian homeomorphism counterexamples do not themselves give smooth diffeomorphisms. All five manuscripts here claim smooth constructions. M5 also cites Jiao’s September 27, 2026 preprint reporting a two-fixed-point smooth map on the equal-area product of two spheres; that distinct construction is not an input to this family. Jiao.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Stable Morse counterexamples: M1–M3

All three examples are simply connected closed Kähler manifolds. Every fixed point is nondegenerate, every orbit loop is contractible, and the count includes all fixed points.

The source column gives the manuscript and the real dimension in parentheses.

SourceFixed pointsStable Morse number
M1 (22)FS
M2 (3332)1,872,2321,872,264
M3 (1412)318,952318,968

In M1, mmm is any positive integer, and the table’s two counts are

F=80+1952m,S=80+1968m.\begin{aligned}F&=80+1952m,\\S&=80+1968m.\end{aligned}FS​=80+1952m,=80+1968m.​

The deficit is 16m16m16m, so it becomes arbitrarily large while the dimension stays twenty-two. The fixed-point count is at most 127/128127/128127/128 of the stable Morse number. The underlying manifold is allowed to vary with mmm.

M2 has minimal Chern number one and attains the cyclic integral Floer bound exactly. Its count is therefore simultaneously optimal for that cited bound and thirty-two below the stable Morse number. M3 supplies a sixteen-point deficit through the original mixed-prime construction; M1 and M2 develop that mechanism in different directions.

Ordinary Morse counterexamples: M4

M4 asserts closed connected symplectic twelve-manifolds with

#Fix⁡(φH1)=χ(M)+128<Morse⁡(M),\#\operatorname{Fix}(\varphi_H^1)=\chi(M)+128<\operatorname{Morse}(M),#Fix(φH1​)=χ(M)+128<Morse(M),

where χ(M)\chi(M)χ(M) is the Euler characteristic. All fixed points are nondegenerate and have contractible trajectories. The deficit can be arbitrarily large among such twelve-dimensional examples, again allowing the manifold to vary.

These examples use a nontrivial fundamental group. They separate ordinary Morse theory from a stabilized construction; they are not the simply connected stable-Morse examples in the first table.

A degenerate example: M5

The complex quadric threefold is the smooth hypersurface

Q3={[z0:⋯:z4]∈CP4:∑j=04zj2=0}.Q^3=\left\{[z_0:\cdots:z_4]\in\mathbb{CP}^4:\sum_{j=0}^4z_j^2=0\right\}.Q3={[z0​:⋯:z4​]∈CP4:j=0∑4​zj2​=0}.

With its restricted standard symplectic form, it has real dimension six. M5 claims a smooth Hamiltonian diffeomorphism φ\varphiφ satisfying

#Fix⁡(φ)=3<4=Crit⁡(Q3)=cuplength⁡(Q3;Q).\#\operatorname{Fix}(\varphi)=3<4=\operatorname{Crit}(Q^3)=\operatorname{cuplength}(Q^3;\mathbb Q).#Fix(φ)=3<4=Crit(Q3)=cuplength(Q3;Q).
