At least one fixed point is degenerate. The manuscript says that three attains Gong’s existing lower bound for this quadric. It does not violate a theorem whose hypotheses require every fixed point to be nondegenerate. Gong’s version cited by M5.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the family would sharply redraw the relationship between Hamiltonian fixed points and geometric critical-point minima. The stable-Morse examples are especially strong because the ambient manifolds are simply connected and Kähler, and every fixed point is nondegenerate.

M1 makes the separation robust in a numerical sense: the dimension is fixed and the deficit grows without bound, with a uniform proportional gap. M2 supplies a different kind of precision by attaining the cyclic integral homological bound exactly while missing the geometric one.

The six-dimensional quadric example addresses the degenerate problem with a very small count. Together, the papers illustrate why an “Arnold bound” must always be stated with its benchmark, coefficient convention, grading, and nondegeneracy hypotheses.

This rating measures the significance of the claims if correct. It does not independently validate any construction or compare priority beyond the sources’ descriptions.

6. The main idea

Convert a fixed submanifold into finitely many fixed points

A common device in M1–M3 and M5 starts with a Hamiltonian map AAA of finite order, whose fixed set is a smooth submanifold FFF. Its fixed tangent vectors must be exactly the tangent vectors to FFF.

Choose a function fff on FFF, extend it to an AAA-invariant Hamiltonian KKK, and let BsB_sBs​ be its flow. If ArA^rAr is the identity, commutation gives

(A∘Bϵ)r=Brϵ.(A\circ B_\epsilon)^r=B_{r\epsilon}.(A∘Bϵ​)r=Brϵ​.

A smooth vector field on a compact manifold has no nonconstant periodic trajectories of arbitrarily short period. For sufficiently small ϵ\epsilonϵ, this identity excludes extra fixed points away from the desired equilibria. Symmetric criticality identifies the remaining ones with the critical points of fff on FFF.

Thus the fixed-point count is controlled by a function on the fixed submanifold, which can require fewer critical points than a function on the entire ambient manifold.

Mixed primes distinguish integer degrees from parity

For finite abelian groups,

d((Z/2)a⊕(Z/3)b)=max⁡{a,b}.d\bigl((\mathbb Z/2)^a\oplus(\mathbb Z/3)^b\bigr)=\max\{a,b\}.d((Z/2)a⊕(Z/3)b)=max{a,b}.

For example, Z/2⊕Z/3\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/3Z/2⊕Z/3 is cyclic of order six and needs only one generator. If the two summands occur in separate homological degrees, however, degreewise Morse theory must account for both separately.

M1–M3 build a simply connected Kähler manifold XXX by blowing up projective space along carefully chosen centers carrying two-primary and three-primary torsion. A blowup replaces a submanifold by its projective normal directions and adds predictable shifted homology groups.

They multiply XXX by a rational surface YYY whose Hamiltonian involution fixes four projective lines. The resulting manifold M=X×YM=X\times YM=X×Y has four fixed components, each X×CP1X\times\mathbb{CP}^1X×CP1. The perturbation device realizes four times the Morse count of that component.

The free homology ranks of CP1\mathbb{CP}^1CP1 and YYY, in even degrees, are respectively (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) and (1,6,1)(1,6,1)(1,6,1). Products combine the torsion sequences with these different patterns. Choosing where each prime dominates makes the component count smaller than the ambient degreewise count.

M1 embeds arbitrarily many disjoint centers in one fixed projective dimension, giving the dimension-twenty-two family. M2 chooses seven centers with a more elaborate degree pattern so that the component count equals the parity-grouped bound exactly. These refine M3’s mechanism; their constructions are not five copies of one identical example.

Group generators drive the twelve-dimensional construction

M4 uses the groups G=A5kG=A_5^kG=A5k​, direct products of the alternating group on five letters. Their minimum number of group generators grows with kkk, while the augmentation ideal in the integral group ring has a generating list of length two. The augmentation ideal consists of formal integer combinations of group elements whose coefficients sum to zero; generating it as a module is different from generating GGG as a group.

Gompf’s construction supplies a symplectic four-manifold XXX with this fundamental group. Relative handle operations produce a Morse model on X×R8X\times\mathbb R^8X×R8 with a controlled count, exactly quadratic outside a compact region. The paper inserts its small-time dynamics into sixteen product-cap regions of X×(S2)4X\times(S^2)^4X×(S2)4, matching rotations outside the caps and excluding additional fixed points.

The resulting count is χ(M)+128\chi(M)+128χ(M)+128, while group generators force a larger ordinary Morse count. The distinction is geometric: a short algebraic complex alone would not produce the required closed Hamiltonian map.

Three points arise from a lower-dimensional fixed surface

For M5, a Hamiltonian involution of Q3Q^3Q3 has fixed set the quadric surface Q2Q^2Q2, diffeomorphic to S2×S2S^2\times S^2S2×S2. The paper supplies a function on that surface with exactly three critical points, one degenerate, and transfers them to fixed points of the ambient map.

Meanwhile, the hyperplane class hhh of Q3Q^3Q3 satisfies h3≠0h^3\ne0h3=0, forcing unit-inclusive rational cup length at least four. A rotation realizes four critical points on Q3Q^3Q3, giving the matching critical-number upper bound. The smaller fixed-set function is therefore the source of the discrepancy.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The examples concern unrestricted strong formulations. They do not contradict stable-Morse theorems with symplectic-asphericity and Chern-class hypotheses, nor the cited nondegenerate homological inequalities. M2 is explicitly designed to attain one such integral inequality.

The degeneracy in M5 is essential to its comparison with nondegenerate bounds. Conversely, degeneracy cannot explain M1–M4 because all their fixed points are stated to be nondegenerate.

The unbounded-deficit families vary the manifold. The manuscripts do not claim an unbounded deficit on a single fixed compact manifold, a lowest possible counterexample dimension, or a complete replacement for every strong Arnold formulation.

All five constructions are reported as stated. The digest does not verify their handle realizations, invariant perturbations, torsion calculations, or exclusion of additional fixed points.

8. Sources and further reading

Golovko’s survey is useful for keeping the formulations separate. The primary sources linked above explain the homological lower bounds and special positive cases. Optional background appears under Hamiltonian vector field, Morse theory, and Floer homology.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Hamiltonian Fixed Points Below the Stable Morse Number in Dimension Twenty-Two (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Sharpness of the Cyclic Integral Floer Bound Below the Stable Morse Number (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Hamiltonian Fixed Points Below the Stable Morse Number (October 5, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, A nondegenerate counterexample to the Morse-number Arnold bound (September 23, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Three fixed points on the symplectic quadric threefold (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The first minimal-hypersurface volume above an equator
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 349 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

An equator is the simplest closed minimal hypersurface in a round sphere. It has the least possible volume. What is the next possible volume level if the image is not an equator?

There is a natural family of candidates: products of two smaller round spheres sitting inside the unit sphere. Their radii can be chosen so that the positive curvatures from one factor balance the negative curvatures from the other. These are the minimal Clifford products.

The Solomon–Yau least-volume conjecture predicts that every non-equatorial closed minimal hypersurface has at least the volume of the smallest such product. Family 349 claims this sharp bound in every hypersurface dimension at least two, including smooth immersions with overlapping sheets.

The question is not whether there is some positive volume gap above the equator; earlier work already established a dimension-dependent gap. It is whether the gap ends at precisely the Clifford threshold, without extra topology, symmetry, or curvature hypotheses.

2. Background and essential definitions

Minimal hypersurfaces in a sphere

A hypersurface has one dimension less than its ambient manifold. A smooth immersion F:Mm→Sm+1F:M^m\to S^{m+1}F:Mm→Sm+1 is locally an embedded hypersurface but may identify different domain points globally. The induced metric F∗groundF^*g_{\mathrm{round}}F∗ground​ measures lengths and volumes on the domain.

The hypersurface is minimal if its mean curvature vanishes. At a point, mean curvature is the average of the principal curvatures, which describe bending in independent tangent directions. Minimality means zero first variation of volume under small deformations; it does not mean that every deformation increases volume.

The image is totally geodesic when its second fundamental form vanishes. For a connected closed hypersurface in the round sphere, the relevant model is an equator, a great mmm-sphere. The theorem excludes a totally geodesic image, even if the domain parametrization has multiplicity.

The Clifford comparison family

For 1≤k<m1\leq k<m1≤k<m, define

Ck,m−k=Sk ⁣(km)×Sm−k ⁣(m−km)⊂Sm+1.C_{k,m-k}=S^k\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\right)\times S^{m-k}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{m-k}{m}}\right)\subset S^{m+1}.Ck,m−k​=Sk(mk​​)×Sm−k(mm−k​​)⊂Sm+1.

The squared radii add to one, so the product lies in the unit sphere. The chosen radii make its weighted sum of principal curvatures zero, hence it is minimal.

Let σj\sigma_jσj​ be the volume of the unit jjj-sphere. The product volume is

Vol⁡(Ck,m−k)=σkσm−k(km)k/2(m−km)(m−k)/2.\operatorname{Vol}(C_{k,m-k})=\sigma_k\sigma_{m-k}\left(\frac{k}{m}\right)^{k/2}\left(\frac{m-k}{m}\right)^{(m-k)/2}.Vol(Ck,m−k​)=σk​σm−k​(mk​)k/2(mm−k​)(m−k)/2.

Write ama_mam​ for the minimum over the finitely many choices of kkk. This definition is enough to make the claimed threshold explicit without needing to classify which index minimizes it in every dimension.

For m=2m=2m=2, the product is the Clifford torus, with both circle radii 1/21/\sqrt21/2​. Its area is 2π22\pi^22π2, while the equatorial sphere has area 4π4\pi4π. Thus the predicted first non-equatorial level is larger than the equator by a factor π/2\pi/2π/2.

Why domain volume matters

For an immersion, the quantity being bounded is

Vol⁡(M,F∗ground).\operatorname{Vol}(M,F^*g_{\mathrm{round}}).Vol(M,F∗ground​).

It counts every sheet. If two domain points map to the same image point, their contributions are not merged into one. Measuring only the area of the image as a set would be a different problem.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Simons’s identities for minimal submanifolds supplied basic curvature rigidity and explained the special role of hypersurfaces with parallel second fundamental form, including Clifford products. Cheng–Li–Yau later obtained a dimension-dependent volume gap above the equator using heat-kernel comparison. A nonzero gap, however, does not identify the sharp next level. Simons, Cheng–Li–Yau.

In dimension two, Marques–Neves’s Willmore theorem yields the sharp area bound and Clifford-torus rigidity. Their proof uses a canonical family of surfaces and min–max theory: topology prevents the whole family from being deformed below a certain area threshold. This variational strategy is an important model for the new manuscript. Marques–Neves.

Higher-dimensional partial results retained geometric assumptions. Cheng–Wei–Zeng treated rotational cases. Viana obtained the sharp Clifford bound when both connected complementary regions are antipodally invariant. Related lower bounds for minimal cones, including work of Bernstein–Wang, connect volume questions to the density of conical singularities under additional topological conditions. Rotational results, Viana.

Nguyen and Ge–Li provided a useful reduction for immersions: an image point with qqq preimages forces domain volume at least qσmq\sigma_mqσm​. Since the Clifford threshold is less than 2σm2\sigma_m2σm​, any hypothetical counterexample would already be embedded. Ge–Li’s more recent general embedded bounds still leave the sharp threshold as the target. Nguyen, Ge–Li.

The new paper also proves an average-curvature estimate and uses an index characterization of Clifford products. It explicitly credits Nifa’s recent preprint with those conclusions through a stronger Schrödinger quadratic-form inequality. Those intermediate statements are therefore not presented here as originating solely in the new volume argument. Nifa’s preprint.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For every integer m≥2m\geq2m≥2, every closed connected smooth manifold MmM^mMm, and every smooth minimal immersion into the unit round sphere,

F:Mm⟶Sm+1,F:M^m\longrightarrow S^{m+1},F:Mm⟶Sm+1,

the manuscript asserts

F(M) not totally geodesic⟹Vol⁡(M,F∗ground)≥am.F(M)\text{ not totally geodesic}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Vol}(M,F^*g_{\mathrm{round}})\geq a_m.F(M) not totally geodesic⟹Vol(M,F∗ground​)≥am​.

Closed means compact without boundary. Embeddedness, orientability of the initial domain, symmetry, and prescribed topology are not additional hypotheses. Covering multiplicities are included in the volume.

The threshold is sharp because a Clifford product realizing the finite minimum has volume ama_mam​. The stated main theorem is the inequality and its attainment by these examples; it should not automatically be expanded into a full classification of every equality case in arbitrary dimension.

For the embedded part of the argument, the manuscript also obtains

∫Σ∣A∣2 dμ≥mVol⁡(Σ),\int_\Sigma |A|^2\,d\mu\geq m\operatorname{Vol}(\Sigma),∫Σ​∣A∣2dμ≥mVol(Σ),

where AAA is the second fundamental form and Σ\SigmaΣ is non-equatorial. Combined with spectral estimates, it identifies an embedded minimal hypersurface of Morse index m+3m+3m+3 as a Clifford product. The Morse index counts independent normal deformation directions that decrease area to second order.

These intermediate conclusions are used to show that a hypothetical smaller-volume counterexample has an extra negative direction beyond those already controlled by the variational family.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem identifies the sharp first nontrivial volume level for minimal hypersurfaces in every round sphere, resolving a longstanding geometric extremal question.

The scope is broad: the statement does not assume a genus, a symmetry group, or embeddedness. The immersion reduction explains why this breadth is possible while keeping multiplicity visible.

The claimed all-dimensional method is also important. In high dimensions, minimizing sequences and min–max constructions can develop singularities. A successful sharp-volume argument must control those limits rather than rely only on the smooth geometry of its starting hypersurfaces.

The family combines a geometric comparison, a topological detection mechanism, and an induction preventing singular subthreshold limits. The score reflects that claimed reach, not independent proof verification.

6. The main idea

Reduce a counterexample to an embedding

Form the Euclidean cone over the immersed hypersurface. Its density at the vertex is the domain volume divided by σm\sigma_mσm​. If an image point has qqq preimages, the corresponding nonzero point of the cone has density at least qqq, including tangent or coincident sheets.

Monotonicity then gives volume at least qσmq\sigma_mqσm​. The manuscript shows am<2σma_m<2\sigma_mam​<2σm​, so a counterexample below ama_mam​ cannot have any image point with two preimages. It must be embedded.

This reduces the hard variational argument to embedded hypersurfaces without weakening the final immersion statement.

Use curvature to find an additional decreasing direction

A two-point comparison looks at the normal direction at one point relative to all other points. The paper treats both signs of principal curvature and derives the integrated estimate for ∣A∣2|A|^2∣A∣2.

A conformal and spectral argument then controls the index. If the index is exactly m+3m+3m+3, the hypersurface is a Clifford product. A counterexample with volume below every Clifford product must consequently have index greater than m+3m+3m+3.

That extra negative direction is the resource used to lower the maximum area in a carefully constructed family. The index statement alone does not produce a smaller minimal hypersurface; the topological family is needed for that step.

Build a family whose topology cannot disappear

Take the signed distance to the Euclidean cone over the hypersurface and view its graph in a space with an additional time coordinate. Lorentz transformations preserve the difference between squared spatial length and squared time. After transforming and intersecting with the unit spatial sphere, level sets provide a family of hypersurfaces.

At closest-point contacts, minimality fixes the trace of a nonnegative Jacobian matrix. A determinant inequality controls the areas of the resulting levels, even when closest points are not unique.

The parameters lead to a projective family of dimension m+3m+3m+3. Along its nontrivial parameter loop, filling regions change to their complements. A degree-one cohomology class therefore has a nonzero (m+3)(m+3)(m+3)-rd power. This detects topology of the family without imposing a separate topological assumption on the original hypersurface.

The original hypersurface is the unique area maximum, with a uniform gap away from the central parameter. Its extra index direction allows that maximum to be lowered strictly while retaining the detecting topology and preventing concentration of area into tiny regions.

Keep the min–max output above the equator

The detecting condition forces the family to contain a boundary enclosing half the sphere’s volume with zero centroid. A hemisphere has half-volume but does not have zero centroid, so the spherical isoperimetric equality case is excluded. The paper obtains a uniform threshold

γm>σm\gamma_m>\sigma_mγm​>σm​

for these boundaries. This keeps the variational construction from collapsing back to an equator.

Min–max theory finds a stationary limiting hypersurface whose area lies between that lower threshold and the family’s maximum. Such an output is initially a varifold, a generalized surface allowing multiplicity and singularities. Smoothness is not automatic in all dimensions.

Rule out singular limits below the Clifford threshold

The proof proceeds by induction on hypersurface dimension. At a nonzero point of a Euclidean cone, a tangent cone splits off the radial line. The remaining geometry has lower cone dimension, allowing the earlier-dimensional volume statements to constrain it.

The manuscript uses this radial splitting to establish regularity and multiplicity one for the specific subthreshold limits arising in the argument. The induction does not apply the still-unproved dimension-mmm theorem to a dimension-mmm link. The base case m=2m=2m=2 requires no lower-dimensional volume hypothesis.

If counterexamples existed, compactness would then produce one of least area HHH, with

σm<γm≤H<am.\sigma_m<\gamma_m\leq H<a_m.σm​<γm​≤H<am​.

The extra index direction lowers its detecting family to a maximum strictly below HHH. Min–max, followed by the same regularity argument, produces a smooth connected non-equatorial minimal hypersurface with area between γm\gamma_mγm​ and HHH. That is a smaller counterexample, contradicting the definition of HHH.

The claimed proof therefore needs both ingredients: topology keeps the new surface above the equator, while cone induction makes it smooth enough to contradict leastness.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The ambient space is a unit round sphere, and the submanifold is a closed minimal hypersurface. The theorem does not cover arbitrary ambient metrics, higher-codimension minimal submanifolds, or hypersurfaces with boundary.

It supplies a sharp lower volume threshold, not a complete volume spectrum or a classification of all minimal hypersurfaces. The existence of a gap above the equator does not imply that subsequent volume levels are discrete.

For immersions, replacing domain volume by the measure of the image would remove multiplicity and change the statement. For equality, the paper’s main theorem provides the sharp examples but does not state a universal equality-classification theorem in the form quoted here.

Finally, the manuscript credits prior average-curvature and index progress while supplying its own variational family and all-dimensional compactness argument. This digest reports that organization without verifying the estimates, the topological detection, or the cone induction.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked primary works explain the earlier volume gap, the two-dimensional sharp result, special higher-dimensional cases, and the curvature input. Optional background appears under Clifford torus, minimal surface.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Solomon–Yau least-volume theorem (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Nodal size: a sharp surface bound and higher-dimensional failures
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 350 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A vibrating membrane has stationary vibration modes. Along the nodal set of a mode, the displacement is zero: these are the lines where sand can gather in a Chladni experiment. On a higher-dimensional manifold, the analogous zero set is usually a hypersurface.

How large can that zero set be as the frequency increases? Yau’s nodal conjecture predicts that its measure is comparable to frequency, with constants depending on the fixed geometry.

Family 350 claims a sharply divided answer in the smooth category. On every smooth closed surface, the predicted upper bound holds. Starting in dimension three, there are fixed smooth metrics with sequences of exact eigenfunctions violating it. In dimensions at least five, the claimed violation even exceeds frequency by a fixed positive power of the eigenvalue.

The phrase fixed metric is central. Choosing a different geometry for every complicated nodal pattern would not contradict Yau’s formulation. Each negative result here claims one metric supporting an entire violating sequence.

2. Background and essential definitions

Eigenvalue and frequency conventions

Let (Md,g)(M^d,g)(Md,g) be a closed connected Riemannian manifold; closed means compact without boundary. Its Laplace–Beltrami operator describes spatial diffusion and vibration. The papers use

−Δgu=λu,λ>0,-\Delta_gu=\lambda u,\qquad \lambda>0,−Δg​u=λu,λ>0,

for a nonzero real eigenfunction uuu. Set k=λk=\sqrt\lambdak=λ​. This kkk is the frequency scale, while λ\lambdaλ is its square. Confusing them would change every exponent in the conjecture.

The nodal set is

Zu={x∈M:u(x)=0}.Z_u=\{x\in M:u(x)=0\}.Zu​={x∈M:u(x)=0}.

Its size is measured by (d−1)(d-1)(d−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure Hgd−1\mathcal H_g^{d-1}Hgd−1​: length on a surface, area in dimension three, and the corresponding hypersurface volume in higher dimensions. Multiplying uuu by a nonzero constant does not change this set.

The conjectured two-sided estimate is

cgλ≤Hgd−1(Zu)≤Cgλ.c_g\sqrt\lambda\leq\mathcal H_g^{d-1}(Z_u)\leq C_g\sqrt\lambda.cg​λ​≤Hgd−1​(Zu​)≤Cg​λ​.

The constants may depend on the manifold and metric, but must work for every nonzero real eigenfunction in every positive eigenspace. The lower and upper bounds are logically separate.

Smooth versus analytic geometry

A smooth metric has derivatives of every order. A real-analytic metric is locally represented by convergent power series, a stronger requirement. Analytic continuation gives additional control unavailable for arbitrary smooth coefficients.

One should also distinguish nodal topology from nodal measure. A zero set can contain a complicated component without violating a total-length or total-area estimate. Conversely, many sign changes in small regions can force large measure without providing a classification of topology.

Growth at the wavelength scale

The natural local length scale is k−1k^{-1}k−1. A doubling or growth index compares the size of uuu on a disk with its size on a larger concentric disk. Large growth indicates strong local oscillation or concentration, but the surface proof does not need every local growth index to be uniformly bounded. It seeks a bound on their average.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Donnelly–Fefferman proved the sharp two-sided estimate for real-analytic manifolds and metrics. This established the predicted frequency scale in the analytic setting, but left the smooth setting open. Donnelly–Fefferman, 1988.

For smooth surfaces, Brüning proved the square-root lower bound. Donnelly–Fefferman and Dong obtained upper bounds of order λ3/4\lambda^{3/4}λ3/4, and Logunov–Malinnikova improved this to λ3/4−β\lambda^{3/4-\beta}λ3/4−β for a universal positive β<1/4\beta<1/4β<1/4. These exponents approach the desired 1/21/21/2 but do not reach it. Surface upper bound, Logunov–Malinnikova.

In all dimensions, Logunov proved the sharp lower bound. He also established a polynomial upper bound in dimensions at least three, replacing earlier nonpolynomial estimates. A polynomial bound with a larger exponent leaves room for the counterexamples claimed here. Lower bound, polynomial upper bound.

Nazarov–Polterovich–Sodin promoted a statistical approach to local growth, and Roy-Fortin made precise its relation to total nodal length on surfaces. M1 supplies the uniform average-growth estimate needed to reach the sharp exponent through that framework. Roy-Fortin, average growth refinement.

Metric flexibility has also been used to prescribe nodal sets. Enciso and Peralta-Salas realized specified separating hypersurfaces by choosing a metric, and related work constructed complicated high-energy nodal components even on fixed analytic spheres and tori. These results concern prescribed topology, not unbounded nodal measure divided by frequency on one smooth metric. The new negative claims require that stronger quantitative feature.

Intermediate regularity assumptions also matter. Hezari obtained stronger estimates for Gevrey metrics and a specified quasianalytic class. Those classes are more restrictive than arbitrary smooth geometry, so the claimed smooth counterexamples do not erase such results.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Every smooth surface: M1

For each fixed closed connected smooth Riemannian surface, M1 asserts a constant C(M,g)C(M,g)C(M,g) such that

Hg1(Zu)≤C(M,g)λ\mathcal H_g^1(Z_u)\leq C(M,g)\sqrt\lambdaHg1​(Zu​)≤C(M,g)λ​

for every nonzero real positive-eigenvalue eigenfunction. No orientation assumption is imposed. Together with the existing lower bound, this gives the two-sided conjecture on smooth surfaces.

Qualitative violations in dimensions three and four: M2

M2 claims that every neighborhood of the round metric on S3S^3S3 in the smooth topology contains a metric g∞g_\inftyg∞​ with exact real eigenfunctions uju_juj​ satisfying

−Δg∞uj=λjuj,λj⟶∞,-\Delta_{g_\infty}u_j=\lambda_ju_j,\qquad\lambda_j\longrightarrow\infty,−Δg∞​​uj​=λj​uj​,λj​⟶∞,

and

Hg∞2(Zuj)λj⟶∞.\frac{\mathcal H_{g_\infty}^2(Z_{u_j})}{\sqrt{\lambda_j}}\longrightarrow\infty.λj​​Hg∞​2​(Zuj​​)​⟶∞.

It separately claims a fixed smooth metric on S2×T2S^2\times T^2S2×T2 with the analogous divergence of nodal three-volume. Here T2T^2T2 is the two-dimensional torus. These are two dimension-specific constructions, not an assertion that one exactification method works unchanged in both dimensions.

Neither result states a fixed positive power-law excess in dimensions three or four. Unbounded ratios may grow more slowly than every chosen positive power.

A fixed power-law excess in dimension five: M3

M3 claims a fixed smooth metric on S4×S1S^4\times S^1S4×S1, a fixed number ϵ0>0\epsilon_0>0ϵ0​>0, and exact real eigenfunctions with

Hg4(Zuj)λj1/2+ϵ0longrightarrow∞.\frac{\mathcal H_g^4(Z_{u_j})}{\lambda_j^{1/2+\epsilon_0}}longrightarrow\infty.λj1/2+ϵ0​​Hg4​(Zuj​​)​longrightarrow∞.

This also disproves the proposed upper bound with an arbitrarily small positive exponent loss, for that metric. Taking products with fixed closed manifolds extends the power-law conclusion to every dimension greater than five.

Together, the papers claim the following distinction:

DimensionUniversal smooth upper bound of order λ\sqrt\lambdaλ​Negative example supplied
2Holds for every fixed closed surfaceNone
3Fails for some fixed metricsS3S^3S3, arbitrarily close to round
4Fails for some fixed metricsS2×T2S^2\times T^2S2×T2
At least 5Fails, even with a small fixed power lossS4×S1S^4\times S^1S4×S1 and products

Failure for some metrics is not failure for every metric or every eigenfunction. Analytic metrics retain their established sharp bounds, and the lower bound remains intact.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the family would give an unexpected dimension threshold for a central conjecture in spectral geometry. The same smooth regularity would permit the sharp universal upper estimate in dimension two and fail to guarantee it in every higher dimension.

The closeness-to-round assertion in dimension three is particularly notable. It says that the exceptional behavior can occur in any prescribed smooth neighborhood of a familiar analytic metric, while still belonging to a single smooth limit metric.

The power-law claim goes further than merely producing an unbounded normalized ratio. It rules out a commonly considered near-sharp relaxation with every positive exponent loss.

These distinctions would reshape the search for upper bounds: dimension, regularity class, and additional geometric assumptions would need to be tracked separately. The rating concerns that stated significance, not proof verification.

6. The main idea

On surfaces, sum average growth rather than worst growth

In local isothermal coordinates, a smooth surface metric is conformal to the Euclidean metric. The eigenfunction equation becomes

Δu+k2p(x)u=0,\Delta u+k^2p(x)u=0,Δu+k2p(x)u=0,

where ppp is a fixed positive smooth function. Divide a coordinate region into squares of side sss comparable to k−1k^{-1}k−1.

A local theorem of Roy-Fortin bounds nodal length in such a square by a constant times sss multiplied by one plus a logarithmic growth index. There are on the order of s−2s^{-2}s−2 squares. If their average growth is bounded, summing gives total length on the order of s−1s^{-1}s−1, hence kkk.

M1 extracts logarithmic profiles from weighted local norms. A Carleman estimate, a weighted inequality for differential equations, makes these limiting profiles subharmonic. Its decisive trace control is specific to two dimensions.

Affine parts of a profile can persist under subdivision, so the argument subtracts them and tracks their slopes separately. The remaining growth improves on average. Excursions of high growth produce witness sets of positive area. These witnesses can lie outside their parent squares, so a separate geometric packing argument controls boundary-collar discrepancies rather than assuming each witness remains inside its original square. The resulting terminal mean-growth bound yields the sharp length estimate.

In higher dimensions, create many stable sign changes

M2 and M3 begin with explicit high-frequency background waves and modify their logarithmic amplitude envelopes in localized regions. Corrugation increases the integrated gradient of the envelope while retaining inequalities needed for localized complex-phase wave packets.

Finite-order phase and transport equations produce quasimodes: functions whose eigenfunction equation has a small error. A Gaussian combination of packets is then used to select a real wave with strong first-derivative control and many strict opposite-sign tests on separated small regions.

These sign tests provide robust lower bounds on nodal measure. If a function has opposite signs on the two ends of a short cylinder, its zero set must separate them. A collection of disjoint cylinders gives an additive lower bound. Strict signs persist under small perturbations, so the construction need not rely solely on delicate pointwise descriptions of the zero set.

Replace approximate waves by exact metric eigenfunctions

Small residual error is not enough: the theorem is about exact eigenfunctions of an ordinary Laplace–Beltrami operator.

For the three-sphere construction, M2 first adjusts a scalar conductivity and an independent density. Those coefficients describe a weighted elliptic equation but need not yet arise from one metric. Division by a positive solution of a semilinear equation imposes the three-dimensional metric identity in the active region, and a transverse tensor repair handles the remaining annulus.

On S2×T2S^2\times T^2S2×T2, a conformal scalar correction has a coercive linearized equation. A further change tangent to the eigenfunction’s level sets enforces the four-dimensional determinant relation without changing the corrected eigenfunction equation. The separate repairs preserve the chosen sign tests.

M3 instead works first with a positive principal tensor and density on S4S^4S4, varied independently. After obtaining a fixed limiting weighted operator, it adds a warped circle. Choosing the circle radius to account for the density makes the Laplacian on functions independent of the circle coordinate equal to the weighted base operator. This produces an ordinary five-dimensional metric.

Preserve infinitely many witnesses in one limit

Each construction must protect earlier eigenfunctions while introducing new high-frequency behavior. The papers perturb the operator or metric while preserving a selected eigenfunction and making its eigenvalue simple. Its strict sign score then persists throughout a neighborhood of that metric.

Nested neighborhoods and summably small changes retain every previous witness and converge to one smooth limit. No uniform spectral gap across the whole sequence is assumed; each finite stage has its own tolerance.

For M3, quantitative control is stronger. Repeated corrugations give a multiplicative gain, while derivatives grow at a controlled exponential rate in the number of generations. Taking the number of generations proportional to log⁡k\log klogk converts this into a fixed power gain in kkk. Constants and frequency thresholds may deteriorate with the desired accuracy, but the positive gain exponent is kept fixed. That distinction makes the final power-law violation survive the infinite construction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The negative results concern smooth metrics, not real-analytic ones. They use exact real eigenfunctions on a single closed manifold and metric for each sequence, not approximate modes or a different metric at every frequency.

M2 gives qualitative divergence in dimensions three and four. M3 gives a fixed positive power excess only from dimension five upward. A corresponding power-law construction in dimensions three or four is not claimed by this family.

The known lower bound is not challenged, and a larger polynomial upper bound remains compatible with the examples. Neither theorem prescribes the optimal universal polynomial exponent for all smooth metrics.

Nor do the claims describe a typical metric, a random eigenfunction, or every high-energy mode. They combine a universal positive statement on surfaces with existential negative statements elsewhere.

This digest reports the manuscripts’ proposed average-growth, exactification, and fixed-limit mechanisms without checking their estimates or independently verifying the conjecture resolutions.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked primary papers explain the analytic theorem, smooth lower and polynomial upper bounds, and the average-growth approach. Optional background appears under nodal set, Laplace–Beltrami operator, and Chladni figures.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Sharp nodal length on smooth surfaces (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Smooth counterexamples to Yau’s nodal upper bound in dimensions three and four (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Power-law violations of Yau’s nodal upper bound (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A Calabi flow that becomes singular before reaching a canonical metric
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 352 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Suppose a space admits an especially well-balanced metric. Can a natural geometric evolution always reach that metric from arbitrary smooth initial data?

Calabi flow was introduced to seek canonical Kähler metrics by reducing variation in scalar curvature while keeping the complex structure and Kähler class fixed. A longstanding conjecture proposed that the smooth flow should exist for all positive time from every smooth Kähler metric on a compact complex manifold.

Family 352 claims a counterexample on complex projective ten-space. The starting metric is smooth, highly symmetric, and belongs to the same Kähler class as the standard Fubini–Study metric, which already has constant scalar curvature. Nevertheless, its Calabi flow develops unbounded scalar curvature in finite time.

The distinction is between the existence of a desirable endpoint somewhere in the class and the behavior of a particular evolution from every starting point. A class can contain an ideal metric while some smooth trajectories become singular before reaching it.

2. Background and essential definitions

Kähler metrics and their class

A Kähler manifold has a complex structure, a compatible Riemannian metric, and a closed two-form ω\omegaω encoding the metric and complex structure together. Within a fixed Kähler class, nearby forms can be written using a real potential φ\varphiφ:

ωφ=ω0+i∂∂ˉφ>0.\omega_\varphi=\omega_0+i\partial\bar\partial\varphi>0.ωφ​=ω0​+i∂∂ˉφ>0.

The operators ∂\partial∂ and ∂ˉ\bar\partial∂ˉ are the complex-coordinate parts of exterior differentiation. Positivity means that the form still defines a positive-definite metric. Adding this exact correction preserves integrals over closed surfaces, hence the cohomology class.

A constant-scalar-curvature Kähler metric has scalar curvature independent of position. It need not have constant sectional curvature. In this article, the scalar convention is the manuscript’s complex trace

S(ω)=tr⁡ωRic⁡(ω).S(\omega)=\operatorname{tr}_{\omega}\operatorname{Ric}(\omega).S(ω)=trω​Ric(ω).

Keeping this convention matters for the numerical constant appearing in the radial formula below.

The flow

Calabi flow evolves the potential by

∂tφ=S(ωφ)−S‾,φ(0)=0.\partial_t\varphi=S(\omega_\varphi)-\overline S,\qquad\varphi(0)=0.∂t​φ=S(ωφ​)−S,φ(0)=0.

The average scalar curvature S‾\overline SS is fixed by the Kähler class. A constant-scalar-curvature metric is stationary for this normalization.

Scalar curvature involves second derivatives of the metric, and the metric already involves second derivatives of the potential. Thus Calabi flow is fourth order in φ\varphiφ. It has smoothing properties, but it lacks some elementary maximum-principle tools familiar from second-order heat equations.

The Fubini–Study form on CPn\mathbb{CP}^nCPn is normalized here by the potential log⁡(1+∣Z∣2)\log(1+|Z|^2)log(1+∣Z∣2) on an affine coordinate chart. Its scalar curvature is n(n+1)n(n+1)n(n+1), hence 110 for n=10n=10n=10.

Smooth and weak continuation

A smooth flow remains a smooth positive metric at every time. A weak flow may continue in a larger space of finite-energy potentials, where smoothness is not required. Convergence in a weak potential-space distance does not imply uniform control of curvature or smooth continuation through every intermediate time.

The manuscript challenges smooth global existence. It does not deny the existence of global weak evolutions.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Calabi introduced the flow as a route toward extremal and constant-scalar-curvature metrics. On compact Riemann surfaces, where the complex dimension is one, Chruściel proved global forward existence and convergence to constant curvature. Chen gave a different approach, and Struwe developed a unified treatment of Calabi and normalized Ricci flows on surfaces. Chen’s surface account.

Higher dimensions brought local existence, uniqueness, and stability near canonical metrics. Chen–He proved short-time theory and stability near constant-scalar-curvature metrics; He–Zeng extended short-time theory to rougher initial data. These results do not say that every smooth metric lies in the basin of smooth global convergence. Chen–He, He–Zeng.

Continuation criteria identify quantities that must become uncontrolled at a singularity. Chen–He obtained extension under a Ricci-curvature bound, and Chen–Cheng obtained extension under a scalar-curvature bound. Further results use spatial or spacetime integrability conditions on scalar curvature. The claimed example is consistent with those criteria precisely because its scalar curvature diverges. Chen–Cheng.

Symmetry has yielded global convergence in particular settings. Guan studied modified Calabi flow on almost homogeneous manifolds with two hypersurface ends. The action in the present example has a point orbit and a hyperplane orbit instead; the point has complex codimension ten, so the two-hypersurface hypothesis does not apply.

Meanwhile, Streets constructed global weak Calabi flows by minimizing movements. Berman–Darvas–Lu identified these with finite-energy trajectories and established convergence in the d1d_1d1​ distance to a smooth constant-scalar-curvature potential when the class contains one. Here d1d_1d1​ extends an L1L^1L1-type path-length distance on potentials. The classical and weak flows agree while the classical flow remains smooth, but the weak theory does not force smoothness at every finite time. Streets, Berman–Darvas–Lu.

4. What the new manuscript claims

There is a smooth U(10)U(10)U(10)-invariant Kähler form ω0\omega_0ω0​ on CP10\mathbb{CP}^{10}CP10, in the Fubini–Study class, whose maximal smooth Calabi flow exists on

[0,T∗),0<T∗<∞.[0,T_*),\qquad0<T_*<\infty.[0,T∗​),0<T∗​<∞.

At a fixed point ppp, its scalar curvature satisfies

S(ω(t))(p)∼a(T∗−t)−1/2,a>0.S(\omega(t))(p)\sim a(T_*-t)^{-1/2},\qquad a>0.S(ω(t))(p)∼a(T∗​−t)−1/2,a>0.

The symbol ∼\sim∼ means that the ratio tends to one. This is an asymptotic at the specified point, not a complete global curvature profile.

The group U(10)U(10)U(10) acts by unitary transformations on the affine coordinates. Its invariance reduces the construction to one spatial variable, but the resulting metric is smooth on the whole compact projective manifold. The example has real dimension twenty.

Because the same class contains Fubini–Study, the result disproves the proposed smooth global existence statement even in a class containing a constant-scalar-curvature metric. It also prevents a universal claim of smooth global existence followed by smooth convergence modulo holomorphic automorphisms from arbitrary initial data.

The paper extends the singularity by products. If (Y,η)(Y,\eta)(Y,η) is a compact connected Kähler manifold with constant scalar curvature, then

Ω(t)=πX∗ω(t)+πY∗η\Omega(t)=\pi_X^*\omega(t)+\pi_Y^*\etaΩ(t)=πX∗​ω(t)+πY∗​η

is the corresponding product Calabi flow, with the same maximal smooth time and the same blowup rate at every (p,y)(p,y)(p,y). Suitable stationary projective factors give examples in every complex dimension at least ten, in classes containing Kähler–Einstein metrics. The theorem does not claim such examples in every lower dimension.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the result disproves a central smooth long-time existence conjecture for a major geometric flow. Its strength is that failure occurs in a familiar projective manifold and a class already known to contain a canonical metric.

The example would show that the existence theory of canonical metrics and the global smooth dynamics of Calabi flow cannot be identified. Weak convergence may remain available even when a particular classical trajectory encounters finite-time curvature blowup.

The explicit pointwise rate also gives more information than an abstract failure of continuation. It identifies the scalar quantity that diverges and the leading temporal scale of that divergence.

This rating measures the consequences of the stated construction, not verification of the profile matching or the nonlinear correction.

6. The main idea

Convert radial geometry into one fourth-order equation

For a radial Kähler potential Φ(ℓ)\Phi(\ell)Φ(ℓ), with ℓ=log⁡∣Z∣2\ell=\log|Z|^2ℓ=log∣Z∣2, introduce the momentum coordinate and profile

x=Φ′(ℓ),v=Φ′′(ℓ).x=\Phi'(\ell),\qquad v=\Phi''(\ell).x=Φ′(ℓ),v=Φ′′(ℓ).

In the fixed Fubini–Study class, 0<x<10<x<10<x<1. The two endpoints correspond to the affine origin and the hyperplane at infinity. Write

v=x(1−x)+x2(1−x)2H.v=x(1-x)+x^2(1-x)^2H.v=x(1−x)+x2(1−x)2H.

The metric extends smoothly across both special orbits when HHH is smooth on the closed interval and

1+x(1−x)H>0.1+x(1-x)H>0.1+x(1−x)H>0.

This representation packages the endpoint behavior into a smooth function and an explicit positivity condition. The manuscript derives a scalar fourth-order equation for HHH, including the affine normalization in the Legendre potential needed to recover the exact Calabi flow.

At the affine origin ppp, its scalar-curvature formula simplifies to

S(t,p)=110(1−H(t,0)).S(t,p)=110\bigl(1-H(t,0)\bigr).S(t,p)=110(1−H(t,0)).

Thus a sufficiently negative divergence of one profile value produces positive scalar-curvature blowup at a fixed geometric point.

Construct an exact shrinking profile in the flat limit

Shift the singular time to zero temporarily and take t<0t<0t<0. Set ρ=−t\rho=\sqrt{-t}ρ=−t​. The approximate compact solution is built from

F(t,x)=ρ−1h(x/ρ),h(y)=G(y)−1y.F(t,x)=\rho^{-1}h(x/\rho),\qquad h(y)=\frac{G(y)-1}{y}.F(t,x)=ρ−1h(x/ρ),h(y)=yG(y)−1​.

The function GGG is positive, bounded above and away from zero, and satisfies G(0)=1G(0)=1G(0)=1 with G′(0)<0G'(0)<0G′(0)<0. The quotient defining hhh extends smoothly at zero, giving

F(t,0)=ρ−1G′(0).F(t,0)=\rho^{-1}G'(0).F(t,0)=ρ−1G′(0).

The profile is chosen to solve the scale-invariant flat-limit equation exactly. It matches an analytic solution near the origin with a half-line solution tending to a positive constant at infinity. The manuscript supports this matching with finite exact-arithmetic inequalities, analytic enclosures, and nonlinear error estimates, providing an executable certificate in its appendices.

That certificate is part of the source’s claimed construction; it has not been run or verified for this digest.

Correct the compact error without assuming stability

The compact projective equation differs from the flat model. The paper seeks an exact solution

H=F+VH=F+VH=F+V

with the correction smaller at the origin:

V(t,0)=O(ρ−1+δ)for some δ>0.V(t,0)=O(\rho^{-1+\delta})\qquad\text{for some }\delta>0.V(t,0)=O(ρ−1+δ)for some δ>0.

The leading negative term then survives, yielding the asserted scalar asymptotic.

To construct VVV, the paper develops a right inverse for the linearized equation on negative times. In similarity variables, its evolution is a compact perturbation of a damped constant-coefficient evolution. A spectral split determines finitely many components from future forcing.

This is permitted because the initial metric has not been prescribed in advance: the construction is free to choose a suitable interior slice afterward. It does not assume that the shrinking profile attracts a neighborhood of initial metrics or prove a general nonlinear stability theorem for it.

Join the shrinking core to the outer region

Near the core, the negative-time inverse controls the singular scale. Away from it, a short-time forward solution handles the compact outer region. The outer forcing cancels the error introduced by the inner cutoff, leaving perturbative operator errors.

Weighted parabolic estimates control spatial derivatives through order four and the needed temporal Hölder behavior. A fixed-point construction then supplies the exact nonlinear correction, its time derivative, and positivity of the Kähler form.

Finally, choose a smooth time slice before the singular time as the initial metric and shift time forward. The flow is smooth and positive at every earlier time, but the scalar asymptotic prevents smooth continuation at T∗T_*T∗​. For products, scalar curvature adds and the stationary factor contributes only its constant value, so the same singularity persists.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem constructs one carefully chosen symmetric initial metric. It does not say that every metric in the Fubini–Study class becomes singular, that the behavior is generic, or that small perturbations of Fubini–Study produce the same singularity.

The construction begins in complex dimension ten and extends upward by products. It does not determine the smallest dimension admitting such a singularity. The established global theory on complex curves remains a distinct positive case.

The result concerns the classical smooth flow. It does not contradict global weak Calabi flow or convergence in a weak potential-space distance. A weak trajectory can pass through times at which no smooth metric continuation is available.

The pointwise scalar asymptotic is not a classification of every blowup model or of the limiting weak metric. Further questions include stability of the constructed singularity, its geometric limit, and which initial-data conditions guarantee smooth global evolution.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary sources linked above explain surface existence, higher-dimensional stability and extension criteria, and weak continuation. Optional background appears under Kähler manifold, Fubini–Study metric, and Calabi flow.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A finite-time singularity of Calabi flow on projective space (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Balls, tubes and slabs: the least-area shapes in a periodic cube
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 354 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

In ordinary three-dimensional space, a ball encloses a prescribed volume using the least surface area. Now imagine a unit cube whose opposite faces are identified: leaving through one face brings you back through the opposite face. Which shape encloses a prescribed fraction of this periodic space with the least boundary area?

For a small amount of material, a ball still looks best. With more material, a circular tube can wrap once around the space and avoid paying for end caps. With still more, a slab bounded by two flat sheets may be cheaper. These simple competitors suggest a ball–tube–slab sequence.

The hard question is whether a more intricate surface, perhaps with several handles and passages through the cube, can ever do better. Family 354 claims a complete answer for the cubic flat three-torus: the three expected types and their complements are all the minimizers, including at the two volumes where the preferred type changes.

This is a geometric phase transition. The quantity being optimized is boundary area, the parameter is enclosed volume, and the minimizing shape changes its topology as that parameter grows.

2. Background and essential definitions

A periodic space with ordinary local geometry

The cubic flat three-torus is

T3=R3/Z3.\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3.T3=R3/Z3.

Points differing by an integer vector represent the same point. Small neighborhoods have the ordinary Euclidean metric, so the space is flat. Globally, however, straight lines in coordinate directions close into loops of length one.

A region E⊂T3E\subset\mathbb T^3E⊂T3 has volume ∣E∣|E|∣E∣ between zero and one. Its perimeter P(E)P(E)P(E) means the area of its boundary. The theorem uses finite-perimeter sets, a generalized class that permits rough competitors as well as smooth regions. One can define perimeter as the total variation of the region’s indicator function; for a smooth boundary this agrees with usual surface area.

The isoperimetric profile is

I(V)=inf⁡{P(E):∣E∣=V}.I(V)=\inf\{P(E):|E|=V\}.I(V)=inf{P(E):∣E∣=V}.

It records the least boundary area needed to enclose volume VVV. A region and its complement have the same separating boundary, so

I(V)=I(1−V).I(V)=I(1-V).I(V)=I(1−V).

It therefore suffices to understand 0<V≤1/20<V\le1/20<V≤1/2.

The three candidates

A sufficiently small embedded ball of radius rrr has volume 4πr3/34\pi r^3/34πr3/3 and area 4πr24\pi r^24πr2. Expressed in terms of its volume, its area is

Pball(V)=(36π)1/3V2/3.P_{\mathrm{ball}}(V)=(36\pi)^{1/3}V^{2/3}.Pball​(V)=(36π)1/3V2/3.

A solid circular tube around a shortest closed coordinate geodesic has length one and no end caps. Its volume is πr2\pi r^2πr2, and its boundary area is 2πr2\pi r2πr, giving

Ptube(V)=2πV.P_{\mathrm{tube}}(V)=2\sqrt{\pi V}.Ptube​(V)=2πV​.

A coordinate slab of width VVV has two boundary tori, each of area one. Its perimeter is consequently

Pslab(V)=2.P_{\mathrm{slab}}(V)=2.Pslab​(V)=2.

Here a boundary torus is a flat two-dimensional periodic sheet, not a doughnut-shaped surface drawn in ordinary space. The periodic identification removes the slab’s apparent side faces.

These formulas give upper bounds for I(V)I(V)I(V). They become the exact profile only if every other possible region has at least as much perimeter.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The ball–cylinder–slab prediction appears in Hauswirth, Pérez, Romon and Ros’s The periodic isoperimetric problem and Ros’s later account of isoperimetry. Reflection also links the periodic problem with relative perimeter in a cube, where boundary lying on the cube’s walls is not counted. The canonical pieces there are an eighth of a ball at a corner, a quarter cylinder along an edge, and a coordinate cut.

Important parts of the prediction were known well before the full classification. Hadwiger established the optimality of a coordinate cut at half volume in the cube. Morgan and Johnson’s small-volume comparison gave balls as minimizers for sufficiently small volumes on compact flat manifolds. Acerbi, Fusco and Morini established the uniqueness of coordinate slabs near half volume in the cubic torus. These results controlled neighborhoods of the ends of the relevant volume range, but did not reach the predicted transition points with matching sharp bounds.

The possible geometry of an unknown minimizer was also progressively constrained. Reflection arguments supplied symmetry; volume-constrained stability supplied restrictions on topology. Ritoré and Ros developed results for stable constant-mean-curvature surfaces in flat three-manifolds. Hauswirth and collaborators obtained the connectedness, genus and curvature–area estimates used in this manuscript.

More recently, Emanuel Milman obtained effective ranges, including the cubic spherical regime through volume fraction approximately 0.1205820.1205820.120582. He also formulated the reduction to the two proposed transition volumes, using the differential comparison method of Hauswirth and collaborators. This is a substantial precursor: knowing the right endpoint information can force the whole profile between those endpoints.

The remaining difficulty was not simply locating where the three elementary formulas cross. It was ruling out nonstandard minimizers at those crossing volumes, including extra shapes tied with the familiar ones. Family 354 claims to complete those endpoint exclusions.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For every V∈(0,1)V\in(0,1)V∈(0,1), set v=min⁡(V,1−V)v=\min(V,1-V)v=min(V,1−V). The manuscript states

I(V)=min⁡{(36π)1/3v2/3,  2πv,  2}.I(V)=\min\left\{(36\pi)^{1/3}v^{2/3},\;2\sqrt{\pi v},\;2\right\}.I(V)=min{(36π)1/3v2/3,2πv​,2}.

For V≤1/2V\le1/2V≤1/2, it gives the following exhaustive classification, up to ambient isometry and modification on a set of volume zero.

Volume rangeMinimizing region
0<V<4π/810<V<4\pi/810<V<4π/81An embedded round ball
V=4π/81V=4\pi/81V=4π/81A ball or a circular tube around a shortest closed geodesic
4π/81<V<1/π4\pi/81<V<1/\pi4π/81<V<1/πSuch a circular tube
V=1/πV=1/\piV=1/πA circular tube or a coordinate slab
1/π<V≤1/21/\pi<V\le1/21/π<V≤1/2A coordinate slab

At the two transitions there are exactly the listed alternatives, with no additional equality cases. For volumes above one half, take the complements of the corresponding small-volume regions.

The transition fractions are approximately 0.15510.15510.1551 and 0.31830.31830.3183. The ball has radius (3V/(4π))1/3(3V/(4\pi))^{1/3}(3V/(4π))1/3, the tube has radius V/π\sqrt{V/\pi}V/π​, and the slab has width VVV. These formulas use the unit cubic torus throughout.

“Up to ambient isometry” allows moving a shape around the torus and applying the symmetries of the cubic lattice. It does not allow an arbitrary rotation that fails to preserve that lattice. In particular, the optimal tubes follow shortest coordinate loops, and the optimal slabs have coordinate directions.

The classification applies to unrestricted finite-perimeter competitors. It does not assume that the region is convex, symmetric, connected or given by one of the three models in advance.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claim. This would settle a classical, concrete isoperimetric conjecture by giving both the optimal value and every optimizer. Exact profiles are much rarer than nonsharp inequalities or classifications restricted to very small volumes.

The example exposes a basic competition between local geometry and global topology. At small scale, a ball behaves as it does in Euclidean space. A tube benefits from closing around a periodic direction. A slab benefits from extending through two periodic directions. The boundary can become simpler in area while the region becomes less localized.

The transition cases are mathematically significant. A formula for the infimum alone would leave open whether unexpected surfaces share the optimum. The manuscript’s strict exclusions claim to remove that ambiguity as well.

Its proposed method also offers a general lesson for slicing arguments. Optimizing each cross-section independently can underestimate the cost of a whole object, because the optimal sections may not fit together. The additional information here is how neighboring sections are nested.

6. The main idea

Reduce a continuum of volumes to two difficult ones

Classical regularity says an isoperimetric boundary in this three-dimensional setting is smooth and has constant mean curvature. The mean curvature describes its first-order area response when the enclosed volume changes. Volume-constrained stability says that small perturbations preserving volume cannot decrease area to second order.

The existing structural theory severely restricts such minimizers. Planar, spherical and circular-cylinder boundaries give the standard candidates. A nonstandard minimizing boundary must be connected and have genus between two and four. The genus counts handles: a sphere has genus zero, a torus genus one, and more elaborate candidates have at least two.

Curvature–area estimates and differential inequalities for the isoperimetric profile then provide the two-volume reduction. If every minimizer at

V1=4π81,V2=1πV_1=\frac{4\pi}{81},\qquad V_2=\frac1\piV1​=814π​,V2​=π1​

is standard, the comparison argument gives the complete profile and the classification in the intervening open ranges. The new work can therefore concentrate on excluding higher-genus competitors at those two values.

Use symmetry to study nested planar slices

Reflection and stability put a hypothetical nonstandard minimizer into a coordinate-monotone form in a cube. Coordinate monotonicity means that its sections shrink as one moves in the appropriate coordinate direction. The remaining configurations have two possible patterns of occupied vertices.

The manuscript relates the area of the three-dimensional boundary to areas, boundary lengths and fluxes of its planar sections. A flux identity integrates a component of the normal vector and links it to the section geometry. The coarea formula expresses an integral over a surface in terms of its level slices, with the appropriate slope factor.

These tools and scalar inequalities exclude one vertex pattern at both transitions and the other pattern at the ball–tube transition. The delicate case is the remaining configuration at the tube–slab transition.

Why nesting improves the bound

A planar isoperimetric inequality supplies a lower bound for the perimeter of each section from its area. But those separate bounds are not always strong enough after integration. Near the difficult curvature range, they leave a small deficit.

The proposed improvement starts with the bottom section. Its complementary corner has two edge extents, which need not be equal. A calibration—here an auxiliary unit vector field paired with the boundary tangent—controls both extents using the corner’s area and boundary data. This step uses monotonicity, without assuming that the corner is circular or convex.

Every intermediate section lies inside the bottom section. Thus either orientation of a strip-like section has an endpoint constrained by one of those extents. The strip cannot simultaneously have the area it needs and the least conceivable planar boundary length. Nesting forces a definite excess.

A useful analogy is packing a sequence of shelves into a tapered cabinet. Each shelf might be optimal when designed alone, but its permitted width is constrained by the cabinet and the shelves around it. Here the constraint is exact set inclusion, and the cost is perimeter.

The manuscript converts this extra section length into a positive gain in total surface area using the flux identity and Jensen’s inequality. The latter controls averages of nonlinear quantities by exploiting convexity. That gain supplies the missing strict margin against a nonstandard minimizer.

Finish with a one-variable estimate

After the geometric reduction, a residual inequality depends on a single curvature parameter. The manuscript supplies outward arithmetic bounds and interpolation estimates between finitely many parameter values, together with exact calculation files. Those are stated components of its argument. This digest does not execute or independently certify them.

The paper performs much of the analysis in a torus of side length two with normalized area. Its final theorem restores the unit torus. Keeping that normalization separate is essential: doubling lengths multiplies physical areas by four and volumes by eight. The profile displayed above is the original unit-torus perimeter, not the intermediate normalized quantity.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The claim concerns the cubic flat three-torus. Changing the lattice, taking unequal side lengths, or moving to higher dimensions changes the available loops, sheet areas and possible competing shapes. The same numerical thresholds cannot be carried over without new analysis.

It is a global minimization and equality theorem, not a classification of all constant-mean-curvature surfaces or all stable surfaces. Complicated periodic surfaces can exist even when none minimizes perimeter at its enclosed volume.

The result also does not by itself provide a quantitative stability estimate: it does not state that a region with nearly optimal perimeter must be close to a canonical optimizer by a particular measured amount. Such a statement becomes especially subtle near a transition, where two distinct types tie.

Further questions include the profiles of rectangular and general flat tori, rates of closeness for almost minimizers, and how the nesting method extends beyond this three-dimensional setting. The manuscript’s full theorem and equality claims are reported here as stated, without proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript’s introduction and Theorem 1.1 give the profile and full equality classification. Sections 2–6 explain the two-volume reduction and the nesting improvement; its appendices describe the scalar estimates.

Primary background includes Hauswirth–Pérez–Romon–Ros, Acerbi–Fusco–Morini, and Milman’s effective isoperimetric comparisons. These distinguish the earlier structural and partial results from the endpoint exclusions claimed here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Isoperimetric Conjecture for the Cubic Flat Three-Torus (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Does every magnification see the same mean-curvature singularity?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 355 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A surface moving by mean curvature tends to smooth itself out, but it can also develop a neck pinch or collapse in finite time. Near such a singularity, one magnifies space and slows down time to see the local shape more clearly.

There is a subtle ambiguity. Different sequences of magnifications might conceivably reveal different limiting shapes. Even if the shape is always a cylinder, its axis could drift as the magnification changes. Existence of a limiting model along some sequence does not show that the singularity has one well-defined model.

Family 355 claims that this ambiguity disappears at the first singular time of every smooth closed embedded surface in R3\mathbb R^3R3. At each fixed singular point, every sufficiently large magnification approaches the same shrinking surface, with the same position and axes in the original coordinates. No mean-convexity assumption and no advance choice of a spherical, cylindrical or other model is required.

The result concerns what happens before the singularity. It does not assert a unique way to continue the original surface after the singular time.

2. Background and essential definitions

Mean-curvature flow and parabolic magnification

Let Mt⊂R3M_t\subset\mathbb R^3Mt​⊂R3 be a smoothly evolving surface. Mean-curvature flow prescribes its normal velocity to be its mean curvature vector H\mathbf HH:

∂tX=H,\partial_t X=\mathbf H,∂t​X=H,

up to tangential changes of parametrization. Here XXX records points on the surface, and the convention uses the trace of the second fundamental form. A round sphere shrinks under this motion.

Suppose the flow first becomes singular at time TTT, and x0x_0x0​ is a singular point. Magnifying lengths by λ\lambdaλ requires magnifying time by λ2\lambda^2λ2, because curvature has units of inverse length. The rescaled surfaces are

Msλ=λ(MT+λ−2s−x0),s<0.M_s^{\lambda}=\lambda\bigl(M_{T+\lambda^{-2}s}-x_0\bigr),\qquad s<0.Msλ​=λ(MT+λ−2s​−x0​),s<0.

The new singular time is zero. For fixed negative sss, increasing λ\lambdaλ examines the original flow closer to TTT. A tangent flow is a limit obtained along a sequence λi→∞\lambda_i\to\inftyλi​→∞.

The center x0x_0x0​ remains fixed. Allowing the center to move with the scale is a different procedure and can reveal different geometric information.

Self-shrinkers and multiplicity

A self-shrinker is a surface SSS satisfying

H+X⊥2=0,\mathbf H+\frac{X^\perp}{2}=0,H+2X⊥​=0,

where X⊥X^\perpX⊥ is the normal component of the position vector. It generates a flow by simple dilation:

Ms=−s S,s<0.M_s=\sqrt{-s}\,S,\qquad s<0.Ms​=−s​S,s<0.

For example, in this convention the round shrinking sphere at time −1-1−1 has radius two, and the round cylindrical model has radius 2\sqrt22​.

A limit has multiplicity one when it represents one sheet of area, rather than several sheets collapsing onto the same support. This is stronger than knowing only the visible set of points. Local smooth convergence means that on each fixed bounded spatial region the surfaces and their derivatives converge smoothly, using suitable local graphical descriptions.

A noncompact shrinker can have several ends, the parts remaining far outside a large ball. An end may approach a cone as it is dilated, or approach a round cylinder as one moves outward along it. Having a cylindrical end does not by itself mean that the entire surface is a cylinder.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Huisken’s monotonicity formula identified self-shrinkers as natural models for blowups of mean-curvature flow. Ilmanen’s work supplied smooth tangent supports at the first singular time for closed embedded surface flows in three dimensions. Smooth support, however, leaves multiplicity and uniqueness as additional issues.

Several major uniqueness cases were subsequently settled. Schulze treated smooth compact multiplicity-one shrinkers. Colding and Minicozzi proved uniqueness for round cylindrical tangents, including the cylinder’s axis. Chodosh and Schulze established uniqueness for multiplicity-one asymptotically conical hypersurface tangents.

These results already resolved large and important classes. They did not amount to a theorem for every first-time singularity without specifying its tangent geometry. In particular, a shrinker with cylindrical ends need not have been classified as an exact round cylinder, and it can require a simultaneous analysis of several ends.

Bamler and Kleiner’s multiplicity-one theory is a major geometric input for the present manuscript. In the setting used here, its tangent structure gives a smooth properly embedded multiplicity-one shrinker with finitely many separated conical and cylindrical ends. Lu Wang’s earlier work established the conical-or-cylindrical end alternative under finite-topology assumptions. The manuscript takes its required finite-end structure directly from Bamler–Kleiner; finite genus alone is not substituted for finite topology.

The analytic strategy has its own history. Simon developed convergence methods based on gradient inequalities, and the preceding tangent-uniqueness theorems adapted them to geometric flows. Zhu developed finite-order obstruction methods for certain exact product shrinkers. Family 355 proposes a stationary analysis covering all the ends supplied by the geometric structure theorem, without assuming a separate cylinder-rigidity conjecture.

4. What the new manuscript claims

Start with a smooth, compact, connected surface M0⊂R3M_0\subset\mathbb R^3M0​⊂R3, embedded without boundary. Let (Mt)0≤t<T(M_t)_{0\le t<T}(Mt​)0≤t<T​ be its maximal smooth mean-curvature flow, and fix a singular point (x0,T)(x_0,T)(x0​,T) at its first singular time.

The theorem claims the existence of one smooth properly embedded self-shrinker SSS such that

Msλ⟶−s Sas λ→∞.M_s^\lambda\longrightarrow\sqrt{-s}\,S\qquad\text{as }\lambda\to\infty.Msλ​⟶−s​Sas λ→∞.

This is convergence of the full family of scales, not merely a selected subsequence. It is locally smooth in space, with multiplicity one, uniformly for sss in every compact interval contained in (−∞,0)(-\infty,0)(−∞,0).

The limit is unique in the original ambient frame. One does not rotate each rescaled surface separately to obtain convergence. The position and axes are part of the conclusion.

There is no mean-convexity condition—that is, no requirement that the mean curvature consistently point toward one chosen side of the initial surface. There is no separately imposed entropy or genus bound beyond those automatically supplied by the compact initial surface, and no assumed list of allowable tangent models.

The manuscript also states an all-negative-time conclusion for weak tangent flows in its specified integral Brakke convention. A Brakke flow describes evolving area measures through an inequality encoding motion by mean curvature. Here the convention requires the relevant local integrability and an inequality for every pair of time endpoints, together with convergence of the rescaled spacetime area measures. Under those conditions, every negative-time slice equals the area measure of −s S\sqrt{-s}\,S−s​S, not just almost every slice.

That endpoint convention matters: spacetime measures alone do not determine what an arbitrarily chosen representative does at isolated times.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claim. Uniqueness of blowups is a fundamental question in singularity analysis. A tangent object is much more informative when it belongs intrinsically to the singularity, rather than depending on which sequence of scales was selected.

The claim unifies several previously separate geometric cases in the basic setting of closed embedded surfaces in three-dimensional space. Fixing the ambient frame strengthens the conclusion beyond uniqueness up to rotation and rules out persistent axis drift during magnification.

The broader methodological significance lies in handling noncompact models whose distant ends can change type under tiny perturbations. Such effects are difficult for ordinary local expansions to see. The paper proposes to combine finite Taylor information with exponentially small geometric effects, then convert that stationary information into actual convergence of the evolving surface.

This significance is conditional on the stated theorem. It does not imply that every singularity is a sphere or cylinder, or that uniqueness of a backward model resolves every issue in weak continuation.

6. The main idea

Rescaling turns the problem into convergence toward a critical point

Introduce logarithmic time and rescaled surfaces by

τ=−log⁡(T−t),M~τ=(T−t)−1/2(Mt−x0).\tau=-\log(T-t),\qquad\widetilde M_\tau=(T-t)^{-1/2}(M_t-x_0).τ=−log(T−t),Mτ​=(T−t)−1/2(Mt​−x0​).

As the original time approaches TTT, the rescaled time tends to infinity. A self-shrinker becomes stationary in these coordinates.

The relevant energy is Gaussian area,

F(S)=∫Se−∣X∣2/4 dμ,F(S)=\int_S e^{-|X|^2/4}\,d\mu,F(S)=∫S​e−∣X∣2/4dμ,

with an inessential normalization constant omitted. The Gaussian factor strongly suppresses contributions far from the origin. The rescaled flow decreases this energy, and its stationary defect is H+X⊥/2\mathbf H+X^\perp/2H+X⊥/2.

Energy decrease alone need not prevent a trajectory from drifting among nearby critical objects. A gradient inequality relates energy difference to the size of the stationary defect. When combined with the flow equation, it can show that the rescaled trajectory has finite total length in a suitable norm and hence approaches one limit.

The difficult directions open cylindrical ends

A Jacobi field is an infinitesimal deformation satisfying the linearized shrinker equation. Certain Jacobi fields grow quadratically along a cylindrical end and begin to change its type. They are not ordinary decaying perturbations.

For a circular comparison profile, an opening parameter β<0\beta<0β<0 gives

Rc(z)2=2(1+βz2).R_c(z)^2=2(1+\beta z^2).Rc​(z)2=2(1+βz2).

Its radius reaches zero at distance z=(−β)−1/2z=(-\beta)^{-1/2}z=(−β)−1/2. At that distance the Gaussian factor is

exp⁡ ⁣(−14∣β∣).\exp\!\left(-\frac1{4|\beta|}\right).exp(−4∣β∣1​).

As β\betaβ tends to zero, this is smaller than every fixed power of ∣β∣|\beta|∣β∣. A major geometric change far along the end can therefore be invisible to any single finite Taylor approximation of the Gaussian energy.

The manuscript does not simply assume that a power series in the opening parameters converges. It retains finite Taylor expansions, called jets, and analyzes the smaller effects separately.

Exclude a hidden family of stationary openings

Compactly supported observations near the core provide finitely many parameters for nearby surfaces. Some parameters preserve end types; others open cylindrical ends. Successive linear solves define a formal stationary action, an algebraic power series not presumed convergent in all directions.

The central proposed obstruction is that a formal curve of critical points cannot have a nonzero opening. To obtain it, the paper constructs two stationary comparison solutions using complex parameter contours passing on opposite sides of a collapsing radius. These are complex coefficients on real spatial domains; it does not analytically continue an arbitrary smooth surface in its spatial variables.

The two constructions share the same formal expansion but differ by an exponentially small Stokes jump. This term describes a difference that ordinary power-series coefficients miss. The collapsing end supplies a nonzero contribution, and the analysis of several ends shows that their relevant contributions cannot cancel. This contradicts the stronger smallness that a stationary opening curve would require.

Real-algebraic and analytic approximation tools then convert that exclusion into a finite-power estimate. One sufficiently high finite truncation is enough to control the opening parameters by the stationary defect. Convergence of the full formal series is unnecessary.

Localize carefully enough to control the actual flow

A noncompact limit cannot be compared globally to each compact rescaled surface without cutoffs. The manuscript derives a localized gradient inequality and estimates the discarded Gaussian tails at the scale of the defect.

Graphical improvement and short-time smoothing let the comparison radius grow. The radius is chosen using accumulated earlier energy drops, so the localization errors have a finite total sum. This closes the graphical comparison near the core and yields finite rescaled length.

The resulting convergence takes place at every intermediate rescaled time in the fixed coordinates, not just along the original extracting sequence. Finally, the all-endpoint Brakke inequality upgrades equality of spacetime weights to equality at each negative time under the stated weak-flow convention.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is about two-dimensional embedded surfaces in R3\mathbb R^3R3, their smooth evolution before the first singular time, and rescalings about one fixed singular center. It does not assert the corresponding statement for arbitrary hypersurface dimensions, immersed initial surfaces, or moving-center blowups.

It establishes uniqueness of the tangent shrinker without classifying all such shrinkers. In particular, a model with a cylindrical end is not declared to be a round cylinder everywhere. The proof is designed to avoid needing that additional rigidity statement.
