The convergence is local on compact negative-time intervals. The theorem does not describe a unique forward evolution through time zero, and the weak representative conclusion relies on its explicit endpoint and integrability conditions.

Questions about later singularities of continued weak flows, higher-dimensional analogues and a complete classification of possible shrinkers remain separate. The stationary obstruction and convergence argument are described here as the manuscript presents them, without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

The source’s introduction gives the precise fixed-center and weak-tangent conventions. Its Sections 3–7 develop the stationary obstruction; Sections 8–9 turn it into convergence.

Primary predecessors include Schulze on compact tangents, Colding–Minicozzi on cylindrical blowups, Chodosh–Schulze on conical tangents, and Bamler–Kleiner on multiplicity one. These supply distinct pieces of the context rather than interchangeable versions of the same theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniqueness of tangent flows at the first singular time of embedded surface mean-curvature flow (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Can scalar curvature detect a Ricci-flow singularity?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 351 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Ricci flow changes a Riemannian metric according to its curvature. It is often compared to a heat equation for geometry: irregularities tend to smooth out, but some regions can also collapse and develop singularities.

Several levels of curvature information are available. The full curvature tensor records all directional bending. Ricci curvature averages some of that information, and scalar curvature is a further trace. If the scalar curvature stays bounded, must the whole flow remain smooth?

Family 351 claims that the answer depends on dimension. One manuscript proves extension on every closed four-manifold. Another constructs closed flows in sufficiently high dimension whose scalar curvature stays uniformly bounded while the full curvature diverges at a finite time. A third provides the static analytic estimate used by the four-dimensional proof.

These conclusions concern smooth continuation on the original manifold. Continuing from a singular limit by an orbifold flow is a different result and does not by itself settle this extension question.

2. Background and essential definitions

The equation and its curvature tensors

A Ricci flow is a family of metrics satisfying

∂g∂t=−2Ric⁡g(t).\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}=-2\operatorname{Ric}_{g(t)}.∂t∂g​=−2Ricg(t)​.

Write Rm⁡\operatorname{Rm}Rm for the full curvature tensor, Ric⁡\operatorname{Ric}Ric for its Ricci contraction, and

R=tr⁡gRic⁡R=\operatorname{tr}_g\operatorname{Ric}R=trg​Ric

for scalar curvature. A bound on a tensor controls its trace, but a bound on the trace need not control the tensor. Ricci-flat geometry can still have nonzero full curvature.

On a closed manifold—compact without boundary—a smooth flow extends while full curvature stays uniformly bounded. Its finite maximal time TTT is the endpoint beyond which no smooth continuation agreeing with the original flow exists.

Scalar curvature satisfies

(∂t−Δ)R=2∣Ric⁡∣2.(\partial_t-\Delta)R=2|\operatorname{Ric}|^2.(∂t​−Δ)R=2∣Ric∣2.

It also controls volume change through ∂tdμ=−R dμ\partial_t d\mu=-R\,d\mu∂t​dμ=−Rdμ. These identities make bounded scalar curvature powerful, but turning that information into full regularity is the central issue.

Rates and geometric scales

The usual parabolic singularity scale is curvature of order (T−t)−1(T-t)^{-1}(T−t)−1, corresponding to lengths of order T−t\sqrt{T-t}T−t​. A finite-time singularity is Type I if a uniform bound of that order holds. It is Type II if

lim sup⁡t↑T(T−t)max⁡M∣Rm⁡∣=∞.\limsup_{t\uparrow T}(T-t)\max_M|\operatorname{Rm}|=\infty.t↑Tlimsup​(T−t)Mmax​∣Rm∣=∞.

This is a limsup condition, not necessarily a monotone limit. The examples in M1 have stronger, two-sided power-law estimates.

When curvature concentrates, magnifying different regions can reveal several nested scales. In dimension four, such limits may be Ricci-flat spaces that approach a Euclidean quotient at infinity. These are called asymptotically locally Euclidean, or ALE, spaces. Several nested limits can be organized as a finite bubble tree, with large pieces containing smaller concentration regions.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hamilton established Ricci flow and its basic existence and continuation theory. Šešum proved that a uniform bound on the Ricci tensor already suffices for extension, even without initially bounding the full curvature tensor. The scalar question asks whether one can replace that tensor bound by a bound on its trace. Šešum.

Bamler–Zhang developed heat-kernel, curvature, and compactness estimates under scalar bounds. In dimension four, their theory gives curvature-energy control and orbifold limits, as well as extension under additional topological assumptions. Bamler’s later convergence theory permits singular sets of codimension at least four. These results constrain possible degeneration but do not automatically remove every singular point from the original manifold. Bamler–Zhang, Bamler.

Positive extension or scalar-blowup conclusions were also known in special settings, including closed Kähler–Ricci flow and Type I singularities. Local Type I results address specified concentration regimes. M2 claims to remove such rate restrictions in real dimension four.

The counterexample direction builds on symmetric singularity constructions. Angenent–Knopf produced neckpinches, Gu–Zhu constructed Type II singularities, and Angenent–Isenberg–Knopf obtained degenerate neckpinches with prescribed rates. These show rapid full-curvature concentration, but do not by themselves give bounded scalar curvature. Degenerate neckpinches.

Stolarski constructed closed doubly warped flows with conical singularities and arbitrarily fast blowup, approaching a Ricci-flat cone at the parabolic scale. He identified bounded scalar curvature as a possible feature. M1 imports quantitative profile estimates from that construction and claims the additional scalar bound for suitable large dimensions and mode indices. Stolarski’s source version.

The four-dimensional static companion has a separate ancestry in Einstein desingularization and analytic inequalities near Ricci-flat ALE metrics. It develops an estimate allowing several neck lengths to diverge simultaneously, rather than staying near one fixed smooth ALE background.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

High-dimensional failure: M1

For some sufficiently large integer q≥10q\geq10q≥10, M1 constructs a smooth Ricci flow on

M=S2×Sq+1M=S^2\times S^{q+1}M=S2×Sq+1

with finite maximal time TTT, such that

sup⁡M×[0,T)∣R∣<∞,lim⁡t↑Tmax⁡M∣Rm⁡∣=∞.\sup_{M\times[0,T)}|R|<\infty,\qquad\lim_{t\uparrow T}\max_M|\operatorname{Rm}|=\infty.M×[0,T)sup​∣R∣<∞,t↑Tlim​Mmax​∣Rm∣=∞.

The real dimension is q+3q+3q+3. The theorem does not claim that the construction works already at the smallest displayed lower bound on qqq.

More precisely, in one sufficiently high fixed dimension, the examples have an unbounded discrete collection of exponents α\alphaα with

c(T−t)−α≤max⁡M∣Rm⁡∣≤C(T−t)−αc(T-t)^{-\alpha}\leq\max_M|\operatorname{Rm}|\leq C(T-t)^{-\alpha}c(T−t)−α≤Mmax​∣Rm∣≤C(T−t)−α

for all sufficiently late times. The flow and constants may vary with the exponent. This is not an assertion that every real exponent is realizable.

Four-dimensional extension: M2

Let g(t)g(t)g(t), 0≤t<T<∞0\leq t<T<\infty0≤t<T<∞, be a smooth Ricci flow on a closed smooth real four-manifold. M2 claims that a uniform absolute scalar bound implies a smooth extension on the same manifold to T+ϵT+\epsilonT+ϵ, agreeing with the original flow at every earlier time.

No orientation assumption, curvature-rate restriction, or additional topology is imposed. Disconnected closed manifolds are handled componentwise. Consequently, at a finite maximal singular time in dimension four,

lim sup⁡t↑Tmax⁡MR(⋅,t)=+∞.\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\max_M R(\cdot,t)=+\infty.t↑Tlimsup​Mmax​R(⋅,t)=+∞.

The conclusion is stated as a limsup. The scalar evolution equation supplies a lower bound on finite intervals, so an upper bound would be enough to contradict maximality.

The static estimate: M3

For metrics degenerating along one fixed finite tree of four-dimensional Ricci-flat pieces, M3 proves a sequential inequality

E=o(M).\mathcal E=o(\mathcal M).E=o(M).

Here E\mathcal EE is a renormalized Einstein–Hilbert functional in fixed root units, and M\mathcal MM is a scale-neutral weighted Ricci error controlling ten scaled derivatives. The end geometry has uniform bounds through twenty derivatives; the root end decays faster than inverse radius, and joined quotient groups are nontrivial.

The notation means E/M→0\mathcal E/\mathcal M\to0E/M→0 as the error tends to zero and all joining lengths diverge under the stated hypotheses. It is not a universal estimate from a small unweighted Ricci norm on arbitrary spaces. M2 uses this companion and supplies the flow-specific constructions needed to apply it.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the family would separate the four-dimensional extension theorem from a false unrestricted all-dimensional statement. It would identify a genuine limitation of scalar curvature as a monitor of geometric singularity.

The high-dimensional examples are particularly strong because they keep scalar curvature bounded while allowing arbitrarily fast power-law full-curvature blowup in one fixed dimension. Their two-sided estimates describe the scale of the singularity, not just an isolated lower bound along a sequence.

The four-dimensional result would close the gap between compactness with possible orbifold points and smooth continuation on the original manifold. Its need to control nested Ricci-flat bubbles explains why a scalar estimate alone is not a short route to extension.

The rating reflects the stated scope and consequences, not verification of the constructions or analytic inequalities.

6. The main idea

Separate the cone scale from the cap scale

M1 uses metrics of the form

g=ds2+ϕ(s,t)2gS2+r(s,t)2gSqg=ds^2+\phi(s,t)^2g_{S^2}+r(s,t)^2g_{S^q}g=ds2+ϕ(s,t)2gS2​+r(s,t)2gSq​

away from two pole orbits. The sphere radii vary along the interval coordinate sss. At each pole, the SqS^qSq factor collapses smoothly, leaving a positive-radius two-sphere that shrinks as the singular time approaches.

There are two relevant length scales. The larger is T−t\sqrt{T-t}T−t​, where the geometry approaches a Ricci-flat cone. The smaller cap scale is (T−t)σ(T-t)^\sigma(T−t)σ, with σ>1/2\sigma>1/2σ>1/2. Near-flat Ricci behavior on the larger annuli does not control the smaller smooth cap automatically.

The paper uses one-sided cone comparisons and a slope estimate to bound the cap, then curvature point selection to control full curvature without assuming convergence to a particular complete cap metric. Dimension-explicit parabolic estimates yield a Ricci bound of the form ∣Ric⁡∣≤Cr−e|\operatorname{Ric}|\leq Cr^{-e}∣Ric∣≤Cr−e with 0<e<10<e<10<e<1.

The square of this estimate can be dominated in the scalar evolution equation by a bounded supersolution. Full curvature still diverges because a tangent plane to the shrinking pole two-sphere has curvature ϕ(0,t)−2\phi(0,t)^{-2}ϕ(0,t)−2. Thus the scalar control and the full-curvature blowup are obtained from separate estimates at the two scales.

In four dimensions, isolate the outermost bubble

Under a hypothetical bounded-scalar singularity, M2 extracts a finite tree of Ricci-flat pieces from spatial rescalings. It tracks the outermost nonflat piece at a scale a(t)a(t)a(t), while permitting arbitrarily smaller descendants.

Attach an ALE exterior beyond a collar of radius NaNaNa, where NNN is large and fixed. The renormalized functional combines an integral of scalar curvature with a boundary-flux subtraction. The two terms may diverge separately; the subtraction is what makes their combined limit meaningful.

The functional’s first variation pairs metric velocity with the Einstein tensor. Along the flow, this relates its change to Ricci energy. The main difficulty is to construct and differentiate the exterior using one fixed material collar, without assuming that the whole bubble tree varies smoothly in time.

Why a multiscale analytic path is needed

M3 reduces the elliptic problem to finite parameters while retaining kernels and cokernels of the linearized equations. Long necks introduce exponential and polynomial-logarithmic terms. An asymptotic expansion to every finite order is not automatically a convergent power series at infinite neck length.

The manuscript therefore proves a path-selection theorem for a specified class of such expansions. A path can retain finite sign conditions and prescribed limits while having finite weighted variation in all length and ordinary parameters. The lengths may diverge at unrelated rates, and no assumption says that infinitesimal Ricci-flat deformations integrate to a smooth moduli space.

Combining this path control with the first variation gives the little-oh improvement E=o(M)\mathcal E=o(\mathcal M)E=o(M) on each fixed limiting tree. No uniform exponent across all possible trees is asserted or needed by M2.

Small energy prevents the prescribed scale change

M2 selects time intervals on which the outermost scale changes by a fixed factor. A divergence constraint removes a problematic radial mode in the Ricci equation on nearly flat annuli, improving exterior decay. A time maximal-function estimate converts spacetime Ricci energy into the weighted single-time error required by M3.

The static smallness of the functional conflicts with the amount of variation that a contracting root would require. The resulting estimate forces normalized Ricci energy to tend to zero. Dense material point sets then preserve distances at the root scale between the interval endpoints, producing a pointed isometry that preserves the geometric quantity defining that scale.

But the intervals were chosen to change the scale by a fixed factor. This contradiction rules out concentration. The flow consequently reaches a smooth terminal metric and extends on the original manifold.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M2 treats closed four-manifolds; M1 supplies counterexamples only in sufficiently high dimension. The family does not identify the smallest dimension where bounded-scalar finite-time singularities occur or settle every intermediate dimension.

A scalar bound must be uniform over the full spacetime interval. The theorems do not replace it by an arbitrary averaged or spatial integral condition.

The static companion applies to a fixed finite limiting tree with detailed decay and regularity hypotheses. Its error is weighted and includes derivatives. It should not be simplified into a general scalar-energy inequality without those assumptions.

Finally, the high-dimensional construction explicitly builds on Stolarski’s singular flows, while the four-dimensional extension explicitly depends on M3. This digest preserves those dependencies and reports the claims without auditing the underlying estimates.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked primary sources explain tensor extension, scalar-bound compactness, and the singular-flow construction. Optional background appears under Ricci flow, scalar curvature, and Einstein–Hilbert action.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A closed Ricci flow with bounded scalar curvature and finite-time curvature blowup (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Bounded scalar curvature and smooth extension of four-dimensional Ricci flow (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Path selection and an elliptic inequality on degenerating Ricci-flat trees (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When affine maximal graphs must be paraboloids—and when they need not be
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 353 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A parabola is the simplest strictly convex curve. Its higher-dimensional relative, an elliptic paraboloid, is the graph of a positive quadratic function. Can a natural geometric equation single out these shapes among all complete convex graphs?

The affine Bernstein problem asks this for hypersurfaces that are stationary for affine area. This area measures curvature as well as ordinary size and behaves naturally under affine coordinate changes. Its stationarity equation is fourth order: it involves four derivatives of the function defining the graph.

Family 353 contains two complementary claims. M2 says that in dimensions three through nine, a smooth strictly convex graph satisfying the classical equation must be a paraboloid if it is complete in the ordinary Euclidean metric. M1 constructs a smooth, everywhere strictly convex, nonquadratic solution on all of ten-dimensional space. Taken with the classical two-dimensional result, these claims put a sharp boundary between rigidity and flexibility for smooth entire graphs at dimension ten.

The word “complete” needs care. Affine geometry supplies its own metric, different from the metric inherited from Euclidean space. The counterexample is Euclidean-complete; the paper does not assert that its affine metric is complete.

2. Background and essential definitions

Convex graphs and their equation

Let Ω⊂Rn\Omega\subset\mathbb R^nΩ⊂Rn be an open convex set and let u:Ω→Ru:\Omega\to\mathbb Ru:Ω→R be smooth. Its graph consists of points (x,u(x))(x,u(x))(x,u(x)) in Rn+1\mathbb R^{n+1}Rn+1. The graph has dimension nnn, even though the surrounding space has dimension n+1n+1n+1.

The Hessian D2u=(uij)D^2u=(u_{ij})D2u=(uij​) is the matrix of second derivatives. Here locally uniformly convex means that this matrix is positive definite at every point. On each compact subset its eigenvalues consequently have a positive lower bound. No single positive lower bound over the whole graph is assumed.

For a compact region of the domain, affine area is given by the integral

A(u)=∫(det⁡D2u)1/(n+2) dx.\mathcal A(u)=\int (\det D^2u)^{1/(n+2)}\,dx.A(u)=∫(detD2u)1/(n+2)dx.

The determinant measures the product of the principal second-derivative contributions. A graph is classically affine maximal when the first variation of this functional vanishes under compactly supported smooth variations. Its equation is

∑i,j=1nUijwij=0,w=(det⁡D2u)−(n+1)/(n+2),\sum_{i,j=1}^n U^{ij}w_{ij}=0,\qquadw=(\det D^2u)^{-(n+1)/(n+2)},i,j=1∑n​Uijwij​=0,w=(detD2u)−(n+1)/(n+2),

where UijU^{ij}Uij are the entries of the cofactor matrix

U=(det⁡D2u)(D2u)−1.U=(\det D^2u)(D^2u)^{-1}.U=(detD2u)(D2u)−1.

Although the equation looks second order in www, that quantity already depends on two derivatives of uuu. This is why the original equation is fourth order. “Maximal” is the established geometric terminology; the formulation used here is stationarity.

A positive quadratic polynomial has constant positive Hessian, hence constant www, and satisfies the equation immediately. The question is whether other complete solutions exist.

Two meanings of completeness

Distances along the graph in ordinary Euclidean space are described by

gij=δij+uiuj.g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+u_i u_j.gij​=δij​+ui​uj​.

Completeness means that a path escaping every compact part of the graph cannot have finite length. An entire graph, with Ω=Rn\Omega=\mathbb R^nΩ=Rn, is complete for this metric because its lengths dominate those of its projection to Rn\mathbb R^nRn.

The affine, or Berwald–Blaschke, metric is instead

gijaff=(det⁡D2u)−1/(n+2)uij.g^{\mathrm{aff}}_{ij}=(\det D^2u)^{-1/(n+2)}u_{ij}.gijaff​=(detD2u)−1/(n+2)uij​.

Its lengths depend directly on second derivatives. Completeness for one metric cannot simply be substituted for completeness for the other.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Chern asked whether an entire locally uniformly convex affine maximal surface must be an elliptic paraboloid. Calabi developed the affine-area framework and proved a surface rigidity theorem under both Euclidean and affine completeness. These works established the geometric problem before the modern regularity machinery was available.

Trudinger and Wang’s 2000 paper proved the Euclidean-complete surface theorem without requiring affine completeness. It also developed higher-dimensional interior estimates: once suitably normalized pieces of a graph retain uniform strict convexity, derivative bounds can force global rigidity. The obstacle was obtaining that convexity control from completeness alone.

The same paper constructed the famous singular ten-dimensional example

u0(x,t)=∣x∣9+t2,(x,t)∈R9×R.u_0(x,t)=\sqrt{|x|^9+t^2},\qquad (x,t)\in\mathbb R^9\times\mathbb R.u0​(x,t)=∣x∣9+t2​,(x,t)∈R9×R.

This showed that unrestricted rigidity could fail for generalized convex solutions. It did not provide a smooth graph with positive-definite Hessian everywhere. Removing the singularity while preserving the classical equation was a separate problem.

Trudinger and Wang subsequently proved that an affine-complete locally uniformly convex hypersurface is Euclidean-complete and established a global graph representation. Li and Jia gave a separate proof of the affine-complete surface theorem. These results explain why graph rigidity can also yield a theorem for certain immersed hypersurfaces that are not initially presented as graphs.

Later analytic approaches included Wang and Zhou’s partial Legendre transform method, with a new surface proof and higher-dimensional results under integral assumptions. Results for modified determinant powers also appeared. Such equations resemble the classical one, but their exponent is part of the problem, not a disposable parameter.

There is an additional contemporary source: Trudinger and Wang’s The higher dimensional affine Bernstein and Plateau problems, posted on 7 October 2026, states smooth counterexamples in dimensions ten and above, interior regularity for the affine Plateau problem in all dimensions, and rigidity under a growth condition. Its arXiv record also notes a February 2026 submission. These claims deserve explicit credit; this digest does not determine priority between constructions. Family 353 is discussed in its own stated scope.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: completeness forces a quadratic in dimensions three through nine

Suppose 3≤n≤93\le n\le93≤n≤9, Ω\OmegaΩ is nonempty, open and convex, and u∈C∞(Ω)u\in C^\infty(\Omega)u∈C∞(Ω) has positive-definite Hessian and satisfies the classical affine maximal equation. M2 claims that Euclidean completeness of its graph implies

Ω=Rn,u(x)=12xTAx+b⋅x+c,\Omega=\mathbb R^n,\qquadu(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Ax+b\cdot x+c,Ω=Rn,u(x)=21​xTAx+b⋅x+c,

where AAA is a constant symmetric positive-definite matrix, bbb a vector, and ccc a constant. Thus an invertible affine transformation takes the graph to the standard elliptic paraboloid.

No growth condition at infinity, global Hessian bound, or integral estimate is assumed. The domain need not be all of space at the outset; the conclusion includes that fact.

M2 also states an affine-complete consequence. A connected, smooth, locally uniformly convex, classically affine maximal immersed hypersurface of dimension three through nine is an elliptic paraboloid if its underlying manifold is noncompact without boundary and its affine metric is complete. This uses the earlier completeness and graph theorems. It does not identify the two metrics.

M1: a smooth ten-dimensional counterexample

M1 claims a function

u∈C∞(R10),D2u>0,u\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^{10}),\qquad D^2u>0,u∈C∞(R10),D2u>0,

which solves the classical equation but is not quadratic. The construction has the form

u(x,t)=F(∣x∣)2+t2,x∈R9,u(x,t)=\sqrt{F(|x|)^2+t^2},\qquad x\in\mathbb R^9,u(x,t)=F(∣x∣)2+t2​,x∈R9,

with FFF positive, smooth as a radial function on R9\mathbb R^9R9, and strictly convex. Its normalization is F(0)=1F(0)=1F(0)=1. Along the last coordinate axis, therefore, u(0,t)=1+t2u(0,t)=\sqrt{1+t^2}u(0,t)=1+t2​, which is visibly nonquadratic.

The graph is Euclidean-complete because it is entire. The theorem does not impose affine completeness or a global uniform lower bound for the Hessian. It is a smooth counterexample to the classical equation, not merely to a related determinant-power equation.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claims. The affine Bernstein problem is a central classification question linking convexity, geometric invariance and nonlinear differential equations. An unconditional rigidity theorem through dimension nine, paired with a smooth failure in dimension ten, would establish a sharp dimensional transition for entire classical solutions.

The two directions illuminate different obstacles. For rigidity, the challenge is preventing a complete graph from becoming arbitrarily poorly shaped after normalization. For flexibility, it is preserving an exact fourth-order equation while replacing the singular center of a model by a smooth cap.

The result also teaches a useful lesson about geometric PDE: a familiar-looking equation can change character when either the dimension or an exponent changes. Convexity alone does not eliminate that sensitivity. The score reflects this structural significance, not a judgment about proof validity or exclusivity relative to other 2026 work.

6. The main idea

Rigidity: control every section of the graph

At a point aaa, the tangent affine function is

ℓa(x)=u(a)+Du(a)⋅(x−a).\ell_a(x)=u(a)+Du(a)\cdot(x-a).ℓa​(x)=u(a)+Du(a)⋅(x−a).

A tangent section of height h>0h>0h>0 is the region

Su(a,h)={x:u(x)<ℓa(x)+h}.S_u(a,h)=\{x:u(x)<\ell_a(x)+h\}.Su​(a,h)={x:u(x)<ℓa​(x)+h}.

It is the part of the domain lying beneath a plane raised a fixed amount above the tangent plane. These sections record how quickly the graph separates from its tangents.

M2 seeks a uniform balance property: reflecting a section through its base point and shrinking it by one fixed factor places it inside the original section. The same factor must work at every point and every height. This rules out increasingly one-sided sections.

The manuscript studies affine rescalings of the epigraph, the convex region above the graph. Degenerate limiting shapes are organized by the number of independent nonnegative directions they contain. Maximizing that number forces their transverse slices to stay centered: otherwise, another rescaling would create an additional direction.

The equation then excludes models with two or more such directions. In logarithmic coordinates, an integral inequality forces a relevant measure to grow exponentially, whereas geometric bounds on normalized pieces allow only polynomial growth. The crucial quadratic estimate is strictly positive in dimensions three through nine. The estimates are applied to smooth approximations on a finite large region; the limiting convex body is not assumed smooth.

With this degeneration excluded, the tangent sections remain uniformly balanced. Trudinger–Wang interior estimates apply after normalizing sections by ellipsoids. Third derivatives of the normalized functions stay bounded. Transforming back along larger and larger sections makes the original third derivatives tend to zero. Thus D3u=0D^3u=0D3u=0, exactly the condition that uuu be quadratic.

Flexibility: replace a singular profile by a controlled radial solution

M1 starts with the square-root ansatz above, but solves for its radial factor rather than smoothing the old example arbitrarily. An auxiliary positive function PPP converts the affine maximal equation into a radial differential system. Writing r=∣x∣r=|x|r=∣x∣ and y=F′(r)y=F'(r)y=F′(r), the ten-dimensional system is

F′=y,y8y′=r8FP−12/11,F'=y,\qquad y^8y'=r^8F P^{-12/11},F′=y,y8y′=r8FP−12/11,
(y8P′)′=−11r8P−1/11.(y^8P')'=-11r^8P^{-1/11}.(y8P′)′=−11r8P−1/11.

The powers reflect the nine radial coordinates and the classical ten-dimensional exponent. Positivity of F,P,y,y′F,P,y,y'F,P,y,y′ is essential: it keeps the equation meaningful and the constructed graph strictly convex.

The origin looks singular in radial coordinates. The manuscript first uses the variable r2/2r^2/2r2/2 and an integral formulation to build a smooth local solution with F(0)=P(0)=1F(0)=P(0)=1F(0)=P(0)=1. The remaining danger is that this solution breaks down at a finite radius, for example because PPP reaches zero.

Logarithmic derivative variables turn the continuation problem into a three-dimensional dynamical system. The paper constructs a bounded box whose faces cannot be crossed outward. Its upper corner is suggested by the old singular profile. Staying inside the box controls the growth and decay of the original functions on every finite radial interval, allowing continuation to all radii.

Thus the singular example guides the large-scale bounds without being used as the final graph. Smoothness at the center and control at infinity are separate parts of the construction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These are claims about smooth, locally uniformly convex solutions of the classical affine maximal equation. Weak solutions, graphs with degenerate Hessian, and equations with another determinant power require separate statements.

The dimensional threshold refers to the dimension of the graph. M1’s example lies in R11\mathbb R^{11}R11 and is a graph over R10\mathbb R^{10}R10. Its theorem is a dimension-ten construction. Extending it by simply adding quadratic variables is not automatic, because changing dimension changes the classical exponent.

The Euclidean-complete counterexample does not resolve the corresponding question under affine completeness. Conversely, M2’s affine-complete corollary has explicit noncompactness, connectedness and convexity assumptions. Neither paper supplies a classification of all high-dimensional nonquadratic solutions.

Natural further questions concern their growth, asymptotic geometry, affine-metric completeness and the extent to which other symmetry classes allow similar constructions. The contemporary Trudinger–Wang paper provides additional results in this direction; comparison of the proofs or their correctness is outside this exposition. The mathematical claims here are reported as stated.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives the radial smooth counterexample; M2 gives the low-dimensional rigidity theorem and its affine-complete consequence. Their introductions distinguish the completeness assumptions and related determinant-power equations.

Historical sources include Trudinger–Wang, The Bernstein problem for affine maximal hypersurfaces, and their Affine complete locally convex hypersurfaces. Their 2026 paper is relevant contemporary work. For the separate range of generalized exponents, see Sun, Xing and Xu.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Smooth Nonquadratic Entire Affine Maximal Graph in Dimension Ten (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The affine Bernstein theorem in dimensions three through nine (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: From a Euclidean tangent to coordinates with controlled distortion
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 357 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

If a space looks increasingly like Rn\mathbb R^nRn when magnified around a point, does a whole neighborhood admit Euclidean coordinates that preserve distances within a fixed factor?

A tangent space only records limiting geometry at one point. A coordinate chart must compare every pair of points in a neighborhood, including pairs much closer to one another than either is to the original center. Small errors across infinitely many scales may accumulate, so a Euclidean tangent does not automatically produce a quantitatively good chart.

Family 357 claims that such coordinates do exist at every regular point of a noncollapsed RCD space. These are metric spaces with a synthetic lower Ricci-curvature bound and their natural dimensional volume measure. The chart is defined on an open neighborhood, lands in an open subset of Rn\mathbb R^nRn, and distorts distances by at most a constant depending only on nnn.

The neighborhood may be very small and depend on the point. The uniform part of the claim is the distortion factor, not the radius of the chart.

2. Background and essential definitions

Curvature without smooth coordinates

A metric measure space (X,d,m)(X,d,m)(X,d,m) consists of a space, a distance and a reference measure. The condition RCD(K,n)\mathrm{RCD}(K,n)RCD(K,n) is a synthetic analogue of a Ricci-curvature lower bound KKK and dimension bound nnn. It combines a curvature-dimension condition expressed through optimal transport with a quadratic energy for weak gradients.

That quadratic structure makes the calculus Riemannian: weak gradients have inner products, the heat equation is linear, and weak Hessians and Laplacians can be defined. A smooth nnn-dimensional Riemannian manifold with Ricci curvature at least KKK, equipped with its volume measure, is a basic example. Singular limits of manifolds motivate the broader theory.

Here noncollapsed has the exact meaning

m=Hn,m=\mathcal H^n,m=Hn,

where Hn\mathcal H^nHn is nnn-dimensional Hausdorff measure. It is not an arbitrary weighted measure. The spaces are complete, separable and geodesic, with full-support measure finite on bounded sets. Full support means every nonempty open ball has positive measure.

Regular points and tangent spaces

A tangent space at ppp is obtained by rescaling distances by 1/ri1/r_i1/ri​, for some ri↓0r_i\downarrow0ri​↓0, and taking a pointed Gromov–Hausdorff limit. This convergence compares bounded metric balls while keeping track of their distinguished center; it does not require a common ambient Euclidean embedding.

The point ppp is nnn-regular if every such tangent is pointed-isometric to Rn\mathbb R^nRn with its usual distance. Thus the infinitesimal limiting shape is unambiguously Euclidean.

A map F:U→V⊂RnF:U\to V\subset\mathbb R^nF:U→V⊂Rn is LLL-bi-Lipschitz when

L−1d(x,z)≤∣F(x)−F(z)∣≤Ld(x,z)(x,z∈U).L^{-1}d(x,z)\le |F(x)-F(z)|\le Ld(x,z)\qquad(x,z\in U).L−1d(x,z)≤∣F(x)−F(z)∣≤Ld(x,z)(x,z∈U).

The right inequality prevents excessive stretching, and the left prevents excessive compression. A bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism is a one-to-one correspondence with this control in both directions.

This is stronger than a bi-Hölder homeomorphism, where powers of distances may appear. For example, a bound involving d(x,z)αd(x,z)^\alphad(x,z)α with α<1\alpha<1α<1 allows the ratio to the original distance to grow without bound as the points approach each other.

Which distance is used inside a neighborhood?

The manuscript uses the original ambient distance ddd restricted to UUU. It does not replace it by the length of the shortest path required to stay inside UUU. These distances can differ because an ambient shortest path may leave the chart domain. The all-pairs estimate is stated for the original distance.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Cheeger and Colding developed the structure theory of noncollapsed limits of manifolds with lower Ricci curvature. They obtained manifold neighborhoods with bi-Hölder parametrizations and raised the possibility of a bi-Lipschitz improvement. This is a historical antecedent of the synthetic regular-point problem.

The RCD theory subsequently extended weak differential geometry beyond spaces explicitly presented as smooth limits. De Philippis and Gigli established important noncollapsed volume-convergence and rigidity results, providing quantitative Euclidean approximation from the geometric hypotheses.

Mondino and Naber proved countable bi-Lipschitz rectifiability for RCD spaces. Roughly, almost all of the space can be covered by measurable pieces that are bi-Lipschitz equivalent to measurable subsets of Euclidean spaces. Such pieces need not be open, and an arbitrary prescribed regular point need not be covered by one open chart. This distinction is precisely relevant here.

Kapovitch and Mondino showed that the regular set of a noncollapsed RCD space lies in an open manifold region with bi-Hölder charts. That gave neighborhood topology, but left the stronger distance control unresolved.

Other results came close from different directions. Colding and Naber obtained bi-Lipschitz embeddings of sufficiently regular quantitative subsets into a Euclidean space that may have higher dimension. They also constructed examples showing that Euclidean tangents do not guarantee coordinates with a Hölder-continuous metric tensor. A bi-Lipschitz chart into the same dimension is therefore a specific intermediate target, not a route to unrestricted smoothness.

Honda and Zhang’s 2026 work recalls the regular-point conjecture and proves stronger geometric regularity under positive injectivity-radius assumptions. Their analytic criteria also use additional uniform control. Family 357 claims the open bi-Lipschitz chart under the noncollapsed RCD assumptions alone, without those extra conditions.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For each integer n≥2n\ge2n≥2, the theorem asserts a constant Ln≥1L_n\ge1Ln​≥1. For any real KKK, any noncollapsed RCD(K,n)\mathrm{RCD}(K,n)RCD(K,n) space (X,d,Hn)(X,d,\mathcal H^n)(X,d,Hn), and any nnn-regular point ppp, there exist:

  • an ambient-open neighborhood UUU of ppp;
  • an open set V⊂RnV\subset\mathbb R^nV⊂Rn;
  • a homeomorphism F:U→VF:U\to VF:U→V;

such that

Ln−1d(x,z)≤∣F(x)−F(z)∣≤Lnd(x,z)for every x,z∈U.L_n^{-1}d(x,z)\le |F(x)-F(z)|\le L_n d(x,z)\qquad\text{for every }x,z\in U.Ln−1​d(x,z)≤∣F(x)−F(z)∣≤Ln​d(x,z)for every x,z∈U.

The constant depends only on dimension. The domain and its size may depend on the space, the curvature bound and the chosen point. No quantitative radius valid for all examples is asserted.

The conclusion holds at every prescribed regular point, rather than only outside an unspecified measure-zero exceptional set. The image is open in Rn\mathbb R^nRn, not just a measurable set and not a subset of a higher-dimensional target.

The paper also states an atlas consequence. There is an open set U⊂X\mathcal U\subset XU⊂X containing every nnn-regular point and satisfying

Hn(X∖U)=0.\mathcal H^n(X\setminus\mathcal U)=0.Hn(X∖U)=0.

It has a countable atlas of LnL_nLn​-bi-Lipschitz charts. On overlaps, transition maps have bi-Lipschitz constant at most Ln2L_n^2Ln2​, by composing one chart with the inverse of another.

The open set U\mathcal UU may include points outside the exact regular locus. The corollary does not assert that the set of points with Euclidean tangents is itself open. Being a point in a bi-Lipschitz manifold and having an exactly Euclidean metric tangent are different conditions.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claim. This would settle the noncollapsed regular-point bi-Lipschitz conjecture and upgrade an open topological description to quantitative metric coordinates.

For analysis, an open chart is more useful than a collection of measurable pieces: it describes an entire local region and compares all nearby pairs. For geometry, a dimension-only distortion constant separates the strength of the coordinate system from the scale at which it becomes available.

The result would also clarify how much regularity a lower Ricci bound provides. It claims genuine control of distances without claiming a smooth or Hölder-continuous metric tensor. This places the conclusion between weak measurable rectifiability and classical smooth differential geometry.

The proposed mechanism is of broader interest because it handles scale-dependent corrections that may accumulate without bound. The essential control is directional and summable, rather than a blanket assumption that every normalization remains uniformly mild.

6. The main idea

Start with harmonic coordinates that may degenerate

At a regular point, rescaling makes the geometry increasingly Euclidean. Volume comparison propagates quantitative flatness to sufficiently small balls around nearby centers. Harmonic functions—weak solutions of Δuj=0\Delta u_j=0Δuj​=0—then approximate Euclidean coordinate functions.

Write the resulting open coordinate map as

u=(u1,…,un).u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n).u=(u1​,…,un​).

Its gradient inner products form the Gram matrix

Gjk=⟨∇uj,∇uk⟩.G_{jk}=\langle\nabla u_j,\nabla u_k\rangle.Gjk​=⟨∇uj​,∇uk​⟩.

If this matrix were uniformly close to the identity at every relevant scale, metric control would be straightforward. The difficulty is that averages of the Gram matrix remain invertible but can become increasingly poorly conditioned at small scales. A harmonic coordinate direction can become compressed.

Simply renormalizing separately at each scale need not produce one limiting chart. The transformations can accumulate, fail to commute, and introduce a Hölder loss.

Separate cumulative stretching from directional error

The manuscript uses a matrix-valued Bochner measure. After rescaling so that the curvature lower bound is −κ-\kappa−κ, it takes the form

M=12ΔG+κG m,\mathsf M=\tfrac12\Delta G+\kappa G\,m,M=21​ΔG+κGm,

with the Laplacian interpreted entry by entry as a measure. Positivity records control of second derivatives of the harmonic functions. Normalized local averages of this measure produce positive matrices governing how much stretching is needed at each dyadic radius ri=2−ir_i=2^{-i}ri​=2−i.

There are two distinct estimates. One compares the accumulated positive matrices to the total normalization needed by the coordinates. This accumulated quantity may be unbounded.

The second evaluates the local matrices only on actual coordinate differences u(x)−u(z)u(x)-u(z)u(x)−u(z). Schematically, the resulting error is bounded by

Cri2(Ei(x)+Ei(z)),sup⁡x∑i≥0Ei(x)⟶0C r_i^2\bigl(E_i(x)+E_i(z)\bigr),\qquad\sup_x\sum_{i\ge0}E_i(x)\longrightarrow0Cri2​(Ei​(x)+Ei​(z)),xsup​i≥0∑​Ei​(x)⟶0

as the initial rescaling becomes flat. The functions EiE_iEi​ are nonnegative defects; their sum, rather than the sum of their square roots, is controlled.

The paper obtains this directional estimate from Poisson replacements of squared distance, radial derivative approximations and a two-center projection estimate. A Poisson replacement solves a prescribed Laplace equation with boundary data chosen to imitate the distance function while providing better analytic control.

The distinction between the two estimates is the main geometric idea. A coordinate system may require large accumulated correction even though its errors on the pairs of points being compared have a small total budget.

Correct coordinates in their value space

Instead of differentiating a possibly irregular metric on XXX, the manuscript works in the open Euclidean domain of coordinate values Ω=u(B1(p))\Omega=u(B_1(p))Ω=u(B1​(p)), in rescaled units. It constructs smooth maps hi:Ω→Rnh_i:\Omega\to\mathbb R^nhi​:Ω→Rn with invertible ordinary Jacobians.

The iteration is

h0(P)=P,hi+1(P)=hi(P)+Dhi(P)−Tvi(P).h_0(P)=P,\qquadh_{i+1}(P)=h_i(P)+Dh_i(P)^{-\mathsf T}v_i(P).h0​(P)=P,hi+1​(P)=hi​(P)+Dhi​(P)−Tvi​(P).

Here PPP is a coordinate value, DhiDh_iDhi​ is the derivative matrix, and viv_ivi​ is a covector field built from the positive local matrices and smooth cutoffs. The inverse transpose arranges that the leading change in squared lengths supplies the required positive stretching.

Differentiating the update creates further terms involving second and higher derivatives. The manuscript controls the diagonal second-derivative terms through a recurrence tied to the directional defects. Separate derivative estimates close the smooth iteration despite a loss of one derivative at each update.

This is designed to sum errors using ∑iEi\sum_iE_i∑i​Ei​, even when ∑iEi\sum_i\sqrt{E_i}∑i​Ei​​ diverges. The elementary distinction is substantial: for example, squares of 1/i1/i1/i have a finite sum, while 1/i1/i1/i itself does not. Taking an unnecessary square root can destroy the entire estimate.

Obtain one chart, not separate maps at separate scales

The limiting map is

F=lim⁡i→∞hi∘u.F=\lim_{i\to\infty}h_i\circ u.F=i→∞lim​hi​∘u.

The cumulative estimate supplies enough correction to prevent compression, and the directional estimate controls the total metric error. Together they yield both sides of the all-pairs bi-Lipschitz inequality.

Finally, the original open coordinate description and invariance of domain give openness of the image. Invariance of domain says that a continuous injective map between open subsets of Rn\mathbb R^nRn has open image. This topological step is needed because metric bounds on an arbitrary subset alone would not establish the claimed open-neighborhood chart.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem assumes integer dimension n≥2n\ge2n≥2, exact Hausdorff reference measure, the full RCD condition and Euclidean tangents at the chosen point. It is not a theorem for arbitrary metric spaces with Euclidean tangents, or for every point of every collapsed RCD space.

The chart is bi-Lipschitz, but its components are not asserted to have bounded Laplacians. Nor is the metric tensor in these coordinates asserted to be Hölder-continuous. Restrictions proved for analytically more regular coordinate maps do not automatically apply to the limiting maps claimed here.

There is no uniform chart radius, no statement that the exact regular set is open, and no elimination of singular points elsewhere in the space. The atlas region has full measure while its complement may still have important geometry.

Natural extensions concern collapsed settings, quantitative control of chart size and additional assumptions that improve coordinate regularity. The manuscript’s estimates and construction are explained as stated; they have not been independently verified by this digest.

8. Sources and further reading

The source’s Theorem 1.1 gives the open chart, and Corollary 1.2 gives the atlas. Its introduction distinguishes rectifiable pieces, bi-Hölder neighborhoods, higher-dimensional embeddings and analytically regular maps.

Primary background includes Mondino–Naber, Kapovitch–Mondino, Colding–Naber, and Honda–Zhang. These explain the different prior regularity conclusions and the extra hypotheses used for stronger structures.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Bi-Lipschitz Coordinates at Regular Points of Noncollapsed RCD Spaces (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Recognizing Alexandrov curvature without a smooth metric
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 356 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

On a smooth curved space, curvature can be described in two very different ways. One differentiates the metric and computes a curvature tensor. The other draws geodesic triangles and compares them with triangles on a sphere, plane or hyperbolic plane.

These descriptions agree in classical Riemannian geometry. But a singular space may have distances and shortest paths without possessing a smooth metric tensor in coordinates. Can a weak, distributional curvature tensor still capture exactly the geometric triangle condition?

Family 356 claims a positive answer to Gigli’s characterization conjecture in every integer dimension at least two. Its first manuscript identifies Alexandrov lower curvature with a lower bound for Gigli’s distributional sectional curvature, within an appropriate synthetic Ricci-curvature framework and with the exact Hausdorff reference measure.

A second manuscript supplies an essential bridge: under precise boundedness assumptions, a distributional Hessian inequality controls a function along every minimizing geodesic. This is stronger than an almost-everywhere assertion, because one particular geodesic may lie entirely inside a set of measure zero.

2. Background and essential definitions

Triangles as curvature detectors

A geodesic is a path realizing the distance between its endpoints, parametrized at constant speed. An Alexandrov space with curvature at least κ\kappaκ, abbreviated CBB(κ)\mathrm{CBB}(\kappa)CBB(κ), satisfies lower triangle comparison with the simply connected two-dimensional model of constant curvature κ\kappaκ.

Informally, its triangles are at least as “fat” as the corresponding model triangles: appropriate distances between points on their sides are no smaller than in the comparison triangle. When κ>0\kappa>0κ>0, the comparison is restricted to the usual model scale. This is a distance-based condition, meaningful even at singular points.

On a smooth manifold, sectional curvature assigns curvature to each two-dimensional tangent plane. If X,YX,YX,Y span that plane, the denominator in its formula is

∣X∣2∣Y∣2−⟨X,Y⟩2,|X|^2|Y|^2-\langle X,Y\rangle^2,∣X∣2∣Y∣2−⟨X,Y⟩2,

the squared area of their parallelogram. The numerator is a component of the Riemann curvature tensor. Ricci curvature sums appropriate sectional curvatures; thus sectional curvature at least κ\kappaκ implies Ricci curvature at least (n−1)κ(n-1)\kappa(n−1)κ in dimension nnn.

The RCD framework

A metric measure space (M,d,m)(M,d,m)(M,d,m) combines a distance ddd with a reference measure mmm. Full support means every nonempty open ball has positive measure. The measure is assumed finite on bounded sets.

The condition RCD(K,N)\mathrm{RCD}(K,N)RCD(K,N) is a synthetic version of a Ricci lower bound KKK and a dimension upper bound NNN. Its curvature-dimension part describes convexity of suitable entropy quantities when probability distributions are moved by optimal transport. “Riemannian” adds that the energy of a function’s gradient is quadratic, so the weak first-order calculus behaves like a Hilbert space rather than a general normed geometry.

This framework permits weak gradients, Laplacians, Hessians and covariant derivatives without assuming a smooth atlas. The manuscripts use the unreduced curvature-dimension convention.

The measure Hn\mathcal H^nHn is nnn-dimensional Hausdorff measure, defined from coverings by small sets and their diameters. On a smooth nnn-manifold it is the usual geometric volume, with the standard normalization. Requiring m=Hnm=\mathcal H^nm=Hn is an exact structural assumption, not just a statement that the measures have the same null sets.

What “distributional” means

A distributional derivative is defined through integration by parts against suitable test functions. It can exist when pointwise derivatives do not.

Gigli’s curvature functional R(X,Y,Z,W)(f)\mathcal R(X,Y,Z,W)(f)R(X,Y,Z,W)(f) similarly pairs a weak curvature expression with a scalar test function fff. In the smooth case it equals the integral of f⟨R(X,Y)Z,W⟩f\langle R(X,Y)Z,W\ranglef⟨R(X,Y)Z,W⟩. In the nonsmooth case integration by parts expresses it using available weak first covariant derivatives, avoiding an assumed classical curvature tensor.

The allowed global test functions are bounded and globally Lipschitz, belong to the L2L^2L2-Laplacian domain, and have Laplacian in W1,2W^{1,2}W1,2. Here W1,2W^{1,2}W1,2 means square-integrable functions with square-integrable weak gradient. Test vector fields are finite sums ∑jaj∇bj\sum_j a_j\nabla b_j∑j​aj​∇bj​ with aj,bja_j,b_jaj​,bj​ in that test class. These domain conditions matter on noncompact spaces.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Lott–Villani and Sturm developed synthetic Ricci lower bounds using optimal transport. Ambrosio, Gigli and Savaré introduced the RCD condition to select a Riemannian subclass, and subsequent work developed its local and second-order analysis.

On the geometric side, Petrunin and Zhang–Zhu connected Alexandrov lower curvature with synthetic Ricci bounds. The Sobolev theory of Kuwae, Machigashira and Shioya supplied the quadratic energy structure. Thus Alexandrov spaces were already known to fit into the analytic framework relevant here.

Gigli’s 2019 paper defined the distributional Riemann tensor on RCD spaces and proposed the characterization at issue. Defining a tensor with the expected algebraic symmetries was not enough to show that its lower bound controls metric triangles.

Several partial connections clarified the remaining obstacles. Ketterer and Mondino characterized sectional and intermediate Ricci bounds by transport in the smooth setting. Lebedeva and Petrunin constructed a weak curvature tensor for Alexandrov spaces admitting suitable noncollapsing smooth approximations. That is a different framework from a characterization using Gigli’s original global test classes on an arbitrary space satisfying the stated assumptions.

Brena and Gigli studied measure representations of weak Hessians and curvature tensors and identified regularity issues in turning a weak Hessian bound into geodesic convexity. Work on C1C^1C1 Riemannian metrics also obtained distributional-to-Alexandrov comparison in that more regular setting.

The companion manuscript builds on earlier changes-of-measure and entropy arguments of Ketterer, Sturm and Han. Its claimed contribution is to justify the required analytic steps under the weaker distributional Hessian hypothesis and to recover the bound on each prescribed geodesic, using Deng’s nonbranching theory.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: an exact characterization

Let n≥2n\ge2n≥2 be an integer, let κ∈R\kappa\in\mathbb Rκ∈R, and let (M,d)(M,d)(M,d) be complete and separable. Completeness means that Cauchy sequences converge; separability means there is a countable dense subset.

M1 claims that the following are equivalent:

  • (M,d)(M,d)(M,d) is an nnn-dimensional Alexandrov space with curvature at least κ\kappaκ.
  • With m=Hnm=\mathcal H^nm=Hn, it is a full-support RCD((n−1)κ,n)\mathrm{RCD}((n-1)\kappa,n)RCD((n−1)κ,n) space and satisfies
R(X,Y,Y,X)(f)≥κ∫Mf(∣X∣2∣Y∣2−⟨X,Y⟩2) dm\mathcal R(X,Y,Y,X)(f)\ge \kappa\int_M f\bigl(|X|^2|Y|^2-\langle X,Y\rangle^2\bigr)\,dmR(X,Y,Y,X)(f)≥κ∫M​f(∣X∣2∣Y∣2−⟨X,Y⟩2)dm

for all global test vector fields X,YX,YX,Y and all nonnegative global test functions fff described above.

In the smooth case this is precisely the integrated sectional-curvature lower bound. In the claimed theorem it includes the singular geometry through the weak functional. It is not merely a curvature inequality on a smooth regular subset, nor a theorem restricted to compactly supported test fields.

M2: from a weak Hessian to every geodesic

Let (M,d,m)(M,d,m)(M,d,m) be any full-support RCD(K,N)\mathrm{RCD}(K,N)RCD(K,N) space with 1<N<∞1<N<\infty1<N<∞. Let FFF be bounded and globally Lipschitz, and let GGG be bounded and continuous. Suppose its distributional Hessian satisfies

HF(∇g,∇g)(h)≤∫MhG∣∇g∣2 dmH_F(\nabla g,\nabla g)(h)\le\int_M hG|\nabla g|^2\,dmHF​(∇g,∇g)(h)≤∫M​hG∣∇g∣2dm

for compactly supported test functions ggg and nonnegative compactly supported Lipschitz weights hhh. The left side is defined by integration by parts using first derivatives of FFF.

M2 claims that every constant-speed minimizing geodesic σ:[0,1]→M\sigma:[0,1]\to Mσ:[0,1]→M, of length ℓ\ellℓ, satisfies

(F∘σ)′′≤ℓ2G∘σ(F\circ\sigma)''\le\ell^2G\circ\sigma(F∘σ)′′≤ℓ2G∘σ

in distributions on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1). Explicitly, for nonnegative smooth φ\varphiφ supported inside that interval,

∫01F(σ(t))φ′′(t) dt≤ℓ2∫01G(σ(t))φ(t) dt.\int_0^1 F(\sigma(t))\varphi''(t)\,dt\le\ell^2\int_0^1 G(\sigma(t))\varphi(t)\,dt.∫01​F(σ(t))φ′′(t)dt≤ℓ2∫01​G(σ(t))φ(t)dt.

For constant G=cG=cG=c, this says F(σ(t))−cℓ2t2/2F(\sigma(t))-c\ell^2t^2/2F(σ(t))−cℓ2t2/2 is concave. M2 does not require the measure to equal Hausdorff measure, and includes collapsed spaces. Infinite total measure is allowed; FFF need not be globally square-integrable.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claims. M1 would identify two fundamental languages of curvature on singular spaces: triangle comparison and distributional tensor calculus. It is an equivalence under the stated hypotheses, providing both a geometric interpretation of the weak tensor bound and an analytic characterization of Alexandrov geometry.

The companion theorem addresses a recurring difficulty in analysis on nonsmooth spaces. An integral inequality sees sets through a measure, while geometry asks questions about individual paths. Moving from almost-everywhere information to every geodesic is therefore a substantive step, not a change of wording.

Together the papers would allow weak differential estimates to recover geometric comparison without first smoothing the entire space. Their scope remains tied to the RCD and measure assumptions; the claim is not that an arbitrary metric space carries a usable curvature tensor.

6. The main idea

Extract curvature from small metric configurations

For the Alexandrov-to-tensor direction, M1 compares small configurations of points and integrates the comparison against transported densities. In smooth geometry, curvature first appears in a higher-order expansion of distances. The manuscript develops an integrated version that uses only the weak derivatives available in the test calculus.

Averaging cancels lower-order terms. The remaining coefficient is the desired curvature functional plus a nonnegative square error. Local choices of gradient tests make that error small; approximation and exhaustion then restore the original global test classes. Controlling changes in the transported densities is necessary because the Hessian coefficients are only square-integrable.

Recover a second-variation inequality from the tensor bound

For the converse, heat flow regularizes transport between densities. A forward heat factor and a suitably normalized backward factor yield a continuity equation describing the movement of mass. Their logarithmic potentials produce a weak version of a Riccati calculation, the matrix differential relation behind classical curvature comparison.

After controlling acceleration and singular measure terms, the zero-viscosity limit yields an index inequality. In smooth geometry an index form measures how the energy of a geodesic changes under transverse variations. Here the inequality is obtained through the weak calculus and weighted transport estimates.

To use it, the paper constructs frames—collections of independent tangent directions—along relevant paths. Spatial almost-everywhere regularity would not automatically provide a frame at every time. The argument combines noncollapsed structure, estimates for exceptional sets, Deng’s continuity of tangent cones, and a countable collection of trial fields. These trials play the role of classical Jacobi variations and yield a radial Hessian comparison.

Change measure to reach an individual path

M2 supplies the next step. For λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, change the reference measure to

mλ=eλFm.m_\lambda=e^{\lambda F}m.mλ​=eλFm.

The proposed weighted Bochner inequality has curvature bound K−λGK-\lambda GK−λG. A Bochner inequality relates the Laplacian of gradient energy to second derivatives and curvature. Its weighted form translates the Hessian information about FFF into an entropy inequality for the new measure.

The delicate point is operator domains. A bounded Lipschitz weight preserves the relevant Laplacian generator domain, but need not preserve the stronger test-function class. The manuscript establishes the needed multiplier regularity and closes the inequality in a common graph domain before applying curvature-dimension results. It does not assume a formal change-of-measure calculation is automatically legitimate.

For a probability measure μ\muμ, the entropy identity is

Ent⁡mλ(μ)=Ent⁡m(μ)−λ∫F dμ.\operatorname{Ent}_{m_\lambda}(\mu)=\operatorname{Ent}_m(\mu)-\lambda\int F\,d\mu.Entmλ​​(μ)=Entm​(μ)−λ∫Fdμ.

Thus, after dividing by λ\lambdaλ, an entropy inequality can become an inequality for averages of FFF. The proof concentrates endpoint measures near a strict interior subsegment of a chosen geodesic. Nonbranching makes that subsegment the unique minimizing connection between its endpoints, forcing the concentrating transports to recover it. Taking λ\lambdaλ sufficiently large removes the residual entropy terms.

This yields the second-derivative inequality along the chosen path, including paths an almost-everywhere statement might miss.

Return from functions to triangles

M1 applies M2 to bounded global modifications of distance functions. These satisfy the required weak Hessian bounds and produce the appropriate one-dimensional model inequality along every geodesic. Ordinary differential comparison then gives local triangle comparison, and the Alexandrov local-to-global theorem supplies the global curvature bound.

M2 is an independent analytic input in this chain. Its proof does not assume the characterization that M1 is trying to establish.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 requires integer dimension n≥2n\ge2n≥2, the exact measure Hn\mathcal H^nHn, full support and the stated unreduced RCD bound. Replacing that measure by an arbitrary positive density, dropping the Ricci framework, or restricting curvature tests to a convenient regular subset changes the assertion.

M2 has broader measure scope but specific function hypotheses: bounded globally Lipschitz FFF, bounded continuous GGG, and finite synthetic dimension greater than one. Its conclusion is distributional along paths; it does not make FFF twice classically differentiable.

Neither result says every RCD space is Alexandrov. The extra distributional sectional bound is decisive. Nor does the characterization provide a smooth atlas or a pointwise classical tensor at every singular point.

Extensions to weaker function bounds, other measures and different dimensional settings are separate questions. The mathematical arguments and equivalences are reported as stated, without proof or novelty verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 states the characterization and identifies precisely where M2 is used. M2 states the independent weak-Hessian theorem and explains its change-of-measure regularity issue.

Useful primary sources are Gigli’s original tensor and conjecture, Brena–Gigli on fine Hessian representations, Deng on tangent cones and nonbranching, and De Philippis–Gigli on noncollapsed RCD spaces.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Gigli’s distributional curvature characterization of Alexandrov spaces (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Weak Hessian bounds along every geodesic in RCD spaces (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Geodesics without focusing on a manifold that forbids nonpositive curvature
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 358 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

On a negatively curved surface, nearby geodesics tend to spread apart. On a sphere, geodesics leaving the north pole meet again at the south pole. The second behavior has an infinitesimal version called the appearance of conjugate points.

Nonpositive sectional curvature prevents conjugate points. But does the converse hold at the level of the underlying manifold? If a closed manifold has some metric without conjugate points, must it also have some possibly different metric of nonpositive sectional curvature?

These are two existence questions about the same topological space. Producing a metric with a small region of positive curvature does not answer them, because that manifold might still admit another negatively curved metric.

Family 358 claims a negative answer in dimension three. It constructs a closed orientable three-manifold with a smooth metric without conjugate points, while its fundamental group obstructs every nonpositively curved metric. The geometry of its geodesics is therefore less restrictive than the existence of a nonpositive-curvature geometry on the same manifold.

2. Background and essential definitions

Conjugate points measure infinitesimal refocusing

A Riemannian metric assigns inner products to tangent spaces and thereby defines lengths and geodesics. Along a geodesic γ(s)\gamma(s)γ(s), an infinitesimal variation through neighboring geodesics is described by a Jacobi field JJJ, satisfying

Ds2J+R(J,γ˙)γ˙=0.D_s^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0.Ds2​J+R(J,γ˙​)γ˙​=0.

Here DsD_sDs​ differentiates vector fields along the path while respecting the metric, and RRR is the curvature tensor. The equation is a geometric version of a linear second-order oscillator equation.

Two points on the geodesic are conjugate when a nonzero Jacobi field vanishes at both times. Intuitively, a family of initially diverging geodesics has refocused to first order. “No conjugate points” excludes this on every geodesic.

For a normal field, meaning J⊥γ˙J\perp\dot\gammaJ⊥γ˙​, nonpositive sectional curvature gives

12d2ds2∣J∣2=∣DsJ∣2−⟨R(J,γ˙)γ˙,J⟩≥0.\frac12\frac{d^2}{ds^2}|J|^2=|D_sJ|^2-\langle R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma,J\rangle\ge0.21​ds2d2​∣J∣2=∣Ds​J∣2−⟨R(J,γ˙​)γ˙​,J⟩≥0.

This convexity explains the implication from nonpositive curvature. Without a pointwise curvature sign, however, one may still control the total effect along whole geodesic segments.

The stronger condition no focal points requires a nonzero normal Jacobi field with J(0)=0J(0)=0J(0)=0 to satisfy

dds∣J(s)∣2>0(s>0).\frac{d}{ds}|J(s)|^2>0\qquad(s>0).dsd​∣J(s)∣2>0(s>0).

This demands persistent growth, not merely the absence of a second zero.

The manifold is assembled from two familiar pieces

Let Σ\SigmaΣ be a torus with the interior of one disk removed. It is a compact surface with one boundary circle. Each product

Ni=Σ×S1N_i=\Sigma\times S^1Ni​=Σ×S1

is a three-dimensional manifold whose boundary is a torus.

On that boundary, let hih_ihi​ denote the loop coming from ∂Σ\partial\Sigma∂Σ, and fif_ifi​ the loop in the circle factor. These generate the torus’s fundamental group Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2. The construction glues the two boundary tori using

h2=h1+f1,f2=h1.h_2=h_1+f_1,\qquad f_2=h_1.h2​=h1​+f1​,f2​=h1​.

The additive notation refers to loops in this abelian torus group. The gluing matrix has determinant −1-1−1, reversing boundary orientation so that the resulting closed manifold is orientable. Such a manifold assembled from circle-fibered pieces is called a graph manifold; “graph” refers to its decomposition, not to the graph of a function.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gulliver’s 1975 work, On the variety of manifolds without conjugate points, showed that a metric without conjugate points can contain regions of positive curvature. Those examples were obtained by modifying negatively curved metrics. They separated two properties of a particular metric, but the underlying manifolds still possessed negatively curved metrics.

The stronger existence question appears in Ivanov and Kapovitch and in Burns and Matveev’s survey of questions about geodesics. Ivanov and Kapovitch specifically identified three-dimensional graph manifolds, including gluings of punctured-torus products, as important test cases.

For closed surfaces the existence question has a positive answer. A metric without conjugate points forces the relevant universal-cover and topological restrictions, giving nonpositive Euler characteristic; uniformization then supplies a flat or negatively curved metric. Thus dimension three is the first place where a counterexample of the present kind can occur.

The topology needed for a candidate was already available. Leeb constructed graph-manifold examples obstructing nonpositive curvature, and Kapovich–Leeb studied the corresponding obstruction to group actions on nonpositively curved spaces. Family 358 uses an instance of that known two-piece obstruction. Its main new claim is a metric without conjugate points on that same manifold.

There is also a useful boundary between nearby conditions. Ivanov and Kapovitch proved that a closed three-manifold admits a metric without focal points if and only if it admits a metric of nonpositive sectional curvature. Consequently, a counterexample for conjugate points would necessarily fail the stronger no-focal-points condition for every metric.

4. What the new manuscript claims

The main theorem asserts a closed, connected, orientable smooth three-manifold MMM with two properties:

  • It admits a C∞C^\inftyC∞ Riemannian metric with no conjugate points.
  • It admits no C∞C^\inftyC∞ Riemannian metric with sectional curvature everywhere at most zero.

The manifold is the explicit two-piece gluing described above. The construction inserts a torus-shaped neck between the pieces; adding this collar does not change the diffeomorphism type.

The topological obstruction is stated in a stronger form. The group π1(M)\pi_1(M)π1​(M), consisting of homotopy classes of based loops, admits no proper cocompact isometric action on a nonempty proper CAT(0)\mathrm{CAT}(0)CAT(0) space.

A CAT(0) space is a geodesic metric space whose triangles are no thicker than their Euclidean comparison triangles. “Proper” for the space means closed bounded sets are compact. A proper action has only finitely many group elements moving one compact set to meet another, and cocompactness means the quotient is compact.

As a consequence, the manifold admits no locally CAT(0) length metric inducing its topology. A length metric measures distance by infima of path lengths. Thus allowing certain nonsmooth notions of nonpositive curvature does not evade the obstruction.

Combining the main theorem with Ivanov–Kapovitch’s equivalence also excludes every metric without focal points on this manifold. The paper therefore separates no conjugate points from both nonpositive sectional curvature and no focal points at the level of metric existence.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claim. The result would answer a longstanding existence question in the smallest possible dimension and distinguish two broad classes of closed manifolds defined by geodesic behavior.

The central point is the quantifier over metrics. The counterexample would not merely show that one metric has some positive curvature. It would show that no replacement metric can make sectional curvature nonpositive, even though another global metric avoids infinitesimal refocusing everywhere.

The construction also illustrates the different strengths of local and integrated conditions. Sectional curvature restricts each tangent two-plane at each point. Absence of conjugate points constrains how curvature acts along an entire geodesic through the Jacobi equation. Carefully controlled positive contributions can coexist with the latter condition.

The obstruction belongs to topology and group theory; the positive existence statement belongs to differential geometry and variational estimates. Making both hold on the same explicit manifold is the essential advance claimed here.

6. The main idea

A short algebraic conflict rules out nonpositive curvature

Suppose the fundamental group acted properly and cocompactly on a proper CAT(0) space. The flat torus theorem makes the common Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2 subgroup act by translations on a Euclidean plane.

In each product piece, the circle fiber commutes with every loop in the surface factor. The surface boundary is a commutator of two such loops. The resulting group relations force the translation vector of the boundary loop to be perpendicular to that of the fiber.

Let uuu and vvv be the translation vectors for h1h_1h1​ and f1f_1f1​. The first product piece requires

⟨u,v⟩=0.\langle u,v\rangle=0.⟨u,v⟩=0.

The gluing makes the second pair of translation vectors u+vu+vu+v and uuu. Its orthogonality requirement gives

0=⟨u+v,u⟩=∣u∣2.0=\langle u+v,u\rangle=|u|^2.0=⟨u+v,u⟩=∣u∣2.

But a generator of the translation lattice has a nonzero vector. This is the incompatibility behind the known obstruction. The manuscript includes the group-theoretic details to obtain the full CAT(0)-action statement.

Build a neck with controlled inverse metric

Each product core is given nonpositive curvature. Between them, use coordinates t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]t∈[0,1] and x∈T2x\in\mathbb T^2x∈T2 and a neck metric

g=dt2+dxTP(t)−1dx.g=dt^2+dx^{\mathsf T}P(t)^{-1}dx.g=dt2+dxTP(t)−1dx.

The positive-definite matrix P(t)P(t)P(t) is the cometric, the inverse of the metric matrix in torus directions. It is chosen concave in the matrix sense:

−P′′(t)≥0,-P''(t)\ge0,−P′′(t)≥0,

meaning that every vector evaluates this matrix to a nonnegative number.

The path has exact product forms near its ends, and smooth warped collars connect it to the cores. A small parameter controls its derivatives. Appropriate unequal torus periods allow a geometrically small shear to realize the fixed integral gluing map. The topology is not being changed continuously into a trivial gluing; the metric scales make the required shear manageable.

Estimate complete neck passages, including their endpoints

The relevant variational quantity is the index form along a unit-speed geodesic, with tangent TTT:

I(V)=∫(∣DsV∣2−⟨R(V,T)T,V⟩) ds.I(V)=\int\bigl(|D_sV|^2-\langle R(V,T)T,V\rangle\bigr)\,ds.I(V)=∫(∣Ds​V∣2−⟨R(V,T)T,V⟩)ds.

It measures the second variation of geodesic energy for a variation field VVV. On the nonpositively curved cores, the integrand is nonnegative. In the neck, the aim is a nonnegative integral over each whole visit, even if some pointwise curvature terms have the wrong sign.

Concavity of the cometric gives a nonnegative coordinate second variation. The intrinsic index form differs from it by endpoint and tangential terms. Those terms cannot simply be discarded, because the variation field generally does not vanish whenever a geodesic enters or leaves the neck.

Passages that cross monotonically, remain at constant height, or stay in simple endpoint collars can be treated separately. The delicate case is a geodesic entering the neck, turning, and returning to the same boundary. Its entire excursion must be controlled with arbitrary field values at both endpoints.

The manuscript uses a positive boundary contribution to control a component of the field’s endpoint change. Cauchy–Schwarz and a quadratic minimization combine that control with the coordinate energy. A strict timing margin for excursions that leave the endpoint collar makes the estimate uniform in entry angle, turning height and duration.

No upper bound on how long the excursion lasts is assumed. This matters because one fixed smooth metric must work for every complete geodesic, including nearly tangent or slowly returning ones.

Assemble local passage estimates into a global conclusion

The same small parameter is chosen for all types of passages. A complete geodesic may enter the neck infinitely many times, but the index integrand of a compactly supported variation field is absolutely integrable. The whole index integral is therefore the sum over its neck visits plus its contribution outside the neck.

Each full visit has a nonnegative intrinsic index form, and the cores contribute nonnegatively. The manuscript then uses the standard index-form argument to exclude any nonzero Jacobi field with two zeros. This establishes absence of conjugate points for the constructed metric, without requiring nonpositive curvature throughout the neck.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is an existence result for a particular closed orientable three-manifold. It does not classify all graph manifolds admitting metrics without conjugate points, nor all possible metrics on this example.

Absence of conjugate points is not absence of focal points, monotonic divergence of every pair of geodesics, or a pointwise curvature bound. The stronger no-focal-points property is explicitly impossible on this manifold by the cited three-dimensional equivalence.

The result also does not assert that the constructed geodesic flow has stronger dynamical features such as uniform hyperbolicity. Those would require separate statements and estimates.

Natural further problems concern how widely the neck construction can be adapted, which gluings permit similar metrics, and how their geodesic dynamics reflect the topology. The construction and its uniform passage estimates are reported as claimed, without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

The source separates the known graph-manifold obstruction in Section 2 from its metric construction and global index estimates in Sections 3–6.

For the existence question and the no-focal-points distinction, see Ivanov–Kapovitch. For the underlying obstruction, see Leeb’s three-manifold paper. Gulliver’s On the variety of manifolds without conjugate points, Transactions of the AMS 210 (1975), 185–201, is the classical precursor separating properties of an individual metric.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Three-Manifold Without Conjugate Points and Without a Nonpositively Curved Metric (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Negative Kähler curvature does not guarantee bounded holomorphic coordinates
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 359 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

The unit disk is a basic meeting point of complex analysis and negative curvature. In complex dimension one, a complete simply connected surface with curvature bounded above by a negative constant is biholomorphic to the disk. Its geometry therefore comes with a bounded global holomorphic coordinate.

Does a similar principle hold in several complex variables? If a simply connected complete Kähler manifold has uniformly negative curvature, must it be biholomorphic to some bounded domain? At a more modest level, must it possess even one nonconstant bounded holomorphic function?

Family 359 contains two independent constructions addressing different versions of these questions. M1 claims a complex three-dimensional example with curvature bounded between two finite negative constants, but no global bounded holomorphic coordinate triple with everywhere independent differentials. M2 claims an example in a sufficiently large fixed finite dimension with curvature at most −1-1−1, but with every bounded holomorphic function constant.

The hypotheses differ critically. M2’s curvature is unbounded below. M1 has two-sided pinching but retains nonconstant bounded functions. Neither paper settles the existence of a single nonconstant bounded holomorphic function under finite two-sided negative pinching.

2. Background and essential definitions

Holomorphic functions, coordinates and domains

A domain in Cm\mathbb C^mCm is a connected open set. A holomorphic function is complex differentiable in its variables; locally it has a convergent power series. It is bounded if its absolute value has a finite global upper bound.

A biholomorphism is a holomorphic bijection with holomorphic inverse. If MMM is biholomorphic to a bounded domain in Cm\mathbb C^mCm, the target’s coordinate functions pull back to bounded holomorphic functions F1,…,FmF_1,\ldots,F_mF1​,…,Fm​ on MMM. Their complex Jacobian determinant is nowhere zero:
