det⁡(∂Fi∂zj)≠0.\det\left(\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial z_j}\right)\ne0.det(∂zj​∂Fi​​)=0.

A bounded holomorphic map with nowhere-zero Jacobian need not be globally injective, so even that condition is weaker than a biholomorphism. Thus a bounded-domain representation gives bounded holomorphic coordinates, which in turn supply a nonconstant bounded holomorphic function.

Reversing these implications requires extra information.

The notation H∞(M)H^\infty(M)H∞(M) denotes the algebra of bounded holomorphic functions. The holomorphic Liouville property is H∞(M)=CH^\infty(M)=\mathbb CH∞(M)=C: every such function is constant. It concerns bounded functions, not all holomorphic functions.

Kähler metrics and curvature bounds

A Kähler metric is a Riemannian metric compatible with a complex structure whose associated two-form is closed. A common way to construct one is from a strictly plurisubharmonic potential Φ\PhiΦ, whose complex Hessian

gijˉ=∂2Φ∂zi∂zˉjg_{i\bar j}=\frac{\partial^2\Phi}{\partial z_i\partial\bar z_j}gijˉ​​=∂zi​∂zˉj​∂2Φ​

is positive definite. A real-metric normalization must then be chosen; constant rescaling changes numerical curvature values.

The papers bound sectional curvature on every real two-plane, not just on complex lines. The latter, more restricted quantity is holomorphic sectional curvature. A two-sided negative bound means

−B≤Kg(σ)≤−A<0-B\le K_g(\sigma)\le-A<0−B≤Kg​(σ)≤−A<0

for fixed finite 0<A≤B0<A\le B0<A≤B, every point and every real tangent two-plane σ\sigmaσ. A one-sided bound Kg≤−1K_g\le-1Kg​≤−1 permits curvature to become arbitrarily negative.

Completeness means that geodesics can continue indefinitely, equivalently that escaping to infinity or to the domain boundary costs infinite metric length. A bounded Euclidean domain can carry a complete metric because that metric becomes large near its boundary.

3. Development history and previous partial results

H. Wu’s work on normal families asked whether complete simply connected Kähler manifolds with nonpositive real sectional curvature and uniformly negative holomorphic sectional curvature must be bounded domains in holomorphic coordinates. Wu and Yau later formulated the version with two-sided negative real-sectional pinching and bounded pseudoconvex conclusion.

Earlier examples showed that the unit ball was too narrow a target. Mostow and Siu constructed compact negatively curved Kähler surfaces not covered by the ball; Deraux obtained related three-dimensional examples. Their universal covers inherit finite negative curvature bounds. But failure to be the ball does not exclude being some other bounded domain. M1 targets that stronger obstruction.

The existence of just one bounded holomorphic function is a separate question, traced in the manuscripts to Yau’s 1982 Problem 38. Seshadri, using radial curvature calculations of Klembeck, exhibited complete strictly negatively curved Kähler metrics on Cn\mathbb C^nCn. Liouville’s theorem makes all bounded entire functions constant there. Some sectional curvatures approach zero, so that example does not provide a uniform negative upper bound such as −1-1−1.

Greene and Wu, and later Wu and Yau, established strong comparisons between intrinsic complex metrics under two-sided pinching. These include the Bergman metric, built from square-integrable holomorphic top-degree forms, and the Kobayashi–Royden metric, built from holomorphic disks mapping into the manifold. Such comparisons do not automatically provide bounded functions mapping out to the disk.

Shcherbina and Zhang constructed a domain that is complete for Bergman and Kobayashi metrics yet has the holomorphic Liouville property. That supplies another warning against identifying completeness of intrinsic metrics with abundance of bounded functions. The additional issue addressed by M2 is real sectional curvature control.

A Cao–Shaw announcement concerning bounded functions under two-sided pinching was withdrawn in 2016. It is not an established input to either construction here.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: two-sided pinching, but no bounded coordinate triple

M1 constructs a contractible domain M⊂C3M\subset\mathbb C^3M⊂C3 with a smooth complete Kähler metric satisfying finite uniform bounds

−B≤Kg≤−A<0.-B\le K_g\le-A<0.−B≤Kg​≤−A<0.

Every bounded holomorphic map F:M→C3F:M\to\mathbb C^3F:M→C3 has a point where its Jacobian determinant vanishes. Consequently, MMM is not biholomorphic to any bounded domain in C3\mathbb C^3C3.

The conclusion does not say that each such determinant vanishes identically. Nor does it say all bounded functions are constant: the construction has two nonconstant bounded base-coordinate functions.

The domain is also Stein, a standard analytic condition expressing strong holomorphic convexity and separation properties. The source obtains this from a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion. Thus the obstruction concerns bounded global coordinates, not a failure of the basic analytic structure supplied by Stein theory.

M2: no bounded functions under a one-sided bound

M2 constructs, for some sufficiently large fixed finite integer mmm, a domain T⊂CmT\subset\mathbb C^mT⊂Cm diffeomorphic to R2m\mathbb R^{2m}R2m and a complete Kähler metric with

Kg≤−1,H∞(T)=C.K_g\le-1,\qquad H^\infty(T)=\mathbb C.Kg​≤−1,H∞(T)=C.

Its sectional curvatures are unbounded below. The dimension is chosen once for the entire construction; the theorem does not give the assertion in every dimension or a specific minimal dimension.

The two examples separate the following conclusions:

ConstructionCurvature hypothesis achievedBounded holomorphic behavior
M1, complex dimension threeFinite two-sided negative pinchingNo everywhere nonsingular bounded coordinate triple; two bounded nonconstant functions remain
M2, a fixed sufficiently large dimensionUniform negative upper bound, no finite lower boundEvery bounded holomorphic function is constant

Their proofs are independent. The stronger function obstruction in M2 is not combined with M1’s stronger curvature hypothesis.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claims. The papers would give negative answers to central higher-dimensional uniformization and bounded-function questions, while identifying precisely which expectations fail.

M1 would show that even uniform negative curvature on all real planes, completeness and contractibility do not force a bounded-domain realization. M2 would show that a uniform negative upper curvature bound does not even guarantee one nonconstant bounded holomorphic function.

The contrast with one complex dimension is substantial. Several-variable holomorphic geometry can impose global compatibility constraints that strong local curvature inequalities do not resolve.

The examples also distinguish intrinsic metrics from bounded coordinate functions. M1 still falls within the two-sided-pinching comparison theory for several complete intrinsic metrics. In M2, the Carathéodory infinitesimal pseudometric—defined by pulling back the disk metric through bounded holomorphic maps—vanishes identically because every such map is constant. Different analytic constructions of metric geometry need not encode the same information.

6. The main idea

M1: vary disk radii over a bounded base

Let B⊂C2B\subset\mathbb C^2B⊂C2 be the unit ball. A smooth real function ϕ\phiϕ defines a Hartogs domain

Mϕ={(z,w)∈B×C:eϕ(z)∣w∣2<1}.M_\phi=\{(z,w)\in B\times\mathbb C:e^{\phi(z)}|w|^2<1\}.Mϕ​={(z,w)∈B×C:eϕ(z)∣w∣2<1}.

The fiber above zzz is a disk of radius e−ϕ(z)/2e^{-\phi(z)/2}e−ϕ(z)/2. The base coordinates are bounded, explaining the two surviving bounded functions.

With ψ(z)=−log⁡(1−∣z∣2)\psi(z)=-\log(1-|z|^2)ψ(z)=−log(1−∣z∣2), the metric comes from the potential

Φ(z,w)=λψ(z)−log⁡(1−eϕ(z)∣w∣2).\Phi(z,w)=\lambda\psi(z)-\log\bigl(1-e^{\phi(z)}|w|^2\bigr).Φ(z,w)=λψ(z)−log(1−eϕ(z)∣w∣2).

The analytic task is to choose ϕ\phiϕ with controlled complex Hessian and derivatives through the order needed for curvature, while preventing any holomorphic function HHH on BBB from satisfying

Re⁡H(z)≤CH+4log⁡11−∣z∣+ϕ(z).\operatorname{Re}H(z)\le C_H+4\log\frac1{1-|z|}+\phi(z).ReH(z)≤CH​+4log1−∣z∣1​+ϕ(z).

Why this particular obstruction? If a bounded map FFF had nonvanishing Jacobian everywhere, restrict its Jacobian to the zero section w=0w=0w=0, obtaining a nowhere-zero holomorphic function d(z)d(z)d(z). Cauchy estimates in base and fiber directions yield

log⁡∣d(z)∣2≤C+4log⁡11−∣z∣+ϕ(z).\log|d(z)|^2\le C+4\log\frac1{1-|z|}+\phi(z).log∣d(z)∣2≤C+4log1−∣z∣1​+ϕ(z).

Because the ball is simply connected, ddd has a holomorphic logarithm. Its real part produces exactly the forbidden inequality.

The potential is built from separated homogeneous polynomial peaks. Positive representing measures preserve the value at the origin of every holomorphic real part, while selected regularized logarithms have increasingly negative averages. Those averages overwhelm the explicit boundary allowance. Representing holomorphic evaluation is weaker than satisfying every logarithmic mean inequality; the construction uses that distinction.

Meanwhile, widely separated polynomial degrees give derivative control in ball coordinates centered at arbitrary points. For a sufficiently large fixed λ\lambdaλ, a full real-sectional curvature calculation gives strict negativity. Near limiting planes where a leading term degenerates, a cancellation in the largest error term is essential. Compact-range bounds and the limiting tensor near the fiber boundary then supply both finite pinching constants.

M2: large testing disks force derivatives to vanish

The second construction uses a tube above a potential ℓ\ellℓ on Cn+1\mathbb C^{n+1}Cn+1:

T={(s,y,w):Im⁡w>ℓ(s,y)},T=\{(s,y,w):\operatorname{Im}w>\ell(s,y)\},T={(s,y,w):Imw>ℓ(s,y)},
Φ=−log⁡(Im⁡w−ℓ(s,y)).\Phi=-\log\bigl(\operatorname{Im}w-\ell(s,y)\bigr).Φ=−log(Imw−ℓ(s,y)).

Here sss has nnn complex components, so the final dimension is m=n+2m=n+2m=n+2. A curvature-transfer lemma says that a complete nonpositively curved Kähler potential metric for ℓ\ellℓ gives a complete tube metric with real sectional curvature at most −1-1−1, in M2’s normalization.

The base must simultaneously permit specially placed large holomorphic disks in the tube. Cauchy’s estimate says that a bounded holomorphic function has small derivative along a sufficiently large disk. The difficulty is arranging enough disk directions and positions to force a global conclusion.

Polynomial systems supply finite grids of spatial points. Their affine lifts occur in root-of-unity cycles; averaging around a cycle separates Taylor degrees modulo the polynomial degree. Carefully selected phases prevent low-order derivative data from hiding among the higher-order contributions. Large-disk estimates then force decay of Taylor coefficients of ∂f/∂w\partial f/\partial w∂f/∂w.

Each finite-order test is repeated infinitely often, with controlled heights. A three-lines argument ultimately gives ∂f/∂w=0\partial f/\partial w=0∂f/∂w=0. The function descends to a bounded entire function on the base Cn+1\mathbb C^{n+1}Cn+1, so it is constant.

Preserve geometry while installing infinitely many tests

The disks require changing fiber centers and directions. A nonholomorphic change of center can damage curvature, so it cannot be dismissed as a coordinate change.

The manuscript uses a partial Legendre transform to organize the fiber metric and its curvature terms. It temporarily widens a fiber profile, moves the center while sufficient margin is available, and restores the profile with controlled offsets. Estimates on matrices of rank at most two handle all real two-planes while keeping key losses independent of dimension.

The recursive construction reserves bounds for later modifications, so each installed testing disk survives. Growth is capped between stages to prevent breakdown at finite spatial radius, and separate length estimates establish completeness. The potential becomes unbounded below; simple functions such as eikwe^{ikw}eikw are therefore not bounded on the resulting tube.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The principal unresolved distinction is explicit: these examples do not decide whether finite two-sided negative real-sectional pinching forces a nonconstant bounded holomorphic function. M1 has such functions, and M2 lacks the lower curvature bound.

M1 excludes bounded maps to C3\mathbb C^3C3 with nowhere-zero Jacobian; it does not say that every bounded map has rank deficiency everywhere. M2 concerns some sufficiently large fixed dimension, not every dimension beginning with two.

Both bounds concern real sectional curvature. Conclusions based only on holomorphic sectional curvature have different hypotheses. The papers also use different constant conventions for the real metric associated with a complex Hessian, so their numerical model intervals should not be identified without rescaling.

Questions about minimal dimensions, stronger pinching and the exact structure of bounded-function algebras remain separate. The curvature constructions and analytic obstructions are reported as stated, without proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 separates its controlled potential and bounded-Jacobian obstruction from the real-sectional pinching argument. M2 separates the large-disk testing criterion from its global geometric realization.

Primary background includes Wu–Yau’s intrinsic-metric comparisons, Seshadri’s strictly negative examples, Hwang–Singer’s momentum construction, and Shcherbina–Zhang’s complete domain with the Liouville property. The Cao–Shaw withdrawal record is included to distinguish an earlier announcement from an available theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A negatively pinched Kähler threefold without bounded holomorphic coordinates (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, One-sided negative sectional curvature and the holomorphic Liouville property (September 25, 2026).

entry.title: Weak transport curvature, convex geodesic domains and continuous optimal maps
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 360 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Imagine redistributing material across a curved closed surface or manifold. The initial and final densities are prescribed, and moving a unit of material from xxx to yyy costs half the squared geodesic distance. An optimal transport map chooses destinations to minimize total cost.

Even when both densities stay positive and bounded, existence of an almost-everywhere defined optimal map does not guarantee continuity. Nearby starting points might be sent to widely separated destinations. The geometry of the squared-distance function determines whether such tearing can occur.

The Ma–Trudinger–Wang condition, or MTW condition, is a curvature condition on that cost. Family 360 claims that its weak nonnegative form has two major consequences on every fixed smooth compact boundaryless manifold. First, every tangent injectivity domain is convex. Second, optimal maps between measurable densities with fixed positive upper and lower bounds have uniformly Hölder-continuous representatives and inverses.

The challenge is the cut locus, where squared distance ceases to be smooth. The papers allow conjugate cut endpoints rather than assuming that all relevant geodesics avoid them.

2. Background and essential definitions

The cost and its geodesic coordinates

Let (M,g)(M,g)(M,g) be a smooth Riemannian manifold, and let ddd denote geodesic distance. The cost is

c(x,y)=12d(x,y)2.c(x,y)=\frac12d(x,y)^2.c(x,y)=21​d(x,y)2.

The exponential map exp⁡x\exp_xexpx​ takes an initial tangent vector p∈TxMp\in T_xMp∈Tx​M to the point reached at time one by its geodesic. The open tangent injectivity domain is

I(x)={p: d(x,exp⁡x(ap))=a∣p∣ for some a>1}.I(x)=\{p:\ d(x,\exp_x(ap))=a|p|\text{ for some }a>1\}.I(x)={p: d(x,expx​(ap))=a∣p∣ for some a>1}.

Thus the geodesic with initial vector ppp remains minimizing slightly beyond its endpoint. In this domain, the minimizing geodesic is unique and the exponential map is nonsingular.

The closed minimizing domain is

Gx={p: d(x,exp⁡xp)=∣p∣}.G_x=\{p:\ d(x,\exp_xp)=|p|\}.Gx​={p: d(x,expx​p)=∣p∣}.

Its boundary can contain cut vectors. At a cut point, another shortest geodesic may compete, or the exponential map may become singular. The latter is conjugacy: infinitesimally different geodesics focus to the same endpoint.

Convexity of I(x)I(x)I(x) means ordinary linear convexity inside the vector space TxMT_xMTx​M. If two initial velocities lie in it, so does every straight interpolation between them. This is not a claim that the manifold itself is a convex subset of Euclidean space.

Weak MTW only tests transverse directions

In the papers’ convention, the MTW quantity is

Sx,p(ξ,η)=−32∂4∂s2∂t2c(exp⁡x(tξ),exp⁡x(p+sη))∣s=t=0.\mathfrak S_{x,p}(\xi,\eta)=-\frac32\left.\frac{\partial^4}{\partial s^2\partial t^2} c\bigl(\exp_x(t\xi),\exp_x(p+s\eta)\bigr)\right|_{s=t=0}.Sx,p​(ξ,η)=−23​∂s2∂t2∂4​c(expx​(tξ),expx​(p+sη))​s=t=0​.

It measures how a second derivative of the cost changes as the destination velocity changes. Weak MTW requires

⟨ξ,η⟩x=0⟹Sx,p(ξ,η)≥0(p∈I(x)).\langle\xi,\eta\rangle_x=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathfrak S_{x,p}(\xi,\eta)\ge0\qquad(p\in I(x)).⟨ξ,η⟩x​=0⟹Sx,p​(ξ,η)≥0(p∈I(x)).

Only orthogonal direction pairs are tested, and the lower bound may be zero. No condition on nonorthogonal pairs or strictly positive lower bound is assumed. The derivatives are taken where the cost is smooth; the condition does not pretend that the fourth derivative exists on the cut locus.

Potentials and supporting functions

A cost potential has the form

u(x)=max⁡y∈M{−c(x,y)−v(y)},u(x)=\max_{y\in M}\{-c(x,y)-v(y)\},u(x)=y∈Mmax​{−c(x,y)−v(y)},

where vvv is a continuous function. A term that attains the maximum is an active supporting function, sometimes called a supporting mountain. It lies below uuu everywhere and touches it at the chosen point.

These potentials are semiconvex: locally, adding a sufficiently large quadratic makes them convex. Their ordinary subdifferential ∂u(x)\partial u(x)∂u(x) records slopes supporting them to first order. On a manifold vectors and covectors are identified using the metric. At a smooth contact, ∇u(x)\nabla u(x)∇u(x) is the initial minimizing velocity to the active target.

3. Development history and previous partial results

McCann’s polar factorization theorem supplied existence and almost-everywhere uniqueness of optimal maps for squared distance under suitable absolute-continuity hypotheses. Regularity is a separate issue.

Ma, Trudinger and Wang introduced a strict cost-curvature condition in their regularity theory; Trudinger and Wang developed its weak form, often called A3w. Loeper established the connection between this geometry, supporting functions and continuity. Kim and McCann supplied a geometric formulation of the supporting-mountain principle.

Villani proposed that weak MTW should force convexity of tangent injectivity domains. Figalli, Gallouët and Rifford proved the implication for nonfocal manifolds, where minimizing geodesics reach their cut points strictly before the first conjugate point. Loeper and Villani obtained related conclusions under stronger curvature and geometric assumptions. The possible coincidence of cut and conjugacy remained a significant obstruction.

For regularity, Caffarelli’s section and contact-volume methods were foundational. Figalli, Kim and McCann obtained Hölder continuity and injectivity for rough densities under weak MTW and appropriate smooth-cost, convexity and nondegeneracy assumptions. Rough densities themselves are therefore not the new feature here. The issue is uniform control on a compact manifold as transport graphs approach singular cost pairs.

Uniform estimates were already known in important settings, including strict MTW with additional assumptions and products of round spheres. Figalli, Rifford and Villani also established necessary conditions for transport continuity and a two-dimensional characterization involving weak MTW together with convex injectivity domains.

M1 claims to derive the missing convexity from weak MTW alone in the compact setting. M2 uses that foundation to obtain a common Hölder estimate across the entire class of densities with fixed positive bounds, without requiring uniform separation from conjugate pairs.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Both papers assume (M,g)(M,g)(M,g) is smooth, connected, compact, without boundary, and of dimension n≥2n\ge2n≥2, satisfying weak MTW as defined above.

M1: global geometric support without density assumptions

M1 claims that both I(x)I(x)I(x) and GxG_xGx​ are convex for every xxx. This is ordinary convexity, with no assertion that their boundaries are smooth or strictly convex.

More generally, every ordinary subgradient p∈∂u(x)p\in\partial u(x)p∈∂u(x) of any cost potential is a minimizing velocity and supplies a global support:

u(x′)≥u(x)+c(x,exp⁡xp)−c(x′,exp⁡xp)(x′∈M).u(x')\ge u(x)+c(x,\exp_xp)-c(x',\exp_xp)\qquad(x'\in M).u(x′)≥u(x)+c(x,expx​p)−c(x′,expx​p)(x′∈M).

The distinction is that an ordinary first-order supporting slope is promoted to a genuine global squared-distance support, even at the minimizing boundary.

For each 0<t<10<t<10<t<1, the map

Ft(x,p)=exp⁡x(tp),(x,p)∈Γu:={(x,p):p∈∂u(x)},F_t(x,p)=\exp_x(tp),\qquad(x,p)\in\Gamma_u:=\{(x,p):p\in\partial u(x)\},Ft​(x,p)=expx​(tp),(x,p)∈Γu​:={(x,p):p∈∂u(x)},

is claimed to be a homeomorphism from the whole subgradient graph onto MMM. Intermediate infimum-regularized potentials are C1,1C^{1,1}C1,1, meaning differentiable with Lipschitz derivative, and the inverse pole and momentum maps have geometry-and-time-controlled Lipschitz bounds. Lifted sections of the dual potential gap are compact and convex.

These statements use no densities. The homeomorphism and intermediate regularity are asserted only for 0<t<10<t<10<t<1. At time one, the support and minimizing-velocity conclusions remain, but an arbitrary potential can send many starting points to one target.

M2: uniform transport and inverse estimates

Fix constants 0<λ≤Λ<∞0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty0<λ≤Λ<∞ for which the density class is nonempty. Let ρ0,ρ1\rho_0,\rho_1ρ0​,ρ1​ be measurable probability densities with

∫Mρi dvol=1,λ≤ρi≤Λalmost everywhere.\int_M\rho_i\,d\mathrm{vol}=1,\qquad\lambda\le\rho_i\le\Lambda\quad\text{almost everywhere}.∫M​ρi​dvol=1,λ≤ρi​≤Λalmost everywhere.

The optimal map pushes ρ0 dvol\rho_0\,d\mathrm{vol}ρ0​dvol to ρ1 dvol\rho_1\,d\mathrm{vol}ρ1​dvol: the mass arriving in each measurable target set equals its prescribed target mass.

M2 claims a homeomorphic representative T~:M→M\widetilde T:M\to MT:M→M of that almost-everywhere unique map, with

d(T~(x),T~(x′))≤Cd(x,x′)α,d(\widetilde T(x),\widetilde T(x'))\le C d(x,x')^\alpha,d(T(x),T(x′))≤Cd(x,x′)α,
d(T~−1(y),T~−1(y′))≤Cd(y,y′)α.d(\widetilde T^{-1}(y),\widetilde T^{-1}(y'))\le C d(y,y')^\alpha.d(T−1(y),T−1(y′))≤Cd(y,y′)α.

Here α>0\alpha>0α>0 and C<∞C<\inftyC<∞ depend only on the fixed manifold and λ,Λ\lambda,\Lambdaλ,Λ. They are common to all such density pairs, independently of density derivatives or oscillations. No continuity of the densities is assumed.

The exponent is obtained by contradiction and is not explicit. The theorem does not give uniform constants while the manifold or its metric varies. Combined with the prior necessity theorem, the source states an equivalence between weak MTW and transport continuity for all positive bounded density pairs in this setting.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claims. This would resolve Villani’s convexity conjecture in the stated compact setting and connect one weak local cost-curvature condition to global geodesic support and quantitative transport regularity.

The common estimate in M2 is stronger than separately proving continuity for each density pair. A sequence of increasingly irregular but uniformly bounded positive densities would retain the same Hölder control on the fixed manifold. The inverse estimate prevents uncontrolled compression as well as uncontrolled stretching.

The treatment of conjugate cut endpoints is central. At those points the usual smooth-coordinate formulas degenerate, and one cannot simply apply a smooth-cost theorem with constants silently depending on distance from the singular set.

The pair of papers also separates two sources of structure. M1 obtains support geometry without any measure bounds. M2 uses actual mass constraints to deduce uniqueness of final contact endpoints and regularity of the transport map.

6. The main idea

Continue the whole subgradient graph

Every ordinary subgradient can be expressed as a convex combination of finitely many active minimizing velocities. The potential may have infinitely many possible targets, but each local representation needs only finitely many. All minimizing velocities to each active cut target are retained.

M1 begins with short geodesic segments, where the geometry is controlled, and continues the projections FtF_tFt​ toward time one. At a hypothetical first failing scale, it must exclude two mechanisms: a conjugacy obstruction and collisions of different points of the subgradient graph.

Radial shortening supplies smooth upper supports for distance and a strictly decreasing divided-action Hessian. Weak MTW controls only directions perpendicular to a velocity segment. The manuscript combines that transverse control with a radial Hessian identity and a Jacobi-field variation to exclude a conjugacy kernel at the first obstruction.

For collisions, it compares the finite active representations before passing to limits. Their first-order relations place relevant velocities in a hyperplane perpendicular to the collision direction. Linear terms are canceled at the finite stage before division by the squared separation. Weak MTW and strict radial comparison then provide the proposed contradiction.

Local injectivity, invariance of domain and a homotopy from the short-time map make the global projection one-to-one and onto. Closure as t↑1t\uparrow1t↑1 gives global supporting mountains. Importantly, closure does not turn the time-one projection of every arbitrary potential into a homeomorphism.

Measure how large a near-contact section can be

For a dual pair (u,v)(u,v)(u,v), define the lifted gap section

Sx(r)={p∈Gx:u(x)+∣p∣22+v(exp⁡xp)≤r}.S_x(r)=\left\{p\in G_x: u(x)+\frac{|p|^2}{2}+v(\exp_xp)\le r\right\}.Sx​(r)={p∈Gx​:u(x)+2∣p∣2​+v(expx​p)≤r}.

The gap is nonnegative and vanishes at exact transport contacts. Thus a small rrr selects almost-optimal destinations from the starting point xxx.

M1 gives convexity of these lifted sets. M2 studies the oscillation of vvv on their endpoint images, and takes the supremum over all density pairs in the fixed class. A power bound for this one scalar quantity yields a power bound for endpoint diameter. At zero height, the endpoint must then be unique.

Taking the supremum from the outset is how the argument aims to obtain class-uniform constants, rather than a separate small scale for each pair.

Control degeneration without assuming cut avoidance

Near a conjugate endpoint, the differential of exp⁡x\exp_xexpx​ can have small singular values. The manuscript factors the relevant Jacobi matrix through an intermediate joining point and a broken-action Hessian. Radial shortening adds a positive term, and transverse MTW supplies comparisons along affine velocity segments.

These estimates compare the degeneracies at related endpoints rather than demanding that all exponential Jacobians have a fixed positive lower bound. This distinction allows the analysis to approach conjugate configurations.

If every power bound for section oscillation failed, the manuscript finds two separated gap scales where that oscillation barely changes. Modified supporting functions then create a controlled interior contact configuration. Lower quadratic tests at selected endpoints transfer information between its center and outer contacts.

The order of this transfer matters. Contact-volume estimates using the original densities first exclude conjugacy at a selected outer endpoint and control its determinant. Only after obtaining the needed nonsingularity does the argument use the almost-everywhere density equation at sampled center endpoints. It does not assign a smooth density equation to an arbitrary singular point.

A determinant gain contradicts the geometric Jacobian comparisons and the fixed mass bounds. This yields a positive power estimate for the sections. Reversing the density pair gives the corresponding result for the inverse map, and compactness extends the local estimates globally.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The claims concern squared geodesic distance on a fixed smooth compact connected manifold without boundary. They are not assertions for arbitrary costs, noncompact manifolds or domains with boundary.

Weak MTW is not replaced by ordinary nonnegative sectional curvature. It is the stated fourth-order cost condition on transverse pairs. No strict MTW inequality, nonfocality or prior convexity of injectivity domains is assumed.

M2 requires both densities to be bounded above and bounded away from zero over the whole manifold. Removing the lower bound, allowing singular measures, or asking for Lipschitz or smooth transport changes the problem. No explicit optimal exponent or uniformity across varying metrics is claimed.

The density-free intermediate homeomorphism in M1 and the final transport homeomorphism in M2 should also remain distinct. The latter uses mass bounds that an arbitrary potential does not possess. The manuscript arguments and claimed consequences are reported without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 provides the convexity, support and intermediate geometry used as an explicit input to M2. M2 develops the class-uniform section estimate and explains the order of its limiting argument near conjugacy.

Primary predecessors include Figalli–Gallouët–Rifford on nonfocal injectivity domains, Figalli–Kim–McCann on Hölder optimal maps, Figalli–Rifford–Villani on continuity criteria, and Villani’s formulation of the geometric conjecture.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Global Support and Convex Injectivity Domains under Weak MTW (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Uniform Bi-Holder Transport from Weak MTW (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: More polynomial-growth harmonic functions than Euclidean space
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 361 · Differential geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A harmonic function models a steady temperature with no internal heat sources. In Euclidean space it satisfies Laplace’s equation. If its growth is bounded by a polynomial of integer degree kkk, then the function itself is a harmonic polynomial of degree at most kkk. There are only finitely many independent possibilities.

What happens on a complete curved space with nonnegative Ricci curvature? Such curvature imposes strong volume and analytic restrictions. Yau asked whether Euclidean space gives the largest possible dimension of the space of harmonic functions with a prescribed polynomial growth bound.

Family 361 claims that the exact comparison fails even when the growth degree is an integer. M1 gives a higher-dimensional construction; M2 gives counterexamples on R3\mathbb R^3R3, with a fixed-factor excess over the Euclidean count. M2 also claims these metrics can be arbitrarily close to the Euclidean metric in global bi-Lipschitz distance.

The mechanism is not to find one cone with too many slow angular modes. Instead, the geometry changes gradually with radius, letting harmonic functions cycle through different growth rates whose averages remain below the chosen degree.

2. Background and essential definitions

Counting harmonic functions by growth

For a complete Riemannian manifold (M,g)(M,g)(M,g), a real-valued function uuu is harmonic if

Δgu=0.\Delta_g u=0.Δg​u=0.

The Laplace–Beltrami operator Δg\Delta_gΔg​ is the geometric version of the ordinary sum of second derivatives. Let Hd(M,g)H_d(M,g)Hd​(M,g) be the real vector space of smooth harmonic functions satisfying

∣u(x)∣≤Cu(1+dg(o,x))dfor every x∈M,|u(x)|\le C_u\bigl(1+d_g(o,x)\bigr)^d\qquad\text{for every }x\in M,∣u(x)∣≤Cu​(1+dg​(o,x))dfor every x∈M,

where ooo is a base point and the finite constant CuC_uCu​ may depend on the function. Changing ooo does not change the space. Write hd=dim⁡RHdh_d=\dim_{\mathbb R}H_dhd​=dimR​Hd​.

For an integer k≥1k\ge1k≥1, the Euclidean count is

hk(Rn,gE)=(n+k−1k)+(n+k−2k−1).h_k(\mathbb R^n,g_E)=\binom{n+k-1}{k}+\binom{n+k-2}{k-1}.hk​(Rn,gE​)=(kn+k−1​)+(k−1n+k−2​).

In three dimensions, homogeneous harmonic polynomials of degree lll have dimension 2l+12l+12l+1, so

hk(R3,gE)=∑l=0k(2l+1)=(k+1)2.h_k(\mathbb R^3,g_E)=\sum_{l=0}^k(2l+1)=(k+1)^2.hk​(R3,gE​)=l=0∑k​(2l+1)=(k+1)2.

For example, degree at most one gives the constant function and the three coordinate functions. The conjectured comparison would bound the corresponding dimension on a Ricci-nonnegative three-manifold by the same square for every integer kkk.

Geometry at infinity

Ricci curvature sums sectional curvature contributions in directions through a tangent vector. Nonnegative Ricci curvature does not require every individual sectional curvature to be nonnegative.

The asymptotic volume ratio is

AVR⁡(g)=lim⁡R→∞vol⁡gBg(o,R)ωnRn,\operatorname{AVR}(g)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{vol}_g B_g(o,R)}{\omega_nR^n},AVR(g)=R→∞lim​ωn​Rnvolg​Bg​(o,R)​,

where ωn\omega_nωn​ is the volume of the Euclidean unit ball. A positive ratio means the manifold retains Euclidean-order volume growth at large distances. Under nonnegative Ricci curvature, volume comparison supplies the limit.

A tangent cone at infinity is a limit obtained by looking at the whole space from farther and farther away, rescaling lengths by 1/Rj1/R_j1/Rj​. Different sequences can produce different limits. A metric cone has the form

gC=dr2+r2h,g_C=dr^2+r^2h,gC​=dr2+r2h,

where hhh is a metric on its angular cross-section, called the link.

If the link has dimension m=n−1m=n-1m=n−1, an angular Laplacian eigenfunction with eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ gives a homogeneous harmonic mode rdφr^d\varphirdφ when

d(d+m−1)=λ.d(d+m-1)=\lambda.d(d+m−1)=λ.

Thus angular spectral data determine growth rates on a fixed cone.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Yau’s questions distinguished finite dimensionality from the sharper Euclidean dimension bound. Li and Tam proved the sharp linear-growth estimate h1≤n+1h_1\le n+1h1​≤n+1 under nonnegative Ricci curvature. Colding and Minicozzi established finite dimensionality at every fixed degree and later bounds with the optimal order dn−1d^{n-1}dn−1 as the degree grows.

Those results do not force the exact Euclidean coefficient or count at each integer. A space can have the correct order of growth in the number of functions and still exceed Euclidean space at a particular degree.

Donnelly constructed counterexamples for a real growth degree strictly between one and two in dimensions at least five. This does not settle degree two: Euclidean harmonic quadratics enter the comparison space at that endpoint, making the allowable count jump.

There are also positive results with additional hypotheses. Cai and Lai obtain the Euclidean bound for locally conformally flat manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Lin, Wang and Xu establish a three-dimensional integer-degree comparison under nonnegative sectional curvature and positive asymptotic volume ratio. These assumptions are stronger than Ricci nonnegativity alone.

At infinity, Huang relates harmonic dimensions to the spectrum of a unique tangent cone under nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth. Earlier constructions of Perelman and Colding–Naber showed that nonunique cones are possible even with favorable Ricci and volume properties. Such flexibility is relevant here.

M1 uses slowly varying Berger-sphere links and exact control in fixed finite-dimensional harmonic spaces. M2 is an independent three-dimensional construction whose angular eigenspaces move and can interact with infinitely many higher modes. It does not invoke M1’s theorem as an input.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: an integer-degree violation in higher dimension

M1 claims a complete smooth metric ggg on Rn\mathbb R^nRn, for some even n≥8n\ge8n≥8, and an integer k≥2k\ge2k≥2, such that

Ric⁡g≥0,hk(Rn,g)>hk(Rn,gE).\operatorname{Ric}_g\ge0,\qquadh_k(\mathbb R^n,g)>h_k(\mathbb R^n,g_E).Ricg​≥0,hk​(Rn,g)>hk​(Rn,gE​).

The metric is Euclidean near the origin, has asymptotic volume ratio strictly between zero and one, and has nonunique tangent cones at infinity. Its finite spectral-selection appendix states that one may take n=16n=16n=16 and k=50000k=50000k=50000. That numerical selection is a stated ingredient, not a calculation independently certified here.

M2: a fixed-factor excess in dimension three

For every

49<v<1,1<c<9v4,\frac49<v<1,\qquad1<c<\frac{9v}{4},94​<v<1,1<c<49v​,

M2 claims a threshold k0(v,c)k_0(v,c)k0​(v,c) such that, for each integer k≥k0k\ge k_0k≥k0​, there is a complete smooth metric gkg_kgk​ on R3\mathbb R^3R3 with

Ric⁡gk≥0,AVR⁡(gk)=v,\operatorname{Ric}_{g_k}\ge0,\qquad\operatorname{AVR}(g_k)=v,Ricgk​​≥0,AVR(gk​)=v,
hk(R3,gk)≥c(k+1)2>(k+1)2.h_k(\mathbb R^3,g_k)\ge c(k+1)^2>(k+1)^2.hk​(R3,gk​)≥c(k+1)2>(k+1)2.

The metric is Euclidean near the origin and has positive Ricci curvature outside a compact set. It has uncountably many pairwise nonisometric pointed tangent cones at infinity. Some radial sectional curvatures are negative at points arbitrarily far out, so it does not satisfy the stronger sectional-curvature hypothesis of the positive comparison theorem above.

The order of quantifiers is important: choose a sufficiently large degree, then construct its metric. M2 does not assert one fixed metric with this excess for all large degrees.

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 and 1<c<9/41<c<9/41<c<9/4, M2 further claims such metrics for all sufficiently large kkk with

(1+ε)−2gE≤gk≤(1+ε)2gE.(1+\varepsilon)^{-2}g_E\le g_k\le(1+\varepsilon)^2g_E.(1+ε)−2gE​≤gk​≤(1+ε)2gE​.

The identity map is therefore globally (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon)(1+ε)-bi-Lipschitz. The volume ratio can be prescribed arbitrarily close to one. The value 9/49/49/4 comes from the construction; no endpoint or optimality assertion is made.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claims. The papers would answer the integer-degree form of a central comparison question negatively, with M2 placing the phenomenon in dimension three and showing a substantial multiplicative excess.

The result would not undermine the established finite-dimensionality or optimal-order bounds. It would show that the stronger intuition “Euclidean space has the most functions at every integer degree” needs additional hypotheses.

The almost-Euclidean examples are particularly instructive. Controlling all distances within a factor close to one does not control how small geometric changes accumulate over infinitely many scales. Harmonic functions solve a global equation, and their long-range growth can record this accumulation.

The method also changes the role of spectral information at infinity. A single frozen cone assigns one growth rate to each mode. A varying geometry can transfer a function between modes, so its eventual exponent reflects a carefully arranged average rather than one fixed eigenvalue.

6. The main idea

Average logarithmic growth rates

On a fixed cone, a mode growing like rdr^drd grows exponentially like edte^{dt}edt in logarithmic radius t=log⁡rt=\log rt=logr. If a mode spends comparable stretches of logarithmic radius at several rates, its total growth can be governed by their mean.

An elementary analogy is alternating between multiplication factors eate^{at}eat and ebte^{bt}ebt: over equal durations, the logarithm accumulates at average rate (a+b)/2(a+b)/2(a+b)/2. In the manuscripts, the difficulty is arranging exact harmonic continuation while changing angular directions. Tiny contamination by a faster-growing mode can eventually dominate, so approximate cycling alone is inadequate.

M1: exchange directions inside fixed harmonic blocks

M1 uses Berger metrics on odd-dimensional spheres. These deform the metric in a distinguished Hopf circle direction while preserving a normalized volume form. The direction itself can rotate.

Each angular Laplacian preserves the same finite-dimensional space of round spherical harmonics of degree lll. A spectral selection finds enough directions whose mean selected growth rate lies below kkk, even though some individual rates may exceed kkk.

Short geometric control pulses are designed to permute these directions simultaneously in finitely many harmonic blocks. Long nonround intervals then supply the desired growth rates. A long round rest regularizes the incoming radial derivative before the next pulse.

The source tunes the transfer across the entire pulse-plus-dwell period, not just the value at the end of the pulse. This avoids a small radial-derivative error feeding an unwanted fast mode during the following long interval. Exact cycling and negligible relative transition costs yield the average exponent.

The link changes slowly enough that a concave radial correction preserves nonnegative Ricci curvature. Estimates between scheduled endpoints then give the growth bound at every radius, not merely at selected spheres.

M2: move eigenlines through crossings on the two-sphere

In three dimensions the link is S2S^2S2. M2 builds a periodic path of near-round sphere metrics with a common area form. Its low eigenvalues are simple except at carefully arranged isolated double crossings.

At a crossing, there are two ways to label modes: order eigenvalues by size at each instant, or continue a smooth eigenline through the equality. Continuing the eigenline exchanges its position in the ordered spectrum. A sequence of crossings cycles a long band through many positions.

Choose a=va=\sqrt va=v​ and a parameter ϑ\varthetaϑ with

c<ϑ<3a2.\sqrt c<\vartheta<\frac{3a}{2}.c​<ϑ<23a​.

A band reaching round degree approximately ϑk\vartheta kϑk provides about ϑ2k2\vartheta^2k^2ϑ2k2 modes. Counting the multiplicities 2l+12l+12l+1 shows that their average round degree is approximately 2ϑk/32\vartheta k/32ϑk/3. The radial scaling contributes a factor 1/a1/a1/a, leaving the average below kkk. The strict inequalities leave room for the small geometric perturbations.

This is the origin of the range c<9v/4c<9v/4c<9v/4. The construction does not find an individual limiting sphere with too many eigenvalues below the threshold. Each frozen link obeys the relevant comparison; the cycling is essential.

Control the high modes and the Euclidean center

Unlike M1’s fixed finite blocks, M2’s moving angular eigenspaces can leak into infinitely many higher modes. The manuscript works with exact inward maps: given boundary data on an outer sphere, extend harmonically across the whole enclosed ball and restrict to an inner sphere.

These maps incorporate smoothness at the Euclidean center from the start. They preserve constants and contract the appropriate L2L^2L2 norm. A gap above the selected low spectrum produces an invariant graph describing the high-mode component in terms of low-mode data.

Small controls near each crossing then match the selected invariant lines to the continued eigenbranches. One solves a scalar recurrence in opposite directions on its contracting and expanding sides; the crossing control changes the mismatch with a definite sign. Finite-dimensional fixed points and a compact limiting argument choose all controls for one resulting metric.

The radial metric has the form

g=dr2+f(r)2H∗(log⁡r),f(r)/r→v.g=dr^2+f(r)^2H_*(\log r),\qquad f(r)/r\to\sqrt v.g=dr2+f(r)2H∗​(logr),f(r)/r→v​.

Slow angular motion and a concave radial tail control the Ricci tensor. The mixed curvature terms are absorbed quadratically using a positive tangential Ricci block, rather than being assumed absent.

Compatible traces on nested spheres yield independent entire harmonic functions. Periodic averaging bounds their logarithmic growth, inward contraction controls intermediate spheres, and local elliptic estimates convert spherical L2L^2L2 bounds into the required pointwise bound everywhere.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The distinction between a fixed metric and a family depending on kkk is essential. M2 proves the claimed excess degree by degree, not an asymptotic lower bound for one common three-manifold metric as k→∞k\to\inftyk→∞.

Neither construction violates Li–Tam’s sharp linear-growth theorem. Nor do they contradict comparison results assuming nonnegative sectional curvature, local conformal flatness or a suitable unique cone at infinity. Their geometry deliberately falls outside those additional hypotheses.

Global bi-Lipschitz proximity to Euclidean space does not mean closeness of curvature or all metric derivatives. Negative radial sectional planes and changing cone limits remain possible despite the distance comparison.

The factor 9/49/49/4 is not claimed to be best possible, and its endpoint is excluded. Questions about optimal excess, smaller integer degrees and a single fixed metric exhibiting repeated large-degree excess remain separate. The spectral selections, transfer arguments and geometric constructions are reported as stated without proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 develops fixed-block Berger-link control and gives the finite spectral-selection appendix. M2 develops crossing control and whole-ball harmonic continuation in dimension three; its theorem explicitly records dependence of the metric on the chosen degree.

Primary background includes Li–Tam’s linear-growth theorem, Donnelly’s noninteger examples, Huang’s cone-spectral comparison, Cai–Lai, and Lin–Wang–Xu.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A counterexample to integer-degree harmonic dimension comparison (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Three-Dimensional Counterexample to Integer-Degree Harmonic Dimension Comparison (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Can a collisionless relativistic plasma remain smooth for all time?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 362 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A collisionless plasma is described by a cloud of charged particles coupled to the electromagnetic field they generate. The field accelerates the particles; the moving particles, in turn, change the field. Even without particle collisions, this feedback makes the evolution nonlinear.

For smooth initial data, the relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell equations have a smooth solution for a short time. The central large-data question is whether that solution can develop a singularity in finite time. Particles never reach the speed of light, but their momenta can become arbitrarily large as their speeds approach that limit. A speed bound alone therefore does not control the evolution.

Family 362 claims global existence and uniqueness of smooth solutions in three spatial dimensions for the one-species model, with no size or symmetry restrictions on admissible initial data. The particle density is initially smooth and compactly supported in both position and momentum; the fields have finite energy and bounded derivatives of every order.

The manuscript’s proposed mechanism is an estimate on the net momentum change along a particle trajectory. It retains cancellation in the force before taking its magnitude, preventing momentum from doubling infinitely often in finite time.

2. Background and essential definitions

Position, momentum and relativistic velocity

Let f(t,x,p)≥0f(t,x,p)\ge0f(t,x,p)≥0 be the particle density in phase space, with position x∈R3x\in\mathbb R^3x∈R3 and momentum p∈R3p\in\mathbb R^3p∈R3. In units where particle mass and the speed of light are one, define

q(p)=1+∣p∣2,u(p)=pq(p).q(p)=\sqrt{1+|p|^2},\qquad u(p)=\frac{p}{q(p)}.q(p)=1+∣p∣2​,u(p)=q(p)p​.

Here qqq is particle energy and uuu is velocity. Always ∣u∣<1|u|<1∣u∣<1, even when ∣p∣|p|∣p∣ is very large. Momentum and velocity are therefore different variables.

Let E(t,x)E(t,x)E(t,x) and B(t,x)B(t,x)B(t,x) be the electric and magnetic fields. The Vlasov equation is

∂tf+u(p)⋅∇xf+(E+u(p)×B)⋅∇pf=0.\partial_t f+u(p)\cdot\nabla_x f+\bigl(E+u(p)\times B\bigr)\cdot\nabla_p f=0.∂t​f+u(p)⋅∇x​f+(E+u(p)×B)⋅∇p​f=0.

It says that density is transported along particle trajectories, with no collision term. Those trajectories satisfy

X′=u(P),P′=E(t,X)+u(P)×B(t,X).X'=u(P),\qquad P'=E(t,X)+u(P)\times B(t,X).X′=u(P),P′=E(t,X)+u(P)×B(t,X).

The force is the Lorentz force. The magnetic part changes momentum direction but does no direct work, since it is perpendicular to velocity.

Maxwell’s equations close the feedback loop

Charge and current densities are

ρ(t,x)=∫R3f(t,x,p) dp,j(t,x)=∫R3u(p)f(t,x,p) dp.\rho(t,x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(t,x,p)\,dp,\qquadj(t,x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(p)f(t,x,p)\,dp.ρ(t,x)=∫R3​f(t,x,p)dp,j(t,x)=∫R3​u(p)f(t,x,p)dp.

The electromagnetic equations in the manuscript’s normalization are

∂tE−∇×B=−j,∂tB+∇×E=0,\partial_t E-\nabla\times B=-j,\qquad\partial_t B+\nabla\times E=0,∂t​E−∇×B=−j,∂t​B+∇×E=0,
∇⋅E=ρ,∇⋅B=0.\nabla\cdot E=\rho,\qquad\nabla\cdot B=0.∇⋅E=ρ,∇⋅B=0.

There is one particle species and no background charge. The last two equations are constraints that compatible initial data must satisfy and that the evolution preserves.

The conserved total energy has the form

E=∬q(p)f(t,x,p) dp dx+12∫(∣E∣2+∣B∣2) dx.\mathcal E=\iint q(p)f(t,x,p)\,dp\,dx+\frac12\int\bigl(|E|^2+|B|^2\bigr)\,dx.E=∬q(p)f(t,x,p)dpdx+21​∫(∣E∣2+∣B∣2)dx.

This integral bound is powerful but does not directly bound the largest particle momentum or the field at every point. A small amount of density can occupy a high-energy region while the integral stays finite.

Classical versus weak solutions

A classical solution has enough derivatives to satisfy the equations pointwise. The theorem ultimately asserts smoothness on every finite time interval. A weak solution satisfies integrated versions of the equations and may have much lower regularity. Global weak existence does not by itself give global smoothness or uniqueness in the classical class.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Wollman established local classical existence and uniqueness. DiPerna and Lions developed global weak existence for large data; Rein later gave a direct treatment of the relativistic one-species formulation. The remaining classical problem was to prevent loss of regularity.

Glassey and Strauss identified a decisive continuation criterion: a classical solution can be extended as long as the momentum support of the particle distribution stays bounded on finite time intervals. Their work also proved global existence for initially dilute plasmas. Later proofs of the criterion used Fourier methods and physical-space wave-kernel decompositions; Bouchut, Golse and Pallard provide one such approach.

Glassey and Schaeffer obtained global classical solutions in several lower-dimensional reductions and in a symmetric relativistic Vlasov–Poisson setting. Small-data and perturbative results were developed by Rein, Schaeffer, Bigorgne, Wang, Wei and Yang, among others. Some allow noncompact particle tails or large electromagnetic fields, but retain smallness of the particle distribution or proximity to a controlled reference solution.

Luk and Strain sharpened continuation theory by showing that control of momentum projected onto a fixed two-dimensional plane suffices. Other criteria use moments or spatial density bounds. Such results identify sufficient controls, but do not automatically establish those controls for arbitrary data.

A relevant recent predecessor is Xuecheng Wang’s July 2026 two-paper treatment of large cylindrically symmetric data: the iterative smoothing construction and pointwise estimates. It imposes rotational covariance about a fixed axis and uses Sobolev and weighted data assumptions. Family 362 removes symmetry for its own compact-particle data class. The two classes should not be treated as identical, since Wang’s formulation permits localized noncompact particle data.

The retarded-field representation, light-cone energy flux and changes from current phase points to particle labels all have classical antecedents. The new claim rests on combining them into a signed impulse bound strong enough to close the unrestricted large-data continuation argument.

4. What the new manuscript claims

The initial particle density is any

f0∈Cc∞(Rx3×Rp3),f0≥0.f_0\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R_x^3\times\mathbb R_p^3),\qquad f_0\ge0.f0​∈Cc∞​(Rx3​×Rp3​),f0​≥0.

The notation Cc∞C_c^\inftyCc∞​ means smooth with compact support. The initial fields satisfy

E0,B0∈Cb∞(R3;R3)∩L2(R3;R3),E_0,B_0\in C_b^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)\cap L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),E0​,B0​∈Cb∞​(R3;R3)∩L2(R3;R3),
∇⋅E0=∫f0 dp,∇⋅B0=0.\nabla\cdot E_0=\int f_0\,dp,\qquad\nabla\cdot B_0=0.∇⋅E0​=∫f0​dp,∇⋅B0​=0.

Here Cb∞C_b^\inftyCb∞​ means that the fields and every spatial derivative are bounded. Only the fields themselves are required to be square-integrable; square-integrability of every derivative is not assumed.

For every such datum, the theorem claims a unique global classical solution. For each finite TTT, the functions f,E,Bf,E,Bf,E,B are smooth on [0,T][0,T][0,T], the particle support stays inside a compact subset of position–momentum space over that interval, and the divergence constraints remain valid.

There is no smallness, spherical symmetry or cylindrical symmetry requirement. Nonzero total charge is allowed: the electric field may have its corresponding Coulomb tail, which is compatible with finite field energy at spatial infinity. The fields are not required to have compact support.

The support bound may grow with TTT. The theorem does not claim a uniform momentum bound for all infinite time, asymptotic scattering, or decay to a particular equilibrium.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claim. Global classical regularity for general large data in the three-dimensional relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system is a central problem in kinetic PDE. The theorem would remove the size and symmetry restrictions for the stated natural class of smooth compact particle data.

The result would establish deterministic smooth evolution for arbitrarily strong initial configurations within this model. That is substantially stronger than producing weak solutions or constructing special large solutions from prescribed asymptotic behavior.

Its analytic significance is the distinction between total force magnitude and net impulse. Bounding the integral of the absolute force can lose cancellations that are crucial at high momentum. The manuscript proposes to retain enough of the signed vector structure to prevent a finite-time cascade of momentum doublings.

The claim remains specific to the one-species collisionless equations and the stated data. It is not a general regularity theorem for all plasma or fluid models.

6. The main idea

Reduce smooth continuation to momentum support

Along characteristics, the distribution function is transported and particle speeds remain below one. Initial compact spatial support therefore stays within a linearly expanding spatial region on every finite horizon. The harder issue is momentum support.

The Glassey–Strauss continuation criterion reduces the global argument to showing that the largest supported momentum cannot become infinite in finite time. The manuscript proves the local theory and smooth persistence in its precise field class, including a finite-horizon modification that connects it to the Sobolev formulation of the continuation theorem.

This modification retains the Coulomb field and changes divergence-free remainders outside the relevant particle region. Finite propagation makes the removed vacuum Maxwell field irrelevant to the particle dynamics during the chosen horizon. Thus extra global square-integrability of all initial field derivatives is not silently added.

Use the light cone to locate the sources of a force

Electromagnetic influence travels at speed one. The force at a particle is therefore expressed through source particles on its backward light cone, not through an instantaneous interaction at the same time.

The argument follows source trajectories to their intersections with that cone and divides contributions into ranges of momentum, separation distance and relative angles. Energy flux through light cones controls suitable field components. Occupation estimates control how long source particles can remain in a given geometric range.

Direct estimates of the absolute force are still too large in a narrow angular configuration: the source velocity is much more closely aligned with the light ray than the receiving particle’s velocity is. At high receiver energy, the loss is of square-root size relative to the desired estimate.

Preserve cancellation along source trajectories

Instead of taking absolute values term by term, the manuscript integrates the force along source trajectories. An identity combines the part independent of source acceleration with the part involving that acceleration. A term generated by differentiating the cone geometry cancels against the first part.

The remaining expression contains a total derivative and less singular bulk terms. One bulk term involves the receiver’s acceleration, which is itself the Lorentz force. The argument must therefore make its coefficient small enough; integration by parts alone is not the conclusion.

The signed identity is used twice. First, under a provisional impulse estimate, its transverse projection bounds changes of particle direction. That directional control improves occupation estimates when both source and receiver momenta are large: between significant turns, relative motion crosses the relevant region in a controlled way.

Second, the argument applies signed cancellation only in ranges where direct estimates exceed a summable threshold. The selection forces troublesome configurations into the angular window covered by the improved occupation estimate. The resulting receiver-force coefficient gains the square-root factor needed to compensate for the earlier loss.

Time weights handle integration by parts away from interval endpoints. The short endpoint pieces are then restored using the provisional estimate, producing a strict improvement and closing a continuity bootstrap.

Why the final estimate rules out finite-time blowup

The central estimate has the following form. Let PPP be a dyadic upper scale, at least a fixed multiple of the maximum supported particle energy on a classical interval. Suppose a receiver stays at energy comparable to a dyadic scale www during an interval of length Δt\Delta tΔt. Then

∣Δp∣≤C1PΔt+C2Δt P2log⁡(2+P)w.|\Delta p|\le C_1P\sqrt{\Delta t}+C_2\Delta t\,\frac{P^2\log(2+P)}{w}.∣Δp∣≤C1​PΔt​+C2​ΔtwP2log(2+P)​.

The constants depend on the datum and a fixed finite time horizon, but not on the provisional maximum PPP. The norm is taken after integrating the force.

If maximum energy were to pass successively through 2j2^j2j, choose a trajectory making each doubling and take PPP and www comparable to that level. The estimate gives a lower bound of the form

Δtj≥clog⁡(2+C2j).\Delta t_j\ge\frac{c}{\log(2+C2^j)}.Δtj​≥log(2+C2j)c​.

These lower bounds have a divergent sum, behaving like the harmonic series in jjj. Infinitely many doublings therefore require infinite total time. The continuation criterion then supplies the claimed global smooth solution.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns three position and three momentum variables, one particle species, and no background charge. It does not state a multispecies extension, a collisional Boltzmann model, or a coupled gravitational system.

Initial compact support of the particle density and the specified smooth finite-energy field class are genuine hypotheses. The result does not automatically cover arbitrary noncompact momentum tails or rough initial data merely because other small-data theories do.

Global classical uniqueness is also distinct from uniqueness among every possible low-regularity weak solution. No such broader uniqueness assertion is made here.

The theorem controls each finite interval, leaving long-time momentum growth, scattering for general large data and extensions to other admissible data classes as separate questions. Its signed-force estimates and global regularity conclusion are reported as stated, without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript’s Theorem 1.1 states the data class and global conclusion; Proposition 2.1 gives the signed increment estimate, and Section 10 supplies the continuation interface.

Primary background includes Bouchut–Golse–Pallard on the Glassey–Strauss criterion, Luk–Strain’s continuation refinement, and Wang’s first and second papers on large cylindrically symmetric data. The manuscript’s bibliography separates weak existence, classical continuation and small-data asymptotics.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Global classical solutions of the three-dimensional relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: What one boundary patch can reveal about an unknown interior
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 365 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Suppose an object is inaccessible inside. You can impose voltages on its surface and measure the resulting currents. Can those measurements determine how well each interior point conducts electricity?

Calderón’s inverse problem asks this mathematically. Its geometric version allows conductivity to depend on direction, so the unknown resembles a Riemannian metric. A further version includes a connection, which describes how vector-valued quantities change when transported through the object.

Family 365 contains three manuscripts with complementary conclusions. M2 claims that any open boundary patch determines an arbitrary smooth metric, up to the unavoidable freedom to change coordinates. M1 adds simultaneous recovery of a smooth unitary connection on a trivial rank-two bundle. M3 claims that, with only bounded measurable scalar conductivity, even measurements on the entire boundary can fail to distinguish different interiors.

The contrast concerns regularity as well as the type of unknown. It does not say that the same class of conductivities is both recoverable and unrecoverable.

2. Background and essential definitions

Voltages, currents and boundary response

For a positive scalar conductivity γ(x)\gamma(x)γ(x) in a domain Ω⊂Rn\Omega\subset\mathbb R^nΩ⊂Rn, a stationary voltage uuu satisfies

div⁡(γ∇u)=0.\operatorname{div}(\gamma abla u)=0.div(γ∇u)=0.

The equation expresses conservation of electric current. A prescribed boundary voltage fff determines an interior solution. The Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, abbreviated DN map, sends fff to its outward conductivity flux γ∂νu\gamma\partial_ u uγ∂ν​u. Knowing this map means knowing the response to every admissible voltage, not just a finite set of experiments.

Its weak formulation uses energy:

⟨Λγf,h⟩=∫Ωγ∇uf⋅∇uh dx.\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h angle=\int_\Omega\gamma abla u_f\cdot abla u_h\,dx.⟨Λγ​f,h⟩=∫Ω​γ∇uf​⋅∇uh​dx.

Here uf,uhu_f,u_huf​,uh​ solve the equation with boundary values f,hf,hf,h. This definition still works for bounded measurable coefficients. Uniform positivity means fixed constants satisfy 0<c≤γ≤C<∞0<c\le\gamma\le C<\infty0<c≤γ≤C<∞ almost everywhere.

For a boundary patch Γ\GammaΓ, both fff and hhh are supported in Γ\GammaΓ; voltages vanish on the rest of the boundary. The measurement is therefore restricted on both the input and observation sides.

Geometry and its unavoidable ambiguity

A metric ggg gives lengths and angles on a manifold MMM. Its harmonic functions solve Δgu=0\Delta_g u=0Δg​u=0, and their boundary response is defined by

⟨Λg,Γf,h⟩=∫M⟨duf,duh⟩g dVg.\langle\Lambda_{g,\Gamma}f,h angle=\int_M\langle du_f,du_h angle_g\,dV_g.⟨Λg,Γ​f,h⟩=∫M​⟨duf​,duh​⟩g​dVg​.

The output includes the boundary density. This matters when the boundary metric is itself unknown: the definition does not silently assume a known surface measure.

A diffeomorphism is a smooth invertible change of coordinates with smooth inverse. If Φ\PhiΦ fixes the measured boundary points, the metrics ggg and Φ∗g\Phi^*gΦ∗g give identical measurements. The notation Φ∗g\Phi^*gΦ∗g means that lengths are computed after applying Φ\PhiΦ. Recovery can at best be up to this coordinate freedom.

For n≥3n\ge3n≥3, scalar Euclidean conductivity corresponds to

g=γ2/(n−2)gEucl.g=\gamma^{2/(n-2)}g_{\mathrm{Eucl}}.g=γ2/(n−2)gEucl​.

This power makes the metric energy equal the conductivity energy. General anisotropic conductivities correspond to more general metrics.

Connections and gauge freedom

In M1, each point carries a copy of C2\mathbb C^2C2, with its usual Hermitian inner product. A connection replaces differentiation by

dAu=du+Au,d_Au=du+Au,dA​u=du+Au,

where AAA is a matrix-valued one-form. Its matrices are skew-Hermitian, A∗=−AA^*=-AA∗=−A, so parallel transport preserves the inner product. The connection Laplacian is Lg,A=dA∗dAL_{g,A}=d_A^*d_ALg,A​=dA∗​dA​; the star here denotes the adjoint with respect to the metric and Hermitian structure.

A unitary matrix U(x)U(x)U(x) changes the basis in each fiber. This is a gauge transformation, producing

A⟼U−1AU+U−1dU.A\longmapsto U^{-1}AU+U^{-1}dU.A⟼U−1AU+U−1dU.

If UUU equals the identity on the measured patch, this basis change is invisible to the boundary experiment. Both coordinate and gauge freedoms must therefore appear in a correct uniqueness statement.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Calderón posed the conductivity problem in 1980 and studied its linearization. Sylvester and Uhlmann established full-boundary uniqueness for smooth scalar conductivities in dimensions at least three in 1987. Their special complex-valued solutions became a central tool in inverse problems.

The anisotropic problem is harder because the geometry is unknown. Lee and Uhlmann obtained boundary determination and real-analytic recovery under additional hypotheses. Lassas and Uhlmann subsequently recovered real-analytic manifolds from a boundary patch without the earlier topological restrictions. Real analyticity supplies strong continuation properties that arbitrary smooth functions need not have.

Partial-data methods then recovered coefficients under particular arrangements of the measurement regions, reflection symmetries, known boundary neighborhoods or special product geometries. Smooth Einstein metrics supplied another important geometric class. Recent results near prescribed backgrounds use smallness, ordering or foliation assumptions. M2 targets arbitrary smooth metrics and an arbitrary common patch without those restrictions.

The Poisson embedding approach of Lassas, Liimatainen and Salo represents an interior point by its values on boundary-generated harmonic functions. This supplies a geometric language for reconstruction; in the general higher-dimensional setting, their global continuation result uses real analyticity.

For connections, previous work recovered connections and potentials on known surfaces or suitable known higher-dimensional geometries. Cekić obtained same-patch recovery for Yang–Mills connections on a fixed smooth metric. Gabdurakhmanov and Kokarev obtained joint recovery of geometry, bundle and connection in the real-analytic category. M1’s distinction is simultaneous smooth recovery without prescribing the metric or imposing the Yang–Mills equation.

Regularity has a different history for scalar conductivities. Astala and Päivärinta proved planar uniqueness with merely bounded measurable, uniformly positive conductivity. In higher dimensions, uniqueness extends below smoothness: Haberman treated specified Sobolev classes in dimensions three and four, and Caro and Rogers treated positive Lipschitz conductivities in all dimensions at least three. M3 concerns the larger three-dimensional measurable class, without derivative control.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: smooth geometry from an arbitrary patch

Let MMM be a compact connected smooth manifold of dimension n≥3n\ge3n≥3, with nonempty smooth boundary. Let Γ\GammaΓ be any nonempty proper relatively open boundary subset. For smooth positive-definite metrics, including smoothness up to the boundary, M2 claims

Λg1,Γ=Λg2,Γ⟹g2=Φ∗g1,Φ∣Γ=Id.\Lambda_{g_1,\Gamma}=\Lambda_{g_2,\Gamma}\quad\Longrightarrow\quadg_2=\Phi^*g_1,\qquad \Phi|_\Gamma=\mathrm{Id}.Λg1​,Γ​=Λg2​,Γ​⟹g2​=Φ∗g1​,Φ∣Γ​=Id.

The diffeomorphism extends smoothly through the boundary. Neither orientability nor a connected boundary is required. The inaccessible boundary need not be fixed pointwise.

Full-boundary data yield a diffeomorphism fixing the whole boundary. A scalar corollary states exact equality γ1=γ2\gamma_1=\gamma_2γ1​=γ2​ for smooth positive conductivities on a bounded connected smooth Euclidean domain from any common open patch. No conductivity values are assumed known near the inaccessible boundary.

M1: simultaneous metric and connection recovery

Under the same geometric hypotheses, take arbitrary smooth unitary connections A1,A2A_1,A_2A1​,A2​ on M×C2M imes\mathbb C^2M×C2. Equality of their zero-frequency local energy forms for all smooth vector-valued inputs supported in Γ\GammaΓ is claimed to imply

g2=Φ∗g1,A2=U−1(Φ∗A1)U+U−1dU, egin{aligned}g_2&=\Phi^*g_1,\A_2&=U^{-1}(\Phi^*A_1)U+U^{-1}dU,\end{aligned}g2​A2​​=Φ∗g1​,=U−1(Φ∗A1​)U+U−1dU,​

with Φ∣Γ=Id\Phi|_\Gamma=\mathrm{Id}Φ∣Γ​=Id and U∣Γ=IU|_\Gamma=IU∣Γ​=I. No field equation is imposed on AjA_jAj​. The bundle is specifically trivial and of complex rank two; the theorem is not stated here as an arbitrary-bundle result.

M3: rough scalar conductivities with identical full data

On B(0,3)⊂R3B(0,3)\subset\mathbb R^3B(0,3)⊂R3, M3 constructs two real scalar conductivities γ0,γ1\gamma_0,\gamma_1γ0​,γ1​, uniformly positive and bounded, both equal to one near the boundary, such that

Λγ0=Λγ1,∣{x:γ0(x)≠γ1(x)}∣>0.\Lambda_{\gamma_0}=\Lambda_{\gamma_1},\qquad|\{x:\gamma_0(x) e\gamma_1(x)\}|>0.Λγ0​​=Λγ1​​,∣{x:γ0​(x)=γ1​(x)}∣>0.

The equality is for the entire weak DN operator. The coefficients are exactly indistinguishable, rather than merely having responses that approach one another in a limit.

A localization corollary places independent copies inside any finite collection of disjoint interior balls of a bounded connected Lipschitz domain in R3\mathbb R^3R3. With mmm balls, there are 2m2^m2m distinct conductivities sharing one full boundary response. That common response is not asserted to equal the response of the constant conductivity one.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the smooth results resolve central forms of the anisotropic Calderón uniqueness problem and extend geometric recovery to coupled transport data. The rough counterexample simultaneously identifies a genuine failure of unrestricted scalar recovery in three dimensions.

Together, these claims would sharpen what boundary measurements can encode. An arbitrarily small open patch can contain enough information for smooth uniqueness, while the entire boundary can fail in a broader coefficient class.

This is information-theoretic uniqueness, however, rather than a promise of practical imaging accuracy. An infinite collection of exact boundary measurements can determine an unknown even when reconstruction from finitely many noisy measurements is extremely unstable.

6. The main idea

Continue a geometric match through the interior

For M2, boundary measurements first determine all boundary derivatives of the metric in suitable coordinates. The argument attaches a small exterior region where the two geometries agree. Equality of boundary response then supplies equality of Green functions there. A Green function describes the response to a concentrated interior source.

Solutions generated from that exterior region distinguish interior points and provide enough harmonic functions to form local coordinates. The task becomes extending an existing match across any proposed frontier.

The manuscript constructs a mixed Green kernel, satisfying one metric’s equation in one variable and the other metric’s equation in the second. Its flux through a small moving sphere transfers harmonic functions from one geometry to the other. The transfer reproduces constants and coordinate functions, so their contributions cancel in a Taylor expansion.

The crucial claimed estimate remains uniform as the spheres shrink. Finite harmonic tests with sufficiently many independent second derivatives convert this control into an improved bound for the difference of normalized inverse metrics: a provisional bound of order rrr improves to order r3/2r^{3/2}r3/2, where rrr is sphere radius. With a single spatial rescaling held fixed, the radius can tend to zero, forcing agreement on an actual neighborhood.

The argument retains second-order terms caused by moving the spheres; treating all geometric errors as lower-order terms would miss the needed estimate. Harmonic coordinates then remove the remaining conformal factor. Global source evaluations prevent ambiguous identifications and eliminate interior frontiers.

Handle matrix-valued transport as well

M1 develops the analogous mechanism for vector-valued solutions. A harmonic frame simplifies the operator, but the transfer still has a matrix-valued first moment. Unlike scalar coordinate displacement, that moment cannot simply be normalized away.

The manuscript organizes its nonscalar components into a differential system related to conformal Killing fields, infinitesimal transformations preserving angles. In dimension at least three, this system has a finite-type property: sufficiently high derivatives are determined by finitely many lower derivatives. This improves the first-moment estimate enough to close the shrinking-sphere argument for both metric and connection.

The scalar companion supplies analytic methods, not a shortcut that applies a scalar uniqueness theorem directly to matrix measurements.

Make every rough harmonic solution share a hidden average

M3 uses a different mechanism. It first constructs a block with one parent and two child torus boundaries. Two selected voltage solutions control all current triples whose sum is zero. An exact scalarization step replaces an anisotropic tensor by one positive scalar coefficient while preserving both selected voltage-and-flux responses.

Nested copies of the block force every global harmonic function uuu to have the same weighted average u∗u_*u∗​ on the relevant internal surfaces. The construction produces a nonzero bounded function www, vanishing near the exterior boundary, with a special source-annihilation identity involving every such uuu.

For small nonzero δ\deltaδ, put

ρ=1+δw,γ~=ρ2γ,u~=u∗+u−u∗ρ. ho=1+\delta w,\qquad\widetilde\gamma= ho^2\gamma,\qquad\widetilde u=u_*+ rac{u-u_*}{ ho}.ρ=1+δw,γ​=ρ2γ,u=u∗​+ρu−u∗​​.

The identity makes u~\widetilde uu solve the new conductivity equation. Since ρ=1 ho=1ρ=1 in an outer collar, voltage and flux there stay unchanged. Thus every boundary response agrees even though the interior coefficient changes.

The intermediate scalarization preserves only two designated responses. The nested construction and the identity for every harmonic uuu are what promote that finite-input statement to equality of the full operator. Mere approximation by rapidly oscillating scalar materials would not establish this exact conclusion.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The smooth results assume exact zero-frequency data, arbitrary smoothness up to a smooth boundary, and dimension at least three. They give uniqueness modulo the stated symmetries, without a quantitative noise-stability estimate or a finite-measurement reconstruction algorithm.

M1 concerns a fixed trivial rank-two Hermitian bundle. More general bundles, other ranks, additional unknown matrix potentials and lower coefficient regularity require separate statements.

M3 gives a three-dimensional counterexample with some finite ellipticity contrast C/cC/cC/c. It does not prescribe arbitrarily small contrast, prove nonuniqueness in every higher dimension, or locate a sharp regularity threshold between known uniqueness classes and bounded measurability. Its conclusion also does not contradict planar measurable uniqueness.

The family therefore leaves substantial questions about intermediate regularity, quantitative reconstruction and the extension of joint recovery to more general geometric systems.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary historical papers linked above trace smooth scalar uniqueness, analytic geometric recovery, the Poisson embedding approach, connection recovery and low-regularity conductivity theory. For background terminology, Wikipedia’s articles on Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps and connections on vector bundles provide optional complements to the definitions here.

The three manuscripts below are read together as one family. Their conclusions are reported as stated; the distinction between smooth recovery and measurable nonuniqueness is essential to interpreting them.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Determination of a metric and a unitary connection from one boundary patch (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Smooth anisotropic uniqueness in the Calderón problem from one boundary patch (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Nonuniqueness for bounded measurable scalar conductivities in three dimensions (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Two Boltzmann evolutions with the same data and exact local conservation
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 363 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

The Boltzmann equation describes a dilute gas through a density of particles in position and velocity. Particles travel freely between binary collisions, while each collision conserves momentum and kinetic energy. The entropy inequality supplies an additional direction of time.

Do these requirements determine the gas’s future uniquely from its initial density? For sufficiently controlled data and solutions, many uniqueness theorems answer yes. For the broad class allowed by finite mass, energy and entropy, the issue is more delicate: the density may concentrate strongly in space even when these global quantities are finite.

Family 363 claims nonuniqueness for one such rough datum on a periodic three-dimensional box. The stronger manuscript, M1, constructs two global solutions with exactly the same initial density, both satisfying the entropy inequality and exact local conservation of mass, momentum and kinetic energy.
