The initial velocities are bounded, but the density amplitudes become unbounded on smaller and smaller spatial scales. The claim is therefore about weak entropy solutions for singular data, not two smooth classical evolutions from a well-controlled smooth initial gas.

2. Background and essential definitions

Transport plus elastic collisions

The position space is the unit three-torus T3=R3/Z3\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3T3=R3/Z3, which imposes periodic boundary conditions. Velocities lie in R3\mathbb R^3R3. A nonnegative density F(t,x,v)F(t,x,v)F(t,x,v) satisfies

∂tF+v⋅∇xF=Q(F,F).\partial_tF+v\cdot\nabla_xF=Q(F,F).∂t​F+v⋅∇x​F=Q(F,F).

The left side is free transport. The collision term splits into gain and loss,

Q(F,F)=Q+(F,F)−Q−(F,F).Q(F,F)=Q^+(F,F)-Q^-(F,F).Q(F,F)=Q+(F,F)−Q−(F,F).

Gain counts collisions producing velocity vvv; loss counts particles leaving that velocity through collisions.

For another velocity v∗v_*v∗​ and a unit collision direction ω∈S2\omega\in S^2ω∈S2, put

a=(v−v∗)⋅ω,v′=v−aω,v∗′=v∗+aω.a=(v-v_*)\cdot\omega,\qquad v'=v-a\omega,\qquad v_*'=v_*+a\omega.a=(v−v∗​)⋅ω,v′=v−aω,v∗′​=v∗​+aω.

These elastic collision rules preserve v+v∗v+v_*v+v∗​ and ∣v∣2+∣v∗∣2|v|^2+|v_*|^2∣v∣2+∣v∗​∣2. With the manuscript’s hard-sphere normalization,

Q(F,F)(v)=∫R3×S2∣a∣(F(v′)F(v∗′)−F(v)F(v∗)) dv∗ dω,Q(F,F)(v)=\int_{\mathbb R^3\times S^2}|a|\bigl(F(v')F(v_*')-F(v)F(v_*)\bigr)\,dv_*\,d\omega,Q(F,F)(v)=∫R3×S2​∣a∣(F(v′)F(v∗′​)−F(v)F(v∗​))dv∗​dω,

where every factor has the same t,xt,xt,x. The relative normal speed ∣a∣|a|∣a∣ is the hard-sphere collision kernel.

Entropy and renormalization

Finite mass, energy and absolute entropy mean

∫T3×R3F0(1+∣v∣2+∣log⁡F0∣) dx dv<∞,\int_{\mathbb T^3\times\mathbb R^3}F_0\bigl(1+|v|^2+|\log F_0|\bigr)\,dx\,dv<\infty,∫T3×R3​F0​(1+∣v∣2+∣logF0​∣)dxdv<∞,

with 0∣log⁡0∣=00|\log0|=00∣log0∣=0. These integral bounds allow high narrow peaks. Because collisions are quadratic in FFF, they do not automatically make the collision term integrable.

A renormalized solution therefore satisfies equations for bounded-growth transformations of the density. Using the reference Maxwellian

M(v)=(2π)−3/2e−∣v∣2/2,M(v)=(2\pi)^{-3/2}e^{-|v|^2/2},M(v)=(2π)−3/2e−∣v∣2/2,

the manuscripts test the equation through Mβ(F/M)M\beta(F/M)Mβ(F/M), where β(0)=0\beta(0)=0β(0)=0 and ∣β′(z)∣≤C/(1+z)|\beta'(z)|\le C/(1+z)∣β′(z)∣≤C/(1+z). This weakens the effect of large amplitudes while retaining the transport and collision structure.

The relative entropy is

HM(F)=∫(Flog⁡(F/M)−F+M) dx dv.H_M(F)=\int\bigl(F\log(F/M)-F+M\bigr)\,dx\,dv.HM​(F)=∫(Flog(F/M)−F+M)dxdv.

The entropy inequality states that this quantity plus accumulated nonnegative Boltzmann collision dissipation does not exceed its initial value. In the mathematical sign convention, entropy decreases; physical thermodynamic entropy has the opposite sign.

Local conservation is stronger than a total bound

The five collision invariants are

ψ(v)∈{1,v1,v2,v3,∣v∣2/2}.\psi(v)\in\{1,v_1,v_2,v_3,|v|^2/2\}.ψ(v)∈{1,v1​,v2​,v3​,∣v∣2/2}.

Exact local conservation means

∂t∫Fψ dv+∇x⋅∫vFψ dv=0\partial_t\int F\psi\,dv+\nabla_x\cdot\int vF\psi\,dv=0∂t​∫Fψdv+∇x​⋅∫vFψdv=0

in distributions, including the prescribed initial traces. These are mass, three momentum components and kinetic energy. They describe balances in each spatial region, not merely a global energy inequality. The energy flux involves a third velocity moment, so its integrability is part of the issue.

3. Development history and previous partial results

DiPerna and Lions established global existence and weak stability for renormalized Boltzmann solutions with finite mass, energy and entropy. Their theory is a foundational existence result, but it does not automatically give uniqueness at that level of regularity. Passing momentum and energy identities through weak limits can also introduce defects, even when local mass conservation survives.

Uniqueness holds in stronger classes. Kaniel and Shinbrot used Maxwellian upper bounds in local theory, while Ukai proved global uniqueness for small periodic perturbations of a Maxwellian in weighted Sobolev spaces. Duan, Huang, Wang and Yang allowed large bounded amplitudes under additional smallness conditions. The unbounded spatial peaks in the present construction place it outside those classes; small relative entropy alone is not enough to invoke their uniqueness theorem.

The spatially homogeneous problem is different. Mischler and Wennberg established uniqueness for conservative hard-sphere evolution with finite mass and energy. Wennberg’s homogeneous nonuniqueness examples for hard potentials permit increasing energy. Family 363 instead uses spatial concentration and, in M1, preserves energy locally.

Recent ill-posedness results also require a distinction. Chen and Holmer, Chen–Shen–Zhang, and Chen–Guo–Shen–Zhang for hard spheres study failures of uniform continuity of solution maps in various rough norms. They compare nearby initial states. Two evolutions from exactly the same datum are a stronger type of failure of well-posedness.

Within this family, M2 develops the concentrating-jet mechanism and obtains nonuniqueness in a global admissible entropy class. M1 retains that mechanism but constructs the global continuation directly, with additional estimates that preserve all local conservation laws. This stronger conservation statement is the principal distinction between the two manuscripts.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: two global solutions with all five local balances

The October manuscript claims one nonnegative datum F0F_0F0​, supported in a bounded velocity ball, with finite mass, energy and absolute entropy, for which there are two distinct global entropy solutions. They differ on a set of positive spacetime–velocity measure, not just on a choice of values on a null set.

Both satisfy the renormalized equation, the full entropy-dissipation inequality and exact local mass, momentum and kinetic-energy conservation with the given initial traces. Both are strongly continuous for all time in L1L^1L1:

F∈C([0,∞);L1(T3×R3)).F\in C([0,\infty);L^1(\mathbb T^3\times\mathbb R^3)).F∈C([0,∞);L1(T3×R3)).

This means the integral of ∣F(t)−F(s)∣|F(t)-F(s)|∣F(t)−F(s)∣ tends to zero as t→st\to st→s, including at the initial time.

For every finite TTT and every polynomial weight exponent k≥0k\ge0k≥0, each solution also satisfies

∫0T∫⟨v⟩k(Q+(F,F)+Q−(F,F)) dx dv dt<∞,\int_0^T\int \langle v\rangle^k\bigl(Q^+(F,F)+Q^-(F,F)\bigr)\,dx\,dv\,dt<\infty,∫0T​∫⟨v⟩k(Q+(F,F)+Q−(F,F))dxdvdt<∞,

where ⟨v⟩=1+∣v∣2\langle v\rangle=\sqrt{1+|v|^2}⟨v⟩=1+∣v∣2​. The gains and losses are separately integrable, so the conclusion is not based on canceling two undefined infinite collision terms. This control permits the ordinary distributional equation and the local invariant balances.

M2: the earlier entropy-class construction

M2 claims two global renormalized solutions for one finite-entropy datum with bounded velocity support. They conserve local mass and total momentum, and satisfy global energy and entropy-dissipation inequalities. On a common initial interval they are strongly L1L^1L1-continuous and have integrable gain and loss terms.

M2 does not require exact local momentum and energy conservation in its admissibility definition. Its initial-interval integrability statement is also narrower than M1’s weighted collision integrability on every finite horizon. These qualifications should not be erased by describing both results simply as “nonuniqueness for Boltzmann.”

The existence statements concern constructed data and solution pairs. They do not assert nonuniqueness for every finite-entropy datum or for a dense class of data.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claims. Nonuniqueness in the large-data entropy theory would be a major boundary on determinism at weak regularity for a central kinetic equation. M1 strengthens that boundary by retaining the local conservation laws built into individual elastic collisions.

The example would show that imposing positivity, entropy dissipation, strong initial traces and exact mass–momentum–energy balances is still insufficient to select one evolution for all rough data. Additional regularity or another selection principle would be needed to recover uniqueness in such a broad class.

This is a statement about the mathematical solution class. It does not claim that the deterministic motion of a specified finite collection of hard spheres has two futures, nor that the well-posed smooth or perturbative Boltzmann theories are invalid.

The global continuation estimate is significant in its own right: it keeps collision products integrable despite an initial density with arbitrarily high spatial amplitudes.

6. The main idea

Concentrate cold jets while keeping total entropy finite

The datum contains narrow velocity distributions near two opposite axial directions. These are called cold jets because their velocity spread is small, not because they have zero kinetic energy.

At a spatial scale sss, a jet occupies a thin transverse annulus. Its velocity-integrated density can be of order 1/s1/s1/s, while its total mass is of order s2s^2s2. The entropy contribution is of order s2(1+∣log⁡s∣)s^2(1+|\log s|)s2(1+∣logs∣). Choosing geometrically decreasing scales makes the total mass and entropy finite despite unbounded amplitudes.

Opposite streams occupy fine alternating spatial stripes. At the original scale, separation suppresses their direct interactions. Under dilation near the accumulating spatial singularity, the stripes average to a medium containing both streams.

The argument assigns auxiliary colors to cold components. Same-color collisions retain their color; interactions between colors or with a designated hot component contribute to that hot component. This is bookkeeping: summing the colored equations gives the original Boltzmann equation, with no extra physical species.

Amplify a seed that disappears from the initial data

One approximation family starts with no extra hot population and remains comparatively dormant. Another starts with a smooth hot seed whose mass, energy and entropy tend to zero as more jet scales are included.

The seed is adjusted until the hot component reaches a prescribed time-dependent weighted bound, or cap. Both approximation families approach the same initial datum. A sufficiently strong gain mechanism can nevertheless make their later limits differ.

A cap hit alone is not enough. Its height might be carried by a set of vanishing mass and disappear in the weak limit. The source therefore analyzes gain kernels to prevent concentration from erasing the event.

Carleman’s representation expresses gain through integrals over velocity planes. Near the velocity axis, two successive gains give the needed nonconcentration. Away from the axis, repeated gains spread the relevant parameters into time, position and velocity. These estimates show that dilation at a cap time produces a nonzero hot limit.

A linear branching limit separates the evolutions

Under the dilation, the cold jets form a two-stream background, while the normalized hot component obeys a linear Boltzmann equation in that background. Strong convergence of suitable velocity averages identifies the cold–hot interaction; weak convergence alone would not justify multiplying the limits.

The linear equation has a branching interpretation in the color bookkeeping: one hot particle colliding with a cold particle produces two hot outputs. Selected finite collision histories yield definite mass growth inside expanding boxes.

If the rescaled observation horizon were infinite, repeated growth would exceed the polynomial bound inherited from the cap. The horizon must therefore remain finite, making the cap scale comparable to the original observation horizon.

The dormant solution has a vanishing normalized limit away from the velocity axis. If the two global solutions coincided at arbitrarily short relevant horizons, comparison of their dilations would force the nonzero hot limit to vanish. This is the proposed separation argument. Branching here concerns the auxiliary labels, not creation of physical particles or energy.

M1 keeps the construction conservative for all time

Periodic space creates a new difficulty: jets eventually encounter their periodic copies. M1 chooses an irrational axis and gives each scale a finite lifetime as a separate cold component. The geometric separation lasts long enough for that schedule.

A surrounding nearly Maxwellian bath supplies a positive collision frequency after a fixed short time. Cold jets then decay, allowing each component to be transferred into a controlled remainder at the end of its lifetime. The decomposition changes, but the total density still solves the same equation.

The global estimate combines small velocity mass, small spatially integrated excess over the Maxwellian, and averaging along free flights. Together these control the nonlinear gain and close a weighted supremum estimate for the remainder, even though no common finite bound holds for all initial cold amplitudes.

The contributions of small scales to weighted collision integrals are summable. This is what lets local momentum and energy conservation, as well as strong time traces, pass to the global limit. M1 therefore does more than attach an arbitrary weak continuation to the early-time nonuniqueness construction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The equation is the spatially inhomogeneous periodic three-dimensional hard-sphere Boltzmann equation with its stated elastic collision kernel. The theorem is not a homogeneous nonuniqueness result and does not automatically extend to other kernels or the whole-space problem.

The datum has bounded velocity support but unbounded spatial amplitudes. These are not smooth bounded-data counterexamples to classical uniqueness. The construction’s small relative entropy does not put it inside uniqueness classes that also require weighted amplitude control.

M1’s exact local conservation is stronger than global inequalities; M2’s original class does not include all those local identities. Both distinctions remain relevant when comparing to other weak-solution theories.

Questions about additional uniqueness criteria, physical approximation procedures that select one solution, and the range of data exhibiting this behavior remain separate. The two construction mechanisms and their conservation claims are reported as stated, without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 is the October 5 manuscript with global local-conservation and weighted collision-integrability claims. M2 supplies the earlier concentrating-jet mechanism and a weaker global admissibility class.

Primary background includes DiPerna–Lions on global existence and weak stability, Mischler–Wennberg on conservative homogeneous uniqueness, Duan–Huang–Wang–Yang on large bounded amplitudes, and the hard-sphere instability result. They address different solution classes or different meanings of ill-posedness.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Nonuniqueness with local conservation for the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Nonuniqueness for the periodic hard-sphere Boltzmann equation (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why seven is the first dimension for singular Bernoulli minimizers
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 367 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Many variational problems choose both a function and the region where that function is active. The edge of that region is a free boundary: it is part of the answer rather than part of the prescribed data.

In the one-phase Bernoulli problem, energy penalizes both changes in the function and the volume of its positive region. Minimizers usually have smooth free boundaries, but in sufficiently high dimension a singular cone can also minimize energy. What is the first dimension in which this happens?

Family 367 claims that the answer is seven. More precisely, every nonzero homogeneous global minimizer in dimensions at most six is flat, while a nonflat example exists in dimension seven. The seven-dimensional example is an established result of De Silva and Jerison. The new contribution is the claimed exclusion of dimensions five and six without a symmetry assumption.

This threshold also governs singularities of general local minimizers. Below seven there would be no interior singular points; in dimension seven they would be locally finite; above seven their Hausdorff dimension would be at most the ambient dimension minus seven.

2. Background and essential definitions

An energy with an unknown active region

For a nonnegative function vvv on a ball B⊂RdB\subset\mathbb R^dB⊂Rd, consider

J(v;B)=∫B(∣∇v∣2+1{v>0}) dx.J(v;B)=\int_B\bigl(|\nabla v|^2+\mathbf1_{\{v>0\}}\bigr)\,dx.J(v;B)=∫B​(∣∇v∣2+1{v>0}​)dx.

The symbol 1{v>0}\mathbf1_{\{v>0\}}1{v>0}​ equals one in the positive region and zero elsewhere, so its integral is the volume of that region. The gradient term favors gentle variation; the volume term discourages spreading the positive phase unnecessarily.

The function belongs to H1(B)H^1(B)H1(B), the Sobolev space of square-integrable functions with square-integrable weak first derivatives. A competitor has the same boundary values in the Sobolev trace sense. Equivalently, its difference from the original function lies in H01(B)H^1_0(B)H01​(B), the closure of compactly supported smooth functions in the H1H^1H1 norm.

A global minimizer on Rd\mathbb R^dRd minimizes this energy in every ball against all such competitors. This does not mean that its total energy over the whole space is finite. A local minimizer in an open set DDD has the corresponding comparison property on every ball compactly contained in DDD.

Inside {u>0}\{u>0\}{u>0}, a minimizer is harmonic:

Δu=0.\Delta u=0.Δu=0.

At a smooth free boundary the normalized Bernoulli conditions are u=0u=0u=0 and ∣∇u∣=1|\nabla u|=1∣∇u∣=1, with the gradient taken from the positive side. These conditions describe the balance between changing Dirichlet energy and changing positive-phase volume.

Flat solutions and cones

The simplest solution is

u(x)=(x⋅e)+,∣e∣=1,u(x)=(x\cdot e)_+,\qquad |e|=1,u(x)=(x⋅e)+​,∣e∣=1,

where s+=max⁡{s,0}s_+=\max\{s,0\}s+​=max{s,0}. Its positive region is a half-space and its free boundary is a hyperplane. This is called a flat solution.

A function is one-homogeneous if

u(rx)=r u(x)(r>0).u(rx)=r\,u(x)\qquad(r>0).u(rx)=ru(x)(r>0).

Its positivity region is unchanged by dilation, hence is a cone. A nonflat homogeneous minimizer has geometry that cannot be smoothed away by simply zooming in at its vertex.

The critical dimension d∗d_*d∗​ is the smallest dimension containing a nonzero, nonflat, one-homogeneous global minimizer. It concerns global energy minimality, not merely solutions of the differential equation or cones stable under a restricted set of perturbations.

Blow-ups and singular points

At a free-boundary point x0x_0x0​, the natural rescaling is

ux0,r(y)=u(x0+ry)r.u_{x_0,r}(y)=\frac{u(x_0+ry)}{r}.ux0​,r​(y)=ru(x0​+ry)​.

Established compactness and monotonicity theory yields homogeneous global minimizers as limits along suitable sequences r↓0r\downarrow0r↓0. Such limits are called blow-ups.

A point is regular if at least one blow-up is flat. Improvement-of-flatness theory then makes the nearby free boundary smooth. A point is singular if no flat blow-up exists. Thus classifying minimizing cones controls the local geometry of far more general functions.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Alt and Caffarelli established the basic existence and regularity theory for this energy. Caffarelli’s later Harnack-inequality method connected flatness to regularity. De Silva developed another improvement-of-flatness approach, and work with Ferrari and Salsa supplied higher regularity for relevant free boundaries.

Weiss’s monotonicity and dimension-reduction theory connected singularities to homogeneous minimizing blow-ups. This explains why identifying d∗d_*d∗​ is a structural question: its value determines a general bound on the size of singular sets.

Caffarelli, Jerison and Kenig obtained three-dimensional rigidity for the relevant stable homogeneous solutions. Jerison and Savin extended flatness through dimension four for stable cones with smooth spherical cross-section, implying that minimizing free boundaries are regular there. Consequently, the critical dimension was at least five.

In the other direction, De Silva and Jerison constructed a singular homogeneous global minimizer in dimension seven. Its minimality is against all Sobolev competitors with the same boundary trace, not just symmetric or homogeneous competitors. These results left

5≤d∗≤7.5\le d_*\le7.5≤d∗​≤7.

Recent work by Firester, Tsiamis and Wang studies stability of cones with specified bi-orthogonal symmetry, showing a threshold at seven within that family. Their capillary-cone work constructs further minimizing examples, including another in dimension seven. Such symmetry-based classifications do not exclude arbitrary nonsymmetric minimizing cones in dimensions five and six.

Two other advances address related but distinct questions. Fernández-Real and Serra treat arbitrary entire classical stable solutions in dimension four, without a homogeneity assumption. Fernández-Real and Yu obtain regularity through dimension six for almost every parameter in an admissible increasing family of boundary data. A generic-data theorem allows exceptional parameters; the present claim concerns every minimizer in the stated class.

4. What the new manuscript claims

The main theorem states that every nonzero one-homogeneous global minimizer in Rd\mathbb R^dRd, for 1≤d≤61\le d\le61≤d≤6, is a half-space solution. Combining this with the established seven-dimensional example gives

d∗=7.d_*=7.d∗​=7.

For every nonnegative local minimizer in an open set D⊂RnD\subset\mathbb R^nD⊂Rn, the manuscript then claims that the interior free boundary is smooth away from its singular set Sing⁡(u)\operatorname{Sing}(u)Sing(u), with:

  • No singular points when n≤6n\le6n≤6.
  • Only finitely many singular points in every compact interior region when n=7n=7n=7.
  • The bound dim⁡HSing⁡(u)≤n−7\dim_{\mathrm H}\operatorname{Sing}(u)\le n-7dimH​Sing(u)≤n−7 for n≥7n\ge7n≥7.

Hausdorff dimension extends the idea of dimension to irregular sets. A zero-dimensional bound alone need not mean local finiteness, so the seven-dimensional conclusion is stronger than simply substituting n=7n=7n=7 into the displayed dimension bound.

The bound is claimed sharp in every n≥7n\ge7n≥7. Let UUU be the De Silva–Jerison minimizer on R7\mathbb R^7R7, and define

Un(x,y)=U(x),(x,y)∈R7×Rn−7.U_n(x,y)=U(x),\qquad (x,y)\in\mathbb R^7\times\mathbb R^{n-7}.Un​(x,y)=U(x),(x,y)∈R7×Rn−7.

This remains a global minimizer. Its singular set contains {0}×Rn−7\{0\}\times\mathbb R^{n-7}{0}×Rn−7, giving dimension at least n−7n-7n−7; the upper bound makes the dimension exactly that value.

The theorem does not classify all seven-dimensional minimizing cones or assert that all singularities resemble one unique cone.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the result determines the exact singularity threshold for a central free-boundary variational problem and yields optimal regularity conclusions in every ambient dimension.

Its force comes from the passage between scales. A statement about scale-invariant global objects rules out local singularities for arbitrary minimizers in dimensions up to six. Above the threshold, the same classification fixes the maximal dimension of the singular set.

The result also clarifies the analogy with minimal-surface theory, where curvature, stability and dimension determine when singular cones become possible. The Bernoulli problem has its own energy and boundary conditions, so that analogy motivates methods without making the two theories identical.

6. The main idea

Reduce the unknown cases to one spherical problem

Assume the first nonflat minimizing cone occurs in dimension five or six. Any singularity away from its vertex would, after another blow-up, give a lower-dimensional nonflat minimizer. By the choice of the first dimension, this cannot happen. Its intersection with the unit sphere is therefore smooth away from the special points introduced below.

A five-dimensional minimizer can be extended to six dimensions by making it independent of an extra coordinate. This preserves minimality. Its spherical cross-section acquires two suspension tips, corresponding to the two directions of the added axis. Both possible dimensions can then be studied on a region Ω⊂S5\Omega\subset S^5Ω⊂S5, with smooth boundary except possibly at those two tips.

Write ggg for the restriction of the cone function to the sphere. The tensor

T=∇S52g+gI,w=∣T∣,T=\nabla^2_{S^5}g+gI,\qquad w=|T|,T=∇S52​g+gI,w=∣T∣,

encodes the relevant angular Hessian; III is the identity on tangent directions. For a flat linear solution this tensor vanishes. A nonflat component supplies a nonzero tensor somewhere.

Keep the shape of the Hessian

Stability is a necessary consequence of minimality: the second variation cannot be negative. It compares the energy of a test function with a curvature contribution on the free boundary.

Earlier approaches used a power of the Hessian norm, roughly waw^awa, as the test function. The difficulty is that interior and boundary estimates impose competing restrictions. Taking only the norm discards how the Hessian’s eigenvalues are arranged, even though that arrangement affects both estimates.

The manuscript builds two objects together: a scalar test hhh, and a vector field ZZZ whose divergence controls the test’s energy. Both depend on the normalized tensor T/wT/wT/w, together with ggg, its gradient and suitable derivative data. Keeping the same tensor information in both constructions is the proposed way around the incompatible estimates.

Create a strict surplus against stability

With a fixed exponent a∈(1/2,1)a\in(1/2,1)a∈(1/2,1), the claimed pointwise inequalities have the form

div⁡Z≥∣∇h∣2+4h2+ε∗w2a,\operatorname{div}Z\ge |\nabla h|^2+4h^2+\varepsilon_*w^{2a},divZ≥∣∇h∣2+4h2+ε∗​w2a,

and, on the regular boundary,

N⋅Z+Hh2≥0.N\cdot Z+Hh^2\ge0.N⋅Z+Hh2≥0.

Here ε∗>0\varepsilon_*>0ε∗​>0, NNN is the inward unit normal, and HHH is the specified sum of principal curvatures. The positive term ε∗w2a\varepsilon_*w^{2a}ε∗​w2a is the decisive surplus. After integration, the divergence theorem and stability give incompatible bounds unless the Hessian vanishes.

The coefficient four comes from the six-dimensional spherical stability formulation. These are dimension-specific estimates, not inequalities asserted on arbitrary manifolds.

Two cancellations reduce the calculation to finitely many normalized tensors. Interior contractions cancel fourth derivatives; boundary reflection removes derivative components not determined by the boundary conditions. The manuscript supplies weighted sums of tensor squares and rational remainder bounds for the resulting algebraic inequalities. These finite calculations are part of its stated argument.

Do not ignore the places where normalization fails

The expression T/wT/wT/w is undefined where w=0w=0w=0. The suspension tips also prevent direct integration over a wholly smooth compact region. Removing these sets without control would leave a gap in the intended comparison.

The manuscript uses a regularized Bochner identity to obtain an integrable derivative weight near Hessian zeros. Explicit suspension formulas provide integrable powers of distance near the two tips. Smooth cutoffs then remove both kinds of exceptional set, with errors tending to zero.

A genuinely nonflat component retains positive surplus in the limit, contradicting stability. This excludes both candidate dimensions. Standard dimension reduction and the known seven-dimensional example then yield the sharp singular-set statement.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The energy has constant volume coefficient one and a single nonnegative phase. Variable coefficients, two-phase problems and other free-boundary energies require their own statements. The conclusions are interior; boundary-contact behavior is not included.

The central classification concerns homogeneous global minimizers. It does not say that every entire stable solution in dimensions five or six is one-dimensional, nor that every stationary cone is flat. Minimality against arbitrary Sobolev competitors is the operative hypothesis.

In dimension seven, local finiteness allows infinitely many singular points approaching the boundary of the ambient domain or escaping to infinity. In higher dimensions, the Hausdorff bound alone is not a complete structural description of the singular set.

Classification of all cones at and above the threshold, uniqueness of singular blow-ups and sharper quantitative geometry remain distinct questions from identifying the critical dimension.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary papers linked above trace the Alt–Caffarelli theory, Weiss’s dimension reduction, Jerison–Savin rigidity and the De Silva–Jerison singular example. Velichkov’s Regularity of the One-phase Free Boundaries develops the background used to pass from cone classification to local regularity.

The manuscript below supplies the claimed exclusion in dimensions five and six. Its finite tensor calculations are reported as part of the source’s argument, not independently certified here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The critical dimension for one-phase Bernoulli minimizers (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why optimal image edges should consist of arcs, tips and triple junctions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 366 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

An image contains gradual shading and sharp boundaries. A useful mathematical reconstruction should smooth noise without blurring every edge. The Mumford–Shah model balances these two goals by choosing both a reconstructed image and a set of edges.

The resulting question is surprisingly geometric: must an optimal edge set look locally like an ordinary curve, a curve ending at a tip, or three curves meeting at equal angles? Or could minimizing energy produce infinitely complicated branching and accumulating tiny cracks?

Family 366 claims the expected interior classification for planar absolute minimizers with bounded image data. It also claims that only finitely many connected components of the entire edge set can meet any region strictly inside the image domain. A consequence gives a sharp form of control on how large the image gradient can become near crack tips.

The result concerns the continuum variational problem. It is not a convergence theorem for a particular image-processing algorithm or a statement that every stationary numerical output has this geometry.

2. Background and essential definitions

The three costs

Let Ω⊂R2\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2Ω⊂R2 be a bounded domain with Lipschitz boundary, meaning that its boundary is locally a graph with bounded slope. Let ggg be a bounded real-valued image, interpreted as intensity. We choose a function uuu and a relatively closed set K⊂ΩK\subset\OmegaK⊂Ω, across which uuu may jump.

The normalized energy is

Fg(u,K)=∫Ω∖K∣∇u∣2 dx+H1(K)+∫Ω∣u−g∣2 dx.F_g(u,K)=\int_{\Omega\setminus K}|\nabla u|^2\,dx+\mathcal H^1(K)+\int_\Omega|u-g|^2\,dx.Fg​(u,K)=∫Ω∖K​∣∇u∣2dx+H1(K)+∫Ω​∣u−g∣2dx.

The first term penalizes rapid variation away from edges. The second charges their length; H1\mathcal H^1H1 is one-dimensional Hausdorff measure, which agrees with ordinary arc length on curves. The third is the fidelity term, penalizing disagreement with the observed image.

Allowing a jump can reduce the gradient cost, but creating an edge is not free. For example, replacing a sharp brightness transition by a very narrow smooth ramp makes the gradient large. An actual jump avoids that cost while paying for the separating curve.

Admissibility requires finite edge length, u∈L2(Ω)u\in L^2(\Omega)u∈L2(Ω), and square-integrable weak derivatives on Ω∖K\Omega\setminus KΩ∖K. The Sobolev notation for the last condition is u∈W1,2(Ω∖K)u\in W^{1,2}(\Omega\setminus K)u∈W1,2(Ω∖K). No initial assumption says that KKK is already made of curves.

Absolute minimality and reduction

An absolute minimizer cannot be improved by any admissible change supported compactly inside Ω\OmegaΩ. Both the function and the edge set may change. This is stronger than vanishing first variation, and it is not restricted to small deformations preserving the topology of the cracks.

A pair is reduced if every interior disk centered on KKK contains positive length of KKK. This removes irrelevant decorations such as an isolated point added to an otherwise valid edge set: such additions cost no length and do not change the energy, but would spoil a geometric classification of the literal closed set.

A C1,αC^{1,\alpha}C1,α arc has a continuous tangent that varies Hölder continuously. Informally, tangent changes over distance rrr are bounded by a constant times rαr^\alpharα, for some α>0\alpha>0α>0. This gives a quantitative form of having no corner along an individual arc.

Weak integrability at a tip

The model crack-tip function, in polar coordinates around its endpoint, is

u(r,θ)=2rπsin⁡θ2,−π<θ<π.u(r,\theta)=\sqrt{\frac{2r}{\pi}}\sin\frac\theta2,\qquad -\pi<\theta<\pi.u(r,θ)=π2r​​sin2θ​,−π<θ<π.

The crack is the negative horizontal ray. Its gradient behaves like r−1/2r^{-1/2}r−1/2, so it becomes unbounded near the endpoint while retaining finite Dirichlet energy.

A function qqq is in weak L4L^4L4, written L4,∞L^{4,\infty}L4,∞, if its large-value sets satisfy an estimate of the form

∣{x:∣q(x)∣>t}∣≤Ct−4.|\{x:|q(x)|>t\}|\le C t^{-4}.∣{x:∣q(x)∣>t}∣≤Ct−4.

The vertical bars here denote area. This is weaker than integrability of ∣q∣4|q|^4∣q∣4, but stronger than an arbitrary LpL^pLp bound with one fixed p<4p<4p<4.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Mumford and Shah’s original work introduced the model through image segmentation and formulated the expectation that optimal edges should have simple geometry. Establishing existence already required a framework that permits discontinuities while controlling their size.

De Giorgi and Ambrosio developed the free-discontinuity setting, and Ambrosio established compactness and existence results. De Giorgi, Carriero and Leaci connected weak minimizers to a formulation with a closed discontinuity set. These results make it possible to study minimizers without assuming their edges are smooth in advance.

Bonnet developed planar blow-up and monotonicity methods and classified global minimizers with connected crack set. David and Ambrosio–Fusco–Pallara established regularity on large portions of the edge set; David also developed triple-junction regularity. Bonnet and David proved that the crack-tip model is globally minimizing. David and Léger classified global minimizers whose crack disconnects the plane.

These achievements left a specific obstruction in the limiting geometry: bounded components of a generalized global crack when its complement remains connected. Excluding such compact pieces is the new manuscript’s central task.

Higher-integrability results by De Lellis–Focardi and De Philippis–Figalli strengthened analytic control of gradients and exceptional sets. Crack-tip regularity received separate treatment by Andersson–Mikayelyan and De Lellis–Focardi–Ghinassi, including a correction to the latter work. The De Lellis–Focardi monograph assembles the compactness, classification and endpoint regularity statements used by this manuscript.

There is also an immediately preceding claim. Deangelis’s September 2026 preprint gives a compact-translation argument for global classification and the resulting interior regularity. The present manuscript explicitly credits it. Deangelis uses relaxed second variations, a planar Hodge identity and holomorphic rigidity; this manuscript uses finite translations and a scalar harmonic interaction. The family should therefore be read as a claimed resolution with a related contemporary predecessor, not as the first appearance of every conclusion it states.

4. What the new manuscript claims

Let (u,K)(u,K)(u,K) be a reduced absolute minimizer for the energy above, with bounded fidelity datum ggg. The manuscript claims that every point x∈Kx\in Kx∈K has an interior neighborhood in which exactly one of the following descriptions applies:

  • One embedded C1,αC^{1,\alpha}C1,α arc passes through xxx.
  • One such arc ends at xxx.
  • Three such arcs meet only at xxx, with pairwise angles of 120∘120^\circ120∘.

The arcs are locally non-self-intersecting. The conclusion rules out crossings, higher-order junctions and other irregular interior points for this minimizing class.

For every open UUU whose closure is compact and contained in Ω\OmegaΩ, it also claims

#{C: C is a connected component of K, C∩U≠∅}<∞.\#\{C:\ C\text{ is a connected component of }K,\ C\cap U\ne\varnothing\}<\infty.#{C: C is a connected component of K, C∩U=∅}<∞.

The counted objects are global connected components of KKK. They are not components of the truncated set K∩UK\cap UK∩U, nor components of the complement Ω∖K\Omega\setminus KΩ∖K. Those are different topological questions.

The gradient consequence is

∇u∈Lloc4,∞(Ω),∇u∈Llocp(Ω)(0<p<4).\nabla u\in L^{4,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega),\qquad\nabla u\in L^p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)\quad(0<p<4).∇u∈Lloc4,∞​(Ω),∇u∈Llocp​(Ω)(0<p<4).

The subscript “loc” means on every region strictly inside Ω\OmegaΩ. Constants can depend on that region and the minimizing pair. The theorem does not assert a universal bound for all images and all domains.

The exponent four has a concrete interpretation. For the tip model, ∣∇u∣>t|\nabla u|>t∣∇u∣>t occurs roughly within radius t−2t^{-2}t−2, whose area is of order t−4t^{-4}t−4. But the fourth-power integral near the tip behaves like ∫0εr−1 dr\int_0^\varepsilon r^{-1}\,dr∫0ε​r−1dr, which diverges. Weak L4L^4L4, rather than strong L4L^4L4, is the natural endpoint.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the claim resolves the interior regularity problem for one of the central models of free-discontinuity calculus of variations. It turns a qualitative picture of optimal edges into a classification at every interior point.

The gradient estimate connects geometry to analysis. Knowing all possible local edge models controls the frequency and size of extreme gradients. Conversely, the established theory relates endpoint gradient control to the absence of irregular points.

The significance extends beyond visual segmentation: the functional is a basic example of an energy that chooses its own discontinuity set. Understanding how bulk energy and crack length interact informs the broader study of variational problems with unknown interfaces.

6. The main idea

Zoom until the image data disappear

Near a point xxx, magnify space by a factor 1/r1/r1/r. The gradient and length terms have a natural common scaling if function values are rescaled by r−1/2r^{-1/2}r−1/2, after subtracting suitable constants. The bounded fidelity contribution becomes lower order as rrr tends to zero.

Limits therefore minimize the homogeneous whole-plane energy

E0(v,H;V)=∫V∖H∣∇v∣2 dx+H1(H∩V).E_0(v,H;V)=\int_{V\setminus H}|\nabla v|^2\,dx+\mathcal H^1(H\cap V).E0​(v,H;V)=∫V∖H​∣∇v∣2dx+H1(H∩V).

Here HHH is the limiting crack. Additive constants on different complementary regions must be tracked carefully; the limiting objects are generalized global minimizers, not automatically homogeneous cones.

Before taking these limits, the manuscript derives local boundedness of uuu and rectifiability of the given KKK. Rectifiability means coverage by countably many curves up to a set of zero length. This step ensures that the original finite-length formulation fits the established geometric theory without replacing the original pair by an unrelated minimizer.

Isolate a compact obstruction

Known classification results reduce the unresolved case to a bounded component of HHH with connected complement. A bounded component need not itself have positive distance from the rest of HHH: other pieces might accumulate near it.

The manuscript enlarges it to a compact subset A⊂HA\subset HA⊂H, possibly containing several components, separated from the remainder B=H∖AB=H\setminus AB=H∖A. This permits small translations of the whole piece without collisions with BBB.

Why translate it? Translation preserves its length. If its interaction with the surrounding field cannot have a strict energy minimum, then such a piece cannot be energetically trapped in place.

Split the field and translate the jump

The gradient of the limiting function is decomposed into a finite-energy field carrying the jumps across AAA and a field harmonic through AAA. A whole-plane orthogonal projection supplies the decomposition.

Moving the compact piece and its own field leaves their individual energy unchanged. What changes is an interaction term I(t)I(t)I(t), where t∈R2t\in\mathbb R^2t∈R2 is the translation vector. The manuscript shows that this interaction is harmonic as a function of ttt.

Absolute minimality makes t=0t=0t=0 a local minimum. A harmonic function with an interior minimum is constant. Thus the interaction cannot supply a restoring energy force.

This resembles the impossibility of stable electrostatic equilibrium in a source-free region, but the analogy alone is insufficient. The comparison has long tails, while admissible variations must be compactly supported. The argument inserts a distant cutoff and controls its error using the whole-plane field decay and the linear energy-growth bound.

Vary the jump values independently

Constancy under translation does not by itself remove the compact crack. The manuscript also changes the jump values independently along a regular subarc of AAA. The resulting identities force the surrounding harmonic potential to be affine.

Its gradient must then vanish: a nonzero constant gradient would have energy proportional to disk area, conflicting with the available linear-in-radius growth bound. The value-variation identity next forces the remaining jump-carrying field to vanish.

At that point removing AAA loses no needed gradient structure but saves positive length. This contradicts minimality and excludes the compact obstruction.

Return from limiting models to actual curves

The remaining nonempty blow-up cracks are a line, a halfline or a three-ray junction. Established epsilon-regularity results say that sufficient closeness to one of these models forces the actual nearby crack to be a regular arc, tip or triple junction.

Finally, compactness supplies a finite cover by connected model neighborhoods, giving the claimed local count of global crack components. The known equivalence between regularity and endpoint gradient control yields weak L4L^4L4.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is planar and interior. It does not classify higher-dimensional Mumford–Shah singularities, prove finiteness up to the domain boundary, or prescribe how edges meet that boundary. Accumulation approaching ∂Ω\partial\Omega∂Ω is outside its conclusion.

Absolute minimality is essential to the comparison argument. The result does not cover every critical point, every topologically constrained local minimizer or every approximate numerical solution. The datum is bounded measurable; greater smoothness may permit stronger descriptions, but those should not be silently inserted into this statement.

The weak endpoint estimate allows genuine crack-tip blow-up. It therefore says neither that the gradient is bounded nor that its fourth power is locally integrable.

Questions about boundary regularity, quantitative complexity bounds and robust approximation of these geometric features remain separate from the interior classification reported here.

8. Sources and further reading

The original Mumford–Shah paper linked above explains the image-segmentation motivation. Bonnet’s paper develops the blow-up viewpoint, and the De Lellis–Focardi monograph provides a detailed route through the regularity theory. Deangelis’s preprint is the contemporary classification result explicitly discussed by the source.

For optional background, Sobolev spaces explain the weak-derivative framework, while Lorentz spaces include the weak integrability notation used at the endpoint.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Interior regularity of planar Mumford–Shah minimizers (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Smoothing three-dimensional deformations without folding or changing the target
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 368 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Imagine deforming a solid object without allowing different material points to occupy the same location. A mathematical deformation should therefore be one-to-one. It may nevertheless be rough: its local stretching can exist only as a weak derivative, rather than as a continuously varying matrix.

Can every such rough deformation be approximated by perfectly smooth, invertible deformations, while keeping both the positions and the local stretching close?

This is the Ball–Evans approximation problem. Ordinary smoothing controls derivatives but can destroy injectivity. Purely topological approximation can preserve injectivity but say little about derivatives. Reconciling the two requirements is the difficulty.

Family 368 claims a complete positive answer in three dimensions for every finite exponent 1≤p<∞1\le p<\infty1≤p<∞. M1 treats 1≤p≤21\le p\le21≤p≤2; M2 treats 2<p<∞2<p<\infty2<p<∞. Every approximating map has exactly the original target, even when the source and target domains have irregular boundaries.

2. Background and essential definitions

Topology and derivatives impose different conditions

A homeomorphism f:Ω→Λf:\Omega\to\Lambdaf:Ω→Λ is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. Here Ω,Λ⊂R3\Omega,\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^3Ω,Λ⊂R3 are nonempty bounded connected open sets. A homeomorphism preserves the topology of the object and prevents interpenetration, but need not possess classical derivatives everywhere.

A diffeomorphism is a smooth bijection whose inverse is also smooth. Smoothness and injectivity alone are insufficient: the one-dimensional map x↦x3x\mapsto x^3x↦x3 is smooth and bijective, but its inverse is not differentiable at zero. A diffeomorphism must have an invertible derivative at every interior point.

The Sobolev condition f∈W1,p(Ω;R3)f\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)f∈W1,p(Ω;R3) says that its three components and their weak first derivatives belong to LpL^pLp. Write DfDfDf for the resulting matrix field. The larger ppp is, the more strongly the norm penalizes large derivatives.

Strong approximation means

∫Ω(∣fj−f∣p+∣Dfj−Df∣p) dx⟶0.\int_\Omega\bigl(|f_j-f|^p+|Df_j-Df|^p\bigr)\,dx\longrightarrow0.∫Ω​(∣fj​−f∣p+∣Dfj​−Df∣p)dx⟶0.

This controls both where material points move and how their local deformation matrices differ. Uniform convergence of positions alone would not imply it: functions can have very small oscillation amplitude and very large oscillating derivatives.

Fixed target and interior smoothness

The fixed-target requirement is

fj(Ω)=Λfor every j.f_j(\Omega)=\Lambda\qquad\text{for every }j.fj​(Ω)=Λfor every j.

It is stronger than having target domains converge to Λ\LambdaΛ, or merely having maps whose images lie inside Λ\LambdaΛ. No part of the target may be omitted by an individual approximant.

Smoothness is required only on the open domains. If their boundaries are rough, the theorem does not claim that the maps extend smoothly to their closures. Nor does it prescribe agreement with a boundary trace that may not exist continuously.

A homeomorphism can have a singular derivative

The Jacobian determinant det⁡Df\det DfdetDf measures oriented local volume change where the derivative exists. It can vanish on a large set for a Sobolev homeomorphism. Global injectivity does not force every infinitesimal linear approximation to be invertible.

This matters because a rank-one or rank-two derivative can carry substantial Sobolev energy even though its determinant is zero. For example,

A=(100000000)A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}A=​100​000​000​​

has determinant zero but squared matrix norm one. Ignoring all points with singular derivatives would therefore discard energy that strong approximation must reproduce.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ball formulated the approximation question in connection with nonlinear elasticity and explicitly attributed it to Evans. The motivation is to understand whether weakly differentiable admissible deformations can be replaced by smoother ones without violating the geometric constraints of the material.

The planar case was resolved earlier. Iwaniec, Kovalev and Onninen first treated p=2p=2p=2 using harmonic replacements and smoothing. Their general theorem covers 1<p<∞1<p<\infty1<p<∞, using coordinatewise ppp-harmonic replacements. Hencl and Pratelli proved the endpoint p=1p=1p=1, with geometric extensions and an adapted grid. These results already preserve the target and do not assume Sobolev regularity of the inverse.

Stronger input assumptions lead to stronger approximation conclusions. Daneri and Pratelli treated bi-Lipschitz planar maps, meaning both directions have bounded local stretching globally. Pratelli obtained simultaneous forward and inverse Sobolev approximation for planar maps with both directions in W1,1W^{1,1}W1,1. These are distinct from merely requiring each approximant to have a smooth inverse.

Higher dimensions introduce real obstructions. Following Hencl and Vejnar, Campbell, Hencl and Tengvall constructed examples in dimensions n≥4n\ge4n≥4, for 1≤p<⌊n/2⌋1\le p<\lfloor n/2\rfloor1≤p<⌊n/2⌋, with Jacobian determinants of both signs on sets of positive measure. Strong derivative approximation by diffeomorphisms cannot reproduce that sign pattern, because a diffeomorphism on a connected domain has one orientation.

Three dimensions behave differently. Hencl and Malý showed that a sense-preserving Wloc1,1W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}Wloc1,1​ homeomorphism has nonnegative Jacobian almost everywhere. This removes the sign-changing obstruction but does not make the determinant strictly positive or construct an approximation.

A separate line of work smooths maps that are already piecewise affine. Campbell and Soudský obtained C1C^1C1 homeomorphic approximation in arbitrary dimension. Campbell, D’Onofrio and Vítek obtained diffeomorphic smoothing in dimensions three and four with derivative control. The remaining challenge for arbitrary Sobolev inputs is reaching such a tractable intermediate map while retaining strong derivative accuracy.

M1 and M2 claim to supply that missing approximation step in three dimensions, through two different constructions.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Together the papers state the following: if Ω,Λ⊂R3\Omega,\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^3Ω,Λ⊂R3 are bounded domains and f:Ω→Λf:\Omega\to\Lambdaf:Ω→Λ is a W1,pW^{1,p}W1,p homeomorphism for a finite p≥1p\ge1p≥1, there exist C∞C^\inftyC∞ diffeomorphisms

fj:Ω⟶Λf_j:\Omega\longrightarrow\Lambdafj​:Ω⟶Λ

that themselves belong to W1,pW^{1,p}W1,p and converge strongly to fff in that space.

M1 covers the endpoint and critical range 1≤p≤21\le p\le21≤p≤2; M2 covers 2<p<∞2<p<\infty2<p<∞. Neither range theorem invokes the other. Their common smoothing component is supplied within each manuscript.

The theorem assumes no boundary regularity, no continuous extension of fff to the boundary, no Sobolev regularity of f−1f^{-1}f−1, and no nonvanishing-Jacobian condition. Orientation-reversing maps are included by reflecting the target before construction and undoing that reflection afterward.

A shared intermediate statement concerns locally bi-Lipschitz homeomorphisms HHH. Given any Sobolev error tolerance ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 and any positive continuous function ξ\xiξ on Ω\OmegaΩ, it claims a smooth diffeomorphism ggg onto the same target with

∥g−H∥W1,p(Ω)<ε,∣g(x)−H(x)∣<ξ(x).\|g-H\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}<\varepsilon,\qquad |g(x)-H(x)|<\xi(x).∥g−H∥W1,p(Ω)​<ε,∣g(x)−H(x)∣<ξ(x).

The variable tolerance can become arbitrarily small near the boundary. This fine positional control is useful for preserving the exact target while smoothing an intermediate map.

The main theorem concerns forward convergence. It does not claim fj−1→f−1f_j^{-1}\to f^{-1}fj−1​→f−1 in a Sobolev norm, and it does not include p=∞p=\inftyp=∞.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the family resolves a central approximation problem at the interface of nonlinear elasticity, geometric mapping theory and three-dimensional topology across the entire finite-exponent range.

Strong approximation is the bridge between weak analytic models and smooth deformations. The theorem would show that, in three dimensions, retaining injectivity and the original target does not itself obstruct approximation in the forward Sobolev norm.

Its importance should not be confused with automatic convergence of every physical energy. An elastic energy may strongly penalize tiny determinants or depend on inverse derivatives. Those quantities need additional control beyond Dfj→DfDf_j\to DfDfj​→Df in LpL^pLp.

6. The main idea

Separate topology from energy estimates

Both papers first construct a locally bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism close to fff, then smooth it. Three-dimensional triangulation and piecewise-linear topology provide ways to modify maps while preserving injectivity and matching prescribed local pieces.

Those topological tools are qualitative. They do not give a useful bound for the derivative of an arbitrary extension. The construction therefore measures selected curves, surfaces or scalar coordinates directly, rather than treating the existence of an injective extension as an energy estimate.

It also separates points by the rank of DfDfDf. Full-rank data admit local affine or smooth invertible models. Rank-one and rank-two data require special treatment because their nonzero derivative energy cannot simply be thrown into an exceptional set. Rank-zero points contribute no derivative energy to retain.

M1: measure curves and surfaces before filling cells

For p≤2p\le2p≤2, the construction selects source curves and, at p=2p=2p=2, source surfaces. It compares their images with complementary-dimensional pieces of a target triangulation. Counting intersections supplies budgets for image lengths and areas, including multiplicity.

On retained rank-one regions, a curve with nearly minimal length and nearly affine endpoints must move mostly in the desired direction. This recovers its derivative rather than merely bounding its energy.

At rank two and p=2p=2p=2, the analogous tool is a sharp disk-parametrization estimate: a surface with nearly minimal area and controlled boundary parametrization can be reparametrized with nearly minimal Dirichlet energy and derivative close to the desired planar map. The boundary parametrization matters; area alone does not control how quickly a parametrized surface is traversed.

Remaining cells are filled using their already chosen boundaries. Radial compression has finite ppp-energy when ppp is below the cell dimension. Thus it fills two-dimensional faces for p<2p<2p<2 and three-dimensional cells throughout this range. The endpoint p=2p=2p=2 needs the disk estimate for faces instead of that subcritical argument.

Additional critical-exponent tools select reverse rays and measure generic image surfaces, using known consequences of three-dimensional W1,2W^{1,2}W1,2 homeomorphism theory. Inverse bounded-variation regularity is used as a derived fact, not imposed as a hypothesis.

At p=1p=1p=1, ordinary uniform-convexity arguments are unavailable. M1 instead uses a squared length-defect estimate to recover derivative accuracy along the selected lines.

M2: retain two scalar coordinates

For p>2p>2p>2, the principal construction represents rank-deficient data through two scalar coordinates. On small retained patches these coordinates have prescribed affine first-order models. Their values determine mean gradients through boundary integrals; nearly sharp upper bounds on their gradient norms then force strong gradient closeness by uniform convexity.

The target is organized into a polyhedral two-dimensional complex outside protected full-dimensional regions. On its faces, two parameters describe radial position and position around the perimeter. In the source, families of surfaces realize their level sets.

These surfaces must be routed without creating unwanted intersections or multiplying derivative errors at every change of route. Reference paths constrain where the realized coordinate levels can lie: a substantially misplaced level would force too much path energy across many small spheres. The relevant lower bound grows under refinement precisely because p>2p>2p>2.

The construction controls the derivatives of the two parameters directly. It does not substitute the potentially enormous derivative of a topologically chosen chamber-filling map into the main energy estimate.

For 2<p<32<p<32<p<3, a separate compression handles certain exceptional interiors. For p≥3p\ge3p≥3, the volume Lusin property—the relevant preservation of measure-zero sets—removes that particular obstruction. These distinctions explain why the higher-exponent proof is not just the low-exponent construction repeated with a larger power.

Smooth without losing the target

The intermediate locally bi-Lipschitz map is approximated by a locally finite piecewise-affine map and then smoothed near edges and vertices. Local errors are chosen summably, so the final estimate is global on Ω\OmegaΩ, not merely valid on each compact subset.

To preserve the target, the positional error is kept smaller than a fixed fraction of the distance to its boundary. The resulting deformation stays inside Λ\LambdaΛ and gives a proper homotopy to the original homeomorphism. Combined with positive local degree and global degree one, this yields bijectivity onto the whole target for each approximant.

Throughout the construction, finite geometric constants are fixed before the error regions they multiply are made small. This ordering is how qualitative topology and quantitative energy control are kept compatible.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The combined claim concerns bounded domains in R3\mathbb R^3R3 and finite ppp. It does not resolve every higher-dimensional Ball–Evans problem; the sign-changing examples already prevent a universal positive theorem in some higher-dimensional ranges.

Smoothness is interior, with no claimed smooth boundary extension or exact prescribed boundary trace. Although every approximant has a smooth inverse, convergence of those inverses in a chosen Sobolev space requires separate assumptions and estimates.

Strong derivative convergence also does not control an arbitrary singular determinant penalty. For example, a function of det⁡Dfj\det Df_jdetDfj​ that diverges as the determinant approaches zero need not have convergent integrals merely because the matrices converge in LpL^pLp.

Quantitative distortion bounds, simultaneous approximation in both directions, determinant-sensitive energy convergence and analogous results on other geometric spaces remain separate questions.

8. Sources and further reading

The planar approximation papers linked above establish the main positive precedents; the Campbell–Hencl–Tengvall paper explains the higher-dimensional sign obstruction. The recent piecewise-affine smoothing paper isolates the final regularization stage from the more difficult approximation of arbitrary Sobolev input.

For background, Sobolev spaces, diffeomorphisms and topological degree provide complementary introductions to the analytic and topological language used here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Strong diffeomorphic approximation in three dimensions for 1≤p≤2 (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Strong diffeomorphic approximation in three dimensions for p>2 (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Where the slowest heat mode reaches its hottest and coldest values
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 369 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Take a thin insulated plate with an uneven initial temperature. As heat diffuses, the temperature approaches its spatial average. The slowly decaying part of the remaining temperature variation is described by the lowest nonconstant Neumann eigenfunctions.

Must the hottest and coldest points of such an eigenfunction lie on the plate’s boundary? This is the spectral hot-spots problem associated with Rauch.

Family 369 claims a positive answer for every bounded smooth simply connected planar domain, with no convexity or symmetry assumption. It claims more: the gradient of every nonzero first-positive Neumann eigenfunction is nonzero everywhere in the interior. Thus the result would exclude interior saddle points as well as interior maxima and minima.

The statement applies even when the eigenvalue is multiple. It concerns every nonzero eigenfunction in the relevant eigenspace, rather than the possibility of choosing one particularly favorable eigenfunction.

2. Background and essential definitions

Insulation leads to Neumann boundary conditions

Let Ω⊂R2\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2Ω⊂R2 be the plate. With thermal diffusivity normalized to one, temperature TTT satisfies

∂tT=ΔT,∂νT=0on ∂Ω.\partial_tT=\Delta T,\qquad \partial_ u T=0\quad ext{on }\partial\Omega.∂t​T=ΔT,∂ν​T=0on ∂Ω.

Here ν uν is the outward unit normal. The zero normal derivative expresses insulation: no heat crosses the boundary.

Separation of variables leads to the eigenvalue problem

−Δu=μuin Ω,∂νu=0on ∂Ω.-\Delta u=\mu u\quad ext{in }\Omega,\qquad \partial_ u u=0\quad ext{on }\partial\Omega.−Δu=μuin Ω,∂ν​u=0on ∂Ω.

The constant functions have eigenvalue zero. The first positive eigenvalue is the smallest μ>0\mu>0μ>0 for which a nonzero solution exists. This digest denotes it by μ1\mu_1μ1​; conventions that count the constant mode first often call the same eigenvalue μ2\mu_2μ2​.

Its eigenfunctions have mean zero and therefore take both signs. Variationally,

μ1=inf⁡v∈H1(Ω), v≠0∫Ωv=0∫Ω∣∇v∣2 dx∫Ω∣v∣2 dx.\mu_1=\inf_{\substack{v\in H^1(\Omega),\ v e0\\int_\Omega v=0}} rac{\int_\Omega| abla v|^2\,dx}{\int_\Omega|v|^2\,dx}.μ1​=v∈H1(Ω), v=0∫Ω​v=0​inf​∫Ω​∣v∣2dx∫Ω​∣∇v∣2dx​.

The space H1H^1H1 consists of square-integrable functions with square-integrable weak first derivatives. The quotient measures gradient energy relative to the size of the function.

Why the first mode describes late-time behavior

An eigenfunction contributes a term e−μtu(x)e^{-\mu t}u(x)e−μtu(x) to heat flow. Among nonconstant modes, the first positive eigenspace decays slowest. If the initial temperature has a nonzero projection onto that space, the leading deviation from the average at large times is a fixed eigenfunction from it.

If that projection vanishes, a higher mode leads instead. Also, an asymptotic statement about the leading mode is not automatically a theorem locating the exact hottest point at every finite time. The manuscript’s theorem is stated for eigenfunctions.

Three distinctions in the conjecture

An interior point xxx is critical if ∇u(x)=0 abla u(x)=0∇u(x)=0. A local extremum is critical, but a saddle point can be critical without being an extremum.

The nonstrict hot-spots statement permits an interior value tied with the global boundary maximum or minimum. The strict statement says every interior value lies strictly between the two boundary extremes. Nonvanishing gradient is stronger still because it excludes saddle points.

A domain is simply connected if every closed loop can be contracted to a point within the domain. For a smooth bounded planar region, this means there are no holes. It permits severe indentations and narrow passages; it does not imply convexity.

Multiplicity means that several linearly independent eigenfunctions share μ1\mu_1μ1​. Any linear combination remains an eigenfunction. A result for one basis vector would not settle the statement for the entire eigenspace.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Rauch discussed the problem in connection with long-time heat flow in the 1970s. Bañuelos and Burdzy later distinguished strict and nonstrict formulations and the quantifier over eigenfunctions, distinctions that become essential when multiplicities occur.

Topology soon proved important. Burdzy and Werner constructed a planar counterexample with two holes and a simple first positive eigenvalue. Bass and Burdzy obtained examples with both extrema strictly inside. Burdzy’s one-hole construction showed that even one hole can allow failure. The remaining simply connected planar assertion is therefore a substantive topological restriction.

Positive results developed under geometric assumptions. Jerison and Nadirashvili obtained a positive directional derivative for every relevant eigenfunction on convex planar domains with two perpendicular reflection symmetries. Pascu treated antisymmetric eigenfunctions on suitable convex domains with one reflection symmetry. Atar and Burdzy treated lip domains, bounded between graphs with Lipschitz constants at most one. Miyamoto excluded interior critical points under a spectral-diameter condition, including nonsymmetric nearly circular convex examples.

Polygons have their own theory. Siudeja treated a class of acute triangles. Judge and Mondal, together with their subsequent erratum, excluded interior critical points for every first-positive Neumann eigenfunction on every Euclidean triangle. Chen, Gui and Yao later gave a finer classification of nonvertex critical points. These corner-domain results are distinct from the smooth-domain theorem reported here.

Recent quantitative work, including de Dios Pont, Hsu and Taylor, bounds the ratio between an eigenfunction’s supremum over a domain and its boundary maximum. Such estimates measure possible failure of hot spots but do not by themselves exclude saddle points.

The main methodological starting point is Rohleder’s variational approach. It treats eigenfunction gradients as tangent vector fields and gives an analytic route to hot spots on lip domains. The manuscript seeks a replacement for the preferred directions available in those geometries, using scalar boundary multipliers and Green kernels.

4. What the new manuscript claims

Let Ω⊂R2\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2Ω⊂R2 be a nonempty bounded simply connected open set with C∞C^\inftyC∞ boundary. Let VVV be the real eigenspace for its first positive Neumann eigenvalue.

The main theorem states that for every 0≠u∈V0 e u\in V0=u∈V,

∇u(x)≠0for every x∈Ω. abla u(x) e0\qquad ext{for every }x\in\Omega.∇u(x)=0for every x∈Ω.

Consequently,

min⁡y∈∂Ωu(y)<u(x)<max⁡y∈∂Ωu(y)(x∈Ω).\min_{y\in\partial\Omega}u(y)<u(x)<\max_{y\in\partial\Omega}u(y)\qquad(x\in\Omega).y∈∂Ωmin​u(y)<u(x)<y∈∂Ωmax​u(y)(x∈Ω).

All global maxima and minima over the closed domain therefore lie on its boundary. Smoothness supplies a continuous boundary extension, so these extrema are attained.

No convexity, reflection symmetry, preferred direction, eigenvalue simplicity or small deformation from a standard domain is assumed. The conclusion includes any nonzero linear combination in a multiple first-positive eigenspace.

The nonvanishing-gradient statement is not a uniform numerical lower bound over the entire domain. The gradient may approach zero as a point approaches the boundary, where extrema are expected. Nor does it assert that one fixed directional derivative is positive throughout the domain.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the result settles a central geometric spectral conjecture on the full smooth simply connected planar class and strengthens it by excluding all interior critical points.

The claim would identify a striking constraint on the lowest nonconstant mode: complicated geometry without holes cannot create an interior stationary point. This is much stronger than expecting the hottest point to sit near the boundary in familiar symmetric pictures.

The proposed method also connects two areas that are usually presented separately. A variational principle for PDE vector fields is combined with positivity properties of kernels and Hilbert-space geometry. That connection is part of the family’s mathematical significance, independently of the heat-flow interpretation.

6. The main idea

Use both derivatives together

Each Cartesian derivative of uuu solves the same Helmholtz equation (Δ+μ1)v=0(\Delta+\mu_1)v=0(Δ+μ1​)v=0. But neither derivative has a useful fixed sign on an arbitrary domain. The Neumann condition instead says that the vector ∇u abla u∇u is tangent to the boundary.

Rohleder’s variational principle uses this joint constraint. For tangent vector fields X=(X1,X2)X=(X_1,X_2)X=(X1​,X2​), define

Q(X)=∫Ω(∣div⁡X∣2+∣curl⁡X∣2) dx,Q(X)=\int_\Omega igl(|\operatorname{div}X|^2+|\operatorname{curl}X|^2 igr)\,dx,Q(X)=∫Ω​(∣divX∣2+∣curlX∣2)dx,

where curl⁡X=∂1X2−∂2X1\operatorname{curl}X=\partial_1X_2-\partial_2X_1curlX=∂1​X2​−∂2​X1​ in the plane. The principle gives

Q(X)≥μ1∫Ω∣X∣2 dx,Q(X)\ge\mu_1\int_\Omega|X|^2\,dx,Q(X)≥μ1​∫Ω​∣X∣2dx,

with equality exactly for gradients of functions in VVV.

Simple connectivity removes an extra harmonic-field obstruction in this decomposition. The strict inequality between the first positive Neumann eigenvalue and the first Dirichlet eigenvalue separates the unwanted vector-field component from the equality space.

Convert the problem to boundary data on a circle

A smooth conformal parametrization Φ\PhiΦ maps the unit disk DDD onto Ω\OmegaΩ. Pull back the boundary gradient to obtain a vector-valued function ggg on S1S^1S1.

Solving the scalar Helmholtz equation in each component produces a nonnegative quadratic form EEE on tangent boundary data. Its zero-energy vectors correspond precisely to first-eigenfunction gradients; in particular, E(g)=0E(g)=0E(g)=0.

Multiplication by any real scalar boundary function bbb preserves tangency. The manuscript derives the identity

E(bg)=12∫S1∫S1N(s,t)(b(s)−b(t))2 g(s)⋅g(t) ds dt.E(bg)= rac12\int_{S^1}\int_{S^1}N(s,t)(b(s)-b(t))^2\,g(s)\cdot g(t)\,ds\,dt.E(bg)=21​∫S1​∫S1​N(s,t)(b(s)−b(t))2g(s)⋅g(t)dsdt.

The kernel NNN is positive off the diagonal. Nevertheless, the dot product can change sign, so positivity of NNN alone does not solve the problem.

Choose multipliers through a distance kernel

Let K(p,s)K(p,s)K(p,s) be the kernel evaluating a solution at an interior disk point ppp from its boundary values. The central analytic claim concerns

Dp(s,t)=K(p,s)K(p,t)N(s,t)(s≠t),Dp(s,s)=0.D_p(s,t)= rac{K(p,s)K(p,t)}{N(s,t)}\quad(s e t),\qquad D_p(s,s)=0.Dp​(s,t)=N(s,t)K(p,s)K(p,t)​(s=t),Dp​(s,s)=0.

The manuscript proves, as stated, that this is conditionally negative semidefinite: for any finitely many boundary points and real coefficients whose sum is zero,

∑i,jcicjDp(si,sj)≤0.\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jD_p(s_i,s_j)\le0.i,j∑​ci​cj​Dp​(si​,sj​)≤0.

Schoenberg’s correspondence interprets this as squared distances in a Hilbert space. There is an injective Lipschitz map b:S1→Hb:S^1 o\mathcal Hb:S1→H such that

Dp(s,t)=∥b(s)−b(t)∥H2.D_p(s,t)=\|b(s)-b(t)\|_{\mathcal H}^2.Dp​(s,t)=∥b(s)−b(t)∥H2​.

Take the scalar coordinates bjb_jbj​ of this map as multipliers. Summing the energy identity cancels the troublesome kernel factor and yields

∑jE(bjg)=12∣∇u(Φ(p))∣2.\sum_jE(b_jg)= rac12| abla u(\Phi(p))|^2.j∑​E(bj​g)=21​∣∇u(Φ(p))∣2.

This is the desired bridge from an interior critical point to many boundary equality cases.

A critical point would produce too many first modes

If Φ(p)\Phi(p)Φ(p) were critical, the right side would vanish. Every term on the left is nonnegative, so every bjgb_jgbj​g must itself be the boundary gradient of another function in VVV.

The manuscript establishes that VVV has real dimension at most two, using planar separation and the boundary sign pattern of a first eigenfunction. An injective image of a circle cannot lie in a line. When the nonzero set of ggg is dense, the multipliers therefore produce at least three independent gradient traces, contradicting that dimension bound.

If the nonzero set is not dense, ggg vanishes on an open boundary arc. Two independent generated eigenfunctions then yield a nonzero combination with both zero value and zero normal derivative on that arc. Boundary uniqueness forces that combination to vanish identically, another contradiction.

Where the kernel theorem enters

The distance-kernel property is the main analytic work. The manuscript regularizes Green functions and studies finite kernel matrices whose entrywise reciprocals have at most one positive eigenvalue. Rank-one updates, positive quadrature and limits transfer that property to the Green resolvent and then to the boundary kernels.

The matrix condition comes from complete Nevanlinna–Pick kernel theory. The argument must handle singular kernels and the order of boundary limits carefully; a boundary Poisson kernel cannot simply be assumed square-integrable. This analytic construction supplies the special multipliers that ordinary sign arguments lack.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is for smooth bounded simply connected planar domains and the first positive Neumann eigenspace. It does not extend the claim to domains with holes, where counterexamples exist, to arbitrary higher-dimensional domains, or to higher eigenfunctions.

The statement does not classify boundary critical points or prove that extrema are unique. It permits eigenvalue multiplicity and does not provide a domain-independent lower bound for the interior gradient.

The heat-flow interpretation remains asymptotic and depends on which modes are present initially. The theorem does not say that every temperature profile has boundary-only hot spots at every time.

Lower boundary regularity, quantitative gradient estimates and extensions of the reciprocal-kernel method are separate questions beyond the stated theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

The counterexamples, geometric special cases and Rohleder papers linked above supply the historical setting. The triangle result should be read together with its erratum. Optional background on Neumann boundary conditions and conformal maps complements the definitions used here.

The manuscript below supplies the strict hot-spots and noncriticality claims. Its kernel theorem is also formulated independently for bounded nonnegative disk potentials satisfying the specified subcritical Dirichlet inequality.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Strict hot spots and absence of interior critical points on smooth simply connected planar domains (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The critical boundary between existence and nonexistence for Lane–Emden systems
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 370 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Can two positive fields sustain one another everywhere in space when each acts as the source of the other’s elliptic equation? The Hénon–Lane–Emden system asks this through

−Δu=∣x∣Avp,−Δv=∣x∣Buq.-\Delta u=|x|^A v^p,\qquad-\Delta v=|x|^B u^q.−Δu=∣x∣Avp,−Δv=∣x∣Buq.

The powers p,q>0p,q>0p,q>0 describe nonlinear coupling. The real numbers A,BA,BA,B make the source strength depend on distance from the origin. Setting A=B=0A=B=0A=B=0 gives the unweighted Lane–Emden system.

The conjecture predicts that one inequality in the exponents forbids positive solutions on all of Rn\mathbb R^nRn, with no need to assume symmetry, boundedness or decay. Family 370 claims this nonexistence theorem in every dimension n≥2n\ge2n≥2, including singular weights and powers below one.

Together with an earlier radial existence theorem, the claim gives an exact existence–nonexistence classification when n≥3n\ge3n≥3 and A,B>−2A,B>-2A,B>−2. The new manuscript supplies the nonexistence half; it does not claim to have newly constructed the complementary radial solutions.

2. Background and essential definitions

Entire positive solutions

The Laplacian is Δu=∑i=1n∂i2u\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_i^2uΔu=∑i=1n​∂i2​u. An equation −Δu=f>0-\Delta u=f>0−Δu=f>0 says that uuu is superharmonic: its local curvature is constrained by a positive source. Superharmonic functions need not be constant, and in higher dimensions a source can generate a positive decaying potential. Positivity alone therefore does not settle the coupled problem.

An entire solution is defined throughout the whole space, rather than just a bounded domain. The solution class here is

u,v∈C2(Rn∖{0})∩C(Rn),u,v>0on Rn.u,v\in C^2(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})\cap C(\mathbb R^n),\qquad u,v>0\quad\text{on }\mathbb R^n.u,v∈C2(Rn∖{0})∩C(Rn),u,v>0on Rn.

The equations hold classically away from zero. At zero the functions are only required to be continuous and strictly positive. This matters because a negative weight, such as ∣x∣−1|x|^{-1}∣x∣−1, is singular there. No differentiability at the origin is initially assumed.

A Liouville-type theorem rules out nontrivial entire solutions in a specified class. Here the conclusion is that no strictly positive pair exists. It does not rule out solutions on bounded regions with boundary conditions, or functions singular at the origin outside this class.

The critical hyperbola

The claimed subcritical condition is

n+Ap+1+n+Bq+1>n−2.\frac{n+A}{p+1}+\frac{n+B}{q+1}>n-2.p+1n+A​+q+1n+B​>n−2.

Equality defines the critical hyperbola in the exponent plane. “Subcritical” refers to the strict inequality above; it does not mean simply that both powers are less than some universal number.

In the unweighted case this becomes

1p+1+1q+1>n−2n.\frac1{p+1}+\frac1{q+1}>\frac{n-2}{n}.p+11​+q+11​>nn−2​.

On the diagonal p=q=sp=q=sp=q=s, for n≥3n\ge3n≥3, it reduces to s<(n+2)/(n−2)s<(n+2)/(n-2)s<(n+2)/(n−2), the familiar scalar Sobolev critical exponent. The system has two potentially different powers, however, so a single scalar threshold is not enough.

Scaling reveals the relevant energy

In the nontrivial remaining range pq>1pq>1pq>1 and A,B>−2A,B>-2A,B>−2, choose positive numbers α,β\alpha,\betaα,β satisfying

pβ=α+2+A,qα=β+2+B.p\beta=\alpha+2+A,\qquad q\alpha=\beta+2+B.pβ=α+2+A,qα=β+2+B.

Then the rescaled functions

uR(x)=Rαu(Rx),vR(x)=Rβv(Rx)u_R(x)=R^\alpha u(Rx),\qquad v_R(x)=R^\beta v(Rx)uR​(x)=Rαu(Rx),vR​(x)=Rβv(Rx)

solve the same weighted system. These dilations are centered at the origin; arbitrary translations would move the spatial weights and change the equation.
