The two natural energy densities are ∣x∣Buq+1|x|^B u^{q+1}∣x∣Buq+1 and ∣x∣Avp+1|x|^A v^{p+1}∣x∣Avp+1. Their integrals scale with the same power Rα+β+2−nR^{\alpha+\beta+2-n}Rα+β+2−n. Subcriticality makes that exponent positive, which is the eventual source of the contradiction.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The scalar theory supplied the first major model. Gidas and Spruck established subcritical nonexistence for positive scalar solutions, along with local consequences. For systems, Mitidieri developed Rellich identities and obtained early nonexistence regions.

Serrin and Zou proved the unweighted three-dimensional assertion under a growth condition. Poláčik, Quittner and Souplet removed that additional condition, and Souplet settled the four-dimensional Lane–Emden conjecture. Higher dimensions remained more difficult because spherical estimates lose strength as dimension grows.

A recent partial result by Kui Li, Mingxiang Li and Juncheng Wei covers, for n≥5n\ge5n≥5 and p,q≥1p,q\ge1p,q≥1, a region satisfying

1p+1+1q+1≥1−2n+4n2.\frac1{p+1}+\frac1{q+1}\ge1-\frac2n+\frac4{n^2}.p+11​+q+11​≥1−n2​+n24​.

This lies strictly inside the full conjectured subcritical range. Family 370 claims the remaining region as well, including exponents below one.

For the weighted problem, Bidaut-Véron and Giacomini identified the critical hyperbola in the regular radial theory. Phan formulated the unrestricted weighted question for A,B>−2A,B>-2A,B>−2 and proved bounded, low-dimensional and conditional cases.

Fazly and Ghoussoub obtained results under boundedness and stability assumptions for nonnegative weights. Li and Zhang proved the weighted three-dimensional conjecture without boundedness. Other work covered restricted exponent regions in dimensions four and five. Huang and Zou formulated the broader origin-continuous, all-real-weight assertion and proved cases with stability, decay or energy hypotheses.

The new claim removes those extra restrictions in the nonradial higher-dimensional problem. Its method continues the tradition of scaling and Rellich–Pohozaev identities, but obtains the needed local energy bound without first assuming finite total energy or a decay rate.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For every integer n≥2n\ge2n≥2, every p,q>0p,q>0p,q>0, and every real A,BA,BA,B, the manuscript claims that

n+Ap+1+n+Bq+1>n−2\frac{n+A}{p+1}+\frac{n+B}{q+1}>n-2p+1n+A​+q+1n+B​>n−2

excludes all strictly positive pairs in the origin-continuous solution class defined above.

The conclusion requires no radial symmetry, global boundedness, integrability, finite energy, stability, or prescribed growth or decay at infinity. With zero weights it yields the usual subcritical Lane–Emden nonexistence statement for positive classical entire solutions.

The source also makes preliminary exclusions independent of the subcritical inequality: a pair in this solution class would necessarily have n≥3n\ge3n≥3, A,B>−2A,B>-2A,B>−2, and pq>1pq>1pq>1. Continuity and positivity at zero are what make the weight restriction unavoidable; the two-dimensional exclusion follows from spherical averages and positivity at large radius.

For n≥3n\ge3n≥3 and A,B>−2A,B>-2A,B>−2, combining the new result with the cited radial existence theorem gives the exact classification:

a positive entire pair exists⟺n+Ap+1+n+Bq+1≤n−2.\text{a positive entire pair exists}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{n+A}{p+1}+\frac{n+B}{q+1}\le n-2.a positive entire pair exists⟺p+1n+A​+q+1n+B​≤n−2.

In the existence range a pair can be chosen radial, including equality on the critical hyperbola. This is an existence statement, not a claim that all positive solutions are radial or unique.

The broader all-real-weight formulation belongs to the nonexistence theorem. The complementary existence classification is specifically restricted to n≥3n\ge3n≥3 and A,B>−2A,B>-2A,B>−2.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the manuscript resolves the full subcritical Lane–Emden conjecture and its weighted extension, central nonexistence questions for nonlinear elliptic systems.

Liouville theorems have consequences beyond whole-space equations. In a blow-up argument, a sequence of increasingly large solutions on bounded domains can be rescaled around its peaks. If a nontrivial entire limit would violate a Liouville theorem, such blow-up is impossible. This mechanism underlies a priori bounds and singularity estimates, although each application has its own hypotheses.

The weighted result also adds information that cannot be obtained by merely inserting the same powers into the unweighted theorem. Spatial weights alter the critical inequality, the scaling and the geometry of the source layers.

6. The main idea

Express each field through the other’s source

For n≥3n\ge3n≥3, let

K(x)=cn∣x∣2−n,cn=1(n−2)∣Sn−1∣,K(x)=c_n|x|^{2-n},\qquad c_n=\frac1{(n-2)|S^{n-1}|},K(x)=cn​∣x∣2−n,cn​=(n−2)∣Sn−1∣1​,

be the Newton kernel, the fundamental solution of −Δ-\Delta−Δ. Define source densities

f=∣x∣Buq,g=∣x∣Avp.f=|x|^B u^q,\qquad g=|x|^A v^p.f=∣x∣Buq,g=∣x∣Avp.

After the preliminary reductions, the manuscript obtains

u=K∗g,v=K∗f.u=K*g,\qquad v=K*f.u=K∗g,v=K∗f.

Convolution means integration against the translated kernel. Initially nonnegative additive constants may occur; source-mass estimates rule them out. These same estimates control source masses on origin-centered balls and distant contributions to potentials on a fixed ball.

The key issue is that source-mass control is weaker than energy control. Integrals of fff and ggg do not immediately bound integrals of fufufu and gvgvgv, because the potential may be large where its source concentrates.

Localize the scaling identity

The interaction between the two sources can be written as a nonnegative measure

dπ(x,y)=f(x)g(y)K(x−y) dx dy.d\pi(x,y)=f(x)g(y)K(x-y)\,dx\,dy.dπ(x,y)=f(x)g(y)K(x−y)dxdy.

Integrating out one variable produces fufufu or gvgvgv. Thus the two energy densities are the two marginals of the same interaction.

A compactly supported radial cutoff gives a localized virial identity, a version of the Rellich–Pohozaev scaling identity. It retains the exact coefficients involving n+An+An+A and n+Bn+Bn+B, together with terms generated near the cutoff’s edge.

Using a compact cutoff avoids assuming that boundary terms vanish at infinity. But it creates an obligation: those cutoff terms must be controlled without already knowing the energy bound being sought.

Compare intervals in weighted source layers

The manuscript decomposes each source into superlevel sets. This is the layer-cake idea: a nonnegative function is the integral of indicators of the sets where it exceeds a level.

Intersecting these sets with lines produces intervals. An elementary comparison of pairs of intervals relates their Newtonian interaction to endpoint contributions and a directional pressure term. The comparison is organized with nonnegative quantities, avoiding undefined subtraction when an interaction integral over an unbounded interval diverges.

Weights make the endpoints subtle. If ∣x∣Bu(x)q=t|x|^Bu(x)^q=t∣x∣Bu(x)q=t, then

u(x)=(t∣x∣B)1/q,u(x)=\left(\frac{t}{|x|^B}\right)^{1/q},u(x)=(∣x∣Bt​)1/q,

which varies with the endpoint location. It is not the constant t1/qt^{1/q}t1/q available in the unweighted problem.

The argument therefore uses short intervals and directions close to the local radial direction. On each retained interval the weight changes only slightly. Long or poorly positioned intervals are discarded with estimates based on polar integration, source masses and a high/low decomposition of source levels.

The resulting errors have the form εE+Cε\varepsilon E+C_\varepsilonεE+Cε​, where EEE is the localized energy and CεC_\varepsilonCε​ is independent of the particular solution. Obtaining this estimate without assuming an upper bound on EEE is the central claimed advance.

Absorb errors, then dilate

Let

γ=n+Ap+1+n+Bq+1−(n−2)>0.\gamma=\frac{n+A}{p+1}+\frac{n+B}{q+1}-(n-2)>0.γ=p+1n+A​+q+1n+B​−(n−2)>0.

The localized identity, pressure estimate and comparison of the two energy marginals lead to an inequality of the schematic form

γ2E≤CεE+Cε.\frac\gamma2 E\le C\varepsilon E+C_\varepsilon.2γ​E≤CεE+Cε​.

Choosing ε\varepsilonε small compared with the fixed positive gap γ\gammaγ absorbs the energy term on the right. This yields a universal bound for the energy on the unit ball.

Apply that same bound to every rescaled solution (uR,vR)(u_R,v_R)(uR​,vR​). The exact scaling relation is

∫B1(∣x∣BuRq+1+∣x∣AvRp+1) dx=Rα+β+2−n∫BR(∣x∣Buq+1+∣x∣Avp+1) dx.\begin{aligned}&\int_{B_1}\bigl(|x|^B u_R^{q+1}+|x|^A v_R^{p+1}\bigr)\,dx\\&\qquad=R^{\alpha+\beta+2-n}\int_{B_R}\bigl(|x|^B u^{q+1}+|x|^A v^{p+1}\bigr)\,dx.\end{aligned}​∫B1​​(∣x∣BuRq+1​+∣x∣AvRp+1​)dx=Rα+β+2−n∫BR​​(∣x∣Buq+1+∣x∣Avp+1)dx.​

The exponent is positive under subcriticality. For R≥1R\ge1R≥1, the last integral is at least its fixed strictly positive value on B1B_1B1​. The right side therefore grows without bound, contradicting the uniform estimate for the left side.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Strict positivity includes the origin, and continuity there is part of the solution class. Singular profiles that blow up at zero, or different notions of weak solution, require separate analysis. Sign-changing solutions are also outside the theorem.

The subcritical inequality is strict. On the critical hyperbola the absorption gap disappears, and the cited radial theory supplies positive solutions in the admissible existence range. The nonexistence conclusion cannot be extended there unchanged.

The result concerns the second-order Laplacian with radial power weights. Higher-order, fractional or nonradial-weight systems require their own estimates. The existence classification does not describe every solution, its uniqueness or its detailed asymptotic behavior.

Applications to bounded-domain estimates likewise need explicit rescaling and compactness hypotheses. The manuscript supplies a strong entire-solution obstruction, rather than every possible application of that obstruction.

8. Sources and further reading

The Gidas–Spruck and Souplet papers linked above explain the scalar and low-dimensional precedents. Phan’s paper formulates the weighted classification, while Bidaut-Véron–Giacomini supply the radial existence theorem used for its complementary half.

For optional background, the Laplace operator and fundamental solutions explain the differential and potential formulations. The manuscript below is the source for the unrestricted subcritical nonexistence claim.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Subcritical Hénon–Lane–Emden Conjecture (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Stable blowup in a defocusing Schrödinger equation
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 371 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

The word “defocusing” suggests that a wave spreads rather than concentrates. For the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, its most immediate mathematical meaning is that the nonlinear part of the conserved energy has a positive sign. Yet positive energy need not control all the derivatives required to keep a solution smooth.

Can a defocusing wave develop a singularity that survives small changes in its initial state? And if it can, does making random initial data arbitrarily regular guarantee global evolution with probability one?

Family 371 claims stable finite-time blowup for a scalar, unforced defocusing Schrödinger equation on the twelve-dimensional torus, for a sufficiently large odd power. The blowup data contain a nonempty open set in a high Sobolev space.

That openness is the decisive feature. The manuscript uses it to show that a prescribed family of Gaussian Fourier laws has positive probability of blowup, even with arbitrarily high finite Sobolev regularity. This is not a claim of probability-one blowup or of instability for every defocusing equation.

2. Background and essential definitions

The equation and its positive energy

On the periodic space

Td=(R/2πZ)d,\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^d,Td=(R/2πZ)d,

consider a complex-valued function u(t,x)u(t,x)u(t,x) satisfying

i∂tu+Δu=∣u∣p−1u,i\partial_tu+\Delta u=|u|^{p-1}u,i∂t​u+Δu=∣u∣p−1u,

where p≥3p\ge3p≥3 is odd. Opposite faces of a periodic cell are identified. There is no boundary where conditions must be imposed.

For sufficiently regular solutions, the conserved mass and energy are

M(u)=∫Td∣u∣2 dx,M(u)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}|u|^2\,dx,M(u)=∫Td​∣u∣2dx,

and

E(u)=∫Td(12∣∇u∣2+1p+1∣u∣p+1) dx.E(u)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\left(\frac12|\nabla u|^2+\frac1{p+1}|u|^{p+1}\right)\,dx.E(u)=∫Td​(21​∣∇u∣2+p+11​∣u∣p+1)dx.

Both energy terms are nonnegative. This distinguishes the defocusing sign from the focusing sign, where the nonlinear energy term is negative.

Nevertheless, these integrals allow a very tall feature concentrated on a very small region. In a supercritical regime, their conservation does not bound the high Sobolev norm needed for classical continuation.

Scaling and supercriticality

The Euclidean version has the scaling

uλ(t,x)=λ2/(p−1)u(λ2t,λx).u_\lambda(t,x)=\lambda^{2/(p-1)}u(\lambda^2t,\lambda x).uλ​(t,x)=λ2/(p−1)u(λ2t,λx).

Its invariant homogeneous Sobolev order is

sc=d2−2p−1.s_c=\frac d2-\frac2{p-1}.sc​=2d​−p−12​.

“Energy-supercritical” means sc>1s_c>1sc​>1: the scale-invariant regularity lies above the first-derivative level controlled by energy. Although changing scale does not preserve one fixed torus globally, it still describes a concentrating region much smaller than the periodic cell.

The space Hk(Td)H^k(\mathbb T^d)Hk(Td) controls square-integrable derivatives through order kkk. For large enough kkk, standard local theory gives a unique solution from HkH^kHk data. The question is whether that solution can continue for all time.

Blowup, self-similarity and openness

Finite-time blowup here means that the solution cannot be extended continuously in HkH^kHk through a finite time TTT. The manuscript proves a stronger visible symptom: its amplitude diverges at a point.

With a=1/(p−1)a=1/(p-1)a=1/(p−1), the claimed core has spatial scale (T−t)1/2(T-t)^{1/2}(T−t)1/2 and amplitude scale (T−t)−a(T-t)^{-a}(T−t)−a, together with a logarithmically rotating complex phase. This is called self-similar, or type-I, blowup in the manuscript.

An open set of blowup data means that some entire HkH^kHk ball consists of data leading to blowup. Nearby data may have different blowup times, locations and phases. Stability permits those parameters to adjust; it does not demand that every perturbed solution blow up at exactly the same spacetime point.

A finite-codimension family is weaker: it can require several exact constraints on the initial data and need not contain any open ball.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Classical Schrödinger Cauchy theory establishes local solutions and many global results in appropriate regimes. In certain whole-space supercritical settings, Killip and Visan showed that a bounded critical Sobolev norm implies scattering. The unresolved issue in such a criterion is obtaining that bound from the initial data or conserved quantities.

Tao constructed blowup for a specially designed vector-valued forced defocusing system, showing that conservation and scaling alone are not enough to settle all regularity questions. That model differs from the unforced scalar equation considered here.

Merle, Raphaël, Rodnianski and Szeftel constructed radial whole-space defocusing blowup on finite-codimension families for selected dimension–power pairs, with a stated profile nondegeneracy condition. Cao-Labora, Gómez-Serrano, Shi and Staffilani developed nonradial periodic blowup, including the cubic equation in dimension eight. Those constructions use hydrodynamic profiles at spatial scales (T−t)1/r(T-t)^{1/r}(T−t)1/r with r>2r>2r>2.

A more immediate predecessor is Buck, Carballeira, Gómez-Serrano and Shi. They construct asymptotically self-similar scalar defocusing blowup from smooth radial compactly supported data on Rd\mathbb R^dRd for (d,p)=(3,27),(4,9),(5,7)(d,p)=(3,27),(4,9),(5,7)(d,p)=(3,27),(4,9),(5,7). Their construction is finite-codimensional; it does not assert an open set in the physical Sobolev space.

Open sets of self-similar blowup data have precedents for focusing NLS, including work of Merle–Raphaël–Szeftel and Li. The sign and spectral analysis are different. Family 371 claims to establish the profile and the full stability mechanism needed for an open set in the defocusing periodic problem.

The Gaussian question is motivated by an energy-supercritical branch of an open problem in Deng, Nahmod and Yue. The source explicitly gives its own precise quantifiers rather than identifying its corollary with every possible formulation of that problem. Global-flow results for particular invariant random ensembles also concern different probability measures.

4. What the new manuscript claims

A deterministic open set

There exist an odd power ppp, a finite integer k>8k>8k>8, and a nonempty open set

U⊂Hk(T12;C)\mathcal U\subset H^k(\mathbb T^{12};\mathbb C)U⊂Hk(T12;C)

such that every initial datum in U\mathcal UU produces a unique solution on [0,T)[0,T)[0,T), for some finite TTT, with

u∈C([0,T);Hk)∩C1([0,T);Hk−2),u\in C([0,T);H^k)\cap C^1([0,T);H^{k-2}),u∈C([0,T);Hk)∩C1([0,T);Hk−2),

and no continuous HkH^kHk extension through TTT.

More precisely, for some x∗∈T12x_*\in\mathbb T^{12}x∗​∈T12 and c0>0c_0>0c0​>0,

lim⁡t↑T(T−t)1/(p−1)∣u(t,x∗)∣=c0.\lim_{t\uparrow T}(T-t)^{1/(p-1)}|u(t,x_*)|=c_0.t↑Tlim​(T−t)1/(p−1)∣u(t,x∗​)∣=c0​.

The power is chosen sufficiently large and odd; kkk is fixed afterward. The theorem is existential and does not provide an explicit smallest permissible power.

Positive probability under a prescribed Gaussian law

Let gng_ngn​, indexed by n∈Z12n\in\mathbb Z^{12}n∈Z12, be independent standard complex Gaussian random variables. For every α>k+6\alpha>k+6α>k+6, consider

u0ω(x)=∑n∈Z12gn(ω)⟨n⟩αein⋅x,⟨n⟩=(1+∣n∣2)1/2.u_0^\omega(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^{12}}\frac{g_n(\omega)}{\langle n\rangle^\alpha}e^{in\cdot x},\qquad \langle n\rangle=(1+|n|^2)^{1/2}.u0ω​(x)=n∈Z12∑​⟨n⟩αgn​(ω)​ein⋅x,⟨n⟩=(1+∣n∣2)1/2.

The manuscript states that these data belong to HkH^kHk almost surely and have positive probability of finite-time blowup. Increasing α\alphaα gives arbitrarily high finite Sobolev regularity. A single fixed polynomial decay exponent does not mean that samples are almost surely C∞C^\inftyC∞.

The probability may depend on α\alphaα. No uniform positive lower bound and no almost-sure blowup assertion are made.

This refutes the universal assertion that every energy-supercritical pair admits a finite Gaussian-decay threshold beyond which all the indicated high-regularity local solutions extend globally almost surely. One fixed pair (12,p)(12,p)(12,p) suffices for that logical conclusion.

The source also obtains smooth deterministic blowup examples on product tori of every dimension d≥12d\ge12d≥12 by making the solution independent of the extra coordinates. It does not infer higher-dimensional openness or Gaussian blowup probability from that extension.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the family shows robust singularity formation for an unforced scalar defocusing equation and converts it into a failure of a broad proposed random-data global-existence principle.

The deterministic robustness is stronger than producing one special singular solution. It says that blowup occupies a genuine neighborhood in a high-regularity phase space, after allowing the singularity parameters to adjust.

The probabilistic conclusion is equally specific: regularity and full support of the Gaussian law do not remove that neighborhood. Randomness in this setting does not automatically protect the evolution from a stable deterministic singularity.

6. The main idea

Build a profile in the large-power limit

Set a=1/(p−1)a=1/(p-1)a=1/(p−1). For large ppp, this is a small parameter. In the limit a→0a\to0a→0, the radial profile develops a nearly flat core and an exterior governed by a simpler equation.

The exterior equation is expressed through confluent hypergeometric functions. Matching its value and derivative to the core becomes a finite-dimensional problem involving the phase frequency and core radius. The manuscript supplies analytic tail estimates and exact rational certificates for the matching and low-angular spectral calculations.

It then constructs genuine profiles at finite, sufficiently large odd powers. These are not merely formal asymptotic series. The finite calculations are reported as part of the manuscript’s argument; no independent certification is asserted by this digest.

Identify all relevant perturbation modes

Use similarity variables

y=x−x∗T−t,s=log⁡TT−t.y=\frac{x-x_*}{\sqrt{T-t}},\qquad s=\log\frac{T}{T-t}.y=T−t​x−x∗​​,s=logT−tT​.

Physical blowup at finite time corresponds to s→∞s\to\inftys→∞. Near its center the leading form is

u(t,x)≃eiθ(T−t)−aexp⁡ ⁣(iblog⁡T−tT)Q(y),u(t,x)\simeq e^{i\theta}(T-t)^{-a}\exp\!\left(ib\log\frac{T-t}{T}\right)Q(y),u(t,x)≃eiθ(T−t)−aexp(iblogTT−t​)Q(y),

where QQQ is the profile and bbb its phase-rotation frequency. This expression describes the concentrating core; the actual periodic solution uses a localized profile plus a decaying perturbation.

Linearization around QQQ separates perturbations into spherical-harmonic angular degrees. The claimed spectral classification leaves only the modes corresponding to phase, twelve spatial translations and blowup time in the relevant nondecaying spectral region.

Controlling only finitely many low modes would be insufficient. A uniform outgoing estimate excludes modes escaping to arbitrarily large temporal or angular frequencies. A compact limiting argument preserves algebraic multiplicities in the bounded spectral region.

Transfer stability to the periodic problem

In similarity coordinates, the torus expands as the singularity scale shrinks. Local convergence toward the whole-space profile does not automatically control perturbations far from the core: norm could escape into distant regions of the expanding torus.

The manuscript combines local compact-error estimates with global dissipative control in its similarity-space norms. This transfers decay to expanding tori while retaining the part of the norm that a purely local limiting argument could lose. The dissipation is in the rescaled perturbation estimates, not a claim that the original Schrödinger mass or energy ceases to be conserved.

A nonlinear argument then constructs a graph of perturbations that decay in similarity time.

Let physical parameters absorb the remaining modes

A stable graph by itself could still describe only a finite-codimension set. The source varies the phase, center and blowup time—fourteen real parameters in total—and shows that their variations account for all complementary modes.

A degree argument solves the matching equations for every physical datum in a small HkH^kHk ball around a smooth localized reference profile. This is the step that turns a constrained perturbation construction into an open set of actual initial data.

At the center, Q(0)≠0Q(0)\ne0Q(0)=0, and the perturbation tends to zero. Undoing the similarity variables gives the stated amplitude limit. Since high HkH^kHk regularity controls pointwise values, that divergence prevents continuous HkH^kHk continuation.

Use Gaussian support, not random forcing

For α>k+6\alpha>k+6α>k+6, the expected squared HkH^kHk norm of the Fourier series is finite because

∑n∈Z12⟨n⟩2k−2α<∞.\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^{12}}\langle n\rangle^{2k-2\alpha}<\infty.n∈Z12∑​⟨n⟩2k−2α<∞.

Its law has full support in HkH^kHk: every nonempty open ball has positive probability. A finite collection of Fourier coefficients has a positive Gaussian density everywhere, while the remaining tail can be small with positive probability.

The deterministic blowup neighborhood is one such open ball. The random solution therefore blows up with positive probability. No stochastic forcing is added to the PDE, and no separate random singularity construction is needed.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The stable theorem concerns dimension twelve and a sufficiently large odd power. It does not show open blowup sets for every energy-supercritical dimension–power pair or settle the optimal dimension and power range.

The Gaussian consequence concerns the specific independent Fourier law above. It does not contradict global existence for other ensembles, especially measures supported on special sets of initial data. It also leaves the blowup probability unquantified.

The result permits changes in blowup time, center and phase under perturbation. It does not assert that arbitrary large data blow up, that the same singularity is the only possible one, or that conservation of mass and energy fails before blowup.

The product construction gives higher-dimensional deterministic examples only. Extending openness, spectral stability or the Gaussian statement to those dimensions requires additional analysis.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary blowup papers linked above locate the contribution relative to whole-space, periodic, type-II and self-similar constructions. The Deng–Nahmod–Yue paper provides the random-data motivation, while the source gives the exact universal assertion it refutes.

For background, nonlinear Schrödinger equations and Sobolev spaces introduce the equation and regularity framework. The manuscript below supplies the deterministic openness and Gaussian consequence reported here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Stable self-similar blowup for a supercritical defocusing Schrödinger equation on the torus (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: From Newtonian particles to Boltzmann evolution and Gaussian fluctuations
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 364 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

A gas can be described by tracking every particle through Newton’s equations, or by evolving one density through the Boltzmann equation. The second description is far simpler, but why should it correctly summarize the first?

The Boltzmann–Grad limit makes this question precise. Particle interaction ranges shrink while particle numbers grow so that collisions remain frequent enough to matter. At leading order, one expects a deterministic kinetic density. At the next order, random initial sampling produces fluctuations around the mean, even though subsequent particle motion is deterministic.

Family 364 makes two claims on these two levels. M1 derives the nonlinear Boltzmann equation for a broad class of stable radial finite-range interaction potentials, allowing attractive wells. M2 derives Gaussian fluctuations for hard spheres away from equilibrium.

Both extend through any prescribed finite interval on which the corresponding classical Boltzmann solution exists with the stated Gaussian velocity bound. That is a conditional lifespan statement. Neither manuscript proves global regularity of the Boltzmann equation for arbitrary data.

2. Background and essential definitions

The dilute scaling and initial ensemble

Work in the whole position space R3\mathbb R^3R3, with velocities in R3\mathbb R^3R3. Let ε\varepsilonε be the interaction range or hard-sphere diameter. The activity parameter is

με=ε−2.\mu_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-2}.με​=ε−2.

The collision cross-sectional area is of order ε2\varepsilon^2ε2, so particle number of order ε−2\varepsilon^{-2}ε−2 keeps a typical collision frequency of order one. Meanwhile, occupied volume is of order μεε3=ε\mu_\varepsilon\varepsilon^3=\varepsilonμε​ε3=ε, which tends to zero.

The papers use a grand-canonical law: the number NNN is random. Given a probability density f0(z)f_0(z)f0​(z), with z=(x,v)z=(x,v)z=(x,v), the initial configuration law is proportional to

μεNN!∏i=1Nf0(zi) 1{∣xi−xj∣>ε for i≠j}.\frac{\mu_\varepsilon^N}{N!}\prod_{i=1}^N f_0(z_i)\,\mathbf1_{\{|x_i-x_j|>\varepsilon\ \text{for }i\ne j\}}.N!μεN​​i=1∏N​f0​(zi​)1{∣xi​−xj​∣>ε for i=j}​.

An exact normalizing constant makes this a probability measure, including the empty configuration. The exclusion prevents particles from starting within interaction range. For M1 it is an initial-law restriction only: the later Newtonian evolution is not artificially forbidden from creating close interacting groups.

Once initial data are sampled, the dynamics are deterministic. There is no stochastic collision rule or repeated resampling.

Stable potentials and the kinetic equation

M1 uses Φε(x)=Φ(x/ε)\Phi_\varepsilon(x)=\Phi(x/\varepsilon)Φε​(x)=Φ(x/ε), where Φ\PhiΦ is radial and zero outside the unit ball. Thermodynamic stability means that for some fixed B≥0B\ge0B≥0, every finite configuration satisfies

∑i<jΦ(qi−qj)≥−BN.\sum_{i<j}\Phi(q_i-q_j)\ge-BN.i<j∑​Φ(qi​−qj​)≥−BN.

Attraction is allowed, but total potential energy cannot decrease faster than linearly with particle number. The potential is C2C^2C2 everywhere, or C2C^2C2 away from a repulsive singularity with Φ(q)→+∞\Phi(q)\to+\inftyΦ(q)→+∞ at the origin.

The limiting density solves

∂tf+v⋅∇xf=QΦ(f,f),\partial_tf+v\cdot\nabla_xf=Q_\Phi(f,f),∂t​f+v⋅∇x​f=QΦ​(f,f),

where the collision operator is determined by actual two-body scattering for Φ\PhiΦ. M2 instead uses instantaneous elastic hard-sphere collisions.

Independence and fluctuations are different scales

The rescaled factorial marginal FsεF_s^\varepsilonFsε​ describes ordered selections of sss distinct particles, divided by μεs\mu_\varepsilon^sμεs​. Convergence to f⊗sf^{\otimes s}f⊗s means asymptotic independence of any fixed number of sampled particles, often called propagation of chaos.

For a smooth compactly supported test function aaa, the empirical observable is

πtε(a)=με−1∑i=1Na(zi(t)).\pi_t^\varepsilon(a)=\mu_\varepsilon^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N a(z_i(t)).πtε​(a)=με−1​i=1∑N​a(zi​(t)).

Its leading value is ∫aft\int af_t∫aft​. Central-limit fluctuations use the larger magnification

ζtε(a)=με(πtε(a)−Eπtε(a)).\zeta_t^\varepsilon(a)=\sqrt{\mu_\varepsilon}\bigl(\pi_t^\varepsilon(a)-\mathbb E\pi_t^\varepsilon(a)\bigr).ζtε​(a)=με​​(πtε​(a)−Eπtε​(a)).

An error that disappears at the first scale may survive at the second. This is why the exact microscopic expectation appears in the definition.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Grad introduced the dilute kinetic scaling, and Lanford proved the hard-sphere Boltzmann limit for a short time interval. King treated positive finite-range potentials. Gallagher, Saint-Raymond and Texier developed detailed geometric control of recollisions for hard spheres and repulsive interactions.

Pulvirenti, Saffirio and Simonella obtained a short-time theorem for the stable radial class relevant to M1, including attractive parts and scattering maps that need not have a globally single-valued differential cross-section. Global-time results for sufficiently rare dispersive gases were also obtained by Illner and Pulvirenti.

A major recent advance is Deng, Hani and Ma’s hard-sphere derivation throughout every regular finite kinetic interval. Their layered expansion retains correlations from earlier times rather than restarting a short-time theorem as if particles had become independent again. M1 extends this regular-lifespan objective to finite-duration interactions governed by stable potentials.

Fluctuation theory has a parallel history. Van Beijeren, Lanford, Lebowitz and Spohn obtained short-time equilibrium covariance results; Spohn treated nonequilibrium second moments. A Gaussian limit additionally requires control of higher correlations, not just the covariance.

Bodineau, Gallagher, Saint-Raymond and Simonella developed short-time nonequilibrium fluctuation theory, including process convergence, and later proved a long-time equilibrium Gaussian limit. Their fluctuation setting is periodic. M2 works in the whole space with integrable initial data, extends the time interval away from equilibrium, and claims finite-dimensional laws rather than convergence of entire random paths.

These distinctions locate the contributions accurately: neither long-time hard-sphere kinetic limits nor Gaussian Boltzmann fluctuations originate with this family. The new claims concern the stated interaction class, nonequilibrium lifespan and sharper control required at fluctuation scale.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Common regular-interval assumptions

The initial probability density has Gaussian velocity decay that is summable over spatial unit cells, as does its spatial gradient. Explicitly, for some β>0\beta>0β>0, the relevant sums include

∑k∈Z3 sup∣x−k∣≤1, v∈R3e2β∣v∣2(∣f0(x,v)∣+∣∇xf0(x,v)∣)<∞.\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}\ sup_{|x-k|\le1,\ v\in\mathbb R^3} e^{2\beta|v|^2}\bigl(|f_0(x,v)|+|\nabla_xf_0(x,v)|\bigr)<\infty.k∈Z3∑​ sup∣x−k∣≤1, v∈R3​e2β∣v∣2(∣f0​(x,v)∣+∣∇x​f0​(x,v)∣)<∞.

M1 assumes f0∈C1f_0\in C^1f0​∈C1; M2 assumes smoothness. Both take as input a nonnegative classical probability-density solution on [0,T][0,T][0,T] with

sup⁡0≤t≤Tsup⁡x,ve2β∣v∣2f(t,x,v)<∞.\sup_{0\le t\le T}\sup_{x,v}e^{2\beta|v|^2}f(t,x,v)<\infty.0≤t≤Tsup​x,vsup​e2β∣v∣2f(t,x,v)<∞.

No near-equilibrium or small-data condition replaces this lifespan hypothesis.

M1: all fixed marginals converge in full phase-space norm

For every fixed positive integer sss, M1 claims

sup⁡0≤t≤T∥Fsε(t)−f(t)⊗s∥L1((R6)s)⟶0.\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|F_s^\varepsilon(t)-f(t)^{\otimes s}\|_{L^1((\mathbb R^6)^s)}\longrightarrow0.0≤t≤Tsup​∥Fsε​(t)−f(t)⊗s∥L1((R6)s)​⟶0.

The potential and TTT are fixed independently of ε\varepsilonε. Attractive wells, long scattering delays, noninjective scattering maps, simultaneous interactions, recollisions and dynamically formed clusters are allowed in the actual process.

For each fixed observable, empirical averages consequently converge in probability to their kinetic values, uniformly over deterministic observation times. This means sup⁡tP(∣error at t∣>η)→0\sup_t\mathbb P(|\text{error at }t|>\eta)\to0supt​P(∣error at t∣>η)→0, not a probability bound on the supremum of the error along an entire sample path.

M2: Gaussian hard-sphere fluctuations at finitely many times

For hard spheres, M2 claims that every finite vector

(ζt1ε(a1),…,ζtmε(am))\bigl(\zeta_{t_1}^\varepsilon(a_1),\ldots,\zeta_{t_m}^\varepsilon(a_m)\bigr)(ζt1​ε​(a1​),…,ζtm​ε​(am​))

converges in distribution to the corresponding centered Gaussian vector from the linear fluctuating Boltzmann equation. The times and smooth compactly supported real tests are fixed in [0,T][0,T][0,T].

The limiting field has weak evolution

dζt(a)=ζt(Ata) dt+dWt(a),d\zeta_t(a)=\zeta_t(A_ta)\,dt+dW_t(a),dζt​(a)=ζt​(At​a)dt+dWt​(a),

where AtA_tAt​ is the dual linearization of transport and collisions about ftf_tft​, and WWW is Gaussian noise with independent increments. This noise describes the limiting statistics of deterministic collisions with random initial data.

For one elastic collision, define

Δa=a(x,v′)+a(x,v∗′)−a(x,v)−a(x,v∗).\Delta a=a(x,v')+a(x,v_*')-a(x,v)-a(x,v_*).Δa=a(x,v′)+a(x,v∗′​)−a(x,v)−a(x,v∗​).

With B=[(v−v∗)⋅ω]+B=[(v-v_*)\cdot\omega]_+B=[(v−v∗​)⋅ω]+​, the covariance rate of the noise is

Ct(a,b)=12∫Bft(x,v)ft(x,v∗)Δa Δb dx dv dv∗ dω.\mathcal C_t(a,b)=\frac12\int B f_t(x,v)f_t(x,v_*)\Delta a\,\Delta b\,dx\,dv\,dv_*\,d\omega.Ct​(a,b)=21​∫Bft​(x,v)ft​(x,v∗​)ΔaΔbdxdvdv∗​dω.

This incoming-flux normalization fixes the collision-rate constant. The initial covariance is

E[ζ0(a)ζ0(b)]=∫f0ab.\mathbb E[\zeta_0(a)\zeta_0(b)]=\int f_0ab.E[ζ0​(a)ζ0​(b)]=∫f0​ab.

There is no subtraction of (∫f0a)(∫f0b)(\int f_0a)(\int f_0b)(∫f0​a)(∫f0​b), because particle number is random. Initial fluctuations are independent of the collision noise.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, conditional on the claims. The family would strengthen the mathematical connection between microscopic mechanics and kinetic statistics at both the law-of-large-numbers and central-limit levels.

M1 would cover stable interactions with attraction through the full assumed regular kinetic interval, rather than only short times or purely repulsive settings. It treats actual interacting clusters instead of removing them from the microscopic model by definition.

M2 would explain nonequilibrium fluctuations over the same kind of regular lifespan. Identifying the Gaussian covariance and eliminating higher cumulants gives information that leading-order independence cannot provide.

The importance is conditional on kinetic regularity. Deriving a PDE from particle mechanics on its smooth lifespan and proving that the PDE remains smooth forever are different problems.

6. The main idea

Retain correlations across time layers

A collision-tree expansion tracks which particles have influenced an observed particle. Over longer times, those histories proliferate and create correlations. One cannot simply declare independence again at the start of each short interval.

Both manuscripts use coarse time layers, with finer subdivisions inside them, and center parts of the expansion against the known Boltzmann solution. Correlated remainders retain their earlier histories. Exact finite identities are established before limits and cutoffs are removed.

In M1, interactions last for positive time and several particles may interact together. The expansion therefore follows whole connected interaction components, rather than breaking every event into isolated instantaneous binary collisions. Keeping components intact preserves their potential-energy bookkeeping.

Thermodynamic stability provides one energy budget across the history. Each particle input is charged once rather than repeatedly at every layer. Combined with the time factors, this yields a summable expansion when the fixed number of coarse layers is chosen sufficiently large.

Expose exceptional encounters in causal order

Recollisions, crowded cells and long interactions are treated through geometric estimates. Fresh scattering parameters give small sets for an extra encounter with a trajectory independent of those parameters.

To multiply such small factors, the exposure order matters. For a genuine scattering, both not-yet-exposed outgoing branches must remain hidden until the fresh parameters are integrated. A virtual overlap between independently evolved components requires different bookkeeping. Exposing a branch too early could destroy the independence on which the small-factor estimate relies.

The manuscript combines these causal estimates with finite-history counting and chronological cutoff removal. Close configurations and any clusters in the real dynamics are finally controlled through their small nonnegative marginal mass; they were not excluded from the evolution.

Fluctuations require sharp connected estimates

A cumulant records the part of a correlation not explained by products of lower-order correlations. For Gaussian variables, cumulants above order two vanish.

M2 obtains connected factorial-cumulant bounds at scale μ1−h\mu^{1-h}μ1−h for hhh observed particle histories. Geometric mergers contribute the powers of ε2\varepsilon^2ε2 needed for that scale. After central-limit normalization, higher ordinary cumulants vanish, while the surviving two-particle terms and the same-particle diagonal contribution yield the stated covariance.

Observation marks attached to particle histories encode several fixed times in one calculation. This gives joint Gaussian laws for any finite list without asserting tightness in a space of whole trajectories.

Exact centering cannot be replaced by the kinetic mean

The initial exclusion already changes the empirical expectation at fluctuation scale. Writing ρ0(x)=∫f0(x,v) dv\rho_0(x)=\int f_0(x,v)\,dvρ0​(x)=∫f0​(x,v)dv, M2 states

μ(Eπ0ε(a)−∫f0a)⟶−4π3∫f0(x,v)a(x,v)ρ0(x) dx dv.\sqrt\mu\left(\mathbb E\pi_0^\varepsilon(a)-\int f_0a\right)\longrightarrow-\frac{4\pi}{3}\int f_0(x,v)a(x,v)\rho_0(x)\,dx\,dv.μ​(Eπ0ε​(a)−∫f0​a)⟶−34π​∫f0​(x,v)a(x,v)ρ0​(x)dxdv.

Thus centering by ∫aft\int af_t∫aft​ alone generally introduces a deterministic shift already at time zero. Leading-order convergence of the mean is not accurate enough.

The proof first obtains fluctuation limits for a modified, truncated dynamics. It then bounds the probability that this dynamics ever differs from the true one before TTT by O(ε1+η)O(\varepsilon^{1+\eta})O(ε1+η) for some η>0\eta>0η>0. Together with moments of N/μN/\muN/μ, this stronger estimate transfers expectations at order o(μ−1/2)o(\mu^{-1/2})o(μ−1/2), and hence transfers exact centering. A discrepancy probability merely tending to zero would not suffice for that step.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 treats fixed stable finite-range radial potentials in its stated smooth or repulsively singular class. It does not include arbitrary long-range forces, unstable attractions or nonspherical interactions. M2’s fluctuation theorem is for hard spheres; it is not automatically a fluctuation theorem for every potential in M1.

Both rely on a classical kinetic solution with uniform Gaussian velocity decay over the chosen finite interval. Neither extends the conclusion past a kinetic singularity or chooses among rough nonunique Boltzmann solutions.

M1 controls each fixed marginal order, not an order growing with particle number. Its empirical corollary is uniform over deterministic times, while M2 gives finite-dimensional distributions rather than process convergence or a path-space tightness theorem.

Extending fluctuations to stable attractive potentials, establishing full path-space convergence on the regular nonequilibrium lifespan, and weakening the kinetic envelope assumptions are separate questions. The expansions and convergence claims are reported as stated without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 states the stable-potential theorem and deterministic-time empirical corollary. M2 specifies the exact microscopic centering, grand-canonical covariance and finite-dimensional fluctuation limit.

Primary predecessors include Pulvirenti–Saffirio–Simonella on stable short-range potentials, Deng–Hani–Ma on the regular-lifespan hard-sphere limit, BGSS on short-time statistical dynamics, and their equilibrium fluctuation theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Boltzmann–Grad limit for stable radial potentials on regular kinetic intervals (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Hard-sphere fluctuations on the regular Boltzmann lifespan (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Can static boundary measurements determine an elastic body’s two moduli?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 372 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Suppose an elastic object has unknown stiffness inside. You prescribe a small displacement on its surface and measure the force required to hold that displacement. Repeating this for every possible boundary displacement gives a complete static boundary response.

Can those measurements determine both interior elastic moduli? In three-dimensional isotropic elasticity, one modulus controls shear and another controls compression. Their spatial variation is coupled through a vector-valued equilibrium equation, so recovering them is more complicated than recovering a single conductivity from voltage measurements.

Family 372 claims that the full static boundary map determines both smooth Lamé moduli on every bounded connected smooth domain in R3\mathbb R^3R3, under positive shear and bulk modulus assumptions. No small variation from constant coefficients, real analyticity or prior agreement near the boundary is required.

This is a uniqueness theorem for exact complete data in a fixed Euclidean domain. It does not supply a practical reconstruction algorithm or a bound for errors caused by measurement noise.

2. Background and essential definitions

Displacement, strain and stress

Let u:Ω→R3u:\Omega o\mathbb R^3u:Ω→R3 be the displacement of an elastic body. Its derivative matrix ∇u abla u∇u contains both deformation and infinitesimal rotation. The symmetric part

e(u)=∇u+(∇u)T2e(u)= rac{ abla u+( abla u)^T}{2}e(u)=2∇u+(∇u)T​

is the linearized strain. Taking the symmetric part removes pure infinitesimal rotation, which should not cost elastic energy.

An isotropic material has the same local response in every direction. Its stress tensor is determined by two scalar functions, the Lamé moduli λ(x)\lambda(x)λ(x) and μ(x)\mu(x)μ(x):

σλ,μ(u)=λ(div⁡u)I+2μe(u).\sigma_{\lambda,\mu}(u)=\lambda(\operatorname{div}u)I+2\mu e(u).σλ,μ​(u)=λ(divu)I+2μe(u).

Here III is the identity matrix and div⁡u=tr⁡e(u)\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{tr}e(u)divu=tre(u) measures first-order volume change. The shear modulus is μ\muμ; the bulk modulus is λ+2μ/3\lambda+2\mu/3λ+2μ/3.

Static equilibrium without body forces means

div⁡σλ,μ(u)=0.\operatorname{div}\sigma_{\lambda,\mu}(u)=0.divσλ,μ​(u)=0.

The divergence acts on the rows of the stress tensor. This is the Lamé system, a coupled elliptic PDE for the three components of uuu.

Why the positivity assumptions have this form

The energy density is

λ(tr⁡e)2+2μ∣e∣2.\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e)^2+2\mu|e|^2.λ(tre)2+2μ∣e∣2.

Decompose strain into its trace-free part e0e_0e0​ and its pure-volume part:

e=e0+tr⁡e3I.e=e_0+ rac{\operatorname{tr}e}{3}I.e=e0​+3tre​I.

Then the same density becomes

2μ∣e0∣2+(λ+2μ3)(tr⁡e)2.2\mu|e_0|^2+\left(\lambda+ rac{2\mu}{3} ight)(\operatorname{tr}e)^2.2μ∣e0​∣2+(λ+32μ​)(tre)2.

Thus the assumptions

μ>0,3λ+2μ>0\mu>0,\qquad 3\lambda+2\mu>0μ>0,3λ+2μ>0

give positive energy for both shear and compression. The coefficient λ\lambdaλ itself need not be positive. For smooth coefficients on the compact closure, strict positivity gives uniform positive lower bounds.

The measured operator

Prescribe boundary displacement fff, and let ufu_fuf​ be the equilibrium solution with that boundary value. The measured traction is the force per unit area,

Λλ,μf=σλ,μ(uf)n,\Lambda_{\lambda,\mu}f=\sigma_{\lambda,\mu}(u_f)n,Λλ,μ​f=σλ,μ​(uf​)n,

where nnn is the outward normal. The displacement-to-traction map Λ\LambdaΛ records this response for every fff.

Its weak form is

⟨Λf,g⟩=∫Ω[λ(div⁡uf)(div⁡vg)+2μe(uf):e(vg)],dx,\langle\Lambda f,g angle=\int_\Omega igl[\lambda(\operatorname{div}u_f)(\operatorname{div}v_g)+2\mu e(u_f):e(v_g) igr],dx,⟨Λf,g⟩=∫Ω​[λ(divuf​)(divvg​)+2μe(uf​):e(vg​)],dx,

where vgv_gvg​ is any Sobolev extension of the boundary displacement ggg, and A:B=∑i,jAijBijA:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}A:B=∑i,j​Aij​Bij​. Equilibrium makes the value independent of the chosen extension.

The natural trace spaces are H1/2H^{1/2}H1/2 for displacement and H−1/2H^{-1/2}H−1/2 for traction. They allow the boundary work pairing to remain meaningful when the data are less regular than classical smooth functions.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Calderón’s conductivity problem and the Sylvester–Uhlmann complex geometric optics method established the broader inverse-boundary framework. Elasticity adds two coefficient fields and vector coupling; scalar uniqueness cannot simply be applied component by component.

Nakamura and Uhlmann recovered the boundary Taylor series of the elastic coefficients. Their 1994 global uniqueness claim was subsequently corrected by a 2003 erratum. The corrected theorem assumes sufficiently small derivatives of the shear moduli in a suitable smooth norm.

The erratum identifies difficulties in a prescribed planar matrix transport problem and in the type of equation obtained from corrected complex geometric optics solutions. This is part of the mathematical development history: the unrestricted smooth three-dimensional theorem should not be attributed to the original claim without its correction.

Eskin and Ralston developed matrix complex geometric optics expansions and restricted elasticity uniqueness results. Their auxiliary vector–scalar reductions are useful, but an auxiliary field can contain information not determined by the corresponding physical displacement. Equality of physical boundary measurements must therefore be transferred with care.

In two dimensions, Imanuvilov and Yamamoto proved global uniqueness for smooth Lamé coefficients under the appropriate positivity assumptions, without a smallness condition. The different dimension changes the available analytic methods.

For three dimensions, Lin and Nakamura developed boundary reconstruction at finite regularity. Tan and Liu recovered boundary jets on smooth Riemannian manifolds and obtained global recovery under analytic hypotheses. Recent work by Chen, Jiang, Liu and Tao treats structured shear moduli under specified symmetry, separation or quasianalyticity assumptions.

The new manuscript claims global uniqueness for the unrestricted smooth isotropic class under positive elastic energy. Its method combines physical displacement transfer, compatible complex geometric optics solutions and holomorphic dependence on complex directions.

4. What the new manuscript claims

Let Ω⊂R3\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3Ω⊂R3 be any bounded connected domain with C∞C^\inftyC∞ boundary. For j=1,2j=1,2j=1,2, let λj,μj\lambda_j,\mu_jλj​,μj​ be real functions smooth on the closure and satisfying

μj>0,3λj+2μj>0on Ω‾.\mu_j>0,\qquad3\lambda_j+2\mu_j>0\quad ext{on }\overline\Omega.μj​>0,3λj​+2μj​>0on Ω.

The theorem states

Λλ1,μ1=Λλ2,μ2⟹λ1=λ2,μ1=μ2throughout Ω.\Lambda_{\lambda_1,\mu_1}=\Lambda_{\lambda_2,\mu_2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda_1=\lambda_2,\qquad\mu_1=\mu_2\quad ext{throughout }\Omega.Λλ1​,μ1​​=Λλ2​,μ2​​⟹λ1​=λ2​,μ1​=μ2​throughout Ω.

The measured map is the full zero-frequency displacement-to-traction operator. Both inputs and observations range over the whole boundary. Unlike the local conductivity claims discussed in family 365, this theorem is not stated for one arbitrary boundary patch.

The domain and Euclidean coordinates are fixed. The conclusion is exact equality of the two scalar coefficient fields, not equality modulo an arbitrary interior coordinate transformation.

No simple-connectivity assumption is imposed. The boundary may have several components. The moduli need not be close to constants, and agreement in a boundary neighborhood is not an input hypothesis: the source derives the required matching boundary information from the measurements.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the manuscript resolves a central smooth inverse problem for three-dimensional isotropic elasticity. It establishes that the full static response contains enough information to separate and recover both shear and compressional behavior.

The result concerns identifiability before computation. If two different admissible interiors could produce identical complete data, no algorithm could distinguish them from those data alone. The claimed theorem excludes that ambiguity in the stated class.

Its proposed method also addresses a recurring issue in inverse systems: an analytically convenient augmented equation may have more solutions than the physical model. Recovery must use the boundary information actually available for physical displacements, not stronger measurements of auxiliary variables that were never prescribed.

6. The main idea

Transfer genuine displacements between the two media

Equality of boundary maps first gives equality of all boundary derivatives of the moduli. The manuscript extends both coefficient pairs smoothly outside Ω\OmegaΩ, making them identical there and constant sufficiently far away.

Take an exact equilibrium displacement in the first extended medium. In the second medium, solve the interior problem with the same boundary displacement and glue it to the first solution outside. Equality of traction cancels the interface term in the weak equation, so the glued field is an exact physical solution of the second system.

The two displacements and their actual divergences agree outside the object. This exterior agreement is the starting information for the analytic comparison; it is obtained from the physical map itself.

Add divergence without forgetting its meaning

Adjoining a scalar variable ddd, intended to equal div⁡u\operatorname{div}udivu, turns the system into an augmented vector–scalar equation whose highest-order part is the ordinary Laplacian on each component.

That simplification is useful for estimates, but arbitrary augmented solutions need not satisfy d=div⁡ud=\operatorname{div}ud=divu. The manuscript retains a compatibility identity for this difference and constructs exact physical displacements after correcting approximate solutions. Thus the scalar component remains the true divergence in the comparisons that use measured data.

The normalized augmented operators for two coefficient pairs have the same highest-order part. Their difference contains only first derivatives and zeroth-order terms, which is crucial for controlling transferred solutions.

Probe with complex exponential solutions

Choose a nonzero complex vector θ hetaθ with

θ⋅θ=0. heta\cdot heta=0.θ⋅θ=0.

The dot product here is complex bilinear, without complex conjugation. Such vectors exist: (1,i,0)(1,i,0)(1,i,0) is an example. The null condition makes the largest Laplacian term vanish when testing with an exponential eτθ⋅xe^{ au heta\cdot x}eτθ⋅x, leaving transport equations for its amplitude.

The real and imaginary parts of θ hetaθ span a plane. On that plane, Dθ=θ⋅∇D_ heta= heta\cdot ablaDθ​=θ⋅∇ acts like a complex Cauchy–Riemann derivative. Leading displacement amplitudes aaa satisfy θ⋅a=0 heta\cdot a=0θ⋅a=0; together with a scalar divergence amplitude they form a three-dimensional complex space.

The manuscript constructs a full local frame in this constrained space using exact physical solutions. High-order transport expansions and weighted estimates control both the leading amplitudes and their first derivatives. This is stronger than constructing formal auxiliary solutions with no physical compatibility.

Compare transport frames as direction varies

After an invertible normalization, each medium’s leading transport has a universal upper equation of the form

DθP=θs,D_ heta P= heta s,Dθ​P=θs,

where P∈θ⊥P\in heta^\perpP∈θ⊥ and sss is scalar. The coefficient dependence enters the remaining equation.

Transfer a first-medium frame through the physical solution construction. Limits of the transferred amplitudes produce a comparison matrix GGG, equal to the identity outside a fixed ball. Only the original frame must be invertible; the argument does not initially assume that the transferred columns form a frame.

Supported transport uniqueness joins the local comparisons and makes them vary holomorphically with the complex direction. Directions are considered up to nonzero complex multiples; the null directions form a compact complex curve, the projective null conic.

The spaces θ⊥ heta^\perpθ⊥ vary with direction and form a vector bundle: a smoothly and holomorphically organized family of vector spaces. The manuscript uses this bundle’s restricted holomorphic sections, together with the universal upper transport equation, to force GGG to be the identity. A rank comparison on the two-dimensional space θ⊥ heta^\perpθ⊥ removes the remaining off-diagonal freedom.

Recover the moduli from identical transports

Equality of transport coefficients first determines the ratio

λ+μλ+2μ. rac{\lambda+\mu}{\lambda+2\mu}.λ+2μλ+μ​.

The remaining difference is expressed through

η=log⁡μ1−log⁡μ2.\eta=\log\mu_1-\log\mu_2.η=logμ1​−logμ2​.

The manuscript derives a system of the form

∇2η=B(x)∇η+q(x)I, abla^2\eta=B(x) abla\eta+q(x)I,∇2η=B(x)∇η+q(x)I,

where B(x)B(x)B(x) is a known smooth linear map from vectors to matrices and qqq is an auxiliary scalar. Differentiating and commuting mixed derivatives closes a homogeneous first-order system for (∇η,q)( abla\eta,q)(∇η,q).

These quantities vanish in the common exterior. Along any path the system becomes a linear ordinary differential equation with zero initial values, so uniqueness propagates their vanishing throughout the connected region. The exterior normalization fixes the remaining constant in η\etaη, giving μ1=μ2\mu_1=\mu_2μ1​=μ2​. The already determined ratio then gives λ1=λ2\lambda_1=\lambda_2λ1​=λ2​.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns smooth real isotropic coefficients in three dimensions with positive shear and bulk moduli. Rough, complex, anisotropic or degenerating coefficients are outside its statement. It also concerns static linearized elasticity, not nonlinear material response or an unknown mass density in a time-dependent problem.

Full boundary data mean an entire operator, not finitely many loading experiments. The result does not quantify reconstruction stability, give a noise tolerance or specify a numerical recovery method.

Partial-boundary recovery, lower regularity and quantitative estimates remain separate questions. The connection to family 365 is methodological, through complex transport and inverse-boundary geometry; its different operator and measurement assumptions should be retained.

8. Sources and further reading

The Nakamura–Uhlmann erratum is essential to the historical account. The Imanuvilov–Yamamoto, Lin–Nakamura and Tan–Liu papers linked above describe the two-dimensional and boundary-determination precedents. Eskin–Ralston supply important matrix complex geometric optics methods.

For optional background, Lamé parameters and linear elasticity explain the material interpretation. The manuscript below is the source of the unrestricted smooth three-dimensional uniqueness claim.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Global Uniqueness for the Smooth Isotropic Elasticity Inverse Problem (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How sensitively does an optimal transport map depend on its target?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 374 · Partial differential equations
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

An optimal transport map rearranges one probability distribution into another with the least mean squared travel distance. If the target distribution changes only a little, should the optimal map change only a little as well?

Continuity alone gives no rate. A numerical or statistical application needs to know how an error in the target distribution translates into an error in the map assigning destinations to individual source points.

Family 374 claims the sharp uniform rate when the source is uniformly distributed on a compact convex body. In every dimension at least two, the map varies Hölder continuously with exponent one-third in the target’s quadratic Wasserstein distance. The constant works for every target in a fixed compact set, including discrete targets with vanishingly small atom masses.

A three-atom construction on a fixed cube is claimed to show that no larger exponent works uniformly. In particular, it disproves a conjectured square-root rate in this class.

2. Background and essential definitions

The Brenier map

Let K⊂RdK\subset\mathbb R^dK⊂Rd be compact and convex with nonempty interior. The fixed source probability measure is

ρ=1K∣K∣ dx, ho= rac{\mathbf1_K}{|K|}\,dx,ρ=∣K∣1K​​dx,

where ∣K∣|K|∣K∣ is its volume. Let μ\muμ be a target probability measure supported in a compact set YYY.

Among maps TTT satisfying T#ρ=μT_\# ho=\muT#​ρ=μ, quadratic optimal transport minimizes

∫K∣x−T(x)∣2 dρ(x).\int_K|x-T(x)|^2\,d ho(x).∫K​∣x−T(x)∣2dρ(x).

The pushforward condition means that if xxx is sampled from ρ hoρ, then T(x)T(x)T(x) has distribution μ\muμ. Brenier’s theorem gives an almost-everywhere unique optimal map of the form

Tμ=∇φμ,T_\mu= abla\varphi_\mu,Tμ​=∇φμ​,

where φμ\varphi_\muφμ​ is convex. The potential is determined only up to an additive constant; its gradient is unaffected by that freedom.

Even though the source has a density, the target may consist of atoms. In that case the map is typically constant on cells and jumps across their boundaries. Stability here cannot rely on every transport map being a smooth function.

Two different distances

The quadratic Wasserstein distance between targets is

W2(μ,ν)=inf⁡π∈Π(μ,ν)(∫∣y−z∣2 dπ(y,z))1/2.W_2(\mu, u)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu, u)}\left(\int|y-z|^2\,d\pi(y,z) ight)^{1/2}.W2​(μ,ν)=π∈Π(μ,ν)inf​(∫∣y−z∣2dπ(y,z))1/2.

A coupling π\piπ matches target mass from μ\muμ to target mass from ν uν. It may choose whichever matching is cheapest.

The map error instead compares the destinations of the same source point:

∥Tμ−Tν∥L2(ρ)=(∫K∣Tμ(x)−Tν(x)∣2 dρ(x))1/2.\|T_\mu-T_ u\|_{L^2( ho)}=\left(\int_K|T_\mu(x)-T_ u(x)|^2\,d ho(x) ight)^{1/2}.∥Tμ​−Tν​∥L2(ρ)​=(∫K​∣Tμ​(x)−Tν​(x)∣2dρ(x))1/2.

These are different comparisons. Two target distributions can be close because their atoms barely move, while their optimal source partitions change enough to send some source points to entirely different atoms.

A Hölder bound with exponent α\alphaα has the form

∥Tμ−Tν∥L2(ρ)≤CW2(μ,ν)α.\|T_\mu-T_ u\|_{L^2( ho)}\le C W_2(\mu, u)^\alpha.∥Tμ​−Tν​∥L2(ρ)​≤CW2​(μ,ν)α.

For small distances, a larger exponent gives a stronger bound. “Uniform” means one constant works for every pair of targets in the prescribed class.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Brenier’s polar-factorization theorem supplies the representation by convex gradients. Quantitative stability asks how reliably that representation changes when the measure changes.

Early estimates included a local square-root bound along target curves near regular data, attributed to Ambrosio and recorded by Gigli. Berman obtained quantitative estimates under geometric and density assumptions in a different source–target variation setting.

Mérigot, Delalande and Chazal used duality to obtain target-uniform bounds, including a dimension-independent exponent 2/152/152/15 measured in W1W_1W1​. Here W1W_1W1​ is the optimal expected travel distance without squaring it.

Delalande and Mérigot obtained an L2L^2L2 map bound of order W11/6W_1^{1/6}W11/6​ for source densities bounded above and below on convex domains. Their route—first compare potentials, then interpolate to control gradients—is an important predecessor of this manuscript’s final step. Letrouit and Mérigot later extended potential stability to John domains using local-to-global methods.

Divol, Niles-Weed and Pooladian obtained a one-third W2W_2W2​ bound for regular sources and nondegenerate finite targets. Its constant depends on atom count, lower mass bounds and geometric separation conditions. Thus the exponent itself has a precedent; the present theorem claims a constant uniform even as those target features degenerate.

At the regular end of the subject, Caja-Lopez, Delgadino and Kitagawa obtain Lipschitz stability under strong positive-density and domain-regularity hypotheses. Better rates in such classes are compatible with a worse optimal rate when arbitrary atomic targets are allowed.

For unrestricted targets, recent work also gives stronger W1W_1W1​ estimates, including a sharp quarter-power bound of Mérigot reported in the literature cited by the manuscript. Since W1≤W2W_1\le W_2W1​≤W2​, that comparison alone does not give a one-third W2W_2W2​ estimate.

Letrouit exhibited a one-third obstruction for a nonconvex source and conjectured a uniform square-root rate for a uniform convex source. Family 374 claims that convexity does not remove the obstruction: three atoms on a fixed cube already force one-third, and its upper bound attains that endpoint.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For every compact convex body K⊂RdK\subset\mathbb R^dK⊂Rd with interior, every nonempty compact set Y⊂RdY\subset\mathbb R^dY⊂Rd, and every d≥2d\ge2d≥2, there is a finite constant C(K,Y)C(K,Y)C(K,Y) such that

∥Tμ−Tν∥L2(ρ)≤C(K,Y)W2(μ,ν)1/3\|T_\mu-T_ u\|_{L^2( ho)}\le C(K,Y)W_2(\mu, u)^{1/3}∥Tμ​−Tν​∥L2(ρ)​≤C(K,Y)W2​(μ,ν)1/3

for all Borel probability measures μ,ν\mu, uμ,ν supported in YYY.

Targets may be atomic, singular or absolutely continuous. The constant is independent of the number of atoms, their positive masses, site separation and target density bounds. It can depend on the fixed source and target sets, hence on their geometry and dimension.

No smoothness or strict convexity of KKK is required. The compact set YYY need not be convex. The source, however, is specifically uniform on KKK; the theorem does not assert this same endpoint for every nonuniform bounded source density.

Sharpness is stated on K=Y=[−1,1]dK=Y=[-1,1]^dK=Y=[−1,1]d. Even restricting each target to exactly three atoms, every exponent larger than 1/31/31/3 fails with a target-independent constant.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the result determines the optimal uniform stability exponent for a broad and useful class of quadratic transport maps, while resolving the proposed square-root improvement negatively.

The uniformity is practically significant. Discrete approximations can introduce tiny masses, nearly merging sites or changing atom counts. A bound whose constant deteriorates with those features may be unsuitable for a refinement limit. The claimed estimate remains valid throughout those degenerations.

The theorem also quantifies the limits of representing a distribution by its optimal map from one fixed reference measure. That representation is stable, but its worst-case sensitivity is inherently nonlinear. Additional target regularity can improve the rate; arbitrary compact support alone cannot.

6. The main idea

A thin cell creates the sharp obstruction

On the uniform cube, choose 0<a<1/20<a<1/20<a<1/2, let b=a/2b=a/2b=a/2, and consider convex potentials

φa(x)=max⁡{−x1,x1,a},\varphi_a(x)=\max\{-x_1,x_1,a\},φa​(x)=max{−x1​,x1​,a},

and

φ~a(x)=max⁡{−x1,x1,a+bx2}.\widetilde\varphi_a(x)=\max\{-x_1,x_1,a+bx_2\}.φ​a​(x)=max{−x1​,x1​,a+bx2​}.

A maximum of affine functions is convex. Its gradient equals the slope of the winning affine function almost everywhere, so each potential defines a three-valued optimal map to its own target law.

For the first potential, the central cell is ∣x1∣<a|x_1|<a∣x1​∣<a. Tilting the central affine function changes that cell to ∣x1∣<a+bx2|x_1|<a+bx_2∣x1​∣<a+bx2​. Its total mass remains aaa, but some source points switch between the central and outer destinations.

The targets are

μa=1−a2(δ−e1+δe1)+aδ0,\mu_a= rac{1-a}{2}(\delta_{-e_1}+\delta_{e_1})+a\delta_0,μa​=21−a​(δ−e1​​+δe1​​)+aδ0​,
νa=1−a2(δ−e1+δe1)+aδbe2. u_a= rac{1-a}{2}(\delta_{-e_1}+\delta_{e_1})+a\delta_{be_2}.νa​=21−a​(δ−e1​​+δe1​​)+aδbe2​​.

Here δy\delta_yδy​ denotes unit point mass at yyy. Only the small central atom moves. The manuscript gives the exact identities

W2(μa,νa)2=ab2,W_2(\mu_a, u_a)^2=ab^2,W2​(μa​,νa​)2=ab2,

and

∥Tμa−Tνa∥L2(ρ)2=b2+ab2.\|T_{\mu_a}-T_{ u_a}\|_{L^2( ho)}^2= rac b2+ab^2.∥Tμa​​−Tνa​​∥L2(ρ)2​=2b​+ab2.

Thus target distance has order a3/2a^{3/2}a3/2, while map error has order a1/2a^{1/2}a1/2. Their relation is precisely a cube root. The larger map error comes from source points reassigned between destinations separated by order-one distances, not from the tiny movement of the central atom alone.

For the same example W1=abW_1=abW1​=ab, of order a2a^2a2. Its map error therefore also fits a quarter-power W1W_1W1​ obstruction. The two sharp exponents are compatible because the two target distances scale differently here.

Control finite cells without a separation assumption

For the upper bound, first take a finite target with sites yiy_iyi​. Its potential has the form

φc(x)=max⁡i{x⋅yi+ci}.\varphi_c(x)=\max_i\{x\cdot y_i+c_i\}.φc​(x)=imax​{x⋅yi​+ci​}.

The intercepts cic_ici​ determine convex cells PiP_iPi​ on which the map equals yiy_iyi​. Let

Mi=ρ(Pi),Bi=∫Pix dρ(x)M_i= ho(P_i),\qquad B_i=\int_{P_i}x\,d ho(x)Mi​=ρ(Pi​),Bi​=∫Pi​​xdρ(x)

be each cell’s mass and first moment.

The source’s central estimate compares how moments and masses change when the intercepts vary. If dots denote these derivatives and K⊂B(0,R)K\subset B(0,R)K⊂B(0,R), the claimed inequality is

∑i∣B˙i∣2Mi≤C0R2∑i∣M˙i∣2Mi.\sum_i rac{|\dot B_i|^2}{M_i}\le C_0R^2\sum_i rac{|\dot M_i|^2}{M_i}.i∑​Mi​∣B˙i​∣2​≤C0​R2i∑​Mi​∣M˙i​∣2​.

Its constant stays controlled even when cells or faces become small. The proof couples uniform measures on nearby cells and controls the density of their midpoint distribution using convexity and a triangular rearrangement. Testing a concave quadratic function and summing over the partition turns that geometric comparison into the moment estimate.

Move target sites while preserving their masses

An optimal coupling between two finite targets gives a way to move their sites while retaining the coupling masses. Keeping the source-cell masses fixed determines how the intercepts must change.

The resulting linear equation is a weighted graph-Laplacian equation: neighboring cells exchange mass through shared faces. Direct inversion can be poorly conditioned when cells become tiny. The manuscript instead tests the equation in a direction chosen to exploit the moment inequality, obtaining a bound for the weighted intercept velocity without a quantitative inverse-Laplacian estimate.

After integrating the motion, this yields a potential estimate of the form

∥φμ−φν∥L2(ρ)≤CW2(μ,ν),\|\varphi_\mu-\varphi_ u\|_{L^2( ho)}\le C W_2(\mu, u),∥φμ​−φν​∥L2(ρ)​≤CW2​(μ,ν),

with additive constants normalized appropriately.

Turn potential control into gradient control

Potential values can be much closer than their gradients near moving cell boundaries. Convexity supplies an interpolation estimate. For a step length h>0h>0h>0, comparison with finite differences along coordinate slices gives

∥∇φμ−∇φν∥L2(ρ)2≤C(h−2∥φμ−φν∥L2(ρ)2+h).\| abla\varphi_\mu- abla\varphi_ u\|_{L^2( ho)}^2\le C\left(h^{-2}\|\varphi_\mu-\varphi_ u\|_{L^2( ho)}^2+h ight).∥∇φμ​−∇φν​∥L2(ρ)2​≤C(h−2∥φμ​−φν​∥L2(ρ)2​+h).

Convexity makes every nonempty coordinate slice an interval and bounds the accumulated derivative changes along it. Boundary slices contribute the term proportional to hhh, without requiring a smooth boundary.

Insert the potential estimate and balance the terms with hhh of order W22/3W_2^{2/3}W22/3​. The squared map error is then of order W22/3W_2^{2/3}W22/3​, giving the one-third bound after taking a square root.

Finally, finite approximations of arbitrary target measures and supporting inequalities for convex potentials extend the result beyond discrete targets. Uniformity of the finite-cell estimates is what makes that passage possible.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Sharpness concerns one constant valid for all targets in a compact set. It does not prevent a better local rate near a regular target or a better uniform rate on a class with density and nondegeneracy bounds.

The source is fixed and uniform on a convex body. Nonuniform sources, changing sources, nonconvex supports, other transport costs and manifold settings require separate hypotheses. Dimension one is not part of the sharpness statement.

The norm is an averaged L2L^2L2 map error. It does not give uniform pointwise closeness of maps, continuity of discontinuous cell assignments, or a universal numerical convergence rate independent of an approximation scheme.

The theorem identifies the endpoint in this source class; understanding which weaker or different source assumptions retain it is a distinct question.

8. Sources and further reading

The Brenier, Delalande–Mérigot, Divol–Niles-Weed–Pooladian and Letrouit papers linked above locate the representation, interpolation method, finite-target predecessor and conjectured exponent. Kitagawa, Mérigot and Thibert develop the semi-discrete cell calculus and graph-Laplacian viewpoint used in this area.

Optional background on Brenier’s theorem and Wasserstein distance complements the definitions. The manuscript below supplies the claimed uniform endpoint and matching three-atom example.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Sharp One-Third Stability of Brenier Maps (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why monotone Allen–Cahn transitions must be planar through dimension eight
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 375 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Imagine a material with two preferred phases, labeled −1-1−1 and 111. A transition between them occupies a thin layer. The simplest equilibrium has parallel, flat layers: the phase changes only with distance in one direction.

Could an equilibrium transition be curved everywhere, even if the phase always increases as we move upward? This is the question behind De Giorgi’s conjecture for the Allen–Cahn equation. It connects a nonlinear differential equation to the geometry of minimal surfaces.

The manuscript in this family claims that every bounded equilibrium in eight-dimensional Euclidean space, strictly increasing in one fixed direction, is a flat one-dimensional transition. It assumes neither a bound on the amount of transition energy in large balls nor prescribed phases at the two ends of that direction. Those properties are conclusions of its argument.

Eight is significant. Nonplanar monotone solutions are already known in dimensions nine and higher. A second threshold is equally important: the manuscript claims a classification of stable solutions in dimension seven, while stable nonplanar solutions are known in dimension eight. Monotonicity and stability are related conditions, but they have different endpoints.

2. Background and essential definitions

A diffuse interface equation

The scalar Allen–Cahn equation considered here is

Δu=u3−u.\Delta u=u^3-u.Δu=u3−u.

Here u:Rn→[−1,1]u:\mathbb R^n\to[-1,1]u:Rn→[−1,1] describes the phase and Δ\DeltaΔ is the sum of the second derivatives. The potential

W(s)=14(1−s2)2W(s)=\frac14(1-s^2)^2W(s)=41​(1−s2)2

has minima at the two preferred values. On a region Ω\OmegaΩ, the energy is

E(u;Ω)=∫Ω(12∣∇u∣2+W(u)) dx.E(u;\Omega)=\int_\Omega\left(\frac12|\nabla u|^2+W(u)\right)\,dx.E(u;Ω)=∫Ω​(21​∣∇u∣2+W(u))dx.

The first term discourages abrupt spatial changes; the second discourages intermediate phase values. Equilibria satisfy the displayed differential equation.

An explicit transition is g(s)=tanh⁡(s/2)g(s)=\tanh(s/\sqrt2)g(s)=tanh(s/2​). If eee is a unit vector and ccc a real number, then

u(x)=g(e⋅x−c)u(x)=g(e\cdot x-c)u(x)=g(e⋅x−c)

is a solution. Its level sets are parallel hyperplanes. Such a solution is called a planar heteroclinic: it connects the two constant equilibria as its one relevant coordinate runs from one end of the real line to the other. “Entire” means defined on all of Rn\mathbb R^nRn, with no finite boundary.

Stability versus minimization

A solution vvv is stable if small, compactly supported perturbations cannot lower its energy to second order. Precisely, every continuously differentiable test function φ\varphiφ of compact support must satisfy

Qv(φ)=∫Rn(∣∇φ∣2+(3v2−1)φ2) dx≥0.Q_v(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\left(|\nabla\varphi|^2+(3v^2-1)\varphi^2\right)\,dx\geq0.Qv​(φ)=∫Rn​(∣∇φ∣2+(3v2−1)φ2)dx≥0.

A global minimizer satisfies a stronger requirement: in every ball it has least energy among all Sobolev competitors with the same boundary values. Stability tests the quadratic response near a solution; minimization compares it with potentially large changes.

Strict monotonicity means ∂nu>0\partial_nu>0∂n​u>0 everywhere, after choosing coordinates. This positive derivative solves the linearized equation and supplies stability. But a general stable solution need not have a preferred direction of increase.

Energy density

A planar transition has infinite energy in the whole space, but its energy in a ball of radius RRR grows like surface area, Rn−1R^{n-1}Rn−1. The normalized density is

MR(y)=E(v;BR(y))s0ωn−1Rn−1,s0=223.M_R(y)=\frac{E(v;B_R(y))}{s_0\omega_{n-1}R^{n-1}},\qquad s_0=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}.MR​(y)=s0​ωn−1​Rn−1E(v;BR​(y))​,s0​=322​​.

Here BR(y)B_R(y)BR​(y) is the ball centered at yyy, ωn−1\omega_{n-1}ωn−1​ is the volume of the unit ball in Rn−1\mathbb R^{n-1}Rn−1, and s0s_0s0​ is the energy per unit area of the one-dimensional transition. Its limiting density is one. A finite-density assumption bounds sup⁡R>0MR(0)\sup_{R>0}M_R(0)supR>0​MR​(0); it does not require finite total energy.

3. Development history and previous partial results

De Giorgi proposed the monotonicity question in the late 1970s, in the setting of phase transitions and the Bernstein problem for minimal graphs. The connection comes from sharpening the interface: appropriately rescaled phase energies converge to surface tension times perimeter.

The geometric analogy contains a crucial distinction. Nonflat minimizing cones occur in ambient dimension eight. Nonaffine entire minimal graphs first occur in ambient dimension nine. A graph has directional structure that an arbitrary minimizing surface lacks; likewise, a monotone phase transition carries more information than stability alone.

Ghoussoub and Gui established the Allen–Cahn conjecture in dimension two in 1998. Ambrosio and Cabré proved the three-dimensional result in 2000. These were classifications without an assumption that the solution already approaches the two wells along the monotone direction.

Savin’s 2009 theorem reached dimensions through eight with an additional hypothesis: for each fixed transverse point x′x'x′, the solution tends to −1-1−1 as the last coordinate tends to minus infinity and to 111 as it tends to plus infinity. These are pointwise directional limits, not a requirement of uniform convergence in x′x'x′. They supply substantial information about the global interface.

Del Pino, Kowalczyk and Wei subsequently constructed nonplanar strictly monotone solutions in every ambient dimension at least nine, using large dilations of nonaffine minimal graphs. Thus the proposed dimension-eight conclusion is at the expected sharp threshold.

For stability, Pacard and Wei constructed nonplanar stable solutions in dimension eight. Recent work cited by the manuscript includes stable rigidity in dimension three and monotone rigidity in dimension four, obtained independently by Liu, Luo, Wang, Juncheng Wei, Yong Wei and Wu, and by Chan, Fernández-Real, Figalli, Florit-Simon and Serra. Florit-Simon and Serra also proved stable rigidity in dimension four under bounded energy density.

The present manuscript therefore addresses two gaps together: extending the stable classification to dimension seven and dispensing with the density assumption there. That stable theorem then feeds a geometric reduction to the monotone theorem in dimension eight. The earlier reduction through minimizing end profiles is credited to Alberti–Ambrosio–Cabré and Jerison–Monneau.

4. What the new manuscript claims

Monotone rigidity in dimension eight

Theorem 1.1 states that if u∈C2(R8,(−1,1))u\in C^2(\mathbb R^8,(-1,1))u∈C2(R8,(−1,1)) satisfies

Δu=u3−u,∂8u>0,\Delta u=u^3-u,\qquad \partial_8u>0,Δu=u3−u,∂8​u>0,

then there are a unit vector e∈S7e\in\mathbb S^7e∈S7, with e8>0e_8>0e8​>0, and a real number ccc such that

u(x)=tanh⁡(e⋅x−c2).u(x)=\tanh\left(\frac{e\cdot x-c}{\sqrt2}\right).u(x)=tanh(2​e⋅x−c​).
