Here S7\mathbb S^7S7 denotes the unit sphere in R8\mathbb R^8R8. The theorem does not assume minimization, surface-order energy growth, or directional limits at the wells.

Stable rigidity in dimension seven

Theorem 1.2 states that every stable C2C^2C2 solution v:R7→[−1,1]v:\mathbb R^7\to[-1,1]v:R7→[−1,1] is either the constant 111, the constant −1-1−1, or a planar heteroclinic. There is no energy-growth assumption.

A subsidiary theorem first gives the same classification in dimensions four through seven when sup⁡RMR(0)<∞\sup_R M_R(0)<\inftysupR​MR​(0)<∞. Removing this extra assumption in dimension seven is a separate part of the manuscript, not a consequence of merely restating the finite-density result.

Together with the known counterexamples, these claims give sharp dimension endpoints for the stated scalar quartic equation: seven for stable rigidity and eight for strictly monotone rigidity.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the claims settle a central symmetry problem linking nonlinear elliptic equations, variational phase transitions and minimal-surface geometry. The significance includes both the endpoint conjecture and a stable classification requiring no global energy bound.

A density bound can quietly encode much of the desired simplicity. It limits how many transition layers can accumulate as one looks farther away. Proving rigidity without that bound means controlling configurations whose large-scale complexity has not been restricted in advance.

The two dimension thresholds also clarify a physical and geometric distinction. Resistance to small perturbations does not force the same structure as a globally consistent direction of increase. The manuscript’s conclusion uses this extra directional information at exactly the dimension where stable nonplanar patterns are already possible.

6. The main idea

Measure departure from the one-dimensional profile

For a nonconstant solution, introduce the inverse-profile coordinate U=g−1(v)U=g^{-1}(v)U=g−1(v). For a planar transition, UUU is affine with unit gradient. Set

q=1−v2,D=1−∣∇U∣2.q=1-v^2,\qquad D=1-|\nabla U|^2.q=1−v2,D=1−∣∇U∣2.

Modica’s gradient bound gives D≥0D\geq0D≥0. The quantity DDD measures failure to follow the ideal one-dimensional profile. Testing stability with qηq\etaqη, where η\etaη is a compactly supported cutoff, yields the identity

0≤Qv(qη)=∫q2∣∇η∣2 dx−∫q3Dη2 dx.0\leq Q_v(q\eta)=\int q^2|\nabla\eta|^2\,dx-\int q^3D\eta^2\,dx.0≤Qv​(qη)=∫q2∣∇η∣2dx−∫q3Dη2dx.

This converts stability into control of a nonnegative defect. It remains useful near irregular portions of the zero set, where describing the transition as a smooth surface is harder.

Under finite density, the manuscript combines diffuse estimates with descriptions of separated sheets. When sheets lie close together, their interaction constrains the gaps between them. Comparing those constraints with what stability allows gives the finite-density classification through dimension seven. Estimates for transition layers developed in earlier work of Wang and Wei enter after the required local regularity has been obtained.

Obtain the missing density bound

Without finite density, one cannot begin by assuming a uniformly manageable collection of sheets. The manuscript introduces a penalized version of geometric reach: a local scale sensitive both to bending of a sheet and to the proximity of other sheets.

Near that scale, local density control permits use of the preceding regularity estimates. The argument combines curvature information on good interface regions with ambient stability tests that also cover bad regions. Fourth-moment estimates control the accumulation of curvature and profile defect.

A delicate issue is joining test functions on neighboring layers. Joining arbitrary amplitudes could consume the positive margin needed in dimension seven. The construction arranges that the cost depends on squared differences of neighboring amplitudes; close layers receive nearly equal amplitudes. The same radial weight is then used in both the geometric reach estimate and the ambient stability estimate.

According to the manuscript, the remaining positive margin contradicts the amount of interface area that unbounded density would force. This establishes the missing density bound and closes the stable classification. The argument is not simply an appeal to a corresponding minimal-surface theorem.

Recover the monotone theorem

For a monotone solution in eight variables, boundedness supplies end profiles

u±(x′)=lim⁡t→±∞u(x′,t),x′∈R7.u_\pm(x')=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}u(x',t),\qquad x'\in\mathbb R^7.u±​(x′)=t→±∞lim​u(x′,t),x′∈R7.

They are stable seven-dimensional solutions. At this stage the classification allows planar transitions as well as constant wells; the argument must not assume that the end profiles are already −1-1−1 and 111.

Each allowed end profile is a global minimizer. By clipping competitors between the profiles and sliding translates of the original solution, the manuscript applies the classical reduction to show that uuu is itself a global minimizer. Comparison with a constant phase then supplies E(u;BR)≤CR7E(u;B_R)\leq CR^7E(u;BR​)≤CR7.

Zooming out gives a minimizing boundary preserved by dilations, called a minimizing cone. The argument identifies the full limiting energy as surface tension times its perimeter, excluding additional hidden energy. Directional monotonicity gives a consistent sign to a component of the cone’s normal.

In ambient dimension eight, the minimizing cone can have at most a singular vertex. The directed-cone argument forces a hyperplane, including the case where the distinguished normal component vanishes identically. Finally, a near-unit-density theorem of Wang returns from this flat limit to the original solution. The one-dimensional equation fixes its profile and orientation.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The claims concern the scalar equation with the particular quartic potential above. They are not stated here for vector-valued systems, arbitrary double-well potentials, fractional operators, or curved ambient spaces.

The monotonicity hypothesis is an everywhere strictly positive derivative in a fixed direction. The result does not classify all bounded eight-dimensional solutions. The stable theorem concerns dimension seven; known stable nonplanar examples prevent extending that conclusion unchanged to dimension eight.

Likewise, known monotone nonplanar examples in dimension nine rule out an unrestricted extension of the monotone theorem. Further questions concern what other hypotheses recover rigidity beyond these endpoints, and which parts of the density-removal method extend to other phase-transition energies.

The manuscript’s mathematical conclusions and analytical mechanisms are reported as stated. This digest explains the role of its assumptions and reductions without independently establishing the claimed classifications.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Ghoussoub and Gui, On a conjecture of De Giorgi and some related problems: the two-dimensional theorem.
  • Ambrosio and Cabré, Entire solutions of semilinear elliptic equations in three space dimensions and a conjecture of De Giorgi: the three-dimensional theorem.
  • Savin, Regularity of flat level sets in phase transitions: the result through dimension eight with directional well limits.
  • Del Pino, Kowalczyk and Wei, On De Giorgi’s conjecture in dimension N ≥ 9: nonplanar monotone solutions above the threshold.
  • Pacard and Wei, Stable solutions of the Allen–Cahn equation in dimension 8 and minimal cones: the different endpoint for stability.
  • Liu and collaborators and Chan and collaborators: recent stable three-dimensional and monotone four-dimensional classifications cited by the manuscript.
  • Florit-Simon and Serra, their bounded-density stable rigidity work: a preceding finite-density result.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A positive resolution of De Giorgi’s conjecture in dimension eight (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When optimal Coulomb transport must split mass
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 373 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Suppose three repelling particles each have the same prescribed spatial probability density. How should their positions be correlated to minimize their average Coulomb repulsion?

One economical description chooses the first particle’s position xxx, then places the others deterministically at T2(x)T_2(x)T2​(x) and T3(x)T_3(x)T3​(x). If these maps preserve the prescribed density, all three particles have the correct distribution. This is the Monge, or co-motion, ansatz.

Must some optimal arrangement always have this deterministic form when the density is smooth?

Family 373 claims a counterexample. It constructs a smooth compactly supported density on R3\mathbb R^3R3 for which an optimal joint distribution exists, but no pair of density-preserving Borel maps is optimal. Nevertheless, maps can approach the optimal cost arbitrarily closely. The failure is attainment, not a positive gap between the best possible cost values.

2. Background and essential definitions

Marginals describe individual particles; couplings describe correlation

Let μ=ρ(x) dx\mu=\rho(x)\,dxμ=ρ(x)dx be a probability measure. A coupling π\piπ is a joint probability distribution for (x1,x2,x3)∈(R3)3(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in(\mathbb R^3)^3(x1​,x2​,x3​)∈(R3)3 such that each coordinate separately has distribution μ\muμ.

This leaves enormous freedom. Independent particles have coupling μ⊗μ⊗μ\mu\otimes\mu\otimes\muμ⊗μ⊗μ, while correlated particles can avoid configurations that put them close together.

The Coulomb cost is

c(x1,x2,x3)=1∣x1−x2∣+1∣x1−x3∣+1∣x2−x3∣.c(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\frac1{|x_1-x_2|}+\frac1{|x_1-x_3|}+\frac1{|x_2-x_3|}.c(x1​,x2​,x3​)=∣x1​−x2​∣1​+∣x1​−x3​∣1​+∣x2​−x3​∣1​.

It is infinite when two positions coincide. The Kantorovich problem allows every coupling with the prescribed marginals:

E∗(μ)=inf⁡π∈Π(μ,μ,μ)∫c dπ.E_*(\mu)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\mu,\mu)}\int c\,d\pi.E∗​(μ)=π∈Π(μ,μ,μ)inf​∫cdπ.

The symbol Π(μ,μ,μ)\Pi(\mu,\mu,\mu)Π(μ,μ,μ) denotes this set of admissible joint distributions. The objective minimizes expected repulsion, not the distance traveled from an initial configuration.

Deterministic maps are a restricted class

A Borel map is measurable with respect to the sets generated by open sets; no continuity or differentiability is required. Its pushforward satisfies

T#μ(A)=μ(T−1(A)).T_\#\mu(A)=\mu(T^{-1}(A)).T#​μ(A)=μ(T−1(A)).

The condition T#μ=μT_\#\mu=\muT#​μ=μ means that TTT preserves the probability distribution.

A Monge coupling is

π=(Id,T2,T3)#μ,(T2)#μ=(T3)#μ=μ.\pi=(\mathrm{Id},T_2,T_3)_\#\mu,\qquad (T_2)_\#\mu=(T_3)_\#\mu=\mu.π=(Id,T2​,T3​)#​μ,(T2​)#​μ=(T3​)#​μ=μ.

Conditioned on the first coordinate xxx, there is no remaining randomness: the other two coordinates are fixed. A general coupling can instead divide the conditional mass among several possible pairs.

The theorem concerns every preserving Borel pair. It does not merely reject smooth maps, a particular radial recipe, or cyclic maps satisfying an additional relation such as T3=T22T_3=T_2^2T3​=T22​.

Infimum and minimum need not coincide

An infimum is the greatest lower bound of attainable costs. A minimum is an attainable cost equal to that bound. For example, positive numbers have infimum zero, but no smallest positive number.

Here the set of deterministic plans is rich enough to approximate the best cost, yet can fail to contain an optimizer. Limits of deterministic plans may acquire conditional randomness through increasingly fine rearrangements.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Coulomb multi-marginal transport arises in the strong-interaction limit of density functional theory. Seidl, Gori-Giorgi and Savin developed the co-motion formulation for strictly correlated electrons. The prescribed one-particle density is retained while correlation minimizes repulsion.

For two particles, Cotar, Friesecke and Klüppelberg established existence and uniqueness of optimal maps for absolutely continuous marginals. This is an important positive precedent, but adding a third particle changes the geometry of the correlation problem.

For any number of particles on the line, Colombo, De Pascale and Di Marino constructed optimal cyclic maps for identical nonatomic marginals with finite transport value. The higher-dimensional three-particle question is therefore different from the one-dimensional theory.

Colombo and Di Marino proved equality between the Coulomb Kantorovich minimum and the infimum over measure-preserving cyclic maps for identical nonatomic marginals. That theorem supplies approximating maps; equality of values does not assert existence of a minimizing map.

Several earlier negative results concerned narrower assertions. Pass constructed non-Monge Coulomb optimizers for radial data, but the existence of one non-Monge optimizer does not rule out another optimizer of Monge form. Colombo and Stra disproved specific radial quantile-cyclic prescriptions. Bindini, De Pascale and Kausamo constructed smooth densities for a reduced radial three-particle cost for which four prescribed maps fail. That reduced cost minimizes over angular variables and is not the Coulomb cost on the line.

Gerolin, Kausamo and Rajala established nonexistence of optimal maps for a different interaction, the repulsive harmonic cost. Their shared-component mass-splitting mechanism is a methodological predecessor of the present construction.

The general higher-dimensional map-attainment question is discussed in the Friesecke–Gerolin–Gori-Giorgi account, and the three-particle Coulomb case remained explicitly posed in Friesecke’s January 2026 preprint. Family 373 claims to exclude every deterministic preserving pair for one smooth identical marginal, rather than only selected candidate maps.

4. What the new manuscript claims

The manuscript constructs a nonnegative density ρ\rhoρ with

∫R3ρ dx=1,ρ∈Cc∞(R3),ρ∈Cc∞(R3).\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,dx=1,\qquad \rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3),\qquad \sqrt\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3).∫R3​ρdx=1,ρ∈Cc∞​(R3),ρ​∈Cc∞​(R3).

The notation Cc∞C_c^\inftyCc∞​ means smooth with compact support. Smoothness of the square root is an extra condition; it is not automatic for every smooth nonnegative function near its zeros.

For μ=ρ dx\mu=\rho\,dxμ=ρdx, the Kantorovich value is finite and attained. Yet every preserving Borel pair satisfies

∫c(x,T2(x),T3(x)) dμ(x)>E∗(μ).\int c(x,T_2(x),T_3(x))\,d\mu(x)>E_*(\mu).∫c(x,T2​(x),T3​(x))dμ(x)>E∗​(μ).

The left side is allowed to be infinite. The theorem therefore rules out every Monge optimizer, regardless of regularity or cyclic relations.

At the same time,

inf⁡(T2)#μ=(T3)#μ=μ∫c(x,T2(x),T3(x)) dμ(x)=E∗(μ).\inf_{(T_2)_\#\mu=(T_3)_\#\mu=\mu}\int c(x,T_2(x),T_3(x))\,d\mu(x)=E_*(\mu).(T2​)#​μ=(T3​)#​μ=μinf​∫c(x,T2​(x),T3​(x))dμ(x)=E∗​(μ).

The source directly constructs finite-cost maps approaching the optimum for its example.

Symmetrizing an admissible Monge plan by averaging over particle permutations does not restore optimality. Permutation averaging preserves both the marginals and the symmetric cost, so it preserves the original strict excess cost as well.

The construction extends to every dimension d≥2d\ge2d≥2 and every exponent s>0s>0s>0 for the inverse-power interaction

cs(x1,x2,x3)=∑i<j∣xi−xj∣−s.c_s(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\sum_{i<j}|x_i-x_j|^{-s}.cs​(x1​,x2​,x3​)=i<j∑​∣xi​−xj​∣−s.

For each such pair (d,s)(d,s)(d,s), the manuscript gives a smooth identical marginal with nonattainment by maps and equality of infima.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the family resolves a central existence question for Coulomb multi-marginal transport and shows that smooth one-particle densities do not guarantee an exact deterministic co-motion description.

The practical distinction is subtle. Restricting to maps need not produce a wrong limiting energy, because the infima agree. But an exact optimizer may require mass splitting, so a method that expects a convergent pair of optimal maps can be asking for an object that does not exist.

With particle-density normalization n=3ρn=3\rhon=3ρ, the example has total mass three and n∈H1\sqrt n\in H^1n​∈H1. It therefore belongs to the usual density-regularity class discussed in the source’s density-functional setting. This does not assert realization as the ground-state density of a specified external potential.

6. The main idea

Arrange five small components

Take a small central ball BBB around the origin and four disjoint outer regions near e1,−e1,e2,−e2e_1,-e_1,e_2,-e_2e1​,−e1​,e2​,−e2​, where e1,e2e_1,e_2e1​,e2​ are perpendicular unit vectors. Construct smooth diffeomorphisms Yk,WkY_k,W_kYk​,Wk​, for k=1,2k=1,2k=1,2, from BBB to the outer regions.

The two allowed families of optimal triples are

(x,Y1(x),W1(x))and(x,Y2(x),W2(x)),x∈B,(x,Y_1(x),W_1(x))\quad\text{and}\quad(x,Y_2(x),W_2(x)),\qquad x\in B,(x,Y1​(x),W1​(x))and(x,Y2​(x),W2​(x)),x∈B,

together with all coordinate permutations. Each triple contains one central point and the two outer points belonging to the same branch.

Let ν\nuν be a smooth probability measure inside BBB. Define the common marginal by

μ=13ν+16∑k=12((Yk)#ν+(Wk)#ν).\mu=\frac13\nu+\frac16\sum_{k=1}^2\bigl((Y_k)_\#\nu+(W_k)_\#\nu\bigr).μ=31​ν+61​k=1∑2​((Yk​)#​ν+(Wk​)#​ν).

The central component has mass 1/31/31/3; each of the four outer components has mass 1/61/61/6. Choose a central point with law ν\nuν, select either branch with equal probability, then randomly permute the three positions. This gives a coupling with marginal μ\muμ in every coordinate.

Force every optimizer onto those families

The remaining geometric task is to show that the proposed coupling really is optimal and that every optimizer uses only the allowed families.

The source constructs a common supporting potential φ\varphiφ on the five components such that

c(x1,x2,x3)≥φ(x1)+φ(x2)+φ(x3),c(x_1,x_2,x_3)\ge\varphi(x_1)+\varphi(x_2)+\varphi(x_3),c(x1​,x2​,x3​)≥φ(x1​)+φ(x2​)+φ(x3​),

with equality precisely on the prescribed triples. Integrating gives the same lower bound 3∫φ dμ3\int\varphi\,d\mu3∫φdμ for every admissible coupling. The constructed coupling attains it.

The center triples (0,ek,−ek)(0,e_k,-e_k)(0,ek​,−ek​) have equal cost and equal central gradient, making it possible for the two branches to share the same central potential. Strongly concave quadratic terms and the implicit function theorem produce the nearby smooth branches. Strict cost gaps exclude other triples of distinct component centers, while the Coulomb singularity excludes triples containing two points in one sufficiently small component.

Thus optimality forces a concrete geometric constraint, not just a favorable numerical comparison for one candidate plan.

A deterministic choice sends twice too much mass

Suppose a preserving map T2T_2T2​ belonged to an optimal Monge pair. When its input lies in BBB, it must choose one of the four outer branch images. Fix one branch map HHH, and let S⊂BS\subset BS⊂B be the measurable set where T2(x)=H(x)T_2(x)=H(x)T2​(x)=H(x).

By construction,

μ(S)=13ν(S),μ(H(S))=16ν(S).\mu(S)=\frac13\nu(S),\qquad \mu(H(S))=\frac16\nu(S).μ(S)=31​ν(S),μ(H(S))=61​ν(S).

But all of SSS maps into H(S)H(S)H(S). Measure preservation would require

13ν(S)≤μ(T2−1(H(S)))=μ(H(S))=16ν(S).\frac13\nu(S)\le\mu(T_2^{-1}(H(S)))=\mu(H(S))=\frac16\nu(S).31​ν(S)≤μ(T2−1​(H(S)))=μ(H(S))=61​ν(S).

Hence ν(S)=0\nu(S)=0ν(S)=0. The same reasoning applies to every branch, so no positive central mass can be assigned anywhere allowed by optimality.

Matching only the total mass of each outer component would miss this contradiction. The exact image-measure relation holds for every selection set SSS, and therefore excludes arbitrarily irregular Borel choices as well as continuous ones.

Fine rearrangements still approach the optimum

Partition the five components into increasingly small cells. Record how much mass the optimal coupling assigns to each product of three cells. Split each source cell into pieces of those masses, then map each piece to the required target-cell distributions.

These maps preserve the marginal exactly and reproduce the optimal coupling’s cell-level mass table. Their configurations need not lie exactly on the optimal branches, which is why the preceding obstruction does not apply to approximate optimality.

All active triples stay in three different components separated by a fixed positive distance. On this separated region the Coulomb cost varies continuously, with a bound proportional to cell diameter. Refining the cells makes the excess cost tend to zero.

The separation controls the singular cost on the approximating plans themselves. The argument does not assume that weak convergence alone allows passage through the Coulomb singularity.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result is existential: some smooth density has this behavior. It does not say that all smooth densities lack optimal maps. The construction uses several separated support components, so it does not resolve every version with connected support or strict positivity on a prescribed region.

There are three marginals, all identical. The theorem does not contradict two-particle map existence or the one-dimensional cyclic-map theory. The inverse-power extension still concerns three particles.

No positive gap separates deterministic and general optimal values. Near-optimal maps exist, but the source does not give a universal complexity bound for them or classify all optimal couplings.

The physical regularity condition on the density does not identify an external potential whose quantum ground state realizes it. Questions about such realizability, robust nonattainment under perturbations and favorable classes admitting maps remain distinct.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary papers linked above distinguish two-particle and one-dimensional existence, equality of infima, failures of prescribed radial maps and the repulsive harmonic predecessor. The Friesecke–Gerolin–Gori-Giorgi account explains the strong-interaction density-functional interpretation.

For optional background, optimal transport and pushforward measures explain the difference between maps and general couplings. The manuscript below supplies the smooth Coulomb nonattainment construction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A counterexample to the Monge ansatz for the three-marginal Coulomb cost (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Programming a viscous fluid to detect whether a computation halts
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 376 · Partial differential equations
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Start a viscous fluid at rest. Fix one marked particle and a region in space. Can a finite description of an external force make that particle enter the region exactly when a given computer program eventually stops?

This family of nine manuscripts claims several ways to do so in three-dimensional flat geometry. The force encodes the machine and its finite input. The fluid motion carries out the instructions, and entry into a fixed detector reports halting.

The resulting prediction problem is undecidable: no algorithm can take every force description in the constructed class and always answer correctly whether detection will occur. This is a statement about exact mathematical trajectories over arbitrarily long times. It does not mean the fluid computes answers to undecidable problems in finite time: a machine that never halts produces no finite-time halting signal.

The family also distinguishes several experiments. Some forces repeat periodically, another becomes stationary, and others decay. Most detectors follow a particle; one manuscript instead tests the evolving velocity. These alternatives have different guarantees, so they should not be combined into one imagined construction possessing every property at once.

2. Background and essential definitions

The fluid equation

For velocity u(t,x)u(t,x)u(t,x), pressure p(t,x)p(t,x)p(t,x), viscosity ν>0 u>0ν>0, and external body force f(t,x)f(t,x)f(t,x), the equations are

∂tu+(u⋅∇)u=−∇p+νΔu+f,∇⋅u=0.\partial_tu+(u\cdot abla)u=- abla p+ u\Delta u+f,\qquad abla\cdot u=0.∂t​u+(u⋅∇)u=−∇p+νΔu+f,∇⋅u=0.

The divergence condition expresses incompressibility. A solenoidal vector field is simply a divergence-free one. The nonlinear term is the acceleration due to particles moving through a spatially varying velocity; the Laplacian represents viscous diffusion.

Several constructions use the flat unit torus T3=(R/Z)3\mathbb T^3=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^3T3=(R/Z)3: a cube with opposite faces identified. Others use R3\mathbb R^3R3 or R2×T\mathbb R^2 imes\mathbb TR2×T. All begin with u(0,x)=0u(0,x)=0u(0,x)=0, and viscosity is fixed before the machine is supplied.

A particle with initial label aaa follows

X˙(t)=u(t,X(t)),X(0)=a.\dot X(t)=u(t,X(t)),\qquad X(0)=a.X˙(t)=u(t,X(t)),X(0)=a.

The event “X(t)∈OX(t)\in OX(t)∈O for some finite ttt” is a material-particle observation. An Eulerian observation instead inspects the velocity at locations in space, without following one label.

What counts as a finite program for a force?

A Turing machine has finitely many control states and instructions but an unbounded tape. A finite input uses only finitely many nonblank cells initially. Its halting problem asks whether its instructions eventually reach a designated stop state.

An effective smooth force is described by a finite program that evaluates the force and each requested derivative to arbitrary rational accuracy at computably specified arguments. The program also supplies the relevant derivative bounds. No efficiency bound is claimed.

Crucially, the construction installs all local instruction branches. It does not first discover the machine’s future execution and then replay a precomputed particle path. Unqualified effectiveness assumes a positive computable viscosity; for an arbitrary fixed real viscosity, evaluation is relative to access to that parameter.

Infinite information in bounded coordinates

A tape can be represented by a positional expansion. In base BBB, a word a0a1…a_0a_1\ldotsa0​a1​… can be encoded as

z=∑j≥0d(aj)B−j−1,z=\sum_{j\geq0}d(a_j)B^{-j-1},z=j≥0∑​d(aj​)B−j−1,

where the digits d(aj)d(a_j)d(aj​) represent symbols. Choosing separated digits leaves gaps between the intervals identifying different first symbols. Removing a first symbol becomes an affine expansion; inserting one becomes an affine contraction.

The unbounded tape is stored in arbitrarily fine digits of an exact real coordinate. This explains both the computational capacity and the absence of a uniform finite-precision guarantee.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Turing’s undecidability theorem supplies the logical obstruction. Moore’s work in 1990–1991 connected symbolic computation with generalized shifts, piecewise affine maps, and smooth dynamical systems. It established a route from local tape instructions to continuous trajectories.

There is an obstacle to using fluid trajectories: a smooth flow is invertible between finite times, while an ordinary instruction can erase information. Landauer discussed retaining intermediate information, and Bennett’s 1973 reversible simulation explicitly recorded instruction history. The present manuscripts use related retention principles, with several different placements of the record.

Fluid computation itself also has substantial predecessors. Cardona, Miranda, Peralta-Salas and Presas constructed Turing-complete stationary Euler flows on a three-sphere with an adapted Riemannian metric. Cardona, Miranda and Peralta-Salas obtained universal stationary Beltrami fields in Euclidean three-space; those universal fields have infinite energy and a noncompact computational set. Their work also gives robust tape-bounded simulations on the flat torus, including a viscous realization from nonzero initial velocity.

Dyhr, González-Prieto, Miranda and Peralta-Salas constructed stationary unforced Navier–Stokes computation with an adapted metric and Hodge viscosity. In that setting a harmonic velocity makes the viscous term vanish. These are important results, but the choices of geometry, initial data and observation differ from the fixed flat, externally forced, initially resting experiments here.

For velocity observations, earlier work by Cardona and collaborators encoded computation in the Euler evolution on a constructed higher-dimensional compact manifold. M7 changes the setting to positive viscosity in three flat dimensions and supplies pointwise or integral detectors.

The claimed advance is therefore a collection of explicit forced-fluid realizations under carefully separated constraints, rather than the first connection between computation and fluid dynamics.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A common decision statement

Each particle construction fixes its geometry, viscosity, initial velocity, label aaa, and detector OOO before receiving a machine MMM and word www. It constructs a force with a unique global smooth solution in its declared comparison class such that

(∃t<∞: X(t,a)∈O)⟺M halts on w. igl(\exists t<\infty:\ X(t,a)\in O igr)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M ext{ halts on }w.(∃t<∞: X(t,a)∈O)⟺M halts on w.

The fixed label and detector may differ between constructions. Uniqueness on the torus is among classical solutions on every finite time interval. Whole-space statements specify additional Sobolev and pressure conditions; they do not assert uniqueness without a declared solution class.

How the nine manuscripts fit together

SourceMain additional feature
M1, Finite Instructions and Solenoidal Shear FlowsUnit-torus particle detection with directly solenoidal, mean-zero forcing, zero pressure, and period one after initialization. All mixed derivatives are bounded.
M2, A Fixed Particle TestThe ordinary machine writes its history into a third coordinate. Longer steps compensate for finer gates, making every mixed derivative of force and velocity bounded and square-integrable in time in spatial supremum norm.
M3, Eventually Stationary ForcingA spatial clock drives a finite mechanism. The mean-zero force becomes independent of time after time one; the fixed particle continues computing.
M4, Geometric ProgramsSolenoidal mean-zero forcing is periodic from time zero, with zero initial velocity and pressure. Separate geometric results handle area-changing sheet maps and reciprocal maps on thick boxes.
M5, Prefix InstructionsSeveral history processors realize finite prefix replacements. Normal compensation handles changes of planar area; separate variants change support, initialization, clocks and detectors.
M6, Rapidly Vanishing ForcingThree memory constructions give decay faster than every inverse power of time for every fixed derivative. Each machine step takes one unit of physical time, with progressively smaller spatial signals.
M7, Velocity-Field DetectionHalting is detected by a velocity component exceeding a fixed threshold on the torus, or by its integral on R2×T\mathbb R^2 imes\mathbb TR2×T. The two regimes have different bounds and support properties.
M8, Scalar Potentials and Slow ClocksA compactly supported whole-space particle construction has derivative decay O((1+t)−1−j)O((1+t)^{-1-j})O((1+t)−1−j) for time-derivative order jjj. Other constructions provide invariant-plane and spatial-clock mechanisms.
M9, Incompressible Box TransportDeterminant-one diagonal maps are realized on neighborhoods of entire solid boxes. A balanced three-stack recorder gives compactly supported forcing, periodic after loading, with a fixed open cube as detector.

M9 is the October 6 manuscript; the other eight are dated September 27.

M7 deserves an additional qualification. On the torus it detects whether u3>1/2u_3>1/2u3​>1/2 somewhere in a fixed strip at some time, but force derivatives need only be bounded on each finite time interval. On R2×T\mathbb R^2 imes\mathbb TR2×T, all force derivatives are globally bounded, and the detector asks whether the integral of u3u_3u3​ over a fixed half-space times the circle exceeds 1/21/21/2. That construction expands spatially and claims neither fixed compact support for all time nor uniformly bounded total kinetic energy.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, this is a broad constructive contribution linking computability, incompressible geometry and dissipative PDEs. Its significance lies in explicit realizations with fixed flat geometry, zero initial velocity, and several sharply distinguished restrictions on the force and observer.

Smoothness and uniqueness do not guarantee that every long-term event is algorithmically decidable. A perfectly smooth, explicitly described solution can carry a decision problem whose answer is not uniformly computable over all descriptions.

The decaying constructions make this especially striking. A particle may travel only a finite total distance while carrying an unbounded computation in finer spatial scales. The exact observer is essential to that conclusion. The work does not establish a robust physical computer with unlimited storage at fixed measurement accuracy.

6. The main idea

Preserve information before moving fluid

Two tape halves occupy two positional coordinates. An instruction reads finitely many symbols, so it acts on an entire rectangle of codes sharing those prefixes. For reciprocal maps, expansion in one direction is balanced by contraction in the other.

Information that would be overwritten must remain somewhere. M1 and M3 use finite reversible recording tables. M2 stores branch indices in a third real coordinate and reads the newest digit through a fine periodic gate. M5 explores other prefix and history arrangements. M9 uses three stacks with balanced total prefix lengths, making the corresponding three-dimensional affine map have determinant one.

The distinction between injectivity on one chosen run and injectivity on the full allowed instruction domain matters: the latter separates target blocks for arbitrary unused tails.

Route whole neighborhoods and control the journey

Even when source blocks are mutually disjoint and target blocks are mutually disjoint, a target can overlap another source. Moving one block directly may disturb information waiting elsewhere.

The geometric constructions use private heights or temporary storage, followed by delivery along separated routes. Local curls and shear pulses preserve divergence-free motion. In M9, obstacle detours transport full solid boxes, not just a zero-thickness coding surface. When a planar map changes area, a compensating normal expansion or contraction preserves three-dimensional volume.

Endpoint correctness alone is insufficient: a nonhalting particle must avoid the detector throughout every intermediate motion. The manuscripts therefore include coordinate bounds, height guards or detours appropriate to each observer.

Convert the mechanism into a forced solution

Once a smooth divergence-free velocity UUU has been prescribed, define

f=∂tU+(U⋅∇)U−νΔU.f=\partial_tU+(U\cdot abla)U- u\Delta U.f=∂t​U+(U⋅∇)U−νΔU.

Then (U,0)(U,0)(U,0) satisfies the fluid equations. The substantive construction is the effective computational velocity and its all-time detector bounds. A classical difference-energy estimate gives uniqueness for these constructed data in the specified classes.

For certain shear schedules, the active velocity is transverse to its own spatial variation, so (U⋅∇)U=0(U\cdot abla)U=0(U⋅∇)U=0. The resulting force is directly solenoidal with zero pressure. Other torus forces can be projected to their divergence-free part, changing the pressure while preserving velocity. This projection should not be confused with the direct shear property or assumed to preserve compact support in Euclidean space.

Slow time or shrink space

A clock τ(t) au(t)τ(t) replaces a recurring velocity VVV by

U(t,x)=τ′(t)V(τ(t),x).U(t,x)= au'(t)V( au(t),x).U(t,x)=τ′(t)V(τ(t),x).

It preserves the entire trajectory only if accumulated computational time remains unbounded. A logarithmic clock achieves decay of order 1/t1/t1/t while still traversing infinitely many steps.

Decay faster than every inverse power makes a nonnegative clock speed integrable, so this simple slowdown cannot drive infinitely many steps of the same recurring mechanism. M6 instead retains unit physical step lengths and shrinks the spatial displacement much faster than the cost of differentiating its selectors grows. Its three memories use moving localized curls, alternating fractional coordinates, or periodic lattice selectors. Late halting signals can be arbitrarily small.

Carry a signal through diffusion

M7 uses a velocity U=(a,w)U=(a,w)U=(a,w) independent of the third coordinate, where aaa is planar and divergence free. The vertical component satisfies

∂tw+a⋅∇w=νΔw+h.\partial_tw+a\cdot abla w= u\Delta w+h.∂t​w+a⋅∇w=νΔw+h.

The horizontal velocity and scalar source hhh are prescribed; the scalar www is solved for. Thus the force does not conceal an unknown solution in its definition.

On the torus, increasingly short stirring bursts keep fresh signals close to pure transport, while waiting intervals dissipate older signals. In the expanding construction, a cutoff moving with the computational address controls escaped scalar mass. These two methods pay for diffusion with different resources.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All conclusions concern specially constructed external forces. They give no general regularity theorem or blowup result for arbitrary three-dimensional Navier–Stokes data, and no resolution of the unforced global regularity problem.

The reductions use exact real encodings and unlimited observation time. They assert neither efficient simulation nor uniform tolerance to force perturbations, measurement error, or finite-precision replacement. Even M7’s strict detection thresholds do not themselves imply stability under arbitrary perturbations of the forcing.

Periodicity, eventual stationarity and decay are separate choices. Directly solenoidal forces, zero pressure, fixed compact support and globally bounded derivatives are asserted only where the individual construction supplies them.

A natural further direction is to understand which computational behaviors persist under specified noise or finite storage constraints. The existing robust tape-bounded predecessors illustrate why that is a different question from unrestricted exact universality.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Bennett, Logical Reversibility of Computation: history retention in reversible simulation.
  • Moore, Generalized shifts: unpredictability and undecidability in dynamical systems: positional coding and smooth dynamical realizations.
  • Cardona, Miranda, Peralta-Salas and Presas, Constructing Turing complete Euler flows in dimension 3: adapted-geometry stationary Euler computation.
  • Cardona, Miranda and Peralta-Salas, Computability and Beltrami fields in Euclidean space, version 3: Euclidean universality and the distinct tape-bounded torus results.
  • Dyhr, González-Prieto, Miranda and Peralta-Salas, Turing complete Navier–Stokes steady states via cosymplectic geometry: the unforced construction with adapted geometry and Hodge viscosity.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Finite Instructions and Solenoidal Shear Flows (September 27, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Fixed Particle Test for Computation in a Forced Viscous Flow (September 27, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary Navier–Stokes Forcing (September 27, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Geometric Programs for Solenoidal Forcing (September 27, 2026).

entry.title: How smooth is the least-steep extension of a function?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 377 · Partial differential equations
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-26

1. The question

Suppose heights are prescribed around the edge of a region. We want to fill in the interior while making the steepest slope as small as possible. We also want the same optimality in every smaller region, with its own boundary values held fixed.

This is an absolute minimization problem. Its solutions are called infinity-harmonic functions. They need not be twice differentiable, even when considered well inside the region. The central regularity question is how smoothly their slopes vary.

A tangent plane can exist at every point without those tangent planes depending continuously on the point. Earlier work established everywhere differentiability in all dimensions. The manuscript in this family claims the stronger conclusion that the gradient is locally Hölder continuous in every dimension at least three, with a uniform estimate depending only on dimension and the function’s oscillation.

The exponent is positive but unspecified. The manuscript does not claim the sharp exponent 1/31/31/3, nor any regularity at the boundary.

2. Background and essential definitions

Minimizing the largest slope

A function is Lipschitz if there is a finite constant LLL such that

∣u(x)−u(y)∣≤L∣x−y∣.|u(x)-u(y)|\leq L|x-y|.∣u(x)−u(y)∣≤L∣x−y∣.

This says that changes in height never exceed LLL times distance. For a sufficiently regular function, the local version is a bound on ∣∇u∣| abla u|∣∇u∣, the magnitude of its gradient.

An absolute minimizer cannot improve its largest gradient by changing the function inside any relatively compact subregion VVV while leaving its boundary values fixed. For every Lipschitz competitor www with the same boundary values, it satisfies

∥Du∥L∞(V)≤∥Dw∥L∞(V).\|Du\|_{L^\infty(V)}\leq\|Dw\|_{L^\infty(V)}.∥Du∥L∞(V)​≤∥Dw∥L∞(V)​.

Here DDD denotes the gradient, and the L∞L^\inftyL∞ norm is the essential supremum. “Absolute” emphasizes local optimality on every subregion, stronger than just solving one global extension problem.

The infinity Laplacian

For a twice differentiable function, the relevant equation is

Δ∞u=⟨D2u ∇u,∇u⟩=∑i,j=1duiujuij=0.\Delta_\infty u=\langle D^2u\, abla u, abla u angle=\sum_{i,j=1}^d u_i u_j u_{ij}=0.Δ∞​u=⟨D2u∇u,∇u⟩=i,j=1∑d​ui​uj​uij​=0.

The matrix D2uD^2uD2u is the Hessian. Only its component along the gradient is tested. By comparison, the usual Laplacian sums second derivatives in all coordinate directions. The infinity Laplacian is therefore highly degenerate: it does not directly constrain all directions of bending.

Continuous solutions are interpreted in the viscosity sense. If a smooth test function φ\varphiφ touches uuu locally from above at zzz, one requires Δ∞φ(z)≥0\Delta_\infty\varphi(z)\geq0Δ∞​φ(z)≥0; touching from below requires the opposite inequality. This is the sign convention for the unnormalized operator used here. Tests with zero gradient are included.

Viscosity solutions need not have classical second derivatives. The theory allows the equation to express the minimizing property even at nonsmooth points.

What Hölder continuity of the gradient means

A function is C1,αC^{1,\alpha}C1,α when it has a continuous gradient satisfying a local estimate

∣∇u(x)−∇u(y)∣≤C∣x−y∣α| abla u(x)- abla u(y)|\leq C|x-y|^\alpha∣∇u(x)−∇u(y)∣≤C∣x−y∣α

for some α>0\alpha>0α>0. The exponent quantifies how quickly neighboring tangent planes approach one another.

The Hölder seminorm is

[g]C0,α(E)=sup⁡x≠y in E∣g(x)−g(y)∣∣x−y∣α.[g]_{C^{0,\alpha}(E)}=\sup_{x e y ext{ in }E} rac{|g(x)-g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.[g]C0,α(E)​=x=y in Esup​∣x−y∣α∣g(x)−g(y)∣​.

The oscillation osc⁡Eu=sup⁡Eu−inf⁡Eu\operatorname{osc}_E u=\sup_Eu-\inf_EuoscE​u=supE​u−infE​u measures vertical variation. It is unchanged when a constant is added to uuu, as a gradient estimate should be.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Aronsson developed absolute minimization and its differential equation in the 1960s. Jensen later established the viscosity characterization and uniqueness for the associated Dirichlet problem. Crandall, Evans and Gariepy developed comparison with cones, an equivalent way to characterize solutions using simple functions shaped like distance cones.

These results supply existence, uniqueness and local slope control, but finer regularity is a separate problem. Crandall and Evans showed that infinitesimal rescalings at a fixed point have affine limits. An affine function has the form a+p⋅xa+p\cdot xa+p⋅x: a constant plus a plane with slope ppp. Knowing that limits are planes does not by itself supply a common rate of approximation, or identify the same slope along every sequence of scales.

In the plane, Savin proved continuous differentiability in 2005. Evans and Savin obtained interior C1,αC^{1,\alpha}C1,α regularity for some positive exponent in 2008. Their method introduced thin-cylinder rescalings and a limiting equation that also appear in the present manuscript.

Evans and Smart proved everywhere differentiability in every dimension in 2011. This identifies a derivative at each point. It does not, by itself, imply that derivatives at nearby points are close. A further higher-dimensional special case is the work of Peng, Zhang and Zhou on infinity-harmonic potentials in convex rings, where they established interior continuous differentiability and nonvanishing of the gradient.

The planar endpoint has recent developments. Brustad’s June 2026 preprint gives 1/31/31/3-Hölder continuity under additional assumptions that the gradient is nonzero and has a Lipschitz inverse. Xu’s July 2026 preprint states unrestricted planar local C1,1/3C^{1,1/3}C1,1/3 regularity, while separately leaving a universal endpoint norm estimate open.

The present October 4 manuscript concerns arbitrary solutions in dimensions d≥3d\geq3d≥3, and its main statement is uniform over a normalized family of solutions. It seeks a positive dimension-dependent exponent, not the planar endpoint conclusion.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For every integer d≥3d\geq3d≥3, Theorem 1.1 asserts the existence of constants

0<αd≤13,Cd<∞,0<\alpha_d\leq rac13,\qquad C_d<\infty,0<αd​≤31​,Cd​<∞,

depending only on ddd, such that every bounded continuous infinity-harmonic function on the Euclidean unit ball B1⊂RdB_1\subset\mathbb R^dB1​⊂Rd belongs to C1,αd(B1/2)C^{1,\alpha_d}(B_{1/2})C1,αd​(B1/2​) and obeys

∥∇u∥L∞(B1/2)+[∇u]C0,αd(B1/2)≤Cdosc⁡B1u.\| abla u\|_{L^\infty(B_{1/2})}+[ abla u]_{C^{0,\alpha_d}(B_{1/2})}\leq C_d\operatorname{osc}_{B_1}u.∥∇u∥L∞(B1/2​)​+[∇u]C0,αd​(B1/2​)​≤Cd​oscB1​​u.

No nonvanishing-gradient assumption is imposed. Neither smooth boundary data nor a special shape for distant parts of the domain enters this interior estimate.

Rescaling gives the corresponding statement in a ball B2r(x0)B_{2r}(x_0)B2r​(x0​) contained in an open domain:

∥∇u∥L∞(Br(x0))+rαd[∇u]C0,αd(Br(x0))≤Cdrosc⁡B2r(x0)u.\| abla u\|_{L^\infty(B_r(x_0))}+r^{\alpha_d}[ abla u]_{C^{0,\alpha_d}(B_r(x_0))}\leq rac{C_d}{r}\operatorname{osc}_{B_{2r}(x_0)}u.∥∇u∥L∞(Br​(x0​))​+rαd​[∇u]C0,αd​(Br​(x0​))​≤rCd​​oscB2r​(x0​)​u.

The powers of rrr reflect the change in scale: gradients measure height per unit distance. In particular, every continuous infinity-harmonic function on an open subset of Rd\mathbb R^dRd is locally continuously differentiable. Global boundedness of the function on that entire domain is unnecessary, because the estimate can be applied on smaller balls.

The constants and exponent arise through compactness. The manuscript supplies neither a numerical value of αd\alpha_dαd​ nor an endpoint claim that αd=1/3\alpha_d=1/3αd​=1/3.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, a uniform positive Hölder exponent for arbitrary higher-dimensional solutions resolves a central regularity problem for a fundamental degenerate equation. It upgrades the existence of a tangent plane at each point to quantitative control of how those planes vary.

Uniformity is part of the advance. For all solutions with oscillation at most one on B1B_1B1​, the same dimension-dependent constants control the gradient on B1/2B_{1/2}B1/2​. A statement assigning an unrelated modulus of continuity to each individual solution would be weaker.

The regularity ceiling has a concrete illustration. Aronsson’s example is

u(x)=∣x1∣4/3−∣x2∣4/3,u(x)=|x_1|^{4/3}-|x_2|^{4/3},u(x)=∣x1​∣4/3−∣x2​∣4/3,

independent of any additional coordinates. It is infinity-harmonic, and along the first coordinate axis its gradient changes by

∣Du(he1)−Du(0)∣=43∣h∣1/3.|Du(he_1)-Du(0)|= rac43|h|^{1/3}.∣Du(he1​)−Du(0)∣=34​∣h∣1/3.

Here e1e_1e1​ is the first coordinate unit vector. Thus no exponent greater than 1/31/31/3 can hold for all solutions, even locally. The claimed theorem gives some positive exponent below or at this natural ceiling, without determining the best one.

6. The main idea

Turn individual flatness into uniform flatness

The manuscript first normalizes the oscillation and adds one linear coordinate:

U(y,b)=u(y)+b.U(y,b)=u(y)+b.U(y,b)=u(y)+b.

The lifted function remains infinity-harmonic, and its affine approximations have a nonzero slope because of the extra coordinate. This avoids dividing the argument into regions where the original gradient vanishes and regions where it does not.

A three-point estimate controls a midpoint’s departure from the average of two endpoint values. Its relevance is that it works even when the endpoints are much closer together than the scale on which the function is already approximately affine.

Combining that control with affine blow-ups at fixed centers gives uniform small-scale approximation over all normalized solutions and all interior centers. Ordinary compactness of the functions alone would not provide such a common rate for their slopes.

Seek a power rate using thin cylinders

Next the argument uses cylinders elongated along an approximate slope. A fitting parameter λ\lambdaλ allows axial size rrr, transverse size λ r\sqrt\lambda\,rλ​r, and error λr\lambda rλr. The geometry distinguishes directions that the equation treats differently.

If the fitting error decreases at a uniform power rate, successive affine slopes converge at a power rate too, producing the Hölder estimate. Suppose instead that every such bound fails. The manuscript selects nearly worst scales and centers, with enough control on nearby fits to take a limit after anisotropic rescaling.

The limiting function v(x,t)v(x,t)v(x,t), defined for all (x,t)∈Rm×R(x,t)\in\mathbb R^m imes\mathbb R(x,t)∈Rm×R, solves

D2v[(∇xv,1)]=0,D2v[ξ]=ξTD2v ξ.D^2v[( abla_xv,1)]=0,\qquad D^2v[\xi]=\xi^{\mathsf T}D^2v\,\xi.D2v[(∇x​v,1)]=0,D2v[ξ]=ξTD2vξ.

The coordinate ttt is an axial variable of the rescaled elliptic problem, not physical time. In addition, the limit has controlled affine fits at every center and radius, in boxes sheared according to their fitted horizontal slopes.

A Liouville theorem is a rigidity statement for an entire solution. The required theorem says that every limit with these equation and fitting properties must be affine. That contradicts the retained failure of improvement and yields a power rate. The added fit assumptions are essential: the claim is not that every entire solution of the limiting equation is affine.

Compare values through quadratic envelopes

To establish that rigidity, the manuscript uses forward and backward quadratic envelopes. For example,

Pℓv(x,t)=sup⁡y{v(y,t+ℓ)−∣y−x∣22ℓ},ℓ>0.P_\ell v(x,t)=\sup_y\left\{v(y,t+\ell)- rac{|y-x|^2}{2\ell} ight\},\qquad \ell>0.Pℓ​v(x,t)=ysup​{v(y,t+ℓ)−2ℓ∣y−x∣2​},ℓ>0.

The quadratic penalty prevents distant points from contributing without cost. A backward envelope uses an infimum at t−ℓt-\ellt−ℓ, with the quadratic penalty added instead. The affine-fit bounds control growth so that these extrema are attained.

Appropriate envelope difference quotients are monotone in ℓ\ellℓ and share a small-length limit at each point. Constancy of both slopes across all lengths at one point forces affinity. The challenge is to reach such a situation while retaining evidence that the limiting function is nonaffine.

Preserve a defect while moving toward one terminal point

For an affine function, the average of its values equals its value at the average of the input points. The argument measures failure of this identity by a horizontal averaging defect. It normalizes configurations approaching the largest relevant defect ratio and obtains an extremal solution.

A variance-penalized averaging envelope then gives a subsolution touching the original solution at a positive axial coordinate, while retaining a positive gap before a linear correction. The variance penalty is chosen so that the viscosity inequality survives the averaging operation.

Forward and backward envelope optimizers define two possible steps. A discrete averaging argument controls the accumulated squared discrepancy of their velocities. This propagates contacts toward zero axial coordinate while keeping one common terminal point inside controlled fitted frames.

Using the same terminal point matters: there, both envelope slopes have one finite small-length limit. After rescaling the successive contacts, differences of slopes at fixed lengths converge to zero. The final limit therefore has constant envelope slopes and must be affine, yet it still carries the positive averaging defect. The manuscript uses this contradiction to prove its Liouville theorem and then the regularity estimate.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The statement is interior regularity for the unnormalized infinity Laplace equation in Euclidean space. It does not give boundary estimates, an explicit Hölder exponent, or the sharp 1/31/31/3 endpoint in dimensions at least three.

It also does not claim twice differentiability. Aronsson’s example already shows why a smoothness conclusion comparable to ordinary harmonic functions would be inappropriate.

Everywhere differentiability, continuous differentiability, qualitative Hölder continuity for each solution, and a uniform oscillation-controlled Hölder estimate are distinct levels of information. The main theorem claims the last of these, with constants depending only on dimension.

Determining the optimal higher-dimensional exponent and obtaining endpoint estimates remain natural questions beyond the stated result. Extensions to more general absolute-minimization equations would require their own hypotheses and arguments. The analytical claims here are explained as presented by the manuscript, without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Aronsson, Extension of functions satisfying Lipschitz conditions, and his singular-solution paper: the variational foundations and the regularity obstruction.
  • Jensen, Uniqueness of Lipschitz extensions: minimizing the sup norm of the gradient: the viscosity and uniqueness theory.
  • Savin, C1 regularity for infinity harmonic functions in two dimensions, and Evans–Savin, their planar Hölder regularity paper: earlier planar results and the anisotropic method.
  • Evans and Smart, Everywhere differentiability of infinity harmonic functions: the prior all-dimensional differentiability result.
  • Peng, Zhang and Zhou, Regularity from p-harmonic potentials to infinity-harmonic potentials in convex rings: a higher-dimensional special class.
  • Brustad, Infinity-harmonic functions in the plane: Regularity by injectivity, and Xu, Infinity-harmonic functions and inverse mean curvature flow clusters: the recent planar endpoint work distinguished above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniform Interior C^{1,\alpha} Estimates for Infinity-Harmonic Functions (October 4, 2026).

Sources consulted on 26 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How much mass does a black hole require? Penrose inequalities beyond time symmetry
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 260 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

How much mass must a universe contain if a black-hole boundary of a given size is already present? In three spatial dimensions, the simplest proposed answer is

m≥A16π.m\geq\sqrt{\frac{A}{16\pi}}.m≥16πA​​.

Here units are chosen so that the gravitational constant and speed of light are one. Mass therefore has units of length. The Schwarzschild black hole, the ideal nonrotating and uncharged black hole, attains equality: its horizon has area 16πm216\pi m^216πm2.

The difficult words are “mass,” “boundary,” and “size.” General relativity allows moving spatial slices, electric and magnetic fields, rotating configurations, and different geometries far away. A surface indicating trapped light need not itself be the smallest surface enclosing that region. Changing one of these choices can change a true inequality into a false one.

Family 260 contains thirteen manuscripts addressing these distinctions. They claim spacetime Penrose inequalities, classifications of equality, charged and rotating extensions, results for negative cosmological constant, and a Bondi-mass version. One manuscript supplies counterexamples to an insufficiently qualified rotating formulation. The common aim is to relate quantities on a single spatial slice without first solving the entire future evolution.

2. Background and essential definitions

An initial data set consists of a spatial manifold with a Riemannian metric ggg, which measures lengths, and a symmetric tensor KKK, which describes how the slice bends in spacetime. Time-symmetric data have K=0K=0K=0. Maximal data satisfy the weaker condition tr⁡gK=0\operatorname{tr}_gK=0trg​K=0; their full tensor can be nonzero.

The dominant energy condition says that the matter energy density μ\muμ is at least the magnitude of its momentum density jjj: μ≥∣j∣g\mu\geq |j|_gμ≥∣j∣g​. This is a local condition. For charged data, the manuscripts specify separately whether electromagnetic energy and momentum have been removed from these densities.

On a boundary surface SSS, take the unit normal toward the exterior. Let HHH be its mean curvature, the sum of its principal curvatures. The future outward light expansion is

θ+=H+tr⁡SK.\theta_+=H+\operatorname{tr}_S K.θ+​=H+trS​K.

The condition θ+≤0\theta_+\leq0θ+​≤0 means outward-directed light initially fails to expand. Equality defines a marginally outer trapped surface, or MOTS. This is information on the slice; an event horizon is defined using the global spacetime and is a different object.

An asymptotically flat end approaches Euclidean space at large distance. Its ADM energy EEE and linear momentum PPP are fluxes measured at spatial infinity. When E>∣P∣E>|P|E>∣P∣, the invariant mass is

m=E2−∣P∣2.m=\sqrt{E^2-|P|^2}.m=E2−∣P∣2​.

Using EEE alone would make the bound depend on the asymptotic observer’s motion.

The relevant area is usually Amin⁡A_{\min}Amin​, the infimum of the areas of full enclosing cuts. Such a cut is the entire compact boundary of a connected exterior region containing the distant end. Every component counts, including portions coinciding with SSS. Cuts need not be trapped or connected. A smooth minimizer need not exist. “Outer area-minimizing” means that every such cut has area at least that of SSS; only then can one replace Amin⁡A_{\min}Amin​ by the original boundary area without further argument.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Penrose’s 1973 proposal combined gravitational collapse, the expected hiding of singularities, and black-hole area increase. If a configuration settles to a black hole while radiation removes energy, its initial mass should already cover the final black hole’s area cost. This physical argument motivates the inequality; an initial-data theorem must establish its own geometric statement. See Penrose’s Naked singularities.

The time-symmetric problem became a theorem through two different geometric flows. Huisken and Ilmanen developed weak inverse mean curvature flow, allowing the evolving surface to jump across troublesome regions. Their three-dimensional bound uses the area of each connected component of an outermost minimal boundary. Bray’s conformal flow changes the ambient metric and handles the total area of a possibly disconnected horizon. Both papers appeared in 2001.

Bray and Lee extended the Riemannian method to dimensions below eight. In higher dimensions, area-minimizing boundaries can have singularities. M9 and M10 explicitly place their treatment of such frontiers in the line of Bray, Bray–Lee, and Bi–Zhu; they do not present conformal flow or the high-dimensional program as originating here.

For general KKK, Jang-type graph deformations offered a route back to scalar-curvature inequalities. The problem is to preserve enough area and control mass while repairing curvature. Bray and Khuri developed this perspective. Counterexamples by Ben-Dov, and by Carrasco and Mars for a different horizon definition, also showed why the area convention cannot be ignored; M1, M9 and M12 discuss those precedents.

Charge introduced another branch condition. Khuri, Weinstein and Yamada established a charged Riemannian inequality for multiple black holes. Rotation required electromagnetic corrections to angular momentum and earlier harmonic-map comparisons. For negative cosmological constant, prior work treated graphs and perturbations of Schwarzschild–anti-de Sitter geometry. The local result of Khuri and Kopiński imposed a quantitative condition comparing a seed tensor’s interior and boundary behavior. M8 claims to remove that additional condition in its fixed-seed setting.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Neutral data and original-data equality

M9 claims, in every spatial dimension n≥3n\geq3n≥3,

m≥12(Amin⁡ωn−1)n−2n−1,m\geq\frac12\left(\frac{A_{\min}}{\omega_{n-1}}\right)^{\frac{n-2}{n-1}},m≥21​(ωn−1​Amin​​)n−1n−2​,

where ωn−1\omega_{n-1}ωn−1​ is the area of the unit sphere in Rn\mathbb R^nRn. The exterior is smooth, complete with its compact boundary included, and has one asymptotically flat end. It obeys the dominant energy condition, finite ADM fluxes, integrable constraint densities, and weak future trapping.

Its all-dimensional version assumes positive enclosing area and differentiated decay through six metric derivatives and five derivatives of KKK, with decay exponent (n−2)/2<q<n−2(n-2)/2<q<n-2(n−2)/2<q<n−2. Future timelikeness is obtained in a corollary. In dimensions three and four, M9 also claims a weaker-decay version requiring only two metric derivatives and one tensor derivative, with q>(n−2)/2q>(n-2)/2q>(n−2)/2; positive enclosing area and timelikeness are then conclusions. These are bounds at infinity on otherwise smooth data.

M10 supplies the Riemannian comparison for locally perimeter-minimizing, outer-minimizing frontiers, including the permitted high-dimensional singular sets. M12 supplies boundary graph deformations in dimensions three and four. M3 includes weak-decay neutral results and designated-end versions for finitely many ends, whose enclosing-cut conventions must be kept separate.

M11 treats equality on the original data. Under its additional horizon and decay assumptions, equality identifies both ggg and KKK with a spacelike slice of Schwarzschild–Tangherlini spacetime, smoothly attached to a horizon. The all-dimensional strong-decay theorem has connected boundary. Its three-dimensional finite-component theorem uses an ambient complete-data hypothesis and stronger outermostness allowing partial coincidence with existing components; equality then forces connectedness. M3 also presents neutral rigidity in its stated three- and four-dimensional classes.

Charge and rotation

For M1’s three-dimensional source-free electric and magnetic fields, write Q=QE2+QB2Q=\sqrt{Q_E^2+Q_B^2}Q=QE2​+QB2​​ and rA=Amin⁡/(4π)r_A=\sqrt{A_{\min}/(4\pi)}rA​=Amin​/(4π)​. It claims

m≥Q,rA≤m+m2−Q2.m\geq Q,\qquad r_A\leq m+\sqrt{m^2-Q^2}.m≥Q,rA​≤m+m2−Q2​.

The boundary can be disconnected, KKK arbitrary, and ADM momentum nonzero. The non-electromagnetic matter obeys its charged dominant energy condition. Fields are divergence-free on the exterior, with the stated decay and finite fluxes. On each boundary component the theorem even permits a fixed future or past trapping sign.

The familiar rearrangement

m≥12(rA+Q2rA)m\geq\frac12\left(r_A+\frac{Q^2}{r_A}\right)m≥21​(rA​+rA​Q2​)

is asserted on the outer branch rA>Qr_A>QrA​>Q, not for every positive radius. Under connected, outermost, outer-area-minimizing future-horizon assumptions and m>Qm>Qm>Q, equality in M1 recovers a slice of dyonic Reissner–Nordström, including both original electromagnetic fields. “Dyonic” means that both charge types are allowed.

M2 gives a purely electric higher-dimensional reduction using the companion neutral theorem. Replace rAr_ArA​ above by rAn−2r_A^{n-2}rAn−2​, with the paper’s normalized signed charge taken in absolute value. Its nonextremal rigidity conclusion is Reissner–Nordström–Tangherlini and includes only slices whose induced magnetic two-form vanishes. M3 supplies related three-dimensional charged numerical statements, without itself asserting charged rigidity.

M4 claims the rotating bound

m2≥A16π+Q22+π(Q4+4J2)A.m^2\geq\frac{A}{16\pi}+\frac{Q^2}{2} +\frac{\pi(Q^4+4J^2)}{A}.m2≥16πA​+2Q2​+Aπ(Q4+4J2)​.

This is for its one-ended axisymmetric electrovacuum exterior class, a connected outermost and outer-area-minimizing future MOTS, zero ADM momentum, and Coulomb leading electromagnetic tails. The physical branch A≥4πQ4+4J2A\geq4\pi\sqrt{Q^4+4J^2}A≥4πQ4+4J2​ is an explicit assumption. The angular momentum JJJ is the conserved total, including its electromagnetic contribution. Strict-branch equality identifies admissible Kerr–Newman slices. Maximality is not assumed.

M5 supplies a complementary warning: if one instead uses bare gravitational ADM angular momentum and merely permits fields of order r−2r^{-2}r−2 with angularly varying leading terms, it constructs violations and nonrigid equality examples. Their total electric and magnetic charges vanish, although their fields do not. These counterexamples do not contradict M4’s stronger conventions.

Curved infinity and Bondi mass

With cosmological constant normalized to −3-3−3, M6 claims

mAH≥rA+rA32.m_{\mathrm{AH}}\geq\frac{r_A+r_A^3}{2}.mAH​≥2rA​+rA3​​.

The data have one spherical asymptotically anti-de Sitter end, weighted differentiable decay with exponent between 3/23/23/2 and 333, weighted integrable constraint sources, the dominant energy condition, and the same future trapping sign on all boundary components. The hyperbolic metric mass four-flux is assumed future timelike. Its Lorentz norm is mAHm_{\mathrm{AH}}mAH​; its spatial entries are not ADM linear momentum. No maximality is required. The connected horizon subclass has original-data Schwarzschild–anti-de Sitter rigidity, with explicit matching of the slice’s metric mass.

M7 gives a maximal-data theorem and a time-symmetric time-component comparison. M8, also reflected in M3, treats small maximal vacuum conformal perturbations of a positive-mass Schwarzschild–anti-de Sitter exterior. For each fixed decaying transverse-traceless seed and prescribed solution branch, its bound uses the boundary’s own area. Small positive parameters give equality for radial seeds and strictness otherwise. This is a local branch statement, without a uniform neighborhood over all seeds.

Finally, M13 replaces an end in the precise Cha–Khuri–Sakovich hyperboloidal class by asymptotically flat ends while protecting every enclosing area. Using M9, it obtains the three-dimensional bound with invariant Bondi initial-data mass. It assumes strictly future-timelike charge and positive enclosing area, and gives sharp Schwarzschild examples. Identification with a Bondi–Sachs charge at null infinity requires the compatible spacetime development described in its scope discussion.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The claimed general spacetime inequalities address a central connection between black-hole physics and geometric analysis. Moving beyond time symmetry means retaining the tensor that records motion of the slice, rather than treating spatial geometry alone.

The equality results add substantial content. A numerical bound can survive a deformation even when much of the original geometry is lost. Recovering the original metric, second fundamental form, fields, and horizon attachment says which configurations exhaust the mass budget.

The family also clarifies the mathematical question itself. Enclosing area, charge branches, conserved angular momentum, and the choice of mass at infinity are structural ingredients. Its positive and negative statements together explain why a single unqualified “Penrose inequality” cannot represent all thirteen papers.

6. The main idea

The numerical arguments build comparison geometries. A graph height and conformal factors change the original data until scalar curvature has a useful sign. Their estimates must simultaneously protect every enclosing cut and prevent an excessive increase in mass. An artificial filling or carefully controlled boundary allows the elliptic equations to be solved before a minimizing enclosure is selected.

One elementary principle explains the area bookkeeping. If a comparison metric hhh satisfies h≥cgh\geq c gh≥cg as quadratic forms, then every hypersurface has hhh-area at least c(n−1)/2c^{(n-1)/2}c(n−1)/2 times its ggg-area. Thus a single metric estimate controls all competing cuts, even when the minimizing surface changes or is singular. The papers combine such estimates with sharper constructions where a pointwise bound alone is insufficient.

Charged reductions turn conserved flux into a controlled energy decrease, then invoke a neutral comparison. Rotating arguments retain electric, magnetic and twist potentials, which encode the angular momentum constraints. Anti-de Sitter arguments must also account for the cubic area-radius term and for all four hyperbolic mass fluxes. M13 instead changes the distant end while leaving each fixed compact interior intact.

Equality is handled separately. Varying the original mass-minus-area deficit produces stationary equations through constraint multipliers. These identify a static or stationary model and then reconstruct the original spacelike slice. The claim is therefore stronger than observing that some auxiliary comparison metric resembles a black hole.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These are initial-data claims, not proofs of cosmic censorship or of convergence of gravitational evolution to a stationary black hole. They classify exteriors in specified equality classes and generally say nothing about the region behind the boundary.

There is no universal substitution of apparent-horizon area for enclosing area, no unrestricted polynomial charged bound below the charge threshold, and no rotating theorem here for arbitrary asymptotic electromagnetic tails. The all-dimensional neutral result, weak-decay low-dimensional results, and multi-end results have different assumptions. The charged higher-dimensional paper explicitly depends on the stated neutral companion input.

Extremal charged or rotating equality is not covered by the stated nondegenerate classifications. The local conformal anti-de Sitter result does not provide one parameter bound valid for every seed. Natural further questions include quantitative stability near equality and extensions beyond the stated end, topology, and asymptotic classes. None follows merely from the sharp inequalities presented here.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked historical papers in section 3 explain the original proposal and the two principal Riemannian flow methods. For precise earlier charged and deformation results, see the references to Khuri–Weinstein–Yamada and Bray–Khuri in M1, and the detailed historical discussions in M6, M8 and M9. M4 and M5 should be read together when comparing angular-momentum conventions. All thirteen source manuscripts are listed below; their theorem-level hypotheses take precedence over abbreviated descriptions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The spacetime Penrose inequality with charge and original-data rigidity (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Charged Reduction of the Spacetime Penrose Inequality in Spatial Dimensions at Least Four (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Spacetime Penrose inequalities: enclosing area, charge, and rigidity (October 5, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, The Kerr–Newman Penrose Inequality for Axisymmetric Electrovacuum Exteriors (October 5, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Electromagnetic tails and the Kerr–Newman Penrose inequality (October 5, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, The nonmaximal anti-de Sitter Penrose Inequality and original-data rigidity (October 5, 2026).
  • M7. OpenAI, The Penrose inequality for maximal asymptotically hyperbolic initial data (October 5, 2026).
  • M8. OpenAI, A local Penrose inequality for conformal perturbations of Schwarzschild–anti-de Sitter data (October 5, 2026).
  • M9. OpenAI, The spacetime Penrose inequality and enclosing area (September 27, 2026).
  • M10. OpenAI, Conformal flow and the Riemannian Penrose inequality with minimizing frontiers (September 27, 2026).
  • M11. OpenAI, Equality and rigidity in the spacetime Penrose inequality (September 27, 2026).
  • M12. OpenAI, Boundary graph deformations for the spacetime Penrose inequality (September 27, 2026).
  • M13. OpenAI, Area-controlled end replacement and the Bondi Penrose inequality in the CKS class (September 27, 2026).

entry.title: When disorder traps a quantum particle—and when extended states survive
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 261 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Imagine a particle moving through an infinite crystal. In an ideal lattice, the local environment repeats, and wave interference can support states spread across the material. Now independently change the energy at every lattice site. Does arbitrarily weak disorder trap the particle, or can extended states survive?

The Anderson model turns this question into a random operator on an integer lattice. Family 261 contains two complementary claims for independent uniformly distributed site energies. One concerns two dimensions at every fixed positive disorder strength. The other concerns every fixed dimension at least three, at sufficiently weak positive disorder.

Their conclusions concern spectral type: the kind of energy decomposition supplied by the spectral theorem. This is closely related to transport, but it is not interchangeable with a quantitative statement that a wave packet diffuses at a specified rate. Keeping that distinction visible is essential to understanding both manuscripts.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let Zd\mathbb Z^dZd be the integer lattice in ddd dimensions. A wave function ψ\psiψ assigns a complex amplitude to each site, with

∑x∈Zd∣ψ(x)∣2<∞.\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^d}|\psi(x)|^2<\infty.x∈Zd∑​∣ψ(x)∣2<∞.

These functions form the Hilbert space ℓ2(Zd)\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d)ℓ2(Zd). The Hamiltonian combines hopping to nearest neighbors with a random diagonal potential:

(Hλψ)(x)=−∑j=1d(ψ(x+ej)+ψ(x−ej))+λVxψ(x).(H_\lambda\psi)(x)=-\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(\psi(x+e_j)+\psi(x-e_j)\bigr)+\lambda V_x\psi(x).(Hλ​ψ)(x)=−j=1∑d​(ψ(x+ej​)+ψ(x−ej​))+λVx​ψ(x).

Here eje_jej​ is the jjj-th coordinate vector, the variables VxV_xVx​ are independent uniforms on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], and λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 measures disorder. Changing the hopping sign gives a unitarily equivalent model on this lattice, so the different sign convention in the two-dimensional paper does not change its spectral claim.

The spectrum consists of energies at which the operator cannot be inverted continuously. In infinite dimension it is not just a list of eigenvalues. For a state ψ\psiψ, the spectral theorem gives a measure μψ\mu_\psiμψ​: its mass on an energy set describes how much of ψ\psiψ lies in that spectral range.

There are three basic types. A pure-point measure is concentrated on countably many atoms, corresponding to eigenvectors. An absolutely continuous measure has a density with respect to ordinary length on the energy axis. A singular continuous measure has no atoms but is concentrated on a set of length zero. Thus excluding eigenvectors alone does not establish absolute continuity.

Pure-point spectral type for the entire operator means that its eigenvectors form a complete orthonormal basis. It does not mean that every point in its spectrum is an eigenvalue. A countable dense collection of eigenvalues can have an interval as its closure.

By contrast, purely absolutely continuous spectrum on an interval means every state restricted to that energy interval has an absolutely continuous spectral measure. This is stronger than merely finding a nonzero absolutely continuous component there.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Anderson’s 1958 paper introduced random site energies as a mechanism suppressing transport. It provided the physical origin of the problem, rather than a modern proof of the particular almost-sure spectral assertions discussed here. The 1979 scaling theory of Abrahams, Anderson, Licciardello and Ramakrishnan sharpened the expected distinction between two and higher dimensions; M2 cites that work as physical motivation.

Rigorous localization developed through several methods. Fröhlich and Spencer’s 1983 multiscale analysis controlled Green functions and diffusion in strong-disorder or suitable extreme-energy regimes. The subsequent work of Fröhlich, Martinelli, Scoppola and Spencer established pure-point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions in such regimes. The distinction matters: information at almost every fixed energy is not automatically a complete decomposition of a random spectral measure.

Aizenman and Molchanov’s fractional-moment method provided another powerful route to localization. Here one estimates an average of a fractional power of a resolvent entry, which is less sensitive to rare large values. These methods settled substantial regions of parameters without giving all-energy localization at arbitrarily weak disorder in two dimensions. M2 also distinguishes later spectral-edge localization for Bernoulli and broader bounded distributions from its own whole-spectrum uniform-law claim.

Delocalization was established earlier on trees, including Klein’s absolutely continuous spectrum results for the Bethe lattice. A tree has exponentially branching geometry; it is not a Euclidean lattice. Such theorems therefore do not automatically settle the problem on Z3\mathbb Z^3Z3.

Barry Simon’s Schrödinger Operators in the Twenty-First Century separated the higher-dimensional absolutely continuous energy-range question, the planar pure-point question, and diffusion. Both manuscripts use that separation. More recently, Black, Drogin and Hernández obtained quantitative weak-disorder diffusion and resolvent results for Gaussian potentials on disorder-dependent scales. Those finite-scale or weak-coupling statements have a different order of limits from a spectral-type theorem at fixed positive coupling.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Two dimensions: a complete eigenbasis

M2 claims that for every fixed λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, the square-lattice operator almost surely has pure-point spectral type throughout its spectrum. In the centered uniform convention,
