σ(Hλ)=[−4−λ, 4+λ].\sigma(H_\lambda)=[-4-\lambda,\,4+\lambda].σ(Hλ​)=[−4−λ,4+λ].

The eigenvalues are dense in this interval, and the eigenvectors form a complete orthonormal basis. An arbitrary nondegenerate uniform interval is covered after subtracting its midpoint as a constant energy shift.

The probability-one event is allowed to depend on λ\lambdaλ. The theorem does not assert exponential decay of every eigenfunction, dynamical localization, or an estimate uniform in energy. Its asserted advance is the pure-point conclusion for every positive disorder, including arbitrarily small disorder, over the entire spectrum for this single-site law.

At least three dimensions: a nonempty continuous range

M1 claims that for each fixed d≥3d\geq3d≥3, there is a positive threshold λd\lambda_dλd​. For every fixed 0<λ<λd0<\lambda<\lambda_d0<λ<λd​, the operator almost surely has purely absolutely continuous spectrum with nonzero weight on a specified open interval IdI_dId​. The interval does not shrink with λ\lambdaλ.

For d≥4d\geq4d≥4, the paper chooses

Id=−2d+(1200,1100).I_d=-2d+\left(\frac1{200},\frac1{100}\right).Id​=−2d+(2001​,1001​).

For d=3d=3d=3, it chooses

I3=(−6+ε/2,−6+ε),I_3=(-6+\varepsilon/2,-6+\varepsilon),I3​=(−6+ε/2,−6+ε),

where ε\varepsilonε is a fixed sufficiently small positive constant. These intervals sit just above the lower edge of the free hopping band, not at the lower edge of the full disordered spectrum.

The conclusion excludes both point and singular continuous spectral mass on IdI_dId​. The thresholds may depend on dimension. The higher-dimensional threshold is specified through probability conditions for finite matrices, without an effective numerical bound; the three-dimensional threshold is existential.

M1 also combines its theorem with established edge localization. At the same fixed weak coupling, a separate interval near −2d−λ-2d-\lambda−2d−λ has pure-point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions. Thus the manuscript claims coexistence of a localized edge region and an absolutely continuous region. It does not locate a unique transition energy between them or classify everything in between.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The spectral-type questions addressed here are central problems in disordered quantum systems. The two claims would establish a particularly clear dimension-dependent contrast for the same elementary random potential law.

The planar result reaches arbitrarily weak disorder, where finite samples can look very different from the infinite-volume spectral conclusion. The higher-dimensional result establishes purity, rather than just a small extended component. It also gives an interval independent of the sufficiently small fixed coupling.

Their significance lies in the order of quantifiers. Fixing a nonzero disorder and then reaching the infinite-volume, real-energy boundary is stronger in a different direction from following transport for longer and longer times while simultaneously taking disorder to zero. Neither kind of theorem makes the other unnecessary; they describe different aspects of the model.

6. The main idea

Both papers work with resolvents, finite-volume matrices and controlled ways of revealing random potentials. The resolvent is

G(z)=(H−z)−1,Im⁡z>0.G(z)=(H-z)^{-1},\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.G(z)=(H−z)−1,Imz>0.

Its entries measure the response at one site to a source at another. Approaching the real energy axis reveals spectral information, but near-resonances can make individual entries large. The technical task is to retain useful control as the artificial imaginary part disappears.

For M1, the starting operator has damping at selected sites. Each uniform random variable is represented by independent binary digits. Revealing digits gradually replaces artificial regularization with the actual random potential. A Schur complement eliminates completed sites while retaining their influence on the remaining matrix.

Three controls travel through this procedure: a self-consistency estimate, bounds preventing a resolvent row from concentrating at a few sites, and a spatial energy form derived from the Ward identity. Failed local updates leave a record; they cannot simply be retried as though already observed random values were fresh. The manuscript organizes pending sites and their later completion to preserve the true product distribution. The final finite-volume certificate keeps a positive spectral response on many sites. Spectral averaging then upgrades this response to pure absolute continuity.

M2 uses absorbing channels, called ports, and scattering matrices. Their squared amplitudes define an energy measuring differences between input values at different ports. Rare resonant cells and a hierarchy of progressively sparser ports produce comparisons under the original uniform law.

Two-dimensional geometry enters through logarithmic voltage profiles. A large annulus can separate inner and outer values at arbitrarily small capacity cost. The paper uses this feature to force a limiting affine scattering energy to vanish. It then obtains the resolvent summability needed for a rank-one spectral argument. Averaging over one independent site value transfers fixed-energy information to the random spectral measure, yielding the complete pure-point conclusion.

These are explanations of the stated mechanisms, not physical replacements of the random potential by a different distribution. The auxiliary ports, damping and conditioning belong to the analysis; the final claims concern the original Anderson operator.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The two primary theorems use independent uniform site potentials and nearest-neighbor hopping. They do not automatically extend to Gaussian, Bernoulli, correlated or continuum disorder, nor to interacting particles.

The planar theorem does not claim exponential localization or uniform dynamical bounds. The higher-dimensional theorem does not give a full mobility-edge diagram, a diffusion coefficient, or effective usable disorder thresholds. Its probability-one event may depend on the fixed coupling, just as in the planar result. There is no asserted uniformity as dimension tends to infinity.

Natural further questions concern quantitative localization lengths, transport at fixed disorder, the spectral region between the specified intervals, and robustness under other potential laws. The manuscripts’ stated conclusions should therefore be read as sharp answers to their spectral-type questions, with these additional transport and classification questions kept separate.

8. Sources and further reading

Anderson’s original article and Black–Drogin–Hernández are linked in section 3. Other primary historical sources discussed by the manuscripts include Fröhlich–Spencer, Absence of diffusion in the Anderson tight binding model for large disorder or low energy, and Fröhlich–Martinelli–Scoppola–Spencer, Constructive proof of localization in the Anderson tight binding model. The spectral readout is related to Simon and Wolff’s rank-one perturbation and localization theorem. M1 and M2 give the precise versions and parameter regimes used in their comparisons with earlier work.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Absolutely Continuous Spectrum for Weak-Disorder Anderson Models in Dimensions at Least Three (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Pure-Point Spectrum for the Two-Dimensional Anderson Model at Every Positive Disorder (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The sharp cost of binding: Lieb–Thirring inequalities and their equality cases
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 262 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

An attractive potential can bind a quantum particle. If we give the potential a fixed budget, measured by an integral of a power of its strength, how much total binding can it create? Is one carefully shaped well more efficient than many interacting bound states?

The Lieb–Thirring inequality answers this with an upper bound on a sum of powers of negative energy levels. The outstanding issue in the one-dimensional range considered here is the best constant: an inequality can be valid while still losing some of the true efficiency.

Family 262 contains three claims. M3 gives the sharp scalar constant for the remaining exponents between one half and three halves. M2 extends that constant to every finite matrix size, allowing internal channels to mix as position changes. M1 classifies every equality case. Its conclusion is that exact optimality forces the channels to stop rotating: one constant basis separates independent scalar one-bound-state profiles.

2. Background and essential definitions

On the real line, consider the Schrödinger operator

HW=−d2dx2−W(x).H_W=-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}-W(x).HW​=−dx2d2​−W(x).

For a scalar potential, W(x)≥0W(x)\geq0W(x)≥0 describes attraction because it enters with a minus sign. For a matrix potential, a wave function takes values in Cm\mathbb C^mCm, and W(x)W(x)W(x) is an m×mm\times mm×m Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix. Hermitian means W∗=WW^*=WW∗=W; positive semidefinite means v∗Wv≥0v^*Wv\geq0v∗Wv≥0 for every vector vvv.

The operator is defined through its energy form,

∫R∥ψ′(x)∥2 dx−∫R⟨ψ(x),W(x)ψ(x)⟩ dx.\int_{\mathbb R}\|\psi'(x)\|^2\,dx-\int_{\mathbb R}\langle\psi(x),W(x)\psi(x)\rangle\,dx.∫R​∥ψ′(x)∥2dx−∫R​⟨ψ(x),W(x)ψ(x)⟩dx.

Its natural form domain is H1H^1H1, the space of square-integrable wave functions with square-integrable weak derivative. This formulation accommodates measurable potentials rather than requiring a classical differential equation at every point.

Write the negative eigenvalues as λj<0\lambda_j<0λj​<0, counted with multiplicity. Their magnitudes measure binding below the free-particle threshold zero. For γ>0\gamma>0γ>0, the spectral moment is

Sγ(W)=∑λj<0∣λj∣γ.S_\gamma(W)=\sum_{\lambda_j<0}|\lambda_j|^\gamma.Sγ​(W)=λj​<0∑​∣λj​∣γ.

The exponent changes how heavily deep states are weighted relative to shallow ones. The associated potential cost is

Pγ(W)=∫Rtr⁡(W(x)γ+1/2) dx.P_\gamma(W)=\int_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(W(x)^{\gamma+1/2}\bigr)\,dx.Pγ​(W)=∫R​tr(W(x)γ+1/2)dx.

Matrix powers are formed by applying the scalar power to each eigenvalue; the trace is the ordinary, unnormalized sum of diagonal entries. A sharp inequality asks for the smallest CγC_\gammaCγ​ such that Sγ(W)≤CγPγ(W)S_\gamma(W)\leq C_\gamma P_\gamma(W)Sγ​(W)≤Cγ​Pγ​(W) for every admissible potential.

There are two natural benchmarks. A single optimally shaped bound state gives the one-state constant. A broad well with many levels gives a semiclassical constant, obtained by replacing spectral sums with phase-space integrals. The conjecture predicts which benchmark wins in each exponent range.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Lieb and Thirring introduced these inequalities in the 1970s in their work on fermionic kinetic energy and stability of matter. The one-state optimization has an earlier source in Keller’s 1961 work on Schrödinger eigenvalues. The full problem is harder because an arbitrary potential may have many, even infinitely many, negative levels.

At γ=3/2\gamma=3/2γ=3/2, inverse-scattering identities connected to the Korteweg–de Vries equation supplied the sharp scalar constant 3/163/163/16. Aizenman and Lieb’s integration argument transfers sharp semiclassical estimates to larger exponents. Laptev and Weidl developed matrix and operator-valued versions and a dimension-lifting method. These are established foundations of the subject, not claims introduced by this family.

At the lower endpoint γ=1/2\gamma=1/2γ=1/2, Weidl established finiteness, and Hundertmark, Lieb and Thomas obtained the sharp scalar constant 1/21/21/2. Hundertmark, Laptev and Weidl treated operator-valued extensions and improved bounds in the open interval. Work on orthonormal functions, including that of Dolbeault, Laptev and Loss, further narrowed the gap.

An especially important immediate predecessor is Read and Schulz’s September 2026 theorem. It establishes the sharp value

C1=433 πC_1=\frac{4}{3\sqrt3\,\pi}C1​=33​π4​

at exponent one and includes an operator-valued extension. Both the scalar and matrix manuscripts explicitly acknowledge this priority. Their additional claimed exponent range is therefore 1/2<γ<3/21/2<\gamma<3/21/2<γ<3/2 with γ≠1\gamma\ne1γ=1, rather than a first solution of the exponent-one case.

Numerical studies had suggested concentration into a one-state profile or separation into distant copies. Such evidence does not control all possible orthonormal families. The claimed new action estimate addresses that uniform many-state obstruction, and the equality paper asks what exact saturation forces beyond the numerical value of the constant.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The sharp scalar and matrix bounds

For every 1/2<γ<3/21/2<\gamma<3/21/2<γ<3/2, every finite m≥1m\geq1m≥1, and every measurable positive semidefinite Hermitian WWW with finite Pγ(W)P_\gamma(W)Pγ​(W), M2 claims

Sγ(W)≤CγPγ(W),S_\gamma(W)\leq C_\gamma P_\gamma(W),Sγ​(W)≤Cγ​Pγ​(W),

with

Cγ=(γ−1/2γ+1/2)γ−1/2Γ(γ+1)π Γ(γ+3/2).C_\gamma=\left(\frac{\gamma-1/2}{\gamma+1/2}\right)^{\gamma-1/2}\frac{\Gamma(\gamma+1)}{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(\gamma+3/2)}.Cγ​=(γ+1/2γ−1/2​)γ−1/2π​Γ(γ+3/2)Γ(γ+1)​.

Here Γ\GammaΓ is the gamma function, the extension of factorial satisfying Γ(n+1)=n!\Gamma(n+1)=n!Γ(n+1)=n! for nonnegative integers. The formula is the scalar one-state constant, independent of matrix size.

All negative eigenvalues are included. The potential can be rough and unbounded, and its matrices need not commute at different positions. In particular, the theorem is not restricted to a potential that is already diagonal in one fixed basis. M3 gives the scalar case, including the full negative spectral sum, and a separate signed-potential extension on its natural form domain. The displayed matrix theorem uses positive semidefinite potentials.

Every equality case

Set

r=(γ−1/2)−1>1.r=(\gamma-1/2)^{-1}>1.r=(γ−1/2)−1>1.

M1 claims that equality holds precisely when, almost everywhere,

W(x)=Udiag⁡(w1(x),…,wk(x),0,…,0)U∗,W(x)=U\operatorname{diag}(w_1(x),\ldots,w_k(x),0,\ldots,0)U^*,W(x)=Udiag(w1​(x),…,wk​(x),0,…,0)U∗,

where 0≤k≤m0\leq k\leq m0≤k≤m, UUU is a constant unitary matrix, and

wj(x)=(r+1)aj2sech⁡2(raj(x−xj)).w_j(x)=(r+1)a_j^2\operatorname{sech}^2\bigl(ra_j(x-x_j)\bigr).wj​(x)=(r+1)aj2​sech2(raj​(x−xj​)).

The scale aja_jaj​ is positive, the center xjx_jxj​ is real, and sech⁡t=1/cosh⁡t\operatorname{sech}t=1/\cosh tsecht=1/cosht. Each nonzero channel has exactly one negative eigenvalue, −aj2-a_j^2−aj2​. The parameters can be chosen independently; repeated scales and coincident profiles are allowed. The case k=0k=0k=0 includes the zero potential.

Thus an extremal matrix potential has at most mmm negative eigenvalues. This is a conclusion, not an assumption used to exclude infinitely many levels at the start. In the scalar case it leaves precisely one nonzero bound state, up to translation and scaling.

The endpoint γ=3/2\gamma=3/2γ=3/2 is excluded from this classification. There the equality structure is different: scalar multisolitons can support several bound states in a single channel. Extending the interior formula to the endpoint would lose that distinction.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Sharp Lieb–Thirring constants are central quantities in spectral theory and mathematical physics. The claimed resolution completes the remaining one-dimensional open-interval cases and simultaneously shows that noncommuting finite internal channels cannot improve the optimal constant.

The equality theorem supplies more than an attractive example. It says that exact optimality removes a whole class of possible behavior: position-dependent channel rotation and multiple bound states in one scalar channel. This turns an optimization problem into a structural classification.

One can also see why the matrix result is substantial. Diagonalizing W(x)W(x)W(x) separately at each point does not reduce the problem to independent scalar operators. A changing basis contributes derivative terms to the kinetic energy. The theorem must control that extra freedom rather than silently discard it. Its dimension-independent constant gives the same cost-to-binding limit at every finite channel count.

6. The main idea

The source papers begin on a bounded interval with finitely many orthonormal trial functions. Their individual binding scales are recorded in a diagonal matrix KKK, whose entries are square roots of positive binding energies. A lower triangular coefficient matrix combines the trial functions while preserving their successive spans. This matters because spectral inequalities remain valid on those nested spans.

The central object is an action: a functional containing kinetic energy, the chosen spectral scales, and a nonlinear density penalty. The papers bound this action from two sides. The eigenfunction equations give an upper comparison involving the potential cost. A specially constructed matrix path gives a lower comparison involving the desired sum of eigenvalue moments.

The path joins KKK to −K-K−K. A regularized matrix field and a continuation argument arrange the necessary endpoint conditions. An integrated resolvent comparison controls the nonlinear term. In the scalar-potential paper, the relevant pointwise density has rank at most one. The matrix paper’s additional estimate allows arbitrary rank and retains the noncommutative terms that the scalar argument does not encounter.

Passing from finite intervals to the line, and from finite lists to the full spectral sum, is part of the claim. It is why finding the explicit optimizing well alone would be insufficient: an arbitrary potential might bind many shallow states whose collective contribution matters.

For equality, M1 retains nonnegative errors instead of throwing them away after obtaining an inequality. Zero total deficit forces these errors to vanish. Some measure failure of first-order differential relations; others measure failure of matrix commutation and density identities.

A key compactness observation is that an increasing list of trial states still has only mmm internal columns. The retained errors control the contribution of shallow tail states, allowing the equality analysis to begin without assuming a finite spectrum. The resulting identities separate different energy blocks, force their row spaces to be independent of position, and leave at most mmm orthogonal directions.

Within each fixed channel, a Riccati-type first-order equation determines the hyperbolic-secant profile. The explicit formula in section 4 is therefore the endpoint of the claimed rigidity argument, rather than an ansatz imposed on all competitors.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The new matrix theorem and complete equality classification are stated for finite matrix size and the strict exponent interval. A constant independent of mmm does not by itself constitute the paper’s proof of every infinite-dimensional operator-valued extension. Earlier operator-valued results at particular exponents retain their own hypotheses.

This family does not settle sharp Lieb–Thirring constants in every spatial dimension. The relation between one-state and semiclassical optimization changes with dimension and exponent. Likewise, the scalar signed-potential statement should not be substituted for the positive semidefinite assumption in the matrix theorem without consulting its separate formulation.

Exact equality also differs from quantitative stability. The classification does not itself provide a universal estimate saying how close a nearly optimal potential must be to a direct sum of solitons. Widely separated profiles and independent scales suggest why such a question requires careful choice of distance and normalization.

8. Sources and further reading

Read–Schulz’s primary paper is linked in section 3. The sources’ bibliographies identify Keller’s Lower bounds and isoperimetric inequalities for eigenvalues of the Schrödinger equation (1961), Lieb–Thirring’s original spectral and kinetic-energy papers, Hundertmark–Lieb–Thomas’s sharp lower-endpoint result, and Laptev–Weidl’s Sharp Lieb–Thirring inequalities in high dimensions (2000). M3 explains the scalar action method; M2 isolates its arbitrary-rank extension; M1 retains the equality defects and derives the fixed-channel classification.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Equality cases in the sharp one-dimensional matrix Lieb–Thirring inequality (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Sharp one-dimensional Lieb–Thirring inequalities for matrix potentials (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Sharp one-dimensional Lieb–Thirring constants (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The outer electrons of large atoms: ionization bounds and universal scales
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 263 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A nucleus of charge ZZZ attracts electrons, while the electrons repel one another. How many extra electrons can remain bound? How much energy does it take to remove one electron from a neutral atom? And how far from the nucleus are its outermost electrons?

These questions concern the edge of the electron cloud. They are surprisingly difficult even when the leading total energy of a large atom is understood. The total energy grows on a large scale, while a few outer electrons account for only a small difference between two large numbers.

Family 263 contains three manuscripts claiming uniform ionization bounds and the energy and radius parts of the generalized ionization conjecture. Their model is the full nonrelativistic Coulomb Hamiltonian with two electron spin states. In particular, the claims allow correlated many-electron wave functions, rather than restricting the state to a mean-field approximation.

2. Background and essential definitions

For one fixed nucleus, the NNN-electron Hamiltonian in atomic units is

HZ,N=∑i=1N(−12Δi−Z∣xi∣)+∑1≤i<j≤N1∣xi−xj∣.H_{Z,N}=\sum_{i=1}^N\left(-\frac12\Delta_i-\frac{Z}{|x_i|}\right)+\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\frac1{|x_i-x_j|}.HZ,N​=i=1∑N​(−21​Δi​−∣xi​∣Z​)+1≤i<j≤N∑​∣xi​−xj​∣1​.

The first term is kinetic energy, the second attraction to the nucleus, and the last electron-electron repulsion. The wave function is antisymmetric under exchange of the full position and spin labels of two electrons. This implements the Pauli principle. The nucleus is held fixed, and there are two possible spin states per electron.

Let EZ(N)E_Z(N)EZ​(N) be the bottom of the spectrum, the smallest possible energy in the sector with NNN electrons. Sending an electron arbitrarily far away shows why these energies are nonincreasing with NNN. A sector binds strictly when

EZ(N)<EZ(N−1).E_Z(N)<E_Z(N-1).EZ​(N)<EZ​(N−1).

Strict binding is stronger than equality with a threshold, where a ground state might or might not exist.

A neutral atom has N=ZN=ZN=Z. Its energy for removing mmm electrons is

Im(Z)=EZ(Z−m)−EZ(Z).I_m(Z)=E_Z(Z-m)-E_Z(Z).Im​(Z)=EZ​(Z−m)−EZ​(Z).

This is the total cost of removing mmm electrons, not the cost of only the last electron in that sequence.

For a normalized neutral ground state ΨZ\Psi_ZΨZ​, let ρΨZ(x)\rho_{\Psi_Z}(x)ρΨZ​​(x) be its spin-summed one-electron density. Its integral is ZZZ. Define an outer-electron radius by

Rm(ΨZ)=inf⁡{r≥0:∫∣x∣>rρΨZ(x) dx≤m}.R_m(\Psi_Z)=\inf\left\{r\geq0:\int_{|x|>r}\rho_{\Psi_Z}(x)\,dx\leq m\right\}.Rm​(ΨZ​)=inf{r≥0:∫∣x∣>r​ρΨZ​​(x)dx≤m}.

The quantity outside the sphere is an expected electron number. A radius leaving half an electron outside is meaningful even though an actual measurement counts integer electrons. Also, this definition concerns a neutral atom with ZZZ electrons; it does not mean that mmm electrons have physically been removed.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Thomas and Fermi introduced a statistical approximation replacing the many-electron wave function by a density. Lieb and Simon established its variational theory and leading large-charge energy and bulk-density limits. The total energy scale is Z7/3Z^{7/3}Z7/3, and the bulk length scale is Z−1/3Z^{-1/3}Z−1/3.

Those successes do not settle ionization. If two energy formulas each have a large error, subtracting them need not accurately determine a much smaller difference. Similarly, an outer tail containing one electron represents only a fraction 1/Z1/Z1/Z of a neutral atom. Convergence of the bulk density can miss precisely that tail.

For the full quantum model, Lieb obtained charge bounds linear in nuclear charge. Lieb, Sigal, Simon and Thirring established asymptotic neutrality: the largest strictly bound electron number divided by ZZZ tends to one for large atoms. Subsequent sublinear and explicit estimates improved the excess-charge bound. But a statement such as “the excess is small compared with ZZZ” still permits an excess tending slowly to infinity.

Seco, Sigal and Solovej obtained quantitative bounds on first ionization energy and an outer-electron radius for the full model. Their estimates depended on powers of ZZZ, leaving uniform bounds distinct. M1 and M2 explain the relevant normalizations and the improved exponent recorded in that earlier paper.

Uniform ionization results were achieved earlier in approximate models, including Thomas–Fermi–von Weizsäcker theory and reduced Hartree–Fock theory. Solovej’s unrestricted Hartree–Fock theorem established bounded excess charge, bounded first ionization energy, and outer-radius control. These results are major predecessors, but their variational spaces differ from the fully correlated Schrödinger model.

Solovej’s A new look at Thomas–Fermi theory formulates generalized ionization laws using upper and lower large-ZZZ limits, followed by a large outer-electron-number limit. The current family claims the corresponding full-model conclusions, with a stronger joint limit for energy but the stated iterated limits for radii.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Uniform charge, energy and outer radius

M1 first considers a molecule with MMM fixed nuclei at arbitrary distinct positions, real charges zj≥1z_j\geq1zj​≥1, and total charge Z=∑jzjZ=\sum_j z_jZ=∑j​zj​. It claims a universal constant CCC such that

E(N)<E(N−1)⟹N≤Z+CM.E(N)<E(N-1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N\leq Z+CM.E(N)<E(N−1)⟹N≤Z+CM.

The same constant is independent of the nuclear charges and separations. For N>Z+CMN>Z+CMN>Z+CM, adjacent sector energies are equal. This resolves the paper’s strict-binding formulation of the excess-charge conjecture; it does not exclude all possible ground states at threshold.

For a neutral atom with integer Z≥1Z\geq1Z≥1, M1 additionally claims constants 0<c≤C<∞0<c\leq C<\infty0<c≤C<∞, independent of ZZZ, with

c≤I1(Z)≤C,c≤R1/2(ΨZ)≤C.c\leq I_1(Z)\leq C,\qquadc\leq R_{1/2}(\Psi_Z)\leq C.c≤I1​(Z)≤C,c≤R1/2​(ΨZ​)≤C.

The radius statement holds for every normalized neutral ground state. No uniqueness or spherical symmetry of the state is assumed. The positive lower bound on first ionization energy is an additional conclusion beyond the usual boundedness assertion.

Removing many outer electrons

M2 claims the energy asymptotic

Im(Z)m7/3⟶aTF>0\frac{I_m(Z)}{m^{7/3}}\longrightarrow a_{\mathrm{TF}}>0m7/3Im​(Z)​⟶aTF​>0

whenever the integers satisfy m→∞m\to\inftym→∞ and Z/m→∞Z/m\to\inftyZ/m→∞. Thus many electrons are removed, but their number remains negligible compared with the nuclear charge.

The constant is the Thomas–Fermi coefficient for two spin states and kinetic energy −Δ/2-\Delta/2−Δ/2. It is characterized using the classical Thomas–Fermi functional, rather than a fitted coefficient. M2 also obtains the conjectured iterated upper and lower limits: take Z→∞Z\to\inftyZ→∞ at fixed mmm, using limsup or liminf, normalize by m7/3m^{7/3}m7/3, and then let m→∞m\to\inftym→∞.

No convergence of Im(Z)I_m(Z)Im​(Z) at a fixed mmm is asserted. In particular, this theorem does not say that the first ionization energies approach one universal number as ZZZ grows.

Radii in neutral atoms

M3 claims, for every choice of neutral ground states,

lim⁡m→∞m1/3[lim sup⁡Z→∞Rm(ΨZ)]=bTF,\lim_{m\to\infty}m^{1/3}\left[\limsup_{Z\to\infty}R_m(\Psi_Z)\right]=b_{\mathrm{TF}},m→∞lim​m1/3[Z→∞limsup​Rm​(ΨZ​)]=bTF​,

and the same formula with liminf, where

bTF=(81π22)1/3.b_{\mathrm{TF}}=\left(\frac{81\pi^2}{2}\right)^{1/3}.bTF​=(281π2​)1/3.

All limits are over integers with Z>mZ>mZ>m. The inner limit keeps mmm fixed. Neither convergence at fixed mmm nor an arbitrary joint-limit radius theorem is part of this statement. The result is uniform over the choice of vector in each ground eigenspace.

M2 and M3 use screening and localization estimates supplied by M1. M3 shares an intermediate-scale strategy with M2, but states that its own proof uses the foundation companion and supplies its own neutral-profile and tail arguments.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Ionization is a central test of how quantum mechanics controls matter beyond its leading bulk behavior. The claimed results describe a small exterior portion of a potentially enormous electron cloud, with constants that do not grow with nuclear charge.

The molecular bound is especially uniform: arbitrary nuclear arrangements cost only a constant number of excess electrons per nucleus. The atomic results then identify two distinct levels of information. A fixed outer tail has a bounded physical radius; a large but relatively small exterior population follows a universal Thomas–Fermi scaling law.

The full correlated model is the decisive setting. Electron correlations can alter local behavior, so results in a restricted variational model do not automatically carry over. The family claims a mechanism for recovering the relevant screening laws directly from correlated states while preserving the exact leading coefficients.

6. The main idea

The physical mechanism is screening. Electrons nearer the nucleus partly cancel its Coulomb attraction, leaving outer electrons to see a reduced effective field. A Thomas–Fermi description relates local density to the positive part of this screened field FFF:

ρ≈k(F+)3/2,k=23/23π2,\rho\approx k(F_+)^{3/2},\qquadk=\frac{2^{3/2}}{3\pi^2},ρ≈k(F+​)3/2,k=3π223/2​,

where F+=max⁡(F,0)F_+=\max(F,0)F+​=max(F,0). The challenge is to justify the appropriate comparisons for a correlated quantum state, rather than assume this relation as the model.

M1 localizes particles while recording the positions and spins removed from each region. The remaining conditional state still carries the correlations relevant to that region. Local trial-electron insertions and lower energy comparisons are arranged with matching semiclassical kinetic coefficients. A coarse kinetic inequality controls density, while the sharp coefficient comes from separate phase-space and eigenvalue-counting comparisons.

Noisy observations then produce conditional densities and screened fields. Conditioning changes probability laws and costs energy; the estimates keep those costs explicit. Positive comparison fields are propagated outward through successive spatial scales, controlling the accumulated errors. For molecules, the geometry is organized so the cost is proportional to the number of nuclei, rather than to the number of scales.

For M2, particle number is first allowed to vary with a price λ>0\lambda>0λ>0:

P(λ)=min⁡N≥0(EZ(N)+λN).P(\lambda)=\min_{N\geq0}\bigl(E_Z(N)+\lambda N\bigr).P(λ)=N≥0min​(EZ​(N)+λN).

A price makes local insertion and deletion compatible with the optimization. At length scale s=λ−1/4s=\lambda^{-1/4}s=λ−1/4, the missing charge is of order s−3s^{-3}s−3. The manuscript identifies its universal coefficient for every minimizing sector, including prices where several sectors tie. Integrating the slopes of this priced energy and bracketing fixed particle numbers recovers the m7/3m^{7/3}m7/3 law without assuming convexity of EZ(N)E_Z(N)EZ​(N).

For M3, the limiting neutral screened field has the homogeneous form F(x)=A∣x∣−4F(x)=A|x|^{-4}F(x)=A∣x∣−4. Its Thomas–Fermi density is proportional to ∣x∣−6|x|^{-6}∣x∣−6, whose exterior mass is proportional to r−3r^{-3}r−3. Solving “exterior mass equals mmm” therefore gives rrr proportional to m−1/3m^{-1/3}m−1/3. The substantial work is obtaining this profile from all allowed quantum ground states, without assuming spherical symmetry, and transferring conditional smoothed densities back to the actual expected electron tail.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These claims concern fixed nuclei, nonrelativistic kinetic energy, Coulomb interactions and two spin states. They do not directly describe relativistic heavy atoms, moving nuclei, magnetic fields or finite-temperature states. The universal constants depend on the stated physical normalization even when they are independent of ZZZ.

Strict binding must remain distinct from threshold-state existence. The generalized energy theorem requires both a growing number of removed electrons and a much larger nuclear charge. The radius theorem retains its iterated limit order. Neither theorem predicts individual chemical shell oscillations or fixed-mmm convergence.

The manuscripts provide universal bounds and asymptotic coefficients rather than a numerical table of ionization energies for particular elements. Effective error rates, sharper constants in the uniform bounds, and extensions to other physical Hamiltonians are separate questions. They should not be inferred from the leading laws alone.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical links in section 3 lead to Solovej’s Hartree–Fock theorem and formulation of generalized ionization. Other primary predecessors are Lieb and Simon’s The Thomas–Fermi theory of atoms, molecules and solids and Seco, Sigal and Solovej’s Bound on the ionization energy of large atoms. M1 is the common foundation for the present family; M2 gives the energy limit and its price construction; M3 gives the radius limits and records its foundation inputs explicitly.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniform excess charge for Coulomb molecules and the outer radius of neutral atoms (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Generalized ionization energies for full Coulomb atoms (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Generalized outer-electron radii of neutral Coulomb atoms (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Predictability beyond a rotating black hole: three levels of strong cosmic censorship
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 264 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Einstein’s equations evolve a spatial geometry into spacetime. But does the initial geometry determine everything that can happen, or can the evolution reach a boundary beyond which several continuations are possible?

The rotating Kerr black hole makes this question concrete. Its exact mathematical solution has an inner Cauchy horizon, beyond the region uniquely controlled by its initial data. Strong cosmic censorship proposes that such extendibility should disappear for generic data. A perfectly symmetric or specially tuned solution can be exceptional.

Family 264 contains three manuscripts claiming local forms of this principle near each fixed rotating subextremal Kerr bridge. They exclude progressively rougher continuations: first twice continuously differentiable metrics, then continuously differentiable metrics, and finally continuous metrics whose weak connection is locally square-integrable. The regularity threshold and the meaning of “generic” are part of the mathematical result, not optional qualifications.

2. Background and essential definitions

Vacuum initial data consist of a spatial metric hhh and a second fundamental form KKK, describing intrinsic geometry and how the spatial slice bends in spacetime. They cannot be chosen independently. They satisfy the vacuum constraint equations

R(h)+(tr⁡hK)2−∣K∣h2=0,R(h)+(\operatorname{tr}_hK)^2-|K|_h^2=0,R(h)+(trh​K)2−∣K∣h2​=0,
div⁡h(K−(tr⁡hK)h)=0.\operatorname{div}_h\bigl(K-(\operatorname{tr}_hK)h\bigr)=0.divh​(K−(trh​K)h)=0.

Here R(h)R(h)R(h) is scalar curvature. The equations are the restrictions of the Einstein vacuum equations to the initial slice.

The maximal globally hyperbolic development, abbreviated MGHD, is the largest spacetime development uniquely governed by those Cauchy data. Global hyperbolicity provides the causal structure needed for a well-posed initial-value problem. “Maximal” in this class does not automatically mean that the spacetime cannot sit inside a larger Lorentzian manifold.

An extension is such a larger manifold with a nondegenerate metric agreeing with the original metric on a proper open subset. The papers require a future-directed timelike curve to reach the boundary of that subset. Thus the extension is accessible in the future, rather than merely being an unrelated added region. No vacuum equation or global-hyperbolicity requirement is imposed outside the original image.

A C2C^2C2 metric has two continuous derivatives; a C1C^1C1 metric has one; a C0C^0C0 metric is continuous. The Sobolev condition Wloc1,2W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}Wloc1,2​ means that first derivatives exist in the weak, distributional sense and are square-integrable on compact coordinate regions. The strongest paper excludes extensions with regularity

C0∩Wloc1,2.C^0\cap W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}.C0∩Wloc1,2​.

For a continuous nondegenerate metric, this is equivalent locally to square-integrability of its weak connection coefficients. It is not enough merely to compute derivatives wherever a continuous function happens to be differentiable.

Finally, Baire generic is topological. A meagre set is a countable union of nowhere dense sets. Its complement contains a residual set, a countable intersection of open dense sets. In the Baire spaces used here, residual sets are dense. This is not a probability-one assertion, and it need not describe an open set.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The local Cauchy theory of Fourès-Bruhat and the maximal-development theorem of Choquet-Bruhat and Geroch established the mathematical framework for deterministic evolution. Kerr’s rotating solutions and Carter’s analysis of their global geometry then exposed the distinction between maximal Cauchy evolution and unrestricted spacetime continuation.

Penrose’s strong cosmic censorship formulation connects this issue with instability at Cauchy horizons. The physical mass-inflation analyses of Poisson–Israel and Ori suggested that incoming radiation could be increasingly blueshifted near the inner horizon. A metric might remain continuous while its derivatives become singular. That possibility is why “singular” alone does not specify the desired theorem.

Dafermos developed nonlinear stability and instability results for a spherically symmetric Einstein–Maxwell–scalar-field system. Luk and Oh’s two-part theorem, with its exterior analysis, established generic C2C^2C2 future inextendibility for the stated two-ended data in that matter model. The symmetry, matter fields and topology are essential parts of those earlier results.

For nonsymmetric vacuum interiors, Luk constructed weak null singularities. Dafermos and Luk proved continuous extension across a nontrivial Cauchy-horizon portion from appropriate data already inside a black hole. This is compatible with failure of stronger extension regularity: continuity and control of derivatives answer different questions.

More recent interior results discussed by the manuscripts, including work of Gurriaran and Luk–Sbierski, use specified radiation asymptotics or quantitative lower bounds to establish singular behavior and obstruct locally Lipschitz extensions through covered horizon portions. Sbierski’s holonomy methods provide a geometric way to test extension regularity.

The present family claims to start instead from a neighborhood of complete vacuum Cauchy data and to cover every future exit of the full development. It builds finite perturbations that violate extension tests, without imposing a radiation lower bound on each initial datum in advance.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The data neighborhood

Fix a Kerr black hole with mass M>0M>0M>0 and rotation parameter aaa, strictly between the nonrotating and extremal cases. M1 allows 0<∣a∣<M0<|a|<M0<∣a∣<M; M2 and M3 formulate their theorems with positive rotation and discuss the relevant geometric reductions.

The reference initial surface is the complete two-ended bridge through the bifurcation sphere, with topology R×S2\mathbb R\times S^2R×S2. Nearby data are smooth, complete vacuum data on that surface, with no symmetry imposed. Their differences from the reference metric and tensor decay like r−1r^{-1}r−1 and r−2r^{-2}r−2, respectively, with corresponding derivative weights.

The topology tests every finite derivative order through weighted seminorms pmp_mpm​. The actual neighborhood requires only

p10(h−h∗,K−K∗)<ε.p_{10}(h-h_*,K-K_*)<\varepsilon.p10​(h−h∗​,K−K∗​)<ε.

Higher seminorms must be finite, but need not be small. No prescribed leading asymptotic coefficient, parity condition or fixed charge value is imposed beyond the stated data conditions. This differs from assuming a particular asymptotic expansion at infinity.

Three extension obstructions

M3 claims that data whose full MGHD admits a future C2C^2C2 extension form a meagre subset of such a neighborhood. M2 gives the corresponding C1C^1C1 result. M1 gives the strongest stated conclusion: data permitting a future C0∩Wloc1,2C^0\cap W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}C0∩Wloc1,2​ extension are meagre.

On a common restriction of the neighborhoods, the extension classes satisfy

C2⊂C1⊂C0∩Wloc1,2.C^2\subset C^1\subset C^0\cap W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}.C2⊂C1⊂C0∩Wloc1,2​.

Excluding the largest class is the strongest obstruction. A residual set of nearby data therefore has no extension with even the weak derivative control specified in M1. Each manuscript may choose its own neighborhood, whose size depends on the fixed Kerr center.

The conclusion concerns the full MGHD and all future timelike exits in the stated definition. It is not limited to the edge of one chosen coordinate chart or to a predetermined portion of a comparison horizon. Ambient extensions may be nonvacuum.

The papers are linked through intermediate results. M3 supplies near-Kerr comparison geometry, constrained packets and correction of initial constraints. M2 develops further geometric and transport tools. M1 uses specified intermediate interfaces from both, together with its own nonlinear comparison and averaging argument. It does not take either weaker paper’s final inextendibility theorem as the premise of its stronger conclusion.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Strong cosmic censorship addresses determinism in general relativity. The claimed local vacuum result treats rotating black holes without imposing symmetry on perturbations, and reaches a regularity threshold relevant to weak geometric formulations.

The distinction between whole-development and partial-horizon statements is substantial. An obstruction in one constructed region would leave open the possibility of an extension elsewhere. The family claims a reduction that begins with an arbitrary future exit and brings it into the perturbative test.

The weighted smooth topology also makes the claim precise. It describes a robustly dense collection in a specified mathematical sense while allowing broad asymptotic tails. It does not promote “generic” into “every,” nor convert a local neighborhood theorem into a theorem for all gravitational initial data.

6. The main idea

The organizing strategy is to turn a hypothetical extension into a finite observation that small perturbations can defeat. This avoids needing an explicit asymptotic radiation law for every starting datum.

A C2C^2C2 extension controls curvature in suitable regular frames near an exit. A C1C^1C1 extension controls connection coefficients but need not bound curvature, because curvature involves another derivative. The appropriate test then uses parallel transport around small loops. Returning a vector around a loop can change it; that change is its holonomy, and the leading small-loop term records curvature.

The papers organize possible regular exits into countably many tests with specified bounds. A strict violation occurs on a finite part of the evolution and persists under sufficiently small changes in initial data. Showing each test to be nowhere dense yields the Baire-category conclusion.

To violate a test, the construction launches a small oscillatory gravitational packet that produces a large enough signal deep in the interior. The packet must arise from exact vacuum data, so the initial constraints are corrected while a protected inner region is left unchanged. The comparison then follows the signal through exterior and interior regions and attaches it to the development of the entire corrected bridge.

For the C1C^1C1 argument, M2 uses two perturbations with opposite linear parts. Subtracting their evolutions cancels a shared quadratic contribution. This allows the difference in observed curvature to dominate errors even when an individual nonlinear error would be too large. A sufficiently short loop and a finite interpolation formula extract the curvature signal from transport data, contradicting the hypothesized extension bound.

M1 needs an additional idea. An L2L^2L2 connection cannot generally be evaluated on a chosen individual curve. The argument therefore averages over families of observation positions and loops. Square-integrability controls most observations outside a small exceptional set. A stopping argument keeps sampled loops in the relevant extension chart. The packet creates a signal on a positive portion of the observing family, while the averaged holonomy estimate would force a smaller signal there.

This explains why the final regularity improvement is not a matter of replacing one derivative count by another. It changes the kind of observation available and requires a measure-theoretic family of tests.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The neighborhood is centered at one fixed rotating subextremal Kerr bridge. No estimate is claimed uniformly as ∣a∣|a|∣a∣ approaches zero or MMM, and the nonrotating and extremal endpoints are excluded. The result does not cover arbitrary vacuum data or the one-ended collapse problem.

The conclusion is Baire generic, not universal or probabilistic, and inextendibility is not asserted to be open. Exact Kerr remains an exceptional extendible solution. The theorem also does not rule out all merely continuous extensions: the additional Wloc1,2W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}Wloc1,2​ requirement is central.

These claims do not supply a complete classification of the singular boundary or a uniform blow-up rate for every generic datum. Quantitative estimates approaching the excluded parameter endpoints, other initial topologies, and broader data neighborhoods remain distinct directions. The source statements should retain their extension definitions and topology whenever compared with other versions of cosmic censorship.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary papers linked in section 3 explain the earlier spherically symmetric censorship theorem and continuous stability of Kerr interiors. The three current manuscripts give detailed accounts of the Cauchy theory, localized constraint deformations, radiation estimates and holonomy precedents they use. For reading order, M3 provides the geometric foundation, M2 explains the pointwise transport obstruction, and M1 explains the averaged obstruction at square-integrable-connection regularity.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Generic Future Inextendibility with Square-Integrable Connection Near a Fixed Kerr Spacetime (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Generic C1 Future Inextendibility Near Rotating Subextremal Kerr Spacetimes (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Quantitative Near-Kerr Evolution and Generic C2 Future Inextendibility (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why a gapped quantum sheet should have only boundary-sized entanglement
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 265 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A sheet of quantum spins has an enormous state space. If there are nnn sites and each has qqq states, a general pure state requires qnq^nqn complex amplitudes. Yet ground states of local physical systems often appear much simpler. How much information can a region share with the rest of the sheet?

An area law says that this shared quantum information grows with the boundary of the region, rather than with its volume. In two spatial dimensions, “area” means boundary length. Family 265 claims such an entropy bound for unique ground states of finite-range square-lattice Hamiltonians using only a positive gap above the full system’s ground state.

A companion manuscript then claims a compact tensor-network approximation on an open square grid. These are related but separate statements: controlling each cut’s entropy does not automatically produce one globally consistent approximation across all cuts.

2. Background and essential definitions

At each lattice site place a copy of Cq\mathbb C^qCq. The full Hilbert space is their tensor product. A local Hamiltonian has the form

H=∑XhX,H=\sum_X h_X,H=X∑​hX​,

where each Hermitian term hXh_XhX​ acts only on a small set XXX. The interaction range RRR bounds the diameter of these supports, and ∥hX∥≤J\|h_X\|\leq J∥hX​∥≤J bounds their strength. The manuscript indexes at most one term per support, so fixed range and strength also bound the total interaction strength touching each site.

Let Ω\OmegaΩ be the unique normalized ground vector, up to its physically irrelevant phase, and let E0E_0E0​ be its energy. A spectral gap Δ>0\Delta>0Δ>0 means

H−E0I≥Δ(I−∣Ω⟩⟨Ω∣).H-E_0 I\geq\Delta\bigl(I-|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|\bigr).H−E0​I≥Δ(I−∣Ω⟩⟨Ω∣).

Every state orthogonal to the ground vector costs at least Δ\DeltaΔ additional energy. For a family of growing systems, the claimed uniform conclusion requires a lower bound on Δ\DeltaΔ independent of system size.

For a region AAA, discard the other sites by taking a partial trace. This gives its reduced density matrix

ρA=Tr⁡Ac∣Ω⟩⟨Ω∣.\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{A^c}|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|.ρA​=TrAc​∣Ω⟩⟨Ω∣.

Its von Neumann entropy is S(A)=−Tr⁡(ρAlog⁡ρA)S(A)=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_A\log\rho_A)S(A)=−Tr(ρA​logρA​), with 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0. For a pure global state, this measures entanglement between the two sides. The elementary bound is S(A)≤∣A∣log⁡qS(A)\leq |A|\log qS(A)≤∣A∣logq, proportional to the number of sites.

A projected entangled-pair state, or PEPS, replaces the full amplitude table by local tensors. Each site tensor has a physical index and virtual indices joined along lattice edges. Summing over paired virtual indices gives the many-body vector. The largest virtual index size is the bond dimension DDD. Small DDD limits the tensor sizes, although finding or contracting the tensors may still be difficult.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Early links between entropy and boundary area arose in quantum-field studies motivated by black-hole entropy, including work of Bombelli and collaborators and Srednicki. These provided important models and physical motivation. The finite-dimensional lattice-spin question asks for a theorem under explicit locality and gap assumptions.

Hastings’s one-dimensional area law established a size-independent entropy bound for unique gapped ground states of local spin chains. It also connected the gap to matrix-product-state approximation. Later work by Arad, Landau, Vazirani and collaborators sharpened the method using approximate ground-state projectors: operators that preserve the ground state while suppressing excitations without introducing too much entanglement.

Exponential decay of correlations is another consequence of a spectral gap, but it does not by itself transparently bound the entire reduced-state spectrum. Entropy sums contributions from all eigenvalues of ρA\rho_AρA​, including many individually small ones. Brandão and Horodecki’s one-dimensional result uses decay of correlations between arbitrary separated regions, a stronger information condition than a statement just about pairs of single-site observables.

Higher-dimensional area laws were known in restricted settings, such as suitable Gaussian oscillator systems. Other results used low-energy counting, heat-capacity assumptions, local gaps, or frustration-free interactions. A Hamiltonian is frustration-free when its ground state minimizes each local term simultaneously; a general ground state need not do this.

In two dimensions, Anshu, Arad and Gosset obtained subvolume estimates and subsequent area-law results under local-gap and frustration-free hypotheses, with specified cuts. M1’s historical discussion distinguishes those hypotheses and geometric settings from the global-gap, arbitrary-region theorem it claims here.

PEPS were introduced as higher-dimensional counterparts of matrix product states. Earlier approximation results addressed local observables, stronger entropy hypotheses, extra low-energy spectral assumptions, or tensor networks on an enlarged lattice. Those variants remain distinct from a small global vector error on the original grid. M2 expressly develops more than the entropy bound to reach that conclusion.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

An entropy law for every region

M1 considers any finite induced subgraph Λ\LambdaΛ of the square lattice. “Induced” means that every nearest-neighbor edge between included sites is present. The domain may have holes or disconnected components. Interaction range is measured in the graph distance within that domain, with infinite distance between different components.

For fixed q,R,J,Δq,R,J,\Deltaq,R,J,Δ, it claims a finite constant CCC such that every admissible unique gapped ground state satisfies

S(A)≤C ∣∂ΛA∣(A⊆Λ).S(A)\leq C\,|\partial_\Lambda A|\qquad(A\subseteq\Lambda).S(A)≤C∣∂Λ​A∣(A⊆Λ).

Here ∂ΛA\partial_\Lambda A∂Λ​A is the set of nearest-neighbor edges with one endpoint in AAA and the other in Λ∖A\Lambda\setminus AΛ∖A. The constant is independent of domain size, domain shape, the chosen region and the individual Hamiltonian.

The gap assumption is imposed only on the full Hamiltonian. There is no requirement that every restriction to a smaller region remain gapped. Nor are commutativity, translation invariance or frustration freeness assumed. If the boundary is empty, the stated inequality gives zero entropy; the induced-graph interaction convention and uniqueness are relevant to that degenerate case.

A global PEPS approximation

M2 specializes to an open L×LL\times LL×L square grid, L≥2L\geq2L≥2, with bounded on-site and nearest-neighbor interactions. For fixed q≥2q\geq2q≥2, JJJ and Δ\DeltaΔ, it claims constants C,c>0C,c>0C,c>0 and a nonzero PEPS Φ\PhiΦ on that same grid with

D≤CLc,D\leq C L^c,D≤CLc,

and

min⁡θ∈R∥Φ∥Φ∥−eiθΩ∥≤L−1.\min_{\theta\in\mathbb R}\left\|\frac{\Phi}{\|\Phi\|}-e^{i\theta}\Omega\right\|\leq L^{-1}.θ∈Rmin​​∥Φ∥Φ​−eiθΩ​≤L−1.

The norm is the Hilbert-space norm of the entire state. The minimization accounts for global phase. The tensors can have arbitrary complex entries and need not be isometries. Constants are uniform over Hamiltonians with the fixed local parameters.

This is an existence theorem. It does not assert that the tensors can be found efficiently, that the resulting PEPS can be contracted efficiently, or that the approximant has an injective structure or a gapped parent Hamiltonian. It also does not silently replace the open square by a torus or claim the same representation theorem for every irregular domain covered by M1.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. A general two-dimensional gap-to-area theorem would resolve a central structural question about quantum many-body ground states. The asserted removal of local-gap and frustration-free assumptions is particularly significant, because physical interactions often compete and restricted Hamiltonians can behave differently from the full system.

The PEPS result adds a global representation statement with polynomial bond dimension. It gives a mathematical explanation for compact tensor-network descriptions in the claimed class, while keeping the computational task separate. A concise representation can exist even when discovering its coefficients is hard.

The two manuscripts also show why the distinction matters conceptually. An entropy estimate concerns a bipartition at a time. A state representation must make all those local descriptions compatible, control their accumulated errors, and route the required indices through the actual grid. That extra work is a substantive part of the family.

6. The main idea

M1 compares information gained with excitation energy spent. Its gap says that a state with very little excess energy must lie mostly in the ground-state direction. The proof seeks constructions that would create too much independent information at too little energy if the desired area bound failed.

The first step obtains a weaker entropy estimate, below volume growth, on suitable boxes. Local spectral filters then replace the Hamiltonian by positive constraints that individually annihilate Ω\OmegaΩ, retain a global gap, and have rapidly decaying spatial tails. This is an analytical construction; the original Hamiltonian need not have been frustration-free.

A useful information quantity is mutual information:

I(B:C)=S(B)+S(C)−S(B∪C)I(B:C)=S(B)+S(C)-S(B\cup C)I(B:C)=S(B)+S(C)−S(B∪C)

for disjoint regions. The proof moves partitions through a collar separating a target region from the remote system. It encodes entropy comparisons using operators on many symmetric copies of the state. The same interpolating family controls both information and energy, allowing the global gap to constrain the information cost.

The resulting collar estimate is strengthened using localized products of the positive constraints. Finally, the planar geometry permits two ordered families of separated regions after removing only a boundary-sized collection of sites. Two entropy-chain-rule comparisons cancel the interior contributions. The remaining exceptional sites and summed information errors have boundary size, yielding the claimed area law.

M2 imports the area law and stronger collar estimates from M1. It does not infer PEPS approximation from entropy alone. Its construction imagines distributing physical registers among auxiliary parties, beginning with one party holding the whole vector and ending with one party per site. This starting point is legitimate for an existence theorem and also makes clear why it is not an algorithm for discovering the ground state.

At successive geometric scales, small information across buffers allows registers to change owners with controlled error. Small patches near junctions need separate encodings, because ordinary separation disappears there. The protocol is arranged so each party participates in only boundedly many interactions over its lifetime.

A compression theorem then replaces large auxiliary pair resources by polynomial-size sums in a density-operator calculation. A suitable product-basis column recovers an approximate vector. Finally, the connections are routed through the original square grid with bounded congestion, so polynomial virtual dimensions remain polynomial. The error budget is chosen to control the normalized global vector, rather than only individual reduced states.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Uniqueness of the ground state, finite local dimension, bounded local interactions and a positive full-system gap are explicit hypotheses. The displayed theorem does not address arbitrary degenerate ground spaces, gapless systems, unbounded oscillator sites or all higher spatial dimensions.

The area law covers finite induced square-lattice domains with intrinsic graph-range interactions. The PEPS theorem has the narrower open-square nearest-neighbor setting and the stated inverse-linear accuracy. Alternative boundary conditions, stronger approximation guarantees and additional tensor structure require their own arguments.

Neither compact entanglement nor polynomial bond dimension alone settles efficient simulation. Searching for the tensors, representing their entries with controlled numerical precision, and contracting the network are separate problems. The manuscript explicitly leaves those algorithmic claims outside its theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

Hastings and the Anshu–Arad–Gosset papers linked in section 3 provide primary background for the one-dimensional theorem and restricted two-dimensional advances. M1’s historical discussion separates correlation decay, entropy, local gaps and global gaps. M2 compares global PEPS approximation with local-observable and enlarged-lattice formulations, and its Appendix A records the stronger companion estimates used beyond the entropy inequality itself.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A two-dimensional area law from a global spectral gap (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Polynomial PEPS approximation of gapped square-grid ground states (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Three complementary measurements in dimension six—and why a fourth is excluded
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 266 · Mathematical physics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Some quantum measurements are maximally incompatible in a precise sense: knowing the outcome of one leaves every outcome of another equally likely. How many such measurements can coexist in a six-dimensional quantum system?

Represent each measurement by an orthonormal basis of C6\mathbb C^6C6. Two bases are mutually unbiased when every cross-basis squared inner product equals 1/61/61/6. Three pairwise mutually unbiased bases are known to exist. The long-standing question is whether a fourth can exist.

M1 claims that the maximum is exactly three, through a computer-assisted exclusion covering arbitrary complex bases under specified arithmetic and compiler conditions. M2 proves a different structural claim about Fourier sums of complex Hadamard matrices and gives an exact-arithmetic obstruction to a complete seven-basis family. The two conclusions should remain distinct: M2’s basis-count consequence is an upper bound of five, not three.

2. Background and essential definitions

In Cd\mathbb C^dCd, let B={b1,…,bd}B=\{b_1,\ldots,b_d\}B={b1​,…,bd​} and C={c1,…,cd}C=\{c_1,\ldots,c_d\}C={c1​,…,cd​} be orthonormal bases. They are mutually unbiased if

∣⟨bi,cj⟩∣2=1d(1≤i,j≤d).|\langle b_i,c_j\rangle|^2=\frac1d\qquad(1\leq i,j\leq d).∣⟨bi​,cj​⟩∣2=d1​(1≤i,j≤d).

The quantum interpretation follows directly from the rule for measurement probabilities. If a state is one vector of BBB, measurement in CCC gives a uniform distribution. “Unbiased” here is a relation between two whole bases, rather than a statement about statistical estimation bias.

Write N(d)N(d)N(d) for the largest number of pairwise mutually unbiased bases. The general upper bound is d+1d+1d+1. Complete families reaching that bound exist when ddd is a power of a prime. Six is the smallest dimension outside that construction, since 6=2⋅36=2\cdot36=2⋅3.

A common unitary change of coordinates can make one basis the standard coordinate basis. Every vector in a second unbiased basis must then have coordinates of modulus 1/d1/\sqrt d1/d​. Writing its vectors as columns gives a normalized complex Hadamard matrix H/dH/\sqrt dH/d​, where

∣Hij∣=1,HH∗=dI.|H_{ij}|=1,\qquad HH^*=dI.∣Hij​∣=1,HH∗=dI.

The entries may be arbitrary complex phases. Restricting them to a finite set of roots of unity would change the problem.

Multiplying rows or columns by phases, or permuting them, preserves the relevant Hadamard equivalence. One may make the first row and first column all ones; this is called dephasing. It removes redundant coordinates without claiming that all remaining matrices belong to a known parametrized family.

For M2, a balanced integer vector a=(a0,…,a5)a=(a_0,\ldots,a_5)a=(a0​,…,a5​), with ∑iai=0\sum_i a_i=0∑i​ai​=0, defines a character sum

gH(a)=16∑k=05∏i=05Hikai.g_H(a)=\frac16\sum_{k=0}^5\prod_{i=0}^5H_{ik}^{a_i}.gH​(a)=61​k=0∑5​i=0∏5​Hikai​​.

It averages a phase monomial over the columns. Balance makes it invariant under column rephasing. These sums are Fourier coordinates on the torus of possible phases, and orthogonality imposes relations among them.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Mutually unbiased bases arose in the mathematical description of complementary quantum measurements. Schwinger’s unitary-operator framework, Ivanović’s state-determination work, and Wootters–Fields constructions connected them to quantum tomography and prime-power dimensions. The general d+1d+1d+1 bound and its prime-power attainability leave composite dimensions with a different arithmetic structure.

The conjecture N(6)=3N(6)=3N(6)=3 is associated with Zauner. The lower bound follows from tensor products: take three mutually unbiased bases in dimension two and three chosen bases in dimension three, and pair corresponding factors. For cross-basis tensor vectors, squared overlaps multiply to (1/2)(1/3)=1/6(1/2)(1/3)=1/6(1/2)(1/3)=1/6.

The upper bound resisted several approaches. Grassl excluded four bases containing the standard–Fourier pair. Numerical searches and algebraic studies examined many Hadamard families, but failure to find a fourth basis is not a universal exclusion.

A close predecessor is Jaming, Matolcsi, Móra, Szöllősi and Weiner’s certified Fourier-family analysis. It ruled out extending the standard basis together with any member of a specified two-parameter Fourier family to four bases. Their method combined phase intervals, error bounds, subdivision and exhaustive compatibility tests. Jaming, Matolcsi and Móra subsequently outlined an unrestricted discretization program.

A separate line uses Fourier and combinatorial identities. Matolcsi, Ruzsa and Weiner conjectured a particular degree-six character cancellation outside one exceptional cubic Hadamard class. Maxwell and Brierley established that cancellation for the Karlsson family. M2 claims to remove the family restriction and adds a finite positivity certificate for the complete-family problem.

Thus the two manuscripts extend different partial solutions: exhaustive covering beyond previously specified second bases, and universal Fourier identities beyond previously specified Hadamard families.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Exactly three bases, with a computational contract

M1 states that, under its binary64 arithmetic and compiler assumptions, the complete execution documented in its section 7.5 excludes four arbitrary pairwise mutually unbiased bases in C6\mathbb C^6C6. Combined with the elementary construction of three, it claims

N(6)=3.N(6)=3.N(6)=3.

The second basis is unrestricted. The method covers all complex Hadamard matrices of order six rather than relying on a classification into familiar families.

The computational premises are explicit. They include the stated floating-point rounding model, separately evaluated operations, specified square-root behavior, and compiler conditions excluding transformations incompatible with the error analysis. The paper reports a complete execution accounting for initially unresolved records. These are descriptions of the manuscript’s result and evidence; they are not a separate execution or verification performed for this digest.

Universal Fourier vanishing

Let

α=(1,1,1,−1,−1,−1).\alpha=(1,1,1,-1,-1,-1).α=(1,1,1,−1,−1,−1).

M2 claims that every order-six complex Hadamard matrix outside Tao’s cubic equivalence class satisfies

gH(πα)=0g_H(\pi\alpha)=0gH​(πα)=0

for every coordinate permutation π\piπ. The exceptional class has entries that, after the allowed equivalences, are cube roots of unity. The manuscript notes that its displayed representative also appeared in Moorhouse’s earlier work.

A related structural step says that if both HHH and its entrywise square are Hadamard, then HHH belongs to that cubic class. Entrywise squaring means squaring each entry, not matrix multiplication H2H^2H2. This classification is used to identify the exception in the Fourier argument.

M2 also claims there is no complete family of seven mutually unbiased bases in dimension six. It then invokes Weiner’s completion theorem: any ddd mutually unbiased bases in Cd\mathbb C^dCd extend to a complete d+1d+1d+1-basis family. Excluding seven therefore excludes six as well, giving

N(6)≤5.N(6)\leq5.N(6)≤5.

Its certificates use integer and rational arithmetic, and it includes a verifier. This structural and exact-arithmetic contribution is meaningful independently of M1’s sharper count.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The six-dimensional MUB problem is a prominent finite-dimensional question in quantum information and discrete mathematics. Six is the first place where prime-power constructions do not settle the maximal count, so a complete exclusion of four bases would mark a major boundary of those constructions.

The Fourier result has its own value. It constrains every individual order-six Hadamard matrix, including matrices not assumed to participate in any large unbiased family. Such structural identities can support further analysis of complementary measurements and complex Hadamard geometry.

The rating reflects a major resolution within a focused dimension and problem class. It does not imply a classification of all composite dimensions or of all triples in dimension six. The two papers also illustrate complementary ways of obtaining a universal conclusion: a finite covering with controlled numerical error and exact identities derived from positivity.

6. The main idea

Cover every possible second basis

M1 first removes phase and permutation redundancies. A small initial block leaves nine phases to cover. Necessary interval tests remove impossible seed regions while retaining all feasible choices.

For a surviving seed, the remaining block must satisfy both unitary and fixed-modulus conditions. The argument compresses part of the unknown completion to a two-dimensional unitary problem. A closed cover of U(2)U(2)U(2), together with Taylor remainder bounds, either excludes a cell or places its possible completions inside certified phase balls.

The balls are refined using approximate tangent directions to the Hadamard equations plus a bound on normal displacement. The numerical directions need not parametrize a smooth manifold. Their role is only to give a controlled cover of every exact solution still possible.

Inside each final ball, the method covers vectors unbiased to the first two bases. These vector balls become vertices in two graphs. One graph retains pairs that might be orthogonal; the other retains pairs that might be unbiased. Two further bases would require two disjoint six-vertex cliques in the orthogonality graph, with all cross-pairs connected in the unbiasedness graph.

The claimed execution excludes this pattern everywhere. A failed numerical certification or an exhausted search cap is retained as unresolved, rather than counted as a contradiction. The logical distinction is between proposing a useful center and certifying an exclusion for the whole region around it.

Derive an exact positivity contradiction

M2 averages monomials over distinct row and column indices. Orthogonality supplies linear relations among these averages. Products of character sums can be expanded into the same moment coordinates by tracking which sampled columns coincide.

The first certificate expresses an average of nonnegative quantities as zero. Each summand must therefore vanish. This forces a dichotomy: either the desired character sums vanish, or the entrywise square of the matrix is also Hadamard. Algebraic identities for row ratios then identify the second alternative with the cubic class.

For a complete unbiased family, further moments involve several transition matrices and shared columns. Explicit positive quadratic forms would have a combined value forced to be negative by their exact coefficient identities and the bound that every normalized moment has modulus at most one. That contradicts positivity.

The certificate coefficients are rational, but the actual Hadamard entries need not be. Exact arithmetic verifies identities valid for arbitrary complex phases. This is why the approach is not restricted to a rational or root-of-unity sample of the original problem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1’s strongest claim retains its stated arithmetic and complete-execution conditions. M2’s rational certificates establish the Fourier theorem and the weaker upper bound described above. They should not be conflated into an assertion that the exact Fourier calculation alone proves N(6)=3N(6)=3N(6)=3.

The family does not classify every triple of mutually unbiased bases, every order-six complex Hadamard matrix, or the maximum number of bases in all non-prime-power dimensions. Nor does nonexistence of an exact fourth basis quantify how close an approximate fourth basis can come to satisfying the conditions.

Questions about approximate complementarity, structural classifications of triples, and analogous obstructions in other composite dimensions remain separate. The source statements are reported at their stated scope, including the computational premises of the sharper theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary links in section 3 lead to the Fourier-family exclusion, the unrestricted discretization proposal, and the Fourier/combinatorial approach. M1 explains the exhaustive covering and the contract for its reported computation. M2 gives the individual-matrix Fourier theorem, the cubic exception, the complete-family certificate and the use of Weiner’s completion theorem. Its appendix contains the exact verifier as part of the source exposition.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The maximum number of mutually unbiased bases in dimension six (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Exact Fourier certificates for complex Hadamard matrices of order six (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Condensation in an interacting Bose gas—and the particles left outside it
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 267 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Bose–Einstein condensation means that a macroscopic fraction of particles occupies the same one-particle state. For an ideal gas this follows from particle statistics. Interactions make the problem much harder: repulsion changes the many-particle state, and even at zero temperature some particles remain outside the condensate.

Can one establish condensation for an exact interacting gas while keeping its density and interaction fixed as the sample grows without bound? And in a dilute gas, can one determine the fraction left outside the condensate, rather than merely show that the condensate exists?

Family 267 contains five manuscripts addressing these questions in three dimensions. They treat hard spheres and fixed bounded repulsive potentials, including positive-temperature condensation and zero-temperature depletion. Their central convention is the ordinary thermodynamic limit at fixed physical parameters, followed, where needed, by a separate dilute limit.

2. Background and essential definitions

Place NNN identical bosons on a periodic cube of side LLL, mathematically the torus (R/LZ)3(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3(R/LZ)3. Their wave function is symmetric under particle exchange. Density is ρ=N/L3\rho=N/L^3ρ=N/L3, and the thermodynamic limit sends N,L→∞N,L\to\inftyN,L→∞ while this ratio tends to a fixed positive number.

For a bounded repulsive potential vvv, the Hamiltonian is

HN,L=−∑i=1NΔi+∑i<jvL(xi−xj),H_{N,L}=-\sum_{i=1}^N\Delta_i+\sum_{i<j}v_L(x_i-x_j),HN,L​=−i=1∑N​Δi​+i<j∑​vL​(xi​−xj​),

where vLv_LvL​ is the periodic version of vvv. Units are chosen so that ℏ2/(2mparticle)=1\hbar^2/(2m_{\mathrm{particle}})=1ℏ2/(2mparticle​)=1, and the thermal papers also set Boltzmann’s constant to one.

For hard spheres, configurations with two centers at distance at most aaa are forbidden. The Hamiltonian is the kinetic operator on the allowed configurations, with Dirichlet boundary conditions at contact. The parameter aaa is the exclusion distance between centers, not a separately doubled geometric radius.

The scattering length summarizes low-energy two-body repulsion. For a bounded radial potential it is determined by the zero-energy scattering solution

(−Δ+12v)f=0,f(x)=1−a∣x∣\left(-\Delta+\frac12v\right)f=0,\qquad f(x)=1-\frac{a}{|x|}(−Δ+21​v)f=0,f(x)=1−∣x∣a​

outside the potential’s range. For the hard-core model, the scattering length equals the exclusion distance. The dimensionless gas parameter is η=ρa3\eta=\rho a^3η=ρa3; small η\etaη means dilute.

For an NNN-particle state Γ\GammaΓ, its one-particle density matrix is γ(1)=NTr⁡2,…,NΓ\gamma^{(1)}=N\operatorname{Tr}_{2,\ldots,N}\Gammaγ(1)=NTr2,…,N​Γ, with trace NNN. Let u0=L−3/2u_0=L^{-3/2}u0​=L−3/2 be the normalized constant orbital. Its occupation fraction is

B=⟨u0,γ(1)u0⟩N.B=\frac{\langle u_0,\gamma^{(1)}u_0\rangle}{N}.B=N⟨u0​,γ(1)u0​⟩​.

A positive lower limit of BBB establishes condensation in that orbital. The fraction 1−B1-B1−B is its depletion. At positive temperature the exact canonical state is e−H/T/Tr⁡(e−H/T)e^{-H/T}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-H/T})e−H/T/Tr(e−H/T); at zero temperature the papers use ground states or density matrices supported on the ground eigenspace.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Bose’s counting and Einstein’s extension to material particles led to the ideal-gas condensation prediction. Penrose and Onsager formulated the interacting version through a macroscopic eigenvalue of the one-particle density matrix. Bogoliubov’s quasiparticle theory then predicted excitations and depletion around a macroscopically occupied mode. Lee, Huang and Yang calculated the leading hard-sphere energy correction and depletion coefficient.

Rigorous control of the energy came through Dyson’s bounds and Lieb–Yngvason’s leading dilute asymptotics. Later Lee–Huang–Yang estimates reached the next energy term. Fournais and Solovej’s general lower bound includes hard cores; the manuscripts credit Basti, Brooks, Cenatiempo, Olgiati and Schlein with the matching sharp hard-sphere upper bound. These are crucial energy inputs, but the occupation of a single orbital is a separate observable.

The reason is visible in a large box. The first nonzero one-particle kinetic energy is of order L−2L^{-2}L−2.
