Moving particles into extremely long-wavelength modes can cost little energy as LLL grows. An accurate energy formula alone therefore need not distinguish the global constant orbital from nearby modes.

Lieb and Seiringer established complete condensation in the trapped Gross–Pitaevskii regime. Further work established thermal condensation and Bogoliubov depletion in other coupled scaling regimes, where scattering length, density or box size vary together. Those results have their own substantial content. They do not automatically permit unrestricted growth of volume at a fixed positive gas parameter.

Fixed-parameter condensation also has precedents for lattice gases and continuum interactions under different assumptions, including positivity of both the potential and its Fourier transform. A literal hard core falls outside some such hypotheses. The present family’s claimed advance is exact canonical or ground-state occupation in the stated fixed-interaction thermodynamic setting, followed by sharp depletion information.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Condensation for hard spheres

M5 claims absolute constants η0,c0>0\eta_0,c_0>0η0​,c0​>0 such that, whenever fixed a,ρ>0a,\rho>0a,ρ>0 satisfy ρa3<η0\rho a^3<\eta_0ρa3<η0​, every thermodynamic sequence of hard-sphere ground states obeys

lim inf⁡B≥c0.\liminf B\geq c_0.liminfB≥c0​.

This includes arbitrary complex ground vectors and mixtures supported on the ground eigenspace. The positive fraction is uniform throughout the sufficiently dilute interval. The volume threshold may depend on aaa and ρ\rhoρ. M5 itself establishes a positive fraction, without claiming the optimal depletion law.

M1 adds positive temperature. For every fixed a>0a>0a>0, each sufficiently small fixed density admits a fixed temperature T(a,ρ)>0T(a,\rho)>0T(a,ρ)>0 at which the exact canonical Gibbs state has a positive lower limiting constant-orbital fraction. Exclusion distance, density and temperature all stay fixed while volume grows. The theorem does not locate the transition temperature or state a sharp thermal depletion formula.

A uniform bound for bounded repulsion

M4 assumes vvv is bounded, measurable, nonnegative, radial, finite-range and not zero almost everywhere. It claims constants ρ∗(v),c∗(v)>0\rho_*(v),c_*(v)>0ρ∗​(v),c∗​(v)>0 such that, for each 0<ρ<ρ∗0<\rho<\rho_*0<ρ<ρ∗​, all sufficiently large boxes with

ρ/2≤N/L3≤2ρ\rho/2\leq N/L^3\leq2\rhoρ/2≤N/L3≤2ρ

satisfy B≥c∗B\geq c_*B≥c∗​ for every 0≤T≤ρ20\leq T\leq\rho^20≤T≤ρ2, in its stated units. The interaction is not weakened with particle number. The fraction bound is independent of density within the admitted interval, although the required box size is not. Neither radial monotonicity nor positivity of the Fourier transform is assumed.

The leading quantum depletion

At zero temperature, M2 for hard spheres and M3 for fixed bounded potentials claim

1−B=83πρa3+o(ρa3).1-B=\frac{8}{3\sqrt\pi}\sqrt{\rho a^3}+o\bigl(\sqrt{\rho a^3}\bigr).1−B=3π​8​ρa3​+o(ρa3​).

The thermodynamic limit is taken first at each fixed density, then ρ↓0\rho\downarrow0ρ↓0. More precisely, all thermodynamic accumulation values have this same dilute asymptotic, uniformly over the stated ground-state density matrices. The claim does not require that occupation have a unique thermodynamic limit at every fixed positive density.

The bounded-potential theorem keeps the potential itself fixed throughout both limits. Its hypotheses are the same type of bounded, nonnegative, radial finite-range repulsion, with positive scattering length. M3 reports uniqueness of the finite-volume ground state in that class but formulates occupation using density matrices.

Where the depleted hard-sphere particles go

M2 claims the full scaled nonzero-momentum occupation measure for hard spheres. For periodic momenta k∈(2π/L)Z3k\in(2\pi/L)\mathbb Z^3k∈(2π/L)Z3, let n(k)n(k)n(k) be the occupation of L−3/2eik⋅xL^{-3/2}e^{ik\cdot x}L−3/2eik⋅x. Define

νN,L=1Nη∑k≠0n(k) δk/8πρa.\nu_{N,L}=\frac1{N\sqrt\eta}\sum_{k\ne0}n(k)\,\delta_{k/\sqrt{8\pi\rho a}}.νN,L​=Nη​1​k=0∑​n(k)δk/8πρa​​.

In the same thermodynamic-then-dilute sense, this converges against every bounded continuous test function to the finite measure

νBog(dt)=(8π)3/2(2π)3g(t) dt,\nu_{\mathrm{Bog}}(dt)=\frac{(8\pi)^{3/2}}{(2\pi)^3}g(t)\,dt,νBog​(dt)=(2π)3(8π)3/2​g(t)dt,
g(t)=∣t∣2+12∣t∣4+2∣t∣2−12.g(t)=\frac{|t|^2+1}{2\sqrt{|t|^4+2|t|^2}}-\frac12.g(t)=2∣t∣4+2∣t∣2​∣t∣2+1​−21​.

The value at t=0t=0t=0 is irrelevant to the integral. The density is integrable both near zero and at infinity, and the total measure is 8/(3π)8/(3\sqrt\pi)8/(3π​). Testing with the constant function one gives the depletion coefficient. This momentum-profile theorem is asserted for hard spheres; M3’s stated headline is the total depletion for bounded potentials.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Condensation in a fixed-density interacting continuum gas is a central many-body question. The claims address coherence across arbitrarily large samples, not just an energy expansion or a regime in which interactions simultaneously vanish with the box size.

The family then reaches the next level of precision: a universal leading depletion coefficient depending on the interaction through scattering length. For hard spheres it identifies the distribution of those depleted particles on the natural momentum scale, rather than just their total number.

The positive-temperature result is also substantial, but its role is an existence theorem at a sufficiently low fixed temperature. It should not be inflated into a determination of the critical temperature or a complete phase diagram. The importance comes from the stated coherence and occupation claims themselves.

6. The main idea

The core obstacle is long-distance coherence. Local energy estimates can show that particles prefer a nearly constant mode inside a moderate box. They do not automatically make the phases or amplitudes in far-apart boxes agree.

The papers use positive imaginary-time path representations. Roughly, a quantum state or thermal kernel is represented using Brownian trajectories with interaction weights; hard spheres enforce avoidance of forbidden contacts. One compares configurations in which a distinguished particle has been moved between distant cells while the observed remaining particles—the bath—are matched.

Multiplying a fixed loss at every step of a long route would destroy the desired bound as the sample grows. Instead, the construction averages over many routes before taking a second moment. Exact conditional normalizations cancel away from encounters between two sampled routes. The remaining cost depends on how often the routes meet, rather than on their total lengths. Probabilistic paths with controlled intersection tails, plus detours around rare unusable cells, provide the geometric input.

M5 first handles the modulus of a ground wave function and then controls phase transfer to cover arbitrary complex ground states. M1 must additionally handle a mixed thermal state. It factors the Gibbs kernel through its square root, retaining the same bath in the two factors whose overlap gives constant-orbital occupation. Joint spatial and trajectory estimates ensure that enough movable particles remain available under the interacting thermal law.

The depletion papers separate two contributions. Let PℓP_\ellPℓ​ project a one-particle function onto functions constant on cubes of side ℓ\ellℓ, and let P0P_0P0​ project onto the global constant. Since P0≤PℓP_0\leq P_\ellP0​≤Pℓ​, for a normalized bosonic ground vector,

1−B=⟨Ψ,(1−Pℓ)1Ψ⟩+∥(Pℓ−P0)1Ψ∥2.1-B=\langle\Psi,(1-P_\ell)_1\Psi\rangle+\|(P_\ell-P_0)_1\Psi\|^2.1−B=⟨Ψ,(1−Pℓ​)1​Ψ⟩+∥(Pℓ​−P0​)1​Ψ∥2.

The subscript means action on one particle. The first term measures variation inside cubes; the second measures differences between their averages.

Local energy bounds retaining positive quasiparticle terms control the first contribution at the Bogoliubov scale. Sharper comparisons of particle-deletion measures control the second below the depletion scale, using fourth moments locally and second moments over long distances. M2 then tests one-body observables to recover the whole momentum distribution. M3 adapts the method to bounded interactions while preserving their exact Boltzmann weights.

The companion roles are explicit. M5 uses M4’s geometric route construction; M1 develops the additional thermal hard-core estimates; M2 uses M5’s spatial and path inputs; M3 uses bounded-potential density tails from M4 and route/comparison methods from M2. These are related arguments with model-specific work, not five interchangeable formulations of one theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All five papers concern three-dimensional homogeneous periodic systems and the specified repulsive interactions. They do not directly cover attractive gases, arbitrary long-range forces, disordered systems or every trapping geometry. The hard-core and bounded-potential hypotheses must remain separate.

Condensation, superfluid response, energy asymptotics and a critical-temperature formula are different properties. The family does not claim all of them from the same occupation bound. The temperature produced for hard spheres is positive and volume-independent, but not claimed optimal. The exact depletion law is a zero-temperature statement.

The sharp occupation asymptotics retain their order of limits and accumulation-value interpretation. No unique fixed-density thermodynamic occupation limit is assumed or supplied by that wording. Rates of convergence, finite-temperature depletion coefficients and transition-temperature shifts remain additional questions beyond the displayed claims.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary links in section 3 lead to Lieb–Seiringer’s trapped condensation theorem and Fournais–Solovej’s energy analysis including hard cores. The manuscripts’ bibliographies give the original Bogoliubov and Lee–Huang–Yang predictions and the later sharp upper bounds. M4 and M5 introduce the fixed-parameter condensation mechanisms, M1 extends the hard-core setting to positive temperature, and M2–M3 give the sharper zero-temperature occupation statements.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Bose–Einstein condensation at positive temperature in the dilute hard-sphere gas (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Quantum Depletion and Momentum Distribution in the Dilute Hard-Sphere Bose Gas (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Quantum Depletion for Fixed Bounded Repulsive Potentials (October 5, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, A density-uniform condensate bound for dilute Bose gases (September 27, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Ground-state condensation in the dilute hard-sphere gas (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The spin-one Haldane gap: rings, boundary fields and a topological index
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 268 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A quantum spin chain can have excitations whose energy becomes arbitrarily small as the chain grows. Alternatively, every nontrivial excitation can cost a fixed positive amount. That difference separates a gapless system from a gapped one.

Haldane predicted a striking distinction between antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chains with integer spin and those with half-odd-integer spin. For spin one, the expected excitation gap is positive. Physical arguments, numerical calculations and experiments supplied strong evidence, but they are different from a uniform mathematical lower bound for the exact Hamiltonian.

Family 268 contains two manuscripts claiming such bounds for the pure bilinear spin-one Heisenberg interaction. M1 treats even periodic rings. M2 treats odd open chains with a specified magnetic field at both endpoints, then uses Tasaki’s index theorem to identify a nontrivial topological index for the resulting boundary-selected infinite-chain states.

2. Background and essential definitions

A spin-one site has a three-dimensional state space C3\mathbb C^3C3. Its spin operators Sx,Sy,SzS^x,S^y,S^zSx,Sy,Sz are Hermitian matrices satisfying the angular-momentum commutation rules and

(Sx)2+(Sy)2+(Sz)2=2I.(S^x)^2+(S^y)^2+(S^z)^2=2I.(Sx)2+(Sy)2+(Sz)2=2I.

The eigenvalues of SzS^zSz are −1,0,1-1,0,1−1,0,1. On a chain, SjαS_j^\alphaSjα​ acts on site jjj and as the identity elsewhere.

For a ring of nnn sites, with coupling constant one, the Hamiltonian is

Hnper=∑j=0n−1Sj⋅Sj+1,Sn=S0.H_n^{\mathrm{per}}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mathbf S_j\cdot\mathbf S_{j+1},\qquad \mathbf S_n=\mathbf S_0.Hnper​=j=0∑n−1​Sj​⋅Sj+1​,Sn​=S0​.

The dot product means the sum of the three component products. The positive coupling is antiferromagnetic: neighboring spins favor antiparallel correlations. Quantum terms on overlapping bonds need not commute, so minimizing every bond separately is generally impossible.

Let E0(n)E_0(n)E0​(n) be the ground energy and E1(n)E_1(n)E1​(n) the next distinct energy. The periodic gap is γn=E1(n)−E0(n)\gamma_n=E_1(n)-E_0(n)γn​=E1​(n)−E0​(n). Each finite nonconstant matrix has a positive gap above its full ground eigenspace. The difficult assertion is a lower bound that survives arbitrarily large nnn.

For an open chain with sites −L,…,L-L,\ldots,L−L,…,L, M2 uses

HL(h)=∑j=−LL−1Sj⋅Sj+1−h(S−Lz+SLz).H_L(h)=\sum_{j=-L}^{L-1}\mathbf S_j\cdot\mathbf S_{j+1}-h(S_{-L}^z+S_L^z).HL​(h)=j=−L∑L−1​Sj​⋅Sj+1​−h(S−Lz​+SLz​).

There is no bond joining the ends, and both fields have the same sign. Here the two lowest eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity, so a positive gap also implies a unique ground state.

A thermodynamic state is described by expectations of local observables, matrices acting on finitely many sites. A subsequential local limit means these expectations converge along a selected sequence of longer chains, without assuming convergence of the entire sequence.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Lieb–Schultz–Mattis theorem supplied a rigorous low-energy obstruction for the cyclic spin-one-half chain. Affleck and Lieb extended the half-odd-integer picture in their setting, retaining the possibility of ground-state degeneracy. Integer spin escapes that obstruction, but escaping a no-go theorem does not prove a gap.

Haldane’s 1983 field-theoretic work predicted the integer versus half-odd-integer distinction. The Affleck–Kennedy–Lieb–Tasaki model then provided a rigorous gapped spin-one example. Its bond interaction includes a biquadratic term: if q=Sj⋅Sj+1q=\mathbf S_j\cdot\mathbf S_{j+1}q=Sj​⋅Sj+1​, it is proportional, up to an additive constant, to q+q2/3q+q^2/3q+q2/3. The pure Heisenberg chain uses qqq alone.

This distinction is essential. Stability of the AKLT gap under sufficiently small perturbations, as established by Yarotsky in the relevant class, controls a neighborhood of that interaction. It does not by itself give a gapped path all the way to the pure bilinear point.

White and Huse’s numerical study estimated the spin-one bulk gap near 0.410500.410500.41050 in the unit-coupling normalization and identified effective spin-one-half behavior at free ends. Experiments in nearly one-dimensional spin-one materials supplied additional evidence. Boundary effects explain why a periodic gap does not automatically settle a particular open-chain gap.

Finite-size gap criteria also developed, notably for frustration-free chains. Those methods have powerful scope, but the pure Heisenberg model requires an argument suited to its competing interactions. M1 uses finite thermal traces and trial-state energy bounds followed by an analytic recurrence, rather than importing a frustration-free criterion unchanged.

For topology, Tasaki’s conditional theorem proves that the spin-one Heisenberg ground state has a nontrivial index under a precise fixed-boundary-field gap assumption. M2 claims to establish that assumption at one explicit field. The topological implication is credited to Tasaki, not presented as a new independent index theorem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Even periodic rings

M1 claims uniqueness of the periodic ground state for every even n≥60n\geq60n≥60, together with

γn>4105log⁡8079(n≥60, n even),\gamma_n>\frac4{105}\log\frac{80}{79}\qquad(n\geq60,\ n\text{ even}),γn​>1054​log7980​(n≥60, n even),

and the stronger eventual estimate

γn>log⁡20784(n≥2304, n even).\gamma_n>\frac{\log20}{784}\qquad(n\geq2304,\ n\text{ even}).γn​>784log20​(n≥2304, n even).

Consequently the lower limit along even rings is at least (log⁡20)/784>0(\log20)/784>0(log20)/784>0. This is the positive even-periodic formulation of the spin-one Haldane conjecture stated by the paper.

The finitely many smaller even rings have a positive gap above their full ground sector simply because they are finite-dimensional nonconstant Hamiltonians. Combining that fact with the uniform large-ring estimate gives a positive infimum over all even n≥4n\geq4n≥4. This observation does not provide a numerical bound or a uniqueness assertion for those smaller rings. M1 also states a corresponding bound for local excitations in subsequential periodic ground-state limits.

Odd open chains with one fixed field

M2 claims, at the fixed field h=3/5h=3/5h=3/5,

E1(L,3/5)−E0(L,3/5)>log⁡10392(L≥960).E_1(L,3/5)-E_0(L,3/5)>\frac{\log10}{392}\qquad(L\geq960).E1​(L,3/5)−E0​(L,3/5)>392log10​(L≥960).

The chain has 2L+12L+12L+1 sites, so the threshold refers to half-length, not total length. The same-field endpoint Hamiltonian above is part of the theorem. It is not a free-end chain, nor a model with extra spin-one-half endpoint sites.

The boundary-selected index

For every subsequential local limit ω\omegaω of those open-chain ground states, M2 derives a locally unique gapped ground-state inequality, invariance under rotations about the zzz-axis and site reflection, and Tasaki index −1-1−1.

The index is defined through a slowly varying local twist. In the source convention,

Uε=exp⁡[−i∑∣j∣≤π/ε(π+εj)Sjz].U_\varepsilon=\exp\left[-i\sum_{|j|\leq\pi/\varepsilon}(\pi+\varepsilon j)S_j^z\right].Uε​=exp​−i∣j∣≤π/ε∑​(π+εj)Sjz​​.

After taking the infinite-chain state limit first, the index is lim⁡ε↓0ω(Uε)\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\omega(U_\varepsilon)limε↓0​ω(Uε​), which the cited theorem restricts to {−1,1}\{-1,1\}{−1,1}. The value −1-1−1 is the nontrivial alternative for this diagnostic.

This does not assume that the full finite-chain sequence converges, establish global uniqueness of every infinite-chain ground state, or identify all possible boundary constructions with these selected states.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The Haldane gap is a central example of a qualitative quantum effect that depends on spin parity. A uniform lower bound for the pure spin-one interaction would place this prediction on a mathematical footing in the stated finite-volume formulations.

The explicit lower bounds are much smaller than the familiar numerical gap estimate. Their purpose is different: they remain strictly positive at every sufficiently large allowed length. They are not claimed to locate the true gap accurately.

The second manuscript matters independently because boundaries can carry low-energy degrees of freedom even when the bulk is gapped. Its fixed-field result supplies the specific hypothesis needed for a nontrivial topological index. This connects spectral control to a robust property of selected infinite-chain states without conflating several different notions of string order, edge behavior and topological index.

6. The main idea

M1 reads one partition function in two directions. The physical expression is a trace of a thermal exponential, a sum of positive Boltzmann weights. A time-ordered bond-history expansion also expresses it as a spatial moment

Zn(β)=Tr⁡(Xβn)Z_n(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}(X_\beta^n)Zn​(β)=Tr(Xβn​)

of a compact self-adjoint transfer operator. A common energy shift is included in the source’s definition of ZnZ_nZn​; it cancels from the probability ratios used for gaps. For even nnn, the powers of the spatial eigenvalues contribute nonnegative weights, even though XβX_\betaXβ​ itself need not be positive.

Normalize each collection of weights to a probability distribution. Its purity is ∑ipi2\sum_i p_i^2∑i​pi2​. Purity close to one means that one weight dominates. Squaring and renormalizing weights improves that concentration rapidly once a suitable initial threshold is reached.

On the physical side, squaring weights doubles inverse temperature β\betaβ. On the spatial side, it doubles chain length. Exact identities couple these two operations. Starting from finite purity bounds, the manuscript propagates increasingly strong concentration as both scales double. Moment inequalities fill the intermediate even lengths.

Why does purity imply a gap? The ratio of an excited-state weight to a ground-state weight is e−β(E−E0)e^{-\beta(E-E_0)}e−β(E−E0​). A sufficiently strong exponential suppression as β\betaβ grows forces E−E0E-E_0E−E0​ to stay positive. The argument tracks the full physical Gibbs distribution, so ground-state multiplicity is also relevant.

The finite starting estimates use explicitly specified thermal trace enclosures and matrix-product trial vectors. The source describes integer arithmetic, rational interval bounds and controlled polynomial truncation errors. These finite inputs initialize an analytic argument for all larger sizes; the digest reports that construction without rerunning its certificates.

For an open chain, the transfer expression becomes a boundary pairing rather than a trace. Spatial eigenspaces are weighted by overlap with a boundary vector, and that vector changes with temperature. Periodic concentration alone therefore leaves a missing step.

M2 controls boundary-weighted residual moments together with Gibbs purity for an auxiliary opposite-field chain. A rotation then relates the leading spatial contribution to the same-field Hamiltonian. The coupled recurrence yields the claimed uniform open-chain gap. Tasaki’s theorem subsequently fixes the twist-index sign: symmetry keeps the twist expectation real, and the gap prevents the interpolation from crossing zero in the relevant regime.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These claims concern spin one, unit antiferromagnetic coupling and the specified pure bilinear interaction. They do not settle the entire integer-spin Haldane prediction, arbitrary anisotropies, all boundary conditions or odd periodic rings.

The open-chain field is fixed at 3/53/53/5. A gap there should not be quoted as a free-boundary gap. The topological result concerns subsequential boundary-selected states and Tasaki’s particular twist index; stronger global uniqueness conclusions require additional hypotheses.

The papers provide explicit positive lower bounds, not the exact gap, a complete excitation spectrum or a uniform description of every perturbation of the model. Sharper quantitative bounds and extensions to other interactions remain separate questions from the claimed positive-gap resolution.

8. Sources and further reading

Haldane’s original field-theoretic paper and Tasaki’s conditional index theorem are linked in section 3. The manuscripts cite the Lieb–Schultz–Mattis and Affleck–Lieb obstructions, the AKLT construction, White–Huse numerical results and finite-size gap methods in their respective scopes. M1 supplies the periodic transfer and finite inputs used by M2; M2 proves the boundary-specific estimates before applying Tasaki’s theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The periodic spin-one Haldane gap (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A boundary-field gap for the spin-one Heisenberg chain (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The Laughlin gap: a quantum Hall state that resists weak disorder
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 269 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

An exact ground-state formula can be extraordinarily informative without answering a basic physical question: how much energy does it cost to leave that state? If the cost tends to zero as a sample grows, a beautiful finite-system formula may describe a fragile thermodynamic state.

This distinction is central to the fractional quantum Hall effect. Electrons restricted to a plane, placed in a strong magnetic field and cooled to low temperature can form strongly correlated states. Laughlin’s wavefunction describes one of the most famous examples, at filling fraction one third. A specially chosen repulsive interaction has this wavefunction as its exact zero-energy ground state. The longstanding spectral question asks whether every orthogonal state costs at least a fixed positive energy, independently of the number of electrons.

Family 269 reports such a bound for the full spherical interaction and a planar consequence. Its companion asks a further question: does the gap survive a weak, spatially irregular external potential? The claimed answer is uniform even when that potential changes with the size of the system. The manuscripts are labeled M1 and M2 below; the unperturbed gap in M2 supplies an input to the stability theorem in M1.

2. Background and essential definitions

Restricting the available states

A magnetic field organizes single-particle energies into Landau levels. The model retains only the lowest level, treating excitation to higher levels as unavailable. On a sphere carrying an integer number QQQ of magnetic flux quanta, its one-particle space UQU_QUQ​ has dimension Q+1Q+1Q+1. It is also the spin-Q/2Q/2Q/2 representation of the rotation group.

For NNN identical fermions, the space is the antisymmetric product ⋀NUQ\bigwedge^N U_Q⋀NUQ​: exchanging two particle labels reverses the wavefunction’s sign. The interaction is

HN,Q=∑1≤i<j≤NPij(1).H_{N,Q}=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}P_{ij}^{(1)}.HN,Q​=1≤i<j≤N∑​Pij(1)​.

Each Pij(1)P_{ij}^{(1)}Pij(1)​ is an orthogonal projection onto pair relative angular momentum one, equivalently pair total spin Q−1Q-1Q−1. A projection has eigenvalues zero and one. Thus each pair pays for occupying one specified relative-motion channel. Every unordered pair has coefficient one; there is no size-dependent normalization. This convention matters when reading numerical gap bounds.

The operator is positive. At the Laughlin flux Q=3(N−1)Q=3(N-1)Q=3(N−1), its zero space is a single line generated by

ΨL,N=∏i<j(uivj−ujvi)3.\Psi_{L,N}=\prod_{i<j}(u_i v_j-u_j v_i)^3.ΨL,N​=i<j∏​(ui​vj​−uj​vi​)3.

Here (ui,vi)(u_i,v_i)(ui​,vi​) are homogeneous coordinates for particle iii on the sphere. Cubing makes the polynomial antisymmetric and imposes a third-order zero when two particles meet. Each particle has degree 3(N−1)3(N-1)3(N−1), explaining the flux relation. The finite-size correction by one is the spherical shift; the ratio of particle number to flux tends to one third.

Gaps and limits

For a normalized ground state Ω\OmegaΩ, a gap at least Δ>0\Delta>0Δ>0 means

⟨ψ,HN,Qψ⟩≥Δ∥ψ∥2,⟨Ω,ψ⟩=0.\langle\psi,H_{N,Q}\psi\rangle\geq\Delta\|\psi\|^2,\qquad \langle\Omega,\psi\rangle=0.⟨ψ,HN,Q​ψ⟩≥Δ∥ψ∥2,⟨Ω,ψ⟩=0.

Uniformity means the same positive Δ\DeltaΔ works as NNN grows. With magnetic length set to one, the sphere has radius Q/2\sqrt{Q/2}Q/2​ and area 2πQ2\pi Q2πQ. Increasing flux therefore gives a genuinely expanding two-dimensional sample, rather than a fixed-radius thin cylinder.

The Fock space FQ=⨁n=0Q+1⋀nUQ\mathcal F_Q=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{Q+1}\bigwedge^n U_QFQ​=⨁n=0Q+1​⋀nUQ​ simply collects every allowed particle number. Its Hamiltonian HQH_QHQ​ acts as Hn,QH_{n,Q}Hn,Q​ in each sector. This larger space is useful because removing particles reveals relations between states at different fillings.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Laughlin’s 1983 paper proposed the correlated wavefunction and a description of fractional excitations. Haldane’s spherical construction organized the problem through angular momentum and pair interactions. Trugman and Kivelson subsequently identified exact Laughlin ground states for suitable repulsive interactions in a vanishing-range limit. These developments explained why a particular polynomial is special; they did not themselves bound every competing excitation from below.

Finite-size calculations by Haldane and Rezayi supported a gap. The density-wave picture of Girvin, MacDonald and Platzman supplied a physical description of collective excitations. A variational trial excitation, however, provides an upper bound on an excitation energy. A uniform gap requires a lower bound valid for all orthogonal wavefunctions, including ones not captured by the trial construction.

Rigorous progress became possible in more restricted geometries and interactions. Nachtergaele, Warzel and Young established gaps for a truncated pseudopotential in the thin-cylinder regime. Warzel and Young treated a thin torus and distinguished bulk behavior from open-chain edge effects. Algebraic work by Ortiz, Nussinov, Dukelsky, Seidel and collaborators clarified the zero spaces. These are substantive predecessors, but truncating the interaction or keeping a cylinder thin changes the problem addressed by an expanding round sphere.

Another route concerns incompressibility: density estimates for Laughlin wavefunctions multiplied by analytic symmetric factors. Work of Rougerie and Yngvason, and of Lieb, Rougerie and Yngvason, established strong restrictions within that correlated class. Such information differs from a spectral bound on arbitrary states. M2 does not assume a density-screening hypothesis.

Stability has its own history. Lattice theorems of Bravyi, Hastings and Michalakis, and of Michalakis and Zwolak, relate gap stability to additional local conditions. A bulk gap alone is not their entire input. M1 develops the corresponding local control for the spherical lowest-Landau-level setting, using M2 as its unperturbed starting point.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A uniform gap for the full interaction

M2 states that, for every 0<γ<γ∗0<\gamma<\gamma_*0<γ<γ∗​, all sufficiently large fluxes satisfy

HQ2≥γHQ,γ∗=46167333190011014>125.H_Q^2\geq\gamma H_Q,\qquad\gamma_*=\frac{4616733319001}{10^{14}}>\frac1{25}.HQ2​≥γHQ​,γ∗​=10144616733319001​>251​.

The flux threshold is independent of particle number. For a nonnegative eigenvalue EEE, this inequality says E2≥γEE^2\geq\gamma EE2≥γE, so either E=0E=0E=0 or E≥γE\geq\gammaE≥γ. At Laughlin filling, where the zero state is unique, M2 obtains

HN,3(N−1)≥125(I−PL,N)H_{N,3(N-1)}\geq\frac1{25}(I-P_{L,N})HN,3(N−1)​≥251​(I−PL,N​)

for every sufficiently large NNN, with PL,NP_{L,N}PL,N​ the ground-line projection. The threshold is existential. The finite-sphere theorem does not assert the endpoint coefficient γ∗\gamma_*γ∗​.

In a particle sector having no zero mode, the Fock-space inequality only bounds its lowest energy away from zero. It does not automatically give a gap between that sector’s first two energies.

M2 also reports a planar consequence for the full fermionic relative-degree-one pair interaction, still with coefficient one and unrestricted center-of-mass degree. Its positive spectrum is bounded below by γ∗\gamma_*γ∗​, uniformly over particle number N≥2N\geq2N≥2 and total polynomial degree. This includes the cubic fermionic case of the planar folklore gap conjecture described in Rougerie’s survey. The planar endpoint conclusion should not be transferred back to finite spheres.

Stability under bounded scalar disorder

M1 fixes Q=3(N−1)Q=3(N-1)Q=3(N−1). For a real bounded measurable function φ\varphiφ on the sphere, let

TQ(φ)=ΠQMφΠQ∣UQ,VN,Q(φ)=∑i=1NTQ(φ)(i).T_Q(\varphi)=\Pi_Q M_\varphi\Pi_Q\big|_{U_Q},\qquadV_{N,Q}(\varphi)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_Q(\varphi)^{(i)}.TQ​(φ)=ΠQ​Mφ​ΠQ​​UQ​​,VN,Q​(φ)=i=1∑N​TQ​(φ)(i).

Here MφM_\varphiMφ​ multiplies by the potential and ΠQ\Pi_QΠQ​ projects to the lowest Landau level. This projected multiplication is called a Toeplitz operator. The perturbed Hamiltonian is HN,Q+λVN,Q(φ)H_{N,Q}+\lambda V_{N,Q}(\varphi)HN,Q​+λVN,Q​(φ).

M1 claims constants λ∗,Δ∗>0\lambda_*,\Delta_*>0λ∗​,Δ∗​>0 and N∗N_*N∗​ such that, whenever N≥N∗N\geq N_*N≥N∗​, ∥φ∥∞≤1\|\varphi\|_\infty\leq1∥φ∥∞​≤1 and ∣λ∣≤λ∗|\lambda|\leq\lambda_*∣λ∣≤λ∗​, the two lowest eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, obey

E1(N,λ,φ)−E0(N,λ,φ)≥Δ∗.E_1(N,\lambda,\varphi)-E_0(N,\lambda,\varphi)\geq\Delta_*.E1​(N,λ,φ)−E0​(N,λ,φ)≥Δ∗​.

Thus the ground state remains unique. No symmetry, derivative bound or randomness assumption on φ\varphiφ is required. Both constants are uniform over its profile and system size. They are existential, rather than optimized numerical disorder thresholds. The ground vector and ground energy may change.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The family addresses a central spectral problem for a canonical fractional quantum Hall Hamiltonian and adds a robustness statement on a fixed perturbation interval. Its importance rests on these claimed mathematical conclusions, not on a verification of their proofs.

The full interaction and expanding geometry are decisive. A gap surviving only in a thin or truncated model would leave open whether the two-dimensional parent Hamiltonian has arbitrarily cheap bulk excitations. The all-particle-sector estimate also provides information beyond one selected ground state, which becomes useful in the stability argument.

Disorder stability connects an exact, highly symmetric model to imperfect external environments. The theorem allows irregular scalar profiles without making the perturbation strength shrink as the number of particles grows. It concerns a particular projected interaction, so its physical significance should not be confused with a theorem covering every experimental quantum Hall material.

6. The main idea

Compare the square with the energy itself

M2 expands HQ2H_Q^2HQ2​ into terms involving two, three and four particles. It then constructs a positive auxiliary operator from squares of combinations of particle-removal and particle-creation operations, averaged over rotations. Rotation symmetry sorts the comparison into angular-momentum blocks.

Some comparisons reduce to finite matrices with rational data. The manuscript reports the needed finite inequalities; the role of these matrices is to support a bound for the full interaction, not to replace it with a truncated Hamiltonian.

The difficult passage is from limiting blocks to large finite spheres. An absolute error on a growing many-body space could overwhelm the desired gap. M2 instead controls the error by a small multiple of HQH_QHQ​ itself. It therefore vanishes on the zero space and remains uniform in particle number. The resulting comparison has the form HQ2≥KQ+(γ∗−o(1))HQH_Q^2\geq K_Q+(\gamma_*-o(1))H_QHQ2​≥KQ​+(γ∗​−o(1))HQ​, with KQ≥0K_Q\geq0KQ​≥0.

Pay for disorder with interaction energy

Even if ∥φ∥∞≤1\|\varphi\|_\infty\leq1∥φ∥∞​≤1, the many-particle perturbation can have norm of order NNN. Ordinary perturbation estimates using that full norm would allow a disorder interval shrinking like 1/N1/N1/N. M1 seeks a local, energy-relative estimate instead.

First it analyzes zero modes with fewer electrons at fixed flux. An orthogonal branching construction records missing flux or particles. Pinning zeros at a pole and transporting between nearby fluxes turn this algebra into quantitative control of local observables. After averaging rotations, the change in a suitable observable is bounded by a constant times the number of missing electrons.

Second, local particle-loss operations reduce interaction energy while controlling how many particles are removed. M1 retains additional positive four-body information from M2 to establish this descent. Combining descent with the zero-mode estimates bounds centered local perturbations by an appropriate energy operator.

Finally, spectral transport follows the moving ground line along the perturbation. A gap bootstrap closes the argument on a fixed interval of λ\lambdaλ. The local estimates are the extra ingredient that turns an unperturbed spectral gap into uniform stability.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The principal model is the fermionic cubic Laughlin parent interaction at filling one third. The statements do not automatically extend to other filling fractions, bosonic versions, Coulomb interactions, Landau-level mixing or arbitrary two-body disorder.

M1 concerns real scalar one-body potentials projected to the lowest level on expanding spheres. Its amplitude-only hypothesis is broad within that class, but it is not a general theorem for every local perturbation. The planar gap consequence in M2 is likewise distinct from a planar disorder-stability theorem.

The constants leave quantitative questions: what is the actual excitation gap, what finite sizes are covered, and how large can the stable disorder interval be? Edge spectra, transport coefficients and fractional quasiparticle statistics require additional statements beyond the displayed inequalities. A unique spherical ground state also says nothing by itself about the ground-state degeneracies appropriate to other spatial topologies.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary historical links in section 3 introduce the wavefunction, spherical model and earlier thin-geometry gap results. M2 supplies the unperturbed Fock-space inequality and planar consequence; M1 supplies the local estimates and disorder-stability theorem. Their claims are reported as stated.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniform Stability of the Spherical Laughlin Gap (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Fock-space inequality and the Laughlin spectral gap (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Bound states in BFSS matrix mechanics: one at zero, infinitely many above it
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 270 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A quantum particle may remain bound even when classical motion offers a route to infinity. Transverse quantum vibrations can make escape expensive. Supersymmetry complicates this picture: bosonic and fermionic contributions can cancel that expense, allowing scattering at arbitrarily small energy.

The BFSS matrix model brings these effects together. Its variables are nine matrices rather than an ordinary particle position. When the matrices commute, the classical interaction vanishes, creating unbounded escape directions. Nevertheless, string-theoretic arguments predict exactly one normalizable zero-energy state after the freely moving center of mass is removed.

Family 270 contains two claims about this same spectral landscape. M1 reports the unique zero-energy state for every finite matrix size. M2 reports infinitely many positive-energy normalizable eigenstates when the matrices have size two. The latter challenges a separate exclusion stated in the original BFSS paper. These conclusions concern different energies and can coexist: uniqueness at zero does not mean uniqueness of all bound states.

2. Background and essential definitions

From positions to matrices

Fix N≥2N\geq2N≥2. The bosonic variables are nine traceless Hermitian N×NN\times NN×N matrices X1,…,X9X_1,\ldots,X_9X1​,…,X9​. A Hermitian matrix equals its conjugate transpose. Tracelessness removes the scalar matrix coordinates that describe the free center of mass. Since the real dimension of traceless Hermitian matrices is N2−1N^2-1N2−1, the bosonic configuration space is

R9(N2−1).\mathbb R^{9(N^2-1)}.R9(N2−1).

There are also finitely many fermionic degrees of freedom, represented by a finite-dimensional complex space FNF_NFN​. Wavefunctions are square-integrable FNF_NFN​-valued functions on that Euclidean space.

The group SU(N)SU(N)SU(N), consisting of unitary matrices with determinant one, acts by simultaneous conjugation on the bosonic variables and by a corresponding action on the fermions. Physical states are invariant under this action: conjugating every matrix describes a gauge change, not a new physical configuration. Thus

HN=[L2(R9(N2−1))⊗FN]SU(N).\mathcal H_N=\bigl[L^2(\mathbb R^{9(N^2-1)})\otimes F_N\bigr]^{SU(N)}.HN​=[L2(R9(N2−1))⊗FN​]SU(N).

The bosonic potential is built from squared commutators [Xi,Xj]=XiXj−XjXi[X_i,X_j]=X_iX_j-X_jX_i[Xi​,Xj​]=Xi​Xj​−Xj​Xi​. Commuting matrices therefore have zero potential even when their entries become large. Their simultaneous eigenvalues suggest separated clusters, but this geometric picture does not by itself determine the quantum spectrum.

Supersymmetry and normalizability

Sixteen differential operators QαQ_\alphaQα​, called supercharges, combine momentum terms with matrix commutators and fermionic matrices. The manuscripts specify the Hamiltonian through the closed quadratic form

qN(Ψ)=116∑α=116∥QαΨ∥2.q_N(\Psi)=\frac1{16}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{16}\|Q_\alpha\Psi\|^2.qN​(Ψ)=161​α=1∑16​∥Qα​Ψ∥2.

One begins with smooth compactly supported gauge-invariant functions and closes this form. The associated operator HNH_NHN​ is nonnegative and self-adjoint. This specification matters: an operator restricted to a valley with an imposed boundary condition is a different spectral problem.

A normalizable eigenstate is a nonzero square-integrable vector satisfying HNΨ=EΨH_N\Psi=E\PsiHN​Ψ=EΨ. After normalization, its squared norm integrates to one. A formal solution or a scattering wave need not satisfy this requirement.

The spectral set begins at zero and extends through nonnegative energies. A zero eigenstate is consequently at the threshold of the continuum, rather than below an isolated band of scattering energies. Positive normalizable eigenstates lie inside that spectral interval; such embedded eigenstates are logically compatible with the interval being the whole spectral set.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Supersymmetric matrix mechanics arose in supermembrane regularization. The BFSS conjecture of Banks, Fischler, Shenker and Susskind proposed a large-matrix-size description of M-theory. A prediction associated with Witten’s D0-brane analysis was that each finite size should have one relative zero-energy bound state. In the proposed interpretation, that internal state supports a single supergraviton carrying the corresponding longitudinal momentum.

De Wit, Lüscher and Nicolai established the nonnegative continuous spectral interval for the matrix Hamiltonians they studied. Their analysis explicitly left room for normalizable states inside it. Confusing a statement about the spectral set with an exclusion of eigenvectors would erase the distinction at issue here.

Supersymmetric indices supplied substantial evidence for the zero state. Such an index counts even zero modes minus odd zero modes. On a noncompact configuration space, contributions from infinity must be controlled. Yi analyzed the two-particle bulk contribution; Sethi and Stern included a boundary contribution to establish the two-particle bound state. Moore, Nekrasov and Shatashvili evaluated relevant matrix integrals. Green and Gutperle, and Konechny, developed general-rank cluster and asymptotic arguments.

M1 identifies a remaining analytic issue in passing from such calculations to a full-space kernel count: eigenvalue separations need not all grow at the same rate. Clusters can split into smaller clusters on nested scales, and normalizable mass must not disappear between those scales. Earlier rotation-invariance results of Sethi–Stern and Hasler–Hoppe are also important: in the grading used by M1, they make normalizable zero states even, allowing a signed count to become a dimension count.

Mass deformations offered another approach. Porrati–Rozenberg and Kac–Smilga emphasized normalizability when removing a deformation. The confining plane-wave deformation of Berenstein, Maldacena and Nastase has vacua indexed by partitions of NNN. Asymptotic wavefunction constructions by Halpern–Schwartz, Graf–Hoppe, Fröhlich and collaborators, and Lin–Yin clarified local cluster behavior. M1’s claimed advance is global control sufficient to remove the deformation without losing or inventing states.

Positive-energy binding has a separate history. Danielsson, Ferretti and Sundborg found excited normalizable wavefunctions in a Born–Oppenheimer approximation and discussed metastability beyond it. Symmetry-restricted confinement also appeared in related, simpler matrix models. M2 claims exact eigenvectors of the undeformed relative SU(2)SU(2)SU(2) operator, beyond those approximate conclusions.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Exactly one threshold state

M1 states

dim⁡ker⁡HN=1for every finite integer N≥2.\dim\ker H_N=1\qquad\text{for every finite integer }N\geq2.dimkerHN​=1for every finite integer N≥2.

The kernel is the zero-energy eigenspace. Its states are invariant under Spin⁡(9)\operatorname{Spin}(9)Spin(9), the spin group implementing spatial rotations, and even in the specified fermion grading. Square integrability is over the entire configuration space. Constants may depend on the fixed value of NNN; this is not a uniform large-NNN estimate.

The free U(1)U(1)U(1) center of mass is absent. Adding it back introduces free motion, so the statement should not be rewritten as a normalizable bound state of all center-of-mass coordinates. Nor does uniqueness of a kernel supply a positive gap above it.

Infinitely many positive-energy states at size two

M2 uses the same full-space, gauge-invariant supercharge-form realization for the relative SU(2)SU(2)SU(2) model. It states that there are orthonormal vectors Ψj\Psi_jΨj​ in the operator domain and numbers Ej>0E_j>0Ej​>0 such that

H2Ψj=EjΨj,Ej⟶∞.H_2\Psi_j=E_j\Psi_j,\qquad E_j\longrightarrow\infty.H2​Ψj​=Ej​Ψj​,Ej​⟶∞.

In particular, there are infinitely many distinct positive eigenvalues. M2 presents this as a counterexample, at N=2N=2N=2, to the original BFSS paper’s exclusion of other normalizable relative bound states beyond the threshold states. It does not present it as a disproof of the separate large-NNN Matrix Theory conjecture.

The positive states occur in selected rotation sectors. They do not contradict the rotation-invariance theorem for zero-energy states, whose energy hypothesis is essential. M2 also does not assert that the entire operator has discrete spectrum.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The threshold-state prediction is a central finite-size consistency question in matrix theory. A full-space existence-and-uniqueness theorem for every finite NNN, together with exact positive embedded states at N=2N=2N=2, would substantially sharpen the spectral foundations of this model.

The family is also instructive beyond its physical interpretation. It illustrates two distinct roles of symmetry: supersymmetry can permit escape channels, while a specified rotation type can prevent a state from using the low transverse modes needed for escape. The same operator can therefore support scattering and confined sectors.

This rating concerns the significance of the claims if correct. Their exposition does not independently establish the claimed proofs or settle the wider physical conjectures motivating the model.

6. The main idea

Count states without losing norm at infinity

M1 begins with a massive, confining deformation. A suitable restricted real supercharge has a Fredholm index equal to p(N)p(N)p(N), the number of unordered integer partitions of NNN. A Fredholm index is a stable signed kernel count for an operator with controlled range and finite-dimensional defects.

As the mass is removed, the partitions acquire a second meaning. A proper partition describes separated blocks of smaller matrix sizes. Each block contributes its own internal zero state, while the block centers carry relative-motion variables. The intended accounting is one line for each of the p(N)−1p(N)-1p(N)−1 proper partitions, leaving one line for a bound state in which the whole system remains together.

That subtraction becomes meaningful only after proving that every limiting norm is accounted for. M1 separates fast transverse oscillators from slow cluster coordinates, corrects approximate test states so their charge outputs converge, and uses induction on block size. An exterior estimate based on the Hardy inequality controls intermediate scales; a separate massive estimate prevents escape to infinity.

The resulting decomposition preserves norms and inner products. Extraction forces existence of a whole-system zero state. Recovery of proposed profiles and a spectral-gap estimate in the massive comparison bound its multiplicity by one. This is the manuscript’s mechanism for turning a deformation count into the undeformed full-space statement.

Let rotation types forbid cheap escape

For SU(2)SU(2)SU(2), write the bosonic coordinates as three vectors x1,x2,x3∈R9x^1,x^2,x^3\in\mathbb R^9x1,x2,x3∈R9. The potential in M2’s normalization is

V(x)=∑a<b∣xa∧xb∣2.V(x)=\sum_{a<b}|x^a\wedge x^b|^2.V(x)=a<b∑​∣xa∧xb∣2.

It vanishes when the vectors are collinear. Fixing a nonzero vector uuu exposes sixteen transverse coordinates for the other two vectors. They behave like an oscillator whose frequency grows with ∣u∣|u|∣u∣.

The rotations fixing uuu form Spin⁡(8)\operatorname{Spin}(8)Spin(8). Representation theory constrains which transverse oscillator levels can appear in a chosen Spin⁡(9)\operatorname{Spin}(9)Spin(9) sector. If its highest-weight label is λ=(λ1,λ2,λ3,λ4)\lambda=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\lambda_4)λ=(λ1​,λ2​,λ3​,λ4​), the relevant bound forces an oscillator level nnn to satisfy n≥λ2−Mn\geq\lambda_2-Mn≥λ2​−M, where MMM depends only on the finite fermionic space.

Making the second weight coordinate large excludes many low oscillator levels. The remaining positive oscillator energy dominates the potentially negative fermionic term, which grows only linearly in the coordinates. The chosen sector then has compact resolvent: its spectrum consists of eigenvalues escaping to infinity. M2 constructs infinite-dimensional physical sectors with the required weights, so their eigenvectors are also eigenvectors of the full Hamiltonian.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 is a theorem claimed for each fixed finite NNN, with the center of mass removed and a specified operator domain. It supplies neither an explicit closed-form wavefunction nor uniform control as N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞. The existence of a threshold state does not separate it from the continuum by a gap.

M2 proves its positive-state statement only for relative SU(2)SU(2)SU(2). It does not classify every eigenstate, determine exact energies, or extend the result to all matrix sizes. Its confined rotation sectors coexist with escape in other sectors. The stability of these embedded states under symmetry-breaking perturbations is a further question.

Scattering theory, detailed cluster asymptotics and the large-NNN physical interpretation require additional work beyond the two headline statements. Keeping these boundaries explicit preserves the difference between resolving a precise spectral question and establishing an entire proposed physical duality.

8. Sources and further reading

The original BFSS and Sethi–Stern papers linked above provide the physical proposal and a major two-particle predecessor. For the spectral distinction, see de Wit, Lüscher and Nicolai, The supermembrane is unstable. For earlier approximate excited states, see Danielsson, Ferretti and Sundborg, D-particle dynamics and bound states. M1 and M2 below supply the claims and their stated operator conventions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The unique threshold bound state of the SU(N) BFSS model (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Positive eigenvalues of the relative SU(2) BFSS Hamiltonian (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How a quantum ferromagnet orders: Bloch’s law and the magnetization sphere
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 271 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A ferromagnet favors neighboring spins pointing in the same direction. Yet its interaction may have no preferred direction at all. How can an equilibrium system choose one? And if a finite sample preserves rotation symmetry, what becomes of the magnetization that one expects in the ordered phase?

Family 271 addresses these questions for the quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet. Four manuscripts report increasingly detailed statements: existence of magnetized equilibrium states; the leading low-temperature reduction known as Bloch’s law; its first correction from the lattice; and the distribution of magnetization in a symmetric periodic sample.

The last conclusion is especially useful for intuition. A random vector can have mean zero while having a fixed nonzero length, if its direction is uniform. The claimed spherical law makes this picture precise in a quantum system without assuming that its noncommuting spin components admit a joint measurement.

2. Background and essential definitions

Spins and equilibrium

At each lattice site put a spin S∈{12,1,32,…}S\in\{\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\ldots\}S∈{21​,1,23​,…}, acting on a space of dimension 2S+12S+12S+1. Its three self-adjoint components obey

[Sa,Sb]=i∑cϵabcSc,∑a(Sa)2=S(S+1)I.[S^a,S^b]=i\sum_c\epsilon_{abc}S^c,\qquad \sum_a(S^a)^2=S(S+1)I.[Sa,Sb]=ic∑​ϵabc​Sc,a∑​(Sa)2=S(S+1)I.

The symbol [A,B]=AB−BA[A,B]=AB-BA[A,B]=AB−BA is the commutator; ϵabc\epsilon_{abc}ϵabc​ encodes the signs of cyclic permutations. Thus spin is a quantum vector whose components generally cannot be measured simultaneously.

For the nearest-neighbor model in a finite box Λ⊂Zd\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^dΛ⊂Zd, the energy is

HΛ=−∑{x,y}Sx⋅Sy,MΛz=∑x∈ΛSxz.H_\Lambda=-\sum_{\{x,y\}}\mathbf S_x\cdot\mathbf S_y,\qquad M_\Lambda^z=\sum_{x\in\Lambda}S_x^z.HΛ​=−{x,y}∑​Sx​⋅Sy​,MΛz​=x∈Λ∑​Sxz​.

The sum counts each unordered nearest-neighbor edge once. Its negative sign favors alignment. Lattice spacing, the coupling, Boltzmann’s constant and ℏ\hbarℏ are set to one. Temperature is T=β−1T=\beta^{-1}T=β−1, where β\betaβ is inverse temperature.

A field hhh adds −hMΛz-hM_\Lambda^z−hMΛz​. The thermodynamic pressure and spontaneous magnetization are

pβ(h)=lim⁡Λ↑Zdlog⁡Tr⁡e−β(HΛ−hMΛz)β∣Λ∣,mS(β)=pβ′(0+).p_\beta(h)=\lim_{\Lambda\uparrow\mathbb Z^d}\frac{\log\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta(H_\Lambda-hM_\Lambda^z)}}{\beta|\Lambda|},\qquad m_S(\beta)=p_\beta'(0+).pβ​(h)=Λ↑Zdlim​β∣Λ∣logTre−β(HΛ​−hMΛz​)​,mS​(β)=pβ′​(0+).

The volume tends to infinity before the field tends to zero from above. Reversing this order would retain the zero mean of a symmetric finite-volume state. Convexity of pressure guarantees the right derivative.

An infinite-volume state assigns consistent expectations to every local observable. The KMS condition is the equilibrium condition expressed through analytic continuation of time correlations to imaginary time iβi\betaiβ; it generalizes the finite Gibbs formula. Translation invariance says expectations do not depend on where an observable is placed.

Magnons and dispersion

A magnon is a spin-wave excitation that reduces magnetization by one unit. For the three-dimensional unit-coupling nearest-neighbor model its one-particle energy is

εS(k)=2S∑j=13(1−cos⁡kj),k∈[−π,π]3.\varepsilon_S(k)=2S\sum_{j=1}^{3}(1-\cos k_j),\qquad k\in[-\pi,\pi]^3.εS​(k)=2Sj=1∑3​(1−coskj​),k∈[−π,π]3.

Near zero momentum it is S∣k∣2+O(∣k∣4)S|k|^2+O(|k|^4)S∣k∣2+O(∣k∣4). Treating magnons as independent bosons gives their density

nSsw(β)=∫[−π,π]3d3k(2π)3(eβεS(k)−1).n_S^{\mathrm{sw}}(\beta)=\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^3}\frac{d^3k}{(2\pi)^3(e^{\beta\varepsilon_S(k)}-1)}.nSsw​(β)=∫[−π,π]3​(2π)3(eβεS​(k)−1)d3k​.

Rescaling small momenta by βS\sqrt{\beta S}βS​ suggests a T3/2T^{3/2}T3/2 deficit. The challenge is to justify this independent-particle prediction for the interacting finite-spin system and for its zero-field pressure derivative.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Heisenberg’s exchange model supplied a quantum mechanism for ferromagnetism. Bloch’s 1930 analysis predicted the T3/2T^{3/2}T3/2 reduction using long-wavelength spin waves. Holstein and Primakoff introduced a bosonic representation of spin, and Dyson developed the effects of spin-wave interactions.

The power series contains different mechanisms. Terms of orders T5/2T^{5/2}T5/2 and T7/2T^{7/2}T7/2 already arise from the nonquadratic lattice dispersion of ideal magnons. Dyson’s leading interaction contribution to magnetization is of order T4T^4T4. M2 addresses the first lattice correction, so it should not be described as establishing that interaction term.

Rigorous ordering results also distinguish models. The Mermin–Wagner theorem excludes positive-temperature spontaneous order for finite-range isotropic Heisenberg systems in dimensions one and two. Infrared bounds established ordering for classical continuous spins and important quantum antiferromagnets in higher dimensions. Those theorems did not directly settle the corresponding nearest-neighbor quantum ferromagnet.

Probabilistic representations developed by Powers, Conlon–Solovej, Tóth and Nachtergaele converted quantum spins into permutations, walks and exchange cycles. They yielded pressure and free-energy bounds. Correggi, Giuliani and Seiringer established the leading low-temperature free-energy asymptotic in three dimensions at every fixed spin. This was a major partial result, but a zero-field free-energy estimate alone does not control the field derivative defining spontaneous magnetization.

The spherical distribution had antecedents too. Ueltschi derived its transform conditionally from a proposed law for macroscopic loop lengths. Björnberg, Fröhlich and Ueltschi proved it for the complete-graph quantum Heisenberg model. M3 concerns the three-dimensional nearest-neighbor lattice and does not assume a macroscopic-loop length distribution.

Within this family, M4 supplies the ordering and finite pin estimates; M1 develops the leading magnetization asymptotic; M2 sharpens its precision; M3 adds spatial and pressure arguments for the symmetric zero-field law. Their conclusions and hypotheses differ despite this shared foundation.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Existence at a fixed positive temperature

M4 states that for every d≥3d\geq3d≥3 and fixed allowed spin SSS, there is a finite β0(d,S)\beta_0(d,S)β0​(d,S) such that every finite β≥β0(d,S)\beta\geq\beta_0(d,S)β≥β0​(d,S) admits a translation-invariant zero-field KMS state ω\omegaω with

ω(S0z)≥S/4.\omega(S_0^z)\geq S/4.ω(S0z​)≥S/4.

This is a statement about a selected ordered infinite-volume state. Averaging it over rotations may erase its mean. M4 also gives a spin-one-half consequence for the particle–hole-symmetric attractive hard-core hopping model: a rotated state has density one half and averaged off-diagonal long-range order. Its uniform-mode occupation is at least 1/321/321/32 of the expected particle number in every finite restriction of that state. This is not a claim about finite-volume Gibbs states of that boson model.

Bloch’s law with spatially anisotropic couplings

M1 works in Z3\mathbb Z^3Z3 with a fixed finite-support interaction J(z)≥0J(z)\geq0J(z)≥0, satisfying J(0)=0J(0)=0J(0)=0, J(z)=J(−z)J(z)=J(-z)J(z)=J(−z), whose positive support generates the whole lattice as an additive group. The Hamiltonian is −12∑x,yJ(y−x)Sx⋅Sy-\tfrac12\sum_{x,y}J(y-x)\mathbf S_x\cdot\mathbf S_y−21​∑x,y​J(y−x)Sx​⋅Sy​.

Define the positive definite matrix

DS,J=S2∑zJ(z)zzT.D_{S,J}=\frac S2\sum_z J(z)zz^{\mathsf T}.DS,J​=2S​z∑​J(z)zzT.

It is the quadratic coefficient of the magnon dispersion. M1 claims

lim⁡β→∞β3/2[S−mS,J(β)]=ζ(3/2)8π3/2det⁡DS,J.\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\beta^{3/2}[S-m_{S,J}(\beta)]=\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{8\pi^{3/2}\sqrt{\det D_{S,J}}}.β→∞lim​β3/2[S−mS,J​(β)]=8π3/2detDS,J​​ζ(3/2)​.

Here ζ(s)=∑n≥1n−s\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\geq1}n^{-s}ζ(s)=∑n≥1​n−s. Spin and interaction remain fixed. The order is volume first, positive field removal second, temperature tending to zero last. For unit nearest-neighbor couplings, DS,J=SID_{S,J}=SIDS,J​=SI.

The first lattice correction

For the three-dimensional nearest-neighbor model, M2 claims that the deficit differs from the full ideal-magnon density by o((βS)−5/2)o((\beta S)^{-5/2})o((βS)−5/2). Equivalently,

S−mS(β)=ζ(3/2)8π3/2(βS)−3/2+3ζ(5/2)128π3/2(βS)−5/2+o((βS)−5/2).\begin{aligned}S-m_S(\beta)={}&\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{8\pi^{3/2}}(\beta S)^{-3/2}\\&+\frac{3\zeta(5/2)}{128\pi^{3/2}}(\beta S)^{-5/2}+o((\beta S)^{-5/2}).\end{aligned}S−mS​(β)=​8π3/2ζ(3/2)​(βS)−3/2+128π3/23ζ(5/2)​(βS)−5/2+o((βS)−5/2).​

The little-ooo error becomes negligible after division by (βS)−5/2(\beta S)^{-5/2}(βS)−5/2. The assertion is for every fixed spin, rather than a simultaneous large-spin limit.

A sphere of magnetization directions

M3 fixes sufficiently low but positive temperature in the three-dimensional nearest-neighbor model and takes even periodic cubes of side LLL, volume V=L3V=L^3V=L3. Writing ML\mathbf M_LML​ for total spin and m=pβ′(0+)>0m=p_\beta'(0+)>0m=pβ′​(0+)>0, it claims

lim⁡L→∞, L even⟨et⋅ML/V⟩β,L=sinh⁡(m∣t∣)m∣t∣(t∈R3).\lim_{L\to\infty,\ L\ \mathrm{even}}\left\langle e^{\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf M_L/V}\right\rangle_{\beta,L}=\frac{\sinh(m|\mathbf t|)}{m|\mathbf t|}\qquad(\mathbf t\in\mathbb R^3).L→∞, L evenlim​⟨et⋅ML​/V⟩β,L​=m∣t∣sinh(m∣t∣)​(t∈R3).

The value at t=0\mathbf t=0t=0 is one. The right side is the transform of mnm\mathbf nmn, with n\mathbf nn uniform on the unit sphere. In addition, the volume-averaged two-point correlation converges to m2m^2m2. The formula uses each self-adjoint linear combination separately; it does not posit a joint finite-volume measurement of all three components.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. These claims address the central ordering problem for the quantum ferromagnet and quantify both the size and distribution of its magnetization. They connect a fixed-temperature equilibrium state, a low-temperature expansion and a symmetric finite-volume observable.

Each stage answers something the previous one leaves unresolved. Nonzero order does not determine its exact thermal reduction. Bloch’s leading coefficient does not determine the first lattice correction. Rotation symmetry does not force a single magnetization radius: it could permit a mixture of several radii. The spherical law excludes that latter possibility in its stated setting.

The general finite-range coefficient also explains how spatial anisotropy enters through det⁡DS,J\det D_{S,J}detDS,J​. Spin-rotation symmetry is retained even when bonds differ by spatial direction. This distinction helps separate physical anisotropies that are often grouped together informally.

6. The main idea

Turn spin information into return probabilities

Represent a spin SSS by 2S2S2S spin-one-half slots, projected onto their symmetric subspace. Random exchanges between slots trace cycles around an imaginary-time circle of circumference β\betaβ. Each cycle receives an up or down color. A pin requires a cycle passing through a chosen point to be up.

M4 estimates how often interior cycles avoid boundary pins. Adding pins creates an induction: information under a more constrained law controls a less constrained one. After exposing certain cycles, a one-particle walk moves through the available slots. Diffusive estimates and finite-energy flows around obstacles bound its returns. A boundary pinning cost of surface order then permits selection of a magnetized equilibrium state by a field tending to zero.

Recover the coefficient and its correction

For M1, the ideal walk’s return probability behaves as (4πt)−3/2/det⁡DS,J(4\pi t)^{-3/2}/\sqrt{\det D_{S,J}}(4πt)−3/2/detDS,J​​. Returns after one, two and more time periods generate the sum ∑n−3/2\sum n^{-3/2}∑n−3/2, explaining the zeta factor. The argument must control late returns in the same repeatedly encountered environment, rather than silently replacing each period with an independent environment.

M2 needs greater accuracy. An obstacle both removes possible transitions and transports the remaining walk when it moves. Keeping these signed effects together produces a cancellation governed by obstacle displacement. A capacity comparison with a free trial potential retains the full Bose sum and pushes the error below the first lattice correction. Expanding the lattice heat kernel then supplies its coefficient.

Establish one radius

M3 combines spatial control across many scales with a pressure argument. The spatial estimates prevent local magnetizations from canceling through increasingly large patterns. The pressure analysis excludes translation-ergodic equilibrium states with different magnetization lengths, using zero-free traces and auxiliary replicated systems.

Finally, rotation representation theory converts concentration of the total-spin magnitude into the spherical transform. The randomness of direction survives; randomness of the macroscopic radius disappears. This extra argument is why the symmetric distribution is more than a consequence of merely constructing one ordered state.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The four settings should remain distinct. M4 covers nearest neighbors in every dimension at least three. M1 permits general nonnegative finite-range couplings in three dimensions. M2 and M3 concern the three-dimensional nearest-neighbor model, with M3 taking even periodic cubes at fixed positive temperature.

The results do not identify a critical temperature, classify all equilibrium states, or establish Dyson’s T4T^4T4 interaction coefficient. The low-temperature expansion is not asserted uniformly as spin or the interaction changes. The spherical law is a thermodynamic moment statement, not a claim that the finite quantum components commute.

Quantitative temperature thresholds, further expansion terms and extensions of the spherical law to other interactions remain natural questions beyond the claims presented here.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical links in section 3 give Bloch’s prediction, Dyson’s expansion, rigorous fixed-spin free-energy progress and the complete-graph spherical-law predecessor. The four source manuscripts below specify the respective limits, normalizations and companion dependencies. Mathematical claims are reported as stated.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Bloch’s Law for Finite-Range Heisenberg Ferromagnets in Three Dimensions (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The first lattice correction to Bloch’s law (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The spherical magnetization law for the three-dimensional quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet (October 5, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Spontaneous magnetization in the quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Entanglement without a secret key
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 272 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Entanglement is a resource, but a resource for which task? Two laboratories may share a state that cannot be prepared by mixing independent local states. That fact alone does not immediately tell them how to produce identical random bits hidden from an eavesdropper.

Secret-key distillation asks whether many copies of a noisy shared state can be converted into such private bits using local quantum operations and public discussion. Public messages may coordinate the laboratories, but the eavesdropper hears them too. The central question is whether every entangled state contains some recoverable secrecy.

Family 272 reports a negative answer under its specified local-instrument protocol model. It constructs an entangled state on two ten-dimensional systems and claims that no number of copies can even approximate one ideal secret bit beyond a fixed error threshold. The same construction also yields counterexamples to conjectures about composing quantum maps that preserve positivity after partial transposition.

These conclusions distinguish three tasks: possessing entanglement, distilling pure entangled pairs, and distilling classical secret key. Earlier work separated the second from the third. This manuscript claims a separation between the first and the third.

2. Background and essential definitions

States, entanglement and Eve

A quantum state is a positive semidefinite matrix ρ\rhoρ of trace one. For laboratories AAA and BBB, it acts on a tensor product HA⊗HB\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal H_BHA​⊗HB​. It is separable if it can be written

ρ=∑jpjρA(j)⊗ρB(j),pj≥0,∑jpj=1.\rho=\sum_j p_j\rho_A^{(j)}\otimes\rho_B^{(j)},\qquad p_j\geq0,\quad\sum_jp_j=1.ρ=j∑​pj​ρA(j)​⊗ρB(j)​,pj​≥0,j∑​pj​=1.

Otherwise it is entangled. A product vector is a vector a⊗ba\otimes ba⊗b. Every nonzero separable positive matrix has at least one nonzero product vector in its range, a useful geometric obstruction to separability.

A purification of ρAB\rho_{AB}ρAB​ is a pure state on a larger system ABEABEABE whose partial trace over EEE equals ρAB\rho_{AB}ρAB​. Giving Eve the purifying system models all information compatible with the input state, rather than assuming that its apparent randomness is private.

An ideal shared secret bit has joint state

γKAKBE′=12∑i=01∣i,i⟩⟨i,i∣⊗σE′.\gamma_{K_AK_BE'}=\frac12\sum_{i=0}^{1}|i,i\rangle\langle i,i|\otimes\sigma_{E'}.γKA​KB​E′​=21​i=0∑1​∣i,i⟩⟨i,i∣⊗σE′​.

The registers KA,KBK_A,K_BKA​,KB​ agree, each bit is uniform, and Eve’s state σE′\sigma_{E'}σE′​ does not depend on the bit. The enlarged register E′E'E′ includes her initial purification and the entire public transcript.

The trace norm is ∥X∥1=Tr⁡X∗X\|X\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^*X}∥X∥1​=TrX∗X​. The conventional trace distance between states is half the trace norm of their difference. This factor of two matters for the manuscript’s numerical bound.

Positive maps and channels

A linear map F:Ma(C)→Mb(C)F:M_a(\mathbb C)\to M_b(\mathbb C)F:Ma​(C)→Mb​(C) is completely positive, or CP, if id⁡k⊗F\operatorname{id}_k\otimes Fidk​⊗F preserves positive matrices for every ancillary dimension kkk. A trace-preserving CP map is a quantum channel.

Coordinate transposition is denoted TTT. A CP map is called PPT here when T∘FT\circ FT∘F is also CP. Equivalently, its Choi matrix

J(F)=∑i,j=1a∣i⟩⟨j∣⊗F(∣i⟩⟨j∣)J(F)=\sum_{i,j=1}^{a}|i\rangle\langle j|\otimes F(|i\rangle\langle j|)J(F)=i,j=1∑a​∣i⟩⟨j∣⊗F(∣i⟩⟨j∣)

is positive and remains positive after transposition of one tensor factor. A map is entanglement breaking if applying it to part of any bipartite positive input always produces a separable output. This is equivalent to separability of J(F)J(F)J(F), and makes sense even without trace preservation.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Classical key agreement established how public discussion and privacy amplification can turn suitable correlated data into secrecy. Entanglement purification then provided a quantum route: nearly pure shared entangled pairs are nearly independent of a purifying adversary.

The discovery of bound entanglement showed that some entangled states cannot yield pure entangled pairs by local operations and classical communication. In particular, positive-partial-transpose entangled states have zero distillable entanglement. But Horodecki, Horodecki, Horodecki and Oppenheim showed that some such states still yield secret key. Their private-state framework explains how auxiliary quantum systems can shield a classical secret even when singlet distillation is impossible.

The remaining converse was harder: could an entangled state have no distillable key at all? The manuscript traces the explicit question to the 2005 “Secret key from all entangled states” entry in Krüger and Werner’s problem collection. Earlier distance bounds between PPT states and private bits depended on the size of an auxiliary shield. A protocol can enlarge that shield as more copies become available, so those bounds did not give the copy-independent obstruction claimed here.

A related classical development is Pauwels, Gisin and Renner’s Bipartite Bound Information Exists, cited by the manuscript in its September 2026 revision. It separates classical secrecy formation cost from asymptotic secret-key rate. The quantum input and purifying adversary in the present family are different. The same cited revision also obtains positive quantum key for a particular two-qutrit family, so those states are not the zero-key example used here.

On the map side, the PPT-composition conjecture asked whether composing two PPT maps must destroy entanglement. Christandl, Müller-Hermes and Wolf proved affirmative cases, including dimension three and Gaussian channels, and developed equivalent formulations. Results on eventual entanglement breaking under repeated iteration addressed another timescale. Failure at the second iterate is compatible with eventual loss after a map-dependent number of iterations.

4. What the new manuscript claims

An entangled state with a uniform secrecy obstruction

The manuscript specifies a density operator ρ\rhoρ on C10⊗C10\mathbb C^{10}\otimes\mathbb C^{10}C10⊗C10 whose range contains no nonzero product vector. It claims that every admitted completed bit-output protocol on every ρ⊗n\rho^{\otimes n}ρ⊗n, n≥1n\geq1n≥1, obeys

∥τKAKBE′−12∑i=01∣i,i⟩⟨i,i∣⊗σE′∥1≥15\left\|\tau_{K_AK_BE'}-\frac12\sum_{i=0}^{1}|i,i\rangle\langle i,i|\otimes\sigma_{E'}\right\|_1\geq\frac15​τKA​KB​E′​−21​i=0∑1​∣i,i⟩⟨i,i∣⊗σE′​​1​≥51​

for every state σE′\sigma_{E'}σE′​. In conventional trace distance, the lower bound is 1/101/101/10. Thus the error cannot approach zero even for one bit; in particular the distillable key rate KD(ρ)K_D(\rho)KD​(ρ) is zero.

The protocol permits joint processing of all copies within each laboratory, local auxiliary systems and private randomness, and unlimited two-way authenticated public communication. The supplied input is the only shared private resource. Any initial shared randomness is public, independent of input and reference, and recorded for Eve. Conditional on it, the two private auxiliary resources are independent of each other and of the input-reference state.

Definition 4.1 allows ordinary finite protocols with finite records, with the number of rounds growing with input length, as well as specified countable processes. Its measurable histories, local readouts and any aggregated subroutines must define compatible quantum operations on arbitrary inputs with untouched finite references. A completed protocol produces the required outputs almost surely with normalized joint output. Eve retains messages, speaker choices and stopping information. These conditions are part of the theorem’s scope, not optional technical decoration.

The manuscript separately extends the bound to conditioning on any positive-probability event in the complete public transcript. It also excludes approaching an ideal accepted bit with vanishing abort probability, and treats trace-norm limits of outputs when Eve’s full purification and transcript remain recoverable.

Two map counterexamples with different dimensions

The ten-dimensional construction gives PPT maps Φ1,Φ2:M10(C)→M10(C)\Phi_1,\Phi_2:M_{10}(\mathbb C)\to M_{10}(\mathbb C)Φ1​,Φ2​:M10​(C)→M10​(C) such that

Z=J(Φ2∘Φ1)≠0,ρ=Z/Tr⁡Z.Z=J(\Phi_2\circ\Phi_1)\ne0,\qquad \rho=Z/\operatorname{Tr}Z.Z=J(Φ2​∘Φ1​)=0,ρ=Z/TrZ.

The range of ZZZ contains no nonzero product vector, so the composition is not entanglement breaking. The two maps may differ and are not required to preserve trace or the identity.

A separate construction produces a trace-preserving PPT channel Θ:M21(C)→M21(C)\Theta:M_{21}(\mathbb C)\to M_{21}(\mathbb C)Θ:M21​(C)→M21​(C) whose square Θ∘Θ\Theta\circ\ThetaΘ∘Θ is not entanglement breaking. This second example uses the same channel twice. Neither dimension is claimed to be minimal.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. A finite-dimensional entangled state with zero distillable key would answer a central resource question in quantum information. The uniform one-bit obstruction is stronger than merely showing a vanishing asymptotic rate: it prevents an increasingly accurate isolated secret bit from arbitrarily many copies in the stated protocol model.

The accompanying map examples challenge the proposed two-step boundary between PPT noise and complete destruction of entanglement. Together, the results connect an operational impossibility statement to the geometry of positive matrices and quantum maps.

The implication is not that entanglement is useless. It is that usefulness depends on the task and available operations. A state can fail at private-key extraction while retaining mathematical and potentially operational properties absent from separable states. The score measures the significance of the reported claims if correct, without independently verifying them.

6. The main idea

A class closed under taking copies

The operational argument begins with states obtained by applying a PPT map locally on each side of a pure bipartite input. This represented class remains closed under tensor powers. A Choi composition identity places the normalized matrix ZZZ in that class.

The manuscript analyzes a complete public transcript and the four possible final bit pairs. It obtains common positive product factors for their local effects. Auxiliary product inputs and untouched references are used to identify those factors without assuming independence of the actual entangled input. This is why reference compatibility and retention of the full public record enter the protocol definition.

Let eee be the probability that the laboratories’ bits disagree. Let fff measure overlap between Eve’s unnormalized states for the two agreeing outcomes, summed over the transcript. The manuscript derives

f≤e(1−e)+e.f\leq\sqrt{e(1-e)}+e.f≤e(1−e)​+e.

A nearly ideal bit requires both small disagreement and substantial overlap of Eve’s conditional states: she should not distinguish the two values. If the unhalved trace-norm error is η\etaη, the reported bounds give e≤η/2e\leq\eta/2e≤η/2 and f≥(1−η)/2f\geq(1-\eta)/2f≥(1−η)/2. These conditions are incompatible for η<1/5\eta<1/5η<1/5. Taking the first bit of a longer key cannot increase trace distance, transferring the obstruction to key rates.

Make a state in that class entangled

The construction starts from a PPT map on four-dimensional matrices and twenty special projective directions. Its algebraic arrangement ensures that no nonzero homogeneous quadratic in four variables vanishes at ten of those directions.

The ten-dimensional symmetric square stores quadratic monomials. If the resulting Choi range contained a product vector, its factors would define two nonzero quadratics whose zero sets together cover all twenty directions. Each could cover at most nine, giving the contradiction 9+9<209+9<209+9<20.

The manuscript supplies integer data and exact arithmetic certificates for this arrangement. Their role is to specify and support the construction; no certificate execution is needed to understand the geometric mechanism. A separate larger construction uses projective measurements and restricted intersections to obtain entanglement under two PPT maps through a different argument.
