Finally, to obtain a channel, two ten-dimensional coordinate blocks alternate the original maps and an additional one-dimensional flag receives missing trace. The resulting dimension is 10+10+1=2110+10+1=2110+10+1=21. A local corner of the square’s Choi matrix retains a positive multiple of ZZZ; separability of the whole matrix would force that corner to be separable too.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The secrecy statement is tied to the stated resource rules and admitted local-instrument processes. It includes broad finite two-way protocols and specified countable extensions, but should not be paraphrased as covering an unspecified larger model. Presupplying shared secret key or hiding part of the public transcript changes the problem.

The maps in dimension ten are not channels merely because their normalized Choi matrix is a state. Trace preservation is supplied by the distinct dimension-21 construction. The result also does not say that every PPT entangled state has zero key; earlier positive-key examples remain part of the picture.

Minimal dimensions, further characterizations of zero-key entanglement, and behavior under other resource combinations remain questions beyond these claims. Failure of a channel’s second iterate to break entanglement does not exclude entanglement breaking at later iterates.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked private-key and PPT-composition papers explain the principal historical questions. The source manuscript below provides the state, exact map conventions, arithmetic data and Definition 4.1 of the protocol model. Its mathematical and operational claims are reported as stated.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Entanglement with zero distillable secret key in local dimension ten (September 27, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How much uncertainty survives when two quantum light beams mix?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 273 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Mix two independent light beams on a beam splitter and keep one output. How uncertain must that output be, given the uncertainties of the inputs? The answer cannot depend only on their average brightness: highly ordered and highly disordered quantum states can carry the same mean number of photons.

A natural comparison uses thermal light. For each input, find a thermal state with the same entropy, then ask whether mixing these thermal references gives the least possible output entropy. This is the entropy photon-number conjecture.

Family 273 reports the inequality for every finite number of modes and finite mean input energy. The two incoming groups must be independent, but the modes inside either group may be arbitrarily entangled. The manuscript then derives an exact constrained output-entropy minimum for identical thermal attenuators and the classical capacity region of a degraded two-receiver pure-loss broadcast channel.

2. Background and essential definitions

Entropy expressed as a photon number

A bosonic mode is a quantum harmonic oscillator with number states ∣0⟩,∣1⟩,…|0\rangle,|1\rangle,\ldots∣0⟩,∣1⟩,…. The annihilation operator aaa removes a photon, and a†aa^\dagger aa†a counts photons. An nnn-mode state ρ\rhoρ has finite mean energy in the manuscript’s sense when

Tr⁡ρ∑j=1naj†aj<∞.\operatorname{Tr}\rho\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j^\dagger a_j<\infty.Trρj=1∑n​aj†​aj​<∞.

Its von Neumann entropy is S(ρ)=−Tr⁡ρlog⁡ρS(\rho)=-\operatorname{Tr}\rho\log\rhoS(ρ)=−Trρlogρ. All logarithms here are natural, so information is measured in nats. Divide by log⁡2\log2log2 to convert nats to bits.

A one-mode thermal state with mean photon number r≥0r\geq0r≥0 has geometric number probabilities and entropy

g(r)=(r+1)log⁡(r+1)−rlog⁡r,g(0)=0.g(r)=(r+1)\log(r+1)-r\log r,\qquad g(0)=0.g(r)=(r+1)log(r+1)−rlogr,g(0)=0.

This function increases continuously from zero to infinity, so its inverse g−1g^{-1}g−1 exists. For an arbitrary nnn-mode state define its entropy photon number by

Nent(ρ)=g−1(S(ρ)/n).N_{\mathrm{ent}}(\rho)=g^{-1}(S(\rho)/n).Nent​(ρ)=g−1(S(ρ)/n).

This is the mean photon number per mode of a product of identical thermal states with the same total entropy. It is generally not the actual mean photon number of ρ\rhoρ. A pure coherent state, for example, has zero entropy even when it carries nonzero energy.

A beam splitter as a quantum sum

Let aja_jaj​ and bjb_jbj​ describe corresponding modes at two independent input ports. A passive beam splitter retains modes

cj=η aj+1−η bj,0≤η≤1.c_j=\sqrt\eta\,a_j+\sqrt{1-\eta}\,b_j,\qquad 0\leq\eta\leq1.cj​=η​aj​+1−η​bj​,0≤η≤1.

The other output is discarded. “Passive” means the full mixing preserves total photon number; η\etaη is the power transmissivity. The joint input is ρA⊗ρB\rho_A\otimes\rho_BρA​⊗ρB​, while ρA\rho_AρA​ or ρB\rho_BρB​ need not factor across their own modes.

If each input is a product of identical thermal states, with means rA,rBr_A,r_BrA​,rB​, the retained output is thermal with mean ηrA+(1−η)rB\eta r_A+(1-\eta)r_BηrA​+(1−η)rB​. This exact formula motivates a sharp entropy inequality for general states.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The classical entropy power inequality begins with Shannon’s communication theory and was developed through Fisher-information arguments by Stam and Blachman. It bounds the entropy of a sum of independent random vectors. Beam-splitter mixing is a quantum counterpart of addition, but the appropriate thermal entropy function changes the sharp comparison.

Guha, Erkmen and Shapiro formulated the entropy photon-number inequality and explained how it would imply minimum-output-entropy statements relevant to optical communication. The capacity of a single pure-loss bosonic channel had already been determined; noisy and broadcast settings raised sharper constrained entropy questions.

König and Smith established quantum entropy power bounds using Fisher information and heat evolution. De Palma, Mari and Giovannetti obtained the exponential form for every transmissivity,

eS(ρC)/n≥ηeS(ρA)/n+(1−η)eS(ρB)/n.e^{S(\rho_C)/n}\geq\eta e^{S(\rho_A)/n}+(1-\eta)e^{S(\rho_B)/n}.eS(ρC​)/n≥ηeS(ρA​)/n+(1−η)eS(ρB​)/n.

Subsequent work treated more general mixing and gave rigorous finite-energy heat-flow formulations. These were multimode results permitting entanglement within each independent input group.

The desired photon-number inequality is sharper when input entropies differ. Thermal inputs of unequal entropy attain its proposed bound, whereas the exponential inequality does not reproduce their exact output entropy. At equal input entropies, the already known linear entropy bound gives the required photon-number comparison. The full inequality was also known for independent Gaussian inputs, including Gaussian correlations among their modes.

Minimum-output optimization had additional successes. Giovannetti, Holevo and García-Patrón settled broad unconstrained Gaussian optimizer questions. Fixing a positive input entropy imposes a different constraint. De Palma, Trevisan and Giovannetti proved thermal optimality for one-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels. Multimode progress covered inputs diagonal in a product basis and, in further work of De Palma, entanglement-breaking parameter regimes. Beigi and Rahimi-Keshari provided another one-mode variational route.

The new manuscript claims the two-input comparison without Gaussian, diagonal, product-across-modes or separability restrictions within either port. This is the enlargement that drives its channel consequences.

4. What the new manuscript claims

The two-input inequality

For every finite n≥1n\geq1n≥1, independent finite-energy inputs ρA,ρB\rho_A,\rho_BρA​,ρB​, and 0≤η≤10\leq\eta\leq10≤η≤1, the retained state ρC\rho_CρC​ is claimed to satisfy

g−1 ⁣(S(ρC)n)≥ηg−1 ⁣(S(ρA)n)+(1−η)g−1 ⁣(S(ρB)n).g^{-1}\!\left(\frac{S(\rho_C)}n\right)\geq\eta g^{-1}\!\left(\frac{S(\rho_A)}n\right)+(1-\eta)g^{-1}\!\left(\frac{S(\rho_B)}n\right).g−1(nS(ρC​)​)≥ηg−1(nS(ρA​)​)+(1−η)g−1(nS(ρB​)​).

Thermal products with a common mean within each port attain equality, including unequal means between the ports. The statement gives these equality examples, not a complete classification of every possible equality case.

The finite-energy assumption ensures the entropies are finite and supports the infinite-dimensional limiting arguments. A finite number of modes does not mean a finite-dimensional Hilbert space: each oscillator can contain arbitrarily many photons.

An exact constrained minimum

A thermal attenuator Eη,NB\mathcal E_{\eta,N_B}Eη,NB​​ mixes one input mode with an independent thermal environment of mean NBN_BNB​. Its nnn-fold tensor power uses identical parameters and a product thermal environment. For finite s,NB≥0s,N_B\geq0s,NB​≥0, the manuscript obtains

min⁡ρ finite energyS(ρ)=ns1nS ⁣(Eη,NB⊗n(ρ))=g ⁣(ηg−1(s)+(1−η)NB).\min_{\substack{\rho\ \mathrm{finite\ energy}\\S(\rho)=ns}}\frac1nS\!\left(\mathcal E_{\eta,N_B}^{\otimes n}(\rho)\right)=g\!\left(\eta g^{-1}(s)+(1-\eta)N_B\right).ρ finite energyS(ρ)=ns​min​n1​S(Eη,NB​⊗n​(ρ))=g(ηg−1(s)+(1−η)NB​).

The input may be entangled across all nnn modes. A product thermal input of mean g−1(s)g^{-1}(s)g−1(s) attains the minimum. This is attainment, not uniqueness. Vacuum cases and η=0,1\eta=0,1η=0,1 are included.

Broadcasting to two receivers

One input mode per use is split with independent vacuum auxiliary modes into outputs for receivers B,CB,CB,C and an inaccessible loss output. Assume

0≤ηC<ηB,ηB+ηC≤1.0\leq\eta_C<\eta_B,\qquad \eta_B+\eta_C\leq1.0≤ηC​<ηB​,ηB​+ηC​≤1.

The weaker receiver’s marginal can be obtained by further attenuating the stronger one’s, which is the meaning of “degraded.” It does not say the physical output systems are independent.

The sender transmits two independent classical messages. Each receiver may collectively measure its own outputs over many uses, with vanishing average decoding error. There is no feedback or receiver cooperation. Codewords have finite energy and may be entangled across uses. The mean photon budget Nˉ\bar NNˉ is averaged over the full codebook and all uses, not imposed separately on every codeword.

The claimed capacity region is the closed convex hull of nonnegative pairs obeying, for some 0≤α≤10\leq\alpha\leq10≤α≤1,

RB≤g(ηBαNˉ),RC≤g(ηCNˉ)−g(ηCαNˉ).\begin{aligned}R_B&\leq g(\eta_B\alpha\bar N),\\R_C&\leq g(\eta_C\bar N)-g(\eta_C\alpha\bar N).\end{aligned}RB​RC​​≤g(ηB​αNˉ),≤g(ηC​Nˉ)−g(ηC​αNˉ).​

Rates are in nats per use. The parameter α\alphaα divides the coding resource between the two messages; taking the convex hull allows time sharing between choices. If the weaker output is vacuum, its rate is zero and the formula reduces to the known single-receiver expression.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The inequality is a central proposed sharp relation between entropy and passive quantum mixing. Its importance includes both the unrestricted multimode input structure and exact communication consequences.

Entanglement across channel uses often prevents a one-use optimization from settling a capacity question. Here the claimed entropy minimum already permits arbitrary finite-block entanglement. For the specified identical thermal attenuators, such correlations cannot lower the constrained output entropy below the thermal benchmark.

The broadcast consequence also gives an operational meaning to the inequality’s sharpness. A bound that misses the thermal output for unequal entropies may leave a gap between achievable rates and a converse. The photon-number form supplies the exact comparison needed to close that gap in the stated degraded pure-loss setting.

The rating concerns mathematical significance if the manuscript’s claims hold; it does not represent independent proof verification.

6. The main idea

Turn a violation into an optimization problem

The manuscript argues by contradiction. Suppose two inputs strictly violate the proposed inequality. Their entropy levels determine thermal reference parameters, which are then held fixed. This converts the violation into a negative value of a functional involving the two input entropies and the output entropy.

Working directly with that functional is delicate. Entropy derivatives can be singular, the Hilbert spaces are infinite dimensional, and creation or annihilation operators are unbounded. The proof therefore adds several regularizations: an auxiliary thermal port, a small thermal replacement at the output, a relative-entropy penalty and a fourth-moment penalty.

These additions serve different purposes. They control energy, make minimizers sufficiently regular, bound output logarithms and justify the traces used later. The argument does not simply assume that entropy can be differentiated along an arbitrary unbounded evolution.

Use curvature adapted to thermal relaxation

At a regularized minimizer, varying one input at a time gives a comparison involving the entropy Hessian, its second-order response. This yields a contraction in a logarithmic-mean metric at those minimizers. The manuscript does not assert that this particular contraction holds universally for every channel and every state.

An independent interpolation theorem combines four comparisons between positive quadratic forms. Its conclusion controls a centered thermal-balance defect: a quantity measuring how creation and annihilation fail to balance as they would in a thermal state, after subtracting the state’s mean.

Pairing the stationarity identities with relaxation generators cancels the centered energy terms. As the fourth-moment penalty is removed, the remaining defects and means vanish. Their number-basis identities force the limiting inputs to be thermal. Entropy continuity then contradicts the strictly negative value that started the construction.

The thermal states are thus reference points and forced limiting optimizers, rather than assumptions about the original inputs. The distinction is what allows non-Gaussian and internally entangled states into the theorem.

Convert entropy into communication bounds

The attenuator minimum follows by choosing the second port to be its thermal environment. For broadcasting, choose a vacuum environment and apply the finite-block bound to conditional states at the stronger receiver. Degradation then bounds the weaker receiver’s conditional entropy. Standard information inequalities supply the converse, following the earlier Guha–Shapiro–Erkmen framework; coherent-state superposition coding supplies achievability.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Independence is required between the two input ports. Arbitrary entanglement within either port is allowed, but correlations across the ports change the problem. The theorem is stated for finite mean energy and finitely many modes; it does not automatically extend to infinite-energy states or infinitely many modes.

The constrained minimum concerns identical passive thermal attenuators. It is not asserted here for mode-dependent transmissivities, amplifiers or additive-noise channels. Thermal attainment does not settle uniqueness of optimizers.

The broadcast region uses independent messages, average energy and error constraints, separate receivers and no feedback. Cooperative decoding, other noise models and different constraints require separate analyses. A full equality classification and extensions beyond the stated finite-energy setting are further questions, rather than consequences assumed in this digest.

8. Sources and further reading

The original entropy photon-number proposal explains the thermal comparison. The earlier quantum entropy power inequality and one-mode constrained optimizer theorem supply key partial results. Guha, Shapiro and Erkmen’s broadcast analysis provides the communication framework. The source below supplies the new claims and precise hypotheses.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The entropy photon-number inequality (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why shallow quantum circuits cannot compute parity
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 274 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Given a string of bits, parity asks whether the number of ones is odd or even. Its definition is elementary:

PARITY⁡n(x)=x1⊕⋯⊕xn,\operatorname{PARITY}_n(x)=x_1\oplus\cdots\oplus x_n,PARITYn​(x)=x1​⊕⋯⊕xn​,

where ⊕\oplus⊕ means addition modulo two. Flipping any one input flips the answer. This makes parity a useful test of whether a computation can combine information from every input.

Quantum circuits can use superpositions and interference, so classical circuit lower bounds do not automatically apply. Moreover, the shallow quantum model considered here includes gates acting on arbitrarily many qubits at once. A simple argument that information can reach only a small number of wires therefore fails.

Family 274 contains two manuscripts claiming that these resources still cannot compute parity at constant depth with polynomially many qubits and any fixed positive worst-case advantage over guessing. They allow the inputs to be destroyed and arbitrary unwanted final states to be discarded. Only one measured output bit needs to be correct.

2. Background and essential definitions

The circuit model

A qubit has state space C2\mathbb C^2C2, with basis ∣0⟩,∣1⟩|0\rangle,|1\rangle∣0⟩,∣1⟩. An NNN-qubit system has tensor-product space (C2)⊗N(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}(C2)⊗N. Gates are unitary linear transformations, preserving inner products and total probability.

The allowed gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitaries and generalized Toffoli gates. A Toffoli gate with controls z1,…,ztz_1,\ldots,z_tz1​,…,zt​ and target bbb acts as

∣z1,…,zt,b⟩⟼∣z1,…,zt,b⊕z1z2⋯zt⟩.|z_1,\ldots,z_t,b\rangle\longmapsto|z_1,\ldots,z_t,b\oplus z_1z_2\cdots z_t\rangle.∣z1​,…,zt​,b⟩⟼∣z1​,…,zt​,b⊕z1​z2​⋯zt​⟩.

It flips the target exactly when every control is one. The number of controls is unbounded, and a gate has unit cost regardless of that number.

A parallel layer contains gates with disjoint supports: no qubit belongs to two gates in the same layer. Circuit depth counts sequential layers. There is no geometric restriction on which qubits interact. Ancillary qubits, the extra workspace beyond the input, begin in zero. The circuit starts on ∣x⟩∣0⟩⊗(N−n)|x\rangle|0\rangle^{\otimes(N-n)}∣x⟩∣0⟩⊗(N−n), applies its unitary gates, and measures one designated qubit at the end.

There are no intermediate measurements, postselection or primitive unbounded-fanout gates. The gates may depend arbitrarily on the input length, including their complex matrix entries, but not on the particular input string. Thus this is a nonuniform model with no gate-description computability restriction.

The class QAC0\mathrm{QAC}^0QAC0 uses fixed depth and polynomially many total qubits as nnn grows. Since each disjoint layer has at most NNN nonempty gates, this also bounds the gate count polynomially.

Three output requirements

An exact coherent parity operation maps ∣x,b⟩|x,b\rangle∣x,b⟩ to ∣x,b⊕PARITY⁡(x)⟩|x,b\oplus\operatorname{PARITY}(x)\rangle∣x,b⊕PARITY(x)⟩ on superpositions as well as basis inputs. A clean implementation also restores workspace to zero. A measured-output computation asks only for a correct final classical bit; all other registers may be arbitrary.

The last requirement is weaker. A lower bound for it consequently rules out the stronger tasks too. Worst-case advantage ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 means success probability at least 1/2+ε1/2+\varepsilon1/2+ε on every input. The familiar bounded-error threshold 2/32/32/3 corresponds to ε=1/6\varepsilon=1/6ε=1/6.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Classical AC0\mathrm{AC}^0AC0 allows constant-depth circuits of unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates, with NOT gates and unrestricted wire reuse. Furst, Saxe and Sipser, and independently Ajtai, proved that parity requires superpolynomial size. Yao and Håstad strengthened these bounds, with Håstad’s switching lemma becoming a central tool.

Moore’s 1999 paper formulated quantum analogues and connected parity to fanout. Fanout sends a control bit coherently to many targets by exclusive-or. It is not cloning an arbitrary unknown quantum state; its action is a specified unitary on the computational basis. Conjugating fanout by Hadamard gates exchanges its control-target pattern with coherent parity. Høyer and Špalek subsequently showed how powerful constant-depth circuits become when fanout is supplied as a primitive.

Early lower bounds exposed the importance of workspace. Fang, Fenner, Green, Homer and Zhang obtained logarithmic depth bounds for exact clean parity when the number of ancillas is restricted. Later work ruled out exact clean simulation at entangling depth two, then removed the final-cleanliness requirement there. Entangling depth counts only multiqubit layers, permitting arbitrary one-qubit layers between them; it should not be confused with the total layer convention used in the headline theorem.

Rosenthal studied approximate parity unitaries and related cat-like states, with constant-depth constructions using superpolynomial resources. Pauli-spectrum and low-degree methods of Nadimpalli and collaborators, Anshu–Dong–Ou–Yao, and Dong–Ou–Yao expanded the permitted ancilla counts but retained depth-dependent resource restrictions.

Joshi, Tal, Vasconcelos and Wright established stronger depth-specific results, including exact parity obstructions at entangling depth three and approximate single-output bounds at depth two. The source manuscripts also cite Kintali’s September 2026 preprint for further depth-three correlation and depth-four exact-computation bounds. These precedents do not cover every fixed depth together with every polynomial workspace bound.

Gretta, Gupta and Joshi related the general parity question to Fourier concentration and state preparation. Their work also shows that shallow quantum circuits can approximate majority well on average, an important reason not to infer a sweeping classical-style average-case limitation from a parity lower bound.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The common parity theorem

Both M1 and M2 state that for every fixed depth, fixed polynomial bound on total qubits and fixed 0<ε≤1/20<\varepsilon\leq1/20<ε≤1/2, sufficiently large input lengths admit no allowed circuit with success at least 1/2+ε1/2+\varepsilon1/2+ε on every input.

For example, fix ddd, c≥1c\geq1c≥1 and ε\varepsilonε. Eventually no depth-at-most-ddd circuit on at most ncn^cnc total qubits meets that guarantee. M2 also states the bound with an arbitrary fixed prefactor C(n+1)kC(n+1)^kC(n+1)k. The threshold may depend on all these fixed parameters; finitely many small input lengths are not excluded.

Ancillas start in zero, only one output is measured, the input need not be preserved, and every other final register can be discarded. The manuscripts therefore report a resolution of Moore’s parity conjecture in this more permissive measured-output model. Hadamard conjugation also excludes a constant-depth polynomial-resource coherent fanout implementation.

A structural localization theorem

M1 proves a stronger operator statement in an enlarged model of product-state reflections. Choose reference vectors viv_ivi​ on some qubits and count mismatches with

M=∑i∈S(I−∣vi⟩⟨vi∣)i.M=\sum_{i\in S}(I-|v_i\rangle\langle v_i|)_i.M=i∈S∑​(I−∣vi​⟩⟨vi​∣)i​.

Its integer eigenvalue counts how many selected factors differ from their references. Brackets such as [M=0][M=0][M=0] and [M≥r][M\geq r][M≥r] denote projections onto the indicated eigenspaces.

For a product projection AAA, a fixed-depth circuit UUU and fixed exponents 0≤s<t0\leq s<t0≤s<t, M1 claims, for sufficiently large total size NNN,

∥[M≥Nt]UAU†[M=0]∥≤e−Ns.\bigl\|[M\geq N^t]UAU^\dagger[M=0]\bigr\|\leq e^{-N^s}.​[M≥Nt]UAU†[M=0]​≤e−Ns.

The norm is the operator norm. The estimate is uniform in the product tests and circuit; the uncounted register can have arbitrary internal entanglement. For nontrivial thresholds below NNN, it says that a conjugated product condition barely connects a completely matching state to a state with very many mismatches.

Further consequences

M1 reports strong concentration of the output’s Fourier spectrum below every fixed power nδn^\deltanδ. Here the output function is its expected sign, probability of zero minus probability of one; Fourier characters are products ∏i∈S(−1)xi\prod_{i\in S}(-1)^{x_i}∏i∈S​(−1)xi​. The total squared Fourier weight on subsets of size at least nδn^\deltanδ decays faster than any inverse power of nnn.

The stated reductions also exclude strict-majority computation with worst-case advantage 1/(log⁡n)γ1/(\log n)^\gamma1/(logn)γ for fixed γ>0\gamma>0γ>0. They give state-preparation obstructions, including sufficiently accurate Dicke states: uniform superpositions of strings with exactly kkk ones. For fixed 0<δ<10<\delta<10<δ<1 and nδ≤k≤n/2n^\delta\leq k\leq n/2nδ≤k≤n/2, the claimed trace-distance lower bound is 1/(80k)1/(80k)1/(80k) for sufficiently large nnn. The two papers establish their own parity proofs; neither uses the other’s structural theorem as an input.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The claim addresses a foundational lower-bound problem for shallow quantum computation. It permits arbitrary fixed polynomial workspace, all fixed depths and the weak measured-output task, removing restrictions that shaped earlier progress.

The distinction between large gates and fanout is central. A single Toffoli can inspect many controls, but disjoint layer supports prevent one qubit from controlling arbitrarily many simultaneous operations. The result would show that quantum interference and wide controlled gates do not eliminate this limitation within the stated model.

The structural consequences also explain why parity is a useful benchmark rather than an isolated puzzle. High-order Fourier dependence and certain macroscopic state-preparation tasks would provide routes to parity. A general obstruction constrains all these routes. This rating measures significance if the claims hold, not proof verification.

6. The main idea

Reflections instead of light cones

A generalized Toffoli can be written I−2PI-2PI−2P, where PPP is a product projection: all controls are fixed to one and the target to ∣−⟩=(∣0⟩−∣1⟩)/2|-\rangle=(|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2∣−⟩=(∣0⟩−∣1⟩)/2​. This representation tracks failed local product conditions even when the gate touches many qubits.

M1 uses two inductions. For projections supported on few qubits, only a few gates in a disjoint layer can meet the support. Expanding their reflections reduces the comparison to smaller depth. For a large product projection, a low-degree polynomial in a mismatch count approximates the zero-count test over a suitable interval.

That polynomial may behave badly outside the interval. M1 controls this remaining error through a same-depth inverse-circuit argument at a larger mismatch threshold. A finite sequence of increasing thresholds ends beyond the maximum possible count, where the estimate is automatic. Working backward closes the localization statement. Keeping projections unnormalized preserves the small amplitudes that the argument needs.

The final parity coefficient can be expressed using matrix elements between complementary Hadamard product states. These differ on all nnn input qubits. Localization makes those elements small when NNN is polynomial in nnn, whereas a fixed worst-case parity advantage forces their average to remain nonzero.

A second route through regular trajectories

M2 studies how low-degree operators propagate along particular state trajectories. A trajectory is regular when product-test mismatch counts have rapidly decaying tails for suitable collections of gates. Polynomial filters transport these tails forward and backward and show that regularity survives insertion of a product projection.

A state-dependent pruning rule then supplies regularity: reflections with very small projection probability on the current state are deleted. Each deletion changes the state only slightly, and the accumulated error stays controlled across a fixed number of layers.

For the parity contradiction, the argument copies basis inputs into untouched reference qubits and considers a uniform coherent input. The copied reference retains a parity sign corresponding to exactly nnn excitations in an initial product basis. The pruned computation’s conjugated output projection has a negligible tail at that scale. Their pairing cannot support the required acceptance advantage.

Projection insertion and pruning are analytical devices. They do not add physical postselection or intermediate measurements to the allowed circuit model.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns constant depth and polynomially many total qubits, with the specified gates and zero-initialized ancillas. It does not rule out growing depth, superpolynomial resources, a primitive fanout operation or different measurement-enabled models.

The headline statement excludes a fixed positive worst-case advantage. M1 gives additional quantitative correlation and Fourier consequences, but it should not be replaced by an unproved optimal size-depth tradeoff. Its majority bounds also do not imply a constant average-case error barrier: the manuscript explicitly distinguishes its inverse-polynomial near-perfect-success obstruction from weaker approximation guarantees.

The two proofs offer different structural tools—uniform operator localization and state-dependent trajectory control. Their usefulness for other circuit classes, sharper resource bounds and broader state-preparation questions remains a separate direction from the common parity conclusion.

8. Sources and further reading

Moore’s formulation, the recent depth-specific lower bounds and the Fourier-concentration equivalence are linked above. For the role of an added fanout gate, see Høyer and Špalek, Quantum Fan-out is Powerful. M1 and M2 below provide the new claims, their precise depth conventions and independent proof strategies.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Product-projection localization and the QAC0 parity lower bound (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Regular trajectories, pruning and quantum parity (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The computational difficulty of Coulomb energy in the full continuum
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 275 · Mathematical physics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Given fixed nuclei and a number of electrons, determine the lowest possible electronic energy. This is a basic problem of quantum chemistry. Its mathematical definition is simple enough to write on one line, yet the electrons may occupy an enormous space of correlated wavefunctions.

Complexity theory asks a worst-case question: can instances of a general difficult quantum problem be encoded into this apparently rigid Coulomb system? The rigidity matters. A physical nuclear potential is a sum of attractive point-charge potentials; one cannot simply choose arbitrary matrix entries or an arbitrary external field.

Family 275 reports two reductions establishing QMA-hardness for the full continuum problem. M1 allows positive integer nuclear charges written in binary. M2 goes further by using charge one at every nucleus. Neither supplies an orbital basis that restricts the electron states. The crucial task is to control all continuum states, including those that a finite-dimensional approximation would omit.

2. Background and essential definitions

The electronic operator

Let nuclei have distinct positions R1,…,RM∈R3R_1,\ldots,R_M\in\mathbb R^3R1​,…,RM​∈R3 and positive charges Z1,…,ZMZ_1,\ldots,Z_MZ1​,…,ZM​. With nuclei clamped in place, the electronic Hamiltonian in atomic units is

H=−12∑i=1NΔxi−∑i=1N∑α=1MZα∣xi−Rα∣+∑1≤i<j≤N1∣xi−xj∣.H=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{x_i}-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{M}\frac{Z_\alpha}{|x_i-R_\alpha|}+\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\frac1{|x_i-x_j|}.H=−21​i=1∑N​Δxi​​−i=1∑N​α=1∑M​∣xi​−Rα​∣Zα​​+1≤i<j≤N∑​∣xi​−xj​∣1​.

The terms are kinetic energy, electron–nucleus attraction and electron–electron repulsion. Each electron also has a two-dimensional spin space. The admissible Hilbert space is ⋀NL2(R3;C2)\bigwedge^N L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^2)⋀NL2(R3;C2): exchanging two electrons’ positions and spins reverses the wavefunction’s sign.

The operator is defined through its lower-bounded closed energy form on antisymmetric wavefunctions with square-integrable first derivatives. This fixes its realization despite the Coulomb singularities. No total-spin sector is selected. The target is

E0=inf⁡Spec⁡H.E_0=\inf\operatorname{Spec}H.E0​=infSpecH.

An infimum need not be attained by a normalizable ground eigenvector. The decision problem is meaningful even without a binding assumption. Nuclear–nuclear repulsion is omitted because the stated convention is electronic energy with clamped nuclei.

A promise problem

Rather than demand an exact real number, the input gives rational thresholds a<ba<ba<b. A YES instance has E0≤aE_0\leq aE0​≤a; a NO instance has E0≥bE_0\geq bE0​≥b. Nothing is required when the energy lies between them. The separation is an accuracy promise, not the spacing between physical energy levels.

The total input length LLL counts bits used for rational positions, charges where applicable, thresholds and electron number. Rational numbers have signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Electron number is unary: describing NNN uses order NNN symbols. This prevents an exponentially large electron count from being hidden in a short binary input.

QMA is the class of promise problems whose YES answers admit polynomial-size quantum witnesses checked by a polynomial-time quantum verifier, with bounded error. QMA-hardness means every such problem can be transformed into the Coulomb decision problem by a deterministic classical polynomial-time map preserving YES and NO answers. It is a reduction statement, not an unconditional proof that all algorithms take exponential time.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Electronic-structure complexity developed through several related but distinct formulations. Liu, Christandl and Verstraete established QMA-completeness of the finite-mode representability problem for reduced density matrices. General fermionic interaction coefficients were important there; requiring actual Coulomb coefficients imposes additional structure.

Schuch and Verstraete proved hardness for Hubbard models with local magnetic fields and developed continuum realizations using designed scalar and spin-dependent potentials. Their route through effective spin interactions and control of complementary one-particle states are methodological predecessors. The nuclear-only potential here is a more restrictive input class.

O’Gorman, Irani, Whitfield and Fefferman proved QMA-completeness for electronic structure in a supplied finite orbital basis. Their published work includes positive unit nuclear charges, but the supplied basis remains part of the problem. It explicitly raises the complete-space question.

Why is that distinction substantial? If PPP projects onto chosen orbitals, the variational principle gives

inf⁡Spec⁡H≤min⁡Spec⁡(PHP∣Ran⁡P).\inf\operatorname{Spec}H\leq\min\operatorname{Spec}(PHP|_{\operatorname{Ran}P}).infSpecH≤minSpec(PHP∣RanP​).

A low projected energy supplies a valid trial state for the continuum. A high projected energy does not exclude a lower state outside the chosen space. Thus a finite-basis hardness reduction can transfer its YES instances while failing to transfer its NO instances.

The present manuscripts start from a field-free square-lattice Heisenberg hardness result of Cubitt, Montanaro and Piddock. They use singlet mediators associated with Piddock and Montanaro and the superexchange mechanism introduced by Anderson. The claimed new continuum constructions realize the effective interactions using positive point nuclei while bounding the omitted states from below.

M2’s unit-charge theorem logically implies hardness of the larger binary-charge class. Its proof nevertheless starts directly from the same spin source rather than invoking M1’s hardness theorem. M1 retains a distinct construction involving exponentially large charges and calibrated hydrogenic tunneling.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Binary-encoded positive charges

M1 uses distinct rational positions Rα∈Q3R_\alpha\in\mathbb Q^3Rα​∈Q3, positive integer charges ZαZ_\alphaZα​ encoded in binary, unary NNN, and rational thresholds with b−a≥L−1b-a\geq L^{-1}b−a≥L−1. It claims this promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions.

The reduction can produce the stronger threshold separation b−a≥1b-a\geq1b−a≥1, while all output descriptions have polynomial bit length. Charges and inverse nuclear separations may have exponentially large numerical values. Binary notation makes those values compatible with polynomial-length descriptions.

There is no supplied basis, magnetic field, electronic state or independently adjustable external potential. The minimization is over the full spinful antisymmetric continuum space and every spin sector. The theorem does not assert membership in QMA.

Only unit nuclear charges

M2 claims the same type of hardness with

Zα=1for every nucleus α.Z_\alpha=1\qquad\text{for every nucleus }\alpha.Zα​=1for every nucleus α.

Its reduction outputs polynomially many nuclei and electrons, distinct rational positions with polynomial bit lengths, and rational thresholds separated by at least one. The only variable output data are the nuclear positions, electron number and thresholds.

No neutrality, strict binding, normalizable ground state, molecular spectral gap or lower nuclear-separation promise is imposed. In particular, “unit charges” does not mean ordinary stable hydrogen molecules under familiar chemical conditions. These are general promised instances of the specified operator.

Both statements are about approximation of the spectral infimum to the promised decision precision. The number one in the constructed threshold separation is not a lower bound on any excitation energy.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The family claims a worst-case hardness result for the unrestricted Coulomb continuum with nuclear-only external data, including the strong unit-charge restriction. It closes a conceptual gap between encoding difficulty in a selected basis and encoding it in the actual variational problem over all wavefunctions.

The unit-charge result shows that large nuclear charge is not essential to the claimed complexity phenomenon. The geometric arrangement and collective electronic interactions suffice in M2’s construction. M1, meanwhile, contributes a different quantitative route for controlling extremely small tunneling amplitudes and high-accuracy one-well energies.

The practical interpretation has limits. Worst-case hardness does not say that every molecule is difficult or that successful approximate chemistry methods cannot work on useful families. It says that a uniformly efficient solver for every promised instance would also solve every problem in QMA through these reductions. The rating concerns the significance of that claim if correct, not an independent proof audit.

6. The main idea

Build a finite spin problem inside electron motion

Both reductions begin with a hard Heisenberg spin Hamiltonian with signed couplings on a sparse square-lattice layout. Strongly coupled ancillary spin pairs have a singlet ground state, meaning total spin zero. Coupling other spins to suitable members of these pairs produces effective interactions with the desired signs using positive exchange terms.

Next, a repulsive Hubbard model supplies those exchanges. It has localized spatial sites, electron hopping between sites and an energy penalty for double occupancy. At half filling, one electron per site is favored. Virtual excursions through doubly occupied configurations produce an effective spin interaction proportional to the square of the hopping amplitude divided by an occupancy-energy scale.

Single occupancy is obtained through this low-energy analysis. It is not imposed as a restriction on continuum trial states. Keeping that distinction is necessary for a genuine full-space reduction.

M1: large charges and tiny tunneling

M1 chooses a large integer scale Z∗Z_*Z∗​ of exponential magnitude but polynomial binary length. In coordinates y=Z∗xy=Z_*xy=Z∗​x, primary nuclear wells resemble hydrogen ground states. Weaker secondary nuclei tune isolated-well energies to high accuracy.

Small geometric displacements calibrate the required tunneling ratios. Absolute closeness to a hydrogenic orbital is insufficient when the overlap itself is exponentially small: the reduction needs relative accuracy in that overlap. M1 develops relative tail estimates and a certified polynomial-time eigenvalue computation with exponentially small error.

The effective energy uses a shift and division by Z∗Z_*Z∗​. Errors must remain controlled after the large physical rescaling, and all numerical precision must be describable and computable with polynomially many bits. These requirements are part of the reduction, not free numerical assumptions.

M2: a positive density replaced by unit nuclei

M2 instead uses a polynomially large dilation y=λxy=\lambda xy=λx. After dividing energy by λ2\lambda^2λ2, a physical unit nucleus has coupling 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ. The construction first designs a nonnegative continuous nuclear charge density that creates the needed wells and transverse confinement.

A broad positive slab supplies enough background density to keep the modified density nonnegative. Adjustments to well depths compensate for long-range direct electron repulsion. This direct repulsion is retained in the effective model rather than discarded at polynomial scales.

A transport of density and an equal-mass cubature rule replace the continuous density by point masses of exactly 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ. Cubature is numerical integration by weighted samples; equal masses here ensure that every physical nucleus has charge one after rescaling. Rational rounding is included in the error estimates, and the point positions remain distinct.

Exclude every omitted continuum state

Both approaches need a lower bound on the one-particle complement of the selected modes. Localization provides an energy penalty there. Bounds on electron interactions control coupling between selected and omitted states; completing a square makes the resulting energy loss manageable.

Together with trial states from the selected modes, this produces matching lower and upper comparisons between the continuum infimum and the effective finite model. The lower comparison is what transfers NO instances. Explicit scalar energy shifts and rational threshold adjustments then preserve the original promise under the complete classical reduction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Neither manuscript claims QMA membership, so “QMA-complete” would overstate the result. Infinite-dimensional witness encoding and verification raise questions beyond a hardness reduction.

The input models have no neutrality, separation or binding promise. Hardness under additional chemically motivated constraints is a distinct question. M1’s exponentially large charges cannot be replaced by individually listed unit nuclei without potentially exponential output size; M2 requires its separate polynomial-scale construction.

The theorem also does not give a ground-state preparation algorithm, a dynamical simulation hardness statement or a universal claim about physically accessible chemical processes. Those tasks have different input and output requirements. The precise conclusion is a worst-case decision reduction for the clamped-nuclei electronic spectral infimum.

8. Sources and further reading

The Schuch–Verstraete and O’Gorman–Irani–Whitfield–Fefferman papers linked in section 3 explain earlier designed-potential and supplied-basis formulations. The source manuscripts below specify the continuum domains, numerical encodings, finite spin inputs and error budgets. Their claims are reported as stated.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Continuum Coulomb hardness with binary nuclear charges (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, QMA-hardness of continuum Coulomb energy with unit nuclear charges (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The classical capacity of a relaxing qubit
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 276 · Mathematical physics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A qubit can carry a classical message, but relaxation makes different signals harder to distinguish. Ordinary amplitude damping describes decay toward a ground state. Generalized amplitude damping also permits upward transitions, with a nonzero stationary excited-state population.

The communication question is how many classical bits per channel use can be transmitted with error tending to zero. Optimizing a single qubit is only the beginning. A sender may encode a message in an entangled state across many channel uses, and a receiver may measure the entire output jointly. Such collective coding can outperform a one-use calculation for some quantum channels.

Family 276 reports that this additional input entanglement gives no capacity advantage for any qubit generalized amplitude-damping channel. The capacity equals a maximum over one real variable, attained at the level of Holevo information by a pair of pure signals. The manuscript also claims additivity when this channel is paired with any finite-dimensional quantum channel.

2. Background and essential definitions

Two parameters for relaxation

Write a qubit state as

ρ=(1−qzz‾q),0≤q≤1,∣z∣2≤q(1−q). ho= egin{pmatrix}1-q&z\\overline z&q\end{pmatrix},\qquad 0\leq q\leq1,\quad |z|^2\leq q(1-q).ρ=(1−qz​zq​),0≤q≤1,∣z∣2≤q(1−q).

The population qqq is the probability of finding the excited state ∣1⟩|1 angle∣1⟩; zzz describes coherence between the basis states. For damping strength γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1]γ∈[0,1] and stationary excited-state population ν∈[0,1] u\in[0,1]ν∈[0,1], the channel is

Aγ,ν(ρ)=(1−t1−γ z1−γ z‾t),t=(1−γ)q+γν.\mathcal A_{\gamma, u}( ho)= egin{pmatrix}1-t&\sqrt{1-\gamma}\,z\\sqrt{1-\gamma}\,\overline z&t\end{pmatrix},\qquad t=(1-\gamma)q+\gamma u.Aγ,ν​(ρ)=(1−t1−γ​z​1−γ​zt​),t=(1−γ)q+γν.

Population moves toward ν uν, while coherence shrinks. This explicit convention avoids ambiguity about which thermal parameter denotes excited-state occupation. Ordinary downward damping is ν=0 u=0ν=0. At γ=0\gamma=0γ=0 the channel is the identity; at γ=1\gamma=1γ=1 it replaces every input by the same diagonal state.

A quantum channel is a completely positive trace-preserving linear map. Complete positivity means positivity survives when the channel acts on part of a larger system. Independent, memoryless uses are represented by tensor powers A⊗n\mathcal A^{\otimes n}A⊗n, even when the input to those uses is entangled.

Holevo information and capacity

For a state σ\sigmaσ, let S(σ)=−Tr⁡σln⁡σS(\sigma)=-\operatorname{Tr}\sigma\ln\sigmaS(σ)=−Trσlnσ. The entropy of an ensemble’s average output, minus its average individual output entropy, gives its Holevo information. Optimizing finite input ensembles yields

χ(N)=1ln⁡2sup⁡{pa,ρa}[S ⁣(∑apaN(ρa))−∑apaS(N(ρa))].\chi(\mathcal N)= rac1{\ln2}\sup_{\{p_a, ho_a\}}\left[S\!\left(\sum_a p_a\mathcal N( ho_a) ight)-\sum_a p_aS(\mathcal N( ho_a)) ight].χ(N)=ln21​{pa​,ρa​}sup​[S(a∑​pa​N(ρa​))−a∑​pa​S(N(ρa​))].

The factor converts natural-log entropy to bits. Operationally, the unassisted classical capacity allows arbitrary block inputs and collective output measurements, but no preshared entanglement or feedback. The coding theorem gives

C(N)=sup⁡n≥11nχ(N⊗n).C(\mathcal N)=\sup_{n\geq1} rac1n\chi(\mathcal N^{\otimes n}).C(N)=n≥1sup​n1​χ(N⊗n).

This optimization over all block lengths is called regularization. Showing C=χC=\chiC=χ requires an upper bound on every block, not just a good one-use ensemble.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The coding theorems of Hausladen and collaborators, Holevo, and Schumacher–Westmoreland established the role of collective measurements and Holevo information. Hastings subsequently showed that general Holevo additivity fails. Consequently a simple-looking one-use optimizer cannot, by itself, settle unrestricted capacity.

For ordinary amplitude damping, Bennett, Shor, Smolin and Thapliyal described a two-signal scalar optimization, and Giovannetti and Fazio explicitly derived the one-use expression and attaining ensemble. Cortese and Berry studied the geometry of two-state qubit optimizers. Hou and Fang characterized the generalized channel’s one-use optimum, while Khatri, Sharma and Wilde placed it alongside bounds on unrestricted capacity.

The historical gap was regularization: could entangled blocks exceed the known one-use value? Approximate-additivity work of Leditzky, Kaur, Datta and Wilde addressed bounds rather than an exact general formula. Fang’s September 2026 preprint, in the version cited by the manuscript, supplied a close converse throughout the generalized family but generally left a gap.

An important direct predecessor is Tang, Zhu, Bai and Wang. They established capacity additivity with arbitrary finite-dimensional partners for qubit channels admitting a pure output, including ordinary amplitude damping. Their triangular block-matrix entropy inequality supplies the zero-block estimate used here. The present manuscript credits that result; ordinary damping is a recovered special case, not its new unresolved target.

At strictly interior thermal occupation and positive damping, generalized amplitude damping has no pure output, so that criterion does not apply. Other regions were already covered by King’s unital-qubit theorem and Shor’s entanglement-breaking theorem. The claimed advance extends the entropy argument across the entire parameter square, including the remaining thermal channels.

4. What the new manuscript claims

Define binary entropy in nats by h(q)=−qln⁡q−(1−q)ln⁡(1−q)h(q)=-q\ln q-(1-q)\ln(1-q)h(q)=−qlnq−(1−q)ln(1−q), with endpoint values understood continuously. A two-by-two state of determinant uuu has entropy

g(u)=h ⁣(1+1−4u2),0≤u≤14.g(u)=h\!\left( rac{1+\sqrt{1-4u}}2 ight),\qquad 0\leq u\leq rac14.g(u)=h(21+1−4u​​),0≤u≤41​.

For a pure input with excitation probability ppp, the output determinant is

vγ,ν(p)=γν(1−ν)+γ(1−γ)(p−ν)2.v_{\gamma, u}(p)=\gamma u(1- u)+\gamma(1-\gamma)(p- u)^2.vγ,ν​(p)=γν(1−ν)+γ(1−γ)(p−ν)2.

The manuscript states, for every γ,ν∈[0,1]\gamma, u\in[0,1]γ,ν∈[0,1],

C(Aγ,ν)=χ(Aγ,ν)=1ln⁡2max⁡0≤p≤1[h((1−γ)p+γν)−g(vγ,ν(p))].C(\mathcal A_{\gamma, u})=\chi(\mathcal A_{\gamma, u})= rac1{\ln2}\max_{0\leq p\leq1}\left[h((1-\gamma)p+\gamma u)-g(v_{\gamma, u}(p)) ight].C(Aγ,ν​)=χ(Aγ,ν​)=ln21​0≤p≤1max​[h((1−γ)p+γν)−g(vγ,ν​(p))].

More strongly, every finite block obeys χ(Aγ,ν⊗n)=nχ(Aγ,ν)\chi(\mathcal A_{\gamma, u}^{\otimes n})=n\chi(\mathcal A_{\gamma, u})χ(Aγ,ν⊗n​)=nχ(Aγ,ν​). If ppp maximizes the formula, the equiprobable pure states

∣ϕ±⟩=1−p ∣0⟩±p ∣1⟩|\phi_\pm angle=\sqrt{1-p}\,|0 angle\pm\sqrt p\,|1 angle∣ϕ±​⟩=1−p​∣0⟩±p​∣1⟩

attain the one-use optimum. Their independent product ensemble attains each finite-block Holevo optimum. Reliable communication at rates approaching capacity still uses the coding theorem and collective decoding; optimal Holevo information is not a claim of zero-error single-use distinguishability.

For every finite-dimensional partner channel N\mathcal NN, the manuscript additionally claims

χ(A⊗N)=χ(A)+χ(N),Smin⁡(A⊗N)=Smin⁡(A)+Smin⁡(N),C(A⊗N)=C(A)+C(N). egin{aligned}\chi(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal N)&=\chi(\mathcal A)+\chi(\mathcal N),\S_{\min}(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal N)&=S_{\min}(\mathcal A)+S_{\min}(\mathcal N),\C(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal N)&=C(\mathcal A)+C(\mathcal N).\end{aligned}χ(A⊗N)Smin​(A⊗N)C(A⊗N)​=χ(A)+χ(N),=Smin​(A)+Smin​(N),=C(A)+C(N).​

Here Smin⁡(N)=min⁡ρS(N(ρ))S_{\min}(\mathcal N)=\min_ ho S(\mathcal N( ho))Smin​(N)=minρ​S(N(ρ)), and A=Aγ,ν\mathcal A=\mathcal A_{\gamma, u}A=Aγ,ν​. The partner retains its own regularization: the assertion does not force C(N)=χ(N)C(\mathcal N)=\chi(\mathcal N)C(N)=χ(N).

At the unital midpoint ν=1/2 u=1/2ν=1/2, the formula simplifies to

C(Aγ,1/2)=1−1ln⁡2h ⁣(1+1−γ2).C(\mathcal A_{\gamma,1/2})=1- rac1{\ln2}h\!\left( rac{1+\sqrt{1-\gamma}}2 ight).C(Aγ,1/2​)=1−ln21​h(21+1−γ​​).

The endpoints give one bit per use at zero damping and zero bits at complete replacement. Exchanging the basis states gives symmetry under ν↦1−ν u\mapsto1- uν↦1−ν.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. The family determines a fundamental noise model’s classical capacity over all parameters and claims a strong arbitrary-partner additivity property. It is a major channel-specific advance rather than a general restoration of additivity, which is known to fail.

The scalar formula makes the distinction between thermal relaxation and input coding explicit. The first entropy term describes the average output; the second measures noise remaining in each pure signal. Their difference is the available information. Entangling signals across uses is permitted in the optimization but, according to the theorem, cannot improve that difference per use.

The partner result is broader than tensor-power additivity alone. It says this relaxation channel cannot produce an extra joint capacity benefit when paired with any finite-dimensional channel, even one whose own capacity requires regularization. The score reflects this significance if the claims hold, without assessing proof correctness.

6. The main idea

Keep track of populations

For a pure nnn-qubit state, let pjp_jpj​ be the probability of an excited-state outcome at site jjj. The central entropy estimate is

S ⁣(A⊗n(∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣))≥∑j=1ne(pj),e(p)=g(vγ,ν(p)).S\!\left(\mathcal A^{\otimes n}(|\psi angle\langle\psi|) ight)\geq\sum_{j=1}^{n}e(p_j),\qquad e(p)=g(v_{\gamma, u}(p)).S(A⊗n(∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣))≥j=1∑n​e(pj​),e(p)=g(vγ,ν​(p)).

Retaining each population is essential. A lower bound only by the unconstrained minimum output entropy would discard information needed to optimize the ensemble average.

Split the input according to its first qubit. The two normalized conditional vectors on the remaining qubits may be nonorthogonal and entangled. Applying a channel to those branches produces two matrices of Kraus columns; their Gram matrices describe branch outputs and cross terms. This converts the problem into an entropy inequality for block matrices.

Extend the triangular estimate

The predecessor inequality treats a factor with one zero block. Its entropy has a scalar contribution determined by the masses of the corner blocks, in addition to weighted entropies within them. The manuscript reproduces that estimate using an integral of log-determinant differences, averaging over coordinate signs and scalar concavity.

The thermal extension mixes two zero-block factorizations with the same scalar contribution. Entropy concavity preserves that common term. Allowing rectangular matrices is important because a channel’s output dimension and number of Kraus operators need not agree.

The resulting one-step bound separates the first-qubit entropy from conditional branch entropies. Convexity of eee combines conditional populations into the original populations. Iteration gives the displayed bound without assuming a product input.

Match the upper bound with two signals

For any input ensemble, the entropy of its average output is at most the sum of binary entropies of its average output populations. The population-sensitive lower bound controls the average entropy of individual outputs. Subtracting leaves one scalar objective per site, bounded by the claimed maximum.

The opposite-phase pair cancels coherence in its average while preserving the same excitation probability in each pure signal. It therefore attains both sides of this comparison. With a general partner channel, the same rectangular argument leaves the partner’s Holevo optimization intact; iterating before regularization yields the capacity identity.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The capacity is unassisted and classical. It is not the quantum capacity, private capacity or entanglement-assisted capacity. Collective decoding remains allowed and may be needed; the conclusion concerns the lack of benefit from entangled input ensembles for the stated rate.

The channel is memoryless, and the arbitrary partner is finite dimensional. Correlated environmental noise or infinite-dimensional partners require separate hypotheses. The maximum is an exact one-variable characterization, not a universal elementary expression for its optimizing population or a claim of unique optimizers.

The extension from a pure-output criterion to thermal block structure suggests further entropy questions for other channel families. It does not establish additivity for general qubit channels beyond those covered by the stated arguments.

8. Sources and further reading

The Tang–Zhu–Bai–Wang predecessor establishes ordinary-damping capacity and the triangular inequality. Khatri, Sharma and Wilde discuss the generalized model and earlier bounds. The source below supplies the full-parameter theorem and arbitrary-partner conclusions, reported as stated.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Classical capacity and entropy inequalities for generalized amplitude damping (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Repeating an entangled game: why unusually many wins become exponentially rare
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 277 · Mathematical physics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Suppose two separated players can win a game with probability at most v<1v<1v<1. Repeat the game many times using independently sampled questions. If the players independently repeat their original strategy, elementary probability says their fraction of wins will rarely exceed vvv by much.

But the players need not behave independently. They can receive all questions at once, share an entangled quantum state and make joint measurements across every repetition. The individual wins can then be correlated. Ordinary concentration bounds for independent trials no longer apply to an arbitrary strategy.

Family 277 claims that an exponential threshold bound nevertheless holds for every finite two-player game. It permits correlated questions within each game, arbitrary finite-dimensional shared entanglement and joint strategies over all repetitions. A second estimate improves the dependence on the excess winning fraction when the question distribution is fixed.

2. Background and essential definitions

A nonlocal game

A finite one-round game has question sets X,YX,YX,Y, answer sets A,BA,BA,B, a distribution μ\muμ on question pairs and an acceptance rule

V:X×Y×A×B⟶{0,1}.V:X\times Y\times A\times B\longrightarrow\{0,1\}.V:X×Y×A×B⟶{0,1}.

A referee draws (x,y)(x,y)(x,y), sends xxx to Alice and yyy to Bob, then checks their answers. The players cannot communicate after receiving questions. They may have agreed on a strategy and shared entanglement beforehand.

A finite-dimensional quantum strategy consists of a unit vector ψ∈HA⊗HB\psi\in\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal H_Bψ∈HA​⊗HB​ and local measurements. For each question, a measurement is a collection of positive matrices summing to the identity, called a POVM. If its effects are Mxa,NybM_x^a,N_y^bMxa​,Nyb​, the answer probability is

Pr⁡[a,b∣x,y]=⟨ψ,Mxa⊗Nybψ⟩.\Pr[a,b\mid x,y]=\langle\psi,M_x^a\otimes N_y^b\psi\rangle.Pr[a,b∣x,y]=⟨ψ,Mxa​⊗Nyb​ψ⟩.

The entangled value ω∗(G)\omega^*(G)ω∗(G) is the supremum of the winning probability over all finite dimensions and strategies. There need not be a strategy attaining this supremum. No fixed dimension bound is built into the definition.

Repetition and thresholds

For kkk repetitions, the referee independently samples kkk pairs from μ\muμ, then gives each player its entire question string. Each player’s measurement may depend on that whole string and return a whole answer string.

Let Ii∈{0,1}I_i\in\{0,1\}Ii​∈{0,1} indicate a win in coordinate iii, and let Wk=∑i=1kIiW_k=\sum_{i=1}^k I_iWk​=∑i=1k​Ii​. The threshold event is

Wk≥⌈(v+δ)k⌉,v=ω∗(G),0<δ<1−v.W_k\geq\lceil(v+\delta)k\rceil,\qquad v=\omega^*(G),\quad0<\delta<1-v.Wk​≥⌈(v+δ)k⌉,v=ω∗(G),0<δ<1−v.

The ceiling makes the noninteger threshold precise. Independence applies to question pairs across coordinates, not to the resulting wins under a joint strategy. Within a coordinate, Alice’s and Bob’s questions may be correlated and some pairs may have probability zero.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Raz’s parallel repetition theorem established exponential decay for winning every coordinate in classical two-player games. Holenstein simplified the argument using information theory and correlated sampling. Rao then obtained exponential concentration above the classical game value.

The threshold formulation is stronger than an all-wins statement. If winning 90 percent of the repetitions is already exceptional, then winning all of them is exceptional too. The converse implication does not follow: an all-wins bound alone can leave substantial probability of winning a large but imperfect fraction.

Early entangled-game results used additional structure. Cleve, Slofstra, Unger and Upadhyay proved perfect repetition for XOR games. Kempe, Regev and Toner treated unique games, and Dinur, Steurer and Vidick treated projection games while developing quantum correlated sampling. Jain, Pereszlényi and Yao handled independent question distributions, with improvements by Chailloux and Scarpa. Complete-support correlated distributions also admitted exponential all-wins bounds with distribution-dependent constants.

Yuen obtained polynomial all-wins decay for arbitrary finite entangled games. Bavarian, Vidick and Yuen established exponential amplification through anchoring, which modifies the game by adding questions. Their threshold result concerns that modified setting.

More directly, Chapter 6 of OpenAI’s Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science, in its August 2026 version, reports exponential all-wins repetition for arbitrary finite entangled games. Song improved the all-wins gap dependence using a smoother quantum sampling construction.

The present manuscript credits these inputs. Its universal threshold theorem uses Song’s conditioning estimate, rather than claiming a new independent origin for the entire repetition machinery. The additional contribution is a quantitative passage from tested-coordinate conditioning to threshold concentration, together with a separate fixed-distribution cubic estimate. A cubic all-wins rate does not automatically give cubic concentration above an arbitrary value.

4. What the new manuscript claims

Write d=∣A∣∣B∣d=|A||B|d=∣A∣∣B∣, the product of answer-alphabet sizes. The manuscript claims a universal constant κ0>0\kappa_0>0κ0​>0 such that every finite game with v<1v<1v<1, every allowed δ\deltaδ, every k≥1k\geq1k≥1, and every finite-dimensional joint strategy satisfy

Pr⁡[Wk≥⌈(v+δ)k⌉]≤exp⁡ ⁣(−κ0δ51+log⁡d k).\Pr[W_k\geq\lceil(v+\delta)k\rceil]\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\kappa_0\delta^5}{1+\log d}\,k\right).Pr[Wk​≥⌈(v+δ)k⌉]≤exp(−1+logdκ0​δ5​k).

Logarithms are natural. Neither question-alphabet size nor entanglement dimension enters the displayed rate. The same bound holds after taking the supremum over strategies. The distribution may have zero entries or disconnected support.

A complementary bound records that support geometry. Make a graph whose vertices are positive-probability question pairs, joining pairs when they share either question. For each connected component HjH_jHj​, let μj\mu_jμj​ be the distribution conditioned on that component and μj,min⁡\mu_{j,\min}μj,min​ its smallest positive probability. Set

κμ=8max⁡j∣Hj∣−1μj,min⁡.\kappa_\mu=8\max_j\frac{|H_j|-1}{\mu_{j,\min}}.κμ​=8jmax​μj,min​∣Hj​∣−1​.

A singleton contributes zero. The second claimed bound is

Pr⁡[Wk≥⌈(v+δ)k⌉]≤exp⁡ ⁣(−δ316384(1+κμ)(1+log⁡d) k).\Pr[W_k\geq\lceil(v+\delta)k\rceil]\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\delta^3}{16384(1+\kappa_\mu)(1+\log d)}\,k\right).Pr[Wk​≥⌈(v+δ)k⌉]≤exp(−16384(1+κμ​)(1+logd)δ3​k).

Both bounds apply to the same strategy, so the larger exponential rate may be used. The cubic dependence is not universal in the question distribution: its constant can deteriorate when support probabilities become small. When v=0v=0v=0, the manuscript obtains the sharper conclusion that the threshold probability is zero.

For error amplification, suppose a verification game has completeness at least ccc and soundness at most s<cs<cs<c. Accept a repeated game when the win fraction reaches (c+s)/2(c+s)/2(c+s)/2. With Δ=c−s\Delta=c-sΔ=c−s, the manuscript gives completeness at least 1−e−Δ2k/81-e^{-\Delta^2k/8}1−e−Δ2k/8 and soundness at most

exp⁡ ⁣(−κ0(Δ/2)51+log⁡d k).\exp\!\left(-\frac{\kappa_0(\Delta/2)^5}{1+\log d}\,k\right).exp(−1+logdκ0​(Δ/2)5​k).

The number of players and communication rounds remains unchanged, though question and answer strings grow with kkk.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. Threshold repetition is a substantial general amplification theorem for entangled games. It applies directly to the original game, including imperfect honest strategies and correlated question distributions with missing pairs.

The operational gain is clear. Requiring every coordinate to be won can reject an honest strategy that occasionally fails. A threshold tolerates those failures while still suppressing strategies whose single-game value lies below the acceptance level. The theorem claims this suppression even against arbitrary joint quantum measurements.

The two rates also distinguish uniformity from precision. One bound depends only on answer size and the excess fraction; the other uses additional information about the question law to improve the power of that fraction. This rating concerns the significance of these claims if correct, not independent verification of the conditioning arguments.

6. The main idea

Charge a budget for conditioning

Choose a set CCC of tested coordinates and condition on winning every one of them. If that event has probability p>0p>0p>0, the manuscript assigns a cost per remaining coordinate

τ(C)=log⁡(1/p)+∣C∣log⁡dk−∣C∣.\tau(C)=\frac{\log(1/p)+|C|\log d}{k-|C|}.τ(C)=k−∣C∣log(1/p)+∣C∣logd​.

The first term measures how rare the conditioning event is; the second accounts for the information in tested answers. Song’s estimate bounds the average conditional success on untested coordinates by v+Bτ1/4v+B\tau^{1/4}v+Bτ1/4 when the budget is small, for a universal constant BBB.

Intuitively, a little conditioning information cannot turn an intrinsically limited game into a substantially easier one. The difficulty is making that principle valid for entangled strategies without giving players illicit information about each other’s questions.

Extract a useful test set from too many wins

If the upper-tail event were too likely, sampling a short list of coordinate indices with replacement would identify a fixed tested set with two properties: its all-wins event is not too rare, and conditioning on it raises success elsewhere too much.

The selection uses only the joint distribution of the binary win indicators. A generic transfer then turns a conditioning error of order τ1/4\tau^{1/4}τ1/4 into the fifth-power exponential rate. Independent tensor copies of a short strategy extend the conclusion from sufficiently large lengths to every kkk, preserving the rounded threshold.

Use support geometry for the cubic rate

The second argument represents conditional measurements by vectors in common finite-dimensional spaces. It reveals Alice’s earlier questions and Bob’s later questions in a fixed coordinate order. Moving the dividing point gives two telescoping entropy estimates, controlling the information spent.

Within each connected component of question support, paths compare these vectors to one reference state. Each player can identify the component from its own question, so the component strategies can be combined without communication. The resulting loss is controlled at square-root scale in the conditioning budget, with constants depending on μ\muμ. The same transfer then gives cubic dependence on δ\deltaδ.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The model has two players, one round, finite question and answer sets, Boolean acceptance and finite-dimensional tensor-product strategies. The dimension may grow arbitrarily with repetition length. The theorem does not automatically cover infinite-dimensional or commuting-operator strategy models, more players, or other payoff conventions.

The reference value is entangled value, not classical value. A quantum strategy may exceed the latter without violating the conclusion. The theorem also does not compute vvv, guarantee an optimizing strategy or make the repeated wins independent.

Optimal dependence on the gap and alphabet sizes remains a separate quantitative question. The distribution-dependent cubic rate should not be advertised as a universal cubic threshold theorem. The manuscript’s universal claim has fifth-power dependence.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical links above trace classical repetition, general entangled-game progress and the direct conditioning input. The source below supplies the threshold transfer, support-dependent rate and amplification corollary, reported with its finite-dimensional strategy convention.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Threshold parallel repetition for finite-dimensional entangled games (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Quantum factoring with certainty and a fixed finite gate set
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 279 · Mathematical physics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Shor’s algorithm made integer factorization a landmark example of quantum speedup. Its standard guarantee is bounded error: a polynomial-time run succeeds with sufficiently high probability, and repetition reduces the chance of failure.

Can one instead demand the complete prime factorization with probability exactly one, while retaining polynomial worst-case resources and using one fixed finite collection of gates? Each qualification matters. Retrying until success may have unbounded worst-case duration. Approximating a rotation extremely accurately does not make it exact. Supplying information about an unknown order can change the input problem.

Family 279 reports a positive answer to this stricter question. The manuscript constructs a uniform circuit family that factors every integer using a finite set of bounded-arity gates, with polynomial gate and qubit counts. Its central device is to arrange an exactly known success probability and then amplify it to certainty.

2. Background and essential definitions

What the algorithm must output

The input is a binary integer N≥2N\geq2N≥2, with length approximately log⁡2N\log_2Nlog2​N. The output is its complete nondecreasing list of prime factors, including multiplicities. For example, factoring 727272 means producing 2,2,2,3,32,2,2,3,32,2,2,3,3, not merely finding one divisor.

A polynomial-time uniform circuit family has a deterministic classical algorithm that generates the circuit for each input length in polynomial time. The circuit then works for every integer of that length. This rules out hiding a separate factorization in a circuit chosen for each individual input.

Worst-case polynomial resources mean fixed polynomial bounds on gates and qubits for every input and every computational history. Probability-one correctness refers to the distribution obtained from ideal exact gates and the final measurement.

Orders and factorization

If aaa is coprime to mmm, its multiplicative order rrr is the least positive integer with

ar≡1(modm).a^r\equiv1\pmod m.ar≡1(modm).

When rrr is even and ar/2a^{r/2}ar/2 is a nontrivial square root of one modulo a composite mmm, greatest common divisors of ar/2−1a^{r/2}-1ar/2−1 or ar/2+1a^{r/2}+1ar/2+1 with mmm yield nontrivial factors. This is the familiar arithmetic bridge from order information to factoring. A recursive procedure must also handle primes, prime powers and unsuccessful choices.

A dyadic rational is a number A/2TA/2^TA/2T with integer numerator and power-of-two denominator. Such probabilities can be generated exactly with Hadamard gates: prepare a uniform TTT-bit string uuu, then reversibly test whether u<Au<Au<A. Exactly AAA of the 2T2^T2T labels pass.

Exact amplitude amplification

Suppose a unitary preparation has a marked successful component of squared norm sin⁡2θ\sin^2\thetasin2θ. Ordinary amplitude amplification uses reflections about the initial state and the successful subspace; one iteration changes the success probability to sin⁡2(3θ)\sin^2(3\theta)sin2(3θ).

If the initial probability is exactly 1/41/41/4, then θ=π/6\theta=\pi/6θ=π/6, and one iteration reaches probability one. The challenge is therefore to create that exact probability with efficiently implementable gates and a success predicate that really certifies a complete factorization.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Shor established polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete logarithms with bounded error. The order-based arithmetic reduction builds on Miller’s earlier work. A proposed factorization is efficiently checkable, but checking and retrying does not by itself produce a polynomial worst-case exact algorithm.

Exact quantum algorithms exist in several gate models. Mosca and Zalka developed exact Fourier transforms using computed rotations and exact discrete-logarithm procedures with known group orders. Their discussion also records an exact factoring algorithm in a generalized model allowing gate parameters obtained during computation. Imran’s exact order-finding procedure receives a suitable multiple of the unknown order. That extra information is not initially supplied by the ordinary factoring problem.

Approximate universality of a finite gate set does not bridge these distinctions. It allows approximation of a desired transformation, with a nonzero error, while the present target is exact success. Work of Nishimura and Ozawa formalizes the significance of finitely generated uniform circuit models.

More recent algorithms of Regev, with unconditional correctness results for modified constructions by Pilatte, address resource efficiency. Their success guarantees retain a nonzero failure probability. The present manuscript pursues certainty in a specified gate model and explicitly does not present its large polynomial parameters as a practical resource improvement.

The final amplification step is established machinery, originating in quantum search and amplitude amplification. Brassard and Høyer used exact probability engineering for Simon’s problem; Mosca and Zalka explicitly used probability 1/41/41/4 followed by one ordinary amplification step. The claimed novelty here lies in constructing the required exact factoring success law without unknown-order advice or input-dependent rotation gates.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For every integer N≥2N\geq2N≥2, the manuscript claims a polynomial-time uniform quantum circuit that outputs its complete prime factorization with probability one. Both gate count and number of qubits are bounded by fixed polynomials in the bit length.

One fixed finite gate set suffices: NOT, CNOT, Toffoli, Hadamard, the phase gate diag⁡(1,i)\operatorname{diag}(1,i)diag(1,i), their inverses and their singly controlled versions. Each gate acts on only a bounded number of qubits. Additional controls are implemented through reversible Boolean computations, rather than supplied as gates of growing arity.

A central intermediate trial has a more specific guarantee. With nnn at least the input bit length and a fixed constant cutoff, put B=2nB=2^nB=2n. For a unit aaa modulo 2≤m<B2\leq m<B2≤m<B, of unknown order rrr, the trial returns either no candidate or an integer ddd satisfying

1≤d<B,r∣d.1\leq d<B,\qquad r\mid d.1≤d<B,r∣d.

Its probability of returning the true order is exactly

Pr⁡[d=r]=φ(r) 2−⌈log⁡2r⌉−10,\Pr[d=r]=\varphi(r)\,2^{-\lceil\log_2r\rceil-10},Pr[d=r]=φ(r)2−⌈log2​r⌉−10,

where φ(r)\varphi(r)φ(r) counts residues coprime to rrr, with φ(1)=1\varphi(1)=1φ(1)=1. Neither rrr nor its factorization is supplied to the trial.

The theorem receives only the integer to be factored. It does not assume a supplied multiple of an order, a factorization oracle or continuously adjustable exact rotations. Its final success flag is coherently amplified; intermediate selected events retain their actual probabilities rather than being treated as free postselection.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. Exact factoring in a fixed finite gate model would sharpen a central quantum algorithmic result and clarify the role of randomness, gate precision and worst-case complexity.

The gain is conceptual certainty under stricter computational rules. It is not a new classical factoring algorithm or a claim that practical quantum factoring suddenly needs fewer resources. The manuscript’s construction deliberately accepts large polynomial overheads to make every relevant probability exactly controllable.

The broader technique also separates two issues often conflated in randomized constructions: producing useful outcomes with some probability, and knowing that probability exactly enough to eliminate failure. Here auxiliary arithmetic data generated during a successful run allow deferred verification of earlier transitions. The importance score concerns these claims if correct, not independent verification.

6. The main idea

Engineer an exact order-trial probability

Standard order sampling uses phases associated with a Fourier transform. The manuscript instead employs a four-phase step register and a piecewise-linear interpolation of the complex exponential. Controlled modular shifts implement the selected branch with its actual, unnormalized amplitude.

The resulting residue probabilities admit dyadic majorants. Their sums are evaluated exactly using finitely many polynomial pieces and power sums. Two correction branches then adjust the mass at each reduced fraction so that the true order has precisely the displayed probability.

This does not require knowing the true order during execution. The formula describes the trial’s behavior; later arithmetic data make its relevant probabilities evaluable on completed runs.

Generate the data needed for deferred tests

The factoring process also recursively factors p−1p-1p−1 for prime factors p>2p>2p>2 that arise. This creates an auxiliary occurrence tree of polynomial size.
