Understanding which geometric restrictions restore assembly or projectionlessness remains meaningful even if the unrestricted conjectures fail.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Higson, Lafforgue and Skandalis, Counterexamples to the Baum–Connes conjecture, for the earlier coefficient and groupoid obstructions.
  • M1’s historical discussion identifies the low-degree maximal-assembly nonvanishing theorem and the corrected exotic-completion statement used to delimit its conclusion.
  • M2 and M3 explain why a uniform spectral gap is needed in addition to a nonintegral or irrational von Neumann dimension; their bibliographies give the original projection, trace and expander references.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A torsion-free counterexample to reduced Baum–Connes injectivity (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A torsion-free counterexample to the Kadison–Kaplansky projection conjecture (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, An irrational-trace counterexample to reduced Baum–Connes (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Recovering arithmetic groups from their operator algebras
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 286 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Starting with a group, one can turn its multiplication into operators on a Hilbert space and then take limits. How much of the original group survives this process? Could two different groups become indistinguishable once their operators are completed?

In general, they can. Family 286 claims a strong recovery theorem for a particular class of lattice groups: their operator algebras determine the groups, any scalar twisting of multiplication, and even the particular isomorphism used to compare the algebras. The recovery survives passing to matrix corners, an operation that often makes classification less rigid.

The two manuscripts also describe all finite correspondences between these algebras. Such a correspondence is a more flexible relation than an isomorphism. The claimed classification says that every one still arises from concrete finite-index subgroup data and finite-dimensional projective representations.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a countable group Γ\GammaΓ, let ugu_gug​ denote the operator of translation by ggg on square-summable functions on the group. The group von Neumann algebra L(Γ)L(\Gamma)L(Γ) is the closure of their linear span in the weak operator topology, which tests convergence through matrix coefficients rather than operator norms.

A factor is a von Neumann algebra whose center consists only of scalar multiples of the identity. An infinite group is ICC if every nonidentity conjugacy class is infinite; this ensures its group algebra is a factor. The factors here are of type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​: they have a normalized trace but no minimal nonzero projections, so their geometry resembles a continuous version of matrix dimensions.

A scalar twist replaces multiplication by

uguh=ω(g,h)ugh,∣ω(g,h)∣=1.u_g u_h=\omega(g,h)u_{gh},\qquad |\omega(g,h)|=1.ug​uh​=ω(g,h)ugh​,∣ω(g,h)∣=1.

Here the displayed ugu_gug​ are the canonical unitaries; ω\omegaω is a cocycle, meaning its phases satisfy the identity needed for associativity. It is normalized by ω(e,g)=ω(g,e)=1\omega(e,g)=\omega(g,e)=1ω(e,g)=ω(g,e)=1. The resulting factor is written Lω(Γ)L_\omega(\Gamma)Lω​(Γ). Changing each canonical unitary by a phase changes the cocycle without changing the underlying algebraic structure.

A lattice is a discrete subgroup of a locally compact group with finite-volume quotient. Two groups are abstractly commensurable when some finite-index subgroups are actually isomorphic. A group has property (T) when every unitary representation with almost invariant unit vectors has a nonzero invariant vector.

Finally, an amplification MtM^tMt is a corner pMn(M)ppM_n(M)ppMn​(M)p where the unnormalized matrix trace of ppp is t>0t>0t>0. A bifinite correspondence between factors M,NM,NM,N is a Hilbert space with commuting left MMM- and right NNN-actions and finite module dimensions on both sides. Its ordinary Hilbert-space dimension can still be infinite.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Connes showed that property-(T) group factors have countable fundamental groups, where the fundamental group records which amplification scales produce an isomorphic factor. His questions about recovering property-(T) groups helped motivate modern operator-algebra rigidity. A stronger formulation, discussed by Popa, asks to recover the actual isomorphism up to the expected group-theoretic and inner symmetries.

Popa’s deformation/rigidity methods led to powerful reconstruction theorems. Ioana recovered certain Bernoulli actions from their crossed-product algebras, while Ioana–Popa–Vaes obtained groups recoverable from their bare group factors. Later work produced property-(T) examples using wreath-like products. Recovering an action with its extra structure and recovering a group from its factor are related but distinct achievements.

For lattices, character rigidity, approximation invariants and boundary methods already detect significant information. For example, Cowling–Haagerup’s invariant distinguishes the parameter in certain quaternionic hyperbolic lattice families. These results do not by themselves classify every finite correspondence to an arbitrary comparison group.

The finite-correspondence framework comes from Jones’s index theory, Pimsner–Popa inequalities and Connes’s relative tensor product. Vaes and later Donvil–Vaes obtained detailed classifications involving subgroup isomorphisms and projective cocycle ratios in other group constructions. Family 286 extends this kind of description to its stated local-field lattice class.

Property (T) alone is insufficient. The manuscripts explicitly acknowledge independent, concurrent constructions by OpenAI and Zhou of nonisomorphic ICC property-(T) groups with isomorphic factors. Their positive theorem therefore depends on the specified lattice geometry, not merely on an abstract rigidity slogan.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The precise class of groups

Let K\mathcal KK consist of countably infinite ICC groups commensurable with lattices in finite products of noncompact groups Hi(ki)+H_i(k_i)^+Hi​(ki​)+. Each HiH_iHi​ is connected, adjoint and absolutely simple over its field; the superscript means the subgroup generated by unipotent radicals of proper parabolic subgroups. Each factor must have property (T).

The fields kik_iki​ may be R\mathbb RR, C\mathbb CC, or finite extensions of Qp\mathbb Q_pQp​, the field of p-adic numbers. Different primes may occur. The real rank-one cases include the quaternionic groups locally modeled on Sp⁡(n,1)\operatorname{Sp}(n,1)Sp(n,1), n≥2n\geq2n≥2, and the exceptional Cayley case. No irreducibility, cocompactness or torsion-free assumption is imposed. In particular, SL3(Z)\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb Z)SL3​(Z) is included.

M1: exhaustion by arithmetic models

For Γ∈K\Gamma\in\mathcal KΓ∈K, any countably infinite ICC group Λ\LambdaΛ, and arbitrary scalar cocycles μ,ω\mu,\omegaμ,ω, M1 states that every bifinite correspondence between their twisted factors is a closed summand of a finite sum of elementary models.

Each model uses finite-index subgroups A≤ΓA\leq\GammaA≤Γ, B≤ΛB\leq\LambdaB≤Λ, an isomorphism δ:A→B\delta:A\to Bδ:A→B, and a nonzero finite-dimensional projective representation σ\sigmaσ satisfying

σ(a)σ(b)=μ(a,b)ω(δ(a),δ(b))σ(ab).\sigma(a)\sigma(b)=\frac{\mu(a,b)}{\omega(\delta(a),\delta(b))}\sigma(ab).σ(a)σ(b)=ω(δ(a),δ(b))μ(a,b)​σ(ab).

Only this ratio of cocycles must admit such a representation. Neither endpoint cocycle individually is required to have finite order or finite-dimensional realization. The image of σ\sigmaσ need not be finite.

M2: stable recovery and all finite neighbors

M2 uses M1 as its geometric input and claims

Lω(Γ)t≅Lν(Λ)sL_\omega(\Gamma)^t\cong L_\nu(\Lambda)^sLω​(Γ)t≅Lν​(Λ)s

exactly when t=st=st=s and a group isomorphism δ:Γ→Λ\delta:\Gamma\to\Lambdaδ:Γ→Λ matches the cocycles up to a normalized phase function bbb:

ω(g,h)=b(g)b(h)b(gh)−1ν(δ(g),δ(h)).\omega(g,h)=b(g)b(h)b(gh)^{-1}\nu(\delta(g),\delta(h)).ω(g,h)=b(g)b(h)b(gh)−1ν(δ(g),δ(h)).

At unit scale every specified factor isomorphism has the form

θ(ug)=w b(g)vδ(g)w∗\theta(u_g)=w\,b(g)v_{\delta(g)}w^*θ(ug​)=wb(g)vδ(g)​w∗

for a unitary www in the target. At general scales M2 supplies an implementing partial isometry in the actual matrix corners. In particular, each factor in the class has trivial fundamental group: only amplification scale one returns the same factor.

M2 also starts with an arbitrary II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factor having separable predual as a finite-index neighbor. It claims that any such neighbor is an amplification of a twisted group factor, with the same finite-index subgroup and projective-ratio criterion. Thus a group presentation need not be assumed at the unknown endpoint.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this gives a broad reconstruction and classification theorem for natural arithmetic operator algebras, including familiar integer-matrix groups. It recovers considerably more than a numerical invariant or the abstract isomorphism type of one factor.

The conclusion also organizes relations between factors: their finite correspondences, maps between correspondences, subobjects and compositions all receive group-theoretic descriptions. In an analogy with linear algebra, it describes not only which spaces are isomorphic, but the structured transformations and decompositions allowed between them.

The strength depends on its reach toward arbitrary ICC comparison groups and arbitrary finite-factor neighbors. Their geometry is not supplied in advance. Recovering it from the analytic relation is a central part of the claimed advance.

6. The main idea

Reconstruct geometry from a finite module

M1 begins with the correspondence rather than an assumed group isomorphism. The source lattice has rich boundary geometry, encoding directions toward infinity and incidence relations between them. The proof constructs compatible geometric information on the comparison side from Fourier coefficients and finite-module realizations.

Its major stages force boundary data to preserve incidence and metric behavior, then turn that data into actual finite-index subgroup isomorphisms. Real and nonarchimedean places require different local arguments; reducible products and rank-one property-(T) factors are included explicitly. Finite-dimensional projective fibers retain the mismatch between the two scalar twists.

This is an exhaustion statement: the familiar arithmetic models exist, but the difficult claim is that no other finite correspondences survive.

Resolve summands before using dimensions

A closed summand of an elementary model need not visibly have the elementary model’s whole dimension. M2 therefore refines M1’s classification using subgroup isomorphisms regarded as the same when they agree on a common finite-index subgroup. These are called virtual-isomorphism germs.

Grouping data by the full stabilizer of a germ identifies all bounded intertwining maps and every projection selecting a summand. M2 then obtains integer left and right module dimensions for the actual nonzero correspondences, not merely their presenting models.

An isomorphism after amplification defines an equivalence correspondence whose two dimensions are reciprocal. If both are positive integers, both must equal one. This is the dimension mechanism behind equal scales and the recovery of the specified isomorphism.

Retain multiplication as well as vector spaces

To reconstruct an unknown finite-index factor neighbor, M2 uses products of its finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces. Their multiplication supplies group and cocycle data. Composition of correspondences is described by Connes fusion, the operator-algebra analogue of tensoring compatible modules, with explicit projective induction rules. This additional structure makes the classification compatible with how relations actually combine.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the exact class K\mathcal KK, not all lattices, all property-(T) groups or all group factors. Isomorphisms are normal, unital, complex-linear and adjoint-preserving. Correspondences are separable, and the arbitrary-factor-neighbor statement assumes separable predual.

The cocycle-ratio condition cannot be replaced by separate finite-type assumptions on both cocycles. The identity correspondence already shows why a common arbitrary twist must be allowed to cancel against itself. Similarly, finite-dimensional projective representation does not mean finite image.

These are structural classifications, not algorithms deciding isomorphism from arbitrary group presentations. M2’s strongest conclusions depend on M1’s geometric exhaustion theorem. Additional consequences concerning recovery from reduced C*-algebras require the stated unique-trace condition; they are not blanket consequences for every C*-completion. Extending recovery beyond this lattice class remains a separate question, especially because general property-(T) counterexamples already exist.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Popa, Deformation and rigidity for group actions, for the historical rigidity program.
  • Zhou, ICC property (T) groups without W*-superrigidity, for why property (T) alone does not imply group recovery.
  • M1 and M2 give detailed comparisons with the earlier finite-correspondence classifications and specify the local-field and cocycle conventions used throughout.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Arithmeticity of twisted finite correspondences for lattices over local fields (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The arithmetic category and stable recovery of lattice factors (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How large can a quantum query advantage be? The quartic boundary
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 284 · Mathematical physics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Suppose an unknown binary string is stored behind an interface. An algorithm may request individual bits, and its task is to compute a specified yes-or-no property of the string. How many requests can quantum computation save?

For the property “at least one bit equals one,” classical randomized computation needs a number of requests proportional to the string length, while quantum search needs only its square root. More elaborate properties allow larger advantages. But if the property must be defined on every binary string, there is a universal restriction: classical queries never need to exceed a constant times the fourth power of quantum queries.

Family 284 claims that this fourth power is optimal, even when the classical algorithm may use randomness and make a small error. Its constructed examples approach a quartic separation and thereby disprove a proposed cubic upper bound. The distinction between a completely defined problem and a problem restricted to promised inputs drives the story.

2. Background and essential definitions

A total Boolean function is a map f:{0,1}n→{0,1}f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}f:{0,1}n→{0,1}. “Total” means that every possible input has an assigned output. A partial function is defined only on some inputs; an algorithm for it need be correct only when the input satisfies that promise.

Write R(f)R(f)R(f) for bounded-error randomized query complexity and Q(f)Q(f)Q(f) for bounded-error quantum query complexity. Both require success probability at least 2/32/32/3 on every relevant input. Both count the worst-case number of queries, including the worst case over random choices or measurement outcomes. Time spent computing between requests is unrestricted.

A quantum query can access a superposition of addresses. Its standard reversible form is

Ox∣i,b,z⟩=∣i,b⊕xi,z⟩.O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle.Ox​∣i,b,z⟩=∣i,b⊕xi​,z⟩.

Here iii is an address, bbb a one-bit register, xix_ixi​ the requested input bit, and zzz other working memory; ⊕\oplus⊕ denotes addition modulo two. Applying this operation to a superposition does not reveal all bits at once. Interference and the final measurement determine what information can actually be extracted.

A certificate is a collection of specified input bits sufficient to force an output. For OR, a single observed one certifies acceptance, whereas certifying rejection requires seeing every bit. Certificate size, deterministic query complexity D(f)D(f)D(f), and randomized query complexity are different measures. A large separation involving one does not automatically establish the same separation involving another.

The notation O(g)O(g)O(g) means an upper bound by a constant multiple of ggg for sufficiently large parameters; Ω(g)\Omega(g)Ω(g) means the analogous lower bound. Logarithmic factors matter for precise bounds but do not change the limiting power discussed here.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Grover’s search algorithm supplies the basic quadratic advantage. The polynomial method of Beals, Buhrman, Cleve, Mosca and de Wolf established a much broader restriction: for total Boolean functions, deterministic queries are at most a sixth power of bounded-error quantum queries. Thus the spectacular exponential separations available for some promise problems cannot simply carry over to total functions.

Constructing larger total-function separations nevertheless proved difficult. Pointer functions made certificates navigable in ways that favored quantum algorithms and produced nearly quartic deterministic-versus-quantum separations. Randomized algorithms were harder to defeat: they can explore many possible witnesses without committing to a deterministic search pattern.

Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari’s cheat-sheet framework hid useful certificates at addresses determined by hard partial-function instances. It gave a randomized-versus-quantum exponent of 5/25/25/2, ignoring logarithms. Subsequent work by Tal raised the exponent to nearly 8/38/38/3; work by Bansal and Sinha and, independently, Sherstov, Storozhenko and Wu brought it arbitrarily close to three.

On the other side, the consequences of Huang’s sensitivity theorem gave the known quartic upper bound for deterministic complexity and hence also for randomized complexity. The associated conjecture proposed that randomness should improve the exponent to three. Family 284 targets precisely the remaining gap between this conjectured cubic restriction and the known quartic restriction.

Its main external lower-bound ingredient is Bansal and Sinha’s result about generalized Forrelation, a promise problem comparing several sign vectors through Fourier transforms. Quantum queries can estimate the relevant correlation with very few accesses, while classical randomized queries need almost the full input length. The new manuscript combines this existing ingredient with a different organization of witnesses.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that the optimal universal power is four. More explicitly, for every fixed integer k≥2k\geq2k≥2, it constructs total Boolean functions Fk,mF_{k,m}Fk,m​, for sufficiently large powers of four mmm, with

Q(Fk,m)≤Ckm (log⁡m)bk,Q(F_{k,m})\leq C_k\sqrt m\,(\log m)^{b_k},Q(Fk,m​)≤Ck​m​(logm)bk​,

and

R(Fk,m)≥ckm2−1/k(log⁡m)2.R(F_{k,m})\geq c_k\frac{m^{2-1/k}}{(\log m)^2}.R(Fk,m​)≥ck​(logm)2m2−1/k​.

The positive constants ck,Ck,bkc_k,C_k,b_kck​,Ck​,bk​ may depend on kkk. The parameter mmm describes the construction’s columns, not its total number of input bits; the latter also includes large arrays of certificate cells.

Combining the two estimates gives an exponent approaching 4−2/k4-2/k4−2/k, apart from logarithmic losses. For any proposed universal exponent α<4\alpha<4α<4, one first fixes kkk large enough that 4−2/k>α4-2/k>\alpha4−2/k>α, and then lets mmm grow. Polynomial growth eventually dominates the logarithms. Consequently, M1 rules out every bound

R(f)≤Cα(1+Q(f))αR(f)\leq C_\alpha(1+Q(f))^\alphaR(f)≤Cα​(1+Q(f))α

holding for all total Boolean functions with α<4\alpha<4α<4. The additive one handles constant functions harmlessly.

This is a nearly quartic separation, not a statement that the displayed examples satisfy an exact lower bound proportional to Q(f)4Q(f)^4Q(f)4. The known universal quartic upper bound supplies the other side of the optimal-exponent conclusion; that upper bound is credited to earlier work.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, this resolves a central quantitative question in quantum query complexity and disproves a specific proposed limitation on quantum advantages. It shows that randomized classical access can be almost as far from quantum access, in exponent, as deterministic classical access is allowed to be.

The conceptual gain is also substantial. Promise problems offer unusually favorable terrain for quantum algorithms, but real total-function separations must remain well-defined and correctly handled when every internal promise fails. M1 explains how to preserve useful quantum behavior while making malformed local data merely invalidate a candidate witness.

The rating concerns a basic computational model rather than an immediate experimental application. Query complexity deliberately ignores potentially expensive computation between oracle calls. The construction identifies a boundary of information access; it does not by itself supply a practical fourth-power speedup for an everyday numerical task.

6. The main idea

Hide the certificate’s address

The input has mmm columns. Column iii contains a string XiX_iXi​ of mmm bits, several Forrelation instances, and an array of certificate cells. The answers to the Forrelation instances determine the address of the relevant cell.

A column is a winner if its own string is all ones, its address instances satisfy their promises, and its correctly addressed certificate verifies those answers while pointing to a zero in every other column. The function accepts exactly when a winner exists. At most one column can win: a purported second winner would have to contain a zero identified by the first.

Certificates include transcripts of ordinary Boolean circuits that check the address claims. Thus validity is a definite condition on the input bits even when the Forrelation promises fail. Invalid instances produce no winning certificate. The outer function is genuinely total.

Let the winner defeat unreliable opponents

Quantumly, the address information is cheap to obtain on valid instances, and quantum search accelerates certificate checking. The harder issue is locating a winner without thoroughly checking every column.

Pointers point outward from the winning column to zeros in its competitors. This orientation gives a reliable comparison whenever a genuine winner participates: its evidence can defeat an opponent, while an opponent cannot point to a zero in the winner’s all-one string. Comparisons between two non-winners may behave arbitrarily, including when their address promises fail.

M1’s tournament procedure is designed for exactly this uneven reliability. It uses comparison probabilities as weights, with coherent workspaces and amplitude amplification, to obtain a short list containing any true winner. Subsequent checking gives the stated square-root dependence on the number of columns, up to logarithmic factors. The argument does not assume that all pairwise comparisons define a consistent ranking.

Make classical discovery expensive

For the classical lower bound, begin with one independently hidden zero in every column and blank certificate cells. This is a rejecting input. Select a random column, erase its zero, and fill its correctly addressed certificate cell. The modified input has a winner.

A randomized algorithm distinguishes the two only by encountering the erased zero or the filled cell. Finding the relevant hidden zero across many possible columns is costly. Finding the filled cell requires learning enough hard address information or successfully guessing a whole vector of answers.

An adaptive direct-product argument controls the second possibility even when the algorithm chooses its next column from everything observed so far. This is where simply analyzing one fixed hard instance would be insufficient: the algorithm can spread its effort among many candidate winners.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The claims concern bounded-error, worst-case bit queries for total Boolean functions. They do not compare gate counts, memory, communication, energy use, or classical and quantum wall-clock running time. The quantum routines retain a fixed query cap even on inputs that violate the internal promises.

The parameter kkk is fixed before mmm tends to infinity. Constants may deteriorate with kkk, and the theorem leaves logarithmic losses and exact constant factors unresolved. It settles the best universal exponent, not the sharpest possible relationship at every finite input size.

The construction is deliberately elaborate: certificate arrays, address instances and transcripts form part of the actual input. Replacing them by a succinct representation would change the access model and would require a separate analysis. A more natural or smaller-input realization of the same extremal behavior would be a further contribution, rather than an automatic consequence of the theorem.

Finally, the lower bound uses an established Forrelation theorem. M1’s contribution is the total-function construction and its quantum and randomized analyses, not the discovery of that underlying partial-function separation.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Aaronson and collaborators, Quantum Implications of Huang’s Sensitivity Theorem, for the quartic upper bound and the surrounding complexity measures.
  • Bansal and Sinha, k-Forrelation Optimally Separates Quantum and Classical Query Complexity, for the partial-function ingredient.
  • Aaronson and Ambainis, Forrelation: A Problem that Optimally Separates Quantum from Classical Computing, for the original correlation problem and its query interpretation.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Nearly Quartic Separation Between Randomized and Quantum Query Complexity (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Can an operator algebra forget how many free generators it had?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 287 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

The free group on two generators and the free group on three generators are different groups. Their elements are words, with cancellation of a letter against its inverse as the only rule. The number of independent generators is an essential algebraic distinction.

Now replace each group element by its translation operator on square-summable functions, and take the weak operator closure. Does this much larger algebra still remember whether the original group had two or three generators?

Family 287 claims that it does not:

L(F2)≅L(F3).L(\mathbb F_2)\cong L(\mathbb F_3).L(F2​)≅L(F3​).

This would resolve the free group factor isomorphism problem, a foundational question in operator algebras. Through earlier classification results, the manuscript derives that all interpolated free group factors, including the countably infinite-rank one, are isomorphic. The proposed mechanism gradually absorbs an extra free generator while preserving the statistical behavior and eventual generating power of the remaining generators.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a discrete group GGG, left translation acts on ℓ2(G)\ell^2(G)ℓ2(G) by

(λ(g)ξ)(h)=ξ(g−1h).(\lambda(g)\xi)(h)=\xi(g^{-1}h).(λ(g)ξ)(h)=ξ(g−1h).

The group von Neumann algebra L(G)L(G)L(G) is the weak operator closure of finite linear combinations of these translations. Weak closure permits limits tested through inner products of vectors. The canonical trace is τ(x)=⟨xδe,δe⟩\tau(x)=\langle x\delta_e,\delta_e\rangleτ(x)=⟨xδe​,δe​⟩, with τ(1)=1\tau(1)=1τ(1)=1.

For the nonabelian free groups Fn\mathbb F_nFn​, n≥2n\geq2n≥2, this algebra is a type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factor: its center is just the scalars, it has a finite normalized trace, and it has no minimal nonzero projections. The trace gives an additional norm

∥x∥2=τ(x∗x)1/2,\|x\|_2=\tau(x^*x)^{1/2},∥x∥2​=τ(x∗x)1/2,

which measures average quadratic size. It differs from the operator norm, which measures the largest effect on a unit vector.

A unitary UUU is Haar when τ(Uk)=0\tau(U^k)=0τ(Uk)=0 for every nonzero integer kkk, analogous to a uniformly distributed point on the unit circle. A tuple U1,…,UnU_1,\ldots,U_nU1​,…,Un​ is a free Haar tuple when every nontrivial reduced word in the unitaries and their adjoints has trace zero. It is freely generating if its weakly closed algebra is the whole factor.

That final requirement matters. A free Haar tuple can sit inside a much larger algebra without generating it. Matching all its moments identifies the algebra it generates, not automatically the surrounding algebra.

An amplification MtM^tMt, t>0t>0t>0, is a normalized corner of a matrix algebra over MMM, cut out by a projection with unnormalized trace ttt. The fundamental group F(M)\mathcal F(M)F(M) consists of scales ttt for which Mt≅MM^t\cong MMt≅M. Here “fundamental group” names an invariant of a factor, not the loop group of a topological space.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Free group factors appeared in Murray and von Neumann’s foundational work. Their nonhyperfiniteness separated them from the hyperfinite factor, which is built by approximating with finite-dimensional algebras. But this distinction did not distinguish one free rank from another. Kadison is credited in the historical literature with raising the rank-isomorphism question.

Voiculescu’s free probability supplied models in terms of freely independent noncommuting random variables. Semicircular variables, the free-probability counterparts of Gaussian variables, generate free group factors. Compression calculations related the number of such variables to the size of a corner.

Dykema and Rădulescu independently introduced interpolated factors L(Fr)L(\mathbb F_r)L(Fr​) for real r>1r>1r>1. The noninteger symbol is a parameter for a factor; it does not mean an ordinary free group with a fractional number of generators. Their amplification formula is

L(Fr)t≅L(F1+(r−1)/t2).L(\mathbb F_r)^t\cong L(\mathbb F_{1+(r-1)/t^2}).L(Fr​)t≅L(F1+(r−1)/t2​).

The classical alternative says that these factors are either all isomorphic or pairwise nonisomorphic. Rădulescu’s version includes the infinite parameter. Thus a single isomorphism between distinct finite ranks would settle the alternative.

Free entropy dimension offered a possible route toward distinguishing ranks. A semicircular nnn-tuple has dimension nnn. If that dimension depended only on the generated factor, different ranks would be different. However, this required a generator-invariance statement, not merely computing the dimension for familiar tuples.

Other methods constructed isomorphisms in perturbative settings. Guionnet–Shlyakhtenko’s free monotone transport changes noncommuting variables while retaining the generated algebra under appropriate analytic assumptions. M1 also discusses a recent Shlyakhtenko construction involving Fuchsian group factors, but states that it uses no result from that preprint. The present claim specifically requires changing the number of free generators.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s direct construction gives, for every integer n≥3n\geq3n≥3, a unital normal trace-preserving *-isomorphism

L(Fn)≅L(Fn+1).L(\mathbb F_n)\cong L(\mathbb F_{n+1}).L(Fn​)≅L(Fn+1​).

A *-isomorphism preserves multiplication, complex linear combinations, adjoints and the identity. Normality gives the appropriate continuity for von Neumann algebras. The claim is an actual isomorphism, not only agreement of selected invariants or an approximation by maps.

The construction produces a freely generating Haar nnn-tuple inside L(Fn+1)L(\mathbb F_{n+1})L(Fn+1​). To reach ranks two and three, M1 first combines the direct comparisons at ranks three and four, obtaining L(F3)≅L(F5)L(\mathbb F_3)\cong L(\mathbb F_5)L(F3​)≅L(F5​). Amplifying both sides by 2\sqrt22​ and applying the classical formula yields ranks two and three.

The earlier all-or-nothing alternative then implies

L(Fr)≅L(Fs),1<r,s≤∞,L(\mathbb F_r)\cong L(\mathbb F_s),\qquad 1<r,s\leq\infty,L(Fr​)≅L(Fs​),1<r,s≤∞,

and

F(L(Fr))=R>0.\mathcal F(L(\mathbb F_r))=\mathbb R_{>0}.F(L(Fr​))=R>0​.

M1 also states that four free entropy dimensions, δ,δ0,δ∗,δ⋆\delta,\delta_0,\delta^*,\delta^\starδ,δ0​,δ∗,δ⋆, fail to depend only on the generated von Neumann algebra. Each takes every integer value n≥2n\geq2n≥2 on some finite self-adjoint generating tuple of L(F2)L(\mathbb F_2)L(F2​). The tuples used for the microstates and nonmicrostates versions need not be the same. This does not claim that all four dimensions disagree on every tuple.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this settles one of the central classification problems for finite factors and determines the isomorphism type of an entire interpolated family. It would establish a striking loss of information: the completed operator algebra forgets a rank distinction that the original free group retains.

It would also change how free entropy dimensions can be used. A quantity may remain highly informative about a chosen family of noncommuting variables while failing to be an invariant of the algebra they generate. The claimed result separates those two roles decisively.

The conclusion does not make all II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factors isomorphic. Free group factors would still differ from the hyperfinite factor and from many other factors. What collapses is this particular rank parameter, not the entire classification theory.

6. The main idea

Move generators without changing their law

Begin with a free Haar tuple (A1,…,An,C)(A_1,\ldots,A_n,C)(A1​,…,An​,C) generating L(Fn+1)L(\mathbb F_{n+1})L(Fn+1​). The goal is to hide the information carried by CCC inside small changes to the first nnn variables.

The manuscript takes a bounded logarithm S=arg⁡(C)S=\arg(C)S=arg(C), so eiS=Ce^{iS}=CeiS=C, and uses its conjugates by words in the AjA_jAj​. These feed a polynomial differential equation. M1’s moment identity and analyticity argument show that the resulting flow preserves traces of words and extends to automorphisms of the factor.

This is more specific than a formal change of symbols. The maps must respect the actual operator relations and norms before they can serve as automorphisms.

Make a long word carry the missing variable

The flow is controlled by finitely supported coefficient vectors on a free group. Their values on generators are small, while a suitable long word accumulates a coefficient close to a unit point mass. A cocycle identity organizes that accumulation, much as repeatedly applying a product rule organizes a long algebraic expression.

M1 obtains the coefficients using spectral estimates for sums of free translations and a truncated inverse. Small generator coefficients keep each AjA_jAj​ almost fixed in operator norm, yet the selected word can move enough to encode the extra variable. After a change of free basis, a word in the moved first nnn coordinates approximates the old CCC.

Take a limit and preserve generation

The absorption step is repeated with decreasing errors. The first nnn coordinates converge in norm; their joint free Haar moments therefore persist in the limit. The complementary coordinate is allowed to change at each stage.

Generation requires a separate argument. Once an approximating word has been chosen, its length controls how sensitive it is to future changes in the generators. M1 chooses later error budgets only after knowing that word. This keeps earlier approximations useful throughout the iteration.

The resulting word algebra is claimed to be dense in the ambient tracial L2L^2L2 space. A trace-preserving conditional expectation, which acts as orthogonal projection onto a von Neumann subalgebra’s L2L^2L2 space, then identifies the limiting generated algebra with the whole factor. The construction thus needs both preservation of distribution and recovery of all ambient operators.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The direct absorption theorem begins at n=3n=3n=3. The ranks-two-and-three statement uses the established amplification calculus afterward. The extension to every real parameter and infinite rank uses the classical dichotomy, rather than a separate direct construction at each parameter.

The theorem concerns tracial von Neumann algebras. It does not identify the original free groups, their algebraic group rings, or their reduced group C*-algebras. Taking weak closure is essential to the setting.

The argument is constructive in its mathematical presentation but does not provide a practical finite formula evaluating the isomorphism on arbitrary operators. It relies on limiting procedures and generation in a topology weaker than norm closure of the word algebra.

Finally, failure of generator invariance for free entropy dimensions leaves many questions about their behavior on particular tuples. Their definitions and local analytic uses remain meaningful. M1’s conclusion is that the generated factor alone cannot determine these four numerical values.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Dykema, Interpolated free group factors, for interpolation and amplification theory.
  • Guionnet and Shlyakhtenko, Free Monotone Transport, for an earlier analytic method of constructing isomorphisms through changes of variables.
  • M1’s Sections 6–7 specify the classical dichotomy used, its inclusion of infinite rank, and the separate consequences for the four entropy dimensions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An isomorphism of the free group factors (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When nearby operator algebras are the same—and when they are not
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 289 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Suppose two collections of operators are so close that every unit-sized operator in either collection can be approximated in norm by one in the other. Must the collections describe the same algebra in slightly different coordinates?

The Kadison–Kastler perturbation problem asks this for operator algebras. Family 289 claims a positive answer, with a uniformly small coordinate change, for arbitrary unital von Neumann algebras. Its other two manuscripts show why nearby formulations have different answers: one-sided approximation need not admit a small spatial embedding, and arbitrarily close separable C*-algebras need not be spatially conjugate at all.

These are compatible conclusions. They change either the approximation hypothesis or the kind of closure defining the algebras. The family is therefore a study of the exact boundary between stable and unstable operator-algebraic structure.

2. Background and essential definitions

All algebras here act on a common complex Hilbert space HHH, with the same identity operator. A C*-algebra is closed under adjoints and operator-norm limits. A von Neumann algebra is also closed in the weak operator topology, which tests operators through their matrix coefficients. The latter closure can add many operators.

For an algebra MMM, write M1={x∈M:∥x∥≤1}M_1=\{x\in M:\|x\|\leq1\}M1​={x∈M:∥x∥≤1}. The Kadison–Kastler distance is the Hausdorff distance of unit balls:

d(M,N)=max⁡{sup⁡x∈M1inf⁡y∈N1∥x−y∥,sup⁡y∈N1inf⁡x∈M1∥y−x∥}.d(M,N)=\max\left\{\sup_{x\in M_1}\inf_{y\in N_1}\|x-y\|,\sup_{y\in N_1}\inf_{x\in M_1}\|y-x\|\right\}.d(M,N)=max{x∈M1​sup​y∈N1​inf​∥x−y∥,y∈N1​sup​x∈M1​inf​∥y−x∥}.

Small distance gives approximants in both directions. It does not supply a preferred linear or multiplicative map matching the operators.

A spatial conjugacy is an equality uMu∗=NuMu^*=NuMu∗=N for a unitary operator uuu on the given Hilbert space. Requiring ∥u−I∥\|u-I\|∥u−I∥ to be small is stronger: it says that the concrete positions of the algebras differ only slightly. An abstract *-isomorphism need not be implemented by such a unitary in the given representation.

For one-sided approximation, M2 uses

γ(M,N)=sup⁡x∈M1inf⁡y∈N∥x−y∥.\gamma(M,N)=\sup_{x\in M_1}\inf_{y\in N}\|x-y\|.γ(M,N)=x∈M1​sup​y∈Ninf​∥x−y∥.

Here the approximating yyy need not be contractive, and there is no reverse condition. If uMu∗⊆NuMu^*\subseteq NuMu∗⊆N, then γ(M,N)≤2∥u−I∥\gamma(M,N)\leq2\|u-I\|γ(M,N)≤2∥u−I∥. The question is whether a small gap forces a converse with a small unitary.

An algebra is norm separable if a countable set is dense in its operator norm. This differs from having separable predual as a von Neumann algebra. M3’s norm-separability assumption is part of its stated counterexample.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kadison and Kastler introduced the metric in 1972. Early work treated type I algebras, followed by the amenable case through results of Christensen, Johnson and Raeburn–Taylor. Christensen also established a one-sided embedding theorem when the source von Neumann algebra is amenable.

Other positive results required additional structure, such as placing both algebras inside one common finite von Neumann algebra. Merely knowing that each algebra is finite does not supply that common ambient hypothesis. Later work of Cameron and collaborators produced strongly stable nonamenable factors using crossed products and a hyperfinite tensor factor, and studied which structural properties transfer under small perturbations.

The C*-algebra story differs. Christensen, Sinclair, Smith, White and Winter proved spatial conjugacy for sufficiently close norm-separable nuclear algebras on a separable Hilbert space. Nuclearity is an approximation property that makes these algebras particularly tractable.

Earlier negative examples stopped short of M3’s target. Johnson constructed close separable nuclear algebras for which implementing unitaries cannot uniformly approach the identity, but spatial conjugacies still exist. Choi–Christensen constructed close nonisomorphic algebras using norm nonseparability. M3 claims failure of any spatial conjugacy while retaining norm separability.

Similarity theory supplies another part of the background. Bounds on commutators at every matrix level control the passage between representations, but do not themselves construct a multiplicative correspondence between nearby algebras. M1 develops that additional step. Its commutator argument is stated to be independent of the companion similarity manuscript in family 288.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: universal strong stability for von Neumann algebras

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, M1 states that there exists δ(ε)>0\delta(\varepsilon)>0δ(ε)>0 such that

d(M,N)<δ(ε)d(M,N)<\delta(\varepsilon)d(M,N)<δ(ε)

implies the existence of a unitary u∈B(H)u\in B(H)u∈B(H) with

uMu∗=N,∥u−I∥<ε.uMu^*=N,\qquad \|u-I\|<\varepsilon.uMu∗=N,∥u−I∥<ε.

The tolerance is independent of the algebras, their types, their representations and the cardinalities of their Hilbert spaces and preduals. The hypothesis uses ordinary operator-norm unit-ball distance, not an assumed distance at every matrix level.

M2: one-sided gaps do not force small embeddings

M2 constructs pairs Mn,Nn⊆B(Hn)M_n,N_n\subseteq B(H_n)Mn​,Nn​⊆B(Hn​) on separable Hilbert spaces such that γ(Mn,Nn)→0\gamma(M_n,N_n)\to0γ(Mn​,Nn​)→0, but a fixed ε0>0\varepsilon_0>0ε0​>0 satisfies

uMnu∗⊆Nn⟹∥u−I∥≥ε0uM_nu^*\subseteq N_n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\|u-I\|\geq\varepsilon_0uMn​u∗⊆Nn​⟹∥u−I∥≥ε0​

for all sufficiently large nnn. Spatial embeddings do exist in these examples. The failure concerns their unavoidable displacement from the identity, not nonexistence of embeddings. No reverse near inclusion is asserted.

M3: close separable C*-algebras without any spatial conjugacy

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, M3 constructs unital norm-separable C*-algebras A,BA,BA,B on a separable Hilbert space with

d(A,B)<ε,A′′=B′′,d(A,B)<\varepsilon,\qquad A''=B'',d(A,B)<ε,A′′=B′′,

but no unitary uuu satisfying uAu∗=BuAu^*=BuAu∗=B. The notation A′′A''A′′ denotes the weak operator closure, equivalently the double commutant. Thus the two algebras even have the same von Neumann closure.

M3 does not assert that AAA and BBB are abstractly nonisomorphic. Failure of spatial conjugacy in a particular representation is its precise conclusion.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, M1 settles the unrestricted strong perturbation conjecture for von Neumann algebras. The uniform tolerance would make the result independent of representation size and algebra type, rather than a collection of separate stability theorems.

M2 and M3 make the boundary informative. Approximation of every source operator is insufficient if the target has uncontrolled extra structure. Likewise, norm-closed subalgebras may retain positional information that disappears entirely on taking weak closure.

The family therefore distinguishes three questions often compressed into “nearby means the same”: whether an isomorphism exists, whether it is spatial in the given Hilbert space, and whether its implementing unitary is close to the identity. The manuscripts answer different versions with carefully different hypotheses.

6. The main idea

Build the missing multiplicative map

For finite factors, M1 combines matrix-level commutator control with a construction of a near-identity isomorphism. After arranging a common tracial position and a shared hyperfinite subfactor, it chooses nearby unitaries. These choices almost multiply correctly, but need correction.

Boundary averaging first turns them into a measurable cocycle over an amenable action. This does not assume that the underlying group is amenable. An additional ergodicity argument yields a map preserving adjoints and squares; closeness rules out reversing multiplication. Commutator estimates then implement the resulting isomorphism by a small unitary on the original Hilbert space.

Infinite factors require modular theory, which associates a canonical time evolution to a faithful state. M1 compares suitably rescaled graphs of the operators defining that evolution, aligns the modular actions, and passes to crossed products. Finite corners bring the problem back to the finite-factor theorem. Completely positive maps, which preserve positivity at every matrix size, then permit descent to the original algebras. Centers and separable restrictions finish the arbitrary-Hilbert-space case.

Encode almost-commuting matrices

M2 starts with clock and shift matrices that nearly commute but remain a fixed distance from every commuting unitary pair. Their obstruction is topological, expressed through a winding number.

A family of free-group representations inserts those matrices as parameters. Uniform Fourier estimates turn their small commutator into a small one-sided gap for the entire source unit ball. If a near-identity spatial embedding existed, weak operator limits and compression would recover genuinely commuting matrices close to the original pair, contradicting the starting obstruction.

The construction thus transfers a finite-dimensional instability into a problem about infinite-dimensional operator algebras. Existence of some spatial embedding is retained throughout.

Record an inclusion at the end of a sequence

M3 starts with subalgebras P,QP,QP,Q inside a common algebra DDD. It forms an algebra of norm-convergent sequences

ED(P)={(xn):xn∈D, xn→p∈P}.E_D(P)=\{(x_n):x_n\in D,\ x_n\to p\in P\}.ED​(P)={(xn​):xn​∈D, xn​→p∈P}.

Changing PPP changes only which limits are allowed. Coordinate projections are intrinsic central projections, so any spatial conjugacy of sequence algebras must permute coordinates and normalize DDD there.

A tensor-norm identity distinguishes the positions of the chosen close P,QP,QP,Q inside DDD. That identity survives the coordinate normalizations and limiting operations forced by a hypothetical conjugacy. The sequence construction therefore upgrades a relative inclusion obstruction into failure of every spatial conjugacy, while preserving closeness and a common weak closure.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The positive theorem requires two-sided distance and weakly closed algebras with common identity. M2 changes the first requirement; M3 changes the second. Neither is a counterexample to M1’s stated theorem.

M1 asserts a universal tolerance but does not provide an optimal modulus relating algebra distance to unitary displacement. Its independent commutator estimate is only one component; the multiplicative correction and return to the original representation are essential additional claims.

M2 does not rule out arbitrary spatial embeddings. M3 does rule out arbitrary spatial conjugacies, but makes no abstract nonisomorphism claim and does not apply to the nuclear class covered by earlier positive results. Determining sharper tolerances and identifying intermediate structural assumptions for other stability notions remain meaningful questions.

The three source versions also matter: M1 is dated September 23, while the two counterexample manuscripts used here are dated October 5. Their conclusions are reported with the scope of these pinned versions.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Christensen and collaborators, Perturbations of nuclear C*-algebras, for the separable nuclear positive theorem.
  • Cameron and collaborators, Kadison–Kastler stable factors and Type II1 factors satisfying the spatial isomorphism conjecture, for earlier nonamenable stability results.
  • M2 explains its clock-and-shift obstruction; M3 distinguishes Johnson’s displacement examples from its stronger failure of spatial conjugacy.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Universal strong Kadison–Kastler stability (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Near Inclusions of von Neumann Algebras Without Small Spatial Embeddings (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Close Separable C*-Algebras Without Spatial Conjugacy (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Simpler subalgebras that preserve every modular commutation constraint
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 290 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Can a complicated operator algebra contain a simpler subalgebra that imposes exactly the same commutation constraints on everything around it? The answer depends on what counts as “around it.” In modular theory, the surrounding algebra includes not only the original operators but also unitaries recording a canonical time evolution.

Family 290 claims that an expected inclusion of von Neumann algebras contains an amenable expected subalgebra preserving the commutant in this enlarged continuous core. A companion manuscript develops a bounded-recovery principle: a signal detected on narrow spectral bands of Hilbert-space vectors can also be detected by uniformly bounded algebra elements.

The papers connect these two statements to bicentralizers. They also give alternative arguments for the absolute bicentralizer theorem, explicitly crediting an earlier September 2026 announcement by Houdayer and Marrakchi. The relative inclusion theorem and the analytical recovery tool are the family’s distinct contributions.

2. Background and essential definitions

A von Neumann algebra MMM is an adjoint-closed algebra of bounded operators closed in the weak operator topology. For a subalgebra N⊆MN\subseteq MN⊆M, its relative commutant in MMM is

N′∩M={x∈M:xn=nx for every n∈N}.N'\cap M=\{x\in M:xn=nx\text{ for every }n\in N\}.N′∩M={x∈M:xn=nx for every n∈N}.

An inclusion is expected if there is a faithful normal conditional expectation EN:M→NE_N:M\to NEN​:M→N. This is a positive, identity-preserving projection compatible with multiplication by elements of NNN; it acts like averaging away the information outside NNN. Faithfulness detects positive elements, and normality is the relevant continuity for monotone operator limits.

A faithful normal state φ\varphiφ assigns normalized positive expectations to operators. It determines a modular automorphism group σtφ\sigma_t^\varphiσtφ​, a canonical real-parameter evolution. Its fixed algebra

Mφ={x:σtφ(x)=x for all t}M_\varphi=\{x:\sigma_t^\varphi(x)=x\text{ for all }t\}Mφ​={x:σtφ​(x)=x for all t}

is the state’s centralizer. The continuous core c(M)=M⋊σφRc(M)=M\rtimes_{\sigma^\varphi}\mathbb Rc(M)=M⋊σφ​R adjoins unitaries implementing this evolution. Changing the faithful state gives a canonical core identification fixing MMM, so the commutant assertion below is independent of that choice.

An amenable von Neumann algebra here means an injective one, a particularly tractable class possessing strong approximation and extension properties. This does not mean that the larger algebra is amenable.

The bicentralizer BC(M,φ)\mathrm{BC}(M,\varphi)BC(M,φ) consists of operators commuting asymptotically with every uniformly bounded sequence that asymptotically centralizes the state. State centralization is measured in the norm of the predual, the space of normal linear functionals. A scalar bicentralizer means that only multiples of the identity pass all these tests.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Connes introduced the bicentralizer problem in the classification of injective factors. Haagerup proved triviality for amenable type III1\mathrm{III}_1III1​ factors, completing the uniqueness theorem for the injective factor of that type. Type III factors lack the finite trace used in II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ theory; the subscript one describes the case with full modular scaling behavior.

Popa’s work on maximal abelian subalgebras and irreducible inclusions supplied a related strategy: find a tractable subalgebra retaining the required commutation constraints. Haagerup linked bicentralizer triviality to states with irreducible centralizers. “Irreducible centralizer” means its relative commutant is scalar; it does not mean that the centralizer itself is scalar.

Masuda introduced a relative bicentralizer in a finite-index setting. Ando, Haagerup, Houdayer and Marrakchi developed a canonical relative bicentralizer flow. Marrakchi’s later work formulated the general relative conjecture and related it to commutants inside the continuous core and to averaging of unitary orbits.

A preceding theorem of Marrakchi supplies an expected amenable P⊆NP\subseteq NP⊆N preserving N′∩MN'\cap MN′∩M. M1 seeks equality inside c(M)c(M)c(M), which is stronger. One cannot simply replace the upper algebra by its core in that theorem: the original expectation onto NNN does not automatically extend to an expectation from the core.

On September 10, 2026, Houdayer and Marrakchi announced absolute bicentralizer triviality for every type III1\mathrm{III}_1III1​ factor admitting a faithful normal state, without a separability restriction in the statement. Both manuscripts acknowledge that result. Their absolute arguments are alternatives for the separable-predual case, rather than claims of first resolving the absolute problem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: preserve the full core commutant

Suppose N⊆MN\subseteq MN⊆M is a unital inclusion with separable preduals and a faithful normal conditional expectation M→NM\to NM→N. M1 states that there is a unital amenable P⊆NP\subseteq NP⊆N, itself the range of a faithful normal conditional expectation from NNN, such that

P′∩c(M)=N′∩c(M).P'\cap c(M)=N'\cap c(M).P′∩c(M)=N′∩c(M).

This allows arbitrary centers and types. The smaller algebra imposes exactly the same commutation constraints as NNN, even on the added modular operators.

M1 also obtains an expected maximal abelian subalgebra A⊆NA\subseteq NA⊆N satisfying

A′∩c(M)=c(A)∨(N′∩c(M)).A'\cap c(M)=c(A)\vee\bigl(N'\cap c(M)\bigr).A′∩c(M)=c(A)∨(N′∩c(M)).

The symbol ∨\vee∨ means the von Neumann algebra generated by the two indicated subalgebras. The expectations specify the compatible embeddings of the cores. A further conclusion that AAA is maximal abelian in MMM uses the additional core condition stated in M1; it is not asserted for every inclusion solely from the displayed formula.

M2: recover spectral signals with bounded operators

Assume a faithful normal state has scalar centralizer, Mφ=C1M_\varphi=\mathbb C1Mφ​=C1. On the standard Hilbert space put ξ=φ1/2\xi=\varphi^{1/2}ξ=φ1/2, D=log⁡ΔφD=\log\Delta_\varphiD=logΔφ​, and Ut=eitDU_t=e^{itD}Ut​=eitD, where Δφ\Delta_\varphiΔφ​ is the modular operator.

Fix an arbitrary bounded Hilbert-space operator TTT and a real spectral point sss. Suppose unit vectors hnh_nhn​ have DDD-spectral support in [s−δn,s+δn][s-\delta_n,s+\delta_n][s−δn​,s+δn​], with δn→0\delta_n\to0δn​→0, and

lim sup⁡nmt∥TUthn∥2>0.\limsup_n m_t\|TU_t h_n\|^2>0.nlimsup​mt​∥TUt​hn​∥2>0.

Here mmm is the fixed translation-invariant mean obtained from symmetric interval averages as specified by M2, rather than an assumed ordinary time limit.

M2 claims a subsequence njn_jnj​, elements vj∈Mv_j\in Mvj​∈M, and constants C∗<∞C_*<\inftyC∗​<∞, η>0\eta>0η>0 with

∥vj∥≤C∗,∥Tvjξ∥≥η,\|v_j\|\leq C_*,\qquad \|Tv_j\xi\|\geq\eta,∥vj​∥≤C∗​,∥Tvj​ξ∥≥η,

whose vectors vjξv_j\xivj​ξ have support in [s−4δnj,s+4δnj][s-4\delta_{n_j},s+4\delta_{n_j}][s−4δnj​​,s+4δnj​​]. Thus the signal survives on algebra elements with one uniform operator-norm bound.

M2 applies this to a spectral-intertwining rigidity theorem and derives BC(M,φ)=C1\mathrm{BC}(M,\varphi)=\mathbb C1BC(M,φ)=C1 for type III1\mathrm{III}_1III1​ factors with separable predual.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, M1 resolves the general relative bicentralizer conjecture in its separable-predual expected-inclusion setting. The core formulation retains information invisible to ordinary commutants and makes the theorem useful across different operator-algebra types.

The bounded-recovery result addresses a recurrent analytical obstacle. Hilbert-space approximation can produce vectors represented by algebra elements whose operator norms grow without bound. Such approximations cannot be inserted into hypotheses about uniformly bounded sequences. M2 supplies a way across that gap while retaining increasingly narrow spectral localization.

The significance is not that the absolute bicentralizer conjecture was previously untouched. The earlier Houdayer–Marrakchi announcement is part of the baseline. The family adds a relative core statement and a general recovery mechanism with its own precise assumptions.

6. The main idea

Turn commutation into comparison of multiplication maps

For the type III1\mathrm{III}_1III1​ part of M1, let BBB be the relative bicentralizer and Ω\OmegaΩ the vector representing the state. On suitable tensor-product vectors, consider the two orders of multiplication:

R(xΩ⊗aΩ)=xaΩ,L(xΩ⊗aΩ)=axΩ.R(x\Omega\otimes a\Omega)=xa\Omega,\qquadL(x\Omega\otimes a\Omega)=ax\Omega.R(xΩ⊗aΩ)=xaΩ,L(xΩ⊗aΩ)=axΩ.

The manuscript proves these maps are isometries and relates them through the generators of modular evolution and bicentralizer flow. This comparison packages the failure of ordinary commutation into an explicit spectral phase.

A tensor argument controls words of arbitrary length and intervening flow shifts uniformly. Randomized repeated tests eliminate a possible discrepancy between the proposed spectral comparison and the actual multiplication maps. Passing to the core then identifies the fixed algebra of the relative flow with the desired core commutant.

Existing characterizations convert that fixed-point result into the expected amenable subalgebra. Other factor types and central decompositions extend the conclusion beyond the initial type III1\mathrm{III}_1III1​ case.

Average, truncate and restore the band

M2 starts with spectral vectors that need not come from uniformly bounded algebra elements. It first approximates them by individual bounded representatives; their bounds may depend on the vector.

Modular orbit averages and independent phases provide second- and fourth-moment control. Fourth moments limit how much mass can hide in very large operator values, allowing one fixed polar-truncation threshold to produce a uniformly bounded sequence without losing the signal.

Truncation can spoil spectral localization. A final Fourier filter restores support near the original spectral point. Its norm estimate is independent of the shrinking interval width, which is why the uniform bound survives this last step. The output band may be four times wider, but still shrinks to the same point.

Extract rigidity from joint spectra

For a state-preserving action satisfying the manuscript’s asymptotic intertwining condition, its implementing unitaries commute with modular evolution. Their generators have a joint spectral support in the plane. Bounded recovery lets the sequence-level intertwining hypothesis constrain this support.

Applying the spectral comparison in both directions forces a restrictive symmetric phase relation. The scalar-centralizer assumption rules out the unwanted modular eigenvalues, leaving the action trivial. Standard bicentralizer reductions then yield the absolute application.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 requires separable preduals and a faithful normal conditional expectation for the original inclusion. It does not claim the same conclusion for arbitrary nonexpected inclusions. The core equality is independent of the state used to construct the core, but not independent of these structural hypotheses.

M2 requires a scalar centralizer, not merely an irreducible one. Its input is a positive averaged limsup for a fixed TTT and fixed spectral point; its conclusion passes to a subsequence and allows constants depending on the data. It is not a norm-bounded representation of every spectral vector, nor a universal quantitative recovery rate.

The expected maximal abelian subalgebra obtained for a factor need not preserve the particular scalar-centralizer state used in the recovery argument. Keeping those two existence statements separate avoids an extra conclusion absent from the manuscripts. Extensions beyond the stated hypotheses and sharper recovery bounds are distinct further questions.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Houdayer and Marrakchi, The classification of flows on II1 factors and Connes’ bicentralizer problem, the September 10 absolute theorem acknowledged by both sources.
  • Marrakchi, Kadison’s problem for type III subfactors and the bicentralizer conjecture, for the relative-core characterization.
  • Marrakchi, Ergodicity of the bicentralizer flow and Kadison’s problem, for the preceding expected-subalgebra result used by M1.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Expected amenable subalgebras preserving core commutants (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Bounded recovery for modular spectral averages (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Three forms of regularity become one: comparison, dimension and Jiang–Su absorption
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 291 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

An infinite-dimensional operator algebra can be regular in several apparently different ways. Positive operators may be ordered by their numerical sizes. Finite-dimensional approximations may need only a bounded number of pieces. Tensoring with a particular infinite-dimensional algebra may leave its isomorphism type unchanged.

The Toms–Winter program asks when these properties coincide. Family 291 claims the missing comparison-to-absorption implication in broad simple settings, a dimension-and-absorption equivalence beyond simplicity, and an equivariant version for amenable group actions. A fourth manuscript develops trace-splitting constructions underlying these regularity phenomena.

The four papers have different hypotheses. In particular, the dynamical theorem assumes the original algebra is already Jiang–Su stable, and the nonsimple dimension equivalence excludes elementary ideal subquotients. Keeping those restrictions visible is essential to understanding what has been claimed.

2. Background and essential definitions

A C*-algebra is a norm-closed algebra of operators closed under adjoints. It is simple if it has no nonzero proper closed two-sided ideals, and separable if a countable set is norm dense. Nuclearity means that its identity map admits finite-dimensional completely positive approximations. Completely positive maps preserve positivity even when applied entrywise to matrices.

The Jiang–Su algebra Z\mathcal ZZ is a distinguished simple, unital, infinite-dimensional C*-algebra whose standard classification invariant resembles that of the complex numbers. An algebra is Jiang–Su stable if

A≅A⊗Z.A\cong A\otimes\mathcal Z.A≅A⊗Z.

Tensor products are spatial unless explicitly marked maximal. Absorption expresses a strong internal regularity, not finite dimensionality.

For positive elements in A⊗KA\otimes\mathcal KA⊗K, where K\mathcal KK denotes compact operators, write a≾ba\precsim ba≾b if vj∗bvj→av_j^*bv_j\to avj∗​bvj​→a in norm for some sequence. This Cuntz comparison is a flexible version of fitting one positive operator inside another. Mutual comparison gives classes forming the ordered Cuntz semigroup Cu(A)\mathrm{Cu}(A)Cu(A), with addition and increasing suprema.

A trace τ\tauτ gives a rank-like quantity

dτ(a)=lim⁡n→∞τ(a1/n),d_\tau(a)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\tau(a^{1/n}),dτ​(a)=n→∞lim​τ(a1/n),

using the unnormalized matrix trace after stabilization. Traces and ranks may be infinite. Functionals on Cu(A)\mathrm{Cu}(A)Cu(A) preserve addition, order and increasing suprema, taking values in [0,∞][0,\infty][0,∞].

Nuclear dimension bounds the number of orthogonality-preserving pieces in finite-dimensional approximations. Dimension at most one means two such pieces suffice. Uniform property Gamma provides approximately central partitions splitting every coefficient trace evenly, simultaneously for all traces. Equal traces of the partition pieces alone are insufficient.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Jiang and Su introduced their algebra in the classification program. Rørdam showed that its absorption forces strong comparison properties. Toms and Winter linked absorption, finite nuclear dimension and strict comparison as three manifestations of regularity.

Winter established absorption from finite nuclear dimension in the simple setting. Work culminating in Castillejos–Evington–Tikuisis–White–Winter supplied the converse dimension bound, with Castillejos–Evington treating the nonunital simple case. Thus comparison-to-absorption was the remaining direction of the simple regularity triangle addressed here.

Matui–Sato proved that direction with finitely many extremal traces. Sato, Kirchberg–Rørdam and Toms–White–Winter extended methods to suitable compact finite-dimensional trace boundaries. Later uniform-Gamma criteria isolated the missing central divisibility: strict comparison plus uniform property Gamma yields absorption. Pointwise information at each trace was not enough; one construction had to work across the whole trace space.

Outside simplicity, ideals create new obstacles. A trace can be finite on one ideal and infinite elsewhere, and finite and purely infinite behavior can coexist. Robert–Tikuisis developed a nonsimple absorption strategy and identified central splitting conditions. Prior dimension-collapse results covered several special nonsimple classes, including purely infinite absorption and locally subhomogeneous settings.

For dynamics, Szabó proposed automatic equivariant Jiang–Su stability for amenable actions on already stable algebras. Szabó–Wouters established an equivariant uniform-Gamma criterion. M1 uses that existing absorption theorem after constructing invariant trace splittings without restricting how the action moves traces.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: comparison gives absorption

For a separable simple nuclear non-elementary algebra, M2 claims that strict comparison implies Jiang–Su stability, including nonunital algebras and unbounded traces. “Non-elementary” excludes algebras of compact operators on any Hilbert space.

Its precise extended-functional comparison convention says that x≤yx\leq yx≤y follows whenever every functional fff satisfies f(x)≤f(y)f(x)\leq f(y)f(x)≤f(y), with strict inequality whenever 0<f(y)<∞0<f(y)<\infty0<f(y)<∞. Zero and infinite target values therefore remain part of the convention; they are not discarded by normalizing traces.

More generally, for separable nuclear algebras, M2 obtains absorption from almost unperforation and full almost divisibility:

(ℓ+1)x≤ℓy⟹x≤y,(\ell+1)x\leq\ell y\Longrightarrow x\leq y,(ℓ+1)x≤ℓy⟹x≤y,

and, for every positive integer NNN and class xxx, existence of one class uuu satisfying

Nu≤x≤(N+1)u.Nu\leq x\leq(N+1)u.Nu≤x≤(N+1)u.

The same uuu must satisfy both inequalities. As a consequence, M2 claims

A≅A⊗Z⟺Cu(A)≅Cu(A⊗Z)A\cong A\otimes\mathcal Z\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathrm{Cu}(A)\cong\mathrm{Cu}(A\otimes\mathcal Z)A≅A⊗Z⟺Cu(A)≅Cu(A⊗Z)

for separable nuclear AAA. The right-hand isomorphism may be abstract in the Cuntz-semigroup category, preserving its full order and supremum structure; it need not come from a *-homomorphism. The canonical first-factor map is a special case.

M3: nonsimple dimension collapses to at most one

For separable nuclear AAA with no nonzero elementary ideal subquotient, M3 claims equivalence of finite nuclear dimension, Jiang–Su stability, and nuclear dimension at most one. An ideal subquotient is I/JI/JI/J for ideals J⊆I⊆AJ\subseteq I\subseteq AJ⊆I⊆A; the excluded elementary algebras are K(H)\mathcal K(H)K(H).

The broader dimension statement is

dim⁡nuc(A0⊗Z)≤1\dim_{\mathrm{nuc}}(A_0\otimes\mathcal Z)\leq1dimnuc​(A0​⊗Z)≤1

for every separable nuclear A0A_0A0​. The exclusion is needed for the reverse implication from finite dimension to absorption: a matrix algebra has dimension zero but does not absorb Z\mathcal ZZ.

M3 also gives an independent splitting theorem: a nonzero unital C*-algebra without characters has two full orthogonal positive elements in some finite maximal tensor power. A character is a nonzero *-homomorphism to C\mathbb CC, and “full” means generating the whole algebra as an ideal. This auxiliary theorem assumes neither nuclearity nor separability.

M4: three routes to central trace splitting

For simple separable unital infinite-dimensional nuclear stably finite AAA with traces, M4 claims that real rank zero of the uniform tracial ultrapower of its uniform tracial completion implies uniform property Gamma. Real rank zero means norm approximation of self-adjoint elements by finite-spectrum ones. The completion and ultrapower are specified constructions, not interchangeable with an arbitrary norm ultrapower.

Independently, M4 proves the unital strict-comparison-to-absorption implication. Its traceless case uses comparison with every nonzero positive target; absence of traces alone is not the hypothesis.

A third route treats simple separable nuclear stably projectionless algebras: every densely finite lower-semicontinuous trace must be bounded, the normalized trace base must be nonempty and compact, and comparison is tested on rays with positive finite target rank. Under these conditions M4 claims uniform Gamma and absorption. This route does not assume the real-rank-zero condition of the first theorem.

M1: absorb the trivial action

Let AAA be simple, separable, unital, infinite-dimensional, nuclear, stably finite and already Jiang–Su stable. For every action α\alphaα of a countable discrete amenable group, M1 claims cocycle conjugacy to α⊗idZ\alpha\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal Z}α⊗idZ​.

Concretely, there are an isomorphism Φ:A→A⊗Z\Phi:A\to A\otimes\mathcal ZΦ:A→A⊗Z and unitaries ugu_gug​ satisfying, with βg=αg⊗id\beta_g=\alpha_g\otimes\mathrm{id}βg​=αg​⊗id,

ugh=ugβg(uh),Φαg=Ad⁡(ug)βgΦ.u_{gh}=u_g\beta_g(u_h),\qquad\Phi\alpha_g=\operatorname{Ad}(u_g)\beta_g\Phi.ugh​=ug​βg​(uh​),Φαg​=Ad(ug​)βg​Φ.

Here Ad⁡(u)(x)=uxu∗\operatorname{Ad}(u)(x)=uxu^*Ad(u)(x)=uxu∗. No outerness, Rokhlin, UCT, trace-boundary or trace-orbit restriction is imposed. The theorem resolves the unital stably finite case of the equivariant conjecture, not its entire nonunital formulation.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, these results connect numerical order, approximation complexity, tensorial regularity and dynamics across a large portion of nuclear C*-algebra theory. The comparison implication completes the simple regularity triangle under the stated conventions, while the nonsimple theorem incorporates arbitrary ideal structure subject to its elementary-subquotient exclusion.

The dimension bound is striking: after absorbing Z\mathcal ZZ, arbitrarily complicated separable nuclear input would admit two-piece approximations. This is a statement about noncommutative approximation dimension, not the ordinary dimension of a space underlying every algebra.

The dynamical result adds that regularity can coexist with arbitrary amenable symmetries in the specified finite unital setting. It does not require choosing an action that leaves each trace fixed.

6. The main idea

Convert numerical divisibility into central structure

M2 first turns comparison into division of Cuntz classes. In nonunital settings it measures rounding errors against one fixed spectral cut with controlled support rank. This accommodates unbounded traces without pretending that a compact normalized trace space always exists.

Nuclear approximations and positive maps preserving orthogonality then produce central matrix structures. Separate arguments handle visibility in ideals and largeness in traces. Packing those structures yields a copy of Z\mathcal ZZ in the appropriate central-sequence quotient, which gives absorption.

Assemble approximations across ideals and traces

M3 localizes finite-dimensional approximations in hereditary corners, rounds weights and compares positive elements with extended rank functions. Two weighted conjugacies produce the two-color dimension bound. For the reverse implication, a finite tensor splitting construction supplies full orthogonal central elements, feeding the established Robert–Tikuisis absorption criterion.

M4 works directly with projections and coefficient identities. Nuclear averaging and controlled packing make trace splittings central. Conditional central-limit arguments and bounded truncations preserve uniform estimates over all traces. Its three routes supply their own hypotheses and constructions; they are not one theorem with freely interchangeable assumptions.

Make the splitting invariant under the action

M1 places many commuting orbit algebras in a uniform tracial central-sequence algebra. Their trace distributions permit a central-limit construction. Amenability provides finite Følner sets whose boundaries are small relative to their size.

A covariance-normalized quadratic construction prevents degeneracy even when orbit variables are highly correlated. It produces almost invariant distributions uniformly across the trace space. Diagonal selections give invariant equal-trace central projections, establishing equivariant uniform Gamma. The existing Szabó–Wouters theorem supplies the final cocycle-conjugacy step.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Nuclearity and separability remain central hypotheses of the main absorption and dimension results. Simple strict comparison is not the same as merely comparing a selected family of bounded traces. M2 explicitly uses the extended functional cone; M4’s projectionless theorem states its own finite-target-rank convention and compact-base assumptions.

M3’s elementary-subquotient exclusion cannot be omitted from the finite-dimension-to-absorption implication. Its abstract Cuntz-semigroup equivalences invoke M2. The independent maximal-tensor splitting theorem should not be confused with spatial tensor products throughout the main nuclear statements.

M1 assumes existing Jiang–Su stability and proves cocycle conjugacy, allowing the specified unitary correction. It does not assert literal conjugacy with no cocycle, extend to nonamenable groups, or settle the nonunital equivariant case. These boundaries remain part of the mathematical question after the claimed advances.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Castillejos and collaborators, Nuclear dimension of simple C*-algebras, for the earlier simple dimension theorem.
  • Robert and Tikuisis, Nuclear dimension and Z-stability of non-simple C*-algebras, for the nonsimple absorption framework.
  • Szabó and Wouters, Equivariant property Gamma and the tracial local-to-global principle for C*-dynamics, for the absorption criterion used by M1.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Equivariant Jiang–Su Stability for Amenable Actions in the Unital Stably Finite Case (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Cuntz comparison and Jiang–Su absorption (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Nuclear dimension and Jiang–Su stability without elementary subquotients (September 23, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Tracial projection methods and uniform property Gamma (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A concrete algebra that cannot fit inside any nuclear norm ultrapower
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 292 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A complicated object can sometimes be placed inside a simpler universal one. For operator algebras, the Cuntz algebra O2\mathcal O_2O2​ plays a remarkable universal role: every separable unital exact C*-algebra embeds into it.

What if exactness is dropped, but the target is enlarged to an ultrapower? An ultrapower allows an entire sequence of approximate realizations to act as one limiting realization. Kirchberg’s embedding problem asks whether every separable unital C*-algebra embeds into O2ω\mathcal O_2^\omegaO2ω​.

Family 292 claims an explicit negative answer. Its example is the full C*-algebra of a countable group defined using dyadic rational translations, integer matrices and dilation by two. The obstruction is stronger than failure for O2\mathcal O_2O2​: the same algebra cannot embed unitally into the norm ultrapower of any nonzero unital nuclear C*-algebra.

2. Background and essential definitions

A C*-algebra is a complete normed algebra with an adjoint operation satisfying ∥a∗a∥=∥a∥2\|a^*a\|=\|a\|^2∥a∗a∥=∥a∥2. An embedding is an injective *-homomorphism. “Unital” additionally requires the identity to map to the identity.
