For a discrete group GGG, the full group C-algebra* C∗(G)C^*(G)C∗(G) completes its complex group ring using all unitary representations. This differs from the reduced algebra, which uses only the regular translation representation. The full completion is part of the theorem’s hypothesis.

The Cuntz algebra O2\mathcal O_2O2​ is generated by two isometries s1,s2s_1,s_2s1​,s2​ with

si∗si=1,s1s1∗+s2s2∗=1.s_i^*s_i=1,\qquad s_1s_1^*+s_2s_2^*=1.si∗​si​=1,s1​s1∗​+s2​s2∗​=1.

Each isometry copies the entire space into one of two orthogonal ranges. This makes O2\mathcal O_2O2​ very different from a finite matrix algebra.

A free ultrafilter ω\omegaω on the positive integers chooses a coherent notion of which infinite sets of indices are large. The norm ultrapower is

Bω=ℓ∞(N,B)/{(bn):lim⁡ω∥bn∥=0}.B^\omega=\ell^\infty(\mathbb N,B)\big/\{(b_n):\lim_\omega\|b_n\|=0\}.Bω=ℓ∞(N,B)/{(bn​):ωlim​∥bn​∥=0}.

Thus bounded sequences differing by an operator-norm-null sequence represent the same element. The quotient uses operator norm, not a trace-based quadratic norm.

Nuclearity means that finite sets of algebra elements admit arbitrarily accurate factorizations through finite-dimensional algebras by completely positive maps. Exactness means that spatial tensoring preserves short exact sequences. Nuclearity implies exactness, but they are not the same property. A subalgebra of a nuclear algebra can be exact without itself being nuclear.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kirchberg–Phillips’s embedding theorem established the universality of O2\mathcal O_2O2​ for separable exact algebras. The ultrapower question asks whether sequences in this one nuclear algebra can represent algebras beyond that class. Nonexactness alone does not settle the ultrapower problem: ultrapowers have different permanence behavior from a single copy of the target.

Goldbring and Sinclair studied the problem using model theory. They connected a positive answer with good nuclear witnesses, a local condition asking whether satisfiable finite norm constraints can be realized by tuples admitting good nuclear approximations. They also related the question to existentially closed algebras, in which passing to an extension cannot improve finite existential tests.

More recent approaches explored computability and tensor norms. The source discusses computability consequences obtained by Fox–Goldbring–Hart and a conditional tensor-norm route of Goldbring–Sinclair. M1 instead claims a direct representation-theoretic obstruction from a specified group.

That group configuration has predecessors. De Cornulier recorded the property-(T) affine group and its finite-index dilation maps. Sauers and Eckhardt used related constructions to show nonfiniteness of full group algebras and to construct non-MF groups, meaning groups that cannot be represented faithfully by asymptotic finite matrices in the relevant norm sense.

Those facts alone do not answer the present question. A proper isometry obstructs finiteness, but O2\mathcal O_2O2​ already contains proper isometries. Failure of approximation by matrices also does not automatically imply failure of embedding into a nuclear algebra’s norm ultrapower. M1 adds a finiteness principle for approximate representation types inside arbitrary nuclear targets.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let

G=Z[1/2]3⋊(SL3(Z)×Z),G=\mathbb Z[1/2]^3\rtimes\bigl(\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb Z)\times\mathbb Z\bigr),G=Z[1/2]3⋊(SL3​(Z)×Z),

where Z[1/2]\mathbb Z[1/2]Z[1/2] consists of rational numbers whose denominators are powers of two. The action is

(M,k)⋅v=2kMv.(M,k)\cdot v=2^kMv.(M,k)⋅v=2kMv.

Here MMM is an integer three-by-three matrix of determinant one, and kkk is an integer dilation parameter. The semidirect product combines translations with these linear transformations; explicitly,

(v,M,k)(w,N,ℓ)=(v+2kMw,MN,k+ℓ).(v,M,k)(w,N,\ell)=(v+2^kMw,MN,k+\ell).(v,M,k)(w,N,ℓ)=(v+2kMw,MN,k+ℓ).

M1 states that the separable unital algebra A=C∗(G)A=C^*(G)A=C∗(G) has no unital embedding into BωB^\omegaBω for any nonzero unital nuclear complex C*-algebra BBB and any free ultrafilter on N\mathbb NN. No separability assumption is imposed on BBB. The group is fixed independently of both the target and the ultrafilter.

Taking B=O2B=\mathcal O_2B=O2​ gives the negative answer to Kirchberg’s embedding problem. The source recalls that the universal question formulated without unit preservation is equivalent to its unital formulation. Its stronger arbitrary-target theorem is explicitly stated for unital embeddings.

Using established model-theoretic equivalences, M1 derives three further consequences. No exact or nuclear unital C*-algebra is existentially closed among all unital C*-algebra extensions. Embeddability into O2ω\mathcal O_2^\omegaO2ω​ can fail after taking a crossed product by an action of Z\mathbb ZZ. And some satisfiable finite norm condition lacks good nuclear witnesses, with a fixed positive approximation-error obstruction for every realizing tuple.

The last two witnesses are existential consequences of the equivalences. M1 does not identify them explicitly through the displayed group construction.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this fixes a fundamental limit of nuclear universality. Allowing infinitely many norm-approximate realizations in a nuclear algebra still would not accommodate every separable C*-algebra.

The explicit source algebra makes the claim particularly informative. Its obstruction is encoded by familiar ingredients—integer matrices, dyadic translations and a finite-index self-embedding—rather than only by a nonconstructive existence argument. At the same time, the theorem treats every nuclear target, not just the special geometry of O2\mathcal O_2O2​.

The consequences also show that local approximation and global embeddability interact with algebraic operations. Even a crossed product by the amenable group Z\mathbb ZZ can leave the class of embeddable algebras. This is a limitation of that class, not a claim that nuclear algebras themselves fail their defining approximation property.

6. The main idea

A rigid group with a shrinking translation lattice

Inside GGG, consider

Γ=Z3⋊SL3(Z).\Gamma=\mathbb Z^3\rtimes\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb Z).Γ=Z3⋊SL3​(Z).

It has property (T): sufficiently almost invariant unit vectors in a unitary representation force an actual invariant vector. The map θ(v,M)=(2v,M)\theta(v,M)=(2v,M)θ(v,M)=(2v,M) embeds Γ\GammaΓ as a subgroup of index eight. In the larger group, conjugating by the dilation generator implements θ\thetaθ.

Choose a finite-dimensional irreducible representation π∗\pi_*π∗​ that factors through reduction modulo two and is nontrivial on translations. Every positive iterate of θ\thetaθ makes its translation action trivial after that reduction, so π∗\pi_*π∗​ cannot be equivalent to π∗∘θj\pi_*\circ\theta^jπ∗​∘θj for j≥1j\geq1j≥1. This is a built-in nonperiodicity condition.

Nuclearity permits only finitely many approximate matches

Assume an ultrapower embedding exists and choose unitary representatives in BBB for its group elements. At each coordinate, the representatives satisfy group relations only approximately. Treating them as genuine representations would lose an essential part of the problem.

M1 tests a coordinate tuple against finite-dimensional irreducible representations using a spectral measure of how nearly the corresponding tensor-product operators have invariant vectors. Property (T) supplies a gap separating matches from nonmatches.

The new finiteness lemma says that, inside a nuclear algebra, only finitely many representation classes can pass the chosen test at one coordinate. Its estimate works for arbitrary unitary tuples without requiring exact group relations. It also controls varying matrix dimensions, since the representation class may change with the coordinate.

Finite chains contradict nonperiodicity

Faithfulness ensures that π∗\pi_*π∗​ appears among the approximate matches on an ultrafilter-large set of coordinates. The dilation relation and finite-index induction force every matched representation to have a predecessor in the same finite set, with predecessor defined through composition with θ\thetaθ.

Iterating predecessors must eventually revisit a representation. M1’s representation-theoretic argument converts that repetition into periodicity of π∗\pi_*π∗​ under a positive iterate of θ\thetaθ, contradicting its construction.

The logical hinge is simultaneous control at one coordinate. A separate approximation for each representation would not produce a finite closed chain on which the contradiction could operate. The dimension-independent spectral estimate and nuclear finiteness lemma provide that uniformity.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

This is a norm-ultrapower embedding question. It is distinct from Connes’ embedding problem for tracial von Neumann algebras and from the tensor-norm formulation often also called Kirchberg’s conjecture. Their names and connections do not make them interchangeable.

The explicit algebra is the full group C*-algebra. The theorem does not automatically transfer to the reduced completion, to nonnuclear targets, or to every type of sequence quotient. The target may be nonseparable, but must be nonzero, unital and nuclear; the ultrapower is indexed by N\mathbb NN.

The example’s nonfiniteness and earlier non-MF constructions are context, not sufficient substitutes for the new obstruction. Conversely, failure to embed here does not prevent representations on Hilbert spaces, which every C*-algebra possesses.

The model-theoretic corollaries establish existence of additional obstructions without explicit witnesses. Producing concrete crossed-product examples and concrete finite norm conditions realizing those consequences would add information beyond the source’s stated construction.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Goldbring and Sinclair, On Kirchberg’s Embedding Problem, for the norm-ultrapower formulation and model-theoretic equivalences.
  • Eckhardt, Non-MF groups and non-finite full group C*-algebras, for the earlier group configuration and the distinct nonfiniteness obstruction.
  • M1 specifies the finite-dimensional representation, the nuclear approximate-matching lemma, and which consequences are explicit versus existential.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An explicit obstruction to nuclear norm-ultrapower embeddings (September 23, 2026).

entry.title: Can every bounded representation be made to respect adjoints?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 288 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Matrices carry two kinds of structure: multiplication and the adjoint operation, which transposes a matrix and conjugates its entries. A map can preserve multiplication without preserving adjoints. Sometimes the apparent mismatch comes only from using the wrong inner product.

Kadison’s similarity problem asks whether this is always the explanation for a bounded representation of a C*-algebra. Can one bounded, invertible change of coordinates make every represented adjoint correct simultaneously?

Family 288 claims a positive answer without restrictions on the algebra or the Hilbert space beyond the stated complex, unital setting. Its central estimate also gives a universal way to measure how close an operator is to an arbitrary von Neumann algebra by testing how badly it mixes invariant subspaces.

2. Background and essential definitions

A C-algebra* is a complete normed algebra with an adjoint operation satisfying ∥a∗a∥=∥a∥2\|a^*a\|=\|a\|^2∥a∗a∥=∥a∥2. Bounded operators on a Hilbert space form a basic example. A unital algebra homomorphism π:A→B(H)\pi:A\to B(H)π:A→B(H) preserves multiplication, complex linear combinations and the identity. Boundedness means that one constant controls ∥π(a)∥\|\pi(a)\|∥π(a)∥ by ∥a∥\|a\|∥a∥.

An adjoint-preserving homomorphism additionally satisfies π(a∗)=π(a)∗\pi(a^*)=\pi(a)^*π(a∗)=π(a)∗. Two representations are similar if one is obtained from the other by conjugating with a bounded invertible operator SSS:

ρ(a)=Sπ(a)S−1.\rho(a)=S\pi(a)S^{-1}.ρ(a)=Sπ(a)S−1.

Such a change corresponds to replacing the original Hilbert norm by the equivalent norm ∥ξ∥S=∥Sξ∥\|\xi\|_S=\|S\xi\|∥ξ∥S​=∥Sξ∥. “Equivalent” means that each norm bounds the other by fixed constants; it excludes a singular or unbounded change of geometry.

For a linear map uuu, its matrix amplification u(n)u^{(n)}u(n) applies uuu entry by entry to nnn-by-nnn matrices. It is completely bounded if

∥u∥cb=sup⁡n≥1∥u(n)∥<∞.\|u\|_{\mathrm{cb}}=\sup_{n\geq1}\|u^{(n)}\|<\infty.∥u∥cb​=n≥1sup​∥u(n)∥<∞.

Ordinary boundedness controls individual elements. Complete boundedness additionally controls all finite matrix arrangements of elements with one constant. The distinction is central to the problem.

A derivation behaves like differentiation of a product: for a represented algebra, d(ab)=d(a)π(b)+π(a)d(b)d(ab)=d(a)\pi(b)+\pi(a)d(b)d(ab)=d(a)π(b)+π(a)d(b). It is inner if it has the form d(a)=Yπ(a)−π(a)Yd(a)=Y\pi(a)-\pi(a)Yd(a)=Yπ(a)−π(a)Y. The difference [Y,X]=YX−XY[Y,X]=YX-XY[Y,X]=YX−XY is called a commutator and measures failure to commute.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kadison formulated the similarity problem in 1955. The question concerns one simultaneous coordinate change for an entire representation, rather than separately adjusting each operator. Multiplicativity is a strong constraint, but ordinary boundedness does not directly provide the matrix-level estimates needed to construct that change.

Bunce and Christensen established the nuclear C*-algebra case. Nuclearity is a finite-dimensional approximation property, and it gives especially strong similarity estimates. Haagerup solved the cyclic representation case, where one vector generates a dense subspace under the representation, and linked similarity to complete boundedness. He also obtained the similarity property for C*-algebras without tracial states. Christensen covered type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factors with property Gamma, a condition providing suitable approximately central unitaries.

Paulsen’s similarity theorem gives the general completely bounded homomorphism criterion and controls the best similarity condition number. Christensen established the corresponding criterion for derivations. Kirchberg then connected the similarity property of a given C*-algebra with innerness of derivations in its faithful *-representations. These results turn the original coordinate question into a problem about uniform operator estimates.

Pisier organized quantitative versions using similarity degree and matrix factorization length. More recently, work of Eleftherakis and Paulsen connected the similarity problem to hyperreflexivity of von Neumann algebras: whether distance to an algebra can be controlled by invariant-subspace tests.

The remaining difficulty addressed by M1 is uniformity across finite factors and their representations. Good estimates for a fixed matrix size or a favorable cyclic representation do not automatically survive arbitrary multiplicity and unbounded matrix size.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Similarity in the unrestricted unital setting

M1 states that for every unital complex C*-algebra AAA, every complex Hilbert space HHH, and every bounded complex-linear unital algebra homomorphism π:A→B(H)\pi:A\to B(H)π:A→B(H), there is a bounded invertible SSS such that

Sπ(a∗)S−1=(Sπ(a)S−1)∗S\pi(a^*)S^{-1}=\bigl(S\pi(a)S^{-1}\bigr)^*Sπ(a∗)S−1=(Sπ(a)S−1)∗

for every a∈Aa\in Aa∈A.

There is no separability, nuclearity, finite-generation, faithfulness or normality assumption. The operator SSS may depend on the whole homomorphism. The headline theorem asserts existence; it does not state an optimal universal bound for ∥S∥∥S−1∥\|S\|\|S^{-1}\|∥S∥∥S−1∥.

A uniform estimate at every matrix size

For a represented unital von Neumann algebra P⊆B(K)P\subseteq B(K)P⊆B(K), define

gP(Y)=sup⁡a∈P, ∥a∥≤1∥Ya−aY∥.g_P(Y)=\sup_{a\in P,\,\|a\|\leq1}\|Ya-aY\|.gP​(Y)=a∈P,∥a∥≤1sup​∥Ya−aY∥.

M1 claims an absolute constant C<∞C<\inftyC<∞ such that, for every positive integer hhh and every matrix X∈Mh(P)X\in M_h(P)X∈Mh​(P),

∥[Y(h),X]∥≤C gP(Y) ∥X∥.\|[Y^{(h)},X]\|\leq C\,g_P(Y)\,\|X\|.∥[Y(h),X]∥≤CgP​(Y)∥X∥.

Here Y(h)Y^{(h)}Y(h) is diagonal repetition of YYY on KhK^hKh. The constant is independent of the algebra, its representation, the Hilbert space and hhh. Scalar commutator control therefore controls all amplifications.

A universal distance estimate

Let M′M'M′ denote the commutant of MMM, consisting of operators commuting with every element of MMM. For T∈B(H)T\in B(H)T∈B(H), set

αM(T)=sup⁡e=e∗=e2∈M′∥(1−e)Te∥.\alpha_M(T)=\sup_{e=e^*=e^2\in M'}\|(1-e)Te\|.αM​(T)=e=e∗=e2∈M′sup​∥(1−e)Te∥.

The projection eee selects a reducing subspace for MMM; the displayed block measures how much TTT sends that subspace outside itself. M1 states

dist⁡(T,M)≤2C αM(T).\operatorname{dist}(T,M)\leq2C\,\alpha_M(T).dist(T,M)≤2CαM​(T).

This is universal hyperreflexivity. No optimality of 2C2C2C is claimed.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem resolves a long-standing structural question about all bounded representations of C*-algebras. It says that a representation preserving algebraic multiplication cannot possess an irreparable mismatch with the adjoint, provided it is bounded.

The result also unifies different languages. Similarity is a coordinate-change problem; complete boundedness concerns matrices of operators; derivations express infinitesimal algebraic behavior; hyperreflexivity concerns distance detected by subspaces. M1’s universal estimate would connect all of them without special assumptions on the represented algebra.

The distance conclusion has an especially concrete interpretation. If an operator almost respects every reducing subspace of MMM, it lies close to an element of MMM, with a constant independent of the particular algebra. This is stronger than merely knowing which operators respect all those subspaces exactly.

6. The main idea

First control cyclic pieces

The argument begins with derivations between two representation spaces when the domain representation is cyclic. Combining row and column estimates produces a bounded implementing operator with controlled norm. This is a local building block: arbitrary representations need not be cyclic, but can be analyzed through collections of cyclic pieces.

The obstacle is preventing constants from growing when those pieces are combined or when the representation is amplified to large matrices. M1 devotes its central argument to a dimension-independent estimate in a finite tracial setting.

Enlarge the algebra with free variables

A tracial free product joins two operator algebras so that alternating centered products have trace zero. M1 uses one algebra assembled from increasing full matrix algebras and another arbitrary finite tracial algebra. Their free-product word structure supplies a Hilbert-space decomposition on which commutator information can be tracked.

The key intermediate statement starts with control in a small corner, cut out by a projection of trace 1/N1/N1/N, and concludes an estimate for compressed commutators with trace-zero self-adjoint unitaries. Crucially, its constant is independent of NNN.

Averaging over matrix unitary groups constrains the possible actions on words. Estimates on long words then propagate local control. The final comparison uses a Hankel matrix, whose entries depend on the sum of their indices; its lower bound cancels the small trace factors in the upper estimate. In the manuscript’s account, this cancellation prevents the bound from deteriorating as the corner becomes tiny.

Transfer the estimate and return to similarity

Popa’s relative independence theorem places the needed free-product configuration inside a tracial ultrapower after matrix amplification. An ultrapower packages a bounded sequence of approximations into a single limiting algebra. M1 passes the relevant operator through a Hilbert-space ultrapower and compresses it while retaining the required commutator data.

The argument next moves from separable finite factors to arbitrary normal factor representations, then uses central decomposition and separable reducing subspaces to remove the remaining restrictions. This is why the theorem’s arbitrary-Hilbert-space scope needs more than its initial tracial calculation.

Finally, cyclic implementations of a derivation are assembled using the uniform commutator bound. The derivation becomes completely bounded, established implementation results make it inner, and Kirchberg’s equivalence yields similarity. Applying the same estimate to a commutant gives the hyperreflexivity consequence through the standard commutant-distance formula.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The statement requires a bounded complex-linear unital algebra homomorphism from a unital complex C*-algebra. It does not assert that every algebraic representation is automatically bounded, nor that the original representation already preserves adjoints. The necessary similarity can be nonunitary.

A uniformly bounded representation of a discrete group is another matter. Such a representation automatically extends to the group’s ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1-algebra, but need not extend boundedly to its full or reduced group C*-algebra. Consequently M1’s theorem does not make every uniformly bounded group representation unitarizable. The manuscript explicitly separates that issue from Kadison similarity.

The universal constant concerns commutators and hyperreflexivity; the paper does not claim its optimal value or an optimal condition-number formula for the resulting similarity. Quantitative improvements and concrete construction of the best equivalent inner product remain distinct questions.

The exposition reports the uniform estimates and their stated dependencies. The passage through free products and ultrapowers is part of the manuscript’s argument, not an independent verification of the claimed solution.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Ozawa, An Invitation to the Similarity Problems, for the homomorphism, derivation and group-representation distinctions.
  • Eleftherakis and Paulsen, Hyperreflexivity of von Neumann algebras and similarity of finitely generated C*-algebras, for the hyperreflexivity connection discussed by M1.
  • M1’s introduction attributes the nuclear, cyclic, property-Gamma and complete-boundedness results and states the unrestricted hypotheses of its new estimate.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Kadison’s similarity theorem through uniform derivation estimates (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Operators with invariant subspaces but no hyperinvariant ones
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 293 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A matrix has invariant subspaces: subspaces that it maps into themselves. For a bounded operator on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, the general invariant-subspace question is much subtler. One can also ask for a subspace preserved by every operator commuting with the given operator. Such a subspace is called hyperinvariant.

Family 293 claims operators with no nontrivial closed hyperinvariant subspace. One manuscript obtains them from weighted irrational rotations with no invariant projection in a specified containing factor. The other gives a direct construction whose ordinary invariant subspaces are plainly present, while additional commuting operators prevent any of them from being hyperinvariant.

The distinction is essential. The family claims a negative answer to the hyperinvariant-subspace problem and a related transitive-algebra question. It does not claim a negative answer to the ordinary Hilbert-space invariant-subspace problem.

2. Background and essential definitions

A closed subspace L⊆HL\subseteq HL⊆H is invariant for T∈B(H)T\in B(H)T∈B(H) if T(L)⊆LT(L)\subseteq LT(L)⊆L. If ppp is its orthogonal projection, this is equivalent to

(1−p)Tp=0.(1-p)Tp=0.(1−p)Tp=0.

It does not require pT=TppT=TppT=Tp; that stronger condition would make both LLL and its orthogonal complement invariant.

The commutant of TTT is {T}′={A:AT=TA}\{T\}'=\{A:AT=TA\}{T}′={A:AT=TA}. Hyperinvariance requires invariance under every element of this commutant. An operator algebra is transitive when its only common closed invariant subspaces are zero and the whole Hilbert space. Thus a transitive commutant is precisely the absence of nontrivial hyperinvariant subspaces.

A bounded operator is norm-quasinilpotent if

lim⁡n→∞∥Tn∥1/n=0.\lim_{n\to\infty}\|T^n\|^{1/n}=0.n→∞lim​∥Tn∥1/n=0.

Its spectrum is then {0}\{0\}{0}. Unlike a finite-dimensional nilpotent matrix, it need not have a power that is exactly zero.

A type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factor MMM is a von Neumann algebra with scalar center and a normalized trace τ\tauτ, but no minimal nonzero projections. An invariant subspace is affiliated with MMM when its orthogonal projection lies in MMM. This restricts which invariant subspaces are being considered.

If T∈MT\in MT∈M, every hyperinvariant subspace has its projection in MMM. Indeed, the unitaries in the commutant M′M'M′, and their inverses, commute with TTT, so hyperinvariance makes the subspace reducing for them. Its projection therefore belongs to M′′=MM''=MM′′=M. Excluding affiliated invariant projections consequently excludes hyperinvariant subspaces, though it need not exclude all invariant subspaces.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Invariant-subspace theory has many positive results under additional assumptions. In finite factors, Brown measure supplies a spectral distribution for nonnormal operators. Haagerup–Schultz associate invariant projections to regions of the complex plane, with projection trace equal to the region’s Brown mass. A Brown measure that is not concentrated at one point therefore gives a nontrivial projection.

The point-mass case is not settled by that construction. It does not automatically have no invariant subspaces: Dykema–Haagerup’s quasinilpotent DT-operator has a rich family of affiliated hyperinvariant subspaces, and Tucci constructed other quasinilpotent examples with invariant projections.

For weighted irrational rotations, earlier work identifies Brown measure as uniform measure on a circle with radius given by the weight’s Fuglede–Kadison determinant. Zhu, Fang and Shi studied the zero-determinant case and asked whether nontrivial affiliated invariant subspaces must still exist. They had already exhibited continuous one-zero weights with zero determinant. M1 adds the claimed exclusion of every invariant projection for suitable such weights.

A second history connects hyperinvariance with transitive algebras. Arveson’s density theorem says that a transitive algebra containing a maximal abelian self-adjoint subalgebra of B(H)B(H)B(H) is strongly dense in B(H)B(H)B(H). M2’s scalar multipliers have infinite multiplicity and are not maximal abelian in B(H)B(H)B(H), so that hypothesis does not apply.

Classical work of Domar and Grabiner analyzes shifts with tightly ordered invariant-subspace lattices. M2 uses those ideas while coupling different fibers through an additional commuting operator. The source also notes that a Kérchy–Pearcy preprint claiming an equivalence between ordinary invariance and hyperinvariance was withdrawn. Such an equivalence is not used here.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: a counterexample at every irrational angle

Fix any irrational θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1)θ∈(0,1). In the irrational-rotation factor RθR_\thetaRθ​, let the generating unitaries satisfy

VU=e2πiθUV.VU=e^{2\pi i\theta}UV.VU=e2πiθUV.

M1 constructs a continuous weight f:T→[0,1]f:\mathbb T\to[0,1]f:T→[0,1], on the unit circle, such that

f−1(0)={1},∫Tlog⁡f dm=−∞,f^{-1}(0)=\{1\},\qquad \int_{\mathbb T}\log f\,dm=-\infty,f−1(0)={1},∫T​logfdm=−∞,

where mmm is normalized circle measure. Nevertheless, for T=Uf(V)T=Uf(V)T=Uf(V), every projection p∈Rθp\in R_\thetap∈Rθ​ satisfying (1−p)Tp=0(1-p)Tp=0(1−p)Tp=0 is zero or one.

The angle is prescribed before the weight is chosen; no Diophantine restriction is imposed. The operator is nonzero and norm-quasinilpotent. The logarithmic integral means that the determinant exp⁡(∫log⁡f dm)\exp(\int\log f\,dm)exp(∫logfdm) is zero, although fff is positive almost everywhere.

By the projection observation above, M1 obtains a nonzero norm-quasinilpotent operator with no nontrivial hyperinvariant subspace on every separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space.

M2: an explicit mechanism with ordinary invariant tails

M2 works on

H0=L2(Z2;ℓ2(Z)),H_0=L^2(\mathbb Z_2;\ell^2(\mathbb Z)),H0​=L2(Z2​;ℓ2(Z)),

where Z2\mathbb Z_2Z2​ is the compact probability group of 2-adic integers, not the two-element group. Its translation x↦x+1x\mapsto x+1x↦x+1 is an ergodic probability-preserving transformation.

The operator acts fiberwise as a weighted bilateral shift,

Sxej=βj(x)ej+1,βj(x)>0.S_xe_j=\beta_j(x)e_{j+1},\qquad \beta_j(x)>0.Sx​ej​=βj​(x)ej+1​,βj​(x)>0.

M2 states that every fiber’s closed invariant subspaces are exactly the coordinate tails K≥hK_{\geq h}K≥h​, together with zero and the full fiber. It also gives

∥S∥=e−10,∥Sn∥≤exp⁡(−10⌊(n+1)24⌋).\|S\|=e^{-10},\qquad\|S^n\|\leq\exp\left(-10\left\lfloor\frac{(n+1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor\right).∥S∥=e−10,∥Sn∥≤exp(−10⌊4(n+1)2​⌋).

A bounded contraction VVV commutes with SSS, transports the base point from xxx to x+1x+1x+1, and moves fiber coordinates backward. Together with all scalar multiplication operators and SSS, it generates a transitive algebra.

Hence {S}′\{S\}'{S}′ is a proper strongly closed unital transitive algebra. This also contradicts the assertion that every unital transitive operator algebra must be strongly dense in B(H)B(H)B(H). Ordinary invariant subspaces remain: every fixed tail space L2(Z2;K≥h)L^2(\mathbb Z_2;K_{\geq h})L2(Z2​;K≥h​) is invariant under SSS.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, these constructions resolve the hyperinvariant-subspace problem negatively and establish a sharp separation between invariance under one operator and invariance under all its commuting symmetries.

The rotation result also answers a specific question inside the hyperfinite factor, one of the most tractable infinite-dimensional operator algebras. It shows that zero-determinant weighted rotations can behave more radically than the existence of earlier quasinilpotent examples suggested.

M2 makes the mechanism understandable: ordinary invariant tails exist in abundance, but a commuting operator pushes them in a direction incompatible with a globally invariant measurable choice. Its explicit power bound additionally controls the whole operator, not merely its individual fibers.

6. The main idea

Force a projection to contradict weighted orthogonality

M1 first constructs a measurable weight. If an invariant projection existed, the shift representation would express it as a measurable field of projections. Finite trace and ergodicity force its central diagonal coordinate strictly between zero and one almost everywhere. Both the projection and its complement therefore contain vectors with nonzero central coordinates.

Invariance imposes weighted orthogonality identities. The constructed weight has rare but very deep drops: a selected finite window remains controlled, while sufficiently distant terms are strongly suppressed. A finite convolution coefficient forced by the central coordinates cannot be canceled by the suppressed tail, contradicting the identity.

The source then smooths and rearranges the logarithmic drops to obtain a continuous weight with exactly one zero. The change is expressed through a measurable coboundary and an intertwining multiplier, possibly unbounded. A separate domain-and-trace argument transfers any hypothetical invariant projection back to the measurable model. This transfer is needed; smoothing alone would not preserve the obstruction automatically.

Couple forward shifts to a backward operator

M2 chooses weights whose logarithms have controlled quadratic behavior at both ends of the bilateral sequence. This gives the stated classification of fiber invariant subspaces and the uniform decay of powers.

To construct the backward intertwiner, write its fiber action as Vxej=bj(x)ej−1V_xe_j=b_j(x)e_{j-1}Vx​ej​=bj​(x)ej−1​. Requiring VS=SVVS=SVVS=SV determines a recurrence for the coefficients. Opposite logarithmic changes at the two ends make the solution decay in both directions. A measurable normalization produces one bounded contraction over the entire probability space.

A tail cannot move downward forever in distribution

A subspace invariant under all scalar multipliers has a measurable projection field. Invariance under SSS then makes each fiber a tail, described by a measurable label h(x)h(x)h(x) taking integer values or the symbols for full and zero fibers.

The backward intertwiner forces

h(x+1)≤h(x)−1h(x+1)\leq h(x)-1h(x+1)≤h(x)−1

where the label is finite. Probability preservation rules out this perpetual strict descent for an integer-valued measurable label. Ergodicity rules out mixing full and zero fibers nontrivially. Only the whole space and zero remain.

All the operators used in this transitivity argument commute with SSS. Thus their lack of a common invariant subspace excludes a hyperinvariant subspace for SSS, even though SSS alone preserves the fixed coordinate tails.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 excludes invariant projections inside the specified rotation factor. It does not exclude arbitrary invariant projections in B(H)B(H)B(H). M2 explicitly retains ordinary invariant tails, so the ordinary invariant-subspace problem remains outside the conclusion.

The nonzero quasinilpotent operators are nonscalar, ensuring their commutants are proper. Strong closedness means closure under pointwise norm convergence on vectors; the resulting transitive algebras are not claimed to be self-adjoint. Arveson’s theorem is avoided by failure of its maximal-abelian hypothesis, not by contradicting that theorem.

The two constructions are different. M2 imports only the elementary commutant and measurable-field facts identified in its introduction from M1; M1 uses no result from M2. The quantitative power bound belongs to the 2-adic construction, not automatically to every rotation example.

Both sources used here are dated September 27. Their claims are reported with these precise distinctions between factor affiliation, ordinary invariance and hyperinvariance.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Haagerup and Schultz, Invariant Subspaces for Operators in a General II1-factor, for the Brown-measure projection theorem.
  • Kérchy and Pearcy, Hyperinvariant subspaces of block-triangular operators on Hilbert space, whose withdrawal notice is relevant to the distinction discussed above.
  • M1 cites the original Zhu–Fang–Shi question and earlier quasinilpotent examples; M2 specifies its weighted-translation criterion and its relation to Arveson’s density theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Invariant-projection counterexamples for every irrational rotation (September 27, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Backward intertwiners and a transitive commutant (September 27, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A quasitrace that cannot be a trace—and finite algebras with an infinite tensor product
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 294 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

The trace of a matrix measures size additively: Tr⁡(a+b)=Tr⁡(a)+Tr⁡(b)\operatorname{Tr}(a+b)=\operatorname{Tr}(a)+\operatorname{Tr}(b)Tr(a+b)=Tr(a)+Tr(b). It also assigns the same value to x∗xx^*xx∗x and xx∗xx^*xx∗. In more general operator algebras, a quasitrace retains positivity and this symmetry, but initially requires additivity only for commuting operators.

Does compatibility with two-by-two matrices force full additivity? Kaplansky’s quasitrace problem asks whether these weaker size functions must actually be traces. Family 294 claims a negative answer, with a fixed pair of positive operators witnessing a definite additive defect for every normalized 2-quasitrace on the example.

An established chain of implications then yields another striking conclusion: two simple stably finite C*-algebras can have a properly infinite spatial tensor product. The paper distinguishes several different algebras used for these conclusions; no single example is asserted to have every listed property.

2. Background and essential definitions

A C*-algebra is a norm-complete adjoint algebra satisfying ∥x∗x∥=∥x∥2\|x^*x\|=\|x\|^2∥x∗x∥=∥x∥2. A tracial state is a positive linear functional τ\tauτ with τ(1)=1\tau(1)=1τ(1)=1 and τ(xy)=τ(yx)\tau(xy)=\tau(yx)τ(xy)=τ(yx). It is a normalized analogue of matrix trace.

A quasitrace is positive on positive elements, respects τ(x∗x)=τ(xx∗)\tau(x^*x)=\tau(xx^*)τ(x∗x)=τ(xx∗), is linear on commutative subalgebras, and is compatible with real and imaginary parts. A 2-quasitrace additionally extends consistently to M2(A)M_2(A)M2​(A). Its extension takes value two on the two-by-two identity when the original quasitrace takes value one on 1A1_A1A​. This is an unnormalized matrix extension.

An isometry satisfies v∗v=1v^*v=1v∗v=1. It is unitary if also vv∗=1vv^*=1vv∗=1. An algebra is finite if every isometry is unitary, and stably finite if this holds in every finite matrix algebra over it. It is properly infinite if it contains two isometries with orthogonal ranges, so that two full copies of its unit fit inside the unit.

“No matrix algebra is properly infinite” is weaker than stable finiteness. It excludes two orthogonal full copies at every matrix size, but does not by definition exclude every individual nonunitary isometry. This distinction matters for the constructed algebra.

An AW-algebra* has an intrinsic projection structure modeled on von Neumann algebras. Kaplansky asked whether every type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ AW*-factor is a von Neumann algebra. Here that means an abstract W*-algebra admitting a Banach-space predual, not merely an algebra given some representation on a Hilbert space. The finite-factor question is equivalent to the general 2-quasitrace problem used by the manuscript.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kaplansky introduced AW*-algebras in 1951 to describe operator-algebra structure without choosing a Hilbert-space representation. The factor types behave differently: type I AW*-factors are W*-algebras, while type III counterexamples exist. The type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ question isolates the finite case.

Cuntz’s dimension functions and the work of Blackadar–Handelman connected quasitraces with size and comparison of positive operators. A key existence theorem says that a unital algebra admits a normalized 2-quasitrace if no matrix algebra over it is properly infinite. This offers a route to a counterexample: arrange that obstruction to proper infiniteness while separately ruling out tracial states.

Haagerup proved that 2-quasitraces on unital exact C*-algebras are traces. Exactness is a tensor-product preservation property satisfied by nuclear algebras and many other examples. His argument circulated from 1991 and was published in 2014. Therefore any counterexample to full additivity must lie outside exactness.

The matrix-extension requirement cannot be skipped. A previously reported example of a 1-quasitrace failing to be a 2-quasitrace already shows that weaker quasitraces need not be linear, but does not answer the present question.

Milhøj–Rørdam connected the quasitrace problem to whether spatial tensor products preserve stable finiteness for simple unital algebras. They also described how a negative quasitrace answer would yield a properly infinite tensor product with a reduced free-group algebra. M1 constructs the missing example and states that the two-generator free group suffices.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 constructs a separable unital complex C*-algebra AAA admitting a normalized 2-quasitrace and positive contractions a,b∈Aa,b\in Aa,b∈A such that every normalized 2-quasitrace satisfies

τ(a+b)−τ(a)−τ(b)≥1144.\tau(a+b)-\tau(a)-\tau(b)\geq\frac1{144}.τ(a+b)−τ(a)−τ(b)≥1441​.

A positive contraction is a positive operator of norm at most one. The inequality makes nonadditivity uniform over the quasitraces, not merely a feature of one specially chosen functional. In particular, AAA has no tracial state. By Haagerup’s theorem it is necessarily nonexact.

The construction begins with another separable unital algebra

B=C∗(1,x1,…,x24)B=C^*(1,x_1,\ldots,x_{24})B=C∗(1,x1​,…,x24​)

satisfying

∑i=124xi∗xi=1,∑i=124xixi∗≤23,1,\sum_{i=1}^{24}x_i^*x_i=1,\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{24}x_ix_i^*\leq\frac23,1,i=1∑24​xi∗​xi​=1,i=1∑24​xi​xi∗​≤32​,1,

while no Mm(B)M_m(B)Mm​(B) is properly infinite. These relations rule out a tracial state: additivity and the trace symmetry would assign equal values to the two sums, contrary to the bounds. The main quantitative example is obtained in A=M48(B)A=M_{48}(B)A=M48​(B).

M1 then derives three related consequences:

  • Two unital simple stably finite complex C*-algebras can have a properly infinite minimal tensor product. One factor can be Cr∗(F2)C_r^*(\mathbb F_2)Cr∗​(F2​), the reduced algebra of the free group on two generators.
  • The separable algebra BBB admits a normalized 2-quasitrace, but B⊗min⁡Cr∗(F2)B\otimes_{\min}C_r^*(\mathbb F_2)B⊗min​Cr∗​(F2​) is properly infinite and admits none.
  • A separable unital stably finite complex C*-algebra can have no tracial state.

The first uses a type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ AW*-factor with no asserted separability. The second uses the explicit BBB, for which stable finiteness is not claimed. The third uses a finitely generated subalgebra of the AW*-factor, with no simplicity assertion. These qualifications prevent an unjustified stronger combined theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the construction separates quasitracial size from linear trace in the general C*-algebra setting and answers Kaplansky’s finite AW*-factor question negatively. The explicit positive pair makes the failure quantitative.

The tensor consequence would show that stable finiteness is not preserved by combining arbitrary simple unital algebras through the spatial tensor product. One factor may be the familiar reduced free-group algebra, so the phenomenon does not require both factors to be newly invented examples.

The result leaves Haagerup’s exact-algebra theorem intact. Rather than making quasitraces unreliable everywhere, it identifies behavior that exactness prevents. It also highlights why several definitions containing the word “finite” must be tracked separately.

6. The main idea

Preserve a trace obstruction with finitely many generators

The two displayed sums provide a compact certificate that no tracial state exists. Keeping the generator count fixed is important: the same finite obstruction must survive while infinitely many possible matrix-isometry constructions are excluded.

M1 realizes the generators as shifts between finite-rank vector bundles. A vector bundle is a family of finite-dimensional vector spaces varying continuously over a compact base. Nontrivial topology can prevent a prescribed trivial bundle from fitting into another bundle, even when a naive pointwise rank comparison looks plausible.

Test every matrix size and every polynomial complexity

For each pair (m,R)(m,R)(m,R), the construction chooses a compact base and bundles designed to obstruct a candidate pair of isometries in Mm(B)M_m(B)Mm​(B) expressed by words of length at most RRR.

Such a polynomial matrix restricts to a map from a trivial bundle into a finite sum of the chosen bundles. If it approximated the required isometries sufficiently well, its image would force a forbidden trivial subbundle. A nonzero Chern class, a topological invariant measuring twisting, obstructs that inclusion.

All these finite tests are assembled in one bounded operator product. The generated C*-algebra remains separable because it has finitely many generators. Any hypothetical pair of isometries can be approximated by finite words; its matrix size and word length select a test already included in the product.

Normalize without destroying the topology

The bundle maps must simultaneously satisfy the column-sum identity and strict row-sum bound. M1 uses an operator-scaling construction based on a convex determinant potential. A unique minimizing normalization varies continuously and respects changes of bundle coordinates.

Different collections of maps handle small and large source subspaces, keeping the total at 24 as the topological tests grow. This uniform finite length preserves the trace obstruction through the product construction.

Extract a definite nonlinear defect

The absence of proper infiniteness in every matrix size gives normalized 2-quasitraces by the established existence theorem. Passing to M48(B)M_{48}(B)M48​(B), a finite telescoping argument uses linearity only where the relevant elements commute. It produces the fixed pair a,ba,ba,b and the lower bound 1/1441/1441/144, without requiring an explicit formula for any chosen quasitrace.

The tensor-product and AW*-factor conclusions then use established implications from the quasitrace problem. Their examples inherit only the properties explicitly retained by those deductions.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All tensor products in the stated consequences are minimal, or spatial, C*-tensor products. The paper does not replace them by arbitrary tensor norms. Its nonexact examples do not contradict trace additivity for exact algebras.

The algebra BBB is known in the manuscript to have no properly infinite matrix amplification, which suffices for quasitrace existence. Calling it stably finite would add an unproved property. Similarly, the simple AW*-factor used in the tensor example is not asserted separable, and the separable stably finite traceless algebra is not asserted simple.

The main theorem gives a uniform additive gap but does not classify all nonlinear 2-quasitraces or provide a simple closed formula for them. Understanding more explicit quasitrace values and determining which further structural assumptions restore tensor-product finiteness are questions beyond the stated conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Haagerup, Quasitraces on exact C*-algebras are traces, for the exactness boundary and the historical equivalences.
  • Milhøj and Rørdam, Around traces and quasitraces, for the tensor-product question and its connection to quasitraces.
  • M1 distinguishes the three algebras in its consequences and identifies the characteristic-class and scaling ingredients of its construction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A counterexample to Kaplansky’s quasitrace conjecture and failure of tensor-product stable finiteness (September 23, 2026).
