entry.title: Every bounded cocycle has a primitive: the Kadison–Ringrose cohomology claim
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 295 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

In calculus, a closed differential form need not have a global antiderivative; cohomology records the obstruction. An analogous construction applies to algebras. Multilinear maps satisfying an algebraic compatibility equation are called cocycles, and one asks whether they come from simpler maps called primitives.

For operator algebras, boundedness matters: a formal solution is not enough if its norm is uncontrolled. The Kadison–Ringrose conjecture asks whether every bounded Hochschild cocycle on a von Neumann algebra, taking values in that same algebra, has a bounded primitive.

Family 295 claims a positive answer in every degree at least two, without separability or special structural assumptions on the algebra. Combined with the classical degree-one theorem for derivations, this would settle the conjecture in all positive degrees. Its new mechanism averages over a specially constructed random walk on the unitary group.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let MMM be a complex von Neumann algebra. A bounded kkk-cochain is a complex multilinear map f:Mk→Mf:M^k\to Mf:Mk→M with finite norm

∥f∥=sup⁡∥a1∥,…,∥ak∥≤1∥f(a1,…,ak)∥.\|f\|=\sup_{\|a_1\|,\ldots,\|a_k\|\leq1}\|f(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\|.∥f∥=∥a1​∥,…,∥ak​∥≤1sup​∥f(a1​,…,ak​)∥.

The Hochschild differential combines multiplication in the inputs with multiplication on the output:

(df)(a1,…,ak+1)=a1f(a2,…,ak+1)+∑j=1k(−1)jf(a1,…,ajaj+1,…,ak+1)+(−1)k+1f(a1,…,ak)ak+1.\begin{aligned}(df)(a_1,\ldots,a_{k+1})={}&a_1f(a_2,\ldots,a_{k+1})\\&+\sum_{j=1}^k(-1)^jf(a_1,\ldots,a_ja_{j+1},\ldots,a_{k+1})\\&+(-1)^{k+1}f(a_1,\ldots,a_k)a_{k+1}.\end{aligned}(df)(a1​,…,ak+1​)=​a1​f(a2​,…,ak+1​)+j=1∑k​(−1)jf(a1​,…,aj​aj+1​,…,ak+1​)+(−1)k+1f(a1​,…,ak​)ak+1​.​

It satisfies d2=0d^2=0d2=0. A cocycle obeys df=0df=0df=0; a coboundary has the form f=dgf=dgf=dg. The cohomology group Hbk(M,M)H_b^k(M,M)Hbk​(M,M) is the quotient of bounded cocycles by bounded coboundaries. Vanishing means every cocycle has an actual bounded primitive. The quotient uses the image of ddd, not merely its closure.

In degree one, the cocycle equation becomes

f(ab)=af(b)+f(a)b,f(ab)=af(b)+f(a)b,f(ab)=af(b)+f(a)b,

the product rule for a derivation. A degree-zero primitive is an element c∈Mc\in Mc∈M, giving f(a)=ac−caf(a)=ac-caf(a)=ac−ca. Thus degree-one vanishing says that every derivation into MMM is inner.

For a bilinear cocycle, the equation is

af(b,c)−f(ab,c)+f(a,bc)−f(a,b)c=0.af(b,c)-f(ab,c)+f(a,bc)-f(a,b)c=0.af(b,c)−f(ab,c)+f(a,bc)−f(a,b)c=0.

A primitive is a bounded linear map g:M→Mg:M\to Mg:M→M satisfying f(a,b)=ag(b)−g(ab)+g(a)bf(a,b)=ag(b)-g(ab)+g(a)bf(a,b)=ag(b)−g(ab)+g(a)b. This low-degree example captures the main question without requiring the full higher-degree notation.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kadison and Sakai proved the inner-derivation theorem, settling degree one. Kadison, Ringrose and Johnson developed the higher-degree theory and its continuity reductions. The self-coefficient conjecture is traced in the literature to 1967.

Kadison–Ringrose obtained vanishing for type I and hyperfinite von Neumann algebras. They also proved an extended-cobounding theorem: for a concrete algebra M⊆B(H)M\subseteq B(H)M⊆B(H), an MMM-valued cocycle can admit a primitive with values in the larger algebra B(H)B(H)B(H). That does not settle the self-coefficient problem, because the primitive must remain inside MMM.

Completely bounded methods resolved additional classes, including algebras without a type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ central summand and finite summands absorbing the hyperfinite factor. Complete boundedness controls all matrix amplifications, a stronger hypothesis than the ordinary boundedness in the conjecture.

For finite factors, further positive cases included Cartan subalgebras and property Gamma, a source of approximately central unitaries. Christensen–Pop–Sinclair–Smith proved vanishing for all property-Gamma factors, including nonseparable ones. In degree two, Pop–Smith established vanishing for tensor products of arbitrary type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ algebras.

Earlier Cartan arguments also showed the usefulness of averaging one cocycle variable until it satisfies a module identity. M1 follows that broad strategy, but replaces the special structure with a single random walk whose harmonic maps satisfy a strong rigidity theorem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that, for every complex von Neumann algebra MMM and every integer k≥2k\geq2k≥2,

df=0⟹f=dgdf=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f=dgdf=0⟹f=dg

for some bounded complex (k−1)(k-1)(k−1)-linear map g:Mk−1→Mg:M^{k-1}\to Mg:Mk−1→M, whenever fff is a bounded kkk-linear map into MMM.

Consequently Hbk(M,M)=0H_b^k(M,M)=0Hbk​(M,M)=0 for all k≥2k\geq2k≥2. Together with the established degree-one theorem, this gives vanishing in every positive degree. It does not assert degree-zero vanishing: degree zero records the center, which need not be zero.

The theorem requires neither separable predual, a factor assumption, property Gamma, a Cartan subalgebra, nor hyperfinite absorption. Boundedness is ordinary multilinear operator-norm boundedness. The initial cocycle need not be completely bounded or separately normal.

A central intermediate theorem concerns a type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ algebra with separable predual and faithful normal trace τ\tauτ. M1 constructs a symmetric, countably supported probability measure μ\muμ on its unitary group such that

T(x)=EU∼μ[T(xU)U∗]⟹T(x)=T(1)x.T(x)=\mathbb E_{U\sim\mu}\bigl[T(xU)U^*\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T(x)=T(1)x.T(x)=EU∼μ​[T(xU)U∗]⟹T(x)=T(1)x.

Here T:M→MT:M\to MT:M→M is any bounded linear map continuous in ∥x∥2=τ(x∗x)1/2\|x\|_2=\tau(x^*x)^{1/2}∥x∥2​=τ(x∗x)1/2 on each operator-norm ball. Positivity and complete boundedness are not assumed. The measure is fixed before choosing TTT.

For separately normal cocycles in the intermediate tracial setting, the construction gives a primitive bounded by the cocycle norm. The final unrestricted theorem uses classical normality reductions and further assembly; it should not be read as claiming that same sharp norm bound for every initial cocycle without qualification.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this completes the bounded self-coefficient cohomology theory in a central class of operator algebras. All bounded compatibility defects satisfying the cocycle equation would be removable by bounded primitives inside the original algebra.

The significance lies partly in eliminating the remaining finite-algebra restrictions. The classical properly infinite and type I results did not solve arbitrary type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ behavior. M1’s random-walk method is designed to supply the module identity without a Cartan subalgebra or approximately central unitaries.

The result is also connected to perturbation theory: Hochschild cohomology measures algebraic obstructions arising when multiplication is varied. Such connections motivate the conjecture, though a particular quantitative perturbation theorem still needs its own hypotheses and estimates. Cohomology vanishing alone should not be expanded into every conceivable stability statement.

6. The main idea

Reduce to a finite tracial problem

Classical results replace an arbitrary bounded cocycle, up to a bounded coboundary, by one separately normal in its inputs. Other established results dispose of the non-II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ central part. The new argument focuses on the finite tracial part.

A faithful normal trace turns the algebra into a Hilbert space under its quadratic norm. This allows probabilistic averaging and Hilbert-space martingales while retaining the ordinary operator norm for the bounded maps being studied.

Design a random walk with free limiting behavior

M1 constructs a countably supported unitary probability measure from increasingly rare, increasingly large configurations of approximately free unitaries. Popa’s independence results supply the finite configurations.

Long independent products along this random walk approach joint free Haar moments on a subsequence. Free Haar unitaries are a noncommutative analogue of independent uniform circle variables: nontrivial reduced words have trace zero. Only convergence of moments is required here, not convergence of the unitaries in operator norm.

The special measure supplies a Liouville property for maps satisfying the displayed harmonic equation. The term echoes the classical principle that bounded harmonic objects can be forced to be constant, although the conclusion here is the module form T(x)=T(1)xT(x)=T(1)xT(x)=T(1)x.

Rule out two different limiting multipliers

The harmonic equation produces a Hilbert-space-valued martingale. If its limit were nonconstant, M1 derives two distinct elements a,b∈Ma,b\in Ma,b∈M governing the map on different signed words in free Haar unitaries inside a tracial ultrapower.

A separate rigidity argument shows this incompatible with boundedness and the required quadratic-norm continuity. It averages free generators, controls repeated indices through free-group length estimates, and uses polar decomposition to pass to a unitary. Uniformly bounded sine sums and a spectral partition force the two proposed multipliers to agree.

This step provides the new module identity. It is a claim about bounded linear maps, independent of the particular degree of the original cocycle.

Average the cocycle and assemble its primitive

M1 takes Cesàro averages in the last cocycle input. A cluster point need not remain normal, so the argument explicitly preserves the weaker continuity needed by the Liouville theorem. That theorem identifies the averaged last-variable map as a right module map.

Averaging the cocycle equation then produces the primitive, with a uniform bound in the intermediate setting. Compactness removes separability, central decompositions handle finite algebras without one global faithful trace, and mixed inputs from different central pieces receive a separate correction. The classical reductions then return to arbitrary MMM.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The coefficient module is MMM itself, with left and right multiplication. The theorem does not claim vanishing for every arbitrary bimodule over every operator algebra. Nor does it assert the same result for general C*-algebras that are not von Neumann algebras.

The bounded primitive is an exact solution, not a limit of approximate coboundaries. Ordinary boundedness, complete boundedness and separate normality are distinct conditions; the latter two enter intermediate tools but are not assumptions of the main theorem.

The random-walk Liouville statement does have a continuity hypothesis and initially assumes separable predual and a faithful normal trace. Those restrictions are removed for the cohomology conclusion through additional arguments, not by silently dropping them from the intermediate theorem.

The paper’s structural conclusion leaves room for sharper bounds on primitives, more explicit constructions in particular algebras, and extensions to other coefficient modules. None is required for the stated self-coefficient vanishing claim.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Christensen, Pop, Sinclair and Smith, Hochschild Cohomology of Factors with Property Gamma, for a major earlier finite-factor case.
  • Pop and Smith, Vanishing of second cohomology for tensor products of type II1 von Neumann algebras, for the degree-two tensor-product theorem.
  • M1’s opening sections state the classical normality reductions and distinguish bounded self-coefficients from primitives allowed to take values in a larger operator algebra.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Vanishing of higher bounded Hochschild cohomology (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: One operator can generate a whole von Neumann algebra
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 296 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A large algebra may be generated by a surprisingly small set. Two matrices, together with their adjoints, sums and products, can already generate a full matrix algebra. For an infinite-dimensional von Neumann algebra, generation also permits weak operator limits.

The generator problem asks whether every von Neumann algebra with separable predual can be generated by a single bounded operator. That operator need not be self-adjoint: its real and imaginary parts provide two self-adjoint generators.

Family 296 claims a positive answer for all type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factors with separable predual, the remaining case in an established reduction of the general problem. Its main intermediate theorem is stronger in a relative direction: if a subfactor already has trivial relative commutant, a generic single unitary added to it generates the ambient factor.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a set of operators SSS, write W∗(S)W^*(S)W∗(S) for the smallest unital von Neumann algebra containing it. This includes adjoints and closure in the weak operator topology. Thus “generated by xxx” means generated by both xxx and x∗x^*x∗, followed by the appropriate closure.

If a,ba,ba,b are self-adjoint and x=a+ibx=a+ibx=a+ib, then

a=x+x∗2,b=x−x∗2i.a=\frac{x+x^*}{2},\qquadb=\frac{x-x^*}{2i}.a=2x+x∗​,b=2ix−x∗​.

Consequently W∗(a,b)=W∗(x)W^*(a,b)=W^*(x)W∗(a,b)=W∗(x). A single self-adjoint operator, by contrast, generates an abelian algebra, so it cannot generate a noncommutative factor by itself.

A factor has scalar center. A type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factor has a faithful normalized trace τ\tauτ, has no minimal nonzero projections, and is infinite-dimensional. Its quadratic norm is

∥x∥2=τ(x∗x)1/2.\|x\|_2=\tau(x^*x)^{1/2}.∥x∥2​=τ(x∗x)1/2.

The hypothesis separable predual makes the corresponding tracial Hilbert space separable. It does not require the algebra to be separable in operator norm; infinite von Neumann algebras usually are not.

An inclusion P⊆MP\subseteq MP⊆M of factors is irreducible if P′∩M=C1P'\cap M=\mathbb C1P′∩M=C1. In other words, no nonscalar element of MMM commutes with all of PPP. This does not imply that P=MP=MP=M.

A dense GδG_\deltaGδ​ subset is a countable intersection of open sets that is dense. Such a set is often called generic in the Baire-category sense. Genericity is topological, not a claim about a probability distribution on operators.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The generator problem has long been central to the structure of von Neumann algebras. Pearcy handled type I cases; Suzuki and Saitô treated hyperfinite cases; Wogen established properly infinite cases. Willig’s direct-integral theorem reduced the remaining general separable-predual question to type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factors.

Progress on finite factors often used additional internal structure. Tensor products of two finite factors are singly generated. Popa treated factors with Cartan subalgebras, while Ge–Popa covered property Gamma and recovered tensor-product cases. Ge–Shen obtained arithmetic examples with generators supported on suitably small projections.

Shen introduced a generator invariant that organized many positive cases. Dykema–Sinclair–Smith–White calculated its exact amplification behavior and related it to the number of self-adjoint generators. Sherman showed that proving finite generation for every countably generated finite factor would already suffice to solve the problem.

More recently, Gao, Kunnawalkam Elayavalli, Patchell and Tan obtained single generation when a countable generating family can be linked through specified chains of commuting unitaries in an ultrapower. Such results enlarge the known classes but retain structural conditions on the generators.

Relative generation by one unitary was also known for finite-index inclusions through the basic construction. M1 claims it for every irreducible inclusion, with no finite-index assumption, and adds density and GδG_\deltaGδ​ structure of the successful unitaries.

A different problem asks for generators varying continuously in a family of factors. Hayes constructed a continuous tracial bundle with no finite family of continuous sections generating every fiber. M1’s pointwise theorem does not remove that continuity obstruction.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1’s relative theorem states that, for an irreducible inclusion P⊆MP\subseteq MP⊆M of type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factors with MMM of separable predual, the set

{u∈U(M):W∗(P,u)=M}\{u\in\mathcal U(M):W^*(P,u)=M\}{u∈U(M):W∗(P,u)=M}

is dense GδG_\deltaGδ​ in the unitary group U(M)\mathcal U(M)U(M), equipped with the trace quadratic-norm topology. Therefore an arbitrarily small quadratic-norm perturbation of any unitary can be chosen to generate the whole ambient algebra together with PPP.

Its main absolute conclusion is that every type II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​ factor MMM with separable predual admits two self-adjoint generators, or equivalently

M=W∗(x)M=W^*(x)M=W∗(x)

for one bounded operator x∈Mx\in Mx∈M. Combining this with the established direct-integral reduction gives single generation for every von Neumann algebra with separable predual, not only factors.

The paper also deduces that the generator invariants G\mathcal GG and Gsa\mathcal G_{\mathrm{sa}}Gsa​ vanish for every such finite factor. Since every amplification is again a separable-predual finite factor, the conclusion holds at all amplification scales.

A free-entropy consequence is stated precisely: for every integer n≥3n\geq3n≥3, L(Fn)L(\mathbb F_n)L(Fn​) has finite self-adjoint generating tuples on which both microstates dimensions δ\deltaδ and δ0\delta_0δ0​ take different values. A standard semicircular nnn-tuple has dimension nnn, while a two-self-adjoint generating tuple has dimension at most two. This argument does not itself identify different free group factors; the stronger isomorphism claim belongs to family 287.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this completes the long-standing generator problem in its separable-predual formulation. Every algebra in that broad class could be encoded by one operator together with its adjoint, even when its original description used countably many generators.

The relative statement is valuable in its own right. It says that an irreducible subfactor needs only one additional unitary, and that suitable choices are dense in a natural topology. This gives structural information about inclusions, not just a bound on the total number of generators.

Single generation does not make the classification of factors trivial. Different operators can generate very different algebras, and one may still face difficult questions about the relations and limiting structure encoded by a generator. The result concerns the number of required coordinates, not the complexity of their content.

6. The main idea

Amplify a tiny perturbation through a long word

Begin with a unitary u∈Mu\in Mu∈M and a target unitary zzz one wants the generated algebra to detect. M1 perturbs uuu slightly and examines a long word with coefficients in PPP, using the perturbed unitary repeatedly.

With a small parameter α\alphaα fixed and word length parameter ℓ\ellℓ, the perturbation has quadratic norm of order α/ℓ\alpha/\sqrt\ellα/ℓ​. It therefore becomes arbitrarily small as the word grows. Yet its repeated contributions are coordinated so that the word retains a fixed positive correlation with the target information.

A naive estimate would accumulate an error proportional to word length. The manuscript instead controls nonlinear terms by a free-group convolution operator and Haagerup’s length-one norm estimate. This yields a remainder bound uniform in ℓ\ellℓ, making the limiting perturbation useful.

Popa’s free-independence theorem supplies the required auxiliary unitaries in a tracial ultrapower. For each fixed finite word length, choosing a sufficiently good coordinate returns the construction to the original MMM and PPP. The final theorem is not merely generation in an ultrapower.

Use continuity points to force full generation

For a vector ξ∈L2(M,τ)\xi\in L^2(M,\tau)ξ∈L2(M,τ), consider the norm of its orthogonal projection onto

L2(W∗(P,u),τ).L^2(W^*(P,u),\tau).L2(W∗(P,u),τ).

As a function of uuu, this is bounded and lower semicontinuous. Baire-category arguments provide common continuity points for a countable dense collection of vectors, and contractivity extends continuity to every vector.

Suppose the algebra generated at such a continuity point were proper. A nonzero bounded vector could be chosen orthogonal to it, so its projection norm would be zero. The long-word perturbation gives arbitrarily nearby unitaries for which that projection norm has a fixed positive lower bound. This contradicts continuity.

Thus the common continuity points give full relative generation. A separate description of the generating condition supplies the claimed GδG_\deltaGδ​ property of the whole locus.

Compress four self-adjoint generators into two

Popa’s irreducible hyperfinite embedding theorem provides an appropriate P⊆MP\subseteq MP⊆M. The hyperfinite subfactor has two self-adjoint generators. Adding the relative unitary contributes its real and imaginary parts, giving four self-adjoint generators for every separable-predual finite factor.

The same uniform bound applies to a corner cut out by a projection of trace one half. Reconstructing MMM as a two-by-two matrix algebra over that corner allows an explicit matrix encoding to package the data into two self-adjoint operators. This final compression uses established matrix-generation techniques; relative generation alone initially yields the larger bound.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The absolute result assumes separable predual, not arbitrary cardinality. The relative genericity theorem uses the trace quadratic-norm topology, not operator-norm density and not probabilistic almost-sure language. Its irreducibility assumption is part of the statement.

The single generator is generally nonselfadjoint. Generation is in the von Neumann sense, including adjoints and weak closure. The theorem does not claim that every C*-algebra is singly generated in norm, nor that every element is a finite polynomial in the chosen operator.

The result also does not produce continuously varying generators for arbitrary bundles of factors. The cited bundle obstruction concerns that additional requirement and is compatible with single generation of each individual fiber.

The entropy consequence concerns δ\deltaδ and δ0\delta_0δ0​ on different finite self-adjoint tuples in the same factor. It is separate from classification of factors by free rank, and it does not claim a particular exact entropy value for every two-generator tuple. More explicit generator constructions and control of their additional analytic properties remain further questions.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Dykema, Sinclair, Smith and White, Generators of II1 Factors, for generator invariants, amplification and matrix encoding.
  • Gao, Kunnawalkam Elayavalli, Patchell and Tan, Internal sequential commutation and single generation, for a recent structural positive case.
  • M1 identifies the established direct-integral reduction and distinguishes its finite-factor construction from continuously varying generators in bundles.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Relative generation and the generator problem for finite factors (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Two free entropies disagree even when both are finite
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 298 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Entropy can describe how many microscopic configurations realize a macroscopic law. In free probability, the variables are operators that need not commute, and there are two major definitions of entropy.

One counts the volumes of large matrix tuples approximating the variables’ moments. The other uses an analytic measure of sensitivity to freely independent noise. A general theorem says the matrix-volume entropy is no larger than the analytic entropy. Are they equal whenever the matrix-volume entropy is finite?

Family 298 claims a negative answer: one bounded self-adjoint tuple has two finite entropies separated by at least one half in the stated normalization. The construction keeps a hidden block pattern visible in matrices even after enough noise has been added to make the analytic entropy almost Gaussian.

2. Background and essential definitions

A tracial von Neumann algebra (M,τ)(M,\tau)(M,τ) provides a noncommutative probability space. Self-adjoint operators are real-valued random variables in this language, and τ(Xi1⋯Xik)\tau(X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k})τ(Xi1​​⋯Xik​​) are their joint moments. The trace is faithful and normalized, so τ(1)=1\tau(1)=1τ(1)=1.

For a bounded self-adjoint tuple X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)X=(X1​,…,Xn​), a microstate is a tuple of self-adjoint ddd-by-ddd matrices whose normalized trace moments approximate those of XXX. The set ΓR(X;m,d,ε)\Gamma_R(X;m,d,\varepsilon)ΓR​(X;m,d,ε) requires coordinate norms at most RRR and accuracy ε\varepsilonε for every word of length at most mmm.

The original microstates entropy is

χR(X)=inf⁡m,εlim sup⁡d→∞[d−2log⁡Vol⁡ΓR(X;m,d,ε)+n2log⁡d],\chi_R(X)=\inf_{m,\varepsilon}\limsup_{d\to\infty}\left[d^{-2}\log\operatorname{Vol}\Gamma_R(X;m,d,\varepsilon)+\frac n2\log d\right],χR​(X)=m,εinf​d→∞limsup​[d−2logVolΓR​(X;m,d,ε)+2n​logd],

followed by χ(X)=sup⁡RχR(X)\chi(X)=\sup_R\chi_R(X)χ(X)=supR​χR​(X). Volume uses the Euclidean structure from the unnormalized Hilbert–Schmidt inner product. The normalization compensates for growth of matrix dimension. This is a differential-entropy-type quantity and can be negative.

The analytic entropy χ∗\chi^*χ∗ uses conjugate variables, free analogues of score functions, and their squared norms summed as free Fisher information Φ∗\Phi^*Φ∗. Its normalization is

χ∗(X)=n2log⁡(2πe)+12∫0∞[n1+s−Φ∗(X+s S)]ds.\chi^*(X)=\frac n2\log(2\pi e)+\frac12\int_0^\infty\left[\frac n{1+s}-\Phi^*(X+\sqrt s\,S)\right]ds.χ∗(X)=2n​log(2πe)+21​∫0∞​[1+sn​−Φ∗(X+s​S)]ds.

Here SSS is a variance-one semicircular family free from XXX. Semicircular variables play the role of Gaussians in free probability; freeness replaces classical independence through vanishing traces of alternating centered products. A variance-one free semicircular nnn-tuple has entropy n2log⁡(2πe)\frac n2\log(2\pi e)2n​log(2πe).

The two definitions ask different questions: how much matrix volume realizes the law, and how its analytic noise response integrates over time.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Voiculescu introduced microstates free entropy and later its nonmicrostates counterpart. They agree for one self-adjoint variable. Agreement for several variables became part of the broader program of unifying free-entropy theories.

Biane, Capitaine and Guionnet proved the general inequality χ≤χ∗\chi\leq\chi^*χ≤χ∗ using matrix Brownian-motion large deviations. Jekel and Pi later gave an elementary proof through classical entropy and Fisher information and extended the comparison to conditional free entropy.

Without a finiteness assumption, equality can fail because some noncommutative laws have no sufficiently good matrix approximations: their microstates entropy is minus infinity while analytic entropy is larger. That does not answer the sharper question posed explicitly in Guionnet’s formulation: does χ(X)>−∞\chi(X)>-\inftyχ(X)>−∞ force equality?

Substantial positive results support equality under stronger regularity assumptions. Dabrowski proved it for suitable strictly convex potentials with Lipschitz derivatives and polynomial approximation properties. Jekel obtained matrix entropy and Fisher-information convergence for regular convex potentials with appropriate concentration and approximation control.

M1 targets the gap between these structured settings and mere finiteness. Its matrix argument also draws on older methods controlling microstate volumes through commutation constraints and projection geometry. The new claim is that residual simultaneous block structure can produce a strict entropy deficit even after smoothing ensures finite microstates entropy.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that there is a finite integer n≥2n\geq2n≥2 and a bounded self-adjoint tuple XXX in a von Neumann algebra with faithful normal tracial state such that

−∞<χ(X)≤χ∗(X)−12<∞.-\infty<\chi(X)\leq\chi^*(X)-\frac12<\infty.−∞<χ(X)≤χ∗(X)−21​<∞.

Both values are finite, and the inequality concerns the same tuple. The definition of χ\chiχ is the original operator-norm-cutoff version with a limsup over matrix sizes, not an alternative entropy defined by a preferred matrix ensemble or by a liminf.

The tuple has a large but fixed number of coordinates. The theorem does not establish the same phenomenon for every prescribed smaller number, such as exactly two variables.

The construction begins with

C=(B1,…,Bp,Y),C=(B_1,\ldots,B_p,Y),C=(B1​,…,Bp​,Y),

where the BiB_iBi​ are free variance-one semicircular variables and YYY, in a separate tensor factor, is uniformly distributed on ppp equally spaced points in [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1]. Thus YYY commutes with every BiB_iBi​. With SSS free from CCC, the tuple is

X=C+h SX=C+\sqrt h\,SX=C+h​S

for a suitably small positive hhh, after choosing one sufficiently large finite ppp. An additional noise time t=p3/4t=p^{3/4}t=p3/4 is used in the comparison argument. All matrix-size limits are then taken with ppp and hhh fixed.

The result is distinct from the entropy-dimension consequences in families 287 and 296. Those compare different generating tuples of one algebra; M1 compares two entropy definitions on a single tuple.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem separates the two principal free-entropy theories even in the finite regime where a simple failure of matrix approximability cannot explain the difference.

This would change the role of regularity assumptions in equality theorems. Convexity, concentration and approximation hypotheses would be substantive reasons for agreement, rather than technical routes toward an equality implied by finite entropy alone.

The construction also identifies a mechanism. Analytic noise estimates can become nearly Gaussian while a matrix ensemble retains collective geometry restricting its volume. Two variables can have the same broad variance scale without erasing all joint block information. The discrepancy is structural, not just a mismatch in additive normalization constants.

6. The main idea

Build a shared block signal

Because YYY commutes with all the BiB_iBi​, its spectral projections divide the original tuple into simultaneous blocks. In a matrix approximation, the last coordinate organizes subspaces on which much of the energy of the first coordinates is concentrated.

Adding the small free noise h S\sqrt h\,Sh​S makes the microstates entropy finite while leaving enough of this pattern detectable. M1 then compares what happens after a larger positive noise time.

Make the analytic deficit small

Free cumulants organize joint moments into contributions associated with noncrossing partitions. A semicircular family has only second-order cumulants; higher cumulants measure departures from semicircular behavior.

M1 bounds a Fisher-information deficit by squared sums of higher cumulant arrays, using semicircular Wick-polynomial orthogonality. The signal’s cumulants are sparse enough that additional noise makes χ∗\chi^*χ∗ close to the entropy of a semicircular family with matching coordinate variances.

This is an analytic comparison with a Gaussian-type reference, not a claim that the entire tuple becomes exactly semicircular.

Keep a rare matrix event visible

For the matrix side, the source chooses increasingly accurate cutoff microstate sets for XXX, takes uniform laws on them, and evolves those laws by independent Gaussian unitary ensemble noise. GUE matrices are the standard self-adjoint Gaussian matrix model whose large-size law is semicircular.

The evolved selected ensembles retain a simultaneous block-energy event with probability bounded away from zero. For independent GUE reference matrices with the same limiting variances, that event has probability at most e−cd2e^{-cd^2}e−cd2 for some fixed c>0c>0c>0.

Relative entropy cannot increase when observations are simplified to an event indicator. Comparing these two event probabilities therefore produces a deficit of order d2d^2d2, which remains nonzero after the entropy normalization by d2d^2d2.

Balance the two scales and retain the same ensembles

The analytic deficit becomes small when t/pt/\sqrt pt/p​ grows, while the matrix block estimate survives when tlog⁡p/pt\log p/ptlogp/p becomes small. The choice t=p3/4t=p^{3/4}t=p3/4 satisfies both as ppp grows.

A finite-time classical-to-free Fisher comparison transfers the positive-time matrix deficit back to the original tuple. M1 keeps the same selected terminal ensembles throughout this step. Their normalized entropy limsup need not equal the microstates entropy of the limiting law, so replacing one by the other would lose precisely the distinction being exploited.

After selecting sufficiently large finite ppp and then small hhh, the estimates yield the stated fixed gap.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the original χ\chiχ and χ∗\chi^*χ∗ with the displayed conventions. It does not assert an exact formula for either entropy of the constructed tuple. The lower bound on their gap is quantitative, but the minimal number of variables realizing a finite gap is not determined.

The parameter choices are made before matrix size tends to infinity. The result is not merely a sequence of tuples with increasing coordinate count whose limiting entropies disagree. Likewise, the selected noisy matrix laws are analytical tools, not a redefinition of microstates entropy.

The known one-variable equality and regular convex equality theorems remain outside the counterexample’s scope. The paper does not claim that every finite-entropy tuple has a gap, nor that the two theories lose their general comparison inequality.

Further questions include identifying broader equality classes, reducing the coordinate count of counterexamples, and understanding which matrix structures analytic Fisher information can fail to capture. These go beyond the stated finite-entropy separation.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Jekel and Pi, An Elementary Proof of the Inequality chi ≤ chi* for Conditional Free Entropy, for the comparison used in the scale-transfer argument.
  • Dabrowski, A Laplace Principle for Hermitian Brownian Motion and Free Entropy I, for a substantial convex equality class.
  • M1 fixes both entropy normalizations and explains why the terminal matrix ensembles must be retained through its finite-time comparison.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A finite-entropy separation of microstates and nonmicrostates free entropy (September 25, 2026).

entry.title: No scalar shadows in central sequences: a criterion for Jiang–Su stability
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 299 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

An operator algebra can contain sequences that increasingly commute with every fixed element. These central sequences reveal internal structure that may be invisible in the algebra’s ordinary center.

The Kirchberg–Rørdam character question asks whether one very weak-looking condition on this sequence algebra already forces a strong regularity property: if central sequences admit no one-dimensional representation, must the original algebra absorb the Jiang–Su algebra?

Family 299 claims yes for every nonzero unital separable complex C*-algebra, without nuclearity, simplicity or trace assumptions. It also claims that the infinite spatial tensor power of every such characterless algebra absorbs, and contains a unital copy of, the Jiang–Su algebra. The main ingredient is a finite maximal-tensor construction of a dimension-drop algebra image.

2. Background and essential definitions

A C*-algebra is a norm-complete algebra closed under adjoints, with ∥a∗a∥=∥a∥2\|a^*a\|=\|a\|^2∥a∗a∥=∥a∥2. A character is a nonzero *-homomorphism from the algebra to C\mathbb CC. For a unital algebra it automatically preserves the identity. Characters are one-dimensional representations, so having none means that no nonzero representation reduces all algebraic behavior to scalars.

For a free ultrafilter ω\omegaω on N\mathbb NN, the norm ultrapower is

Aω=ℓ∞(N,A)/{(an):lim⁡ω∥an∥=0}.A_\omega=\ell^\infty(\mathbb N,A)/\{(a_n):\lim_\omega\|a_n\|=0\}.Aω​=ℓ∞(N,A)/{(an​):ωlim​∥an​∥=0}.

Bounded sequences are identified when their difference tends to zero in operator norm along the ultrafilter. The norm central-sequence algebra is

Fω(A)=Aω∩A′,F_\omega(A)=A_\omega\cap A',Fω​(A)=Aω​∩A′,

where AAA sits as constant sequences. Its elements have representatives asymptotically commuting with every fixed element of AAA. This is not a tracial ultrapower, which would discard sequences small in a trace-based quadratic norm.

The Jiang–Su algebra Z\mathcal ZZ is a distinguished infinite-dimensional algebra whose absorption expresses regularity:

A≅A⊗min⁡Z.A\cong A\otimes_{\min}\mathcal Z.A≅A⊗min​Z.

The minimal tensor product is the spatial completion obtained from Hilbert-space representations. The maximal tensor product uses the largest C*-norm allowed by representations of the algebraic tensor product. They need not coincide for the nonnuclear algebras allowed here.

A subhomogeneous algebra has a common finite upper bound on dimensions of its irreducible representations. A full positive element generates the entire algebra as a closed two-sided ideal. Fullness says that the element is visible in every nonzero irreducible representation, not that it is invertible.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Toms–Winter’s theory of strongly self-absorbing algebras formalized how central copies of a fixed algebra imply tensorial absorption. For Z\mathcal ZZ, Kirchberg–Rørdam proved a useful criterion: a unital separable algebra absorbs Z\mathcal ZZ exactly when its norm central-sequence algebra contains a same-unit separable subhomogeneous algebra without characters.

The necessary direction is immediate at the level of characters: if the central-sequence algebra had a character, restricting it to that unital subalgebra would give a forbidden character there. The open question was whether the absence of characters on the whole central-sequence algebra suffices to construct the required subalgebra.

Dadarlat–Toms related absorption to infinite tensor powers. They showed that a suitable characterless subhomogeneous subalgebra inside such a tensor power gives Jiang–Su stability. Their dimension-drop constructions covered recursive subhomogeneous algebras whose matrix sizes are sufficiently large relative to topological dimension.

Other regularity criteria involved stronger hypotheses. Robert–Tikuisis used full orthogonal central positive elements under finite nuclear dimension. Perera–Thiel–Vilalta characterized absorption through comparison and divisibility properties of the central-sequence Cuntz semigroup. M1 seeks a criterion requiring none of those comparison or dimension conditions.

The companion dimension manuscript in family 291 constructs two full orthogonal positive elements in a finite maximal tensor power of a characterless algebra. M1 describes a different representation-label construction and then carries the process further, to a unital dimension-drop map. It also uses the companion’s commuting-copy lemma, with the earlier reindexing provenance credited to Kirchberg–Rørdam.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every nonzero unital separable complex C*-algebra AAA and every free ultrafilter ω\omegaω on N\mathbb NN, M1 states

Fω(A) has no characters⟺A≅A⊗min⁡Z.F_\omega(A)\text{ has no characters}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quadA\cong A\otimes_{\min}\mathcal Z.Fω​(A) has no characters⟺A≅A⊗min​Z.

There is no nuclearity, simplicity, trace, dimension or comparison assumption. The condition is imposed on Fω(A)F_\omega(A)Fω​(A), not merely on AAA itself. The statement holds for each free ultrafilter, so the resulting absorption property does not depend on choosing a favorable one.

The finite construction applies more broadly. For any nonzero unital complex C*-algebra DDD with no characters, even nonseparable, M1 claims that some finite m≥1m\geq1m≥1 admits a unital *-homomorphism

I(2,3)⟶D⊗max⁡m.I(2,3)\longrightarrow D^{\otimes_{\max}m}.I(2,3)⟶D⊗max​m.

The prime dimension-drop algebra here is

I(2,3)={f∈C([0,1],M2⊗M3): f(0)∈M2⊗13, f(1)∈12⊗M3}.\begin{aligned}I(2,3)=\{f\in C([0,1],M_2\otimes M_3):&\ f(0)\in M_2\otimes1_3,\\&\ f(1)\in1_2\otimes M_3\}.\end{aligned}I(2,3)={f∈C([0,1],M2​⊗M3​):​ f(0)∈M2​⊗13​, f(1)∈12​⊗M3​}.​

Its interior fibers are six-by-six matrices, while endpoint restrictions have sizes two and three. These dimensions explain the absence of one-dimensional representations and its role as a building block for Z\mathcal ZZ.

The map need not be injective. Its image is nevertheless a unital subhomogeneous algebra without characters, which is the property required by the absorption criteria. The finite exponent depends on DDD, and M1 does not claim that this finite tensor power itself absorbs Z\mathcal ZZ.

For nonzero unital separable characterless DDD, the infinite minimal tensor power

B=D⊗min⁡∞=lim→⁡(D⊗min⁡n,x↦x⊗1)B=D^{\otimes_{\min}\infty}=\varinjlim\bigl(D^{\otimes_{\min}n},x\mapsto x\otimes1\bigr)B=D⊗min​∞=lim​(D⊗min​n,x↦x⊗1)

is claimed to satisfy B≅B⊗min⁡ZB\cong B\otimes_{\min}\mathcal ZB≅B⊗min​Z and to contain a unital copy of Z\mathcal ZZ. The finite theorem uses maximal products; this infinite conclusion uses minimal products. They are deliberately different statements.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem characterizes a major regularity property by an elementary representation-theoretic obstruction in central sequences. It would replace substantial comparison or approximation assumptions with the absence of scalar representations.

Its scope extends beyond the nuclear classification setting. Nonnuclear, nonsimple algebras and algebras with complicated traces are included, provided they are nonzero, unital and separable. That breadth is part of what makes the criterion striking.

The infinite-tensor conclusion also explains how repeated composition can create regularity. A single characterless algebra need not already absorb Z\mathcal ZZ, but infinitely many spatial tensor copies would supply enough distributed structure. This should not be compressed into the false stronger slogan that characterlessness of AAA alone implies its absorption.

6. The main idea

Detect noncommutativity in every representation

The absence of characters means that every irreducible representation has dimension at least two. M1 first extracts finite-dimensional spaces of self-adjoint elements whose images detect this noncommutativity.

A tensor-label construction keeps selected vectors linearly independent after arbitrary rank-at-least-two maps on individual tensor factors. These robust labels produce self-adjoint elements that fail to commute in every irreducible representation of a suitable finite tensor power.

A double commutator then yields full positive and negative parts. A further labeling step combines finitely many connections between them into one full square-zero element. “Square zero” means v2=0v^2=0v2=0, allowing its source and range pieces to behave like off-diagonal matrix coordinates.

Go beyond two full orthogonal pieces

The square-zero element supplies a homomorphism from a matrix cone, equivalently an orthogonality-preserving completely positive map on a matrix algebra. Its first corner is full, but fullness alone does not give a unital dimension-drop map.

The next stage arranges two exactly equivalent orthogonal positive contractions, represented by v∗vv^*vv∗v and vv∗vv^*vv∗, and controls the part of the identity they leave unused. A simplex of matrix embeddings organizes the construction over a finite tensor power. Regions near coordinate axes supply room to absorb the remaining defect after a further finite amplification.

This is the comparison input needed for the Rørdam–Winter dimension-drop criterion. It upgrades full orthogonal elements to the specific unital I(2,3)I(2,3)I(2,3) image, without assuming stable rank one.

Place the finite construction centrally

Inside a central-sequence algebra, reindexing supplies commuting copies of a suitable separable characterless subalgebra. Commuting copies define a map from a maximal tensor product, so the finite theorem produces the required dimension-drop image centrally. Kirchberg–Rørdam’s established criterion then gives Z\mathcal ZZ-absorption of AAA.

For the infinite minimal tensor power, disjoint tensor blocks provide the needed copies. The finite image and the Dadarlat–Toms absorption theorem give the infinite-power conclusion. Unitality is preserved through these passages, which matters because a zero or nonunital map would not supply the stated criterion.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The main theorem is for nonzero unital separable complex C*-algebras. It does not simply assert the same formula for nonunital algebras, where central-sequence annihilator quotients require additional care. Its ultrapower is defined with the operator norm, not a chosen collection of traces.

The auxiliary finite theorem drops separability but uses maximal tensor products. Its conclusion is a homomorphism with a useful image, not necessarily an embedding of I(2,3)I(2,3)I(2,3), and not finite-power Jiang–Su absorption. No uniform exponent is given independently of DDD.

The infinite-power theorem returns to separability and minimal tensor products. It asserts both absorption and an actual unital copy of Z\mathcal ZZ at that infinite stage. Whether stronger finite-stage conclusions hold under additional assumptions is a different question.

Finally, M1’s dimension-drop comparison and its reindexing dependencies are essential parts of the claimed construction. Merely finding two full orthogonal elements would not, without further hypotheses or steps, reproduce the entire theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Kirchberg and Rørdam, When central sequence C*-algebras have characters, for the character criterion question and its connection to tensor powers.
  • Kirchberg and Rørdam, Central sequence C*-algebras and tensorial absorption of the Jiang–Su algebra, for the earlier central-sequence absorption framework.
  • M1 states the precise Dadarlat–Toms and Rørdam–Winter criteria used to pass from its finite construction to absorption.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Kirchberg–Rørdam character criterion (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Paving every maximal abelian subalgebra with a uniform number of pieces
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 300 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Imagine partitioning the coordinates of a matrix into groups, then deleting entries joining different groups. Can the remaining blocks be made small after removing an appropriate diagonal part?

This is the idea of paving, central to the Kadison–Singer problem. For general operator algebras there may be no coordinate basis, but projections in a maximal abelian subalgebra play the role of diagonal coordinate blocks. Ordinary operator-norm paving is too strong in this generality.

Family 300 claims two universal replacements. One allows a nearby bounded operator before norm paving. The other paves the original operator after compressing to a projection arbitrarily close to the identity on any prescribed finite collection of vectors. The latter uses a number of pieces proportional to the inverse square of the error, the optimal general exponent.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let M⊆B(H)M\subseteq B(H)M⊆B(H) be a complex von Neumann algebra, and let A⊆MA\subseteq MA⊆M be a maximal abelian self-adjoint subalgebra, abbreviated MASA. Its elements commute with one another, and it cannot be enlarged within MMM while remaining abelian. The ordinary diagonal matrices are the basic finite-dimensional example.

Choose mutually orthogonal projections p1,…,pr∈Ap_1,\ldots,p_r\in Ap1​,…,pr​∈A summing to the identity. Their pinching map is

CP(x)=∑i=1rpixpi.C_P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^r p_i x p_i.CP​(x)=i=1∑r​pi​xpi​.

It retains the block-diagonal part associated with the partition. Zero projections are allowed, so a bound on the number of pieces can be expressed using one fixed partition length.

Ordinary norm paving asks for CP(x)C_P(x)CP​(x) to be close in operator norm to some a∈Aa\in Aa∈A. Operator norm controls all unit vectors at once. The strong operator topology is weaker: a neighborhood of xxx asks that (y−x)ξ(y-x)\xi(y−x)ξ be small only for a specified finite set of vectors ξ\xiξ.

In approximation paving, one first chooses such a nearby self-adjoint yyy, with a uniform norm bound, and then norm-paves yyy. In strong-operator paving, one keeps xxx but finds a projection q∈Mq\in Mq∈M close to the identity on the prescribed vectors and controls

q(CP(x)−a)q.q(C_P(x)-a)q.q(CP​(x)−a)q.

The projection qqq need not belong to AAA. Being close to the identity strongly does not mean ∥1−q∥\|1-q\|∥1−q∥ is small: a nonzero orthogonal projection always has norm one.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kadison–Singer’s pure-state extension problem concerned the atomic diagonal MASA of B(ℓ2)B(\ell^2)B(ℓ2). Anderson formulated its paving counterpart, and Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava solved it through mixed characteristic polynomials.

Moving to arbitrary MASAs changes the problem. Popa–Vaes showed that, in the separable-predual setting, norm paving characterizes type I algebras with a normal expectation onto the MASA. Thus a universal norm-paving theorem for arbitrary MASAs is not the right target.

Popa introduced finite-factor methods, obtaining norm paving in ultraproducts of singular MASAs and hence strong-operator paving in the original inclusions. Popa–Vaes formulated the strong-operator and approximation-paving conjectures and proved major special cases, including type I algebras and certain Cartan inclusions.

The two structural extremes behaved differently. Cartan MASAs have many normalizing symmetries and can be described using measured equivalence relations. Singular MASAs have few such symmetries and admit free-probabilistic methods. Earlier combinations of the methods could multiply partition counts, worsening a quadratic or quartic bound to a sixth-power bound.

Ravichandran–Srivastava obtained asymptotically optimal finite-dimensional multipaving estimates. M2 uses their finite polynomial bound while coordinating the Cartan and complementary parts with one partition. This avoids multiplying the number of colors and is central to the claimed quadratic rate.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: norm paving after a bounded strong perturbation

For every 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<10<ε<1, M1 claims a universal integer R(ε)≤Capε−6R(\varepsilon)\leq C_{\mathrm{ap}}\varepsilon^{-6}R(ε)≤Cap​ε−6 with the following property. For any MASA A⊆M⊆B(H)A\subseteq M\subseteq B(H)A⊆M⊆B(H), self-adjoint x∈Mx\in Mx∈M, finite F⊆HF\subseteq HF⊆H, and δ>0\delta>0δ>0, there are a self-adjoint y∈My\in My∈M, an R(ε)R(\varepsilon)R(ε)-piece partition in AAA, and self-adjoint a∈Aa\in Aa∈A such that

∥y∥≤3∥x∥,∥(y−x)ξ∥<δ(ξ∈F),\|y\|\leq3\|x\|,\qquad\|(y-x)\xi\|<\delta\quad(\xi\in F),∥y∥≤3∥x∥,∥(y−x)ξ∥<δ(ξ∈F),

and

∥a∥≤∥y∥,∥CP(y)−a∥≤ε∥y∥.\|a\|\leq\|y\|,\qquad\|C_P(y)-a\|\leq\varepsilon\|y\|.∥a∥≤∥y∥,∥CP​(y)−a∥≤ε∥y∥.

The error is relative to the approximant’s own norm. The count is fixed before choosing the inclusion, operator or strong neighborhood. No separability or conditional-expectation assumption is imposed.

M1 also obtains a quadratic approximation-paving bound when the MASA is the range of a normal conditional expectation, using the companion strong-operator theorem. It does not claim that quadratic approximation rate for arbitrary expectation-free MASAs.

M2: quadratic strong-operator paving of the original operator

M2 gives

rε=lceil400000000ε−2⌉+⌈4/ε⌉+1≤500000000ε−2.r_\varepsilon=lceil400000000\varepsilon^{-2}\rceil+\lceil4/\varepsilon\rceil+1\leq500000000\varepsilon^{-2}.rε​=lceil400000000ε−2⌉+⌈4/ε⌉+1≤500000000ε−2.

For every inclusion and self-adjoint xxx as above, and every finite-vector neighborhood, it claims a partition with rεr_\varepsilonrε​ pieces, self-adjoint a∈Aa\in Aa∈A, and projection q∈Mq\in Mq∈M satisfying

∥(1−q)ξ∥<δ(ξ∈F),\|(1-q)\xi\|<\delta\quad(\xi\in F),∥(1−q)ξ∥<δ(ξ∈F),
∥a∥≤∥x∥,∥q(CP(x)−a)q∥≤ε∥x∥.\|a\|\leq\|x\|,\qquad\|q(C_P(x)-a)q\|\leq\varepsilon\|x\|.∥a∥≤∥x∥,∥q(CP​(x)−a)q∥≤ε∥x∥.

Again there is no separability or expectation hypothesis. The exponent two is optimal in general by an existing finite-factor obstruction that survives the permitted compressions. The numerical constant is not optimized.

For countably decomposable expected MASAs, M2 also transfers the quadratic bound to norm paving in the associated Ocneanu von Neumann ultrapower. That corollary retains both its countable-decomposability and normal-expectation assumptions.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the pair resolves the general approximation-paving and quadratic strong-operator-paving conjectures. It extends the paving framework far beyond the atomic diagonal setting of Kadison–Singer.

The uniform partition count is substantive. The number of pieces is chosen from the desired error before the algebra, representation and finite-vector tests are known. Arbitrarily large or nonseparable representations do not require more colors.

The quadratic exponent places a sharp quantitative boundary on strong-operator paving, even though its displayed constant is large. Approximation paving gives a different useful conclusion: the entire nearby operator is norm-paved, without discarding a corner. Neither statement should be conflated with universal norm paving of the original operator.

6. The main idea

Separate normalizing structure from diffuse behavior

When a suitable faithful normal state centralizes the MASA, let NNN be the algebra generated by its partial normalizers. Conditional expectations give the decomposition

x−EA(x)=(EN(x)−EA(x))+(x−EN(x)).x-E_A(x)=\bigl(E_N(x)-E_A(x)\bigr)+\bigl(x-E_N(x)\bigr).x−EA​(x)=(EN​(x)−EA​(x))+(x−EN​(x)).

The first term belongs to a Cartan-type measured-relation setting. The second has diffuse, or atomless, left-right kernels. These kernels describe how the operator connects points of the abelian algebra without concentration on discrete matching pairs.

The challenge is to pave both contributions while retaining a uniform count. M2 arranges for the same color projections to handle them, rather than first paving one term and refining every resulting piece for the other.

Transfer finite matrix choices to measurable colorings

Mixed determinantal or characteristic polynomials encode finite paving choices through their roots. The manuscripts use spectral-root estimates to assign colors while controlling an accumulated cost.

For measured equivalence relations, the choices must be measurable and compatible across overlapping finite regions. Nonsingular actions need not preserve the initial measure, so an auxiliary real coordinate converts the problem to an invariant mass-transport setting. Uniform estimates then descend the color choices back to the original space.

M1 uses buffered pinning and sparse updates to construct its approximation paving. M2 works with a relative Bernoulli extension, giving independent site labels and uniform conditional color marginals. The latter support both the measured Cartan estimate and a free-compression estimate for the diffuse term.

Return from the auxiliary model to actual projections

M2 puts the algebra and its Bernoulli model in an amalgamated free product. It then transfers fixed mixed moments back to projections in the original MASA. Atomless kernels make unwanted collisions disappear, while modular analytic approximation handles the lack of a tracial state.

Clipping produces bounded approximants, and a sufficiently high moment estimate yields a spectral cut qqq with the required strong-neighborhood control. The number of colors is fixed before choosing these later approximation parameters.

Remove expectation and separability assumptions

The arbitrary-MASA arguments split the representation into a corner supporting centralizing normal functionals and a complementary corner. The first admits state-based methods; the second uses almost disjoint conjugate states and additional randomization.

Careful corner assembly controls off-diagonal terms. In M2, disjoint palettes make counts add across corners. Separable reductions preserve the bounds before returning to arbitrary Hilbert spaces. M1 additionally uses a norming vector and final clipping so the paving error is measured against ∥y∥\|y\|∥y∥, as its theorem requires.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The input operators are self-adjoint. The main quadratic result concerns one operator at a time; it does not claim a partition count independent of the size of an arbitrarily prescribed family of operators that must all be paved simultaneously.

M1’s general bound is sixth-power approximation paving, with norm inflation at most three. M2’s quadratic bound controls a compression of the original operator. The expected-MASA conversion gives quadratic approximation paving only under its stated normal-expectation hypothesis.

The original operators need not admit norm paving at all. Strongly large projections may discard a nonzero subspace, and strong approximants need not be close in operator norm. These allowances are exactly what makes the general formulations plausible.

The two main proofs are independent, while particular corollaries use established transfer results or the companion theorem. Improving constants, determining optimal approximation-paving rates without expectations, and understanding simultaneous-family bounds remain separate quantitative questions.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Popa and Vaes, Paving over arbitrary MASAs in von Neumann algebras, for the conjectures, definitions and transfer results.
  • Popa and Vaes, On the optimal paving over MASAs in von Neumann algebras, for sharp singular-MASA bounds.
  • Ravichandran and Srivastava, Asymptotically Optimal Multi-Paving, for the finite-dimensional input used by M2.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Approximation Paving over Arbitrary Maximal Abelian Subalgebras (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Quadratic Strong-Operator Paving over Arbitrary Maximal Abelian Subalgebras (September 25, 2026).
