entry.title: One irreducible representation does not determine the compact operators
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 297 · Operator algebras
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

An algebra of operators can be studied through its irreducible representations, the representations that cannot be split into smaller invariant pieces. The compact operators on a Hilbert space have a special feature: every nonzero irreducible representation is equivalent to the defining one.

Naimark asked whether this feature characterizes the compact operators. Family 297 claims an algebra with only one irreducible representation up to unitary equivalence that nevertheless is not an algebra of compact operators. The construction uses ZFC, the usual axioms of set theory with choice, without an additional prediction principle.

The manuscript explicitly credits an earlier ZFC construction by Ryotaro Tanaka. Its contribution is an alternative method: selectively join pure-state representation classes, preserve unique extensions, and ensure every pure state of the final algebra is eventually captured by the recursion.

2. Background and essential definitions

A representation of a complex C*-algebra AAA is a *-homomorphism π:A→B(H)\pi:A\to B(H)π:A→B(H). It is irreducible if it is nonzero and its only closed invariant subspaces are zero and HHH. Two representations are unitarily equivalent if a unitary between their Hilbert spaces intertwines their actions.

The algebra K(H)\mathcal K(H)K(H) consists of compact operators, the norm closure of finite-rank operators. It is unital exactly when HHH is finite-dimensional. Therefore a unital infinite-dimensional algebra cannot be isomorphic to K(H)\mathcal K(H)K(H) for any HHH.

A state is a positive linear functional of norm one. It is pure if it is an extreme point of the state space, meaning it cannot be a nontrivial convex mixture of two different states. The Gelfand–Naimark–Segal construction associates a representation to each state; purity is equivalent to irreducibility of that representation.

Two pure states can be different while their GNS representations are equivalent. Naimark’s property concerns one equivalence class of irreducible representations, not a single pure state or a single state of any kind.

A trace satisfies τ(ab)=τ(ba)\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)τ(ab)=τ(ba); it is faithful if τ(a∗a)>0\tau(a^*a)>0τ(a∗a)>0 for every nonzero aaa. A simple algebra has no nonzero proper closed two-sided ideals. These additional properties appear in the claimed example but do not force it to be norm separable.

The density of an algebra is the smallest size of a norm-dense subset. Set-theoretic size is crucial here: the known positive results for separable situations are compatible with large counterexamples.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Naimark’s problem dates to 1951. Classical affirmative results apply when the unique nonzero irreducible representation acts on a separable Hilbert space. That condition concerns the irreducible representation itself. Merely possessing some faithful representation on a separable Hilbert space is weaker, since that representation can be reducible.

Akemann and Weaver constructed a counterexample using Jensen’s diamond principle, a set-theoretic prediction principle consistent with but not provable from the usual axioms, assuming those axioms are consistent. They also established independence for the existence of a counterexample generated by ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​ elements. This is a statement with a cardinality bound, not a proof that unrestricted counterexamples cannot be constructed in ZFC.

Later work refined both the additional axioms and the possible algebraic structure. Calderón–Farah used a weaker diamond-like principle together with the continuum hypothesis. Vaccaro constructed traced counterexamples with prescribed metrizable trace simplices under diamond. The presence of a trace therefore was already compatible with negative examples.

Tanaka’s September 22, 2026 preprint states a ZFC counterexample with a faithful trace and a faithful representation on a separable Hilbert space. Its irreducible representations remain nonseparable, preserving the classical positive theorem’s scope. M1, dated September 24, expressly says that its existence conclusion is already present in Tanaka’s work.

The new approach follows an earlier suggested route through separable subalgebras that uniquely determine states. Rather than predicting unknown future states with a diamond principle, it claims enough control of extensions and countable dependencies to find every relevant state by ordinary transfinite bookkeeping.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states the existence in ZFC of a unital infinite-dimensional simple complex C*-algebra AAA with a faithful tracial state such that all nonzero irreducible representations are unitarily equivalent.

Because AAA is unital and infinite-dimensional, it cannot be K(H)\mathcal K(H)K(H). Thus it is a counterexample to Naimark’s characterization. No separability assumption is placed on AAA, and the source does not claim the additional separable faithful representation supplied by Tanaka’s different construction.

The recursion has length c+\mathfrak c^+c+, where c=2ℵ0\mathfrak c=2^{\aleph_0}c=2ℵ0​ is the cardinality of the continuum and c+\mathfrak c^+c+ its successor cardinal. M1 explicitly does not identify that recursion length with the density of the resulting algebra. It also does not claim a counterexample with only ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​ generators in every model of ZFC.

Two intermediate assertions organize the construction. A selective extension joins a chosen pair of pure-state equivalence classes while preserving unique state extensions for every old pure state and preventing unintended joins of other old classes. A countable-determination theorem then makes every pure state of the full algebra the unique extension of its restriction to a suitable separable subalgebra built from countably many dependency-closed steps.

These are existence and structural claims about the construction. They do not provide a finite presentation or a practical algorithm listing all states of the resulting algebra.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The family addresses a classical representation-theoretic problem at the boundary of operator algebras and set theory. If correct, its method explains how unrestricted counterexamples can be built without a state-guessing axiom, using unique extensions and countable determination instead.

The rating reflects the manuscript’s explicit priority qualification: the same ZFC existence conclusion already appears in Tanaka’s earlier preprint. The new value is the alternative construction and the proposed general-purpose extension machinery, rather than first establishing the headline existence statement.

The result also illustrates how coarse a representation-class invariant can be. Having only one irreducible representation class does not force an algebra to resemble compact operators once large nonseparable structures are permitted. Distinct pure states and a faithful trace can coexist with that single class.

6. The main idea

Describe a pure state by shrinking projections

A decreasing sequence of projections pnp_npn​ is said to peak at a state φ\varphiφ if φ\varphiφ is the only state taking value one on every pnp_npn​. Such a sequence concentrates the state’s defining information into countably many algebra elements.

M1 begins with faithfully tracial algebras having no finite-dimensional irreducible representations. For two suitable inequivalent pure states, it chooses peaking sequences with matching trace values decreasing to zero. Matching traces makes it possible to adjoin a unitary connecting the two sequences while retaining the tracial structure.

Join exactly the intended classes

The adjunction is a reduced HNN extension, an operator-algebra version of adding a new symmetry that identifies two prescribed pieces. It is realized through a matrix corner of a reduced amalgamated free product.

The crucial property is selective control. Every old pure state must have a unique extension among all states, not merely among pure states. The intended two representation classes become equivalent, while other inequivalent old classes remain distinct unless the prescribed join requires otherwise.

Pure-state excision supplies norm estimates expressing how compression near a pure state behaves like multiplication by its scalar value. Cross-excision estimates distinguish inequivalent states. M1 uses these estimates on reduced words to establish its extension claims.

Track countable dependencies

At each active successor step the construction adjoins one unitary; at limit stages it takes norm closures of unions. Each new unitary depends on only countably many earlier generators.

A collection of steps is dependency closed if it includes all earlier data required by its chosen adjunctions. The manuscript proves that a pure state on such a subiteration has a unique extension to the whole construction. Its argument reorders omitted adjunctions, postponing them past retained ones. The selective no-unintended-join property keeps that reordering under control.

Excision then finds, for every pure state of the final algebra, a separable dependency-closed subalgebra on which its restriction is pure and determines its entire extension. This is the claimed replacement for guessing future states.

Schedule every state into one class

With countable determination available, a transfinite schedule can eventually process the relevant states. At stages below c+\mathfrak c^+c+, the construction controls the state count by c\mathfrak cc, and suitable homogeneity on separable determining subalgebras supplies new peaking sequences.

Repeated selective joins merge all pure-state GNS classes into one. A final countable-determination argument ensures that no pure state appearing only at the limit escapes the schedule. The trace is maintained along the chain, giving the faithful tracial state in the conclusion.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is unrestricted in algebra size, but does not settle every cardinally bounded version of Naimark’s problem. In particular, a ZFC counterexample at some large density is compatible with independence results for a prescribed number of generators.

A faithful representation and an irreducible representation must also remain distinct. The source’s theorem does not claim that the unique irreducible representation acts on a separable Hilbert space; the classical affirmative result would preclude that. Tanaka’s separable faithful representation is reducible.

The faithful trace does not mean that all states coincide or that every representation is a direct copy of one finite-dimensional matrix representation. The algebra is infinite-dimensional, and the uniqueness concerns unitary equivalence classes of nonzero irreducible representations only.

M1 does not assert uniqueness of the tracial state, an exact density value, or equivalence of its construction with Tanaka’s. Its stated advance is an alternative ZFC route and its extension machinery. The exposition takes those mathematical claims as stated, without treating the transfinite argument as independently verified.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Akemann and Weaver, Consistency of a counterexample to Naimark’s problem, for the diamond construction and cardinally bounded independence result.
  • Tanaka, A separably representable counterexample to Naimark’s problem in ZFC, the September 22 theorem explicitly credited by M1.
  • Calderón and Farah, Can you take Akemann–Weaver’s diamond away?, for the intervening set-theoretic and unique-extension questions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A counterexample to Naimark’s problem in ZFC (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When every extended trace determines a stabilized operator algebra
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 301 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Can an operator algebra be reconstructed from all its ways of measuring positive elements? Usually traces alone lose too much information: projection classes, ideals and other invariants may distinguish algebras with similar ordinary trace spaces.

Family 301 claims a setting in which a suitably complete trace invariant is enough. After tensoring a separable nuclear C*-algebra with the Razak–Jacelon algebra and with compact operators, its isomorphism type is determined by the topological cone of all extended lower-semicontinuous tracial weights.

“All” is crucial. The invariant includes weights taking only zero and infinity, and these encode the ideal structure. The theorem allows arbitrary ideals, nonunital algebras, and mixtures of finite and infinite behavior. It also claims that an algebra isomorphism can realize a prescribed isomorphism of trace cones.

2. Background and essential definitions

A C*-algebra is an adjoint algebra complete in a norm satisfying ∥a∗a∥=∥a∥2\|a^*a\|=\|a\|^2∥a∗a∥=∥a∥2. Its positive elements form A+A_+A+​. Separability means a countable norm-dense subset exists; nuclearity means finite sets admit completely positive finite-dimensional approximations.

An extended tracial weight is a map τ:A+→[0,∞]\tau:A_+\to[0,\infty]τ:A+​→[0,∞] that is additive, positively homogeneous, vanishes at zero, and satisfies τ(x∗x)=τ(xx∗)\tau(x^*x)=\tau(xx^*)τ(x∗x)=τ(xx∗). Lower semicontinuity means its value cannot jump upward under a norm-convergent approximation in the forbidden direction: τ(a)≤lim inf⁡τ(ai)\tau(a)\leq\liminf\tau(a_i)τ(a)≤liminfτ(ai​) when ai→aa_i\to aai​→a.

The weight need not be finite on a dense subset. For every closed two-sided ideal III, the cone includes

τI(a)={0,a∈I+,∞,a∈A+∖I+.\tau_I(a)=\begin{cases}0,&a\in I_+,\\\infty,&a\in A_+\setminus I_+.\end{cases}τI​(a)={0,∞,​a∈I+​,a∈A+​∖I+​.​

These are not normalized states. Omitting them would discard information central to the classification claim.

The cone T(A)T(A)T(A) has addition, multiplication by positive real scalars, and a canonical topology. With (a−ε)+(a-\varepsilon)_+(a−ε)+​ denoting the positive part obtained by cutting off the spectrum below ε\varepsilonε, convergence is characterized by

lim sup⁡iτi((a−ε)+)≤τ(a)≤lim inf⁡iτi(a)\limsup_i\tau_i((a-\varepsilon)_+)\leq\tau(a)\leq\liminf_i\tau_i(a)ilimsup​τi​((a−ε)+​)≤τ(a)≤iliminf​τi​(a)

for every positive aaa and every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0. A cone isomorphism must be a homeomorphism preserving addition, zero and positive scalar multiplication.

The Razak–Jacelon algebra W\mathcal WW is simple, nuclear, stably projectionless and has a unique tracial state. Stably projectionless means no nonzero projection appears even after tensoring with compact operators. Write K=K(ℓ2(N))\mathcal K=\mathcal K(\ell^2(\mathbb N))K=K(ℓ2(N)). The theorem classifies A⊗W⊗KA\otimes\mathcal W\otimes\mathcal KA⊗W⊗K, not AAA itself; both tensor factors are part of the conclusion.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Razak classified certain simple inductive limits of stably projectionless building blocks using traces and scale. Jacelon isolated W\mathcal WW, with trivial K-theory and a unique trace, as a central example. Its tensorial role suggests removing K-theoretic distinctions while retaining numerical size information.

Elliott, Robert and Santiago developed the full topological cone of extended traces and its relationship to functionals on the Cuntz semigroup. The latter records comparison classes of positive operators. Robert showed that tensoring with W\mathcal WW corresponds to a realification of that semigroup. Thus the trace cone already determines the stabilized order invariant; the remaining question is whether the invariant can be realized by actual algebra isomorphisms.

Robert’s trace-cone classification question was recorded in 2012 and appears in the later Schafhauser–Tikuisis–White problem collection. Simple tracial cases were covered by classification results under their respective contractibility and regularity hypotheses. Other results show absorption of W\mathcal WW for suitable simple monotracial algebras.

The traceless branch behaves differently. If every extended trace takes only zero and infinity, the cone mainly records ideals, and purely infinite classification tools address the corresponding stabilization. Neither that branch nor the simple tracial branch automatically handles an algebra with both finite and infinite regions.

Restricted nonsimple classification results treated particular extensions with additional hypotheses. M1 claims the full cone-only theorem for arbitrary ideal structure, without a universal coefficient theorem assumption. Its historical discussion emphasizes that even one proper nonzero ideal introduces difficulties absent from simple classification.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let A,BA,BA,B be separable nuclear complex C*-algebras. M1 states that an isomorphism of their full topological trace cones implies

A⊗W⊗K≅B⊗W⊗K.A\otimes\mathcal W\otimes\mathcal K\cong B\otimes\mathcal W\otimes\mathcal K.A⊗W⊗K≅B⊗W⊗K.

All tensor products are spatial. The conclusion is an actual C*-algebra isomorphism, not just agreement of trace data, Cuntz semigroups, or asymptotic models.

Put P=A⊗W⊗KP=A\otimes\mathcal W\otimes\mathcal KP=A⊗W⊗K and Q=B⊗W⊗KQ=B\otimes\mathcal W\otimes\mathcal KQ=B⊗W⊗K. After transporting the given cone map to the stabilized cones in the contravariant direction,

F:T(Q)⟶T(P),F:T(Q)\longrightarrow T(P),F:T(Q)⟶T(P),

M1 constructs an isomorphism Φ:P→Q\Phi:P\to QΦ:P→Q satisfying

τ∘Φ=F(τ)(τ∈T(Q)).\tau\circ\Phi=F(\tau)\qquad(\tau\in T(Q)).τ∘Φ=F(τ)(τ∈T(Q)).

Thus the specified invariant map is realized, not merely some map between isomorphic cones.

The algebras may be nonunital, need not be simple, and may have arbitrary primitive ideal spaces. Weights may have nondense finite domains. No extra dimension, trace-boundary or UCT condition is imposed in the main theorem.

The source also observes that these stabilizations have nuclear dimension at most one, using the separate dimension theorem in family 291 and absorption of Z\mathcal ZZ by W\mathcal WW. It explicitly states that its classification argument does not use that dimension bound.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this is a broad nonsimple classification theorem with a single integrated invariant. It would show that, after the stated stabilization, trace data encode not only finite numerical sizes but also the ideal geometry needed to distinguish the algebras.

The invariant is richer than the familiar simplex of tracial states. For instance,

I⊆J⟺τI+τJ=τI.I\subseteq J\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\tau_I+\tau_J=\tau_I.I⊆J⟺τI​+τJ​=τI​.

The cone’s arithmetic therefore remembers inclusion between ideals. Its topology and scaling also distinguish where general weights are finite and where they vanish.

Realizing a prescribed cone map adds classification strength. It connects not just objects but the way their invariants are identified. This matters when one wants a particular trace correspondence respected by an algebra isomorphism.

6. The main idea

Recover positive-element order and ideal supports

Cuntz comparison writes a≾ba\precsim ba≾b when vn∗bvn→av_n^*bv_n\to avn∗​bvn​→a in norm. Its classes form Cu(A)\mathrm{Cu}(A)Cu(A), an ordered semigroup with increasing suprema. For a positive contraction, the rank associated with a weight is

dτ(a)=lim⁡k→∞τ(a1/k).d_\tau(a)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\tau(a^{1/k}).dτ​(a)=k→∞lim​τ(a1/k).

Robert’s realification result converts the cone isomorphism into a compatible Cuntz-semigroup isomorphism for P,QP,QP,Q. It also identifies their ideal spaces. M1 then tries to build algebra maps implementing this data.

Measure errors where a weight is finite

In a simple normalized-trace setting, an error can often be bounded uniformly over a compact trace space. Here a weight may be finite only on a proper ideal. A full positive element may even have infinite rank for every relevant nonzero weight, making a small scalar multiple of that rank useless as an error estimate.

M1 therefore fixes local controllers: spectral cuts and ideal supports on which finite quantities can be compared. Upper bounds keep errors small there, while lower support estimates prevent a map from accidentally erasing the regions where the prescribed weight is infinite.

This two-sided control is the central bookkeeping difficulty. Matching all finite numerical values would not suffice if the resulting map changed which elements had infinite weight.

Build sequence models and correct them in norm

The first maps land in a sequence algebra Q∞=ℓ∞(Q)/c0(Q)Q_\infty=\ell^\infty(Q)/c_0(Q)Q∞​=ℓ∞(Q)/c0​(Q), where errors may vanish along coordinates. Regularized limits of weights retain lower semicontinuity through spectral cuts.

Finite-dimensional nuclear approximations and von Neumann algebra uniqueness tools produce tracial models. Small stabilizing pieces simultaneously satisfy upper trace estimates and lower ideal-support comparisons. Ideal-related absorption and stable-uniqueness methods then remove differences in operator norm, rather than leaving only agreement under traces.

The manuscript explicitly treats correction on the original module and recovery of the full trace formula, including infinite values. These are the steps turning a numerical model into an algebraic one.

Pass from models to an actual isomorphism

A suspension-and-corner construction converts point and interval models into actual maps with the required trace normalization. Approximate intertwining builds maps in both directions and adjusts successive compositions to approach the identity on increasing finite sets.

Separability permits this countable approximation scheme. The limiting maps are mutually inverse and realize the prescribed cone correspondence. The final output is therefore an isomorphism of the stabilized C*-algebras, not just an embedding into a sequence quotient.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem classifies after tensoring with both W\mathcal WW and K\mathcal KK. It does not claim that equal trace cones classify the original algebras, nor that either stabilization can always be omitted. It also does not classify all C*-algebras without nuclearity or separability.

The cone must include every extended lower-semicontinuous tracial weight with the specified topology. Restricting to bounded traces, normalized states or densely finite weights would change the invariant and could lose ideal information. A set-theoretic bijection of weights or an affine identification of one trace base is not the theorem’s hypothesis.

The map-realization statement is an existence assertion, not uniqueness of the implementing algebra isomorphism. Likewise, the separate nuclear-dimension consequence is not a hidden assumption in the classification construction.

Understanding which additional hypotheses permit removing compact stabilization, or using a smaller trace invariant in particular classes, remains a separate classification question. M1’s claim is the full-cone theorem in the stated stabilized setting.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Jacelon, A simple, monotracial, stably projectionless C*-algebra, for the construction and role of W\mathcal WW.
  • M1’s introduction gives the precise Robert realification theorem, the earlier simple and traceless classification cases, and the formulation of the full trace-cone question.
  • The source’s Sections 2–3 specify the extended-weight topology and local error ideals; Section 8 states realization of the prescribed cone map.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The trace cone classifies Razak–Jacelon stabilizations (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Half the mean dimension: an exact bridge from dynamics to operator comparison
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 302 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A dynamical system can generate new geometric complexity as its orbit is observed for longer times. Mean dimension measures the number of continuous parameters needed per time step. An associated operator algebra has a different measure of complexity: how much extra tracial size is needed before one positive operator can be fitted inside another.

The Phillips–Toms conjecture predicts a precise bridge between these quantities. Family 302 claims that for every minimal homeomorphism of an infinite compact metrizable space,

rc⁡(C(X)⋊hZ)=12mdim⁡(X,h).\operatorname{rc}(C(X)\rtimes_h\mathbb Z)=\frac12\operatorname{mdim}(X,h).rc(C(X)⋊h​Z)=21​mdim(X,h).

The equality includes infinity. One manuscript proves the dynamical statement using an established upper bound; the other supplies a topological compression theorem needed for the new lower bound. The factor one half reflects the relation between complex vector-bundle rank and real covering dimension.

2. Background and essential definitions

A homeomorphism h:X→Xh:X\to Xh:X→X is minimal if every orbit is dense. For infinite compact XXX, minimality rules out periodic points. Metrizability gives a countable, metric framework without requiring finite covering dimension.

For a finite open cover U\mathcal UU, join its translates over NNN steps to obtain the orbit cover U[0,N)\mathcal U^{[0,N)}U[0,N). Let DDD be the smallest order of a finite open refinement, where order is one less than the largest number of sets meeting at one point. Then

mdim⁡(X,h)=sup⁡Ulim⁡N→∞D(U[0,N))N.\operatorname{mdim}(X,h)=\sup_{\mathcal U}\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{D(\mathcal U^{[0,N)})}{N}.mdim(X,h)=Usup​N→∞lim​ND(U[0,N))​.

It measures average covering complexity along orbits, rather than the dimension of XXX alone.

The crossed product C(X)⋊hZC(X)\rtimes_h\mathbb ZC(X)⋊h​Z combines continuous functions on XXX with a unitary implementing the dynamics. Invariant probability measures yield normalized tracial states on this algebra.

For positive matrix elements a,ba,ba,b, Cuntz subequivalence a≾ba\precsim ba≾b means that vj∗bvj→av_j^*bv_j\to avj∗​bvj​→a in norm after placing the matrices in compatible larger corners. For a normalized trace τ\tauτ, define

dτ(a)=lim⁡m→∞(τ⊗Tr⁡)(a1/m),d_\tau(a)=\lim_{m\to\infty}(\tau\otimes\operatorname{Tr})(a^{1/m}),dτ​(a)=m→∞lim​(τ⊗Tr)(a1/m),

with the matrix trace unnormalized. The radius of comparison is the infimum of numbers r≥0r\geq0r≥0 such that

dτ(a)+r<dτ(b) for all τ⟹a≾b.d_\tau(a)+r<d_\tau(b)\text{ for all }\tau\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a\precsim b.dτ​(a)+r<dτ​(b) for all τ⟹a≾b.

If no finite rrr works, the radius is infinity. It records a dimension-like obstruction left over after numerical ranks are compared.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gromov introduced mean dimension, developed systematically by Lindenstrauss and Weiss. Toms introduced the radius of comparison in C*-algebra classification, where vector bundles show that numerical rank alone need not determine comparison.

Giol–Kerr connected these ideas by constructing minimal systems with positive mean dimension and large comparison radii. Phillips obtained a general upper bound with a larger constant and additive term. Elliott–Niu settled the zero-mean-dimension case through Jiang–Su stability.

Niu then proved the optimal upper bound

rc⁡(C(X)⋊hZ)≤12mdim⁡(X,h)\operatorname{rc}(C(X)\rtimes_h\mathbb Z)\leq\frac12\operatorname{mdim}(X,h)rc(C(X)⋊h​Z)≤21​mdim(X,h)

in a setting including all systems considered here. M2 credits this result; the new problem is the reverse inequality.

Hirshberg–Phillips obtained lower bounds through mean cohomological independence, detecting persistent cup products of translated cohomology classes. These gave strong estimates for particular minimal subshifts. But a general cover may carry dimensional complexity not captured by the required cohomological independence hypothesis.

M1’s topological tools draw on complex cobordism and the Devinatz–Hopkins–Smith nilpotence theorem, with quantitative connective refinements. M2 uses them to turn a comparison assumption directly into a reduction of open-cover complexity, avoiding a separate cohomological independence assumption.

A subsequent October 8 preprint of Elliott and Niu states related equalities for amenable actions with the uniform Rokhlin property and Cuntz comparison of open sets, explicitly using these topological ideas. That is later work with its own hypotheses; the pinned family’s main dynamical theorem concerns integer actions generated by one minimal homeomorphism.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: exact equality and the zero endpoint

For every minimal homeomorphism hhh of an infinite compact metrizable XXX, M2 claims the equality in Section 1 in [0,∞][0,\infty][0,∞]. No finite-dimensionality or cohomological independence condition on XXX is assumed.

It also derives equivalence of zero mean dimension, the small boundary property, Jiang–Su stability of the crossed product, finite nuclear dimension, and nuclear dimension at most one.

The small boundary property means that neighborhoods can be chosen whose boundaries have orbit capacity zero: the largest fraction of visits to the boundary over long orbit segments tends to zero. Jiang–Su stability means absorption of Z\mathcal ZZ; nuclear dimension counts pieces in finite-dimensional positive-map approximations.

The zero-mean-dimension-to-regularity directions use earlier theorems. The new lower bound supplies the converse from operator-algebraic comparison. Positive or infinite mean dimension consequently forces failure of Jiang–Su stability and infinite nuclear dimension in this class.

M1: coherent vanishing on product unions

For a finite pointed CW pair G⊆EG\subseteq EG⊆E and a map v:E→Sdv:E\to S^dv:E→Sd, suppose the restriction to GGG becomes null in complex cobordism. Here a finite CW complex is built from finitely many cells, and complex cobordism is a generalized cohomology theory encoding stable complex-geometric information.

M1 claims that sufficiently large smash powers of vvv are stably null on the whole union where at least a fixed positive proportion of factors lie in GGG. A smash product is a pointed product with all basepoint-coordinate subsets collapsed; stable nullity means nullity after passing to stable homotopy. The conclusion gives one compatible nullhomotopy on the union, not unrelated nullhomotopies on its pieces.

M1: boundary-preserving cube compression

Let a continuous map from any compact metrizable space have nnn cube-valued slots of dimension 2p+12p+12p+1. A specified torus locus over sparse translations carries a complex bundle of rank pnpnpn. If that bundle has one continuous embedding over the entire parameter locus into a trivial bundle of rank K<2pnK<2pnK<2pn, M1 obtains compression on arbitrarily large Cartesian powers.

For a sparsity parameter 0<a<1/160<a<1/160<a<1/16, the output places at least an a/8a/8a/8 fraction of slots on their boundaries. Every slot already on the boundary is preserved as its entire vector, including coordinates that were interior within that slot. There is no covering-dimension bound on the input space.

The strict inequality K<2pnK<2pnK<2pn is essential to this general criterion: M1 gives a cube example at equality where the required compression is impossible. The embedding must vary continuously as the sparse parameter’s support changes.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the equality identifies an exact numerical operator-algebra invariant from topological dynamics across all minimal homeomorphisms in the stated class. It also makes zero mean dimension precisely the boundary of the crossed product’s Jiang–Su and finite-dimensional approximation regularity.

The new lower-bound mechanism is important beyond improving a constant. It detects arbitrary orbit-cover complexity, including infinite-dimensional spaces where a selected cohomological invariant may miss information.

M1 supplies a reusable topological principle: local or restricted vanishing must remain compatible across product intersections before it can support a global compression. Its boundary-preservation requirement is what lets the compression improve a cover without destroying its original refinement information.

6. The main idea

Assume comparison is too easy

Fix a finite comparison bound rrr and an open cover whose mean cover rate exceeds 2r2r2r. M2 represents a long orbit block by a finite simplicial complex. After subdivision, vertices receive colors distinct on each simplex.

Groups of 2p+22p+22p+2 colors become packets whose proportions define cube-valued slots of dimension 2p+12p+12p+1. Zero colors record absent members of the original cover. A useful compression must preserve these absences, or the resulting map may no longer describe a refinement.

Turn a comparison witness into a bundle embedding

Each slot carries a small torus and a rank-ppp bundle assembled from degree-one line bundles. Niu’s open tower theorem aligns most orbit blocks with a small uniform remainder.

A finite-propagation Cuntz comparison witness gives a bundle embedding on the aligned pieces. Additional linear maps handle sparse support changes and imperfect alignment. M2 obtains the single continuous embedding over the full parameter locus required by M1, with target rank strictly below twice the source rank.

Compress coherently and reconstruct a smaller cover

M1 first converts cobordism vanishing into stable vanishing on a constrained product union. Compatible local duality then turns this into avoidance of a sparse arrangement. A padding construction removes the dimension restriction that would otherwise obstruct conversion from stable data to an actual map.

Radial normalization produces boundary slots while restoring original boundary vectors exactly. M2 interprets each new boundary slot as at least one missing color. Small packets are discarded carefully, and boundary preservation prevents any originally absent color from reappearing.

The reconstructed map lands in a complex of smaller dimension while still refining the full orbit cover. That contradicts the chosen cover rate. The ratio of ppp complex lines to 2p+22p+22p+2 colors tends to one half, producing the exact constant after controlling the other losses.

Include infinite mean dimension

The argument bounds every finite-cover rate by 2r2r2r. Taking the supremum over covers gives mean dimension at most 2r2r2r. If mean dimension is infinite, no finite comparison bound can exist. Combining this lower bound with Niu’s established upper bound completes the stated equality.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The main theorem concerns minimal homeomorphisms of infinite compact metrizable spaces. It does not by itself settle the conjecture for every action of every amenable group, and the later cited extension retains additional dynamical assumptions.

The topological compression theorem requires a continuous bundle monomorphism over the full sparse-parameter locus, not separate embeddings at individual parameters. It gives arbitrarily large suitable powers, rather than specifying compression at every power or a universal small power.

The equality uses normalized algebra traces with unnormalized matrix traces. Changing rank normalization changes the comparison convention and can obscure the factor one half. The point at infinity is part of the theorem, not an extrapolation from finite examples.

M2 depends on M1’s compression theorem and on Niu’s upper-bound and tower results. The regularity corollary also invokes published simple-algebra theorems. These dependencies are part of the claimed result’s structure, rather than independent verifications performed for this digest.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Hirshberg and Phillips, Radius of comparison and mean cohomological independence dimension, for earlier dynamical lower bounds.
  • Elliott and Niu, Mean dimension and radius of comparison, for the later extension under its stated hypotheses.
  • M2 gives the precise Niu upper-bound and tower inputs; M1 states the compatible product-vanishing and strict-rank compression theorems used in the new lower bound.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Filtered products and boundary-preserving compression in complex cobordism (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Radius of comparison equals half the mean dimension (September 25, 2026).

entry.title: From local infinite size to Cuntz-algebra absorption
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 303 · Operator algebras
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Infinite-dimensional objects can sometimes contain two copies of themselves. For positive operators in a C*-algebra, Cuntz comparison makes this idea precise: an element is properly infinite if two copies can be fitted into one in the comparison sense.

Several versions of pure infiniteness ask whether this happens for every positive element, only after a fixed matrix amplification, or with simultaneous control of interactions between two elements. In nonsimple algebras, these requirements were not interchangeable by definition.

Family 303 claims that ordinary pure infiniteness already implies the strong simultaneous version for every complex C*-algebra. Under exactness, it also removes a fixed finite amplification. For separable nuclear algebras, established absorption theorems then identify all these conditions with tensorial absorption of the Cuntz algebra O∞\mathcal O_\inftyO∞​.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let CCC be a complex C*-algebra, possibly nonunital. For positive elements in its stabilization C⊗KC\otimes\mathcal KC⊗K, write a≾ba\precsim ba≾b if some sequence satisfies vj∗bvj→av_j^*bv_j\to avj∗​bvj​→a in norm. Here K\mathcal KK is the compact operators, allowing different matrix sizes to be compared by adding zero corners.

A positive element hhh is properly infinite if

h⊕h≾h.h\oplus h\precsim h.h⊕h≾h.

The symbol ⊕\oplus⊕ denotes a block-diagonal direct sum. The convention includes zero as properly infinite. Ordinary pure infiniteness in the Kirchberg–Rørdam nonsimple sense is equivalent to requiring this for every positive element.

The fixed-amplification form of weak pure infiniteness requires one integer n≥1n\geq1n≥1 such that h⊕nh^{\oplus n}h⊕n is properly infinite for every h∈C+h\in C_+h∈C+​. The integer is chosen before hhh; allowing a different uncontrolled integer for each element would change the hypothesis.

Strong pure infiniteness demands compatible comparison for pairs. One formulation says that for positive x,yx,yx,y and every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, there are s,t∈Cs,t\in Cs,t∈C with

∥s∗x2s−x2∥<ε,∥t∗y2t−y2∥<ε,\|s^*x^2s-x^2\|<\varepsilon,\qquad\|t^*y^2t-y^2\|<\varepsilon,∥s∗x2s−x2∥<ε,∥t∗y2t−y2∥<ε,

and

∥s∗xyt∥<ε.\|s^*xyt\|<\varepsilon.∥s∗xyt∥<ε.

The first two inequalities retain the diagonal information, while the third suppresses the mixed interaction. No norm bound on s,ts,ts,t is part of this definition.

An algebra is exact if spatial tensoring preserves short exact sequences. Nuclearity, the existence of completely positive finite-dimensional approximations, implies exactness. The algebra O∞\mathcal O_\inftyO∞​ is generated by countably many isometries with mutually orthogonal ranges. Absorption means A≅A⊗min⁡O∞A\cong A\otimes_{\min}\mathcal O_\inftyA≅A⊗min​O∞​.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kirchberg and Rørdam developed weak, ordinary and strong pure infiniteness to extend the simple-algebra theory to algebras with ideals. Strong pure infiniteness naturally supports O∞\mathcal O_\inftyO∞​-absorption, but an individual positive-element comparison need not visibly control mixed entries.

Several structural classes were already understood. Kirchberg–Rørdam treated simple, real-rank-zero and approximately divisible cases. Blanchard–Kirchberg obtained ordinary-to-strong pure infiniteness when the primitive ideal space is Hausdorff. Rørdam obtained the same implication for Jiang–Su-absorbing purely infinite algebras.

Other results used ideal structure. Pasnicu–Rørdam proved equivalence of the notions when projections separate ideals. Work on topological dimension zero, where the primitive ideal space has a basis of compact open sets, gave additional ordinary-to-strong and weak-to-ordinary implications.

The weak-to-ordinary direction is connected to the Global Glimm Property, which produces suitably large square-zero elements inside hereditary subalgebras. Such an element supplies orthogonal equivalent source and range pieces. Earlier results show that enough of this halving structure permits removal of a fixed amplification.

Finally, Kirchberg–Rørdam established the relationship between strong pure infiniteness and O∞\mathcal O_\inftyO∞​-absorption in stable or projection-approximate-unit settings. Kirchberg’s later central-sequence results cover general nonunital separable nuclear algebras. M1 uses that established absorption bridge after proving its new comparison implications.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Ordinary implies strong without additional regularity

Suppose every positive element of a complex C*-algebra CCC is properly infinite. M1 claims that for all positive a,ba,ba,b, every c∈Cc\in Cc∈C, and every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, there exist s,t∈Cs,t\in Cs,t∈C such that

∥s∗as−a∥<ε,∥t∗bt−b∥<ε,∥s∗ct∥<ε.\|s^*as-a\|<\varepsilon,\qquad\|t^*bt-b\|<\varepsilon,\qquad\|s^*ct\|<\varepsilon.∥s∗as−a∥<ε,∥t∗bt−b∥<ε,∥s∗ct∥<ε.

The cross term ccc is arbitrary, not necessarily a product of the diagonal inputs. Choosing (a,b,c)=(x2,y2,xy)(a,b,c)=(x^2,y^2,xy)(a,b,c)=(x2,y2,xy) gives strong pure infiniteness. This theorem assumes neither exactness, nuclearity, separability, unitality nor a restriction on the ideal space.

Exactness removes one fixed amplification

If CCC is exact and one integer nnn makes every h⊕nh^{\oplus n}h⊕n properly infinite, M1 claims that every hhh itself is properly infinite. The first theorem then makes CCC strongly purely infinite.

Thus the three notions agree for exact algebras, including nonseparable and nonunital ones. The paper also supplies an independent nuclear argument, while explaining how quotient exactness extends that route further. Its direct exact proof uses a different quantitative construction.

Nuclear absorption

For every separable nuclear complex C*-algebra AAA, the fixed-amplification condition therefore implies

A≅A⊗min⁡O∞.A\cong A\otimes_{\min}\mathcal O_\infty.A≅A⊗min​O∞​.

Together with established reverse implications, M1 identifies weak pure infiniteness, ordinary pure infiniteness, strong pure infiniteness and O∞\mathcal O_\inftyO∞​-absorption in this class. No simplicity or unit is required.

The weak-to-ordinary implication for arbitrary nonexact algebras is explicitly left outside the conclusions. The general ordinary-to-strong theorem must not be read as removing the exactness assumption from the other direction.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, these results remove major distinctions among notions of infiniteness in broad nonsimple settings. A local condition on each positive element would already guarantee the compatibility needed to suppress arbitrary mixed entries.

For separable nuclear algebras, a single finite amplification test would characterize a global tensorial regularity property. This connects positive-element comparison with the structure of the whole algebra while allowing arbitrary ideals and nonunital examples.

The scope includes algebras with no nonzero projections. For example, the cone C0((0,1])⊗O∞C_0((0,1])\otimes\mathcal O_\inftyC0​((0,1])⊗O∞​ absorbs O∞\mathcal O_\inftyO∞​, yet any continuous projection-valued function vanishing at the missing endpoint must be zero. Positive-element comparison therefore reaches beyond reasoning only with projections or visible isometries in a unitized picture.

6. The main idea

Separate two hereditary corners

For positive hhh, the hereditary subalgebra Her⁡(h)=hCh‾\operatorname{Her}(h)=\overline{hCh}Her(h)=hCh is the part supported by hhh. The ideal generated by hhh records where it remains visible in irreducible representations.

M1 first seeks positive contractions in the hereditary subalgebras of aaa and bbb whose support projections make the mixed term a strict contraction. At the same time, those contractions must retain a definite norm in every representation detecting the relevant inputs. Otherwise the mixed term could become small simply because important diagonal information had been discarded.

A graph construction inside several orthogonal copies introduces freely chosen algebra entries. If the required separation failed in a detecting representation, equality cases would force those entries to equal predetermined measurements. Under ordinary pure infiniteness, four carefully chosen entries contradict those forced identities through an isometry with a nonzero defect.

Iterate a uniform strict improvement

The first separation only reduces the mixed compression below one. A bounded-product argument gives a uniform contraction factor, and iteration makes the compression arbitrarily small while retaining the represented norm signals.

High spectral cutoffs of the original positive elements are then compared into the separated corners. The order of choices controls the coefficients independently of the final mixed-entry accuracy. This produces simultaneous diagonal recovery and off-diagonal suppression.

Build enough orthogonal copies under exactness

Removing a fixed amplification requires a different step: constructing enough equivalent orthogonal pieces in a scalar hereditary subalgebra before using the amplified comparison.

The exact argument uses a quantitative obstruction coming from a nonexact universal algebra. Finite matrix tests force a positive error threshold for exact targets. This obstruction helps construct square-zero elements retaining a nonzero image throughout a prescribed slice of primitive quotients.

These slices are determined by a lower bound on the norm of a positive element in the quotient. They are quasi-compact even when the primitive ideal space is not Hausdorff. Repeated halving on the same slice creates sufficiently many copies to remove the fixed amplification while preserving the necessary ideal support.

A separate nuclear route

The nuclear argument uses finite tuples witnessing nonexactness as an obstruction to failure of the graph construction. A hypothetical persistent failure would place their limiting matrix norms inside a quotient of a nuclear algebra, contradicting exactness there.

Representation-dependent hereditary witnesses are then merged into one element retaining all the required norm signals. A finite ideal argument covers each spectral cutoff, and comparison returns two copies of that cutoff to the original element. This supplies ordinary pure infiniteness independently of the direct exact route.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The fixed integer in weak pure infiniteness is uniform over all scalar positive elements and their spectral cutoffs. The hypothesis is not merely that some matrix amplification of the algebra contains a properly infinite unit or that selected generators have the property.

Ordinary-to-strong pure infiniteness is claimed in complete generality, but amplification removal requires exactness. The unrestricted nonexact weak-to-ordinary question remains open within the source’s stated conclusions. The absorption equivalence additionally requires separability and nuclearity.

The mixed-entry theorem permits arbitrary ccc, and its definition does not impose fixed coefficient bounds. Quantitative bounds obtained during the proof depend on the specified cutoff data; they should not be replaced by an unstated universal norm bound for every input.

The paper develops two routes for amplification removal, with different external inputs. Their existence does not weaken the assumptions of the main statements. The digest reports those comparison and absorption claims without auditing the constructions.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Kirchberg and Rørdam, Infinite Non-simple C*-Algebras: Absorbing the Cuntz Algebra O∞, for the three infiniteness notions and their absorption framework.
  • Blanchard and Kirchberg, Non-simple purely infinite C*-algebras: the Hausdorff case, for an earlier ideal-space case.
  • M1 specifies the fixed-amplification convention, the exactness boundary, and the separate direct-exact and nuclear constructions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Weak pure infiniteness and O-infinity absorption (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The same metric shape can hide different linear Banach spaces
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 324 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A bounded linear isomorphism between Banach spaces preserves distances up to fixed multiplicative constants. Does the converse hold if a bijection preserves distances to that same accuracy but is allowed to be nonlinear?

Family 324 claims that the answer is no even for separable real Banach spaces. One manuscript distinguishes the spaces by whether they contain a linear copy of a sequence space with Hilbert-valued coordinates. The other gives a stronger ordinary-sequence obstruction: a space containing no linear copy of c0c_0c0​ is nevertheless bi-Lipschitz equivalent to itself with an entire c0c_0c0​ summand added.

These are global, whole-space equivalences with fixed two-sided distance bounds. They are stronger than earlier examples involving only uniform continuity or coarse control at large distances.

2. Background and essential definitions

A map F:X→YF:X\to YF:X→Y is bi-Lipschitz if constants 0<c≤C<∞0<c\leq C<\infty0<c≤C<∞ satisfy

c∥x−x′∥≤∥F(x)−F(x′)∥≤C∥x−x′∥c\|x-x'\|\leq\|F(x)-F(x')\|\leq C\|x-x'\|c∥x−x′∥≤∥F(x)−F(x′)∥≤C∥x−x′∥

for all pairs. It is a bi-Lipschitz equivalence if it is onto; the lower bound then makes it a bijection with Lipschitz inverse. A linear isomorphism additionally preserves addition and scalar multiplication and has bounded inverse.

A uniform homeomorphism requires both directions to be uniformly continuous, but need not provide linear bounds at every scale. A coarse-Lipschitz map can allow additive errors, which weaken its control of small distances. Neither automatically yields the theorem’s global inequalities.

The real Banach space c0c_0c0​ consists of scalar sequences tending to zero, with supremum norm. More generally,

c0(H)={(vi):vi∈H, ∥vi∥→0},∥(vi)∥=sup⁡i∥vi∥.c_0(H)=\{(v_i):v_i\in H,\ \|v_i\|\to0\},\qquad \|(v_i)\|=\sup_i\|v_i\|.c0​(H)={(vi​):vi​∈H, ∥vi​∥→0},∥(vi​)∥=isup​∥vi​∥.

For H=ℓ2H=\ell^2H=ℓ2, each coordinate is a whole infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. Containing a linear copy of c0(ℓ2)c_0(\ell^2)c0​(ℓ2) is therefore a stronger structural condition than containing ordinary c0c_0c0​.

The sum X⊕∞YX\oplus_\infty YX⊕∞​Y has norm max⁡{∥x∥,∥y∥}\max\{\|x\|,\|y\|\}max{∥x∥,∥y∥}. A linear copy means a closed subspace linearly isomorphic to the indicated space, not merely a nonlinear image with comparable distances.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ribe’s theorem shows that uniform homeomorphisms preserve finite-dimensional linear structure up to a uniform distortion bound. This is a powerful reason to expect metric geometry to constrain linear geometry, but it does not recover an entire infinite-dimensional linear isomorphism.

Aharoni–Lindenstrauss constructed nonseparable bi-Lipschitz equivalent Banach spaces that are not linearly isomorphic and asked for separable examples. Ribe later gave separable uniformly homeomorphic nonisomorphic spaces. Further work separated uniform equivalence from Lipschitz equivalence and expanded the collection of uniform counterexamples.

Positive rigidity results obstruct straightforward constructions. Godefroy–Kalton–Lancien proved that a space bi-Lipschitz equivalent to c0c_0c0​ must be linearly isomorphic to c0c_0c0​, and similarly preserved being isomorphic to a subspace of c0c_0c0​. These concern whole-space equivalences, not merely containing a bi-Lipschitz image of c0c_0c0​.

Godefroy–Kalton’s Lipschitz-free lifting theorem supplies another constraint: a Lipschitz right inverse of a bounded linear quotient onto a separable Banach space yields a bounded linear right inverse. A construction claiming to lift arbitrary quotient maps nonlinearly must therefore distinguish exactly what it is lifting.

Separable quasi-Banach counterexamples existed for exponents below one, but they do not settle the Banach-norm case. Kalton recorded the separable Lipschitz-isomorphism problem separately from the question whether a Lipschitz image of c0c_0c0​ forces a linear copy.

M1 claims the former using a Hilbert-block obstruction. M2 addresses the ordinary c0c_0c0​ embedding question and proves an onto absorption statement. Both identify earlier uniform or coarse constructions while retaining their weaker distance hypotheses.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: separable spaces with different Hilbert-block subspaces

M1 constructs separable real Banach spaces X,YX,YX,Y and an onto map Ψ:X→Y\Psi:X\to YΨ:X→Y with

421∥s−t∥X≤∥Ψ(s)−Ψ(t)∥Y≤7625∥s−t∥X.\frac4{21}\|s-t\|_X\leq\|\Psi(s)-\Psi(t)\|_Y\leq\frac{76}{25}\|s-t\|_X.214​∥s−t∥X​≤∥Ψ(s)−Ψ(t)∥Y​≤2576​∥s−t∥X​.

The space XXX contains a linearly isometric copy of c0(ℓ2)c_0(\ell^2)c0​(ℓ2), while YYY contains no closed subspace linearly isomorphic to it. Therefore the spaces cannot be linearly isomorphic.

The obstruction does not say that YYY contains no ordinary c0c_0c0​. M1 states neither reflexivity nor a complex-scalar analogue.

M2: metric absorption without a linear copy

M2 constructs a separable real Banach space ZZZ with no closed linear subspace isomorphic to c0c_0c0​, together with an onto bi-Lipschitz map

F:Z⊕∞c0⟶Z.F:Z\oplus_\infty c_0\longrightarrow Z.F:Z⊕∞​c0​⟶Z.

Restricting to the added summand embeds c0c_0c0​ bi-Lipschitzly into ZZZ, even though no linear copy exists. The whole spaces are bi-Lipschitz equivalent but not linearly isomorphic, since the domain visibly has a linear c0c_0c0​ subspace.

Aharoni’s theorem says every separable metric space embeds bi-Lipschitzly into c0c_0c0​. Composing with the displayed embedding makes this same ZZZ a bi-Lipschitz universal target for separable metric spaces. This means existence of embeddings, not isometric universality or a claim that all those spaces become linearly embedded.

M2’s construction is independent of M1’s Hilbert-block and localized Lipschitz-free argument. Its source is dated September 26, while M1 is dated September 24.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, these examples settle a central rigidity question in nonlinear Banach-space geometry. Global distance equivalence would fail to determine linear isomorphism even under separability.

M2 sharpens the separation in a particularly recognizable way. An entire c0c_0c0​ direction can be absorbed metrically by one space that cannot contain that direction linearly. Metric embeddings of all separable metric spaces can coexist with this linear exclusion.

The conclusions do not contradict exact-distance rigidity, such as the sphere-isometry theorem claimed in family 322. Fixed multiplicative distortion permits behavior that exact distance preservation forbids. They also do not contradict Ribe’s preservation of finite-dimensional structure; the distinguishing subspace properties are infinite-dimensional.

6. The main idea

Lift a correction, not a quotient inverse

Both constructions use a triangular change of variables. A nonlinear map rearranges coordinates, and an auxiliary space lifts the difference between that map and a simple projection. This is weaker than finding a Lipschitz right inverse for a linear quotient, so the Godefroy–Kalton splitting theorem does not directly force the unwanted linear structure.

In M2 the data are a bi-Lipschitz map g:E⊕∞U→Ug:E\oplus_\infty U\to Ug:E⊕∞​U→U, a bounded linear map Q:Z→UQ:Z\to UQ:Z→U, and a Lipschitz correction KKK satisfying

QK=g−P,QK=g-P,QK=g−P,

where PPP projects onto UUU. They yield

F(b,t)=b+K(t,Qb).F(b,t)=b+K(t,Qb).F(b,t)=b+K(t,Qb).

The identity makes an explicit inverse possible. No surjectivity or right-inverse property is demanded of QQQ.

M1: local orthogonality becomes a linear obstruction

M1 first constructs a bi-Lipschitz change of Hilbert-space coordinates h:U⊕2ℓ2→Uh:U\oplus_2\ell^2\to Uh:U⊕2​ℓ2→U. Its nonlinear correction has a local orthogonality property: near finitely many distinct input points, sufficiently high output coordinates occupy mutually orthogonal regions.

The Lipschitz-free space over the domain turns this correction into a bounded linear map qqq. A Lipschitz-free space is built from point evaluations so that zero-preserving Lipschitz maps admit linearizations. M1 proves that the local geometry makes qqq completely continuous, sending weakly null sequences to norm-null sequences.

Sequence graph spaces combine a weighted summable norm with a supremum norm on their qqq-images. The nonlinear coordinate change acts on each sequence coordinate and gives the desired bi-Lipschitz equivalence. The domain visibly retains c0(ℓ2)c_0(\ell^2)c0​(ℓ2); complete continuity and a disjoint-support argument exclude it from the target.

M2: coordinate shifts with controlled nonlinear weights

For ordinary c0c_0c0​, M2 builds ggg using finite coordinate blocks arranged in rows. With weights frozen, the construction shifts scalar slots and has an explicit linear inverse. The actual weights depend on the input, so global invertibility requires controlling their variation, not just inverting the frozen map.

Finite-row arguments use Brouwer’s theorem, with an extra scalar balancing dimensions and controlling spillover. Uniform bounds and a closed-image argument then yield an onto map on the infinite space.

Design a norm that excludes linear c0

M2 records the coordinate corrections as localized scalar Lipschitz tests. It builds ZZZ from finite mass-zero combinations of points, using selected test lists and a norm combining exponents approaching one with an outer square sum.

If a linear c0c_0c0​ basis existed, its finite signed sums would remain uniformly bounded. The test construction extracts one detecting function per basis vector while retaining uniform Lipschitz control on signed sums of those tests. Separated supports or carefully controlled nested supports then force the vector sums’ norms to grow, a contradiction.

The same tests define QQQ and the lifted correction KKK, connecting the exclusion argument to the metric absorption map rather than constructing two unrelated spaces.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Both manuscripts concern real separable Banach spaces and global bi-Lipschitz maps. They do not establish complex-linear counterexamples, reflexive examples, or a universal optimal distortion constant.

M1 excludes c0(ℓ2)c_0(\ell^2)c0​(ℓ2), not ordinary c0c_0c0​; M2 supplies the latter exclusion by a different construction. Its universality statement concerns metric embeddings, not whole-space equivalences with every separable metric space.

The rigidity theorem for spaces bi-Lipschitz equivalent to c0c_0c0​ remains compatible with M2. The target ZZZ contains a nonlinear image of c0c_0c0​, but is not asserted bi-Lipschitz equivalent to c0c_0c0​ itself. Likewise, the correction-lifting identity is not a nonlinear section of a linear quotient.

The examples leave many structured versions of nonlinear rigidity meaningful: imposing reflexivity, additional smoothness, or particular linear classes may change the answer. The present claims settle the unrestricted separable real questions stated above, not every such refinement.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Godefroy, Kalton and Lancien, Subspaces of c0 and Lipschitz isomorphisms, for the positive whole-space rigidity results.
  • Godefroy and Kalton, Lipschitz-free Banach spaces, for linearization and the quotient-section constraint.
  • M1 and M2 state their distinct linear obstructions and explain why their correction lifts do not violate the established linear splitting theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Lipschitz Equivalent Separable Banach Spaces Need Not Be Linearly Isomorphic (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Bi-Lipschitz Absorption of c0 Without a Linear Copy of c0 (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A sharp numerical-range bound for matrix functions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 325 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A matrix is more than its eigenvalues. A normal matrix, one that commutes with its conjugate transpose, behaves particularly well: evaluating a polynomial at the matrix has norm equal to the largest absolute value of that polynomial on its spectrum. For a nonnormal matrix, eigenvalues alone can badly underestimate this norm. Even a nonzero nilpotent matrix has only the eigenvalue zero.

The numerical range provides a larger picture of a matrix. Instead of asking only which scalars are eigenvalues, it records the quadratic expressions obtained from every unit vector. Crouzeix’s question asks whether this region always controls polynomial evaluation up to the universal factor two.

Family 325 concerns the complete version: the polynomial can itself have matrix coefficients of any finite size. The two manuscripts claim the sharp factor two in this setting. One takes a direct route to the inequality; the other constructs a single change of inner product and a single positive boundary representation that work for every coefficient size and every admissible analytic function.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a complex matrix AAA, its numerical range is

W(A)={x∗Ax: x∗x=1}.W(A)=\{x^*Ax:\ x^*x=1\}.W(A)={x∗Ax: x∗x=1}.

Here x∗x^*x∗ is conjugate transpose. This is a convex, compact subset of the complex plane containing the eigenvalues. For a bounded operator on an infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, the same definition applies, but one generally uses its closure when making compact-set statements.

Write a matrix polynomial as

P(z)=∑j=0dzjBj,P[A]=∑j=0dAj⊗Bj.P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}z^jB_j,\qquadP[A]=\sum_{j=0}^{d}A^j\otimes B_j.P(z)=j=0∑d​zjBj​,P[A]=j=0∑d​Aj⊗Bj​.

The coefficients BjB_jBj​ are mmm-by-mmm matrices. The tensor product means that AAA acts on the original Hilbert-space coordinate and BjB_jBj​ on an additional mmm-dimensional coordinate. All norms are operator norms for the Hilbert-space norm.

A complete numerical-range estimate is uniform in mmm. Merely proving the scalar case m=1m=1m=1 does not automatically give it: matrix coefficients need not commute, and a scalar rearrangement of factors can cease to be legitimate.

A similarity replaces AAA by SAS−1SAS^{-1}SAS−1, with SSS invertible. Its cost is the condition number ∥S∥∥S−1∥\|S\|\|S^{-1}\|∥S∥∥S−1∥. Equivalently, a positive definite matrix HHH defines a new inner product, and S=H1/2S=H^{1/2}S=H1/2 converts that inner product back to the usual one. A contraction is an operator of norm at most one.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The classical spectral theorem explains polynomial evaluation for normal operators. Von Neumann’s inequality gives another model: a contraction is controlled by the supremum of its polynomial on the unit disk. Numerical-range estimates seek an analogous principle for arbitrary operators, using a region adapted to the particular operator.

Crouzeix posed the factor-two question in 2004 and obtained a universal complete bound of 11.08 in 2007. Positive boundary integral formulas, including work of Delyon and Delyon, supplied an important mechanism. Crouzeix and Palencia subsequently proved the complete bound 1+21+\sqrt21+2​, bringing the universal constant close to the conjectured endpoint. Their argument also made the role of a positive boundary kernel especially clear.

The source manuscripts situate themselves after several 2026 scalar claims by Jin, Lorist and Schwenninger, and Luo. In particular, Lorist and Schwenninger’s August 17 version states the scalar result for bounded Hilbert-space operators and discusses the obstruction to simply transferring its argument to matrix coefficients. A further cited 2026 preprint establishes the complete factor-two estimate when the base matrix has order at most three.

Thus the family should be read as an all-dimensions complete result, together with a structural representation theorem. It is not presented here as the first scalar factor-two claim. The distinction matters because controlling every coefficient size is precisely what connects the inequality to powerful similarity and dilation principles.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The complete inequality

M1 states that for every finite complex matrix AAA and every finite matrix polynomial,

∥P[A]∥≤2max⁡z∈W(A)∥P(z)∥.\|P[A]\|\leq 2\max_{z\in W(A)}\|P(z)\|.∥P[A]∥≤2z∈W(A)max​∥P(z)∥.

There is no dependence on the size of AAA, the coefficient size, or the degree. Numerical ranges that are points or line segments are included.

M2 obtains the same estimate and extends it to every bounded operator on an arbitrary complex Hilbert space, including nonseparable spaces. Its closed numerical range is a complete 2-spectral set: the factor-two bound also holds for finite matrix-valued functions holomorphic on a neighborhood of that closed set. In particular, it covers rational functions whose poles lie outside it.

The constant cannot be improved universally. For

A=(0100),P(z)=z,A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P(z)=z,A=(00​10​),P(z)=z,

one has ∥A∥=1\|A\|=1∥A∥=1, while W(A)W(A)W(A) is the disk of radius 1/21/21/2. This scalar example already requires the factor two.

A common metric and boundary density

The additional structural statement is finite-dimensional. Enclose W(A)W(A)W(A) strictly inside a bounded convex domain Ω\OmegaΩ with regular real-analytic boundary, and choose a conformal bijection fff from Ω\OmegaΩ to the unit disk. Set T=f(A)T=f(A)T=f(A).

M2 claims that the optimization problem

κ2=min⁡{τ: I≤H≤τI, T∗HT≤H}\kappa^2=\min\{\tau:\ I\leq H\leq\tau I,\ T^*HT\leq H\}κ2=min{τ: I≤H≤τI, T∗HT≤H}

has an attained minimum with 1≤κ2≤41\leq\kappa^2\leq41≤κ2≤4. The inequalities compare Hermitian matrices by positivity. For a minimizing HHH, the matrix S=H1/2S=H^{1/2}S=H1/2 makes f(SAS−1)f(SAS^{-1})f(SAS−1) contractive, and its condition number is κ≤2\kappa\leq2κ≤2.

For this same similarity, the manuscript constructs a continuous positive matrix density Λ\LambdaΛ on a boundary parameter circle. Its integral is the identity. If GGG parametrizes the boundary and dσd\sigmadσ is normalized angular measure, then

v[SAS−1]=∫TΛ(t)⊗v(G(t)) dσ(t).v[SAS^{-1}]=\int_{\mathbb T}\Lambda(t)\otimes v(G(t))\,d\sigma(t).v[SAS−1]=∫T​Λ(t)⊗v(G(t))dσ(t).

The same density works for every finite coefficient size and every matrix-valued vvv holomorphic near the closed domain. The metric is chosen once, rather than separately for each test function.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family claims the sharp answer to a central operator inequality in its complete form. Its strength is both quantitative and structural: a universal best constant is paired with a representation that explains how all matrix-valued evaluations can be controlled together.

For readers coming from numerical analysis, the numerical range is a way to retain information lost by looking only at eigenvalues. Bounds on matrix functions underlie estimates for approximations, evolution operators, and iterative methods. The theorem provides a universal norm bound; exploiting it efficiently in a particular computation is a further problem.

For operator theory, the complete estimate is particularly consequential. Complete boundedness is the language in which controlled similarities and normal dilations become available. M2 makes this relationship concrete through an optimal metric and a positive density, rather than only asserting an abstract existence principle.

The rating concerns these claimed mathematical consequences. It does not assign a reliability score to the manuscripts or determine priority among the surrounding preprints.

6. The main idea

Both approaches turn complex-analytic boundary information into positivity, then use positivity to control the size of matrix evaluation. The difficult part is preserving the order of matrix multiplications throughout.

M1 begins with a polynomial and vectors witnessing its largest singular value. It uses an exterior conformal coordinate to express boundary functions through a Faber-type expansion, a version of power-series expansion adapted to the exterior of the numerical range. A positive kernel controls the associated boundary operation in an L2L^2L2 norm.

The proof then tests products in both orders. Its resolvent expressions involve the original matrix, and the positive block matrix built from them controls the off-diagonal terms responsible for the norm. The manuscript attributes the sharp factor two to this paired comparison. Looking only at a scalar expression would conceal the order issue that the complete problem requires one to retain.

M2 reverses the starting point. It first chooses an optimal inner product making the disk-coordinate operator contractive. From that contraction it constructs the common positive density. Positivity and total mass equal to the identity make evaluation a compression of multiplication on a boundary function space: embed a vector into boundary functions, multiply pointwise, and project back.

The remaining task is to show that the optimal change of metric costs at most two. When its cost exceeds one, finite-dimensional separation supplies extremal vectors and an auxiliary matrix-valued analytic function linking them. Boundary identities turn these extremal data into positive block matrices. Orthogonality of Fourier components separates certain cross terms, and comparison of their squared norms yields the stated bound on κ\kappaκ.

Finally, enclosing domains shrink toward the numerical range. Finite compressions and holomorphic approximation transfer the resulting inequality to arbitrary Hilbert spaces. These passages extend the norm estimate; they should not be confused with a claim that the finite-dimensional continuous density itself has the same form in every infinite-dimensional setting.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The main inequality concerns complex Hilbert-space operator norms, with finite matrix coefficient sizes. It is not a theorem for arbitrary Banach-space norms. The sharp example shows optimality over all operators, not that every individual operator needs the factor two; normal operators already have constant one.

The common continuous boundary density and the attained matrix optimization are stated for finite matrices and regular analytic convex enclosing domains. Degenerate numerical ranges enter the final inequality by approximation. One should retain this distinction between a convenient domain for the construction and the exact compact set in the endpoint estimate.

The results do not by themselves give a cheap algorithm for computing the optimal metric, evaluating a conformal map, or estimating the numerical range in very high dimensions. More refined constants for special classes, equality and stability phenomena, and computational versions remain separate questions.

The claims and their mechanisms are reported as stated in the two manuscripts. The earlier scalar and small-dimension results remain part of the development of the problem.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Crouzeix and Palencia, the complete 1+21+\sqrt21+2​ bound.
  • Lorist and Schwenninger, A solution to Crouzeix’s conjecture, version 2.
  • The cited small-dimensional predecessor, Square functions and the complete Crouzeix conjecture in dimension three.
  • Optional background: numerical range.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A direct proof of the complete Crouzeix inequality (September 26, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The complete Crouzeix theorem: optimal similarity and a common positive boundary representation (September 23, 2026).
