entry.title: Can every Banach space have a separable infinite-dimensional quotient?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 323 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Every infinite-dimensional Banach space contains a separable infinite-dimensional closed subspace: take the closed span of countably many linearly independent vectors. Can one always obtain such a space as a quotient instead?

A quotient collapses a closed subspace to zero. It describes the information retained by a bounded linear surjection, rather than information found by looking inside the original space. The separable quotient problem asks whether every infinite-dimensional Banach space admits a separable infinite-dimensional quotient.

Family 323 claims that the unrestricted statement is independent of ZFC, relative to the consistency of a measurable cardinal. Under the continuum hypothesis it constructs counterexamples; under a different set-theoretic measure hypothesis it proves the positive statement. For spaces of density exactly ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​, it claims independence assuming only consistency of ZFC.

2. Background and essential definitions

A Banach space is a complete normed vector space. It is separable if it has a countable norm-dense subset. Its density character is the smallest cardinality of a norm-dense set.

If M⊆XM\subseteq XM⊆X is closed, the quotient X/MX/MX/M has norm

∥x+M∥=inf⁡m∈M∥x+m∥.\|x+M\|=\inf_{m\in M}\|x+m\|.∥x+M∥=m∈Minf​∥x+m∥.

It is again a Banach space. A bounded linear surjection Q:X→YQ:X\to YQ:X→Y identifies YYY, up to equivalent norm, with X/ker⁡QX/\ker QX/kerQ by the open mapping theorem.

The dual X∗X^*X∗ is the Banach space of bounded linear functionals on XXX. A predual of a space EEE is a Banach space XXX with X∗X^*X∗ isomorphic to EEE. Different preduals can give different evaluation behavior even when their duals are isomorphic.

ZFC denotes the usual set-theory axioms with choice. The continuum hypothesis, CH, says c=2ℵ0=ℵ1\mathfrak c=2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1c=2ℵ0​=ℵ1​. A measurable cardinal is a large-cardinal assumption stronger than ZFC alone in the consistency hierarchy.

M1 uses the condition that c\mathfrak cc is real-valued measurable: there is a probability measure on every subset of a set of size c\mathfrak cc, vanishing on singletons and additive over disjoint families of size less than c\mathfrak cc. This is substantially stronger than ordinary Lebesgue measure on a sigma-algebra of measurable sets.

Relative independence means that appropriate models of the axioms give opposite answers. It does not mean a particular specified Banach space simultaneously has and lacks a quotient inside one fixed model.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The problem is traditionally attributed to Banach and Mazur, although historical accounts note that it is not explicitly stated in Banach’s 1932 book. Rosenthal’s 1969 work is an early written formulation.

Many positive cases are known. Johnson–Rosenthal developed weak-star basic-sequence methods and showed that every separable infinite-dimensional Banach space has an infinite-dimensional quotient with a Schauder basis. A Schauder basis permits unique norm-convergent coordinate expansions.

Argyros, Dodos and Kanellopoulos proved the positive answer for every dual Banach space. Another useful criterion, based on Hagler–Johnson, says that an unconditional basic sequence in X∗X^*X∗ yields a separable infinite-dimensional quotient of XXX. Unconditionality means convergence is stable under sign changes and rearrangements in the appropriate basis sense.

Set theory already influenced positive results. Let b\mathfrak bb be the smallest size of a family of functions N→N\mathbb N\to\mathbb NN→N unbounded under eventual domination. Saxon–Sánchez Ruiz proved the quotient statement for infinite-dimensional spaces with density below b\mathfrak bb. Thus b>ℵ1\mathfrak b>\aleph_1b>ℵ1​ gives the positive assertion at density ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​.

Earlier large-cardinal consistency results covered certain large density ranges. M1 claims a positive implication covering all infinite-dimensional spaces from real-valued measurability of the continuum, together with a new CH construction giving failure already at the smallest nonseparable density.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For either scalar field F=R\mathbb F=\mathbb RF=R or C\mathbb CC, let SQF\mathrm{SQ}_{\mathbb F}SQF​ denote the assertion that every infinite-dimensional Banach space over F\mathbb FF has a separable infinite-dimensional quotient.

M1 states that ZFC proves both implications

c real-valued measurable⟹SQF,\mathfrak c\text{ real-valued measurable}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathrm{SQ}_{\mathbb F},c real-valued measurable⟹SQF​,

and

CH⟹¬SQF.\mathrm{CH}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\neg\mathrm{SQ}_{\mathbb F}.CH⟹¬SQF​.

The CH counterexamples have norm density ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​. A standard model construction from a measurable cardinal supplies the positive measure hypothesis. Consequently, if ZFC with a measurable cardinal is consistent, the unrestricted quotient assertion is independent of ZFC. Consistency of its failure needs only consistency of ZFC, because CH is available in the constructible model.

For the restricted statement that every space of density exactly ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​ has such a quotient, M1 claims independence relative to consistency of ZFC alone. The positive side uses the earlier density-below-b\mathfrak bb theorem together with a model of Martin’s axiom where b>ℵ1\mathfrak b>\aleph_1b>ℵ1​. The negative side uses M1’s CH example.

The two consistency strengths should not be conflated. M1 does not establish that the unrestricted positive statement has exactly the consistency strength of a measurable cardinal; that cardinal is a sufficient assumption for the stated relative-independence conclusion.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this would resolve a central existence question in Banach-space theory by locating it at a set-theoretic boundary. The simple analogy between subspaces and quotients would fail in some models even though it succeeds for broad familiar classes.

The density-ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​ result is especially sharp in location: it places counterexamples at the first possible nonseparable density, while established axioms yielding a larger bounding cardinal give a positive answer at that same density.

The real and complex conclusions also match. The phenomenon would not be an artifact of choosing one scalar field. The manuscript includes explicit transfers between the two settings rather than assuming that realification automatically preserves every quotient issue.

6. The main idea

Test quotients through dual evaluation

For a closed subspace F⊆X∗F\subseteq X^*F⊆X∗, define

RF:X→F∗,(RFx)(f)=f(x).R_F:X\to F^*,\qquad (R_Fx)(f)=f(x).RF​:X→F∗,(RF​x)(f)=f(x).

M1 establishes a common criterion: a separable infinite-dimensional quotient exists exactly when some infinite-dimensional closed FFF has norm-separable evaluation image RF(X)R_F(X)RF​(X). In the necessary direction FFF can itself be chosen separable.

Separability of FFF does not imply separability of F∗F^*F∗ or of the evaluation image. Also, an image with a useful topology is not automatically an onto map to a Banach quotient; the source supplies the additional surjectivity step. Both constructions use this criterion in opposite directions.

Use a measure to force an unconditional sequence

For the positive implication, assume a counterexample XXX and choose a separable infinite-dimensional subspace of its dual. The measure hypothesis first forces its evaluation image to have full continuum density; a smaller dense set would permit a basic-sequence construction yielding a quotient.

The large image then supplies a family of dual functionals with controlled norms that vanishes almost everywhere at each fixed vector of XXX. Sequential bidual approximations and Borel coding allow an integration argument to select an unconditional basic sequence.

The source uses ordinary Borel Fubini after coding; it does not assume an unrestricted interchange theorem for arbitrary power-set measures. The resulting unconditional sequence contradicts the established dual criterion for a separable quotient.

Construct a dual with many separating paths

For the negative implication, M1 builds a dual space E=X0∗E=X_0^*E=X0∗​ with coordinates indexed by ω1\omega_1ω1​, the first uncountable ordinal. Successive finitely supported norming functionals form paths with bounded partial sums, hence define functionals on EEE.

Integer weights and coding make different paths share only finitely many relevant weights. A block argument produces uncountably many norm-separated restrictions of these path functionals on every infinite-dimensional subspace of EEE. The goal is to prevent the evaluation image required by the quotient criterion from ever becoming separable.

Change the predual while retaining the dual

CH permits assigning all the needed paths to the available coordinates. A small perturbation of a quotient map involving E∗/X0E^*/X_0E∗/X0​ produces a new predual XXX, with X∗X^*X∗ isomorphic to EEE, whose evaluations approximate the path information.

For every separable infinite-dimensional subspace of X∗X^*X∗, those evaluations are nonseparable. The common criterion therefore excludes every separable infinite-dimensional quotient of XXX.

This does not contradict the positive theorem for dual Banach spaces: the counterexample is the new predual XXX, not the dual space EEE used to organize its construction. The distinction between a space and its dual is part of the mechanism.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The unrestricted independence claim is relative to consistency of ZFC with a measurable cardinal. It is not an unconditional proof that ZFC is consistent, nor a claim that the positive statement requires a measurable cardinal in every possible model.

The sharper ZFC-consistency-only conclusion concerns spaces of density exactly ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​. It cannot be promoted to the unrestricted statement merely because the negative examples already occur there.

All separability and density conditions on evaluation images use the norm topology, unless the source explicitly says otherwise. Weak or weak-star separability would not replace the criterion. The quotient must be infinite-dimensional and arise through a bounded linear surjection, not just a nonlinear map or a dense nonclosed image.

The manuscript’s consistency and construction claims are taken as stated. Determining the optimal consistency strength of the unrestricted positive assertion, or describing additional geometric classes with a ZFC positive answer, remains beyond its stated conclusion.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Saxon and Sánchez Ruiz, Barrelled Countable Enlargements and the Bounding Cardinal, for the earlier density criterion.
  • Argyros, Dodos and Kanellopoulos, Unconditional families in Banach spaces, for the positive dual-space result.
  • M1’s final section states the Solovay measure-model input and separates the unrestricted and density-ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​ consistency bounds.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Relative independence of the separable quotient problem (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When cotype on both sides forces nontrivial type
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 326 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Take several vectors, attach independent random plus or minus signs, and add them. How large is the resulting vector, on average? In Euclidean space, squared lengths add in expectation. In a general Banach space, the answer reflects the geometry of its unit ball.

Two families of inequalities, called type and cotype, measure opposite sides of this behavior. A longstanding question asks whether good cotype for both a space and its continuous dual forces nontrivial type. The dual is the space of bounded linear scalar measurements, so the question combines the geometry of vectors with the geometry of ways to measure them.

Without an additional assumption, the answer is known to be negative. Family 326 claims a positive characterization under the ordinary approximation property: finite-rank operators can approximate the identity uniformly on compact sets. Crucially, their operator norms need not have a common bound.

The manuscript therefore concerns how three different ideas fit together: random cancellation, duality, and approximation by finite-dimensional operations.

2. Background and essential definitions

A real Banach space XXX is a complete normed real vector space. Its dual X∗X^*X∗ consists of bounded linear maps from XXX to R\mathbb RR, with their operator norm. Let εi\varepsilon_iεi​ be independent signs, each equally likely to be 111 or −1-1−1.

For 2≤q<∞2\leq q<\infty2≤q<∞, cotype qqq means that some constant CCC, independent of the number and choice of vectors, satisfies

(∑i∥xi∥q)1/q≤C(E∥∑iεixi∥2)1/2.\left(\sum_i\|x_i\|^q\right)^{1/q}\leq C\left(\mathbb E\left\|\sum_i\varepsilon_i x_i\right\|^2\right)^{1/2}.(i∑​∥xi​∥q)1/q≤C​E​i∑​εi​xi​​2​1/2.

It says that a collection of substantial vectors cannot have an arbitrarily small random signed sum relative to the indicated aggregate size. The least admissible constant is denoted Cq(X)C_q(X)Cq​(X). Finite cotype means that such an estimate holds for at least one finite qqq.

Type ppp, for 1<p≤21<p\leq21<p≤2, reverses the direction of control:

(E∥∑iεixi∥2)1/2≤D(∑i∥xi∥p)1/p.\left(\mathbb E\left\|\sum_i\varepsilon_i x_i\right\|^2\right)^{1/2}\leq D\left(\sum_i\|x_i\|^p\right)^{1/p}.​E​i∑​εi​xi​​2​1/2≤D(i∑​∥xi​∥p)1/p.

Having some p>1p>1p>1 is called nontrivial type. Euclidean spaces have both type two and cotype two. The distinction between the two inequalities is essential: knowing a lower bound on random sums does not directly provide an upper bound.

The approximation property, or AP, says that for every compact M⊂XM\subset XM⊂X and δ>0\delta>0δ>0, there is a bounded finite-rank linear operator S:X→XS:X\to XS:X→X with

sup⁡x∈M∥Sx−x∥<δ.\sup_{x\in M}\|Sx-x\|<\delta.x∈Msup​∥Sx−x∥<δ.

Finite rank means that the image is finite-dimensional. The bounded approximation property, BAP, adds one uniform bound on the norms of all required approximants. AP alone permits these norms to grow.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Maurey and Pisier developed the relationship between random-sign estimates and the finite-dimensional structures that occur inside Banach spaces. Their theory and Pisier’s work identify nontrivial type with K-convexity, a boundedness property of a particular Fourier projection on sign cubes.

This has a geometric interpretation. Nontrivial type is equivalent to not containing the spaces ℓ1n\ell_1^nℓ1n​ with uniformly bounded distortion as nnn grows. Here ℓ1n\ell_1^nℓ1n​ is Rn\mathbb R^nRn with norm ∑i∣xi∣\sum_i|x_i|∑i​∣xi​∣; distortion measures how far a linear identification changes relative lengths. In that geometry, summing distinct coordinate vectors produces no random cancellation at all.

The two-sided cotype question has important earlier positive cases. Pisier proved that cotype two for both the space and its dual, together with AP, gives the stronger conclusion of being isomorphic to a Hilbert space. Other work established K-convexity under restrictions on the cotype exponents and stronger approximation assumptions, including BAP. Removing the exponent restriction became the cotype–cotype conjecture in the relevant literature.

The approximation hypothesis is not cosmetic. Pisier’s 1983 construction can embed a cotype-two space into another space whose primal and dual both have cotype two. Starting with ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ produces a space that cannot be K-convex. These counterexamples fail AP.

Meanwhile, Enflo showed that even separable reflexive spaces can fail AP, and Figiel and Johnson separated AP from BAP. Thus replacing BAP by AP is a real strengthening. Family 326 claims to remove the exponent restriction while working with this weaker approximation assumption.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For every nonzero real Banach space XXX with AP, M1 states

X is K-convex⟺Cq(X)<∞ and Cr(X∗)<∞X\text{ is K-convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quadC_q(X)<\infty\ \text{and}\ C_r(X^*)<\inftyX is K-convex⟺Cq​(X)<∞ and Cr​(X∗)<∞

for some finite exponents q,r≥2q,r\geq2q,r≥2. The two exponents may differ. By the classical equivalence, the left side can equally be described as nontrivial type. The forward implication requires no approximation hypothesis; the new content is the reverse implication under AP.

For completeness, K-convexity can be defined without invoking any geometric picture. On a sign cube, the Rademacher projection retains just the first-order Fourier terms:

(Rsf)(ε)=∑i=1sεi Eη[ηif(η)].(\mathcal R_s f)(\varepsilon)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\varepsilon_i\,\mathbb E_\eta[\eta_i f(\eta)].(Rs​f)(ε)=i=1∑s​εi​Eη​[ηi​f(η)].

The norm on these vector-valued functions is the square-mean norm. K-convexity means that the operator norms of Rs\mathcal R_sRs​ stay bounded as the cube dimension sss grows.

M1 also states a uniform form: bounds on the two cotype constants and their exponents give a bound on the K-convexity constant depending only on those data. No common norm bound for the AP approximants enters.

One consequence concerns covering convex bodies. For symmetric convex bodies K,L⊂RnK,L\subset\mathbb R^nK,L⊂Rn, let N(K,tL)N(K,tL)N(K,tL) count the minimum number of translates of tLtLtL covering KKK. The polar body is

K∘={y: ∣⟨x,y⟩∣≤1 for every x∈K}.K^\circ=\{y:\ |\langle x,y\rangle|\leq1\text{ for every }x\in K\}.K∘={y: ∣⟨x,y⟩∣≤1 for every x∈K}.

Under fixed primal and dual cotype bounds for the norm with unit ball either KKK or LLL, M1 obtains constants a,b≥1a,b\geq1a,b≥1, independent of dimension, such that

b−1log⁡N(L∘,atK∘)≤log⁡N(K,tL)≤blog⁡N(L∘,a−1tK∘).b^{-1}\log N(L^\circ,atK^\circ)\leq\log N(K,tL)\leq b\log N(L^\circ,a^{-1}tK^\circ).b−1logN(L∘,atK∘)≤logN(K,tL)≤blogN(L∘,a−1tK∘).

This consequence uses an existing entropy-duality theorem once the new uniform K-convexity bound is available.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claimed characterization resolves a central relationship between type, cotype, and approximation. It also identifies the role of a hypothesis whose absence is already known to allow counterexamples.

The result would allow one to infer an upper random-sum estimate from lower random-sum estimates on the space and its dual, without assuming a basis or uniformly bounded finite-dimensional approximations. That is a substantial strengthening of the way these geometric properties interact.

The covering-number corollary illustrates its reach beyond random vectors. It says that the complexity of covering one convex body by another can be compared with the corresponding dual covering problem, with constants controlled by the stated geometric data rather than ambient dimension.

The manuscript also derives a tensor-norm consequence for the Grothendieck-pair framework studied by Gupta, Misra, and Ray. That application concerns uniform operator estimates between two tensor norms. It should not be conflated with Grothendieck’s original tensor-product conjecture, which Pisier disproved.

6. The main idea

The argument first studies finite-rank operators between potentially different spaces. It applies such an operator to a family of vectors, then mixes the outputs with a normalized Walsh transform. This is the Fourier transform on a finite cube: its entries are signs determined by dot products modulo two.

For a fixed finite-rank operator, factoring through a Hilbert space gives decay as the cube dimension increases. The obstacle is that the constant may depend on that particular operator. The manuscript seeks decay controlled only by the cotype information.

Its amplification argument says that decay cannot remain too slow. If it does, a moment-lifting construction produces bounded sign-indexed families with specified first moments. Averaging turns these into scalar functions carrying row and column information. Their Fourier expansion must contain a binary-matrix index of rank at least two, supplying two independent Walsh factors.

This allows the alleged failure of decay to reproduce itself at a larger dimension. Iterating would conflict with the known Hilbert-space-factorization estimate for the same fixed operator. M1 uses this to obtain an operator-independent decay bound.

The second stage is where ordinary AP matters. Given a finite-dimensional piece E⊂XE\subset XE⊂X, the manuscript constructs an auxiliary space and a compact map into XXX that reproduces the vectors of EEE. The auxiliary dual has the needed controlled moment estimate.

Because the map is compact, AP permits finite-rank approximations that converge to it in operator norm, even though the norms of the approximating identity operators need not be uniformly bounded. The finite-rank decay bound then passes to the compact map and ultimately to all finite Walsh inputs in XXX.

Uniform copies of increasingly large ℓ1n\ell_1^nℓ1n​ would contradict this decay. Excluding those copies yields K-convexity through the classical characterization. This route explains both the use of two-sided cotype and the precise point at which compact-set approximation replaces a stronger bounded approximation assumption.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is stated for nonzero real Banach spaces. It requires finite cotype for both the space and its full continuous dual, together with AP. Neither one-sided cotype nor the omission of AP is the asserted result.

The constants in the uniform theorem are existential. The manuscript does not give an explicit quantitative formula for the K-convexity constant in terms of the cotype data. Likewise, its general conclusion is nontrivial type, not a specified optimal type exponent or a Hilbert-space structure for arbitrary cotype exponents.

The entropy application is restricted to bodies with the stated uniform geometric control. It does not establish dimension-free duality for every pair of symmetric convex bodies. Family 329 concerns a different, unrestricted entropy-duality question, so the hypotheses must be retained when comparing the two families.

More effective bounds and more precise information about the type exponent are natural further questions. The present account reports the manuscript’s characterization and consequences without checking its proof.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Gupta, Misra, and Ray, the Grothendieck-pair framework and related conjectures.
  • Pisier, Counterexamples to a conjecture of Grothendieck, for the earlier obstruction without approximation.
  • Milman, entropy duality with geometric hypotheses.
  • Optional background: type and cotype.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The cotype–cotype conjecture under the approximation property (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Fixed points for nonexpansive maps in reflexive spaces
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 328 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A map is nonexpansive if it never increases distances. Does such a map, acting inside a bounded closed convex region, have to leave some point unchanged?

In finite-dimensional Euclidean space the answer follows from classical fixed-point theory. In infinite-dimensional spaces, bounded closed sets need not be compact in the norm topology, and the question becomes sensitive to the geometry of the space. A strict contraction is manageable by repeated iteration; a map that only satisfies a distance factor of one can behave very differently.

Family 328 claims a positive answer for every real reflexive Banach space, using its given norm. That last qualification is central. Earlier work showed that a reflexive space can be equipped with a suitable equivalent norm having the fixed-point property. Changing the norm, however, changes which maps count as nonexpansive. The manuscript addresses the original metric, without replacing it.

2. Background and essential definitions

A Banach space is a complete normed vector space. A subset CCC is convex when it contains the segment joining any two of its points. It is bounded when all its points lie in some finite-radius ball, and norm closed when it contains the limits of norm-convergent sequences from the set.

A selfmap F:C→CF:C\to CF:C→C is nonexpansive if

∥F(x)−F(y)∥≤∥x−y∥(x,y∈C).\|F(x)-F(y)\|\leq\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in C).∥F(x)−F(y)∥≤∥x−y∥(x,y∈C).

A fixed point is a point xxx with F(x)=xF(x)=xF(x)=x. By comparison, a contraction has a uniform multiplier strictly smaller than one on the right. The contraction theorem then supplies a unique fixed point and convergence of iterates. Neither uniqueness nor convergence of unmodified iterates follows merely from nonexpansiveness.

The dual X∗X^*X∗ consists of bounded linear real-valued functionals on XXX. Each vector xxx defines a functional on the dual by evaluation, f↦f(x)f\mapsto f(x)f↦f(x). The space is reflexive when every bounded linear functional on X∗X^*X∗ arises in this way.

The weak topology records convergence under all members of X∗X^*X∗, rather than convergence in norm. In a reflexive Banach space, every norm-closed bounded convex set is weakly compact. This is a powerful substitute for finite-dimensional compactness, but a nonexpansive map need not be weakly continuous. Consequently, one cannot simply apply a compact fixed-point theorem in the weak topology.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Browder and Göhde proved the fixed-point property for uniformly convex spaces in the 1960s. Uniform convexity ensures that separated points on the unit ball have midpoints uniformly inside it. This gives a strong geometric mechanism preventing a fixed-point-free map from spreading approximate fixed points across an invariant set.

Kirk established a broader criterion using normal structure. Roughly, a nontrivial bounded convex set should contain a point whose maximum distance to the rest is strictly smaller than its diameter. The diameter is the supremum of all pairwise distances. Such a point provides a center that obstructs the extreme geometry of a minimal fixed-point-free invariant set.

Normal structure is sufficient, but not necessary. Karlovitz gave a particular norm on ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ with the fixed-point property without normal structure. Other advances covered reflexive subspaces of L1L_1L1​ in their inherited norm, spaces with a 1-unconditional basis in the weakly compact setting, and uniformly nonsquare spaces. These results progressively weakened the geometric conditions while retaining some additional structure.

Two developments clarify the remaining gap. Alspach constructed a weakly compact convex subset of L1[0,1]L_1[0,1]L1​[0,1] admitting a fixed-point-free nonexpansive map. Thus weak compactness of the domain inside an arbitrary Banach space is insufficient. Domínguez Benavides proved that every reflexive Banach space admits an equivalent norm with the fixed-point property, but this leaves the given-norm question distinct.

M1 also records earlier claims of the full given-norm assertion by Hanebaly, alongside more recent literature treating the general problem as unresolved. This digest preserves that attribution without adjudicating those earlier arguments. M1 presents its own claimed proof through adaptive choices, compact families, and a tree construction.

4. What the new manuscript claims

M1 states the following theorem. Let XXX be any real reflexive Banach space and let C⊂XC\subset XC⊂X be nonempty, norm closed, bounded, and convex. Then every nonexpansive selfmap of CCC has a fixed point:

F:C→C,∥F(x)−F(y)∥≤∥x−y∥⟹∃x∈C: F(x)=x.F:C\to C,\qquad\|F(x)-F(y)\|\leq\|x-y\|\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists x\in C:\ F(x)=x.F:C→C,∥F(x)−F(y)∥≤∥x−y∥⟹∃x∈C: F(x)=x.

There is no assumption of separability, a basis, uniform convexity, normal structure, or a specially selected equivalent norm. Separability enters an internal reduction, not the theorem’s hypothesis.

M1 further combines this assertion with an existing theorem of Bruck. For any pairwise commuting family S\mathcal SS of nonexpansive selfmaps of the same set CCC, the common fixed-point set

Fix⁡(S)={x∈C: T(x)=x for every T∈S}\operatorname{Fix}(\mathcal S)=\{x\in C:\ T(x)=x\text{ for every }T\in\mathcal S\}Fix(S)={x∈C: T(x)=x for every T∈S}

is nonempty and is a nonexpansive retract of CCC. This means that there is a nonexpansive map from CCC onto that common fixed set which leaves every point already in the set unchanged.

The family may be infinite. Pairwise commuting means that applying two maps in either order gives the same result. The corollary uses Bruck’s established framework after the main theorem supplies its fixed-point hypotheses; it is not an unrelated new construction of a retraction.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claimed theorem resolves a central fixed-point question at the level of all reflexive Banach spaces and their actual metrics. It removes the additional geometric assumptions that drove many of the earlier positive results.

Fixed points represent equilibria: a state is unchanged by the operation defining the model. Nonexpansive maps appear in approximation, optimization, and nonlinear analysis, often exactly at the boundary where contraction arguments stop working. An existence theorem valid for every reflexive norm would provide a broad structural foundation for such problems.

The significance is an existence statement, however. It does not automatically produce an effective approximation procedure, a convergence rate, or uniqueness. The identity map already has every point fixed, while a rotation can prevent the raw sequence of iterates from converging.

The commuting-family consequence also enlarges the interpretation from one equilibrium condition to many compatible ones. Compatibility is essential: arbitrary noncommuting maps need not share a fixed point even when each has its own.

6. The main idea

The argument starts with a hypothetical fixed-point-free map and uses a classical minimal-invariant-set reduction. It arrives at a separable weakly compact convex set KKK, normalized to diameter one, with no smaller nonempty closed convex invariant subset.

An approximate fixed-point sequence satisfies ∥T(xj)−xj∥→0\|T(x_j)-x_j\|\to0∥T(xj​)−xj​∥→0. The Goebel–Karlovitz lemma says that, in the minimal counterexample, such a sequence becomes asymptotically as far as possible from every fixed point of the set:

∥xj−z∥⟶1for every fixed z∈K.\|x_j-z\|\longrightarrow1\qquad\text{for every fixed }z\in K.∥xj​−z∥⟶1for every fixed z∈K.

Here “fixed” means a point selected independently of jjj, not a fixed point of TTT. This distinction avoids assuming the very object whose existence is in question. The condition says that approximate equilibria are forced toward an extreme diametral configuration.

M1 then introduces an adaptive anchor. A compact semigroup of nonexpansive maps supplies a point x∈Kx\in Kx∈K for which convex combinations of increasingly accurate approximate fixed-point images can return close to xxx. The required accuracy can depend on earlier choices, which is important when assembling a large construction with accumulated errors.

These images label an ordered tree. At each node, a compact family records possible limiting outputs at the root, retaining parameters for convex coefficients that have not yet been chosen. This allows the argument to anticipate later replacements without pretending that nonlinear maps preserve convex combinations.

The leaves are replaced from right to left by a common approximate fixed point. The resulting root values form an actual sequence, so their consecutive differences telescope. Nonlinearity remains present, but it no longer prevents the elementary cancellation between successive outputs.

Weighted estimates then produce, at every finite depth, a vector detected by all the functionals along one branch. The functionals are bounded linear measurements that arise from separating geometric configurations. A summable error budget controls the total deficit even when individual branch weights become very small.

Finally, reflexivity supplies weak compactness for the unit ball of the closed span of differences of points of KKK. Passing to a limit yields one vector detected along an infinite branch. The same functionals were arranged to converge pointwise to zero on that space, giving the claimed contradiction. The manuscript identifies the adaptive anchor, compact output families, and weighted switching as the additions beyond the classical diametral reduction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All four domain assumptions matter to the statement: the set is nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex, and the map sends it into itself. The ambient space is real and reflexive. The result does not assert a fixed-point theorem for every weakly compact convex subset of every Banach space; Alspach’s example prevents that extension.

The conclusion uses the original norm. Multiplying the norm by a scalar during the diameter normalization preserves nonexpansiveness, whereas replacing it by an arbitrary equivalent norm need not do so. Keeping these two operations separate is essential to understanding the claim.

No uniqueness or universal algorithmic convergence assertion is included. Quantitative rates, reliable iterative schemes under additional hypotheses, and versions for broader classes of maps are separate issues. The common-fixed-point corollary also retains pairwise commutativity.

The account reports M1’s result and its description of the surrounding literature. It does not settle the validity or priority of earlier proposed proofs.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Alspach, A fixed point free nonexpansive map.
  • Domínguez Benavides, a renorming theorem for the fixed-point property.
  • Hanebaly, the earlier claimed reflexive-space theorem.
  • Nourouzi, Reflexivity of Hilbert K(H)-modules and fixed-point property for nonexpansive mappings, for the later discussion cited by M1.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Fixed Points of Nonexpansive Maps in Reflexive Banach Spaces (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Random walks detect superreflexive Banach spaces
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 327 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Imagine drawing a finite reversible random walk inside a normed vector space. How far can the walk travel after many steps, compared with the size of one step? In Euclidean geometry, cancellation makes random motion much slower than a journey whose steps all point in the same direction.

Markov type asks for a uniform version of this phenomenon across every finite stationary reversible chain and every placement of its states in the space. It is a metric test: it only observes distances. Superreflexivity, by contrast, is a structural property of Banach spaces, expressed through the possibility of changing the norm to make its unit ball uniformly convex.

Family 327 claims that these viewpoints identify the same class of real Banach spaces. More precisely, any nontrivial Markov type forces superreflexivity. The converse was already known. The proposed result says that controlling an extensive family of random walks is enough to guarantee a deep improvement of the space’s linear geometry.

2. Background and essential definitions

A finite Markov chain has a finite state set SSS and transition probabilities PijP_{ij}Pij​. Its distribution π\piπ is stationary when starting with π\piπ leaves that distribution unchanged at each step. Reversibility is the balance identity

πiPij=πjPji.\pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_jP_{ji}.πi​Pij​=πj​Pji​.

It means that the stationary flow from iii to jjj matches the reverse flow. Throughout the Markov-type test, the walk starts in its stationary distribution.

A real Banach space XXX has Markov type ppp if there is a finite constant KKK such that, for every such chain, map f:S→Xf:S\to Xf:S→X, and integer t≥1t\geq1t≥1,

E∥f(Zt)−f(Z0)∥p≤Kpt E∥f(Z1)−f(Z0)∥p.\mathbb E\|f(Z_t)-f(Z_0)\|^p\leq K^p t\,\mathbb E\|f(Z_1)-f(Z_0)\|^p.E∥f(Zt​)−f(Z0​)∥p≤KptE∥f(Z1​)−f(Z0​)∥p.

The constant must be independent of the chain, map, and time. For p>1p>1p>1, this prevents displacement of order ttt from occurring with a fixed positive probability when one-step distances stay bounded: that would give growth of order tpt^ptp on the left but only order ttt on the right.

Two norms are equivalent if each bounds the other up to fixed positive multiplicative constants. A norm ∣⋅∣|\cdot|∣⋅∣ is uniformly convex if, for each separation ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, there is a depth δ>0\delta>0δ>0 such that

∣x∣,∣y∣≤1,∣x−y∣≥ε⟹∣x+y2∣≤1−δ.|x|,|y|\leq1,\quad |x-y|\geq\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\left|\frac{x+y}{2}\right|\leq1-\delta.∣x∣,∣y∣≤1,∣x−y∣≥ε⟹​2x+y​​≤1−δ.

Thus well-separated points of the unit ball have a midpoint a definite distance inside it, uniformly over all directions. A Banach space is superreflexive precisely when it admits an equivalent uniformly convex norm. The original norm itself need not have that property.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ball introduced Markov type in the study of Lipschitz extension: extending a map from part of a metric space while keeping its distance distortion controlled. This connected random walks with questions traditionally studied through linear operators.

The broader Ribe program seeks metric descriptions of linear-geometric properties of Banach spaces. Bourgain characterized superreflexivity through the distortion required to embed increasingly large binary trees. Diamond graphs provide another family of finite tests. These results show that a property defined by renorming can leave a detectable signature in distances alone.

A related notion, Markov convexity, was introduced by Lee, Naor, and Peres. Its inequalities compare walks with a shared past that subsequently evolve independently. Mendel and Naor characterized superreflexivity through this stronger-looking comparison scheme. Ordinary Markov type uses just the displacement of a single stationary reversible walk, so its converse relationship with superreflexivity remained a separate question.

In the positive direction, Naor, Peres, Schramm, and Sheffield proved that a uniformly smooth norm with a suitable power-type modulus gives Markov type. Uniform smoothness controls how the norm changes under small perturbations, uniformly over directions. Combined with Pisier’s renorming theorem, their result implies that every superreflexive space has Markov type for some exponent greater than one.

Naor asked whether the converse could fail. Ordinary Rademacher type, which controls independent random signed sums, does not settle the issue: James constructed nonreflexive spaces with type two. The proposed theorem singles out the richer test supplied by reversible Markov chains.

4. What the new manuscript claims

M1 states that every real Banach space with Markov type ppp for at least one p>1p>1p>1 is superreflexive. Together with the known converse, this gives

superreflexivity⟺Markov type p for some p>1.\text{superreflexivity}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{Markov type }p\text{ for some }p>1.superreflexivity⟺Markov type p for some p>1.

The statement has no separability, approximation-property, or basis assumption. It concerns the existence of a nontrivial exponent; it does not claim that a prescribed Markov exponent determines an optimal convexity modulus.

Because equivalent uniformly smooth and uniformly convex renormings exist for exactly the superreflexive spaces, M1 also answers Naor’s equivalent formulation positively: nontrivial Markov type guarantees an equivalent uniformly smooth norm.

The central quantitative construction concerns spaces that fail superreflexivity. It produces a specially ordered sequence norm, finitely representable in the original space, and, for every nnn, a finite reversible marked walk with unit-size edge labels ggg satisfying

P(∥∑i=1ng(Ei)∥≥n24)≥320.\mathbb P\left(\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}g(E_i)\right\|\geq\frac n{24}\right)\geq\frac3{20}.P(​i=1∑n​g(Ei​)​≥24n​)≥203​.

The chain and its dimension may depend on nnn; the displayed constants do not. The labels change sign when an edge is reversed.

An additional transfer lemma makes Markov type apply to these labels, even when they are not initially differences of values of a map on the state space. It would then bound the same expected ppp-th power by KpnK^pnKpn. The lower estimate grows like npn^pnp, producing the claimed contradiction for every p>1p>1p>1.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claimed theorem completes a central metric characterization of superreflexivity and answers an explicit question about the geometric force of Markov type.

It identifies a particularly economical kind of information: the distances traveled by single reversible walks. No linear operations appear in the definition of Markov type, yet the conclusion is the existence of a new norm with strong uniform convexity and smoothness properties.

This matters conceptually even alongside earlier tree and Markov-convexity characterizations. Different metric tests are useful in different settings. Markov type arises naturally in probability and Lipschitz extension, so identifying its exact Banach-space meaning creates a direct connection to renorming theory.

It also clarifies why good behavior for independent random signs need not be enough. A Markov chain can organize its steps through a state-dependent geometry, testing features that a single signed sum may miss. The manuscript’s constructed walks are designed to exploit precisely that additional freedom.

6. The main idea

The proof argues by contradiction. A classical James–Enflo characterization says that a space is superreflexive exactly when every Banach space finitely representable in it is reflexive. Here finite representability means that every finite-dimensional piece can be linearly embedded with distortion arbitrarily close to one.

Starting from failure of superreflexivity, M1 uses a nonreflexive model to construct a norm on finitely supported sequences. In this norm, inserting zeros does not change lengths, and merging adjacent coordinates by adding their coefficients cannot increase the norm. These ordered features let the argument turn oscillating partial sums into lower bounds on vector length.

The next task is to build a reversible walk whose accumulated labels retain many such oscillations. The manuscript describes the motion using words in letters and their inverses. Canceling adjacent inverse letters gives a reduced word. With a fixed positive probability, the reduced length after nnn random letters is proportional to nnn.

Selected prefix sums of the associated coefficient sequence alternate between two levels separated by this reduced length. Merging consecutive blocks then converts the oscillation into the desired norm lower bound. A finite Ramsey averaging construction supplies compatible increasing coordinate charts, so the ordering mechanism can coexist with reversibility.

There is a subtle mismatch to overcome. Markov type measures differences f(Zt)−f(Z0)f(Z_t)-f(Z_0)f(Zt​)−f(Z0​), whereas the construction initially gives labels on transitions. A cycle may have a nonzero total label, so these labels need not come from a function on the original states. Even a marked transition that leaves the state unchanged may carry a nonzero label.

M1 addresses this by enlarging the finite state space with bounded integer coordinates recording the traversed oriented edges. On this lifted chain, a potential has the desired increments except near a boundary. Moves rejected at the boundary preserve reversibility, and increasingly large coordinate boxes make the boundary effect negligible for the fixed time being considered.

This transfer lets the usual Markov-type inequality constrain the labeled walk. Finite representability carries the constraint from the original Banach space to the ordered model, with arbitrarily small distortion loss. The linear-displacement lower bound then conflicts with the sublinear moment bound whenever p>1p>1p>1.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is a characterization within real Banach spaces. Markov type is defined for much more general metric spaces, but a general metric space has no vector operations to renorm, so the conclusion cannot simply be transferred verbatim.

Superreflexivity asserts the existence of an equivalent favorable norm. It does not say that the supplied norm is uniformly convex or uniformly smooth. This distinction is also why the theorem is stronger than reflexivity alone and different from a statement about strict convexity of a particular unit ball.

The existential choice of exponent matters. The manuscript does not provide a sharp formula translating a Markov-type constant and exponent into optimal renorming constants, nor does the characterization identify all exponents available in each individual space.

The auxiliary chains grow with the time scale. They are witnesses to an obstruction, rather than a single universal finite chain or a practical finite test deciding superreflexivity from numerical input. Quantitative refinements and connections to specific extension estimates remain further directions. The construction and conclusion are reported as claims of M1.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Naor, Peres, Schramm, and Sheffield, Markov chains in smooth Banach spaces and Gromov hyperbolic metric spaces, for the earlier positive direction.
  • Naor, Comparison of metric spectral gaps, including the question addressed by this family.
  • Optional background: uniformly convex spaces.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Nontrivial Markov Type Forces Superreflexivity (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A claimed failure of universal entropy duality
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 329 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

How many small shapes are needed to cover a larger shape? This elementary-sounding question is a way to measure complexity: each translate in a cover represents a collection of points that need not be distinguished at the chosen resolution.

For symmetric convex bodies, there is a natural duality operation called polarity. It exchanges a body with the set of linear measurements bounded by one on that body. Pietsch’s entropy-duality conjecture asks whether covering complexity is preserved, up to universal constants, when one reverses the roles of two bodies and takes their polars.

Family 329 claims a negative answer to the unrestricted, dimension-free conjecture. For every proposed pair of universal constants, it constructs bodies violating the required comparison. The covering body can already be an ordinary cube.

The result does not say that polarity destroys every useful comparison. Strong positive theorems remain available for ellipsoids, geometrically controlled spaces, and comparisons with dimension-dependent losses. The issue is whether one fixed pair of constants works for all symmetric convex bodies in every dimension.

2. Background and essential definitions

A convex body in Rn\mathbb R^nRn is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. It is origin-symmetric when xxx belongs exactly when −x-x−x does. For bounded sets A,BA,BA,B, with BBB having interior, the covering number N(A,B)N(A,B)N(A,B) is the smallest number of translates of BBB whose union contains AAA. The centers of the translates can lie anywhere in the ambient space.

The quantity log⁡N(A,B)\log N(A,B)logN(A,B), using natural logarithms, is called covering entropy. Taking the logarithm turns multiplicative increases in the number of approximations into additive increases in complexity.

For an origin-symmetric convex body KKK, its polar is

K∘={y: ∣⟨x,y⟩∣≤1 for every x∈K}.K^\circ=\{y:\ |\langle x,y\rangle|\leq1\text{ for every }x\in K\}.K∘={y: ∣⟨x,y⟩∣≤1 for every x∈K}.

The absolute value can be omitted for symmetric KKK. A larger body has a smaller polar. The polar of the cube [−1,1]n[-1,1]^n[−1,1]n is the unit ball {y:∑i∣yi∣≤1}\{y:\sum_i|y_i|\leq1\}{y:∑i​∣yi​∣≤1}.

The conjectured comparison asks for absolute constants a,b≥1a,b\geq1a,b≥1 satisfying

b−1log⁡N(L∘,aK∘)≤log⁡N(K,L)≤blog⁡N(L∘,a−1K∘)b^{-1}\log N(L^\circ,aK^\circ)\leq\log N(K,L)\leq b\log N(L^\circ,a^{-1}K^\circ)b−1logN(L∘,aK∘)≤logN(K,L)≤blogN(L∘,a−1K∘)

for every dimension and every pair K,LK,LK,L. The constant aaa permits a fixed change of resolution; bbb permits a fixed multiplicative change in entropy. Both allowances are important: the question is much weaker than equality of the two covering numbers.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The problem originated in Pietsch’s 1972 work on entropy numbers of linear operators. These numbers measure how efficiently the image of a unit ball can be approximated by finitely many balls. Passing from an operator to its adjoint leads to the geometric polar-body formulation.

Early results already established substantial dual control. König and Milman compared the appropriate roots of covering numbers, allowing an additive error proportional to dimension on the logarithmic scale. Bourgain, Pajor, Szarek, and Tomczak-Jaegermann obtained estimates under geometric or sequence-regularity assumptions, and estimates involving rank-dependent losses.

Artstein, Milman, and Szarek proved the dimension-free conjecture when one body is a Euclidean ball, hence also when one body is an ellipsoid. This settled a central Hilbert-space case. It did not cover arbitrary unit balls of arbitrary norms.

Artstein, Milman, Szarek, and Tomczak-Jaegermann also introduced convexified packing and proved a universal duality theorem for that quantity. In an ordinary packing, points are separated pairwise. In convexified packing, each new translated neighborhood must avoid the convex hull of its predecessors. This ordered requirement is stronger and changes the quantity being counted.

The same work gave ordinary entropy duality under a bound on a K-convexity constant, which measures a space’s random-sign geometry. Emanuel Milman later obtained comparisons for general symmetric bodies with logarithmic losses in scale and entropy. These results identify important positive regimes but leave room for failure of one universal pair of constants across all dimensions.

4. What the new manuscript claims

M1 states that for every a,b≥1a,b\geq1a,b≥1, there are an integer n≥1n\geq1n≥1 and an origin-symmetric convex body K⊂RnK\subset\mathbb R^nK⊂Rn such that, with L=[−1,1]nL=[-1,1]^nL=[−1,1]n,

log⁡N(K,L)>blog⁡N(L∘,a−1K∘).\log N(K,L)>b\log N(L^\circ,a^{-1}K^\circ).logN(K,L)>blogN(L∘,a−1K∘).

Thus the upper inequality of the conjecture fails for every proposed universal pair. That is sufficient to disprove the two-sided formulation. The construction gives bodies with nonempty interior in their full ambient dimension; it is not exploiting a lower-dimensional set whose polar behaves degenerately.

The dimension and body depend on the proposed constants. There is no claim of a fixed dimension in which all possible constants fail. The quantifier order is the point: choose the constants first, and the construction supplies a sufficiently demanding example afterward.

M1 also derives a separation between ordinary covering entropy and convexified-packing entropy, even after a fixed change of scale. This explains why the earlier universal convexified-packing theorem need not extend to ordinary covering numbers.

The manuscript formulates its main result for arbitrary translation centers, the usual definition of covering number. Its compression construction therefore has to account carefully for whether approximation centers belong to the set being approximated; the geometric conversion includes that bookkeeping.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family claims a counterexample to a central universal duality conjecture in the local theory of Banach spaces and convex geometry. A negative resolution would substantially change the boundary between useful dual comparisons and comparisons that demand additional hypotheses.

The cube makes the statement particularly striking. One need not choose two unfamiliar bodies: even covering by a standard coordinate box can display the alleged failure. The complexity is carried by the other body and the dimension-dependent construction.

The result also separates notions that can initially appear interchangeable. Pairwise distinguishability, ordered convexified packing, and approximation by a small list all express complexity, but they need not obey the same duality principles. Understanding these distinctions matters when transferring geometric results into approximation or learning problems.

At the same time, the proposed counterexample leaves the ellipsoid theorem and bounded-geometric-constant results intact. Family 326’s conditional entropy consequence has precisely such additional geometric control, so its positive statement and this negative one concern different ranges of hypotheses.

6. The main idea

The construction begins with a finite matrix whose entries lie between zero and one. Think of rows as objects to distinguish and columns as measurements on those objects. M1 seeks two properties that pull in opposite directions: many rows are well separated in the maximum-coordinate norm, while all signed convex combinations of columns admit a short uniform approximation list.

A support-function calculation translates this discrepancy into convex bodies. The support function of a body assigns to each linear measurement its largest value on that body. Taking a symmetric hull of the rows creates large primal covering complexity, while the compressed column combinations control the polar covering complexity. A small cube is added to ensure nonempty interior.

The column compression uses a finite collection of partitions of a set. Selected partitions define a graph: two points are linked when they share a class in one of those partitions. Columns are profiles that decrease logarithmically with graph distance from a chosen center and become zero beyond a cutoff.

For a convex combination of columns, averaging identifies a partition used by most of the coefficient mass. At each distance scale, a greedy choice of a few pivots captures nearly all relevant mass. A pivot can then be replaced by a fixed representative of its class in that common partition.

This replacement is the compression step. One stores a class label instead of an arbitrary original point. Although replacement enlarges graph-distance radii, the logarithmic profile makes the resulting error uniformly small. Positive and negative coefficient parts are treated separately to cover the absolutely convex hull, meaning the convex hull of the columns and their negatives.

The separated rows come from symmetric multilinear forms over a finite field. A symmetric hhh-linear form takes hhh vectors as input, is linear in each, and is unchanged when inputs are permuted. Carefully chosen directions ensure a nonvanishing condition after deleting a small fraction of them. A short graph path would contradict this condition, forcing different rows to be separated.

The numerical advantage comes from the different sizes of the forms and their contracted labels. With rrr field coordinates, write

Dj=(r+j−1j).D_j=\binom{r+j-1}{j}.Dj​=(jr+j−1​).

There are pDhp^{D_h}pDh​ possible rows but at most pDh−1p^{D_{h-1}}pDh−1​ labels per partition, where ppp is a sufficiently large prime. Their logarithmic size ratio satisfies

Dh−1Dh=hr+h−1.\frac{D_{h-1}}{D_h}=\frac{h}{r+h-1}.Dh​Dh−1​​=r+h−1h​.

For fixed hhh, this tends to zero as rrr increases. The remaining encoding costs are fixed before ppp is chosen, so a large prime makes those costs negligible. This ordered choice of parameters turns the row-versus-column discrepancy into a violation of any prescribed universal constants.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The claim concerns finite-dimensional real symmetric convex bodies, but dimensions are allowed to grow. It does not contradict the existence of constants depending on dimension, nor comparisons with logarithmic or geometric losses.

The counterexample is an existence construction. The main statement does not advertise a small, practical-dimensional pair of bodies or an efficient numerical procedure for finding the first failure for given constants. Its purpose is to defeat uniformity, not to optimize the size of a counterexample.

The result also does not identify the best possible replacement for the conjecture. Determining sharp dimension-dependent losses, finding broader positive geometric classes, and clarifying exactly when ordinary and convexified entropy remain comparable are separate questions.

The manuscript’s definitions must be kept fixed when comparing these claims: covering uses arbitrary translates, the bodies have full interior, and the polar pair reverses their order. The construction and its consequences are reported as stated, without a proof audit.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Artstein, Milman, and Szarek, Duality of metric entropy, for the Euclidean-ball and ellipsoid case.
  • Artstein, Milman, Szarek, and Tomczak-Jaegermann, On convexified packing and entropy duality.
  • E. Milman, A remark on two duality relations, for comparisons with losses.
  • Optional background: polar sets.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Counterexamples to the duality conjecture for metric entropy (September 24, 2026).

entry.title: Discrete distances do not guarantee bounded approximation
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 330 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

A discrete metric space may seem easy to approximate: distinct points stay apart, so there are no arbitrarily small geometric features to resolve. But linearizing its geometry can produce a Banach space with much subtler approximation behavior.

A Lipschitz-free space is a canonical linear space built from a metric space. It preserves the original distances between designated point vectors and turns Lipschitz maps into linear operators. Kalton asked whether uniform separation of the original points guarantees that this free space has the bounded approximation property.

Family 330 claims a counterexample. It constructs a countable metric space in which every two distinct points are at least one unit apart, but the associated free space cannot approximate its identity using finite-rank operators with one common norm bound.

Ordinary approximation still works. Every compact set can be approximated as accurately as desired by some bounded finite-rank operator. The obstruction is the need to let the operator norm grow as the approximation tasks become more demanding.

2. Background and essential definitions

A pointed metric space (M,d,o)(M,d,o)(M,d,o) is a metric space with a selected basepoint ooo. Let Lip⁡0(M)\operatorname{Lip}_0(M)Lip0​(M) be the real-valued Lipschitz functions vanishing at ooo, with norm

∥f∥Lip=sup⁡x≠y∣f(x)−f(y)∣d(x,y).\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}=\sup_{x\ne y}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{d(x,y)}.∥f∥Lip​=x=ysup​d(x,y)∣f(x)−f(y)∣​.

Each point xxx defines an evaluation functional δx(f)=f(x)\delta_x(f)=f(x)δx​(f)=f(x). The real Lipschitz-free space F(M)\mathcal F(M)F(M) is the closed linear span of these evaluations inside the dual of Lip⁡0(M)\operatorname{Lip}_0(M)Lip0​(M). Its norm satisfies

∥δx−δy∥=d(x,y),δo=0.\|\delta_x-\delta_y\|=d(x,y),\qquad \delta_o=0.∥δx​−δy​∥=d(x,y),δo​=0.

Thus the original metric embeds isometrically in a linear space. A basepoint-preserving Lipschitz map into a Banach space has a corresponding bounded linear map on the free space, with the same norm as its Lipschitz constant. This is the construction’s linearization principle.

A Banach space has the approximation property, AP, if its identity can be approximated uniformly on every norm-compact set by bounded finite-rank linear operators. It has λ\lambdaλ-BAP if these operators can always be chosen with norm at most λ\lambdaλ. BAP means λ\lambdaλ-BAP for some finite λ\lambdaλ, and the metric approximation property, MAP, means 1-BAP.

Uniform discreteness means that all nonzero distances have one common positive lower bound. This is stronger than merely requiring every point to be isolated. A metric space is proper when every closed bounded ball is compact. A bounded infinite uniformly discrete set is not compact, so uniform discreteness alone does not imply properness.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The free-space construction goes back to the molecular spaces of Arens and Eells. Godefroy and Kalton developed its role in relating Lipschitz geometry to linear Banach-space structure. It provides a setting where a question about distances can become a question about operators.

Kalton established AP for free spaces over uniformly discrete metric spaces and asked whether BAP always follows. Godefroy and Ozawa restated the question in their work on free spaces and approximation properties; it also appears in Godefroy’s survey.

Several positive and negative results approached the boundary. Dalet proved MAP for free spaces over countable proper metric spaces. For bounded uniformly discrete spaces, the free space is isomorphic to ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​, the space of absolutely summable sequences, and therefore has BAP. These cases leave room for an unbounded, nonproper example assembled from increasingly difficult bounded pieces.

Smith constructed countable complete discrete spaces whose free spaces have AP but fail BAP. M1 emphasizes that these examples do not assert one uniform positive lower bound on all distances. The proposed new example supplies exactly that stronger condition.

Cúth and Kalenda’s April 2026 work proves a quantitative Schur property for uniformly discrete free spaces: weakly convergent sequences must converge in norm, with a quantitative strengthening. This is substantial sequential regularity, yet their introduction still records the BAP question. M1 claims that this regularity and ordinary approximation can coexist with failure of every bounded approximation constant.

4. What the new manuscript claims

M1 constructs a countable, unbounded, nonproper pointed metric space MMM satisfying

d(x,y)≥1(x≠y)d(x,y)\geq1\qquad(x\ne y)d(x,y)≥1(x=y)

such that F(M)\mathcal F(M)F(M) has AP but fails λ\lambdaλ-BAP for every finite λ≥1\lambda\geq1λ≥1.

The main local ingredient is more quantitative. For each integer p≥1p\geq1p≥1, M1 constructs a bounded countably infinite metric block MpM_pMp​ and a finite set of anchors ApA_pAp​, including the basepoint. Distinct points remain at least one apart, and

diam⁡(Mp)≤Bp,Bp=300p2+150p+5.\operatorname{diam}(M_p)\leq B_p,\qquad B_p=300p^2+150p+5.diam(Mp​)≤Bp​,Bp​=300p2+150p+5.

Every finite-rank operator TTT on F(Mp)\mathcal F(M_p)F(Mp​) with norm at most ppp must make a visible error at an anchor:

max⁡a∈Ap∥Tδa−δa∥≥12.\max_{a\in A_p}\|T\delta_a-\delta_a\|\geq\frac12.a∈Ap​max​∥Tδa​−δa​∥≥21​.

Each block nevertheless has 2Bp2B_p2Bp​-BAP. Thus a block defeats a prescribed small bound without losing all bounded approximation. Joining all the blocks defeats every finite bound simultaneously.

The block also yields an equivalent norm on real ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ with 2Bp2B_p2Bp​-BAP but without ppp-BAP. In the manuscript’s coefficient coordinates,

12∥c∥1≤∥c∥p≤Bp∥c∥1.\frac12\|c\|_1\leq\|c\|_p\leq B_p\|c\|_1.21​∥c∥1​≤∥c∥p​≤Bp​∥c∥1​.

For p=1p=1p=1, this gives a renorming of ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ without MAP.

Finally, M1 derives a nonlinear consequence through an existing theorem of Kalton: the separable space F(M)\mathcal F(M)F(M) is not approximable in Kalton’s uniform sense. There is no equi-uniformly continuous sequence of maps with relatively compact ranges converging pointwise to its identity. Equi-uniform continuity requires one continuity bound to work for every map in the sequence.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claimed construction answers Kalton’s uniformly discrete free-space question negatively and separates several approximation principles that might otherwise appear closely tied.

It shows why ordinary AP is weaker than BAP in a concrete metric setting. At every finite stage, approximation is possible. What fails is uniform control across all stages. The metric space has no arbitrarily small distances, so this failure must arise from how large-scale pieces interact with linear approximation.

The result also warns against confusing an obstruction to a special projection with an obstruction to all finite-rank approximations. Earlier finite metric extension problems can force large projection norms onto a prescribed range. But in a finite-dimensional free space, the identity itself is already a norm-one finite-rank operator. M1’s infinite blocks aim at the stronger obstruction needed here.

The nonlinear consequence adds another distinction: linear AP does not by itself imply uniformly controlled nonlinear approximation by compact-range maps. These implications concern different quantifiers and different kinds of control, even though all describe ways to approximate the identity.

6. The main idea

The global assembly is straightforward once the blocks exist. Identify their basepoints and define the distance between points in different blocks as the sum of their distances to the common basepoint. This produces a metric wedge.

Each block has a 1-Lipschitz retraction from the wedge: keep its points and send the other blocks to the basepoint. Linearization gives contractive inclusion and retraction maps between the corresponding free spaces. Any BAP bound for the whole space would therefore work for every block, contradicting the obstruction for sufficiently large ppp.

AP survives for a different reason. On a fixed compact set, first retain only finitely many blocks. Then approximate within each retained block using its own finite BAP constant. Only finitely many constants occur in this particular task, so their maximum is finite. AP permits that maximum to grow for later tasks.

The difficult work lies inside a block. M1 uses a sequence of finite colored graphs and attaches their vertices to finitely many anchors. Labels record capped distances to color classes. Long attachment edges keep the whole block bounded while preserving useful local graph geometry.

Suppose a small-norm finite-rank operator approximates all anchor evaluations. A small perturbation lets its range be supported on one finite subset of the metric block. Its values can then be represented by signed measures on that support, after adding a basepoint coefficient to normalize total mass. The measures need not be positive.

Lipschitz bump functions near the anchor labels force these signed measures to give large pairings with certain tests. On the other hand, a long nonbacktracking walk in a source graph is unlikely to be tracked by nearby support points with matching labels. Nonbacktracking means that a step never immediately reverses the preceding edge.

At most one direction can be exceptional for each support point in the relevant local comparison. This permits opposing scalar tests at the two ends of an edge. A scalar Lipschitz extension principle makes the tests globally defined, and averaging over many graph directions keeps the exceptional contribution small.

The resulting lower bound on an averaged pairing conflicts with the operator-norm upper bound on adjacent vertices. Importantly, the entire graph sequence and anchor set are fixed first. The operator and its support come later, after which the argument chooses a sufficiently large graph. This order is necessary to obstruct every candidate finite-rank operator, rather than only a preselected collection.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The example is uniformly discrete and countable, but unbounded and nonproper. It does not contradict the bounded uniformly discrete case or Dalet’s theorem for countable proper spaces. The local blocks retain BAP; failure arises from their unbounded sequence of required constants.

The scalar field in the manuscript is real. The principal conclusion is failure of every uniform finite bound, not failure of AP. The additional nonlinear statement uses Kalton’s specific definition involving equi-uniform continuity and relatively compact ranges.

The construction does not classify all uniformly discrete spaces whose free spaces have BAP or supply optimal constants for the individual blocks. Finding simpler examples, sharper growth of the block constants, and geometric conditions guaranteeing BAP remain separate questions. The results and the construction mechanism are reported as stated in M1.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Godefroy and Ozawa, Free Banach spaces and the approximation properties.
  • Dalet, Free spaces over some proper metric spaces.
  • Smith, Lipschitz-free spaces and Bossard’s reduction argument.
  • Cúth and Kalenda, Lipschitz-free spaces over uniformly discrete metric spaces are 3-Schur.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A uniformly discrete counterexample to bounded approximation in Lipschitz-free spaces (September 26, 2026).

entry.title: Midpoint convexity without asymptotically convex renormings
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 331 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Convexity says that the midpoint of two points in a ball remains in the ball. Stronger forms ask how far inside it must lie. In infinite-dimensional spaces, one can also ignore finitely many directions and study the geometry that remains.

Two versions of this asymptotic question look similar. One asks for growth in every sufficiently far-out direction from a unit vector. The other allows a direction and its opposite to be tested together, through the average of the two endpoint norms. Does this weaker midpoint growth imply that some equivalent norm has the stronger one-sided property?

The general implication already had a negative answer before this family. The seven manuscripts develop more explicit examples, exact moduli, and quantitative metric consequences. A central claim is a reflexive counterexample: midpoint growth persists, no equivalent asymptotically uniformly convex norm exists, and increasingly deep countably branching diamond graphs require unbounded distortion to embed.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let XXX be an infinite-dimensional real Banach space with norm NNN. A closed subspace has finite codimension when its quotient space has finite dimension. Restricting perturbations to such a subspace discards finitely many linear measurements.

For a unit vector xxx, first choose a finite-codimensional subspace FFF, then consider every unit vector y∈Fy\in Fy∈F. The one-sided and averaged midpoint moduli are

δ‾N(t)=inf⁡N(x)=1sup⁡Finf⁡y∈FN(y)=1(N(x+ty)−1),\overline\delta_N(t)=\inf_{N(x)=1}\sup_F\inf_{\substack{y\in F\\N(y)=1}}\bigl(N(x+ty)-1\bigr),δN​(t)=N(x)=1inf​Fsup​y∈FN(y)=1​inf​(N(x+ty)−1),
δ^N(t)=inf⁡N(x)=1sup⁡Finf⁡y∈FN(y)=1(N(x+ty)+N(x−ty)2−1).\widehat\delta_N(t)=\inf_{N(x)=1}\sup_F\inf_{\substack{y\in F\\N(y)=1}}\left(\frac{N(x+ty)+N(x-ty)}2-1\right).δN​(t)=N(x)=1inf​Fsup​y∈FN(y)=1​inf​(2N(x+ty)+N(x−ty)​−1).

The space is asymptotically uniformly convex, AUC, when the first is positive for every t>0t>0t>0. It is asymptotically midpoint uniformly convex, AMUC, when the second is positive for every t>0t>0t>0.

The historical AMUC definition uses the maximum of the two endpoint norms. It has the same positivity property, but different numerical constants. All midpoint formulas below use the average. Some manuscripts allow directions of norm at least one; even convexity along each line gives the same infimum.

An equivalent norm changes lengths by at most fixed multiplicative factors. Saying that a space has no equivalent AUC norm is stronger than saying that its displayed norm is not AUC.

A countably branching diamond begins with one edge and repeatedly replaces each edge by countably many two-edge paths sharing the endpoints. An embedding has distortion DDD if, after one overall rescaling, every distance is preserved between factors one and DDD. Uniform embedding means that one finite distortion works for all depths.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Dilworth, Kutzarova, Randrianarivony, Revalski, and Zhivkov introduced AMUC and exhibited a norm on ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ that is AMUC but not AUC. Since ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ has its usual uniformly convex norm, this did not settle the question about equivalent renormings.

Baudier subsequently answered the general renorming question negatively using the Kadets–Werner modification of the Bourgain–Rosenthal space. The example is a real L1L_1L1​ subspace with special compactness in measure and the Daugavet property. That earlier negative answer is credited throughout this family; the present claims are refinements and different constructions, including reflexive examples.

Diamond graphs supplied a related metric question. Earlier work showed that an equivalent AMUC norm prevents uniform embeddings of countably branching diamonds. Conversely, for reflexive spaces with unconditional asymptotic structure, failure of AUC renormability implies uniform diamond embeddings. This additional structure controls the effect of signs in asymptotic configurations. Swift and Perreau developed related embedding and dual-space formulations while retaining corresponding structural hypotheses.

The proposed reflexive examples show why the unconditional assumption cannot simply be omitted from that converse. They fail AUC renormability but still obstruct uniform diamond embeddings.

Tree spaces have an older role in Banach-space geometry. James’s norm sums squared coefficients over disjoint segments of a tree. Girardi proved AUC for the canonical predual and full dual of the classical binary James tree space. These manuscripts use different branching, completions, constraints, and root conventions; the earlier binary-tree theorem does not automatically describe them.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Segment forests and diamond distortion

M1 uses a forest containing a separate countably branching tree of each finite height. For finitely supported real arrays uuu, define

ρ(u)=sup⁡S1,…,Sm(∑i=1m∣∑v∈Siu(v)∣2)1/2,\rho(u)=\sup_{S_1,\ldots,S_m}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left|\sum_{v\in S_i}u(v)\right|^2\right)^{1/2},ρ(u)=S1​,…,Sm​sup​​i=1∑m​​v∈Si​∑​u(v)​2​1/2,

where the SiS_iSi​ are pairwise disjoint segments along ancestral chains. Complete this normed space to obtain JJJ, then take its dual X=J∗X=J^*X=J∗.

M1 claims that XXX is separable and reflexive, has no equivalent AUC norm, and satisfies

δ^X(t)≥1+t2/12−1.\widehat\delta_X(t)\geq\sqrt{1+t^2/12}-1.δX​(t)≥1+t2/12​−1.

It also gives the distortion bound D2≥1+k/12D^2\geq1+k/12D2≥1+k/12 for a depth-kkk diamond.

M2 studies both this forest dual and a separate infinite-height coordinate space B∞B_\inftyB∞​, the closed span of coordinate evaluations in the dual of the infinite-tree segment space. For either model, it claims the following lens estimate. If a center xxx is supported on a finite ancestral set HHH, and QHQ_HQH​ removes those coordinates, then

∥x+y∥,∥x−y∥≤R⟹∥QHy∥≤2R2−∥x∥2.\|x+y\|,\|x-y\|\leq R\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\|Q_Hy\|\leq2\sqrt{R^2-\|x\|^2}.∥x+y∥,∥x−y∥≤R⟹∥QH​y∥≤2R2−∥x∥2​.

The same head HHH works for every displacement in the lens, including displacements with a nonzero head. Both specified norms are AMUC and neither space admits an AUC renorming. Reflexivity is asserted for the finite-height forest dual.

Using this stronger lens estimate, M3 obtains

D2≥1+k/4D^2\geq1+k/4D2≥1+k/4

for diamonds in either of these two spaces. Its normalized edge lengths differ from M1’s convention only by an overall scale at each depth, which does not change distortion. M3 also develops direct tree-energy arguments and power-type bounds for other norms in the family.

Exact curves in an L1 model

M4 assumes that EEE is an infinite-dimensional closed real subspace of a probability L1L_1L1​ space, its unit ball is totally bounded for convergence in measure, and its inherited norm has the Daugavet property:

∥I+T∥=1+∥T∥\|I+T\|=1+\|T\|∥I+T∥=1+∥T∥

for every rank-one bounded operator TTT. Total boundedness in measure means that finitely many measure-metric balls cover the unit ball at each positive resolution.

Under these hypotheses, M4 claims exact formulas, valid at every unit center and hence for the moduli:

δ^E(t)=max⁡{t/2,t−1},δ‾E(t)=max⁡{0,t−2}.\widehat\delta_E(t)=\max\{t/2,t-1\},\qquad\overline\delta_E(t)=\max\{0,t-2\}.δE​(t)=max{t/2,t−1},δE​(t)=max{0,t−2}.

It separately excludes every equivalent AUC norm and supplies a quantitative realization of the earlier Kadets–Werner construction satisfying the assumptions. The formulas describe the inherited norm, not all equivalent norms.

Further explicit constructions

M5 constructs four tree norms whose scalar tests have bounded sums along root paths and different quadratic constraints: on sibling groups, antichains, or the whole coefficient family. An antichain consists of mutually incomparable vertices. All four have

δ^(t)≥1+t2/4−1(0<t<1)\widehat\delta(t)\geq\sqrt{1+t^2/4}-1\qquad(0<t<1)δ(t)≥1+t2/4​−1(0<t<1)

and admit no AUC renorming. Further path-cost and segment-start constructions yield reflexive AMUC examples with the same renorming obstruction. These are distinct norms; the constants are not interchangeable.

M6 gives a probabilistic construction. Put independent copies of a positive, nonconstant, mean-one random variable WWW at the nonroot vertices of a countably branching tree. Multiply along each root path, then take the closed real L1L_1L1​ span of the resulting products. For every such WWW with finite second moment, M6 excludes an equivalent AUC norm. Positive averaged midpoint bounds are proved specifically for exponential multipliers and squares of standard Gaussian variables. It makes no claim that all multiplier laws give AMUC, or that these product spaces are reflexive or Daugavet spaces.

M7 defines norms through two least nonnegative fields on a tree whose difference equals the vector and whose values dominate the Euclidean size of their children. Root sums give an infinite-tree model and a reflexive joining-root model with

δ^(t)≥t3/128(0<t<1).\widehat\delta(t)\geq t^3/128\qquad(0<t<1).δ(t)≥t3/128(0<t<1).

A separate fixed-zero-root normalization gives a homogeneous cubic estimate. Height-dependent aggregation exponents yield further sixth-power and cubic bounds. The stated models again admit no equivalent AUC norm.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The main significance is the claimed separation within reflexive spaces and its consequence for a natural metric characterization. Failure of AUC renormability would no longer force uniform diamond embeddings without additional structural assumptions.
