The family also gives unusually concrete ways to see why two-sided and one-sided asymptotic behavior differ. The exact L1L_1L1​ curves show positive averaged growth at every positive radius while one-sided growth remains zero through radius two. The tree examples turn a qualitative separation into estimates that accumulate over graph depth.

These claims refine an already established general negative answer rather than replacing its history. Their value lies in the reflexive setting, explicit constructions, exact or quantitative geometry, and different mechanisms that lead to the separation.

6. The main idea

A recurring obstruction to AUC renorming is a bounded tree of path vectors. A root-path sum or product has uniformly bounded norm, while moving to a new child adds a weakly null increment with norm bounded away from zero. Weakly null means that every bounded linear measurement tends to zero along the child sequence.

A hypothetical AUC norm would allow the successive choice of children giving a definite multiplicative increase at each step. Arbitrarily long paths would then have unbounded norm. Equivalence with the original norm contradicts the bounded path construction.

Midpoint growth requires a different argument. In the segment models, tests crossing from a finite head into a tail can have troublesome mixed terms. M1 adds corrections at first-exit vertices so their evaluations cancel between the two endpoints. M2 instead uses atomic segment representations and controls cancellations where segments leave the head. The resulting squared-radius budget bounds the whole tail of a symmetric lens.

Infinite branching connects this estimate to diamonds. Among infinitely many midpoint images, two finite-dimensional projections can be made very close. Their difference therefore retains substantial tail size. The lens estimate forces a loss in squared stretch at each replacement level; summing the losses gives M3’s depth-dependent bound.

The other models implement related ideas with different tools. M5 directs scalar potential perturbations inward so they stay within the allowed interval while sharing a quadratic budget. M7 propagates a defect through a recursion where at least one child inequality is tight, avoiding a loss that multiplies at every level.

In L1L_1L1​, the real scalar identity

∣a+b∣+∣a−b∣2=max⁡{∣a∣,∣b∣}\frac{|a+b|+|a-b|}{2}=\max\{|a|,|b|\}2∣a+b∣+∣a−b∣​=max{∣a∣,∣b∣}

turns midpoint gain into mass outside an overlap region. M4 combines clipping and finite sign tests with the weak-neighborhood geometry supplied by the Daugavet property. M6 conditions on a finite subtree; fresh independent multipliers beyond its first exits force positive excess uniformly over the remaining directions. The arguments have a shared theme but do not identify the underlying spaces.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All constructions here use real scalars. Numerical formulas refer to the specified averaged modulus and specified norms. Maximum-based moduli have the same positivity property but need not have the same values.

Reflexivity belongs to particular forest and joining-root models. It should not be transferred to every space in the seven manuscripts, especially the independent-product examples. Likewise, the exact L1L_1L1​ formulas require both measure-total-boundedness and the Daugavet property.

The diamond bounds concern countably branching graphs, which have infinitely many vertices even at finite depth. They are not automatically the same statement for finite binary diamonds. The distortion convention controls every pair of vertices.

Most constants are presented as quantitative bounds, not optimal values. The exact curves in M4 are a separate stronger assertion. Sharp constants, relations among the different constructions, and converse embedding theorems under other structural hypotheses remain further questions. The manuscript claims are explained without proof or novelty verification.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Baudier, the earlier negative answer to the general renorming question.
  • Baudier and collaborators, On the geometry of the countably branching diamond graphs, for the midpoint obstruction and conditional converse.
  • Kadets and Werner, A Banach space with the Schur and the Daugavet property, for the earlier L1L_1L1​ construction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Asymptotic midpoint uniform convexity and unbounded diamond distortion in a reflexive tree space (September 27, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Midpoint lenses in segment spaces (September 27, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Distortion of countably branching diamonds from midpoint and tree energies (September 27, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Exact asymptotic moduli in a Daugavet subspace of L1 (September 27, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Midpoint convexity from bounded tree potentials and path costs (September 27, 2026).
  • M6. OpenAI, Independent products in real L1: asymptotic midpoint convexity without AUC renormings (September 27, 2026).
  • M7. OpenAI, Midpoint convexity from two recursive potentials (September 27, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Markov cotype of ℓ1 and Lipschitz extension
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 332 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Suppose a function is defined on only part of a Hilbert space, and nearby inputs always have nearby outputs in ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​, the space of absolutely summable sequences. Can it be extended to every input while increasing its Lipschitz constant by at most one universal factor?

This is Ball’s extension problem for the target ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​. The factor must work independently of the dimension, the subset, and the function. Extending coordinates separately is not enough: their errors can accumulate when the target norm adds absolute values.

Family 332 claims a positive answer through a random-walk property called metric Markov cotype two. The main theorem says that values assigned to the states of a finite chain can be adjusted to reduce their one-step variation, while paying a controlled cost for moving them.

The adjustment is nonlinear. Rather than taking a prescribed linear average, the manuscript constructs new values using the expected coordinatewise median of three independent random-walk endpoints. This freedom is the feature that allows the proposed result to coexist with earlier negative statements about linear averaging and subspaces.

2. Background and essential definitions

The real Banach space ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ consists of sequences x=(x(k))k≥1x=(x(k))_{k\geq1}x=(x(k))k≥1​ with

∥x∥1=∑k≥1∣x(k)∣<∞.\|x\|_1=\sum_{k\geq1}|x(k)|<\infty.∥x∥1​=k≥1∑​∣x(k)∣<∞.

A map fff is Lipschitz when some finite LLL satisfies d(f(u),f(v))≤Ld(u,v)d(f(u),f(v))\leq Ld(u,v)d(f(u),f(v))≤Ld(u,v) for all inputs. The least such constant is Lip⁡(f)\operatorname{Lip}(f)Lip(f). An extension agrees with fff everywhere on its original domain.

A stochastic matrix A=(aij)A=(a_{ij})A=(aij​) has nonnegative entries and rows summing to one. It specifies a finite Markov chain. A probability vector π\piπ is stationary when πA=π\pi A=\piπA=π, and reversible when

πiaij=πjaji.\pi_i a_{ij}=\pi_j a_{ji}.πi​aij​=πj​aji​.

Reversibility implies stationarity. The entry (As)ij(A^s)_{ij}(As)ij​ is the probability of traveling from iii to jjj in sss steps.

To define metric Markov cotype two, start with arbitrary points x1,…,xnx_1,\ldots,x_nx1​,…,xn​ in a metric space and choose a time t≥1t\geq1t≥1. One must find replacement points y1,…,yny_1,\ldots,y_ny1​,…,yn​ so that

∑iπid(xi,yi)2+t∑i,jπiaijd(yi,yj)2≤C2∑i,jπiBijd(xi,xj)2,\sum_i\pi_i d(x_i,y_i)^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_i a_{ij}d(y_i,y_j)^2\leq C^2\sum_{i,j}\pi_i B_{ij}d(x_i,x_j)^2,i∑​πi​d(xi​,yi​)2+ti,j∑​πi​aij​d(yi​,yj​)2≤C2i,j∑​πi​Bij​d(xi​,xj​)2,

where

B=1t∑s=1tAs.B=\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^{t}A^s.B=t1​s=1∑t​As.

The first term is the cost of modifying the data. The second is the remaining one-step variation, multiplied by time. The right side measures the original variation averaged over times one through ttt. One constant CCC must work for every chain, dataset, and time. Its optimal value is denoted N2(X)N_2(X)N2​(X).

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ball introduced Markov type and cotype in his work on Lipschitz maps. Markov type controls how far a stationary reversible walk travels relative to its one-step motion. Markov cotype asks for a complementary smoothing operation on the target values.

There are different cotype formulations. Ball’s Banach-space condition uses specified linear averages, and ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ fails that stronger condition. His metric formulation allows more freedom. Mendel and Naor developed the time-averaged definition above, established its relationship with Ball’s metric definition, and explicitly asked whether N2(ℓ1)N_2(\ell_1)N2​(ℓ1​) is finite.

For 1<p≤21<p\leq21<p≤2, uniformly convex theory gives metric Markov cotype two for ℓp\ell_pℓp​, with known bounds deteriorating as ppp approaches one. Consequently, simply taking an endpoint limit does not settle the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ question.

Mendel and Naor also used a construction of Kalton to find a closed linear subspace of ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ failing metric Markov cotype at every finite exponent. This may initially sound incompatible with a positive theorem for the whole space. The distinction is that the replacement points may leave the subspace containing the original data. The metric condition is not automatically inherited by arbitrary subspaces.

Their extension framework already showed why the endpoint question mattered: a positive answer for ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ would yield the desired Hilbert-to-ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ extension theorem. M1 claims the missing cotype result and then invokes that existing implication, rather than presenting the extension principle itself as new.

4. What the new manuscript claims

For real scalars, M1 states

N2(ℓ1)≤1221.N_2(\ell_1)\leq12\sqrt{21}.N2​(ℓ1​)≤1221​.

Thus C2=3024C^2=3024C2=3024 works in the defining inequality, independently of the number of data points, sequence coordinates, or time parameter. The manuscript does not claim that this numerical constant is optimal. Zero entries of the stationary probability vector are allowed.

The proof is stated to use only stationarity, so M1 also records the same smoothing inequality and construction for stationary stochastic matrices without detailed balance. Reversibility remains part of the standard definition that the main theorem answers.

A real-linear comparison between complex sequences and their interlaced real and imaginary parts gives the additional bound

N2(ℓ1(C))≤1242.N_2(\ell_1(\mathbb C))\leq12\sqrt{42}.N2​(ℓ1​(C))≤1242​.

The main extension consequence is formulated for a real Hilbert space HHH. For every subset S⊂HS\subset HS⊂H and every Lipschitz map f:S→ℓ1f:S\to\ell_1f:S→ℓ1​, M1 states that there is an extension F:H→ℓ1F:H\to\ell_1F:H→ℓ1​ satisfying

F∣S=f,Lip⁡(F)≤KLip⁡(f),F|_S=f,\qquad\operatorname{Lip}(F)\leq K\operatorname{Lip}(f),F∣S​=f,Lip(F)≤KLip(f),

where K<∞K<\inftyK<∞ is universal. The subset need not be finite or convex, and no finite-dimensional hypothesis is imposed on HHH. The extension constant is obtained through the existing extension theorem; the manuscript does not identify its optimal value with the displayed cotype constant.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The family claims a positive resolution of an explicit metric Markov cotype question and, through it, a universal extension theorem for an important classical target space.

Hilbert spaces express quadratic geometry, whereas ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ measures length by adding absolute coordinate contributions. Moving between these geometries is difficult because a coordinatewise construction can lose uniform control. A constant independent of all dimensions and datasets is therefore the substantive conclusion.

The result would also emphasize the power of nonlinear smoothing. Choosing replacement points freely can succeed where a prescribed linear averaging rule fails. The expected-median construction makes that distinction concrete rather than merely existential.

Its compatibility with a bad subspace of ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ is equally instructive. Having room in the ambient target can be essential. An extension or smoothing theorem for the whole space need not preserve every linear subspace containing the input data.

6. The main idea

The first step encodes a finite subset of ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ by weighted cuts. A cut separates the indices of the data points into two groups. Thresholding each original coordinate produces such cuts, and the coordinate gaps supply nonnegative weights.

After collecting them, each original point xix_ixi​ has a finite binary encoding ziz_izi​. For a weighted Hilbert norm and a weighted ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm on the cut coordinates, the encoding satisfies

∥xi−xj∥1=∥zi−zj∥1,w=∥zi−zj∥H,2.\|x_i-x_j\|_1=\|z_i-z_j\|_{1,w}=\|z_i-z_j\|_{H}^{,2}.∥xi​−xj​∥1​=∥zi​−zj​∥1,w​=∥zi​−zj​∥H,2​.

Binary coordinate differences have equal absolute value and square, explaining the last equality. M1 also retains an affine reconstruction map TTT with T(zi)=xiT(z_i)=x_iT(zi​)=xi​, contractive from the weighted ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm back to the original ambient ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​. The construction therefore remembers more than just pairwise distances.

Next, run the chain for an independent geometric number of steps with mean ttt, and average the binary endpoint encoding. Starting at state iii gives a vector hih_ihi​ in the unit cube. Apply the cubic function

ϕ(r)=3r2−2r3(0≤r≤1)\phi(r)=3r^2-2r^3\qquad(0\leq r\leq1)ϕ(r)=3r2−2r3(0≤r≤1)

to each coordinate, then reconstruct:

yi=T(Φ(hi)).y_i=T(\Phi(h_i)).yi​=T(Φ(hi​)).

The cubic fixes zero and one and has zero derivative at both endpoints. Its flatness near binary values is central to the estimate. The manuscript uses a fourth-power Hilbert potential to control squared weighted-ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ increments after applying Φ\PhiΦ.

To accumulate the estimate, M1 forms a martingale from the walk and its stopping event. A martingale is a process whose current value equals the conditional expectation of its next value. While the walk is alive, its attached value is the expected binary endpoint; on stopping, the actual binary endpoint is revealed.

The potential inequality telescopes in expectation because its linear remainder has conditional mean zero. The final stopping jump accounts for the cost of replacing xix_ixi​ by yiy_iyi​. The expected preceding jumps account for ttt times the remaining one-step variation. A separate comparison converts the geometric stopping cost to the average over times one through ttt, producing the stated constant.

There is a useful interpretation in the original coordinates. For three independent geometric-walk endpoints started at iii, take the coordinatewise median of their data vectors and then its expectation. The result is exactly yiy_iyi​. Indeed, if a threshold is exceeded with probability rrr, at least two of three independent samples exceed it with probability 3r2−2r33r^2-2r^33r2−2r3.

Finally, Hilbert spaces have Markov type two with constant one, and ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ is the dual of c0c_0c0​, the space of sequences tending to zero. These facts and the new cotype bound satisfy the hypotheses of the cited extension theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem allows replacement points anywhere in the full target. Requiring them to remain in a prescribed closed subspace, or to equal fixed linear averages, changes the problem and can make the corresponding assertion false.

Metric Markov cotype is also distinct from ordinary metric cotype and from Rademacher cotype, which concerns random signed sums of vectors. A theorem about one invariant cannot be substituted for another merely because their names are similar.

The displayed constants are upper bounds, not sharp values. The extension corollary guarantees existence with universal loss but does not provide an optimized algorithm for arbitrary infinite subsets. Determining optimal constants and effective constructions for concrete finite data remains separate work.

The source’s direct smoothing construction, its stationarity extension, and its Hilbert-space corollary are reported as stated. The mathematical proof is not independently checked here.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Ball, Markov chains, Riesz transforms and Lipschitz maps, for the original probabilistic extension framework.
  • Mendel and Naor, Spectral calculus and Lipschitz extension for barycentric metric spaces, for the metric cotype question, subspace obstruction, and extension theorem.
  • Optional background: Lipschitz continuity and martingales.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Metric Markov Cotype Two of ℓ1 (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Does the unit sphere remember the whole Banach space?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 322 · Functional analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-25

1. The question

Suppose you know only the unit sphere of a normed vector space, together with distances measured by the ambient norm. You are given a distance-preserving bijection from that sphere to the unit sphere of another space. Does it necessarily come from a linear isometry of the entire spaces?

This is Tingley’s problem. The proposed extension is easy to write: keep the distance from the origin and apply the sphere map to the direction. What is difficult is proving that this radial extension respects distances between points at different radii, and hence respects addition.

Family 322 claims a positive solution for all nonzero real Banach spaces. There is no finite-dimensionality, separability, reflexivity, smoothness or strict-convexity assumption. Applied to complex spaces, the conclusion is real linearity, not necessarily complex linearity.

2. Background and essential definitions

A Banach space is a vector space with a complete norm. Its unit sphere is SX={x:∥x∥=1}S_X=\{x:\|x\|=1\}SX​={x:∥x∥=1}, with distance d(x,y)=∥x−y∥d(x,y)=\|x-y\|d(x,y)=∥x−y∥. This is the ambient chord distance, not distance measured by traveling along the sphere.

An isometry f:SX→SYf:S_X\to S_Yf:SX​→SY​ preserves every pairwise distance. Surjectivity means every target sphere point is reached; together these properties make fff a bijection.

If a linear extension exists, it is forced to be

T(0)=0,T(x)=∥x∥f(x∥x∥)(x≠0).T(0)=0,\qquadT(x)=\|x\|f\left(\frac{x}{\|x\|}\right)\quad(x\ne0).T(0)=0,T(x)=∥x∥f(∥x∥x​)(x=0).

This map automatically preserves norms and is homogeneous for positive real scalars. It also preserves distances between points with the same norm, by scaling the sphere isometry. Neither fact alone proves additivity.

A supporting functional at a unit vector is a linear functional φ\varphiφ with ∥φ∥=1\|\varphi\|=1∥φ∥=1 and φ(x)=1\varphi(x)=1φ(x)=1. It describes a supporting hyperplane of the unit ball. When two unit vectors share a support, convex combinations between them remain on the same supporting face. Norms with flat faces make this geometry different from a Euclidean sphere.

A space is strictly convex when its sphere has no nontrivial line segment, and smooth when each nonzero vector has a unique norming support. M1 assumes neither property, so supports and directions can have nonunique behavior.

The Mazur–Ulam property for a space means that every surjective sphere isometry from it to any real Banach target extends linearly. This is stronger than an extension theorem restricted to a specified target class.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Mazur and Ulam proved that a surjective isometry between entire real normed spaces is affine. If it fixes zero, it is linear. Mankiewicz extended this kind of result to convex sets with nonempty interiors. A sphere has empty ambient interior, so these theorems do not directly extend a sphere map.

Tingley’s original work established antipodal preservation in finite dimensions: opposite sphere points map to opposite points. That is necessary for a real-linear extension, but it does not by itself recover distances between unequal radii.

Early positive results treated concrete spaces, including continuous-function spaces and sequence spaces. Subsequent work distinguished class-to-class theorems from the arbitrary-target Mazur–Ulam property. Tan proved that property for real LpL^pLp spaces over sigma-finite measure spaces in the stated range 1<p<∞1<p<\infty1<p<∞, p≠2p\ne2p=2.

Facial geometry supplied another approach. Sphere isometries preserve maximal convex subsets of spheres, allowing support and face structure to constrain possible maps. In operator algebras, Fernández-Polo–Peralta treated von Neumann algebras, Mori treated their preduals, and Mori–Ozawa proved the arbitrary-target property for unital complex C*-algebras viewed as real spaces and for real von Neumann algebras.

Banakh established the property for every two-dimensional real Banach space. Other recent results covered specific sphere self-isometries and noncommutative LpL^pLp or Schatten settings. M1 claims to remove all structural restrictions in the Banach-space problem rather than add another special class.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that for any nonzero real Banach spaces X,YX,YX,Y and any surjective sphere isometry f:SX→SYf:S_X\to S_Yf:SX​→SY​, the radial map in Section 2 is a surjective real-linear isometry. It is the unique linear extension of fff.

There is no dimension or cardinality restriction. The spaces may have flat sphere faces, nonsmooth norms, or nonreflexive behavior. Completeness is included through the Banach-space hypothesis.

For complex spaces regarded as real ones, the theorem guarantees a real-linear extension. It does not guarantee T(ix)=iT(x)T(ix)=iT(x)T(ix)=iT(x). Complex conjugation on C\mathbb CC already illustrates why a metric sphere map need not preserve multiplication by iii.

The source organizes the key metric obstruction using

Dq(x,y)=∥f(x)−qf(y)∥−∥x−qy∥,0≤q≤1,D_q(x,y)=\|f(x)-qf(y)\|-\|x-qy\|,\qquad 0\leq q\leq1,Dq​(x,y)=∥f(x)−qf(y)∥−∥x−qy∥,0≤q≤1,

for x,y∈SXx,y\in S_Xx,y∈SX​. This measures distortion between two radius levels. It vanishes at q=0q=0q=0 and q=1q=1q=1, while the unresolved values lie strictly between them.

M1 proves that the maximal absolute defect is zero. Once every DqD_qDq​ vanishes, scaling handles arbitrary pairs of nonzero vectors, and surjectivity supplies the whole-space isometry. The classical midpoint-reflection principle then yields real linearity.

The theorem is exact. It does not state a quantitative stability result for maps that preserve sphere distances only approximately.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this resolves a central metric extension problem and establishes that the unit sphere’s ambient metric determines the real linear geometry of the entire Banach space.

The conclusion is stronger than recognizing a normed space up to some nonlinear equivalence. It recovers the unique linear isometry compatible with the specified sphere map. Thus both the object and the actual correspondence are determined.

The absence of regularity assumptions matters. Euclidean intuition relies on roundness and unique normal directions; general Banach balls can have corners, large flat faces and noncompact spheres. M1’s proposed method is designed to work without replacing those spaces by smooth or finite-dimensional models.

6. The main idea

Make a hypothetical largest error occur

Assume some sphere isometry has positive maximal defect

M=sup⁡x,y∈SX, 0≤q≤1∣Dq(x,y)∣>0.M=\sup_{x,y\in S_X,\,0\leq q\leq1}|D_q(x,y)|>0.M=x,y∈SX​,0≤q≤1sup​∣Dq​(x,y)∣>0.

The supremum might not be attained because unit spheres can be noncompact. M1 passes to a possibly enlarged pair of Banach spaces built from bounded sequences and an ultrafilter. The sphere isometry acts coordinatewise, and its inverse ensures the induced map remains onto.

The construction preserves the universal defect bound while making one positive defect attain MMM. Replacing the original map by its inverse if necessary fixes the sign. This is a contradiction device; it does not claim that every original sphere is compact or that its supremum was attained there.

Propagate extremality through supports

At a maximizing configuration, supporting functionals turn equality and near-equality in triangle inequalities into geometric restrictions. Common supports propagate the extremal configuration along appropriate directions.

The source constructs a nonempty closed bounded convex set of directions and an opposite-endpoint return map preserving it. The goal is to find a fixed direction, which aligns two relevant chords and makes their length relations directly comparable.

Ordinary compactness is unavailable. Instead, M1 estimates the Kuratowski measure of noncompactness, which measures how small finite coverings by bounded-diameter sets can be made. The return map strictly contracts this measure. Darbo’s fixed-point theorem then supplies the aligned direction. It is contraction of noncompactness, not necessarily an ordinary Lipschitz contraction of distances.

Eliminate the aligned configuration

Once the chords are aligned, the manuscript divides the possible parameters into two regimes. In one, a small radial perturbation would produce a defect larger than the supposed maximum. In the other, support and convexity estimates contradict one of the original sphere distances, which fff preserves exactly.

Thus the positive maximal defect cannot occur. This is the proof-specific geometric stage: the ultrapower and fixed-point theorems provide the setting, while the invariant direction set, return-map estimate and chord contradiction do the new work.

Recover distances and then addition

For nonzero vectors of norms r≥sr\geq sr≥s, write them as rxrxrx and sysysy with unit vectors x,yx,yx,y. The ratio q=s/rq=s/rq=s/r lies in [0,1][0,1][0,1]. Vanishing of DqD_qDq​ gives

∥T(rx)−T(sy)∥=r∥f(x)−qf(y)∥=r∥x−qy∥.\|T(rx)-T(sy)\|=r\|f(x)-qf(y)\|=r\|x-qy\|.∥T(rx)−T(sy)∥=r∥f(x)−qf(y)∥=r∥x−qy∥.

This is the original distance. The radial extension is therefore a surjective isometry fixing zero, and the whole-space Mazur–Ulam argument supplies additivity and real homogeneity. Uniqueness was already forced by the radial formula.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Surjectivity of the sphere map is essential to the stated theorem and to the use of its inverse. M1 does not claim that every distance-preserving embedding of one sphere into another has an onto linear extension.

The conclusion is real linearity even for complex spaces. It concerns Banach spaces, not arbitrary incomplete normed spaces, quasi-Banach spaces, or unrelated metric spheres. Results for those settings need their own hypotheses.

The proof’s passage to enlarged spaces is used only to rule out positive defect. The resulting extension is defined on the original spaces by the explicit radial formula. No additional choice of values away from the sphere is required.

Finally, exact rigidity does not automatically give a bound for approximately distance-preserving maps. Quantitative versions, extension from only part of a sphere, and weaker surjectivity assumptions remain separate questions beyond the manuscript’s main claim.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Mori and Ozawa, Mankiewicz’s theorem and the Mazur–Ulam property for C*-algebras, for a broad earlier arbitrary-target theorem.
  • Banakh, Every 2-dimensional Banach space has the Mazur–Ulam property, for the complete two-dimensional case.
  • M1 explains its defect-maximization, common-support and Darbo fixed-point steps, with the exact Banach-space and real-linearity conventions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A positive solution to Tingley’s problem (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 25 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A sphere at infinity determines hyperbolic three-dimensional geometry
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 246 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Imagine exploring an infinite network from one vertex. Nearby junctions describe its local structure, but the directions in which an explorer can escape describe another object: its boundary at infinity. Could the shape of that boundary determine the geometry of the entire network?

For a group, the network can be its Cayley graph, whose edges represent multiplication by generators. Cannon’s conjecture concerns groups whose graphs have a form of negative curvature. It asks whether a boundary shaped like an ordinary two-dimensional sphere forces the group to act as the symmetries of a tiling of hyperbolic three-dimensional space.

The manuscript in family 246 claims an affirmative answer without additional algebraic or geometric assumptions. Its central step is to turn a merely topological sphere into a quantitatively controlled sphere. Established uniformization and group-action theorems then supply the three-dimensional action.

The distinction between topology and geometry is the heart of the problem. A rubber sheet can remain a sphere while distances on it become extremely distorted. Recognizing its topology does not immediately provide coordinates that respect the geometry inherited from the group.

2. Background and essential definitions

A group as a geometric object

Let GGG be a group generated by a finite set SSS. Its Cayley graph has one vertex for each element of GGG, with an edge from ggg to gsgsgs for each generator sss. Give every edge length one. Distance then measures the smallest number of generator steps needed to travel between elements.

Different finite generating sets can alter these distances, but only within controlled multiplicative and additive bounds. Large-scale properties such as hyperbolicity therefore belong to the group rather than to a particular drawing of the graph.

A graph is hyperbolic when there is a constant δ\deltaδ such that every side of every shortest-path triangle lies within distance δ\deltaδ of the other two sides. These are called uniformly thin triangles. Trees provide the simplest example: their triangles collapse into three branches meeting at a point.

This condition expresses negative curvature at large scales. It does not require the graph to be a smooth space, nor does it assign an ordinary differential-geometric curvature to each vertex.

Directions at infinity

A geodesic ray is an infinite path that realizes distance along each finite segment. Two rays represent the same boundary point when they remain within bounded distance of each other, with the usual adjustment of starting points. The resulting space is written ∂G\partial G∂G.

The infinite cyclic group has two boundary points, corresponding to its two directions of escape. A nonabelian free group has a tree-like Cayley graph and a Cantor-set boundary. Groups acting properly and cocompactly on hyperbolic three-space have sphere boundaries.

A visual metric on the boundary makes two directions close when their rays travel together for a long time before separating. Schematically,

d(ξ,η)≍a−L(ξ,η),a>1,d(\xi,\eta)\asymp a^{-L(\xi,\eta)},\qquad a>1,d(ξ,η)≍a−L(ξ,η),a>1,

where L(ξ,η)L(\xi,\eta)L(ξ,η) measures their common initial travel and ≍\asymp≍ means equality up to fixed multiplicative constants. Thus a difference far from the observer corresponds to a small boundary distance.

The assumption ∂G≅S2\partial G\cong S^2∂G≅S2 means a homeomorphism exists: a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. It does not say that the visual metric is the usual round metric.

The action we want

Hyperbolic three-space, denoted H3\mathbb H^3H3, is the simply connected three-dimensional geometry of constant curvature −1-1−1. An isometric group action preserves its distances.

An action is proper when, for each compact region KKK, only finitely many group elements move KKK so that it still meets itself. It is cocompact when translates of one compact region cover the whole space. Together these conditions say that the group describes the space with finite local complexity and a compact fundamental region.

The kernel consists of elements acting trivially everywhere. Properness permits a finite kernel. A group is torsion-free when its only element of finite order is the identity; in that case, a proper action has trivial point stabilizers and trivial kernel.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Cannon’s 1994 combinatorial Riemann mapping theorem developed a way to recover analytic geometry from combinatorial coverings. Instead of beginning with angles and derivatives, it studied discrete measurements of how curves cross annular regions. Cannon and Swenson’s 1998 work formulated the group-boundary recognition problem and linked it to conformality of natural boundary coverings.

Cannon, Floyd and Parry subsequently gave sufficient conditions involving annuli whose separating-curve moduli remain bounded away from zero. Their work on finite subdivision rules supplied another language for recursively refining the relevant tilings. These developments converted a qualitative recognition question into estimates that must hold at every scale.

Bonk and Kleiner established uniformization results for metric two-spheres. Their 2005 theorem proved Cannon’s conjecture when a particular conformal-dimension infimum is attained. Here conformal dimension asks how small the Hausdorff dimension can become after controlled changes of boundary metric. Attainment was an additional hypothesis, not something guaranteed by the boundary’s topology alone.

Bourdon and Kleiner later supplied the specific combinatorial-modulus criterion used in the new paper. For an approximately self-similar metric sphere, a uniform bound on a suitable discrete two-modulus leads to a controlled parametrization by the round sphere. The difficult remaining task was to establish that bound for every sphere boundary in the conjecture.

Another route sought surfaces and cube complexes inside the group. Kahn and Marković constructed surface subgroups in closed hyperbolic three-manifold groups. Bergeron and Wise related suitable separating subgroups to actions on cube complexes, and Agol obtained powerful virtual-structure theorems for hyperbolic groups with such actions.

In the recognition direction, Marković proved a criterion using sufficiently many quasiconvex surface subgroups. Haïssinsky established a virtual Kleinian criterion under cubulation and planarity assumptions. Work of Groves, Haïssinsky, Manning, Osajda, Sisto and Walsh connected a relative version of Cannon’s conjecture to recognition for residually finite groups.

These results explain both the strength and the remaining gap of earlier approaches. They identify extra structures that would force hyperbolic three-dimensional geometry, but those structures are not part of Cannon’s original hypothesis. The new manuscript instead claims to derive the needed analytic control directly from hyperbolicity and sphere topology.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The paper, dated 23 September 2026, states that every hyperbolic group GGG with ∂G\partial G∂G homeomorphic to S2S^2S2 admits a homomorphism

ρ:G⟶Isom⁡(H3)\rho:G\longrightarrow\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb H^3)ρ:G⟶Isom(H3)

whose action is proper and cocompact. Its kernel is finite.

There is no torsion-free assumption in this main statement. The action may include orientation-reversing isometries, so the conclusion does not require a preselected orientation preserved by the group.

When GGG is torsion-free, the quotient H3/G\mathbb H^3/GH3/G is a closed hyperbolic three-manifold with fundamental group GGG. It may be nonorientable. Here closed means compact and without boundary.

For this torsion-free case, the paper combines the claimed realization with existing three-manifold results. A finite-index subgroup has the form

π1(Σ)⋊Z,\pi_1(\Sigma)\rtimes\mathbb Z,π1​(Σ)⋊Z,

where Σ\SigmaΣ is a closed orientable surface. This describes a finite cover that fibers over a circle, with the integer direction recording repeated travel around the circle.

The paper also records virtual compact specialness and residual finiteness in the torsion-free case. Residual finiteness means that each nonidentity element remains nonidentity in some finite quotient. These consequences use the earlier geometric theorems once the hyperbolic manifold has been obtained; they are not separate new proofs of those earlier theorems.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. Cannon’s conjecture is a central recognition problem in geometric group theory. Its claimed resolution would show that the topology of a hyperbolic group’s boundary already forces a highly specific three-dimensional geometry.

The conclusion is stronger than saying that the Cayley graph resembles some negatively curved space. It produces an actual action by isometries of H3\mathbb H^3H3, with properness and cocompactness controlling the quotient. In the torsion-free case, an abstract algebraic object becomes the fundamental group of a closed hyperbolic manifold.

The method would also close the gap between a qualitative sphere and the quantitative curve estimates required by uniformization. That is a substantial analytic advance within a problem whose original statement uses only groups and topology.

The rating concerns the significance of the stated claim. It does not express an independent assessment of the proof.

6. The main idea

Measure how hard it is to cross the boundary

Cover the boundary by small balls at scale a−na^{-n}a−n. Give each ball BBB a nonnegative weight w(B)w(B)w(B). Require every continuous path of some fixed minimum diameter to meet balls whose total weight is at least one.

Among all such admissible assignments, minimize the squared-weight cost:

M(n)=inf⁡w∑Bw(B)2.M(n)=\inf_w\sum_B w(B)^2.M(n)=winf​B∑​w(B)2.

This is a discrete two-modulus. The crossing requirement prevents weights from being tiny everywhere, while minimization distributes the cost efficiently. The exponent two is tied to the two-dimensional geometry sought on the boundary.

The classical criterion used by the manuscript reduces the problem to showing that M(n)M(n)M(n) stays bounded as the covers become finer. The source applies this criterion to continuous curves of controlled diameter, without assuming an ordinary smooth metric on the boundary.

Turn a hypothetical failure into a scalar function

The paper argues by contradiction. If the modulus becomes unbounded, selected record scales let it compare large values with nearby finer or coarser scales. Planar crossing duality produces low-energy weights for a complementary crossing problem.

The manuscript regularizes those weights into continuous scalar functions on a coordinate rectangle. A limiting function remains nonconstant and has level sets that separate opposite portions of the rectangle. A finite measure controls how much the function can oscillate inside a small ball.

This is the bridge from combinatorics to analysis: an assumed failure of uniformization would create a function with substantial variation but unusually small local energy. The sphere’s topology supplies separating sets, while the group supplies controlled magnifications of small regions.

Compare magnified copies

The proof separates two possible growth regimes. If the record moduli grow exponentially, the scalar limit has quantitative continuity. Magnifying its variation gives a nonconstant limit on a punctured sphere. Comparisons between different magnifications force incompatible restrictions on where that limit can vary.

If growth is subexponential, a single magnification does not provide the same contradiction. The paper instead distributes variation through a tree of separated balls. Nested intervals of function values carry a probability flow, so some variation must survive through many generations.

At a common depth, many group elements expand these small regions into two comparable target regions. Pairwise comparisons charge definite amounts of the controlling measure to small source balls. The manuscript’s overlap estimates bound the total charge from above, while the number of contributing pairs forces a larger lower bound.

The two branches exclude unbounded modulus. The existing uniformization theorem then identifies the boundary with a controlled round sphere. Sullivan’s and Tukia’s methods straighten the boundary action into conformal or anticonformal transformations, which extend to isometries of H3\mathbb H^3H3. The source retains orientation-reversing elements throughout this final step.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The boundary hypothesis is specifically a topological two-sphere. The statement does not classify hyperbolic groups with arbitrary boundaries, nor does it say that every topological sphere equipped with any metric admits the same uniformization. The self-similarity and expansion properties supplied by the group are essential ingredients of the claimed argument.

The main action can have a finite kernel. Replacing that conclusion by a faithful action for every group would strengthen the statement. The clean manifold interpretation is made for torsion-free groups, where finite stabilizers disappear.

Residual finiteness is a consequence here for the stated sphere-boundary, torsion-free class. It is not a conclusion about all hyperbolic groups. This distinction matters when comparing this family with other constructions in the collection.

The proof is an existence argument through limiting functions, measures and uniformization. It does not by itself supply a practical algorithm that takes a finite group presentation and outputs a geometric fundamental region in H3\mathbb H^3H3.

Questions about explicit quantitative bounds, effective reconstruction and recognition from presentations remain separate from the qualitative existence theorem explained here.

8. Sources and further reading

Cannon, The combinatorial Riemann mapping theorem, Acta Mathematica 173 (1994), 155–234, supplies the original analytic-combinatorial framework. Cannon and Swenson, Recognizing constant curvature discrete groups in dimension 3, Transactions of the AMS 350 (1998), 809–849, formulates the recognition problem.

Bonk and Kleiner, Conformal dimension and Gromov hyperbolic groups with 2-sphere boundary, Geometry & Topology 9 (2005), 219–246, proves the attained-infimum case. Bourdon and Kleiner, Combinatorial modulus, the combinatorial Loewner property, and Coxeter groups, Groups, Geometry, and Dynamics 7 (2013), 39–107, supplies the criterion used by the manuscript.

Marković’s recognition criterion, Haïssinsky’s planar-boundary theorem, and Agol’s virtual Haken theorem describe the complementary geometric route and the virtual consequences.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Modulus Proof of Cannon’s Conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why Thompson’s group F cannot have almost invariant finite sets
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 248 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

The integers can be approximated by long finite intervals that barely change when shifted one step. Only the two endpoints are lost or gained, while the interval’s total size grows. Amenability asks for an analogous way to average over a group without favoring one location over another.

Thompson’s group FFF is a famous test case. Its elements are simple-looking piecewise linear transformations of an interval, but the group resists several familiar classifications. It contains no nonabelian free subgroup, so one standard source of nonamenability is absent. Yet that absence does not guarantee amenability.

The manuscript in family 248 claims that FFF is nonamenable. It constructs a fixed finite collection of translations for which every nonempty finite subset of FFF has a definite relative boundary. No sequence of larger and larger sets can make all those boundary proportions vanish.

Its proposed argument connects three subjects: interval subdivisions, averaging in groups, and the geometry of infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.

2. Background and essential definitions

What is Thompson’s group F?

An element of FFF is an increasing piecewise linear homeomorphism from [0,1][0,1][0,1] onto itself. It has finitely many linear pieces, its breakpoints are dyadic rationals, and each slope is an integer power of two. A dyadic rational is a number of the form k/2rk/2^rk/2r, with integers kkk and r≥0r\geq0r≥0.

For example, the following map belongs to FFF:

g(x)={x/2,0≤x≤1/2,x−1/4,1/2≤x≤3/4,2x−1,3/4≤x≤1.g(x)=\begin{cases}x/2,&0\leq x\leq1/2,\\x-1/4,&1/2\leq x\leq3/4,\\2x-1,&3/4\leq x\leq1.\end{cases}g(x)=⎩⎨⎧​x/2,x−1/4,2x−1,​0≤x≤1/2,1/2≤x≤3/4,3/4≤x≤1.​

Its pieces fit continuously, it is increasing, and its slopes are 2−1,20,212^{-1},2^0,2^12−1,20,21. Composition and inversion preserve the defining conditions. The manuscript uses hg=h∘ghg=h\circ ghg=h∘g and treats FFF as a discrete group.

A basic dyadic interval is one cell of a uniform dyadic grid, such as [3/8,4/8][3/8,4/8][3/8,4/8]. Finite partitions into such intervals give a convenient combinatorial model. Restricting a partition to one of its dyadic subintervals and stretching that interval back to [0,1][0,1][0,1] produces a smaller normalized partition.

Almost invariant finite sets

For a finite subset AAA of a group and an element hhh, write hA={ha:a∈A}hA=\{ha:a\in A\}hA={ha:a∈A}. The symmetric difference hA△AhA\triangle AhA△A consists of points in exactly one of the two sets.

The Følner criterion says that a discrete group is amenable precisely when, for every finite set SSS of translations and every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, there is a nonempty finite AAA with

∣hA△A∣∣A∣<εfor every h∈S.\frac{|hA\triangle A|}{|A|}<\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }h\in S.∣A∣∣hA△A∣​<εfor every h∈S.

For the additive group of integers, long intervals have this property for any fixed finite collection of shifts. Their boundaries grow much more slowly than their interiors.

An equivalent formulation uses an invariant mean: a positive normalized linear rule for averaging all bounded real functions on the group, unchanged by translation. It is not an ordinary countably additive uniform probability distribution on an infinite group.

Nonamenability means that some fixed finite set SSS and some fixed positive tolerance defeat every finite candidate AAA. The order of these choices matters: the translations must not be chosen anew after seeing each candidate.

A Hilbert-space obstruction

A real Hilbert space has an inner product and the associated norm. Its closed unit ball is convex, so averages of its points remain inside it.

A map fff is Lipschitz if a constant LLL satisfies ∥f(x)−f(y)∥≤L∥x−y∥\|f(x)-f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|∥f(x)−f(y)∥≤L∥x−y∥. An approximate fixed point would be a point with small ∥f(x)−x∥\|f(x)-x\|∥f(x)−x∥.

Benyamini and Sternfeld proved that an infinite-dimensional Hilbert ball admits a Lipschitz self-map whose displacement is uniformly positive:

∥f(x)−x∥≥δ>0for every point x in the ball.\|f(x)-x\|\geq\delta>0\quad\text{for every point }x\text{ in the ball}.∥f(x)−x∥≥δ>0for every point x in the ball.

This does not contradict Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem, which concerns finite-dimensional compact balls. The infinite-dimensional ball is not compact in its norm topology.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Thompson introduced FFF in 1965. Cannon, Floyd and Parry’s introductory account records Geoghegan’s 1979 conjecture that it is nonamenable. The question became a central example in the study of amenability because standard structural tests did not settle it.

Brin and Squier proved that FFF contains no nonabelian free subgroup. Meanwhile, FFF is not elementary amenable. The elementary amenable class is generated from finite and abelian groups by several natural closure operations, including extensions and directed unions. It is only a subclass of amenable groups, so being outside it is insufficient to establish nonamenability.

Brown and Geoghegan showed that FFF has strong topological finiteness properties: it has a classifying space with finitely many cells in every dimension. Thus the difficulty is not simply that the group lacks a manageable finite description.

Moore studied possible Følner sets quantitatively and proved tower-type lower bounds on their sizes. Such bounds say that almost invariant sets, if they exist, must be extraordinarily large. They do not alone rule out their existence.

Moore also characterized amenability of FFF through a scalar convex Ramsey property for finite ordered binary trees. This connected averaging over the group to finite combinatorial structures. Guba developed estimates for densities of finite Cayley subgraphs and restrictions on invariant means using diagram-defined classes.

Haagerup and Olesen found an operator-algebraic implication: simplicity of the reduced group operator algebra of Thompson’s group TTT would imply nonamenability of FFF. This is a conditional route, not a deduction from the bare definition of FFF.

The manuscript also discusses earlier complete-resolution claims. It notes Akhmedov’s 2021 nonamenability claim, Shavgulidze’s amenability claim and Moore’s criticism of that approach, and a separately withdrawn amenability manuscript of Moore. The withdrawn work is distinct from Moore’s published Ramsey characterization. These are reported as part of the source’s historical context, without independently adjudicating their arguments.

The new proposed route uses finite averages of scalar correlations. It aims to turn approximate translation invariance into an approximate fixed point of a map specifically chosen to have none.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The main theorem of the manuscript dated 23 September 2026 is simply that Thompson’s group FFF is not amenable.

More concretely, the paper constructs a finite set S⊂FS\subset FS⊂F and a positive constant ccc such that every nonempty finite A⊂FA\subset FA⊂F satisfies

max⁡h∈S∣hA△A∣∣A∣≥c.\max_{h\in S}\frac{|hA\triangle A|}{|A|}\geq c.h∈Smax​∣A∣∣hA△A∣​≥c.

The translations and the constant are fixed before AAA is chosen. This is exactly the kind of uniform obstruction that contradicts the Følner criterion.

The source also records two consequences that use separate companion theorems. First, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, it obtains a representation of FFF by bounded invertible operators on a separable complex Hilbert space with operator norms at most 1+ε1+\varepsilon1+ε, but with no bounded change of Hilbert coordinates making all operators unitary. This uses the unitarizability theorem discussed in family 251.

Second, it applies the percolation theorem of family 214 to every simple Cayley graph from a finite symmetric generating set of FFF. In Bernoulli bond percolation, each edge is independently retained with probability ppp. The source obtains a nonempty interval between the threshold for an infinite cluster and the threshold for a unique infinite cluster.

It also states the stronger operator bound from that companion and an interval on which infinitely many infinite clusters occur simultaneously in the usual coupled percolation process. These consequences are not inputs to the proof of nonamenability.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The amenability problem for FFF is a longstanding central question about one of the most intensively studied finitely presented groups. Its claimed resolution would settle a test case that evades the usual free-subgroup argument.

The result would give a specific, highly structured example where finite subsets cannot approximate translation-invariant averaging, even though the group contains no nonabelian free subgroup. Nonamenable groups without such subgroups were already known; the significance lies in resolving the question for this particular group and its rich interval and tree models.

The argument’s proposed mechanism also links an elementary-looking partition structure to an infinite-dimensional geometric obstruction. Its companion-dependent consequences connect the conclusion to representation theory and random connectivity on Cayley graphs.

6. The main idea

Recursively color partitions

Choose a Lipschitz map fff on a Hilbert unit ball with displacement at least δ\deltaδ. Then choose DDD separated internal dyadic intervals, called parents, and put an affine copy of this family inside every parent.

The manuscript assigns a Hilbert-ball color to each finite dyadic partition. If the partition does not respect every parent interval, its color is zero. Otherwise, restrict to the parents, normalize those restrictions, average their colors, and apply fff.

This recursion terminates because each restriction has fewer cells than the original partition. It does not require solving a fixed-point equation in order to define the coloring.

For a sufficiently fine partition transformed by g∈Fg\in Fg∈F, let Xi(g)X_i(g)Xi​(g) be its parent colors and Yij(g)Y_{ij}(g)Yij​(g) its descendant colors. Set

m(g)=1D∑iXi(g),zi(g)=1D∑jYij(g).m(g)=\frac1D\sum_iX_i(g),\qquadz_i(g)=\frac1D\sum_jY_{ij}(g).m(g)=D1​i∑​Xi​(g),zi​(g)=D1​j∑​Yij​(g).

The recursive rule gives the exact relation Xi(g)=f(zi(g))X_i(g)=f(z_i(g))Xi​(g)=f(zi​(g)). Thus m(g)m(g)m(g) is the average of the f(zi(g))f(z_i(g))f(zi​(g)).

Almost invariance compares scalar correlations

Elements of FFF can carry any ordered pair of separated internal basic intervals affinely onto another such pair. The source chooses finitely many of these transports once and for all, forming the set SSS.

Given a candidate finite set AAA, it chooses one partition level fine enough for every element of AAA and every translated set hAhAhA, with h∈Sh\in Sh∈S. This level may depend on AAA; the transport set does not.

If the relative boundaries are small, averages over AAA barely change under these translations. Applying this elementary cancellation observation to scalar inner products makes the averaged correlations of separated interval colors nearly equal.

Not every pair is separated. A descendant is nested inside its own parent, and diagonal pairs repeat the same interval. Those exceptions occupy only a proportion of order 1/D1/D1/D among the relevant pairs.

An approximate fixed point becomes unavoidable

Expand the squared distance ∥zi(g)−m(g)∥2\|z_i(g)-m(g)\|^2∥zi​(g)−m(g)∥2 using inner products. The common correlation of separated pairs cancels. Unit-ball bounds control the exceptional pairs, while the translation error contributes the relative-boundary quantity

η=max⁡h∈S∣hA△A∣∣A∣.\eta=\max_{h\in S}\frac{|hA\triangle A|}{|A|}.η=h∈Smax​∣A∣∣hA△A∣​.

The manuscript derives a bound of size D−1+ηD^{-1}+\etaD−1+η for the averaged squared distance. Convexity and the Lipschitz property then transfer this to the displacement of m(g)m(g)m(g) under fff. Its stated estimate is

δ2≤4L2(D−1+(1−D−1)η).\delta^2\leq4L^2\bigl(D^{-1}+(1-D^{-1})\eta\bigr).δ2≤4L2(D−1+(1−D−1)η).

Choose DDD large enough that the first term is too small to account for δ2\delta^2δ2. The inequality forces η\etaη to stay positively bounded away from zero, independently of AAA.

The nonlinear map is handled through its Lipschitz estimate; the argument does not simply commute it with an average. The contradiction is that sufficiently good Følner sets would force displacement below the map’s known positive lower bound.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result concerns the discrete group FFF. It is not a general assertion that all groups of interval transformations are nonamenable, nor does it concern every possible topology on a homeomorphism group.

The boundary obstruction is given for a particular finite collection of translations. The paper does not claim an optimal expansion constant for the usual two-generator Cayley graph, or an exact random-walk spectral radius.

Nonamenability also does not produce a nonabelian free subgroup. The classical absence of such a subgroup in FFF remains part of the problem’s distinctive structure.

The representation and percolation conclusions require their cited companion claims. They should not be read as independent consequences of elementary definitions alone, and they are not used to establish the main theorem.

Quantitative optimization of the transport set and boundary constant, and related amenability questions for other transformation groups, are separate from the stated qualitative resolution for FFF.

8. Sources and further reading

Cannon, Floyd and Parry, Introductory notes on Richard Thompson’s groups, L’Enseignement Mathématique 42 (1996), 215–256, gives the group models and historical conjecture. Brin and Squier, Groups of piecewise linear homeomorphisms of the real line, proves the relevant free-subgroup restriction.

Følner’s original criterion connects amenability to finite boundaries. Moore’s Følner-function lower bounds and Ramsey characterization give major earlier approaches.

Benyamini and Sternfeld, Spheres in infinite-dimensional normed spaces are Lipschitz contractible, provides the fixed-point obstruction. The source’s historical discussion also cites Akhmedov’s 2021 version and Moore’s note on Shavgulidze’s argument.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Thompson’s group F is nonamenable (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A group whose algebra needs two dimensions but whose space needs three
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 249 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A group can be studied through a space whose loops record its multiplication. The space may use vertices, edges, filled triangles and higher-dimensional cells. How many dimensions are really necessary?

There are two ways to ask. One is geometric: build an actual classifying space for the group and minimize its dimension. The other is algebraic: replace the space by a chain of modules recording its homological information and minimize the length of that chain.

The algebraic answer cannot exceed the geometric one. For most dimensions, classical theorems say that the answers agree. Dimension two is the exceptional case, and the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture asks whether equality holds there as well.

Family 249 claims a counterexample: a finitely generated residually finite group whose integral cohomological dimension is two but whose geometric dimension is three. The source rules out every two-dimensional classifying space, including spaces with infinitely many cells. Its group is not finitely presented, a distinction that matters when interpreting the result.

2. Background and essential definitions

Spaces assembled from cells

A CW complex is a space built by attaching cells: points, intervals, disks, three-dimensional balls and their higher-dimensional analogues. Its dimension is the largest dimension of a cell used. A complex can have infinitely many cells while still being two-dimensional.

The fundamental group π1(X)\pi_1(X)π1​(X) records loops in a connected space XXX, with loops identified when one can be continuously deformed into the other. A classifying space K(G,1)K(G,1)K(G,1) has fundamental group GGG and contractible universal cover.

Contractible means that the entire space can be continuously collapsed to a point. The universal cover removes the loops encoded by the fundamental group; requiring it to be contractible ensures that no additional higher homotopy remains.

The geometric dimension gd⁡G\operatorname{gd}GgdG is the least dimension of a classifying space for GGG. A circle is a one-dimensional classifying space for Z\mathbb ZZ, because its universal cover is a line. More generally, a bouquet of circles gives a one-dimensional model for a free group.

The algebraic dimension

The group ring Z[G]\mathbb Z[G]Z[G] consists of finite integer linear combinations of group elements, with multiplication extended from the group. Modules over this ring are abelian groups equipped with compatible GGG-actions.

A projective resolution of the trivial module Z\mathbb ZZ is an exact sequence of projective modules ending in Z\mathbb ZZ. Exactness means that the output of one map is precisely the part killed by the next. Projective modules behave like direct summands of free modules and are the natural building blocks for this algebraic problem.

The integral cohomological dimension cd⁡ZG\operatorname{cd}_{\mathbb Z}GcdZ​G is the shortest possible resolution length. For a classifying space, the cellular chains of its universal cover provide such a resolution. Consequently,

cd⁡ZG≤gd⁡G.\operatorname{cd}_{\mathbb Z}G\leq\operatorname{gd}G.cdZ​G≤gdG.

The issue is whether a short algebraic resolution can always be realized by an equally low-dimensional contractible covering space.

Acyclic does not mean contractible

A connected space is acyclic over the integers when all its reduced integral homology groups vanish. Homology measures cycles modulo boundaries using additive algebra. It forgets some nonlinear information about how paths are composed.

A contractible space is acyclic, but an acyclic space can still have nontrivial fundamental group. This is the crucial gap. A two-dimensional acyclic complex may supply the desired short algebraic resolution without being the universal cover of a classifying space.

A group is residually finite if each nonidentity element has a nonidentity image in some finite quotient. Finite generation means that finitely many elements generate the group; finite presentation additionally requires finitely many defining relations. The new example has the former property but not the latter.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Eilenberg and Ganea proved in 1957 that geometric and integral cohomological dimensions agree when the latter is at least three. In cohomological dimension one, Stallings proved freeness under finite generation, and Swan removed that restriction. Free groups have one-dimensional classifying spaces.

The unresolved case was therefore sharply localized: could cohomological dimension two force geometric dimension three?

Bestvina and Brady’s 1997 work produced a rich supply of candidates using kernels of height homomorphisms on right-angled Artin groups. Their examples separated homological finiteness conditions from geometric ones. For suitable flag complexes related to a spine of the Poincaré homology sphere, they proved that at least one of the Eilenberg–Ganea and Whitehead conjectures must fail.

Whitehead’s asphericity conjecture asks whether every connected subcomplex of an aspherical two-dimensional CW complex is itself aspherical. Aspherical means that the universal cover is contractible. The Bestvina–Brady alternative did not decide which conjecture fails, and did not by itself identify the geometric dimension of a particular height kernel.

Dicks and Leary gave presentations of these kernels using edge generators and power relations associated with cycles. Howie studied related examples through the plus construction and obtained free relation modules. These works established much of the algebraic and geometric setting used by the new manuscript.

A recent comparison by Leary and Petrosyan, cited by the source, relates Coxeter and Bestvina–Brady candidates under an additional conjectural condition. The new paper instead claims a direct obstruction for one specified height kernel.

The central historical difficulty is easy to state: showing that one two-dimensional acyclic model is not contractible does not exclude a completely different two-dimensional classifying space. The source’s proposed advance is a comparison argument that addresses every hypothetical model, regardless of how many cells it has.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The manuscript dated 23 September 2026 asserts the existence of a finitely generated residually finite group GGG with

cd⁡ZG=2,gd⁡G=3.\operatorname{cd}_{\mathbb Z}G=2,\qquad\operatorname{gd}G=3.cdZ​G=2,gdG=3.

These are ordinary group dimensions with integral coefficients. They are not dimensions defined using a family of allowed stabilizers or a special kind of proper group action.

The source specifies a construction. Start with a finite acyclic flag triangulation LLL of the presentation complex

⟨x,y∣x2=y5,x2=(xy−1)3⟩.\langle x,y\mid x^2=y^5,\quad x^2=(xy^{-1})^3\rangle.⟨x,y∣x2=y5,x2=(xy−1)3⟩.

A simplicial complex is flag if every finite collection of pairwise adjacent vertices spans a simplex. This condition makes its associated right-angled Artin group geometrically well behaved.

With one generator ava_vav​ for each vertex vvv of LLL, define

AL=⟨av∣[av,aw]=1 whenever {v,w} is an edge of L⟩.A_L=\langle a_v\mid [a_v,a_w]=1\text{ whenever }\{v,w\}\text{ is an edge of }L\rangle.AL​=⟨av​∣[av​,aw​]=1 whenever {v,w} is an edge of L⟩.

Thus adjacent generators commute, and no other relations are imposed. The height homomorphism λ:AL→Z\lambda:A_L\to\mathbb Zλ:AL​→Z sends each ava_vav​ to 111. The claimed example is the kernel G=ker⁡λG=\ker\lambdaG=kerλ.

The paper further supplies a length-two resolution of Z\mathbb ZZ by finitely generated free Z[G]\mathbb Z[G]Z[G]-modules. This is the finiteness condition called type FL, and implies type FP∞, meaning that there is a projective resolution with finitely generated terms in every degree.

Nevertheless, GGG is not finitely presented. The seed complex has nontrivial fundamental group, so the Bestvina–Brady finite-presentability criterion excludes that property. A finite algebraic resolution must therefore not be mistaken for a finite presentation or a finite classifying space.

The geometric nonexistence statement is unrestricted: no two-dimensional K(G,1)K(G,1)K(G,1) exists, even if arbitrary infinite sets of cells are allowed. A three-dimensional model supplies the upper bound and hence the exact geometric dimension.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The claimed result settles the exceptional case in a basic comparison between algebraic and geometric dimensions of groups. It would show that a two-dimensional homological description can fail to have any two-dimensional geometric realization.

The example is finitely generated and residually finite. Its obstruction is therefore compatible with both finite generation and separation by finite quotients, rather than arising solely from a very large uncontrolled group.

The stronger exclusion of models with infinitely many cells matters. Merely ruling out a finite two-dimensional model would leave geometric dimension undecided, because geometric dimension does not impose a finite-cell requirement.

The proposed small-labeling obstruction also illustrates a general phenomenon: additive cycle data may fail to capture the order-sensitive products that determine actual topology.

6. The main idea

Slice a three-dimensional cubical space

The right-angled Artin group ALA_LAL​ has a standard cubical classifying space assembled from coordinate tori. Its universal cover EEE is contractible and three-dimensional. The height homomorphism extends to a real-valued function on EEE, affine on each cube.

Take the level set

X=λ−1(0)⊂E.X=\lambda^{-1}(0)\subset E.X=λ−1(0)⊂E.

The kernel GGG acts freely on this two-dimensional complex. The paper establishes that XXX is acyclic and has finitely many cell orbits. Its cellular chains provide the short free resolution. The quotient E/GE/GE/G, meanwhile, is a three-dimensional classifying space.

What remains is to prevent some other two-dimensional space from doing better.

Label edges by small rotations

The source uses H=SU(2)H=\mathrm{SU}(2)H=SU(2), which can be represented by unit quaternions. It is a compact noncommutative group with a notion of distance from the identity.

Assign an element of HHH to every oriented edge of XXX, and assign the inverse to the reversed edge. Multiplying labels along a path gives its transport. The product around a closed path is called holonomy.

A labeling is flat on triangles when each triangular boundary has product 111. Even if every edge label is very close to 111, triangle-flatness need not make the product around every long closed path trivial. Global topology can survive local flatness.

The paper claims that a hypothetical two-dimensional classifying space would force precisely such global triviality for all sufficiently small labelings of this particular XXX. It then constructs arbitrarily small counterexamples.

Compare chains with actual words

The triangular boundary chains of XXX form a specified free basis of its cycle module. Chains record signed edge counts but forget traversal order. Group-valued path products retain that order, so equality of chains is weaker than equality of products.

The comparison argument starts from an actual presentation associated with the hypothetical classifying space. It adjusts generators and relators so that distinguished boundary chains match the triangular ones. These triangular words alone need not present GGG; that is why an arbitrary actual presentation must enter.

Near the identity of SU(2)\mathrm{SU}(2)SU(2), errors caused by changing multiplication order are quadratic in the sizes of the labels. Exact signed-count identities cancel the linear discrepancies. The resulting estimate provides a barrier keeping selected products near the identity.

To solve the remaining relator equations, the source uses a localized version of the Gerstenhaber–Rothaus word-map degree argument. The localization keeps solutions in the portion of the equation space controlled by that barrier. Residual finiteness handles finite collections of constraints on finite quotients; compactness passes to all constraints. A single finite quotient need not carry the entire final labeling.

Preserve a global loop while shrinking every edge

The seed complex LLL has a nontrivial representation of its fundamental group into SU(2)\mathrm{SU}(2)SU(2). The manuscript constructs maps from the graph of XXX into LLL for which individual edge images and triangle boundaries become uniformly small, but certain long closed paths trace prescribed loops exactly.

Pulling back transport from the representation makes every edge label arbitrarily close to the identity. Small triangle images give exactly trivial triangular products. A long path representing a loop detected by the representation keeps nontrivial holonomy.

This conflicts with the claimed consequence of any two-dimensional classifying space. The three-dimensional upper bound then gives gd⁡G=3\operatorname{gd}G=3gdG=3.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The example is finitely generated but not finitely presented. The manuscript therefore does not establish the same counterexample under finite presentation, nor does it give a finite three-dimensional classifying space for this group.

Type FL and FP∞ are homological finiteness conditions. They do not repair that missing finite presentation, and they should not be confused with having finitely many cells in every dimension of a classifying space.

The theorem uses integral cohomological dimension. Changing coefficients or changing the kind of group action being classified leads to different invariants and potentially different questions.

The conclusion also does not settle Whitehead’s asphericity conjecture. It resolves the Eilenberg–Ganea side of an earlier alternative, without deciding every other conjecture that appeared in that alternative.

More broadly, identifying which groups of cohomological dimension two do admit two-dimensional classifying spaces remains a meaningful structural problem. A counterexample to the universal statement does not provide a classification of the positive cases.

8. Sources and further reading

Eilenberg and Ganea, On the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category of abstract groups, Annals of Mathematics 65 (1957), 517–518, is the foundational dimension theorem. Swan, Groups of cohomological dimension one, completes the one-dimensional case.

Bestvina and Brady, Morse theory and finiteness properties of groups, Inventiones Mathematicae 129 (1997), 445–470, supplies the height-kernel construction and the earlier alternative. Dicks and Leary’s presentations and Howie’s plus-construction work develop the relevant algebraic models.

Gerstenhaber and Rothaus, The solution of sets of equations in groups, is the degree-theoretic predecessor. Hatcher’s Algebraic Topology gives background on CW complexes, covering spaces, homology and homotopy.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A finitely generated counterexample to the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: An infinite group described by finitely many rules, with only finite-order elements
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 247 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A group element has finite order if repeating it sufficiently many times returns to the identity. If every element has this property, can the group nevertheless be infinite?

The answer has long been yes, even when finitely many elements generate the group. The harder question asks whether finitely many defining relations can also suffice. A finite list of rules must then force every possible combination of generators to have finite order, while leaving infinitely many distinct combinations alive.

Family 247 claims such a construction. Its earlier manuscript builds an infinite finitely presented periodic group and an accompanying algebra with unusual nilpotence properties. A later companion strengthens the group result to an infinite finitely presented residually finite 222-group: every element has power-of-two order, and finite quotients can distinguish every nonidentity element.

The orders are not uniformly bounded. That qualification is indispensable, because existing theorems rule out the stronger bounded-exponent conclusion in this residually finite setting.

2. Background and essential definitions

Generators, relations and finite-order behavior

A group is finitely generated if a finite list of elements and their inverses produces every element by multiplication. A finite presentation

G=⟨s1,…,sk∣r1,…,rm⟩G=\langle s_1,\ldots,s_k\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangleG=⟨s1​,…,sk​∣r1​,…,rm​⟩

adds a finite list of words required to equal the identity. All other equalities must follow from those relations and the group axioms.

For example, ⟨s∣sN=1⟩\langle s\mid s^N=1\rangle⟨s∣sN=1⟩ is a finite cyclic group. With several generators, imposing finite order on each generator does not automatically impose finite order on their products. That is why an infinite periodic group is much harder to describe than a collection of generators that happen to be torsion elements.

Periodic means that for every g∈Gg\in Gg∈G, some positive integer n(g)n(g)n(g) satisfies gn(g)=1g^{n(g)}=1gn(g)=1. Bounded exponent means one integer works for every element. A 222-group has element orders 1,2,4,8,…1,2,4,8,\ldots1,2,4,8,…, possibly with no common upper bound.

The presentations here are ordinary presentations of abstract discrete groups. They do not conceal an additional infinite family of periodicity axioms, and they are not presentations in the category of topological pro-222 groups.

Finite quotients can see an infinite group

A group is residually finite when each nonidentity element has a nonidentity image in some finite group. Different elements may require different finite quotients. Thus residual finiteness provides an unlimited collection of finite windows onto an infinite object.

If every element of the original group has power-of-two order, the same holds in every finite image. Such a finite image is a finite 222-group. There is no implication that a single finite image captures the entire original group.

Nil is weaker than nilpotent

An associative algebra is a vector space with a bilinear associative multiplication. It need not be commutative, and it need not have an identity element.

A nonunital algebra III is nil if every element aaa satisfies aN(a)=0a^{N(a)}=0aN(a)=0 for some exponent depending on aaa. It is nilpotent if there is one NNN for which every product of NNN elements vanishes. Nilpotence is therefore a uniform statement about mixed products, not just repeated copies of one element.

Adjoining an identity gives the unitization R=F2⊕IR=\mathbb F_2\oplus IR=F2​⊕I, where F2\mathbb F_2F2​ is the two-element field. If aaa is nilpotent, then 1+a1+a1+a is invertible: a finite geometric series provides its inverse. This is the elementary bridge between nil algebras and groups.

The construction needs more than elementwise nilpotence. It claims that every finite square matrix with entries in III is nilpotent, with an exponent allowed to depend on the matrix. The paper calls this property matrix-nil.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Burnside’s 1902 questions initiated the study of how finite generation interacts with finite element orders. Several distinct problems emerged, and their different conclusions should not be conflated.

Golod’s 1964 work, using the Golod–Shafarevich dimension argument, produced infinite finitely generated periodic groups. It also gave residually finite groups with torsion restricted to one prime. The underlying nil-algebra method already connected algebraic nilpotence to group-theoretic finite orders.

Novikov and Adian constructed infinite finitely generated groups of bounded exponent. Their result answered a stronger torsion question in one direction, but did not supply the additional ordinary finite presentation sought here.

Grigorchuk gave a concrete infinite finitely generated residually finite 222-group. Its original construction is not finitely presented. It therefore demonstrates that residual finiteness and power-of-two torsion can coexist, while leaving the finite-presentation requirement open.

Zel’manov’s solution of the restricted Burnside problem goes in a different direction. In particular, a finitely generated residually finite group with a fixed power-of-two exponent is finite. Any example with the new manuscript’s other properties must consequently have elements of arbitrarily large order.

Ol’shanskii and Sapir constructed finitely presented torsion-by-cyclic groups. Those groups have infinite cyclic quotients, so they are not periodic. Their work shows how powerful finite-presentation constructions can be without resolving the fully periodic case.

There is a parallel algebraic history. Golod’s nil algebras already refuted the broad finite-generation form of Kurosh’s algebraic finiteness question. The remaining strengthening asks for finitely many defining algebra relations. Ufnarovskij’s question about finitely presented nil algebras, and Amitsur’s related question for Jacobson radical algebras, impose this additional constraint.

The new sources also credit finite local-rule constructions. Durand, Romashchenko and Shen developed hierarchical simulations by tile sets. Ivanov-Pogodaev and Kanel-Belov constructed a finitely presented infinite nilsemigroup.
