A semigroup result controls individual words; the present algebra construction additionally needs cancellation for arbitrary sums and matrices. That additional step is essential to the claimed group construction.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: the algebra and the periodic group

The manuscript dated 23 September 2026 constructs an infinite-dimensional, finitely presented, graded algebra

R=F2⊕I,I=⨁d≥1Rd,R=\mathbb F_2\oplus I,\qquad I=\bigoplus_{d\geq1}R_d,R=F2​⊕I,I=d≥1⨁​Rd​,

with each homogeneous component RdR_dRd​ finite-dimensional and with III matrix-nil. Grading means multiplication adds degrees.

It asserts that III, viewed as a nonunital algebra, is finitely presented, nil and not nilpotent. It is also Jacobson radical: every 1−a1-a1−a is invertible in the unitization. The unital algebra RRR is finitely presented, algebraic over F2\mathbb F_2F2​, and infinite-dimensional. Algebraic means each element satisfies some nonzero polynomial over the field; the polynomial degree may depend on the element.

From this ring it constructs

Γ=St⁡12(R),\Gamma=\operatorname{St}_{12}(R),Γ=St12​(R),

an infinite ordinarily finitely presented periodic group. The notation denotes a Steinberg group, an abstract group encoding elementary matrix operations and their relations. Its relation to actual matrices has a kernel that must be controlled separately.

M2 also applies an existing theorem of Ershov and Jaikin-Zapirain to give Γ\GammaΓ Kazhdan’s property (T)(T)(T), a rigidity condition for almost invariant vectors in unitary representations. Since Γ\GammaΓ is infinite, this implies nonamenability.

M1: residual finiteness and a fixed torsion prime

The companion dated 5 October 2026 uses M2’s algebra and hierarchy as essential inputs. It asserts that Γ\GammaΓ is residually finite and considers

G=ker⁡(St⁡12(R)⟶St⁡12(F2)).G=\ker\bigl(\operatorname{St}_{12}(R)\longrightarrow\operatorname{St}_{12}(\mathbb F_2)\bigr).G=ker(St12​(R)⟶St12​(F2​)).

The target is finite, so GGG has finite index in Γ\GammaΓ. The claimed result is that GGG is infinite, ordinarily finitely presented and residually finite, with every element of finite power-of-two order.

The subgroup step matters: M2’s whole periodic group and M1’s 222-group are not identical statements. M1 strengthens the construction, rather than providing an unrelated alternative proof of M2’s algebra theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The claimed construction resolves the finitely presented Burnside question and several parallel finite-presentation problems for algebras. It combines properties that earlier examples achieved only in weaker combinations.

A finite presentation is a particularly strong form of finite description. The proposed example would show that finitely many rules can force periodicity of every group element without forcing the whole group to be finite.

Residual finiteness adds another significant constraint: the group’s infinitude is compatible with separating all elements by finite images. The result therefore cannot be understood merely as a group whose unusual behavior becomes invisible in every finite quotient.

On the algebra side, the same construction distinguishes elementwise nilpotence from uniform nilpotence even under finite presentation. Its matrix-nil property supplies a bridge powerful enough to support the group theorem.

6. The main idea

Finite rules generate a hierarchy

The algebra uses a finite alphabet, word replacements that preserve length, and declarations that certain words equal zero. Nonzero replacement classes form a vector-space basis. A surviving word of large degree witnesses that the algebra has not collapsed to finite dimension.

The rules encode larger-scale letters by blocks of smaller-scale letters. Clean encodings preserve nonzero words through the hierarchy, producing survivors at arbitrarily large degrees. Yet the construction must also control every allowed word, including malformed intermediate verification states.

For sufficiently long nonzero words, the source obtains a decomposition into bounded end pieces and recognizable tokens. Long runs of specially colored letters can be permuted. In characteristic two, summing suitable matrix weights over these permutations produces cancellation.

A weighted automaton keeps track of how tokens can be segmented when passing between hierarchy levels. The paper uses increasing palette sizes to make the cancellation dominate the increased matrix dimension. A separate bookkeeping variable distinguishes the number of multiplied factors from their word lengths. The resulting claim is nilpotence of each fixed matrix over III, not merely of each basis word.

Matrices give torsion, but their abstract lifts need more

For a nilpotent matrix AAA in characteristic two,

(1+A)2k=1+A2k=1(1+A)^{2^k}=1+A^{2^k}=1(1+A)2k=1+A2k=1

once 2k2^k2k exceeds its nilpotence index. This explains the source of power-of-two torsion near the identity.

The elementary matrix group over RRR is infinite because its off-diagonal entries can vary through the infinite ring. Existing finite-presentation results for Steinberg groups turn the finite ring presentation into a finite group presentation.

However, a torsion matrix image does not ensure that its abstract preimage is torsion. M2 therefore controls the central kernel of the map from the Steinberg group to the elementary matrix group. It compares substitutions of cyclic and truncated shift matrices into a graded expression. Rational homological stability then brings the resulting torsion information back to the fixed rank twelve.

Finite truncations must also detect the kernel

Discarding sufficiently high degrees gives finite rings R/R≥dR/R_{\geq d}R/R≥d​. These truncations readily detect a nonzero matrix entry. The harder issue is an element of the abstract group that maps to the identity matrix.

M1 assigns start and end phases to sufficiently long nonzero words, modulo arbitrarily large odd integers LLL. Compatible phases constrain products and allow roots to be moved between phase-labeled coordinates.

Suppose a central element escapes every degree truncation. One calculation makes a sufficiently long cyclic transfer vanish. The phase calculation identifies the same transfer with the LLL-th power of that element. It already has power-of-two order, while LLL is odd, so these conclusions force it to be trivial.

A stabilization theorem connects this stable calculation back to rank twelve. Finite truncations then separate the whole group, and the finite-index kernel of reduction to F2\mathbb F_2F2​ gives the final 222-group.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The construction uses characteristic two and produces a 222-group. It does not state an analogous ordinary finite-presentation theorem for every prime.

The element orders are unbounded, and the nilpotence indices of algebra elements and matrices can grow. Replacing any of these element-dependent bounds by one global bound would change the problem substantially.

The matrices are over a special noncommutative ring. This is not a finite-dimensional linear representation over a field that contradicts classical finiteness theorems for finitely generated periodic linear groups.

Finite presentation is an existence conclusion with a construction by hierarchical rules. The sources do not turn it into a small practical multiplication table for the infinite group. Likewise, residual finiteness asserts the existence of detecting finite quotients, without the digest supplying efficient bounds on their size.

Finally, the algebra and group conclusions have distinct logical requirements. Surviving words give infinitude; matrix cancellation gives periodicity of the matrix image; central-kernel arguments supply torsion and finite-quotient detection for the abstract group. Omitting the last stage would leave the strongest claims unsupported by the stated construction.

8. Sources and further reading

Burnside, On an unsettled question in the theory of discontinuous groups (1902), is the original source. Golod’s nil-algebra and finite-approximation paper (1964) and Grigorchuk’s On Burnside’s problem on periodic groups (1980) give earlier infinite residually finite torsion examples.

Zel’manov’s restricted Burnside theorem for 2-groups explains why the new group cannot have bounded exponent. Ol’shanskii and Sapir’s torsion-by-cyclic construction addresses a different finite-presentation problem.

For the construction’s inputs, see Durand, Romashchenko and Shen, Fixed-point tile sets and their applications; Krstić and McCool, Presenting GLn(k⟨T⟩); and Weibel, Module structures on the K-theory of graded rings.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An infinite finitely presented residually finite 2-group (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An infinite finitely presented periodic group (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When an algorithmic group fits inside a simple group with finite structure in every dimension
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 250 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Suppose a group comes with an algorithm that decides whether any word in its generators equals the identity. Can that computational fact be recognized purely from the group’s position inside a larger algebraic object?

The Boone–Higman conjecture predicts a striking answer: a finitely generated group has such an algorithm exactly when it embeds in a finitely presented simple group. The larger group combines a finite description with the absence of proper nontrivial normal subgroups.

Family 250 contains three related claims. The first resolves that conjecture. The second asks for more geometric finiteness in the simple overgroup and claims it in every dimension. The third removes the word-problem hypothesis and constructs one universal group with the same higher finiteness property containing every finitely presented group, but does not require this universal target to be simple.

These are different embedding questions. In particular, the last universal target must accommodate groups with undecidable word problem, whereas a finitely presented simple group has decidable word problem.

2. Background and essential definitions

Algorithms for equality

Choose a finite generating set for a group GGG. A word is a finite string of generators and their inverses. The word problem asks whether that string represents the identity.

A decider must halt on every input and answer correctly both when the word is trivial and when it is not. This is stronger than an enumeration procedure that eventually lists all trivial words but may never settle a nontrivial one.

A recursively presented group has finitely many generators and a recursively enumerable list of defining relations. A finite presentation is a special case. Recursive presentation does not imply decidability of the word problem; finitely presented groups with undecidable word problem exist.

An embedding G↪HG\hookrightarrow HG↪H is an injective homomorphism. It preserves every equality and inequality between elements, so it identifies GGG with a subgroup of HHH.

Simplicity is an algebraic restriction

A subgroup is normal if conjugation by every ambient group element preserves it. A nontrivial group is simple when its only normal subgroups are the identity subgroup and the whole group.

Simplicity does not mean that multiplication is easy to compute, that the group is finite, or that it has few ordinary subgroups. A simple group can contain complicated subgroups that are not normal.

Finite presentation means a finite list of generators and relators determines the entire group. It does not generally pass to subgroups. Thus placing a group inside a finitely presented group is weaker than giving the subgroup itself a finite presentation.

Finiteness in every dimension

A classifying space K(H,1)K(H,1)K(H,1) is a connected cell complex whose fundamental group is HHH and whose universal cover is contractible. Its cells encode generators, relations, and successively higher relations among those relations.

A group has type FnF_nFn​ if such a space can be chosen with finitely many cells through dimension nnn. Type F1F_1F1​ is finite generation, and type F2F_2F2​ is finite presentation.

Type F∞F_\inftyF∞​ means that one classifying space has finitely many cells in each dimension. It may still have infinitely many dimensions and infinitely many cells altogether. In particular, this condition does not imply torsion-freeness or finite cohomological dimension.

Homological conditions denoted FPnFP_nFPn​ instead concern finite generation of modules in a projective resolution. They are related to geometric finiteness but should not be silently substituted for FnF_nFn​. The manuscripts’ final claims are geometric F∞F_\inftyF∞​ statements.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Higman’s 1961 embedding theorem characterized the finitely generated subgroups of finitely presented groups: they are exactly the finitely generated recursively presented groups. It connected an effective enumeration of relations to a finite algebraic description in an overgroup.

Boone and Higman obtained a sharper characterization in 1974. A finitely generated group has decidable word problem exactly when it sits in a chain

G≤S≤P,G\leq S\leq P,G≤S≤P,

where SSS is simple and PPP is finitely presented. The two desirable properties belonged to different groups. Their conjecture asked whether the intermediate simple group could itself be finitely presented. Finite presentation of PPP alone cannot justify that conclusion for its subgroup SSS.

Thompson later obtained a finitely generated simple overgroup while preserving decidability of the word problem. That advanced the finite-generation side, but finite generation remained weaker than finite presentation.

Recent positive cases include hyperbolic and contracting self-similar groups, through work of Belk, Bleak, Matucci and Zaremsky. Bux, Llosa Isenrich and Wu treated groups acting on locally finite trees, including Baumslag–Solitar groups and finite-rank free-by-cyclic groups. Belk, Fournier-Facio, Hyde and Zaremsky established results for automorphism groups of finite-rank free groups and mapping class groups of punctured surfaces.

Thompson-type constructions also supplied simple groups with strong higher finiteness properties. Brown proved type F∞F_\inftyF∞​ for the Thompson–Higman families. Belk and Zaremsky constructed one simple F∞F_\inftyF∞​ group containing all finitely generated right-angled Artin groups, while Belk, Hyde and Matucci obtained a simple F∞F_\inftyF∞​ group containing every countable abelian group.

The general obstacle was to build such an overgroup from an arbitrary word-problem decider. Belk and Zaremsky’s twisted Brin–Thompson construction provides a final transfer theorem, but its input requires a suitable permutation action and finiteness properties of stabilizers. Zaremsky later weakened the conditions needed for finite presentation alone.

A separate higher-dimensional Higman question asks for F∞F_\inftyF∞​ overgroups without decidability of the word problem. Leary obtained broad embeddings under the weaker homological condition FP2FP_2FP2​. Fournier-Facio and Zaremsky analyzed how homological embeddings could yield geometric ones and identified limitations of particular rope-trick constructions. M3 addresses this separate direction with a single universal target.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: finite presentation and simplicity together

M1 asserts that a finitely generated group GGG has decidable word problem exactly when there is an embedding

G↪HG\hookrightarrow HG↪H

into some finitely presented simple group HHH.

For the constructive direction, the input includes a finite generating set and a word-problem decider. The input group need not be finitely presented, and the algorithm’s running time is unrestricted.

Its principal intermediate theorem embeds GGG in a finitely presented group with a faithful two-transitive action on a countably infinite set and finitely generated point stabilizers. Faithful means that no nonidentity element acts trivially. Two-transitive means that any ordered pair of distinct points can be sent to any other such pair.

M2: a simple target of type F∞

M2 strengthens the target to a nontrivial simple group HHH of type F∞F_\inftyF∞​. The input conditions remain finite generation and decidable word problem. The source also notes that its chosen target can be generated by two finite-order elements, using a further conclusion of the earlier twisted Brin–Thompson theorem.

The converse is classical. In a nontrivial finitely presented simple group, run two searches in parallel: one for a proof that a given word is trivial, and one for a proof that adding it as a relator collapses the whole group. A nontrivial element normally generates a simple group, so exactly the appropriate search terminates. Restricting this decision procedure to a finitely generated subgroup decides its word problem.

M2 imports specific tools from M1, including its bounded compiler, corner construction and Steinberg-kernel calculation. Its higher-finiteness assertion is not obtained merely by applying M1’s final theorem.

M3: one universal higher-finiteness group

M3 asserts the existence of a single group U∞U_\inftyU∞​ of type F∞F_\inftyF∞​ containing every finitely presented group. No word-problem assumption is imposed on those subgroups.

Equivalently, its finitely generated subgroups, up to isomorphism, are exactly the finitely generated recursively presented groups. The forward construction uses Higman’s embedding theorem; the reverse direction follows by enumerating relations inside the finitely presented ambient group.

M3 shares the finite-diagram and ascending-torus method with M2 and gives local proofs of the relevant identities and finiteness criterion. It does not assert simplicity of the universal target. All three manuscripts are dated 23 September 2026.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The family claims a general algebraic characterization of decidable word problems, resolving a central embedding conjecture and extending it to geometric finiteness in every dimension.

M1 joins two properties that earlier general embeddings placed in different overgroups. M2 controls not only generators and relations but also the higher-dimensional relations needed to construct finite skeleta throughout a classifying space.

M3 has a different breadth: one F∞F_\inftyF∞​ group accommodates all finitely presented groups, including those with undecidable word problem. It would show that strong geometric finiteness of an ambient group can coexist with very complicated subgroup algorithms.

The significance is the exact match between computational hypotheses and algebraic embedding possibilities. The claims do not say that every group becomes computationally easy after embedding.

6. The main idea

Build a permutation action that a known theorem can use

The final simplicity step is supplied by the twisted Brin–Thompson construction. It turns a suitable faithful action on a countable set into an embedding in a simple group. The new task is to manufacture the required action while controlling its finiteness properties.

For M1, the action is affine: translations move one chosen point to zero, while a linear part moves nonzero vectors. A simple algebra helps provide the needed linear operations, because every nonzero element generates the entire algebra as a two-sided ideal.

The source keeps this simple algebra inside a different, finitely presented algebra. Passing to a later stage moves a finite set of coordinates into the simple part. This avoids assuming that one algebra automatically has both simplicity and finite presentation.

Elementary matrix operations are first represented in an abstract Steinberg group. Elements in the kernel of its map to actual matrices would spoil faithfulness. M1 constructs a transition that removes this whole kernel, then adjoins a stage-shifting element to package the sequence into a finitely presented group.

The algebra itself is built by encoding computation into finite word rules. A bounded evaluator ensures that recursive calls concern shorter inputs. A fixed-point construction supplies the self-referential program, and induction on input length supplies termination. The role of this mechanism is to preserve the original group’s equality information while creating the extra algebraic operations.

Higher finiteness requires stabilizers too

M2 constructs a highly transitive action: any two ordered tuples of distinct points of the same finite length lie in one orbit. It also arranges type F∞F_\inftyF∞​ for the acting group and every finite-point stabilizer, the subgroup fixing a prescribed finite set point by point.

This extra work is essential. A good action of a finitely presented group need not have stabilizers with the higher finiteness required by the transfer theorem. The source builds the action and stabilizers together through compatible matrix and ring constructions.

The shared device is an ascending torus, also called an ascending HNN extension. For an injective endomorphism f:V→Vf:V\to Vf:V→V, it has the form

T(V,f)=⟨V,t∣t−1vt=f(v) for v∈V⟩.T(V,f)=\langle V,t\mid t^{-1}vt=f(v)\text{ for }v\in V\rangle.T(V,f)=⟨V,t∣t−1vt=f(v) for v∈V⟩.

The new element ttt records movement through successive copies of VVV. A factorization through a finitely presented group supplies finite presentation. Additional finite diagrams of commuting homomorphisms control higher-dimensional cycles.

Two primes force the same obstruction to vanish

The diagrams arise from systems of idempotents, elements satisfying e2=ee^2=ee2=e, over F2\mathbb F_2F2​ and F3\mathbb F_3F3​. Once lower-dimensional error terms have been removed, the two systems force the same relevant homology class zzz to satisfy

2z=0,3z=0.2z=0,\qquad3z=0.2z=0,3z=0.

Then z=3z−2z=0z=3z-2z=0z=3z−2z=0. The difficult input is making both relations apply to the same class with enough uniform control.

For each finite set of allowed simplex types, the sources obtain one iteration and one finite set of output types that fill all relevant cycles. The lengths and coefficients of the filling chains need not be uniformly bounded. This specific uniformity lets the argument handle products of group-ring modules and apply the Bieri–Eckmann finiteness method. Finite presentation then helps convert the homological control into actual finite skeleta.

M3 begins instead with a classical universal finitely presented group VVV. It embeds a finite diagram enlargement back into VVV, obtaining an injective endomorphism fff. The same ascending-torus method makes T(V,f)T(V,f)T(V,f) type F∞F_\inftyF∞​, while retaining VVV and therefore every finitely presented subgroup already inside it.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The simple-overgroup theorems require decidability of the word problem. M3 removes that condition by making a different assertion about a universal target without simplicity. Combining the strongest adjectives from all three statements would produce a claim the sources do not make.

Type F∞F_\inftyF∞​ means finitely many cells in each dimension, not a finite-dimensional or finite classifying space. It gives no automatic bound on cohomological dimension and does not exclude torsion.

The embedding constructions preserve the group as a subgroup, but the stated theorems do not promise polynomial-time word-problem algorithms, small presentations, or controlled geometric distortion of the embedding. A decider supplied as input may take arbitrarily long to halt.

The higher-finiteness proof also requires uniformity over finite simplex types, not a universal bound on filling lengths. Confusing these different quantitative statements would overstate the result.

Questions about efficient embeddings, explicit small targets and additional geometric properties of the overgroups remain separate from the existence theorems summarized here.

8. Sources and further reading

Higman, Subgroups of finitely presented groups, and Boone–Higman, An algebraic characterization of groups with soluble word problem, supply the foundational embedding theorems. Thompson’s word-problem-preserving simple embeddings gives the finite-generation predecessor.

Belk and Zaremsky, Twisted Brin–Thompson groups, supplies the final simplicity and finiteness transfer. Zaremsky’s finite-presentability theorem weakens the action hypotheses needed for M1.

For the higher-dimensional background, see Bieri and Eckmann’s finiteness criteria, Brown’s geometric finiteness theory, and Fournier-Facio and Zaremsky’s Finiteness properties and Higman’s rope trick.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Finite algebraic envelopes and the Boone–Higman conjecture (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Simple F∞ overgroups of groups with decidable word problem (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, A universal group of type F∞ (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Amenability decides when bounded actions can be made unitary and approximate actions repaired
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 251 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A unitary operator preserves lengths and angles. A representation of a group by unitary operators therefore realizes every group element as an exact symmetry of a Hilbert space.

There are two natural ways to relax this ideal. One can keep the group law exact but allow operators that distort lengths by a uniformly bounded amount. Alternatively, one can keep every operator unitary but permit small errors in the multiplication law.

Family 251 asks when these defects can always be repaired. Its first manuscript claims that every uniformly bounded representation can be made unitary by a bounded change of coordinates exactly when the discrete group is amenable. Its second claims that, for countable discrete groups, sufficiently accurate unitary approximate representations can always be corrected exactly when the group is amenable.

The conclusions concern all Hilbert spaces, including infinite-dimensional ones. Restricting the second question to finite-dimensional matrices changes the answer and is not the theorem stated here.

2. Background and essential definitions

Bounded representations and changes of inner product

A complex Hilbert space HHH is a complete inner-product space. It may be finite-dimensional, such as Cn\mathbb C^nCn, or infinite-dimensional, such as the square-summable complex sequences.

A representation π:G→GL(H)\pi:G\to\mathrm{GL}(H)π:G→GL(H) assigns a bounded invertible operator to each group element and satisfies

π(gh)=π(g)π(h),π(e)=I.\pi(gh)=\pi(g)\pi(h),\qquad \pi(e)=I.π(gh)=π(g)π(h),π(e)=I.

Here eee is the group identity and III the identity operator. The operator norm measures the largest stretching of unit vectors.

The representation is uniformly bounded if

∣π∣=sup⁡g∈G∥π(g)∥<∞.|\pi|=\sup_{g\in G}\|\pi(g)\|<\infty.∣π∣=g∈Gsup​∥π(g)∥<∞.

This bound is required over the whole group, not just over a generating set. Since inverses are also group elements, it controls the inverse operators as well.

The representation is unitarizable if there is one bounded invertible operator SSS such that every Sπ(g)S−1S\pi(g)S^{-1}Sπ(g)S−1 is unitary. Equivalently, one can choose an equivalent Hilbert inner product preserved by the action. Equivalent means that the new and old norms bound each other by fixed positive constants.

A group is unitarizable when this is possible for every uniformly bounded representation. The change of coordinates may depend on the representation; the definition does not prescribe a common bound on its condition number ∥S∥∥S−1∥\|S\|\|S^{-1}\|∥S∥∥S−1∥.

Amenability as an averaging property

A discrete group is amenable when bounded functions on it admit a positive normalized translation-invariant mean. This is a generalized averaging rule that assigns average one to the constant function one and respects translations.

Finite groups have an ordinary uniform average. The integers admit generalized averages obtained from long intervals. For amenable groups, such averaging can be used to turn a uniformly bounded family of distorted inner products into one invariant inner product.

The question is whether the ability to repair every representation already forces that averaging property to exist.

Approximate multiplication

Let μ:G→U(H)\mu:G\to\mathcal U(H)μ:G→U(H) assign unitary operators, with μ(e)=I\mu(e)=Iμ(e)=I, but without assuming exact multiplication. Its defect is

def⁡(μ)=sup⁡g,h∈G∥μ(gh)−μ(g)μ(h)∥.\operatorname{def}(\mu)=\sup_{g,h\in G}\|\mu(gh)-\mu(g)\mu(h)\|.def(μ)=g,h∈Gsup​∥μ(gh)−μ(g)μ(h)∥.

The group is strongly Ulam stable if, for every desired accuracy ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, some δ>0\delta>0δ>0 guarantees that any such map of defect at most δ\deltaδ is uniformly within ε\varepsilonε of a genuine unitary representation on the same HHH.

The tolerance must work for every Hilbert space. It can depend on the group and the desired accuracy, but not on the dimension of the chosen representation. Distance is measured uniformly over all group elements in operator norm.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Sz.-Nagy proved in 1947 that an invertible Hilbert-space operator with uniformly bounded positive and negative powers is similar to a unitary operator. This is the representation problem for the infinite cyclic group.

Day and Dixmier extended the averaging mechanism to amenable groups. Dixmier’s 1950 question asked for the converse: does unitarizability characterize amenability?

Early nonunitarizable representations showed that uniform boundedness alone was insufficient. Pytlik and Szwarc constructed families for free groups. Induction carries such an obstruction from a subgroup to its ambient group, covering groups with nonabelian free subgroups but leaving many other nonamenable groups untreated.

Pisier developed quantitative criteria. Amenability follows when every uniformly bounded representation admits a unitarizer with a suitable polynomial condition-number bound of exponent below three. Ordinary unitarizability yields a polynomial bound with some finite exponent, but not automatically below that threshold. The missing quantitative improvement was therefore substantive.

Epstein and Monod used random forests to obtain nonunitarizability from numerical invariants such as first L2L^2L2-Betti number and cost under additional hypotheses. Osin constructed nonunitarizable groups without nonabelian free subgroups. Monod and Ozawa, using measurable-action ideas of Gaboriau and Lyons, established results for wreath-product extensions. Those extensions are larger groups; an obstruction there does not by itself give one for the original group.

Vergara obtained another route under approximation-property assumptions, including classes related to actions on finite-dimensional cube complexes. M1 claims to remove the remaining restrictions for all discrete groups.

The approximate-representation problem has a separate history. Kazhdan’s 1982 theorem proves strong Ulam stability for amenable groups. Burger, Ozawa and Thom showed failure for groups containing nonabelian free subgroups and asked whether amenability is exactly the dividing line. Alpeev established instability for further wreath products using measured equivalence relations.

Meanwhile, Glebsky, Lubotzky, Monod and Rangarajan proved finite-dimensional stability for broad classes of nonamenable higher-rank lattices. Fournier-Facio and Rangarajan developed further finite-dimensional results, including examples related to Thompson groups. These positive theorems are compatible with M2 because strong stability also quantifies over infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: the discrete Dixmier problem

M1, dated 23 September 2026, asserts that a discrete group is amenable if and only if it is unitarizable.

Its nonamenable direction is stronger than merely finding one bounded counterexample. For every nonamenable discrete GGG and every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, it supplies a representation π\piπ with

∣π∣≤1+ε|\pi|\leq1+\varepsilon∣π∣≤1+ε

that admits no bounded similarity making it unitary. Thus the operators can have uniform norm bound arbitrarily close to one while still resisting every change of equivalent Hilbert norm.

If GGG is countable, the witness Hilbert space can be separable, meaning it has a countable dense subset. For an uncountable group, the construction may use a nonseparable space. The definition in the theorem quantifies over all complex Hilbert spaces.

M2: strong Ulam stability

M2, dated 5 October 2026, asserts that a countable discrete group is strongly Ulam stable if and only if it is amenable.

For every nonamenable countable GGG and every δ>0\delta>0δ>0, it constructs a separable Hilbert space and a normalized unitary-valued map μ\muμ with defect less than δ\deltaδ, such that every genuine unitary representation ρ\rhoρ on that same space satisfies

sup⁡g∈G∥μ(g)−ρ(g)∥>110.\sup_{g\in G}\|\mu(g)-\rho(g)\|>\frac1{10}.g∈Gsup​∥μ(g)−ρ(g)∥>101​.

The multiplication error can therefore tend to zero while the distance from every genuine representation stays bounded below by one fixed positive number.

The two papers use different constructions. M2 does not present its instability theorem as an immediate conversion of M1’s nonunitarizable representation. The underlying repair questions are related, but exact multiplication with nonunitary operators and approximate multiplication with unitary operators are distinct requirements.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The family claims two general characterizations of amenability by representation-theoretic repair properties. M1 addresses Dixmier’s longstanding problem, and M2 supplies the converse to Kazhdan’s strong stability theorem.

The significance is the elimination of extra assumptions such as free subgroups, special approximation properties or passage to a larger wreath-product group. Each nonamenable group in the stated range would carry its own obstruction.

The quantitative forms sharpen the qualitative contrast. Arbitrarily small norm excess in M1 does not guarantee an invariant equivalent inner product. Arbitrarily small multiplication defect in M2 does not guarantee even moderately close correction on the same space.

These statements identify amenability as an exact structural dividing line for both problems, while preserving the essential difference between finite- and infinite-dimensional stability.

6. The main idea

M1: bounded changes that have no global implementer

Start with a unitary representation UUU. An operator cocycle is a family of bounded operators D(g)D(g)D(g) satisfying

D(gh)=D(g)+U(g)D(h)U(g)−1.D(gh)=D(g)+U(g)D(h)U(g)^{-1}.D(gh)=D(g)+U(g)D(h)U(g)−1.

It is inner if a single bounded operator BBB gives

D(g)=B−U(g)BU(g)−1D(g)=B-U(g)BU(g)^{-1}D(g)=B−U(g)BU(g)−1

for every ggg. In that case, the family of changes comes from one global choice of coordinates.

A bounded cocycle produces a triangular representation on H⊕HH\oplus HH⊕H:

π(g)=(U(g)D(g)U(g)0U(g)).\pi(g)=\begin{pmatrix}U(g)&D(g)U(g)\\0&U(g)\end{pmatrix}.π(g)=(U(g)0​D(g)U(g)U(g)​).

A similarity making this representation unitary would force the cocycle to be inner. The source therefore seeks a bounded cocycle with no bounded implementer.

It constructs operators whose changes under every group translation remain uniformly bounded, while their distance from all translation-commuting operators grows without bound. A direct sum packages these increasingly difficult finite stages into one obstruction. Scaling the cocycle gives the arbitrarily small norm excess in the theorem.

Nonamenability supplies a finite collection of group steps with a sparse assignment of their edges to endpoints. The paper weights those edges by positive rank-one matrix projections. Random-matrix estimates keep the relevant row and column norms under control even when many edges are present.

At the same time, the total squared matrix energy grows relative to the size of the matrix fibers. This forces the operator away from every translation-commuting operator. Repeated group products can coincide, so the construction retains edge labels as separate coordinates; positivity prevents those coincidences from canceling the energy needed for the obstruction.

For arbitrary discrete groups, a finitely generated nonamenable subgroup supplies the witness. Induction extends it to the full group without increasing the uniform bound. The established Day–Dixmier averaging argument supplies the amenable direction.

M2: almost compatible circuits that cannot come from an action

The second construction begins with a nontrivial boundary action of a nonamenable group on a compact space. Here the relevant boundary property means that group translates can concentrate probability measures toward point masses, and every orbit is dense.

From that action, the source constructs finite lists of group steps marked in two ways. Most steps leaving a fixed point have one mark, while most steps arriving at a fixed point have the other. A compatibility rule prevents a step of the first kind from being followed by one of the second kind.

These marked paths define unitary circuits on a Hilbert space with several levels. Comparisons made using one fixed collection of markings compose exactly. But the approximate representation uses comparisons from different pairs of markings, so the main estimate must control the change caused by adding a third marking.

Simply summing the errors over all levels would be too costly. The source chooses the isometries between slightly different coordinate metrics so that principal errors can be moved onto mutually orthogonal levels. Their norms then combine by a maximum rather than by a sum. This produces a multiplication defect as small as desired.

A separate quadratic-form test prevents correction to a true representation. Signed sums from two orthonormal bases make the test vanish on vectors coming from any genuine action. In the constructed approximate action, the initial inner product gives the same test the value 1/21/21/2.

Most marked paths transport the relevant final vectors back toward these initial ones. If a genuine representation were uniformly within 1/101/101/10, the two values of the quadratic form would have to be too close. The source chooses the parameters so that this contradicts the fixed discrepancy while the multiplication defect still tends to zero.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 treats all discrete groups. M2’s stated characterization is for countable discrete groups. Neither statement here automatically extends to nondiscrete locally compact groups, where continuity requirements for representations enter.

Infinite-dimensional spaces are essential to the strong stability formulation. The theorem does not assert that finite-dimensional Ulam stability characterizes amenability; the historical positive results for some nonamenable groups show why that substitution would be wrong.

All approximation estimates use the operator norm and are uniform over the entire group, or over all pairs of group elements for the defect. Other norms, estimates only on generators, and correction after changing the Hilbert space define different stability questions.

M1 does not merely rule out well-conditioned similarities. It asserts that no bounded invertible similarity works at all for its witness. Conversely, its small bound 1+ε1+\varepsilon1+ε does not say that the representation is uniformly close to one fixed unitary representation.

M1 additionally discusses extensions to group operator algebras using a separate companion similarity theorem. That application has an extra input; it is not needed for the amenability characterization explained here.

The manuscripts leave room for further quantitative questions about optimal correction estimates in amenable cases and about restricted classes of representations. Their principal claims concern the existence or failure of uniform repair under the precise hypotheses above.

8. Sources and further reading

Day’s invariant-mean work and Dixmier’s Les moyennes invariantes dans les semi-groupes et leurs applications (1950) give the classical amenable direction and the original question. Pisier’s Are unitarizable groups amenable? explains the quantitative framework.

Epstein and Monod, Nonunitarizable representations and random forests, and Monod–Ozawa, The Dixmier problem, lamplighters and Burnside groups, give important preceding approaches.

Kazhdan, On ε-representations, proves amenable strong stability. Burger, Ozawa and Thom, On Ulam stability, formulates the converse question. Fournier-Facio and Rangarajan’s finite-dimensional results clarify why the dimensional convention matters.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Unitarizability implies amenability for discrete groups (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Strong Ulam Stability Characterizes Amenability (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Negative curvature does not guarantee detection by finite groups
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 252 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Finite quotients provide a way to study an infinite group through finite calculations. If two elements are different, one hopes that some finite image of the group will still distinguish them.

Residual finiteness says that this hope always succeeds. Hyperbolicity imposes a very different kind of control: the group’s large-scale geometry has uniformly thin triangles, resembling negative curvature. Does that geometric discipline force enough finite quotients to detect every element?

Family 252 claims a negative answer. Its manuscript constructs a torsion-free word-hyperbolic group with a nonidentity element killed by every homomorphism to a finite group.

The same element is then invisible to every finite-dimensional linear representation over every commutative field. The source proves the existence of such an element among a fixed finite family, but does not identify which member of that family it is. That distinction is part of the stated result.

2. Background and essential definitions

Seeing an infinite group through finite images

A homomorphism ϕ:G→Q\phi:G\to Qϕ:G→Q preserves multiplication. When QQQ is finite, it gives a finite image of GGG. Its kernel consists of elements that become the identity in that image.

The group is residually finite if every g≠1g\neq1g=1 has some finite image in which ϕ(g)≠1\phi(g)\neq1ϕ(g)=1. Equivalently, the finite residual

Rf(G)=⋂ϕ:G→Q, Q finiteker⁡ϕR_f(G)=\bigcap_{\phi:G\to Q,\ Q\text{ finite}}\ker\phiRf​(G)=ϕ:G→Q, Q finite⋂​kerϕ

contains only the identity.

For example, the integers are residually finite: a nonzero integer remains nonzero modulo some positive integer. No single modulus distinguishes every pair, but the whole family of finite quotients does.

Failure of residual finiteness means that at least one nonidentity element disappears in every finite image. It does not mean that all finite images are trivial. Other elements may remain visible.

Hyperbolicity and torsion

Choose a finite generating set for GGG, and form its Cayley graph. Vertices are group elements; edges multiply by generators; distance counts the fewest generator steps.

The group is word-hyperbolic if some constant δ\deltaδ makes every shortest-path triangle δ\deltaδ-thin: every point on one side is within distance δ\deltaδ of the other two sides. Changing the finite generating set changes constants but not the property.

Trees are the simplest examples. Products of two infinite trees behave differently: they contain flat planes, so the required uniform thinness fails. Thus nonpositive curvature is a broader notion than word-hyperbolicity.

An element is torsion if some positive power equals the identity. A torsion-free group has no such elements except the identity. The new claim retains torsion-freeness, so the failure of finite detection is not blamed on finite-order elements.

Linear representations

A finite-dimensional linear representation over a commutative field KKK is a homomorphism

ρ:G⟶GLn(K),n≥1.\rho:G\longrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_n(K),\qquad n\geq1.ρ:G⟶GLn​(K),n≥1.

The group is linear over KKK if one such representation is injective. A classical theorem of Malcev says that finitely generated linear groups over commutative fields are residually finite, including in positive characteristic.

Consequently, a finitely generated group with a nontrivial finite residual cannot be faithfully represented by finite matrices over any such field. The manuscript records the stronger common-kernel formulation: every element of Rf(G)R_f(G)Rf​(G) lies in the kernel of every one of these representations.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The residual-finiteness question is part of the program surrounding Gromov’s theory of hyperbolic groups. Hyperbolicity gives powerful control over geometry and algorithms, but it does not directly produce finite quotients.

Ilya Kapovich and Wise proved equivalences between several class-wide statements. All hyperbolic groups are residually finite if and only if every nontrivial hyperbolic group has a nontrivial finite quotient. They also related the same universal assertion to every hyperbolic group being virtually torsion-free, meaning torsion-free after passage to a finite-index subgroup.

These equivalences do not say that each individual failure has all the corresponding properties. For example, a particular group may fail residual finiteness while still having nontrivial finite quotients.

Agol, Groves and Manning showed that a positive answer for all hyperbolic groups would imply separability of every quasiconvex subgroup of every hyperbolic group. Quasiconvexity means geodesics joining subgroup elements stay uniformly near the subgroup. Separability asks that elements outside a subgroup can be distinguished from it in finite quotients. Their argument needs residual finiteness of certain hyperbolic quotient groups, explaining the importance of the class-wide hypothesis.

Additional geometric structure does give positive results. Haglund and Wise developed special cube complexes, whose groups have strong linear and residual properties. Agol proved that a hyperbolic group acting properly and cocompactly on a CAT(0) cube complex is virtually special. Such a group is residually finite.

Earlier examples showed that nonpositive curvature by itself was insufficient. Wise constructed compact nonpositively curved square complexes with non-residually-finite fundamental groups. Burger and Mozes constructed finitely presented simple groups acting on products of trees. Those products contain flat planes, so these were not counterexamples to the hyperbolic-group question.

Nonlinearity was also already known among hyperbolic groups. Michael Kapovich constructed examples with severe restrictions on finite-dimensional representations, and Tholozan and Tsouvalas constructed residually finite nonlinear hyperbolic groups. The latter result makes the logical distinction especially clear: lack of a faithful linear representation does not alone establish failure of residual finiteness.

The proposed advance is to combine torsion-free hyperbolicity with a genuinely nontrivial finite residual in one group.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The manuscript dated 23 September 2026 asserts that there exists a torsion-free word-hyperbolic group GGG that is not residually finite.

Its group is the fundamental group of a finite Euclidean triangle complex. Such a complex is assembled from finitely many vertices, edges and Euclidean triangles, with compatible edge lengths. In particular, the resulting fundamental group has a finite presentation.

The construction supplies a fixed finite family of nontrivial elements represented by rectangular edge loops. The paper shows that one member of this family belongs to Rf(G)R_f(G)Rf​(G). The family and the complex are fixed independently of any finite quotient under consideration.

The proof is existential about the selected member. It establishes that one fixed nonidentity element is killed by every finite quotient; it does not choose a potentially different element for each quotient and stop there.

As a classical consequence, for every commutative field KKK, every finite dimension nnn, and every representation ρ:G→GLn(K)\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_n(K)ρ:G→GLn​(K),

Rf(G)⊆ker⁡ρ.R_f(G)\subseteq\ker\rho.Rf​(G)⊆kerρ.

Thus one common nonidentity element is killed simultaneously by all these representations, across all fields and dimensions. The group is not linear over any commutative field.

Using the Kapovich–Wise equivalences, the paper also records existence of some nontrivial hyperbolic group with no nontrivial finite quotient and of some hyperbolic group that is not virtually torsion-free. These are further existence consequences about the class. They are not additional descriptions of the torsion-free group explicitly constructed here.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The claimed example resolves a central question about whether coarse negative curvature forces finite-quotient approximation. It separates a powerful geometric condition from a fundamental algebraic finiteness property.

The torsion-free conclusion strengthens the separation. The finite residual survives even when finite-order phenomena are excluded, and the group still has the finite description supplied by a finite triangle complex.

The common-kernel statement also gives a strong limitation on matrix models. Every finite-dimensional linear representation over every commutative field misses the same nonidentity element. This is more informative than simply saying that each candidate faithful representation fails somewhere.

The result would also clarify the role of cubulation and specialness in positive theorems. Their extra geometry cannot be discarded and replaced by hyperbolicity alone.

6. The main idea

Make geometry and finite algebra pull in opposite directions

The construction must satisfy two demands simultaneously. Local geometry must force hyperbolicity and torsion-freeness, and must certify that the chosen rectangular loops represent nonidentity elements. Algebraic relations must then prevent all those loops from surviving together in any finite quotient.

The source begins with affine lines in a vector space over a large finite prime field. Each line has a marked point, which is removed from its incidence list. A point and a line label are adjacent when the point lies on the line away from its mark.

Random sampling followed by deletion removes short cycles from the incidence graph while retaining many incidences outside a small exceptional set. A graph’s girth is the length of its shortest cycle, so this produces large girth together with substantial degree.

The remaining incidences are arranged into blocks with Cartesian-product coordinates. Each line label contributes an array of edges between two vertices. Additional edges through a third vertex complete suitable triples to triangles. Shifts in the array coordinates are chosen so that the relevant vertex links inherit the large-girth control.

Angular links certify nontrivial loops

The link of a vertex records the directions of edges leaving that vertex and the angles between them inside incident triangles. Traveling around a loop in the link measures the total angle encountered around the vertex.

The manuscript proves a criterion requiring every nonempty cyclically reduced closed link walk to have angular length at least

2π+η2\pi+\eta2π+η

for some fixed η>0\eta>0η>0. It claims that the resulting finite triangle complex has torsion-free hyperbolic fundamental group.

The criterion also says that a closed edge path whose turns all have link distance at least π\piπ cannot be nullhomotopic. The specially chosen rectangular loops satisfy this local condition, so they are nontrivial in the original group.

The geometric argument uses reduced planar fillings and angular Gauss–Bonnet estimates. The strict angle excess controls interiors of filling diagrams, leading to thinness estimates and then to thin triangles in a Cayley graph. This geometry supplies the nontriviality that the finite-quotient contradiction will need.

Finite separation would make one matrix both large-rank and small-rank

Suppose every rectangular word survived in some finite quotient. Since there are only finitely many such words, take the product of their detecting quotient maps. This gives one finite image in which all of them survive simultaneously.

Represent that finite image by permutation matrices acting on its elements. The edge arrays become block matrices. Survival of the rectangular words forces substantial real rank in these arrays.

On the other hand, the triangle relations make sums over each Cartesian block factor through comparatively small spaces. Factorization bounds matrix rank from above.

The argument must compare these constraints over the finite prime field fixed when the complex was built. It cannot select a new characteristic after learning the size of the finite quotient. The source uses bounds on integer minors, including Hadamard’s determinant inequality and divisibility, to preserve a fixed fraction of the rank uniformly in that quotient size.

Finally, product Lagrange interpolation at the marked points gives a tensor identity. One side has large rank contributed by the edge arrays. The other has small rank because of the local factorizations and the small exceptional set. The initial parameters make these bounds incompatible.

Therefore simultaneous finite separation is impossible. If no individual rectangular word lay in the finite residual, the product construction would have supplied exactly that simultaneous separation. Hence one fixed nontrivial word lies in every finite-quotient kernel.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem produces an example, not a classification of hyperbolic groups with nontrivial finite residual. The positive results for virtually special and other residually finite classes remain separate statements.

The source does not identify which member of the specified finite family is invisible in every finite quotient. Nor does it assert that this particular group has no nontrivial finite quotients at all.

The linear corollary concerns finite-dimensional representations over commutative fields. It does not claim that every representation is trivial, and it makes no assertion about skew fields or infinite-dimensional representations.

The finite-field parameters and the complex are fixed before any finite quotient is tested. This uniformity is essential: a family of examples adapted to larger and larger quotients would not establish a single non-residually-finite group.

There is also no conflict with the sphere-boundary recognition claim in family 246, which has a special boundary hypothesis and gives additional structure in that restricted class. The present theorem concerns hyperbolic groups without that sphere-boundary assumption.

Further questions include describing the constructed finite residual more explicitly and understanding which additional geometric conditions ensure finite-quotient detection. The claimed counterexample establishes that hyperbolicity and torsion-freeness alone do not suffice.

8. Sources and further reading

Gromov, Hyperbolic groups (1987), provides the general framework. Ilya Kapovich and Wise, The equivalence of some residual properties of word-hyperbolic groups, Journal of Algebra 223 (2000), 562–583, gives the class-wide equivalences. Agol, Groves and Manning, Residual finiteness, QCERF and fillings of hyperbolic groups, Geometry & Topology 13 (2009), 1043–1073, explains the separability implications.

Haglund and Wise, Special cube complexes (2008), and Agol’s The virtual Haken conjecture give important positive cases. Wise’s Complete square complexes (2007) and Burger–Mozes’ Finitely presented simple groups and products of trees (1997) concern the broader nonpositively curved setting.

Malcev’s On isomorphic matrix representations of infinite groups (1940) supplies the linear residual-finiteness theorem. Tholozan and Tsouvalas, Residually finite non-linear hyperbolic groups, Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici 100 (2025), 1–9, explains why nonlinearity alone is a different conclusion.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A torsion-free hyperbolic group that is not residually finite (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: An infinite simple amenable group with a finite presentation
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 253 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Can an infinite group be simple, amenable, and finitely presented at the same time? Each adjective describes a different kind of structure. Simplicity forbids decomposition through normal subgroups. Amenability supplies finite sets that are almost unchanged by translation. Finite presentation says that finitely many generators and finitely many relations describe the entire group.

There are many infinite groups with two of these features. Making all three coexist has been substantially harder. The manuscript claims such a group, constructed from exchanges of polygonal pieces in finitely many squares. Its achievement is therefore about the compatibility of algebraic rigidity, averaging, and a finite description.

An especially striking consequence concerns finite approximations. An infinite simple group has no nontrivial homomorphism to a finite group. The claimed example nevertheless has the finite, almost invariant subsets required by amenability. These are different notions of approximation: finite subsets inside a group need not produce finite quotient groups.

2. Background and essential definitions

Finite rules and simplicity

A presentation

G=⟨s1,…,sr∣R1,…,Rt⟩G=\langle s_1,\ldots,s_r\mid R_1,\ldots,R_t\rangleG=⟨s1​,…,sr​∣R1​,…,Rt​⟩

constructs a group from words in generators and their inverses, with the displayed relations and their consequences imposed. It is a finite presentation when both lists are finite. A finitely generated group can require infinitely many relations; this is exactly the distinction that matters here.

A subgroup NNN is normal if conjugation by any group element preserves it. A nontrivial group is simple if its only normal subgroups are the identity subgroup and the whole group. Kernels of homomorphisms are normal. Consequently, a homomorphism from an infinite simple group to a finite group must be trivial: otherwise it would be injective, which is impossible.

A group is perfect if it equals its commutator subgroup, generated by elements aba−1b−1aba^{-1}b^{-1}aba−1b−1. Every nonabelian simple group is perfect. Perfectness will also help turn a finite presentation of a related group into a finite presentation of the desired example.

Averaging without a finite quotient

For a discrete group, amenability can be expressed by the Følner condition. For every finite subset K⊂GK\subset GK⊂G and every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, there is a nonempty finite D⊂GD\subset GD⊂G such that

∣gD△D∣∣D∣<ε(g∈K).\frac{|gD\mathbin{\triangle}D|}{|D|}<\varepsilon\qquad(g\in K).∣D∣∣gD△D∣​<ε(g∈K).

Here △\triangle△ means symmetric difference. Thus multiplication by any of the finitely many prescribed elements changes only a small fraction of DDD. The sets DDD need not be subgroups, and their size may grow rapidly as the requested error decreases.

For example, large boxes work for the integer lattice under addition. The construction in this manuscript is considerably less direct: its elements use different translations on different polygonal pieces. The fact that individual translations commute does not make a group of piecewise translations automatically amenable.

Exchanging polygonal pieces

An interval exchange cuts an interval into finitely many pieces and translates them into a new order. Polygon exchanges use two-dimensional pieces instead. One specifies the allowed polygons and translations so that compositions and inverses remain in the same class.

The paper uses finitely many copies of a square, called tracks. Its alternating subgroup is generated by local even permutations of disjoint translated copies of the same polygon. A three-cycle, which cyclically moves three such pieces, is the basic example. The number of tracks is fixed once and for all; the final group is not a union obtained by continually adding tracks.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The historical route runs through dynamics on a Cantor set, a compact space with many subsets that are simultaneously open and closed. Given a minimal homeomorphism, its topological full group consists of maps that agree locally with integer powers of that homeomorphism. Minimality means that every orbit is dense.

Giordano, Putnam and Skau developed the structural setting, and Matui identified simple commutator subgroups and strong finite-generation properties. In the minimal-subshift setting, these commutator groups are finitely generated, but Matui also proved that they are not finitely presented. Thus the missing finite presentation was already a concrete obstruction, not merely an omitted calculation.

Juschenko and Monod proved amenability of full groups of minimal Cantor systems. Combined with the simplicity results, this produced infinite finitely generated simple amenable groups. Their 2013 theorem settled the finite-generation problem, leaving the finite-presentation question addressed here.

Grigorchuk and Medynets established strong local approximation properties for these groups. In particular, being locally embeddable into finite groups means that every finite portion of the multiplication table can be reproduced in some finite group. A finitely presented group with this property is residually finite: its nonidentity elements can be separated in finite quotients. That is incompatible with infinite simplicity. The new construction must therefore escape an obstruction built into an important earlier source of examples.

Further constructions produced simple amenable groups with other remarkable features. Nekrashevych obtained finitely generated simple periodic groups of intermediate growth, and Kionke and Schesler obtained two-generated simple amenable groups. These developments do not supply the finite presentation claimed here, nor do their additional properties automatically transfer to the new example.

Moving from one-dimensional dynamics to polygon exchanges offers more geometric freedom, but creates an amenability problem. Elek and Monod showed that a topological full group associated with a free minimal action of Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2 can contain a nonabelian free group. An abelian acting group alone is therefore insufficient. Related work on higher-dimensional full groups, Penrose-type constructions, and rectangle exchanges supplies context without already giving the required combination of properties.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The September 23, 2026 manuscript claims the existence of an infinite finitely presented simple amenable group.

More specifically, it constructs a polygon-exchange group FmF_mFm​ and its alternating subgroup AmA_mAm​, for one sufficiently large finite number mmm of tracks. It claims that FmF_mFm​ is amenable and that

Am=[Fm,Fm]A_m=[F_m,F_m]Am​=[Fm​,Fm​]

is infinite, simple and finitely presented. Amenability passes to subgroups, giving the remaining property of AmA_mAm​.

Two intermediate statements are important to interpreting finite presentation. The paper claims that the second integral homology group H2(Am;Z)H_2(A_m;\mathbb Z)H2​(Am​;Z) is finitely generated and that there is a finitely presented central extension

1⟶K⟶G^⟶Am⟶1.1\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow \widehat G\longrightarrow A_m\longrightarrow 1.1⟶K⟶G⟶Am​⟶1.

A central extension means that every element of the kernel KKK commutes with every element of G^\widehat GG. The second homology of a perfect group is also called its Schur multiplier; roughly, it measures possible central extensions. Finite generation of that multiplier alone would not prove finite presentation. The manuscript combines it with the separately constructed finitely presented central extension.

All these properties concern a fixed group. Stabilization by adding tracks is used as a tool in the argument, but the theorem does not merely describe an infinite union of groups with progressively better properties.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the claim resolves a central existence problem about simple amenable groups by adding the finite-presentation property that earlier constructions lacked.

Finite presentation changes what it means to have an example. Infinite families of local permutation relations can define a group precisely, yet still fail to reduce to finitely many rules. The manuscript claims that a finite collection of relations controls all the geometric configurations needed for simplicity and amenability.

The example would also sharpen the separation between averaging and finite quotient approximation. Its amenability supplies Følner sets, while infinite simplicity eliminates all nontrivial finite quotients. It therefore cannot be residually finite. This does not conflict with amenability: the two properties ask for different ways to approximate an infinite object.

Methodologically, the claim combines arithmetic polygon geometry, probability, group homology, and explicit relations. Its significance lies in making these ingredients work together for one group, rather than obtaining each desired property in a different construction.

6. The main idea

Two views of the same arithmetic

Let

τ=1+52,O=Z[τ],λ=τa,\tau=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad\mathcal O=\mathbb Z[\tau],\qquad\lambda=\tau^a,τ=21+5​​,O=Z[τ],λ=τa,

where aaa is a sufficiently large positive integer. The ring O\mathcal OO consists of numbers u+vτu+v\tauu+vτ with integers u,vu,vu,v. The allowed polygon edges lie on level lines of four functions:

x,y,y−λx,x−λy,x,\qquad y,\qquad y-\lambda x,\qquad x-\lambda y,x,y,y−λx,x−λy,

with levels in O\mathcal OO. Translations by vectors in O2\mathcal O^2O2 preserve this collection of lines. Boundaries are handled through a precise splitting convention, so pieces touching an edge do not create an ambiguity in composition.

The second real embedding sends τ\tauτ to

τ‾=1−52.\overline\tau=\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}.τ=21−5​​.

Since ∣τ‾∣<1|\overline\tau|<1∣τ∣<1, making λ\lambdaλ large in ordinary geometry makes its conjugate λ‾\overline\lambdaλ small. This expanding-and-contracting pair of viewpoints is used both to organize polygon subdivisions and to control induction on their arithmetic data.

Local three-cycles can move pieces through spare regions. An area-comparison argument provides enough room to implement these moves. The manuscript uses them to establish perfectness, simplicity and infinitude of the alternating group.

Making random partitions almost invariant

To prove amenability, the paper starts with finitely many polygon exchanges and seeks finite probability distributions on group elements that are almost unchanged by those exchanges.

It constructs random polygon partitions adapted to the regions on which each prescribed exchange is a single translation. Two correlated random fields control subdivision points and selected boundary segments. Their multiscale correlations, organized through the conjugate embedding, make bounded translations change the distributions only slightly while keeping fluctuations under control.

On a high-probability event, cells respect the translation regions. Translating a cell therefore produces a cell of the same shape. Randomly matching cells of each shape converts the partitions into almost invariant probability distributions on the group. The Følner formulation then supplies the finite sets required for amenability.

The difficult issue is compatibility across boundaries. This is why a collection of abelian translations is only the starting material, not an amenability proof by itself.

From infinitely many configurations to finitely many relations

Finite presentation is handled through the central extension rather than by immediately listing every relation in AmA_mAm​.

The paper chooses finitely many generators, including track permutations and balanced translations, whose translation vectors sum to zero. It imposes finitely many true relations to obtain G^\widehat GG. Coordinate-cut relations are first controlled in a bounded arithmetic range. Inclined edges then let the argument separate small rectangles in ordinary geometry, while contraction in the conjugate coordinate keeps the induction within previously controlled arithmetic ranges.

Rectangle decompositions extend these laws to general allowed polygons. Exact conjugation rules eventually show that an element acting trivially on all tracks commutes with every generator of G^\widehat GG. This identifies the kernel as central; it does not yet discard the kernel.

A separate homology argument proves finite generation of H2(Am;Z)H_2(A_m;\mathbb Z)H2​(Am​;Z). It uses complexes of polygon embeddings, stabilization, and the fact that the allowed geometry has finitely many relevant corner types up to translation. A fixed reserve of tracks brings the needed low-degree information back to the chosen finite mmm.

Finally, the homology exact sequence for the central extension relates H2(Am;Z)H_2(A_m;\mathbb Z)H2​(Am​;Z), KKK, and the abelianization of G^\widehat GG. Both outer pieces needed to control KKK are finitely generated, so KKK is finitely generated as an abelian group. Adding finitely many kernel generators as relators to the finite presentation of G^\widehat GG gives the claimed finite presentation of AmA_mAm​.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is an existence statement with a specific arithmetic construction. It does not assert that arbitrary polygon-exchange groups are amenable or finitely presented. Restricting the allowed slopes, levels and translations is essential to the stated method.

The number of tracks is finite but chosen sufficiently large for several parts of the argument. The headline does not identify an optimal number of generators, an optimal presentation size, or a practical algorithm for finding efficient Følner sets.

The manuscript’s theorem should also be separated from properties of earlier examples. It does not by its headline claim make this group periodic, torsion-free, two-generated, or of intermediate growth. Those are distinct questions requiring additional information.

Finally, the local approximation obstruction remains instructive: this infinite simple finitely presented group cannot be locally embeddable into finite groups. Understanding its approximation properties therefore requires more than transferring the methods used for earlier Cantor full groups.

8. Sources and further reading

For the earlier simple-group constructions, see Matui’s study of Cantor minimal systems, Juschenko–Monod’s amenability theorem, and Grigorchuk–Medynets on local approximation. Elek–Monod’s two-dimensional example explains why amenability cannot be inferred from the translation group alone.

Nekrashevych’s intermediate-growth construction and Kionke–Schesler’s two-generator construction describe different refinements of the earlier existence results. The source manuscript supplies the specific arithmetic geometry and central-extension argument summarized here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An infinite finitely presented simple amenable group (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Artin groups: complete topological models, controlled subgroups, and a curvature obstruction
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 254 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Ordinary braids give a vivid example of a group. Place strands between two rows of points, multiply braids by stacking them, and identify motions that can be continuously deformed into one another. Artin groups generalize the familiar relations between adjacent crossings without requiring an underlying picture of strands.

Their definitions are short, but three basic questions have resisted uniform answers. Does the standard space built from an Artin presentation have a contractible universal cover? Do the natural subgroups remain natural after taking intersections? Can every Artin group act geometrically on a space of nonpositive curvature?

This family claims affirmative answers to the first two questions for every Artin group with finitely many standard generators, and a negative answer to the third. Together they draw a useful boundary: having a complete topological model and well-behaved subgroups does not force the strongest expected metric geometry.

2. Background and essential definitions

The defining relations

Choose a finite set SSS and symmetric labels mstm_{st}mst​, with mss=1m_{ss}=1mss​=1 and, for distinct indices, mst∈{2,3,4,…,∞}m_{st}\in\{2,3,4,\ldots,\infty\}mst​∈{2,3,4,…,∞}. The Artin group has a generator σs\sigma_sσs​ for each s∈Ss\in Ss∈S. When mstm_{st}mst​ is finite, the two alternating words of that length are equal. For example,

mst=2:σsσt=σtσs,mst=3:σsσtσs=σtσsσt.\begin{aligned}m_{st}=2&:\quad \sigma_s\sigma_t=\sigma_t\sigma_s,\\m_{st}=3&:\quad \sigma_s\sigma_t\sigma_s=\sigma_t\sigma_s\sigma_t.\end{aligned}mst​=2mst​=3​:σs​σt​=σt​σs​,:σs​σt​σs​=σt​σs​σt​.​

An infinite label imposes no relation on that pair. Finite rank means that SSS is finite; it does not mean the group itself is finite.

Adding the relations σs2=1\sigma_s^2=1σs2​=1 gives the associated Coxeter group WWW. A subset T⊆ST\subseteq ST⊆S is spherical when its Coxeter subgroup WTW_TWT​ is finite. The Artin subgroup ATA_TAT​ generated by those same indices is generally infinite even when TTT is spherical.

A parabolic subgroup is a conjugate gATg−1gA_Tg^{-1}gAT​g−1. Thinking of ATA_TAT​ as using selected generators is helpful, but conjugation makes intersections far less transparent than intersections of subsets of SSS.

Topology versus curvature

The Salvetti complex is a space made by attaching cells. It has one cell of dimension ∣T∣|T|∣T∣ for every spherical subset TTT, including a vertex for the empty subset. Its loops represent generators and its two-dimensional cells record braid relations. Higher-dimensional cells are essential parts of the construction.

A connected space is a K(G,1)K(G,1)K(G,1) if its fundamental group is GGG and its universal cover is contractible. Contractibility means that the identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map. Equivalently, for this cell complex there are no higher homotopy groups: every sphere of dimension at least two maps into the space in a null-homotopic way.

A CAT(0) space instead satisfies a metric condition: distances inside each geodesic triangle are no greater than the corresponding distances in a Euclidean comparison triangle. Such spaces are contractible, but contractibility alone does not provide a CAT(0) metric.

Here a geometric action is a proper, cocompact isometric action on a nonempty proper CAT(0) space. Properness of the space means that closed bounded subsets are compact. Properness of the action limits how many group elements can move a compact set back into itself; cocompactness means that translates of one compact set cover the space.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The classifying-space question grew from configuration spaces and hyperplane complements. Classical braid groups supplied early positive examples. Deligne proved the spherical Artin case in 1972, using the structure of finite reflection arrangements. Salvetti’s constructions turned the relevant spaces into explicit cellular models.

Charney and Davis developed a complex built from spherical parabolic cosets and connected its contractibility to the general conjecture. They proved important classes, including FC type and the case where the largest spherical subset has size at most two. This dimension need not equal the number of generators.

Paolini and Salvetti resolved all affine types. More recently, Huang and Przytycki treated the dimension-at-most-three case and further classes, while Hoda and Huang treated groups whose irreducible spherical parabolics have specified types. These are broad positive results, but the first manuscript claims to remove the restrictions on the finite-rank Coxeter matrix altogether.

The intersection problem developed alongside this topology. Van der Lek’s embedding theorem ensures that standard parabolic subgroups have the expected Artin presentation. That does not say that intersections of arbitrary conjugates are parabolic. Earlier intersection theorems covered right-angled groups, spherical type, large type, selected affine types, and other substantial classes. In FC type, some theorems required one or both intersected parabolics to be spherical; those hypotheses should not be confused with a theorem about arbitrary parabolics.

The CAT(0) question has its own positive history. Right-angled Artin groups act on natural CAT(0) cube complexes. Results also cover several large-label classes, including Haettel’s XXL-type groups, and classical braid groups with up to seven strands through work by several authors. Brady and Crisp found examples whose smallest CAT(0) dimension exceeds the dimension of a classifying space. Their obstruction was dimensional; the new counterexample claims to exclude geometric CAT(0) actions in every dimension.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

All three manuscripts are dated September 23, 2026.

M1 claims the Artin K(π,1)K(\pi,1)K(π,1) conjecture in finite rank. For every finite Coxeter matrix, the full standard Salvetti complex has contractible universal cover. Finite and infinite labels, disconnected diagrams, and nonspherical Coxeter groups are all allowed.

The manuscript also records consequences using established theorems: torsion-freeness; a description of the center as Zk\mathbb Z^kZk, where kkk counts the spherical irreducible diagram components; and the classifying-space comparison with the positive Artin monoid. These are consequences of the asphericity input combined with earlier work, rather than independent new arguments for every conclusion.

M3 claims the parabolic intersection conjecture in the same finite-rank scope. In particular,

gAXg−1∩hAYh−1=kAZk−1gA_Xg^{-1}\cap hA_Yh^{-1}=kA_Zk^{-1}gAX​g−1∩hAY​h−1=kAZ​k−1
