for suitable Z⊆SZ\subseteq SZ⊆S and k∈Ak\in Ak∈A. Neither intersected subgroup needs to be spherical. The paper further claims that every intersection of parabolics is already the intersection of at most ∣S∣|S|∣S∣ members of the family. The empty intersection is understood to be the whole group.

Consequently, every subset of AAA has a unique smallest containing parabolic subgroup. M3 also claims a uniform algorithm deciding membership in a supplied conjugate of a standard parabolic, with the Coxeter matrix and words as input. Taking the trivial parabolic gives a solution of the word problem. No running-time bound is asserted.

M2 claims an explicit counterexample to the CAT(0) conjecture. Its Artin group has 116 generators and only the off-diagonal labels 2,3,∞2,3,\infty2,3,∞. It admits no geometric action on any nonempty proper CAT(0) space, without a dimension bound. The other manuscripts’ asphericity statements are not inputs to this obstruction.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The family addresses several central structural questions about the entire finite-rank class, rather than extending a theorem to one additional diagram type.

If M1 is correct, a concrete finite cell complex becomes a classifying space for every such Artin group. That turns the defining diagram into a uniform topological tool for computing and studying group invariants.

If M3 is correct, parabolic subgroups acquire a robust closure operation. Intersections and smallest containing parabolics become available without repeatedly checking special-type hypotheses. The claimed membership algorithm adds an effective counterpart to the structural theorem.

M2 would establish that this strong topology cannot always be upgraded to geometric CAT(0) structure. Its force comes from excluding all dimensions and metrics allowed by the definition. It therefore rules out repairing the example simply by choosing a larger complex or a more ingenious nonpositively curved metric.

6. The main idea

Measuring spherical cosets by harmonic heights

M1 replaces the universal-cover problem by a classical equivalent problem: contract the space assembled from spherical cosets ATxA_TxAT​x, ordered by inclusion. The challenge is that the whole group need not be spherical even though the pieces indexing this space are.

The paper builds an algebraic action of the Artin group on complexes of modules. A complex is a sequence of vector-space-like objects with differentials whose successive compositions vanish. Counting generators in its graded layers produces nonnegative numerical data, one coordinate for each original generator and an extra framing coordinate.

Inside a spherical subset, the exterior coordinates are extended harmonically. The extension solves equations of the form

2pi=∑j≠ibijpj,2p_i=\sum_{j\ne i} b_{ij}p_j,2pi​=j=i∑​bij​pj​,

where the coefficients encode Coxeter labels, with bij=2cos⁡(π/mij)b_{ij}=2\cos(\pi/m_{ij})bij​=2cos(π/mij​) for finite labels and 222 for infinite labels. Sphericity gives the positive-definiteness needed for a unique extension in the relevant subsystem.

These vectors define a height on cosets. The paper orders cosets by height and studies how each new vertex attaches to the earlier part. Two algebraic estimates control the process: a comparison preventing competing minimal candidates, and an obstruction to an isolated positive harmonic layer. Special equality cases require a modified tie rule, not just strict descent everywhere. The resulting earlier links are empty or contractible, and connectedness then yields the claimed contraction.

Turning intersections into stabilizers

M3 uses a related categorical framework with a relative frame adapted to a chosen standard parabolic AXA_XAX​. The framing object is arranged so that its stabilizer is exactly AXA_XAX​. Transporting that object by a group element converts an intersection of conjugate parabolics into a stabilizer problem inside another parabolic.

Harmonic heights now organize the set of minimal configurations. The paper claims that these minima are connected, including paths with tied heights. This forces a stabilizer into a smaller parabolic unless a whole factor acts trivially. A separate positive-height argument handles spherical cases where the first reduction would not lower rank. Induction then identifies the stabilizer as parabolic.

For the algorithm, the finite algebra has computable algebraic coefficients. Tensoring the complexes corresponding to an input word and cancelling invertible differential entries reduces membership to a finite exact calculation. The claim is termination and correctness as a decision procedure, not practical efficiency. M3 develops its needed stabilizer argument without assuming M1’s asphericity theorem.

A short angular circuit that cannot exist

M2 begins with the three-generator group

T=⟨a,b,c∣aba=bab, bcb=cbc, cac=aca⟩.T=\langle a,b,c\mid aba=bab,\ bcb=cbc,\ cac=aca\rangle.T=⟨a,b,c∣aba=bab, bcb=cbc, cac=aca⟩.

It attaches a 40-strand braid group along each of the three braid pairs. Each attachment contributes 37 new generators. Two further generators centralize a,b,ca,b,ca,b,c, giving the total 3+3⋅37+2=1163+3\cdot37+2=1163+3⋅37+2=116.

Suppose a geometric CAT(0) action existed. The stable translation length

ℓ(g)=lim⁡n→∞d(x,gnx)n\ell(g)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{d(x,g^nx)}{n}ℓ(g)=n→∞lim​nd(x,gnx)​

measures the distance moved per iterate at large scale. For commuting elements, these lengths behave like lengths of Euclidean translation vectors. The long braid blocks impose quantitative constraints on the lengths associated with each of the three braid pairs.

Those constraints yield six asymptotically Euclidean sectors, each with angle less than π/3\pi/3π/3, forming a circuit with total angle less than 2π2\pi2π. Converting that circuit into a contradiction in arbitrary dimension is the key step. The paper compares a sector disk with a CAT(0) geodesic disk, transfers the comparison to finite triangular diagrams, and uses a winding count: one part forces nonzero signed multiplicity, while a folding argument forces it to vanish.

One further issue matters. A subgroup of a group acting geometrically need not itself act cocompactly. The two extra generators make TTT their simultaneous centralizer. The paper uses this to obtain a suitable closed convex region on which TTT does act geometrically, so the length constraints and the angular obstruction apply to the same action.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The universal statements in M1 and M3 concern finite rank. Their wording does not by itself supply a theorem for arbitrary infinite generating sets. M1 concerns the full Salvetti complex, not merely its two-dimensional presentation complex.

The counterexample excludes geometric CAT(0) actions. It does not exclude every action on every CAT(0) space, such as actions lacking properness or cocompactness. Its 116-generator construction is explicit, but the headline does not establish that this size is minimal.

The membership result supplies no complexity bound. Likewise, the intersection theorem does not mean that simply intersecting the visible generator sets finds the answer for conjugated parabolics.

Finally, M3 explicitly credits earlier work for acylindrical hyperbolicity in its stated non-clique scope. Its deduction through the new intersection theorem is another route to that conclusion, not a new class of groups with that property.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 and M3 give detailed historical references for spherical, affine, FC, and large-type results. For the categorical background, see Heng–Licata’s Artin–Tits actions and stability conditions. The earlier three-dimensional asphericity result and ABI-type theorem show how broad partial results preceded the general claim.

For the metric side, compare Haettel’s XXL-type theorem, Jeong’s seven-strand braid theorem, and Brady–Crisp’s dimension obstruction. Bridson–Haefliger’s book on nonpositive curvature develops the CAT(0) background.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Harmonic heights and the Artin K(pi,1) conjecture (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An Artin group with no geometric CAT(0) action (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Parabolic intersections in Artin groups (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Recognizing polycyclic groups from their large-scale shape
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 255 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Imagine drawing the Cayley graph of a finitely generated group: vertices are group elements, and an edge records multiplication by a generator. Now step so far back that bounded errors and fixed changes of scale become invisible. How much algebra can still be recovered from the resulting shape?

The manuscript asks this for virtually polycyclic groups, a broad class built from cyclic groups by finitely many extensions, allowing a final finite extension. It claims that any finitely generated group with the same large-scale geometry must also be virtually polycyclic.

The comparison group is not assumed solvable, linear, or equipped with a useful presentation. The point is to recover its algebraic structure from geometry alone. The statement recognizes a class of groups; it does not say that two groups with the same large-scale shape are isomorphic.

2. Background and essential definitions

Word metrics and quasi-isometries

Fix finitely many generators and their inverses. The word distance d(g,h)d(g,h)d(g,h) is the shortest length of a word representing g−1hg^{-1}hg−1h. Different finite generating sets give different distances, but those distances agree up to fixed multiplicative bounds.

A map F:X→YF:X\to YF:X→Y is a quasi-isometry if there are constants K≥1K\geq1K≥1 and C≥0C\geq0C≥0 such that

K−1dX(x,x′)−C≤dY(F(x),F(x′))≤KdX(x,x′)+C,\begin{aligned}K^{-1}d_X(x,x')-C&\leq d_Y(F(x),F(x'))\\&\leq Kd_X(x,x')+C,\end{aligned}K−1dX​(x,x′)−C​≤dY​(F(x),F(x′))≤KdX​(x,x′)+C,​

and every point of YYY lies within distance CCC of the image. Thus distances cannot be distorted too much at large scales, and no large part of the target is missed. The map need not preserve multiplication, be continuous, or be one-to-one.

For example, the integer lattice Zn\mathbb Z^nZn, with a word metric, is quasi-isometric to Euclidean nnn-space. Passing to a finite-index subgroup also leaves a finitely generated group’s quasi-isometry type unchanged. This explains why a geometrically detectable property often appears with the qualifier virtually.

Polycyclic groups and Lie models

A group PPP is polycyclic if it has a finite chain

1=P0◃P1◃⋯◃Pr=P1=P_0\triangleleft P_1\triangleleft\cdots\triangleleft P_r=P1=P0​◃P1​◃⋯◃Pr​=P

in which every quotient Pi/Pi−1P_i/P_{i-1}Pi​/Pi−1​ is cyclic, finite or infinite. Each subgroup is normal in the next; it need not be normal in all of PPP. A virtually polycyclic group contains such a group with finite index.

These groups are solvable, meaning that repeatedly taking commutator subgroups eventually gives the identity. The converse is false: finite generation and solvability do not by themselves imply polycyclicity.

A Lie group is a group with a compatible smooth-manifold structure. A lattice is a discrete subgroup whose quotient has finite invariant volume; it is uniform when the quotient is compact. Classical structure theorems relate virtually polycyclic groups, after finite-index changes, to uniform lattices in connected simply connected solvable Lie groups. These continuous groups provide geometric models for the discrete question.

Growth and amenability

A group has polynomial growth if its radius-RRR word ball contains at most a constant times a fixed power of RRR elements. Virtually nilpotent groups have this property. Many polycyclic groups instead have exponential growth, so growth degree alone cannot recognize the whole class.

Amenability means that finite subsets can have arbitrarily small relative boundary under any prescribed finite collection of translations. Polycyclic groups are amenable. Among finitely generated groups this property is preserved by quasi-isometry, supplying one initial piece of algebraic information about the unknown comparison group.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gromov’s polynomial-growth theorem is the basic model for this kind of recognition. It says that a finitely generated group with polynomial growth is virtually nilpotent. Since polynomial growth is preserved by quasi-isometry, the virtually nilpotent part of the present problem was already settled.

The exponential-growth case is subtler. A familiar model is Sol\mathrm{Sol}Sol, where one direction expands while another contracts as a third, height-like coordinate changes. Farb and Mosher formulated recognition and height-preservation problems for such solvable geometries. Eskin, Fisher and Whyte developed coarse differentiation and established recognition for Sol\mathrm{Sol}Sol, while explicitly formulating the broader lattice-recognition conjecture addressed here.

Peng extended height methods to nondegenerate unimodular split abelian-by-abelian Lie groups, including examples with nontrivial Jordan blocks. Her work made local height maps affine and compared them across large regions, obtaining both quasi-isometry information and virtual-polycyclic recognition in that class.

Other approaches extract actions on boundaries from height control. Dymarz treated particular diagonalizable models; Dymarz, Fisher and Xie developed a boundary-conjugation theorem involving nilpotent groups and applied it under specified structural and amenability hypotheses. These results are stronger than recognition in some directions, but do not already give the unrestricted theorem claimed here.

Shalom had shown that a finitely generated group quasi-isometric to an infinite polycyclic group has a finite-index subgroup with infinite abelianization. This detects a significant algebraic feature without recovering the complete polycyclic structure. Le Boudec established recognition under the stronger geometric relationship of commability, which uses chains of proper homomorphisms with cocompact image. A quasi-isometry need not supply such homomorphisms.

The new manuscript claims recognition for the entire virtually polycyclic class, with no algebraic premise on the comparison group beyond finite generation.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The September 24, 2026 manuscript states:

If a finitely generated group HHH is quasi-isometric to a finitely generated virtually polycyclic group PPP, then HHH is virtually polycyclic.

Equivalently in the lattice formulation, if HHH is quasi-isometric to a lattice in a connected simply connected solvable Lie group, then a finite-index subgroup of HHH is a uniform lattice in some connected simply connected solvable Lie group.

The word some matters. The ambient Lie group in the conclusion may differ from the original one. The theorem does not assert a classification of all quasi-isometries or an isomorphism between the two lattice groups.

The main geometric input is a uniform bounded-height theorem. In a connected simply connected real-triangulable unimodular Lie model GGG, let π:G→W\pi:G\to Wπ:G→W be its canonical exponential-height homomorphism to a real vector space. Here real-triangulable means that the infinitesimal adjoint actions can be simultaneously put in upper triangular real form, and unimodular means that left invariant volume is also right invariant.

The paper claims that a finite group AG\mathcal A_GAG​ of invertible linear maps of WWW controls every self quasi-isometry FFF:

∥π(F(g))−π(F(1))−AFπ(g)∥≤B,AF∈AG.\|\pi(F(g))-\pi(F(1))-A_F\pi(g)\|\leq B,\qquad A_F\in\mathcal A_G.∥π(F(g))−π(F(1))−AF​π(g)∥≤B,AF​∈AG​.

For fixed quasi-isometry constants, BBB is uniform over all such maps and all g∈Gg\in Gg∈G. This is a bounded error, not merely an error growing more slowly than distance.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the theorem settles a central recognition conjecture for a major class of solvable groups. It recovers a finite algebraic construction from a metric comparison that need not respect any multiplication.

The bounded-height statement is also significant as a mechanism. Expansion rates provide geometric coordinates even when arbitrary quasi-isometries scramble the small-scale structure. The manuscript claims that those coordinates are preserved up to one of finitely many linear symmetries and a uniformly bounded error.

The scope includes models with nonabelian nilpotent directions and more complicated interactions than the simplest diagonal examples. Retaining those interactions is what lets the conclusion extend from familiar special geometries to the whole virtually polycyclic class.

This remains class recognition rather than complete rigidity. That distinction preserves the theorem’s strength without assigning it a classification conclusion it does not claim.

6. The main idea

Height records how many endpoints are reachable

In Sol\mathrm{Sol}Sol, a height ttt scales two horizontal directions by ete^tet and e−te^{-t}e−t. A path can move in the first direction at a high level and in the second at a low level. The range of available heights therefore controls the exponential number of separated endpoints the path can reach.

For a general solvable model, the paper defines a function P(E)P(E)P(E) of an allowed convex height region EEE. Roughly, paths of length proportional to rrr, constrained to heights in rErErE, can reach

exp⁡(rP(E)+o(r))\exp\bigl(rP(E)+o(r)\bigr)exp(rP(E)+o(r))

points separated at a fixed scale. Here o(r)o(r)o(r) denotes an error whose ratio to rrr tends to zero. The calculation includes directions produced by brackets, the infinitesimal version of commutators. Counting only the visibly expanding coordinates would miss part of the geometry.

A quasi-isometry preserves separated endpoint counts up to controlled changes. Comparing these counts for a map and its inverse constrains the possible changes of height. The inverse must be paired with the same candidate slope; unrelated forward and reverse estimates would not suffice.

From averaged slopes to one global height map

The proof first studies probability distributions on normalized quasi-isometries, obtained by moving the basepoint and recentering. Existing cohomological results provide linear height slopes in this averaged setting. The endpoint-volume comparison restricts the slopes to a finite collection.

The next task is to pass from averaged information to every individual map. The manuscript examines large coordinate regions, rescales their height profiles, and claims that limiting profiles are affine. Stationary increments constrain the profiles, while volume estimates prevent folding.

Different neighboring regions might still have different slopes or offsets. The paper compares paths that switch between them. Incompatible slopes would create more target endpoints than the source geometry permits. Further volume comparisons in appropriate nilpotent quotients control the offsets. This produces one global linear part with a uniform sublinear error.

Sublinear control is not the endpoint. Contracting rays define maps of quotient boundaries, and invariant volumes on those boundaries record height changes. Averaging translated sets converts this volume information into the uniform bounded error stated in the theorem.

Recovering the group structure

Transport left multiplication by HHH to the Lie model through a quasi-isometry. The result is a quasi-action: compositions agree with the group law only up to bounded error. The height theorem associates a linear part in the finite group AG\mathcal A_GAG​ to each element.

Passing to a finite-index subgroup H0H_0H0​ removes those linear parts. Amenability then corrects the remaining approximate height translations to an actual homomorphism

τ:H0⟶W.\tau:H_0\longrightarrow W.τ:H0​⟶W.

Every finitely generated subgroup of ker⁡τ\ker\taukerτ has word paths staying within bounded height. The endpoint estimates now give polynomial, rather than exponential, growth. Gromov’s theorem makes each such subgroup virtually nilpotent.

This yields elementary amenability, a class built from finite and abelian groups through standard subgroup, quotient, extension, and directed-union operations. It does not yet yield polycyclicity. The final step uses finiteness and duality properties transferred from the original lattice model, together with structure theorems for elementary amenable groups, to obtain a polycyclic subgroup of finite index.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Finite generation is part of the recognition statement. The theorem is not a claim about arbitrary countable groups equipped with arbitrary metrics.

The Lie models play two separate roles. A solvable lattice model provides compact-quotient topology and finiteness properties; a suitable real-triangulable model provides the height geometry. The proof does not require the original lattice to sit inside every auxiliary model used for the geometric analysis.

The kernel argument establishes that each finitely generated subgroup of the height kernel is virtually nilpotent. It does not simply assert that the whole kernel is finitely generated and nilpotent. The final structural step remains necessary.

Questions about determining the exact ambient Lie group, classifying all quasi-isometries, or computing effective bounds for a given presentation go beyond the headline recognition theorem. The distinction between bounded and merely sublinear height error is also essential: only bounded control supplies the path estimates used in the final algebraic deduction.

8. Sources and further reading

Eskin–Fisher–Whyte’s recognition conjecture and overview and their rigidity theorem for Sol describe the central historical problem. Compare Peng’s second paper on solvable Lie groups and Dymarz–Fisher–Xie’s nilpotent-boundary theorem.

Gromov’s polynomial-growth theorem and Shalom’s large-scale cohomological results supply important earlier recognition mechanisms. The source manuscript gives the general height construction and the precise finiteness results used to finish the argument.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Quasi-isometric recognition of virtually polycyclic groups (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Solving independent equations without collapsing the coefficient group
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 256 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

An equation can require enlarging the system in which we work. The equation x2=2x^2=2x2=2 has no rational solution, but it has a solution after adjoining 2\sqrt22​, while the rational numbers remain intact.

There is an analogous problem for groups. Equations involve fixed coefficients from a group GGG, unknown group elements, multiplication and inverses. Can we enlarge GGG to solve the equations without making two originally distinct elements equal?

The family claims that a simple linear independence condition on exponent sums always suffices, for every coefficient group. A companion manuscript treats the Kervaire question: can adjoining just one generator and imposing just one relation turn a nontrivial group into the trivial group? It claims that this can never happen.

The linear algebra is only a test on the equations. The groups themselves may be highly noncommutative, and the conclusion is not obtained by pretending that their coefficients commute.

2. Background and essential definitions

Equations over a group

An equation over GGG might look like

x2ay=1,x^2ay=1,x2ay=1,

where a∈Ga\in Ga∈G is fixed and x,yx,yx,y are unknown. A solution over GGG consists of a group HHH containing an isomorphic copy of GGG, together with choices of x,y∈Hx,y\in Hx,y∈H making the equation true. The solution need not lie in GGG itself.

The free product G∗FnG*F_nG∗Fn​, where FnF_nFn​ is the free group on x1,…,xnx_1,\ldots,x_nx1​,…,xn​, formally adds the unknowns without adding any new relations. Imposing words w1,…,wmw_1,\ldots,w_mw1​,…,wm​ as equations gives the quotient

Q=(G∗Fn)/⟨ ⁣⟨w1,…,wm⟩ ⁣⟩.Q=(G*F_n)/\langle\!\langle w_1,\ldots,w_m\rangle\!\rangle.Q=(G∗Fn​)/⟨⟨w1​,…,wm​⟩⟩.

The double brackets mean normal closure: the subgroup generated by all conjugates of the relators and their inverses. The universal solution group QQQ always exists, but the natural map G→QG\to QG→Q might identify distinct coefficients.

Thus solvability in an overgroup is equivalent to injectivity of that map. If it is injective, QQQ itself supplies a solution. Conversely, any solution in an overgroup forces the original coefficients to remain distinct in QQQ.

The exponent-sum test

For each equation, count occurrences of each unknown with signs: xjx_jxj​ contributes +1+1+1, and xj−1x_j^{-1}xj−1​ contributes −1-1−1. Ignore coefficients for this calculation. The counts form an integer matrix A=(aij)A=(a_{ij})A=(aij​), one row per equation and one column per variable.

The system is nonsingular when its rows are linearly independent over Q\mathbb QQ:

rank⁡QA=m.\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}A=m.rankQ​A=m.

For instance, the equations

x2ay=1,xby2=1x^2ay=1,\qquad xby^2=1x2ay=1,xby2=1

have exponent matrix

A=(2112),det⁡A=3.A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det A=3.A=(21​12​),detA=3.

The claimed theorem applies for arbitrary coefficients a,ba,ba,b in any group. The determinant need not be ±1\pm1±1; nonzero rational rank is enough.

For one variable and one equation, nonsingularity means a nonzero exponent sum. The stronger condition that this sum is ±1\pm1±1 is called unimodularity. These two hypotheses distinguish the companion manuscript’s main injectivity theorem from the later system theorem.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kervaire’s problem arose in the study of high-dimensional knot groups, where normal generation by one element is an important condition. The universal nontriviality question and its stronger equation-solving variants subsequently became central problems about relative group presentations.

Gerstenhaber and Rothaus established a foundational theorem in 1962. For compact connected Lie groups, they related the degree of a word map to the determinant of its exponent matrix. A nonzero degree forces surjectivity, producing simultaneous solutions. Their work also gives finite solution overgroups for finite coefficient groups. Rectangular nonsingular systems can be reduced to square ones by selecting a nonzero maximal minor.

Howie proved solvability for finite independent systems over locally indicable groups, meaning groups whose nontrivial finitely generated subgroups map onto Z\mathbb ZZ. Klyachko proved unimodular one-variable injectivity for torsion-free groups. Chen later recovered that result using estimates for the complexity of surfaces. These theorems imposed useful conditions on the coefficient group that the new family claims to remove.

The compact-unitary approach also extends to hyperlinear groups, which admit faithful approximations through metric ultraproducts of finite-dimensional unitary groups. Pestov described this route, and Nitsche and Thom stated a nonsingular-system theorem and stronger variants using homology of covering spaces. The coefficient-group approximation assumption remains part of those results.

Other work controls the solution overgroup more precisely, for example within suitable solvable classes or power-series groups. Such structural conclusions are different from unrestricted existence in some overgroup.

The companion manuscript also acknowledges Kawauchi’s published proposed resolution of the universal Kervaire nontriviality statement by a different topological route. It presents its own spectral and planar-surface argument independently of that construction. This digest reports that attribution without deciding the status of competing proofs.

Within the present family, the September 24 manuscript develops the one-relator unimodular method. The October 5 manuscript extends it to several equation types and arbitrary nonsingular exponent matrices. That extension is an explicit dependency in the account of the method, not simply two unrelated assertions with similar titles.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated October 5, 2026, claims Howie’s nonsingular-system conjecture for arbitrary groups. For any group GGG, any finite number nnn of variables, and m≤nm\leq nm≤n equations with exponent matrix of row rank mmm over Q\mathbb QQ, the map

G⟶(G∗Fn)/⟨ ⁣⟨w1,…,wm⟩ ⁣⟩G\longrightarrow(G*F_n)/\langle\!\langle w_1,\ldots,w_m\rangle\!\rangleG⟶(G∗Fn​)/⟨⟨w1​,…,wm​⟩⟩

is injective. There is no torsion, countability, residual finiteness, or presentation hypothesis on GGG.

The paper also records an extension to arbitrary sets of variables and equations whose finite-support exponent rows are linearly independent over Q\mathbb QQ. Any purported collapse of a coefficient uses only finitely many relations, so the finite theorem applies to that witness.

M2, dated September 24, 2026, claims injectivity for every unimodular one-variable equation over every group. It then deduces the full Kervaire nontriviality statement: if G≠1G\ne1G=1, then

(G∗⟨t⟩)/⟨ ⁣⟨w⟩ ⁣⟩≠1(G*\langle t\rangle)/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle\ne1(G∗⟨t⟩)/⟨⟨w⟩⟩=1

for every word www, with no condition on its exponent sum.

For exponent sum d=±1d=\pm1d=±1, injectivity preserves the nontrivial coefficient group. For all other integers ddd, the quotient maps onto the nontrivial cyclic group Z/dZ\mathbb Z/d\mathbb ZZ/dZ, using Z/0Z=Z\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb ZZ/0Z=Z. Thus universal nontriviality covers even singular one-variable equations, while the claimed coefficient-injectivity theorem requires the stated nonsingularity condition.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the family resolves fundamental universal solvability questions by making rational independence of exponent rows sufficient for completely arbitrary coefficient groups.

The surprising point is the gap between the simplicity of the hypothesis and the complexity of the conclusion. Exponent sums discard all commutators and all coefficient positions. Nevertheless, the manuscript claims that their independence prevents every possible hidden relation from collapsing a nonidentity coefficient.

The theorem also removes approximation assumptions from the unitary approach. Finite-dimensional topology is still used, but the coefficient group itself need not embed into finite groups or admit finite-dimensional unitary approximations.

This is an existence theorem about extensions. It does not provide an algorithm that lists explicit solution words in the original group, nor does it require the larger group to retain all desirable properties of the original one.

6. The main idea

A collapsed coefficient would give a planar diagram

Suppose a nonidentity g∈Gg\in Gg∈G became trivial after imposing the equations. By the definition of normal closure, there would be a finite expression for ggg as a product of conjugates of relators and their inverses.

Draw a disk for each relator occurrence and connect occurrences of the same variable with opposite signs by rectangular bands. The remaining boundary segments carry coefficients. The manuscript carefully constructs these bands from level sets in a punctured disk, obtaining planar surfaces whose boundary curves read words in GGG.

The key obstruction says that on a connected such surface, one boundary word cannot be the only nontrivial boundary word. Removing innermost components then turns the supposed collapse into a contradiction.

Full row rank supplies a first conservation law. Since variable occurrences are paired with opposite signs, the signed number of disks of each equation type must be zero. Positive and negative copies of each type therefore occur in equal numbers. Their multiplicities may differ between types, which is why the system theorem needs more than the single-relator argument.

Measuring a boundary by spectral phase

Every group acts faithfully on the Hilbert space with one orthonormal basis vector for each group element, by left translation. This regular representation exists even for uncountable groups. The associated operator algebra has a faithful finite trace, a replacement for summing diagonal entries of a matrix.

For a unitary operator, think of each spectral value as e2πiθe^{2\pi i\theta}e2πiθ, with 0≤θ<10\leq\theta<10≤θ<1. The trace of these fractional angles defines a nonnegative phase quantity L(U)L(U)L(U). The manuscript proves the inequalities and detection property

L(UV)≤L(U)+L(V),L(U)=0⟺U=I.L(UV)\leq L(U)+L(V),\qquadL(U)=0\Longleftrightarrow U=I.L(UV)≤L(U)+L(V),L(U)=0⟺U=I.

The value zero at the spectral point 111 matters. This phase is not simply the absolute angle or an ordinary distance between operators.

Travel around the diagram boundaries can be encoded by a permutation weighted by coefficient operators. Computing its phase one boundary at a time produces a common combinatorial contribution plus a nonnegative term detecting the potentially nontrivial boundary word.

Mixing copies while keeping coefficients exact

The other estimate comes from finite-dimensional unitary matrices that mix copies of relator disks. In M2, a fixed-space incidence calculation chooses a mixing matrix that forces sufficiently many fixed directions.

M1 replaces this by several independent unitary variables, one for each relator type. A cohomological intersection calculation on their product uses nested nonzero minors of the exponent matrix. This is where rational nonsingularity enters and where different relator multiplicities are accommodated.

The resulting fixed-space lower bound gives an upper bound for the phase. Euler characteristic identifies the common constant in that estimate with the constant from the direct boundary calculation. The remaining nonnegative phase term must vanish, forcing the exceptional boundary word to be the identity.

The two uses of unitary operators are deliberately separate. Finite matrices mix a finite number of disk copies, while the group coefficients remain in their exact regular representation. No finite-dimensional approximation of the coefficient group is inserted between these steps.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Solutions are obtained in an overgroup. Even the elementary equation x2=ax^2=ax2=a may require adding a square root that is absent from the original group. The theorem does not say that every coefficient group is already closed under solving nonsingular equations.

For singular systems, coefficient injectivity can fail. The equation a=1a=1a=1, with a nonidentity coefficient and no occurrence of an unknown, simply kills aaa. Its exponent row is zero. The general theorem therefore cannot discard the independence hypothesis, although particular singular equations may still be solvable.

The Kervaire nontriviality conclusion is weaker than coefficient injectivity. A quotient can remain nontrivial while some original coefficients collapse; this explains why the zero-exponent case is not a nonsingular solvability theorem in disguise.

The universal statements impose no finite-dimensional, finite-overgroup, or computational efficiency conclusion for arbitrary GGG. Earlier results for special coefficient classes can contain such additional information. Understanding which further properties a solution overgroup can preserve remains a separate direction from the existence assertion summarized here.

8. Sources and further reading

Gerstenhaber–Rothaus’s 1962 theorem, Howie’s independent-system theorem, and Klyachko’s torsion-free unimodular result give the principal earlier solvability results. Chen’s surface-complexity approach explains the topological side of the problem.

For approximation-based results, see Nitsche–Thom’s universal solvability paper. Kawauchi’s proposed Kervaire resolution is the separate approach acknowledged by M2. The two source manuscripts below supply the precise operator and incidence statements used in the present family.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Nonsingular systems of equations over arbitrary groups (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Kervaire theorem for groups (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A hyperbolic group that cannot act geometrically on a CAT(0) space
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 257 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A group can look negatively curved from far away without arriving with a particular curved space on which it acts. Does that large-scale geometry guarantee a concrete geometric realization?

For a word-hyperbolic group, the strongest familiar examples come from trees and hyperbolic manifolds. In both cases the group acts properly and cocompactly by isometries on a space satisfying a precise curvature comparison. It has long been natural to ask whether every hyperbolic group admits such an action on some CAT(0), or even CAT(−1), space.

The manuscript claims a counterexample. Its group has a finite two-dimensional classifying space and a linear disk-filling inequality, yet admits no geometric CAT(0) action in any dimension. The obstruction survives replacing the original finite complex by any homotopy-equivalent finite simplicial complex.

2. Background and essential definitions

Large-scale negative curvature

Given a finite generating set, the Cayley graph of a group has one vertex for each element and edges for multiplication by generators. A group is word-hyperbolic if geodesic triangles in this graph are uniformly thin: each side stays within a fixed distance of the other two sides.

For finitely presented groups, an equivalent condition is a linear isoperimetric inequality. A word representing the identity can be filled by a disk diagram, a tiled disk whose faces record defining relations. If the boundary has length ℓ\ellℓ, linear filling means that the number of faces needed is at most

Area⁡≤Cℓ\operatorname{Area}\leq C\ellArea≤Cℓ

for one fixed constant CCC. The constant may depend on the presentation. This is a combinatorial statement about how efficiently relations explain a null word.

A finite cell complex is aspherical when its universal cover is contractible. It is then a classifying space for its fundamental group: its loops encode the group, with no additional higher homotopy. The theorem here supplies a finite two-dimensional simplicial complex, built from vertices, edges and triangles, with this property.

CAT(0) geometry and actions

A geodesic space is CAT(0) if each geodesic triangle is no thicker than its Euclidean comparison triangle. This gives convexity of distance, unique geodesics, and contractibility. CAT(−1) uses comparison triangles in the hyperbolic plane and is a stronger curvature condition.

An isometric action is geometric when it is proper and cocompact. Properness means that only finitely many group elements can move a given compact set to meet itself. Cocompactness means that translates of one compact set cover the space. A metric space is proper if its closed bounded subsets are compact; completeness means that every Cauchy sequence converges.

These action hypotheses matter. The theorem does not forbid the trivial action on a point, which is not proper for an infinite group. Nor does it assert that every action on every CAT(0) space has a fixed point.

Why a finite metric model would produce an action

If a finite complex has a compatible locally CAT(0) geodesic length metric, its universal cover inherits a global CAT(0) metric. Here compatible means that the metric induces the given topology, and a length metric measures distance through path lengths.

Deck transformations of the universal cover give a geometric action of the fundamental group. Thus excluding geometric actions also excludes finite locally CAT(0) models. The same implication applies to CAT(−1) models.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Linear filling entered geometric group theory as a group-theoretic form of negative curvature in Gromov’s development of hyperbolic groups. The associated realization problem asks how far that combinatorial curvature can be upgraded to an actual metric model.

Many important classes admit such models. Free groups act on trees. Fundamental groups of closed hyperbolic manifolds act on hyperbolic space. Cubulation, which constructs actions on spaces assembled from Euclidean cubes, supplies further CAT(0) realizations.

Random groups also provide positive examples. Ollivier and Wise proved that in the standard density model, density below 1/61/61/6 yields free cocompact actions on CAT(0) cube complexes with probability tending to one as relator length grows. Thus randomness and hyperbolicity do not by themselves produce a curvature obstruction. The new construction needs relations designed for an additional purpose. Ollivier–Wise

Brady and Crisp established earlier dimension obstructions. They constructed two-dimensional torsion-free hyperbolic groups that cannot act properly on proper two-dimensional CAT(0) spaces, and examples where CAT(0) and CAT(−1) dimensions differ. Such a theorem leaves open the possibility of an action in a larger dimension. The present manuscript claims an obstruction independent of dimension. Brady–Crisp

A separate line of work uses energy and averaging to study actions of random groups. Gromov and Izeki–Nayatani developed harmonic-map methods; Izeki, Kondo and Nayatani obtained fixed-point results for target classes satisfying specified nonlinear spectral bounds. Toyoda supplied relevant bounds for prescribed finite families of certain CAT(0) spaces, with constants depending on the family.

The quantifier changes in the new problem: a hypothetical target space can be chosen after the group is constructed, with no dimension bound or previously fixed spectral constant. The manuscript’s statistical estimates are designed to remain valid for every such later choice.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The September 25, 2026 manuscript claims the existence of a finite connected two-dimensional aspherical simplicial complex KKK and a constant C<∞C<\inftyC<∞ such that every combinatorial loop of length ℓ\ellℓ in its universal cover bounds a disk diagram with at most CℓC\ellCℓ triangular faces.

At the same time, its fundamental group

G=π1(K)G=\pi_1(K)G=π1​(K)

admits no proper cocompact isometric action on a proper complete CAT(0) space. The linear filling statement makes GGG word-hyperbolic.

The paper deduces that no finite simplicial complex homotopy equivalent to KKK admits a locally CAT(0) geodesic length metric inducing its topology. Consequently, no such finite model admits a compatible locally CAT(−1) metric either.

The construction is an existence argument. The manuscript explicitly does not give an effective size for KKK. The filling constant belongs to the selected finite presentation; a common constant for every group in the auxiliary sequence is not required.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the result resolves a fundamental geometric realization problem by separating word hyperbolicity from geometric CAT(0) actions altogether.

The finite two-dimensional classifying space strengthens the contrast. The obstruction does not come from lacking a finite topological model, nor from needing to discard higher homotopy before constructing one. Even with a finite aspherical model and efficient fillings, the desired metric geometry is claimed to be impossible.

The conclusion also allows the entire finite model to change within its homotopy type. It therefore says more than “this particular triangulation has no suitable metric.” Adding dimensions, subdividing, or choosing another finite homotopy model cannot create the excluded geometric action.

This is distinct from the Artin-group CAT(0) obstruction in family 254. Here the group is specifically word-hyperbolic, so the theorem directly addresses the gap between large-scale negative curvature and metric comparison geometry.

6. The main idea

Relations sparse enough for filling, rich enough for obstruction

The construction begins with the incidence pattern of the projective plane over the two-element field. This small geometry has seven points and seven lines, with three points on each line. The paper modifies its incidence graph by doubling selected point vertices and treating one incidence asymmetrically.

Edges receive signed generator labels. Closed walks in selected labelled graphs become relations. Small subgraphs, called fans, are selected first; a larger labelled graph is admitted only when its required fans have already been selected. Four-letter relations close certain two-edge paths into squares, while six-letter relations control individual generator displacements in hypothetical actions.

This nested sampling creates dependencies. If several large graphs share a fan, its probability cost can only be charged once. A disk diagram can also use the same relator repeatedly. The counting argument tracks both repeated relators and shared prerequisites with multiplicity weights.

Local estimates leave a positive deficit proportional to diagram area that must be paid for by boundary length. A planar-separator argument extends bounded-diagram estimates to arbitrary diagrams. This supplies the claimed linear filling inequality and asphericity without assuming any CAT(0) metric on the constructed complexes.

Statistics that apply to a space chosen later

The geometric obstruction compares labels in several matched copies of the incidence pattern. Ordinary approximate independence is not sufficient, because conditioning on shared labels can make some configurations rare.

The paper builds couplings in which selected conditioning labels agree, each graph match is nearly uniform, and additional labels are nearly independent uniform generators. The error is measured in total variation, which controls expectations of every bounded test function. Hence the same estimate applies to bounded distance-based tests from an action chosen after the random tables are revealed.

The six-letter relations give a uniform bound on each generator’s displacement after normalization. This makes the relevant tests bounded. Without that step, a small probability error could be magnified by a few arbitrarily large displacements.

Passing from energy estimates to an impossible configuration

Suppose infinitely many groups in the selected sequence admitted geometric CAT(0) actions. For each action, minimize the average squared displacement of the generators and rescale so that this positive energy has a common normalization.

Closed-walk relations realize the incidence graph by orbit points. Averaging estimates, using the statistical couplings, bound distances along short paths. Products and limits of these configurations produce a configuration in a complete CAT(0) space. The limiting space need not be proper; properness is used for the original actions.

In the limit, the square relations force exact two-step distance identities. Certain six-cycles acquire a common center, and the triangles from that center become flat. The doubled point vertices then determine four unit directions in the tangent cone at the center. A tangent cone records the infinitesimal geometry of directions and distances from a point.

Incidence constraints force one pair of these directions to have nonnegative scalar product. The exceptional incidence forces another pair to be opposite. Splitting the geometry along the resulting line exposes a flat square in a transverse part, which forces the first pair to be opposite as well. Its scalar product would then be −1-1−1, contradicting the earlier nonnegative bound.

The contradiction rules out infinitely many geometric actions in the chosen sequence. Thus a sufficiently late finite presentation provides the required example. The passage to a finite simplicial model preserves asphericity and transfers the linear filling inequality with a presentation-dependent constant.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem excludes proper cocompact actions on proper complete CAT(0) spaces. It does not classify actions that omit one of these conditions, and it is not a universal fixed-point theorem for all CAT(0) targets.

Its finite-model statement allows arbitrary finite simplicial complexes in the same homotopy type, but requires a geodesic length metric compatible with the given topology. These hypotheses are what let the universal-cover argument recover a forbidden geometric action.

The probabilistic construction chooses parameters for finitely many statistical tests before increasing the generator alphabet. A diagonal selection then handles progressively stronger lists of tests. The claimed existence result should not be read as an explicit small presentation or a practical sampling algorithm with a stated success threshold.

Finally, failure of CAT(0) realization does not remove the group’s hyperbolic features. Thin triangles, linear combinatorial fillings, and the finite aspherical model remain part of the conclusion. The point is precisely that these properties can persist while geometric CAT(0) realization fails.

8. Sources and further reading

Bridson–Haefliger’s book on nonpositive curvature develops CAT(0) geometry, group actions and covering-space consequences. Brady–Crisp’s dimension examples and Ollivier–Wise’s random cubulation theorem give important contrasting precedents.

For the energy method, see Izeki–Kondo–Nayatani’s work on random-group actions. Stark’s survey of hyperbolic boundaries records the realization questions in their recent context. The source manuscript supplies the nested sampling construction and the specific limiting incidence obstruction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A hyperbolic group with no geometric CAT(0) action (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: One relation, negative curvature, and finite special covers
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 258 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

How complicated can a group become when just one equation is imposed on freely generated elements? One-relator groups include free groups, surface groups, and groups with severe geometric distortion. A short presentation is no guarantee of simple geometry.

Gersten’s conjecture proposes a precise dividing line. Among finitely generated one-relator groups, are the familiar Baumslag–Solitar groups the only subgroup obstructions to hyperbolicity? A second question asks whether every hyperbolic one-relator group has, after passing to finite index, the particularly useful geometry of a compact special cube complex.

The two manuscripts claim yes to both. They also combine the second theorem with earlier work of Kielak and Linton to obtain virtual free-by-cyclic structure. The conclusion is unusually broad, but its wording requires care: the free kernel for a general one-relator group may have infinite rank.

2. Background and essential definitions

One relation and the obstruction groups

A one-relator group has a presentation

G=⟨X∣r⟩,G=\langle X\mid r\rangle,G=⟨X∣r⟩,

where XXX is a finite set of generators and rrr is one word in those generators and their inverses. The relation means that rrr, every conjugate of rrr, and all their consequences become trivial.

For nonzero integers m,nm,nm,n, the Baumslag–Solitar group is

BS⁡(m,n)=⟨a,t∣tamt−1=an⟩.\operatorname{BS}(m,n)=\langle a,t\mid ta^mt^{-1}=a^n\rangle.BS(m,n)=⟨a,t∣tamt−1=an⟩.

The relation identifies two possibly different powers of aaa by conjugation. For example, BS⁡(1,2)\operatorname{BS}(1,2)BS(1,2) contains the identity tkat−k=a2kt^ka t^{-k}=a^{2^k}tkat−k=a2k, exhibiting exponential distortion of powers. The case BS⁡(1,1)\operatorname{BS}(1,1)BS(1,1) is Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2, whose flat geometry is another obstruction.

A word-hyperbolic group has uniformly thin geodesic triangles in a Cayley graph. Such groups contain no Baumslag–Solitar subgroup with both parameters nonzero. The first manuscript claims the converse within the one-relator class.

Finite special cubical geometry

A cube complex is built by gluing Euclidean cubes along faces. Nonpositive curvature is a local condition ensuring that the universal cover is CAT(0), with geodesic triangles no thicker than Euclidean comparison triangles.

A special cube complex has additional control over its hyperplanes, the surfaces formed by joining cube midsections. An equivalent description useful here is that it admits a cubical local isometry to the Salvetti complex of a right-angled Artin group. A right-angled Artin group has one generator per vertex of a graph, with commuting relations for its edges. The local isometry preserves the relevant local cubical geometry and induces an embedding of fundamental groups.

A group is virtually compact special if a finite-index subgroup is the fundamental group of a compact special cube complex. Both qualifiers matter: the special model may require a finite cover, and compactness is stronger than merely embedding in a right-angled Artin group.

A subgroup is quasiconvex if geodesics between its elements stay within a fixed distance of it. This controls how subgroup geometry sits in the ambient hyperbolic group and is the condition needed in many cubical combination theorems.

Free-by-cyclic, with a rank convention

The manuscripts use a subgroup-closed meaning of free-by-cyclic:

1⟶K⟶H⟶Q⟶1,K free,Q≤Z.1\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow H\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow1,\qquad K\text{ free},\quad Q\leq\mathbb Z.1⟶K⟶H⟶Q⟶1,K free,Q≤Z.

The free group KKK may have infinitely many generators, and QQQ may be trivial. “Virtually” means that such an HHH has finite index in the original group. This is weaker than saying that a finite-index subgroup is a mapping torus of an automorphism of a finite-rank free group.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Magnus’s Freiheitssatz established that omitting an appropriate generator appearing in a one-relator presentation leaves a free subgroup. His subsequent solution of the word problem made induction through simpler presentations a central method in the subject.

Newman’s spelling theorem handles proper-power relators, the source of torsion in the classical one-relator setting, and yields hyperbolicity there. Thus the main new difficulty in the first manuscript lies in the non-power case, even though its final theorem includes all relators.

Gersten formulated the subgroup-obstruction conjecture in the early 1990s. Recent progress made the remaining gap more precise. Louder and Wilton developed negative-immersion methods, and Linton established hyperbolicity and virtual specialness in broad classes using one-relator hierarchies. Further criteria involved additional stability or primitivity-rank conditions. These did not automatically settle hyperbolicity for every Baumslag–Solitar-free one-relator group.

Combination theorems of Bestvina and Feighn explain when negatively curved pieces remain negatively curved after gluing. Brinkmann’s expansion theorem treats mapping tori of free-group automorphisms, and Mutanguha extended the Baumslag–Solitar criterion to ascending HNN extensions of finite-rank free groups under injective endomorphisms. The first manuscript extends the needed combination analysis to the more general splittings occurring in its one-relator induction.

The special-cube-complex story developed through Haglund–Wise, Wise’s quasiconvex hierarchy theorem, and Agol’s virtual special theorem. Wise had already proved virtual compact specialness for one-relator groups with torsion, resolving and strengthening an earlier residual-finiteness conjecture of Baumslag in that class.

For torsion-free groups, Linton’s work reduced the remaining problem to particular primitive extension groups and specified how a terminal result would propagate up a hierarchy. Kielak and Linton showed that virtual compact specialness would also give Wise’s proposed virtual free-by-cyclic conclusion for hyperbolic one-relator groups. The new second manuscript claims to provide that missing geometric hypothesis.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Both manuscripts are dated September 25, 2026.

M1 claims Gersten’s conjecture: every finitely generated one-relator group containing no subgroup isomorphic to BS⁡(m,n)\operatorname{BS}(m,n)BS(m,n), for any nonzero integers m,nm,nm,n, is word-hyperbolic. Negative parameters are included. In particular, excluding only visibly distorted examples while allowing Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2 would not satisfy the hypothesis.

The theorem includes trivial relators and proper-power relators and has no torsion-free assumption. Under its non-power graph-presentation hypotheses, M1 also records injectivity and quasiconvexity of Magnus subgraphs, crediting the established subgroup theorems used for that conclusion.

M2 claims that every word-hyperbolic one-relator group is virtually compact special. Precisely, some finite-index subgroup is the fundamental group of a finite nonpositively curved cube complex admitting a cubical local isometry into a finite right-angled Artin Salvetti complex.

M2 also claims the same conclusion for every hyperbolic ascending mapping torus

F∗ϕ=⟨F,t∣t−1ft=ϕ(f), f∈F⟩,F*_{\phi}=\langle F,t\mid t^{-1}ft=\phi(f),\ f\in F\rangle,F∗ϕ​=⟨F,t∣t−1ft=ϕ(f), f∈F⟩,

where FFF is free of finite rank and ϕ:F→F\phi:F\to Fϕ:F→F is injective, possibly nonsurjective.

Combining the one-relator theorem with Kielak–Linton gives a finite-index embedding

H↪Fd⋊αZ,H\hookrightarrow F_d\rtimes_{\alpha}\mathbb Z,H↪Fd​⋊α​Z,

where ddd is finite and α\alphaα is an automorphism. Restricting projection to Z\mathbb ZZ gives the free-by-cyclic sequence above. Its kernel H∩FdH\cap F_dH∩Fd​ may have infinite rank: subgroups of finitely generated free groups need not be finitely generated.

For the ascending mapping tori, M2 gives a stronger separate conclusion: a finite-index subgroup maps onto Z\mathbb ZZ with a finite-rank free kernel. The new homomorphism is not identified with the original ascending height.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the family supplies both a central hyperbolicity criterion and a strong geometric structure theorem throughout the hyperbolic one-relator class.

The first result identifies exactly what prevents hyperbolicity in this class through a family of embedded subgroup obstructions. The second connects hyperbolicity to finite covers, cube complexes and right-angled Artin groups.

Using established implications, M2 obtains integral linearity and residual finiteness for the whole group, not merely the chosen finite-index subgroup. Residual finiteness means that every nonidentity element survives in some finite quotient. It also records conjugacy-separation and quasiconvex-subgroup consequences, with their appropriate hypotheses.

This restricted positive theorem contrasts with the claimed general hyperbolic counterexamples in families 252 and 257. The one-relator assumption is doing substantial work; those broader phenomena cannot simply be imported into this narrower class.

6. The main idea

An induction that needs genuine expansion

The Magnus method rewrites a one-relator group as simpler pieces joined through free subgroups. An HNN extension, for example, adds a stable letter that conjugates one specified subgroup to another. Such a decomposition acts on a tree whose vertices represent the pieces and whose edges represent the gluing subgroups.

M1 uses a decreasing complexity measure to reach simpler one-relator vertex groups. Once a vertex group is hyperbolic, existing results provide quasiconvexity of the relevant free edge groups. The remaining task is to prove annular flaring: long corridors passing through successive pieces must expand rather than maintaining uniformly narrow sides indefinitely.

Failure of flaring is encoded by a free-group current, an invariant measure on pairs of distinct points at infinity, or equivalently on unoriented geodesic lines. Long nonexpanding corridors produce a stationary current whose typical lines can be transferred through the tree.

Intersection and rank bounds organize persistent path stabilizers into finitely many subgroup carriers. Returns to a carrier induce automorphisms with no periodic nontrivial conjugacy classes; Brinkmann’s theorem then forces expansion. This makes the carrier-line sets have zero current mass.

Zero mass is not the same as absence from the support of a measure. M1 addresses this distinction separately. It transports positive-mass neighborhoods along carrier returns. A failed transfer produces a long periodic overlap; a successful one would concentrate mass on a set already shown to have zero mass. Further control of whole periods excludes the periodic alternative.

The remaining support has only finitely many relevant branching-ray types. A return then creates infinitely many disjoint positive-mass translates inside a compact region, contradicting local finiteness. This supplies flaring and closes the hyperbolicity induction.

Building special quotients and recovering the original group

M2 first reduces the problem, using Linton’s hierarchy, to primitive extension groups. It uses M1 to establish hyperbolicity of certain embedded terminal groups and the geometry of their Magnus subgroups. This is a specific dependency: it does not assume that every finitely generated subgroup of a hyperbolic group is hyperbolic, which would be false.

The construction proceeds through suitable fillings, meaning quotients obtained by imposing extra relations in designated subgroups. The aim is to make these quotients virtually compact special while retaining enough information to recover specialness of the unfilled group.

Persistent intersections along the hierarchy are controlled by joint injections into finite-dimensional homology. Keeping the joint map, rather than only separate rank inequalities, distinguishes contributions from different paths. Periodic end groups are organized into peripheral subgroups, and exact intersection control makes the filled hierarchy sufficiently acylindrical: long tree segments have tightly constrained stabilizers.

Within the filled pieces, binary labels and attached panels build separating walls. These walls give enough boundary separation for a known cubulation criterion. Agol’s theorem then supplies virtual compact specialness of the filled groups.

Good quotients alone do not automatically imply that the original group is special. A separate recovery criterion uses selective fillings that retain prescribed finite coefficient data. That information is transferred into two opposite Novikov completions, formal series rings organized by increasing or decreasing values of a character to Z\mathbb ZZ. The two-sided homological control produces a finite-index subgroup with a finite-rank free kernel in the cases needed by the construction. Established cubulation and hierarchy results then recover specialness and propagate it upward.

The later general one-relator free-by-cyclic conclusion uses Kielak–Linton. It retains the possibly infinite-rank kernel, rather than extending the stronger intermediate fibering conclusion to every one-relator group.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The subgroup hypothesis excludes actual embedded Baumslag–Solitar groups, not just presentations that visibly contain their defining relation. The theorem is a structural criterion; it does not by itself give a stated efficient algorithm for detecting every such subgroup.

M1’s technical combination theorem has hypotheses on hyperbolic vertex groups, free edge groups, their intersections and rank behavior. It is not a theorem that every Baumslag–Solitar-free HNN extension is hyperbolic.

M2’s compactness and finite-index qualifications should both be retained. An abstract right-angled Artin embedding alone does not provide the claimed finite special model. Quasiconvex-subgroup consequences also cannot be silently upgraded to all finitely generated subgroups.

Finally, the finite rank of the ambient free group FdF_dFd​ does not make the general subgroup kernel finite rank. The stronger virtual finite-rank fibering statement is separately established for the hyperbolic ascending tori, and its character may differ from their canonical height. The related quadratic-filling problem for nonhyperbolic ascending tori lies outside these claims.

8. Sources and further reading

For the classical starting point, see Magnus’s Freiheitssatz and Newman’s one-relator spelling theorem. Linton’s hierarchy paper and primitive-extension reduction explain the recent reductions used here.

Haglund–Wise’s special cube complexes, Wise’s quasiconvex hierarchy monograph, and Kielak–Linton’s virtual free-by-cyclic theorem supply the geometric and fibering background. Mutanguha’s endomorphism theorem gives the earlier ascending-torus criterion.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Baumslag-Solitar-free one-relator groups are hyperbolic (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Virtual compact specialness of hyperbolic one-relator groups (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The same group can have actions with different costs
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 259 · Group theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Suppose a countable group acts on a probability space. Each point has an orbit, consisting of all points reachable by applying group elements. How many edges, on average, are needed to connect every orbit?

The answer is called the cost of the action. One may use different group moves on different measurable subsets, so the minimum can be much smaller than the number of generators in a presentation. The fixed-price problem asks whether all essentially free probability-preserving actions of the same group nevertheless have the same cost.

The manuscript claims a negative answer. It gives one finitely generated group with a Bernoulli action whose cost stays strictly above one, while actions obtained by adding a finite height coordinate have costs approaching one. The group is unchanged; the measurable organization of its orbits changes the minimum cost.

2. Background and essential definitions

Actions and orbit relations

A probability-measure-preserving action of a countable group Γ\GammaΓ on (X,μ)(X,\mu)(X,μ) assigns a measurable, measure-preserving bijection to each group element. The paper uses right actions, so (xg)h=x(gh)(xg)h=x(gh)(xg)h=x(gh).

The orbit relation is

RΓ↷X={(x,xg):x∈X, g∈Γ}.R_{\Gamma\curvearrowright X}=\{(x,xg):x\in X,\ g\in\Gamma\}.RΓ↷X​={(x,xg):x∈X, g∈Γ}.

It records which points are connected by the action, without recording which particular group element makes the connection.

An action is essentially free if every nonidentity element fixes a set of measure zero. After discarding one invariant null set, every remaining point has trivial stabilizer. This condition prevents stabilizers from artificially reducing the complexity of orbits.

Graphings and cost

A graphing is a countable collection of partial measure-preserving bijections

φi:Di⟶Ei\varphi_i:D_i\longrightarrow E_iφi​:Di​⟶Ei​

whose graphs lie inside the orbit relation. These are allowable edges between points in the same orbit. The graphing generates the relation if finite paths using the maps and their inverses connect all orbit-related points outside a null set.

Its cost is

C({φi})=∑iμ(Di),C(\{\varphi_i\})=\sum_i\mu(D_i),C({φi​})=i∑​μ(Di​),

and the cost of the relation is the infimum over generating graphings. An inverse edge is available for traversing a path; it is not separately charged when it is the inverse of a listed map.

Using every group generator on all of XXX gives an immediate upper bound. Better graphings can restrict expensive moves to small sets and reach those sets through other available moves. Cost is therefore a measurable optimization problem, not simply the size of a generating set.

A group has fixed price if this infimum is the same for all its essentially free probability-preserving actions. Free groups of rank rrr have fixed price rrr, while many groups with commuting or amenable structure have fixed price one.

Bernoulli actions and height extensions

The Bernoulli space [0,1]Γ[0,1]^\Gamma[0,1]Γ assigns an independent uniform random label to every group element. The group shifts the coordinate labels. Its action is essentially free; the paper restricts to the invariant set XXX of points with trivial stabilizer, which has full measure.

A finite height extension adds a uniformly distributed coordinate in Z/MZ\mathbb Z/M\mathbb ZZ/MZ. Group elements move both the Bernoulli configuration and the height. The finite coordinate does not introduce stabilizers because the Bernoulli coordinate already makes the action free.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Levitt introduced cost as an invariant of measured equivalence relations in the 1990s. Gaboriau developed its connection with group theory, including fixed-price results for free groups and a framework for calculating costs of relations assembled from simpler pieces.

These results showed that the invariant can detect substantial algebraic structure. A free group needs a definite average number of orbit edges, whereas commuting directions can let one restrict many moves to small complete sets and reuse them elsewhere. A complete set here means one meeting every orbit of the relation under consideration.

Many positive fixed-price theorems accumulated. The manuscript cites, among recent developments, Khezeli’s theorem that products of two infinite countable groups have fixed price one, Bevilacqua–Bowen’s metric criteria, and Slutsky’s criterion using small product neighborhoods of finite subsets. These results cover important classes without proving that every countable group has fixed price.

The new example deliberately combines two contrasting structures. A free factor supplies many independent directions, while a direct-product factor makes some directions cheap. They are glued along a common subgroup in a way that lets an extra finite height coordinate reduce the cost further.

The lower-bound method has another ancestry: Arzhantseva–Ol’shanskii developed graph-shortening arguments that force large generator rank in suitable groups. Kapovich and Schupp refined this approach. The manuscript connects such finite presentation estimates to graphings of a Bernoulli action, rather than relying only on an abstract cost formula for the amalgam.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The October 5, 2026 manuscript specifies

A=F(a,b1,…,b99),w=ab1ab2⋯ab99a,J=⟨b1,…,b99,w⟩≤A.\begin{aligned}A&=F(a,b_1,\ldots,b_{99}),\\w&=ab_1ab_2\cdots ab_{99}a,\\J&=\langle b_1,\ldots,b_{99},w\rangle\leq A.\end{aligned}AwJ​=F(a,b1​,…,b99​),=ab1​ab2​⋯ab99​a,=⟨b1​,…,b99​,w⟩≤A.​

Thus AAA is free of rank 100. It then forms

Γ=A∗J(J×⟨t⟩).\Gamma=A*_J\bigl(J\times\langle t\rangle\bigr).Γ=A∗J​(J×⟨t⟩).

An amalgamated free product glues two groups by identifying the displayed copies of JJJ. In this example, it can be viewed as adjoining ttt to AAA and requiring ttt to commute with every element of JJJ.

There is a height homomorphism χ:Γ→Z\chi:\Gamma\to\mathbb Zχ:Γ→Z with

χ(a)=1,χ(bi)=χ(t)=0.\chi(a)=1,\qquad \chi(b_i)=\chi(t)=0.χ(a)=1,χ(bi​)=χ(t)=0.

In particular, χ(w)=100\chi(w)=100χ(w)=100. The height is not zero on all of JJJ.

Let XXX carry the free Bernoulli action. On YM=X×Z/MZY_M=X\times\mathbb Z/M\mathbb ZYM​=X×Z/MZ, use the action

(x,r)g=(xg,r+χ(g) mod M).(x,r)g=(xg,r+\chi(g)\bmod M).(x,r)g=(xg,r+χ(g)modM).

The theorem claims a fixed constant η>0\eta>0η>0, independent of MMM, such that

Cost⁡(RΓ↷X)≥1+η,1≤Cost⁡(RΓ↷YM)≤1+99M(M>100).\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Cost}(R_{\Gamma\curvearrowright X})&\geq1+\eta,\\1\leq\operatorname{Cost}(R_{\Gamma\curvearrowright Y_M})&\leq1+\frac{99}{M}\qquad(M>100).\end{aligned}Cost(RΓ↷X​)1≤Cost(RΓ↷YM​​)​≥1+η,≤1+M99​(M>100).​

The paper gives explicit conditions defining a sufficiently small positive η\etaη. Choosing M>99/ηM>99/\etaM>99/η, as well as M>100M>100M>100, separates the two costs strictly. Exact values are unnecessary for disproving fixed price.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the example disproves the general fixed-price assertion, a central question about how much orbit complexity is determined by a group alone.

The phenomenon is particularly clear because the low-cost actions are finite extensions of a familiar Bernoulli action. A finite additional coordinate can organize orbit connections more economically, even though the action remains free and the acting group remains the same.

The theorem does not diminish the earlier fixed-price results for their respective classes. Instead, it identifies a limit to generalizing them. The group is an amalgam involving a product, not itself merely a product of two infinite groups to which a product fixed-price theorem would apply directly.

The argument also offers a bridge between measurable and finite mathematics: a lower bound for an infimum over all measurable graphings is extracted from generator-rank bounds in finite permutation models.

6. The main idea

Why the extra height coordinate makes edges cheap

Write B=J×⟨t⟩B=J\times\langle t\rangleB=J×⟨t⟩. Keep all ttt-edges, at cost one. Choose a small measurable set of measure ppp meeting every ttt-orbit and retain each of the 100 displayed generators of JJJ only on that set.

Because ttt commutes with JJJ, a point can travel along its ttt-orbit to the small set, apply a JJJ-generator there, and travel back. These edges generate the BBB-relation at cost 1+100p1+100p1+100p, arbitrarily close to one.

It remains to supply aaa-edges. In the height extension, keep them only at 99 consecutive heights, costing 99/M99/M99/M. The identity

w=ab1ab2⋯ab99aw=ab_1ab_2\cdots ab_{99}aw=ab1​ab2​⋯ab99​a

propagates availability to the next height. Starting at the first height, the 99 known aaa-moves, interspersed with available bib_ibi​-moves, reach the last missing aaa-edge. The available www-move reaches its endpoint by another route, so that edge is already generated.

Repeating around the finite height cycle supplies every aaa-edge. Letting ppp tend to zero gives the upper bound 1+99/M1+99/M1+99/M.

Measuring what remains after the common subgroup is free

For the Bernoulli action, let RAR_ARA​ and RJR_JRJ​ denote the relations from the subgroups. Define a relative cost

δX=inf⁡{C(E):RJ∨E=RA, E⊆RA}.\delta_X=\inf\{C(\mathcal E):R_J\vee\mathcal E=R_A,\ \mathcal E\subseteq R_A\}.δX​=inf{C(E):RJ​∨E=RA​, E⊆RA​}.

The join symbol means “generate a relation using both kinds of steps.” Thus δX\delta_XδX​ measures how much must still be paid to generate AAA-orbits when all JJJ-steps are supplied without charge.

Adapting Gaboriau’s deployment and compression methods, the manuscript claims

Cost⁡(RΓ↷X)≥1+δX.\operatorname{Cost}(R_{\Gamma\curvearrowright X})\geq1+\delta_X.Cost(RΓ↷X​)≥1+δX​.

The construction subdivides graphing moves into factor moves, enlarges the supplied relation and keeps exact track of the cost saved by compression. This relative estimate is proved for the setting at hand; simply subtracting known costs of the factor groups would not give the needed conclusion.

Finite models force positive relative cost

Take a large finite set VVV with a right action of the free group AAA by permutations. Set u0=1u_0=1u0​=1 and ui=ui−1abiu_i=u_{i-1}ab_iui​=ui−1​abi​. The finite model produces a group

DV=⟨xv (v∈V) | xvxvu1⋯xvu99=1 (v∈V)⟩.D_V=\left\langle x_v\ (v\in V)\ \middle|\x_vx_{vu_1}\cdots x_{vu_{99}}=1\ (v\in V)\right\rangle.DV​=⟨xv​ (v∈V) ∣ xv​xvu1​​⋯xvu99​​=1 (v∈V)⟩.

The symbols record aaa-steps after JJJ-steps have been made free. Let rk⁡(DV)\operatorname{rk}(D_V)rk(DV​) be the least number of generators of this group.

Along finite models in which each fixed nonidentity element of AAA fixes a vanishing fraction of points, the manuscript transfers Bernoulli graphings to the inequality

δX≥lim sup⁡rk⁡(DV)∣V∣.\delta_X\geq\limsup\frac{\operatorname{rk}(D_V)}{|V|}.δX​≥limsup∣V∣rk(DV​)​.

These are finite permutation models of AAA, not asserted finite quotient approximations of the entire amalgam Γ\GammaΓ.

Random permutations give models whose length-100 relation rows expand across many symbols and have few overlaps. The remaining task is a deterministic rank bound: a generating set that was too small could be represented by a minimal labelled graph, and the relations would force a long segment in that graph to admit a shorter replacement. This contradicts minimality without increasing graph rank.

Exceptional symbols are absorbed into their actual generated subgroup before shortening. All true relations of that coefficient subgroup are retained, even if it is not finitely presented. A planar word lemma controls the remaining letters while preserving those coefficient values. Expansion prevents the exceptional set from absorbing everything.

The result is a positive proportional rank bound, rk⁡(DV)≥η∣V∣\operatorname{rk}(D_V)\geq\eta|V|rk(DV​)≥η∣V∣ asymptotically. It forces δX≥η\delta_X\geq\etaδX​≥η and hence the Bernoulli cost lower bound.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The conclusion compares essentially free probability-measure-preserving actions on standard probability spaces. Removing freeness or changing the measure setting would define a different problem.

The displayed bounds show that the finite height-extension costs converge to one. They do not identify the exact cost for each finite MMM, nor do they assert that one particular finite height extension has cost exactly one. The Bernoulli action’s exact cost is likewise not determined by its lower bound.

The constants are chosen to make an expansion estimate work, not to optimize the gap or the number of generators. The construction settles existence as claimed; it does not classify all groups without fixed price.

The example also does not say that every finite extension of an action lowers cost. Its special relation and height homomorphism provide the propagation mechanism. Understanding which other groups and actions admit comparable savings is a separate question from this counterexample.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical foundations are Levitt’s On the cost of generating an equivalence relation (1995) and Gaboriau’s Coût des relations d’équivalence et des groupes (2000), both cited in the manuscript. For recent positive results, see Khezeli’s product theorem, Bevilacqua–Bowen’s metric criteria, and Slutsky’s product-neighborhood criterion.

Kapovich–Schupp’s account of the Arzhantseva–Ol’shanskii method gives background for the finite rank obstruction. The source manuscript below supplies the explicit group, the two actions, and the relative-cost transfer used in this construction.

Source manuscripts
