  • M1. OpenAI, A group without fixed price (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Continuous symmetries of manifolds must form Lie groups
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 304 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Rotations, translations and matrix groups describe familiar continuous symmetries. They are Lie groups: their parameters form smooth manifolds, and their group operations are smooth. Could a much less regular locally compact group act faithfully by continuous transformations on an ordinary finite-dimensional manifold?

The Hilbert–Smith conjecture says no. The underlying manifold is only topological, and the transformations need only be continuous. Differentiability, a preserved metric, and a free action are not assumed.

The manuscript claims the conjecture in every finite dimension. Its central step excludes faithful actions of the additive group of ppp-adic integers. The final contradiction has an elementary numerical shape: a fixed nonzero invariant cannot be divided into arbitrarily many equal parts if those parts must lie in a lattice with a fixed denominator bound.

2. Background and essential definitions

The groups and spaces in the statement

A topological nnn-manifold is a space locally homeomorphic to Rn\mathbb R^nRn. The theorem assumes it is connected, Hausdorff and second countable, and has no boundary. Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint neighborhoods; second countable means that the topology has a countable basis. These are standard conditions that exclude various pathological spaces.

A topological group is locally compact if every point has a compact neighborhood. A Lie group is a finite-dimensional smooth manifold whose multiplication and inversion are smooth. A countable discrete group can also be a Lie group of dimension zero; the conclusion does not require a positive-dimensional connected group.

An action is jointly continuous if the map

G×M⟶M,(g,x)⟼gxG\times M\longrightarrow M,\qquad(g,x)\longmapsto gxG×M⟶M,(g,x)⟼gx

is continuous in the pair of variables. It is faithful when only the identity fixes every point of MMM. A faithful action can have many fixed points for individual elements. This is weaker than a free action, which requires every point stabilizer to be trivial.

The p-adic integers

For a prime ppp, the additive group of ppp-adic integers is

Zp=lim←⁡kZ/pkZ.\mathbb Z_p=\varprojlim_k\mathbb Z/p^k\mathbb Z.Zp​=klim​​Z/pkZ.

An element is a compatible sequence of residues modulo p,p2,p3,…p,p^2,p^3,\ldotsp,p2,p3,…. Two elements are close when they agree modulo a large power of ppp. This makes Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​ compact and totally disconnected, with arbitrarily small nontrivial open subgroups pkZpp^k\mathbb Z_ppkZp​.

It is not a Lie group. Classical transformation-group theory reduces Hilbert–Smith to excluding its faithful actions. The reduction is about this specific compact group; it does not say that every non-Lie locally compact group is itself Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​.

Signature as a discrete quantity

For a nonsingular real symmetric matrix, the signature is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues. It is an integer and is additive under block sums. Witt groups package this kind of information by treating certain cancelling forms as zero.

The paper uses a sheaf-theoretic version. A sheaf records compatible local information over a space, and a direct image along a map can encode the topology of its fibers. Duality supplies analogues of symmetric forms. The essential feature for the argument is an additive invariant whose rational values still have uniformly bounded denominators.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hilbert’s fifth problem asked how far differentiability assumptions could be removed from the theory of continuous groups. Gleason and Montgomery–Zippin resolved the locally Euclidean group formulation in 1952, and Yamabe extended the structure theory of locally compact groups.

Hilbert–Smith is the action problem: the group is not assumed locally Euclidean, but acts faithfully on a manifold that is. The distinction is substantial. Properties of the space on which a group acts do not immediately become local coordinates on the group itself.

The one- and two-dimensional cases were classical. Pardon proved the three-dimensional case in 2013 using local three-manifold topology, incompressible surfaces and mapping class groups. His result allowed arbitrary stabilizers rather than replacing the action by a free or smooth one. Pardon’s theorem

Another route added regularity to the transformations. Bochner–Montgomery established the differentiable precedent. Repovš–Ščepin proved the Lipschitz case on Riemannian manifolds; further results covered specified Hölder and quasiconformal actions. These strengthen continuity by controlling distortion of distances.

Dimension-raising results of Yang and Bredon–Raymond–Williams helped motivate these metric approaches. For example, averaging a metric under a sufficiently regular action can constrain the dimension of the orbit space, conflicting with the dimension increase forced by a hypothetical ppp-adic action. Such arguments need their metric and dimension hypotheses.

There are also more specialized advances, including symplectic results using Floer theory. The present manuscript claims to remove action-regularity restrictions and treat every finite dimension without an assumed dimension bound on the orbit space.

Its signature method has a separate history. Verdier duality, Balmer’s Witt groups, Woolf’s sheaf-theoretic constructions, and Ranicki–Weiss’s local chain methods provide precedents for extracting topological invariants from local duality. The new ingredient claimed here is a uniform integral comparison strong enough to keep denominators bounded for the continuous maps arising from the action.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The September 23, 2026 manuscript states that a locally compact second-countable Hausdorff group acting faithfully and jointly continuously on a connected Hausdorff second-countable finite-dimensional topological manifold without boundary must be a Lie group.

The manifold may be noncompact, nonorientable, or nontriangulable. Fixed points and arbitrary stabilizers are allowed. For positive dimension, the main intermediate statement is that every jointly continuous action of Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​ on such a manifold has nonzero kernel and therefore factors through a finite quotient of Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​.

The last implication uses the closed-subgroup structure of Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​: a nonzero closed subgroup is open and has finite index. In dimension zero, a connected manifold is a point, and a faithful acting group is trivial.

The manuscript also records a dynamical consequence. Suppose a homeomorphism fff is almost periodic in the sense that its powers have compact closure in the homeomorphism group with the compact-open topology. Some positive iterate fmf^mfm is then the time-one map of a continuous real flow:

Φ:R⟶Homeo⁡(M),Φ(1)=fm.\Phi:\mathbb R\longrightarrow\operatorname{Homeo}(M),\qquad \Phi(1)=f^m.Φ:R⟶Homeo(M),Φ(1)=fm.

The compact closure of the powers becomes a compact abelian Lie group. Its identity component is a torus of finite index, and some iterate lies in that torus and hence in a one-parameter subgroup. The statement concerns an iterate, not necessarily fff itself.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the theorem resolves a foundational transformation-group problem in full finite-dimensional scope, with continuity as the only regularity of the action.

It would establish that a manifold constrains its locally compact symmetry groups much more strongly than local compactness alone does. The group must possess finite-dimensional smooth group structure even when the action is not assumed smooth.

The theorem does not say that the full homeomorphism group of a manifold is a Lie group: that group generally does not satisfy the local compactness hypothesis. Nor does it produce a smooth structure on the manifold or smooth every transformation. The rigidity concerns the acting group under the stated assumptions.

The method would also provide a way around the irregularity of orbit spaces. It obtains a discrete obstruction using well-controlled source and test spaces, while allowing the intervening quotient to be topologically complicated.

6. The main idea

Localize the hypothetical action

Assume a faithful Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​-action exists. Using the classical local reduction based on Newman’s rigidity theorem for periodic transformations, the paper passes to an open subgroup acting faithfully and orientation-preservingly on a connected invariant open subset OOO of one coordinate chart.

Choose an odd integer d>nd>nd>n, with d≥3d\geq3d≥3, and enlarge the local space to

W=O×Rd−n,W=O\times\mathbb R^{d-n},W=O×Rd−n,

with the action trivial on the added coordinates. This is a device for making odd-dimensional sphere tests available; it is not a regularity assumption on the original manifold.

Compactify WWW by one point, take its orbit space, and test that quotient by maps into finite-polyhedron spaces. A collapse map from SdS^dSd supplies a fixed compact source. The quotient itself is not assumed to be a manifold or to have a convenient dimension bound.

Build a lattice before dividing anything

The manuscript constructs an abelian group Ed(Sd)E_d(S^d)Ed​(Sd) of signature-type classes and an orientation class udu_dud​. After rationalization,

Ed(Sd)⊗Q=Qud.E_d(S^d)\otimes\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q u_d.Ed​(Sd)⊗Q=Qud​.

More importantly, it claims a positive integer LdL_dLd​ such that every original class has rational image in

1LdZud.\frac1{L_d}\mathbb Z u_d.Ld​1​Zud​.

This is the fixed lattice. Knowing only that the rationalized group is one-dimensional would be insufficient: rational numbers have arbitrarily large denominators.

The categories are generated by proper images of finite polyhedra under arbitrary continuous maps. Such images need not be constructible along a finite stratification, and their sheaf stalks need not have finite dimension. The paper develops duality, localization and homotopy invariance within this generated setting.

A comparison with more controlled semialgebraic maps first supplies ordinary signature integrality. Cutoff arguments and a doubling construction then bound the discrepancy between the two theories by a fixed power of two. A finite cover of the sphere gives the uniform denominator bound. Here “integral class” means a class before tensoring the abelian group with Q\mathbb QQ; the sheaf coefficients themselves are real.

Faithfulness produces arbitrarily many equal parts

Characters of Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​ take values in roots of unity of ppp-power order. For each kkk, the paper partitions the character information into pkp^kpk pieces and constructs corresponding integral signature classes.

There is a subtle extension issue: a projector defined away from the collapsed point need not extend as a direct-summand decomposition over that point. The manuscript instead uses the associated involution 2e−12e-12e−1 and a sum of forms on an existing object. Localization lifts the resulting class without assuming that the projector’s image extends.

Faithfulness supplies a region of the orbit space with pkp^kpk finite-quotient sheets. An odd-sphere homotopy argument concentrates a test map in that region after composing with a positive-degree sphere map. A coefficient symmetry then cyclically permutes the character pieces, making their rational classes equal.

The auxiliary degree may depend on the construction. It is cancelled only after rationalization; the original integral classes remain in the same fixed lattice. Their rational images sum to 4ud4u_d4ud​, so each is

4pkud.\frac4{p^k}u_d.pk4​ud​.

For pk>4Ldp^k>4L_dpk>4Ld​, this is a positive quantity smaller than the smallest positive lattice step ud/Ldu_d/L_dud​/Ld​. It cannot lie in the claimed lattice. The contradiction excludes the faithful ppp-adic action, and the classical reduction then gives Hilbert–Smith.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All topological hypotheses in the theorem matter to its stated scope: local compactness and second countability of the group; connectedness, finite dimension and the standard separation/countability conditions for the boundaryless manifold; and joint continuity and faithfulness of the action.

The proof does not replace faithfulness by freeness. Nor does it assume that orbit spaces admit triangulations, have dimension at most that of the manifold, or carry the duality theory used on the actual manifold sources and test spaces.

The odd-dimensional stabilization is an auxiliary construction. It is not a restriction to odd-dimensional original manifolds, and the manuscript treats both odd congruence classes modulo four in its invariant.

The conclusion leaves separate questions about smoothing an action, choosing invariant geometric structures, and quantitative bounds on symmetry groups. Its flow consequence likewise gives existence of a suitable iterate and a continuous flow, not an effective formula for either.

8. Sources and further reading

Pardon’s three-manifold theorem provides the earlier unrestricted low-dimensional result and the local reduction used here. Repovš–Ščepin’s Lipschitz theorem illustrates the distinct regularity-based approach.

Woolf’s Witt groups of sheaves gives background for the signature machinery. The source manuscript includes the classical locally compact group reduction, the precise generated categories, and the integral comparison on which its new obstruction depends.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Hilbert–Smith conjecture in every finite dimension (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Four-dimensional disk embedding and a duality group with no manifold model
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 305 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

In four dimensions, algebraically cancelling intersections need not be easy to remove geometrically. Two surfaces meet at isolated points, and a disk intended to cancel a pair of intersections can itself intersect the surfaces. This is a central difficulty in four-manifold topology.

The disk-embedding problem asks whether suitable intersection data and auxiliary dual spheres allow immersed disks to be replaced by disjoint embedded disks. The theorem is known under restrictions on the fundamental group. The first two manuscripts claim that removing those restrictions is impossible, even if the replacement disks may change their relative homotopy classes.

The third manuscript turns a related marked obstruction into a different counterexample: a group with the integral duality and finite classifying space expected of a closed aspherical four-manifold, but with no such manifold realization. The common theme is that strong algebraic information can still fail to produce the required four-dimensional geometry.

2. Background and essential definitions

Immersed disks and algebraic duals

An immersed disk is locally embedded but may have self-intersections. A proper disk in a manifold with boundary has its boundary on the ambient boundary and its interior in the ambient interior. A locally flat embedded disk has a neighborhood locally homeomorphic to the standard pair (R4,R2)(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)(R4,R2); it need not be smooth.

The fundamental group π=π1(M)\pi=\pi_1(M)π=π1​(M) records loops up to homotopy. To count intersections of surfaces, choose paths from them to a common basepoint. Each intersection then carries both a sign and a loop label in π\piπ. The equivariant pairing λ\lambdaλ adds these contributions in the group ring Z[π]\mathbb Z[\pi]Z[π], whose elements are finite integer sums of group elements.

Sphere maps gjg_jgj​ are algebraically dual to disks fif_ifi​ when

λ(fi,gj)=δij 1.\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}\,1.λ(fi​,gj​)=δij​1.

Here δij\delta_{ij}δij​ is one when i=ji=ji=j and zero otherwise, and 111 is the identity group element. Algebraic duality allows cancelling intersection pairs. Geometric duality would require exactly one actual intersection with the designated disk and none with the others.

A framing is a trivialization of the normal two-plane bundle. It records how a neighborhood twists. The reduced Wall self-intersection invariant μ~\widetilde\muμ​ records signed self-intersections with group labels, modulo the standard changes from reversing a loop and the identity contribution. Its target is an additive quotient, not a quotient by a group-ring ideal.

Good groups

In Freedman–Quinn theory, a group is called good when specified local disk operations can be performed with double-point loops becoming trivial in that group. This is a technical property designed to make the disk-embedding construction work.

A capped grope is a tree of surfaces attached along curves, with disks capping its terminal curves. Such objects organize repeated attempts to resolve intersections. Their double-point loops explain why the ambient fundamental group enters a problem that initially looks local.

Duality groups and manifold models

A closed oriented nnn-manifold has Poincaré duality, relating homology in complementary dimensions. A Poincaré complex satisfies the corresponding homological duality, including local coefficients, without necessarily being a manifold.

An aspherical space has contractible universal cover. It is a classifying space for its fundamental group, so its homotopy type is determined by that group. An oriented integral Poincaré duality group of dimension four has the algebraic finiteness and duality conditions summarized by

Hi(G;ZG)=0 (i≠4),H4(G;ZG)≅Z,H^i(G;\mathbb ZG)=0\ (i\ne4),\qquad H^4(G;\mathbb ZG)\cong\mathbb Z,Hi(G;ZG)=0 (i=4),H4(G;ZG)≅Z,

with trivial group action on the final copy of Z\mathbb ZZ, together with a finite resolution by finitely generated projective modules. Group-ring coefficients retain information from the universal cover; ordinary Betti-number symmetry alone would be much weaker.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Casson’s handle construction and Freedman’s recognition theorem established the simply connected topological foundation. A Casson handle is an infinite tower of immersed disks; Freedman’s theorem identifies it topologically, relative to its attaching region, with a standard open two-handle. This provides topological disks where smooth intersection-removal methods fail.

Freedman and Quinn developed the general framework using capped gropes and good groups. Freedman–Teichner proved that groups of subexponential growth are good, and Krushkal–Quinn gave another proof while recording a correction to the earlier height-raising argument. The known good-group class also has closure properties that include many exponential-growth groups, such as solvable groups. Growth rate alone therefore does not identify the boundary of the theory.

Powell, Ray and Teichner supplied a missing construction of output geometric dual spheres in the classical theorem. This correction concerns the dual spheres, separately from the height-raising correction. Their modern formulation gives the precise positive theorem that the new manuscripts seek to obstruct without the good-group assumption.

Link and surgery formulations provide further context. Weak and homotopy versions of the A–B slice problem admit important positive results by Krushkal and Freedman–Krushkal. They relax conditions that matter to actual embeddings. There are also positive surgery theorems for free fundamental groups under additional hypotheses on intersection pairings. The claimed counterexamples do not erase these restricted results.

The manifold-realization problem has its own finiteness distinctions. Wall asked whether Poincaré duality groups come from closed aspherical manifolds. Davis constructed integral examples that are not finitely presented, already excluding manifold realization in that unrestricted formulation. Fowler constructed finitely presented rational duality examples without finite classifying spaces.

M3 claims to avoid both explanations: its group has integral duality, is finitely presented, and already has a finite four-dimensional classifying space. Its obstruction concerns turning that finite Poincaré complex into a topological manifold of the same dimension.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

All three manuscripts are dated September 24, 2026.

M2 gives a framed disk counterexample. In a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold, it constructs finitely many proper generically immersed disks with disjoint embedded boundaries and framed algebraic dual spheres satisfying

λ(fi,gj)=δij 1,λ(gi,gj)=0,μ~(gi)=0.\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}\,1,\qquad \lambda(g_i,g_j)=0,\qquad \widetilde\mu(g_i)=0.λ(fi​,gj​)=δij​1,λ(gi​,gj​)=0,μ​(gi​)=0.

Nevertheless, it claims there are no pairwise disjoint locally flat replacement disks with the same boundary maps and induced boundary normal framings. No relative homotopy classes for the output disks are prescribed.

M1 gives a stronger boundary-only obstruction. Its specified boundary circles bound no pairwise disjoint proper locally flat disks at all, even when output framings and output dual spheres are not required. The input dual spheres satisfy the same algebraic conditions; each can individually be chosen smoothly embedded, although different spheres may intersect.

The vanishing conditions concern the dual spheres. The theorem does not require vanishing intersections among the input disks. M1 deduces that the free group F2F_2F2​ is not good, and neither is any group containing it. This deduction uses subgroup and quotient closure of goodness; it does not identify the counterexample manifold’s fundamental group with F2F_2F2​.

M1 also concludes that the unrestricted topological surgery and five-dimensional topological s-cobordism assertions for four-manifolds cannot both hold. That is a statement about their conjunction, not an identification of which separately formulated assertion fails.

M3 gives a manifold-realization counterexample. It claims a finitely presented oriented integral duality group GGG of dimension four with a finite oriented four-dimensional aspherical Poincaré complex QQQ, but no closed aspherical topological four-manifold with fundamental group GGG.

M3 specifically imports M2’s marked geometric and tensor package. The boundary-only headline of M1 is not a substitute for that more detailed input.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the family identifies fundamental limits to two major four-dimensional existence principles: unrestricted disk embedding and realization of finitely presented integral duality groups by manifolds.

The boundary-only statement is particularly strong. It cannot be avoided by choosing different homotopy classes or allowing a different normal framing for the replacement disks. The obstruction lies in the existence of any disjoint locally flat filling of the given circles.

The group-realization result is similarly stronger than a failure of smoothability. It excludes a closed aspherical topological manifold, despite providing a finite aspherical Poincaré complex with the expected integral duality.

The claims are dimension-specific. A counterexample in dimension four refutes an assertion quantified over all dimensions, but does not establish counterexamples in every dimension or invalidate surgery theorems under their established hypotheses.

6. The main idea

Encode boundary information before choosing disks

The first two constructions install a finite family of commutator relations in a smooth plumbing model. A commutator is [x,y]=xyx−1y−1[x,y]=xyx^{-1}y^{-1}[x,y]=xyx−1y−1; triple commutators record interactions among three inputs. The words become trivial if any input is deleted, and independent conjugating paths are included in the fixed data.

Capped gropes realize these relations geometrically. Removing neighborhoods of their base surfaces produces the ambient disk problem; compressed product tori supply algebraic dual spheres. The markings record based loops and paths in this initial construction. They do not impose extra unannounced conditions on hypothetical output disks.

If the requested embedded disks existed, their images would allow the manifold to be cut into pieces separated by smooth three-dimensional walls with torus boundaries. The cuts miss the locally flat disks, so ordinary smooth differential forms can still be used on the cut pieces.

Convert the cuts into incompatible algebra

The papers study deformations of flat connections, equivalently compatible matrix holonomies around loops, using SL2\mathrm{SL}_2SL2​, the determinant-one two-by-two matrices. Wall data give formal potentials whose derivative equations describe flatness. The potentials arise from Chern–Simons transgression, which relates boundary expressions to curvature in the interior.

Restriction from the two sides supplies complementary tangent data. The installed triple commutators force products to belong to actual gradient ideals. This is stronger than saying that the products vanish at every ordinary solution.

The distinction matters because the parameter rings contain nilpotent elements. For example, in a ring with s2=t2=0s^2=t^2=0s2=t2=0, the mixed term ststst may still be nonzero. Passing only to ordinary points would discard precisely such information. The arguments retain the mixed terms and their ideal-membership witnesses.

M2 uses a comparison with algebraic critical charts that preserves the marked holonomies. M1 develops a boundary-polarized replacement and correction argument suited to the unframed boundary obstruction. These are related strategies, but their input requirements and algebraic packages are not identical.

After algebraic replacement and specialization to positive characteristic, truncating coordinate powers makes the relevant differential-form complexes finite. The transverse data determine classes with nonzero pairing. The two families of cubic ideal relations force that same pairing, or a nonzero parameter product times it, to vanish. With sufficiently many wall directions, the claimed finite tensor obstruction gives the contradiction.

Turn a marked chamber into a closed duality complex

M3 starts with a chamber whose boundary has a specified map to a finite graph. Attaching three-cells along a hyperbolic basis of middle-dimensional spheres produces a Poincaré pair with graph homotopy type. The imported marked obstruction says that its boundary cannot be filled by a topological four-manifold with that graph homotopy type while preserving the boundary map.

A reflection construction assembles copies of the chamber into a closed aspherical Poincaré complex QQQ. An auxiliary CAT(0) model supplies the assembly-theorem inputs needed later; it does not itself provide a four-manifold model for QQQ.

Assume a closed aspherical manifold model existed. Stable surgery and a product comparison would then make prescribed sphere pairs standard after stabilization by copies of S2×S2S^2\times S^2S2×S2. The sphere markings must be retained: an unmarked stable equivalence would not supply the needed geometric data.

The paper lifts these data to a finite union of reflected chambers, caps all but the central boundary and removes the standard inner pairs. Direction control far from the central chamber arranges the remaining loop systems inside suitable contractible patches. This supplies the particular null-loop step needed for the remaining disk construction, rather than assuming goodness of the free chamber group.

Surgery would then produce exactly the forbidden marked graph-type filling. That contradiction rules out the hypothetical closed manifold model.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The input manifolds in the disk examples are smooth, but the forbidden output disks are topological and locally flat. Thus the claims are not merely smooth disk obstructions.

M2 preserves boundary framings; M1 removes that output requirement. Both allow changes of relative homotopy class. The marked loops in their constructions are essential to the arguments and should not be confused with additional restrictions on prospective disks.

The nongoodness conclusion for F2F_2F2​ does not explicitly produce a counterexample manifold with that exact fundamental group. The surgery/s-cobordism consequence also retains its logical limitation: the two unrestricted assertions cannot both be true.

M3 concerns integral, oriented duality in dimension four and excludes every closed aspherical topological manifold with the specified group. It does not classify all four-dimensional duality groups or answer the corresponding realization problem in each other dimension. Its finite Poincaré complex remains a valid homotopy-theoretic realization; the missing structure is the manifold structure.

8. Sources and further reading

Freedman–Quinn’s Topology of 4-manifolds develops the disk and surgery framework. Powell–Ray–Teichner’s disk theorem with dual spheres gives the modern positive statement and its group hypothesis.

For the realization problem, compare Davis’s duality constructions, Fowler’s rational examples, and Davis–Hillman’s relative realization results. The source manuscripts give the exact marked interfaces and finite algebraic obstructions summarized here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A boundary-only obstruction to four-dimensional disk embedding (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A marked tensor obstruction to four-dimensional disk embedding (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, A PD4 group without an aspherical manifold model (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A nontrivial knot remembers its surgery slope
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 306 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Remove a tubular neighborhood of a knot from the three-sphere. The remaining space has a torus boundary. Glue back a solid torus in a different way, and the result is a new closed three-manifold. This operation is Dehn surgery.

Could two genuinely different gluing slopes produce the same oriented three-manifold? If so, the surgery would be purely cosmetic: the changed slope would leave no detectable change in the oriented homeomorphism type.

The manuscript claims that this never happens for a nontrivial smooth knot in S3S^3S3. Earlier results had reduced the possible exception to surgery slopes −2-2−2 and 222 on a genus-two knot. The new argument targets that remaining case using two compatible gauge-theoretic counts, one forced to be nonzero and the other forced to have total boundary count zero.

2. Background and essential definitions

Slopes on a boundary torus

A smooth knot is an embedded circle K⊂S3K\subset S^3K⊂S3. Its exterior is

EK=S3∖int⁡(νK),E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(\nu K),EK​=S3∖int(νK),

where νK\nu KνK is a tubular neighborhood, homeomorphic to a solid torus.

The boundary torus has a meridian μ\muμ, going once around the knot, and a preferred longitude λ\lambdaλ, running parallel to the knot with linking number zero. A slope is an unoriented primitive curve class

pμ+qλ,gcd⁡(p,q)=1,p\mu+q\lambda,\qquad \gcd(p,q)=1,pμ+qλ,gcd(p,q)=1,

considered up to changing both signs. It is denoted p/qp/qp/q, with q=0q=0q=0 written ∞\infty∞. Dehn filling attaches a solid torus so that its meridian becomes this curve. Write the result as Sp/q3(K)S^3_{p/q}(K)Sp/q3​(K).

The meridional filling ∞\infty∞ restores S3S^3S3. Integer slopes have q=1q=1q=1, so the remaining candidates ±2\pm2±2 represent ±2μ+λ\pm2\mu+\lambda±2μ+λ.

What “the same” means

Purely cosmetic surgery requires an orientation-preserving homeomorphism between the two filled manifolds. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse; it need not respect the decomposition into a knot exterior and a solid torus.

In particular, the putative homeomorphism need not carry one surgery core to the other. Excluding only maps that preserve those cores or the exterior would be a weaker statement.

Orientation-reversing coincidences are called chirally cosmetic and form a different problem. The orientation condition in this theorem cannot be dropped.

Genus and basic invariants

A Seifert surface is a compact connected oriented surface in S3S^3S3 with boundary KKK. The knot genus g(K)g(K)g(K) is the smallest genus of such a surface. Genus two means that a minimal surface has two handles.

First homology is an elementary invariant of a filled manifold:

H1(Sp/q3(K);Z)≅{Z/∣p∣Z,p≠0,Z,p=0.H_1(S^3_{p/q}(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z,&p\ne0,\\\mathbb Z,&p=0.\end{cases}H1​(Sp/q3​(K);Z)≅{Z/∣p∣Z,Z,​p=0,p=0.​

It immediately distinguishes zero surgery from nonzero finite slopes, but it cannot separate −2-2−2 from 222: both have first homology of order two. The unresolved case therefore needs finer information.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Cosmetic filling questions were formulated in work of Gordon and in Kirby’s problem list, with Bleiler, Hodgson and Weeks developing the terminology and distinctions between different kinds of coincidence.

Gordon and Luecke proved that nontrivial surgery on a nontrivial knot cannot give S3S^3S3. This settles pairs involving the meridional slope. Boyer and Lines obtained obstructions from classical three-manifold invariants and the Alexander polynomial.

Heegaard Floer theory supplied stronger restrictions. The rational surgery formula of Ozsváth and Szabó, Wang’s genus-one result, and Wu’s work on same-sign surgeries progressively narrowed the possibilities. Ni and Wu showed that a purely cosmetic finite pair must have opposite slopes.

Hanselman used graded Floer information expressed through immersed curves to restrict possible pairs to ±2\pm2±2 or ±1/q\pm1/q±1/q, with the ±2\pm2±2 case requiring genus two. Daemi, Lidman and Miller Eismeier then used filtered instanton homology to exclude the ±1/q\pm1/q±1/q cases. Their result, together with the earlier work, leaves precisely the genus-two ±2\pm2±2 possibility, with further polynomial restrictions that the new paper does not need for its reduction. Filtered instanton result

Other approaches settle many classes or finite collections. Polynomial and quantum invariants give additional obstructions; results cover nontrivial cable, composite and pretzel knots. An equivariant theorem for strongly invertible knots requires the comparison map to commute with specified involutions, a restriction absent from the present claim.

Futer, Purcell and Schleimer combined invariants, hyperbolic estimates and verified computations to settle the conjecture through 19 crossings and in a one-cusped census. Their procedure does not guarantee a decision for every possible pair. These computational and special-class results provide substantial evidence and coverage, while the manuscript claims a uniform final argument for the remaining case.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The September 23, 2026 manuscript states that for every smooth nontrivial knot K⊂S3K\subset S^3K⊂S3 and every pair of slopes r,s∈Q∪{∞}r,s\in\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}r,s∈Q∪{∞},

Sr3(K)≅+Ss3(K)⟹r=s.S^3_r(K)\cong_+ S^3_s(K)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=s.Sr3​(K)≅+​Ss3​(K)⟹r=s.

The symbol ≅+\cong_+≅+​ denotes an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of the entire filled manifolds. No condition on surgery cores, peripheral curves, or exterior preservation is imposed.

The proof uses the earlier reduction rather than rederiving every slope restriction. It assumes a genus-two knot and an orientation-preserving identification between its −2-2−2 and 222 surgeries, then constructs a contradiction. Three-dimensional smoothing results allow that identification to be replaced by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism for the gauge-theoretic construction.

The manuscript’s analytic work concerns specially constructed four-dimensional cobordisms and parameter families. It does not claim a general new spinor Floer theory on every knot-surgery manifold as a prerequisite or consequence.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the theorem resolves the purely cosmetic surgery conjecture for all nontrivial knots in the three-sphere.

Dehn surgery is one of the main ways to construct closed three-manifolds. The claim says that for a fixed nontrivial knot, the oriented manifold remembers which slope was used, even when a comparison homeomorphism is free to disregard the visible surgery description.

The result also completes a long sequence of increasingly sharp restrictions. Its novelty is concentrated in the last possible configuration left by earlier Floer and instanton results. That concentration does not make the endpoint narrow: eliminating that case gives the full all-slopes theorem.

The two-count method is a further feature of the manuscript. It tries to arrange a nonzero ordinary instanton count and a one-dimensional spinor family within one compatible set of geometric and analytic choices, so that their boundary contributions can be compared directly.

6. The main idea

Count solutions on four-dimensional cobordisms

A cobordism is a four-dimensional space whose boundary contains the three-manifolds being compared. In gauge theory, one studies connections on bundles over such spaces, modulo changes of bundle coordinates called gauge transformations.

Instantons satisfy a curvature equation. Their solution spaces can be organized into Floer chain complexes at the boundary and maps associated with cobordisms. Suitable zero-dimensional solution spaces have signed counts; these counts can encode information invisible to ordinary homology.

Assuming the cosmetic identification, the paper assembles surgery cobordisms into a repeated closed arrangement. Ordinary surgery families provide maps that behave as units modulo two. The negative direction is more delicate: it uses an interval of metrics, a degree-two sphere test and a signed sum over two determinant lifts. The signs cancel two unwanted minimal lens-space contributions.

Symplectic caps and established Donaldson nonvanishing results provide a nonzero cap pairing. The paper moves the probing conditions into fixed final caps, away from the variable blocks. Repeating the construction on the free part of an integral Floer lattice, with congruences modulo a power of two, yields a nonzero integer count

Ω≠0.\Omega\ne0.Ω=0.

This is a count with signs and compatible determinant data, not just a claim that some solution exists.

Enlarge the equations by adding spinors

A spinor is an auxiliary field coupled to the connection through a Dirac operator. The manuscript repeats the arrangement so that the complex index nDn_DnD​ of that operator is positive while preserving the nonzero ordinary count.

Multiplication of a spinor by a complex phase gives a circle symmetry. Impose η=nD−1\eta=n_D-1η=nD​−1 complex phase conditions and divide by the effective circle action. The expected real dimension becomes

2nD−2η−1=1.2n_D-2\eta-1=1.2nD​−2η−1=1.

The desired output is therefore a compact oriented one-dimensional solution space, after handling its allowed boundary phenomena. An ordinary compact oriented one-manifold has total signed boundary zero: every interval contributes one positive and one negative endpoint. The gauge-theoretic argument aims to use the same conservation principle with the appropriate regularized counts.

Near an ordinary instanton, the phase directions form a complex projective space CPnD−1\mathbb{CP}^{n_D-1}CPnD​−1. Each phase condition represents twice its hyperplane class. The resulting instanton-link boundary contribution is consequently

2ηΩ2^\eta\Omega2ηΩ

up to one common orientation sign. Since Ω\OmegaΩ is a nonzero integer, this contribution cannot vanish over Q\mathbb QQ.

Account for every other possible end

The hard part is ensuring that other ends do not cancel this nonzero contribution. Connections may become reducible, meaning that they preserve a splitting into line bundles. Solutions may also break along long regions or concentrate curvature into bubbles.

The paper constructs simultaneous families of metrics using toric geometric pieces, together with a long spherical tube. Period and curvature estimates constrain possible line-bundle reductions. Index inequalities then exclude unwanted fixed and mixed degenerations, including parameter-family corners.

The analytic choices are made compatibly with the already established ordinary count. Energy bounds and compactness come before the regularization and dimension exclusions; the argument does not simply invoke a generic perturbation and assume that all boundary phenomena disappear.

The remaining ends involve one minimal cap separating along a lens-space boundary, without bubbles. Cylindrical gluing identifies their local neighborhoods. Their two determinant sectors cancel with the same orientation convention used in constructing the negative ordinary unit.

With those lens contributions cancelled and the other ends excluded, the total boundary relation would read

0=±2ηΩ,0=\pm2^\eta\Omega,0=±2ηΩ,

contradicting the nonzero ordinary count. This excludes the genus-two ±2\pm2±2 pair, and the earlier reductions supply the full theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The knot is smooth, nontrivial, and lies in S3S^3S3. The theorem is not a blanket assertion about arbitrary torus-boundary manifolds, links, or knots in other ambient three-manifolds.

The conclusion is explicitly orientation-preserving. Chirally cosmetic surgeries remain a different phenomenon and are not excluded by this statement.

The comparison map is unrestricted with respect to the surgery decomposition. This is stronger than an equivariant or core-preserving theorem, and it is why the ordinary manifold invariants and four-dimensional constructions are needed.

The proof’s intermediate necks have different roles. Some are long but finite surgery seams; the actual infinite boundary faces are specified sphere and lens-space cuts. The manuscript does not require general gluing at positive bubble levels or a general regular spinor Floer theory for the knot surgeries.

Finally, the theorem supplies a qualitative uniqueness result. It does not give a practical algorithm reconstructing the slope from a presentation of the filled manifold, an efficient complexity bound, or a classification of orientation-reversing coincidences.

8. Sources and further reading

Daemi–Lidman–Miller Eismeier’s filtered instanton paper gives the decisive prior reduction used here. The manuscript also cites Ni–Wu’s Cosmetic surgeries on knots in S3 and Hanselman’s Heegaard Floer homology and cosmetic surgeries in S3 for the preceding slope restrictions.

For the gauge-theoretic context, its references include Donaldson’s Floer Homology Groups in Yang–Mills Theory, Kronheimer–Mrowka’s Witten’s conjecture and Property P, and the nonabelian-monopole work of Feehan and Leness. The source below provides the particular compatible counts, metric families and boundary analysis summarized in this digest.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Purely cosmetic surgery on knots in the three-sphere (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Finite spectra that remove the first chromatic parameters
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 308 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Algebraic topology assigns algebraic invariants to spaces, but not every plausible algebraic object comes from a space or spectrum. A realization problem asks when a desired algebraic pattern has an actual topological model.

Smith–Toda complexes are a particularly sharp example. Brown–Peterson homology has a polynomial coefficient ring with generators p,v1,v2,…p,v_1,v_2,\ldotsp,v1​,v2​,… encoding successive chromatic phenomena. Algebraically, one can simply quotient by the first several generators. Topologically, realizing that quotient by a finite spectrum requires a sequence of genuine attaching maps.

The family claims such realizations at every fixed stage if the prime is allowed to depend on the stage. A second manuscript gives a specified-prime example: an ordinary finite V(4)V(4)V(4) at p=1009p=1009p=1009. In both statements, the listed parameters are killed to their first powers, not merely to some sufficiently large powers.

2. Background and essential definitions

From spaces to spectra

Suspending a based space adds a dimension in a controlled way. Repeated suspension often makes homotopy problems more stable and algebraic. A spectrum packages this stabilized setting, allowing suspension to be inverted and generalized homology theories to be represented by objects.

A finite CW spectrum is built from finitely many sphere cells by stable attaching maps. “Finite” refers to this cell construction, not to having finitely many homotopy groups or finitely many elements in every invariant.

At a prime ppp, localization makes every integer not divisible by ppp invertible. The ring

Z(p)={ab∈Q:p∤b}\mathbb Z_{(p)}=\left\{\frac ab\in\mathbb Q:p\nmid b\right\}Z(p)​={ba​∈Q:p∤b}

retains ppp-primary information. In these papers, a finite ppp-local spectrum means a retract of the ppp-localization of a finite CW spectrum. A retract is a direct summand in the homotopy-theoretic sense.

Brown–Peterson homology

Brown–Peterson theory, denoted BPBPBP, is a generalized homology theory related to complex cobordism. At the prime ppp, its coefficient ring is

BP∗=Z(p)[v1,v2,…],∣vi∣=2(pi−1).BP_* = \mathbb Z_{(p)}[v_1,v_2,\ldots],\qquad |v_i|=2(p^i-1).BP∗​=Z(p)​[v1​,v2​,…],∣vi​∣=2(pi−1).

The vertical bars give the degree. The viv_ivi​ are Hazewinkel generators, a standard choice of coordinates. Chromatic homotopy theory organizes stable phenomena through successive parameters of this kind.

For a spectrum XXX, the graded group BP∗XBP_*XBP∗​X is a module over BP∗BP_*BP∗​. It also has a comodule structure over the algebra of cooperations BP∗BPBP_*BPBP∗​BP. This additional structure records how the homology interacts with the operations of the theory; specifying only the underlying module would leave part of the realization problem unanswered.

A Smith–Toda complex V(n)V(n)V(n) is a finite ppp-local spectrum with

BP∗V(n)≅BP∗/(p,v1,…,vn),BP_*V(n)\cong BP_* /(p,v_1,\ldots,v_n),BP∗​V(n)≅BP∗​/(p,v1​,…,vn​),

including the canonical quotient comodule structure and a generator in degree zero. Fixing that degree rules out silently shifting the entire spectrum.

Killing a parameter requires a map

The cofiber of a map is the stable analogue of attaching a cone to make that map null. If a self-map of a spectrum induces multiplication by a nonzerodivisor viv_ivi​ on its homology, the cofiber exact sequence gives the quotient by viv_ivi​.

The algebraic generators form a regular sequence: each next generator is a nonzerodivisor after quotienting by its predecessors. This computes the answer once the self-map exists. It does not construct the map. That gap between algebraic multiplication and an actual topological map is the central difficulty.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Milnor and Novikov established the polynomial structure of complex cobordism coefficients. Brown and Peterson introduced BPBPBP, Quillen identified the formal-group structure behind cobordism, and Hazewinkel supplied explicit integral coordinates. These results explain the algebra that the Smith–Toda problem asks topology to realize.

The mod-ppp Moore spectrum, the cofiber of multiplication by ppp on the sphere, gives V(0)V(0)V(0) at every prime. Classical work of Adams, Smith and Toda constructed V(1)V(1)V(1), V(2)V(2)V(2) and V(3)V(3)V(3) for p>2p>2p>2, p>4p>4p>4 and p>6p>6p>6, respectively.

Hopkins–Smith periodicity provides generalized Moore spectra at arbitrary finite stages when suitable higher powers of the initial generators are allowed. Those exponents are chosen as part of the construction. Requiring all of them to be one is a stricter problem; the new family does not claim to be the first arbitrary-stage finite realization with freely chosen powers.

The manuscripts cite the September 2023 version of Culver–Zhang, which recorded existence of V(4)V(4)V(4) as open at every prime. They also distinguish ordinary finite realization from chromatically localized constructions. Kato, Shimomura and Shimomura obtained a related localized object at 1009 with v5v_5v5​ inverted. Inverting a parameter changes the target and does not supply the unlocalized finite spectrum claimed here.

There are genuine nonexistence results at fixed primes. Nave proved that for p≥7p\geq7p≥7, V((p+1)/2)V((p+1)/2)V((p+1)/2) does not exist, and that V((p−1)/2)V((p-1)/2)V((p−1)/2), if it exists, cannot be a ring spectrum. The first obstruction changes its stage with ppp; the second concerns additional multiplicative structure. Neither contradicts existence at each fixed stage with a suitably chosen prime.

Barthel, Schlank and Stapleton developed asymptotic algebraicity through ultraproducts in chromatically localized categories. M1 uses a related large-prime viewpoint but claims to retain ordinary finite spectra before chromatic localization, which is essential to its conclusion.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Both manuscripts are dated September 23, 2026.

M1 claims all-stage existence with a varying prime. For every integer n≥0n\geq0n≥0, there is a prime ppp and a finite ppp-local spectrum XXX such that

BP∗X≅BP∗/(p,v1,…,vn)BP_*X\cong BP_* /(p,v_1,\ldots,v_n)BP∗​X≅BP∗​/(p,v1​,…,vn​)

as graded comodules, with the canonical quotient coaction and bottom generator in degree zero.

The order of quantifiers is

∀n ∃p ∃X.\forall n\ \exists p\ \exists X.∀n ∃p ∃X.

It is not a statement that one prime works at every stage. The theorem does not provide an explicit bound on the necessary prime or assert a multiplication on the final spectrum.

M2 claims a specified-prime realization of V(4)V(4)V(4). At p=1009p=1009p=1009, it constructs an ordinary finite ppp-local spectrum with

BP∗X≅BP∗/(1009,v1,v2,v3,v4),BP_*X\cong BP_* /(1009,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4),BP∗​X≅BP∗​/(1009,v1​,v2​,v3​,v4​),

with the same comodule and degree conventions. The number 1009 is chosen to make the inequalities in its obstruction calculation sufficiently generous; the manuscript does not claim it is the smallest possible prime.

The two methods are distinct. M1 uses a varying-prime construction and finite descent; M2 works at the stated prime through an Adams–Novikov obstruction calculation.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the family resolves the first-power realization problem at every fixed stage when the prime may vary, and supplies a concrete prime for the first stage beyond the classical V(3)V(3)V(3) constructions.

These spectra would give finite topological models with especially simple Brown–Peterson homology. They isolate chromatic layers with no extra powers inserted into the defining quotient, making them sharper objects than generalized Moore spectra with larger exponents.

The claim also advances a broader realization theme: a regular algebraic quotient can be produced by actual maps while retaining the cooperation structure, not merely matched as a graded list of groups.

The varying-prime theorem and the explicit 1009 theorem provide complementary information. One reaches arbitrary fixed stages without a numerical prime bound; the other locates a particular realization at a named prime. Neither supplies a classification of all primes and stages where Smith–Toda complexes exist.

6. The main idea

M1: construct a finite diagram across varying primes

M1 forms an ultraproduct of ordinary ppp-local stable categories over the odd primes. An ultrafilter specifies which collections of primes count as large; the construction is not a numerical average of primes.

In fixed homotopy degrees, the resulting mapping objects become rational. But the degrees 2(pj−1)2(p^j-1)2(pj−1) themselves vary with ppp, and discarding that variation would lose the attaching classes. Formal weights retain it.

The paper builds a finite sequence of cofibers, beginning with multiplication by ppp. To construct each next attaching class, it uses a ppp-fold permutation power with a cyclic group and its affine symmetries acting on the factors.

The comparison between a power of a cofiber and the expected cofiber diagram grows with ppp. A central claim is that one uniformly chosen Euler map kills the whole comparison object. An Euler map is a sphere map associated with a representation; inverting it makes the power construction exact in an auxiliary setting.

The desired attaching class must nevertheless be recovered before inversion. Otherwise the result might exist only after localization. The manuscript normalizes the power on universal coefficient algebras, preserving selected nullhomotopies as well as homotopy classes. Connectivity estimates and a finite Koszul construction control the needed comparisons. A Koszul construction is the algebraic mechanism that successively kills a specified sequence while recording the associated nullhomotopies.

Detect the first powers and descend to one prime

Construction and detection are kept separate. Complex cobordism power operations identify the leading term of the newly constructed class with the next coefficient of the formal-group ppp-series, the series encoding multiplication by ppp in the formal group law.

Passing through the ordinary multiplicative projection to BPBPBP identifies the generated ideals with (p,v1,…,vn)(p,v_1,\ldots,v_n)(p,v1​,…,vn​). The argument does not assume that this projection preserves the power operations used earlier.

For fixed nnn, only finitely many attaching maps, cofiber sequences, unit maps and specified homotopies are needed. They descend together to a common large set of primes. Choosing one prime there gives actual finite cofibers in the ordinary ppp-local category.

Regularity then calculates the whole homology module at once. There is no need to intersect infinitely many sets of primes, one for each homological degree. The bottom sphere map determines the canonical quotient coaction and places its generator in degree zero. Full commutative structure in the ultraproduct is not asserted to descend to the final spectrum.

M2: eliminate the obstructions at 1009

M2 first constructs Y=V(3)Y=V(3)Y=V(3) with a binary product and a two-sided unit. Associativity of that product is not needed for the final step. A sphere map detecting v4v_4v4​ can then be multiplied by YYY to give the required self-map.

The Adams–Novikov spectral sequence starts from algebraic data in BPBPBP-homology and progressively tests which classes come from actual stable maps. A candidate may be killed by a differential on a later page. Thus being an algebraically allowable coefficient does not by itself produce the sphere map.

The paper lists the possible differential targets of v4v_4v4​. A finite filtered calculation reduces them to four cases. The first is excluded by a relation involving the next coefficient and an injective multiplication. Two others are handled through Frobenius-kernel calculations, using the ppp-th-power structure in characteristic ppp while tracking both polynomial and exterior generators.

The final target requires a topological relation involving a power of the first beta-family sphere class and certain low-filtration classes. Cyclic extended powers and an averaging retract provide the relation. Crucially, the manuscript bounds the page on which the corresponding products vanish. Eventual vanishing in homotopy alone would not rule out the prospective differential at the required time.

Once v4v_4v4​ survives, the spectral-sequence edge supplies a sphere map with the desired Brown–Peterson image. The binary product extends it to a self-map of YYY; its finite cofiber has the claimed quotient homology. The unit again fixes the comodule structure.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Ordinary finiteness is part of both theorems. A realization only after inverting a chromatic parameter, or a compact object only in a localized category, is not the same conclusion.

The statements kill each listed generator to its first power. They do not replace the established higher-power periodicity constructions, and those constructions alone do not imply these first-power claims.

Neither paper requires a product on the final spectrum. Intermediate algebra or binary products are tools in the constructions, not a promise of associative or commutative ring structures on every V(n)V(n)V(n). Nave’s multiplicative nonexistence results therefore remain a separate constraint.

M1 leaves the prime unspecified for a general stage. M2 specifies 1009 for V(4)V(4)V(4) without optimizing it. Determining the exact existence range, minimal primes, and possible multiplicative structures remains beyond the stated conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

Hopkins–Smith’s periodicity theorem supplies the higher-power background. Compare Smith’s bordism realization work, Toda’s classical spectrum constructions, and Nave’s nonexistence theorem.

Culver–Zhang’s September 2023 version records the earlier V(4)V(4)V(4) question, while Kato–Shimomura–Shimomura’s localized realization has the different target discussed above. Ravenel’s Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres develops the coefficient and spectral-sequence background.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Finite Smith–Toda Complexes at Varying Primes (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A finite Smith–Toda complex V(4) at the prime 1009 (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Large-scale topology can disappear under coarse assembly
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 307 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

An index theorem translates topology into information about operators. A simple prototype is the Fredholm index, the dimension of a kernel minus the dimension of a cokernel. In coarse geometry, the analogous index takes values in the K-theory of an algebra of operators that only connect points a controlled distance apart.

The coarse assembly map performs this translation for topology visible at large scales. Rational injectivity asks whether a non-torsion topological class can disappear completely under the translation.

The two manuscripts claim that it can, even for spaces assembled from finite graphs with a uniform bound on vertex degree. The September manuscript treats the ordinary reduced Roe algebra. The October manuscript strengthens the conclusion to the maximal Roe algebra, where vanishing requires a separate argument in a larger norm.

2. Background and essential definitions

Looking at a space through increasing scales

A metric space is uniformly discrete if distinct points stay at least a fixed positive distance apart. It has bounded geometry if, for every radius RRR, all radius-RRR balls contain at most some fixed number of points depending on RRR.

A coarse disjoint union consists of finite graphs placed progressively farther apart, retaining their graph path metrics. At each fixed distance, only finitely many pairs of different components are close. Uniformly bounded vertex degree supplies bounded geometry for such a construction.

For a scale rrr, the Rips complex Pr(X)P_r(X)Pr​(X) fills in a simplex whenever a finite set of vertices has diameter at most rrr. Increasing rrr can fill holes that existed at smaller scales.

Coarse K-homology is the direct limit

KXi(X)=lim→⁡r→∞Kilf(Pr(X)).KX_i(X)=\varinjlim_{r\to\infty}K_i^{\mathrm{lf}}(P_r(X)).KXi​(X)=r→∞lim​​Kilf​(Pr​(X)).

Here KilfK_i^{\mathrm{lf}}Kilf​ is locally finite complex K-homology, a generalized homology theory suitable for noncompact spaces; the degree iii is taken modulo two. One can think of its classes as topological cycles carrying index-theoretic data. A class that vanishes at some later Rips scale is zero in the direct limit.

Consequently, exhibiting a hole at one scale is not enough to obstruct assembly. The relevant class must survive every larger scale.

Controlled operators and two completions

Place an infinite-dimensional auxiliary Hilbert space at each vertex of XXX. An operator has finite propagation if its matrix entry from xxx to yyy is zero whenever d(x,y)d(x,y)d(x,y) exceeds some fixed bound. Local compactness requires compact behavior after restricting near finite regions.

The reduced, locally compact Roe algebra C∗(X)C^*(X)C∗(X) is the closure of these operators in their usual operator norm. The maximal Roe algebra Cmax⁡∗(X)C^*_{\max}(X)Cmax∗​(X) instead uses the universal norm, taking all compatible representations into account. There is a canonical quotient map

Cmax⁡∗(X)⟶C∗(X).C^*_{\max}(X)\longrightarrow C^*(X).Cmax∗​(X)⟶C∗(X).

These are locally compact Roe algebras, with the auxiliary infinite-dimensional spaces; the statement is not silently about a different uniform Roe algebra.

Assembly maps topology to operator-algebra K-theory:

μX:KXi(X)⟶Ki(C∗(X)),\mu_X:KX_i(X)\longrightarrow K_i(C^*(X)),μX​:KXi​(X)⟶Ki​(C∗(X)),

and similarly for μXmax⁡\mu_X^{\max}μXmax​. K-theory records stable classes of projections or invertible operators. The assembly output is an index class, rather than necessarily one integer.

Injectivity is different from surjectivity

Injectivity says that no nonzero domain class is lost. Surjectivity says that every analytic target class comes from topology. The coarse Baum–Connes conjecture asks for an isomorphism; the rational coarse Novikov assertion asks for injectivity after tensoring with Q\mathbb QQ.

An infinite-order class remains nonzero after rationalization. A kernel class of infinite order therefore disproves rational injectivity, whereas a torsion kernel class alone would not.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Roe developed coarse index theory to study noncompact spaces through large-scale geometry. Higson and Roe formulated the coarse Baum–Connes framework, relating geometric hypotheses to the preservation and recovery of topological index information.

Yu proved assembly isomorphism for bounded-geometry spaces of finite asymptotic dimension, a large-scale analogue of dimension, and for bounded-geometry spaces admitting coarse embeddings into Hilbert space. Skandalis, Tu and Yu developed a groupoid approach to these embedding methods. Further positive results cover other controlled geometric settings.

There were earlier injectivity failures, but their hypotheses and domains differ. Yu constructed a kernel example without bounded geometry. Dranishnikov, Ferry and Weinberger obtained integral kernel classes for a map starting from locally finite K-homology; their relevant classes disappear under coarsening. The present manuscripts claim classes in the actual Rips direct limit for bounded-geometry spaces.

Higson, Lafforgue and Skandalis produced major assembly counterexamples in group and groupoid settings. Their coarse-space examples involving congruence expanders establish nonsurjectivity, a different failure from the kernel claimed here. A separate groupoid construction uses an odd topological class and a Kazhdan projection, providing a methodological precedent without already yielding the present coarse-space theorem.

Expander behavior also does not automatically imply noninjectivity. Willett and Yu proved coarse injectivity for graph unions whose girth tends to infinity, even when additional expansion makes surjectivity fail. Girth is the length of a shortest cycle. The new constructions have short cycles in their fibers and do not satisfy that large-girth hypothesis.

For maximal assembly, earlier work by Gong–Wang–Yu and Oyono-Oyono–Yu developed the analytic framework. Chen, Wang and Yu proved the maximal conjecture under fibred coarse embeddings into Hilbert space. The new October manuscript claims that bounded geometry alone is insufficient even for rational injectivity of this maximal version.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2, dated September 23, 2026, claims a counterexample to reduced coarse Novikov. It constructs a uniformly discrete bounded-geometry space XXX, a coarse disjoint union of finite connected graphs of uniformly bounded degree, and an infinite-order class

α∈KX1(X),μX(α)=0.\alpha\in KX_1(X),\qquad \mu_X(\alpha)=0.α∈KX1​(X),μX​(α)=0.

M1, dated October 5, 2026, claims the stronger maximal version. It constructs a graph union with the same geometric restrictions and an infinite-order class satisfying

μXmax⁡(α)=0.\mu_X^{\max}(\alpha)=0.μXmax​(α)=0.

Applying the canonical maximal-to-reduced quotient also kills the reduced index of this second construction. The converse implication would be invalid: a reduced index can vanish while its maximal lift remains nonzero.

The two papers use different graph constructions and different persistent classes. M2 uses boundary cycles over discrete disks. M1 uses a difference of classes at two torus ends. The strengthening is not obtained merely by relabelling the reduced target as maximal.

All K-theory and K-homology here are complex. The statements concern non-equivariant coarse assembly for metric spaces. They are not, by themselves, the classical Novikov conjecture for groups or a coefficient-free group assembly theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the family shows that bounded large-scale local complexity does not suffice to preserve rational topological information under coarse assembly, even in a concrete bounded-degree graph setting.

The persistence requirement is the important topological strengthening. The lost information is not an accidental small-scale cycle that disappears when the Rips scale increases. Every nonzero integer multiple is claimed to remain detectable in the coarse domain.

The maximal result strengthens the analytic side as well. Passing to a universal completion does not rescue injectivity for the constructed example. Its proof must therefore control operator constructions in that universal norm, beyond the reduced Hilbert-space realization.

The examples also clarify the role of positive hypotheses. Finite asymptotic dimension, coarse embeddings, fibred embeddings and other uniform conditions carry information that bounded geometry and finite fibers alone do not supply.

6. The main idea

Reduced assembly: winding persists, but averaging fills it

M2 begins with large triangular-lattice disks DjD_jDj​ and their boundary cycles CjC_jCj​. Over every disk vertex, place a finite congruence quotient of SL3(Z)\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb Z)SL3​(Z), the group of determinant-one integer matrices. Fibers are trivial at the boundary and grow deeper inside. Cayley edges connect points within fibers, while twisted matchings and reduction maps connect neighboring fibers.

The twists make short loops unable to wind around the disk center when jjj is sufficiently large relative to the chosen Rips scale. At each fixed scale, an integral winding cocycle pairs to one with the boundary class in sufficiently remote components. This detects every nonzero multiple of the family of boundary classes, giving an infinite-order coarse class α\alphaα.

Analytically, the fibers look different. Property (T) of SL3(Z)\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb Z)SL3​(Z) gives uniform approximation of projection onto constant vectors in all the finite fibers. Property (T) can be viewed here as a uniform spectral gap separating invariant vectors from the rest.

Averaging into the constant vectors defines an operator-algebra map from the disk union to the total graph union. The twists fix constant vectors and therefore do not obstruct this transfer. On the singleton boundary fibers, averaging is exactly the ordinary inclusion.

The boundary classes bound disks in the base. Naturality of assembly, followed by the averaging map, therefore makes their index vanish in the total graph union. The crucial feature is that this operator transfer need not come from a coarse map carrying an actual topological filling into XXX.

Maximal assembly: two torus ends that topology separates

M1 instead uses three-dimensional discrete tori BjB_jBj​ with increasing side lengths. Finite congruence fibers twist over the first two circle directions. Transport elements commute at one congruence level but fail to commute at a deeper level.

Each graph XjX_jXj​ has two copies of BjB_jBj​ at its ends, joined through a long middle region with nontrivial fibers. Moving toward either end reduces the fibers one congruence level at a time. This gradual change keeps vertex degrees uniformly bounded.

If β\betaβ is the family of torus K-homology classes and i+,i−i_+,i_-i+​,i−​ are the end inclusions, set

α=(i+)∗β−(i−)∗β.\alpha=(i_+)_*\beta-(i_-)_*\beta.α=(i+​)∗​β−(i−​)∗​β.

A line bundle over each continuous base torus has first Chern class given by the first two circle directions. Combined with an odd class from the third circle, it pairs to one with β\betaβ.

At any fixed Rips scale, the lifted commutator computation produces roots of this bundle of increasingly large power-of-two order over the middle. A uniform dimension bound at that scale converts those roots into integral K-theory divisibility. A Mayer–Vietoris argument, comparing the two ends through the middle, prevents any fixed nonzero multiple of their difference from vanishing. The integral argument precedes both the scale limit and rationalization.

Why the maximal index still vanishes

Projection from the middle onto the base induces a surjection on maximal Roe-algebra K-theory. The splitting horizontally transports operator entries and averages onto fiber constants using the Kazhdan projection. Averaging repairs the multiplicative defect of the transport.

These identities require maximal-norm estimates: agreement on finite vertex supports and uniform bounds at fixed propagation. Reduced-norm convergence alone would not establish the claimed maximal result.

Finally, the two end maps agree analytically after composition with the middle projection. Their distances grow, so they are not simply uniformly close maps. The paper places orthogonal copies of an operator at successive heights and rotates them one step, cancelling the common interior copies. Equality first holds modulo compact operators, and an injectivity statement in degree-one K-theory removes that quotient.

Surjectivity of the middle projection and naturality of assembly then give zero maximal index for the same endpoint difference already shown to have infinite order.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The examples are infinite metric spaces assembled from finite graphs. The finite nature of each component does not make the whole coarse assembly question finite-dimensional linear algebra.

Short fiber cycles remain present, so the constructions do not contradict injectivity theorems for graph unions with girth tending to infinity. Nor does arranging vertices into finite fibers establish the uniform embedding or fibration hypotheses of other positive results.

The claims concern the actual coarsened K-homology domain and locally compact Roe targets. Replacing either with a related domain or operator algebra can change the statement. The maximal and reduced conclusions must likewise be kept distinct.

The results identify failure of injectivity for particular spaces, not the fate of every assembly map associated with every group or geometry. Understanding which additional uniform geometric conditions retain injectivity remains a separate classification problem.

8. Sources and further reading

Roe’s coarse index monograph and Higson–Roe’s coarse Baum–Connes formulation provide the framework. Yu’s Hilbert-space embedding theorem and Chen–Wang–Yu’s maximal fibred-embedding theorem give major positive results.

Compare Higson–Lafforgue–Skandalis’s assembly counterexamples and Willett–Yu’s large-girth and expander analysis. The source manuscripts distinguish these predecessors from their claimed infinite-order kernels in the bounded-geometry Rips domain.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Failure of rational injectivity for maximal coarse assembly (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A counterexample to the coarse Novikov conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Exactly three survivors in the prime-three Kervaire family
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 309 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Stable homotopy theory studies maps between spheres after allowing repeated suspension. Its algebraic approximations produce many candidate classes, but some candidates disappear before they represent actual maps. Even a surviving candidate can leave uncertainty about the additive order of the represented element.

The prime-three Kervaire problem asks these questions for a distinguished sequence of candidates in the mod-three Adams spectral sequence. The manuscript claims a complete answer: exactly the classes with indices 0,2,30,2,30,2,3 survive, and each has a representative of additive order three.

The new positive case lies in stable stem 322. The negative result excludes every index at least four. This is the standard odd-primary Adams-family problem at the prime three, not the classical prime-two Kervaire invariant-one problem with its different indexing and dimensions.

2. Background and essential definitions

Stable stems and prime-three information

For sufficiently large NNN, repeated suspension stabilizes the groups of based maps

[SN+k,SN].[S^{N+k},S^N].[SN+k,SN].

Their stable value is the kkk-th stable homotopy group of spheres, written πkS\pi_k^SπkS​. The integer kkk is the stem. Addition comes from the stable homotopy structure, and an element has order three if it is nonzero but three times it is zero.

Working at the prime three isolates the part associated with powers of three. Positive stable stems are finite, so the relevant three-local and three-complete versions carry the same finite three-primary information for this question.

A spectral sequence is a sequence of tests

The mod-three Adams spectral sequence starts from algebra built from mod-three cohomology operations, organized in the Steenrod algebra A3\mathcal A_3A3​. Its first computational page is

E2s,t=Ext⁡A3s,t(F3,F3).E_2^{s,t}=\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal A_3}^{s,t}(\mathbb F_3,\mathbb F_3).E2s,t​=ExtA3​s,t​(F3​,F3​).

Here F3\mathbb F_3F3​ is the three-element field. The Ext group measures algebraic extension data; no calculation of Ext is needed to understand the statement. The indices are filtration sss and internal degree ttt, with stable stem t−st-st−s.

Successive pages have differentials that eliminate candidates. A nonzero class surviving to E∞E_\inftyE∞​ is called a permanent cycle and detects an associated-graded part of actual stable homotopy.

Associated-graded information is not the full group. For example, a filtered group of order nine can have two successive quotients of order three without itself being a direct sum of two order-three groups. Thus survival of a mod-three class does not automatically give a representative killed by three. The possible actual representatives form a detection coset, differing by higher-filtration elements.

The standard Kervaire candidates

The family studied here consists of classes

bj∈E22, 4⋅3j+1,j≥0.b_j\in E_2^{2,\,4\cdot3^{j+1}},\qquad j\geq0.bj​∈E22,4⋅3j+1​,j≥0.

They lie on the Adams two-line, meaning filtration two. Their candidate stable stems are

4⋅3j+1−2.4\cdot3^{j+1}-2.4⋅3j+1−2.

These distinguished classes arise from relations among primary cohomology operations. The problem is not to classify every element of three-primary stable homotopy, only the fate of this particular sequence and the order of its surviving representatives.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The terminology reflects an analogy with the classical Kervaire invariant. Browder related the prime-two framed-manifold question to particular squares on the Adams two-line. At odd primes, the standard classes bjb_jbj​ play a corresponding algebraic role, but the family and geometric conventions differ.

Toda proved that b1b_1b1​ supports a nonzero differential at every odd prime. Ravenel subsequently used formal-group and Morava-theoretic methods to exclude every bjb_jbj​ with j≥1j\geq1j≥1 at odd primes at least five. Prime three behaves differently.

The classes in stems 10 and 106 were known to survive with order-three representatives. The stem-106 case illustrates an important distinction between two spectral sequences. Its mod-three Adams class is detected by a corrected combination of Adams–Novikov beta-family terms, even though one obvious beta-family representative by itself supports a differential. Killing one chosen preimage does not necessarily kill the Adams class when other corrected preimages remain.

Selick formulated the strong odd-primary condition through maps involving a Moore spectrum and a nonzero primary operation. Amelotte connected this order-sensitive condition to decompositions of loop spaces and to multiplications on Anick spaces. These applications require actual order-three representatives, not merely permanence of an associated-graded class.

Hill, Hopkins and Ravenel proposed examining an action of the cyclic group C9C_9C9​ on height-six Morava E-theory at three. Their equivariant norm and fixed-point machinery provides tools for this program independently of its famous prime-two application.

Belmont and Ray established detection results and calculated relevant group cohomology under an explicit coefficient-action hypothesis. The present manuscript claims the needed completed coefficient model and finite-page differential constraints. It also departs from one proposed route: it claims that a literal full vanishing gap in degree −2-2−2 is false, and uses outgoing differentials instead. This distinction prevents a broad vanishing assumption from replacing the particular obstruction actually needed.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The September 24, 2026 manuscript defines two sets: the indices whose bjb_jbj​ survive, and the indices whose detection cosets contain an element of additive order three. It claims that both sets equal

{0,2,3}.\{0,2,3\}.{0,2,3}.

The resulting classification is:

IndexCandidate stemClaimed outcome
00010Survives; an order-three representative exists
11134Does not survive
222106Survives; an order-three representative exists
333322Survives; an order-three representative exists
j≥4j\geq4j≥44⋅3j+1−24\cdot3^{j+1}-24⋅3j+1−2Does not survive

The order statement is existential within each detection coset. It does not assert that every representative of the same associated-graded class has order three.
