Using Selick’s and Amelotte’s results, the paper also claims a complete product-decomposition criterion for a family of unstable spaces. Let S2n+1{3}S^{2n+1}\{3\}S2n+1{3} be the homotopy fiber of the degree-three map of a sphere, and let Ω\OmegaΩ denote the based loop space. For every n>1n>1n>1, after localization at three,

ΩS2n+1{3}\Omega S^{2n+1}\{3\}ΩS2n+1{3}

has a nontrivial product decomposition exactly when n∈{3,27,81}n\in\{3,27,81\}n∈{3,27,81}. Nontrivial means that both factors are noncontractible. A homotopy fiber records points together with paths witnessing their image at a chosen basepoint, so it retains the homotopical failure of the degree-three map to be an equivalence.

The manuscript further gives corresponding associativity results for Anick spaces and an explicit decomposition at n=81n=81n=81, through the cited earlier equivalences.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the theorem completes the standard prime-three Kervaire-family problem, supplying both a new high-dimensional survivor and a uniform exclusion of all later candidates.

The stem-322 element is not merely an algebraic entry in a chart. The claimed construction produces an actual stable sphere element killed by three. That order refinement is what activates the unstable-space consequences.

The negative branch also addresses a subtle detection issue. It retains all relevant corrected preimages rather than treating the fate of one beta-family expression as decisive. This matters precisely because the known stem-106 survivor already demonstrates that corrections can change the outcome.

The result organizes an infinite family with a finite list of exceptions. Its reach is substantial within stable homotopy theory, while remaining distinct from a computation of all three-primary stable stems.

6. The main idea

Use a detector sensitive to every possible survivor

The exclusion branch uses height-six Morava E-theory E6E_6E6​, a generalized cohomology theory encoding deformations of a height-six formal group. Its coefficients carry a C9C_9C9​-action. The homotopy fixed-point object E6hC9E_6^{hC_9}E6hC9​​ records invariance together with the necessary coherent homotopies, rather than taking only ordinary fixed coefficients.

The paper first claims that an actual sphere class detected by bjb_jbj​, for j≥2j\geq2j≥2, must have a nonzero finite-order image in this detector. This prevents a hypothetical survivor from simply escaping the test.

It constructs the completed coefficient action and analyzes the geometry of fixed deformations. Character and determinant constraints rule out certain possible maps in coefficient cohomology. Equivariant norms and geometric fixed points give finite Euler-class bounds, which impose deadlines for differentials after Euler localization.

Euler localization is the operation called Tate localization in this argument. It is not rationalization, and the proof does not rely on an unrestricted claim that every relevant localized homotopy group vanishes.

An outgoing differential is the decisive obstruction

A subtle point is the direction of a differential. Passing to a localized spectral sequence can introduce an incoming differential that kills an image even when the original class was genuine. Mere disappearance after localization would therefore not exclude a sphere class.

The paper instead forces every higher detector to support a nonzero outgoing differential. It organizes the remaining possibilities into a finite array of one-dimensional groups with tightly restricted degrees and characters. Translation classes are used only on pages where they and their inverses have been shown to survive.

The known b2b_2b2​ survivor fixes one incoming pairing in the array. The resulting differential constraints then force outgoing differentials on the pattern containing every detector with j≥4j\geq4j≥4. This contradicts the required image of an actual sphere class and supplies the infinite exclusion.

Construct the stem-322 element with its order intact

The positive branch starts from the known order-three stem-106 class. Let M=S/3M=S/3M=S/3 be the Moore spectrum, the cofiber in

S→ 3 S⟶M⟶ΣS.S\xrightarrow{\,3\,}S\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow\Sigma S.S3​S⟶M⟶ΣS.

The exact sequence associated with this cofiber keeps track of elements killed by three. This makes it useful for producing the strong order statement, not just an Adams permanent cycle.

A truncated extended cube, based on Toda’s construction, turns a Moore-spectrum map from the known class into a new map involving a four-cell spectrum. Its cone carries a nonzero primary operation P81P^{81}P81, an operation on mod-three cohomology that detects the desired Kervaire behavior.

The initial map has obstruction components preventing the required lift. The manuscript constructs a correction of Adams–Novikov filtration at least two with the same quotient image. Subtracting it makes the map lift to the Moore spectrum while preserving the nonzero primary operation. The resulting actual Moore boundary is a nonzero sphere element killed by three, hence of exact order three, detected by b3b_3b3​.

Finite calculations support the correction

The correction needs particular finite-page Adams–Novikov information: a cubic boundary, a multiplication that vanishes on an indicated page, and higher-filtration vanishing estimates.

The paper presents finite algebraic resolutions, product rules and elimination procedures for these assertions. It constrains possible differentials by affine equations and by the condition that a differential squares to zero. The stated bounds apply to every differential satisfying those constraints; the exposition does not select an arbitrary favorable differential from the possibilities.

These finite calculations serve the specific lifting argument. They are not presented as a full computation of all homotopy in the relevant range, and the positive Moore-spectrum construction is separate from the height-six exclusion branch.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the standard classes bjb_jbj​ in the mod-three Adams spectral sequence. It does not classify all order-three elements, all beta-family elements, or the classical prime-two Kervaire invariant-one classes.

Survival and additive order remain separate conclusions. The manuscript claims that each surviving coset contains an order-three representative, not that its associated-graded appearance alone determines the order of every representative.

The unstable product classification assumes n>1n>1n>1 and localization at three. Its index conversion is n=3j+1n=3^{j+1}n=3j+1, giving 3,27,813,27,813,27,81 from j=0,2,3j=0,2,3j=0,2,3; confusing these two index systems would shift the claimed dimensions.

The source’s rejection of a proposed full vanishing gap does not reject every other conjectural feature of the detector. It explicitly leaves separate periodicity and torsion assertions untouched. Its proof route uses finite-page outgoing differentials instead.

8. Sources and further reading

Ravenel’s odd-primary nonexistence theorem and Miller–Ravenel–Wilson’s Adams–Novikov calculations provide the classical algebraic background. Toda’s extended-power construction underlies the positive geometric branch.

Amelotte’s degree-three fiber and Anick-space results explain the order-sensitive unstable consequences. Belmont–Ray’s height-six detector study gives the recent program and conditional coefficient calculations addressed by the source manuscript.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Kervaire invariant problem at the prime three (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Recovering spaces from paths and all their higher homotopies
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 312 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A space can be explored by recording its points, paths between points, deformations between paths, and deformations between those deformations. Continuing indefinitely produces a hierarchy of geometric information. Can this hierarchy be described algebraically without losing the space’s homotopy type?

Grothendieck’s homotopy hypothesis proposes that suitably weak infinity-groupoids do exactly this. “Weak” means that composition laws hold through specified higher homotopies, rather than through rigid equalities at every level. The challenge is to make a particular algebraic definition recover the same homotopy theory as spaces.

Family 312 claims this for every Grothendieck coherator in the Ara–Henry convention. Its central assertion is deceptively concrete: adding a new cell together with a higher cell identifying it with an old one does not change any homotopy group. The difficulty is that the algebraic construction also generates many composites and coherence operations.

2. Background and essential definitions

Two continuous maps are homotopic if one can be continuously deformed into the other. The homotopy groups πj(X,x)\pi_j(X,x)πj​(X,x) record based maps from the jjj-sphere into a space XXX, up to homotopy. The set π0(X)\pi_0(X)π0​(X) records path components. A weak homotopy equivalence induces a bijection on components and isomorphisms on all these based groups.

A groupoid is a category in which every arrow is invertible. A space gives a familiar example: points are objects and homotopy classes of paths are arrows. This fundamental groupoid captures components and fundamental groups, but it forgets higher-dimensional information. A sphere such as S2S^2S2, for instance, has important two-dimensional homotopy despite being simply connected.

An infinity-groupoid adds cells in all dimensions. A 1-cell joins objects; a 2-cell joins parallel 1-cells; a 3-cell joins parallel 2-cells; and so on. “Parallel” means having the same source and target. The globular organization treats each cell as a disk with a source hemisphere and a target hemisphere.

Composition introduces choices. Three paths may be composed with either parenthesization. In a weak structure, the two composites are connected by a specified 2-cell. Relations among these 2-cells require 3-cells, and the process continues.

A coherator is an algebraic theory specifying enough such operations freely. Its models are globular sets equipped with interpretations of those operations. In the convention used here, a generating operation with output dimension jjj has a pasting diagram of dimension at most jjj. This restriction concerns the generators, not every composite operation.

Write DjD^jDj for the free algebraic model on one jjj-globe and ∂Dj\partial D^j∂Dj for its boundary. A model is cellular if it is built by successively attaching these globes along boundaries, allowing a transfinite sequence. “Free” is consequential: adjoining one generator also produces all composites demanded by the theory.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Algebraic models of spaces existed well before this conjecture. Simplicial sets, for example, recover the homotopy theory of spaces through geometric realization and the singular-complex construction. Grothendieck’s proposal in Pursuing Stacks asked for a model organized directly around paths and higher invertible cells.

Maltsiniotis made the coherator formulation precise. Berger’s work organized higher operations by globular pasting diagrams, while Ara developed homotopy groups and weak-equivalence tests for Grothendieck infinity-groupoids. Bourke established structural properties of freely generated theories, including faithfulness results needed to control their stages. These developments supplied a well-defined algebraic setting.

The word “weak” cannot simply be removed. Ara showed that, under a realization preserving homotopy groups, the simply connected types represented by strict globular infinity-groupoids are precisely products of Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces. Such a space has homotopy concentrated in one specified degree before products are taken. General spaces contain interactions that this rigid format misses.

Henry isolated a particular pushout conjecture and proved that it would imply both the canonical semi-model structure and the desired comparison with spaces. Lanari constructed substantial parts of a globular path object, but the compatible interpretation of every higher operation remained an issue. In dimension three, Lanari and then Henry–Lanari obtained the corresponding semi-model and comparison results for the relevant groupoids.

M1 presents its advance as the all-dimensional elementary-expansion theorem for an arbitrary fixed coherator in the stated convention. The final comparison uses Henry’s existing framework. It is therefore a resolution of a specific remaining algebraic obstruction, rather than the first discovery that spaces admit algebraic descriptions. These historical steps are documented in the primary references listed in Section 8 and M1.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 24 September 2026, fixes any such coherator CCC. Let XXX be a cellular CCC-infinity-groupoid, and choose any nnn-cell aaa, for n≥0n\geq0n≥0. Form

X+=X⨿DnDn+1,X^+=X\mathbin{\amalg}_{D^n}D^{n+1},X+=X⨿Dn​Dn+1,

where Dn→Dn+1D^n\to D^{n+1}Dn→Dn+1 selects the source face and Dn→XD^n\to XDn→X selects aaa. The pushout is formed inside models of the fixed theory.

Concretely, this adds a parallel cell a′a'a′ and a higher cell from aaa to a′a'a′. The theorem claims that

X⟶X+X\longrightarrow X^+X⟶X+

is a weak equivalence: components and all based homotopy groups are unchanged. The chosen aaa need not be a generating cell; it can already be a composite or coherence cell. When n=0n=0n=0, the operation adds an object and an arrow joining it to an existing object.

The paper then states that the category Mod⁡(C)\operatorname{Mod}(C)Mod(C) has the canonical left semi-model structure, with weak equivalences defined by those intrinsic homotopy groups. A semi-model structure provides the homotopical lifting and factorization machinery with specified cofibrancy restrictions; it should not silently be called a full model structure.

Finally, geometric realization and the fundamental-infinity-groupoid construction give a Quillen equivalence with spaces. In particular,

Mod⁡(C)[W−1]≃Ho⁡(Spaces),\operatorname{Mod}(C)[W^{-1}]\simeq\operatorname{Ho}(\mathrm{Spaces}),Mod(C)[W−1]≃Ho(Spaces),

where WWW is the class of weak equivalences and the notation on the left means that those maps are formally inverted. Different permitted coherators thus describe the same homotopy theory, even though their categories of algebraic models differ.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the claim completes a central version of Grothendieck’s program connecting geometry with weak higher algebra. It establishes independence from the particular freely chosen coherences within the stated convention.

This independence is conceptually valuable. Choosing composition operations and their higher compatibility data should be a way to describe a homotopy type, rather than an extra geometric invariant. The result says that these algebraic choices disappear after passing to homotopy theory.

The elementary-expansion formulation also identifies a useful local principle. A construction that visibly adds a redundant geometric cell remains redundant after freely completing the entire algebraic structure. That principle connects manageable cell operations to a global equivalence of theories.

6. The main idea

Why a retraction is insufficient

There is an evident map back from X+X^+X+ to XXX: send the new cell to the old one and the connecting cell to an identity. But a retraction alone does not prove that an inclusion preserves homotopy type. A space can be a retract of a much more complicated space.

The missing statement is that all the additional composites and coherences can be contracted in a way compatible with the original theory. It is not enough to contract the newly named generators separately.

Work below a cutoff, then descend

The manuscript first replaces the model by a controlled version in which every boundary above a chosen dimension qqq has a unique filler. Cells through dimension qqq are retained. This supplies a top dimension at which the expansion argument becomes immediate.

At fixed qqq, the proof descends in the expansion dimension nnn. The inductive hypothesis therefore controls expansions of higher dimension. Those already controlled expansions are used to duplicate generators and promote individual homotopies into compatible statements about whole free models.

A geometric intermediate step compares a finite tree-shaped pasting diagram with a string on the same vertices. The comparison is homotopic to the identity on generating edges. Higher expansions then extend that information to all coherences, yielding contractibility of the required tree models.

Build enough paths for the current step

These tree models provide partial cylinders: an nnn-cell moves through an (n+1)(n+1)(n+1)-cell while its lower boundary stays fixed. Higher cylinders describe compatible movements along shared faces. Their representing objects are shown to be contractible using a skeletal gluing calculation.

The paper then interprets the coherator’s operations in their original free stage order. This matters because that order is not the same as ordering operations by output dimension. An operation can depend on choices made at earlier stages across several dimensions.

The resulting partial path construction has two endpoint maps with the lifting properties needed for the current expansion. A retract argument yields the weak-equivalence claim. Finally, each fixed-boundary test involves only finitely many dimensions, so a sufficiently high cutoff retains both the test and its homotopy witness. Removing the cutoff recovers the all-dimensional result.

Henry’s established comparison then converts elementary expansions into the semi-model structure and the equivalence with spaces. The manuscript’s new work is concentrated in making the expansion and coherence control available for every permitted coherator.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem uses the Ara–Henry coherator convention, including its bound on generating arities and its free construction. It is not a statement about every definition ever called a weak infinity-category or infinity-groupoid.

The elementary pushout theorem is stated for cellular objects; the subsequent machinery treats the relevant cofibrant retracts. One should not discard these conditions and assert an arbitrary pushout theorem for every model.

Equivalence of homotopy theories does not mean that a space and its algebraic description are literally equal. Nor does it give a short finite presentation for every homotopy type, an algorithm for computing all homotopy groups, or a strictification to strict globular groupoids.

The conclusion leaves substantial practical questions: which coherators make particular computations convenient, how efficiently geometric constructions can be translated, and how this formulation compares explicitly with other higher-categorical models. Those questions concern the use of the equivalence, beyond the existence claim reported here.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 supplies the claims and the cutoff, tree, and partial-cylinder strategy. For the precise predecessors, see Ara’s homotopy theory of Grothendieck infinity-groupoids and strict-groupoid limitation; Henry’s algebraic models and pushout conjecture; and Lanari’s globular path construction. Maltsiniotis’s coherator formulation gives further foundational context.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Grothendieck homotopy hypothesis via elementary expansions (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Finite arithmetic in every degree of the local sphere
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 313 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Localization can make a mathematical object easier to study by focusing on one kind of information. It can also turn a finite object into something with infinitely many layers. The sphere spectrum illustrates both effects: it is the basic unit of stable homotopy theory, yet its chromatic localizations have homotopy in arbitrarily negative as well as positive degrees.

Family 313 asks whether each individual degree nevertheless contains only finitely much arithmetic data. At a prime ppp and height nnn, is every homotopy group of the local sphere finitely generated over the ppp-adic integers?

M1 claims an affirmative answer for every prime, every positive height, and every integer degree. It does not calculate all these groups. Instead, it asserts that each consists of finitely many ppp-adic directions together with finite torsion.

2. Background and essential definitions

The stable homotopy group of spheres in degree ttt is obtained by repeatedly suspending maps between spheres until suspension no longer changes the answer. A spectrum organizes this stable information. The sphere spectrum SSS is the unit for the smash product of spectra.

For a fixed prime ppp, Morava KKK-theory K(n)K(n)K(n) detects chromatic height nnn. One can think of heights as different periodic layers in stable homotopy theory. The localization LK(n)XL_{K(n)}XLK(n)​X retains precisely the information in XXX seen by K(n)K(n)K(n). Localization need not preserve connectivity, so negative-degree homotopy matters here.

The ring Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​ consists of compatible systems of residues modulo p,p2,p3,…p,p^2,p^3,\ldotsp,p2,p3,…. Its fraction field is Qp\mathbb Q_pQp​. A finitely generated Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​-module has the form

Zp r⊕⨁i=1sZ/pai,\mathbb Z_p^{\,r}\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{s}\mathbb Z/p^{a_i},Zpr​⊕i=1⨁s​Z/pai​,

for finite integers r,s≥0r,s\geq0r,s≥0 and positive aia_iai​. “Finitely generated” therefore does not mean a finite set: even one copy of Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​ is infinite. The theorem instead bounds the number of independent ppp-adic directions and makes the torsion subgroup finite in each degree.

A finite ppp-local spectrum is built from finitely many cells, allowing retracts, with primes other than ppp inverted. The mod-ppp Moore spectrum S/pS/pS/p is the cofiber of multiplication by ppp on the sphere. It plays the role of reduction modulo ppp, although derived constructions retain information about kernels as well as quotients.

The calculation uses Morava EEE-theory, whose coefficient ring contains formal deformation parameters. Its stabilizer group acts on those coefficients. Continuous group cohomology measures the obstructions to descent through that action; “continuous” keeps track of the ppp-adic and deformation-parameter topologies.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hovey and Hovey–Strickland explicitly asked the degreewise finite-generation question. At height one, classical calculations describe the local sphere using an Adams operation on completed topological KKK-theory. At height two and primes at least five, Hovey–Strickland’s analysis of Shimomura’s computations gives the required finiteness for finite torsion inputs, including the Moore spectrum.

Devinatz studied related homotopy fixed-point spectra for smaller stabilizer subgroups. His results used an “essentially finite rank” condition involving periodicity and torsion. Those are important partial approaches, but their hypotheses and finiteness notion differ from the all-height statement for the full local sphere.

A separate advance determined the rational answer at every prime and height. Barthel, Schlank, Stapleton, and Weinstein identify it with an exterior algebra on nnn generators in degrees 1−2i1-2i1−2i, for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n1≤i≤n. This determines potential free ranks, but rationalization cannot control integral torsion.

For example, the compact module

∏j≥1Fp\prod_{j\geq1}\mathbb F_pj≥1∏​Fp​

has exponent ppp and zero rationalization, yet is not finitely generated over Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​. Even a uniform bound on torsion exponent would therefore leave the principal finiteness question open.

The descent machinery was also largely available: Devinatz–Hopkins relate the local sphere to Morava homotopy fixed points, and existing descendability results provide a horizontal vanishing line on a finite page of the relevant spectral sequence. M1 identifies finite coefficient cohomology as the remaining input and develops a geometric argument to supply it. Its introduction gives the precise primary references for these earlier results.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 24 September 2026, states that

πtLK(n)Sp∧is finitely generated over Zp\pi_t L_{K(n)}S_p^{\wedge}\quad\text{is finitely generated over }\mathbb Z_pπt​LK(n)​Sp∧​is finitely generated over Zp​

for every prime ppp, every n≥1n\geq1n≥1, and every integer ttt. Here Sp∧S_p^{\wedge}Sp∧​ denotes the completed sphere.

Equivalently, the same conclusion holds for

πtLK(n)F\pi_tL_{K(n)}Fπt​LK(n)​F

for every finite ppp-local spectrum FFF. Finite cofiber sequences, suspension, and retracts transfer the sphere conclusion to these inputs. The Noetherian property of Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​ ensures that kernels, cokernels, and extensions preserve finite generation.

The algebraic theorem driving the argument says that the continuous stabilizer cohomology of the even Morava coefficients modulo ppp is finite in each cohomological and internal degree. It also treats a carefully specified larger class of coefficients arising from whole finite division-point schemes and associated constructions. It is not asserted for every imaginable semilinear coefficient module.

Combined with the earlier rational calculation, the result determines the free ranks. They are encoded by

Q⊗Zπ∗LK(n)S≅ΛQp(ζ1,…,ζn),∣ζi∣=1−2i.\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\pi_*L_{K(n)}S\cong\Lambda_{\mathbb Q_p}(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_n),\qquad |\zeta_i|=1-2i.Q⊗Z​π∗​LK(n)​S≅ΛQp​​(ζ1​,…,ζn​),∣ζi​∣=1−2i.

An exterior algebra has basis given by products of distinct generators, including the empty product in degree zero. Thus the rank in a degree counts subsets of these degrees with the required sum. The new finiteness assertion concerns the integral groups left after restoring torsion.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, this settles a basic structural problem about the arithmetic size of the local sphere, uniformly across primes and heights.

Degreewise finite generation is a foundation for further computation. It says that each answer can be described by a finite rank and finitely many finite cyclic summands, even though locating those summands may remain difficult. It also separates controlled integral information from the much weaker statement that the rational answer is finite-dimensional.

The method would connect a broad topological finiteness problem with geometry of formal groups and ppp-adic period spaces. The significance lies both in the uniform conclusion and in the claimed passage from geometric support calculations back to integral homotopy.

6. The main idea

Reduce integral finiteness to finite coefficients

The first target is finiteness of the local Moore spectrum’s homotopy groups. Morava descent organizes these groups using continuous stabilizer cohomology. Finite entries on its second page, together with the established finite-page horizontal bound, leave finitely many contributions to each resulting homotopy degree.

One must distinguish that later-page bound from finite cohomological dimension of the full stabilizer. At small primes, the stabilizer can contain ppp-torsion. The paper retains this possibility rather than imposing a large-prime hypothesis.

After treating S/pS/pS/p, finite power cofibers and derived ppp-completeness recover the integral group as a compact Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​-module. Compact Nakayama then turns finiteness modulo ppp into finite generation.

Induct through the deformation strata

The coefficient argument moves downward through formal-group heights. At a step, one deformation parameter is inverted, separating an open stratum from a deeper boundary stratum. The induction hypothesis controls the finite boundary strips. The remaining issue is cohomology on the open part.

A useful intermediate goal is countability. The original coefficient cohomology is compact and Hausdorff; in this setting, proving it countable forces it to be finite. But countability must hold at a sufficiently deep fixed finite marking level, not merely after taking an unlimited union of levels.

Markings choose compatible division-point data. A completed tower of such choices is interpreted using independent tuples of extensions of vector bundles on the Fargues–Fontaine curve. Compact-support calculations on that geometric space yield a finite stable image for a transfer operator.

Return from the completed tower

The transfer is a Cartier-type operation, related to Frobenius in characteristic ppp. Repeated application reduces pole orders up to a controlled loss. The manuscript chooses one normalization and one sufficiently large lattice that work through all subsequent iterates.

A Laurent-series model and residue pairing connect the geometric compact-support calculation with the transpose of this transfer tower. This controls the intersection of all late transfer images. It does not yet prove that the whole open-stratum cohomology is countable.

For that final step, the paper uses finite translation representations and a Koszul extension associated with their distribution algebra. If uncountable cohomology persisted in a highest offending degree, the resulting operation would have countable cokernel but would factor through every sufficiently late transfer image. The finite stable-image calculation would then force its image to be countable too, giving a contradiction.

Keeping a common finite marking level and uniform pole bounds is central to the argument as presented. Once countability descends to the original coefficients, compactness supplies finiteness and closes the height induction. The descent and completion steps then deliver the stated sphere theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is degreewise. It provides no uniform bound on ranks, generator counts, or torsion orders as the prime, height, or degree varies. It also does not compute the finite torsion summands.

The input extension is to localizations of finite spectra. Arbitrary dualizable or invertible local spectra cannot replace those inputs: the cited height-two literature already contains invertible objects whose homotopy is not of finite type. Thus this result has a different scope from the construction-class classification in family 311.

No chromatic splitting conjecture is assumed. Finite generation alone does not describe the maps joining different chromatic layers or imply a wedge decomposition of the local sphere. Those are separate questions, some addressed by the manuscripts in family 318.

The geometric coefficient class is also specific. Its closure properties are designed to survive the height induction and finite marking constructions. Extending the same finiteness assertion to a much larger class of continuous modules would require additional results.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 is the source for the theorem and the coefficient, transfer, and descent strategy. The original problem appears in Hovey–Strickland’s Morava K-theories and localisation and Hovey’s problem list. Devinatz’s earlier finiteness approach provides historical context. Li’s Invertible spectra of finite type explains why arbitrary invertible local objects require a separate analysis.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Finite generation for the K(n)-local sphere (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The topology of elementary subgroups detects a normal p-subgroup
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 310 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A finite group can contain many small abelian subgroups. Arrange those subgroups into a geometric object according to inclusion. Can the shape of that object reveal whether the original group has a nontrivial normal subgroup of prime-power order?

Quillen’s conjecture says that if this subgroup complex is contractible, then such a normal subgroup exists. The manuscript claims a stronger result: when the largest normal ppp-subgroup is trivial, the complex has nonzero reduced rational homology.

This turns a question about normality into one about cycles and boundaries. The odd-prime version was already established in work cited by the manuscript. Its all-prime conclusion completes the remaining prime-two cases through explicit cycles, dimension estimates and propagation from simple components to the whole group.

2. Background and essential definitions

The elementary subgroups

Fix a finite group GGG and a prime ppp. A ppp-subgroup has order a power of ppp. An elementary abelian ppp-group is a product

(Z/pZ)r,(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^r,(Z/pZ)r,

so it is a vector space of dimension rrr over the field Fp\mathbb F_pFp​, viewed as an additive group. Every nonidentity element has order ppp.

Let Ap(G)\mathcal A_p(G)Ap​(G) be the partially ordered set of nonidentity elementary abelian ppp-subgroups, ordered by inclusion. Its order complex has one vertex per subgroup, an edge for each strict inclusion, a triangle for each three-term strict chain, and higher simplices for longer chains.

Thus a simplex is not an arbitrary collection of commuting subgroups. It is a nested chain

E1<E2<⋯<Ek.E_1<E_2<\cdots<E_k.E1​<E2​<⋯<Ek​.

The largest normal ppp-subgroup of GGG is denoted Op(G)O_p(G)Op​(G), the ppp-core. A subgroup is normal when conjugation by every element of GGG preserves it. The ppp-core can be trivial even when GGG has many nontrivial ppp-subgroups.

Contractibility and homology

A space is contractible if it can be continuously deformed to a point. Reduced homology measures holes while removing the unavoidable degree-zero class of a connected nonempty space. A nonzero reduced homology class is a cycle that cannot be filled by a chain of one higher dimension.

Contractibility implies zero reduced homology, but the converse is false for general spaces. The manuscript’s rational nonvanishing claim therefore gives more information than merely proving noncontractibility.

The convention at the empty complex matters. The paper uses augmented reduced homology, with

H~−1(∅;Q)=Q.\widetilde H_{-1}(\varnothing;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q.H−1​(∅;Q)=Q.

If ppp does not divide ∣G∣|G|∣G∣, the subgroup complex is empty and Op(G)=1O_p(G)=1Op​(G)=1. This convention makes the main theorem include that case correctly; the empty space is not treated as a contractible point.

A small example

Take G=S3G=S_3G=S3​, the permutation group on three letters. At p=2p=2p=2, its three transpositions generate three distinct order-two subgroups, with no inclusions between them. The complex is three isolated points, so

H~0(A2(S3);Q)≅Q2.\widetilde H_0(\mathcal A_2(S_3);\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Q^2.H0​(A2​(S3​);Q)≅Q2.

There is no nontrivial normal two-subgroup. At p=3p=3p=3, the unique order-three subgroup is normal, and the complex is a single point. These are elementary instances of the two sides of the proposed characterization.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Brown studied the poset of all nonidentity ppp-subgroups and related its Euler characteristic to Sylow-subgroup information. Quillen proved that restricting to elementary abelian subgroups preserves the homotopy type, making the smaller poset sufficient for the topological question.

Quillen formulated the contractibility conjecture in 1978. He proved it for solvable groups, groups of elementary abelian ppp-rank at most two, and groups of Lie type in defining characteristic. In the solvable case with trivial ppp-core, his method gives homology in the largest possible dimension, a stronger property later used in reductions.

Aschbacher and Kleidman settled the almost-simple case. The remaining challenge was not simply to check more simple groups: one must understand how their extensions interact and whether a component’s nonzero homology survives in an ambient group.

Aschbacher and Smith developed reductions for primes greater than five, leaving specified elementary extensions of unitary groups. Piterman and Smith extended the reduction to all odd primes. Díaz Ramos proved the needed unitary statement and deduced the rational-homology assertion for every finite group at odd primes. The source explicitly credits this prior result; its direct unitary argument gives another route within the new framework. Díaz Ramos, version 6

At the prime two, further reductions constrained a minimal counterexample. Piterman and Smith showed that its components must admit particular outer involutions induced by the ambient group. Piterman eliminated additional exceptional and defining-characteristic cases, leaving specified classical components in characteristic at least five.

The new manuscript uses those reductions rather than claiming an independent classification-free proof. Its remaining work constructs cycles for the linear, unitary, symplectic and orthogonal cases, and develops a propagation argument ensuring that their information survives in the full subgroup complex.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The September 24, 2026 manuscript states that for every finite group GGG and every prime ppp,

Op(G)=1⟹H~∗(Ap(G);Q)≠0.O_p(G)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\widetilde H_*(\mathcal A_p(G);\mathbb Q)\ne0.Op​(G)=1⟹H∗​(Ap​(G);Q)=0.

The star means that at least one degree has nonzero augmented reduced homology. The theorem does not assert that every degree is nonzero, or that the nonzero group always lies in the largest possible degree.

A classical result gives the other direction relevant to contractibility: a nontrivial ppp-core makes the complex contractible. Thus the new nonvanishing statement would settle Quillen’s conjecture without restrictions on primes or composition factors.

The manuscript also records a coefficient consequence. Since the complex is finite, nonzero rational homology comes from a positive free rank in integral homology. The universal coefficient theorem then gives nonzero reduced homology over every field in the same degree. The empty case is handled by augmentation.

Consequently, acyclicity over any chosen field characterizes the existence of a nontrivial normal ppp-subgroup. This field-coefficient conclusion follows from rational nonvanishing and the classical contractibility direction; it is not a claim that all integral homology groups have been calculated.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. If correct, the theorem completes a central connection between finite-group structure and topology, in the stronger rational-homology form.

The subgroup complex contains only elementary abelian ppp-subgroups and their inclusions. The result says that this restricted information still detects a global property: the existence of a nontrivial normal ppp-subgroup in the entire group.

The rational strengthening supplies an actual homological witness when the core is trivial. It avoids a situation where the space is noncontractible for subtler reasons but all rational homology vanishes.

Historically, the new coverage must be located accurately. The all-odd-prime assertion is credited to the earlier theorem. The present family claims to finish the prime-two analysis and assemble a uniform all-prime conclusion, with cycle-construction tools adapted to the difficult remaining component types.

6. The main idea

Reduce a hypothetical counterexample to controlled components

Assume a counterexample exists and choose one of smallest group order, at a fixed prime. Every smaller group then satisfies the desired homological implication.

Published reduction theorems constrain the simple components of such a counterexample. A component is a quasisimple subnormal subgroup; in the relevant reduced cases the components are simple. Distinct components commute, giving a connection between component topology and centralizers.

A centralizer consists of elements commuting with a specified subgroup. Proper-subgroup induction supplies homology in appropriate centralizers, while a faithful elementary extension of the component supplies the other half of a product construction. Faithfulness here means that the extension acts injectively by conjugation on the component.

The difficult part is to preserve a nonbounding cycle when these local pieces are placed inside the full group. An inclusion of complexes can turn a nonzero class into a boundary, so local nonvanishing alone is insufficient.

Construct cycles from linear frames

For classical groups, a frame decomposes the underlying vector space into lines. When a bilinear or Hermitian form is present, the lines are chosen nondegenerate and mutually orthogonal as appropriate.

Independent scalar signs on these lines give elementary abelian projective subgroups. Their complete subgroup flags support apartment-like chains: combinatorial cycles associated with a coordinate decomposition.

The paper imposes relations between frames differing only within a two-dimensional plane. These relations make boundary contributions cancel. Additional commuting automorphisms introduce extra faces, whose cancellation becomes further linear equations on the frame coefficients.

The construction therefore needs a dimension estimate: there must be more available independent coefficient choices than the added cancellation conditions can remove. The estimate must remain useful as vector-space dimension grows over a fixed finite field.

The manuscript encodes merger trees of frame lines using multilinear Lie superbrackets, an algebraic bookkeeping device for combining pieces with signs. A Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt argument, together with a bound on the actual relation kernel, converts plane counts into the required lower bound. Supporting subspaces and their form types remain visible throughout the count.

The output is a nonzero cycle on actual full subgroup flags. Merely finding a nonzero parameter vector describing apartments would not suffice if all its resulting simplex coefficients cancelled.

Restrict and propagate without losing the witness

Some cycles are first built in a larger automorphism group. Intersecting each subgroup in a flag with the desired extension can collapse the flag or merge coefficients. The paper selects a supported elementary subgroup with maximal intersection index, fixes a complementary part, and takes a residue before intersecting the remaining flag.

A residue extracts coefficients along a specified part of a chain. In the chosen setting, the restriction remains injective on the relevant residue, so a known nonzero coefficient survives.

At two, the argument chooses a maximal-rank elementary subgroup within a specified family of faithful component configurations. This need not have the largest elementary rank anywhere in GGG. A product with a centralizer cycle has a residue detecting that centralizer class. A deletion argument removes irrelevant overgroups while preserving the detection of nonbounding in the ambient complex.

For odd primes, the cited reduction needs a different output: top-dimensional homology in specified unitary extensions. The paper establishes the relevant rank formula before constructing those cycles. The top-degree argument and the prime-two propagation argument serve different purposes and are not interchangeable.

Symplectic cases permit direct cycle construction in the desired extension. A final small orthogonal case, represented as PSL4(5)\mathrm{PSL}_4(5)PSL4​(5), uses an equivalent-poset construction retaining a join of component and centralizer homology. These cases exhaust the list left by the reductions and exclude a minimal counterexample.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns finite groups and a specified prime. It is not a statement about arbitrary infinite-group subgroup complexes.

The augmented convention is essential when no nontrivial elementary abelian ppp-subgroup exists. In that case the homology witness is in degree −1-1−1, not an ordinary positive-dimensional hole.

The main conclusion is nonvanishing in some degree. Top-dimensional nonvanishing, often called the Quillen dimension property, is proved where particular reductions require it; it is not asserted universally by the headline theorem.

The argument relies on established component reductions and the structure theory of finite simple groups. Its elementary-looking statement should not obscure that dependence.

Finally, detecting a nontrivial normal ppp-subgroup does not reconstruct that subgroup or the full integral homology. Questions about explicit ranks, torsion, preferred cycle representatives and efficient computation remain finer problems than the existence theorem summarized here.

8. Sources and further reading

Quillen’s original subgroup-poset paper gives the conjecture and foundational cases. Aschbacher–Smith’s component reduction, Piterman–Smith’s equivalent-poset techniques, and Díaz Ramos’s unitary and odd-prime theorem explain the progression to the remaining cases.

Piterman’s 2026 component elimination supplies the recent prime-two reduction used by the manuscript. The source below develops the frame counts, restrictions and propagation arguments that claim to complete the rational-homology theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Rational homology and Quillen’s conjecture (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why square-summable topology should concentrate in dimension two
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 315 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A closed aspherical manifold has a contractible universal cover. Ordinary homology of that cover therefore sees no positive-dimensional holes. Yet a different invariant, built from square-summable chains, can remain nonzero. It measures how topology is distributed through infinitely many copies of a fundamental region.

The Singer conjecture predicts that this L2L^2L2-homology concentrates in the middle dimension. In dimension four, that means only degree two can survive. One consequence is strikingly elementary to state: every closed aspherical four-manifold should have nonnegative Euler characteristic.

Family 315 claims the four-dimensional conjecture for all closed connected topological manifolds, without a curvature, smoothness, orientability, or residual-finiteness assumption. Its statement extends further to finite aspherical complexes satisfying integral Poincaré duality in formal dimension four.

2. Background and essential definitions

A connected space is aspherical when its universal cover is contractible. Examples include tori and closed surfaces of genus at least two. Their fundamental groups retain their homotopy information. “Closed manifold” means compact and without boundary.

For a finite cell complex, the Euler characteristic is the alternating count of cells, equivalently the alternating sum of rational Betti numbers:

χ(X)=∑i(−1)ibi(X;Q).\chi(X)=\sum_i(-1)^i b_i(X;\mathbb Q).χ(X)=i∑​(−1)ibi​(X;Q).

A universal cover usually has infinitely many cells. Its deck-transformation group Γ=π1(X)\Gamma=\pi_1(X)Γ=π1​(X) permutes them. Square-summable chains allow infinite linear combinations whose squared coefficients have finite sum. Taking homology requires closures of boundary spaces, so a contraction of the underlying topological space does not automatically give a bounded contraction of this Hilbert-space chain complex.

The resulting L2L^2L2-Betti number bi(2)b_i^{(2)}bi(2)​ uses von Neumann dimension, a dimension normalized by the action of Γ\GammaΓ. The full Hilbert space can have infinite ordinary dimension while having finite normalized dimension. For a finite base complex these invariants obey an Euler-characteristic formula.

When the group admits a nested normal tower of finite-index subgroups with trivial intersection, they also arise as limits of normalized rational Betti numbers of the corresponding finite covers. This is a useful interpretation, but such a tower is not assumed in the main theorem.

An integral Poincaré complex of formal dimension four is a finite complex with a fundamental class inducing duality for every local coefficient system. Local coefficients can change along loops, recording the fundamental group’s action. Nonorientable examples use an orientation character Γ→{1,−1}\Gamma\to\{1,-1\}Γ→{1,−1} and the corresponding twist. This is stronger than simply having the same ordinary Betti numbers as a four-manifold.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Atiyah’s L2L^2L2 index theorem connected normalized dimensions on covers with ordinary indices downstairs. Dodziuk related analytic and simplicial formulations and developed their homotopy-invariance properties. These results made L2L^2L2-invariants tools for topology rather than only for differential equations.

Singer’s proposal linked vanishing of square-integrable harmonic forms to the expected sign of Euler characteristic. The later aspherical-manifold formulation asks for concentration in degree half the manifold dimension. In odd dimensions, where there is no integral middle degree, it predicts complete vanishing.

In dimension four, Poincaré duality reduces the substantive issue to b1(2)=0b_1^{(2)}=0b1(2)​=0. Earlier work proved this for important classes. Davis–Okun treated right-angled Coxeter constructions with suitable three-sphere nerves. Okun–Schreve established results for groups with geometric hierarchies, where a contractible manifold can be repeatedly cut along controlled hypersurfaces.

Complex geometry supplied other cases. Kähler-group restrictions yield the aspherical Kähler surface result, and Albanese–Di Cerbo–Lombardi treated additional complex surfaces under their stated hypotheses. Avramidi–Okun–Schreve obtained the required vanishing for particular Gromov–Thurston branched-cover constructions.

These arguments rely on additional geometry or decomposition. Integral Poincaré duality alone does not provide such a hierarchy. M1 claims to replace those extra structures by a boundary built from finite-energy functions, then use the topology of that boundary to rule out positive first L2L^2L2-Betti number.

The manuscript separately notes a companion complex-surface result as another route for that special case. It is not an input to the general proof reported here. The historical claims and the precise ranges of the preceding results are set out in M1’s introduction.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 25 September 2026, states that every finite connected aspherical integral Poincaré complex QQQ of formal dimension four satisfies

bi(2)(Q~)=0(i≥0, i≠2).b_i^{(2)}(\widetilde Q)=0\qquad(i\geq0,\ i\neq2).bi(2)​(Q​)=0(i≥0, i=2).

The tilde denotes the universal cover, with dimension normalized using its deck group. The orientation character may be nontrivial. The statement concerns absolute Poincaré duality for a complex, not duality for a pair with boundary.

Every closed connected aspherical topological four-manifold has a suitable finite homotopy model, so the paper deduces the same conclusion for all such manifolds. A finite homotopy model is not a triangulation of the manifold. Consequently, the corollary includes manifolds without a smooth structure or triangulation.

The remaining invariant is determined by Euler characteristic:

χ(Q)=b2(2)(Q~)≥0.\chi(Q)=b_2^{(2)}(\widetilde Q)\geq0.χ(Q)=b2(2)​(Q​)≥0.

Thus χ(Q)=0\chi(Q)=0χ(Q)=0 exactly when all its L2L^2L2-Betti numbers vanish. For an oriented closed aspherical four-manifold, the signature consequence is

χ(M)≥∣σ(M)∣,\chi(M)\geq|\sigma(M)|,χ(M)≥∣σ(M)∣,

where σ(M)\sigma(M)σ(M) is the signature of its middle-dimensional intersection form.

If a suitable normal tower of finite covers exists, the normalized rational Betti numbers converge to zero outside degree two and to χ(M)\chi(M)χ(M) in degree two. This final interpretation has an additional covering-tower hypothesis; the vanishing theorem itself does not.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the result settles the four-dimensional Singer conjecture in its full topological form and in the broader finite integral Poincaré-complex setting.

The Euler-characteristic conclusion turns an analytic-looking vanishing statement into a restriction on an elementary invariant. The signature inequality adds a constraint on four-dimensional intersection forms. The finite-cover interpretation, where available, controls asymptotic growth of ordinary homology.

The extension beyond manifold models is also meaningful. A finite aspherical Poincaré complex need not be a manifold. The paper explicitly applies its statement to the companion construction discussed in family 305, rather than assuming all such duality complexes admit manifold realizations.

6. The main idea

Convert a nonzero class into a boundary

The proof begins by assuming b1(2)>0b_1^{(2)}>0b1(2)​>0. A finite presentation gives a locally finite Cayley graph of Γ\GammaΓ: vertices are group elements and edges multiply by selected generators. The assumed class yields a bounded function with finite Dirichlet energy,

∑{v,w} an edge∣f(v)−f(w)∣2<∞,\sum_{\{v,w\}\text{ an edge}}|f(v)-f(w)|^2<\infty,{v,w} an edge∑​∣f(v)−f(w)∣2<∞,

whose behavior at infinity is nonconstant.

Translates of this function provide coordinates for a compactification of the graph. Additional coordinates distinguish components of suitable neighborhoods. The resulting boundary BBB is a compact connected metric space with more than one point.

Finite energy constrains how group translates can cross level sets. The manuscript uses this to produce a convergence action: a sequence of distinct group elements has a subsequence that collapses compact subsets away from one exceptional point toward another point.

Force incompatible properties on a continuum

The energy estimates give covering dimension at most one. Poincaré duality, expressed through group-ring cohomology, supplies

Hˇ1(B;F2)=0.\check H^1(B;\mathbb F_2)=0.Hˇ1(B;F2​)=0.

Čech cohomology is suited to compact spaces that need not initially have a convenient cell structure. The coefficient field F2\mathbb F_2F2​ avoids orientation signs at this stage.

A cut point is a point whose removal disconnects a connected space. If the boundary has cut points, the paper uses Bowditch’s pretree framework and additional arguments to select a nondegenerate subcontinuum LLL without cut points. It is a retract of BBB, so it retains the dimension and cohomology restrictions.

The crucial remaining property is local connectedness. It cannot be assumed merely because the original Cayley graph is locally finite. The auxiliary graph used after passing to a block can have infinite valence and infinite stabilizers.

Push paths uniformly toward infinity

Nested annuli measure depth inside a boundary neighborhood. Component labels indicate where graph paths can travel. The manuscript proves that, after fixing a neighborhood and finitely many relevant moves, one depth threshold works for every sufficiently deep path, regardless of its length or endpoints.

This uniformity lets paths be pushed to arbitrarily large depth while their endpoints approach nearby prescribed boundary points. Compactness then gives small connected subsets of LLL, establishing local connectedness.

Now LLL is a nondegenerate locally connected compact continuum of dimension at most one with vanishing first Čech cohomology. The dimension and cohomology conditions exclude an embedded circle. Such a locally connected continuum is a dendrite, a tree-like space in which every nontrivial arc has separating interior points.

It must therefore have a cut point, contradicting how LLL was chosen. This rules out positive first L2L^2L2-Betti number. Duality and degree-zero vanishing supply all the other nonmiddle degrees. The argument’s order matters: local connectedness is the conclusion of the path analysis, not an input to the earlier boundary reduction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The claim is four-dimensional. It does not settle Singer vanishing in every higher dimension or the corresponding Euler-characteristic sign questions there.

Asphericity is essential to the statement. Arbitrary closed four-manifolds can have very different homology. Likewise, the extension to complexes requires integral duality with local coefficients, not merely rational duality or an ordinary homology resemblance.

The vanishing concerns L2L^2L2-Betti numbers, not ordinary Betti numbers of the manifold. A four-torus, for example, has substantial ordinary homology while its L2L^2L2-Betti numbers vanish. The theorem also does not force the middle invariant to be positive: Euler characteristic zero is allowed.

No residual-finiteness assumption is made. Finite-cover approximations apply only when a suitable tower is available. The proof does not assert that every group in the theorem has enough finite quotients or a word-hyperbolic boundary.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 supplies the full statement, the historical comparisons, and the finite-energy boundary argument. Its bibliography identifies Atiyah’s original L2L^2L2 index theorem, Dodziuk’s analytic–simplicial work, Davis–Okun’s Coxeter results, and Okun–Schreve’s hierarchy theorem. Lück’s L²-Invariants: Theory and Applications to Geometry and K-Theory provides the standard background. For the topological signature input, see Lück–Schick, Various L²-signatures and a topological L²-signature theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Singer conjecture in dimension four (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Which homology classes really come from stable maps of spheres?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 316 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Homology is often easier to calculate than homotopy. A map from a sphere produces a homology class by sending the sphere’s fundamental class into the target. But many homology classes cannot arise this way. Which ones are genuinely spherical?

For the stable sphere, this becomes Curtis’s conjecture. Its target has a large, explicitly structured homology algebra, while the source contains the notoriously complicated stable homotopy groups of spheres. The conjecture predicts that only a very small collection of exceptional classes survives the map from homotopy to mod-two homology.

Family 316 claims the full positive-degree conjecture. The surviving image is generated by the classical Hopf-invariant-one classes and the Kervaire-invariant-one classes that exist. The claim is a classification of an image, not a calculation of all stable homotopy groups.

2. Background and essential definitions

Suspending a based space adds one dimension in a way compatible with based maps. Repeated suspension eventually stabilizes maps between spheres in a fixed difference of dimensions. Their stable homotopy groups are denoted by πdS\pi_d^SπdS​.

The infinite loop space

QSn=colim⁡rΩrSn+rQS^n=\operatorname*{colim}_{r}\Omega^r S^{n+r}QSn=rcolim​ΩrSn+r

packages these stable maps. Here Ωr\Omega^rΩr means the space of based maps from the rrr-sphere, and the colimit follows repeated suspension. Let Q0S0Q_0S^0Q0​S0 be the component containing the basepoint. For d>0d>0d>0, its ddd-th homotopy group is πdS\pi_d^SπdS​.

The mod-two Hurewicz map is

hd:πdS⟶Hd(Q0S0;F2).h_d:\pi_d^S\longrightarrow H_d(Q_0S^0;\mathbb F_2).hd​:πdS​⟶Hd​(Q0​S0;F2​).

A representative Sd→Q0S0S^d\to Q_0S^0Sd→Q0​S0 sends the fundamental homology class of SdS^dSd to hdh_dhd​ of that element. An element in the target is spherical if it occurs this way. The coefficient field F2\mathbb F_2F2​ has two elements, so the image is a vector space over that field.

This map should be distinguished from ordinary homology of the sphere spectrum itself. The target is the homology of its infinite loop space, which has many positive-degree classes and operations.

The stable classes η,ν,σ\eta,\nu,\sigmaη,ν,σ, in degrees 1,3,71,3,71,3,7, have Hopf invariant one. Roughly, the invariant detects a nontrivial relation between the bottom and top cells of a mapping cone through a cohomology operation.

A Kervaire-invariant-one class corresponds, under the Pontryagin–Thom construction, to a framed manifold whose associated quadratic form has Arf invariant one. The possible degrees are

2j+1−2(j≥1).2^{j+1}-2\qquad(j\geq1).2j+1−2(j≥1).

The notation θj\theta_jθj​ denotes such a class only when it exists. A formula for possible dimensions is not an existence theorem in every dimension.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Curtis proposed the Hopf–Kervaire description in his 1975 study of the Dyer–Lashof and lambda algebras. May later recorded a gap identified by Wellington in the proposed proof. The image problem continued to motivate work connecting homology operations, invariant theory, and the Adams spectral sequence.

Adams’s Hopf invariant one theorem identifies the exceptional Hopf degrees. Browder related the framed Kervaire invariant to filtration-two classes in the mod-two Adams spectral sequence. Hill, Hopkins, and Ravenel ruled out Kervaire-invariant-one elements beyond the last possible dimension 126.

M1 also cites Lin, Wang, and Xu’s preprint proving existence in dimension 126. That endpoint existence result is separate from the upper bound needed for the manuscript’s finite-image corollary. The new Curtis claim is formulated in terms of whichever Kervaire classes exist, without deriving an additional existence theorem.

On the homology side, the calculation of free infinite loop spaces supplies a large algebra generated by Dyer–Lashof operations. Spherical classes must satisfy strong necessary conditions: they are primitive and are killed by positive Steenrod operations. But satisfying those algebraic tests does not by itself produce a map from a sphere.

Eccles and Zare obtained restrictions on spherical squares and excluded higher iterated squares. Hung–Peterson and Hunter connected related problems with Dickson invariant algebras and weight filtrations. Kuhn’s work linked Adams filtration to generalized Hurewicz maps and derived ideal powers. M1 builds on these inputs, explicitly crediting the earlier fourth-power exclusion rather than presenting that conclusion as new.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 25 September 2026, states that

im⁡ ⁣(⨁d>0hd)=operatornamespanF2{h(η),h(ν),h(σ),h(θj):θj exists}.\operatorname{im}\!\left(\bigoplus_{d>0}h_d\right)=operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{h(\eta),h(\nu),h(\sigma),h(\theta_j):\theta_j\text{ exists}\}.im(d>0⨁​hd​)=operatornamespanF2​​{h(η),h(ν),h(σ),h(θj​):θj​ exists}.

The statement is about all positive degrees at the prime two. In particular, using the established Kervaire nonexistence bound, the image vanishes outside

{1,2,3,6,7,14,30,62,126}.\{1,2,3,6,7,14,30,62,126\}.{1,2,3,6,7,14,30,62,126}.

It therefore vanishes above degree 126 and is finite as a vector space and as a set. The displayed degree list is an upper support bound; it does not alone assert a nonzero image in every listed degree or give an exact dimension.

The manuscript also deduces Eccles’s conjecture for every positive-dimensional sphere SnS^nSn. In that case, a nonzero spherical class in H∗(QSn;F2)H_*(QS^n;\mathbb F_2)H∗​(QSn;F2​) is either the bottom class in degree nnn or a nonzero homology suspension of one of the three Hopf images.

The Kervaire images are squares, and their first homology suspension vanishes. This explains why they appear at level Q0S0Q_0S^0Q0​S0 but disappear from the positive-sphere conclusion. The corollary concerns spheres, not all spaces in the general formulation of Eccles’s conjecture.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the result settles a longstanding realization problem at the interface of stable homotopy and explicit homology operations.

Its force comes from the disparity between the two sides. The target contains an enormous algebra of possible classes, but the theorem says actual stable sphere maps occupy only the exceptional Hopf–Kervaire part. This would turn a large collection of algebraic possibilities into a definitive geometric exclusion.

The consequence for positive-dimensional spheres extends that restriction through all infinite loop levels. It also clarifies what the Hurewicz map can detect: most stable homotopy is invisible to this particular mod-two invariant, even when the stable groups themselves are nonzero.

6. The main idea

Follow the final surviving suspension

Start with an actual sphere map whose Hurewicz image is nonzero. Repeatedly take its adjoint at higher infinite loop levels, and let

zj∈Hd+j(QSj;F2)z_j\in H_{d+j}(QS^j;\mathbb F_2)zj​∈Hd+j​(QSj;F2​)

be the corresponding images. These satisfy zj+1=σ∗zjz_{j+1}=\sigma_*z_jzj+1​=σ∗​zj​, where σ∗\sigma_*σ∗​ is homology suspension. Degree bounds ensure that the sequence eventually becomes zero.

Let zez_eze​ be the last nonzero term. The manuscript uses the suspension kernel to show that it is a square,

ze=w2,z_e=w^2,ze​=w2,

with a primitive, Steenrod-annihilated root whose suspension is nonzero. At positive terminal level, the preceding spherical suspension imposes an odd-degree condition on the root. At level zero, the paper supplies an argument excluding fourth powers using spectrum pairings and integral characteristic classes.

The root www need not itself be spherical. This is a key distinction: the method uses the original map and the mapping cone of its next adjoint to obtain additional realization information, rather than assuming every suitable root comes from another sphere map.

Retain the geometric extension in an algebraic calculation

The next adjoint has zero Hurewicz image but carries a nonzero square operation in its cone. This yields an extension of modules over the Steenrod algebra, the algebra of mod-two cohomology operations.

The primitive homology is organized by weight, which counts inputs to an extended-power construction. Its dual modules are described using binary Dickson invariants. Those invariants come from polynomials fixed under general linear changes of variables over F2\mathbb F_2F2​.

The new algebraic obstruction is applied to the specific extension arising from the cone, together with a detecting functional that lifts from the preceding suspension level. These compatibility conditions are stronger than primitivity and Steenrod annihilation alone.

The manuscript’s calculation uses Cartier halving and controlled maps on homological algebra groups to retain exponent information through the comparison. At a positive terminal level, it leaves only the bottom-weight possibility, which gives stable Hopf detection.

Separate the level-zero outcome

When the last nonzero term occurs already at level zero, the argument forces the root to have leading weight two. Its square therefore has leading weight four.

Kuhn’s lifting theorem says that sufficiently high Adams filtration forces the Hurewicz image into correspondingly high derived ideal powers. The surviving weight-four component bounds the Adams filtration by two. Browder’s detection theorem then identifies the class as having Kervaire invariant one.

This is a bound on filtration, not an assertion that weight and Adams filtration are always equal. Finally, the detecting invariants are additive. Subtracting a chosen Hopf or Kervaire representative with the same invariant leaves a class whose Hurewicz image must vanish. That gives the claimed span, rather than merely a list of necessary degrees.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns positive-degree mod-two Hurewicz images for the stable sphere. It does not calculate the full stable stems, identify every element in the kernel, or make an odd-prime assertion. The prime-three Kervaire-family discussion in family 309 is a different problem with different detectors.

The notation for Kervaire classes remains conditional on existence. The finite support corollary uses the nonexistence theorem, while the separately cited dimension-126 result supplies endpoint existence in its own right.

Eccles’s conjecture is obtained here for positive-dimensional spheres. Extending that conclusion to arbitrary path-connected finite-type spaces is not part of the stated result.

The proof strategy also preserves a distinction between an algebraically plausible class and an actual sphere map. The latter supplies the cone extension and its compatibility with suspension. Removing those conditions would enlarge the algebraic problem and would no longer be the realization theorem claimed in M1.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 provides the statement and last-suspension strategy. Relevant primary predecessors include Eccles–Zare’s restrictions on potential spherical classes, Kuhn’s Adams-filtration and Hurewicz theorem, and Hill–Hopkins–Ravenel’s Kervaire nonexistence theorem. The separately cited endpoint result is Lin–Wang–Xu, On the last Kervaire invariant problem. M1’s bibliography supplies the original Curtis, Adams, Browder, and May references.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Stable Hurewicz Image of the Sphere at Two (September 25, 2026).

entry.title: Counting the chromatic layers lost when taking fixed points
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 314 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A symmetry can reveal topology that is invisible before taking fixed points. Classical Smith theory gives an important constraint: if a finite complex has trivial reduced homology modulo a prime ppp, then so does its fixed-point space under a finite ppp-group.

Chromatic homotopy theory asks a more finely graded question. Instead of testing all mod-ppp homology at once, it uses theories K(0),K(1),K(2),…K(0),K(1),K(2),\ldotsK(0),K(1),K(2),…, each detecting a different periodic layer. How many layers can be lost when passing from points fixed by a subgroup to points fixed by the whole group?

Family 314 claims an exact answer for every finite ppp-group and every embedded subgroup. The answer is a group-theoretic number: the fewest cyclic steps in a subnormal chain joining the subgroup to the group. Remarkably, the claimed number is independent of the chromatic height at which the question starts.

2. Background and essential definitions

A finite ppp-group has order a power of the prime ppp. If it acts on a space XXX, the fixed-point set XHX^HXH consists of points unchanged by every element of a subgroup HHH.

The stable version uses genuine equivariant spectra, which remember suspension not only by ordinary spheres but also by spheres carrying linear group actions. Their geometric fixed points, written ΦHX\Phi^H XΦHX, isolate the part associated with the subgroup HHH. On suspension spectra of appropriately based spaces, this construction recovers the corresponding fixed-point information. It is distinct from homotopy fixed points, which encode a different construction.

The theorem concerns finite ppp-local genuine spectra, including compact retracts. Here “finite” refers to a finite cell construction, and “ppp-local” means that all other primes are inverted.

Morava KKK-theory K(i)K(i)K(i) detects chromatic height iii, with K(0)=HQK(0)=H\mathbb QK(0)=HQ, rational homology. A spectrum is K(i)K(i)K(i)-acyclic when its K(i)K(i)K(i)-homology is zero. For a nonzero finite spectrum, the first nonvanishing height is its chromatic type.

For H≤GH\leq GH≤G, define rn(G,H)r_n(G,H)rn​(G,H) to be the least integer r≥0r\geq0r≥0 such that every finite genuine GGG-spectrum satisfies

K(n+r)∗(ΦHX)=0⟹K(n)∗(ΦGX)=0.K(n+r)_*(\Phi^H X)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quadK(n)_*(\Phi^G X)=0.K(n+r)∗​(ΦHX)=0⟹K(n)∗​(ΦGX)=0.

The higher starting height compensates for the information that taking more fixed points can lose.

A subnormal chain with cyclic quotients is a sequence

H=G0◃G1◃⋯◃Gs=GH=G_0\triangleleft G_1\triangleleft\cdots\triangleleft G_s=GH=G0​◃G1​◃⋯◃Gs​=G

such that each group is normal in the next and each quotient Gi/Gi−1G_i/G_{i-1}Gi​/Gi−1​ is cyclic. Let ℓ(G,H)\ell(G,H)ℓ(G,H) be the minimum possible length sss. Such chains exist in finite ppp-groups, even when HHH is not normal in GGG. A cyclic quotient of order pap^apa counts as one step, not aaa steps.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Smith theory established the classical fixed-point acyclicity phenomenon. Floyd strengthened it to inequalities for total mod-ppp Betti numbers. Chromatic versions replace a single homology theory by the hierarchy of Morava theories and ask for the precise change of height.

Balmer and Sanders classified the prime tensor ideals of finite genuine equivariant spectra, reducing the topology of their spectrum to inclusions indexed by subgroups and heights. The cyclic prime-order case already displayed a one-step chromatic loss.

Barthel, Hausmann, Naumann, Nikolaus, Noel, and Stapleton determined the finite abelian ppp-group case. There, the loss is the minimum number of generators of G/HG/HG/H. This corrected an earlier order-based expectation: a cyclic group of order p2p^2p2 has loss one, not two. Balderrama and Kuhn later supplied an elementary proof of the abelian theorem, including rational target height zero.

The nonabelian case is subtler because quotient ranks need not capture the placement of a subgroup. Kuhn and Lloyd proved that the relevant acyclicity implications are equivalent to inequalities between Morava-homology dimensions. They obtained the cyclic-chain answer for subgroup pairs in central extensions of elementary abelian 2-groups by a group of order two.

For example, a noncentral order-two subgroup in the dihedral group of order eight has loss two, although a basic elementary-abelian quotient bound gives only one. Kuhn and Lloyd proposed the general equality with cyclic length and separately asked about independence from height. M1 claims both, with the precise prior statements documented in its introduction and bibliography.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 24 September 2026, states

rn(G,H)=ℓ(G,H)r_n(G,H)=\ell(G,H)rn​(G,H)=ℓ(G,H)

for every prime ppp, every finite ppp-group GGG, every subgroup HHH, and every n≥0n\geq0n≥0.

The assertion includes optimality. If r<ℓ(G,H)r<\ell(G,H)r<ℓ(G,H), there exists a finite genuine GGG-spectrum with

K(n+r)∗(ΦHX)=0,K(n)∗(ΦGX)≠0.K(n+r)_*(\Phi^H X)=0,\qquad K(n)_*(\Phi^G X)\neq0.K(n+r)∗​(ΦHX)=0,K(n)∗​(ΦGX)=0.

Thus the formula is not merely an upper bound obtained by iterating known cyclic results. It says that no smaller loss works uniformly over all finite inputs. When H=GH=GH=G, both sides are zero.

A concrete abelian example illustrates why the embedded subgroup matters. Take

G=Cp2×Cp,H1=pCp2×0,H2=0×Cp.G=C_{p^2}\times C_p,\quad H_1=pC_{p^2}\times0,\quad H_2=0\times C_p.G=Cp2​×Cp​,H1​=pCp2​×0,H2​=0×Cp​.

Both subgroups are cyclic of order ppp, but

G/H1≅Cp×Cp,G/H2≅Cp2.G/H_1\cong C_p\times C_p,\qquad G/H_2\cong C_{p^2}.G/H1​≅Cp​×Cp​,G/H2​≅Cp2​.

The claimed losses are two and one, respectively. Knowing only the abstract isomorphism type of HHH is insufficient.

Combined with the existing conjugacy and ppp-subnormal reductions, the manuscript also gives the remaining finite-height prime-inclusion tests for arbitrary finite groups. Together with the previously known infinite-height information, this determines their thick tensor ideals. The general finite-group conclusion uses those reductions; it does not apply the displayed ppp-group formula without first checking the required subgroup conditions.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the theorem supplies the exact numerical invariant for a central fixed-point problem and completes the corresponding structural description of finite equivariant stable homotopy.

Its appeal is the match between two very different measurements. On one side are vanishing tests in generalized homology, quantified over every finite equivariant spectrum. On the other is the shortest length of a group-theoretic chain. The equality makes the former accessible through the latter.

Height independence is an additional structural statement. Increasing chromatic complexity does not change the amount of loss attached to a fixed subgroup pair. The same group invariant governs rational detection at height zero and all positive target heights.

6. The main idea

The upper bound and the missing converse

The upper bound follows by applying the cyclic chromatic Smith theorem at each step of a shortest chain. Each cyclic quotient costs at most one height, so the total cost is at most ℓ(G,H)\ell(G,H)ℓ(G,H).

Sharpness is harder. One needs examples preventing every smaller proposed bound. Standard generalized character theory is indexed by maps from products of ppp-adic integers, whose images are abelian. That cannot directly see all the nonabelian subgroup configurations responsible for the problem.

Build a source with enough nonabelian information

The manuscript constructs a pro-ppp source group from finite groups detected by telescopic cochains. A pro-ppp group is an inverse limit of finite ppp-groups, retaining compatible information from all of them. The construction bounds the number of generators of every finite section of this source.

Relative integration over finite groupoids then imposes divisibility conditions on its finite actions. A groupoid allows objects with automorphisms; integration weights those automorphisms in a controlled way. Applying it to labeled finite sets produces congruences for fixed-point counts at every open subgroup.

The claimed profinite argument combines these arithmetic congruences with the generator bound to force a subnormal series with Zp\mathbb Z_pZp​ factors of bounded length. Thus a chromatic detection statement imposes a cyclic-length constraint on finite quotients. The paper emphasizes that constraints at all open subgroups, rather than only at the original group, carry essential information.

Turn a vanishing estimate into sharp finite examples

The first estimate is rational. Nilpotence and generalized characters upgrade it to higher heights. Products with increasingly large cyclic ppp-groups separate the target chromatic height from the group’s cyclic length.

A final support argument handles an arbitrary embedded subgroup. The support of a finite spectrum records the prime tensor ideals that do not contain it. At a hypothetical first failure of the desired bound, the new estimates would separate the support into two disjoint nonempty closed pieces. But that support is the closure of one point and must be irreducible, so such a separation is impossible.
