This supplies the necessary prime-inclusion obstruction. Separation of primes then yields the finite spectra witnessing sharpness. The manuscript does not need to write down a small explicit cell model for every subgroup pair.

Telescopic localization is used in these intermediate estimates. On finite spectra its acyclicity tests agree with Morava KKK-theory, but the argument does not identify the two localizations on arbitrary spectra. Keeping that distinction avoids importing an unrelated telescope-conjecture assumption.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem quantifies over finite genuine spectra and their geometric fixed points. It should not be transferred automatically to arbitrary infinite spectra, naive group actions, or homotopy fixed points.

The value is relative to the actual inclusion H≤GH\leq GH≤G, not merely the orders or abstract types of the two groups. A chain may have quotients of different cyclic orders, and each contributes one unit.

The existence of sharpness witnesses is structural. It does not provide a uniform efficient algorithm for constructing a smallest witness or a bound on its number of cells. Likewise, a classification of tensor ideals does not compute every equivariant homotopy group.

For general finite groups, conjugacy and the appropriate common ppp-residual conditions remain part of the prime-inclusion criterion. The ppp-group theorem is the numerical component of that larger description, not a substitute for its hypotheses.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 contains the equality, its historical development, and the character, profinite, and support arguments. Its bibliography identifies Balmer–Sanders, The spectrum of the equivariant stable homotopy category of a finite group (2017); Barthel and collaborators, The Balmer spectrum of the equivariant homotopy category of a finite abelian group (2019); and Kuhn–Lloyd, Chromatic fixed point theory and the Balmer spectrum for extraspecial 2-groups (2024), the principal predecessors of the stated classification. The Hopkins–Smith nilpotence theorem supplies the underlying finite-spectrum chromatic framework.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Cyclic length and chromatic fixed-point loss (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A finite chain of building rules for local stable homotopy
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 311 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Suppose we have a collection of geometric objects and a few ways to construct new ones: take sums, form mapping cones, extract direct summands, and multiply by other objects. Which collections are closed under these operations? A classification would describe the possible building rules, even when individual objects remain difficult to compute.

In stable homotopy theory, the objects are spectra, and chromatic localization isolates one layer of their arithmetic complexity. Family 311 asks this classification question for the dualizable objects at a fixed prime and chromatic height. The manuscript claims that every permitted collection lies in one finite, strictly ordered chain.

Its route passes through an apparently different problem: which algebraic subsets of a formal-group deformation space can be preserved by all sufficiently small symmetries? The claimed answer is that only the familiar height conditions survive. A previously established bridge turns that orbit statement into the topological classification.

2. Background and essential definitions

A spectrum packages spaces and suspension maps so that suspension becomes invertible. Stable homotopy groups measure maps from suspended spheres into a spectrum. The smash product, written X∧YX\wedge YX∧Y, plays the role of multiplication, while a cofiber sequence is the stable analogue of attaching cells.

Fix a prime ppp. Morava KKK-theory K(n)K(n)K(n) detects chromatic height nnn, with n≥1n\geq1n≥1. The localization LK(n)XL_{K(n)}XLK(n)​X retains the information in XXX visible to that theory. In the local category, multiplication means localizing the smash product again.

An object is dualizable when it has a dual with evaluation and coevaluation maps satisfying the usual identities, as a finite-dimensional vector space does. Dualizable local spectra form a category denoted here by D\mathcal DD. They are not simply the compact objects of the local category, and they do not include every local spectrum.

A thick tensor ideal in D\mathcal DD is a collection closed under finite sums, suspension and desuspension, cofibers, direct summands, and multiplication by any object of D\mathcal DD. No closure under arbitrary infinite sums is imposed.

The algebraic side uses a formal group: a power series describing addition near an identity, subject to associativity and commutativity identities. Lubin–Tate theory organizes deformations of a height-nnn formal group through the ring

E0=W(Fpn)[[u1,…,un−1]].E_0=W(\mathbb F_{p^n})[[u_1,\ldots,u_{n-1}]].E0​=W(Fpn​)[[u1​,…,un−1​]].

Here Fpn\mathbb F_{p^n}Fpn​ is the finite field with pnp^npn elements. Its Witt-vector ring W(Fpn)W(\mathbb F_{p^n})W(Fpn​) is a complete unramified extension of the ppp-adic integers, with that residue field. The variables uiu_iui​ are deformation parameters. The standard ideals are

I0=(0),Ih=(p,u1,…,uh−1)(1≤h≤n).I_0=(0),\qquad I_h=(p,u_1,\ldots,u_{h-1})\quad(1\leq h\leq n).I0​=(0),Ih​=(p,u1​,…,uh−1​)(1≤h≤n).

Their vanishing loci describe successive height conditions. The Morava stabilizer group consists of symmetries of the original formal group and acts on its deformations. An open subgroup contains a neighborhood of the identity; invariance under such a subgroup is already a substantial symmetry requirement.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hopkins and Smith classified thick subcategories of finite spectra using chromatic type. This established the basic expectation that a complicated world of constructions might have a short list of possible supports. Hovey and Strickland subsequently proposed an analogue for dualizable objects after fixing one Morava height.

The local problem is different from the finite-spectrum theorem. Localization introduces additional dualizable objects, and the coefficient ring retains deformation directions. Those directions could, in principle, support extra invariant subvarieties and hence extra tensor ideals.

Chai’s rigidity work on formal groups supplied an algebraic direction, often called Chai’s Hope in this setting. The relevant question concerns radical ideals invariant under stabilizer symmetries. A radical ideal records a closed set without its nilpotent thickening: if a power of an element belongs to the ideal, the element itself does too.

Barthel, Heard, and Naumann proved the height-two case and established the implication from the appropriate invariant-ideal classification to the Hovey–Strickland conjecture. Their 2022 paper provides the crucial bridge used here. Consequently, the new manuscript does not claim to invent that passage from algebra to topology.

The remaining task described in M1 is the orbit calculation at arbitrary height and prime. Its characteristic-zero argument develops a Lie-theoretic approach credited to Chai. Its positive-characteristic argument addresses the intermediate height strata, where ordinary tangent-space calculations alone do not capture all the necessary information.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 24 September 2026, states that for every prime and positive height, the proper prime ideals invariant under any open subgroup of the nonextended stabilizer are exactly

I0,I1,…,In.I_0,I_1,\ldots,I_n.I0​,I1​,…,In​.

The invariant radical ideals are those ideals together with the unit ideal E0E_0E0​. The same radical-ideal list holds for the canonical extended stabilizer, which also includes the finite-field Galois symmetries. This is the standard finite-residue-field formulation used in the paper.

For the topological conclusion, choose a finite spectrum F(k)F(k)F(k) of type kkk: its lower Morava theories vanish, while K(k)∗F(k)≠0K(k)_*F(k)\neq0K(k)∗​F(k)=0. Put K(0)=HQK(0)=H\mathbb QK(0)=HQ, ordinary rational homology. Let Dk\mathcal D_kDk​ be the thick tensor ideal generated by LK(n)F(k)L_{K(n)}F(k)LK(n)​F(k), and set Dn+1=0\mathcal D_{n+1}=0Dn+1​=0.

M1 claims that the complete list is

D=D0⊋D1⊋⋯⊋Dn⊋Dn+1=0.\mathcal D=\mathcal D_0\supsetneq\mathcal D_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq\mathcal D_n\supsetneq\mathcal D_{n+1}=0.D=D0​⊋D1​⊋⋯⊋Dn​⊋Dn+1​=0.

Thus there are exactly n+2n+2n+2 ideals, independently of the choices of the finite type-kkk spectra. At height one, for example, there are three: the whole category, one nonzero proper ideal, and zero.

The associated Balmer spectrum records prime tensor ideals, where a product belonging to an ideal forces at least one factor to belong. Its points are precisely D1,…,Dn+1\mathcal D_1,\ldots,\mathcal D_{n+1}D1​,…,Dn+1​. It has n+1n+1n+1 points, with

{Dj}‾={Dℓ:j≤ℓ≤n+1}.\overline{\{\mathcal D_j\}}=\{\mathcal D_\ell:j\leq\ell\leq n+1\}.{Dj​}​={Dℓ​:j≤ℓ≤n+1}.

In particular, the zero ideal is the unique closed point. This topology packages which kinds of support can specialize into others.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the result completes a central classification problem in local chromatic homotopy theory at every prime and height. It also resolves the associated invariant-radical-ideal problem in the stated coefficient setting.

The conclusion replaces an open-ended search for possible construction classes by a finite chain. Given two dualizable objects, their supports determine whether one can be built from the other through the allowed finite operations. That is a structural gain even without an explicit description of either object’s homotopy groups.

The connection is also unusually informative: the allowed topological constructions are controlled by the orbit geometry of formal groups. Symmetry rules out hidden supports. The finite answer therefore expresses a rigidity property, rather than a claim that local spectra themselves are easy to enumerate.

6. The main idea

Orbits must fill their height stratum

The geometric objective is to show that an invariant equation cannot carve out an unexpected subset within a fixed height stratum. In characteristic ppp, the paper studies deformations with connected height hhh, together with an étale part of rank n−hn-hn−h. Compatible systems of division points provide coordinates for the latter information.

Small stabilizer elements move a point by increasingly tiny amounts. These movements involve repeated Frobenius powers, the characteristic-ppp operation x↦xpx\mapsto x^px↦xp. A usual first derivative can miss such motion: a power series can have zero derivative without being constant. The manuscript therefore keeps finite jets and rescales the Frobenius behavior, rather than relying on tangent directions alone.

If a nonzero equation vanished along the entire small orbit, this analysis would produce a formal relation among certain division-point vectors. The next step translates that relation into the geometry of vector bundles on the Fargues–Fontaine curve, an arithmetic curve designed to organize ppp-adic period information.

There, the manuscript uses a degree-one determinant comparison to promote independence of the original vectors to independence at the generic point. The stabilizer’s endomorphism algebra becomes sufficiently large at that point to contradict the proposed relation. This is the mechanism claimed to force orbit density.

From invariant equations to construction classes

Characteristic zero is handled separately through the Gross–Hopkins period map and projective tangent directions. Together, the two arguments rule out additional invariant prime ideals. Passing through the finitely many minimal primes of a radical ideal supplies the radical classification.

For a dualizable spectrum XXX, completed Morava EEE-homology gives a finite module whose support is a closed subset of the prime spectrum of E0E_0E0​. Stabilizer symmetry makes this support invariant. The algebraic classification therefore forces it to be a standard height locus, or empty.

The support theorem supplied by Barthel–Heard–Naumann identifies finite construction from YYY with containment in the support of YYY. Since the possible supports form a finite chain, any nonzero thick tensor ideal has a greatest support among those it contains. That produces the asserted complete list; one need not assume in advance that every ideal has a single generator.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The classification concerns dualizable local spectra and thick tensor ideals. It does not classify all local spectra, all subcategories, or the individual objects inside each ideal. It does not compute all homotopy groups or all maps between spectra.

On the algebraic side, the assertion concerns invariant prime and radical ideals. Nonradical ideals can retain multiplicities and nilpotent information, so the displayed list is not a classification of every invariant ideal.

The finite residue field and canonical stabilizer actions are part of the formulation. The statement should not be transferred without explanation to every possible enlargement of the coefficient field. Likewise, a large-prime restriction appearing in the converse direction of earlier comparison results is not imposed on the forward implication used here.

The finite type-kkk objects required for the construction chain come from established periodicity theory. The argument does not require the first-power Smith–Toda constructions discussed in family 308. Questions about explicit representatives, individual computations, and more refined module structures remain beyond this classification.

8. Sources and further reading

The theorem statements and orbit strategy above follow M1, especially its introduction and final support classification. For the historical bridge, see Barthel–Heard–Naumann, On conjectures of Hovey–Strickland and Chai. Hovey–Strickland’s Morava K-theories and localisation develops the local category and its original problems. Lubin–Tate’s formal-moduli paper supplies the deformation-theoretic starting point.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Stabilizer orbits and thick tensor ideals of dualizable K(n)-local spectra (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Local finiteness does not guarantee a finite global construction
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 319 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Some infinite objects can still be built from a standard object using only finitely many operations. A finite construction can therefore be a useful notion of simplicity even when the underlying object has infinitely many nonzero homotopy groups.

The Hahn–Wilson conjecture proposes such a classification for spectra. Roughly, finite presentation of mod-ppp cohomology, combined with a chromatic height bound, should say exactly when a spectrum can be assembled from a truncated Brown–Peterson spectrum by finite cofibers and retracts.

Family 319 claims counterexamples at height two for every sufficiently large prime. Their local chromatic behavior remains well controlled, including the two relevant telescope comparisons. The asserted obstruction lies in the way the local pieces are joined into a global object.

2. Background and essential definitions

A spectrum is a stable object in which suspension has an inverse. It is connective if its homotopy groups vanish in negative degrees, and bounded below if they vanish below some fixed degree. Derived ppp-completion retains compatible information modulo all powers of a prime ppp.

The Steenrod algebra consists of stable operations on mod-ppp cohomology. A module over it is finitely presented if finitely many generators and finitely many relations describe the module, even though the module itself may be infinite-dimensional over Fp\mathbb F_pFp​.

Following Mahowald–Rezk, a bounded-below ppp-complete spectrum XXX is fp when H∗(X;Fp)H^*(X;\mathbb F_p)H∗(X;Fp​) is finitely presented over the Steenrod algebra. An equivalent test asks for a nonzero finite spectrum VVV such that π∗(V∧X)\pi_*(V\wedge X)π∗​(V∧X) is finite in total: only finitely many degrees are nonzero, and each group is finite.

Morava KKK-theories K(j)K(j)K(j) detect chromatic heights, with K(0)=HQK(0)=H\mathbb QK(0)=HQ. A nonzero finite spectrum has type jjj when jjj is its first nonvanishing Morava height. An fp-spectrum has fp-type at most nnn if the total-finiteness test works with a finite spectrum of type n+1n+1n+1. Exact fp-type two means at most two but not at most one.

The standard completed truncated Brown–Peterson spectrum has coefficients

π∗BP⟨2⟩p∧=Zp[v1,v2],∣vi∣=2(pi−1).\pi_*BP\langle2\rangle_p^{\wedge}=\mathbb Z_p[v_1,v_2],\qquad |v_i|=2(p^i-1).π∗​BP⟨2⟩p∧​=Zp​[v1​,v2​],∣vi​∣=2(pi−1).

The variables record the first two chromatic periodicities. The ordinary thick subcategory generated by this spectrum permits equivalences, finite sums, all integer shifts, cofiber sequences, and retracts. It does not add closure under smashing with arbitrary other spectra.

Write L2L_2L2​ for localization retaining heights zero through two, and L2fL_2^fL2f​ for the corresponding finite localization. The telescope T(2)T(2)T(2) is built by repeatedly applying a periodic self-map to a finite type-two spectrum. Agreement of T(2)T(2)T(2)-localization with K(2)K(2)K(2)-localization is a separate condition, not part of the definition of fp-type.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Hopkins–Smith theorem classifies thick subcategories of finite spectra by chromatic type. The Hahn–Wilson proposal asks for an analogous finite-construction description inside a controlled class of infinite spectra, using truncated Brown–Peterson spectra as generators.

Mahowald–Rezk developed the fp framework and its duality theory. Hahn–Wilson’s redshift theorem supplied further examples through algebraic KKK-theory of suitable truncated Brown–Peterson forms. The very low fp-type cases are classical, and Lee–Pstrągowski proved the global generation conjecture at height one.

Lee–Pstrągowski also established a positive local theorem at every height. The locally fp K(n)K(n)K(n)-local spectra are exactly the ordinary thick closure of Morava EEE-theory EnE_nEn​, equivalently of the localized truncated Brown–Peterson spectrum. The local finiteness test is degreewise after smashing with finite type-nnn spectra; it differs from the global test requiring finiteness in total.

A natural hope was that this local classification, together with good comparison between finite and ordinary chromatic localization, would imply global generation. M1 claims that this hope fails at height two.

The unrestricted telescope conjecture had already been disproved by Burklund, Hahn, Levy, and Schlank at heights at least two. Those examples do not supply the present counterexample: the required finite-smash homotopy is bounded but not finite in total, so the relevant fp condition is missing. M1 instead keeps the telescope comparisons true for its own example.

The manuscript’s history also distinguishes the tensor-ideal classification discussed in family 311. That classification allows multiplication by other dualizable local objects, whereas the Hahn–Wilson problem fixes a single global generator and ordinary thick closure.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 26 September 2026, states that for every sufficiently large prime ppp, there is a connective ppp-complete spectrum XXX of exact fp-type two such that

X∉Thick⁡(BP⟨2⟩p∧).X\notin\operatorname{Thick}(BP\langle2\rangle_p^{\wedge}).X∈/Thick(BP⟨2⟩p∧​).

The same spectrum satisfies

L2fX≃L2X,LT(2)X≃LK(2)X.L_2^fX\simeq L_2X,\qquad L_{T(2)}X\simeq L_{K(2)}X.L2f​X≃L2​X,LT(2)​X≃LK(2)​X.

Thus the counterexample persists even with these localization comparisons imposed as additional hypotheses. It disproves the universally quantified global generation conjecture at height two.

The paper works with a specified standard form of BP⟨2⟩p∧BP\langle2\rangle_p^{\wedge}BP⟨2⟩p∧​, obtained as a regular Brown–Peterson module quotient. It invokes the cited uniqueness results for the underlying standard quotient spectrum at the odd primes in question. This is not a claim about every possible unrelated object sharing the displayed coefficient ring.

Its local object LK(2)XL_{K(2)}XLK(2)​X still belongs to Thick⁡(E2)\operatorname{Thick}(E_2)Thick(E2​) and has the associated local finiteness and duality properties. Those positive conclusions are compatible with failure of the global construction.

“Sufficiently large” is the theorem’s prime range. One algebraic comparison used in the argument is available for p>8p>8p>8, but the operator construction requires larger primes. The comparison’s numerical bound should not be advertised as the final counterexample threshold.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the result refutes a central proposed classification of chromatically finite infinite spectra and identifies a specific limitation of passing from local descriptions to global constructions.

It does more than exploit bad behavior of telescope localization. The example satisfies the relevant comparisons, so those hypotheses cannot repair the conjecture by themselves. Any replacement must also control the gluing between heights.

The coexistence of local finite generation and global failure is broadly instructive. Each local part can belong to the expected finite-construction class while the map identifying the parts over their overlap introduces an obstruction that no finite global tower can remove.

6. The main idea

Move to an algebraic setting while retaining maps

At large primes, chromatic algebraicity compares the relevant homotopy category with a periodic derived category of sheaves on the moduli of formal group laws. A derived category retains complexes and their maps up to the equivalences needed for homological calculations.

The manuscript uses a homology-compatible triangulated comparison, so finite triangles and retracts can be transported. It first performs completion, inverse limits, and gluing in the algebraic category. It does not assume a mere equivalence of underlying categories automatically preserves every construction being used.

On a reduced height-at-most-two stack, a parameter t=v1t=v_1t=v1​ cuts out the height-two locus. Inverting it gives an open part, while completion gives a neighborhood of the closed part. The overlap is described by Laurent-type coefficients, allowing both positive and negative powers.

Choose gluing with controlled but numerous defects

The construction starts with the cone of an operation on the completed standard generator, together with shifts through one period. Call this completed object YYY. On the overlap, the operation has many independent kernel and cokernel classes. A triangular matching of coefficients controls both defects and keeps its image closed.

The paper pairs kernel and cokernel directions inside a discrete cocompact vector subspace. Because the open part is simple, this subspace can be realized by an open periodic complex VVV mapping into the overlap LYLYLY, where LLL means inversion of ttt.

The global object is the homotopy pullback

U=Y×LYhV.U=Y\mathbin{\times}^{h}_{LY}V.U=Y×LYh​V.

The complete part contributes a compact open subspace of overlap homotopy. The discrete part complements it up to finite error. Consequently, the combined map has finite kernel and cokernel in each degree, and the pullback has finite homotopy groups degree by degree. Its completion recovers YYY, which has the desired finite construction locally.

Make every finite global tower impossible

The obstruction compares two growth rates at Laurent precision NNN. A separate operator estimate bounds certain joint kernels by O(N1/3)O(N^{1/3})O(N1/3). The deliberately paired defects grow at least like cNβcN^\betacNβ for a fixed β>1/3\beta>1/3β>1/3, with c>0c>0c>0.

This discrepancy constrains maps from UUU to any finite construction from the global generator. After a flat coefficient extension, a map vanishing on homology must also vanish on the homology of the module dual. The dual condition removes the free part of a potential construction stage; the homology condition then passes the obstruction to the preceding stage.

Backward induction rules out every finite tower and its retracts. This is stronger than showing that one chosen presentation fails or that an object cannot be made with a small number of cofibers.

Finally, the algebraic object is transferred back to spectra. Only after obtaining a suitable localized object with degreewise finite homotopy does the paper take its connective cover. A separate transfer argument proves the total-finiteness test required for fp-type. Additional arguments establish exact type two and both localization comparisons.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result is existential at sufficiently large primes. It does not settle the global conjecture separately at every small prime or provide a smallest counterexample.

The generator and permitted operations matter. Ordinary thick closure is not a tensor ideal, and the global fp classification is not the local classification of dualizable objects. The positive local theorem remains part of the description of the example.

Degreewise finiteness is weaker than finiteness in total. The construction needs an additional argument after taking a connective cover to reach the latter fp test; the two notions are not interchangeable.

Taking connective covers of arbitrary local generators also fails as a shortcut. M1 points out that the connective cover of height-two Morava EEE-theory has an infinite power-series coefficient ring modulo ppp in degree zero, unlike objects in the claimed global thick closure. This simpler obstruction illustrates why a local finite tower cannot automatically be converted to the desired global one.

A revised classification would need conditions controlling the overlap and its maps, beyond the separate local pieces and telescope comparisons. The manuscript gives the obstruction, rather than proposing a complete replacement theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 supplies the counterexample and growth-based gluing obstruction. Primary context includes Lee–Pstrągowski, The monochromatic Hahn–Wilson conjecture; Mahowald–Rezk’s fp-spectrum duality theory; Hahn–Wilson’s redshift theorem; and Pstrągowski’s large-prime algebraicity comparison. The distinct unrestricted telescope counterexamples appear in Burklund–Hahn–Levy–Schlank.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Counterexamples to the Hahn-Wilson conjecture at height two (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A model of spaces inside every strict higher category dimension
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 317 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A category consists of objects and composable arrows. Surprisingly, categories can encode arbitrary homotopy types: the chains of composable arrows form a simplicial space called a nerve. This allows questions about spaces to be studied through algebraic diagrams.

A higher category adds arrows between arrows, then further cells between those, and so on. Family 317 asks whether strict globular higher categories admit the full machinery of a model category matching the homotopy theory of spaces, in every positive dimension.

M1 claims an affirmative answer, including infinitely many dimensions. The new content is not merely that the homotopy categories agree; that was already known. It is the prescribed system of weak equivalences, fibrations, cofibrations, factorizations, and lifting properties on the entire category of strict higher categories.

2. Background and essential definitions

In an ordinary category, arrows compose associatively and have identity arrows. A strict 2-category also has 2-cells between arrows, with compatible compositions. A strict globular nnn-category continues this through dimension nnn. “Globular” means a cell has a source and target of one lower dimension. “Strict” means the associativity, identity, and interchange rules are equalities.

Cells are not required to be invertible. This distinguishes the objects here from strict higher groupoids. A strict ω\omegaω-category has cells in every finite dimension; a finite nnn-category can be viewed as one whose higher cells are identities.

A simplicial set is a system of vertices, edges, triangles, and higher simplices with face and degeneracy maps. It need not be a simplicial complex embedded in Euclidean space. Geometric realization turns it into a topological space.

The Street nerve NnXN_nXNn​X records maps from oriented simplex categories, called orientals, into a strict higher category XXX. It generalizes the ordinary nerve. Its left adjoint cnc_ncn​ freely turns simplicial data into a strict nnn-category.

A model category organizes homotopy theory using three classes of maps. Weak equivalences are maps to be inverted; fibrations and cofibrations control lifting problems and replacements. Two required factorizations split every map into suitable combinations of these classes. A Quillen equivalence means that the resulting derived homotopy theories agree through a compatible adjoint pair.

Subdivision Sd⁡\operatorname{Sd}Sd refines simplices into smaller pieces. Its right adjoint Ex⁡\operatorname{Ex}Ex changes a simplicial set in a way that improves its filling behavior while preserving homotopy type. Applying each twice is part of the specific construction here, not an arbitrary cosmetic choice.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Thomason established the ordinary-category case in 1980. His argument transferred the simplicial model structure through a twice-subdivided nerve adjunction. A central issue was how nerves behave when categories are glued by pushouts. Cisinski later corrected a retract argument while retaining the model structure and its properness.

Street’s orientals supplied the higher-dimensional nerve. Ara and Maltsiniotis developed an abstract transfer framework and established the proper combinatorial structure in dimension two. Together with Chiche’s comparison result, this gave the corresponding Quillen equivalence. Earlier proposed two-dimensional constructions by Worytkiewicz, Hess, Parent, and Tonks required corrections, as discussed in the cited literature.

For all dimensions, Ara–Maltsiniotis reduced the problem to two conditions: a unit comparison on nerves of partially ordered sets, and a compatibility statement for certain categorical pushouts with arbitrary targets. They proved the unit condition. Gagna later gave a direct simplicial approach and showed that localizing strict higher categories at nerve weak equivalences already recovers homotopy types.

Thus a basic equivalence of homotopy categories was available before M1. What remained was the pushout control needed to construct the specified lifting and factorization systems everywhere, including attachments to categories that are neither free nor cofibrant.

Fiore and Paoli also established Thomason structures for nnn-fold categories. Those are built by iterating the internal-category construction and have a different organization of cells. Their theorem does not directly supply the strict globular structure considered here. M1 explicitly distinguishes these historical achievements and claims to settle the remaining globular conjecture.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 25 September 2026, considers every

n∈{1,2,3,…}∪{ω}.n\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\omega\}.n∈{1,2,3,…}∪{ω}.

On small strict globular nnn-categories, it defines

Rn=Ex⁡2Nn,Ln=cnSd⁡2.R_n=\operatorname{Ex}^2N_n,\qquad L_n=c_n\operatorname{Sd}^2.Rn​=Ex2Nn​,Ln​=cn​Sd2.

A functor is a weak equivalence exactly when its Street nerve is a weak homotopy equivalence of simplicial sets. Equivalently, this can be tested after applying Ex⁡2\operatorname{Ex}^2Ex2. A functor is a fibration exactly when RnR_nRn​ sends it to a Kan fibration, the simplicial lifting condition for horns.

Cofibrations are determined by the left lifting property against maps that are both fibrations and weak equivalences. The manuscript claims that these classes form a proper combinatorial model structure, and that

Ln:sSet⇄nCat:RnL_n:\mathrm{sSet}\rightleftarrows n\mathrm{Cat}:R_nLn​:sSet⇄nCat:Rn​

is a Quillen equivalence with the usual homotopy theory of simplicial sets.

“Combinatorial” means the underlying category has suitable presentability properties and the model structure is generated by sets of maps. Here the generators come from twice-subdivided simplex boundaries and horns. “Proper” means weak equivalences behave well under the relevant pushouts along cofibrations and pullbacks along fibrations.

The statement applies to all small strict categories of the specified dimension. It is not restricted to free presentations or cofibrant inputs, and it is a full model structure, rather than only a semi-model structure.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the result completes a central model-structure problem in strict higher-category theory, with one uniform construction across all positive finite dimensions and dimension ω\omegaω.

A model structure gives more than a list of equivalent objects. It provides replacements, derived constructions, and lifting tools compatible with how objects are attached. These are the mechanisms used to calculate homotopy limits and colimits and to compare different algebraic presentations.

The arbitrary-target scope is especially significant. A construction restricted to free inputs might miss the attachments that arise during a factorization or a derived gluing problem. The claim supplies the structure on the full category where those operations actually take place.

6. The main idea

Make a contraction stationary on the attaching part

The central pushout problem begins with a partially ordered set EEE and a downward-closed full subset AAA. Suppose the inclusion has a right adjoint retraction. After turning their nerves into strict higher categories, the manuscript seeks a weak equivalence after attaching the larger object along any map out of the smaller one.

The geometric idea is to contract the added part while fixing the old part throughout the contraction. If that equality holds strictly on the attaching subcategory, the contraction can be glued to the constant cylinder on an arbitrary target category.

Ordinary homotopy intuition is insufficient because a categorical pushout creates new composites. The cylinder must control those composites as well as the named generators.

Construct positive directed prisms

The manuscript works with directed chain complexes, where selected positive chains encode allowed higher-cell directions. Under specific monotonicity hypotheses, it writes an explicit prism map between two maps of posets. Repeated vertices become zero after normalization, and the resulting map preserves positivity.

Through Steiner’s description of orientals and the Gray tensor product, this chain map gives a strict cylinder. Its restriction to the old subcategory remains constant in the interval direction. This is the algebraic reason it survives arbitrary attachments.

When the newly added part has a greatest element, two such cylinders yield a relative contraction by a zigzag. For a general finite poset, the argument removes different maximal new elements and covers the attachment by smaller pieces. Their nerves glue along monomorphisms, so the local weak-equivalence conclusions combine.

The contractions on overlapping pieces need not be chosen compatibly. What glues is the homotopical conclusion, using the precise sieve and intersection descriptions. Passing through finite subposets stable under the retraction treats arbitrary posets.

Transfer from simplicial attachments

Two subdivisions put simplex boundaries and horns into the required poset form. The relative contraction theorem then supplies the comparison between a pushout of nerves and the nerve of the categorical pushout.

That comparison permits the small-object constructions producing both factorization systems. Additional presentability and finite-presentation arguments ensure that the generating objects are small enough for those constructions. The paper then establishes properness and the adjunction-unit comparison for arbitrary simplicial sets, giving the claimed Quillen equivalence.

The infinite-dimensional argument uses finite orientals directly. Reflection to finite dimension carries the same construction to each finite nnn, while respecting the necessary relations in the top retained dimension.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns strict globular categories with possibly noninvertible cells. It does not contradict the limitations of strict globular groupoids discussed in family 312. Noninvertible categorical data can encode a general homotopy type through its nerve, even though a strictly invertible globular model is more restrictive.

A finite category dimension does not bound the dimensions in which its nerve can have homotopy. Already ordinary categories can model arbitrary homotopy types. Thus “nnn-category” here is not synonymous with “space having no homotopy above degree nnn.”

The weak equivalences are detected by the Street nerve, not by literal isomorphism or the usual equivalence relation between higher categories. Different choices of weak equivalence lead to different homotopy theories.

M1 compares its method with the weak-groupoid expansion argument in family 312, but states that the latter is not an input. The results address related foundations with different objects and different model-structure conclusions. Explicit computational models and comparisons with other higher-category frameworks remain further applications to develop.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 supplies the theorem and stationary-cylinder construction. Primary background includes Thomason’s original model structure, Ara–Maltsiniotis’s transfer framework and dimension-two result, Gagna’s equivalence with homotopy types, and Steiner’s directed-chain description. These references distinguish the previously known homotopy-category comparison from the additional structure claimed here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Thomason Model Structures in Every Strict Higher Dimension (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The same homotopy type can hide different aspherical four-manifolds
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 320 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A homotopy equivalence says that two spaces can be deformed into one another in a flexible, shape-preserving sense. A homeomorphism is stronger: it identifies their points continuously and has a continuous inverse. For manifolds with contractible universal covers, the Borel conjecture predicts an exceptional rigidity between these two notions.

Family 320 claims that this rigidity fails in dimension four. It constructs closed aspherical topological four-manifolds that have the same homotopy type but admit no homeomorphism at all. Their common fundamental group is word-hyperbolic, placing the example among groups for which strong higher-dimensional rigidity theorems are known.

The manuscript also claims a separate self-map result: one of the manifolds has a self-homotopy equivalence that no homeomorphism represents. Distinguishing these statements is important. Failure to realize one chosen homotopy class does not automatically produce two manifolds with no homeomorphism in any class.

2. Background and essential definitions

A manifold is closed if it is compact and has no boundary. It is aspherical if its universal cover is contractible. Such a space is a classifying space for its fundamental group: its higher homotopy groups vanish, and its fundamental group determines its homotopy type.

A homotopy equivalence f:M→Nf:M\to Nf:M→N has an inverse up to homotopy. A homeomorphism has an actual continuous inverse. The usual topological Borel conjecture asks whether every homotopy equivalence between closed aspherical manifolds is homotopic to a homeomorphism. The weaker existence version asks only whether homotopy-equivalent manifolds are homeomorphic somehow.

A finitely generated group is word-hyperbolic when triangles in a Cayley graph are uniformly thin: each side stays within a fixed distance of the other two. This is a large-scale condition on the group. It does not say that every manifold with that group has a constant-curvature metric.

For an aspherical manifold, self-homotopy equivalences are described by outer automorphisms of its fundamental group. An outer automorphism is an automorphism modulo conjugation by group elements. The subgroup realized by homeomorphisms can be smaller than the full outer automorphism group.

A finite cover corresponds to a finite-index subgroup of the fundamental group. If w:G→Zw:G\to\mathbb Zw:G→Z is surjective, its connected cyclic cover of degree ddd corresponds to

Gd=w−1(dZ).G_d=w^{-1}(d\mathbb Z).Gd​=w−1(dZ).

The construction exploits a difference between even and odd covers of an auxiliary space. A manifold model of that space means a manifold equipped with a homotopy equivalence to it, not necessarily a literal replacement of each cell by a smooth piece.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Borel’s 1953 letter to Serre already asked whether compact manifolds that are classifying spaces are determined up to homeomorphism by their homotopy type. Low-dimensional rigidity and later geometric results gave substantial evidence.

Hsiang–Wall proved the existence version for homotopy tori in dimensions at least five. Farrell–Jones established topological rigidity for closed negatively curved manifolds in that range. Bartels–Lück proved the prescribed-homotopy-class formulation for a broad class of groups containing word-hyperbolic groups and groups acting geometrically on finite-dimensional CAT(0) spaces, again in dimensions at least five.

Dimension four has an additional geometric obstacle. The relevant applications of surgery and topological s-cobordism require control of embedded disks. Freedman’s good-group condition supplies that control in important cases. The four-dimensional applications of higher-dimensional algebraic rigidity therefore carry an extra hypothesis of this kind.

For torsion-free word-hyperbolic groups, Khan obtained rigidity up to topological s-cobordism. But an s-cobordism is not automatically a product in the four-dimensional setting without the needed geometric input. M1 locates its example at precisely this distinction.

There are also smooth exotic aspherical four-manifolds, including examples of Davis, Hayden, Huang, Ruberman, and Sunukjian that are homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic. Those distinguish smooth structures. The present claim is stronger in a different direction: it excludes homeomorphisms in the topological category.

M1 explicitly depends on two companion constructions in family 305: the marked tensor obstruction to disk embedding and the reflection/realization machinery producing an aspherical Poincaré complex without a manifold model. It imports their marked filling and support results, then adds the cover and symmetry arguments needed for the Borel conclusions.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 4 October 2026, states that there exist closed connected aspherical topological four-manifolds M,NM,NM,N such that

M≃N,M≇Nas topological manifolds.M\simeq N,\qquad M\not\cong N\quad\text{as topological manifolds}.M≃N,M≅Nas topological manifolds.

Their common fundamental group is word-hyperbolic. The notation ≃\simeq≃ means homotopy equivalence; the second assertion excludes every homeomorphism, without prescribing its induced group automorphism or homotopy class.

The same manuscript separately states that this MMM admits a self-homotopy equivalence

f:M⟶Mf:M\longrightarrow Mf:M⟶M

that is not homotopic to any self-homeomorphism. In the construction, the corresponding outer automorphism has square equal to the identity, so f2f^2f2 is homotopic to the identity. The nonrealization assertion does not merely rule out a homeomorphism of order two: it rules out every homeomorphism inducing that outer class, including one of infinite order.

The pair theorem disproves the homeomorphism-existence version of the four-dimensional Borel conjecture. The self-map theorem gives the additional prescribed-class failure on a single manifold. Neither theorem says that all aspherical four-manifolds fail rigidity or that word-hyperbolic groups cease to satisfy the higher-dimensional rigidity results.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the result refutes a central rigidity prediction in a dimension where algebraic and geometric topology interact exceptionally delicately.

Aspherical manifolds have no higher homotopy groups to distinguish them. The pair would therefore show that even the full homotopy type, and hence the fundamental group, can miss a topological distinction in dimension four. The obstruction is not merely a choice of smooth structure.

The word-hyperbolic group strengthens the conceptual message. A group can lie within a well-developed rigidity framework while the four-dimensional realization step still fails. The claimed example isolates the role of dimension rather than attributing the problem to an arbitrary poorly controlled group.

6. The main idea

Create a parity obstruction for marked fillings

The construction starts with a finite four-dimensional Poincaré chamber (P,S)(P,S)(P,S). The chamber has the homotopy type of a finite graph, and its group maps onto Z\mathbb ZZ. Its boundary in a cyclic cover of degree ddd is written SdS_dSd​.

A marked filling is a compact four-manifold filling that boundary while preserving the specified boundary map and graph homotopy type. The claimed chamber has a filling in the double cover, but no such filling in any odd cover of degree at least three.

The parity is encoded by red and blue plumbing caps attached to grope bodies. A grope is a surface built by replacing unresolved disks with further surfaces. In the double cover, alternating color choices separate the relevant sheets and produce the filling.

For an odd cover, the companion tensor obstruction turns a hypothetical filling into an assignment problem on an odd cycle. Between neighboring vertices there are five red and five blue edges. Every edge must be assigned to an endpoint, while at each vertex at least one color receives at most one edge.

Choose such a color at each vertex. Two adjacent vertices cannot choose the same color: together they could receive at most two of the five edges of that color between them. The chosen colors must therefore alternate around the cycle, which is impossible for odd length. The tensor machinery connects this elementary parity contradiction to the marked geometric filling problem.

Convert odd-cover failure into a forbidden symmetry

Davis reflection machinery turns the chamber data into a finite aspherical complex QQQ. Its double cover Q2Q_2Q2​ has a closed manifold model, while sufficiently large odd covers do not.

Conjugation by an element mapping to 1∈Z1\in\mathbb Z1∈Z defines an outer automorphism of the index-two subgroup. Asphericity realizes it by a self-homotopy equivalence of the manifold model.

Suppose a homeomorphism realized that class. Lift it to the infinite cyclic cover and compose it with a sufficiently large deck translation. The combined map moves a proper height function uniformly forward. It therefore generates a free, properly discontinuous, cocompact action, whose quotient is a closed manifold model of an odd cover.

That contradicts the odd-cover obstruction. The use of a large translation is why the argument does not need the hypothetical homeomorphism to have finite order.

Rule out every homeomorphism between two models

The pair theorem needs more work. The manuscript fills the double-cover chambers in two ways: one uses uniform boundary identifications, and the other twists them by the deck involution according to a nonzero binary linear functional.

Both produce manifold models of the same aspherical complex. They realize different finite subgroups of the common outer automorphism group: a horizontal subgroup AAA and a twisted graph subgroup BℓB_\ellBℓ​, inside a group also containing the forbidden involution δ\deltaδ.

The paper then controls the whole outer automorphism group. A bound on square grids gives hyperbolicity of the support construction. Poincaré duality excludes the virtually cyclic splittings that an infinite outer automorphism group would force. A further Coxeter-group argument identifies the normalizer of AAA.

These results make AAA a Sylow 2-subgroup of the automorphisms realized on the first manifold. A homeomorphism to the second manifold would transport its realized subgroup BℓB_\ellBℓ​ into that group and force a conjugacy that the construction excludes. This final symmetry argument upgrades a forbidden chosen homotopy class to the absence of every possible homeomorphism.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result is in the topological category and in dimension four. It does not contradict the cited rigidity theorems in dimensions at least five, nor does it merely exhibit exotic smooth structures.

The marked filling obstruction is part of a larger construction. Failure to fill one chamber is not by itself enough to prove the final pair theorem; reflection, cyclic covers, and control of all outer automorphisms are essential additional steps.

Likewise, an outer automorphism of finite order that has no finite-order geometric realization would be weaker than the self-map assertion here. M1’s criterion excludes any representing homeomorphism.

The theorem is existential and does not classify all failures of four-dimensional Borel rigidity. Determining exactly which group and manifold hypotheses recover rigidity remains a broader problem. The companion dependencies should also be retained when interpreting the claimed construction.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 provides the pair and self-map statements and identifies the two companion inputs from family 305. Borel’s 1953 letter, with historical commentary gives the original question. Farrell–Jones’s negative-curvature rigidity theorem illustrates the higher-dimensional positive theory. The distinct smooth phenomenon appears in Davis and collaborators, Exotic aspherical 4-manifolds. M1’s bibliography gives the Bartels–Lück, Khan, and Freedman–Quinn inputs with their dimensional hypotheses.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Nonhomeomorphic closed aspherical four-manifolds with the same homotopy type (October 4, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Chromatic splitting: the pieces can fit without splitting apart
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 318 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

Chromatic homotopy theory studies spectra one periodic height at a time. Reconstructing a spectrum from those layers requires understanding their overlap. A long-standing prediction proposed that the overlap for the sphere splits into a particularly elegant collection of lower-height spheres.

Family 318 contains five manuscripts that give a more complicated picture. They claim that the predicted pieces can form a finite filtration in a large-prime range, while the corresponding direct-sum decomposition fails already at height three. Elsewhere, even a retraction of the canonical map fails, and one small-prime example cannot be assembled from lower local spheres by any finite sequence of the permitted operations.

These statements address different questions. Knowing the pieces of a filtration does not determine how they attach. Knowing that an object is finitely assembled does not make one specified map split. The family’s main theme is that the attaching maps carry information that a list of pieces misses.

2. Background and essential definitions

A spectrum is a stable object in which suspension is invertible. Write ΣdX\Sigma^dXΣdX for a degree shift. A cofiber sequence

A⟶B⟶C⟶ΣAA\longrightarrow B\longrightarrow C\longrightarrow\Sigma AA⟶B⟶C⟶ΣA

describes BBB as an extension of AAA by CCC. The last map records the attachment. If the extension splits, BBB is a wedge A∨CA\vee CA∨C, the stable analogue of a direct sum. An unsplit extension can have the same pieces without being their direct sum, just as an abelian-group extension can.

Fix a prime ppp, and let S=Sp∧S=S_p^{\wedge}S=Sp∧​ be the derived ppp-completed sphere. Morava localization LK(n)L_{K(n)}LK(n)​ isolates height nnn. Johnson–Wilson localization Lr=LE(r)L_r=L_{E(r)}Lr​=LE(r)​ retains heights zero through rrr, with L0L_0L0​ rationalization. The overlap is

Xn,p=Ln−1LK(n)S.X_{n,p}=L_{n-1}L_{K(n)}S.Xn,p​=Ln−1​LK(n)​S.

The canonical unit gives a distinguished map

in,S:Ln−1S⟶Xn,p.i_{n,S}:L_{n-1}S\longrightarrow X_{n,p}.in,S​:Ln−1​S⟶Xn,p​.

Four notions will be kept separate. Strong splitting prescribes a particular wedge decomposition, usually with specified maps. Weak splitting asks only for a homotopy retraction of in,Si_{n,S}in,S​. A filtration constructs the overlap by successive cofibers with specified layers, allowing nonzero attachments. Ordinary finite assembly allows finite sums, all shifts, cofibers, and retracts from lower local spheres, without prescribing a layer list.

In M4, finite assembly takes place in the category of E(2)E(2)E(2)-local modules over the completed sphere. It is ordinary thick closure: tensoring with arbitrary additional objects is not an extra permitted operation.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hopkins’s chromatic splitting proposal, recorded by Hovey, related sphere overlaps to exterior classes in stabilizer cohomology. At height one the expected behavior is classical. At height two, Shimomura–Yabe’s calculations supported the large odd-prime answer, later reorganized and corrected by Behrens. Goerss–Henn–Mahowald proved the height-two splitting at the prime three.

The prime-two height-two case already showed why formulations matter. Beaudry disproved the original strong wedge formula. Beaudry–Goerss–Henn subsequently supplied a refined decomposition with Moore-spectrum terms while retaining the canonical unit retraction. A failure of the original list therefore did not imply failure of weak splitting or of finite assembly.

Barthel–Schlank–Stapleton–Weinstein determined the rational homotopy of the local sphere at every prime and height. It is an exterior algebra over Qp\mathbb Q_pQp​ with generator degrees 1−2i1-2i1−2i. At height three, its degrees are

0,−1,−3,−4,−5,−6,−8,−9.0,-1,-3,-4,-5,-6,-8,-9.0,−1,−3,−4,−5,−6,−8,−9.

These are exactly the shifts expected in the classical eight-piece pattern. But agreement of rational dimensions does not identify the maps between heights, integral representatives, or extension classes.

The manuscripts also build on Gross–Torii marking towers, recent geometric coheight-one calculations, and descent theory. They distinguish completed geometric coefficient calculations from ordinary spectra: returning from a completion requires control of finite marking stages, pole bounds, and actual comparison maps. The five introductions provide the precise primary sources and the roles of these earlier results.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: the predicted layers form a filtration at generic primes

M1, dated 25 September 2026, states that for every n≥1n\geq1n≥1 and prime p>n+1p>n+1p>n+1, the overlap has an ordered filtration with 2n2^n2n layers. For a subset I⊆{1,…,n}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}I⊆{1,…,n}, put

d(I)=∑i∈I(2i−1).d(I)=\sum_{i\in I}(2i-1).d(I)=i∈I∑​(2i−1).

The empty-set layer is Ln−1SL_{n-1}SLn−1​S. For nonempty III, the layer is

Σ−d(I)Ln−max⁡IS.\Sigma^{-d(I)}L_{n-\max I}S.Σ−d(I)Ln−maxI​S.

The first-stage map to the overlap is the canonical unit. The theorem retains the attachments; it does not assert a wedge or a retraction. One family of sphere classes supplies compatible product bases at all lower positive heights. The final rational block is chosen from rational dimensions and is not identified with all the remaining products of that family.

M2 and M3: eight layers, but no eight-piece wedge

M2, dated 27 September 2026, independently constructs the height-three filtration for every p≥5p\geq5p≥5. In order, its layers are

L2S,Σ−1L2S,Σ−3L1S,Σ−4L1S,Σ−5HQp,Σ−6HQp,Σ−8HQp,Σ−9HQp.\begin{aligned}&L_2S,\quad\Sigma^{-1}L_2S,\quad\Sigma^{-3}L_1S,\quad\Sigma^{-4}L_1S,\\&\Sigma^{-5}H\mathbb Q_p,\quad\Sigma^{-6}H\mathbb Q_p,\quad\Sigma^{-8}H\mathbb Q_p,\quad\Sigma^{-9}H\mathbb Q_p.\end{aligned}​L2​S,Σ−1L2​S,Σ−3L1​S,Σ−4L1​S,Σ−5HQp​,Σ−6HQp​,Σ−8HQp​,Σ−9HQp​.​

It identifies the attachments relative to chosen local maps, a compatibility homotopy, and coherent inverse data. Only the first unit is asserted to be canonical independently of those choices.

M3, dated 25 September 2026, claims that the canonical map

L0LK(3)S⟶L0LK(2)LK(3)SL_0L_{K(3)}S\longrightarrow L_0L_{K(2)}L_{K(3)}SL0​LK(3)​S⟶L0​LK(2)​LK(3)​S

is nonzero on π−3\pi_{-3}π−3​ for every p≥5p\geq5p≥5. Here the use of the ordinary sphere or its completion gives the relevant positive-height local object.

For the proposed eight-piece wedge, the corresponding natural map is zero in that degree. M3 therefore rules out even an equivalence of the underlying E(2)E(2)E(2)-local spectra, without requiring it to preserve named summands. Applied to M2’s explicit filtration, this separate result makes its first height-one attachment nonzero. M2’s construction itself does not depend on M3.

M4: finite assembly fails at the prime three

M4, dated 25 September 2026, states that at p=n=3p=n=3p=n=3,

L2LK(3)S∉Thick⁡{L0S,L1S,L2S}L_2L_{K(3)}S\notin\operatorname{Thick}\{L_0S,L_1S,L_2S\}L2​LK(3)​S∈/Thick{L0​S,L1​S,L2​S}

in the specified module category. The obstruction allows arbitrarily many but finitely many cofibers and retracts, including Moore corrections. It is stronger than failure of a particular finite layer list.

This prime is outside M1’s range at height three. M4 does not by itself claim that the distinguished unit lacks a retraction; ordinary thick membership and splitting a particular map are different tests.

M5: explicit kernels obstruct weak splitting

M5, dated 27 September 2026, claims nonretraction at height ppp for every prime p≥5p\geq5p≥5, and at height p+1p+1p+1 for every prime p≥7p\geq7p≥7, using the completion of the finite sphere as input.

Let β1\beta_1β1​ be the first beta element, of degree 2p(p−1)−22p(p-1)-22p(p−1)−2. The same named sphere product

zp=β1(p−1)2z_p=\beta_1^{(p-1)^2}zp​=β1(p−1)2​

survives in the appropriate lower localization but is killed by the upper unit. At p=5p=5p=5, this gives β116\beta_1^{16}β116​ in degree 608 as a nonzero kernel element for the height-five map. A map with a left inverse cannot kill a nonzero homotopy class, so this obstructs any homotopy retraction, even an unnatural one.

M5 also gives an independent height-ppp obstruction using incompatible descent exponents, rather than a named permanent sphere class.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the family substantially revises a central reconstruction picture in chromatic homotopy theory. It supplies a positive replacement by filtrations in one range and explicit obstructions to several stronger predictions.

The distinction between dimensions and maps is especially instructive. The expected rational degree pattern can be entirely correct while the proposed wedge is wrong. The nonzero degree-minus-three map detects information that counting generators cannot see.

The small-prime and weak-splitting counterexamples also show that one universal repair is unlikely to suffice. Allowing nonsplit attachments works in the generic-prime filtration theorem, but it does not rescue ordinary finite assembly at p=n=3p=n=3p=n=3. Merely asking for a unit retraction also fails in M5’s separate ranges.

6. The main idea

Construct actual compatible bases before gluing

M1 separates two tasks: calculating coefficient cohomology and constructing sphere classes that act on it. Finite marking towers and compact-support geometry on spaces of bundle extensions supply the coefficient calculation. Cartier transfers, pole control, and finite-stage comparisons return that information to ordinary coefficients.

A second construction produces one family of integral stable classes, normalized using regulator and volume calculations. The comparison identifies their products as bases under every lower positive-height test. Successive cofibers then lower the remaining chromatic height, and rational information supplies the last block. This produces an actual filtration with the prescribed first map.

M2 makes the height-three gluing explicit. The unit and determinant class first supply the two height-two pieces. A height-one orientation class supplies the next two. A nonzero rational comparison scalar is matched with the height-one map so that the fracture square glues them using a chosen compatibility homotopy. The remaining cofiber is rational and supplies the final four pieces.

Detect an attachment through a natural map

M3 transports a degree-three stabilizer cohomology class through two descriptions of a modification space on the Fargues–Fontaine curve. One description uses division-algebra symmetries and the other linear-group symmetries. The classical trace expression

(U,V,W)⟼tr⁡red(U[V,W])(U,V,W)\longmapsto\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{red}}(U[V,W])(U,V,W)⟼trred​(U[V,W])

provides the relevant class; [V,W]=VW−WV[V,W]=VW-WV[V,W]=VW−WV and the reduced trace generalizes matrix trace.

The rank-three class restricts nontrivially toward rank two. Integral Witt-coefficient comparisons establish that the transported classes remain nonzero, and descent carries that nonvanishing into ordinary degree-minus-three homotopy. Locality of the detector forces its map to factor through the canonical localization map. Naturality then rules out any proposed wedge equivalence, not just one poorly chosen set of summand maps.

Preserve a character that finite assembly cannot create

M4 uses an exact test involving height-two Morava EEE-theory, reduction modulo three, and inversion of its deformation parameter xxx. Every finite construction from the proposed generators has representation constituents that are powers of the periodicity line.

The overlap instead contains a line twisted by a nontrivial norm character from an unramified quadratic extension of Q3\mathbb Q_3Q3​. The argument retains the full semilinear action over k((x))k((x))k((x)): the group acts on coefficients as well as vectors. Looking only at a residue character would lose essential information.

Finite marking comparisons and all deformation jets carry that character into actual homotopy. Its inequivalence to every periodicity power prevents the relevant differentials from removing it and violates the necessary condition for finite assembly.

Kill the same sphere product at a higher height

For M5, an established ordinary homotopy-fixed-point calculation detects the named beta product at height p−1p-1p−1. At the upper heights, the manuscript constructs a separated multiplicative filtration with the beta element in filtration at least two and a finite upper cutoff. The product’s filtration exceeds that cutoff, forcing its upper image to vanish.

Completion and naturality place these two facts on the precise weak-splitting map. The separate exponent argument compares lengths of finite descent constructions: a retraction would transfer an upper bound that contradicts a lower bound at height p−1p-1p−1. Its lower bound needs survival to a particular finite spectral-sequence page, not a permanent sphere representative.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The prime and height ranges are essential. M1 assumes p>n+1p>n+1p>n+1; M2 and M3 use height three with p≥5p\geq5p≥5; M4 treats height three at three; M5 uses the two ranges stated above. The manuscripts do not claim a sharp universal prime threshold.

A nonzero attachment does not automatically prove failure of the canonical unit retraction. Conversely, finite assembly does not imply a prescribed wedge decomposition. The family keeps these implications separate, and the examples occur in different ranges.

The filtration theorem retains extension data rather than computing all homotopy groups. M2 describes attachments relative to compatible choices, not a universally canonical formula independent of choices. M4’s ordinary thick closure is also distinct from a tensor ideal allowing arbitrary additional tensor factors.

These results leave many prime-height combinations and finer attachment calculations outside their statements. They report specific positive constructions and negative obstructions, rather than a complete classification of every chromatic overlap.

8. Sources and further reading

M1–M5 are the sources for the five claims and their dependencies. Their introductions cite Hovey’s account of Hopkins’s conjecture; the height-two work of Shimomura–Yabe, Behrens, and Goerss–Henn–Mahowald; the prime-two correction of Beaudry–Goerss–Henn; and the rational calculation of Barthel–Schlank–Stapleton–Weinstein. The bibliographies also identify the geometric marking comparisons and the Hopkins–Miller detector used by M5. Reading the theorem statements together is particularly useful because the same word “splitting” covers several distinct assertions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Filtered chromatic splitting at generic primes (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The height-three chromatic overlap: an explicit filtration and its attachments (September 27, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, A rational obstruction to strong chromatic splitting at height three (September 25, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Failure of finite assembly for a chromatic overlap at the prime three (September 25, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, Counterexamples to weak chromatic splitting: sphere kernels and descent exponents (September 27, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A finite complex whose third dimension cannot be removed
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 321 · Topology
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-22

1. The question

A cell complex is built by attaching points, edges, disks, and higher-dimensional cells. Sometimes the higher cells are unnecessary: a complex may be homotopy equivalent to one of lower dimension. Algebraic invariants often detect when such a reduction should be possible.

Wall’s finite D(2)D(2)D(2) problem asks whether particular homology and cohomology vanishing conditions force a finite complex to have a finite two-dimensional homotopy model. The conditions remove the obvious algebraic need for dimension three. The question is whether geometry can still prevent the reduction.

Family 321 claims a negative answer. Its example is a finite three-dimensional complex satisfying an even stronger coefficient-vanishing condition than required, yet having no finite model of dimension at most two. Its fundamental group is infinite; “finite” refers to the cell structure.

2. Background and essential definitions

A CW complex is formed by attaching cells along their boundaries. A presentation complex for a group has one vertex, one edge for each generator, and one disk for each relator. Its fundamental group is the presented group.

For a connected complex XXX, let G=π1(X)G=\pi_1(X)G=π1​(X) and let X~\widetilde XX be its universal cover. The group ring ZG\mathbb ZGZG consists of finite integer combinations of group elements. Modules over it allow coefficients that change when transported around loops.

Such local coefficients contain more information than constant coefficients. A particularly accessible example is a character

ρ:G⟶C×.\rho:G\longrightarrow\mathbb C^{\times}.ρ:G⟶C×.

It gives a one-dimensional complex local system LρL_\rhoLρ​: traversing a loop representing ggg multiplies a coefficient by ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g). Twisted homology is calculated by cellular boundary matrices whose entries include these transport factors.

For a finite three-dimensional complex, the D(2)D(2)D(2) condition is

Hi(X~;Z)=0(i>2),H3(X;M)=0H_i(\widetilde X;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(i>2),\qquad H^3(X;M)=0Hi​(X;Z)=0(i>2),H3(X;M)=0

for every finitely generated ZG\mathbb ZGZG-module MMM. The first condition concerns the universal cover; the second concerns cohomology with all the specified local systems. Neither condition says that XXX is aspherical.

A group is perfect if it equals its commutator subgroup, or equivalently if its abelianization is zero. Quillen’s plus construction kills a chosen perfect normal subgroup of the fundamental group by adding two- and three-dimensional cells while preserving homology with coefficients from the quotient group.

A homotopy model preserves the entire homotopy type, not merely ordinary homology. The question here also requires that the lower-dimensional model have finitely many cells.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Wall introduced these dimension conditions in his work on finiteness of CW complexes in the 1960s and returned to the question in his 1979 problem list. His reductions bring the D(2)D(2)D(2) case to a finite three-dimensional model. The unresolved step was removing the remaining three-cells up to homotopy.

A stable version has a positive answer. Work going back to Cohen shows that adding sufficiently many two-spheres by a wedge makes a finite D(2)D(2)D(2) complex homotopy equivalent to a finite two-dimensional complex. Hambleton gives a bound in terms of the number of three-cells. But adding spheres changes the space, so stable reduction does not settle the original problem.

There are positive results for particular groups. Hambleton established the D(2)D(2)D(2) property for finite subgroups of SO(3)SO(3)SO(3). M1 also cites Hofmann–Nicholson’s results for generalized quaternion groups, including the resolution of a longstanding candidate involving the group of order 32.

Other candidate counterexamples arose from relation gaps: the relator subgroup may appear to need more normal generators than its abelianization needs as a module. Bridson–Tweedale constructed relevant finite D(2)D(2)D(2) complexes, with failure of a two-dimensional model conditional on a relation-gap assertion.

Mannan connected the problem directly with the plus construction. Applied to a finite two-dimensional complex along a finitely normally generated perfect subgroup, it produces a finite D(2)D(2)D(2) complex. He also obtained a converse description for finite cohomologically two-dimensional three-complexes.

M1 uses this established production method. Its claimed new obstruction is a restriction on rank-one twisted homology in a finite two-dimensional complex, obtained by adapting Howie’s cyclic-tower method. The construction and obstruction then meet in a small explicit presentation.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, dated 6 October 2026, states that there is a finite connected three-dimensional CW complex XXX with

Hi(X~;Z)=0(i>2),H3(X;M)=0for every ZG-module M,H_i(\widetilde X;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(i>2),\qquad H^3(X;M)=0\quad\text{for every }\mathbb ZG\text{-module }M,Hi​(X;Z)=0(i>2),H3(X;M)=0for every ZG-module M,

but no homotopy equivalence from XXX to any finite CW complex of dimension at most two. The cohomology assertion covers all modules, not merely finitely generated ones.

The example starts with the presentation

P=⟨x1,a1,x2,a2,s∣  x1a1x1−1=a14,x2a2x2−1=a23,x1=a213,sx2s−1=a15⟩.\begin{aligned}P=\langle x_1,a_1,x_2,a_2,s\mid\;&x_1a_1x_1^{-1}=a_1^4,\quadx_2a_2x_2^{-1}=a_2^3,\\&x_1=a_2^{13},\quad sx_2s^{-1}=a_1^5\rangle.\end{aligned}P=⟨x1​,a1​,x2​,a2​,s∣​x1​a1​x1−1​=a14​,x2​a2​x2−1​=a23​,x1​=a213​,sx2​s−1=a15​⟩.​

Its presentation complex BBB has one vertex, five edges, and four two-cells. Let KKK be the normal closure of x12x_1^2x12​ and x23x_2^3x23​ in PPP. The manuscript shows that KKK is perfect and forms the finite plus construction with group G=P/KG=P/KG=P/K.

This adds two two-cells and two three-cells. Sending sss to 1∈Z1\in\mathbb Z1∈Z and the other generators to zero gives a surjection G→ZG\to\mathbb ZG→Z, so the group is infinite.

The general obstruction states that for a finite two-dimensional complex YYY,

H2(Y;Lρ)=0⟹ρ(g)=1 for every finite-order g∈π1(Y).H_2(Y;L_\rho)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\rho(g)=1\text{ for every finite-order }g\in\pi_1(Y).H2​(Y;Lρ​)=0⟹ρ(g)=1 for every finite-order g∈π1​(Y).

The constructed XXX has a character violating the conclusion while retaining the vanishing hypothesis. Homotopy invariance would transfer both properties to any proposed finite two-dimensional model, which is therefore excluded.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisionally. If correct, the example gives a negative answer to a classical dimension-reduction problem and separates algebraic cancellation from geometric realization in a particularly low dimension.

The obstruction is finer than ordinary homology. A one-dimensional coefficient system remembers how loops act on coefficients, and that small extra piece of information detects the impossibility of a finite two-dimensional model.

The explicit size is also informative. The construction begins with five generators and four relators, then adds a finite plus-construction package. The difficulty is not an uncontrolled infinite complex; it is a mismatch between finite algebraic conditions and finite geometric realizability.

6. The main idea

A tower that cannot keep growing

Suppose a finite two-dimensional complex YYY has H2(Y;L)=0H_2(Y;L)=0H2​(Y;L)=0. The manuscript proves a stronger statement than the torsion obstruction: a map from a finite complex FFF with b1(F;Q)=0b_1(F;\mathbb Q)=0b1​(F;Q)=0 cannot pull LLL back to a system with nontrivial monodromy.

Assume such a map exists and replace its image by a finite simplicial subcomplex AAA. In dimension two, second homology is the kernel of the second boundary map, with no third boundary to quotient out. Its vanishing therefore passes to subcomplexes.

Nontrivial rank-one monodromy gives H0(A;L)=0H_0(A;L)=0H0​(A;L)=0. Together with H2(A;L)=0H_2(A;L)=0H2​(A;L)=0, the Euler-characteristic formula implies χ(A)≤0\chi(A)\leq0χ(A)≤0, hence b1(A;Q)≥1b_1(A;\mathbb Q)\geq1b1​(A;Q)≥1. There is consequently an infinite cyclic cover of AAA.

The map from FFF lifts to that cover because every homomorphism from π1(F)\pi_1(F)π1​(F) to Z\mathbb ZZ is zero. The manuscript shows that the twisted second-homology vanishing also passes to the cover. Its boundary matrix has Laurent-polynomial entries; a nonzero full-rank minor after setting the deck variable to one remains a nonzero polynomial upstairs.

Replace the cover by the image of the lifted map and repeat. Each new image has strictly more simplices, while every image is still the image of the same fixed triangulated FFF. The number of simplices can neither grow indefinitely nor exceed that finite bound. This yields the claimed contradiction.

For a finite-order loop, a suitable finite Moore complex provides FFF. In the order-two case used below, it is simply the real projective plane RP2\mathbb RP^2RP2, whose first rational Betti number is zero.

Arrange the forbidden character

The exponents in the presentation are chosen so that

42−1=15,33−1=26,gcd⁡(15,26)=1.4^2-1=15,\qquad3^3-1=26,\qquad\gcd(15,26)=1.42−1=15,33−1=26,gcd(15,26)=1.

The induced relations in the abelianization of KKK impose coprime annihilators on its normal generators. M1 uses this to show that the abelianization vanishes, making the finite plus construction available.

Choose a primitive cube root of unity ζ\zetaζ. The character is

ρ(x1)=−1,ρ(a1)=ζ,ρ(x2)=ζ2,ρ(a2)=−1,ρ(s)=1.\rho(x_1)=-1,\quad\rho(a_1)=\zeta,\quad\rho(x_2)=\zeta^2,\quad\rho(a_2)=-1,\quad\rho(s)=1.ρ(x1​)=−1,ρ(a1​)=ζ,ρ(x2​)=ζ2,ρ(a2​)=−1,ρ(s)=1.

It respects the relations and kills the two generators of KKK, so it descends to GGG. The element represented by x1x_1x1​ has order exactly two: its square is killed, and its character value −1-1−1 shows that it is not the identity.

The paper computes the twisted cellular boundary of BBB. A four-by-four minor has determinant −4(1−ζ2)≠0-4(1-\zeta^2)\neq0−4(1−ζ2)=0, giving H2(B;Lρ)=0H_2(B;L_\rho)=0H2​(B;Lρ​)=0. This is the manuscript’s reported boundary calculation, used here to explain how the example is arranged.

The plus construction preserves this twisted homology while supplying the D(2)D(2)D(2) conditions. A finite two-dimensional model would therefore have vanishing twisted second homology and a character nontrivial on an order-two element. The tower obstruction forbids that combination.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns Wall’s finite D(2)D(2)D(2) problem. Both the initial complex and the excluded two-dimensional model have finitely many cells. The statement should not be expanded into an exclusion of every possible infinite two-dimensional model.

The example is not assumed aspherical, and its group contains torsion. It is therefore a different construction from the cohomological-versus-geometric dimension problem discussed in family 249.

The positive stabilized theorem remains compatible with this counterexample: adding two-spheres changes the homotopy type and can remove the obstruction. Likewise, positive D(2)D(2)D(2) results for specified finite groups are unaffected by this infinite-group example.

The claimed general rank-one obstruction may be useful in other realization problems, but the manuscript does not classify every group or every finite complex for which dimension reduction fails. Its conclusion is one explicit obstruction and one resulting counterexample.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 supplies the example, tower obstruction, and twisted boundary calculation. The established construction framework is Mannan’s Quillen’s plus construction and the D(2) problem. M1’s bibliography gives Wall’s 1965 finiteness paper and 1979 problem list, Cohen’s stable result, Hambleton’s positive cases, Howie’s cyclic-tower method, and the relation-module work of Bridson–Tweedale. These sources distinguish the existing method for producing finite D(2)D(2)D(2) complexes from the new obstruction claimed for this one.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Counterexample to Wall’s D(2) Problem (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 22 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How many isolated oscillations can a polynomial system sustain
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 143 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
