Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A pendulum with friction eventually stops, but a system that also receives energy can settle into a repeating oscillation. In a two-dimensional phase portrait, such an oscillation appears as a closed trajectory. If nearby closed trajectories do not fill a surrounding band, the orbit is called a limit cycle.

How many distinct limit cycles can a polynomial differential equation in the plane possess? The question is part of Hilbert’s sixteenth problem. Polynomial formulas of small degree look simple, yet their trajectories need not have simple shapes or simple dependence on the coefficients.

Family 143 contains two different claims. The first is a uniform finiteness theorem: fixing the polynomial degree fixes some finite upper bound on the number of limit cycles, regardless of the coefficients. The second gives an exact answer for a special family of oscillators: classical Liénard systems with a primitive of degree at most five have at most two limit cycles, and two can occur.

These statements have different levels of precision. The general theorem does not provide an effective numerical bound. The restricted theorem supplies the sharp number two.

2. Background and essential definitions

Polynomial vector fields and isolated cycles

Consider

x˙=P(x,y),y˙=Q(x,y),\dot x=P(x,y),\qquad \dot y=Q(x,y),x˙=P(x,y),y˙​=Q(x,y),

where the dot denotes differentiation with respect to time and P,QP,QP,Q are real polynomials. The degree of the vector field is the larger of their total degrees. Its coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers.

A periodic solution is a nonconstant motion that repeats after some positive time. Its geometric image is the closed curve traced by the motion. A limit cycle is a periodic orbit with a neighborhood containing no other periodic orbit. We count that image once, even if the same motion is parametrized with a different starting time.

Isolation is essential. The harmonic oscillator x˙=y, y˙=−x\dot x=y,\ \dot y=-xx˙=y, y˙​=−x has circles of periodic trajectories around the origin, but none is a limit cycle: every circle has other periodic circles arbitrarily close to it. Such a region is called a center.

An attracting cycle draws nearby trajectories toward it, while a repelling one pushes them away. The statements in this family also include isolated cycles with more delicate stability behavior; they are not restricted to attractors.

A return map turns an orbit into a zero

Place a short interval across a periodic trajectory, transversely to the direction of motion. Starting at coordinate rrr on the interval, follow the trajectory until it returns. Its new coordinate defines the Poincaré return map Π(r)\Pi(r)Π(r).

The original orbit is a fixed point, and nearby cycles correspond to isolated zeros of

D(r)=Π(r)−r.D(r)=\Pi(r)-r.D(r)=Π(r)−r.

A simple zero satisfies D′(r)≠0D'(r)\ne0D′(r)=0, or equivalently Π′(r)≠1\Pi'(r)\ne1Π′(r)=1; the corresponding cycle is hyperbolic. A multiple zero may still represent an isolated cycle and must not be discarded when counting all cycles.

The special Liénard class

The companion paper treats

x˙=y−F(x),y˙=−x.\dot x=y-F(x),\qquad \dot y=-x.x˙=y−F(x),y˙​=−x.

Eliminating yyy gives the scalar oscillator equation

x′′+F′(x)x′+x=0.x''+F'(x)x'+x=0.x′′+F′(x)x′+x=0.

Thus F′F'F′ is the damping polynomial, and the restoring force is exactly xxx. A quintic primitive means deg⁡F≤5\deg F\leq5degF≤5, so the damping has degree at most four. This convention matters when comparing statements phrased in terms of the damping rather than its primitive.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hilbert’s 1900 problem asked about both the number and the arrangement of limit cycles of polynomial planar systems. A basic distinction soon became central: finiteness for each individual system is weaker than a bound uniform over all systems of a given degree. Every member of a collection can have a finite count while the collection of counts remains unbounded.

Dulac announced an individual-finiteness argument in 1923. After a gap was identified, Écalle and Ilyashenko developed proofs using sophisticated asymptotic and complex analysis of return maps. M1 also discusses Yeung’s later objection to one coefficient-closure mechanism in Ilyashenko’s monograph. That discussion concerns a proof mechanism, not an example with infinitely many cycles. The new manuscript states that its own uniformity argument does not assume individual finiteness as an input.

Important partial results controlled particular degenerations. Bautin obtained the sharp bound of three cycles bifurcating from a quadratic focus or center under quadratic perturbations. Ilyashenko and Yakovenko proved finite cyclicity for elementary polycycles in generic parameter families; Kaloshin subsequently supplied quantitative bounds. A polycycle is a closed chain of trajectories joining equilibrium points. The elementary and genericity assumptions limit the singular behavior these theorems address.

Binyamini, Novikov, and Yakovenko established effective bounds in the infinitesimal Hilbert problem, involving zeros of Abelian integrals and suitable perturbations of Hamiltonian ovals. This is a major restricted setting, rather than the unrestricted polynomial problem.

For classical Liénard systems, Lins, de Melo, and Pugh proposed the bound ⌊(n−1)/2⌋\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor⌊(n−1)/2⌋ when the primitive has degree nnn. Rychkov proved the two-cycle statement for odd quintic primitives. Later counterexamples invalidated the proposed formula in degrees six and above. Li and Llibre established the unrestricted quartic one-cycle bound, and Li and Lu treated certain quintic slow–fast limiting configurations. The gap addressed by M2 is the global quintic case with arbitrary even as well as odd coefficients.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A degree-only bound in the whole plane

M1 states that, for every integer d≥1d\geq1d≥1, there is a finite nonnegative integer B(d)B(d)B(d) such that

#{limit cycles of (P,Q)}≤B(d)whenever max⁡(deg⁡P,deg⁡Q)≤d.\#\{\text{limit cycles of }(P,Q)\}\leq B(d)\qquad\text{whenever }\max(\deg P,\deg Q)\leq d.#{limit cycles of (P,Q)}≤B(d)whenever max(degP,degQ)≤d.

The bound applies throughout R2\mathbb R^2R2. There is no restriction on the size of the coefficients, on how far the cycles lie from the origin, or on their stability. Geometric cycles are counted once, without a multiplicity weight.

This is the uniform boundedness assertion in the second part of Hilbert’s sixteenth problem. The manuscript explicitly does not give an effective formula for B(d)B(d)B(d), the best possible value, or a classification of arrangements.

Exactly two in the quintic Liénard class

M2 states that every classical Liénard system with an arbitrary real polynomial FFF of degree at most five has at most two limit cycles. It also supplies a construction attaining two, so the maximum within this class is exactly two.

No oddness assumption is made on FFF, and its coefficients need not satisfy prescribed signs. Isolated nonhyperbolic cycles are included. The result concerns the whole phase plane, not only small oscillations near an equilibrium or cycles arising in a particular perturbation limit.

The restoring force remains xxx. Replacing it by a general polynomial would produce a larger class not covered by this theorem. Likewise, the result does not restore the Lins–de Melo–Pugh formula in degrees where earlier counterexamples already contradict it.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. A uniform degree-only bound would settle a central finiteness assertion in one of Hilbert’s classical problems. The difficulty is not merely to study a complicated individual system, but to control every coefficient degeneration without excluding exceptional cases.

The quintic theorem adds a different kind of advance: a sharp global answer for a natural oscillator class. It shows how an exact count can become accessible when the equations retain a particular structure, even though the general degree-only bound remains non-effective.

For applications, the distinction between existence and a usable bound remains important. M1 would establish that polynomial degree limits oscillatory complexity in principle. It would not by itself give an engineer a practical maximum to insert into a computation. M2 is numerically explicit, but only within its stated Liénard class.

6. The main idea

Keep track of several competing scales

A trajectory passing close to an equilibrium may spend a very long time there. Even the elementary saddle

x˙=x,y˙=−λy,λ>0,\dot x=x,\qquad \dot y=-\lambda y,\qquad \lambda>0,x˙=x,y˙​=−λy,λ>0,

illustrates the problem. Starting at (r,1)(r,1)(r,1), it reaches (1,rλ)(1,r^\lambda)(1,rλ) after time log⁡(1/r)\log(1/r)log(1/r). If rrr and λ\lambdaλ both vary, the time and the contraction exponent λlog⁡(1/r)\lambda\log(1/r)λlog(1/r) may grow at different rates.

M1 organizes such passages using nested asymptotic expansions on complex domains. It retains exponentially small corrections and distinguishes continuations on opposite sides of a real path. These details matter because an apparently negligible term can become the first nonzero contribution after leading terms cancel.

The claimed analytic machinery is designed to survive differentiation and implicit solving. Those operations arise when one follows a degenerating orbit, so controlling only the original return map would not be enough.

Count matching configurations uniformly

Instead of describing an entire cycle by one unwieldy formula, M1 decomposes it into finitely many local passages and writes equations matching their endpoints. Several choices of cuts can represent the same cycle, so counting every solution would overcount. The argument relates different hyperbolic cycles to different connected components of suitable sets of matching data.

A separate finite-dimensional counting principle then converts finiteness of isolated solutions in auxiliary systems into a uniform bound on those components. The manuscript emphasizes that the auxiliary systems must include the equations created by differentiation, implicit operations, and projection, with their domains preserved.

A bounded-degree geometric decomposition controls how many passage types and crossings are needed. Finally, a small signed rotation handles a prescribed finite collection of isolated nonhyperbolic cycles, while spatial rescaling accounts for cycles arbitrarily far away. These steps connect the local analytic machinery to the whole-plane statement.

Compare the two halves of a Liénard orbit

M2 uses a more specialized geometry. On each half-plane, the change u=x2/2u=x^2/2u=x2/2 turns an orbit into an arch satisfying

dudy=φ(u)−y,φ(u)=F(2u) or F(−2u).\frac{du}{dy}=\varphi(u)-y,\qquad\varphi(u)=F(\sqrt{2u})\ \text{or}\ F(-\sqrt{2u}).dydu​=φ(u)−y,φ(u)=F(2u​) or F(−2u​).

Here yyy serves as an endpoint coordinate, not physical time. At a fixed height, an arch has two endpoints; their half-distance is its width, and their average records its midpoint.

The even coefficients of a quintic primitive contribute the same quadratic part to both profiles, while the odd coefficients change sign. M2 fits quadratic comparison profiles to the arch data and transports their slope and curvature as the height varies. A model inequality controls how these fitted quantities change with width.

A periodic orbit requires the two half-orbits to match. Their midpoint difference is therefore a scalar matching function whose isolated zeros count cycles. The manuscript claims that the quintic coefficient structure constrains its changes of direction strongly enough to permit at most two isolated zeros. This comparison counts degenerate cycles directly. A separate small-parameter construction establishes that two cycles really occur.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Uniform finiteness does not determine the exact maximum for a general degree, its asymptotic growth, or all possible spatial arrangements. Those questions remain distinct from the existence of B(d)B(d)B(d).

The general theorem concerns real planar polynomial vector fields. It is not a statement about arbitrary smooth fields, higher-dimensional systems, or nonisolated families of periodic orbits. The harmonic oscillator’s continuum of circles is compatible with the claim because none is isolated.

For the Liénard result, both the degree convention and the exact restoring force are essential. The maximum two applies to primitive degree at most five, without an oddness assumption. Earlier higher-degree counterexamples remain part of the problem’s history.

The manuscripts present mathematical statements and proposed arguments, rather than a numerical survey of trajectories. A picture showing two apparent cycles would illustrate a system but would not replace either a global upper bound or a proof that the depicted orbits are isolated.

8. Sources and further reading

Hilbert’s Mathematical problems gives the original formulation. Bautin’s quadratic bifurcation theorem and Binyamini, Novikov, and Yakovenko’s constructive infinitesimal result illustrate earlier restricted advances. Ilyashenko’s centennial history supplies broader context.

For the Liénard branch, see Lins, de Melo, and Pugh, On Liénard’s equation; De Maesschalck and Dumortier’s higher-degree counterexamples; and Li and Llibre’s quartic uniqueness theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniform bounds for planar polynomial limit cycles (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Two limit cycles for quintic Liénard systems (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: One observable whose time shifts describe an entire smooth system
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 144 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Imagine observing a deterministic system through one numerical measurement. Record the measurement yesterday, today, tomorrow, and at every other integer time. Could these shifted measurements form an orthonormal basis for every square-integrable observation of the system, after subtracting its average?

The basis requirement has two parts. Different time shifts must be uncorrelated and have unit variance. Yet their linear combinations must also approximate every centered observation, not merely some small collection of signals.

This is a concrete way to formulate the probability-preserving version of Banach’s simple Lebesgue-spectrum problem. Family 144 claims such a system can be realized by an infinitely differentiable, volume-preserving map of the three-dimensional torus. The invariant probability is ordinary smooth volume, rather than a specially chosen measure supported on a complicated subset.

The claimed example would combine strong statistical decorrelation with zero measure-theoretic entropy and zero Lyapunov exponents. Those properties measure different aspects of dynamics, so understanding their coexistence is part of the interest.

2. Background and essential definitions

From trajectories to an operator

Write T=R/Z\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb ZT=R/Z. The three-torus T3\mathbb T^3T3 is a unit cube with opposite faces identified. Let μ\muμ be its normalized volume, so μ(T3)=1\mu(\mathbb T^3)=1μ(T3)=1.

A volume-preserving diffeomorphism TTT is a smooth invertible map with smooth inverse that preserves this measure. An observable is a measurable function ggg on the space. The square-integrable observables form the complex Hilbert space L2(μ)L^2(\mu)L2(μ), with

⟨g,h⟩=∫gh‾ dμ,∥g∥22=∫∣g∣2 dμ.\langle g,h\rangle=\int g\overline h\,d\mu,\qquad\|g\|_2^2=\int |g|^2\,d\mu.⟨g,h⟩=∫ghdμ,∥g∥22​=∫∣g∣2dμ.

The Koopman operator describes how an observable changes after one step:

UTg=g∘T.U_Tg=g\circ T.UT​g=g∘T.

It is unitary because TTT preserves volume and is invertible. Instead of following points, spectral theory studies this linear operator on functions.

Constants are always fixed by UTU_TUT​. They must be separated off when asking for a purely Lebesgue model. The relevant space is

L02(μ)={g∈L2(μ):∫g dμ=0}.L^2_0(\mu)=\left\{g\in L^2(\mu):\int g\,d\mu=0\right\}.L02​(μ)={g∈L2(μ):∫gdμ=0}.

What simple Lebesgue spectrum means

On the unit circle S1⊂CS^1\subset\mathbb CS1⊂C, let mmm be normalized arc length. The model operator is multiplication by the circle coordinate:

(Mg)(w)=w g(w),g∈L2(S1,m).(Mg)(w)=w\,g(w),\qquad g\in L^2(S^1,m).(Mg)(w)=wg(w),g∈L2(S1,m).

Its powers take the constant function one to wnw^nwn, for every integer nnn. These functions form the usual Fourier orthonormal basis.

To say that UTU_TUT​ has simple Lebesgue spectrum on L02(μ)L^2_0(\mu)L02​(μ) means that an inner-product-preserving change of Hilbert-space coordinates identifies it with this one-copy model. “Lebesgue” specifies arc-length spectral type; “simple” means multiplicity one.

Equivalently, there is a function fff for which

⟨f∘Tn,f∘Tk⟩={1,n=k,0,n≠k,\langle f\circ T^n,f\circ T^k\rangle=\begin{cases}1,&n=k,\\0,&n\ne k,\end{cases}⟨f∘Tn,f∘Tk⟩={1,0,​n=k,n=k,​

and the closed linear span of all these shifts is the entire mean-zero space. Indices run through positive and negative integers: this is a bilateral orbit.

Uncorrelated measurements need not be independent random variables. The basis statement is about Hilbert-space geometry and linear approximation, not a claim that repeated observations are independent coin tosses.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The manuscript distinguishes its probability-preserving question from the historical real-line formulation recorded by Ulam and attributed to Banach. Rokhlin explicitly asked for ergodic probability-preserving automorphisms with simple, or at least finite-multiplicity, Lebesgue spectrum. The setting and multiplicity are part of the problem, not optional details.

Earlier constructions achieved pieces of the desired picture. Helson and Parry constructed cocycles whose associated unitary operators have Lebesgue spectrum. A cocycle adds an auxiliary motion over a base transformation; the resulting operator need not already be the complete centered Koopman operator sought here. Mathew and Nadkarni constructed a probability-preserving transformation with a Lebesgue component of multiplicity two.

Guenais related a cocycle version of the question to flat polynomials and obtained a countable abelian group action with simple spectrum of mixed discrete and Haar type. Such results show why both the full space and the precise acting group matter.

Within smooth dynamics, Fayad constructed smooth volume-preserving torus transformations with simple spectrum. That alone did not identify the spectral type as Lebesgue. A separate infinite-measure construction discussed by el Abdalaoui likewise does not directly solve the probability-space problem.

Continuous-time flows provide another important comparison. Prikhod’ko constructed finite-measure flows with simple Lebesgue spectrum. Fayad, Forni, and Kanigowski, and later Abdedou, Fayad, and Kessi, obtained smooth or analytic flows with countably infinite Lebesgue multiplicity in specific torus settings. Sampling a simple Lebesgue flow at a fixed nonzero time does not preserve simplicity: the real frequency line wraps around the circle repeatedly, producing countably many spectral copies.

Finally, successive smooth coordinate changes have a long history in the approximation-by-conjugacy method of Anosov and Katok. The new manuscript uses explicit transitions between smooth integrable maps and supplies its own quantitative spectral control. Its claimed advance is the conjunction of all the desired features: a single discrete-time transformation, finite invariant volume, smooth realization, and multiplicity one on the whole centered space.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript. Its main theorem asserts the existence of a C∞C^\inftyC∞ volume-preserving diffeomorphism

T:T3⟶T3T:\mathbb T^3\longrightarrow\mathbb T^3T:T3⟶T3

and a real-valued f∈L02(T3,μ)f\in L^2_0(\mathbb T^3,\mu)f∈L02​(T3,μ) such that

{f∘Tn:n∈Z}\{f\circ T^n:n\in\mathbb Z\}{f∘Tn:n∈Z}

is an orthonormal basis of the complex mean-zero Hilbert space. Completeness uses complex linear combinations even though the generator itself is real. The measure is standard normalized volume.

The observable fff is only asserted to be square-integrable. The theorem does not claim that the generating observation is smooth or bounded merely because the underlying map is smooth.

The manuscript derives ergodicity and ordinary mixing. Ergodicity means every invariant measurable set has measure zero or one. Mixing means, for fixed measurable sets A,BA,BA,B,

μ(A∩T−nB)⟶μ(A)μ(B)(∣n∣→∞).\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)\longrightarrow\mu(A)\mu(B)\qquad(|n|\to\infty).μ(A∩T−nB)⟶μ(A)μ(B)(∣n∣→∞).

It also states zero Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy and three vanishing Lyapunov exponents at almost every point. The former says that the asymptotic information produced per step by any finite measurable observation partition is zero. Lyapunov exponents measure exponential rates of infinitesimal stretching along typical trajectories; all three rates are claimed to vanish.

Mixing of every finite order is an additional corollary using the separate claim in family 145. It does not follow merely by replacing two observables with several in the spectral calculation. The ordinary mixing, entropy, and Lyapunov conclusions do not depend on that companion theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The proposed construction answers a central existence problem in spectral ergodic theory in a strong smooth setting. It would identify a deterministic volume-preserving system whose entire centered operator theory is one copy of the basic Fourier shift.

The requirement of completeness is crucial. Finding one observation with flat spectral density would give a Lebesgue component, but other observations could live in additional spectral components. The claimed theorem eliminates that hidden remainder.

The example also sharpens the distinction between statistical and geometric notions of complexity. Long-separated observations can decorrelate even when typical infinitesimal separations have no positive exponential growth rate. Zero entropy likewise does not mean that every orbit repeats or that every correlation persists.

6. The main idea

Begin with maps whose spectra can be calculated

The approximating maps are integrable twists. In suitable volume-preserving coordinates (θ,u,a)(\theta,u,a)(θ,u,a), they take the form

S(θ,u,a)=(θ+φ(u),u,a).S(\theta,u,a)=(\theta+\varphi(u),u,a).S(θ,u,a)=(θ+φ(u),u,a).

The angle θ\thetaθ rotates at a speed depending on uuu. A finite angular Fourier signal has pieces of the form A(u,a)e2πimθA(u,a)e^{2\pi i m\theta}A(u,a)e2πimθ. On an arc where the speed varies monotonically, the spectral density of such a piece can be read from how its spatial mass is distributed over rotation speeds.

The paper groups these finite signals according to which target observation they are meant to encode. These labels keep different approximation tasks distinguishable during subsequent changes of coordinates.

Change coordinates while retaining information

A carefully chosen smooth passage replaces a twist by a nearby one whose angular coordinate plays a different role. Oscillatory-integral estimates describe where the old signals move among the new angular frequencies.

The third coordinate supplies a small variation in speed. Large integer parameters separate the frequency bands associated with different labels while leaving the earlier approximation as accurate as needed. At each stage only finitely many signals and error requirements are involved; a parameter can then be chosen sufficiently large for that stage.

This is more than convergence of maps alone. The construction must preserve useful spectral information while the coordinate systems and frequencies change substantially.

Encode labels, then flatten the density

The manuscript introduces small, controlled biases in the spectral densities belonging to the labels. Many such biases form a block. Together they make it possible to predict which target label a signal carries, while spending only a small amount of a separate spectral error budget.

The total density is kept close enough to uniform that whitening, a spectral rescaling that makes it exactly uniform, changes the observable little in physical L2L^2L2 norm. Flat density gives orthogonality of its distinct time shifts. Accurate prediction of labels makes linear combinations of those shifts approximate the selected target observations.

A diagonal construction repeatedly revisits a countable dense collection of centered observables. Errors shrink while the maps and their inverses converge smoothly. In the claimed limit, orthogonality survives and every member of the dense collection lies in the closed orbit span. The latter step supplies completeness, which is the part that a single flat signal would not establish by itself.

Read the dynamical consequences from the model

In the circle model, correlations become Fourier coefficients of integrable functions. Their decay gives ordinary mixing by the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma. Finite spectral multiplicity then invokes Rokhlin’s entropy theorem to obtain zero measure entropy.

For a smooth map preserving volume, Pesin’s entropy formula relates entropy to the positive Lyapunov exponents. Zero entropy rules out positive exponents almost everywhere, and volume preservation makes their sum zero. The manuscript concludes that every exponent vanishes. These are consequences of the claimed construction combined with the cited general theorems, rather than extra properties imposed separately at every approximation stage.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is an existence statement on T3\mathbb T^3T3. It does not provide a short closed formula, establish real analyticity, or claim realization on every compact manifold or in every dimension.

Its spectral assertion excludes constants and includes all remaining square-integrable observables. The generator’s low regularity is compatible with a smooth underlying map. No independence or Gaussian distribution is asserted for its time shifts.

Zero measure-theoretic entropy refers to the specified invariant volume. It should not be silently replaced by a statement about topological entropy, which measures a different form of orbit complexity. Likewise, vanishing Lyapunov exponents do not rule out slower-than-exponential separation.

The stronger multiple-mixing corollary explicitly uses the separate theorem of family 145. Keeping this dependency visible distinguishes the principal construction from conclusions that require another manuscript.

8. Sources and further reading

Primary historical sources include Helson and Parry, Cocycles and spectra, Arkiv för Matematik 16 (1978), 195–206; Mathew and Nadkarni, A measure preserving transformation whose spectrum has Lebesgue component of multiplicity two, Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 16 (1984), 402–406; and Fayad, Partially mixing and locally rank one smooth transformations and flows on the torus, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 64 (2001), 637–654.

For the distinct infinite-measure setting, see el Abdalaoui’s Spectral ergodic Banach problem and flat polynomials. Prikhod’ko, On ergodic flows with simple Lebesgue spectrum, Sbornik: Mathematics 211 (2020), 594–615, concerns continuous time. Optional background on the Koopman operator explains why spectral questions about functions encode properties of a nonlinear dynamical system.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A smooth three-torus diffeomorphism with simple Lebesgue spectrum (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Does mixing two observations force mixing any finite number
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 145 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Suppose a stationary system gradually forgets the relation between two observations made far apart in time. Must it also forget every relation among three, four, or any fixed finite number of well-separated observations?

For arbitrary random variables, the answer is no. Let XXX and YYY be independent fair bits and set Z=X+Y(mod2)Z=X+Y\pmod2Z=X+Y(mod2). Every pair is independent, but knowing two bits determines the third. Pairwise independence can hide a collective constraint.

Rokhlin’s multiple-mixing problem asks whether such a persistent higher-order constraint can survive when all observations come from repeated applications of one measure-preserving transformation. Family 145 claims that it cannot: ordinary mixing implies mixing of every finite order.

The phrase “one transformation” is essential. A system indexed by two independent integer directions can be mixing for pairs while retaining a three-way constraint. The proposed theorem concerns a single time axis, not all group actions.

2. Background and essential definitions

Mixing means asymptotic independence of fixed events

Let (Ω,F,μ)(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)(Ω,F,μ) be a probability space and let TTT be an invertible measurable transformation with measurable inverse. It preserves probability if μ(T−1A)=μ(A)\mu(T^{-1}A)=\mu(A)μ(T−1A)=μ(A) for every measurable set AAA.

An event AAA is a condition imposed on the current state. The preimage T−nBT^{-n}BT−nB means that the state satisfies event BBB after nnn steps. Ordinary mixing is the requirement

μ(A∩T−nB)⟶μ(A)μ(B)(∣n∣→∞)\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)\longrightarrow\mu(A)\mu(B)\qquad(|n|\to\infty)μ(A∩T−nB)⟶μ(A)μ(B)(∣n∣→∞)

for every fixed pair A,BA,BA,B. The limit on the right is what independence would give. The events themselves stay fixed while their observation times separate.

This is stronger than ergodicity, which only rules out invariant events of intermediate probability. It is also stronger than weak mixing, where suitable correlations vanish after time averaging. The theorem starts with ordinary mixing, not merely either of these weaker properties.

Higher orders test genuinely joint behavior

For an integer k≥2k\geq2k≥2, mixing of order kkk means

μ(⋂i=1kT−tiAi)⟶∏i=1kμ(Ai)\mu\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^kT^{-t_i}A_i\right)\longrightarrow\prod_{i=1}^k\mu(A_i)μ(i=1⋂k​T−ti​Ai​)⟶i=1∏k​μ(Ai​)

whenever t1<⋯<tkt_1<\cdots<t_kt1​<⋯<tk​ are integer times and

min⁡1≤i<k(ti+1−ti)⟶∞.\min_{1\leq i<k}(t_{i+1}-t_i)\longrightarrow\infty.1≤i<kmin​(ti+1​−ti​)⟶∞.

Thus all successive gaps grow, but they need not grow at comparable speeds. The theorem is not restricted to equally spaced times such as 0,n,2n0,n,2n0,n,2n.

We count the order by the number of events: ordinary mixing is order two. Some sources call this multiplicity one and shift the terminology by one, so conventions must be checked when comparing papers.

A joining records a possible limiting dependence

A joining is a joint probability law for several copies of a system that retains the required marginal laws and is invariant under simultaneous time evolution. If higher-order mixing fails along a sequence of separated times, a limiting joint law can retain that failure.

Its proper subcollections may nevertheless be independent. The three-bit example illustrates why that information alone does not force the full law to be a product. The challenge is to use the additional structure imposed by a common time evolution.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Rokhlin introduced higher-order mixing in his work on compact commutative groups and established it for ergodic surjective continuous endomorphisms with Haar probability. The unrestricted implication from ordinary mixing became a major problem in ergodic theory.

The two-dimensional contrast emerged sharply in Ledrappier’s 1978 example. Its configurations are binary arrays indexed by Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2, subject to a local three-dot relation. Translating the array in two independent directions gives a mixing action with zero entropy that is not threefold mixing. This demonstrates a real obstruction, while leaving open whether a single generator can sustain it.

Several strong positive results required extra structure. Kalikow proved that twofold mixing implies threefold mixing for rank-one transformations, whose behavior can be approximated by one sequence of increasingly large towers. Host established all orders under a singular-spectrum hypothesis. Ryzhikov obtained all-orders results for mixing finite-rank automorphisms. More recently, Kanigowski and Ravotti treated mixing flows with a suitable local shearing property.

There were also broad results guaranteeing many favorable configurations of observation times. Bergelson and Zelada showed that higher-order good configurations form a strong Ramsey-large set for strongly mixing actions of countable abelian groups. Such abundance is different from convergence along every sequence whose time gaps diverge.

Joining methods, developed from Furstenberg’s work, supplied a language for possible obstructions. Earlier work described how a failure could be sought in a zero-entropy part of a system. De la Rue analyzed the twofold/threefold problem and explained why a direct analogue of the three-dot construction does not work in one dimension.

The new manuscript claims to complete the general single-transformation argument. It supplies an all-orders reduction and then addresses the residual joint dependence, without assuming rank, singular spectrum, group geometry, or a shearing model.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Every finite order for one invertible transformation

The main theorem asserts that every invertible mixing probability-preserving transformation is mixing of every finite order. More explicitly, for fixed measurable sets A1,…,AkA_1,\ldots,A_kA1​,…,Ak​,

μ(A1∩T−n1A2∩⋯∩T−(n1+⋯+nk−1)Ak)⟶∏i=1kμ(Ai)as min⁡ini→∞.\begin{aligned}&\mu\left(A_1\cap T^{-n_1}A_2\cap\cdots\cap T^{-(n_1+\cdots+n_{k-1})}A_k\right)\\&\hspace{2em}\longrightarrow\prod_{i=1}^k\mu(A_i)\qquad\text{as }\min_i n_i\to\infty.\end{aligned}​μ(A1​∩T−n1​A2​∩⋯∩T−(n1​+⋯+nk−1​)Ak​)⟶i=1∏k​μ(Ai​)as imin​ni​→∞.​

The gaps nin_ini​ are positive integers. No standardness or countable-generation assumption is imposed on the original probability space. The manuscript passes to a finite-symbol factor when its argument needs a more manageable measurable setting.

The conclusion is a limit for every diverging-gap configuration. It is not just convergence of a time average, or convergence after excluding a thin collection of times. No quantitative rate is asserted.

Noninvertible maps and flows

A corollary extends the conclusion to mixing measure-preserving endomorphisms: measurable maps that need not be invertible. Observation times are then nonnegative integers, and T−tAT^{-t}AT−tA denotes a preimage under a forward iterate, not an inverse map.

Another corollary treats probability-preserving flows (St)t∈R(S_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}(St​)t∈R​. In addition to mixing, the manuscript assumes strong continuity of their Koopman operators on L1L^1L1. Concretely, for every measurable AAA,

∥1A∘Ss−1A∥1⟶0(s→0),\|\mathbf1_A\circ S_s-\mathbf1_A\|_1\longrightarrow0\qquad(s\to0),∥1A​∘Ss​−1A​∥1​⟶0(s→0),

where 1A\mathbf1_A1A​ is the indicator of AAA, and the norm is the integral of absolute value. Under this hypothesis, the same product limit holds for arbitrary real observation times with diverging successive gaps. Jointly measurable probability-preserving flows on standard probability spaces satisfy the stated continuity condition.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The claim resolves a central structural problem: whether the simplest nontrivial mixing condition already controls every fixed finite pattern of widely separated observations along one time axis.

If correct, it removes an entire hierarchy of additional hypotheses from statements about a general mixing transformation. One would no longer need to establish threefold, fourfold, and higher mixing separately once ordinary mixing is known.

It also clarifies why pairwise-independent counterexamples from elementary probability do not settle the dynamical question. Their joint laws need not be compatible with the repeated action of one transformation and all the limiting configurations that action generates.

The result would have immediate consequences for other proposed examples. For instance, family 144 invokes this theorem to upgrade ordinary mixing of its smooth spectral construction to mixing of all orders. That application is logically separate from constructing the spectral model itself.

6. The main idea

Reduce a hypothetical failure to a small witness

Assume some finite order fails and choose the least such order kkk. All lower orders then mix correctly. The manuscript reduces the obstruction to a stationary process taking values in a finite alphabet, with centered one-coordinate functions whose joint correlation stays away from zero along a sequence of separated layouts.

The process can be chosen to have zero entropy rate. If H(X1,…,Xn)H(X_1,\ldots,X_n)H(X1​,…,Xn​) is the Shannon entropy of an observed block, this means

1nH(X1,…,Xn)⟶0.\frac1nH(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\longrightarrow0.n1​H(X1​,…,Xn​)⟶0.

It does not mean that the process is constant. It means that the typical long words require sublinear information per observed coordinate. This restriction becomes useful against a proposed persistent correlation.

Retain more than one limiting joint law

A single joining may hide the obstruction rather than resolve it. The manuscript therefore builds an ordered family of array laws using repeated limits at sums of observation layouts. Proper collections of coordinate planes retain independence, including specified conditional versions after additional information is recorded.

The order of these limits matters. The construction does not assume that swapping array axes leaves the law unchanged. Nor do the array axes become new independent time directions: the original system still evolves under one transformation.

An extension procedure adds information until certain conditional expectations can no longer improve. Conditional expectation is the best mean-square prediction from the information being retained. At this stage, the paper claims precise local relationships between row and column predictions.

Convert dependence into algebraic labels

The conditional-expectation operators satisfy identities associated with a square of coordinates. The manuscript uses these identities to extract orthogonal one-dimensional spaces of functions whose values have modulus one. Along suitable rows or columns, products of matching functions are constant.

Multiplication of these functions, ignoring constant phase factors, supplies abelian group labels. A measurable construction organizes relevant labels into finite blocks of fixed size. Time moves whole blocks according to one group automorphism. The argument does not require a uniform description of each individual label’s motion inside a block.

This stage translates a probabilistic dependence into algebraic data on which the single time direction imposes strong constraints.

Use one-dimensional time to force cancellation

The manuscript separates label orbits into two behaviors along arithmetic progressions. In one case, labels have enough algebraic independence to produce exponential estimates; zero entropy limits how many likely symbolic words can support a persistent correlation. In the other case, polynomial relations in the orbit allow a degree-reduction argument, with ordinary mixing as the starting case.

Both mechanisms make averaged absolute correlations with moving finite blocks tend to zero. This contradicts a positive quantity that the supposed failure forces time evolution to preserve.

The averaging is internal to the contradiction. It does not weaken the theorem’s final conclusion to an averaged form of higher-order mixing. The proposed argument rules out every least failing finite order.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns repeated use of one transformation. It does not contradict Ledrappier’s action with two independent time generators, and it does not assert the same implication for arbitrary actions of Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2 or other groups.

The number of tested events is fixed before taking the separation limit. Nothing here gives a bound uniform in an increasing number of events, a convergence rate, or control when the events themselves vary with time.

Ordinary mixing remains an assumption. The claim does not upgrade every ergodic or weakly mixing system to ordinary mixing. Likewise, the continuous-time extension retains the specified continuity hypothesis.

The result concerns joint probabilities of observations. It should not be confused with pointwise convergence of multiple ergodic averages along almost every orbit, the different topic of family 154.

8. Sources and further reading

For earlier restricted implications, see Kalikow’s rank-one theorem, Host’s singular-spectrum theorem, and Ryzhikov’s finite-rank results. Bergelson and Zelada’s Strongly mixing systems are almost strongly mixing of all orders makes the distinction between abundant good configurations and unrestricted convergence especially relevant.

De la Rue’s account of twofold and threefold mixing explains the joining viewpoint and the contrast with Ledrappier’s example. Ryzhikov’s 75-year survey of Rokhlin’s problem supplies additional historical context. The source manuscript develops its claimed general argument and the endomorphism and flow corollaries.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Rokhlin’s multiple-mixing problem for one transformation (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Area-visible chaos in the standard map at every large parameter
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 146 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

The standard map is one of the simplest formulas used to study conservative chaos. It repeatedly applies a sinusoidal kick and then a shear. Numerical pictures show intricate mixtures of apparently irregular motion and islands of more orderly behavior.

A picture of complexity leaves a precise mathematical question unanswered: does chaos occupy a set of positive area, or only an exceptional set that a randomly chosen initial point almost surely misses?

Family 146 claims that the exact standard sine map has positive entropy with respect to ordinary area for every sufficiently large positive kick parameter. This would establish chaos visible to the fixed natural probability measure, not merely the existence of complicated invariant trajectories.

The parameter conclusion is also strong. The manuscript claims a whole tail of parameters, rather than isolated examples or an unspecified set of positive parameter measure. It does not claim that almost every initial condition is chaotic or that the whole torus is ergodic.

2. Background and essential definitions

A kick followed by a shear

Let T2=R2/Z2\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2T2=R2/Z2, the unit square with opposite sides identified. With parameter k∈Rk\in\mathbb Rk∈R, the paper uses

fk(x,y)=(x+y+ksin⁡(2πx), y+ksin⁡(2πx))(modZ2).f_k(x,y)=\bigl(x+y+k\sin(2\pi x),\ y+k\sin(2\pi x)\bigr)\pmod{\mathbb Z^2}.fk​(x,y)=(x+y+ksin(2πx), y+ksin(2πx))(modZ2).

First replace yyy by y+ksin⁡(2πx)y+k\sin(2\pi x)y+ksin(2πx), then replace xxx by x+yx+yx+y using the updated value of yyy. Both operations are invertible and preserve area. Their composition therefore preserves normalized Lebesgue area mmm, with m(T2)=1m(\mathbb T^2)=1m(T2)=1.

Different authors place a factor of 2π2\pi2π in the parameter. The displayed formula fixes the normalization for this digest. The theorem concerns this deterministic map, without noise and without changing the sine profile.

Entropy for a specified measure

Divide the torus into finitely many measurable regions and record the region visited at each step. The probabilities of length-nnn records have a Shannon entropy, measuring the information needed on average to describe the record. Its asymptotic growth per step, maximized over finite measurable partitions, is the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy hm(fk)h_m(f_k)hm​(fk​).

The subscript matters: entropy is being measured using ordinary area as the initial-state distribution. A dynamical system can have other invariant probability measures with different entropy values.

Topological entropy asks about the growth of distinguishable orbit patterns without fixing such a probability measure. Positive topological entropy can be supported on a zero-area set. It therefore does not by itself answer the area-based question.

Lyapunov exponents measure infinitesimal growth

The derivative Dfkn(z)D f_k^n(z)Dfkn​(z) describes how a small displacement near an initial point zzz evolves for nnn steps. Its largest asymptotic exponential rate is

λ+(z)=lim⁡n→∞1nlog⁡∥Dfkn(z)∥\lambda_+(z)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log\|D f_k^n(z)\|λ+​(z)=n→∞lim​n1​log∥Dfkn​(z)∥

at points where the multiplicative ergodic theorem supplies the limit. The matrix norm is the Euclidean operator norm. Area preservation makes the two exponents λ+(z)\lambda_+(z)λ+​(z) and −λ+(z)-\lambda_+(z)−λ+​(z), with λ+(z)≥0\lambda_+(z)\geq0λ+​(z)≥0.

For this smooth map and its smooth invariant area measure, Pesin’s entropy formula gives

hm(fk)=∫T2λ+(z) dm(z).h_m(f_k)=\int_{\mathbb T^2}\lambda_+(z)\,dm(z).hm​(fk​)=∫T2​λ+​(z)dm(z).

Thus positive metric entropy is equivalent here to a positive largest exponent on a set of positive area. A few rapidly separating orbits are insufficient; their initial conditions must occupy positive measure.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The standard map developed as a model of conservative instability, prominently in Chirikov’s work. Its attraction is that a short explicit formula creates a difficult interaction between local stretching, folding, recurrence, and regular islands.

Duarte’s large-parameter work constructed hyperbolic basic sets and established elliptic-island and tangency phenomena within the standard family. Hyperbolicity gives a rigorous form of stable and unstable behavior on those sets, but does not automatically give them positive area.

Gorodetski later obtained transitive invariant sets of full Hausdorff dimension for a residual set of large parameters. Full dimension does not imply positive area. Likewise, a residual parameter set is large in the sense of Baire category, but can have zero Lebesgue measure. These two distinctions prevent that result from directly resolving the metric-entropy question.

Obata proved uniqueness of the measure of maximal entropy for sufficiently large parameters. This identifies a distinguished invariant measure, without asserting that it is ordinary area. Oliveira established a positive-topological-entropy result for positive parameters apart from a stated exceptional value in this normalization. Again, topological positivity leaves the entropy of the area measure unresolved.

Other advances concern modified systems. Berger and Turaev resolved Herman’s positive-entropy conjecture through conservative perturbations, including perturbations near standard maps. Such perturbations need not stay within the one-parameter sine family. Positive Lyapunov exponents have also been obtained for random perturbations and for coupled systems with standard-map fibers.

The new manuscript takes Sinai’s positive-parameter-measure conjecture as its central target. Its claimed all-sufficiently-large conclusion would go further: the natural area measure has positive entropy for every parameter in a full tail, for the exact unperturbed map.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A full parameter tail

The main theorem asserts that there is a finite k0>0k_0>0k0​>0 such that

hm(fk)>0for every k≥k0.h_m(f_k)>0\qquad\text{for every }k\geq k_0.hm​(fk​)>0for every k≥k0​.

Equivalently, for each such fixed kkk, the set

Hk={z∈T2:λ+(z)>0}H_k=\{z\in\mathbb T^2:\lambda_+(z)>0\}Hk​={z∈T2:λ+​(z)>0}

has positive area, up to the usual null set on which exponents may be undefined. The set HkH_kHk​ and its area can depend on kkk.

There are two distinct measures in this assertion. Parameter space contains an interval, indeed a whole tail, of successful kkk‘s. Phase space contains a positive-area set of chaotic initial points for each successful parameter. Neither statement is a substitute for the other.

The manuscript does not give an explicit usable threshold, assert a uniform positive lower bound for entropy, or claim that m(Hk)=1m(H_k)=1m(Hk​)=1. It also does not assert ergodicity of area on the whole torus.

A positive-area ergodic component

Using Pesin’s decomposition results, the paper derives an invariant measurable set E=E(k)E=E(k)E=E(k) of positive area on which normalized restricted area is ergodic and the two Lyapunov exponents are nonzero almost everywhere.

It further states that EEE has a finite cyclic partition E0,…,EN−1E_0,\ldots,E_{N-1}E0​,…,EN−1​. The map sends each piece to the next, and the iterate fkNf_k^NfkN​ on each piece, with its normalized restricted measure, is Bernoulli: measure-theoretically equivalent to an independent-symbol shift. The integer NNN and the component may depend on the parameter.

This is a componentwise conclusion, with invariance understood modulo null sets. It does not make the original map globally Bernoulli or globally mixing.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The standard map is a central explicit model of conservative dynamics. Proving area-visible chaos in its unmodified family would connect the striking numerical behavior with a long-sought measure-theoretic statement.

The full parameter tail is particularly consequential. It would show that sufficiently strong kicks always produce a positive-area chaotic component, even though regular structures may coexist with it.

The method also addresses a general obstacle: local derivative expansion does not guarantee sustained growth of a long product. An argument that controls recurrent cancellations without assuming independence could be useful well beyond this particular formula. The rating reflects the significance of the stated result if correct.

6. The main idea

Large one-step stretching can cancel later

A matrix can stretch strongly in one direction, while the next matrix rotates that direction toward a contracting one. Consequently, multiplying large matrices need not produce a large product.

In suitable coordinates, an orbit satisfies

qi+1=2qi+ksin⁡(2πqi)−qi−1(mod1).q_{i+1}=2q_i+k\sin(2\pi q_i)-q_{i-1}\pmod1.qi+1​=2qi​+ksin(2πqi​)−qi−1​(mod1).

Its linearized motion is governed by matrices

Ai=(2+2πkcos⁡(2πqi)−110),det⁡Ai=1.A_i=\begin{pmatrix}2+2\pi k\cos(2\pi q_i)&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det A_i=1.Ai​=(2+2πkcos(2πqi​)1​−10​),detAi​=1.

The cosine creates strong stretching at many locations but also regions where expansion is weaker. Repeated visits and alignments of directions make long-time growth difficult to control.

Rule out too many nearly complete cancellations

The first main input concerns two long orbit segments that each grow nearly at their maximal possible rate. If their concatenation almost cancels that growth, the linearized recurrence has a solution small at both ends.

The manuscript matches the expansion scales on the two sides and converts this situation into many local constraints. An analytic scarcity estimate is then claimed to make such nearly complete cancellations exponentially unlikely with respect to area. Degenerate configurations, including nearly compensating cosine values, are treated within the estimate.

This is not an assumption that successive orbit segments behave like independent random samples. Their dependence is part of the deterministic problem.

Obtain a restricted product estimate across a fast segment

The second input controls observations near opposite ends of a segment whose derivative grows rapidly. Finite boundary-value problems produce two transverse contracting families of graphs. Estimates on their change-of-variable factors yield a weighted product inequality across this fast segment.

The restriction to rapidly growing segments is important. The paper does not first assume global mixing and then use it to prove chaos. It obtains the particular decorrelation estimate needed from finite geometric information.

Compare growth deficits across scales

Set M=2πk+4M=2\pi k+4M=2πk+4, an upper bound for one-step derivative growth in the chosen coordinates. For a transfer matrix from time iii to time jjj, define

g(i,j)=log⁡M∥Ti,j∥.g(i,j)=\log_M\|T_{i,j}\|.g(i,j)=logM​∥Ti,j​∥.

These quantities behave like distances on the integer time axis and satisfy 0≤g(i,j)≤∣i−j∣0\leq g(i,j)\leq|i-j|0≤g(i,j)≤∣i−j∣. The average shortfall

en=E[1−g(0,n)n]e_n=\mathbb E\left[1-\frac{g(0,n)}n\right]en​=E[1−ng(0,n)​]

measures the loss from maximal growth, with expectation taken over area-distributed initial points.

For each fixed length, the manuscript obtains small shortfall as the parameter grows. In contrast, at a parameter where the exponent vanished almost everywhere, shortfall would tend to one as length grew. A hypothetical sequence of arbitrarily large such parameters would therefore require a transition from near-maximal short-time growth to negligible asymptotic growth.

The proof examines the first transition over successively doubled lengths. Cancellation scarcity and the fast-segment product estimate restrict the possible rescaled patterns of slow and fast intervals. A capped version of the shortfall is chosen so that summing its changes over scales telescopes. The manuscript claims the allowed limiting patterns cannot supply the positive total required by that telescoping identity, giving the contradiction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem addresses sufficiently large positive parameters. It does not classify small or intermediate parameters or provide a numerical recipe for locating the threshold.

Positive area is weaker than full area. The claimed chaotic component may coexist with elliptic islands or other invariant regions, and the theorem does not determine their relative sizes. Global ergodicity, uniqueness of a positive-area component, and quantitative entropy asymptotics are separate questions.

The invariant measure is fixed to be normalized area. Results for a maximal-entropy measure, random perturbations, or nearby smooth maps are historically relevant but logically different. The componentwise Bernoulli corollary also requires a finite cyclic decomposition and an iterate; those qualifications should be retained.

Finally, the proof’s probabilistic language refers to the distribution of initial points under area. No external noise is added, and time-separated orbit coordinates are not presumed independent.

8. Sources and further reading

Chirikov’s review of conservative instability explains the model’s origins. Duarte, Plenty of elliptic islands for the standard family of area preserving maps, Annales de l’Institut Henri Poincaré, Analyse non linéaire 11 (1994), 359–409, and Gorodetski’s On stochastic sea of the standard map describe earlier geometric advances.

For distinctions among entropy results, see Obata’s maximal-entropy-measure theorem, Berger and Turaev’s conservative perturbation theorem, and Blumenthal, Xue, and Young’s random-perturbation result. Pesin’s original entropy theory supplies the link between area entropy and Lyapunov exponents used in the manuscript.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Positive Metric Entropy for the Standard Map at Large Parameters (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A full collar of billiard caustics forces an ellipse
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 147 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A billiard ball travels in straight lines inside a planar table and reflects from the boundary with equal incoming and outgoing angles. On an elliptical table, many trajectories stay tangent to one smaller confocal ellipse. That smaller curve acts as a geometric guide, called a caustic.

Near the boundary of an ellipse, these guiding curves fill an entire collar. Every point of the collar lies on one of them. Does such complete organization of near-boundary motion force the table itself to be an ellipse?

Family 147 claims an affirmative answer for infinitely differentiable, strictly convex planar tables with positive curvature. The two manuscripts begin from different formulations of the same geometric organization. One assumes a continuous family of smooth caustics inside the table. The other starts with only continuous invariant curves in the space of billiard states and claims that the necessary smooth caustics emerge automatically.

The word “entire” is crucial. Many nonelliptical tables have large collections of near-boundary caustics with gaps. The claimed rigidity requires a full foliation, with no missing intermediate leaves.

2. Background and essential definitions

Billiards and grazing motion

Let Ω⊂R2\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2Ω⊂R2 be a bounded strictly convex open set. Its boundary is assumed to be a C∞C^\inftyC∞ simple closed regular curve with positive curvature everywhere. Strict convexity prevents boundary segments; the additional positive-curvature assumption rules out flat points as well.

If an incoming unit velocity is vvv and the outward unit normal at impact is nnn, reflection gives

v⟼v−2(v⋅n)n.v\longmapsto v-2(v\cdot n)n.v⟼v−2(v⋅n)n.

The normal component changes sign while the tangential component remains unchanged.

A billiard state can be described by the impact point and the angle of the outgoing ray. Using boundary arclength sss modulo the perimeter LLL, and outgoing angle δ∈(0,π)\delta\in(0,\pi)δ∈(0,π) measured from the positively oriented tangent, the state space is

M=(R/LZ)×(0,π).M=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)\times(0,\pi).M=(R/LZ)×(0,π).

The billiard map TTT takes one outgoing state to the next. Small positive δ\deltaδ describes grazing trajectories that skim along the boundary. A full grazing annulus contains all states with 0<δ<η0<\delta<\eta0<δ<η for some η>0\eta>0η>0, at every boundary point.

Physical caustics and phase curves

A smooth convex caustic is a smooth closed strictly convex curve inside the table such that a segment tangent to it remains tangent after reflection. It is not a wall that the ball strikes. It is an envelope organizing a family of tangent trajectories.

The states tangent to a caustic trace an invariant curve in phase space. Conversely, a merely continuous invariant phase curve does not automatically arrive with a smooth convex envelope. Bridging that gap is a principal task of M1.

A phase curve is essential if it winds around the phase cylinder rather than bounding a disk inside it. A continuous foliation means that the annulus is continuously parametrized by a circle coordinate and a leaf parameter. Every state lies on exactly one leaf, and the billiard map preserves each leaf individually.

A physical caustic collar is a full neighborhood of the boundary in the closed table, continuously parametrized by nested curves. The zero leaf is the boundary, and each positive leaf is a smooth convex caustic. Smoothness of individual leaves does not imply differentiability as one moves from leaf to leaf; the physical theorem assumes only continuity in that transverse direction.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ellipses are the classical integrable examples. Their confocal ellipses provide near-boundary caustics, while a circle has concentric circular caustics. The broader conjecture that integrable convex billiards must be ellipses is traditionally attributed to Birkhoff; an early printed formulation appears in Poritsky’s work on billiards and string constructions.

Lazutkin proved that sufficiently smooth positively curved tables possess a positive-measure Cantor family of near-boundary invariant curves. A Cantor family can accumulate densely at the boundary yet leave gaps between permitted parameters. Its existence for general tables shows why “many caustics” is much weaker than a full collar.

Marvizi and Melrose developed a near-grazing integral accurate up to an error flat at the boundary, meaning that the error vanishes to every finite order there. Such formal accuracy still differs from an exact invariant foliation. Mather’s obstruction to grazing caustics at zero-curvature points also explains why positive curvature is a substantive hypothesis.

Several rigidity theorems imposed stronger global or geometric assumptions. Bialy proved that a foliation of the entire phase cylinder by noncontractible invariant curves forces the table to be a circle. This is stronger information than a narrow grazing annulus and correspondingly gives a narrower conclusion.

Avila, De Simoi, and Kaloshin established local rigidity near ellipses of small eccentricity. Kaloshin and Sorrentino treated perturbations of ellipses with arbitrary eccentricity. Bialy and Mironov obtained ellipse rigidity under central symmetry when the foliated annulus reaches the four-periodic invariant curve. Koval’s local strong result treats small rational-rotation caustics near almost every ellipse, under closeness and regularity conditions.

The present family claims to remove the perturbative and symmetry restrictions for a full near-boundary collar. It also addresses the regularity issue: the initial phase leaves may be merely continuous, even though the conclusion produces jointly analytic geometry.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A continuous phase foliation suffices

M1 assumes a TTT-invariant open annulus U⊂MU\subset MU⊂M containing all sufficiently grazing states and a homeomorphism

H:S1×(0,1)⟶UH:S^1\times(0,1)\longrightarrow UH:S1×(0,1)⟶U

whose circle leaves are essential simple closed curves, each invariant under TTT. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. No differentiability of the leaves or their dependence on the leaf parameter is assumed.

Under these hypotheses, M1 claims that the table is an ellipse. More precisely, for some center ccc and real symmetric positive-definite matrix QQQ,

Ω={x∈R2:(x−c)TQ(x−c)<1}.\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:(x-c)^TQ(x-c)<1\}.Ω={x∈R2:(x−c)TQ(x−c)<1}.

Positive definite means that vTQv>0v^TQv>0vTQv>0 for nonzero vvv; this formula includes circles. The annulus may be arbitrarily thin, and no foliation farther into phase space is assumed.

M1’s intermediate regularity theorem states that the boundary becomes real analytic and that there is a jointly real-analytic family

Γ:S1×[0,λ0]⟶R2,λ0>0,\Gamma:S^1\times[0,\lambda_0]\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad\lambda_0>0,Γ:S1×[0,λ0​]⟶R2,λ0​>0,

whose zero leaf parametrizes the boundary and whose positive leaves are smooth strictly convex caustics filling a physical collar. Analyticity at the parameter endpoints means extension to a neighborhood of those endpoints.

Rigidity from a physical collar

M2 starts with a continuous physical caustic collar. Its individual leaves are smooth closed convex caustics, but differentiability across the leaves is not required. It claims the same elliptical conclusion for the same smooth, strictly convex, positively curved class of boundaries.

The two papers are complementary, not independent proofs of identical statements. M1 uses analytic estimates from M2 to build the physical collar, then applies M2’s rigidity theorem. Its additional contribution is the passage from continuous invariant phase curves to the geometric hypothesis that M2 requires.

Neither theorem assumes that the table is close to an ellipse, centrally symmetric, or algebraic. They do retain the full-foliation and positive-curvature assumptions.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The claimed result settles a central near-boundary form of the Birkhoff conjecture in a broad smooth class. It turns local dynamical organization near the boundary into a global classification of the table’s shape.

The regularity upgrade is also significant. A topological description of phase space would force analyticity of a boundary initially assumed only infinitely differentiable. The hypotheses do not insert an analytic first integral or smooth transverse coordinates at the start.

At the same time, the full collar explains why the statement does not conflict with the abundance of caustics in nonelliptical billiards. The distinction is between a continuous family filling every intermediate layer and a family whose parameter set has gaps.

6. The main idea

Extract periodic trajectories from the foliation

Billiard maps have a twist property: changing the direction at one impact changes the next impact in a strictly ordered way. M1 combines the two relevant twist inequalities with recurrence for the finite invariant area in phase space.

The claimed first step shows that continuous essential leaves are graphs in suitable coordinates. Their rotation number measures the average progress around the boundary per iteration. The full foliation supplies every sufficiently small rational rotation number, and the argument makes the corresponding invariant graph entirely periodic.

This last property is much stronger than finding one periodic orbit of a given period. A whole periodic leaf supplies identities as its starting point moves around the boundary.

Use periodic polygon actions to obtain analyticity

Reflected periodic trajectories can be described by stationary polygonal actions: varying an intermediate impact point gives the reflection law. Along an entirely periodic leaf, the stationary action is constant as the starting state varies.

Taking the resulting equations at many small rational rotations constrains high Fourier modes of the boundary. The manuscripts claim an analytic inversion scheme in which the relevant derivative is a high-frequency projection plus a small operator. A Newton construction first produces analytic data, and a real uniqueness argument identifies it with the original smooth boundary.

A second construction works jointly in the angular and rotation variables. At rational resonances, where a division would otherwise become singular, it uses both the residual values and their first parameter derivatives. These additional compatibility conditions control the previously undetermined coefficients.

Recover physical caustics from tangent lines

An oriented line can be written

z⋅nθ=p,nθ=(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ).z\cdot n_\theta=p,\qquad n_\theta=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta).z⋅nθ​=p,nθ​=(cosθ,sinθ).

For a convex curve, its support function records the value of ppp at its tangent line with normal nθn_\thetanθ​. Once an invariant line graph is analytic and has the necessary curvature positivity, it defines a smooth convex envelope.

M1 constructs these envelopes with strict nesting. Their support values vary in a controlled direction, which makes the curves fill a physical collar rather than leave an uncovered region between them. This supplies exactly the hypothesis needed by M2.

Rule out a nonelliptical analytic boundary

M2 then studies complex continuations of the boundary and of finite reflected chains. A finite chain constrains its intermediate lines through algebraic relations determined by endpoint data. The manuscript uses this to control whether different local continuations can disagree.

The remaining analysis examines possible obstructions at the boundary of a complex continuation domain. Some behaviors of the continued normal force the elliptical form directly. The alternatives are restricted through growth and moment estimates. In the final difficult case, an odd periodic chain and stopped Brownian paths are used as analytic estimation tools to contradict the proposed first obstruction.

These Brownian paths do not add randomness to the billiard motion. They enter the complex-analytic argument for rigidity. The claimed conclusion concerns the original deterministic table and its reflected trajectories.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The claim applies to bounded planar tables with C∞C^\inftyC∞ strictly convex boundary and everywhere positive curvature. It does not establish the same result for rough boundaries, flat points, nonconvex domains, or higher-dimensional billiards.

The phase hypothesis requires every leaf to be invariant individually. Merely preserving a region while moving its leaves among one another is different. Likewise, many periodic trajectories or a large Cantor set of invariant curves do not supply a full foliation.

The family addresses the stated near-boundary interpretation of integrability. Other uses of the word may impose algebraic, measurable, or global conditions, and any implication between those formulations needs its own argument.

The conclusion identifies the table but does not quantify how close an approximately foliated table must be to an ellipse. Such stability questions, and extensions to weaker regularity, remain separate from the exact rigidity assertion.

8. Sources and further reading

Lazutkin’s existence theorem for caustics explains the family-with-gaps baseline. Bialy’s whole-phase-space rigidity theorem illustrates the stronger global hypothesis leading to circles.

The primary local advances include Avila, De Simoi, and Kaloshin’s small-eccentricity theorem, Kaloshin and Sorrentino’s local Birkhoff theorem, and Bialy and Mironov’s centrally symmetric case. Poritsky’s billiard and string-construction paper records the earlier geometric formulation.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Continuous Phase Foliations Create Analytic Caustic Collars (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Rigidity of Smooth Billiards with a Continuous Caustic Collar (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Fractal dimension from the information that exact overlaps leave behind
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 148 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A self-similar fractal is built by repeatedly choosing a shrinking copy of the whole picture. If the copies stay separate, counting choices and measuring their shrinkage predicts the dimension. When copies overlap, different sequences of choices may describe the same small piece, and that count can overstate how much information survives.

Family 148 claims a complete formula for the dimension of finite self-similar probability measures on the real line. The numerator is the rate at which distinct composed maps retain information; the denominator is the average logarithmic contraction. Their ratio is capped at the ambient dimension one.

The claim allows exact coincidences, arbitrarily close distinct copies, unequal contraction ratios, and orientation-reversing maps. It imposes no arithmetic restriction on the coefficients and no quantitative separation between different pieces.

The result concerns dimension. A measure of dimension one need not have a density with respect to length, so the formula is not an absolute-continuity theorem.

2. Background and essential definitions

Randomly applying shrinking affine maps

Take a finite nonempty indexed family

φi(x)=rix+ti,ti∈R,0<∣ri∣<1,\varphi_i(x)=r_i x+t_i,\qquad t_i\in\mathbb R,\quad 0<|r_i|<1,φi​(x)=ri​x+ti​,ti​∈R,0<∣ri​∣<1,

and probabilities pi>0p_i>0pi​>0 summing to one. A negative rir_iri​ reverses orientation as well as shrinking distances. Different indices are allowed to name the same map.

Choose independent symbols I1,I2,…I_1,I_2,\ldotsI1​,I2​,… with probabilities pip_ipi​. The limit of

φI1∘⋯∘φIn(0)\varphi_{I_1}\circ\cdots\circ\varphi_{I_n}(0)φI1​​∘⋯∘φIn​​(0)

exists and has the self-similar probability law μ\muμ. Equivalently,

μ=∑ipi(φi)∗μ,\mu=\sum_i p_i(\varphi_i)_*\mu,μ=i∑​pi​(φi​)∗​μ,

where the pushforward (φi)∗μ(\varphi_i)_*\mu(φi​)∗​μ is the distribution obtained by applying φi\varphi_iφi​ to a μ\muμ-distributed point. The compact set of all possible limits is the attractor KKK.

Count complete maps, not symbolic addresses

A word w=i1⋯inw=i_1\cdots i_nw=i1​⋯in​ describes the composed map φw\varphi_wφw​. An exact overlap occurs when two distinct words of the same positive length define exactly the same affine map. Equality includes both the signed slope and the translation.

Let

Gn=φI1∘⋯∘φIn.G_n=\varphi_{I_1}\circ\cdots\circ\varphi_{I_n}.Gn​=φI1​​∘⋯∘φIn​​.

This random variable takes values in the finite set of composed maps. If several words produce one map, their probabilities are added before its entropy is computed.

Using base-two logarithms, the Shannon entropy of a finite random variable ZZZ is

H(Z)=−∑zP(Z=z)log⁡2P(Z=z).H(Z)=-\sum_z\mathbb P(Z=z)\log_2\mathbb P(Z=z).H(Z)=−z∑​P(Z=z)log2​P(Z=z).

The random-walk entropy rate and average contraction exponent are

hRW=lim⁡n→∞H(Gn)n,χ=−∑ipilog⁡2∣ri∣>0.h_{\mathrm{RW}}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{H(G_n)}n,\qquad\chi=-\sum_i p_i\log_2|r_i|>0.hRW​=n→∞lim​nH(Gn​)​,χ=−i∑​pi​log2​∣ri​∣>0.

The entropy limit exists by subadditivity: a longer composition is determined by two independent shorter compositions. The ratio does not depend on the logarithm base, provided both quantities use the same one.

Dimension of a measure

Hausdorff dimension quantifies how the number and sizes of small covering intervals scale. For a probability measure, one can ask for the smallest dimension of a Borel set carrying positive mass, or of one carrying full mass. These conventions agree here because self-similar measures are exact dimensional by the earlier Feng–Hu theorem.

Exact dimensionality means that, for some constant ddd,

lim⁡s↓0log⁡μ(B(x,s))log⁡s=dfor μ-almost every x.\lim_{s\downarrow0}\frac{\log\mu(B(x,s))}{\log s}=d\qquad\text{for }\mu\text{-almost every }x.s↓0lim​logslogμ(B(x,s))​=dfor μ-almost every x.

The interval B(x,s)B(x,s)B(x,s) has center xxx and radius sss. Informally, typical mass scales approximately like sds^dsd. The constant ddd is the dimension in the claimed formula.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Moran’s work and Hutchinson’s iterated-function-system framework established dimension formulas when the smaller copies satisfy suitable separation conditions. The basic ratio of symbolic entropy to logarithmic contraction is natural in that setting.

Overlaps create a subtler problem. The exact-overlaps conjecture asks whether a dimension drop below the natural upper bound must reflect genuine equality between composed maps. The entropy-rate version incorporates the information already lost through such equalities and asks whether anything further can lower dimension.

Bernoulli convolutions became a central testing ground. They are distributions of random sums ∑j≥0εjλj\sum_{j\geq0}\varepsilon_j\lambda^j∑j≥0​εj​λj, with independent signs and 0<λ<10<\lambda<10<λ<1. Erdős proved singularity for certain arithmetic parameters, while Solomyak established absolute continuity for almost every parameter in (1/2,1)(1/2,1)(1/2,1). Garsia introduced the discrete entropy rate in this context. These developments exposed the interaction between overlaps, arithmetic, dimension, and densities.

Hochman showed that a dimension drop forces superexponential concentration of cylinder maps, using inverse theorems for entropy growth. This yields powerful conclusions under appropriate separation or arithmetic assumptions. Breuillard and Varjú developed approximation methods for Bernoulli convolutions, and Varjú obtained full dimension for every transcendental parameter in (1/2,1)(1/2,1)(1/2,1).

Rapaport established the no-exact-overlap formula for algebraic contraction ratios and arbitrary real translations, including signed unequal ratios. Rapaport and Varjú treated important homogeneous three-map cases and an entropy-rate formula with rational translations. Feng and Feng handled algebraic translations with a common signed contraction. Bárány and Verma supplied a version with exact collisions under weak exponential separation.

A key obstacle remained: absence of exact overlaps does not guarantee any useful minimum distance between distinct maps. Baker and, independently, Bárány and Käenmäki constructed systems without exact overlaps whose distinct cylinders become superexponentially close at prescribed rates. The new manuscript claims to control such closeness without adding a separation assumption.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The main theorem states that every finite indexed system described above satisfies

dim⁡Hμ=min⁡{1,hRWχ}.\boxed{\displaystyle\dim_H\mu=\min\left\{1,\frac{h_{\mathrm{RW}}}{\chi}\right\}.}dimH​μ=min{1,χhRW​​}.​

Exact overlaps, repeated generators, negative contraction ratios, and unequal contraction ratios are all permitted. The probabilities are strictly positive. The theorem includes the threshold hRW=χh_{\mathrm{RW}}=\chihRW​=χ and the regime where the numerator is larger.

The no-overlap consequence

If there are no exact overlaps, distinct words of a given length remain distinct complete maps. Consequently,

H(Gn)=nH(p),H(p)=−∑ipilog⁡2pi,H(G_n)=nH(p),\qquadH(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log_2p_i,H(Gn​)=nH(p),H(p)=−i∑​pi​log2​pi​,

and the formula becomes dim⁡Hμ=min⁡{1,H(p)/χ}\dim_H\mu=\min\{1,H(p)/\chi\}dimH​μ=min{1,H(p)/χ}.

The manuscript also explains why forbidding exact equalities between words of equal length is equivalent, for these nonzero contractions, to forbidding them between arbitrary distinct nonempty words. Thus its convention does not hide a separate class of different-length coincidences.

For the attractor, under the no-exact-overlap hypothesis, it claims

dim⁡HK=min⁡{1,s∗},∑i∣ri∣s∗=1.\dim_H K=\min\{1,s_*\},\qquad\sum_i|r_i|^{s_*}=1.dimH​K=min{1,s∗​},i∑​∣ri​∣s∗​=1.

The number s∗s_*s∗​ is the similarity dimension. This simple set formula is stated with the no-overlap condition; the unrestricted main theorem is formulated for measures using their map entropy rate.

For a positive common contraction λ\lambdaλ, the denominator simplifies to log⁡2(1/λ)\log_2(1/\lambda)log2​(1/λ). The paper records the all-weight consequence for homogeneous systems, including the three maps λx,λx+1,λx+t\lambda x,\lambda x+1,\lambda x+tλx,λx+1,λx+t, whenever they have no exact overlaps.

A simple example of why addresses overcount

Use the map x/3x/3x/3 twice, each indexed copy with probability 1/41/41/4, and the map x/3+2/3x/3+2/3x/3+2/3 with probability 1/21/21/2. After merging the repeated map, these are the ordinary equal-weight Cantor choices.

The original three-symbol entropy is 3/23/23/2 bits per step, but the surviving map entropy is one bit per step. The formula gives log⁡2/log⁡3\log 2/\log 3log2/log3, the dimension of the usual Cantor probability measure. The extra symbolic label carries no geometric information. The main theorem claims that the same accounting principle remains exact for much more complicated collisions between long words.

5. Why the advance matters
