Provisional importance: 5/5. The claim supplies a universal dimension formula in a central class of overlapping fractal measures. It would remove both arithmetic and quantitative separation assumptions while retaining exact coincidences in the correct information quantity.

The formula gives a precise interpretation of dimension loss: after accounting for the ceiling imposed by the real line, the relevant loss is the entropy lost when different addresses become the same map. Distinct maps may be astonishingly close, but the theorem claims that this closeness causes no additional asymptotic dimension deficit.

That is a structural conclusion, not necessarily a computational shortcut. Determining the entropy rate of a complicated system may still be difficult. The importance lies in identifying the exact quantity that governs dimension, including in systems where a simple separation argument cannot work.

6. The main idea

Look for information hidden below the current resolution

Observe a finite distribution only through a grid of small intervals. Several distinct values may fall in one cell and become indistinguishable. The difference between exact entropy and grid-cell entropy measures the information hidden below that resolution.

The manuscript develops an estimate that detects this hidden information through equal-weight two-point distributions at finer scales. Such a pair is the simplest unit of uncertainty: a fair choice between two locations. Crucially, the estimate does not depend on the smallest positive distance between support points.

Averaging over translations of the grid avoids making the argument depend on a fortunate placement of cell boundaries.

Freeze contraction by conditioning on symbol counts

Unequal contractions complicate the relation between symbolic length and physical size. The proof groups symbols into blocks and conditions on how often each symbol occurs in a block. These counts fix the product of the signed contraction ratios, even though the order of the symbols can vary.

With the slope fixed, the translation identifies the complete affine map. This is why the theorem tracks full maps rather than just the endpoint Gn(0)G_n(0)Gn​(0): before conditioning, two maps could share that endpoint and still have different slopes.

Recording symbol counts has a controlled entropy cost. The remaining translation entropy can therefore be bounded using the map entropy rate, including when different words coincide exactly. A hypothetical dimension smaller than both one and hRW/χh_{\mathrm{RW}}/\chihRW​/χ would leave a linear amount of hidden two-point uncertainty across a finite band of finer scales.

Make those hidden choices produce incompatible gains

If the measure’s dimension is below one, its entropy is not saturated at the maximum allowed by the line. The manuscript shows that each suitable two-point choice then produces a positive entropy gain against the still-unobserved tail of the random composition.

The fine-scale bands may extend to arbitrarily deep resolutions. Instead of asserting a bound on their endpoints, the proof chooses later block lengths after earlier endpoints are known. It arranges disjoint windows so the gains can be added without counting the same information twice.

The total entropy increase over the relevant scale intervals is bounded. Yet the proposed deficit supplies a positive contribution from each of arbitrarily many disjoint bands. The resulting contradiction is the mechanism claimed to prove the lower bound. The upper bound comes from grouping equal composed maps and applying ordinary covering estimates.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem is for finite systems of affine similarities on the real line. It does not automatically extend to higher-dimensional self-similar systems, general self-affine maps, or nonlinear contractions.

Dimension one does not imply absolute continuity. A measure can have full Hausdorff dimension while being supported, in the measure-theoretic sense, on a set of zero length. The formula does not assert an integrable density, a smooth density, or a quantitative rate of convergence of scale entropies.

The entropy rate itself is a limit over exact composed-map laws. The paper does not give a universal effective procedure or error bound for computing it. Nor does its no-overlap corollary provide a positive separation estimate between distinct maps.

The assumptions 0<∣ri∣<10<|r_i|<10<∣ri​∣<1 and finiteness of the family remain part of the statement. Repeated maps are explicitly allowed and their probabilities are combined at the map level; they must not be treated as independent geometric branches when applying the formula.

8. Sources and further reading

Hutchinson’s Fractals and self-similarity gives the foundational construction. Feng and Hu’s exact-dimensionality theorem is an explicit input to the new manuscript. Hochman’s entropy and overlap theorem and Rapaport’s algebraic-contraction result describe major preceding advances.

For the obstruction to inferring separation from the absence of exact overlaps, see Baker’s superexponentially close cylinder construction. Varjú’s survey of entropy rates states the conjectural framework. The distinction between dimension and singularity also appears in family 153, devoted to Bernoulli convolutions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The entropy-rate dimension formula for self-similar measures on the line (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: An irrational angle makes a triangular billiard weakly mixing
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 150 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Imagine a frictionless point moving inside a triangle and reflecting off its sides with equal angles of incidence and reflection. The rule is elementary. Its long-term statistics are not: straight walls supply none of the dispersing curvature that makes some other billiards visibly chaotic.

Does a typical trajectory explore all positions and directions according to their natural proportions? More strongly, can the system retain a measurable, perfectly periodic signal? Family 150 addresses these questions for every triangle having at least one angle that is an irrational multiple of π\piπ.

The earlier manuscript claims ergodicity. The later one strengthens the conclusion to weak mixing, which excludes nonconstant periodic spectral signals. The assertion concerns the full phase space, with both position and direction varying, and has no exceptional irrational triangles.

2. Background and essential definitions

The phase space and its probability measure

Let QQQ be a nondegenerate Euclidean triangle, meaning that its area is positive. A unit-speed state consists of a position x∈Qx\in Qx∈Q and an angle θ∈[0,2π)\theta\in[0,2\pi)θ∈[0,2π). The natural probability measure is

dμ(x,θ)=dA(x) dθ2πArea⁡(Q).d\mu(x,\theta)=\frac{dA(x)\,d\theta}{2\pi\operatorname{Area}(Q)}.dμ(x,θ)=2πArea(Q)dA(x)dθ​.

Here dAdAdA is ordinary area. This distribution chooses position uniformly in the triangle and direction uniformly on the circle. The billiard flow Φt\Phi_tΦt​ preserves it.

A path hitting a vertex has no uniquely prescribed reflection. Such paths, in either time direction, form a set of measure zero and are discarded. Statements holding almost everywhere are unaffected by their removal.

Ergodicity, weak mixing, and mixing

Ergodicity says that every measurable set preserved by the flow has probability zero or one. Equivalently, integrable observables have their expected long-time averages along almost every trajectory. This does not assert that every individual trajectory is typical.

Weak mixing says that two independent copies, evolved for the same time, form an ergodic system on the product probability space. One equivalent correlation formulation is that, for measurable sets A,BA,BA,B,

1T∫0T∣μ(A∩Φt−1B)−μ(A)μ(B)∣2 dt⟶0.\frac1T\int_0^T\left|\mu(A\cap\Phi_t^{-1}B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)\right|^2\,dt\longrightarrow0.T1​∫0T​​μ(A∩Φt−1​B)−μ(A)μ(B)​2dt⟶0.

Ordinary mixing would require the correlation difference itself to tend to zero at every sufficiently late time, without averaging. The manuscripts do not claim that stronger conclusion.

A useful spectral language describes an eigenfunction fff satisfying

f∘Φt=eiλtffor every real t,f\circ\Phi_t=e^{i\lambda t}f\quad\text{for every real }t,f∘Φt​=eiλtffor every real t,

as an equality in the space of square-integrable functions. Here λ\lambdaλ is a real frequency. Such an observable evolves with an exact periodic phase. Weak mixing is equivalent to the absence of nonconstant eigenfunctions, including invariant functions at frequency zero.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The classical unfolding construction, developed in the polygonal setting by Zemlyakov and Katok, replaces a reflection of the path by a reflection of the table. A broken billiard path becomes a straight path on a surface assembled from copies of the polygon.

For a rational polygon, every angle is a rational multiple of π\piπ. Only finitely many directions arise from the reflection group, and unfolding produces a compact translation surface. The full phase space splits into invariant directional surfaces. Kerckhoff, Masur, and Smillie proved unique ergodicity for almost every direction on such surfaces. That does not make the full position-and-direction flow ergodic: the directional decomposition itself remains an obstruction.

Their work also gave full-flow ergodicity for a dense GδG_\deltaGδ​ family of polygonal tables. Such a set is a countable intersection of open dense sets, a notion of largeness from topology. It need not have full Lebesgue measure in the space of angle parameters.

Vorobets supplied a quantitative rational-approximation criterion and explicit ergodic irrational examples, including right triangles. These results left open tables without the required exceptionally good approximations.

Chaika and Forni then proved weak mixing of the full billiard flow for a dense GδG_\deltaGδ​ collection of polygons with any fixed number of sides at least three. Their result is already stronger than ergodicity, but its quantifier is genericity, rather than every irrational triangle. Recent work of Arana-Herrera, Chaika, and Forni addresses weak mixing in almost every direction for rational billiards, again a different phase-space question.

The analytic background includes Forni and Moll’s work on geodesic flows on flat surfaces. They obtained rigidity results with assumptions about spatial derivatives. A merely measurable invariant function need not have those derivatives. According to the new manuscripts, proving the missing regularity is the decisive additional step.

Numerical studies have suggested both mixing behavior and failures of ergodicity in particular irrational triangular families. Finite-time trajectories can be misleading when statistical convergence is very slow. The claimed theorems replace this finite-time evidence with statements about all measurable invariants or eigenfunctions.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let the angles of QQQ be α,β,γ>0\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0α,β,γ>0, summing to π\piπ. Suppose at least one of α/π,β/π,γ/π\alpha/\pi,\beta/\pi,\gamma/\piα/π,β/π,γ/π is irrational.

M2, dated 25 September 2026, claims that the full unit-speed billiard flow is ergodic for normalized Liouville measure μ\muμ. M1, dated 5 October 2026, claims that it is weakly mixing for the same measure. There is no symmetry restriction, no Diophantine approximation condition, and no genericity qualifier.

The scope includes irrational right triangles and irrational isosceles triangles. It also includes triangles with one rational angle and two irrational ones. The statement is made for each fixed triangle, not just almost every parameter choice.

Conversely, a rational triangle has a finite reflection group on directions. There are nonconstant functions of direction invariant under that group, hence invariant under the full billiard flow. Its full flow is therefore not ergodic. In this sense, the irrationality assumption is sharp.

As a consequence, weak mixing holds for Lebesgue-almost every angle pair (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)(α,β) in the open region α>0,β>0,α+β<π\alpha>0,\beta>0,\alpha+\beta<\piα>0,β>0,α+β<π. The omitted rational pairs are countable. This measure-theoretic statement follows from the stronger every-irrational-triangle assertion.

Consequences for vibrating triangles

M2 also applies existing quantum-ergodicity theorems. Consider any orthonormal basis of Dirichlet or Neumann Laplace eigenfunctions on the fixed triangle. The manuscript derives interior and boundary quantum ergodicity along a density-one subsequence. Density one means that the fraction of retained eigenfunctions among the first NNN tends to one.

For a real-valued eigenbasis, the number of nodal domains, the connected regions separated by the eigenfunction’s zero set, tends to infinity along a density-one subsequence. These are applications of earlier spectral results, rather than separate new billiard mechanisms. Exceptional subsequences of density zero remain possible.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the family turns a long-standing generic and example-based theory into a classification for all triangular tables at the level of full-flow ergodicity and weak mixing.

The difference in quantifiers is substantial. A theorem about almost every direction on a rational surface, one about a topologically generic collection of tables, and one about every irrational triangle answer different questions. Here the angle condition would become a complete and elementary criterion for weak mixing of the full flow.

The regularity mechanism also matters beyond the headline. Many dynamical arguments can rule out smooth invariants while leaving open irregular measurable ones. The manuscripts claim a method that begins at the measurable level, where ergodicity and weak mixing actually live.

6. The main idea

Double the triangle and separate angular modes

Glue two oppositely oriented copies of the triangle along matching sides. Crossing an open side becomes ordinary straight motion on this flat double. The three vertices become cone points; everything else is locally Euclidean.

On the unit tangent bundle, let XXX denote differentiation in the direction of motion and YYY differentiation in the perpendicular spatial direction. An eigenfunction initially gives only

Xf=iλf.Xf=i\lambda f.Xf=iλf.

It says nothing immediate about YfYfYf. Assuming that missing derivative would bypass the central difficulty.

The manuscripts expand f(x,θ)f(x,\theta)f(x,θ) in angular Fourier modes. In flat charts, the transport equation relates spatial derivatives of neighboring mode coefficients. Smoothing in position away from cone points and using cutoffs first gives a derivative estimate for each individual coefficient. A bound on each coefficient separately does not yet justify summing all their derivative energies.

Recover the missing transverse control

M2 studies frequency zero. Suitable tails of the angular expansion have transport derivatives containing only an endpoint term. Long averages along orbit segments avoiding cone points test these endpoint terms.

Two limits have distinct jobs. At a fixed allowance for discarded trajectories, the smoothing parameter tends to zero and gives an exact local transport equation. A new estimate for that equation removes dependence on the discarded measure. Only then does the second approximation tend to the original measurable function. M2 concludes that the coefficient gradients vanish.

M1 extends this method to every real frequency. Terms involving λ\lambdaλ telescope when coefficient identities are summed, while a boundary-mode pairing controls the remaining endpoint terms. The key claimed estimate is

∥Xf∥22+∥Yf∥22≤λ2∥f∥22.\|Xf\|_2^2+\|Yf\|_2^2\le\lambda^2\|f\|_2^2.∥Xf∥22​+∥Yf∥22​≤λ2∥f∥22​.

Because Xf=iλfXf=i\lambda fXf=iλf, the first term already equals the right-hand side. Thus Yf=0Yf=0Yf=0. The manuscript develops this extension from the earlier method and supplies its own analytic argument.

Reflections eliminate the surviving waves

Inside the triangle, the two differential relations leave a plane wave with an amplitude depending only on direction. Choose the origin at an irrational vertex. Reflections in its two incident sides generate an irrational rotation of the direction circle. A measurable amplitude invariant under that rotation must be constant.

Reflection in the third side includes a nonzero translation. A nonzero-frequency plane wave with constant directional amplitude cannot respect that reflection in every direction. The frequency must therefore be zero, and the function constant.

The argument starts with bounded eigenfunctions. An arbitrary square-integrable one can be changed to the bounded function f/(1+∣f∣)f/(1+|f|)f/(1+∣f∣), which retains its eigenfrequency and preserves the information needed for the conclusion. The spectral criterion then supplies weak mixing.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result concerns triangles, unit speed, specular reflections, and the stated Liouville measure. It should not be extended to every irrational polygon merely because the geometric vocabulary is similar.

Weak mixing gives no rate of correlation decay and does not establish ordinary mixing. It also does not imply unique ergodicity or typical behavior for every initial state. The discarded vertex-hitting paths and other exceptional individual trajectories remain outside such universal orbit claims.

The spectral corollaries preserve their own qualifications. Boundary data differ for Dirichlet and Neumann conditions, with different limiting weights; one cannot treat them as identically normalized boundary distributions. Quantum ergodicity permits exceptional subsequences and is weaker than quantum unique ergodicity. No eigenvalue-spacing law, nodal-count rate, or full-sequence equidistribution is asserted.

Understanding rates of statistical convergence and deciding stronger mixing properties remain separate questions from the classification claimed here.

8. Sources and further reading

Zemlyakov and Katok’s 1975 unfolding paper and Kerckhoff, Masur, and Smillie’s 1986 ergodicity theorem give the classical geometric background. Vorobets’ quantitative approximation work supplies earlier irrational examples.

Chaika and Forni’s Weakly mixing polygonal billiards is the generic weak-mixing predecessor. Forni and Moll’s flat-surface analysis explains the derivative framework. Arana-Herrera, Chaika, and Forni’s rational-billiard manuscript addresses the distinct directional question.

For the spectral applications, M2 cites the interior theorem of Zelditch and Zworski, the boundary theorem of Hassell and Zelditch, and Hezari’s nodal-domain theorem for ergodic billiards.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Weak mixing of triangular billiards with an irrational angle (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Ergodicity of triangular billiards with an irrational angle (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A common safe region for every trajectory of a weakly reversible reaction network
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 149 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Can the wiring diagram of a chemical reaction network prevent any of its species from disappearing? A reaction can consume one substance rapidly, yet a chain of other reactions may regenerate it. The relevant structural condition is weak reversibility: every reaction has a directed route back to its starting combination of species. The reverse need not be a single reaction.

Family 149 asks whether this condition controls all long-term concentrations under mass-action kinetics. Two manuscripts give progressively stronger claims. The earlier one claims that each positive trajectory stays inside some bounded region away from zero. The later one claims that every trajectory with the same conservation constraints eventually enters one common compact region. That uniformity is the distinction between individual persistence and classwise permanence.

The conclusion includes networks whose conservation constraints allow arbitrarily large concentrations. Thus boundedness is an output, rather than an assumption that a finite supply of material has already settled the problem.

2. Background and essential definitions

Reactions become polynomial equations

Suppose there are ddd species with concentration vector x=(x1,…,xd)x=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)x=(x1​,…,xd​). A complex is a vector yyy of nonnegative integers recording a combination of species. For example, with species A,BA,BA,B, the complex 2A+B2A+B2A+B is (2,1)(2,1)(2,1).

A reaction y→y′y\to y'y→y′ has a positive constant rate ky→y′k_{y\to y'}ky→y′​. Mass action assigns it flux ky→y′xyk_{y\to y'}x^yky→y′​xy, where xy=∏ixiyix^y=\prod_i x_i^{y_i}xy=∏i​xiyi​​. The resulting differential equation is

x˙=∑y→y′ky→y′xy(y′−y).\dot x=\sum_{y\to y'}k_{y\to y'}x^y(y'-y).x˙=y→y′∑​ky→y′​xy(y′−y).

Each term multiplies the reaction frequency by the change in species amounts. For 2A⇄B2A\rightleftarrows B2A⇄B, writing concentrations a,ba,ba,b and rates k+,k−k_+,k_-k+​,k−​, this gives

a˙=−2k+a2+2k−b,b˙=k+a2−k−b.\dot a=-2k_+a^2+2k_-b,\qquad\dot b=k_+a^2-k_-b.a˙=−2k+​a2+2k−​b,b˙=k+​a2−k−​b.

Consequently a+2ba+2ba+2b is constant. This elementary example has bounded concentration classes, but general networks need not.

Conservation classes and three kinds of control

Let SSS be the vector space spanned by all reaction changes y′−yy'-yy′−y. Starting from a strictly positive vector ccc, the solution remains in the affine space c+Sc+Sc+S. Its positive stoichiometric compatibility class is

P=(c+S)∩(0,∞)d.P=(c+S)\cap(0,\infty)^d.P=(c+S)∩(0,∞)d.

The adjective “stoichiometric” refers to the species bookkeeping encoded in the reaction changes. Two initial states in the same class obey the same linear conservation constraints.

A trajectory is bounded if no concentration grows without limit. It is persistent if every concentration has a strictly positive lower limit as time tends to infinity. The bounds may depend on the trajectory.

Permanence on PPP is stronger: one compact subset of PPP eventually contains every positive trajectory in that class. Different initial states may take different times to arrive. A set is forward invariant if a trajectory starting there stays there for every later time.

These are statements about deterministic concentrations. They do not say that a finite stochastic population has zero probability of extinction.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Horn and Jackson’s 1972 theory and Feinberg’s work established the special role of complex balance. At a complex-balanced equilibrium, the total flux entering each complex equals the total leaving it. This provides an entropy-like function decreasing along trajectories and a unique positive equilibrium in each positive class. Complex balance depends on rate constants as well as the reaction graph; weak reversibility alone imposes fewer conditions.

Feinberg’s discussion of weakly reversible systems raised the question of excluding limiting states with zero concentrations. Persistence strengthens this by excluding boundary approach even along a sequence of times. Anderson subsequently distinguished the boundedness question from persistence for already bounded trajectories. A proof of one does not automatically supply the other.

Several substantial special cases were known. Craciun, Nazarov, and Pantea established permanence for two-species weakly reversible systems within a broader geometric class called endotactic networks. Pantea established persistence of bounded trajectories when the stoichiometric space has dimension two. These are different restrictions: a system can have many species but only two independent reaction directions.

Gopalkrishnan, Miller, and Shiu proved permanence for strongly endotactic systems, a geometric class including weakly reversible networks with a single connected component of the reaction graph. Boros and Hofbauer later gave another proof in that single-component case. Several such results allow rates to vary with time within fixed positive upper and lower bounds.

The manuscripts also discuss Craciun’s toric differential inclusions. They distinguish the September 2026 revision’s persistence statement for bounded weakly reversible trajectories from its complex-balanced global-convergence application. The general persistence statement does not itself supply the missing upper bound.

The earlier manuscript in this family notes a previous general claim by August and Barahona and identifies an issue in its monomial-dominance argument. This is the manuscript’s account of the literature; the present exposition does not independently assess that proof. Its own construction is presented as an independent route to simultaneous boundedness and persistence.

Finally, the later manuscript explicitly builds on the earlier one’s affine approximation lemma. Its additional contribution is the passage from a trapping region chosen for one initial state to an absorbing region shared by an entire class.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Individual bounds, then uniform eventual bounds

M2, dated 25 September 2026, considers any finite weakly reversible network, in any species dimension, with positive constant reaction rates. For every strictly positive initial state, it claims a unique solution for all forward time and a number ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 such that

ε≤xi(t)≤ε−1for every t≥0 and every species i.\varepsilon\le x_i(t)\le\varepsilon^{-1}\quad\text{for every }t\ge0\text{ and every species }i.ε≤xi​(t)≤ε−1for every t≥0 and every species i.

Here ε\varepsilonε may depend on the initial state. More geometrically, the manuscript constructs a compact convex positive polytope containing that state and invariant under the dynamics.

M1, dated 5 October 2026, strengthens the quantifiers. For each fixed positive class PPP, it claims a nonempty compact convex forward-invariant set KP⊂PK_P\subset PKP​⊂P such that every initial state x0∈Px_0\in Px0​∈P has a finite entry time T(x0)T(x_0)T(x0​), after which its trajectory stays in KPK_PKP​. In particular,

εP≤xi(t)≤εP−1whenever t≥T(x0).\varepsilon_P\le x_i(t)\le\varepsilon_P^{-1}\quad\text{whenever }t\ge T(x_0).εP​≤xi​(t)≤εP−1​whenever t≥T(x0​).

The same εP\varepsilon_PεP​ works for all initial states in that class. It may depend on the network, its fixed rates, and the class. Neither the entry time nor the bound is asserted to be uniform over different classes or rate choices.

There is no restriction on the number of connected components, usually called linkage classes. The class PPP can be unbounded. Initial concentrations must nevertheless be strictly positive.

M2 also recovers the known existence of a positive equilibrium in every positive class, crediting Boros. With the additional complex-balance assumption, it derives convergence to the class’s unique positive equilibrium. General weak reversibility is not claimed to force such convergence.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the family resolves central persistence, boundedness, and permanence questions in chemical reaction network theory for fixed positive rates. Its significance comes from replacing dimension and graph-component restrictions with a basic structural condition.

The common absorbing set is particularly useful. A separate bound for each experiment says that each individual run behaves safely, but gives no shared eventual range for a whole class of starting conditions. Permanence supplies that shared range. It controls the long-term dynamics before one knows whether trajectories settle to equilibria, oscillate, or exhibit more complicated behavior.

The methods also address a general difficulty in polynomial differential equations: some coordinates may become tiny while others become large. A single estimate based on total concentration can miss that mixed behavior. Here the construction compares the individual monomials responsible for the reactions.

6. The main idea

Compare reaction strengths on logarithmic scales

Choose a small number 0<h<10<h<10<h<1 and write positive concentrations in a box as

xi=hpi,−1≤pi≤1.x_i=h^{p_i},\qquad -1\le p_i\le1.xi​=hpi​,−1≤pi​≤1.

Then xy=hp⋅yx^y=h^{p\cdot y}xy=hp⋅y. Because h<1h<1h<1, a smaller exponent means a larger monomial. Thus ordering complexes by a linear function of their exponent vectors reveals which reaction fluxes dominate.

The construction uses a concave piecewise-affine function

Fh(x)=min⁡λ(rλ⋅x+bλ(h)).F_h(x)=\min_{\lambda}\bigl(r_\lambda\cdot x+b_\lambda(h)\bigr).Fh​(x)=λmin​(rλ​⋅x+bλ​(h)).

There are finitely many labels λ\lambdaλ. A label is active where its affine expression achieves the minimum. The central approximation lemma chooses the slopes rλr_\lambdarλ​ so that every active slope closely matches the exponent vector ppp at that point.

The required accuracy is especially delicate near ties between complexes. A careless small error could reverse their order. The lemma permits a tolerance that changes discontinuously near comparison hyperplanes, so all nonzero comparisons have the correct sign. It controls every active label, including several that tie.

Return paths make a barrier point inward

Order the complexes by their value under an active slope and cut the ordered list between consecutive levels. If a reaction crosses the cut in one direction, weak reversibility supplies a crossing in the opposite direction along a return path. The monomial comparison makes an appropriately directed flux dominate the sum of adverse fluxes when hhh is small enough.

Summing over cuts shows that FhF_hFh​ cannot decrease along a trajectory in the relevant box. Its maximum set is a compact convex polytope. Once a trajectory lies on this maximum plateau, nondecrease prevents it from leaving. Choosing the scale to include a prescribed initial state gives M2’s individual trapping region.

M1 adds strictness outside a class’s plateau. A slope perpendicular to SSS is constant on c+Sc+Sc+S, so it cannot be the active obstruction outside the desired maximum set. Every remaining relevant slope gives strict increase. At a fixed scale, compactness turns this into a positive lower bound on the increase, forcing finite-time entry.

The final step connects scales. A trapping set at scale hhh lies inside the box associated with h\sqrt hh​. Repeatedly replacing hhh by its square root, stopping at a scale fixed by the class, brings every trajectory into one common region after finitely many stages. This uses containments in successive boxes; it does not assume that all the trapping polytopes are nested.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The rates are fixed positive constants. Earlier special-case theorems sometimes handle bounded time-varying rates, but that stronger rate flexibility should not be transferred to these general claims.

Permanence also does not give a common entry time for initial states arbitrarily close to the boundary or arbitrarily far away in an unbounded class. The stated uniformity concerns the eventual region. Practical estimates for its size and for entry times are separate quantitative questions.

The claims exclude extinction and escape to infinity from positive initial states. They do not classify attractors or imply uniqueness of equilibrium for arbitrary weakly reversible systems. Nor do they cover boundary initial states, non-mass-action kinetics, infinite reaction networks, or stochastic reaction counts without additional work.

The conceptual separation remains useful: complex balance supports convergence to a particular equilibrium; weak reversibility supplies the broader geometric protection expressed by permanence.

8. Sources and further reading

Horn and Jackson, General mass action kinetics (1972), is a primary source for complex balance and its stability theory. Feinberg’s Chemical reaction network structure and the stability of complex isothermal reactors—I (1987) develops the structural setting and the boundary question.

For earlier partial results, see Craciun, Nazarov, and Pantea, Persistence and permanence of mass-action and power-law dynamical systems (2013); Pantea, On the persistence and global stability of mass-action systems (2012); and Gopalkrishnan, Miller, and Shiu, A geometric approach to the global attractor conjecture (2014). Boros and Hofbauer’s Permanence of weakly reversible mass-action systems with a single linkage class (2020) is the closest earlier absorbing-set result cited here.

Craciun’s toric differential inclusion manuscript, version 3 supplies the separate bounded-trajectory and complex-balanced context. The precise claims and construction summarized above are those of the two pinned manuscripts below.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniform Permanence in Weakly Reversible Mass-Action Systems (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Boundedness and persistence of weakly reversible mass-action systems (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Topological growth without orbit entropy at one derivative
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 151 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

If a map repeatedly wraps a space around itself, must its trajectories become exponentially complicated? Shub’s entropy conjecture makes this intuition precise by comparing two kinds of growth: the number of distinguishable orbit histories and the expansion of topological cycles under iteration.

For infinitely differentiable maps on compact manifolds, the proposed inequality is a theorem. Family 151 claims that it fails for maps with only one continuous derivative. The example has zero topological entropy, yet its action on second homology has eigenvalue two.

Two qualifications are central. The constructed map is noninvertible, and the expanding topological information occurs in an intermediate homology degree. The manuscript therefore does not claim a counterexample among diffeomorphisms, nor does it contradict known inequalities for first homology or topological degree.

2. Background and essential definitions

Counting distinguishable histories

Let f:M→Mf:M\to Mf:M→M be continuous on a compact metric space with distance ddd. To compare two starting points for nnn steps, use

dn(x,y)=max⁡0≤j<nd(fj(x),fj(y)).d_n(x,y)=\max_{0\le j<n}d(f^j(x),f^j(y)).dn​(x,y)=0≤j<nmax​d(fj(x),fj(y)).

Two histories are distinguishable at resolution ε\varepsilonε when this distance exceeds ε\varepsilonε. Let sf(n,ε)s_f(n,\varepsilon)sf​(n,ε) be the largest size of a set of pairwise distinguishable histories. Topological entropy is

htop(f)=lim⁡ε↓0lim sup⁡n→∞1nlog⁡sf(n,ε).h_{\mathrm{top}}(f)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log s_f(n,\varepsilon).htop​(f)=ε↓0lim​n→∞limsup​n1​logsf​(n,ε).

Thus positive entropy means exponential growth in possible histories at sufficiently fine observation scales. Zero entropy permits nontrivial dynamics, but their distinguishable histories have no positive exponential growth rate. This is a property of the map on the whole space, without selecting a probability measure.

Tracking cycles instead of individual points

Real homology Hk(M;R)H_k(M;\mathbb R)Hk​(M;R) is a finite-dimensional vector space recording kkk-dimensional cycles modulo those bounding higher-dimensional pieces. First homology records loop information; second homology can record sphere-like surfaces. A continuous map induces a linear map f∗f_*f∗​ on these spaces.

The spectral radius ρ(f∗)\rho(f_*)ρ(f∗​) is the largest absolute value of an eigenvalue on their direct sum. An eigenvalue two means that repeated application multiplies some homological information at rate 2n2^n2n. The conjectured inequality is

htop(f)≥log⁡ρ(f∗).h_{\mathrm{top}}(f)\ge\log\rho(f_*).htop​(f)≥logρ(f∗​).

The model example is the sphere map z↦z2z\mapsto z^2z↦z2, viewing the sphere as the complex plane together with infinity. A generic target has two preimages, each preserving orientation, so the map has degree two and multiplies its second homology by two.

A C1C^1C1 map has a continuous first derivative. A C∞C^\inftyC∞ map has continuous derivatives of every order. A diffeomorphism must additionally be invertible with a differentiable inverse. These regularity and invertibility distinctions affect the entropy question.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Shub formulated the connection between entropy and homological growth in the 1970s. His later account explicitly discusses both endomorphisms, which need not be invertible, and diffeomorphisms. It also distinguishes earlier Lipschitz counterexamples from the question at C1C^1C1 regularity. A Lipschitz map controls distances but need not have a continuous derivative.

Manning established an entropy lower bound from the induced action on first real homology for continuous maps. Thus a counterexample cannot simply hide exponentially growing loop information in a continuous zero-entropy map.

Misiurewicz and Przytycki established a C1C^1C1 lower bound involving topological degree. On an oriented closed manifold, degree controls the action on the highest-dimensional homology. This leaves intermediate homology as a different issue.

Yomdin’s 1987 work proved the full inequality for C∞C^\inftyC∞ maps by relating entropy to volume growth. Gromov’s exposition explains the geometric estimates behind this result. High regularity bounds the complexity that can be hidden in successively finer geometric features.

Positive results also cover important restricted classes at lower regularity. Saghin and Xia proved the conjectured bound for partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms with one-dimensional center. Liao, Viana, and Yang proved it for diffeomorphisms away from homoclinic tangencies. These hypotheses impose dynamical structure absent from an arbitrary C1C^1C1 self-map.

The claimed counterexample occupies the gap between those results: finite regularity, noninvertibility, and growth in an intermediate-dimensional homology group. It changes the general self-map statement while leaving the cited positive theorems intact.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The single manuscript, dated 25 September 2026, claims that for some positive integer qqq, there is a C1C^1C1 map on the compact boundaryless smooth manifold

M=(R/100Z)×(S2)q+1M=(\mathbb R/100\mathbb Z)\times(S^2)^{q+1}M=(R/100Z)×(S2)q+1

with

htop(f)=0,2 an eigenvalue of f∗:H2(M;R)→H2(M;R).h_{\mathrm{top}}(f)=0,\qquad2\text{ an eigenvalue of }f_*:H_2(M;\mathbb R)\to H_2(M;\mathbb R).htop​(f)=0,2 an eigenvalue of f∗​:H2​(M;R)→H2​(M;R).

The circle factor is a clock with circumference 100; its particular scale is a construction convenience. The remaining factors are spheres. The manifold has dimension 2q+32q+32q+3, at least five, so second homology is neither first nor top-dimensional homology.

Consequently the claimed example satisfies

0=htop(f)<log⁡2≤log⁡ρ(f∗).0=h_{\mathrm{top}}(f)<\log2\le\log\rho(f_*).0=htop​(f)<log2≤logρ(f∗​).

The map is explicitly noninvertible. The claim is an existence statement for a finite-dimensional example, not an assertion that every manifold supports one or that the displayed dimension is minimal.

The construction supplies both parts of the conclusion: a classification of forward-orbit behavior that gives zero entropy, and a homotopy calculation retaining the degree-two action of squaring on one sphere coordinate.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, this gives a negative answer to a central general formulation of the entropy conjecture. It shows that one continuous derivative does not suffice to convert all homological expansion into orbit complexity.

The example also sharpens the role of regularity. The difference between C1C^1C1 and C∞C^\inftyC∞ can look technical in elementary calculus, but here it separates a claimed counterexample from a known universal theorem. Infinitely many increasingly fine features can be compatible with a continuous first derivative while evading the stronger geometric control used in the smooth theorem.

Its significance is not that topology becomes irrelevant to dynamics. First homology and degree still impose their established constraints. The result instead identifies a particular failure of a proposed universal bridge between intermediate topology and entropy.

6. The main idea

A squaring coordinate with delayed interventions

Write a point as (t,z,v1,…,vq)(t,z,v_1,\ldots,v_q)(t,z,v1​,…,vq​). The coordinate ttt is the circular clock, zzz is the main sphere coordinate, and the other sphere coordinates store small complex signals. Most of the time, zzz evolves approximately by squaring.

A clock passage has preparation, possible delay, readout, and reset stages. Near one clock position, its advance can become arbitrarily slow depending on zzz. During preparation, the auxiliary coordinates receive signals designed for possible later readouts. A signal meant for a delay of mmm steps has an angular oscillation of order 2m2^m2m, together with an amplitude of order L−mL^{-m}L−m for a sufficiently large L>2L>2L>2.

The oscillation predicts the direction of a future square. The very small amplitude controls its first derivative. Intervening multiplication by LLL restores the signal’s size when it is read. The manuscript chooses LLL larger than both the angular-growth rate and a derivative bound for the clock-prediction map, making the infinite prediction series converge with its first derivatives.

The auxiliary coordinates live on spheres, so they must use a bounded extension of multiplication away from their small linear region. A separate estimate keeps each relevant signal in that linear region until readout. Each channel is read at most once per passage, and all channels are reset before the next preparation stage.

This is a mathematical construction with infinitely many possible delay terms, not a finite algorithm for predicting arbitrary dynamics. A finite truncation would miss sufficiently long delays. The controlled infinite series is the feature that supplies a response at every required delay while retaining C1C^1C1 regularity.

Force simple asymptotic behavior

At readout, contributions align with the current square rather than cancel it. The manuscript claims that a completed passage forces the main coordinate outside the unit circle. Thereafter repeated squaring drives its modulus toward infinity in the sphere coordinate.

Every orbit approaches one of two compact invariant sets. In one, the clock is fixed at its slow position and z=0z=0z=0; the remaining coordinates have radial dynamics with fixed angles and a nondecreasing radius map. In the other, z=∞z=\inftyz=∞, the auxiliary coordinates vanish, and only a periodic clock rotation remains.

Both restrictions have zero entropy. The first has only polynomially many distinguishable radial itineraries at fixed resolution, and the second is periodic.

An additional entropy-localization lemma handles the fact that entry is not uniform in the initial point. The manuscript derives a bound on the proportion of orbit blocks spent away from neighborhoods of the two invariant sets. Encoding the rare exceptional blocks contributes arbitrarily little exponential complexity. Thus arbitrarily long transients do not create positive entropy in the claimed example.

Retain homological doubling

Let π\piπ project to the main sphere and let g(z)=z2g(z)=z^2g(z)=z2. The main-coordinate update is squaring plus a bounded correction from the auxiliary coordinates. Continuously fading that correction to zero gives a homotopy between π∘f\pi\circ fπ∘f and g∘πg\circ\pig∘π.

Homotopic maps induce the same homology map, so

π∗f∗=g∗π∗=2π∗on second homology.\pi_*f_*=g_*\pi_*=2\pi_*\quad\text{on second homology}.π∗​f∗​=g∗​π∗​=2π∗​on second homology.

Since the projection has a section obtained by fixing the other coordinates, π∗\pi_*π∗​ is onto. The displayed relation therefore forces eigenvalue two for f∗f_*f∗​.

This relation holds on homology. It is not a dynamical factor relation saying that every actual projected orbit follows squaring. The time-dependent corrections can change trajectories drastically while remaining invisible to this homotopy calculation.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The counterexample is a C1C^1C1 self-map, not a diffeomorphism. Its loss of invertibility is explicit: some auxiliary-coordinate regions are collapsed to identical outputs. The manuscript does not settle the unrestricted diffeomorphism version through this construction.

It also does not establish the same phenomenon at an arbitrarily prescribed higher finite regularity. Convergence of the first-derivative series is the stated regularity result. Questions about stronger derivative classes require their own estimates, and the C∞C^\inftyC∞ case is already governed by Yomdin’s positive theorem.

The homology coefficients are real, and the claimed expansion occurs in degree two. No violation of Manning’s first-homology bound or the degree bound is intended. Minimal dimension and simpler explicit realizations are separate questions.

Finally, zero topological entropy does not mean that all points become fixed after a bounded time. The construction uses long, nonuniform delays. Its claim is the more precise one that the global exponential rate of distinguishable histories vanishes despite those delays.

8. Sources and further reading

Shub’s Dynamical systems, filtrations and entropy (1974) is the original conceptual source; All, most, some differentiable dynamical systems (2007) discusses the formulations and regularity distinctions.

Manning’s Topological entropy and the first homology group (1975), Misiurewicz and Przytycki’s Topological entropy and degree of smooth mappings (1977), and Yomdin’s Volume growth and entropy (1987) are primary references for the positive results. Gromov’s Entropy, homology and semialgebraic geometry (1987) explains the smooth geometric framework.

For restricted diffeomorphism classes, see Saghin and Xia’s The entropy conjecture for partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms with 1-D center (2010) and Liao, Viana, and Yang’s The entropy conjecture for diffeomorphisms away from tangencies (2013). Hatcher’s Algebraic Topology provides background on homology, degree, and homotopy invariance.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A C^1 Counterexample to the Entropy Conjecture (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Zero entropy does not guarantee a smooth model with smooth volume
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 152 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

An abstract dynamical system can be described by how it rearranges probability, without mentioning coordinates, distances, or derivatives. Can every statistically simple system nevertheless be represented by smooth motion on a finite-dimensional geometric space?

Finite entropy is a necessary condition for many smooth realizations. It limits the average rate at which observing the system reveals new information. Family 152 claims that even zero entropy is insufficient when the geometric model must preserve a strictly positive smooth probability density.

The qualification about the measure is essential. The manuscript does not claim that its system lacks every smooth model with any invariant probability measure. It claims that one fixed abstract system cannot be represented by a smooth diffeomorphism preserving smooth positive volume, in any finite dimension.

2. Background and essential definitions

Measure-preserving systems and changes of coordinates

A probability-preserving transformation T:X→XT:X\to XT:X→X rearranges a probability space (X,μ)(X,\mu)(X,μ) while leaving probabilities unchanged. Invertibility means that the past as well as the future is defined. Ergodicity means that an invariant measurable set has probability zero or one.

A standard nonatomic probability space is, after ignoring null sets, equivalent to the unit interval with Lebesgue probability. “Nonatomic” rules out individual points carrying positive probability.

Two systems are measurably conjugate if there is a probability-preserving bijection FFF, defined outside null sets, satisfying

F∘T=S∘F.F\circ T=S\circ F.F∘T=S∘F.

Both FFF and its inverse must be measurable, but neither needs to be continuous. Consequently, visible geometric roughness in a symbolic presentation does not by itself obstruct a smooth model. A measurable change of coordinates can be extremely irregular.

Information growth

Choose a finite partition P\mathcal PP of XXX, thought of as a finite-resolution measuring device. Recording which cell contains TjxT^j xTjx produces a word of observations. If a finite distribution has probabilities pap_apa​, its Shannon entropy in bits is

H(p)=−∑apalog⁡2pa,H(p)=-\sum_a p_a\log_2p_a,H(p)=−a∑​pa​log2​pa​,

with 0log⁡20=00\log_2 0=00log2​0=0. The Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy is the greatest asymptotic information rate over all finite partitions:

hμ(T)=sup⁡Plim⁡n→∞1nHμ ⁣(⋁j=0n−1T−jP).h_\mu(T)=\sup_{\mathcal P}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n H_\mu\!\left(\bigvee_{j=0}^{n-1}T^{-j}\mathcal P\right).hμ​(T)=Psup​n→∞lim​n1​Hμ​(j=0⋁n−1​T−jP).

The joined partition records all nnn observations. Zero entropy says their information grows sublinearly for every fixed finite measuring device. It does not mean that observations are constant or that finite stretches lack intricate dependencies.

What counts as smooth volume

The proposed model consists of a compact smooth manifold MMM, a C∞C^\inftyC∞ diffeomorphism SSS, and an invariant probability ν\nuν that locally has the form

dν=f(x) ∣dx1⋯dxd∣,f(x)>0,d\nu=f(x)\,|dx_1\cdots dx_d|,\qquad f(x)>0,dν=f(x)∣dx1​⋯dxd​∣,f(x)>0,

with fff smooth. Absolute values allow densities on nonorientable manifolds. A manifold with smooth boundary is also allowed, with density smooth up to the boundary.

A measure with full support merely assigns positive probability to every nonempty open set. It can still be singular. Even a measure equivalent to volume, meaning that it has exactly the same null sets, need not have a smooth positive density. These distinctions separate different realization problems.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ruelle’s differentiable entropy inequality relates measure entropy to expansion rates of derivatives. On a compact smooth manifold, derivative bounds imply finite entropy. This makes entropy a natural first obstruction to smooth realization.

Positive representation results show that finite entropy is a powerful condition when other requirements are relaxed. Lind and Thouvenot proved that finite-entropy ergodic transformations can be represented by Lebesgue-preserving homeomorphisms of the two-torus. A homeomorphism is continuous with a continuous inverse; differentiability is not required.

They also obtained smooth toral models when one is allowed to choose a suitable invariant Borel probability of full support. Quas and Soo extended the universality results to toral automorphisms with no root-of-unity eigenvalue. Taking a sufficiently high iterate of a hyperbolic toral automorphism provides enough topological entropy to represent any prescribed finite-entropy system with an appropriate invariant measure. That measure need not be smooth volume.

Katok and Thouvenot developed slow entropy invariants to detect complexity below the usual exponential scale. They constructed actions of Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2 without Lipschitz realizations on compact spaces of finite box dimension, even allowing arbitrary invariant measures. An action of Z2\mathbb Z^2Z2 requires two commuting transformations to be realized together. Its obstruction does not directly answer the one-transformation question here.

Another line of work concerns the difficulty of classifying smooth systems up to measurable isomorphism. Foreman and Weiss, and later work on weakly mixing and mixing zero-entropy diffeomorphisms, established strong anti-classification results. Those theorems describe the complexity of equivalence within classes of smooth systems. They do not by themselves exhibit an abstract system with no smooth positive-volume representative.

The new manuscript addresses that existence question for a single invertible transformation. Its proposed obstruction is more refined than ordinary entropy and is designed to survive an arbitrary measurable conjugacy.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The manuscript, dated 25 September 2026, claims an ergodic invertible probability-preserving system (X,μ,T)(X,\mu,T)(X,μ,T) on a standard nonatomic probability space such that

hμ(T)=0,h_\mu(T)=0,hμ​(T)=0,

but no measurable conjugacy identifies it with any C∞C^\inftyC∞ diffeomorphism of a compact finite-dimensional manifold preserving a strictly positive smooth probability density.

The same example excludes all finite dimensions. The construction is fixed before a hypothetical dimension or manifold is chosen. Allowing a nonorientable manifold or a smooth boundary does not evade the claim.

The theorem does not exclude a smooth model with a singular invariant measure. Nor does it exclude all models whose invariant measure is merely equivalent to volume through a nonsmooth density. These are explicit limits of the stated result.

The proof is organized around two ingredients: a quantitative operation available in smooth positive-volume systems that joins one orbit’s future to another’s past, and a symbolic system whose long-range information constraints resist that operation.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the result shows that entropy alone cannot characterize smooth positive-volume realizability, even at its smallest possible value.

This distinguishes two ideas that are easily conflated. A system may generate no positive asymptotic information per step and still impose complicated restrictions on which pasts can coexist with which futures. Smooth geometry with a regular invariant density would impose additional compatibility conditions on those restrictions.

The uniformity over dimension strengthens the result. A family of examples, each requiring a larger manifold than the previous one, would leave open whether every individual system eventually fits somewhere. One example excluding every finite dimension closes that escape route for the stated class of models.

6. The main idea

A geometric operation with statistical control

For a hypothetical smooth model, consider a long time n=2kn=2^kn=2k. Partition the manifold into small cells. First choose a cell with probability equal to its volume, then independently choose two points x,yx,yx,y inside it.

The manuscript’s smooth switching theorem claims that, for most such pairs, one can find a point zzz whose future through time nnn stays close to that of xxx, and whose past back to time −n-n−n stays close to that of yyy. This resembles local product constructions in hyperbolic dynamics, but the argument does not assume that the whole system is uniformly hyperbolic.

Existence of a suitable zzz is not enough. A construction could concentrate all outputs on a statistically exceptional set. The manuscript therefore controls the output distribution: on retained pairs, its unnormalized law is at most twice ν\nuν. In particular, a small-probability exceptional set cannot absorb many switched outputs.

The number of cells has the form

#Dk≤exp⁡(CBk2k),∑kBk16<∞.\#\mathcal D_k\le \exp(CB_k2^k),\qquad \sum_k B_k^{16}<\infty.#Dk​≤exp(CBk​2k),k∑​Bk16​<∞.

The constant CCC and the positive sequence BkB_kBk​ may depend on the chosen smooth model. Summability is stronger than simply saying that the cost per time tends to zero; it forces sufficiently cheap scales that the symbolic construction can exploit.

The analytic work starts with stationary derivative-growth estimates on dyadic intervals. Finite-time changes of basis separate suitable directions, and a boundary-value construction joins the orbit halves. Determinant estimates and injectivity control the volume distortion. The smooth density assumption enters this quantitative distributional control.

Build legal words with incompatible independent halves

The opposing system is constructed from longer and longer finite words. A word at one level is a concatenation of words from the previous level, and additional alignment information records where those blocks begin.

Labels for blocks are nonzero vectors over F2\mathbb F_2F2​, the field with two elements. A fixed alternating bilinear form specifies relations between labels at selected power-of-two separations. Informally, certain distant blocks must be orthogonal under that form.

The construction preserves high information content in selected short lists of labels, even while its overall entropy rate tends to zero as block lengths grow. It also makes distinct words, and words read with incorrect alignment, differ in a definite proportion of symbols. This recognizability prevents an apparent orbit match from silently changing block boundaries.

Two independent label lists with high entropy are unlikely to satisfy most of the imposed pair relations. But the past and future of a single legal symbolic point are required to satisfy them. This creates the mismatch that a smooth switch would expose.

Transfer through a merely measurable conjugacy

A measurable conjugacy need not send nearby manifold points to nearby symbolic sequences. The argument instead approximates a finite symbolic observation on a large-measure set where spatial control is useful. The bounded output law ensures that switched points do not disproportionately land outside this good set.

At selected scales, the small cell-partition cost leaves the two input lists with too much independent information. Yet shadowing and word recognition force most entries to agree with the past and future lists of one legal output point. The manuscript obtains incompatible bounds for the probability that the required label relations hold.

The symbolic scales are chosen first. After any candidate finite-dimensional smooth model is proposed, the summability estimate supplies scales defeating its particular constants. This order is what makes one example work against every finite dimension.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

This is a claim about a smooth map together with a smooth positive invariant density. Removing the density requirement changes the problem, and known realization results already provide smooth models with more general invariant measures.

The theorem also should not be read as ruling out nonsmooth densities equivalent to volume. The manuscript identifies its output-law estimate as the point where the regularity of the density matters; it makes no corresponding assertion for all equivalent measures.

Zero entropy is used in the measure-theoretic sense. It says nothing by itself about the topological entropy of a hypothetical ambient map with a different measure. Nor does the theorem assert mixing, a finite symbolic presentation, or an explicit minimal differentiability threshold for the obstruction.

A natural remaining direction is to identify additional invariants that distinguish realizable zero-entropy systems from nonrealizable ones, and to understand how the answer changes as regularity of the map or its invariant density is weakened.

8. Sources and further reading

Lind and Thouvenot’s torus realization theorem and Quas and Soo’s ergodic universality theorem explain the positive results with different regularity or measure requirements.

Katok and Thouvenot’s slow entropy paper treats commuting transformations and motivates looking below exponential information growth. Ruelle’s entropy inequality gives the classical differentiable obstruction.

Foreman and Weiss’s anti-classification theorem concerns the distinct question of classifying smooth models. The smooth switching statement and the single-transformation counterexample summarized here are the claims of the pinned manuscript below.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A zero-entropy system without a smooth positive-volume model (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When a random geometric series has a density
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 153 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Toss a fair coin repeatedly, turn the outcomes into signs εn=±1\varepsilon_n=\pm1εn​=±1, and form a convergent random series

Yλ=∑n=0∞εnλn,0<λ<1.Y_\lambda=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_n\lambda^n,\qquad 0<\lambda<1.Yλ​=n=0∑∞​εn​λn,0<λ<1.

Its distribution νλ\nu_\lambdaνλ​ is an unbiased Bernoulli convolution. Does it have a density, or does all its probability hide on a set of ordinary length zero?

For small λ\lambdaλ, the possible values form a thin Cantor-like set. When λ>1/2\lambda>1/2λ>1/2, the support is an interval, yet the distribution can still be singular. Overlap between different coin histories creates an arithmetic problem rather than a simple support question.

Family 153 claims a classification for every parameter through an explicitly defined approximation condition. It also claims singular distributions at reciprocals of quartic Salem numbers and at one specified non-Pisot algebraic parameter. The classification is an infinite criterion, not a finite decision algorithm.

2. Background and essential definitions

A measure is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure if it has a density: probabilities can be obtained by integrating a nonnegative function. It is singular if some set of Lebesgue measure zero carries its entire mass. Bernoulli convolutions have pure type, so these alternatives exhaust the possibilities.

For λ<1/2\lambda<1/2λ<1/2, after fixing nnn signs there are 2n2^n2n possible prefixes, each with a remaining tail contained in an interval of length proportional to λn\lambda^nλn. The total covering length tends to zero because (2λ)n→0(2\lambda)^n\to0(2λ)n→0. At λ=1/2\lambda=1/2λ=1/2, binary expansion instead gives the uniform distribution on [−2,2][-2,2][−2,2]. The difficult region is (1/2,1)(1/2,1)(1/2,1).

It is often convenient to use fair bits un∈{0,1}u_n\in\{0,1\}un​∈{0,1}. Their sum Xλ=∑unλnX_\lambda=\sum u_n\lambda^nXλ​=∑un​λn satisfies

Yλ=2Xλ−11−λ,Y_\lambda=2X_\lambda-\frac1{1-\lambda},Yλ​=2Xλ​−1−λ1​,

so the two laws have the same measure type. Differences between finite bit sums are values at λ\lambdaλ of polynomials with coefficients in {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}{−1,0,1}. Exact or approximate polynomial relations therefore encode overlapping histories.

Algebraic conjugates and exceptional parameters

An algebraic integer is a root of a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. Its conjugates are the other roots of its minimal polynomial over the rationals. A Pisot number is a real algebraic integer β>1\beta>1β>1 whose other conjugates all have modulus less than one.

A Salem number is a real algebraic integer β>1\beta>1β>1 whose other conjugates are β−1\beta^{-1}β−1 and numbers on the complex unit circle. In degree four, there is one nonreal conjugate pair on that circle.

These definitions describe how one algebraic relation behaves under all its embeddings. That behavior controls how powers of β\betaβ approach integers and how Fourier phases of the random sum align.

Full Hausdorff dimension is a different property from absolute continuity. A measure can have dimension one and still live on a set of Lebesgue measure zero. This distinction is essential when comparing this family with the dimension formula in family 148.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Erdős proved in 1939 that Bernoulli convolutions are singular when λ−1\lambda^{-1}λ−1 is Pisot. His method shows that their Fourier transforms fail to tend to zero. An integrable density would force Fourier decay, so nondecay excludes absolute continuity.

Garsia subsequently established absolute continuity for a different arithmetic class, including reciprocals of algebraic integers of absolute norm two whose conjugates all lie outside the unit circle. He also connected entropy of finite sums with singularity. The subject thus acquired both arithmetic examples and information-theoretic tools.

Solomyak proved that for Lebesgue-almost every λ∈(1/2,1)\lambda\in(1/2,1)λ∈(1/2,1), the distribution has an L2L^2L2 density. Hochman’s work connected dimension loss with extremely strong concentration of finite-level positions, and Shmerkin proved that the exceptional set for absolute continuity has Hausdorff dimension zero. These results make singular parameters very rare without identifying every one of them.

Varjú proved full dimension for every transcendental parameter in this interval. Breuillard and Varjú showed that dimension-deficient parameters admit very close algebraic approximations by other dimension-deficient parameters. Neither conclusion alone classifies absolute continuity at each exceptional parameter.

Salem’s Fourier result creates a further obstacle: when the reciprocal is not Pisot, the Fourier transform tends to zero. Thus Erdős’s nondecay argument cannot establish singularity at Salem parameters. Recent quantitative decay estimates for Salem convolutions likewise do not settle their measure type.

The new manuscript presents the existence of singular non-Pisot examples as an unresolved issue in the recent literature it cites. Its contribution is claimed at two levels: a universal arithmetic characterization and direct constructions of singular examples beyond the classical Pisot mechanism.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The manuscript, dated 3 October 2026, has three principal claims.

A criterion made entirely from finite algebraic data

For integers n≥1n\ge1n≥1 and d≥2d\ge2d≥2, form a finite set R(n,d)R(n,d)R(n,d) of real algebraic units in (1/2,1)(1/2,1)(1/2,1). An algebraic unit has both itself and its inverse algebraic integral. Here its minimal polynomial must have degree dndndn, coefficients in {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}{−1,0,1}, and irreducible reduction modulo two. Choose its sign so that the constant coefficient is −1-1−1.

For a candidate rrr, inspect other members qqq of this set within distance 4−n4^{-n}4−n. Record the first nnn coefficients of their polynomials, counting distinct coefficient vectors only once. Call this collection Wn(r;d)W_n(r;d)Wn​(r;d).

Each bit word u∈{0,1}nu\in\{0,1\}^nu∈{0,1}n specifies a closed coordinate orthant: coordinate iii is nonnegative when ui=1u_i=1ui​=1, and nonpositive otherwise. Zero coordinates belong to both relevant sign choices. Retain rrr at crowding level jjj if at least 2n/d2^n/d2n/d of these orthants each contain at least

j(2r)nj(2r)^nj(2r)n

distinct vectors from Wn(r;d)W_n(r;d)Wn​(r;d).

The claimed criterion says that νλ\nu_\lambdaνλ​, for λ∈(1/2,1)\lambda\in(1/2,1)λ∈(1/2,1), is singular exactly when there exists a fixed d≥2d\ge2d≥2 such that, for every integer j≥1j\ge1j≥1, retained targets rrr satisfy

r−4−n≤λ<rr-4^{-n}\le\lambda<rr−4−n≤λ<r

for arbitrarily large nnn. The manuscript also claims that “arbitrarily large” can be replaced by “every sufficiently large,” with the threshold depending on jjj.

The order of quantifiers matters: one degree multiplier ddd works for all crowding levels. The target lies strictly above λ\lambdaλ. Every finite target set uses polynomial arithmetic alone, without consulting which Bernoulli convolutions are singular. Parameters failing the criterion are absolutely continuous; the cases at and below 1/21/21/2 are as described earlier.

Explicit non-Pisot singularity

The manuscript claims singularity for ν1/β\nu_{1/\beta}ν1/β​ whenever β∈(1,2)\beta\in(1,2)β∈(1,2) is a quartic Salem number. In particular, it gives the real roots greater than one of

x4−x3−x2−x+1,x4−2x3+x2−2x+1.x^4-x^3-x^2-x+1,\qquad x^4-2x^3+x^2-2x+1.x4−x3−x2−x+1,x4−2x3+x2−2x+1.

A separate claim concerns

p(t)=t31−2t30+∑j=09(t3j+1−t3j).p(t)=t^{31}-2t^{30}+\sum_{j=0}^{9}(t^{3j+1}-t^{3j}).p(t)=t31−2t30+j=0∑9​(t3j+1−t3j).

The specified real root β∈(1.8392,1.8393)\beta\in(1.8392,1.8393)β∈(1.8392,1.8393) is claimed to be non-Pisot, with ν1/β\nu_{1/\beta}ν1/β​ singular. The polynomial has an additional conjugate pair just outside the unit circle, so this example uses a different configuration from quartic Salem numbers.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the family resolves a central measure-type classification question and supplies exceptional examples that the classical Fourier-nondecay mechanism cannot reach.

The universal criterion is valuable even though it is not a short membership test. It translates a statement about concentration of an infinite random series into a prescribed pattern of algebraic approximations and coefficient directions. That identifies what arithmetic data would be sufficient and necessary.

The non-Pisot examples have a complementary role. They would show concretely that Fourier decay does not settle absolute continuity in this classical family. The general criterion and the examples are separate contributions: the manuscript proves the examples directly, then obtains their approximation properties from the criterion.

6. The main idea

From crowded polynomials to concentrated probability

Suppose many coefficient vectors occur near a target root. A vector lying in the orthant specified by a bit word uuu can be subtracted from uuu to produce another bit word. Since the corresponding polynomial nearly vanishes at λ\lambdaλ, these different words have nearby prefix sums.

If this happens in enough orthants, a positive fraction of the probability is covered by unusually few short intervals. Raising the crowding level makes the total interval length arbitrarily small while preserving a fixed positive mass. This rules out absolute continuity; pure type then gives singularity.

Conversely, concentration of a singular measure supplies many pairs of close finite sums with different first bits. Their difference polynomials have the desired nonzero constant coefficient. The manuscript completes their initial coefficients into polynomials with roots strictly above λ\lambdaλ, while keeping the root error small.

Two tools have different jobs. A finite-order nonvanishing estimate maintains a sign change and hence a nearby root. Irreducible polynomials in arithmetic progressions over F2\mathbb F_2F2​ provide the prescribed irreducibility without changing the initial coefficient pattern. The completed roots become the algebraic approximation targets.

Detect singularity despite Fourier decay

For quartic Salem parameters, algebraic trace identities relate the real expanding conjugate to its unit-circle pair. The construction chooses multipliers whose unit-circle contributions become very small while controlling accumulated cosine losses.

Rather than seek one Fourier coefficient that refuses to decay, the manuscript builds averages of many phases. Their relevant random-sign windows can be separated. The averages concentrate under the Bernoulli convolution but tend to zero in Lebesgue mean square. Sets detected by these averages can therefore carry nearly all the random-series mass while having arbitrarily small ordinary length.

For the degree-31 example, finite words are evaluated simultaneously at all roots, placing their values in a lattice. The extra expanding conjugate pair makes a basic lattice count slightly too large. A product of positive trigonometric factors supplies a correction: its Lebesgue integral stays bounded, while it grows exponentially at typical word evaluations. The resulting concentration gain outweighs the extra volume growth.

The manuscript supplies finite recurrences and rational error bounds for numerical constants used in this second construction. Their role here is part of the reported argument; this exposition does not rerun a mathematical verification.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The series uses independent fair signs. Biased Bernoulli convolutions require different statements. The universal criterion covers all real 0<λ<10<\lambda<10<λ<1, but involves infinitely many scales and crowding levels. Finite enumeration at each scale is not a finite procedure deciding membership for an arbitrary real input.

The Salem theorem concerns degree four and 1<β<21<\beta<21<β<2. It does not assert singularity for every Salem number of arbitrary degree. The degree-31 construction likewise gives one specified parameter, not a general theorem for every non-Pisot algebraic reciprocal.

The criterion separates singularity from absolute continuity. It does not automatically provide an L2L^2L2, bounded, or differentiable density in every absolutely continuous case, nor an effective convergence rate for approximating that density.

Understanding how to use the criterion efficiently for concrete parameters, and how far the direct non-Pisot mechanisms extend, remain distinct quantitative and structural questions.

8. Sources and further reading

Erdős’s 1939 singularity theorem and Garsia’s 1962 arithmetic study establish the classical contrasting examples. Solomyak’s almost-everywhere density theorem describes the typical parameter.

Hochman’s entropy and overlap theorem, Shmerkin’s exceptional-set theorem, and Varjú’s transcendental-parameter dimension theorem explain why dimension and measure type must be distinguished. Salem’s Fourier analysis of exceptional sets supplies the classical decay context.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Arithmetic classification and non-Pisot singularity for Bernoulli convolutions (October 3, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Arithmetic-progression observations converge along almost every mixing orbit
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 154 · Dynamical systems and ergodic theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Suppose a dynamical system mixes: observations made far apart become statistically independent in the limit. Start at one point and observe the system at times k,2k,3kk,2k,3kk,2k,3k. As kkk varies, do averages of the three observations settle down along almost every individual orbit?

This is harder than averaging one observable. The three clocks are tied to the same starting point, and the gaps between them change with kkk. Even knowing that the averages converge in a mean-square sense need not rule out exceptional averaging lengths at individual points.

Family 154 contains four manuscripts progressing from three observations to four and then any fixed finite consecutive number. Its broadest claim is pointwise convergence to the product of the individual means for every invertible mixing transformation, with no quantitative rate of mixing. A separate triple result permits any three distinct nonzero integer speeds, including negative ones.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let (X,F,μ)(X,\mathcal F,\mu)(X,F,μ) be a probability space and TTT an invertible measure-preserving transformation with measurable inverse. Think of TkxT^k xTkx as the state after kkk steps. Negative powers describe the past.

The transformation is mixing if, for any measurable sets A,BA,BA,B,

μ(A∩T−rB)⟶μ(A)μ(B)as ∣r∣→∞.\mu(A\cap T^{-r}B)\longrightarrow\mu(A)\mu(B)\quad\text{as }|r|\to\infty.μ(A∩T−rB)⟶μ(A)μ(B)as ∣r∣→∞.

This is a statement about two observations averaged over the initial state. It asserts no speed of convergence.

For bounded measurable functions f1,…,fmf_1,\ldots,f_mf1​,…,fm​, the consecutive multiple ergodic average is

AN(x)=1N∑k=1N∏j=1mfj(Tjkx).A_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(T^{jk}x).AN​(x)=N1​k=1∑N​j=1∏m​fj​(Tjkx).

If fjf_jfj​ is the indicator of a set EjE_jEj​, this measures the frequency with which the states at k,2k,…,mkk,2k,\ldots,mkk,2k,…,mk simultaneously enter their prescribed sets. The proposed limiting value in a mixing system is

∏j=1m∫Xfj dμ.\prod_{j=1}^m\int_X f_j\,d\mu.j=1∏m​∫X​fj​dμ.

Three different kinds of conclusion

Norm convergence in L2L^2L2 says that the mean squared error, integrated over starting points, tends to zero. Pointwise almost-everywhere convergence says that outside one null set, the numerical sequence AN(x)A_N(x)AN​(x) converges as NNN runs through all positive integers.

The latter does not follow automatically from the former. Small exceptional sets can move with NNN, causing the same point to experience infinitely many exceptional lengths. Norm convergence often yields convergence along a suitable subsequence; the full sequence is the issue here.

Multiple mixing is different again. It concerns integrals of products at times separating from one another, without the average over kkk. It is an important input to some manuscripts in this family, not a substitute for their pointwise conclusion.

The word “fixed” also matters. Each theorem fixes the functions and the finite number of observations before taking N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞. It does not promise one exceptional null set that works simultaneously for every possible bounded measurable function.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Birkhoff’s pointwise ergodic theorem treats a single observation. Furstenberg’s ergodic proof of Szemerédi’s theorem brought arithmetic-progression products to the center of recurrence theory. Their convergence questions subsequently developed along separate norm and pointwise tracks.

For weakly mixing transformations, convergence in L2L^2L2 to the product of the integrals is classical. For arbitrary systems, Conze and Lesigne obtained an early three-function norm theorem under total ergodicity. Host and Kra removed restrictions and developed nilpotent characteristic factors, proving norm convergence for every finite consecutive length. Ziegler obtained another general proof through universal characteristic factors. These structures describe which organized parts of a system control its multiple averages.

Bourgain’s double recurrence theorem proved pointwise convergence for two powers of a single transformation. Higher-length pointwise theorems were known under additional assumptions: K-systems, certain spectral restrictions on the zero-entropy part of a weakly mixing system, and independence properties of self-joinings. A joining is a joint probability law for several copies of a system that preserves each marginal and respects the dynamics.

Huang, Shao, and Ye established pointwise convergence of every finite consecutive length on ergodic measure-distal systems. Distal structure is assembled from organized compact extensions and their limits, rather than the relative randomness of weakly mixing extensions.
