Recent polynomial pointwise results provide another route, but hypotheses such as distinct polynomial degrees do not include several linear times k,2k,3k,4kk,2k,3k,4kk,2k,3k,4k: all have the same degree. One cannot import those theorems by treating distinct coefficients as distinct degrees.

The new family also draws on harmonic analysis. Oscillation inequalities, developed by Bourgain and others, control repeated changes of averages across scales. Its analytic foundation is the claimed trilinear Hilbert-transform work in family 086. Its higher-length dynamical arguments use the claimed resolution of Rokhlin’s multiple-mixing problem in family 145. These are substantive dependencies, not four independent proofs of the same conclusion.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

All four manuscripts are dated 4 October 2026. Their principal theorems assume an invertible, bimeasurable, probability-preserving mixing transformation and bounded measurable inputs. They allow arbitrary probability spaces, without requiring standardness or countable generation.

ManuscriptSampling timesClaimed almost-everywhere limit
M4k,2k,3kk,2k,3kk,2k,3kProduct of three integrals
M3a1k,a2k,a3ka_1k,a_2k,a_3ka1​k,a2​k,a3​k, distinct nonzero integers aja_jaj​Product of three integrals
M2k,2k,3k,4kk,2k,3k,4kk,2k,3k,4kProduct of four integrals
M1k,2k,…,mkk,2k,\ldots,mkk,2k,…,mk, every fixed m≥2m\ge2m≥2Product of mmm integrals

All limits are taken through every positive integer averaging length. No rate of mixing, rate of convergence, or uniformity over input functions is asserted. For M3 the slopes may have either sign, and constants in its analytic estimates may depend on those fixed slopes.

M4 extends local estimates from the trilinear Hilbert-transform companion to inputs that vary with scale. M3 adapts the analytic argument to arbitrary distinct integer slopes; a change of time unit alone would not cover all such triples. M2 establishes the fourfold deduction using triple estimates and higher-order mixing. M1 extends the structural argument to every finite consecutive length.

A stronger convergence input than the mixing headline

The triple oscillation estimate itself is claimed on arbitrary invertible probability-preserving systems, without mixing. Mixing is used separately to identify the limit as the product of means.

M1 explicitly derives pointwise convergence along all lengths for at most three bounded functions at distinct positive integer slopes on arbitrary standard invertible systems. It uses this result inside auxiliary systems that need not be mixing. The limiting value there need not be a product of integrals.

This additional input should not be enlarged into a theorem for arbitrary-length products on arbitrary systems. The broadest principal theorem in the family retains mixing and consecutive slopes.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the family establishes full-sequence pointwise convergence for every finite consecutive progression in the mixing class, substantially strengthening the known norm theory and earlier structured special cases.

The gain is about individual trajectories. An experiment or simulation observes one starting state, not an integral over all states. Almost-everywhere convergence says that a typical single trajectory has the predicted limiting progression statistics, even if mixing is arbitrarily slow.

The triple extension also contributes a reusable analytic tool. Its convergence estimate separates the question of whether a limit exists from the question of what that limit is. The higher-length arguments then use that lower-length control inside more complicated extensions, where the original mixing hypothesis may no longer hold.

6. The main idea

Stop averages from oscillating indefinitely

The triple manuscripts first smooth the averaging cutoff. Instead of abruptly stopping at NNN, they use a compactly supported smooth profile at scales 2k2^k2k, producing averages VkV_kVk​.

For any fixed sequence of scale endpoints k1<⋯<kW+1k_1<\cdots<k_{W+1}k1​<⋯<kW+1​, the key estimate has the schematic form

∑i=1W∫Xmax⁡ki≤ℓ≤ki+1∣Vℓ−Vki∣ dμ≤CW.\sum_{i=1}^{W}\int_X\max_{k_i\le\ell\le k_{i+1}}|V_\ell-V_{k_i}|\,d\mu\le C\sqrt W.i=1∑W​∫X​ki​≤ℓ≤ki+1​max​∣Vℓ​−Vki​​∣dμ≤CW​.

If the averages failed to converge on a set of positive measure, one could find arbitrarily many blocks with a definite oscillation. Their total contribution would grow proportionally to WWW, contradicting the square-root bound.

The maximum permits the worst scale to depend on the point. This creates local analytic inputs that vary with depth, beyond a fixed-input Hilbert-transform estimate. M4 develops the required variation control. A transference argument moves estimates for translations on the real line to integer sequences and then to finite pieces of arbitrary orbits.

Smooth profiles are signed and have specified vanishing moments to produce cancellation. They approximate interval cutoffs in L1L^1L1, and finite grids of relative lengths recover every integer NNN, not just powers of two. Mixing identifies the resulting limit through the classical norm argument.

For M3, integer reconstruction and a Vandermonde identity replace special arithmetic-progression formulas. The whole primitive coefficient configuration is used; a pair of slopes need not differ by one. This is why arbitrary slopes require additional analysis rather than a simple rescaling of 1,2,31,2,31,2,3.

Why higher-order mixing is not enough by itself

For longer products, suppose pointwise convergence fails. At each bad starting point, choose an unusually late length where a centered average remains large. The chosen length depends on the point, and this selection can bias joint distributions. Ordinary convergence at predetermined lengths cannot simply be applied after such conditioning.

The manuscripts encode selected configurations as probability laws on several output coordinates. A suspension adds a continuous clock to the discrete system, enabling useful invariance under different coordinate speeds. The laws retain a nonzero correlation from the assumed failure.

Auxiliary outputs are organized into three groups. Those groups have specified independence properties, including independence of the original coordinate from any two groups, but not necessarily from all three jointly. This distinction is real: three independent fair signs have a product independent of each pair, yet conditioning on their product fixes a relation among the triple.

A tensor-packing estimate controls how much selected averages can concentrate in low-dimensional covariance spaces. Combined with higher-order mixing from family 145, it preserves exactly the independence relations needed by the construction without assuming a mixing rate.

Enlarge the system until a contradiction appears

The structural argument chooses extensions where certain conditional expectations cannot improve further. Intuitively, an extension has already exposed all information relevant to specified predictions. This is an energy-maximization method related to sated extensions.

In M2, one maximizes the number of output-only slots in a surviving nonzero correlation. An iterated array construction excludes the largest possibilities. Selecting again creates a square of states, and its row and column laws let the argument replace another original slot by an output slot, contradicting maximality.

M1 first minimizes the number of slots needed for a nonzero correlation, gaining independence for the smaller collections that matter. It then adapts the same three-group mechanism to arbitrary finite length. The repeated selection produces one more output-only slot without changing the minimal slot count. The contradiction eliminates the original failure of pointwise convergence.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The arbitrary-length theorem uses consecutive slopes 1,…,m1,\ldots,m1,…,m. The separate arbitrary-slope statement is for three factors. The exposition does not merge them into an unsupported theorem for every collection of arbitrarily many integer slopes.

The principal theorems assume mixing, invertibility, bounded inputs, and a fixed finite configuration. They do not supply rates, unbounded-function endpoint estimates, or a common full-measure set for all inputs. The general pointwise problem for arbitrary nonmixing systems and longer products is not settled by the stated headlines.

The dependence on companion work is explicit. The family uses local harmonic-analysis estimates from family 086 and, for the higher-length structural step, the higher-order mixing theorem from family 145. M3 extends coefficient-sensitive parts of earlier proofs and imports other local estimates by reference.

For nonstandard probability spaces, the fixed tuple and all its integer translates generate a standard symbolic factor. Convergence there pulls back to the original space. This explains how the conclusion can avoid a global standardness assumption without asserting regularity for every measurable structure at once.

8. Sources and further reading

Furstenberg’s Ergodic behavior of diagonal measures and a theorem of Szemerédi on arithmetic progressions (1977) introduces the recurrence setting. Bourgain’s Double recurrence and almost sure convergence (1990) is the basic pointwise predecessor.

Host and Kra’s Nonconventional ergodic averages and nilmanifolds (2005) and Ziegler’s Universal characteristic factors and Furstenberg averages (2007) establish the general norm theory. Huang, Shao, and Ye’s Pointwise convergence of multiple ergodic averages and strictly ergodic models (2019) supplies the distal pointwise result.

The directly used companion claims are explained in family 086 and family 145, with their pinned manuscript references. The four sources below distinguish the analytic triple work, its coefficient extension, and the later structural deductions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Pointwise Multiple Ergodic Averages for Mixing Transformations (October 4, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Pointwise convergence of fourfold ergodic averages for mixing transformations (October 4, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Triple ergodic averages with distinct integer slopes (October 4, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Pointwise convergence of triple ergodic averages for mixing transformations (October 4, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why a proper algebraic intersection should have positive multiplicity
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 193 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Two transverse curves in a plane meet with multiplicity one. If they are tangent, the meeting counts more heavily. Algebraic geometry extends this local counting idea to higher dimensions and to arithmetic spaces where ordinary pictures no longer suffice.

Serre’s definition uses an alternating sum of algebraic correction terms. The first term is positive, but later terms can subtract from it. Why should a properly dimensioned, isolated intersection still have a strictly positive total?

Family 193 claims a positive answer over every regular local ring, including the general ramified mixed-characteristic case. The theorem removes additional lifting and geometric assumptions from previously known cases. It concerns the strict inequality needed to distinguish a genuine intersection from a total that cancels to zero.

2. Background and essential definitions

A ring describing one neighborhood

A local ring (R,m)(R,\mathfrak m)(R,m) has one maximal ideal m\mathfrak mm, representing a distinguished point. Its residue field is R/mR/\mathfrak mR/m. A Noetherian ring has every ideal finitely generated, making its algebraic geometry locally manageable.

The Krull dimension ddd is the maximum length of a chain of prime ideals. A local ring is regular when its maximal ideal can be generated by exactly ddd elements. This is the algebraic analogue of a nonsingular ambient space.

A finitely generated RRR-module can describe a geometric piece with multiplicities. For instance, R/IR/IR/I describes the equations in an ideal III. Its support is the collection of primes where it remains nonzero after localization, and its dimension is the dimension of that support.

A module of finite length has a finite composition series; its length counts the simple factors. Over a local ring those factors are copies of the residue field. Geometrically, finite length means that the module is concentrated at the distinguished point, with a finite algebraic size.

Correcting the naive intersection

The tensor product M⊗RNM\otimes_R NM⊗R​N is a first approximation to intersecting two modules. Tensoring does not always preserve exact sequences. The groups Tor⁡iR(M,N)\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M,N)ToriR​(M,N) measure this failure: take a free resolution of one module, tensor it with the other, and compute the resulting homology.

If M⊗RNM\otimes_R NM⊗R​N has finite length and RRR is regular of dimension ddd, Serre’s intersection multiplicity is

χR(M,N)=∑i=0d(−1)ilength⁡RTor⁡iR(M,N).\chi_R(M,N)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}(-1)^i\operatorname{length}_R\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M,N).χR​(M,N)=i=0∑d​(−1)ilengthR​ToriR​(M,N).

All the lengths are finite, and higher terms vanish. The degree-zero term is the tensor product itself. The alternating signs are why positivity is a theorem to seek, rather than part of the definition.

For a concrete example, take R=k[[x,y]]R=k[[x,y]]R=k[[x,y]], the formal power-series ring in two variables. The curves y=0y=0y=0 and y=xry=x^ry=xr, with r≥1r\ge1r≥1, give a quotient intersection k[[x]]/(xr)k[[x]]/(x^r)k[[x]]/(xr), of length rrr. Here the higher Tor correction vanishes, so the multiplicity is rrr. The general problem allows much more complicated modules and arithmetic ambient rings.

Mixed characteristic

In equal characteristic, a local ring and its residue field have the same characteristic. In mixed characteristic, the ring has characteristic zero and the residue field characteristic p>0p>0p>0. For a regular local ring, the ramified case has p∈m2p\in\mathfrak m^2p∈m2. Arithmetic and local geometry then interact in ways not visible over a single coefficient field.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Serre introduced the Tor Euler characteristic and proved positivity in equicharacteristic and unramified settings using reduction to the diagonal. His method also treats formal power-series rings over arbitrary complete discrete valuation rings. Thus “ramified” does not mean that every example in that class was previously unknown; the remaining issue is the unrestricted mixed-characteristic situation.

Roberts, and independently Gillet and Soulé, proved the vanishing theorem when the dimensions of the two modules sum to less than the ambient dimension. Their methods use local intersection-theoretic invariants and Adams operations. This result removes lower-dimensional terms in later reductions.

Gabber proved nonnegativity in the remaining mixed-characteristic case using alterations and an intersection calculation on a normal bundle. Nonnegativity is a major advance, but it still permits zero for complementary-dimensional modules. Strict positivity must exclude that last possibility.

Further partial results impose geometric or lifting hypotheses. Skalit proved positivity for regular local rings essentially smooth over a two-dimensional regular local base. KC and Soto Levins proved positivity under a Serre-liftability condition: the module comes from an unramified ambient ring with the appropriate codimension relationship. Their condition is weaker than requiring the usual Tor-vanishing lift, but it is still an additional hypothesis.

Another approach seeks sequences of finite modules that become approximately Cohen–Macaulay after normalization. Cohen–Macaulay behavior means that a full sequence of parameters has no unwanted homological obstruction. Bhatt, Hochster, and Ma showed that appropriate sequences for both quotient domains imply positivity. Perfectoid towers provide related constructions in specified settings.

The present manuscript instead works with complexes after discarding sequences whose normalized free ranks become negligible. It credits normalized-length methods to Faltings and subsequent almost-ring and perfectoid work, and uses algebraic K-theory descent to compare numerical invariants.

The introduction also records a December 2025 public assertion of the prime-quotient statement as a same-scope claim, rather than treating it as an established predecessor theorem. The digest follows that attribution without assessing competing proofs or priority.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The manuscript, dated 23 September 2026, claims the following unrestricted positivity statement. Let (R,m)(R,\mathfrak m)(R,m) be a commutative Noetherian regular local ring of dimension ddd, and let M,NM,NM,N be nonzero finitely generated modules. If

length⁡R(M⊗RN)<∞,dim⁡RM+dim⁡RN=d,\operatorname{length}_R(M\otimes_RN)<\infty,\qquad \dim_R M+\dim_R N=d,lengthR​(M⊗R​N)<∞,dimR​M+dimR​N=d,

then

χR(M,N)>0.\chi_R(M,N)>0.χR​(M,N)>0.

There is no characteristic, residue-field, or ramification restriction, and neither module must lift to an unramified regular local ring.

Two stated consequences

The manuscript applies a theorem of Kurano and Roberts to symbolic powers. For a ramified mixed-characteristic regular local ring and prime ideals P,QP,QP,Q with P+Q=m\sqrt{P+Q}=\mathfrak mP+Q​=m and ht⁡P+ht⁡Q=d\operatorname{ht}P+\operatorname{ht}Q=dhtP+htQ=d, it obtains

P∩Q(r)⊆mr+1(r≥1),Q(r)=QrRQ∩R.P\cap Q^{(r)}\subseteq\mathfrak m^{r+1}\quad(r\ge1),\qquad Q^{(r)}=Q^rR_Q\cap R.P∩Q(r)⊆mr+1(r≥1),Q(r)=QrRQ​∩R.

Here localization at QQQ ignores behavior away from that prime; the symbolic power measures order of vanishing at its generic point. The containment is a consequence of the positivity input, not a separate ingredient establishing it.

A second consequence compares intersection multiplicity with the product of Hilbert–Samuel multiplicities, which measure leading local growth. For prime quotients A/P,A/QA/P,A/QA/P,A/Q meeting in complementary dimensions, set

G=gr⁡(A/P)⊗gr⁡Agr⁡(A/Q).G=\operatorname{gr}(A/P)\otimes_{\operatorname{gr}A}\operatorname{gr}(A/Q).G=gr(A/P)⊗grA​gr(A/Q).

The associated graded ring records successive orders in the maximal ideal, geometrically the tangent cone. Under the additional hypothesis dim⁡G≤1\dim G\le1dimG≤1, the manuscript claims

χA(A/P,A/Q)≥e(A/P)e(A/Q),\chi_A(A/P,A/Q)\ge e(A/P)e(A/Q),χA​(A/P,A/Q)≥e(A/P)e(A/Q),

with equality exactly when dim⁡G=0\dim G=0dimG=0. The dimension restriction is essential to the stated corollary; this is not an unrestricted product lower bound.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem completes a central positivity problem in local algebra and arithmetic intersection theory. It would make the intuitive positive count of a proper intersection valid across all regular local ambient rings.

Its consequences connect an Euler characteristic to ordinary ideal containments and tangent-cone geometry. This illustrates why positivity matters beyond a single numerical inequality: once zero cancellation is excluded, established geometric identities yield stronger algebraic conclusions.

The method is also designed to avoid demanding a finite Cohen–Macaulay module on every singular quotient. Related finite-module existence questions have their own obstructions, discussed in family 195. An asymptotic construction can retain the numerical features needed for intersection theory without producing such a module.

6. The main idea

Replace ordinary size by normalized size

Standard reductions reduce the essential case to two complete local domains D=R/PD=R/PD=R/P and E=R/QE=R/QE=R/Q, whose positive dimensions sum to ddd. Their intersection is supported at the closed point.

The manuscript constructs large auxiliary algebras with additive nonnegative normalized lengths. One can think of these lengths as module sizes divided by the increasing ranks of a tower of extensions. A nonzero module may have normalized length zero, so vanishing in this numerical sense is weaker than actual vanishing.

The useful property is that quotients by parameter sequences have positive finite normalized length, while their higher Koszul homology has length zero. A Koszul complex is the finite complex recording the compatibility of multiplication by the chosen parameters. These algebras behave like Cohen–Macaulay objects for the numerical calculation, even when actual finite modules with that property are unavailable.

Compare averages of conjugate evaluations

Finite extensions with Galois group actions allow the proof to compare ordinary intersection multiplicity with normalized Tor Euler characteristics. Algebraic K-theory organizes the additive relations between complexes needed for this comparison.

The comparison concerns sums over conjugates. It does not assert that the normalized length is invariant under every Galois action, nor that each individual evaluation equals the original multiplicity. After the first comparison, it remains to prove that each term in the relevant sum is positive.

For one such term, choose parameters from the second prime that cut the first domain to finite normalized length. Approximate the resulting module by finite-length modules MnM_nMn​, dividing their ordinary sizes by numbers sns_nsn​. Their higher resolution ranks become negligible compared with sns_nsn​.

The proof then works in a category that identifies free sequences of rank o(sn)o(s_n)o(sn​) with zero. Truncating the resolutions produces supported complexes in that quotient. Support can emerge only after passing to the quotient, so the numerical evaluations must be built there, including for direct summands.

Obtain strict positivity rather than a nonnegative limit

A second comparison, now using the auxiliary algebra for EEE, eliminates higher homological contributions in normalized length. The remaining degree-zero contribution needs a positive lower bound.

All approximating modules are killed by one fixed power ma\mathfrak m^ama. If β0(Mn)\beta_0(M_n)β0​(Mn​) is their minimal generator count, then

length⁡(Mn)≤β0(Mn)length⁡(R/ma),\operatorname{length}(M_n)\le\beta_0(M_n)\operatorname{length}(R/\mathfrak m^a),length(Mn​)≤β0​(Mn​)length(R/ma),

with the corresponding quotient local ring used in the actual argument. A positive limiting normalized length therefore forces a positive normalized generator count. That prevents the final nonnegative quantity from shrinking to zero.

The two conjugate-sum comparisons transfer this strict lower bound back to the original intersection multiplicity. The role of the common annihilator is concrete: it converts positivity of total normalized size into positivity of the surviving degree-zero term.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Regularity of the ambient ring, nonzero finite modules, finite-length tensor product, and complementary dimensions are all part of the theorem. Dropping them changes the problem; arbitrary singular ambient rings need not support the same finite Tor formula or positivity behavior.

The theorem gives strict positivity, hence a positive integer, rather than an unrestricted optimal lower bound in terms of the separate module multiplicities. The product bound in section 4 retains its finite tangent-cone-support restriction.

The auxiliary normalized lengths may vanish on nonzero objects. Their use does not assert that the large algebras are ordinary finite Cohen–Macaulay modules, or that normalized exactness is literal exactness. Likewise, the Galois averaging argument must not be shortened to invariance of individual evaluations.

Further quantitative intersection bounds and broader equality criteria remain different questions from the central positivity claim explained here.

8. Sources and further reading

Serre’s Local Algebra, Chapter V develops the definition and classical cases. Roberts’ vanishing theorem and Gillet–Soulé’s Adams-operation approach establish the dimension-deficient result.

Skalit’s two-dimensional-base theorem and KC–Soto Levins’ lifting theorem provide earlier positivity cases. Kurano and Roberts’ symbolic-power theorem supplies the first consequence above.

Bhatt, Hochster, and Ma’s lim Cohen–Macaulay manuscript and Cai, Lee, Ma, Schwede, and Tucker’s perfectoid length work explain the asymptotic background. The present manuscript states its own normalized-length construction and comparison arguments, with those literature inputs attributed separately.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Positivity of Serre’s Intersection Multiplicity (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Flat local maps cannot lower multiplicity
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 194 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A singular point has an algebraic thickness: its tiny neighborhoods contain more information than equally small neighborhoods of a smooth point. Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity measures the leading coefficient of that local growth.

Lech’s conjecture asks whether this thickness can decrease under a flat local homomorphism. Flatness is an algebraic condition expressing the absence of certain new relations when coefficients are extended. It is the natural language for many well-behaved families, but it does not directly compare the two maximal-ideal filtrations used to measure multiplicity.

Family 194 claims that multiplicity never decreases under such a map, in every dimension and characteristic. The approach works with complexes and normalized lengths rather than requiring special finite modules over every source ring.

2. Background and essential definitions

Measuring infinitesimal neighborhoods

Let (A,a)(A,\mathfrak a)(A,a) be a nonzero Noetherian local ring of dimension ddd. The quotient A/aNA/\mathfrak a^NA/aN describes the point together with information up to order N−1N-1N−1. Its finite length ℓA(A/aN)\ell_A(A/\mathfrak a^N)ℓA​(A/aN) counts residue-field composition factors.

For large NNN, this length grows like a polynomial of degree ddd. The Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity is

e(A)=lim⁡N→∞d! ℓA(A/aN)Nd.e(A)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{d!\,\ell_A(A/\mathfrak a^N)}{N^d}.e(A)=N→∞lim​Ndd!ℓA​(A/aN)​.

It is a positive integer. For the regular power-series ring k[[x1,…,xd]]k[[x_1,\ldots,x_d]]k[[x1​,…,xd​]], the leading growth is Nd/d!N^d/d!Nd/d!, so the multiplicity is one. In dimension zero, multiplicity is simply the length of the ring.

Multiplicity is a numerical measure of local thickness, not a complete classification of singularities. Distinct local rings can have the same multiplicity and very different geometry.

Local maps and flatness

A homomorphism (R,m)→(S,n)(R,\mathfrak m)\to(S,\mathfrak n)(R,m)→(S,n) is local when the maximal ideal of the target pulls back to that of the source. It is flat when tensoring an exact sequence of RRR-modules with SSS preserves exactness. This prevents the coefficient extension from creating unexpected linear relations.

The closed fiber is S/mSS/\mathfrak mSS/mS, the part lying over the source’s distinguished point. A flat local map may change dimension and residue field; the conjecture does not require the map to be a finite extension.

The difficulty is that flatness naturally controls S/mNSS/\mathfrak m^NSS/mNS, whereas the definition of e(S)e(S)e(S) uses S/nNS/\mathfrak n^NS/nN. Since mS\mathfrak mSmS and n\mathfrak nn can differ, comparing lengths from flatness is not already the desired theorem.

Why modules and complexes enter

A maximal Cohen–Macaulay module has depth equal to the ring’s dimension: a full sequence of parameters acts without creating zero divisors successively. An Ulrich module is such a finite nonzero module whose multiplicity equals its minimal number of generators. That equality can turn a geometric growth question into a generator-count comparison.

A finite free complex is a sequence of finite-rank free modules linked by matrices whose consecutive products are zero. Its homology measures the failure of exactness. Complexes can retain useful numerical information even when no single finite module has all the desired properties.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Lech introduced the multiplicity question in work from 1960 and 1964. His results established the inequality for sources of dimension at most two and in important situations with complete-intersection closed fiber. Standard reductions connect his equal-dimensional formulation with the more general flat-local statement.

Ma proved the conjecture for equal-characteristic sources of dimension three. In arbitrary equal-characteristic dimension ddd, he also obtained the weaker bound

e(R)≤max⁡{1,d!/2d} e(S).e(R)\le\max\{1,d!/2^d\}\,e(S).e(R)≤max{1,d!/2d}e(S).

This controls multiplicity but loses the sharp coefficient one in higher dimensions. His use of Cohen factorizations and Hilbert–Kunz multiplicity is a predecessor of the characteristic-ppp argument in the new manuscript.

Hanes developed Ulrich-module methods and asymptotic versions in which generator counts approach multiplicities. Ma’s weakly lim Ulrich sequences relax exact Cohen–Macaulay behavior to suitable negligible homological errors. Their existence over a local domain implies Lech’s inequality for all flat local targets.

Ma used these methods to prove the conjecture when the source is a standard graded algebra over a perfect field, localized at its homogeneous maximal ideal. The target need not be graded. Meng obtained a complementary graded-target result under specified homogeneity and equal-dimension assumptions.

Passing to associated graded rings does not make these theorems universal: the induced graded map need not remain flat. Moreover, Yhee constructed complete two-dimensional nonnormal domains without weakly lim Ulrich sequences. Thus the existence of such sequences over every source is not available as a general solution.

Iyengar, Ma, and Walker developed inequalities for short free complexes using lim Ulrich methods. Their construction combines a finite free resolution with a parameter Koszul complex, providing the immediate model for the new approach. The manuscript also cites the finite-module counterexample in family 195 as a further reason to distinguish module existence from complex-based positivity; that counterexample is not an assumption proving Lech’s inequality.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The manuscript, dated 23 September 2026, claims that every flat local homomorphism of nonzero Noetherian local rings satisfies

e(R)≤e(S).e(R)\le e(S).e(R)≤e(S).

There is no restriction on dimension, residue fields, or characteristics. The source and target need not be domains, complete, graded, or Cohen–Macaulay in the final statement. Those properties appear only in reductions or auxiliary constructions.

The argument’s main technical claim is a uniform lower bound for certain finite free complexes over an auxiliary ring equipped with an additive normalized length. Its constants depend on the number of parameters and free ranks, rather than on the auxiliary extension or the particular length theory. Additional homological and stability hypotheses on that length are required; additivity alone is not enough.

A related positive-characteristic consequence

For a short free complex FFF over a complete local domain of characteristic p>0p>0p>0, the manuscript also claims

χ∞(F)≥e(R).\chi_\infty(F)\ge e(R).χ∞​(F)≥e(R).

Here a short complex is concentrated in degrees 0,…,d0,\ldots,d0,…,d, has finite-length homology, and has nonzero zeroth homology. Its Dutta multiplicity χ∞\chi_\inftyχ∞​ is the limit of its Euler characteristic after raising differential entries to pnp^npn-th powers and dividing by pndp^{nd}pnd.

This consequence is the complete-domain positive-characteristic case of a conjecture of Iyengar, Ma, and Walker. The manuscript does not claim that entire short-complex conjecture for every complete local ring. Nor does it use the full conjecture as an assumption for the main theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, this resolves a central comparison problem in local algebra and replaces dimension-dependent losses with the sharp universal coefficient one.

The theorem would establish a robust monotonicity principle for local multiplicity under flat maps. Such maps occur throughout algebraic geometry and commutative algebra, so a statement without characteristic or dimension restrictions has a broad range of potential applications.

The methodological significance is the move from ideal finite modules to numerical estimates on complexes. That route can remain meaningful even when a desired Cohen–Macaulay or Ulrich module does not exist. It also links characteristic-ppp, mixed-characteristic, and characteristic-zero techniques within one comparison framework.

6. The main idea

Make a complex carry the multiplicity comparison

After reductions, the proof works with a complete domain source and equal source and target dimensions. A Cohen factorization introduces an auxiliary complete local ring TTT and an ideal JJJ with S=T/JS=T/JS=T/J, while keeping e(T)=e(R)e(T)=e(R)e(T)=e(R).

A finite free resolution PPP of SSS is tensored with a Koszul complex on parameters of SSS. The parameters are chosen so that their ideal has the same multiplicity as the target maximal ideal. The combined complex has the appropriate length, degree-zero rank one, and homology supported at the closed point.

This single complex is where the source-side lower estimate and target-side upper estimate can meet.

Obtain a bound independent of the auxiliary ring

The core estimate considers differential matrices whose entries lie deep in a parameter ideal III, say in IsI^sIs. The auxiliary length λ\lambdaλ makes higher parameter Koszul homology negligible and gives controlled growth of parameter quotients. In simplified notation, the claimed bound has the shape

λ(H0F)≥λ(C/I)sh(b0−Ah∑ibis),\lambda(H_0F)\ge\lambda(C/I)s^h\left(b_0-\frac{A_h\sum_i b_i}{s}\right),λ(H0​F)≥λ(C/I)sh(b0​−sAh​∑i​bi​​),

where hhh is the number of parameters, bib_ibi​ are free ranks, and AhA_hAh​ depends only on hhh. The error disappears as the differential entries become deeper.

The manuscript obtains this through a blowup, which separates powers of the parameter ideal geometrically, and a vector bundle with prescribed cohomological vanishing. Its construction builds on Eisenbud and Schreyer’s work. The chosen cohomology pattern makes an Euler characteristic nonnegative, while carefully balanced leading coefficients leave the desired contribution of the zeroth free rank.

The auxiliary ring may be non-Noetherian. Accordingly, the comparison uses finite filtrations and stabilized images, and tracks when negligible-length objects remain negligible under sums and limits. These technical conditions protect the numerical estimate during passage to large extensions.

Three characteristic regimes

In characteristic ppp, Frobenius raises matrix entries to arbitrarily high powers without changing free ranks. Normalized lengths on a perfection, obtained by adjoining compatible ppp-power roots, relate the resulting zeroth homology to Hilbert–Kunz multiplicity. Componentwise inequalities and multiplicity identities then yield the target comparison.

Mixed characteristic has no Frobenius endomorphism of the same kind. The manuscript instead uses roots of parameters, integral-extension results of Heitmann, and perfectoid normalized lengths. Auxiliary extension ranks can grow, so lengths are divided by those ranks before comparison.

The order of limits matters. For a fixed extension, parameter powers first tend to infinity to obtain a target-side upper bound. Only afterward does the depth of the differential entries increase. The upper bound stays independent of the chosen extension, allowing the sharp coefficient to survive.

In residue characteristic zero, the argument reduces to a finite free map over a common coefficient field. A finite system of polynomial identities records algebra structure, freeness, locality, and bounds in the required directions on the two multiplicities. Artin approximation and specialization transfer a hypothetical strict counterexample to positive characteristic. That would contradict the already established characteristic-ppp case.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Flatness and locality are essential hypotheses. A quotient map or an arbitrary homomorphism need not preserve multiplicity in the claimed direction. The theorem also does not assert strict increase or classify all equality cases.

The multiplicities use each ring’s own maximal ideal. Replacing that by the extended source ideal changes the quantity and misses the central issue. Likewise, an argument on associated graded rings must justify flatness there rather than assume it passes automatically.

The proof does not claim that every local domain admits an Ulrich module, a small Cohen–Macaulay module, or a weakly lim Ulrich sequence. Its auxiliary lengths can vanish on nonzero modules, and the associated algebras need not be finite or Noetherian.

The short-complex consequence has the stated complete-domain and positive-characteristic scope. Broader short-complex inequalities, effective descriptions of equality in Lech’s inequality, and sharper bounds using fiber information remain separate problems.

8. Sources and further reading

Lech’s Note on multiplicities of ideals (1960) and Inequalities related to certain couples of local rings (1964) formulate the classical comparison. Ma’s dimension-three work and lim Ulrich approach give major earlier cases and methods.

Iyengar, Ma, and Walker’s short-complex inequalities are a direct predecessor. Yhee’s nonexistence examples explain a limitation of universal module-sequence approaches.

Eisenbud and Schreyer’s vector-bundle and Betti-table work and Cai, Lee, Ma, Schwede, and Tucker’s perfectoid length work supply important inputs. The pinned source below states the uniform complex estimate and the complete claimed deduction of Lech’s inequality.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Lech’s multiplicity conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A three-dimensional singularity that no finite module can make Cohen–Macaulay
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 195 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A singular ring may fail to behave like a smooth coordinate ring, yet a module over it can sometimes restore enough regularity for homological arguments. The small Cohen–Macaulay module question asks whether every complete local domain admits such a finite algebraic substitute.

Family 195 claims a counterexample already in dimension three over the complex numbers. Its ring is complete, normal, and has no zero divisors, but every nonzero finitely generated module has depth less than three.

The strength lies in “every finite module.” Earlier obstructions for finite extension algebras or graded modules leave room for a module with no multiplication or compatible grading. The manuscript’s construction is designed to close those possibilities at its chosen singularity.

2. Background and essential definitions

Depth measures successive regularity

Let (R,m)(R,\mathfrak m)(R,m) be a Noetherian local ring and MMM a nonzero finite module. An element x∈mx\in\mathfrak mx∈m is regular on MMM if multiplication by xxx is injective. A sequence x1,…,xrx_1,\ldots,x_rx1​,…,xr​ is regular on MMM if each element remains regular after quotienting by the preceding ones, with the final quotient nonzero.

The depth of MMM is the longest possible length of such a sequence. It cannot exceed the ring’s dimension. A finite module is maximal Cohen–Macaulay if

depth⁡RM=dim⁡R.\operatorname{depth}_R M=\dim R.depthR​M=dimR.

“Small Cohen–Macaulay module” means the same thing here, with “small” emphasizing finite generation. Over the regular ring C[[x,y,z]]\mathbb C[[x,y,z]]C[[x,y,z]], the ring itself works: multiplication successively by x,y,zx,y,zx,y,z has the required injectivity. A singular ring may fail this test on itself while still possessing another module that passes it.

A domain has no nonzero zero divisors. A normal domain is integrally closed in its fraction field. Completeness means that compatible information modulo all powers of m\mathfrak mm comes from an element of the ring. These conditions make the counterexample a well-controlled local algebra, rather than a pathology caused by dropping standard finiteness assumptions.

Modules, algebras, and infinite substitutes

A finite extension algebra BBB is also a finite RRR-module, but a module need not have multiplication. Ruling out Cohen–Macaulay extension algebras therefore does not rule out all small Cohen–Macaulay modules.

A big Cohen–Macaulay module may require infinitely many generators. In the balanced formulation, every system of parameters acts regularly and the quotient by m\mathfrak mm is nonzero. Big objects can exist even when no small one does. The claimed counterexample concerns finite generation, not the general availability of big Cohen–Macaulay methods.

A cone built from a surface

Let XXX be a smooth projective complex surface and HHH an ample globally generated divisor. “Globally generated” means that its line bundle has sections with no common zero; “ample” supplies sufficiently many sections in large powers to embed the surface projectively.

The section ring is

T(X,H)=⨁j≥0H0(X,OX(jH)).T(X,H)=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(jH)).T(X,H)=j≥0⨁​H0(X,OX​(jH)).

Its geometry is a three-dimensional cone over the surface. Localizing at the positive-degree ideal isolates the vertex, and completing gives the local ring R(X,H)R(X,H)R(X,H). The construction will choose the surface so that its numerical geometry obstructs every hypothetical small module at this vertex.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hochster formulated the finite-module existence problem in early work on Cohen–Macaulay modules and homological conjectures. His later account records both the original existence expectation and a subsequent expectation of counterexamples.

Dimensions at most two have positive answers for complete local domains: finite normalization is Cohen–Macaulay. Dimension three is therefore the first possible dimension for the claimed domain counterexample.

There are also significant positive results in characteristic ppp. Work of Hartshorne, Peskine–Szpiro, and Hochster gives graded small Cohen–Macaulay modules for three-dimensional finitely generated nonnegatively graded domains over perfect fields of positive characteristic. These hypotheses do not include the characteristic-zero cone used here.

Allowing infinite generation changes the landscape. Hochster established big Cohen–Macaulay modules in equal characteristic. Hochster and Huneke showed that absolute integral closures of excellent positive-characteristic domains provide big Cohen–Macaulay algebras. Perfectoid methods later supplied the mixed-characteristic existence theorem. None of these statements promises a finite module.

Nonexistence results for small algebras were known earlier. In characteristic zero, trace makes a normal domain a direct summand of each finite extension domain, so a Cohen–Macaulay extension would force the original ring to be Cohen–Macaulay. Bhatt constructed positive-characteristic examples without finite Cohen–Macaulay extensions. Arbitrary finite modules evade the multiplication and trace framework.

The immediate geometric predecessors involve vector bundles on surfaces. Bogomolov’s inequality and the Hodge index theorem give numerical restrictions on Ulrich bundles. Beauville described such a route under a rank-one divisor-class assumption; Anghel developed a surface inequality without that restriction and used complete-quadrangle covers.

The manuscript carefully records two September 2026 comparisons. Anghel’s 14 September preprint excludes arithmetically Cohen–Macaulay bundles and graded maximal Cohen–Macaulay modules for relevant section rings, using a sharper numerical threshold. Liang Chen’s 21 September preprint proposes a completed-local counterexample under a proportionality condition between the canonical divisor and the polarization. Thus the existential completed-module claim overlaps with that prior proposal. The present manuscript claims a different obstruction without that proportionality hypothesis, and uses an exponent-seven cover rather than the exponent-six example discussed there.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The manuscript, dated 23 September 2026, claims a three-dimensional complete Noetherian normal local domain RRR containing C\mathbb CC, with residue field C\mathbb CC, such that

depth⁡RM<3for every nonzero finitely generated R-module M.\operatorname{depth}_R M<3\quad\text{for every nonzero finitely generated }R\text{-module }M.depthR​M<3for every nonzero finitely generated R-module M.

It imposes no grading, algebra structure, or special rank on the module being excluded.

The principal intermediate claim is a geometric obstruction. Write KXK_XKX​ for the canonical divisor of a smooth projective surface, KX2K_X^2KX2​ for its self-intersection, and c2(X)c_2(X)c2​(X) for the second Chern number, equal here to the topological Euler characteristic. If HHH is ample and globally generated and the completed cone admits a small Cohen–Macaulay module, then

KX2−2c2(X)≤6H2.K_X^2-2c_2(X)\le6H^2.KX2​−2c2​(X)≤6H2.

These are numerical invariants of the chosen surface and polarization. The manuscript constructs a pair with

H2=1715,KX2−2c2(X)=13377>10290=6H2.H^2=1715,\qquadK_X^2-2c_2(X)=13377>10290=6H^2.H2=1715,KX2​−2c2​(X)=13377>10290=6H2.

The claimed obstruction therefore excludes every small Cohen–Macaulay module over its completed cone.

A corollary also excludes such modules over the uncompleted vertex localization of the same section ring. This is a three-dimensional local domain essentially of finite type over C\mathbb CC. If it had a suitable finite module, faithfully flat completion would preserve its nonzeroness and regular sequence, producing the forbidden completed module.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, this gives a negative answer to the domain form of a central finite-module existence question, in the first possible dimension.

The theorem separates the finite and infinite worlds sharply. Big Cohen–Macaulay methods can remain available while no finite module reproduces the required depth. It also explains why approaches to other conjectures cannot universally assume a small Cohen–Macaulay or Ulrich module over each source ring.

The nearby multiplicity problems illustrate this point. Family 194 uses complexes and normalized lengths to formulate its claimed general comparison without making such finite-module existence a prerequisite. A failure of one ideal auxiliary object need not invalidate every numerical method that it once motivated.

6. The main idea

Carry an arbitrary module onto a surface

Choose a finite map f:X→P2f:X\to\mathbb P^2f:X→P2 defined by sections of HHH. The completed cone is finite over the regular ring

A=C[[x0,x1,x2]].A=\mathbb C[[x_0,x_1,x_2]].A=C[[x0​,x1​,x2​]].

A hypothetical depth-three finite module over the cone is free as an AAA-module, by the regular local homological theory. Away from the vertex it determines a vector bundle.

The manuscript replaces the cone vertex by the exceptional surface XXX on a regular model. It extends the actual bundle to a coherent sheaf on that model. This preserves information from an arbitrary nongraded module; it does not assume that the module descends to a graded or Ulrich bundle on XXX.

Balance slopes without changing the punctured bundle

A torsion-free sheaf BBB on the surface has normalized slope

μ(B)=c1(B)⋅Hrank⁡(B)H2.\mu(B)=\frac{c_1(B)\cdot H}{\operatorname{rank}(B)H^2}.μ(B)=rank(B)H2c1​(B)⋅H​.

Here c1(B)c_1(B)c1​(B) records its first Chern class. Slope compares its average twisting in the direction of the polarization. A Harder–Narasimhan filtration separates a sheaf into semistable pieces with decreasing slopes; semistability means that smaller-rank subsheaves cannot have a greater slope.

Elementary modifications supported on the exceptional surface leave the bundle outside that surface unchanged. The manuscript uses them to put the slopes of the restriction’s semistable pieces into an interval of length at most one.

Freeness over AAA yields one Chern-character inequality after pushing this restriction to P2\mathbb P^2P2. Bogomolov’s inequality, the Hodge index theorem, and the bounded slope interval yield an inequality in the opposite direction. Together, they give

0≤Δ≤12−KX2−2c2(X)12H2,0\le \Delta\le\frac12-\frac{K_X^2-2c_2(X)}{12H^2},0≤Δ≤21​−12H2KX2​−2c2​(X)​,

where Δ\DeltaΔ is a normalized Chern-character expression of the pushed-forward sheaf. Its exact value is unimportant for the contradiction: the right-hand side must be nonnegative. This is the claimed surface obstruction.

Choose a surface that violates the bound

Begin with four general points of the projective plane and the six lines joining their pairs, the complete quadrangle. Blow up the four points. The six strict transforms and four exceptional curves form a branch divisor with ten components and fifteen ordinary crossing points.

Adjoin nnn-th roots of five independent ratios of the six line equations and normalize. For prime n≥3n\ge3n≥3, the manuscript obtains a smooth surface covering the blown-up plane with degree n5n^5n5. Its local branch coordinates are ordinary power maps, making the ramification explicit.

Canonical-divisor and Euler-characteristic calculations give

KX2−2c2(X)=n5(1−10n2),H2=5n3.K_X^2-2c_2(X)=n^5\left(1-\frac{10}{n^2}\right),\qquad H^2=5n^3.KX2​−2c2​(X)=n5(1−n210​),H2=5n3.

The polarization is constructed as an integral ample globally generated divisor; having the desired numerical square alone would not suffice. Taking n=7n=7n=7 gives the incompatible numbers in section 4. The resulting completed cone is the asserted ring.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The claim is an existence counterexample, not a classification of all three-dimensional domains without small Cohen–Macaulay modules. Many rings still possess them, including regular and Cohen–Macaulay rings themselves.

The numerical inequality is a necessary condition for the chosen cone construction. Satisfying it is not asserted to guarantee a small module. The constant six also should not be identified with the sharper thresholds in earlier graded-bundle obstructions: those statements exclude different classes of objects.

Characteristic zero and the specified complex surface are part of this construction. The theorem does not negate positive-characteristic graded existence results or big Cohen–Macaulay existence. It also does not prove the absence of every asymptotic substitute, such as the module sequences used in lim Cohen–Macaulay theory.

The prior completed-local proposal is explicitly acknowledged. The significance assigned here concerns the mathematical scope of the claimed obstruction and example, without independently adjudicating novelty or priority.

8. Sources and further reading

Hochster’s Cohen–Macaulay modules (1973), Topics in the Homological Theory of Modules over Commutative Rings (1975), and Homological conjectures and lim Cohen–Macaulay sequences (2017) trace the finite and infinite existence questions. Bhatt’s On the non-existence of small Cohen–Macaulay algebras (2014) concerns the distinct algebra problem.

The closely related sources are Anghel’s surface construction, his graded-module obstruction, and Liang Chen’s completed-local proposal. Hirzebruch’s Arrangements of lines and algebraic surfaces (1983) is the geometric source of the covering construction.

Bhatt, Hochster, and Ma’s lim Cohen–Macaulay work explains asymptotic alternatives. These references supply context for the arbitrary finite-module claim in the manuscript below.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Complete Local Domain without a Small Cohen–Macaulay Module (September 23, 2026).
