entry.title: One finite algebra with arbitrarily long terminating resolutions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 198 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Solving algebraic relations often proceeds in stages: describe generators, then relations among them, then relations among those relations, and so on. A projective resolution records this process. Some modules require infinitely many stages; others eventually terminate.

The little finitistic-dimension conjecture asks a subtle uniformity question. For one fixed finite-dimensional algebra, is there a common upper bound on the lengths of all the resolutions that do terminate?

Family 198 claims a negative answer over the complex numbers. It constructs a single finite-dimensional algebra with finite-dimensional modules whose projective dimensions are finite but arbitrarily large. Changing the module does not change the algebra. That fixed-algebra requirement is the central distinction between the claimed counterexample and familiar families of increasingly complicated algebras.

2. Background and essential definitions

Resolutions and projective dimension

A finite-dimensional complex algebra AAA is a finite-dimensional vector space with associative multiplication and an identity. It need not be commutative. A left AAA-module is a vector space on which algebra elements act linearly and compatibly with multiplication.

A free module is a direct sum of copies of AAA. A projective module is a direct summand of a free module. Projective modules are the building blocks used in resolutions because maps from them lift through surjections.

A finite projective resolution of a module NNN has the form

0⟶Pr⟶⋯⟶P1⟶P0⟶N⟶0,0\longrightarrow P_r\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow P_1\longrightarrow P_0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow0,0⟶Pr​⟶⋯⟶P1​⟶P0​⟶N⟶0,

where each PiP_iPi​ is projective and the sequence is exact. Exactness says that each stage records precisely the relations left by the previous one. The least possible rrr is the projective dimension pd⁡AN\operatorname{pd}_A NpdA​N. If no finite resolution exists, the dimension is infinite.

For a finite-dimensional algebra, a finitely generated module is also finite-dimensional over the coefficient field. Its successive kernels in a projective resolution are called syzygies.

Three suprema with different meanings

The global dimension takes a supremum over projective dimensions without discarding infinite values. The little finitistic dimension instead keeps only finite projective dimensions of finitely generated modules:

fin.dim⁡A=sup⁡{pd⁡AN:N finite-dimensional, pd⁡AN<∞}.\operatorname{fin.dim}A=\sup\{\operatorname{pd}_A N:N\text{ finite-dimensional},\ \operatorname{pd}_A N<\infty\}.fin.dimA=sup{pdA​N:N finite-dimensional, pdA​N<∞}.

The big finitistic dimension, written Fin.dim⁡A\operatorname{Fin.dim}AFin.dimA, permits all modules, including infinitely generated ones, while still retaining only those of finite projective dimension. Therefore the little dimension is at most the big one.

An algebra can have modules of infinite projective dimension and nevertheless have finite finitistic dimension. Such modules are excluded from the defining supremum. The counterexample must supply increasingly long finite resolutions, not simply one infinite resolution.

For a noncommutative algebra, left and right modules need not behave alike. Right AAA-modules are left modules over the opposite algebra AopA^{\mathrm{op}}Aop, whose multiplication reverses the order of factors.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Bass publicized finitistic-dimension questions in 1960. Two questions must be distinguished: whether little and big finitistic dimensions are equal, and whether they are finite.

Huisgen-Zimmermann disproved equality by constructing, for each n≥2n\ge2n≥2, a finite-dimensional monomial algebra with little dimension nnn and big dimension n+1n+1n+1. Those examples vary with nnn, and both dimensions remain finite for each algebra. They therefore do not refute the universal finiteness conjecture.

Several large classes satisfy little finitistic finiteness. Green, Kirkman, and Kuzmanovich proved it for finite-dimensional monomial algebras, whose defining relations are paths rather than linear combinations of paths. Green and Huisgen-Zimmermann proved it for Artin algebras with radical cube zero. The radical is the ideal carrying the algebra’s nonsemisimple behavior; requiring its cube to vanish restricts how long products of such elements can persist.

Igusa and Todorov introduced syzygy invariants giving another proof of the radical-cube-zero case and finiteness for representation dimension at most three. These results show that homological complexity is bounded under important structural restrictions, without settling arbitrary finite-dimensional algebras.

Cummings later proved an equivalence between universal little finitistic finiteness and a universal left–right symmetry assertion for finiteness. This provides a way to convert a counterexample into pronounced asymmetry, but is not itself a construction of infinite finitistic dimension.

Rickard established another connection: if injective modules generate the unbounded derived category in the appropriate sense, then big finitistic dimension is finite. Derived categories organize complexes while identifying maps that preserve homology; allowing arbitrary coproducts permits infinite direct sums. The new counterexample therefore has a consequence for injective generation as well.

The construction draws on universal localization and on formulas for trivial extension algebras developed by Minamoto and Yamaura. A separate characteristic-two construction in family 199 also claims infinite finitistic dimension. The present manuscript emphasizes that its complex example is distinct and constructed independently.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The manuscript, dated 23 September 2026, claims a finite-dimensional unital complex algebra AAA such that for every integer m≥1m\ge1m≥1, there is a finite-dimensional left module NmN_mNm​ with

2m−2≤pd⁡ANm<∞.2m-2\le\operatorname{pd}_A N_m<\infty.2m−2≤pdA​Nm​<∞.

The same AAA works for all mmm. Hence

fin.dim⁡A=Fin.dim⁡A=∞.\operatorname{fin.dim}A=\operatorname{Fin.dim}A=\infty.fin.dimA=Fin.dimA=∞.

The second equality follows because the big supremum includes all the modules already witnessing the first. This also refutes the corresponding universal finiteness statement for Artin algebras, since finite-dimensional complex algebras belong to that class.

By Rickard’s theorem, injective left AAA-modules do not generate the unbounded derived category of all left modules.

An auxiliary algebra with opposite extremes

Combining the example with Cummings’ triangular-algebra construction, the manuscript claims another finite-dimensional complex algebra Λ\LambdaΛ satisfying

fin.dim⁡Λ=Fin.dim⁡Λ=∞,\operatorname{fin.dim}\Lambda=\operatorname{Fin.dim}\Lambda=\infty,fin.dimΛ=Fin.dimΛ=∞,

while

fin.dim⁡(Λop)=Fin.dim⁡(Λop)=0.\operatorname{fin.dim}(\Lambda^{\mathrm{op}})=\operatorname{Fin.dim}(\Lambda^{\mathrm{op}})=0.fin.dim(Λop)=Fin.dim(Λop)=0.

All displayed dimensions use left modules. Thus Λ\LambdaΛ has infinite finitistic dimensions on the left and zero on the right. Its injective left modules do not generate, whereas its injective right modules do.

This is a statement about the auxiliary Λ\LambdaΛ. The manuscript makes no corresponding right-side assertion about the original algebra AAA. Keeping the two algebras separate prevents an unjustified strengthening of the main construction.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the example disproves a central conjecture in the representation theory and homological algebra of finite-dimensional algebras.

Its force comes from the difference between finite description and uniformly bounded homological behavior. A fixed algebra has finitely many basis elements and a finite multiplication table, yet the claimed modules can encode terminating processes of arbitrarily large depth.

The consequences also challenge expectations of symmetry. The auxiliary algebra would support arbitrarily long finite resolutions on one side while every module of finite projective dimension on the other side is already projective. This does not make left and right global behavior identical to those finite suprema; it identifies an extreme asymmetry in the specific finitistic invariants.

6. The main idea

Start with a process that eventually dies, but at no fixed time

The first stage constructs a finitely presented auxiliary complex algebra RRR, a central idempotent eee, and an automorphism α\alphaα. A central idempotent satisfies e2=ee^2=ee2=e and commutes with the algebra, so eYeYeY is a direct summand of every module YYY.

Define a selection operation HHH by taking eYeYeY and changing its action through α\alphaα. The manuscript constructs finite-dimensional modules YmY_mYm​ satisfying

Hj(Ym)≠0(0≤j<m),Hm(Ym)=0.H^j(Y_m)\ne0\quad(0\le j<m),\qquad H^m(Y_m)=0.Hj(Ym​)=0(0≤j<m),Hm(Ym​)=0.

The auxiliary algebra is a group algebra whose group contains an indexed family of central involutions. The automorphism shifts that family. Finite matrix quotients detect arbitrarily long independent segments, and prescribed characters make selection survive for exactly the desired number of rounds.

At this stage, RRR is finitely presented but need not be finite-dimensional. The remaining work is to encode its selection behavior inside one finite-dimensional algebra without changing the encoding when mmm changes.

Simulate selection with a fixed derived tensor operation

A quadratic presentation of RRR is encoded in a directed algebra BBB with three vertices and global dimension at most two. A module M(Y)M(Y)M(Y) places the vector space YYY at each vertex, with arrows recording the generator actions.

The manuscript constructs one bounded complex PPP of BBB-bimodules such that

P⊗BLM(Y)≃M(H(Y))⊕M(H(Y))[3].P\otimes_B^{\mathbf L}M(Y)\simeq M(H(Y))\oplus M(H(Y))[3].P⊗BL​M(Y)≃M(H(Y))⊕M(H(Y))[3].

A bimodule has compatible left and right actions. The derived tensor product uses resolutions so that it retains higher homological information. The symbol [3][3][3] shifts a complex’s degree by three. Thus the formula simulates selection twice in different degrees, rather than demanding that one selected summand lift by itself.

Uniformity is the key issue. Denominators are cleared for a single finite diagram before any test module is chosen. Relations initially hold only up to chain homotopy; extra terms in a three-column differential turn those homotopies into an actual bimodule complex. The separation between the two surviving degrees exceeds BBB‘s global dimension, giving the displayed splitting. The argument does not need a splitting chosen naturally for every module simultaneously.

Turn survival time into resolution length

A further finite-dimensional construction replaces the bounded complex by an ordinary bimodule XXX over an algebra DDD of finite global dimension. Let

F=X⊗DL−.F=X\otimes_D^{\mathbf L}-.F=X⊗DL​−.

Two iterations of FFF simulate one selection step, up to fixed shifts and direct sums. The final algebra is the trivial extension

A=D⋉X,A=D\ltimes X,A=D⋉X,

whose underlying vector space is D⊕XD\oplus XD⊕X, with multiplication

(d,x)(d′,x′)=(dd′,dx′+xd′).(d,x)(d',x')=(dd',dx'+xd').(d,x)(d′,x′)=(dd′,dx′+xd′).

In particular, the ideal XXX has square zero. This does not say that the radical of the whole algebra has cube zero; the earlier positive theorem for that class is not being contradicted.

For an inflated DDD-module NNN, the bar construction decomposes the relevant derived tensor expression according to the number of occurrences of XXX:

D⊗ALN≃⨁r≥0(FrN)[r].D\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}N\simeq\bigoplus_{r\ge0}(F^rN)[r].D⊗AL​N≃r≥0⨁​(FrN)[r].

The manuscript treats derived powers explicitly, including when XXX is not flat. Eventual disappearance of the iterates implies finite projective dimension, while a nonzero rrr-th iterate forces projective dimension at least rrr.

For Nm=M(Ym)N_m=M(Y_m)Nm​=M(Ym​), it obtains F2mNm≃0F^{2m}N_m\simeq0F2mNm​≃0 but F2m−2Nm≄0F^{2m-2}N_m\not\simeq0F2m−2Nm​≃0. These give the finite upper status and the lower bound 2m−22m-22m−2. All algebras, complexes, and bimodules were fixed beforehand; only the test module varies.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The lower bound is not an assertion that pd⁡ANm\operatorname{pd}_A N_mpdA​Nm​ equals exactly 2m−22m-22m−2. The theorem needs finiteness and unboundedness, which are established by different parts of the transfer.

The coefficient field is C\mathbb CC. The manuscript does not claim the identical construction over every field; its characteristic-two comparison comes from a separate companion.

The result does not imply that all modules have finite projective dimension. Nor does it alter the positive theorems for monomial algebras, radical-cube-zero algebras, or the other restricted classes described earlier.

The extreme right-side conclusions belong to Λ\LambdaΛ, not automatically to AAA. More explicit small examples, quantitative upper bounds for the particular test modules, and classifications of the remaining positive classes are separate questions from the universal counterexample.

8. Sources and further reading

Bass’s Finitistic dimension and a homological generalization of semi-primary rings (1960) is the historical starting point. Huisgen-Zimmermann’s survey distinguishes the equality and finiteness questions and describes earlier positive results.

Igusa and Todorov’s On the finitistic global dimension conjecture for Artin algebras (2005) develops syzygy invariants. Cummings’ Left–right symmetry of finite finitistic dimension (2024) supplies the auxiliary asymmetry construction.

Neeman, Ranicki, and Schofield’s universal-localization work and Minamoto–Yamaura’s trivial-extension formulas explain the encoding and transfer background. Rickard’s injective-generation theorem supplies the derived-category consequence.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An algebra of infinite little finitistic dimension (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Zero divisors without finite-order group elements
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 196 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Ordinary nonzero real numbers never multiply to zero. Matrices can: two nonzero matrices may have a zero product. Which behavior should one expect from a group algebra, where formal sums of group elements are multiplied using the group law?

Finite-order group elements create an immediate source of zero divisors. Kaplansky’s zero-divisor conjecture asks whether that is the only obstruction: if a group is torsion-free, must its group algebra over every field have no nonzero zero divisors?

Family 196 claims a negative answer. It constructs a torsion-free group and two nonzero finite sums over the field with two elements whose product vanishes. The algebraic cancellation is driven by a simple parity observation. The difficult part is making that cancellation coexist with torsion-freeness and ensuring that the factors themselves survive the imposed relations.

2. Background and essential definitions

Formal sums with a group multiplication rule

For a field KKK and a group GGG, the group algebra K[G]K[G]K[G] consists of finite sums

α=∑g∈Gagg,\alpha=\sum_{g\in G}a_g g,α=g∈G∑​ag​g,

where only finitely many coefficients ag∈Ka_g\in Kag​∈K are nonzero. Addition combines coefficients, and multiplication distributes using the multiplication in GGG. Thus the coefficient of uuu in a product is the sum of agbha_gb_hag​bh​ over all pairs with gh=ugh=ugh=u.

A zero divisor is a nonzero element that multiplies another nonzero element to zero. If ggg has finite order m>1m>1m>1, then

(1−g)(1+g+⋯+gm−1)=1−gm=0.(1-g)(1+g+\cdots+g^{m-1})=1-g^m=0.(1−g)(1+g+⋯+gm−1)=1−gm=0.

Both factors are nonzero because the indicated group elements are distinct. A group is torsion-free when its identity is the only element of finite order. Removing finite order removes this elementary construction, but the conjecture asks whether more elaborate cancellations remain possible.

The field F2\mathbb F_2F2​ has elements zero and one, with 1+1=01+1=01+1=0. A finite sum over this field vanishes precisely when every group element occurs an even number of times. This turns the desired product cancellation into a parity problem.

Unique product is stronger than torsion-freeness

A group has the unique-product property if every two finite nonempty subsets A,BA,BA,B have some product with exactly one representation ababab. Applying this to the supports of two nonzero group-algebra elements supplies a coefficient that cannot cancel, so their product is nonzero.

Failure of unique product is weaker than having zero divisors. Two or more representations may have odd total multiplicity; over F2\mathbb F_2F2​, three copies still sum to one. The construction needs an even number of occurrences for every product, not merely the absence of unique representations.

A finitely presented group is specified by finitely many generators and relations. A classifying space for a group is a connected space with that fundamental group and contractible universal cover. A finite two-dimensional classifying space gives strong finiteness and topological control; in particular, its fundamental group cannot contain nontrivial finite-order elements.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The question appears in Higman’s 1940 work on units in group rings and in Kaplansky’s 1956 conference problems, published in 1957. Its simplicity conceals the challenge of controlling all finite cancellation patterns at once.

Higman proved positive results for groups whose nontrivial finitely generated subgroups map onto the integers, the local-indicability setting. Kropholler, Linnell, and Moody established the absence of zero divisors for torsion-free elementary amenable groups, even with division-ring coefficients. More recent division-ring embedding results of Fisher and Sánchez-Peralta cover torsion-free virtually compact special groups and substantial classes of three-manifold groups.

These theorems show that torsion-freeness combines with additional structure to give strong algebraic consequences. They do not apply to every torsion-free group.

Rips and Segev constructed torsion-free groups without unique product. Their work showed that one natural route to proving the conjecture could not be universal. Later graphical small-cancellation treatments clarified such constructions. But non-unique-product examples alone did not produce the parity cancellation required here.

The neighboring unit conjecture asks whether every invertible group-algebra element is a scalar multiple of a group element. Gardam disproved it over F2\mathbb F_2F2​ and later over C\mathbb CC. A nontrivial unit is not a zero divisor, so those results address a different conjecture.

Mineyev developed product structures and geometric criteria aimed at constructing units or zero divisors. Garg and Mineyev studied their finite-support combinatorics computationally. Shin established an obstruction to a particular orientable no-fold, triple-girth route. The present manuscript describes its own arrangement-exclusion mechanism rather than invoking those criteria.

Its topological strategy has antecedents in Gromov’s random graphical presentations and subsequent work of Ollivier, Gruber, and Bereznyuk. The new claim combines deliberately prescribed parity with probabilistic control of the relations, rather than taking a generic random presentation with no coefficient constraints.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The manuscript, dated 23 September 2026, claims that there is a finitely presented torsion-free group GGG and elements α,β∈F2[G]\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb F_2[G]α,β∈F2​[G] such that

α≠0,β≠0,αβ=0.\alpha\ne0,\qquad \beta\ne0,\qquad \alpha\beta=0.α=0,β=0,αβ=0.

Moreover, GGG has a finite two-dimensional classifying space. This supplies a counterexample within a class of groups with a finite topological model, rather than relying on infinitely many defining relations.

The construction is probabilistic and existential. It proves that suitable finite graph matchings exist, but does not list matchings from which a concrete presentation and explicit expanded zero-divisor factors can be immediately read off. Finitely presented does not mean that the paper displays a short numerical instance.

The coefficient field in the claimed example is F2\mathbb F_2F2​. This is enough to disprove a conjecture quantified over all fields. The theorem does not assert the same cancellation over characteristic-zero fields or over every characteristic.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the result disproves one of the central structural conjectures about torsion-free group algebras. It shows that eliminating finite-order elements does not eliminate every mechanism for zero multiplication.

The example would also distinguish several neighboring properties sharply: torsion-freeness, unique product, absence of zero divisors, and restrictions on units are related but not interchangeable. Earlier counterexamples to stronger properties did not automatically settle this one.

The construction’s design is useful conceptually. A local parity condition guarantees algebraic cancellation regardless of later random choices. Probability is then used to impose global geometric safeguards. This separates the part that must happen from the bad topological configurations that must be excluded.

6. The main idea

Two labelled graphs supply the factors

Take two finite graphs whose oriented edges carry group-generator labels; reversing an edge replaces its label by the inverse. At each vertex, no outgoing label is repeated. Map both graphs into a rose, a graph with one vertex and one loop for each generator.

Attach cones over the graph components, thereby imposing relations that kill the labels of closed graph paths. In the resulting group, choose a root in one component of each graph. A path from the first root to a vertex xxx has a well-defined group label gxg_xgx​, because alternative paths differ by a closed path. Define hyh_yhy​ in the other component similarly.

Using the full vertex sets A′A'A′ and B′B'B′ of the chosen components, set

α=∑x∈A′gx,β=∑y∈B′hy−1.\alpha=\sum_{x\in A'}g_x,\qquad \beta=\sum_{y\in B'}h_y^{-1}.α=x∈A′∑​gx​,β=y∈B′∑​hy−1​.

These sums can contain repeated group labels. The construction does not require all their non-root labels to be distinct.

Odd degrees force even cancellation

Let SxS_xSx​ and SyS_ySy​ be the outgoing signed-label sets. The graphs are prescribed so that every cross-intersection Sx∩SyS_x\cap S_ySx​∩Sy​ has odd size.

Now form a graph on pairs (x,y)(x,y)(x,y). Connect pairs by taking one step with the same label ttt in both original graphs. The represented product remains unchanged:

(gxt)(hyt)−1=gxhy−1.(g_xt)(h_yt)^{-1}=g_xh_y^{-1}.(gx​t)(hy​t)−1=gx​hy−1​.

Every vertex in this pair graph has odd degree. The degree-sum formula says that a finite graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices, so every connected component has an even number of vertices. All those vertices contribute the same group element to αβ\alpha\betaαβ. Their contributions cancel in F2\mathbb F_2F2​.

This proves the desired zero product once the graphs and their quotient group satisfy the remaining safeguards.

Preserve nonzero factors and forbid torsion

The first safeguard is root separation: a path from a chosen root to any other vertex in its component must have nonidentity label. Then the root contributes the identity exactly once to each factor, so neither factor vanishes. Distinguishing every pair of non-root vertices is unnecessary.

The second safeguard is asphericity of the coned complex, meaning that its higher homotopy groups vanish. The manuscript proves this directly through the exclusion of reduced spherical arrangements. It does not claim that these graphs automatically satisfy a familiar small-cancellation or nonpositive-curvature criterion.

The outgoing labels are arranged using lines in a finite projective plane, together with three extra letters. Distinct projective lines meet once, and the extra-letter intersections preserve odd parity. Random matchings then join compatible label occurrences into edges.

Those vertex types also give exponential decay for a squared-word counting expression, controlling coincidences between labelled paths. The argument must track repeated traversal of the same edges and distinguish genuinely different lifts from coincident paths. It cannot treat all path occurrences as independent random events.

Reduce arbitrarily large diagrams to bounded tests

A bad sphere could involve arbitrarily many paths, so a naive union bound over a fixed diagram size would not suffice. The manuscript uses planar separation, based on the Lipton–Tarjan separator theorem, to extract a bounded configuration from any sufficiently complicated spherical arrangement.

Long boundaries are split and closed at controlled cost, and planar counting limits the number of comparison intervals. The tolerated proportion of unmatched path positions is fixed before the size bounds. The same finite class of forbidden patterns can then detect arbitrarily large bad arrangements.

The probabilistic estimates exclude those patterns for some choice of finite matchings. Cone-picture arguments turn that exclusion into both root separation and asphericity, completing the claimed construction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns existence over F2\mathbb F_2F2​, not an explicit small presentation or a minimum support size for the zero divisors. Finding practical concrete instances is a different problem from the probabilistic existence statement.

The two factors need not have all distinct support labels before coefficient collection. What matters is that the identity coefficient survives in each and every product coefficient cancels. This distinction avoids assuming a stronger graph-embedding statement than the construction uses.

The claimed group need not belong to the classes covered by existing positive theorems, and the result does not negate those theorems. It also makes no general characteristic-zero zero-divisor claim.

Finally, this family should be distinguished from failure of direct finiteness, discussed in family 197. A zero product, a nontrivial unit, and a one-sided inverse without a two-sided inverse are different algebraic phenomena, even when related geometric methods appear in their study.

8. Sources and further reading

Higman’s group-ring work and Kaplansky’s Problems in the theory of rings (1957) give the historical problem. Kropholler, Linnell, and Moody’s positive theorem and Fisher–Sánchez-Peralta’s division-ring embeddings illustrate important cases where zero divisors are excluded.

Rips and Segev’s non-unique-product construction and Gardam’s unit-conjecture counterexample concern distinct neighboring questions. The Lipton–Tarjan separator theorem supplies the planar reduction used in the new argument.

Brown’s Cohomology of Groups and Hatcher’s Algebraic Topology explain classifying spaces and the topological language behind the torsion-free safeguard.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Torsion-Free Group Algebra with Zero Divisors (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A one-sided inverse that cannot be reversed in a group algebra
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 197 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

For square matrices over a field, AB=IAB=IAB=I forces BA=IBA=IBA=I. A left inverse and a right inverse cannot differ. On an infinite-dimensional space, this principle fails: a shift can have a one-sided inverse with a missing direction.

A group algebra lies between these settings. The group may be infinite, but each algebra element is a finite sum. Kaplansky’s direct-finiteness conjecture asks whether that finite support is enough to recover the finite-dimensional implication.

Family 197 claims that it is not. Its strongest group-theoretic version uses a finitely presented torsion-free group over F2\mathbb F_2F2​. Other manuscripts give a torsion-containing characteristic-two construction, one specified odd-characteristic construction, and a dependent counterexample to a determinant inequality. Their hypotheses and dependencies are different and need to be kept separate.

2. Background and essential definitions

One-sided inverses and stable finiteness

The group algebra K[G]K[G]K[G] consists of finite formal sums ∑agg\sum a_g g∑ag​g, with multiplication extended from the group law. Its identity is the group identity with coefficient one.

A unital ring is directly finite if

ab=1⟹ba=1.ab=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad ba=1.ab=1⟹ba=1.

It is stably finite if every finite square matrix ring over it is directly finite. A matrix counterexample shows failure of stable finiteness, but does not automatically provide scalar elements a,ba,ba,b in the original ring. Some manuscripts in this family explicitly enlarge the group to complete that passage.

If ab=1ab=1ab=1 but ba≠1ba\ne1ba=1, the element e=1−bae=1-bae=1−ba is a nonzero idempotent: e2=ee^2=ee2=e. Also ae=0ae=0ae=0. Thus this defect supplies zero divisors, but a zero product by itself does not establish failure of direct finiteness. This is a stronger phenomenon than the headline of family 196.

Finite approximations and local dynamics

A sofic group admits finite approximate permutation models for every finite part of its multiplication table, with small errors and good separation of distinct elements. Soficity is an approximation property, not a requirement that the group itself be finite.

A configuration over a finite alphabet KKK is an arbitrary function x:G→Kx:G\to Kx:G→K. A cellular automaton applies the same rule at every group position using only finitely many nearby coordinates. A group is surjunctive if every injective such automaton is also surjective. Gottschalk’s conjecture proposes this property for every group.

For a=∑auu∈K[G]a=\sum a_u u\in K[G]a=∑au​u∈K[G], one convention for its linear local rule is

(Tax)(g)=∑uaux(gu).(T_a x)(g)=\sum_u a_u x(gu).(Ta​x)(g)=u∑​au​x(gu).

The sum is finite even when the configuration has infinite support, and TaTb=TabT_aT_b=T_{ab}Ta​Tb​=Tab​. A scalar one-sided inverse therefore gives an injective automaton with a local left inverse; a nonzero reverse defect can obstruct surjectivity.

An infinite-dimensional determinant

An integral group-ring matrix acts on square-summable functions on the group. Its Fuglede–Kadison determinant uses the trace of the logarithm of its positive square, extending the absolute value of an ordinary determinant.

For an invertible operator TAT_ATA​ on nnn copies of ℓ2(G)\ell^2(G)ℓ2(G), the convention is

log⁡det⁡N(G)(TA)=12τn ⁣(log⁡(TA∗TA)),\log\det_{\mathcal N(G)}(T_A)=\frac12\tau_n\!\left(\log(T_A^*T_A)\right),logN(G)det​(TA​)=21​τn​(log(TA∗​TA​)),

where τn(I)=n\tau_n(I)=nτn​(I)=n. The trace is built from the identity coefficient in each diagonal entry. The group-ring Determinant Conjecture asserts an analogue of the lower bound one for nonzero integer determinants.

3. Development history and previous partial results

For a finite group, its group algebra and all finite matrix rings are finite-dimensional, so stable finiteness follows from linear algebra in every characteristic. Kaplansky’s characteristic-zero theorem uses finite von Neumann algebras, whose trace replaces ordinary dimension. Montgomery gave a concise operator-algebra proof. The result extends from complex coefficients to every characteristic-zero field.

In positive characteristic, Ara, O’Meara, and Perera proved stable finiteness for free-by-amenable groups over arbitrary division rings. Elek and Szabó extended it to all sofic groups. Consequently, any group supporting the claimed counterexamples here must be nonsofic; this is a deduction from their theorem, not an independently assumed property of the construction.

Dykema, Heister, and Juschenko organized the finite cancellation patterns of one-sided inverses and established positive results for several small supports. Dykema and Juschenko also explained how to convert a matrix defect into a scalar defect after taking a suitable finite-group factor. That distinction is central to the torsion-containing constructions.

The dynamical background begins with Gottschalk’s surjunctivity question. Gromov and Weiss proved surjunctivity for sofic groups, and the linear cellular-automaton theory developed the relation to group-algebra finiteness. Later work of Phung and others established further general connections between surjunctivity and stable finiteness.

For determinants, approximation methods give the lower bound for large classes including amenable and sofic groups. A failure of a determinant approximation formula is a different matter: the manuscript discusses Kammeyer’s example where finite-quotient determinants do not converge to the group determinant, although the relevant determinants remain above one. The claim here violates the lower bound itself.

The torsion-free manuscript develops the parity and coned-graph strategy of family 196. The determinant manuscript instead takes the torsion-containing characteristic-two scalar construction as its exact input. The odd-characteristic construction is presented independently of that binary theorem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

SourceMain algebraic settingClaimed conclusion
M1, 4 October 2026F2[G]\mathbb F_2[G]F2​[G], finitely presented torsion-free GGGab=1ab=1ab=1, ac=0ac=0ac=0, c≠0c\ne0c=0, hence ba≠1ba\ne1ba=1
M2, 23 September 2026A finite characteristic-two field and finitely presented GGG with odd-order torsionScalar ab=1≠baab=1\ne baab=1=ba
M4, 26 September 2026A specified field of order p4p^4p4, one specified odd prime ppp, and finitely generated torsion-containing GGGScalar ab=1≠baab=1\ne baab=1=ba
M3, 23 September 2026An integral square matrix over another finitely generated groupRational group-ring inverse and determinant strictly between zero and one

M1 additionally gives a finite two-dimensional classifying complex, whose universal cover is contractible. Its graph matchings are selected by an existence argument, rather than listed as a practical concrete example.

M2 gives a terminating finite prescription for its field, presentation, and sums. The manuscript states that this prescription has not been executed and need not be computationally practical. Its field is not asserted to be F2\mathbb F_2F2​, and its group contains torsion.

M4 specifies the prime by

m=(1200600),p=min⁡{h>1:h divides (m!)2+1}.m=\binom{1200}{600},\qquadp=\min\{h>1:h\text{ divides }(m!)^2+1\}.m=(6001200​),p=min{h>1:h divides (m!)2+1}.

It claims the result for this prime, not every odd prime. Its field has order p4p^4p4, and its finite formulas likewise are not presented as an executed practical computation. The theorem states finite generation of its group; the stronger finite-presentation conclusion of M1 and M2 should not be silently transferred to it.

M2 and M4 explicitly derive injective nonsurjective cellular automata over their finite fields, giving claimed counterexamples to Gottschalk’s conjecture. The established sofic finiteness theorem makes the direct-finiteness example groups nonsofic.

M3 depends on M2’s scalar characteristic-two defect. It claims an integral matrix invertible over the rational group ring with

0<det⁡N(GD)(TA)<1.0<\det_{\mathcal N(G_D)}(T_A)<1.0<N(GD​)det​(TA​)<1.

Its logarithmic integral is finite and negative, with the spectrum bounded away from zero. This is not an example where a divergent integral or a zero kernel convention creates the failure.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the family overturns central finiteness conjectures connecting algebra, geometric group theory, probability-preserving approximation, and local dynamics.

The torsion-free prime-field result is especially sharp: finite-order elements and a larger coefficient field are not needed for that version. The torsion-containing constructions contribute different explicit prescriptions and, in the odd-characteristic case, a separate coefficient regime.

The consequences extend beyond rearranging products. A nonsurjunctive cellular automaton is locally defined and injective, yet some global configurations never occur. A nonsofic group lacks the finite approximate multiplication models guaranteed for many familiar groups. The determinant construction would show that integral coefficients alone do not enforce the proposed infinite-dimensional volume lower bound.

6. The main idea

Modify parity so that exactly one contribution survives

M1 uses finite labelled graphs attached by cones to a rose of generator loops. Closed graph paths become group relations. Root-to-vertex labels define finite sums, and simultaneous equal-label steps preserve the group element represented by each product pair.

For a zero product, every vertex of a simultaneous-step graph has odd degree. Each component then has even size, causing cancellation over F2\mathbb F_2F2​. To obtain product one, M1 arranges a single even-degree exception at the root pair. Its component has odd size and contributes exactly the identity; all other components cancel.

Seven extra labels organized by the Fano plane create this parity pattern while preserving balanced inverse-label counts. Pairing with a second graph gives ac=0ac=0ac=0, and root protection ensures c≠0c\ne0c=0. If ba=1ba=1ba=1, then c=b(ac)=0c=b(ac)=0c=b(ac)=0, a contradiction.

Random graph estimates, planar separators, and cone surgeries provide asphericity and root protection, adapting the strategy of family 196. The estimates are reproved for the changed vertex types.

From finite incidence data to scalar inverses

M2 starts with finite incidence data and vectors whose outer products sum to zero along specified lines but to a nonzero identity over the whole set. Low-degree interpolation produces these pairing identities. A probabilistic construction with local trades supplies the required incidence regularity and large girth.

Finite groups are glued according to that incidence geometry. A planar argument ensures that the relevant local groups embed, so a later algebraic witness does not collapse in the quotient. Character idempotents and prescribed conjugations pack a rectangular factorization into a matrix one-sided inverse.

The reverse defect is detected inside an embedded subgroup algebra by a rank obstruction. A suitable finite-group algebra then supplies matrix units, allowing an injective encoding of the matrix pair as scalar elements. Adding the complementary identity restores the full scalar identity. The final step is necessary: a matrix defect alone would only prove failure of stable finiteness.

M4 uses a different modular mechanism. A triangle-free graph has a low-rank fitting matrix, while finite-group idempotents have a larger normalized regular rank. Directed zero products along graph edges make these inequalities compatible. Group embeddings, exact rectangular identities, and a finite Heisenberg-group encoding again turn them into a scalar defect. The construction uses the specified odd prime throughout.

Turn a binary defect into a determinant below one

M3 represents the finite characteristic-two field by matrices over F2\mathbb F_2F2​, giving XY=IdXY=I_dXY=Id​ and a nonzero idempotent C=Id−YXC=I_d-YXC=Id​−YX. It enlarges the group by finitely supported copies of the cyclic group of order three, indexed by the original group.

Averages over those cyclic coordinates isolate one coefficient of CCC. The resulting rational orthogonal projection PPP has trace d+θd+\thetad+θ, where θ>0\theta>0θ>0, but its reduction modulo two factors through only ddd columns. Odd denominators make that reduction meaningful.

A modular lift and block-matrix construction turn this discrepancy into an integral matrix with rational inverse. Trace calculations remove block shears and give the exact determinant

det⁡N(GD)(TA)=q−θ<1\det_{\mathcal N(G_D)}(T_A)=q^{-\theta}<1N(GD​)det​(TA​)=q−θ<1

for a suitable power qqq of two. The determinant calculation transfers the binary defect; it does not independently construct the original one-sided inverse.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The four sources do not provide one universal counterexample simultaneously satisfying every field and group condition. M1 is torsion-free over F2\mathbb F_2F2​; M2 and M4 use torsion; M4 concerns one odd prime; and M3 changes the group again and depends specifically on a characteristic-two input.

No claim contradicts direct finiteness in characteristic zero. The determinant bound is a different invariant, so an integral matrix with determinant below one can coexist with the characteristic-zero direct-finiteness theorem.

Existence, a terminating prescription, and an executed small example are different levels of explicitness. The manuscripts state the first two in different places and do not claim practical computations of the full constructions.

Questions about small presentations, minimal supports, other odd primes, and how broadly the determinant transfer applies remain distinct from the stated counterexamples. The explanation reports the constructions and their consequences as claimed, without auditing their proofs.

8. Sources and further reading

Kaplansky’s Fields and Rings, second edition (1972), formulates the finiteness question. Montgomery’s Left and right inverses in group algebras (1969), Ara–O’Meara–Perera’s Stable finiteness of group rings in arbitrary characteristic (2002), and Elek–Szabó’s Sofic groups and direct finiteness (2004) give the principal positive results.

Dykema and Juschenko’s finite-group reduction explains the scalar-versus-matrix distinction. Gottschalk’s Some general dynamical notions (1973), Weiss’s Sofic groups and dynamical systems (2000), and Ceccherini-Silberstein and Coornaert’s linear cellular-automaton work provide the dynamical context.

Fuglede and Kadison introduced the operator determinant; Lück’s L²-Invariants develops the group-ring determinant question. The parity predecessor is explained in family 196. The source list below identifies the four separate claims and their versions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Torsion-Free Group Algebra That Is Not Directly Finite (October 4, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Counterexample to Kaplansky’s Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, A Counterexample to the Group-Ring Determinant Conjecture (September 23, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, A Counterexample to Kaplansky’s Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Odd Characteristic (September 26, 2026).

entry.title: Vanishing self-extensions need not make a module projective
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 199 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A projective module is a particularly flexible algebraic object: maps from it lift through surjections, and its higher extension groups vanish. Could a finite module that looks projective to the right collection of extension tests nevertheless fail to be projective?

The Auslander–Reiten conjecture proposes that vanishing extensions both to itself and to the algebra should suffice. Tachikawa’s second conjecture asks the corresponding question over self-injective algebras, where one of those vanishing conditions is automatic.

Family 199 claims counterexamples to both. One manuscript constructs an explicit triangular algebra and a nonprojective Gorenstein-projective module. The other obtains a symmetric algebra and develops consequences for several related homological conjectures. The setting is noncommutative and characteristic two, over a field containing transcendental parameters.

2. Background and essential definitions

What an extension group measures

For modules M,NM,NM,N over an algebra AAA, the group Ext⁡A1(M,N)\operatorname{Ext}^1_A(M,N)ExtA1​(M,N) classifies short exact sequences

0⟶N⟶E⟶M⟶00\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow00⟶N⟶E⟶M⟶0

up to the usual equivalence. The zero class represents a split sequence, where EEE is a direct sum. Higher groups Ext⁡i\operatorname{Ext}^iExti record longer homological obstructions and can be computed from a projective resolution.

A projective module is a direct summand of a free module. If MMM is projective, then Ext⁡Ai(M,N)=0\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(M,N)=0ExtAi​(M,N)=0 for every target NNN and every i>0i>0i>0. The Auslander–Reiten question asks whether testing only the targets MMM and AAA is enough:

Ext⁡Ai(M,M)=Ext⁡Ai(M,A)=0(i>0).\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(M,M)=\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(M,A)=0\quad(i>0).ExtAi​(M,M)=ExtAi​(M,A)=0(i>0).

A module with no positive self-extensions is called self-orthogonal. Vanishing in every positive degree is much stronger than vanishing only eventually or in a finite initial range.

Special kinds of algebra and module

An Artin algebra is finite over a commutative Artinian central base. Every finite-dimensional algebra over a field is an example. All modules in the main constructions are finite-dimensional left modules.

An algebra is self-injective when its regular module is injective. Injectivity is the dual lifting property to projectivity. For such an algebra, Ext⁡Ai(M,A)=0\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(M,A)=0ExtAi​(M,A)=0 automatically, so Tachikawa’s second conjecture asks whether self-orthogonal finite modules must be projective.

An algebra is symmetric if it is isomorphic to its vector-space dual as a bimodule. Equivalently, it has a nondegenerate symmetric associative bilinear form. Symmetric algebras are self-injective, but the converse need not hold.

A module is Gorenstein-projective if it occurs inside a doubly infinite exact complex of finite projective modules that remains exact after applying Hom⁡A(−,A)\operatorname{Hom}_A(-,A)HomA​(−,A). Such a complex is totally acyclic. This property ensures vanishing of positive Ext into AAA, but need not make the module projective.

Dominant dimension

An injective resolution begins by embedding the algebra into injectives:

0⟶A⟶I0⟶I1⟶⋯ .0\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow I^0\longrightarrow I^1\longrightarrow\cdots.0⟶A⟶I0⟶I1⟶⋯.

The dominant dimension counts how long its initial terms are also projective. Infinite dominant dimension means every term in the minimal injective resolution is projective. It does not, by definition alone, say that the algebra itself is injective or that the resolution terminates.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Auslander and Reiten’s work on the generalized Nakayama conjecture led to the projectivity question. Tachikawa’s 1973 monograph placed its self-injective version among the conjectures surrounding quasi-Frobenius rings and dominant dimension.

Many positive cases are known. Auslander, Ding, and Solberg treated complete local complete intersections in the commutative setting. Huneke and Leuschke proved the conjecture for specified classes including excellent Cohen–Macaulay normal domains containing the rationals. Christensen and Holm showed that Auslander’s condition, a uniform bound on eventual Ext vanishing for each fixed first module, implies the conjecture.

Radical-cube-zero algebras form another important positive class. Work of Huneke, Şega, and Vraciu, Ringel and Zhang, and Zhang and Zhou treats progressively broader versions. Recent results also cover Igusa–Todorov algebras and quantum complete intersections. The new triangular algebra has nonzero fourth radical power, so it does not fall into the radical-cube-zero class.

Earlier examples show why the exact formulation matters. Schulz constructed a nonprojective module without self-extensions using a skew-field setting outside the Artin-algebra framework considered here. His quantum-exterior examples have eventually vanishing self-extensions but retain a nonzero first one. Böhmler and Marczinzik gave a commutative self-injective example with the first two self-extension groups zero and the third nonzero. None meets the all-positive-degree vanishing condition.

The parameter-shifting syzygies in Schulz’s quantum-exterior work are a direct antecedent of the construction. The new manuscripts add two independently scaled actions to remove all positive self-extensions, rather than merely moving them to finitely many degrees.

Recent reductions of Enomoto and Marczinzik connect the universal Auslander–Reiten, Nakayama, and Tachikawa questions. Other work of Chen, Fang, and Xi studies symmetric transfer through endomorphism algebras and related constructions. These implications explain why one sufficiently strong example has several consequences. The present symmetric construction additionally controls negative degrees in a complete resolution; positive Ext vanishing alone would not justify its final transfer.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Both manuscripts are dated 23 September 2026 and work over

k=F2(q,H1,H2),k=\mathbb F_2(q,H_1,H_2),k=F2​(q,H1​,H2​),

where the three displayed variables are algebraically independent. This is a rational-function field, not a finite field.

The triangular and symmetric examples

M1 claims a finite-dimensional algebra Λ\LambdaΛ and a nonprojective finite left module ZZZ with

Ext⁡Λi(Z,Z)=Ext⁡Λi(Z,Λ)=0for every i>0.\operatorname{Ext}^i_\Lambda(Z,Z)=\operatorname{Ext}^i_\Lambda(Z,\Lambda)=0\quad\text{for every }i>0.ExtΛi​(Z,Z)=ExtΛi​(Z,Λ)=0for every i>0.

The module is Gorenstein-projective. The algebra is split with eight simple-module isomorphism classes, meaning its semisimple quotient is k8k^8k8, and its fourth radical power is nonzero. The example therefore claims to refute both Auslander–Reiten and the Gorenstein-projective restriction.

M2 claims a finite-dimensional symmetric algebra AAA and a nonprojective finite module MMM with Ext⁡Ai(M,M)=0\operatorname{Ext}^i_A(M,M)=0ExtAi​(M,M)=0 for every positive iii. This refutes Tachikawa’s second conjecture and also gives a symmetric Auslander–Reiten counterexample.

Both constructions and the stated conclusions persist after every field extension of kkk. Taking an algebraic closure gives examples over an algebraically closed field of characteristic two containing the transcendental parameters. This is not the algebraic closure of a finite field.

Consequences of the symmetric example

For any extension K/kK/kK/k, write AK=K⊗kAA_K=K\otimes_kAAK​=K⊗k​A, MK=K⊗kMM_K=K\otimes_kMMK​=K⊗k​M, and form

ΓK=End⁡AK(AK⊕MK)op.\Gamma_K=\operatorname{End}_{A_K}(A_K\oplus M_K)^{\mathrm{op}}.ΓK​=EndAK​​(AK​⊕MK​)op.

The opposite algebra fixes the left-module convention. M2 claims the following properties:

  • Every term of the minimal injective resolution of ΓK\Gamma_KΓK​ is projective, but its self-injective dimension is infinite. This contradicts the classical Nakayama assertion and the stated Auslander–Gorenstein implication.
  • A nonzero simple module SSS satisfies Ext⁡ΓKi(S,ΓK)=0\operatorname{Ext}^i_{\Gamma_K}(S,\Gamma_K)=0ExtΓK​i​(S,ΓK​)=0 for all i≥0i\ge0i≥0, including Hom in degree zero. This contradicts the generalized and strong Nakayama assertions.
  • There is a projective-injective Wakamatsu tilting module that is not tilting. In this terminology, Wakamatsu tilting permits an infinite exact coresolution with a prescribed Hom-exactness condition; tilting requires a finite one, together with finite projective dimension and self-orthogonality.

The same injective resolution supplies finite modules CnC_nCn​ with

pd⁡ΓKCn=n(n≥1).\operatorname{pd}_{\Gamma_K}C_n=n\quad(n\ge1).pdΓK​​Cn​=n(n≥1).

Thus its little and big left finitistic dimensions are infinite, independently of the complex example in family 198.

Further stated applications use existing results to produce infinitely many distinct one-summand tilting complements for a projective module over ΓKop\Gamma_K^{\mathrm{op}}ΓKop​, and auxiliary symmetric algebras with arbitrarily long idempotent stratifications and associated derived-category decompositions. These are consequences of the main example and established transfer theorems, not additional independent constructions of self-orthogonal modules.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the family refutes a central projectivity criterion and several longstanding conjectures linked to it. The symmetric example is particularly restrictive: even a strong duality between the algebra and its vector-space dual would not force the proposed conclusion.

The common theme is the gap between homological tests and actual projectivity. Vanishing every positive self-extension, and even vanishing every positive extension to the algebra, would still leave a nonprojective module.

The consequences show how this gap propagates. Endomorphism algebras convert a self-orthogonal module into an indefinitely projective injective resolution, failures of detection by Ext, and unbounded finite resolution lengths. The significance comes from this network of precise implications, rather than treating the list of conjectures as unrelated headlines.

6. The main idea

Build a controllable extension algebra

The common starting point is a ten-dimensional algebra CCC with a simple module sss. Its symmetric trivial extension T=C⋉DCT=C\ltimes DCT=C⋉DC, where DDD is vector-space duality, has a claimed self-extension algebra

Ext⁡T∗(s,s)=k[τ],deg⁡τ=3.\operatorname{Ext}^*_T(s,s)=k[\tau],\qquad \deg\tau=3.ExtT∗​(s,s)=k[τ],degτ=3.

Taking two tensor copies gives a module X=s⊗sX=s\otimes sX=s⊗s over the symmetric algebra E=T⊗TE=T\otimes TE=T⊗T, with self-extensions k[τ1,τ2]k[\tau_1,\tau_2]k[τ1​,τ2​], both generators in degree three. This polynomial structure makes the nonzero degrees and the effects of scaling explicit.

The argument works in the stable category, where maps factoring through projective modules are identified with zero. Cones of maps representing τ1\tau_1τ1​ and τ2\tau_2τ2​ act like a Koszul construction that removes most of the polynomial extension structure. The manuscripts track the remaining small collection of stable Hom groups, including negative degrees where needed.

Use two independent twists to remove every positive degree

An automorphism fixes CCC and scales its dual summand by a nonzero parameter HHH. Its action fixes the underlying simple module but rescales a degree-3m3m3m self-extension by H−mH^{-m}H−m.

The construction combines twists with parameters H1,H2H_1,H_2H1​,H2​ through genuine finite bimodule maps. The fact that the maps exist at the bimodule level is important: a map after evaluating on one module would not automatically define a tensor construction for the algebra.

In M1, the comparison on a positive degree reduces to the matrix

(H1−m1H2−m1).\begin{pmatrix}H_1^{-m}&1\\H_2^{-m}&1\end{pmatrix}.(H1−m​H2−m​​11​).

Because H1/H2H_1/H_2H1​/H2​ has infinite multiplicative order, this matrix is invertible for every m>0m>0m>0. The comparison therefore removes positive self-extension classes uniformly over all degrees. In degree zero, a nonzero stable endomorphism survives, certifying nonprojectivity.

A triangular algebra built from EEE and a finite bimodule turns that stable construction into an ordinary finite module. A totally acyclic resolution separately provides the vanishing of Ext into the algebra. The two vanishings have different roles and are both retained.

Add the negative-degree control needed for symmetry

M2 uses a related but different cone and bimodule construction. It obtains a totally acyclic resolution PZP_ZPZ​ such that its complete self-Hom cohomology vanishes for degrees

a>0ora≤−2.a>0\quad\text{or}\quad a\le-2.a>0ora≤−2.

The middle degrees are not simply declared zero. The negative tail is needed because, after passing to the symmetric trivial extension, positive extensions into a dual-tensor term correspond to negative complete-resolution degrees with an index shift.

The transfer forms A=Λ⋉DΛA=\Lambda\ltimes D\LambdaA=Λ⋉DΛ and induces M=A⊗ΛZM=A\otimes_\Lambda ZM=A⊗Λ​Z. The additional negative vanishing makes the induced module self-orthogonal while preserving nonprojectivity. Infinite complexes prove the all-degree statements, but the final algebras, kernels, cokernels, and modules are finite-dimensional.

Finally, the classical endomorphism-algebra correspondence applied to A⊕MA\oplus MA⊕M supplies infinite dominant dimension. Successive cokernels in its projective-injective resolution yield modules with each prescribed finite projective dimension, producing the finitistic-dimension consequence.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Both examples are noncommutative. They do not settle the commutative restriction of the Auslander–Reiten question. Their characteristic-two field and transcendental parameters are also substantive: specialization to arbitrary finite fields or to characteristic zero is not asserted.

All-positive-degree vanishing is essential. Earlier eventual-vanishing or finite-range examples are not equivalent to these claims. Conversely, the degree-zero vanishing in the strong Nakayama consequence applies to its particular simple module over ΓK\Gamma_KΓK​, not to the self-endomorphisms of the original nonzero module.

M1’s eight-simple structural description belongs to its triangular algebra. It should not be transferred to M2’s final symmetric algebra. Similarly, the consequences for ΓK\Gamma_KΓK​ belong to the associated endomorphism algebra, not automatically to AAA itself.

The two manuscripts reproduce the ingredients needed for their respective constructions. They share a starting mechanism, but the symmetric transfer requires extra negative-degree control and is not merely an automatic consequence of M1’s headline.

8. Sources and further reading

Tachikawa’s Quasi-Frobenius Rings and Generalizations develops the classical setting. Schulz’s nonprojective self-extension example and his quantum-exterior work explain important predecessors and their different hypotheses.

Chen and Xi’s theory of self-orthogonal modules, Chen–Fang–Xi’s symmetric and endomorphism-algebra constructions, and Enomoto–Marczinzik’s homological-conjecture reductions describe the implication network.

For positive restricted cases, see Zhang and Zhou’s radical-cube-zero theorem and Xia’s quantum-complete-intersection theorem. The source manuscripts below state the new examples and the precise consequences summarized here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An explicit counterexample to the Auslander-Reiten conjecture (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A counterexample to Tachikawa’s second conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The largest relation counts come from a lex-plus-powers ideal
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 200 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A collection of homogeneous polynomial equations determines how many independent polynomials remain in each degree. It also determines relations among the equations, relations among those relations, and so on. Can a simple monomial model reproduce the first kind of data while maximizing the second?

The Eisenbud–Green–Harris conjecture predicts such a model when the equations contain a regular sequence. Replace that sequence by pure powers of the variables, then arrange the remaining monomials in lexicographic order. The stronger lex-plus-powers conjecture predicts that this same model has at least as many graded syzygies in every position.

Family 200 claims both statements over every characteristic-zero field, for regular sequences of any positive length and arbitrary degrees at least two. One manuscript supplies a division-algebra construction and the Hilbert-function theorem. Its companion transfers entire resolutions to obtain the stronger Betti-number comparison.

2. Background and essential definitions

Count what survives in each degree

Let S=F[x1,…,xn]S=F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]S=F[x1​,…,xn​], with each variable of degree one. A homogeneous ideal III is generated by polynomials whose terms have equal total degree. The quotient splits into finite-dimensional graded pieces, and its Hilbert function is

HS/I(d)=dim⁡F(S/I)d.H_{S/I}(d)=\dim_F(S/I)_d.HS/I​(d)=dimF​(S/I)d​.

It counts independent degree-ddd polynomial classes after imposing the equations.

A sequence f1,…,fcf_1,\ldots,f_cf1​,…,fc​ is regular if multiplication by fif_ifi​ is injective modulo its predecessors. Write their degrees in increasing order as a1≤⋯≤aca_1\le\cdots\le a_ca1​≤⋯≤ac​. Regularity means the equations impose independent codimension in the homological sense; merely having the right number of nonzero equations would not suffice.

When c=nc=nc=n, the quotient by the sequence is finite-dimensional, also called Artinian, with Hilbert series

∏i=1n(1+z+⋯+zai−1).\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1+z+\cdots+z^{a_i-1}).i=1∏n​(1+z+⋯+zai​−1).

The corresponding pure-power ideal is

P=(x1a1,…,xcac).P=(x_1^{a_1},\ldots,x_c^{a_c}).P=(x1a1​​,…,xcac​​).

For full length, monomials outside PPP have exponents in the box 0≤ui<ai0\le u_i<a_i0≤ui​<ai​. This turns polynomial algebra into a finite counting problem.

Lexicographic order and the prescribed model

Fix x1>⋯>xnx_1>\cdots>x_nx1​>⋯>xn​. Among monomials of equal total degree, lexicographic order compares exponents at the first variable where they differ. In two variables, degree-three monomials are ordered

x13>x12x2>x1x22>x23.x_1^3>x_1^2x_2>x_1x_2^2>x_2^3.x13​>x12​x2​>x1​x22​>x23​.

A lex-plus-powers ideal contains PPP and, in each degree, includes the required number of lexicographically greatest monomials outside PPP. The difficult point is that these degree-by-degree choices must fit together under multiplication to form one ideal.

For example, outside (x3,y3)(x^3,y^3)(x3,y3), the allowed degree-three monomials are x2yx^2yx2y and xy2xy^2xy2. If exactly one of them must be removed, the lex rule removes x2yx^2yx2y. The theorem concerns consistency across all degrees, not merely this isolated choice.

Count relations as well as dimensions

A minimal graded free resolution expresses the quotient using free modules with generators of specified degrees. Its graded Betti number

βp,jS(S/I)=dim⁡FTor⁡pS(S/I,F)j\beta_{p,j}^S(S/I)=\dim_F\operatorname{Tor}_p^S(S/I,F)_jβp,jS​(S/I)=dimF​TorpS​(S/I,F)j​

counts generators of internal degree jjj at homological position ppp. Position one records minimal equations; later positions record higher relations. The coefficient field on the right is S/(x1,…,xn)S/(x_1,\ldots,x_n)S/(x1​,…,xn​).

The Hilbert function constrains alternating sums of these numbers but does not determine them individually. Matching Hilbert functions therefore cannot by itself prove the stronger Betti inequalities.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Eisenbud, Green, and Harris proposed the Hilbert-function comparison in work extending Castelnuovo theory, with connections to Cayley–Bacharach questions about how many intersection points force a hypersurface to contain all of them.

Without a prescribed regular sequence, lex ideals already maximize Betti numbers at a fixed Hilbert function by the theorems of Bigatti, Hulett, and Pardue. Prescribed pure powers encode extra information about the equations and should yield a sharper extremal model.

For ideals already containing those powers, Clements–Lindström compression gives the Hilbert-function comparison. The corresponding Betti comparison developed through work of Mermin, Peeva, and Stillman for variable squares, Murai for stable ideals plus powers, and Mermin and Murai for monomial regular sequences over every field. The new manuscripts explicitly credit that monomial comparison as established work.

The harder step is passing from arbitrary polynomial regular sequences to a monomial ideal containing the prescribed powers while retaining the desired invariants. Mermin and Murai isolated a reduction that would preserve the Hilbert function and not decrease any Betti number. M1 claims to obtain precisely that reduction.

Earlier nonmonomial cases include Abedelfatah’s theorem when the forms split into linear factors. Caviglia and Maclagan established Eisenbud–Green–Harris for sufficiently fast-growing degrees, and Caviglia and De Stefani weakened the growth condition. These Hilbert-function results hold over arbitrary fields.

Caviglia and Sammartano obtained characteristic-zero Betti bounds under a related, slightly stronger degree-growth condition. Results for small numbers of quadrics, special liaison configurations, and sufficiently large degrees in bounded comparison ranges supplied further partial progress. Kuzmanovski’s recent asymptotic Betti estimates use a generic initial ideal associated with a lex-plus-powers ideal, rather than asserting the full comparison with that ideal in every degree.

The claimed advance removes the degree-growth, additional-generator, and bounded-degree-range restrictions in characteristic zero. It does not claim the unrestricted positive-characteristic theorem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Both manuscripts are dated 23 September 2026. Let FFF be any characteristic-zero field, 1≤c≤n1\le c\le n1≤c≤n, and

2≤a1≤⋯≤ac.2\le a_1\le\cdots\le a_c.2≤a1​≤⋯≤ac​.

Suppose a homogeneous ideal I⊆SI\subseteq SI⊆S contains a homogeneous regular sequence of these degrees. Form P=(x1a1,…,xcac)P=(x_1^{a_1},\ldots,x_c^{a_c})P=(x1a1​​,…,xcac​​).

M2 claims that the Hilbert function of S/IS/IS/I is realized by a monomial ideal containing PPP, and that the ideal can be chosen lex-plus-powers. M1 claims that this single prescribed ideal JJJ also satisfies

HS/I(d)=HS/J(d)(d≥0),H_{S/I}(d)=H_{S/J}(d)\quad(d\ge0),HS/I​(d)=HS/J​(d)(d≥0),

and

βp,jS(S/I)≤βp,jS(S/J)(p≥0, j∈Z).\beta_{p,j}^S(S/I)\le\beta_{p,j}^S(S/J)\quad(p\ge0,\ j\in\mathbb Z).βp,jS​(S/I)≤βp,jS​(S/J)(p≥0, j∈Z).

No bound is placed on the number or degrees of additional generators of III. The result includes positive-dimensional quotients when c<nc<nc<n and fields that are not algebraically closed.

The foundational construction itself is stated for full regular sequences over C\mathbb CC. Established Artinian reductions of Caviglia–Maclagan and Caviglia–Kummini, together with coefficient-field descent, extend the Hilbert and Betti conclusions to the broader scope above.

Further stated consequences

M2 applies a conditional theorem of Caviglia and Sbarra to bound every graded local-cohomology dimension of S/IS/IS/I by the corresponding one for S/JS/JS/J. Local cohomology measures information supported near the homogeneous maximal ideal. In the Artinian case this reduces to Hilbert-function equality; its additional content concerns positive-dimensional quotients.

It also gives a scheme-theoretic quadratic Cayley–Bacharach consequence. If Ω⊆PFr\Omega\subseteq\mathbb P^r_FΩ⊆PFr​ is a zero-dimensional complete intersection of rrr quadrics, its degree is 2r2^r2r. For a degree-kkk hypersurface XXX, with 1≤k≤r1\le k\le r1≤k≤r,

Ω⊈X⟹deg⁡(Ω∩X)≤2r−2r−k.\Omega\not\subseteq X\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\deg(\Omega\cap X)\le2^r-2^{r-k}.Ω⊆X⟹deg(Ω∩X)≤2r−2r−k.

Degrees mean scheme lengths, so repeated or nonreduced intersection structure is included. Containment of a subscheme of strictly greater length forces containment of all of Ω\OmegaΩ.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, the family resolves two central extremal predictions in graded commutative algebra in characteristic zero.

The Hilbert-function theorem supplies a concrete combinatorial model for every allowed ideal. The stronger theorem says that one model simultaneously bounds all equation and syzygy counts, rather than giving different extremizers for different resolution positions.

This is useful because arbitrary polynomial equations can be difficult to analyze, while monomials in a bounded exponent box are explicit. The model retains the degrees of a regular sequence, giving more information than a general lex bound that ignores those degrees. The geometric corollary shows how such algebraic control returns to questions about forced containment of intersections.

6. The main idea

Enlarge the coefficients to reorganize the equations

M2 constructs an extension field k/Ck/\mathbb Ck/C and a finite-dimensional central division algebra Δ\DeltaΔ over kkk. A division algebra is allowed to be noncommutative, but every nonzero element is invertible. The polynomial variables themselves remain central.

Inside Δ[x1,…,xn]\Delta[x_1,\ldots,x_n]Δ[x1​,…,xn​], it constructs commuting degree-one forms t1,…,tnt_1,\ldots,t_nt1​,…,tn​ satisfying triangular power identities adapted to the original fif_ifi​. Their powers reproduce fif_ifi​, up to earlier equations and later forms. Crucially, all ordered monomials in the tit_iti​ form a left-Δ\DeltaΔ basis of the entire polynomial algebra, not just its finite complete-intersection quotient.

The forms commute with one another, although their individual coefficients need not. Left coefficients and right multiplication by the forms are therefore kept distinct throughout the argument.

The construction combines powers of linear forms in stages. Matrix pencils arising from curves implement binary power addition. Equivariant descent first yields a central simple algebra; an additional index-divisibility argument is needed to ensure it is division. A matrix representation alone would not provide the required coefficient property.

Extract an ordinary monomial ideal

Extend III to the division-coefficient algebra and expand in the ordered ttt-basis. At each leading monomial position, the allowable coefficients form a left ideal of Δ\DeltaΔ. Since Δ\DeltaΔ is division, that coefficient space is either zero or all of Δ\DeltaΔ.

The nonzero positions therefore define an ordinary monomial ideal. The triangular identities ensure that it contains the prescribed pure powers. Counting basis positions gives the Hilbert-function match. Compression then supplies the lex-plus-powers arrangement.

This explains the role of division coefficients: they convert potentially complicated leading coefficient spaces into an all-or-nothing monomial pattern.

Carry the whole resolution through the same construction

M1 uses the stronger full-basis assertion. Introduce a polynomial ring whose variables act on the right by the tit_iti​. The large coefficient algebra is free both over the original polynomial ring and over this new ring, with a common finite multiplicity factor dim⁡kΔ\dim_k\Deltadimk​Δ.

Transferring a minimal resolution multiplies every Betti number by that same factor. A filtered Koszul-complex comparison then passes to the leading monomial ideal without decreasing the relevant homology dimensions. Cancelling the common factor gives a Hilbert-matching monomial ideal with no smaller Betti numbers.

The remaining comparison is the established monomial lex-plus-powers step, which M1 also presents. It stabilizes monomials within the exponent box using allowed transfers from later variables to earlier ones. Degreewise lex compression controls bounded shadows, the multiples that stay inside the box, ensuring the result remains an ideal.

For Betti numbers, splitting according to the last variable leaves only endpoint slices contributing nonzero differential ranks. Their rank comparison, together with equal dimensions of the Koszul terms, gives the desired homology inequalities. This keeps internal degrees separate and yields one ideal bounding every βp,j\beta_{p,j}βp,j​.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Characteristic zero is part of the general claim. Some earlier monomial and fast-degree results hold over every field, but that does not extend these new arbitrary-sequence conclusions to positive characteristic.

The regular sequence has positive length, degrees at least two, and the ideal is homogeneous in a standard graded polynomial ring. The no-prescribed-sequence case is already the classical lex theorem. The manuscripts do not claim that the original ideal is isomorphic to, or has the same resolution as, its lex-plus-powers model.

Equality of Hilbert functions and upper bounds on Betti numbers are different assertions. The full coefficient basis and resolution transfer are necessary parts of the stronger claim; a basis of the Artinian quotient alone would not justify it.

The two manuscripts are dependent: M1 imports M2’s commuting-form construction, then supplies the resolution-level argument. Questions about characteristic-positive analogues, equality cases, and effective computation of the auxiliary division construction remain separate from the stated extremal theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

Eisenbud, Green, and Harris’s Higher Castelnuovo theory and Cayley–Bacharach account give the geometric origins. The Clements–Lindström theorem supplies the monomial compression background.

Mermin and Murai’s pure-powers Betti theorem establishes the earlier monomial comparison. Caviglia and De Stefani’s degree-growth result and Caviglia–Sammartano’s lex-plus-powers theorem describe important nonmonomial cases.

Caviglia and Kummini’s Hilbert and Betti embedding work provides the reduction used to pass beyond Artinian quotients. The two pinned sources below give the claimed division-coefficient construction and its stronger resolution consequence.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Artinian Lex-Plus-Powers Betti Theorem (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Commuting Division-Coefficient Forms and the Artinian Eisenbud–Green–Harris Conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Two algebraic generators can produce an infinite-dimensional division ring
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 201 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

For ordinary fields, adjoining finitely many algebraic elements produces a finite-dimensional extension. If xxx and yyy each satisfy polynomial equations, their powers can be reduced, and commutativity lets every expression be rearranged into a bounded list of monomials.

What happens when multiplication is not commutative, but division by every nonzero element remains possible? Kurosh’s division-ring problem asks whether algebraicity over the center still forces every finitely generated division subring to be finite-dimensional over that center.

Family 201 claims a negative answer. It constructs a countable characteristic-zero division ring generated by just two elements as an algebra over its center. Every element satisfies a polynomial over that center, but the whole ring has infinite dimension over it.

2. Background and essential definitions

Division rings and their centers

A division ring is a ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. Unlike a field, its multiplication need not commute. The familiar quaternions are a finite-dimensional example over the real numbers.

The center F=Z(D)F=Z(D)F=Z(D) consists of elements commuting with every element of DDD. It is an ordinary commutative field. The division ring DDD is algebraic over FFF if every a∈Da\in Da∈D satisfies some nonzero polynomial

c0+c1a+⋯+cnan=0,ci∈F.c_0+c_1a+\cdots+c_na^n=0,\qquad c_i\in F.c0​+c1​a+⋯+cn​an=0,ci​∈F.

The polynomial and its degree may depend on aaa. Algebraicity does not include a common degree bound.

For a subset S⊆DS\subseteq DS⊆D, write F[S]F[S]F[S] for the algebra generated by FFF and SSS: finite sums of finite products. Write F(S)F(S)F(S) for the division subring generated by them, allowing inverses as well. Algebra generation is the stronger finiteness requirement.

The ring is locally finite over its center if

[F(S):F]<∞for every finite subset S⊆D.[F(S):F]<\infty\quad\text{for every finite subset }S\subseteq D.[F(S):F]<∞for every finite subset S⊆D.

Here brackets denote vector-space dimension. The word “locally” refers to finite sets of generators, not to a topology.

Why the field argument breaks

In a commutative algebra, polynomial relations for xxx and yyy reduce every monomial to xiyjx^iy^jxiyj with bounded exponents. In a noncommutative algebra, words such as xyx2yxyxyx^2yxyxyx2yxy cannot generally be rearranged into that form. Bounding individual powers does not immediately bound alternating words.

The hypothesis that every element is algebraic, including all these words and their sums, is much stronger than algebraicity of the generators alone. The difficulty is imposing that hypothesis without eliminating all the remaining infinite-dimensional freedom.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kurosh formulated the question in 1941 in connection with Burnside-type finiteness problems for groups. His original division-ring formulation asks whether algebraicity and finite algebra generation over a central subfield force finite dimension. The chosen central subfield need not be the full center.

A broader question for arbitrary associative algebras has a different answer and mechanism. Golod’s construction, using Golod–Shafarevich estimates, provides finitely generated infinite-dimensional nil algebras. Their unitizations are algebraic but contain nonzero nilpotents. A division ring cannot contain a nonzero nilpotent, so those counterexamples do not settle Kurosh’s division-ring problem.

Positive results show why degree restrictions matter. Jacobson’s bounded-degree theorem leads to a polynomial identity, and Kaplansky’s theorem makes algebraic polynomial-identity algebras locally finite. A polynomial identity is one noncommutative polynomial vanishing under every substitution, unlike an element-specific algebraic equation.

Bell, Drensky, and Sharifi proved a stronger bounded-degree result in a related setting: if elements satisfy polynomial relations of uniformly bounded degree ddd with coefficients on the left in a possibly noncentral subfield, the division ring has dimension at most d2d^2d2 over its center. The new construction deliberately allows unbounded element-dependent degrees.

Amitsur proved that finite algebra generation over an uncountable central field forces algebraicity. That is a theorem about obtaining algebraicity, not a conclusion that the division ring is locally finite. Countability serves another purpose in the present construction: it lets every polynomial expression be put into a schedule.

Recent work of Goodearl and Letzter studies failure of finite algebra generation for classes of transcendental skew fields, explicitly distinguishing that question from the algebraic Kurosh problem. The claimed example here has the opposite combination: finite algebra generation together with algebraicity, yet infinite central dimension.

The technical background includes cyclic and symbol division algebras, trace identities for noncommuting words, and the interpretation of inner derivations as infinitesimal conjugations. The new manuscript combines these tools in a lifting theorem designed to impose one relation while preserving room for further enlargement.

4. What the new manuscripts claim
