The manuscript, dated 23 September 2026, claims a countable division ring DDD of characteristic zero, with actual center F=Z(D)F=Z(D)F=Z(D), and elements x,y∈Dx,y\in Dx,y∈D satisfying

D=F[x,y]=F(x,y),[D:F]=∞,D=F[x,y]=F(x,y),\qquad [D:F]=\infty,D=F[x,y]=F(x,y),[D:F]=∞,

while every element of DDD is algebraic over FFF.

The same pair {x,y}\{x,y\}{x,y} therefore witnesses failure of local finiteness. The theorem asserts algebra generation, not only division generation, and infinite dimension over the actual center, not merely over a smaller field chosen during the construction.

The center is not prescribed in advance. The proof first builds an algebraic division ring over a countable central coefficient field, then separately shows that enlarging to the full center does not make its dimension finite.

The principal intermediate claim is a lifting theorem for formal series in two noncommuting variables over a finite-dimensional central division algebra. It makes one prescribed series algebraic over a larger countable central field while increasing the division algebra’s degree, preserving all earlier polynomial identities, restoring generation, and preserving two independent deformation directions.

The successive division algebras are not asserted to embed into one another. The final construction uses an ultraproduct to retain the compatible identities rather than treating them as an increasing union of division rings.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. If correct, this resolves a central noncommutative finiteness problem negatively in a particularly strong form: countable, characteristic zero, and generated by two elements as an algebra over the center.

The contrast with fields is precise. Algebraicity controls each element separately, but in a division ring that local control would not force a finite common vector-space description, even with only two algebra generators.

The actual-center conclusion is especially important. A division algebra can be infinite-dimensional over a small central subfield for elementary reasons while remaining finite-dimensional over its center. The manuscript explicitly excludes that explanation, so the result addresses the intrinsic noncommutative structure.

6. The main idea

Impose one algebraic relation without exhausting freedom

The construction proceeds through finite-dimensional central division algebras with increasingly large degrees. Formal series in two noncommuting variables record possible deformations of the chosen generators.

At each stage, the constant terms generate the current algebra. Two linear coefficients remain independent after quotienting out changes obtainable by conjugation. Infinitesimal conjugation changes an element aaa by a commutator [T,a]=Ta−aT[T,a]=Ta-aT[T,a]=Ta−aT; directions of this form do not represent genuinely new generator freedom.

Given one expression www, the lifting theorem changes the formal input so that www satisfies an algebraic equation, while keeping both independent directions and increasing the coefficient algebra’s degree. Losing either generation or the available deformation freedom could prevent the next stage from working.

Use matrix responses to solve the formal equations

After extending scalars to split the coefficient division algebra into matrices, the proof studies generic block inputs. Changing a diagonal block gives one type of eigenvalue response; adding an arrow to another block and a return arrow gives a paired response.

The manuscript identifies relations among these responses and transfers each first unsolved word coefficient into the same space. Repeated blocks and auxiliary comparison blocks distinguish local relations from common relations across blocks. Trace identities impose cyclic sums, reflecting the fact that traces do not change when a product is cyclically rotated.

An eleven-block arrangement with two kinds of connections supplies corrections whose obstructions are exactly those cyclic relations. The formal equation is solved one word length at a time through finite affine linear systems.

These matrix calculations must then be realized inside a division algebra. A cyclic-algebra construction supplies that realization, while a translation of the formal input restores generation and the two independent directions. Finally, only countably many scalar coefficients are retained, returning to a countable center for the next step.

This description separates the roles: spectral calculations impose the relation, division realization preserves the ring type, and translation restores the hypotheses required to iterate.

Schedule all expressions and pass to a limit

Every coefficient field at a finite stage is countable, so its polynomial expressions in two noncommuting generators can be enumerated. A diagonal schedule ensures that each expression with coefficients from any stage eventually receives a nonzero algebraic relation. Later stages preserve it.

The fields embed successively, but the division algebras need not. A nonprincipal ultraproduct supplies a common ambient division ring. Informally, it identifies sequences that agree on an ultrafilter-large set of stages, retaining every identity that holds from some point onward.

Let k∞k_\inftyk∞​ be the union of the central fields and form the two-generated subalgebra R=k∞[x,y]R=k_\infty[x,y]R=k∞​[x,y] inside that ultraproduct. Every element of RRR is algebraic by the schedule.

This already makes RRR a division ring. If r≠0r\ne0r=0 has a least-degree relation, its constant coefficient is nonzero. Rearranging gives

r−1=−c0−1(c1+c2r+⋯+cnrn−1)∈R.r^{-1}=-c_0^{-1}(c_1+c_2r+\cdots+c_nr^{n-1})\in R.r−1=−c0−1​(c1​+c2​r+⋯+cn​rn−1)∈R.

Thus adjoining inverses adds nothing. Countability follows from the countable coefficient field and finite algebra generation.

Prove that the full center cannot absorb the growth

At the finite stages, generator words span division algebras of unbounded dimension. For each fixed word-length bound, an ultrafilter selects a fixed finite list that remains linearly independent at sufficiently many stages. These lists show [R:k∞]=∞[R:k_\infty]=\infty[R:k∞​]=∞.

Now suppose RRR were finite-dimensional over its full center FFF. Choose a finite FFF-basis and record its multiplication table and the coordinates of x,yx,yx,y. Only finitely many elements of FFF occur in those data. Since every element of FFF is algebraic over k∞k_\inftyk∞​, they generate a finite field extension E/k∞E/k_\inftyE/k∞​.

The EEE-span of the chosen basis is closed under multiplication and contains both generators. It would contain all of RRR, making RRR finite-dimensional over k∞k_\inftyk∞​, a contradiction. This separate descent argument supplies the actual-center conclusion.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The annihilating polynomial is allowed to vary with the element, with no uniform degree bound. This is compatible with the known positive bounded-degree theorems.

The construction does not prescribe the center or give a small explicit multiplication table for the infinite-dimensional ring. Its ultraproduct is an existence device; the selected two-generated subalgebra is countable even though the ambient ultraproduct can be much larger.

The result is not a claim about commutative fields, where finite algebra generation by algebraic elements still gives finite dimension. Nor does it rely on nilpotents, which are excluded in a division ring.

Determining what additional structural or effective conditions restore local finiteness remains a separate question. The claimed example shows that algebraicity, characteristic zero, and two algebra generators alone would not suffice.

8. Sources and further reading

Kurosh’s Ringtheoretische Probleme, die mit dem Burnsideschen Problem über periodische Gruppen in Zusammenhang stehen (1941) formulates the problem. Jacobson’s Le problème de Kurosch (Bourbaki, 1952) describes early positive theory, while Golod’s 1964 nil-algebra construction addresses the broader algebra question.

Bell, Drensky, and Sharifi’s bounded-degree theorem gives a useful contrast. Amitsur’s Algebras over infinite fields (1956) concerns algebraicity under finite generation, and Goodearl–Letzter’s skew-field work treats a distinct transcendental setting.

Gille and Szamuely’s Central Simple Algebras and Galois Cohomology explains cyclic division algebras. Keisler’s The ultraproduct construction (2010) supplies background on the limiting device used in the manuscript below.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Counterexample to Kurosh’s Division-Ring Problem (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Counting modular representations from local weights
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 202 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A finite group describes a collection of symmetries. A representation turns those abstract symmetries into matrices, making linear algebra available. Over the complex numbers, every representation splits into irreducible pieces. Over a field of prime characteristic, that comfortable picture can fail: a representation may contain an invariant subspace without having an invariant complementary subspace.

The irreducible pieces still exist, but their organization becomes much more subtle. Can their number be recovered from smaller groups associated with the prime? Alperin’s weight conjecture predicts that it can. Its blockwise version makes a separate prediction for each natural component, or block, of the representation theory.

Family 202 contains one manuscript, dated 23 September 2026. It claims the numerical blockwise conjecture for every finite group and every prime. The surprising feature of its approach is that a problem about counting representations is translated into a divisibility problem for covers of algebraic curves.

2. Background and essential definitions

Representations in characteristic p

Fix a finite group GGG, a prime ppp, and an algebraically closed field kkk of characteristic ppp. The group algebra kGkGkG consists of formal sums ∑g∈Gagg\sum_{g\in G}a_g g∑g∈G​ag​g, with multiplication extended from the group law. A representation of GGG over kkk is the same thing as a module over kGkGkG.

A nonzero module is simple if its only submodules are itself and zero. The simple modules are the irreducible representations being counted. Their characters in modular representation theory are called irreducible Brauer characters. For the counting question, one can think of a Brauer character as a label for a simple module; its precise evaluation uses group elements whose orders are prime to ppp.

A block is an indecomposable direct factor of the algebra. More explicitly, a primitive central idempotent eee, satisfying e2=ee^2=ee2=e, determines the factor kGekGekGe. Centrality ensures that every simple module belongs to exactly one block. Write l(B)l(B)l(B) for the number of simple modules in block BBB.

The local objects called weights

A ppp-subgroup QQQ has order a power of ppp; the trivial subgroup is allowed. Its normalizer is

NG(Q)={g∈G:gQg−1=Q}.N_G(Q)=\{g\in G:gQg^{-1}=Q\}.NG​(Q)={g∈G:gQg−1=Q}.

The quotient NG(Q)/QN_G(Q)/QNG​(Q)/Q records symmetries preserving QQQ, after symmetries already inside QQQ have been removed.

For a positive integer aaa, let apa_pap​ denote the largest power of ppp dividing it. A weight is a pair (Q,φ)(Q,\varphi)(Q,φ), where φ\varphiφ is an ordinary irreducible character of NG(Q)/QN_G(Q)/QNG​(Q)/Q satisfying

φ(1)p=∣NG(Q)/Q∣p.\varphi(1)_p=|N_G(Q)/Q|_p.φ(1)p​=∣NG​(Q)/Q∣p​.

Here an ordinary character comes from characteristic-zero representation theory, and φ(1)\varphi(1)φ(1) is the representation’s dimension. This equality is the defect-zero condition. It singles out local representations whose dimensions absorb the entire ppp-part of the quotient’s order.

Conjugating both the subgroup and its character produces an equivalent weight. We therefore count simultaneous GGG-conjugacy classes, not every subgroup embedding separately. A standard procedure, Brauer block induction, assigns each weight to a block of GGG. Let Wp(B)W_p(B)Wp​(B) denote the resulting set of classes assigned to BBB.

This assignment is important: simply adding up weights of normalizers without tracking their blocks would give a weaker, unrefined counting question.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The local viewpoint grows out of Richard Brauer’s modular representation theory. A block has an associated defect group, a ppp-subgroup measuring how far its structure is from the particularly simple defect-zero case. Brauer correspondence relates a block to a distinguished block in the normalizer of its defect group. These constructions suggested that substantial information about a large group should already be visible in its local subgroups.

Alperin formulated the weight conjecture at the 1986 Arcata conference; the account appeared in 1987. It extended a notion of weights arising for finite groups of Lie type to arbitrary finite groups. Alperin and Fong subsequently established major families of cases, including symmetric groups and finite general linear groups in odd modular characteristic.

Knörr and Robinson supplied a different organizing language in 1989: alternating sums over chains of ppp-subgroups. This resembles inclusion–exclusion. Counting contributions with alternating signs can remove overlapping local information and expose exactly the discrepancy that the conjecture says should vanish.

Later reduction theorems shifted much of the work to finite simple groups. Navarro and Tiep developed a reduction for the non-blockwise conjecture; Späth obtained a blockwise reduction. Such reductions do not themselves prove the conjecture: the relevant conditions for the simple groups, including compatibility with automorphisms, still have to be established.

The manuscript cites subsequent progress for special linear and special unitary groups, groups with abelian Sylow 333-subgroups, certain exceptional groups, and inertial blocks. These results illustrate both the breadth of the evidence and the technical work needed to pass from one family to another.

The proposed approach takes a different route. It uses subgroup-chain cancellation but then moves to geometry, rather than completing a classification-based list of inductive conditions. Its geometric ingredients have their own history: Frobenius’s character formulas count group homomorphisms from surface groups; period–index theory constructs curves with restricted divisor degrees; Tate’s genus-change theory controls inseparable maps in positive characteristic. The new manuscript claims to combine suitably strengthened versions of these tools into a uniform divisibility statement.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The central assertion is

l(B)=∣Wp(B)∣ l(B)=|W_p(B)|l(B)=∣Wp​(B)∣

for every prime ppp, every finite group GGG, and every ppp-block BBB. There are no stated restrictions on the defect groups or the type of finite group. Weights with Q=1Q=1Q=1 are included.

This is an equality of cardinalities. It does not assert a preferred bijection between the two sets, and it does not require such a bijection to respect every automorphism or Galois action. These stronger compatibility questions should be distinguished from the numerical theorem.

The paper also supplies consequences previously known to follow from the conjecture. If DDD is a defect group of BBB, and bbb is its Brauer correspondent in NG(D)N_G(D)NG​(D), then

l(B)≥l(b),D abelian ⟹ l(B)=l(b). l(B)\geq l(b),\qquad D\text{ abelian}\ \Longrightarrow\ l(B)=l(b).l(B)≥l(b),D abelian ⟹ l(B)=l(b).

For a Sylow ppp-subgroup PPP, it obtains a corresponding inequality between the total numbers of irreducible Brauer characters of GGG and NG(P)N_G(P)NG​(P). Some special cases of these consequences were already theorems; their significance here is the removal of the remaining restrictions through the claimed general result.

A final functorial identity packages alternating local contributions more richly. The manuscript credits an existing theorem of Boltje, Bouc and Yılmaz for reducing that identity to the numerical conjecture. It is therefore presented as a consequence using earlier machinery, rather than as an independently invented reformulation.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The score reflects a claimed resolution of a central local–global conjecture in modular representation theory, with no restriction on finite groups or primes.

An equality of counts may look modest beside a classification of all representations. Yet such equalities constrain the possible structures of blocks and reveal which local objects contain the right amount of information. They provide tests and inputs for more refined conjectures, even when they do not construct the representations individually.

The method would also be notable. A numerical statement about finite-dimensional algebras is linked to arithmetic properties of curves over carefully chosen fields. The value lies both in the headline conjecture and in a proposed geometric mechanism capable of forcing exact integer identities.

This importance assessment concerns mathematical significance if the claims hold. It does not measure how explicit the resulting correspondence is: the theorem is numerical, and the geometric proof is not offered as a practical enumeration algorithm.

6. The main idea

Turn a discrepancy into tuple counts

The algebraic reduction starts with the difference between the desired local and global counts. Alternating sums over subgroup chains cancel repeated contributions. Calculations in group algebras then express the remaining discrepancy through traces of powers of central elements.

Expanding a trace can turn an algebraic expression into a count of tuples. The tuples here lie in a finite group JJJ with no nontrivial normal ppp-subgroup. Write this condition as Op(J)=1O_p(J)=1Op​(J)=1. For n=psn=p^sn=ps, the tuples have the form (x,y,u1,…,un)(x,y,u_1,\ldots,u_n)(x,y,u1​,…,un​) and satisfy

[x,y]u1⋯un=1,⟨x,y,u1,…,un⟩=J.[x,y]u_1\cdots u_n=1,\qquad\langle x,y,u_1,\ldots,u_n\rangle=J.[x,y]u1​⋯un​=1,⟨x,y,u1​,…,un​⟩=J.

The commutator is [x,y]=xyx−1y−1[x,y]=xyx^{-1}y^{-1}[x,y]=xyx−1y−1. Each uiu_iui​ has order divisible by ppp. Tuples are identified by simultaneous inner conjugation. Their positions remain ordered, even when a multiset of conjugacy classes is prescribed.

The target is strong divisibility: for each fixed hhh, all the relevant counts should be divisible by php^hph once sss is sufficiently large. Crucially, the threshold must work uniformly over the prescribed multisets. Otherwise an increasing number of uncontrolled terms could spoil the trace argument.

Interpret tuples as covers

The displayed relation is the fundamental-group relation for a punctured surface of genus one. The generating condition makes the associated cover connected. Thus the tuples can be interpreted as monodromy descriptions of connected covers, with group JJJ, of a punctured genus-one curve.

The paper constructs a curve in characteristic ppp whose divisor degrees are all divisible by the large power psp^sps. A divisor is a finite integer combination of points, with degrees accounting for their fields of definition. This divisibility is called a large index.

At the same time, the marked points vary independently in the relevant field-differential directions. These are differentials of the field parameters, not many independent regular differentials on a single genus-one curve. The distinction matters because a genus-one curve has only a one-dimensional space of regular differentials.

Exclude small orbits

After lifting to characteristic zero, a Galois group acts on the finite collection of covers. A Sylow ppp-subgroup partitions that collection into orbits whose sizes are powers of ppp. If every orbit has size at least php^hph, then the total number is divisible by php^hph.

The manuscript therefore rules out a small orbit. Such an orbit would lead, through a descent argument, to a cover defined over a field extension with small ppp-part in its degree. Reduction back to characteristic ppp then produces curves whose genera and ramification have to satisfy competing constraints.

One key device upgrades an approximate inequality to an exact one. A geometric error is bounded independently of sss, while the quantity carrying that error is divisible by an increasingly large power of ppp. Once the divisibility step is larger than the possible negative error, a negative value becomes impossible.

The resulting equalities, together with connectedness of a suitable model, force a nontrivial normal ppp-subgroup of JJJ. This contradicts Op(J)=1O_p(J)=1Op​(J)=1. All orbits must therefore be large, giving the required divisibility. The initial algebraic reduction converts that divisibility back into the blockwise counting equality.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The asserted scope is the full numerical blockwise conjecture. The coefficient field is algebraically closed of characteristic ppp; the paper explains why extending such fields does not change the counts or block assignments. Auxiliary fields used to construct curves are separate from these representation-theoretic coefficient fields.

The result does not classify simple modules, give their dimensions, or provide an efficient way to list them. Nor does equality of two finite cardinalities automatically supply a canonical or equivariant matching. Refined local–global questions retain content beyond this numerical conclusion.

The geometric argument also relies on more than a familiar character formula for one surface. Uniformity as the number of punctures grows, descent with the specified group action, and control of inseparable reduction are essential parts of the claimed advance. Omitting them would obscure what the manuscript actually contributes.

A natural further question is how broadly its divisibility mechanism can be used in other representation-theoretic counting problems. The exposition here reports the stated theorem and its mechanism; it does not resolve those extensions.

8. Sources and further reading

For the original problem, see J. L. Alperin, Weights for finite groups, Proceedings of Symposia in Pure Mathematics 47 (1987), 369–379. Alperin and Fong, Weights for symmetric and general linear groups, Journal of Algebra 131 (1990), 2–22, records early large-family cases.

Knörr and Robinson, Some remarks on a conjecture of Alperin, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 39 (1989), 48–60, supplies the subgroup-chain viewpoint. Späth, A reduction theorem for the blockwise Alperin weight conjecture, Journal of Group Theory 16 (2013), 159–220, represents the simple-group reduction approach.

For the functorial consequence, see Boltje, Bouc and Yılmaz, On Alperin’s conjecture and functorial equivalence of blocks, Mathematische Zeitschrift 312 (2026), Article 112. The source manuscript below contains the precise block-assignment convention and geometric statements.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Blockwise Alperin Weight Conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Bounded local defect leaves only finitely many block theories
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 203 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A finite group can be enormous while a particular part of its modular representation theory has only a small local obstruction. Does bounding that obstruction leave only finitely many genuinely different representation theories?

Donovan’s conjecture makes this precise for blocks of finite group algebras. The local datum is a defect group, a finite group of prime-power order. The desired conclusion is finiteness up to Morita equivalence, meaning equivalence of entire module categories, not just equality of the number of irreducible representations.

Family 203 contains two manuscripts. M1, dated 24 September 2026, claims the conjecture over every fixed algebraically closed field of positive characteristic. M2, dated 25 September, claims an integral version over Witt vectors and then over each fixed complete discrete valuation ring of mixed characteristic with algebraically closed residue field. Both include nonabelian defect groups and the prime 222.

2. Background and essential definitions

Blocks and their local size

Fix a prime ppp, a finite group GGG, and an algebraically closed field KKK of characteristic ppp. The group algebra KGKGKG consists of finite formal linear combinations of group elements. Its modules are representations of GGG over KKK.

A primitive central idempotent bbb selects an indecomposable algebra factor KGbKGbKGb, called a block. Every simple module belongs to one block. A defect group DDD is a ppp-subgroup associated with the block, determined up to conjugacy. It measures local modular complexity. Defect zero is the simplest situation; larger defect groups allow more complicated extensions between representations.

The size of DDD does not bound the size of GGG. That is why the conjecture is a genuine uniformity assertion: arbitrarily large ambient groups are allowed.

Equivalence of representation theories

Two KKK-algebras are KKK-linearly Morita equivalent when their module categories are equivalent by a functor respecting scalar multiplication. For example, KKK and the matrix algebra Mn(K)M_n(K)Mn​(K) are Morita equivalent for every positive integer nnn. Their algebra dimensions differ, but the module theories differ only by matrix packaging.

A basic algebra removes these redundant matrix multiplicities. Over an algebraically closed field, it represents the same Morita class with one copy of each simple type and with simple modules of dimension one.

The Cartan matrix (cij)(c_{ij})(cij​) records how often the iii-th simple module occurs among the composition factors of the projective cover of the jjj-th simple module. A projective cover is a minimal projective module mapping onto that simple module. For a basic algebra AAA,

dim⁡KA=∑i,jcij.\dim_K A=\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}.dimK​A=i,j∑​cij​.

Thus Cartan bounds control a concrete size associated with the representation theory, even though the original group algebra may be huge.

What the integral version remembers

A complete discrete valuation ring RRR has a maximal ideal generated by one element, called a uniformizer, and permits convergent expansions in its powers. Mixed characteristic means that RRR has characteristic zero while its residue field R/mR/\mathfrak mR/m has characteristic ppp. The ppp-adic integers are the basic model, although their residue field is not algebraically closed.

Here the initial ring is W(F‾p)W(\overline{\mathbb F}_p)W(Fp​), the Witt-vector ring of the algebraic closure of the prime field. An integral block RGbRGbRGb retains information about modules and lattices over RRR, not merely their reductions modulo m\mathfrak mm. Consequently, integral Morita finiteness is stronger than finiteness of the reduced blocks.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The problem is attributed to Peter Donovan and appears in Alperin’s 1980 discussion of local representation theory. It builds on Brauer’s questions about bounding Cartan invariants in terms of defect groups.

Early progress often used the structure of particular group families. Scopes proved finiteness for symmetric-group blocks through combinatorial reductions. Kessar treated related double covers. Jost developed Morita reductions for general linear groups, and Hiss and Kessar extended the reduction methods to classical groups. These results already addressed substantial uniformity in rank and field size; the general theorem is not the first instance where those parameters can be unbounded.

A second line of work clarified what finiteness actually requires. Bounded Cartan matrices give bounded dimensions of basic algebras, but their multiplication constants could still vary through an infinite field. Hiss emphasized this rationality issue. Kessar separated Donovan finiteness into size control and control of Morita–Frobenius numbers, which measure how many coefficient-Frobenius iterations are needed to recover the same Morita class.

For specific defect groups, the manuscripts cite results for abelian 222-groups, several extraspecial groups, Suzuki 222-groups, and quaternion defect groups. Eaton, Eisele and Livesey developed an integral finiteness criterion combining bounded defect, bounded Cartan data and bounded integral Morita–Frobenius number. Their work also established integral finiteness for abelian 222-groups.

Passing from simple-group components to arbitrary groups introduces another difficulty: extensions carry multiplication data. Külshammer’s crossed-product methods and Eisele’s integral work supplied a framework for retaining these data. Farrell and Kessar obtained uniform rationality bounds for quasisimple blocks, but such bounds alone do not determine how the blocks fit into arbitrary extensions.

The two new manuscripts claim to supply the missing uniform estimates and compatible extension comparisons, then to strengthen the comparison over the integral coefficient ring itself.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: finiteness over a fixed field

Fix ppp, an algebraically closed field KKK of characteristic ppp, and an integer M≥1M\geq1M≥1. M1 asserts that

{KGb: G finite, ∣Db∣≤M}/Morita equivalence over K\{KGb:\ G\text{ finite},\ |D_b|\leq M\}\big/\text{Morita equivalence over }K{KGb: G finite, ∣Db​∣≤M}/Morita equivalence over K

is a finite set. Here DbD_bDb​ denotes a defect group of the block. Neither the order of GGG nor the dimensions of its simple representations are bounded in advance.

Fixing a particular defect group and bounding defect-group order give equivalent finiteness formulations, because only finitely many groups have order at most MMM. The field is fixed before the blocks vary.

The resulting finite list also bounds Cartan entries, Loewy lengths of basic algebras, and extension-space dimensions between simple modules in each fixed degree. The Loewy length counts how many successive powers of the radical are required to reach zero.

M2: finiteness over fixed integral coefficients

M2 first asserts the analogous finiteness of O\mathcal OO-linear Morita classes for

O=W(F‾p).\mathcal O=W(\overline{\mathbb F}_p).O=W(Fp​).

It then extends the conclusion to each fixed complete discrete valuation ring RRR of characteristic zero with algebraically closed residue field of characteristic ppp. Ramified rings are included: the uniformizer need not be ppp. No assumption that the fraction field splits all the finite groups is imposed.

M2 depends on M1’s field theorem for Cartan bounds and on its specified integral comparison constructions. M1 is independent of the integral conclusion. This order matters: reduction of M2 later recovers a field statement, but that recovery is not the premise used to prove M1.

Both papers also use coefficient and block-comparison material from the manuscript in family 202; this should not be confused with deriving Donovan finiteness from the numerical Alperin weight equality alone.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. A general Donovan theorem would establish a central finiteness principle for modular representation theory: a bounded local defect permits only finitely many module-category types, even as the ambient finite group grows without bound.

This is stronger than bounding a list of numerical invariants separately. A finite Morita list controls all categorical information preserved by those equivalences, including systems of extension groups. The integral version retains additional arithmetic information that disappears after passing to a field.

The proposed proof also separates two common sources of uncontrolled variation: the size of a mathematical object and the coefficients needed to define it. This distinction has a broader lesson. A family of small multiplication tables can still be infinite if their entries wander through an infinite field.

The rating concerns the scope and consequences of the claimed finiteness, not an explicit classification. Neither manuscript’s headline theorem supplies a short catalogue for every prescribed defect group.

6. The main idea

Bound both size and arithmetic variation

Over F‾p\overline{\mathbb F}_pFp​, every individual finite multiplication table is defined over some finite field. The difficulty is bounding that field uniformly. If both the dimension and the finite field of definition are bounded, there are only finitely many possible tables.

M1 first attacks Cartan bounds for quasisimple groups, the building blocks closely related to finite simple groups. In groups of Lie type, it constructs projective characters using geometric objects on spaces of pairs of flags. A flag is a nested sequence of vector subspaces. The estimates count projective multiplicities rather than raw vector-space dimensions, so large finite tori do not automatically destroy the bounds.

Rank requires separate treatment. Combinatorial moves on character labels transport cones of projective characters through classical groups. A cone here consists of nonnegative linear combinations of the relevant projective characters. Most moves preserve the needed data exactly after normalization; controlled errors in the remaining moves are summable. Determinant and volume estimates then bound the columns encoding projective multiplicities.

These moves need not themselves be Morita equivalences. Their immediate purpose is to transport a numerical estimate. Special endpoint configurations are handled by modular Harish–Chandra induction, with bounds depending on a weight parameter rather than the potentially unbounded rank.

Keep the multiplication in group extensions

Suppose a larger algebra is assembled from a base algebra BBB and a finite group QQQ. Choose symbols uqu_quq​ for the components. A crossed product has rules such as

uqb=αq(b)uq,uqut=aq,tuqt. u_q b=\alpha_q(b)u_q,\qquad u_q u_t=a_{q,t}u_{qt}.uq​b=αq​(b)uq​,uq​ut​=aq,t​uqt​.

The maps αq\alpha_qαq​ describe actions, while the units aq,ta_{q,t}aq,t​ record corrections in multiplication. Knowing only the outer action is insufficient: different correction factors may produce different algebras.

M1 constructs Frobenius comparisons that retain these factors and the actions of Sylow ppp-subgroups. Combined with structural reductions, integral base finiteness and descent, this yields a finite list over the algebraic closure of the prime field. Scalar extension then gives the statement for every fixed algebraically closed KKK.

Lift exact control to the Witt ring

The integral problem cannot be solved by counting fixed points over a finite field. The Witt ring W(Fq)W(\mathbb F_q)W(Fq​) is infinite. Furthermore, errors that vanish after reduction can survive as principal units, units congruent to 111 modulo the maximal ideal.

M2 refines the comparison so that its particular scalar discrepancies lie in the Teichmüller subgroup, the distinguished multiplicative lifts of nonzero residue-field elements. This restriction permits a cohomological normalization for ppp-group actions; arbitrary principal-unit errors would not permit the same argument.

A rigidity argument then controls the finitely many possible labelled gradings of a fixed total order, retaining the chosen identification of its identity component. Finally, the construction removes a potentially large normal subgroup of order prime to ppp, while preserving these controlled restrictions. An existing integral finiteness criterion completes the finite list. Base change of the Morita bimodules transfers it to a fixed ring RRR.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The conclusions include arbitrary finite groups, arbitrary defect groups, nonprincipal blocks and all primes. The coefficient field or ring is fixed in each finiteness statement. A single classification simultaneously ranging over all coefficient rings is not asserted.

Morita equivalence does not mean algebra isomorphism. The matrix-algebra example explains why infinitely many algebra presentations can represent one categorical type. Likewise, the theorem does not say that only finitely many ambient finite groups realize a given defect group.

The bounds and finite lists should not be read as an efficient algorithm for finding the block associated with an arbitrary input group. Explicit catalogues, sharp bounds and stronger kinds of equivalence remain separate questions.

The integral argument depends on precise compatibility of actions and multiplication factors. Describing it merely as “lift the field theorem” would omit the principal new obstacle addressed by M2.

8. Sources and further reading

Scopes, Cartan matrices and Morita equivalence for blocks of the symmetric groups, Journal of Algebra 142 (1991), 441–455, is an early finiteness result. Kessar, A remark on Donovan’s conjecture, Archiv der Mathematik 82 (2004), 391–394, explains the size-versus-rationality separation.

Eaton, Eisele and Livesey, Donovan’s conjecture, blocks with abelian defect groups and discrete valuation rings, Mathematische Zeitschrift 295 (2020), 249–264, supplies the integral finiteness criterion used by the new work. Farrell and Kessar, Rationality of blocks of quasi-simple finite groups, Representation Theory 23 (2019), 325–349, provides the quasisimple rationality input.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Donovan’s Conjecture over Algebraically Closed Fields (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Integral Donovan Finiteness over Witt Vectors (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Tensor invariants for even spin groups need no extra dilation
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 204 · Algebra
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Suppose three representations can combine to produce a vector unchanged by every symmetry of a group. Such a vector is a tensor invariant. Representation theory often predicts its existence using a continuous geometric problem, but the representations themselves are labelled by discrete data.

This creates an arithmetic gap. A geometric solution may guarantee an invariant only after all the labels have been multiplied by some positive integer. Can the multiplication be removed?

The answer is called a saturation theorem. Family 204 contains a manuscript dated 24 September 2026 claiming saturation for all even spin groups Spin⁡(2n)\operatorname{Spin}(2n)Spin(2n), with the necessary condition imposed by the center. Its scope includes the genuinely spinorial representations, not only those descending to ordinary orthogonal groups.

2. Background and essential definitions

Weights label irreducible representations

The complex group Spin⁡(2n)\operatorname{Spin}(2n)Spin(2n) is the simply connected double cover of SO⁡(2n,C)\operatorname{SO}(2n,\mathbb C)SO(2n,C). Some representations of the covering group do not descend to the orthogonal group; the spin representations are the characteristic examples.

Irreducible finite-dimensional representations are labelled by dominant integral highest weights. Write V(λ)V(\lambda)V(λ) for the representation labelled by λ\lambdaλ. In the coordinate convention used by the manuscript, dominance means

λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥λn−1≥∣λn∣.\lambda_1\geq\lambda_2\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{n-1}\geq|\lambda_n|.λ1​≥λ2​≥⋯≥λn−1​≥∣λn​∣.

The weight lattice consists of vectors whose coordinates are either all integers or all half-odd-integers. Thus “integral weight” means membership in the representation-theoretic weight lattice; it does not require every displayed coordinate to be an integer.

The roots are the vectors ±ei±ej\pm e_i\pm e_j±ei​±ej​, where eie_iei​ are the coordinate basis vectors and i≠ji\ne ji=j. Their integer span is the root lattice

Q(Dn)={a∈Zn:∑iai is even}. Q(D_n)=\left\{a\in\mathbb Z^n:\sum_i a_i\text{ is even}\right\}.Q(Dn​)={a∈Zn:i∑​ai​ is even}.

The distinction between the weight lattice and the root lattice records how the center acts on representations.

Tensor invariants and the central obstruction

The tensor product V(λ)⊗V(μ)⊗V(ν)V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)\otimes V(\nu)V(λ)⊗V(μ)⊗V(ν) carries the diagonal group action: the same group element acts on all three factors. Its invariant subspace is denoted

(V(λ)⊗V(μ)⊗V(ν))G.\bigl(V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)\otimes V(\nu)\bigr)^G.(V(λ)⊗V(μ)⊗V(ν))G.

A nonzero vector in this subspace is fixed by every element of GGG. Equivalently, the trivial representation occurs in the tensor product.

A central group element acts by a scalar on each irreducible representation. For an invariant to exist, the three scalar actions must multiply to one. In highest-weight language this requires

λ+μ+ν∈Q(Dn).\lambda+\mu+\nu\in Q(D_n).λ+μ+ν∈Q(Dn​).

This is a genuine arithmetic restriction. Multiplying weights can erase a nontrivial central character, so occurrence after dilation cannot imply occurrence before dilation without an appropriate congruence assumption.

What saturation asks

Multiplying a weight by NNN produces a new representation V(Nλ)V(N\lambda)V(Nλ). It is not the same operation as taking NNN copies of V(λ)V(\lambda)V(λ), and generally is not its full tensor power.

Saturation asks whether an invariant for some simultaneous dilation already implies an invariant at scale one, once the necessary lattice condition holds. Geometrically, it asks whether a semigroup of allowable lattice points has holes inside its rational cone. A real cone captures continuous feasibility; saturation controls the remaining discrete obstruction.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The best-known predecessor is the type-A saturation theorem of Knutson and Tao, proved using honeycombs. In that setting, tensor multiplicities are Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, and the continuous geometry is closely connected with eigenvalues of sums of Hermitian matrices.

Klyachko had linked eigenvalue inequalities to tensor occurrence after dilation. Berenstein and Sjamaar developed a broader framework connecting moment polytopes and branching multiplicities. These results explain why real geometric feasibility is relevant, while leaving the scale-one arithmetic question to be settled separately.

Other proofs of type-A saturation followed: Derksen and Weyman used semi-invariants of quivers, and Belkale supplied a geometric proof. Kapovich and Millson formulated the corresponding root-lattice saturation conjecture for simply laced groups. Type D, the even spin case, is one major part of that conjectural picture.

Several low ranks were already known. The identifications D2=A1×A1D_2=A_1\times A_1D2​=A1​×A1​ and D3=A3D_3=A_3D3​=A3​ connect the smallest cases with type A. Kapovich, Kumar and Millson proved the case Spin⁡(8)\operatorname{Spin}(8)Spin(8), and Kiers treated Spin⁡(10)\operatorname{Spin}(10)Spin(10) and Spin⁡(12)\operatorname{Spin}(12)Spin(12).

There were also uniform results allowing an extra factor. Building and path methods gave a saturation factor of four in type D. Sam’s symmetric-quiver methods gave factor two for special orthogonal and symplectic groups and factor four for spin groups after passing to doubled weights. Such results control how large a correction may be necessary; they do not eliminate it at the original weights.

Min’s saturation theorem for Newell–Littlewood numbers is another important predecessor. Those numbers describe stable ordinary-weight tensor multiplicities for classical groups. The stable regime does not cover general spin weights or all small-rank interactions of arbitrary weights. M1’s advertised contribution is the full type-D scale-one statement, including those cases.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let G=Spin⁡(2n)G=\operatorname{Spin}(2n)G=Spin(2n), with n≥2n\geq2n≥2, and let λ,μ,ν\lambda,\mu,\nuλ,μ,ν be dominant integral weights satisfying the root-lattice condition. The manuscript asserts that, for every positive integer NNN,

(V(λ)⊗V(μ)⊗V(ν))G≠0⟺(V(Nλ)⊗V(Nμ)⊗V(Nν))G≠0.\begin{aligned}\bigl(V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)\otimes V(\nu)\bigr)^G\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\bigl(V(N\lambda)\otimes V(N\mu)\otimes V(N\nu)\bigr)^G\ne0.\end{aligned}(V(λ)⊗V(μ)⊗V(ν))G=0⟺(V(Nλ)⊗V(Nμ)⊗V(Nν))G=0.​

The difficult direction removes dilation. In particular, if an invariant appears for even one positive dilation, it already appears at the original weights.

Half-integral spin weights are explicitly included. The theorem is not restricted to weights corresponding to representations of the special orthogonal group, to a stable range in rank, or to triples away from chamber walls. Zero coordinates and coincident coordinates are part of the claimed scope.

The statement concerns existence, rather than equality of multiplicities. The invariant space can change dimension drastically as NNN grows. Saturation says that its dimension cannot change from zero to positive solely because dilation fills a hidden lattice gap allowed by the stated congruence.

The manuscript uses D2=A1×A1D_2=A_1\times A_1D2​=A1​×A1​ and notes the familiar type-A interpretation of D3D_3D3​. It does not claim to settle saturation for every remaining simply laced group.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. This would complete a major family of tensor-saturation problems and remove the extra scale factor uniformly in even spin rank, including spinorial and unstable cases.

The conceptual gain is an exact bridge between continuous geometry and discrete representation theory. Real moment feasibility supplies geometric information, while the root-lattice congruence supplies the central arithmetic condition. The claimed theorem says that these two ingredients suffice for occurrence at scale one in type D.

This strengthens the usefulness of eigencone inequalities: an integral triple satisfying the right geometric and lattice conditions would not require a further search through dilations to determine whether any invariant exists.

The score is below the collection’s highest level because the theorem addresses a specific, though broad and central, family of groups. Its proposed tools could have wider applications, but those applications should not be assumed from the saturation statement alone.

6. The main idea

Separate geometry from integrality

Set ξ=ν∗\xi=\nu^*ξ=ν∗, the highest weight of the dual representation. The desired invariant can then be viewed as a nonzero equivariant map

V(λ)⊗V(μ)⟶V(ξ). V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)\longrightarrow V(\xi).V(λ)⊗V(μ)⟶V(ξ).

The manuscript begins with a real moment solution, a geometric configuration equivalent to the relevant continuous feasibility. For a compact form of the group, the configuration involves suitable orbit representatives whose sum is zero.

It converts this solution into a piecewise linear schedule. The schedule starts at λ\lambdaλ, follows Weyl-group transforms of a prescribed shape ending at μ\muμ, and finishes in the Weyl orbit of ξ\xiξ. The Weyl group acts by the coordinate symmetries associated with the root system.

At each switch, a root reflection changes the direction. A scalar switch coefficient measures the corresponding root displacement. The geometric construction gives real coefficients; the arithmetic task is to make them integers while preserving the endpoint and admissibility of the schedule.

Repair the type-D parity obstruction

The switch roots can first be arranged to form a real basis. But a real basis of roots need not generate the entire root lattice over the integers. Linear independence over the reals therefore does not solve the integrality problem.

The paper describes the remaining obstruction using a signed graph. Vertices correspond to coordinates, and roots ei−eje_i-e_jei​−ej​ or ei+eje_i+e_jei​+ej​ become edges carrying different signs. After reduction, the problematic case has two unbalanced components, each carrying an odd coordinate-sum discrepancy.

Joining the components introduces a relation among the roots. Moving halfway along its primitive integer relation changes the switch coefficients without changing the endpoint, and is designed to remove the parity defect.

An arithmetic adjustment alone is insufficient. Switch times must stay ordered, and the signs required by the geometric construction must remain valid. The manuscript uses rank-two reorderings to pass through simultaneous switches, together with a spectral multiplicity argument to force a feasible joining motion even when coordinates tie exactly.

Recover an actual tensor coefficient

An integral schedule is still weaker than a full Lakshmibai–Seshadri path, the standard representation-theoretic object encoding tensor products. The paper does not simply declare that its weaker schedule is such a path.

Instead, it decomposes the moving weight into fundamental columns. Ordinary columns are handled through exterior-power representations; spin columns require the corresponding spin representations. Determinants and skew pairings construct invariant covectors with nonzero coefficients at suitable flags.

A flag is a nested sequence of subspaces. A composition argument arranges the coefficients so their product remains nonzero on the Cartan summand, the irreducible component with the sum of the highest weights. This step converts the integral schedule into the needed equivariant map.

Handle terminal zero coordinates

The first integrality construction requires the moving weight to have at most one zero coordinate. To reach the full theorem, the manuscript removes a common terminal zero block through a construction involving modules over a preprojective algebra, an algebra attached to the underlying graph of the root system.

A filtered intersection estimate for nilpotent operators controls the reduction. Doubling certain Jordan rows helps establish a smaller-rank real moment solution. This intermediate doubling is a geometric device; it does not leave a factor-two dilation in the final theorem. The integral schedule is constructed at the original scale and then padded back to the original rank.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The root-lattice condition must be retained. Without it, dilation can neutralize a central obstruction that is present at scale one. The theorem concerns positive integer stretching parameters, not arbitrary real rescaling of representation labels.

The representations are finite-dimensional representations of complex even spin groups. The manuscript does not assert the same statement in positive characteristic, where complete reducibility and tensor-product behavior can differ substantially.

Existence of an invariant is weaker than computing its multiplicity or constructing an efficient basis of invariant vectors. The geometric method also should not be read as a proven polynomial-time algorithm for every associated decision or counting problem.

Other root systems and refinements of saturation remain separate questions. The useful lesson of the proposed construction is that real geometry, lattice correction and production of a genuine representation coefficient are three distinct steps. Each has to retain the hypotheses needed by the next.

8. Sources and further reading

Knutson and Tao, The honeycomb model of GLn(C) tensor products I: Proof of the saturation conjecture, Journal of the American Mathematical Society 12 (1999), 1055–1090, is the foundational type-A theorem. Derksen and Weyman, Semi-invariants of quivers and saturation for Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, in the same journal 13 (2000), 467–479, gives the quiver approach.

Kapovich, Kumar and Millson, The eigencone and saturation for Spin(8), Pure and Applied Mathematics Quarterly 5 (2009), 755–780, and Kiers, On the saturation conjecture for Spin(2n), Experimental Mathematics 30 (2021), 258–267, record prior type-D cases.

For the path background, see Littelmann, Paths and root operators in representation theory, Annals of Mathematics 142 (1995), 499–525. Sam, Symmetric quivers, invariant theory, and saturation theorems for the classical groups, Advances in Mathematics 229 (2012), 1104–1135, provides the uniform factor results discussed above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Tensor saturation for even spin groups (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A group-algebra trace can remember only finitely many torsion classes
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 207 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

For an ordinary projection matrix, the trace records the dimension of its image. Over a group algebra, a more refined trace can record separate contributions from different conjugacy classes of the group.

Which classes can occur? The Bass trace conjectures predict severe restrictions: infinite-order group elements should contribute nothing. In the analytic algebra ℓ1(G)\ell^1(G)ℓ1(G), where coefficients may have infinite but absolutely summable support, there is an additional demand. Only finitely many finite-order conjugacy classes should survive.

Family 207 contains two manuscripts. M2, dated 24 September 2026, claims the complex group-ring Bass theorem and derives the characteristic-zero Kaplansky idempotent conjecture. M1, dated 5 October, claims the stronger ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1-Bass theorem for every discrete group. Its argument develops the analytic estimates needed to control infinitely supported coefficients.

2. Background and essential definitions

Two algebras built from a group

The complex group ring CG\mathbb CGCG consists of sums ∑gagg\sum_g a_g g∑g​ag​g with only finitely many nonzero complex coefficients. Multiplication extends the group law linearly.

The Banach group algebra ℓ1(G)\ell^1(G)ℓ1(G) allows infinitely many nonzero coefficients, provided

∥a∥1=∑g∈G∣ag∣<∞. \|a\|_1=\sum_{g\in G}|a_g|<\infty.∥a∥1​=g∈G∑​∣ag​∣<∞.

Multiplication is convolution:

(a∗b)(g)=∑h∈Ga(h)b(h−1g). (a*b)(g)=\sum_{h\in G}a(h)b(h^{-1}g).(a∗b)(g)=h∈G∑​a(h)b(h−1g).

Absolute summability makes this well defined. The distinction between finite support and summable support is important: a summable sequence can have infinitely many nonzero entries.

An element eee is idempotent if e2=ee^2=ee2=e. More generally, an idempotent matrix e∈Mq(A)e\in M_q(A)e∈Mq​(A) over an algebra AAA selects a direct summand eAqeA^qeAq of a free module. Such summands are finitely generated projective modules. They generalize vector bundles and provide the objects whose “ranks” are being measured.

A trace indexed by conjugacy classes

Two group elements are conjugate if one has the form hgh−1hgh^{-1}hgh−1 for the other. Let CCC be a conjugacy class. For an idempotent matrix with group-algebra entries, define

τC(e)=∑g∈C∑i=1qeii(g). \tau_C(e)=\sum_{g\in C}\sum_{i=1}^q e_{ii}(g).τC​(e)=g∈C∑​i=1∑q​eii​(g).

First take the usual matrix trace coefficientwise, then sum the coefficients over the class. These sums converge absolutely in the ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 setting. The collection of all τC(e)\tau_C(e)τC​(e) is the Hattori–Stallings trace.

Grouping by conjugacy is what restores the cyclic trace identity in a noncommutative group algebra. The trace is unchanged by similarity and depends only on the corresponding projective module. It therefore extends to K0(A)K_0(A)K0​(A), the abelian group formed from projective modules using direct-sum relations and formal differences.

A finite-order element satisfies gm=1g^m=1gm=1 for some positive integer mmm. “Finite-order conjugacy class” refers to the order of its elements, not the number of elements in the class. A torsion element can have an infinite conjugacy class.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hattori and Stallings introduced the refined rank in the 1960s. Bass connected it with Euler characteristics and formulated trace-support conjectures for group rings. Over the integral group ring ZG\mathbb ZGZG, the conjecture asks for support only at the identity. Over CG\mathbb CGCG, finite-order classes must be allowed.

The reason is already visible for a finite group FFF. Its averaging element

eF=1∣F∣∑g∈Fg e_F=\frac1{|F|}\sum_{g\in F}geF​=∣F∣1​g∈F∑​g

is idempotent. Its trace contribution at a class C⊆FC\subseteq FC⊆F is ∣C∣/∣F∣|C|/|F|∣C∣/∣F∣, which need not vanish away from the identity. Complex and integral versions therefore have different permitted supports.

Bass proved important cases, including complex trace vanishing for linear groups. Burghelea’s computation of cyclic homology separated contributions from finite- and infinite-order conjugacy classes. Eckmann and Emmanouil used cyclic-homological methods to establish further cases under structural or homological hypotheses.

Berrick, Chatterji and Mislin formulated the ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1-Bass conjecture in the finite-support form used here. They proved it for countable groups with rationally surjective degree-zero Bost assembly map. Together with Lafforgue’s work, this includes amenable groups. Their reduction also explains how to pass from suitable countable subgroups to arbitrary groups.

Related work on rapid-decay completions by Ji, Ogle and Ramsey emphasizes a recurring analytic obstacle: moving from finitely supported group-ring elements to completed algebras requires estimates compatible with infinite sums.

The idempotent question has a parallel history. Classical trace arguments show that a scalar idempotent in CG\mathbb CGCG has canonical trace between zero and one, and that the endpoint values force triviality. Known rationality of the trace does not suffice, since rational numbers can lie strictly between the endpoints. M2’s torsion-free trace formula claims the missing integrality by identifying the trace with augmentation rank.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: the full ℓ¹ support assertion

For every discrete group GGG and every idempotent matrix e∈Mq(ℓ1(G))e\in M_q(\ell^1(G))e∈Mq​(ℓ1(G)), M1 asserts that there is a finite set FFF of finite-order conjugacy classes such that

τC(e)=0whenever C∉F. \tau_C(e)=0\qquad\text{whenever }C\notin F.τC​(e)=0whenever C∈/F.

The surviving set can depend on eee. No amenability, growth condition, finite generation or assembly-map assumption is imposed on GGG.

Both parts of the conclusion matter: all infinite-order classes vanish, and only finitely many finite-order classes remain. Absolute summability alone would provide neither this finite cutoff nor its uniformity across conjugacy classes.

M2: the algebraic theorem and idempotents

M2 asserts vanishing on infinite-order classes for every projective class over CG\mathbb CGCG. Finite support is automatic in this algebraic setting. Combining that theorem with the established restriction on integral finite-order coefficients gives the identity-only Bass assertion over ZG\mathbb ZGZG.

For torsion-free GGG, the identity is the only finite-order element. Let τG\tau_GτG​ take the coefficient of the identity, and let the augmentation ϵG\epsilon_GϵG​ sum all coefficients. For an idempotent matrix, M2 obtains

∑iτG(eii)=rank⁡C(ϵG(e)). \sum_i\tau_G(e_{ii}) =\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}\bigl(\epsilon_G(e)\bigr).i∑​τG​(eii​)=rankC​(ϵG​(e)).

The augmentation is applied entrywise. The right side is the ordinary rank of a complex idempotent matrix, hence an integer.

The manuscript then claims that for every torsion-free group and every commutative unital domain RRR of characteristic zero, a scalar idempotent e∈RGe\in RGe∈RG is either 000 or 111. This is the characteristic-zero Kaplansky idempotent conjecture. It concerns elements of the ring itself; nontrivial idempotent matrices are not forbidden.

M1 builds on the weighted-configuration ideas of M2, but states that the complex group-ring theorem is not an input to its proof. It develops the necessary ingredients directly for the analytic setting.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. These are claimed general resolutions of central trace-support problems for group algebras, together with a broad idempotent consequence in characteristic zero.

The trace connects module theory, conjugacy, topology and analysis. Support restrictions limit which group elements can contribute to projective Euler characteristics. The integral theorem also has fixed-point consequences through earlier equivalences involving homotopy-idempotent maps.

The ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 statement is a substantial strengthening of the algebraic one. It says that passing to an algebra allowing infinite tails does not produce an infinite tail of torsion-class contributions in this trace.

The score concerns those structural claims. It does not imply that arbitrary group rings have no zero divisors, or that every completed group algebra has no nontrivial projections. Those are different questions with different hypotheses.

6. The main idea

Idempotency makes weighted paths compatible

Fix an element ggg whose trace coefficient is to be studied. Products of matrix coefficients along lists of group elements assign complex weights to paths whose closing edge is twisted by multiplication by ggg.

The equation e2=ee^2=ee2=e has a useful combinatorial meaning: summing over an intermediate vertex removes that vertex without changing the total weight. Cyclicity of matrix trace gives another compatibility under rotating the list.

These identities let the manuscript build higher-dimensional cycles whose evaluation by a suitable differential or combinatorial expression recovers τ[g](e)\tau_{[g]}(e)τ[g]​(e). The detecting expression involves a Pfaffian, a signed sum over pairings associated with a skew-symmetric matrix. Pfaffians naturally package the repeated two-form contributions arising in even dimensions.

M2 uses finite geometric support

For a group-ring idempotent, only finitely many group steps occur. They define a graph of bounded degree, fixed as the dimension increases. The relevant simplices use connected sets of vertices in that graph.

M2 cuts their supporting complex through a sequence of separating sets. Volume estimates and repeated slicing make the expected number of final zero-dimensional pieces arbitrarily small in high dimension. Equivariant chain comparisons preserve the original cocycle evaluation while allowing it to be bounded by that small quantity.

The construction uses a free probability parameter to separate overlapping translates of local modifications. It does not assume the group is amenable. The resulting high-dimensional vanishing forces the trace coefficient of the chosen infinite-order element to be zero.

M1 first replaces arbitrary tails by exponential decay

An ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 idempotent need not have finite support. M1 approximates it by a finite-support matrix, then applies an analytic correction to obtain a nearby exact idempotent ppp. The correction generally restores an infinite tail, but with an exponential moment in a finitely generated subgroup Γ\GammaΓ:

∑h∈Γ∥p(h)∥ec∣h∣<∞for some c>0. \sum_{h\in\Gamma}\|p(h)\|e^{c|h|}<\infty \quad\text{for some }c>0.h∈Γ∑​∥p(h)∥ec∣h∣<∞for some c>0.

Here ∣h∣|h|∣h∣ is word length for a finite generating set. The corrected matrix is similar to the original, so every conjugacy-class trace coefficient is preserved exactly. The step is not a claim that every projective class has a finite-support idempotent representative.

Timed paths are then averaged over several time scales. Smooth summaries of their spatial distributions provide differential forms whose derivatives remain controlled even when the path support is large. Normalization produces connection forms, and a cyclic Stokes identity relates their curvature Pfaffians to the trace.

Different scales require different estimates: sparse interactions at the initial scale, Hilbert–Schmidt bounds at intermediate scales, and singular-value bounds for ordered kernels at the final scale. Together they give an exponentially decreasing bound as the simplex dimension grows.

One radius gives finite support

The decisive uniformity is a single spatial radius chosen independently of the conjugacy class to be eliminated. The estimate removes every infinite-order class and every finite-order class with no representative in a fixed finite word ball.

Only finitely many conjugacy classes meet that ball. This gives actual finite support. Passing from Γ\GammaΓ back to GGG can merge conjugacy classes but cannot turn a finite surviving list into an infinite one.

For M2’s scalar idempotent consequence, augmentation gives rank zero or one. A classical faithful-trace argument then forces the idempotent to be zero or one. Extension to an arbitrary characteristic-zero domain uses only the finitely generated field containing the finitely many coefficients of the given element, which embeds into C\mathbb CC; no embedding of the whole coefficient domain is required.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The groups are arbitrary discrete groups, possibly uncountable. The analytic statement concerns the complex Banach algebra ℓ1(G)\ell^1(G)ℓ1(G); the idempotent corollary is stated for characteristic-zero commutative domains.

The reduced group C∗C^*C∗-algebra uses a different completion. M2 identifies the trace on the image of algebraic K0(CG)K_0(\mathbb CG)K0​(CG) inside its topological K-theory, but does not assert that every class in that completed K-theory comes from the group ring. It therefore does not claim the full Kadison–Kaplansky conjecture for arbitrary torsion-free groups.

A nontrivial idempotent gives zero divisors through e(1−e)=0e(1-e)=0e(1−e)=0, but excluding idempotents does not exclude all zero divisors. The positive-characteristic constructions in family 196 and the direct-finiteness questions in family 197 should not be conflated with the characteristic-zero scalar conclusion here.

No explicit universal bound on the number of surviving classes is part of M1’s headline theorem. Its finite cutoff depends on the idempotent and the estimates constructed for it.

8. Sources and further reading

Bass, Euler characteristics and characters of discrete groups, Inventiones Mathematicae 35 (1976), 155–196, gives the foundational setting. Berrick, Chatterji and Mislin, From acyclic groups to the Bass conjecture for amenable groups, Mathematische Annalen 329 (2004), 597–621, formulates the analytic conjecture and proves the assembly-based cases.

Burghelea, The cyclic homology of the group rings, Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici 60 (1985), 354–365, supplies the conjugacy-class decomposition. Eckmann, Cyclic homology of groups and the Bass conjecture, in the same journal 61 (1986), 193–202, develops the higher-degree vanishing approach.

Burger and Valette, Idempotents in complex group rings: theorems of Zalesskii and Bass revisited, Journal of Lie Theory 8 (1998), 219–228, explains the classical trace facts used in the scalar corollary.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The ℓ¹-Bass Conjecture for Discrete Groups (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Bass trace conjecture and the characteristic-zero Kaplansky idempotent conjecture (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: One irreducible representation whose square contains every other
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 205 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

The symmetric group SnS_nSn​ contains every permutation of nnn objects. Its irreducible complex representations are the basic linear ways in which those permutations can act. There are many different types, and their number grows rapidly with nnn.

Could one irreducible representation be so rich that combining it with itself produces every irreducible type? This is the universal tensor-square problem. The same representation must work for all targets; choosing a different starting representation for each desired constituent would be a much weaker statement.

Saxl’s conjecture makes a particularly elegant choice at triangular values of nnn: use the representation whose Young diagram is a staircase. Family 205 contains two manuscripts, both dated 24 September 2026. M2 claims Saxl’s conjecture, and M1 uses a strengthened form of that result to claim universal squares for every positive degree except 222, 444 and 999.

2. Background and essential definitions

Partitions and representations

A partition λ⊢n\lambda\vdash nλ⊢n is a decreasing sequence of positive integers with sum nnn. Draw λi\lambda_iλi​ boxes in row iii, aligned on the left, to obtain its Young diagram. For example, (3,2,1)(3,2,1)(3,2,1) is a staircase containing six boxes.

The irreducible complex representations of SnS_nSn​ are indexed by partitions of nnn. Write SλS^\lambdaSλ for the Specht module with label λ\lambdaλ. Transposing the diagram gives the conjugate partition λt\lambda^tλt.

The tensor product Sλ⊗SμS^\lambda\otimes S^\muSλ⊗Sμ uses the diagonal action: a permutation acts on both factors simultaneously. Because the coefficients are complex and the group is finite, the tensor product decomposes as a direct sum of irreducibles:

Sλ⊗Sμ≅⨁ν⊢n(Sν)⊕g(λ,μ,ν). S^\lambda\otimes S^\mu \cong igoplus_{ u\vdash n}(S^ u)^{\oplus g(\lambda,\mu, u)}.Sλ⊗Sμ≅ν⊢n⨁​(Sν)⊕g(λ,μ,ν).

The nonnegative integers g(λ,μ,ν)g(\lambda,\mu, u)g(λ,μ,ν) are Kronecker coefficients. Positivity means that the target representation occurs at least once. A universal square requires g(λ,λ,ν)>0g(\lambda,\lambda, u)>0g(λ,λ,ν)>0 for every partition ν uν of the same integer.

Why the diagram must be self-conjugate

The partition (n)(n)(n) labels the trivial representation, while (1n)(1^n)(1n) labels the sign representation, which assigns +1+1+1 to even permutations and −1-1−1 to odd ones. Tensoring a Specht module with the sign representation transposes its label.

Consequently,

g(λ,λ,(1n))={1,λ=λt,0,λ≠λt. g(\lambda,\lambda,(1^n))= egin{cases} 1,&\lambda=\lambda^t,\ 0,&\lambda e\lambda^t. \end{cases}g(λ,λ,(1n))={1,0,​λ=λt,λ=λt.​

A universal square must therefore start from a self-conjugate diagram. The staircase

ρm=(m,m−1,…,1),Nm=m(m+1)2, ho_m=(m,m-1,\ldots,1),\qquad N_m= rac{m(m+1)}2,ρm​=(m,m−1,…,1),Nm​=2m(m+1)​,

has exactly that symmetry. The conjecture asks whether its square covers every irreducible of SNmS_{N_m}SNm​​.

“Square” here means the full tensor product. It is not the symmetric square alone, which is only one part of the tensor product and has a separate representation-theoretic meaning.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Tensor-square covering questions have precedents for finite simple groups of Lie type, where Steinberg representations provide important examples. Saxl proposed the staircase conjecture in a UCLA seminar in March 2012. Pak, Panova and Vallejo placed it in the broader symmetric-group tensor-square problem and proved positivity for substantial families of targets.

The difficulty is not a shortage of evidence. It is the possibility of an exceptional constituent that remains absent even when almost every other partition occurs.

Ikenmeyer proved the staircase assertion for partitions comparable with the staircase in dominance order. Dominance compares all initial row sums: λ\lambdaλ dominates μ\muμ if the first kkk rows of λ\lambdaλ contain at least as many boxes as those of μ\muμ, for every kkk. His construction with two triangular layers of alternating tensors is an explicit methodological predecessor of M2.

Character-theoretic, spin-character and modular methods established further support families. The papers cite Bessenrodt’s double-hook results, Li’s triple-hook theorem, and Bessenrodt, Bowman and Sutton’s results using modular decomposition numbers. Double and triple hooks here refer to diagrams whose largest square has side two or three.

Luo and Sellke proved that almost every partition occurs in staircase squares, for both the uniform and Plancherel probability distributions. They also obtained universal fourth tensor powers in all sufficiently large degrees. Harman and Ryba later proved universal coverage for every staircase tensor cube.

These achievements leave two precise gaps. Probability tending to one does not eliminate every exceptional target. A cube or fourth power has more room than a square, so its universality does not establish the two-factor claim.

There was also a recent staircase-square theorem for unipotent characters of finite general linear groups, due to Letellier and Nam. It is an analogue in another character theory. Ordinary Kronecker positivity transfers to the relevant unipotent positivity, but that implication does not reverse automatically.

M2 claims to close the staircase-square gap through a specific cyclic generator. M1 then addresses all nontriangular degrees by enlarging staircases in a controlled, self-conjugate way.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: every staircase square is universal

For every m≥1m\geq1m≥1 and every ν⊢Nm u\vdash N_mν⊢Nm​, M2 asserts

g(ρm,ρm,ν)>0. g( ho_m, ho_m, u)>0.g(ρm​,ρm​,ν)>0.

It proves a stronger stated result inside the square. The manuscript specifies one vector wmw_mwm​, built by alternating along rows in one tensor layer and columns in the other. Its orbit span

Wm=span⁡C{σwm:σ∈SNm} W_m=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\sigma w_m:\sigma\in S_{N_m}\}Wm​=spanC​{σwm​:σ∈SNm​​}

already contains every irreducible type. Such an orbit-generated submodule is called cyclic. The assertion is about support, not about containing every multiplicity present in the entire square.

M1: universal squares in all eligible degrees

M1 asserts that, for every positive integer n∉{2,4,9}n otin\{2,4,9\}n∈/{2,4,9}, there is one partition λn⊢n\lambda_n\vdash nλn​⊢n such that

g(λn,λn,ν)>0for every ν⊢n. g(\lambda_n,\lambda_n, u)>0 \quad ext{for every } u\vdash n.g(λn​,λn​,ν)>0for every ν⊢n.

The partition is chosen from nnn before the target ν uν is specified. For large degrees, it comes from a parity-compatible staircase with matching additions to its first two rows and columns. Small degrees are handled separately by the manuscript’s exact character calculations. The reported calculation also finds no covering square in degrees 222, 444 and 999.

The dependence is explicit: M1 uses M2’s cyclic theorem, not merely its bare positivity conclusion. The prescribed generator is needed to ensure constituents survive the construction of enlarged diagrams.

M1 also obtains universal coverage of all unipotent irreducible characters of GL⁡n(Fq)\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)GLn​(Fq​) by squares with these same labels, for every prime power qqq. It credits Letellier’s transfer theorem. Universal unipotent coverage itself already had other witnesses, including the Steinberg character, so the novelty of this corollary is the additional family of labels.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The family claims resolutions of two central tensor-support conjectures, uniformly over all target partitions and all eligible degrees.

Kronecker coefficients are difficult even to understand qualitatively. A universal square theorem supplies a remarkably simple global support pattern inside this complicated landscape: one irreducible can interact with itself to reach every irreducible type.

The cyclic refinement is also meaningful. Knowing that a constituent exists somewhere in a large tensor product does not guarantee that it appears in the submodule preserved by an inductive construction. A specified generator provides information that can be transported to the next step.

The score concerns these structural advances. The manuscripts do not claim a general positive combinatorial formula for arbitrary Kronecker coefficients, and their results should not be presented as solving that broader problem.

6. The main idea

Preserve a particular generator

Arrange NmN_mNm​ positions in a triangular diagram. In the first layer, alternate basis letters within each row; in the second, alternate within each column. Alternation is the familiar signed sum over permutations, analogous to the construction of a determinant.

The two layers produce wmw_mwm​. Rather than changing vectors whenever a new target is considered, M2 studies the orbit span of this one vector throughout the induction.

The first targets are those dominated by the staircase. A sign twist and a permutation-module quotient supply them. The remaining targets are reached by cutting off a narrow band from the triangular position set.

Separate a smaller triangle from a band

Divide the letters into low and high alphabets. A coordinate projection keeps only words whose two letters at each position are both high or both low. The row and column counts force the high positions to form a smaller triangle in the projected generator.

Its projected vector factors into the smaller cyclic staircase vector and a band vector. Different placements of the smaller triangle occupy disjoint coordinate sectors. This separation makes the resulting quotient the full induced representation from the two factors, rather than an uncontrolled part of it.

Here induction means enlarging a representation from a product of symmetric groups on disjoint position sets to the symmetric group on all positions. It is distinct from the diagonal tensor product whose constituents the theorem studies.

Make the width-two band cover four-row targets

A width-two band forms an odd path of alternating pairs. Pairing it with suitable dual tensors becomes a product of two-by-two matrices and their adjugates. A nonzero pairing detects the desired irreducible constituent.

The paper chooses a matrix basis so that alternated path segments of length at most four give invertible matrices. A generic change of basis then makes the required endpoint coefficient nonzero. This proves coverage of every target with at most four rows inside the specific cyclic band module.

The ambient tensor-square coverage of these four-row shapes had already been established by Brown, van Willigenburg and Zabrocki. The generator-specific placement is the extra statement needed here.

A diagram-removal argument completes the induction. A target outside the starting dominance range either allows one horizontal strip to be removed, or allows exactly 2m−12m-12m−1 boxes to be removed in at most four horizontal strips. A horizontal strip has at most one box in each column. The Pieri rule translates these removals into induced-representation constituents, joining the smaller triangle to the band.

Enlarge the staircase without losing targets

M1 adds transposed pairs of cells, preserving self-conjugacy. For example, its degree-49 construction has row and column lengths

(10,9,7,6,5,4,3,2,2,1). (10,9,7,6,5,4,3,2,2,1).(10,9,7,6,5,4,3,2,2,1).

Two complementary tests cover possible target diagrams. One detects a supported band with attachments inside the target; the other handles targets whose first few rows or columns are sufficiently small. If both fail, simultaneous row and column capacity bounds eventually force the target to have fewer boxes than its prescribed size.

The remaining bounded parameters and eligible degrees through 646464 are handled by exact computations supplied in the manuscript. These are stated components of the source argument; the digest does not add a new execution or verification of those programs.
