7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All representations here are finite-dimensional complex representations. The claims do not automatically transfer to modular representations in characteristic dividing n!n!n!, where semisimplicity fails.

The theorem asserts positive multiplicity, not a prescribed multiplicity or an equality with a regular representation. A universal square may contain some constituents many times and others only once.

The existential theorem for arbitrary degree uses particular self-conjugate candidates. It does not say every self-conjugate partition outside the exceptional degrees has a universal square. Stronger conjectures concerning the symmetric and alternating parts of tensor squares also remain distinct.

Finally, the argument’s finite computations and companion dependency are part of its stated scope. M1 should not be summarized as following from the staircase positivity theorem by simply adding boxes: preserving constituents through the actual generator and controlling cancellation are substantive additional tasks.

8. Sources and further reading

Pak, Panova and Vallejo, Kronecker products, characters, partitions, and the tensor square conjectures, Advances in Mathematics 288 (2016), 702–731, gives the conjectures and early support results.

Ikenmeyer, The Saxl conjecture and the dominance order, Discrete Mathematics 338 (2015), 1970–1975, supplies the triangular alternating-tensor predecessor. Luo and Sellke, The Saxl conjecture for fourth powers via the semigroup property, Journal of Algebraic Combinatorics 45 (2017), 33–80, covers asymptotic support and fourth powers.

Harman and Ryba, A tensor-cube version of the Saxl conjecture, Algebraic Combinatorics 6 (2023), 507–511, proves the cube theorem. Brown, van Willigenburg and Zabrocki, Expressions for Catalan Kronecker products, Pacific Journal of Mathematics 248 (2010), 31–48, provides the ambient four-row band result.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Universal Tensor Squares for Symmetric Groups (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A Cyclic Polytabloid Proof of Saxl’s Conjecture (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A regular local ring can lose integral K-theory at its fraction field
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 209 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

A local ring describes geometry near one point. Its fraction field describes the generic point, where all nonzero denominators have been allowed. Passing to that field discards special loci, so some information can disappear. Gersten’s conjecture predicts a particularly strong form of control over this process for algebraic K-theory of regular local rings.

The first requirement is injectivity: a K-theory class that becomes zero over the fraction field should already have been zero in the local ring. Family 209 contains two manuscripts claiming explicit failures of that requirement in ramified mixed characteristic.

M1, dated 25 September 2026, constructs a kernel in integral K5K_5K5​. M2, dated 26 September, constructs one in integral K3K_3K3​ at a different ring. The examples concern regular total rings with singular special fibers. Neither manuscript determines the smallest degree of possible failure or settles the rational-coefficient version.

2. Background and essential definitions

Regularity and ramification are different conditions

A local ring AAA has a unique maximal ideal m\mathfrak mm. Its residue field is A/mA/\mathfrak mA/m. A Noetherian local ring is regular when the minimum number of generators of m\mathfrak mm equals its Krull dimension, the length of the longest chain of prime ideals.

Regularity is the algebraic counterpart of nonsingularity. In the examples, the dimension is two and the maximal ideal has two generators.

Mixed characteristic (0,p)(0,p)(0,p) means that the ring has characteristic zero but its residue field has characteristic ppp. In this setting, the standard unramified condition is p∉m2p\notin\mathfrak m^2p∈/m2. Ramification allows ppp to lie deeper in the maximal ideal.

A regular ring can be ramified. It can also fail to be smooth over a chosen discrete valuation ring. The special fiber, obtained by setting the base uniformizer to zero, can be singular even when the total local ring is regular. These distinctions explain why the examples do not contradict smooth or unramified positive results.

What the K-groups measure

Algebraic K-theory assigns abelian groups Kn(A)K_n(A)Kn​(A) to a ring. The lowest group K0K_0K0​ records finitely generated projective modules and their direct-sum relations. Over a field FFF, K1(F)=F×K_1(F)=F^\timesK1​(F)=F×, its multiplicative group. Higher groups encode more elaborate compatibility information among matrices and algebraic relations.

The digests need no construction of the full K-theory spectrum. The useful properties are functoriality, localization and products: ring maps induce maps on K-groups, removing a closed set fits into exact sequences, and classes can be multiplied.

For a regular local domain with fraction field FFF, the beginning of the Gersten complex is

0⟶Kn(A)⟶Kn(F)⟶⨁ht⁡p=1Kn−1(κ(p))⟶⋯ .0\longrightarrow K_n(A)\longrightarrow K_n(F)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=1} K_{n-1}(\kappa(\mathfrak p))\longrightarrow\cdots.0⟶Kn​(A)⟶Kn​(F)⟶htp=1⨁​Kn−1​(κ(p))⟶⋯.

The fields κ(p)\kappa(\mathfrak p)κ(p) belong to codimension-one points, and the arrows after the generic term are residue maps. Exactness at the initial term requires Kn(A)→Kn(F)K_n(A)\to K_n(F)Kn​(A)→Kn​(F) to be injective.

Integral classes versus finite coefficients

“Integral K-theory” means the original abelian groups, before reducing coefficients or tensoring with Q\mathbb QQ. Finite-coefficient K-theory is not simply the quotient group in every degree. There is an exact sequence

0⟶Kn(A)/5Kn(A)⟶Kn(A;Z/5)⟶Kn−1(A)[5]⟶0,0\longrightarrow K_n(A)/5K_n(A)\longrightarrow K_n(A;\mathbb Z/5)\longrightarrow K_{n-1}(A)[5]\longrightarrow0,0⟶Kn​(A)/5Kn​(A)⟶Kn​(A;Z/5)⟶Kn−1​(A)[5]⟶0,

where Kn−1(A)[5]K_{n-1}(A)[5]Kn−1​(A)[5] denotes elements killed by five. A coefficient class can therefore fail to lift to an integral class. Even a lift may have a nonzero but five-divisible generic image. An integral counterexample must address both issues.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gersten’s questions about transfer and higher K-theory led to the localization problem. Quillen formulated the regular-local conjecture and proved it for regular semilocalizations of finite-type algebras over a field. Sherman treated the equicharacteristic discrete valuation ring case, and Panin established the full equicharacteristic theorem.

Mixed characteristic requires additional care. Gillet and Levine developed a relative theorem reducing smooth local situations over a discrete valuation ring to the associated valuation-ring problem. Geisser and Levine proved finite-coefficient exactness for semilocal rings essentially smooth over such a base, including coefficients of residue-characteristic order.

Skalit proved finite-coefficient exactness for arbitrary unramified regular local rings. The condition excluding deep ramification is therefore mathematically consequential, not an incidental technicality. The new examples deliberately lie outside it.

The manuscripts also discuss Druzhinin’s stated smooth Henselian result. Smoothness over the base excludes the structure maps in the new examples, so that statement has a different scope.

A particularly close predecessor is Feld’s finite-coefficient example in ramified mixed characteristic. It gives a degree-two kernel modulo three at a ring whose integral K2K_2K2​ map is injective. This demonstrates why a coefficient counterexample alone does not disprove integral Gersten injectivity. An integral lift there can retain a nonzero generic image divisible by three.

The new papers adapt the strategy of pushing a class from a divisor and detecting it after a suitable base change or localization. Their claimed advance is to arrange an integral class whose generic restriction is already zero, and only then use finite coefficients to detect that the class is nonzero.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: a quartic example in degree five

Let V0V_0V0​ be the ring of integers in the unramified degree-eight extension of Q5\mathbb Q_5Q5​. Define

A5=(V0[x,y]/(5+x4+y4))(5,x,y). A_5=\left(V_0[x,y]/(5+x^4+y^4)\right)_{(5,x,y)}.A5​=(V0​[x,y]/(5+x4+y4))(5,x,y)​.

The subscript means localization at the displayed maximal ideal. M1 asserts that A5A_5A5​ is a two-dimensional Noetherian regular local domain and

ker⁡(K5(A5)⟶K5(Frac⁡A5))≠0. \ker\bigl(K_5(A_5)\longrightarrow K_5(\operatorname{Frac}A_5)\bigr)\ne0.ker(K5​(A5​)⟶K5​(FracA5​))=0.

Its maximal ideal is generated by x,yx,yx,y, and 5∈(x,y)45\in(x,y)^45∈(x,y)4. Thus the ring is ramified and is not smooth over V0V_0V0​.

M2: a cyclotomic quintic example in degree three

Fix a primitive fifth root of unity ζ\zetaζ, put L=Q5(ζ)L=\mathbb Q_5(\zeta)L=Q5​(ζ), let VVV be its ring of integers, and write π=1−ζ\pi=1-\zetaπ=1−ζ. Consider the projective plane curve model over VVV defined by

(X−Z)5−XY4+Y5+ζZ5=0. (X-Z)^5-XY^4+Y^5+\zeta Z^5=0.(X−Z)5−XY4+Y5+ζZ5=0.

Let A3A_3A3​ be its local ring at the special-fiber point [0:0:1][0:0:1][0:0:1]. M2 asserts that A3A_3A3​ is a two-dimensional regular local domain, with π∈m2\pi\in\mathfrak m^2π∈m2, and constructs a class c∈K3(A3)c\in K_3(A_3)c∈K3​(A3​) satisfying

c∣Frac⁡A3=0,c∣A3[1/π] mod 5≠0. c|_{\operatorname{Frac}A_3}=0, \qquad c|_{A_3[1/\pi]}\bmod5\ne0.c∣FracA3​​=0,c∣A3​[1/π]​mod5=0.

The latter nonvanishing is stated in coherent K-theory with coefficients, denoted G3(−;Z/5)G_3(-;\mathbb Z/5)G3​(−;Z/5). Coherent K-theory permits pushforwards even when auxiliary curves are singular; on the regular rings at issue it agrees with ordinary K-theory.

The two constructions are independent and concern different rings. A degree-three example is a lower-degree failure than a degree-five example, but it does not establish that degree three is the first possible failure in every regular local setting.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The family claims counterexamples to the unrestricted integral form of a foundational conjecture connecting local algebra, K-theory and residue geometry.

Failure occurs at the very first injection, before the more elaborate residue terms become relevant. It would show that regularity alone does not prevent integral K-theory information from disappearing at the generic point in ramified mixed characteristic.

The examples also clarify the role of coefficients. The detecting calculation is performed modulo five, but the objects detected are integral classes already known to vanish generically. That logical order is what separates these claims from earlier finite-coefficient failures.

The rating concerns the unrestricted integral conjecture. The examples leave important positive theories intact and do not justify describing every form of Gersten exactness as false.

6. The main idea

Support guarantees generic vanishing

A class pushed forward from a closed divisor is supported on that divisor. After passing to the fraction field, the divisor disappears, so the pushed-forward class becomes zero.

This supplies one half of the desired counterexample automatically. The hard tasks are to produce the divisor class integrally and to show that its pushforward is not already zero on the local ring.

M2 arranges an integral lift through a Steinberg relation

On the affine chart Z≠0Z\ne0Z=0, M2 uses the divisor y=0y=0y=0. Its local ring S=A3/yA3S=A_3/yA_3S=A3​/yA3​ is a discrete valuation ring with parameter ttt. Its fraction field DDD is a totally ramified degree-five extension of LLL, with

ND/L(t)=π,(1−t)5=ζ. N_{D/L}(t)=\pi,\qquad (1-t)^5=\zeta.ND/L​(t)=π,(1−t)5=ζ.

A Bott-type class β∈K2(L;Z/5)\beta\in K_2(L;\mathbb Z/5)β∈K2​(L;Z/5) has coefficient boundary [ζ][\zeta][ζ]. Multiplying its restriction to DDD by the unit class [t][t][t] produces a degree-three coefficient class.

The obstruction to lifting this class integrally is killed by the displayed fifth-power relation and the Steinberg identity

{1−t,t}=0 \{1-t,t\}=0{1−t,t}=0

in K2(D)K_2(D)K2​(D). The braces denote the standard multiplicative symbol in degree two. Quillen’s finite-field vanishing K2(F5)=0K_2(\mathbb F_5)=0K2​(F5​)=0 then allows the integral class to extend from DDD to SSS. Pushing it into A3A_3A3​ produces the candidate ccc with zero generic restriction.

A norm valuation detects nonvanishing

The special fiber is designed so that every generic-curve point specializing away from [0:0:1][0:0:1][0:0:1] has residue degree divisible by five. The distinguished point on y=0y=0y=0 has residue degree one.

After identifying degree-three coefficient classes over the relevant local fields with units modulo fifth powers, pushforward corresponds to field norm. Normalized valuation gives

vL(NE/L(u))=[kE:F5],vE(u). v_L(N_{E/L}(u))=[k_E:\mathbb F_5],v_E(u).vL​(NE/L​(u))=[kE​:F5​],vE​(u).

Thus points specializing elsewhere contribute zero modulo five. The distinguished class contributes one because its norm is π\piπ.

If the supported class vanished on A3[1/π]A_3[1/\pi]A3​[1/π], localization would express it using points omitted from a suitable affine open. Those points all specialize elsewhere. Proper pushforward and the norm valuation would then equate one with zero modulo five. This is the manuscript’s nonvanishing mechanism.

M1 uses an arithmetic lift and a Picard test

M1 follows a different route. It starts with a cyclotomic coefficient class involving two Bott factors and proves that its obstruction to lifting into integral K5K_5K5​ vanishes. Localization extends the class to a valuation ring, which appears as a divisor of Spec⁡A5\operatorname{Spec}A_5SpecA5​.

After a flat cyclotomic extension, that divisor splits into four points on a Fermat quartic. A specialization criterion translates any hypothetical relation among their supported coefficient classes into a relation in a special-fiber Picard group, the group of line bundles or divisor classes.

A degree-two map from the quartic to a genus-one curve supplies the detector. The four specialized points map to QQQ or −Q-Q−Q, with signs matching the squared cyclotomic character contributed by the two Bott factors. Their weighted sum is 4Q4Q4Q, nonzero modulo five. This detects the already integral, generically vanishing class.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Both examples use ramified regular local rings in mixed characteristic (0,5)(0,5)(0,5), and both fail generic injectivity. They do not contradict the equicharacteristic theorem or the cited smooth and unramified finite-coefficient results.

The nonzero coefficient reductions show that the constructed integral classes are not five-divisible in the relevant K-groups. They do not determine the classes’ orders. In particular, they do not establish that the classes remain nonzero after tensoring with Q\mathbb QQ. The rational-coefficient conjecture is therefore not settled by these examples.

Neither manuscript determines the smallest degree in which integral injectivity can fail. M2’s auxiliary projective generic curve need not be smooth, which is why coherent K-theory is used for its pushforward argument.

M1 includes a separate discussion of a proposed proof in earlier literature. That appendix is not an input to its kernel construction. The mathematical content summarized here is the stated counterexample and its detection, without relying on an independent assessment of that earlier proof.

8. Sources and further reading

Gersten, Problems about higher K-functors, and Quillen, Higher algebraic K-theory: I, appear in Lecture Notes in Mathematics 341 (1973). Panin, The equicharacteristic case of the Gersten conjecture, Proceedings of the Steklov Institute of Mathematics 241 (2003), 154–163, gives the equicharacteristic theorem.

Gillet and Levine, The relative form of Gersten’s conjecture over a discrete valuation ring: The smooth case, Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra 46 (1987), 59–71, supplies the relative framework. Skalit, Regular morphisms and Gersten’s conjecture, states the unramified finite-coefficient result discussed above.

Feld, Finite-coefficient Gersten injectivity fails in ramified mixed characteristic, is the close coefficient-level predecessor. Weibel, The K-book: An introduction to algebraic K-theory (2013), provides background on localization, symbols and coefficient sequences.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An integral counterexample to Gersten’s conjecture (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An integral degree-three Gersten counterexample (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Swapping symmetric powers: the sixth case and a quadratic bound
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 210 · Algebra
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Take symmetric products of vectors, then take symmetric products again. Does it matter which order the two degrees appear in?

For a complex vector space VVV, compare

Sym⁡a(Sym⁡bV)andSym⁡b(Sym⁡aV). \operatorname{Sym}^a(\operatorname{Sym}^b V) \quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{Sym}^b(\operatorname{Sym}^a V).Syma(SymbV)andSymb(SymaV).

They have the same total polynomial degree ababab, but in higher dimensions they are generally different representations of GL⁡(V)\operatorname{GL}(V)GL(V). Foulkes’ conjecture predicts that when a≤ba\leq ba≤b, every irreducible type occurs at least as often in the second as in the first.

Family 210 contains two manuscripts dated 25 September 2026. M1 claims the full case a=6a=6a=6. M2 claims a uniform quadratic bound beyond which a particular canonical map in the reverse direction is surjective. The latter supplies the infinite range of M1’s main argument, leaving finitely many sixth-power comparisons.

2. Background and essential definitions

Symmetric powers and their symmetries

The symmetric power Sym⁡dV\operatorname{Sym}^d VSymdV is formed from ddd-fold tensors by identifying tensors that differ only by permutation of their factors. If VVV has a basis, its symmetric algebra can be viewed as a polynomial algebra in that basis. Products such as v1⋯vdv_1\cdots v_dv1​⋯vd​ are symmetric tensors.

Every invertible linear change of coordinates on VVV acts on all these constructions. A map is GL⁡(V)\operatorname{GL}(V)GL(V)-equivariant if applying the change of coordinates before or after the map gives the same result.

Over C\mathbb CC, finite-dimensional polynomial representations decompose into irreducibles called Schur modules SλVS_\lambda VSλ​V, indexed by partitions λ\lambdaλ. A partition is a decreasing list of nonnegative integers; its size is their sum. A module with too many nonzero parts for dim⁡V\dim VdimV becomes zero.

Complete reducibility means that an equivariant injection exists precisely when every irreducible multiplicity in the source is at most its multiplicity in the target. Thus Foulkes’ conjecture is a whole family of inequalities, not simply a comparison of total dimensions.

Plethysm records composition

The character of a symmetric power is represented by a complete homogeneous symmetric function hdh_dhd​. Composing symmetric-power operations corresponds to plethysm, written with brackets. The stable character of the first representation is ha[hb]h_a[h_b]ha​[hb​].

The conjecture says that

hb[ha]−ha[hb] h_b[h_a]-h_a[h_b]hb​[ha​]−ha​[hb​]

is Schur-positive: its expansion in Schur functions sλs_\lambdasλ​ has nonnegative integer coefficients. These coefficients are the target multiplicities minus the source multiplicities.

One need not manipulate symmetric functions to understand the claim. They are a compact bookkeeping system for the simultaneous comparison of every irreducible type in every dimension.

A canonical map is a stronger requirement

Tensor positions can be arranged in a rectangle, regrouped after transposition, and symmetrized again. This produces a specified Foulkes–Howe map. M2 uses the orientation

μa,b,V:Sym⁡b(Sym⁡aV)⟶Sym⁡a(Sym⁡bV). \mu_{a,b,V}:\operatorname{Sym}^b(\operatorname{Sym}^a V) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^a(\operatorname{Sym}^b V).μa,b,V​:Symb(SymaV)⟶Syma(SymbV).

If this map is surjective, complete reducibility gives an invariant complement to its kernel. Inverting the map on that complement supplies an equivariant injection in the direction predicted by Foulkes.

The injection obtained this way need not be a prescribed canonical map. That distinction matters even when a=ba=ba=b: the two representations then coincide, but a particular canonical endomorphism can still have a kernel.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Foulkes’ conjecture originated in his 1950 work on concomitants of forms. For two-dimensional VVV, classical Hermite reciprocity gives an isomorphism between the two compositions. The difficulty addressed here is uniformity in arbitrary dimension.

The case a=1a=1a=1 is immediate. Thrall’s decomposition formulas imply a=2a=2a=2, and Dent and Siemons proved a=3a=3a=3. Computations combined with McKay’s propagation theorem established the fourth and fifth cases: Müller and Neunhöffer supplied the relevant fourth-case computation, and Cheung, Ikenmeyer and Mkrtchyan supplied a fifth-case injectivity seed at (5,6)(5,6)(5,6).

McKay’s theorem propagates canonical injectivity from a suitable seed to larger second parameters. The seed matters because canonical maps are not always invertible on the diagonal. Nonzero kernels were found at (5,5)(5,5)(5,5) and (6,6)(6,6)(6,6) in suitable dimensions, despite the ordinary representation comparison being automatic there.

Exact character calculations provided another route. Evseev, Paget and Wildon verified Foulkes’ multiplicity inequalities whenever the two parameters sum to at most 191919, covering the sixth case through b=13b=13b=13.

Brion proved eventual truth for fixed aaa, and later gave an effective dimension-dependent bound for surjectivity of the reverse canonical map. Geometrically, that map compares the coordinate ring of the Chow variety of decomposable forms with its normalization.

Raicu, Sam and Weyman developed the invariant-ring and normalization framework further. Their regularity bounds concern related graded modules, but do not by themselves identify the final nonzero degree of the quotient that controls canonical stabilization. M2 claims a sufficient bound depending only quadratically on aaa, independent of dimension. M1 combines its specialization at a=6a=6a=6 with finite multiplicity certificates.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: the sixth symmetric power

For every integer b≥6b\geq6b≥6 and every finite-dimensional complex vector space VVV, M1 asserts an equivariant injection

Sym⁡6(Sym⁡bV)↪Sym⁡b(Sym⁡6V). \operatorname{Sym}^6(\operatorname{Sym}^b V) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}^b(\operatorname{Sym}^6 V).Sym6(SymbV)↪Symb(Sym6V).

Equivalently, hb[h6]−h6[hb]h_b[h_6]-h_6[h_b]hb​[h6​]−h6​[hb​] is Schur-positive for every b≥6b\geq6b≥6. There is no restriction to a fixed dimension or stable-dimensional range. The diagonal case b=6b=6b=6 is immediate as a representation comparison.

M2: quadratic canonical stabilization

For every a≥2a\geq2a≥2, every b≥a(a−1)b\geq a(a-1)b≥a(a−1), and every finite-dimensional complex VVV, M2 asserts that μa,b,V\mu_{a,b,V}μa,b,V​ is surjective. The case a=1a=1a=1 is the identity map.

The bound is sufficient, not claimed to be sharp. It yields Foulkes’ multiplicity comparison throughout that range, but leaves the interval a≤b<a(a−1)a\leq b<a(a-1)a≤b<a(a−1) untreated in general.

For a=6a=6a=6, the threshold is 303030. M1’s main route therefore needs finite comparisons only for 6≤b≤296\leq b\leq296≤b≤29. It also records an independent route: its own chart and polarization argument gives canonical surjectivity for b≥150b\geq150b≥150, and its supplied programs cover the larger finite range through 149149149. The latter route does not use M2’s quadratic theorem.

The finite computations are part of the manuscripts’ claimed arguments. They are reported here as source results, without a new execution or mathematical verification of the certificate programs.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. The family would settle a substantial new case of a longstanding plethysm conjecture and provide a dimension-independent polynomial stabilization bound for all outer degrees.

The two contributions complement each other. A sixth-case theorem addresses every second parameter for one fixed degree. The quadratic bound addresses every degree once the second parameter is sufficiently large. Neither alone is the full Foulkes conjecture, but together they reduce a broad asymptotic question to explicit finite ranges.

The canonical result also has geometric content. It bounds the degrees in which the coordinate ring of decomposable forms can differ from its normalization. This is more specific than knowing that the two nested symmetric powers have compatible dimensions or eventual multiplicities.

The rating reflects major progress with a clearly delimited scope. General multiplicity formulas, optimal stabilization thresholds and the remaining finite ranges for larger aaa are separate questions.

6. The main idea

Turn surjectivity into a vanishing test

M2 realizes the target as equal-multidegree invariants in (Sym⁡V)⊗a(\operatorname{Sym}V)^{\otimes a}(SymV)⊗a. The canonical image is generated by degree-one invariants. More concretely, in degree bbb it is spanned by tensors

P⊗a,P=u1u2⋯ub, P^{\otimes a},\qquad P=u_1u_2\cdots u_b,P⊗a,P=u1​u2​⋯ub​,

where PPP is a product of bbb vectors.

A linear functional annihilating that image corresponds to a symmetric aaa-linear form TTT on Sym⁡bV\operatorname{Sym}^bVSymbV whose diagonal satisfies

T(P,…,P)=0 T(P,\ldots,P)=0T(P,…,P)=0

for every such product. Surjectivity is equivalent to showing that this condition forces T=0T=0T=0.

Differentiate while retaining injectivity

For independent vector variables U=(Ui)U=(U_i)U=(Ui​) and Y=(Yi)Y=(Y_i)Y=(Yi​), consider the directional derivative

DY,U=∑iYi∂∂Ui. D_{Y,U}=\sum_iY_i\frac{\partial}{\partial U_i}.DY,U​=i∑​Yi​∂Ui​∂​.

It lowers the degree in UUU by one and raises the degree in YYY by one. On polynomials homogeneous of degree rrr in UUU and degree sss in YYY, the manuscript uses the standard positive-weight fact that this operator is injective when r>sr>sr>s.

The paper gives an inner-product version: with the Fischer inner product, multiplication and differentiation are adjoint, yielding

∥DY,Uf∥2−∥DU,Yf∥2=(r−s)∥f∥2. \|D_{Y,U}f\|^2-\|D_{U,Y}f\|^2=(r-s)\|f\|^2.∥DY,U​f∥2−∥DU,Y​f∥2=(r−s)∥f∥2.

When r>sr>sr>s, a vanishing forward derivative therefore forces the original polynomial to vanish. Additional independent variables do not alter the criterion.

Factoring a binary form first produces a vanishing identity in which several slots share a common product. One sequence of directional derivatives frees the last slot. Induction on the number of slots then lets the other products vary independently. A second sequence removes their remaining common power.

The second sequence repeatedly raises the degree of the same destination variable. Keeping every derivative injective requires a degree budget, and that accumulation gives the sufficient inequality b≥a(a−1)b\geq a(a-1)b≥a(a−1). The number of coordinates never enters the budget, explaining the dimension-independent bound.

Reduce the sixth case to six-part partitions

M1 denotes the source multiplicity at a partition λ\lambdaλ by F(λ)F(\lambda)F(λ), and the target multiplicity by Q(λ)Q(\lambda)Q(λ). The source has no constituents with more than six parts. It therefore suffices to compare those partitions; longer target constituents already have nonnegative multiplicity.

Stable character specialization allows the calculation in six variables to handle every dimension. Rectangular highest-weight shifts transfer known comparisons to new partitions. A chart calculation also certifies targets whose boxes outside the first row occupy at most bbb positions.

The remaining finite argument combines upper bounds on FFF with lower bounds on QQQ. Source bounds come from a signed-strip recurrence. Target bounds come from multiplying highest-weight polynomials with distinct leading monomials: distinct resulting monomials certify linear independence, so sumset estimates give many independent products.

After the broad certificates are applied, exact character differences are needed only in a narrow band of partition shapes. The manuscript computes that band using seven reused truncated rational-function numerators. It supplies exact programs, arithmetic bounds and reference outputs for the finite checks, rather than relying on floating-point approximations.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The coefficients are complex. The proofs use complete reducibility, nonzero factorials in polarization, factorization of binary forms and a positive Hermitian inner product. No general positive-characteristic extension is asserted.

M1 proves existence of an equivariant injection. It does not claim injectivity of the canonical map in that direction for every sixth-case parameter. M2 proves surjectivity of a specified map in the opposite direction, only in its stated range. Keeping these orientations straight avoids turning a true multiplicity comparison into a stronger unsupported map assertion.

The quadratic bound is not presented as the least stabilization degree. For larger aaa, the finite interval below the bound still contains cases of the full conjecture. The manuscripts do not claim to resolve all of them.

The geometric normalization interpretation also concerns equality in sufficiently high graded pieces. It does not say that the coordinate ring and its normalization agree in every degree, or that the Chow variety is normal in all parameters.

8. Sources and further reading

Foulkes, Concomitants of the quintic and sextic up to degree four in the coefficients of the ground form, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 25 (1950), 205–209, is the original source. Brion, Stable properties of plethysm: on two conjectures of Foulkes, Manuscripta Mathematica 80 (1993), 347–371, supplies the eventual result.

Cheung, Ikenmeyer and Mkrtchyan, Symmetrizing tableaux and the 5th case of the Foulkes conjecture, Journal of Symbolic Computation 80 (2017), 833–843, gives the fifth-case computation and canonical-map distinctions. Ikenmeyer, On McKay’s propagation theorem for the Foulkes conjecture, explains propagation.

Raicu, Sam and Weyman, On some modules supported in the Chow variety, Vietnam Journal of Mathematics 50 (2022), 501–521, provides the invariant-ring framework. Landsberg, Geometric complexity theory: an introduction for geometers, discusses the polynomial-bound question answered by M2’s claim.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Foulkes’ conjecture for the sixth symmetric power (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Quadratic stabilization of the canonical Foulkes–Howe map (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Finite lattices that no finite algebra can realize
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 206 · Algebra
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

An algebra has many possible quotients: one can identify elements in ways compatible with its operations. These identifications form a lattice, an ordered structure recording which quotients refine which others.

Can every finite lattice arise as the complete lattice of compatible identifications of some finite algebra? The operations are entirely unrestricted. We may choose their number, their arities and their tables to suit the desired lattice. The only requirement is that the underlying set remain finite.

Family 206 contains two manuscripts dated 24 September 2026. Both claim a negative answer. M2 constructs an obstruction through subgroup lattices of finite groups. M1 goes further, claiming that no algorithm can decide finite representability from a finite lattice table. It also gives finite certificates for positive instances and a mathematically specified, but not numerically evaluated, smallest negative example.

2. Background and essential definitions

A lattice is an order with meets and joins

A lattice is a partially ordered set in which every pair x,yx,yx,y has a greatest lower bound x∧yx\wedge yx∧y, called the meet, and a least upper bound x∨yx\vee yx∨y, called the join. The subsets of a finite set, ordered by inclusion, form a familiar example: meet is intersection and join is union.

A finite nonempty lattice has a least element 000 and a greatest element 111. It can be specified by a finite order table, so it is a legitimate input to an algorithm.

Congruences record compatible identifications

A finite algebra here is a finite nonempty set AAA equipped with finitely many total operations, each taking finitely many arguments. It need not be a group or a ring. Unary operations, constants and even an empty list of operations are allowed.

A congruence is an equivalence relation θ\thetaθ preserved by every operation. For a binary operation fff, compatibility means

aθa′,bθb′⟹f(a,b)θf(a′,b′). a\mathrel\theta a',\quad b\mathrel\theta b' \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(a,b)\mathrel\theta f(a',b').aθa′,bθb′⟹f(a,b)θf(a′,b′).

This makes the induced operation on equivalence classes well defined. The congruences form a lattice Con⁡(A)\operatorname{Con}(A)Con(A), ordered by inclusion. Its least element identifies only equal elements; its greatest identifies everything. Meets are intersections, while joins are the smallest congruences containing the given relations.

The word full is essential. Finding the desired lattice among some of the congruences is insufficient. A representation requires an isomorphism

L≅Con⁡(A), L\cong\operatorname{Con}(A),L≅Con(A),

with no extra congruences left over.

Group intervals and algorithms

For a subgroup HHH of a finite group GGG, the full subgroup interval is

[H,G]={K:H≤K≤G}, [H,G]=\{K:H\leq K\leq G\},[H,G]={K:H≤K≤G},

ordered by inclusion. It contains every intermediate subgroup, not a selected collection.

A decision algorithm must halt on every input and answer correctly. A semidecision procedure for representability need only halt when a representation exists; it may search forever on a negative instance. The distinction is central here. Every individual proposed finite algebra can be checked, but there may be no computable limit on how large a witness must be sought.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Grätzer and Schmidt proved in 1963 that every algebraic lattice is a congruence lattice of an algebra. Finite lattices belong to that class. The representing algebra in their theorem, however, may be infinite. The finite lattice representation problem asks whether a finite carrier can always be used.

Pudlák developed a graph-based proof of the general representation theorem. Pudlák and Tůma later proved that every finite lattice embeds into the partition lattice of a finite set. A partition lattice is the lattice of all equivalence relations on that set. This is a strong finite embedding result, but it does not ensure that exactly the chosen sublattice is preserved by some operations.

Pálfy and Pudlák established a crucial bridge in 1980: the assertion that every finite lattice has a finite congruence representation is equivalent to the assertion that every finite lattice is an interval in a finite group’s subgroup lattice.

This is an equivalence of universal statements. It does not say that each individual lattice has one representation if and only if it has the other. That logical distinction determines what can be concluded from a particular subgroup obstruction.

Positive results cover all finite lattices of width at most two, where width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements. DeMeo’s analysis left only one possible exception among lattices with at most seven elements. M1 supplies a representation of that remaining small case, so its claimed minimum obstruction has more than seven elements.

On the group side, Baddeley, Lucchini, Börner and Aschbacher developed reductions using finite simple groups and special interval configurations. Repnitskiĭ and Tůma showed that an infinite, countable locally finite group can represent every finite lattice as an interval. Again, allowing an infinite ambient object changes the problem.

The new papers claim obstructions uniform over every possible finite carrier or finite group, regardless of its size. M1 additionally connects that uniformity problem with Diophantine undecidability.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: a negative existence theorem

M2 asserts that some finite nonempty lattice is not the full congruence lattice of any finite algebra of any finite signature. Its direct construction produces a self-dual finite lattice that is not a full subgroup interval in any finite group. Self-dual means that reversing the order gives an isomorphic lattice.

The Pálfy–Pudlák equivalence then gives the negative congruence-lattice conclusion globally. M2 explicitly does not identify its particular decorated subgroup obstruction with the congruence obstruction point by point.

The self-dual subgroup obstruction also cannot be the entire lattice of intermediate fields of a finite separable field extension. Passing to a finite normal closure would, by Galois correspondence, turn that field lattice into the reverse of a finite subgroup interval; self-duality would remove the reversal.

M1: characterization and undecidability

M1 claims a finite colored-graph characterization of representability. Each graph witness is checkable by a finite procedure, and enumerating all possible witnesses eventually finds a representation whenever one exists.

At the same time, it asserts that no deterministic Turing machine always halts and decides whether a given finite lattice is representable. It separately asserts undecidability of recognition as a full subgroup interval of a finite group.

These statements are compatible. Positive certificates can be searchable without there being a stopping rule for unsuccessful searches.

M1 also specifies a nonrepresentable lattice L0L_0L0​ of minimum cardinality, with ∣L0∣>7|L_0|>7∣L0​∣>7. The finite description uses a particular Busy Beaver integer, a maximum associated with halting computations of bounded program size. It does not evaluate that integer, the minimum cardinality or the entries of the lattice’s order table. “Specified” therefore should not be read as “a small diagram explicitly printed and computed.”

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. A negative solution would settle a foundational finite representation problem in universal algebra. The undecidability claim would go further, explaining why no universal recognition procedure can classify all finite instances.

The unrestricted signature makes the negative result especially strong. Failure cannot be repaired by adding a clever operation, increasing its arity, or changing from groups to some other finite algebraic system. The obstruction concerns every finite algebra on every finite carrier.

The decision-theoretic conclusion also gives a structural consequence: there can be no computable bound, depending only on the size of a representable lattice, on the size of the graph witness in M1’s characterization. If such a bound existed, a finite exhaustive search would decide the problem.

The significance is theoretical, not a claim that ordinary small examples are impossible to handle. Indeed, the paper’s small-lattice result points in the opposite direction: substantial finite ranges can have uniformly positive answers while the general recognition problem remains undecidable.

6. The main idea

Replace operations by a colored graph

M1 assigns a lattice element d(a,b)d(a,b)d(a,b) to each pair of vertices in a finite complete graph. Think of the color as the least identification needed to merge aaa and bbb. Diagonal colors are zero, and the labels satisfy a lattice-valued triangle inequality:

d(a,b)≤d(a,c)∨d(c,b). d(a,b)\leq d(a,c)\vee d(c,b).d(a,b)≤d(a,c)∨d(c,b).

For each lattice element xxx, the pairs with d(a,b)≤xd(a,b)\leq xd(a,b)≤x form an equivalence relation. Additional separation conditions ensure that different lattice elements give different relations.

A self-map of the vertices is admissible if it only decreases labels. Give the vertex set all such maps as unary operations. A path condition then ensures that every congruence of this algebra is one of the intended relations. That last condition prevents extra congruences from appearing and turns an embedding into a full representation.

For a fixed number of vertices, all colorings, maps and paths can be checked finitely. The unbounded witness size is where algorithmic difficulty remains.

Force incompatible finite-group configurations

Both manuscripts use carefully decorated finite lattices to impose constraints on any hypothetical subgroup representation. Special intervals test normal subgroups and force nonabelian simple-group components to occur along selected chains.

The challenge is simultaneous compatibility. Recognizing the abstract isomorphism type of a simple group at each step does not control how the actual groups embed into one another. The constructions retain those embeddings and impose tests relative to earlier groups along the chain.

M2 derives an absolute upper bound on the length of certain tested chains with different endpoint labels. It uses finite simple-group classification, restrictions of representations, field parameters and growth estimates. The bound is independent of the size of a hypothetical ambient group.

It then builds a finite lattice whose inserted chains exceed that bound while preserving selected Boolean meets and joins. In a supposed representation, the surviving subgroup data describe homomorphisms extending a common action. The Boolean faces force these extensions to agree locally, while another part of the lattice forbids a common extension. The final gluing argument forces exactly that forbidden extension.

M1 develops a separate obstruction using affine charts and protected chains. Its undecidability argument needs further quantitative constructions beyond the existence of one negative lattice.

Turn a hypothetical decider into bounded arithmetic

M1 encodes positive integer solutions of arithmetic circuits in weighted subgroup templates. Sizes of permutation sets represent numbers; equal totals express addition, and square-size constructions express multiplication.

Two bounds work together. The number of lattice elements is bounded computably by the circuit’s syntax, independently of the sizes of its numerical solution. Conversely, any finite representation gives a fresh numerical reading whose values are computably bounded in the size of that representation.

If a representability decider existed, one could list all representable lattice tables up to the relevant size and search until a witness had been found for each. This would give a computable witness bound, and hence a computable bound on a replacement arithmetic solution whenever any solution existed.

Searching the resulting finite box would decide the Diophantine problem, contradicting its known undecidability. The argument does not need to construct an unknown-solution template directly from the circuit. It uses the bounded collection of possible lattice tables and the hypothetical decider to obtain the replacement bound.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The algebras and lattices are nonempty and finite. Operations are total and finitary. Allowing infinitely many finitary operations on a finite carrier would not add representations: for each unwanted equivalence relation, one could retain a single operation witnessing its incompatibility, leaving a finite list.

The negative conclusion concerns full congruence lattices and full subgroup intervals. It does not contradict the positive embedding theorems or the general representation theorem with infinite carriers.

Undecidability is a statement about one algorithm handling every finite input. It does not say that each individual lattice is unclassifiable, nor that useful restricted classes lack algorithms.

The minimum obstruction’s numerical size remains unevaluated in M1. Producing a manageable explicit order table, determining sharp small-size thresholds, and finding tractable structural subclasses are distinct questions from the claimed existence and undecidability theorems.

8. Sources and further reading

Grätzer and Schmidt, Characterizations of congruence lattices of abstract algebras, Acta Scientiarum Mathematicarum 24 (1963), 34–59, gives the general representation theorem. Pálfy and Pudlák, Congruence lattices of finite algebras and intervals in subgroup lattices of finite groups, Algebra Universalis 11 (1980), 22–27, supplies the global equivalence.

Pudlák and Tůma, Every finite lattice can be embedded in a finite partition lattice, Algebra Universalis 10 (1980), 74–95, is the finite embedding theorem. DeMeo’s Congruence Lattices of Finite Algebras, doctoral thesis (2012), provides small-lattice results and the unary-closure viewpoint.

For the graphical predecessor, see Kenney, Graphical algebras—a new approach to congruence lattices, Algebra Universalis 64, 313–338. Matiyasevich’s Diophantine representation of enumerable predicates, Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya 5 (1971), 1–28, is the arithmetic undecidability input.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Finite congruence lattices: characterization and undecidability (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A common home for finite symmetric tensor categories
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 208 · Algebra
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Many mathematical objects can be added, tensored and dualized. Vector spaces are the basic example; group representations carry the same operations together with symmetry information. A tensor category records these operations abstractly, without first specifying what the objects are made of.

A natural question is whether such an abstract category can always be interpreted inside a familiar concrete setting while preserving its linear and tensor structure. In characteristic zero, supervector spaces provide a remarkably broad answer. Positive characteristic introduces new behavior that ordinary or supervector spaces cannot capture.

Family 208 contains a manuscript dated 24 September 2026 claiming that every finite symmetric tensor category in positive characteristic has a faithful exact interpretation in one finite higher Verlinde category. This is the finite case of the Benson–Etingof–Ostrik conjecture, including characteristic two. The finiteness qualification is a substantive part of the result.

2. Background and essential definitions

Categories that behave like representations

A category has objects and maps between them. In a kkk-linear category, each space of maps is a vector space over the field kkk, and composition is bilinear.

An abelian category supports kernels, quotients and exact sequences, so it provides a setting for linear algebra and extensions. A tensor product combines objects, with a unit object playing the role of the one-dimensional trivial representation. Rigidity means every object has a dual. Symmetry means there are compatible swap maps X⊗Y→Y⊗XX\otimes Y\to Y\otimes XX⊗Y→Y⊗X, whose successive swaps give the identity.

The prototype is the category of finite-dimensional representations of a group. Its tensor product uses the diagonal group action, its dual is the dual representation, and its maps are equivariant linear maps.

Here a finite symmetric tensor category has finite-dimensional map spaces, finite-length objects, finitely many simple isomorphism classes and enough projective objects. Tensoring is exact in each variable, and the endomorphism ring of the unit is kkk. Finite length means that each object has a finite composition series with simple factors. “Finite category” does not mean finitely many objects in total.

What a fiber functor preserves

A fiber functor in this paper is a kkk-linear, exact, faithful, strong symmetric monoidal functor. In more familiar terms, it preserves linear combinations of maps, short exact sequences, tensor products, the unit and the symmetry; it does not identify two distinct maps.

Faithful does not mean full. The target may have maps between the images that did not come from the source. Thus a fiber functor is an interpretation preserving the relevant structure, not necessarily an identification with a full subcategory.

The higher Verlinde tower

Over an algebraically closed field kkk of characteristic p>0p>0p>0, the higher Verlinde categories form a tower

Ver⁡p(k)⊂Ver⁡p2(k)⊂Ver⁡p3(k)⊂⋯ . \operatorname{Ver}_p(k)\subset \operatorname{Ver}_{p^2}(k)\subset \operatorname{Ver}_{p^3}(k)\subset\cdots.Verp​(k)⊂Verp2​(k)⊂Verp3​(k)⊂⋯.

The first level comes from representations of the cyclic group of order ppp, after discarding morphisms invisible to all trace pairings. Its simple objects correspond to Jordan blocks of lengths 1,…,p−11,\ldots,p-11,…,p−1. In particular, Ver⁡2\operatorname{Ver}_2Ver2​ is the category of vector spaces, while Ver⁡3\operatorname{Ver}_3Ver3​ is the category of supervector spaces with the usual sign rule.

A supervector space is a vector space split into even and odd parts; swapping two odd vectors introduces a minus sign. Higher levels of the tower need not be semisimple: objects may be genuine extensions rather than direct sums of simples. They arise from quotients and abelian envelopes of tilting representations of SL⁡2\operatorname{SL}_2SL2​. For the main theorem, their role is a fixed hierarchy of increasingly expressive symmetric tensor targets.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Tannakian theory reconstructs groups from categories of representations together with suitable fiber functors. Deligne’s characteristic-zero theorem extended the common target from vector spaces to supervector spaces for symmetric tensor categories of moderate growth. Moderate growth means that, for each object, the lengths of its tensor powers grow at most exponentially.

Positive characteristic changes the picture. Ostrik proved that symmetric fusion categories admit fiber functors to Ver⁡p\operatorname{Ver}_pVerp​. Fusion categories are semisimple finite tensor categories, so this covers an important but restricted case.

Etingof and Ostrik developed the Frobenius functor for nonsemisimple categories. Coulembier independently constructed its underlying additive functor. Exactness is the decisive issue: the ordinary Frobenius functor need not preserve short exact sequences. Etingof–Ostrik characterized finite categories where it is exact by the existence of a fiber functor to the first Verlinde level. Coulembier, Etingof and Ostrik extended this characterization to moderate-growth categories.

The higher tower is needed to accommodate categories beyond that first-level criterion. Benson and Etingof constructed characteristic-two examples, followed by the all-prime tower of Benson, Etingof and Ostrik. Coulembier independently developed the relevant abelian-envelope constructions.

Coulembier and Flake then introduced higher Frobenius constructions using representations of elementary abelian ppp-groups. Their construction becomes symmetric monoidal under a specific restricted-tilting conjecture. Earlier work established the conjecture in low rank and characteristic, and for substantial module classes, including modules of Loewy length at most two and Carlson modules, together with categories generated from them by standard operations.

The new manuscript claims the full restricted-tilting statement for arbitrary finite-dimensional modules. It then uses that result, together with existing higher-Frobenius machinery, to select an exact functor and obtain the finite-category theorem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every prime ppp, every algebraically closed field kkk of characteristic ppp, and every finite symmetric tensor category C\mathcal CC over kkk, the manuscript asserts the existence of an integer n≥1n\geq1n≥1 and a fiber functor

F:C⟶Ver⁡pn(k). F:\mathcal C\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ver}_{p^n}(k).F:C⟶Verpn​(k).

The height nnn may depend on C\mathcal CC. The theorem does not say that every category maps to the first level or to every prescribed level.

An independent representation-theoretic statement supplies the main new input. Embed

Er=(Z/pZ)r E_r=(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^rEr​=(Z/pZ)r

into the upper unipotent subgroup of SL⁡2(k)\operatorname{SL}_2(k)SL2​(k), and let RRR denote restriction of representations. If St⁡r−1\operatorname{St}_{r-1}Str−1​ is the simple Steinberg module of highest weight pr−1−1p^{r-1}-1pr−1−1, then for every finite-dimensional ErE_rEr​-module DDD, the manuscript claims

R(St⁡r−1)⊗D≅R(T) R(\operatorname{St}_{r-1})\otimes D\cong R(T)R(Str−1​)⊗D≅R(T)

for some tilting SL⁡2\operatorname{SL}_2SL2​-module TTT. Tilting means that the module has both a filtration by Weyl modules and one by their dual counterparts. The assertion applies to every embedding of the specified kind, not only a specially chosen module class.

The fiber theorem also yields consequences through established results. It classifies finite incompressible symmetric tensor categories using the known subcategories of the Verlinde tower. Incompressible means that every exact symmetric tensor functor out of the category is fully faithful.

In characteristic two, a previous uniqueness theorem combines with the new existence claim to give exactly one fiber functor to the union of the tower, up to monoidal natural isomorphism. It has a representative landing in a finite level. The manuscript does not assert this uniqueness for every odd characteristic.

Finally, generalized Tannaka reconstruction realizes C\mathcal CC as a suitable representation category of an affine group scheme internal to the chosen Verlinde level, with the required canonical fundamental-group compatibility.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. This would establish a broad common-target theorem for finite symmetric tensor categories in every positive characteristic, extending far beyond the semisimple and ordinary Frobenius-exact cases.

A common target makes abstract categories more comparable. It provides a setting for reconstruction and separates the universal background structure from the additional internal group symmetry defining a particular category.

The restricted-tilting theorem would also be useful independently: it says that tensoring by one specified restricted Steinberg module brings every elementary-abelian-group representation into the restricted tilting world.

The rating reflects a major finite-case advance while retaining the distinction from the full moderate-growth conjecture. That broader conjecture permits categories without a finite list of simple objects or a projective generator, precisely the features used in the proposed proof.

6. The main idea

Make arbitrary modules accessible to tilting theory

An elementary abelian ppp-group can sit inside the additive upper-unipotent matrices

(1t01). \begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.(10​t1​).

The paper first lifts an individual module for this finite subgroup to a representation of the additive algebraic group, with a bound on its polynomial degree. It does not require this preliminary lifting operation to preserve tensor products.

The lifted representation defines an equivariant vector bundle on the punctured plane. The bundle is then extended across the origin while controlling the highest weights in its fiber there. Tensoring by the specified Steinberg module makes that origin fiber tilting through an established bounded-weight result.

A formal comparison of fibers links the origin construction back to the original module away from the origin. This is the geometric step that the manuscript uses to handle arbitrary DDD, beyond the previously known special classes.

Choose a higher Frobenius functor that is exact

The restricted-tilting result activates the Coulembier–Flake construction. It produces an additive strong symmetric monoidal functor of the form

Φ:C⟶C⊠Ver⁡pr(k). \Phi:\mathcal C\longrightarrow \mathcal C\boxtimes\operatorname{Ver}_{p^r}(k).Φ:C⟶C⊠Verpr​(k).

The symbol ⊠\boxtimes⊠ is the Deligne product, the categorical counterpart of taking modules over a tensor product of finite-dimensional algebras. Initially, Φ\PhiΦ is semilinear: multiplying a map by a∈ka\in ka∈k multiplies its image by apra^{p^r}apr.

Exactness depends on the embedding of ErE_rEr​. Choose a projective generator PPP, an object from which every object is obtained as a quotient of a finite direct sum. Permuting the factors of P⊗prP^{\otimes p^r}P⊗pr gives an ErE_rEr​-module on

Hom⁡C(P,P⊗pr). \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(P,P^{\otimes p^r}).HomC​(P,P⊗pr).

The manuscript finds the first rank where this module is nonprojective. Rank-support methods then select an embedding that makes Φ\PhiΦ exact. The finiteness hypotheses are doing concrete work here by supplying PPP.

Remove the original category from the target

A functor landing in C⊠Ver⁡pr\mathcal C\boxtimes\operatorname{Ver}_{p^r}C⊠Verpr​ has not yet solved the problem: the original unknown category remains in the target.

The paper compares Frobenius–Perron dimensions, positive real sizes determined by tensor multiplication. For a simple object SSS, any first-factor simple constituent AAA arising from Φ(S)\Phi(S)Φ(S) has dimension at most that of SSS. Equality forces the object into the subcategory where the ordinary Frobenius functor is exact.

Draw a finite directed graph with an arrow S→AS\to AS→A for each such possibility. Every cycle lies in that controlled subcategory and cannot escape it. Because there are only finitely many simple objects, repeated application eventually places all first factors in its extension closure.

Earlier theorems give that controlled category a fiber functor to Ver⁡p\operatorname{Ver}_pVerp​ in odd characteristic, or to a specified subcategory of Ver⁡4\operatorname{Ver}_4Ver4​ in characteristic two. Combining the finitely many target factors inside one tower level and correcting the scalar semilinearity produces the claimed kkk-linear fiber functor.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem assumes an algebraically closed field of positive characteristic and a finite symmetric tensor category with the stated exactness, duality and projectivity properties. It includes characteristic two, where the ordinary sign intuition alone is inadequate.

The full Benson–Etingof–Ostrik conjecture for arbitrary moderate-growth categories is not claimed. The proof’s finite directed graph and projective generator do not automatically extend to that setting.

Existence at some finite height is different from a uniform bound on height or an explicit minimum level for every category. The theorem supplies neither a universal prescribed height nor a general classification of all finite symmetric tensor categories by a short list of individual objects.

The internal reconstructed group scheme is asserted to be affine. The manuscript expressly makes no finiteness or finite-type claim for it. Reconstruction includes compatibility with the target category’s canonical fundamental-group action; it is not simply an ordinary group representation category over vector spaces.

8. Sources and further reading

Deligne, Catégories tensorielles, Moscow Mathematical Journal 2 (2002), 227–248, provides the characteristic-zero comparison. Ostrik, On symmetric fusion categories in positive characteristic, Selecta Mathematica 26 (2020), Article 36, gives the semisimple positive-characteristic theorem.

Benson, Etingof and Ostrik, New incompressible symmetric tensor categories in positive characteristic, Duke Mathematical Journal 172 (2023), 105–200, constructs the tower and formulates the conjecture. Coulembier, Etingof and Ostrik, Incompressible tensor categories, Advances in Mathematics 457 (2024), Article 109935, supplies the uniqueness and reconstruction framework.

Coulembier and Flake, Towards higher Frobenius functors for symmetric tensor categories, and A conjecture on the tensor ideal for an elementary p-group generated by the restriction of a Steinberg module, give the higher-functor construction and preceding restricted-tilting results.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Fiber functors for finite symmetric tensor categories in positive characteristic (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Eventual uniqueness of large models, without a prescribed threshold
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 240 · Mathematical logic
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Some axioms determine a mathematical structure completely once its size is specified. For example, vector spaces over a fixed field are classified by the cardinality of a basis. Model theory asks when a similar uniqueness principle holds for classes of structures described by much more general rules.

A class is categorical in a cardinal if it has exactly one model of that size up to isomorphism. Shelah’s eventual categoricity conjecture predicts that uniqueness at one sufficiently large size forces uniqueness at every size beyond a uniform threshold.

Family 240 contains two manuscripts dated 24 September 2026. M2 claims the qualitative conjecture in ZFC, with a threshold depending only on a measure of the class’s complexity. M1 constructs, assuming the continuum hypothesis, an obstruction to one specific proposed threshold. These claims are compatible: a threshold can exist without equalling the proposed explicit bound.

2. Background and essential definitions

Models and categoricity

A structure consists of a set together with named relations and operations. A group, an ordered set and a field are examples. An isomorphism is a bijection preserving that structure.

For a class KKK, let I(K,κ)I(K,\kappa)I(K,κ) count the isomorphism types of models with cardinality κ\kappaκ. Categoricity means

I(K,κ)=1. I(K,\kappa)=1.I(K,κ)=1.

Existence is included. Having no models of a size is not categoricity, even though there are then no two models to distinguish.

An abstract elementary class, or AEC, is a class of structures together with a designated strong-substructure relation ≤K\leq_K≤K​. It is closed under isomorphism and coherent increasing unions. The relation must agree with ordinary substructure in the forward direction and satisfy a coherence condition among nested models.

The Löwenheim–Skolem axiom provides small strong submodels. There is an infinite cardinal ℓ\ellℓ such that every subset AAA of a model MMM lies in a strong submodel N≤KMN\leq_KMN≤K​M with

∣N∣≤∣A∣+ℓ. |N|\leq|A|+\ell.∣N∣≤∣A∣+ℓ.

The least such bound, subject to the language-size convention, is LS⁡(K)\operatorname{LS}(K)LS(K). It measures how much structure must accompany a chosen set of elements. AECs extend the first-order setting without assuming its compactness theorem.

Additional structural properties

Joint embedding means that any two models strongly embed into a common model. Amalgamation asks for such embeddings over a common strong submodel, agreeing there. Tameness says, roughly, that differences between types can be detected over small pieces of their parameter sets.

These are powerful hypotheses in categoricity theorems, but they are not part of the bare AEC axioms used by the new manuscripts.

Thresholds and the beth hierarchy

The cardinals ℶα\beth_\alphaℶα​ start with ℶ0=ℵ0\beth_0=\aleph_0ℶ0​=ℵ0​, satisfy ℶα+1=2ℶα\beth_{\alpha+1}=2^{\beth_\alpha}ℶα+1​=2ℶα​, and take suprema at limit ordinals. They iterate the power-set operation through transfinite stages.

A proposed threshold is

h(κ)=ℶ(2κ)+,H(K)=h(LS⁡(K)), h(\kappa)=\beth_{(2^\kappa)^+},\qquad H(K)=h(\operatorname{LS}(K)),h(κ)=ℶ(2κ)+​,H(K)=h(LS(K)),

where the superscript +++ means the next cardinal, used as an ordinal index for ℶ\bethℶ. It is not an added exponent.

The continuum hypothesis, CH, says 2ℵ0=ℵ12^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_12ℵ0​=ℵ1​. Under CH, a countable Löwenheim–Skolem number gives H(K)=ℶω2H(K)=\beth_{\omega_2}H(K)=ℶω2​​, where ω2\omega_2ω2​ is the initial ordinal of cardinality ℵ2\aleph_2ℵ2​.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Morley’s 1965 theorem is the first-order prototype: a complete theory in a countable language that is categorical in one uncountable cardinal is categorical in every uncountable cardinal. Baldwin and Lachlan’s work on strongly minimal sets explains a central geometric mechanism, in which models are classified by bases and dimensions.

Shelah introduced AECs to organize nonelementary classes, including models of infinitary logics. In that setting, types, independence and amalgamation cannot simply be imported from first-order compactness. Eventual categoricity became a broad test of how much classification theory survives.

Major partial results imposed structural or set-theoretic hypotheses. Makkai and Shelah obtained transfers for infinitary theories using a strongly compact cardinal. Grossberg and VanDieren proved upward transfer from sufficiently large successor categoricity under tameness, amalgamation, joint embedding and arbitrarily large models. Boney derived tameness from large-cardinal assumptions and obtained further eventual-categoricity consequences.

Vasey proved ZFC transfer for universal classes without assuming amalgamation, and other results treated tame classes with primes. Shelah and Vasey developed categoricity through multidimensional diagrams for excellent classes, with broader conclusions under additional hypotheses. These results show why both the structure of the class and the kind of starting cardinal matter.

The literature also distinguishes an unspecified eventual threshold from a prescribed one. An existence bound can ensure that a class has arbitrarily large models without ensuring uniqueness there or guaranteeing that every particular model extends arbitrarily far.

Both manuscripts discuss earlier public claims by Espíndola of general eventual categoricity and explicit-threshold transfer. M2 describes its construction as independent of those preprints. M1 addresses the prescribed-threshold statement and a specific step in the cited argument. These are attributed comparisons in the sources, rather than an independent determination of priority or proof correctness.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: one uniform threshold exists

For every infinite cardinal λ\lambdaλ, M2 asserts that there is a cardinal μ(λ)≥λ\mu(\lambda)\geq\lambdaμ(λ)≥λ such that every AEC KKK with LS⁡(K)≤λ\operatorname{LS}(K)\leq\lambdaLS(K)≤λ satisfies

K categorical in some κ≥μ(λ)⟹K categorical in every κ′≥μ(λ).\begin{aligned}&K\text{ categorical in some }\kappa\geq\mu(\lambda)\\&\qquad\LongrightarrowK\text{ categorical in every }\kappa'\geq\mu(\lambda).\end{aligned}​K categorical in some κ≥μ(λ)⟹K categorical in every κ′≥μ(λ).​

The same threshold appears in the premise and conclusion, and it depends only on the Löwenheim–Skolem bound, not on the particular class.

The theorem is stated in ZFC, without amalgamation, joint embedding, tameness, absence of maximal models or arbitrarily large models as extra assumptions. The initial categoricity cardinal may be a successor, a regular limit or a singular cardinal.

M2 also states an equivalent qualitative form: an AEC categorical in unboundedly many cardinals is categorical on a tail, meaning every cardinal above some bound. It does not give a numerical formula for the uniform threshold.

M1: the proposed endpoint can fail under CH

Assuming CH, M1 constructs an AEC in a countable finitary relational language with LS⁡(K)=ℵ0\operatorname{LS}(K)=\aleph_0LS(K)=ℵ0​, at least two nonisomorphic models of size

H(K)=ℶω2, H(K)=\beth_{\omega_2},H(K)=ℶω2​​,

and categoricity in every cardinal at least

Λ=ℶ(2ℵ1)+. \Lambda=\beth_{(2^{\aleph_1})^+}.Λ=ℶ(2ℵ1​)+​.

This Λ\LambdaΛ is larger than H(K)H(K)H(K). Thus categoricity high above the proposed endpoint does not transfer down to that endpoint. The same class is nevertheless categorical on a higher tail.

Using the relative consistency of CH, the manuscript concludes that, if ZFC is consistent, the specified universal threshold assertion is not provable in ZFC, for the precise formulations discussed there. This is one-sided nonprovability. It is not a claim of independence in both directions, and it does not refute qualitative eventual categoricity.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. M2 claims a general solution of one of the central classification problems for AECs, removing the structural and starting-cardinal restrictions present in major earlier theorems.

The uniform quantifier is particularly strong. It says that a single threshold works for every class with a bounded Löwenheim–Skolem number, even when their internal structures differ greatly.

M1 contributes a complementary warning about quantitative formulations. A threshold motivated by existence theory need not be the correct threshold for uniqueness. Its example would force any general explicit-bound proposal to account for models that coexist at one large size but cannot continue into the final categorical regime.

The importance score concerns those claims together. It does not turn the unspecified bound in M2 into an effective estimate or treat M1’s CH-dependent construction as an unconditional ZFC counterexample.

6. The main idea

M2 constructs geometry from eventual uniqueness

The positive argument first reduces to a fixed AEC categorical in unboundedly many cardinals. It builds models indexed by linear orders, with each element described using a label and finitely many order positions. Order embeddings then induce strong maps.

Specially chosen orders control the possible records of short tuples. The manuscript constructs reversals of strong maps on prescribed bounded tuples directly, rather than assuming an unrestricted syntactic characterization that the cited literature had identified as problematic.

At selected sufficiently closed cardinal levels, these comparisons stabilize. They support amalgamation, homogeneity and an independence calculus for the working models. Here these properties are outputs of the construction at controlled levels, not assumptions on the original class.

The paper then extends the calculus to finite diagrams of models, retaining all specified boundary maps. Completing a boundary in a larger common model and extending an isomorphism onto a prescribed target are treated as separate requirements.

A minimal type supplies a pregeometry, an abstract dependence structure with a basis notion analogous to linear independence. The crucial claim is that a proper strong extension must add a new point of this geometry. Above a threshold, basis cardinality therefore measures the cardinality of the model itself.

The final induction classifies models by basis maps, using coherent unions at limit stages and separate cardinal bookkeeping for successor, regular-limit and singular sizes. This gives a categorical tail for the fixed class.

Uniformity comes from a set of codes

A separate coding argument passes from individual tails to one threshold for all classes with bounded Löwenheim–Skolem number. Up to the relevant coding, there are set-many such AECs.

For each code, either the categoricity spectrum is bounded, or the qualitative theorem gives a categorical tail. Taking a common bound above all bounded spectra and all tail thresholds yields μ(λ)\mu(\lambda)μ(λ). A class categorical above that common bound must belong to the second case.

This is an existence argument for a bound. It does not compute a convenient beth expression for it.

M1 keeps two kinds of models alive at the endpoint

The obstruction uses an index sort III, controlling total size, and a base sort BBB, a dense linear order without endpoints whose bounded intervals are countable. This forces ∣B∣≤ℵ1|B|\leq\aleph_1∣B∣≤ℵ1​.

Attached row and column fibers are torsors: they behave like groups with no distinguished origin. Choosing origins displays binary matrices. Changing row origins alters finitely many entries in each row, while changing column origins alters finitely many in each column.

When BBB is countable, these changes absorb every matrix, leaving one isomorphism type at a fixed large index size. When BBB is uncountable, residual binary-sequence colors remain modulo finite changes. They encode countable extensional relations with ordinal rank labels below ω1\omega_1ω1​.

Under CH, local rank approximations permit an uncountable-base model at ℶω2\beth_{\omega_2}ℶω2​​, alongside a countable-base model of the same size. The base-sort sizes distinguish them.

At sizes at least Λ\LambdaΛ, the color tests would force a coherent global pattern of bounded-rank extensional relations too large to exist. This eliminates uncountable-base models. Only the countable-base regime remains, giving categoricity on the higher tail.

Strong inclusions control newly added columns on old tuples. That detail permits small strong submodels and directed unions even though each tuple can have its own countable exceptional set of columns.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The positive theorem concerns bare AECs with set-sized finitary languages and the stated coherent-union axioms. Categoricity includes existence at every size in the resulting tail.

The negative construction assumes CH and fails both joint embedding and amalgamation. It therefore does not contradict transfer theorems that assume those properties. Nor does the existence of arbitrarily large models somewhere in the class imply that its uncountable-base endpoint model has arbitrarily large extensions.

M2 does not specify the least possible uniform threshold. The classical prescribed ℶω1\beth_{\omega_1}ℶω1​​ question for countable infinitary sentences is also kept separate in the manuscript. M1’s obstruction targets the displayed AEC bound H(K)H(K)H(K), not every proposed threshold in every restricted setting.

The two manuscripts should therefore be read as a qualitative existence claim paired with a limitation on one quantitative proposal. Their constructions are independent: M1’s higher categorical tail is established within its own argument, without invoking M2.

8. Sources and further reading

Morley, Categoricity in power, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 114 (1965), 514–538, is the first-order prototype. Baldwin and Lachlan, On strongly minimal sets, Journal of Symbolic Logic 36 (1971), 79–96, develops the geometric classification background.

Shelah, Classification Theory for Abstract Elementary Classes (2009), formulates the broader program. Boney and Vasey, A survey on tame abstract elementary classes, provides background on tameness and transfer. Their Categoricity and infinitary logics explains the version-sensitive order-presentation issue cited by M2.

Shelah and Vasey, Categoricity and multidimensional diagrams, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 26 (2024), 2301–2372, supplies a major predecessor for the finite-system methods. Espíndola’s eventual-categoricity preprint and explicit-threshold preprint are the earlier public claims discussed in the source manuscripts.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A CH obstruction to a prescribed categoricity threshold (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Eventual categoricity for abstract elementary classes (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 21 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The ordering of computational difficulty has no hidden symmetries
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 241 · Mathematical logic
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-21

1. The question

Imagine sorting all sets of natural numbers by how much computational information they contain. One set is below another if a computer given answers about the second can decide membership in the first.

After identifying sets with exactly the same computational power, we obtain the Turing degrees. Could their entire ordering be relabelled nontrivially while preserving every comparison? Such a relabelling would be a hidden symmetry of relative computation.

Family 241 contains a manuscript dated 24 September 2026 claiming that no such symmetry exists. Every order automorphism of the full Turing-degree structure is the identity. The statement is in ZFC and places no definability or regularity assumption on the automorphism itself.

2. Background and essential definitions

Oracles and degrees

An oracle Turing machine is an ordinary algorithm allowed to ask membership questions about a fixed set B⊆NB\subseteq\mathbb NB⊆N. Write A≤TBA\leq_TBA≤T​B if some such machine decides membership in AAA using oracle BBB.

This is a comparison of available information, not running time. A reduction may take arbitrarily long finite time on successive inputs.

Two sets are Turing equivalent when each computes the other. A Turing degree is an equivalence class under this relation. Let DT\mathcal D_TDT​ denote the degrees, ordered by reducibility. The least degree 0\mathbf00 consists of computable sets.

The join A⊕BA\oplus BA⊕B combines two oracles, for example by putting membership bits of AAA in even positions and those of BBB in odd positions. On degrees it gives a least upper bound, written a∨b\mathbf a\vee\mathbf ba∨b. An automorphism of the order must preserve these joins because least upper bounds are determined by the order alone.

The Turing jump a′\mathbf a'a′ is the degree of the halting problem for machines using an oracle of degree a\mathbf aa. Iteration gives 0′\mathbf0'0′, 0′′\mathbf0''0′′, and higher jumps. A cone above c\mathbf cc consists of every degree a≥Tc\mathbf a\geq_T\mathbf ca≥T​c.

Rigidity

An order automorphism is a bijection π:DT→DT\pi:\mathcal D_T\to\mathcal D_Tπ:DT​→DT​ satisfying

a≤Tb⟺π(a)≤Tπ(b). \mathbf a\leq_T\mathbf b \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \pi(\mathbf a)\leq_T\pi(\mathbf b).a≤T​b⟺π(a)≤T​π(b).

Rigidity says that π(a)=a\pi(\mathbf a)=\mathbf aπ(a)=a for every degree. It concerns the full partial order, not only computably enumerable degrees, a fixed interval or a restricted class of effectively described relabellings.

A topological notion of typicality

The proof uses Baire category. A nowhere-dense set has closure containing no open region. A meager set is a countable union of nowhere-dense sets; a comeager set is its complement. In a complete metric space, a comeager set is topologically large.
