A useful chart must capture enough weighted incidence mass; fitting a polynomial to a negligible exceptional collection would not advance the argument.

A hypothetical dimension deficit forces a tradeoff between the thickness of these polynomial relations and the lengths of line pieces they capture. The paper follows nearly optimal charts through nested scales and distinguishes roughly balanced boxes from increasingly narrow ones.

In the balanced case, several sufficiently independent directions constrain a common approximate polynomial field. In narrow cases, lower-dimensional projections and planar rigidity estimates constrain the trajectories. The stated goal in each regime is to produce better charts than the assumed extremal tradeoff permits.

The manuscript stresses that improved local fits must be returned to the original line family with sufficient coverage and controlled numbers of labels. This is how its local algebraic descriptions are intended to yield a global Hausdorff-dimension conclusion.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The four-dimensional conclusion is full Hausdorff dimension, not positive volume. It does not contradict measure-zero Kakeya constructions, and it does not establish the four-dimensional maximal conjecture.

The three-dimensional theorem allows every positive power loss δ−ε\delta^{-\varepsilon}δ−ε. Improving this to a specific logarithmic bound or a uniform constant is a separate quantitative question. The constant’s dependence on ε\varepsilonε matters if one wants explicit numerical estimates.

The papers also discuss Nikodym and curved-Kakeya consequences through existing transfer theorems. Those applications carry their own curvature and phase assumptions; the Euclidean claims do not imply unrestricted versions on arbitrary manifolds or for arbitrary curves.

Finally, the four-dimensional paper retains a genuine dependency on a weighted estimate from the three-dimensional manuscript. The family is not two interchangeable proofs of one theorem, and neither result should erase the historical credit for the earlier three-dimensional set theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

Wang and Zahl’s set theorem and the streamlined proof by Guth, Wang and Zahl are essential context for the maximal claim. Katz and Zahl’s planebrush paper explains the earlier four-dimensional improvements. The source manuscripts below state their dependencies and geometric consequences in detail.

The Kakeya set article provides optional background on why zero volume and full dimension can coexist.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Kakeya maximal conjecture in three dimensions (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Every four-dimensional Kakeya set has full Hausdorff dimension (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A large fractal must determine many distances
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 073 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Place a collection of points in Euclidean space and measure every distance between two of them. How large must the collection be before its possible distances occupy a positive amount of the real line?

For a solid ball, the answer is immediate: every distance from zero up to the diameter occurs. The interesting case is a fractal, which can have zero ordinary volume while still having substantial dimension. Falconer’s conjecture predicts that a fractal occupying more than half the ambient dimension already determines a set of distances of positive length.

The manuscript in family 073 claims this conclusion in every dimension at least two, with no regularity assumption beyond compactness and the strict Hausdorff-dimension threshold. Its conclusion concerns distances between all pairs. It does not claim that one fixed point sees a positive-length distance set at the same threshold.

2. Background and essential definitions

Three meanings of size

For E⊂RdE\subset\mathbb R^dE⊂Rd, define its distance set by

Δ(E)={∣x−y∣:x,y∈E}.\Delta(E)=\{|x-y|:x,y\in E\}.Δ(E)={∣x−y∣:x,y∈E}.

Here ∣x−y∣|x-y|∣x−y∣ is the ordinary Euclidean distance. The set Δ(E)\Delta(E)Δ(E) lies in [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞), regardless of the dimension of EEE.

Lebesgue measure on the real line is length. A set of positive length need not contain an interval, but it cannot be covered by intervals whose total lengths are arbitrarily small. This is stronger than saying that the set is uncountable or has Hausdorff dimension one.

Hausdorff dimension measures how efficiently a set can be covered at small scales. For a proposed exponent sss, cover EEE by sets of diameter at most δ\deltaδ and add their diameters raised to the power sss. The threshold at which the best possible sums change from large to arbitrarily small is dim⁡HE\dim_H EdimH​E. A smooth curve has dimension one, a surface has dimension two, and a fractal can have a noninteger value.

Packing dimension is another small-scale size notion. It can exceed Hausdorff dimension for irregular sets. Equality of the two is a meaningful extra hypothesis, not a consequence of knowing only dim⁡HE\dim_H EdimH​E.

Turning a fractal into a distribution of mass

A useful bridge from dimension to analysis is a Frostman measure. If s<dim⁡HEs<\dim_H Es<dimH​E, one can put a probability measure μ\muμ on compact EEE such that

μ(B(x,r))≤Crs.\mu(B(x,r))\le C r^s.μ(B(x,r))≤Crs.

The ball B(x,r)B(x,r)B(x,r) has center xxx and radius rrr. The inequality says that no small ball captures too much of the mass. It is an upper bound; it does not say every ball centered on EEE carries mass comparable to rsr^srs.

Choose two independent points according to μ\muμ, and record their distance. The resulting distance measure ν\nuν is characterized by

∫g(t) dν(t)=∬g(∣x−y∣) dμ(x) dμ(y)\int g(t)\,d\nu(t)=\iint g(|x-y|)\,d\mu(x)\,d\mu(y)∫g(t)dν(t)=∬g(∣x−y∣)dμ(x)dμ(y)

for continuous test functions ggg. Its support lies in Δ(E)\Delta(E)Δ(E). If a nonzero such measure has a density with respect to ordinary length, then the distance set must have positive length. This converts a geometric question into a question about the concentration of a measure.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Falconer’s 1985 paper, On the Hausdorff dimensions of distance sets, proved the conclusion when dim⁡HE>(d+1)/2\dim_H E>(d+1)/2dimH​E>(d+1)/2. Lattice-based constructions explained why half the ambient dimension is the natural lower threshold in the conjecture.

Mattila developed a criterion involving spherical averages of the Fourier transform of a measure on EEE. This connected distance geometry with oscillatory cancellation: a measure sufficiently spread out in frequency can force its distances to be spread out on the line.

Wolff reached the planar threshold 4/34/34/3, and Erdoğan obtained d/2+1/3d/2+1/3d/2+1/3 in dimensions at least three. Later weighted restriction and decoupling methods improved these bounds further. They exploit the way frequency pieces pointing in different directions interact.

Guth, Iosevich, Ou and Wang proved a stronger, pinned conclusion in the plane when dim⁡HE>5/4\dim_H E>5/4dimH​E>5/4: some point of EEE sees a positive-length distance set. Du, Ou, Ren and Zhang obtained the corresponding conclusion in dimensions d≥3d\ge3d≥3 above

d2+14−18d+4.\frac d2+\frac14-\frac1{8d+4}.2d​+41​−8d+41​.

Other advances approached the conjecture through regularity assumptions or weaker conclusions. Shmerkin and Wang established full dimension of the distance set for certain critical-dimensional sets whose Hausdorff and packing dimensions agree. Liu’s regular-pin theorem reaches the planar positive-measure conclusion above dimension one when the relevant pin set has equal Hausdorff and packing dimensions.

These distinctions explain the remaining gap addressed by the manuscript. Full dimension need not mean positive length, and a result assuming equal Hausdorff and packing dimensions does not cover an arbitrary compact fractal.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The principal theorem is

E⊂Rd compact,d≥2,dim⁡HE>d2⟹L1(Δ(E))>0.E\subset\mathbb R^d\text{ compact},\quad d\ge2,\quad\dim_H E>\frac d2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathcal L^1(\Delta(E))>0.E⊂Rd compact,d≥2,dimH​E>2d​⟹L1(Δ(E))>0.

The symbol L1\mathcal L^1L1 denotes one-dimensional Lebesgue measure. No product structure, Fourier decay, equality of dimensions, or uniform lower mass estimate is required.

For example, in the plane a compact set of Hausdorff dimension 1.011.011.01 satisfies the hypothesis. In three-dimensional space the threshold is strictly greater than 1.51.51.5; in four dimensions it is strictly greater than two. These examples illustrate the stated theorem, not additional regularity conclusions about the fractal.

The manuscript constructs a nonzero absolutely continuous measure carried by the distance set. Absolute continuity means that every set of length zero has measure zero for this new measure. This is the mechanism by which the claimed analytical estimates imply positive length.

The theorem does not assert a quantitative lower bound for that length depending only on dimension. Rescaling EEE already changes all its distances, so any quantitative statement would need additional normalization and geometric information.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem resolves a central problem linking fractal geometry, harmonic analysis and incidence geometry. The advance is the sharp strict dimension threshold for arbitrary compact sets in every dimension, rather than an improvement restricted to a particular family of fractals.

Distances are among the simplest nonlinear geometric measurements. A universal theorem about them shows that enough small-scale complexity in a set forces a substantial range of outcomes under that measurement. The threshold is particularly striking because the original set can occupy no ordinary volume at all.

The proposed methods also address a recurring difficulty in analysis: information may be good at each scale without being uniformly good along one fixed limiting object. Preserving enough positive mass while combining estimates across infinitely many scales is relevant well beyond the distance problem itself.

6. The main idea

Separate directions from distances

Start with two separated portions of a Frostman measure. Separation avoids the singular geometry of pairs whose endpoints nearly coincide. The direction from xxx to yyy is

y−x∣y−x∣∈Sd−1,\frac{y-x}{|y-x|}\in S^{d-1},∣y−x∣y−x​∈Sd−1,

where Sd−1S^{d-1}Sd−1 is the unit sphere. The distribution of these directions controls how pairs concentrate in narrow tubes.

A subtle point arises in higher dimensions. A measure supported on a set of dimension just above d/2d/2d/2 cannot automatically acquire a smooth density on the (d−1)(d-1)(d−1)-dimensional sphere. The paper instead seeks upper bounds on the mass in small spherical caps. These are weaker than smoothness, but are tailored to the later Fourier estimates.

Auxiliary projections into lower-dimensional spaces help prepare these directional bounds. The actual distance ∣x−y∣|x-y|∣x−y∣ remains the original Euclidean distance in Rd\mathbb R^dRd. Projected distances are not substituted into the final conclusion.

Track how mass changes with scale

The manuscript divides space into successively smaller dyadic cubes, whose side lengths halve at each step. It groups portions of the measure with similar mass behavior and records a profile describing the mass in occupied cubes at each depth.

The useful information is the profile’s excess over the critical dimension d/2d/2d/2. That excess may appear unevenly across scales. The described recursion alternates between counting pairs with almost equal distances and controlling angular Fourier energies. A bookkeeping quantity involving two separated depths is used to pay for the losses in these alternations.

The strict hypothesis dim⁡HE>d/2\dim_H E>d/2dimH​E>d/2 supplies a positive margin. According to the manuscript, this margin eventually gives decay on successive frequency shells, meaning bands of frequencies with magnitudes comparable to powers of two.

Keep the limiting measure nonzero

At successive scales, the argument discards exceptional pairs with badly concentrated directions. Discarding independently at every scale would risk losing all the useful mass or changing the object being estimated without control.

The paper organizes a decreasing sequence of positive measures with a nonzero limit. It combines that monotonicity with approximating measures whose errors and Fourier-shell contributions are summable. Its stated reconstruction lemma then yields absolute continuity of the limit.

The overall strategy therefore has two complementary requirements: enough oscillatory cancellation to prevent concentration of distances, and enough retained positive mass to make the eventual conclusion substantive. Neither requirement alone would establish the theorem.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The inequality in the dimension hypothesis is strict. The manuscript makes no universal positive-length assertion at dim⁡HE=d/2\dim_H E=d/2dimH​E=d/2.

A pinned distance set is

Δx(E)={∣x−y∣:y∈E}.\Delta_x(E)=\{|x-y|:y\in E\}.Δx​(E)={∣x−y∣:y∈E}.

The claimed theorem concerns the union over all pairs and does not prove that one fixed xxx has L1(Δx(E))>0\mathcal L^1(\Delta_x(E))>0L1(Δx​(E))>0 at the conjectured threshold. Earlier pinned results above larger thresholds remain stronger in this different respect.

Positive length also does not guarantee an interval of distances, every sufficiently small distance, or a prescribed finite configuration inside EEE. Such conclusions require their own arguments. Finally, the theorem uses Euclidean distance; replacing it with an arbitrary norm or a distance on a curved space changes the problem.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript’s introduction compares its claim with the positive-measure, pinned and full-dimension results separately. Useful primary references are the planar pinned theorem, the higher-dimensional improvement, and Shmerkin and Wang’s critical-dimension work.

The Hausdorff dimension and Frostman’s lemma articles offer optional background for the size and mass notions used above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Falconer distance conjecture in all dimensions (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Nearly constant waves made only from plus and minus signs
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 076 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Can a sum of waves, each carrying only a plus or minus sign, have almost the same amplitude at every point of a circle?

With arbitrary complex coefficients, the phases can be adjusted continuously. Restricting every coefficient to +1+1+1 or −1-1−1 removes most of that freedom. Yet the question still asks for uniform control at every angle, including places where many waves might reinforce or cancel one another.

The three manuscripts in family 076 describe a progression. The first chronological paper claims an asymptotically smallest possible maximum amplitude. A refinement also keeps the minimum away from zero. The strongest paper claims that both extrema approach the same natural value, giving real ultraflat Littlewood polynomials at every sufficiently large integer length. The family also states consequences for binary sequences with small autocorrelations.

2. Background and essential definitions

The unavoidable square-root scale

A real Littlewood polynomial of length NNN is

P(z)=∑k=0N−1εkzk,εk∈{−1,1}.P(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\varepsilon_k z^k,\qquad \varepsilon_k\in\{-1,1\}.P(z)=k=0∑N−1​εk​zk,εk​∈{−1,1}.

Length counts the coefficients, so the degree is N−1N-1N−1. On the unit circle, write z=e2πitz=e^{2\pi it}z=e2πit, where 0≤t<10\le t<10≤t<1. Orthogonality of the exponential waves gives Parseval’s identity:

∫01∣P(e2πit)∣2 dt=N.\int_0^1|P(e^{2\pi it})|^2\,dt=N.∫01​∣P(e2πit)∣2dt=N.

The root-mean-square amplitude is therefore exactly N\sqrt NN​. In particular, the maximum cannot be smaller than N\sqrt NN​. The challenge is whether the maximum can approach that value without large exceptional peaks or deep troughs.

Constant-factor flatness means keeping the modulus between cNc\sqrt NcN​ and CNC\sqrt NCN​, for fixed positive constants. Ultraflatness asks for the stronger condition

sup⁡∣z∣=1∣∣P(z)∣N−1∣⟶0.\sup_{|z|=1}\left|\frac{|P(z)|}{\sqrt N}-1\right|\longrightarrow0.∣z∣=1sup​​N​∣P(z)∣​−1​⟶0.

The coefficients and even the entire polynomial may change with NNN. This definition does not require successive polynomials to be partial sums of one infinite sign sequence.

Binary correlations and merit factor

A binary word A=(a0,…,aN−1)A=(a_0,\ldots,a_{N-1})A=(a0​,…,aN−1​) with entries in {−1,1}\{-1,1\}{−1,1} has aperiodic autocorrelations

Cu(A)=∑j=0N−1−uajaj+u,1≤u<N.C_u(A)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1-u}a_j a_{j+u},\qquad 1\le u<N.Cu​(A)=j=0∑N−1−u​aj​aj+u​,1≤u<N.

These compare the word with a shifted copy over their overlapping positions. “Aperiodic” means that entries are not wrapped around the ends.

Its merit factor is

F(A)=N22∑u=1N−1Cu(A)2.F(A)=\frac{N^2}{2\sum_{u=1}^{N-1}C_u(A)^2}.F(A)=2∑u=1N−1​Cu​(A)2N2​.

A large value means that the total squared correlation away from zero shift is small. Such questions arise when one wants a signal to resemble itself strongly only at its correct alignment.

For PA(z)=∑ajzjP_A(z)=\sum a_jz^jPA​(z)=∑aj​zj, orthogonality also gives

∫01∣PA(e2πit)∣4 dt=N2+2∑u=1N−1Cu(A)2.\int_0^1|P_A(e^{2\pi it})|^4\,dt=N^2+2\sum_{u=1}^{N-1}C_u(A)^2.∫01​∣PA​(e2πit)∣4dt=N2+2u=1∑N−1​Cu​(A)2.

Thus flattening the polynomial’s modulus suppresses the correlation energy. This identity is the bridge between the analytic and binary-sequence statements.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Littlewood and Erdős posed several related flatness problems with different coefficient constraints. It is essential to distinguish real signs from arbitrary complex coefficients of modulus one.

The Rudin–Shapiro construction produces real-sign polynomials whose maximum is at most 2N\sqrt{2N}2N​ at dyadic lengths. This gets the correct order of growth, but leaves a fixed multiplicative gap above the Parseval minimum.

Kahane constructed ultraflat polynomials with complex unimodular coefficients in 1980. Bombieri and Bourgain later supplied quantitative refinements. Those coefficients can point anywhere on the unit circle; replacing them by real signs is an additional problem.

Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe and Tiba’s Flat Littlewood polynomials exist, published in the Annals of Mathematics in 2020, established two-sided constant-factor flatness for real signs. Their construction controlled both extrema at once, but did not make both constants converge to one.

On the sequence side, Jedwab, Katz and Schmidt’s 2013 paper Littlewood polynomials with small L4 norm constructed families with limiting merit factor approximately 6.3420616.3420616.342061. The conjecture commonly attributed to Turyn predicts a universal bound on binary merit factors. The new family claims that no such bound exists.

Some recent obstructions concern stronger or different quantifiers. Erdélyi’s lower bound on the maximum modulus permits an additive gap above NNN in the squared maximum while its relative size tends to zero. Another obstruction discussed in the strongest manuscript concerns all partial sums of one fixed power series. Neither statement has the same form as choosing a new sign pattern independently at each length.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Three levels of flatness

The September manuscript states that the best normalized maximum tends to one:

min⁡εk∈{−1,1}1Nmax⁡∣z∣=1∣∑k=0N−1εkzk∣⟶1.\min_{\varepsilon_k\in\{-1,1\}}\frac1{\sqrt N}\max_{|z|=1}\left|\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\varepsilon_kz^k\right|\longrightarrow1.εk​∈{−1,1}min​N​1​∣z∣=1max​​k=0∑N−1​εk​zk​⟶1.

This holds through all integer lengths. By itself it supplies no uniform positive lower bound for the same polynomial.

The first October refinement states that, for every η>0\eta>0η>0 and every sufficiently large NNN, one choice of signs gives

N16≤∣P(z)∣≤(1+η)N(∣z∣=1).\frac{\sqrt N}{16}\le |P(z)|\le(1+\eta)\sqrt N\qquad(|z|=1).16N​​≤∣P(z)∣≤(1+η)N​(∣z∣=1).

The strongest October manuscript replaces the fixed lower constant by an asymptotically optimal one. For every 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<10<ε<1, all sufficiently large NNN admit signs satisfying

(1−ε)N≤∣P(z)∣≤(1+ε)Nfor every ∣z∣=1.(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt N\le|P(z)|\le(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt N\qquad\text{for every }|z|=1.(1−ε)N​≤∣P(z)∣≤(1+ε)N​for every ∣z∣=1.

The same polynomial satisfies both bounds, including at z=1z=1z=1 and z=−1z=-1z=−1. The signs may be chosen separately for different lengths.

Correlation consequences

Already the asymptotically minimal maximum implies that the largest merit factor among binary words of length NNN tends to infinity as N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞. The fourth-moment identity explains why: a squared modulus with mean NNN and maximum nearly NNN has fourth moment nearly N2N^2N2, leaving a vanishing relative contribution from nonzero autocorrelations.

The September paper further applies a theorem of Downarowicz and Lacroix to obtain a symbolic dynamical system with a specified absolutely continuous spectral measure. This is a consequence through an existing theorem, not an assertion that every binary sequence has such spectral behavior.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, real ultraflatness settles a central restricted-coefficient problem and overturns a long-standing boundedness prediction for binary merit factors. The claim controls every angle and every sufficiently large length, which is substantially stronger than average flatness or a construction along a sparse subsequence.

The family also illustrates a powerful connection between continuous analysis and discrete design. The modulus of a complex polynomial encodes many correlations of a finite sign sequence simultaneously. Improving a uniform analytic bound can therefore force a qualitative change in what binary patterns can achieve.

The significance is asymptotic and structural. The manuscripts do not provide a practical signing algorithm or numerical length at which a prescribed degree of flatness becomes available, so immediate engineering performance is not part of the claim.

6. The main idea

First permit almost-sign coefficients

Directly choosing NNN signs while controlling infinitely many angles is difficult. The construction first allows coefficients Xk∈[−1,1]X_k\in[-1,1]Xk​∈[−1,1]. These continuous choices can be shaped using oscillatory analysis.

If their mean-square mass is nearly maximal, most of their total coefficient mass must be close to sign size. The deficit can be recorded by

D(X)=12∑k=0N−1(1−∣Xk∣).D(X)=\frac12\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(1-|X_k|).D(X)=21​k=0∑N−1​(1−∣Xk​∣).

A discrepancy estimate then rounds the coefficients to signs while controlling the change in the polynomial uniformly on the circle. Small total deficit makes the rounding error small relative to N\sqrt NN​. Independent rounding would not supply the same coordinated control over all angles.

Spread and coordinate the waves

The manuscripts build auxiliary trigonometric polynomials on a higher-dimensional torus. Quadratic phases spread their Fourier contributions across assigned intervals. A packing argument arranges these contributions so that the largest terms do not all reinforce one another at the same angle.

Stationary phase is the analytical guide: an oscillatory integral is largest near points where its phase derivative matches the requested frequency. Choosing the curvature and placement of each wave controls where its Fourier contribution appears and how large it is.

The first construction obtains nearly full mean-square mass with an almost minimal maximum, but some arcs can still have small amplitude. The intermediate paper repairs those arcs with phase-matched corrections whose coefficient cost stays small. This secures a fixed lower bound before rounding.

Keep the minimum close to the maximum

The ultraflat paper strengthens the wave construction itself. Its waves have almost constant modulus, and their phases coordinate the main Fourier contributions through the auxiliary polynomial. Near wave endpoints, increased phase curvature suppresses unwanted Fourier contributions without lowering the wave amplitude.

Joining the waves requires matching values and leading phase derivatives across the gaps. The described matching cancels leading boundary terms and keeps the Fourier mass outside the permitted degrees small. Projection to the desired coefficient interval and the final rounding can then preserve both upper and lower bounds.

All auxiliary choices are fixed before the final length tends to infinity. That order of parameters is how the manuscripts obtain every sufficiently large length rather than only a selected sequence of lengths.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The strongest theorem chooses a separate polynomial at each length. It does not produce one infinite sign sequence whose every sufficiently long initial segment is ultraflat.

Uniform modulus does not mean the polynomial itself is nearly constant: its complex argument can vary substantially around the circle. Nor is exact constant modulus asserted for a finite nontrivial Littlewood polynomial.

The first paper’s upper bound, the second paper’s fixed lower bound and the final ultraflat claim should remain distinct. A small maximum plus Parseval’s identity gives strong averaged flatness, but does not alone rule out narrow deep troughs. The later lower-bound constructions address that extra difficulty.

The sequence consequence concerns the stated aperiodic merit-factor normalization. It does not automatically transfer to periodic correlations or other signal-quality objectives. Effective rates, practical constructions and the dependence of the threshold length on the accuracy remain separate quantitative questions.

8. Sources and further reading

The three source manuscripts below preserve the progression from maximum control to a positive minimum and then ultraflatness. Primary historical references include Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe and Tiba, Flat Littlewood polynomials exist (2020); Kahane, Sur les polynômes à coefficients unimodulaires (1980); and Jedwab, Katz and Schmidt, Littlewood polynomials with small L4 norm (2013).

Downarowicz and Lacroix’s Merit factors and Morse sequences provides the cited spectral connection. Optional background on Littlewood polynomials and autocorrelation explains the two sides of the problem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Ultraflat real Littlewood polynomials (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Nearly minimal maxima and positive minima of Littlewood polynomials (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Asymptotically minimal maxima of real Littlewood polynomials (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Fourier convergence at the L log L threshold
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 075 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

A periodic signal can be decomposed into pure frequencies. If we add back successively more of those frequencies, do the resulting Fourier sums approach the original signal at almost every point?

For smooth signals, this is a familiar success of Fourier analysis. For rough functions, summing more frequencies can produce large oscillations rather than straightforward improvement. The twentieth-century theory established convergence under LpL^pLp integrability for every p>1p>1p>1, but ordinary integrability alone is insufficient.

Family 075 claims the classical intermediate sufficiency conjecture: every function in Llog⁡LL\log LLlogL has ordinary symmetric Fourier partial sums converging almost everywhere along the full sequence. The result concerns the actual partial sums, without averaging them or selecting a favorable subsequence.

2. Background and essential definitions

Fourier coefficients and symmetric sums

Represent the circle by T=R/(2πZ)\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)T=R/(2πZ), with normalized length measure dμ(x)=dx/(2π)d\mu(x)=dx/(2\pi)dμ(x)=dx/(2π). For an integrable complex-valued function fff, define

f^(k)=∫Tf(x)e−ikx dμ(x),SNf(x)=∑k=−NNf^(k)eikx.\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)e^{-ikx}\,d\mu(x),\qquadS_Nf(x)=\sum_{k=-N}^{N}\widehat f(k)e^{ikx}.f​(k)=∫T​f(x)e−ikxdμ(x),SN​f(x)=k=−N∑N​f​(k)eikx.

The integer kkk is a frequency. The sum is symmetric because it includes all frequencies from −N-N−N through NNN. For a real-valued function, positive and negative frequencies combine into the familiar sine and cosine terms.

Almost-everywhere convergence means that there is a set of measure zero outside which SNf(x)→f(x)S_Nf(x)\to f(x)SN​f(x)→f(x). The exceptional set may depend on fff. This does not mean convergence at every point or uniform convergence over the circle.

How much larger than Lp is L log L

The class used in the theorem is

Llog⁡L(T)={f:∫T∣f(x)∣log⁡(2+∣f(x)∣) dμ(x)<∞}.L\log L(\mathbb T)=\left\{f:\int_{\mathbb T}|f(x)|\log(2+|f(x)|)\,d\mu(x)<\infty\right\}.LlogL(T)={f:∫T​∣f(x)∣log(2+∣f(x)∣)dμ(x)<∞}.

The added two simply keeps the logarithm well behaved for small values. At large amplitudes the extra cost beyond L1L^1L1 is one logarithm. On this finite-measure space,

Lp⊂Llog⁡L⊂L1(p>1).L^p\subset L\log L\subset L^1\qquad(p>1).Lp⊂LlogL⊂L1(p>1).

These inclusions allow strictly different classes of functions. For example, near zero a function behaving like

f(x)=1x(log⁡(1/x))3,0<x<e−2,f(x)=\frac1{x(\log(1/x))^3},\qquad 0<x<e^{-2},f(x)=x(log(1/x))31​,0<x<e−2,

and set to zero elsewhere belongs to Llog⁡LL\log LLlogL, but to no LpL^pLp with p>1p>1p>1. Substituting u=log⁡(1/x)u=\log(1/x)u=log(1/x) turns its Llog⁡LL\log LLlogL integral near zero into an integral comparable to ∫u−2 du\int u^{-2}\,du∫u−2du, which is finite. Its power singularity makes every higher LpL^pLp integral diverge. This illustrates the additional roughness admitted by the claimed theorem.

Why averaging changes the problem

Fejér sums average the initial Fourier partial sums. Their kernels are nonnegative, allowing convergence arguments based on local averaging. Ordinary Fourier sums instead use an oscillatory kernel with positive and negative parts. A theorem for Fejér means therefore does not settle the question asked here.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kolmogorov constructed an integrable function whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere in 1923. That example shows why a theorem for every L1L^1L1 function is impossible.

Carleson’s 1966 theorem established almost-everywhere convergence for L2L^2L2, resolving a landmark problem. Hunt extended it to every LpL^pLp, p>1p>1p>1, in 1968. The resulting Carleson–Hunt theorem leaves open how close one can come to ordinary integrability while retaining convergence for an entire function class.

Progress near L1L^1L1 was measured by slowly growing logarithmic corrections. Sjölin obtained a class with an additional iterated logarithm, while Soria developed extrapolation methods giving larger convergence spaces. Antonov’s 1996 theorem reached the class customarily written Llog⁡Llog⁡log⁡log⁡LL\log L\log\log\log LLlogLlogloglogL, with the iterated logarithms understood as regularized near zero.

Arias de Reyna introduced a larger quasi-Banach convergence space, denoted QAQAQA. Carro, Mastyło and Rodríguez-Piazza developed related spaces, and Lie provided a direct time-frequency approach to a maximal bound near the endpoint. Di Plinio and Fragkos later obtained weak-type estimates with sharp order as ppp approaches one.

The source manuscript cites these original works and distinguishes them from the proposed Llog⁡LL\log LLlogL conclusion. Removing an extra iterated logarithm can look minor in notation, but functions can concentrate on increasingly rare, increasingly high spikes. Even a very slowly growing factor changes which such functions are admitted.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The main theorem states that every complex-valued f∈Llog⁡L(T)f\in L\log L(\mathbb T)f∈LlogL(T) has a measurable exceptional set NfN_fNf​ with μ(Nf)=0\mu(N_f)=0μ(Nf​)=0 such that

lim⁡N→∞SNf(x)=f(x)(x∉Nf).\lim_{N\to\infty}S_Nf(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\notin N_f).N→∞lim​SN​f(x)=f(x)(x∈/Nf​).

The limit uses every integer N=0,1,2,…N=0,1,2,\ldotsN=0,1,2,…. No assumption of positivity, bounded variation or piecewise smoothness is imposed on fff.

The paper’s central analytical estimate treats a nonnegative input ρ\rhoρ of total mass one and height at most ede^ded, for large ddd. Let MρM\rhoMρ be its spatial maximal average: the supremum of the averages of ρ\rhoρ over circle arcs containing the given point. With h=log⁡log⁡dh=\log\log dh=loglogd, the paper removes the set where Mρ>e4hM\rho>e^{4h}Mρ>e4h and claims

∫{Mρ≤e4h}sup⁡N≥0∣SNρ∣ dμ≤Cd.\int_{\{M\rho\le e^{4h}\}}\sup_{N\ge0}|S_N\rho|\,d\mu\le Cd.∫{Mρ≤e4h}​N≥0sup​∣SN​ρ∣dμ≤Cd.

The excluded set has measure at most Ce−4hCe^{-4h}Ce−4h. These estimates have different jobs: one bounds the Fourier oscillations on the retained set, while the other limits how much of the circle was discarded.

The manuscript also states a weak-L1L^1L1 maximal consequence in the Luxemburg norm of Llog⁡LL\log LLlogL. This is a distributional bound on the maximal partial sum, not a strong L1L^1L1 estimate for its integral over the whole circle.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem settles the classical Llog⁡LL\log LLlogL sufficiency problem for Fourier convergence and extends one of harmonic analysis’s central convergence theorems to a substantially larger class of rough functions.

The hypothesis is easy to express directly in terms of the function’s amplitude. A reader need not know its Fourier coefficients in advance to recognize the class. The conclusion then controls the full sequence of reconstructions from those coefficients, despite their oscillatory nature.

The proposed improvement also sharpens the conceptual boundary between two facts: Fourier analysis reconstructs every sufficiently integrable function almost everywhere, yet it can fail dramatically for general integrable functions. The theorem supplies a distinguished class between these regimes without claiming a necessary condition for each individual function.

6. The main idea

Break a rough function into height layers

A general Llog⁡LL\log LLlogL function may be unbounded. Divide it into portions according to the size of its values. Each normalized portion is bounded, so the good-set estimate can be applied to it.

The challenge is to sum the resulting bounds. If the analytical cost grew too rapidly with the layer height, the Llog⁡LL\log LLlogL integral would not pay for it. If the exceptional sets were too large, infinitely many bad events could cover a positive portion of the circle.

The paper uses layers with doubly exponential heights. Its stated integral bounds sum using the logarithmic integrability hypothesis, while the measures of the discarded sets are also summable. Approximation by well-behaved functions then supplies the convergence conclusion.

Organize many frequencies without paying for each one

The hard estimate behind this summation is first formulated on a finite tree of intervals, where each interval splits into two children. Differences between averages on the children are Haar-type coefficients, a discrete model for oscillation at a specified scale.

Modulation multiplies an input by eiuxe^{iux}eiux, shifting its frequency. To control all Fourier cutoffs, the argument must handle many possible modulations together. Paying a separate full cost for every frequency would make the bound useless.

The manuscript groups frequencies whose phases behave similarly on a common region. It uses noisy observations of an input point to identify such groups. Entropy records how much information those observations reveal; a compression argument says that a large collection of frequencies with controlled information cost contains a useful common phase structure.

One distribution samples the input point in proportion to its mass. Another samples the output location uniformly on the circle. These distributions are not interchangeable. The paper’s bookkeeping converts information bounds under the first into estimates for transforms under the second.

Return from the tree to Fourier sums

Averaging translated and rescaled dyadic kernels produces a multiple of the Hilbert-transform kernel, together with a controlled error. The periodic Hilbert transform is a singular integral closely related to projection onto positive and negative Fourier frequencies.

This passage connects the finite tree estimate to ordinary symmetric Fourier sums. It is essential that the control survives the averaging and limiting operations, because convergence for the discrete model alone would not answer the original Fourier question.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem asserts almost-everywhere convergence, allowing an exceptional null set that depends on the function. It does not supply a universal exceptional set, uniform convergence or a rate of convergence.

The result is a sufficiency theorem. It does not characterize all functions whose Fourier series converge almost everywhere, and many individual functions outside Llog⁡LL\log LLlogL can still have convergent Fourier series. Kolmogorov’s counterexample prevents replacing the hypothesis by unrestricted L1L^1L1 membership.

The paper concerns one-dimensional ordinary symmetric Fourier sums. Other summation orders, higher-dimensional frequency regions and non-Fourier orthogonal systems require their own analysis. Nor should the weak maximal consequence be rewritten as a strong integral bound over the entire circle.

8. Sources and further reading

The source manuscript’s references include Carleson’s On convergence and growth of partial sums of Fourier series (1966), Hunt’s On the convergence of Fourier series (1968), Antonov’s Convergence of Fourier series (1996), and Lie’s On the boundedness of the Carleson operator near L1 (2013). These works describe the historical progression from power integrability toward logarithmic endpoint classes.

Optional background on Fourier series, Carleson’s theorem, and Fejér’s theorem helps distinguish ordinary partial sums from averaged reconstruction.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Almost-everywhere Fourier convergence in L log L (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How much smoothing makes spherical Fourier sums bounded
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 078 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

A natural way to reconstruct a function from its Fourier transform is to keep all frequencies inside a large ball and discard the rest. In more than one dimension, that sharp spherical cutoff can behave badly: its boundary creates oscillations that destroy expected norm bounds.

Bochner–Riesz summation softens the cutoff. Frequencies near the boundary receive a weight that decreases to zero, and a parameter specifies how gently or sharply this happens. The conjecture asks for the exact amount of smoothing needed to preserve an LpL^pLp norm.

The manuscript in family 078 claims the full conjectured strict-order range in three dimensions. Its central statement is boundedness on L3(R3)L^3(\mathbb R^3)L3(R3) for every positive smoothing order. Interpolation and duality then supply the other exponents. The strict positivity of the smoothing is part of the result.

2. Background and essential definitions

A multiplier changes each frequency separately

For a rapidly decreasing smooth function fff on R3\mathbb R^3R3, use

f^(ξ)=∫R3f(x)e−2πix⋅ξ dx.\widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.f​(ξ)=∫R3​f(x)e−2πix⋅ξdx.

A Fourier multiplier multiplies f^(ξ)\widehat f(\xi)f​(ξ) by a specified function of frequency and then takes the inverse transform. The Bochner–Riesz operator of order δ>0\delta>0δ>0 and unit radius is

Tδf(x)=∫R3(1−∣ξ∣2)+δf^(ξ)e2πix⋅ξ dξ,T_\delta f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1-|\xi|^2)_+^\delta\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,d\xi,Tδ​f(x)=∫R3​(1−∣ξ∣2)+δ​f​(ξ)e2πix⋅ξdξ,

where a+=max⁡{a,0}a_+=\max\{a,0\}a+​=max{a,0}. Frequencies outside the unit ball are removed. Inside the ball, their weight approaches zero at the boundary. Larger δ\deltaδ gives more smoothing there.

Replacing ∣ξ∣2|\xi|^2∣ξ∣2 by ∣ξ∣2/R2|\xi|^2/R^2∣ξ∣2/R2 defines the means Tδ,RT_{\delta,R}Tδ,R​ at radius RRR. Increasing RRR gradually restores higher frequencies. A dilation relates the bounds at different radii.

The formal order-zero case is the indicator of the frequency ball. It has a jump discontinuity at the sphere, which is the source of the ball-multiplier obstruction.

Norm boundedness, convergence and maximal bounds

Boundedness on LpL^pLp means that

∥Tδf∥p≤C∥f∥p\|T_\delta f\|_p\le C\|f\|_p∥Tδ​f∥p​≤C∥f∥p​

with a constant independent of fff. This is a stability statement: the operation cannot amplify the total ppp-power size arbitrarily.

Uniform bounds for the individual radii, together with approximation by smooth functions, give convergence in LpL^pLp for finite ppp. They do not automatically give almost-everywhere convergence. For pointwise control, one often needs a maximal operator such as

Tδ,∗f(x)=sup⁡R>0∣Tδ,Rf(x)∣,T_{\delta,*}f(x)=\sup_{R>0}|T_{\delta,R}f(x)|,Tδ,∗​f(x)=R>0sup​∣Tδ,R​f(x)∣,

which selects a potentially different radius at each point. This supremum is a stronger operation than fixing one radius before taking a norm.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The problem grows out of Riesz’s summation methods and Bochner’s spherical means for multiple Fourier series. In one dimension, ordering frequencies is comparatively simple. In higher dimensions, the curved boundary of a ball brings geometric interactions between many directions into the reconstruction problem.

Fefferman’s 1971 ball-multiplier theorem showed that the sharp cutoff is unbounded on LpL^pLp in dimensions at least two whenever p≠2p\ne2p=2. This made clear that an arbitrarily small positive smoothing order could be qualitatively different from no smoothing.

Carleson and Sjölin established the conjectured positive-order range in the plane. Córdoba and Bourgain developed connections with tube overlap and Fourier restriction. These connections explain why a summation problem also requires geometric estimates about long thin sets.

Bilinear restriction advances by Wolff and Tao, combined with Lee’s multiplier reduction, yielded sharp-order estimates in part of the three-dimensional exponent range. Later polynomial partitioning and multiscale arguments moved closer to the central exponent three. Wu reached the range with max⁡{p,p′}≥13/4\max\{p,p'\}\ge13/4max{p,p′}≥13/4, where 1/p+1/p′=11/p+1/p'=11/p+1/p′=1.

The manuscript reports Gao, Wu and Xi’s subsequent threshold 22/722/722/7, and places its method beside Guo, Oh, Wang, Wu and Zhang’s pseudoconformal approach. It also explicitly acknowledges an earlier proposed all-dimensional proof by Zipeng Wang. The present digest reports this manuscript’s stated theorem and approach rather than deciding the status or priority of competing proof claims.

The remaining target for this paper is a direct L3L^3L3 estimate with any fixed positive order. That point closes the central gap in the strict-order formulation through interpolation.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The main theorem states that, for every δ>0\delta>0δ>0, there is a finite CδC_\deltaCδ​ such that

∥Tδf∥L3(R3)≤Cδ∥f∥L3(R3).\|T_\delta f\|_{L^3(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_\delta\|f\|_{L^3(\mathbb R^3)}.∥Tδ​f∥L3(R3)​≤Cδ​∥f∥L3(R3)​.

The initial statement for rapidly decreasing smooth functions extends uniquely to all L3L^3L3 data.

The stated full consequence is boundedness on Lp(R3)L^p(\mathbb R^3)Lp(R3) whenever

1≤p≤∞,δ>max⁡{3∣1p−12∣−12, 0}.1\le p\le\infty,\qquad\delta>\max\left\{3\left|\frac1p-\frac12\right|-\frac12,\,0\right\}.1≤p≤∞,δ>max{3​p1​−21​​−21​,0}.

At every 3/2≤p≤33/2\le p\le33/2≤p≤3, any positive order suffices. At p=4p=4p=4, the displayed condition is δ>1/4\delta>1/4δ>1/4. At p=1p=1p=1 or p=∞p=\inftyp=∞, it is δ>1\delta>1δ>1. These examples help read the formula’s two regimes.

Dilation gives the same norm bounds for Tδ,RT_{\delta,R}Tδ,R​, uniformly in R>0R>0R>0. For finite ppp in the stated range, the means converge to fff in LpL^pLp as R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞.

The paper also invokes Tao’s established implication from Bochner–Riesz to spherical restriction, obtaining the bounded-data sphere extension estimate for every output exponent above three. The general positively curved surface theorem in family 077 is a separate statement, not automatically the same consequence.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the theorem settles the three-dimensional Bochner–Riesz conjecture in its strict-order form, one of the central questions about multidimensional Fourier summation.

The result identifies a delicate boundary: the unsmoothed ball cutoff fails on L3L^3L3, while every fixed positive smoothing order would work. There is no smallest positive order demanded at the central exponents, although constants may deteriorate as the order approaches zero.

Its importance also comes from the surrounding network of implications. Fourier restriction, Kakeya geometry, oscillatory integrals and wave propagation all confront related concentration patterns. A direct multiplier theorem supplies another route through this network while retaining the precise distinctions between norm convergence and pointwise reconstruction.

6. The main idea

First study positive mass moving along lines

A localized wave packet follows a thin region of space with a direction and a position. Before handling oscillation, the manuscript studies a positive model: weighted particles move along affine lines

X(t)=A+tV,X(t)=A+tV,X(t)=A+tV,

where AAA is an initial position and VVV a velocity. An observation records approximate position, approximate velocity and the orientation of the observing rectangle.

The key quantity measures how much information these observations reveal across scales. Thin eccentric rectangles receive a penalty, preventing a highly elongated observation from being treated as if it were a round one of the same nominal resolution.

If concentration grew too rapidly, the argument selects nearly extreme configurations. It then uses planar projection estimates and comparisons between observations at different times to constrain how their coordinate information can change. The paper describes these constraints as incompatible with the assumed growth.

Oscillatory packets have an extra limitation

Real waves cannot be modeled solely as independently moving positive particles. Their coefficients are complex, and nearby packets can interfere. Moreover, position and frequency cannot both be resolved arbitrarily sharply; this is the uncertainty principle behind wave-packet analysis.

Away from the limiting uncertainty scale, the positive-mass estimate can be transferred to squared packet amplitudes. At that scale, an earlier packet may be too spatially broad to fit a later position observation. The manuscript records the mismatch as additional fine information about velocity.

The claimed recursive argument shows that excessive packet growth would force this information to accumulate faster than its finite range of possible values allows. Repeating a bounded number of carefully controlled steps yields the proposed contradiction. This is the role of the information bookkeeping: it retains what is lost when one treats a wave packet as a sharply located particle.

Let positive smoothing pay for the final sum

The final multiplier kernel is divided into spatial shells of radius comparable to λ\lambdaλ, with λ\lambdaλ taking dyadic values. The paper obtains shell operator norms of the form

Cδ,νλ−δ+νC_{\delta,\nu}\lambda^{-\delta+\nu}Cδ,ν​λ−δ+ν

for any chosen small positive loss ν\nuν. Taking 0<ν<δ0<\nu<\delta0<ν<δ makes the dyadic shell sum converge.

This last step explains why a strict positive order is useful. The geometric and oscillatory estimates permit an arbitrarily small loss, and the smoothing factor absorbs it. Setting δ=0\delta=0δ=0 would remove that margin and would also conflict with the known ball-multiplier obstruction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The strict-order range does not settle estimates on its boundary. In particular, the theorem does not claim order-zero boundedness at p=3p=3p=3. At p=2p=2p=2, the unsmoothed multiplier is bounded by elementary Fourier orthogonality, but that special fact does not extend to neighboring exponents.

Uniform fixed-radius bounds imply the stated LpL^pLp convergence for finite ppp; they do not alone establish the maximal bound or almost-everywhere convergence for all those exponents. The local-smoothing manuscript in family 079 states additional maximal consequences in its own range.

The paper fixes dimension three and spherical frequency smoothing. Other dimensions, different frequency surfaces and weighted norm versions remain distinct questions. Its constants may depend on the positive smoothing order, so no stable limit of those constants as δ↓0\delta\downarrow0δ↓0 is asserted.

The historical existence of other proposed proofs is recorded with attribution. The exposition here takes the source’s claims as stated and does not resolve mathematical disagreements between manuscripts.

8. Sources and further reading

Fefferman’s ball-multiplier paper explains why the zero-order problem is different. Carleson–Sjölin provides the planar antecedent, and Guo and collaborators develop the modern pseudoconformal approach used in the source’s historical comparison. The manuscript gives its exact shell estimates and interpolation argument.

For optional background, see Bochner–Riesz means and Fourier multipliers.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Bochner–Riesz multipliers in three dimensions (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Fourier extension from positively curved surfaces
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 077 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Suppose we superimpose plane waves whose frequencies lie on a sphere. Each wave extends throughout space, but their phases usually cancel. How much cancellation must occur when the frequency surface is curved?

Fourier restriction theory asks questions of this kind. The geometry of a surface in frequency space controls how strongly the resulting wave can concentrate in physical space. Curvature spreads directions, yet many localized pieces of the wave can still overlap along thin tubes.

Family 077 contains two claimed sharp open-range results in three-dimensional space. One concerns bounded data on the sphere. The other treats data in an LpL^pLp space on any compact smooth positively curved surface, including smooth boundary patches. The second paper uses both the first paper’s packet theorem and the Kakeya maximal theorem from family 074.

2. Background and essential definitions

Extension as a superposition of waves

Let Σ⊂R3\Sigma\subset\mathbb R^3Σ⊂R3 be a smooth surface with area measure dσd\sigmadσ. Its extension operator is

EΣf(x)=∫Σf(ξ)e2πix⋅ξ dσ(ξ).E_\Sigma f(x)=\int_\Sigma f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,d\sigma(\xi).EΣ​f(x)=∫Σ​f(ξ)e2πix⋅ξdσ(ξ).

The point ξ\xiξ is a frequency vector, and e2πix⋅ξe^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}e2πix⋅ξ is its plane wave. The function fff specifies the amplitude and phase attached to each frequency. The output is defined on all of physical space, even though the input lives on a two-dimensional surface.

Why is this called restriction theory? A general Fourier transform of an LpL^pLp function need not have well-defined values on a surface of zero volume. Restriction estimates make such a trace meaningful in appropriate norms. By duality, these estimates can be expressed as extension bounds. The manuscripts use the extension formulation.

An LpL^pLp norm measures (∫∣f∣p)1/p(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}(∫∣f∣p)1/p. The L∞L^\inftyL∞ norm is the essential supremum. An estimate with bounded input and an estimate with LpL^pLp input are different assertions: the latter can admit arbitrarily large amplitudes on small subsets of the surface.

Positive curvature and the number three

Positive curvature here means that the second fundamental form is definite at every point. Locally, after choosing the normal appropriately, the surface is the graph of a function whose Hessian is positive definite. Sphere patches and elliptic paraboloid patches are standard examples. A saddle surface has a different geometry.

For the unit sphere and constant input, direct integration gives

ES21(x)=2sin⁡(2π∣x∣)∣x∣(x≠0).E_{S^2}1(x)=\frac{2\sin(2\pi|x|)}{|x|}\qquad(x\ne0).ES2​1(x)=∣x∣2sin(2π∣x∣)​(x=0).

Its amplitude typically decays like ∣x∣−1|x|^{-1}∣x∣−1. A shell of radius rrr has volume proportional to r2 drr^2\,drr2dr, so the integral of its ppp-th power has the large-radius behavior of ∫r2−p dr\int r^{2-p}\,dr∫r2−pdr. This converges only when p>3p>3p>3. Thus the threshold three already appears in the simplest smooth example.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The restriction problem originates in Stein’s work. The Tomas–Stein theorem gives the classical extension estimate from L2L^2L2 on a positively curved surface to L4L^4L4 in R3\mathbb R^3R3. Improving the output exponent toward three requires more detailed control of how oscillatory pieces interact.

Bilinear methods study pairs of separated frequency pieces. Multilinear methods study several pieces whose normal directions span space. The Bennett–Carbery–Tao theorem supplied a central estimate for these transverse interactions. Bourgain and Guth developed methods to turn such information back into estimates for one full extension operator.

Guth’s polynomial partitioning argument reached bounded-data estimates for p>13/4p>13/4p>13/4. It divides physical space into cells separated by an algebraic surface. Most tubes pass through relatively few cells, while the difficult remaining ones linger near that surface.

Wang’s broom method improved bounded-data restriction for the truncated paraboloid to p>42/13p>42/13p>42/13. The method exploits the fact that tubes clustered near one region must spread elsewhere, restricting repeated concentration. Wang and Wu subsequently combined refined decoupling with two-ends incidence estimates to obtain diagonal bounds for p>22/7p>22/7p>22/7 on compact positively curved surfaces.

The input norms in this history matter. A diagonal bound uses the same ppp on the surface and in space, while a bounded-data theorem uses L∞L^\inftyL∞ on the surface. The new family claims the full open output range p>3p>3p>3, with the second manuscript supplying the general-surface diagonal form.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Bounded sphere data

The first manuscript states that every p>3p>3p>3 has a finite constant CpC_pCp​ such that

∥ES2g∥Lp(R3)≤Cp∥g∥L∞(S2)\|E_{S^2}g\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_p\|g\|_{L^\infty(S^2)}∥ES2​g∥Lp(R3)​≤Cp​∥g∥L∞(S2)​

for every bounded measurable complex-valued ggg. The norm is global in physical space. The constant depends on ppp, not on the input.

The constant-input example above rules out extending this strong estimate to p≤3p\le3p≤3. The stated result is therefore the sharp open range in this formulation.

General positively curved surfaces

The companion states that every compact smooth positively curved Σ⊂R3\Sigma\subset\mathbb R^3Σ⊂R3, possibly with smooth boundary, satisfies

∥EΣf∥Lp(R3)≤CΣ,p∥f∥Lp(Σ)(3<p<∞).\|E_\Sigma f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_{\Sigma,p}\|f\|_{L^p(\Sigma)}\qquad(3<p<\infty).∥EΣ​f∥Lp(R3)​≤CΣ,p​∥f∥Lp(Σ)​(3<p<∞).

The surface is fixed, and the constant may depend on its geometry. This is not a uniform assertion over all surfaces with arbitrarily degenerating curvature.

For a compact paraboloid patch, a known transfer theorem yields a free Schrödinger local-smoothing consequence in two spatial dimensions:

∥eitΔf∥Lp(R2×[0,1])≤Cp,s∥(I−Δ)s/2f∥Lp(R2),s>2−6p,p>3.\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2\times[0,1])}\le C_{p,s}\|(I-\Delta)^{s/2}f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)},\qquad s>2-\frac6p,\quad p>3.∥eitΔf∥Lp(R2×[0,1])​≤Cp,s​∥(I−Δ)s/2f∥Lp(R2)​,s>2−p6​,p>3.

Here Δ\DeltaΔ is the Laplacian and eitΔe^{it\Delta}eitΔ is the free Schrödinger evolution. The operator (I−Δ)s/2(I-\Delta)^{s/2}(I−Δ)s/2 measures sss derivatives in the Bessel-potential sense. The time interval is bounded but space is not. The Sobolev inequality is strict.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, these estimates reach a central conjectured boundary in three-dimensional Fourier restriction. The second manuscript also moves from one highly symmetric surface to general smooth positively curved surfaces and permits rough LpL^pLp data.

Restriction estimates are useful because many oscillatory problems become local versions of the same geometry. A dispersion relation for an evolution equation traces out a surface in frequency-time space; extension from that surface describes a superposition of propagating waves. The stated Schrödinger consequence is one concrete instance.

The family also connects geometric overlap estimates with genuinely complex oscillation. A tube bound counts where packets can be large, while an extension estimate must handle their phases and interference. Passing from one to the other without losing the conjectured exponent is the core significance of the claimed method.

6. The main idea

Resolve a wave into packets

Divide the frequency surface into small caps. Localizing the input within one cap produces a wave packet concentrated near a long thin tube in physical space. Its direction is determined by the surface normal, while another label records its spatial position.

The packets can carry arbitrary complex coefficients. Consequently, a method that works only for equally weighted positive tubes cannot immediately estimate their sum. The first paper formulates a packet theorem that retains this coefficient information through repeated changes of scale.

Its geometric control uses ellipses with semiaxes L≥wL\ge wL≥w. The weight

W(E)=L1+κw1−κ=Lw(Lw)κW(E)=L^{1+\kappa}w^{1-\kappa}=Lw\left(\frac Lw\right)^\kappaW(E)=L1+κw1−κ=Lw(wL​)κ

is ordinary area multiplied by a small eccentricity penalty. The parameter κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 is small. Long narrow concentration is therefore recorded differently from concentration in a round region of the same area.

The paper tracks the joint distribution of direction and position labels. It does not replace that joint distribution by an independent one. Elliptic tests, planar incidence estimates and entropy calculations are used to control how concentration can propagate along packet trajectories.

Combine oscillation with positive tube estimates

The companion applies the packet theorem to general surface charts. A second input, the three-dimensional Kakeya maximal estimate, controls the positive weighted tube density. These inputs serve different purposes: one retains complex coefficients and oscillatory synthesis, while the other bounds geometric concentration.

Grouping packets according to their concentration allows the two estimates to be combined. The paper then obtains a joint bound on sparse collections of spatial balls. This controls the extension on far-separated regions without a constant that worsens with their separation.

An epsilon-removal argument turns local estimates carrying a small power of the spatial scale into a global estimate for every strictly larger exponent. Finally, finitely many charts cover the compact surface. Their Jacobians and the finite-measure inclusion between surface LpL^pLp spaces produce the stated diagonal inequality.

The smooth-boundary case is included by extending the local graph smoothly and extending its input by zero. This does not impose an artificial vanishing condition on the original boundary data.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The estimates are for positively curved surfaces in R3\mathbb R^3R3. Surfaces with zero curvature or mixed curvature are not included. Nor does the family resolve restriction in every ambient dimension.

The lower endpoint p=3p=3p=3 is excluded. Strong global boundedness already fails there for constant sphere data. Separate endpoint formulations, such as suitable weak estimates, are different questions.

The companion records how constants depend on its theorem inputs but does not claim a simple polynomial bound as ppp decreases to three. The finiteness of the constant at each fixed p>3p>3p>3 should not be confused with uniform boundedness near the endpoint.

The Schrödinger consequence uses two spatial dimensions and s>2−6/ps>2-6/ps>2−6/p. It is distinct from the three-spatial-dimensional wave local-smoothing result in family 079. The diagonal surface theorem also retains its dependency on the Kakeya maximal manuscript rather than following from bounded sphere data alone for arbitrary surfaces.

8. Sources and further reading

Primary background includes Bennett, Carbery and Tao’s multilinear theorem, Guth’s polynomial partitioning paper, and Bourgain and Demeter’s decoupling theorem. The source manuscripts give the comparisons with Wang’s and Wang–Wu’s later estimates and state the exact packet and Kakeya inputs.

For optional terminology, see restriction of the Fourier transform. The definitions above suffice to read the claimed inequalities without that reference.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Elliptic capacity propagation and Fourier restriction to the sphere (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Diagonal Fourier extension for positively curved surfaces in three dimensions (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Time averaging smooths waves in every dimension
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 079 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-27

1. The question

A wave can concentrate sharply when many rays meet. At that instant its spatial profile may be much larger than the initial profile in a norm sensitive to peaks. But a focus is temporary. How much control can we recover by averaging the wave’s size over time?

This is the local-smoothing problem. “Local” refers to a bounded time interval; the spatial region can be all of Euclidean space. The desired gain measures how much less regularity of the initial data is needed for a spacetime estimate than for an estimate at one fixed time.

Family 079 contains a three-dimensional argument and a broader manuscript claiming the conjectured gain in every spatial dimension at least two. The latter also states consequences for reconstructing functions from their Fourier transforms and for the size of sets containing line segments in every direction. The connection is that a localized wave travels along a thin tube, so controlling waves also constrains how such tubes overlap.

2. Background and essential definitions

Waves, norms, and derivative costs

For x∈Rnx\in\mathbb R^nx∈Rn, use the Fourier transform with phase e−ix⋅ξe^{-ix\cdot\xi}e−ix⋅ξ. A half-wave is

U(t)f(x)=1(2π)n∫Rnei(x⋅ξ−t∣ξ∣)f^(ξ) dξ.U(t)f(x)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{i(x\cdot\xi-t|\xi|)}\widehat f(\xi)\,d\xi.U(t)f(x)=(2π)n1​∫Rn​ei(x⋅ξ−t∣ξ∣)f​(ξ)dξ.

Here fff is the initial profile and ξ\xiξ its frequency variable. This evolution solves the wave equation ∂t2u−Δu=0\partial_t^2u-\Delta u=0∂t2​u−Δu=0, with Δ\DeltaΔ the spatial Laplacian. The other sign in the phase gives the second half-wave needed for general initial displacement and velocity.

For finite p≥1p\ge1p≥1, the LpL^pLp norm is (∫∣f∣p)1/p(\int |f|^p)^{1/p}(∫∣f∣p)1/p; L∞L^\inftyL∞ measures the essential supremum. Larger exponents emphasize large values. The spacetime norm integrates over both xxx and ttt; throughout the main wave estimate the time interval is I=[1,2]I=[1,2]I=[1,2].

Write Js=(1−Δ)s/2J^s=(1-\Delta)^{s/2}Js=(1−Δ)s/2. In Fourier space this multiplies by (1+∣ξ∣2)s/2(1+|\xi|^2)^{s/2}(1+∣ξ∣2)s/2, so ∥Jsf∥p\|J^sf\|_p∥Jsf∥p​ measures sss derivatives, including fractional values. At frequencies of size NNN, this costs approximately NsN^sNs. The estimates start with Schwartz functions—smooth functions whose derivatives decay faster than every power—and extend to the indicated normed spaces by approximation.

The critical exponent

For p>2p>2p>2, controlling a half-wave at a fixed nonzero time costs

sfixed(p)=(n−1)(12−1p)s_{\mathrm{fixed}}(p)=(n-1)\left(\frac12-\frac1p\right)sfixed​(p)=(n−1)(21​−p1​)

derivatives. The proposed spacetime threshold is

s+(p)=max⁡{0,n−12−np},pc=2nn−1.s_+(p)=\max\left\{0,\frac{n-1}{2}-\frac np\right\},\qquad p_c=\frac{2n}{n-1}.s+​(p)=max{0,2n−1​−pn​},pc​=n−12n​.

Above pcp_cpc​, the difference between the two thresholds is 1/p1/p1/p. At p=pcp=p_cp=pc​, the spacetime threshold reaches zero. The values are pc=4p_c=4pc​=4 in two dimensions and pc=3p_c=3pc​=3 in three.

An arbitrarily small positive loss means a bound for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, with a constant allowed to depend on ε\varepsilonε. It does not mean a bound with ε=0\varepsilon=0ε=0: even N0.001N^{0.001}N0.001 eventually grows.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Sogge’s 1991 paper formulated local smoothing through the study of wave propagation and maximal averages over circles. It established positive smoothing gains in the plane and connected the question to Fourier summation. Mockenhaupt, Seeger and Sogge developed methods that split waves into angular pieces while retaining information about their overlap.

Wolff’s wave-packet and induction-on-scale arguments obtained sharp gains for large exponents. Bourgain and Demeter’s decoupling theorem subsequently gave the conjectured gain, up to arbitrarily small loss, for

p≥2(n+1)n−1.p\ge\frac{2(n+1)}{n-1}.p≥n−12(n+1)​.

This is an important range, but its lower endpoint exceeds pcp_cpc​. In three dimensions it begins at four, leaving the critical exponent three untouched.

Guth, Wang and Zhang’s 2020 cone square-function theorem reached the critical exponent four for waves in two spatial dimensions. The cone lives in three-dimensional spacetime, which explains the dimension appearing in their title. In three spatial dimensions, Gao, Liu, Miao and Xi obtained a Sobolev loss above 1/91/91/9 at p=3p=3p=3. Gan, He, Li and Wu’s January 2026 version gives full gain for p≥10/3p\ge10/3p≥10/3; interpolation supplies losses above 1/121/121/12 at p=3p=3p=3.

The September manuscript in this family claims every positive loss at that critical three-dimensional exponent. The October manuscript gives a different construction in all dimensions, together with a quantitative logarithmic estimate at one frequency scale.

The geometric consequences also have their own history. In particular, Wang and Zahl’s 2025 work already established full Hausdorff dimension for three-dimensional Kakeya sets. The all-dimensional claims here should be understood alongside that earlier result, not as the first resolution of its three-dimensional case. The new manuscript additionally states maximal-operator estimates, which contain more quantitative information than a dimension conclusion alone.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Local smoothing and a logarithmic bound

Theorem 1.1 of the October manuscript states that for n≥2n\ge2n≥2, 2≤p<∞2\le p<\infty2≤p<∞, and every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0,

∥U(t)f∥Lp(Rn×I)≤Cn,p,ε∥Js+(p)+εf∥Lp(Rn).\|U(t)f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n\times I)}\le C_{n,p,\varepsilon}\|J^{s_+(p)+\varepsilon}f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}.∥U(t)f∥Lp(Rn×I)​≤Cn,p,ε​∥Js+​(p)+εf∥Lp(Rn)​.

The constant is independent of fff. At p=2p=2p=2, zero loss is permitted by the usual energy identity. For 2<p≤pc2<p\le p_c2<p≤pc​, every positive Sobolev order suffices; above pcp_cpc​, the order must exceed the displayed threshold.

Theorem 1.2 is more quantitative. For data fNf_NfN​ supported in a fixed frequency annulus of size N≥2N\ge2N≥2, it gives

∥U(t)fN∥Lpc(Rn×I)≤Cn[log⁡(2+N)]2/pc∥fN∥pc.\|U(t)f_N\|_{L^{p_c}(\mathbb R^n\times I)}\le C_n[\log(2+N)]^{2/p_c}\|f_N\|_{p_c}.∥U(t)fN​∥Lpc​(Rn×I)​≤Cn​[log(2+N)]2/pc​∥fN​∥pc​​.

Every fixed power of a logarithm grows more slowly than NεN^\varepsilonNε. This estimate therefore supplies the small-loss theorem after interpolation and frequency summation. In dimension three it gives logarithmic power 2/32/32/3, while recovering the September paper’s critical L3L^3L3 claim as a consequence.

Fourier reconstruction and restriction

Bochner–Riesz means reconstruct a function by multiplying its Fourier transform by

(1−∣ξ∣2R2)+α,\left(1-\frac{|\xi|^2}{R^2}\right)_+^\alpha,(1−R2∣ξ∣2​)+α​,

where R>0R>0R>0, a+=max⁡(a,0)a_+=\max(a,0)a+​=max(a,0), and α\alphaα softens the frequency cutoff. Theorem 10.1 claims uniform LpL^pLp bounds for the individual means, for 1≤p≤∞1\le p\le\infty1≤p≤∞, whenever

α>max⁡{0,n∣1p−12∣−12}.\alpha>\max\left\{0,n\left|\frac1p-\frac12\right|-\frac12\right\}.α>max{0,n​p1​−21​​−21​}.

For 2≤p<∞2\le p<\infty2≤p<∞, it also bounds the pointwise supremum over all radii at the same strict threshold, and obtains almost-everywhere convergence to the original function. Taking a supremum inside the norm is stronger than bounding every radius separately. Stein’s square function instead measures changes with radius by a squared integral; Theorem 11.1 claims its bound for α>1/2+s+(p)\alpha>1/2+s_+(p)α>1/2+s+​(p) in this same range of ppp.

Fourier extension assembles waves from frequencies lying on a surface. For the unit sphere, it is

Eg(x)=∫Sn−1eix⋅ωg(ω) dσ(ω),Eg(x)=\int_{S^{n-1}}e^{ix\cdot\omega}g(\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega),Eg(x)=∫Sn−1​eix⋅ωg(ω)dσ(ω),

where ggg is the amplitude and σ\sigmaσ surface measure. Corollary 9.3 claims LaL^aLa-to-LbL^bLb bounds throughout the conjectured interior:

b>2nn−1,b>n+1n−1a′,1a+1a′=1,b>\frac{2n}{n-1},\qquadb>\frac{n+1}{n-1}a',\qquad\frac1a+\frac1{a'}=1,b>n−12n​,b>n−1n+1​a′,a1​+a′1​=1,

with 1<a≤∞1<a\le\infty1<a≤∞ and finite bbb. Companion bounds concern the truncated cone and compact paraboloid. The latter yields local smoothing for Schrödinger waves, whose phase uses ∣ξ∣2|\xi|^2∣ξ∣2 instead of ∣ξ∣|\xi|∣ξ∣. In ddd spatial dimensions, Corollary 12.1 states the exact spacetime Sobolev order d−2(d+1)/pd-2(d+1)/pd−2(d+1)/p for p>2(d+1)/dp>2(d+1)/dp>2(d+1)/d on compact time intervals.

Tubes and sets containing every direction

A Kakeya set contains a unit line segment in every direction. Its Hausdorff dimension describes its size through covers at arbitrarily small scales; full dimension does not require positive volume.

Let Kδf(ω)K_\delta f(\omega)Kδ​f(ω) be the largest average of ∣f∣|f|∣f∣ over any unit-length tube of radius δ\deltaδ pointing in direction ω\omegaω. Corollary 9.1 states

∥Kδf∥Ln(Sn−1)≤Cn[log⁡(2/δ)]4/pc∥f∥Ln(Rn),0<δ≤1.\|K_\delta f\|_{L^n(S^{n-1})}\le C_n[\log(2/\delta)]^{4/p_c}\|f\|_{L^n(\mathbb R^n)},\qquad 0<\delta\le1.∥Kδ​f∥Ln(Sn−1)​≤Cn​[log(2/δ)]4/pc​∥f∥Ln(Rn)​,0<δ≤1.

This implies the usual conjectured bound allowing every δ−ε\delta^{-\varepsilon}δ−ε loss, and full Hausdorff dimension nnn for every Euclidean Kakeya set. A projective transformation gives the corresponding Nikodym estimate, in which tubes are selected through observation points rather than indexed by direction.

The September companion also states a wave maximal bound in three dimensions: for 3≤p<∞3\le p<\infty3≤p<∞, controlling sup⁡0<t<1∣U(t)f∣\sup_{0<t<1}|U(t)f|sup0<t<1​∣U(t)f∣ requires Sobolev order s>1−2/ps>1-2/ps>1−2/p. This pointwise-in-time conclusion has a stronger regularity requirement than spacetime smoothing.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the all-dimensional theorem resolves a central conjecture about how oscillatory waves concentrate. Its consequences connect several major questions in harmonic analysis: derivative gains for evolution equations, stability of Fourier reconstruction, restriction to curved frequency surfaces, and overlap of thin tubes.

The logarithmic estimate provides more information than an unspecified small power loss. It quantifies the residual growth at the critical exponent and carries that growth into restriction and maximal estimates. This makes it possible to compare the proposed bound with explicit focusing obstructions.

The geometric implication is especially striking. A statement about averaging an oscillating function over time leads to a constraint on every set containing all line directions, without assuming that the set arose from a particular wave. The method’s significance would lie both in the conjectures resolved and in the proposed conservation-law construction connecting them.

6. The main idea

Preserve interference while selecting directions

At one frequency scale, the wave is a superposition of plane waves moving in different directions. Their interference creates the peaks that the estimate must control. Squaring the pieces before adding them would discard this information.

The October argument instead continues a finite superposition to carefully chosen complex spacetime points. An imaginary displacement along a light ray multiplies each frequency by a Gaussian weight in its angular separation from that ray. It thus selects nearby directions while retaining the sum and its interference.

Using a symmetric first-order formulation of the wave equation, the paper constructs a positive tensor in an enlarged space of physical and auxiliary variables. Its columns have zero divergence. This is a conservation law: changes inside a region are related to flux through its boundary.

An auxiliary equation turns conservation into an estimate

On slices of the enlarged space, the argument solves a nonlinear boundary-value problem for a potential. Its prescribed determinant is tied to a nonnegative density μ\muμ that detects the squared wave amplitude.

The determinant is formed from a quaternionic matrix of second derivatives. Quaternions extend complex numbers to four real components; the relevant positive Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues whose product defines their determinant. The role of this machinery is to build an energy sensitive to concentration while permitting integration by parts with the conserved current.

A background potential contributes curvature in one direction. The remaining determinant estimate makes the resulting energy detect the power μn/(n−1)\mu^{n/(n-1)}μn/(n−1). Since μ\muμ corresponds to a squared wave amplitude, this produces ∣U(t)f∣2n/(n−1)|U(t)f|^{2n/(n-1)}∣U(t)f∣2n/(n−1)—exactly the critical exponent pcp_cpc​.

The paper corrects this energy so that difficult interior determinant terms cancel after differentiation. The surviving boundary flux is controlled by Gaussian decay. The result is a scalar differential inequality for the energy in physical time and two auxiliary time variables.

Why two logarithms appear

The final comparison moves from a small circle in the two auxiliary variables to a circle of fixed radius, transfers the estimate toward initial time, and returns to a small circle. Radial harmonic functions in two dimensions depend on the logarithm of the radius. The two annular comparisons each contribute a logarithmic factor.

The resulting bound for the pcp_cpc​-th power of the norm has a squared logarithm. Taking its pcp_cpc​-th root gives the power 2/pc2/p_c2/pc​. Removing an intermediate spatial period and summing frequency scales yields the Euclidean Sobolev estimate.

The September companion follows a separate path: it tracks wave-packet masses across changing scales and sheared coordinate frames. Lower-dimensional wave and incidence estimates constrain an entropy quantity describing packet configurations. Its contradiction argument rules out excessive concentration in three dimensions. The two papers therefore offer different mechanisms for the overlapping three-dimensional conclusion.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The main wave theorem concerns the free Euclidean equation. Variable coefficients and curved manifolds can focus rays differently; the Euclidean critical exponent is not a universal threshold for every wave equation.

At the critical exponent, the manuscript gives an annular lower obstruction of logarithmic power 1/pc1/p_c1/pc​, compared with its upper power 2/pc2/p_c2/pc​. Thus a frequency-independent lossless critical bound is excluded by its focusing examples, while the optimal logarithmic power for unrestricted data remains between those values. Additional angular regularity permits sharper statements in Appendix B.

The restriction conclusions use strict inequalities, and the displayed Bochner–Riesz and square-function orders are also strict. They should not be read as every possible endpoint theorem. Likewise, bounded-time smoothing is different from a global-in-time estimate or regularity improvement at each individual instant.

Full Kakeya dimension permits zero volume. The maximal estimate is quantitative, but it does not say that all collections of thin tubes have a volume bounded below independently of their thickness.

The repository’s formalization description reports local smoothing and specified Bochner–Riesz, spherical extension, square-function and Kakeya results. Its scope statement should be consulted for those formalization claims; the exposition here follows the two manuscripts’ mathematical statements.

8. Sources and further reading

In the October manuscript, Theorems 1.1–1.2 state local smoothing and the annular logarithmic bound. Sections 2–7 develop the auxiliary equation and energy argument; Section 8 gives endpoint obstructions; Sections 9–12 derive the applications. The September paper supplies its independent three-dimensional packet argument and maximal consequences.

The primary historical sources linked above trace Sogge’s formulation, Bourgain–Demeter decoupling, the Guth–Wang–Zhang planar theorem, the Gan–He–Li–Wu three-dimensional range, and Wang–Zahl’s Kakeya dimension theorem. Optional background: Sobolev spaces, Fourier restriction, and Kakeya sets.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation (October 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Critical local smoothing for the three-dimensional wave equation (September 24, 2026; also retained in the current source revision).

Sources consulted on 27 October 2026 at repository revision 7ef5c0c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Riesz transform bounds reveal hidden surface geometry
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 081 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Suppose a set carries roughly the same amount of mass as an nnn-dimensional surface at every small scale, but no parametrization is known. Can an integral operator detect whether substantial parts of that set really behave like surfaces?
