The Riesz transform compares directions between pairs of points, weighted more strongly when the points are close. Its boundedness expresses cancellation in this directional interaction. The David–Semmes question asks whether this analytical condition forces quantitative geometric regularity.

Family 081 claims the remaining higher-codimension implication: for integer-dimensional Ahlfors–David regular measures, a uniform L2L^2L2 bound for the truncated Riesz transforms forces uniform rectifiability. The theorem starts with a two-sided mass condition, not an arbitrary measure, and concludes the existence of substantial Lipschitz-parametrized pieces at every relevant location and scale.

2. Background and essential definitions

A measure with surface-like growth

A Radon measure μ\muμ is a Borel measure finite on compact sets, with the usual regularity properties. Its support EEE consists of points around which every ball has positive mass.

The measure is nnn-Ahlfors–David regular, or AD regular, if a constant CAD≥1C_{\mathrm{AD}}\ge1CAD​≥1 satisfies

CAD−1rn≤μ(B(x,r))≤CADrnC_{\mathrm{AD}}^{-1}r^n\le\mu(B(x,r))\le C_{\mathrm{AD}}r^nCAD−1​rn≤μ(B(x,r))≤CAD​rn

for x∈Ex\in Ex∈E and 0<r≤diam⁡E0<r\le\operatorname{diam}E0<r≤diamE. Thus ball masses have the order expected on an nnn-dimensional plane. Both inequalities matter: an upper growth bound alone allows much sparser local behavior.

The ambient space is Rd\mathbb R^dRd, and the codimension is d−nd-nd−n. A surface of dimension two inside R4\mathbb R^4R4 has codimension two. The new theorem addresses 2≤n≤d−22\le n\le d-22≤n≤d−2, where neither the one-dimensional methods nor the codimension-one theorem directly applies.

Truncating a singular directional kernel

The nnn-dimensional Riesz kernel is

Kn(z)=z∣z∣n+1.K_n(z)=\frac{z}{|z|^{n+1}}.Kn​(z)=∣z∣n+1z​.

It is vector-valued and odd: Kn(−z)=−Kn(z)K_n(-z)=-K_n(z)Kn​(−z)=−Kn​(z). Its size blows up at zero, so the manuscript first uses hard truncations

Rμ,εf(x)=∫∣x−y∣>εx−y∣x−y∣n+1f(y) dμ(y).R_{\mu,\varepsilon}f(x)=\int_{|x-y|>\varepsilon}\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^{n+1}}f(y)\,d\mu(y).Rμ,ε​f(x)=∫∣x−y∣>ε​∣x−y∣n+1x−y​f(y)dμ(y).

“Hard” means an actual exclusion of the ball of radius ε\varepsilonε, rather than a smooth transition. Uniform boundedness requires one constant CRC_RCR​ such that

∥Rμ,εf∥L2(μ;Rd)≤CR∥f∥L2(μ)for every ε>0.\|R_{\mu,\varepsilon}f\|_{L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d)}\le C_R\|f\|_{L^2(\mu)}\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.∥Rμ,ε​f∥L2(μ;Rd)​≤CR​∥f∥L2(μ)​for every ε>0.

The input is scalar, and the output norm uses the Euclidean length of its vector values. This condition controls every truncation separately; it does not assume pointwise convergence as the hole shrinks.

Big pieces of Lipschitz images

A map ggg is MMM-Lipschitz if ∣g(u)−g(v)∣≤M∣u−v∣|g(u)-g(v)|\le M|u-v|∣g(u)−g(v)∣≤M∣u−v∣. It cannot stretch distances by more than a fixed factor, although it need not be injective.

Uniform rectifiability means there are fixed θ>0\theta>0θ>0 and M<∞M<\inftyM<∞ such that every admissible ball B(x,r)B(x,r)B(x,r) contains mass at least θrn\theta r^nθrn lying in the image of an MMM-Lipschitz map from the nnn-dimensional ball of radius rrr. The map may change with xxx and rrr, but its quantitative constants do not.

3. Development history and previous partial results

David and Semmes developed uniform rectifiability to connect geometry with singular integral estimates. Ordinary rectifiability says, roughly, that almost all of a set can be covered by countably many Lipschitz images. Uniform rectifiability adds consistent control at every scale, making it suitable for norm inequalities.

Mattila, Melnikov and Verdera established the planar implication through the relationship between the Cauchy integral and curvature. Related curvature methods also handle one-dimensional Riesz transforms in higher ambient dimensions.

Nazarov, Tolsa and Volberg proved the codimension-one implication. Their method uses a maximum principle whose analogue in higher codimension was a central obstacle. A surface with several independent normal directions presents more geometric freedom than a hypersurface with one normal direction.

Mas and Tolsa characterized uniform rectifiability through a stronger variation bound for Riesz truncations. Variation controls accumulated changes as the cutoff scale varies. A common bound for individual truncations does not immediately provide that stronger control.

Tolsa also characterized ordinary rectifiability under an almost-everywhere principal-value hypothesis for sets of finite Hausdorff measure. That is another distinct starting point: existence of pointwise limits is not the same assumption as the uniform operator bound used here.

The new manuscript claims that the individual-truncation bound alone supplies uniform rectifiability in the remaining integer-dimensional range 1<n<d−11<n<d-11<n<d−1. Together with the previous cases, this would complete the AD-regular Riesz-transform implication across codimensions.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let d≥4d\ge4d≥4 and 2≤n≤d−22\le n\le d-22≤n≤d−2 be integers. The theorem assumes that μ\muμ is an nnn-AD-regular Radon measure on Rd\mathbb R^dRd and that its hard Riesz truncations have the common L2L^2L2 bound above.

It concludes that there exist θ>0\theta>0θ>0 and M<∞M<\inftyM<∞, depending only on d,n,CAD,CRd,n,C_{\mathrm{AD}},C_Rd,n,CAD​,CR​, such that for every admissible x,rx,rx,r, some map

g:BRn(0,r)⟶Rdg:B_{\mathbb R^n}(0,r)\longrightarrow\mathbb R^dg:BRn​(0,r)⟶Rd

is MMM-Lipschitz and satisfies

μ(B(x,r)∩g(BRn(0,r)))≥θrn.\mu\bigl(B(x,r)\cap g(B_{\mathbb R^n}(0,r))\bigr)\ge\theta r^n.μ(B(x,r)∩g(BRn​(0,r)))≥θrn.

The conclusion is quantitative. It does not merely say that some parametrized pieces exist with constants deteriorating unpredictably as one zooms in.

The source imposes no separate principal-value assumption and no initial graph representation of the support. It also does not assume variation bounds. Those stronger analytical consequences are derived later using the resulting uniform rectifiability and established theory.

The theorem allows bounded or unbounded supports, with the radius range stated in the definition. The source treats the degenerate zero-diameter case as having no admissible positive radii; the geometric assertion is then vacuous.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the result answers the remaining range of a central question about whether a single natural singular integral detects quantitative surface geometry.

The analytical hypothesis sees only pairwise directional interactions and their cancellation. The conclusion supplies local parametrizations with uniform control. That bridge is powerful because singular integrals arise naturally in boundary-value problems even when the boundary is too rough to be given initially as a smooth graph.

The higher-codimension setting is especially significant. It removes reliance on a one-normal-direction geometry and would show that the Riesz transform still detects substantial flat structure when several transverse directions are available.

The rating reflects this broad characterization. It does not mean the theorem turns every regular set into one smooth global manifold; big Lipschitz pieces are the precise geometric conclusion.

6. The main idea

Find flat pieces and make flatness persist

The manuscript measures deviation from an affine nnn-plane by a scale-normalized average squared distance, called excess. Small excess says that most of the relevant mass lies near a plane. A stronger bilateral comparison also checks that the plane itself has no large holes relative to the support.

The operator bound is used to find flat descendants among nested cells of the support, apart from a family whose total size has a controlled packing bound. A descendant is simply a smaller cell reached by repeated subdivision.

Finding occasional flat pieces is not enough. The main challenge is to show that flatness improves or persists at smaller scales unless the transform exhibits enough detectable oscillation to be charged to the available analytical bound.

Magnify the deviation from a plane

Suppose the support is close to a plane. Record its normal heights, the components perpendicular to that plane, and divide them by the initial deviation scale. Without this normalization, a limit would merely flatten everything to zero and lose the information needed to measure relative improvement.

Testing Riesz interactions against these heights gives a positive fractional-energy bound. Such an energy controls differences of the height function between pairs of points, allowing compactness even though both the measure and its support are changing.

The manuscript passes to a limiting height equation when suitably normalized Riesz oscillations vanish. Its stated rigidity argument forces each limiting height to be affine. An affine height describes a tilted plane, so choosing that improved plane gives a better relative excess estimate in the original configuration.

This is the replacement for a direct higher-codimension maximum principle: the proposed limiting equation constrains the possible shapes of small deviations.

Count the scales where improvement fails

Nested cells form a tree across scales. If a chain starts with a flat cell and later loses flatness, the propagation result forces an intervening cell with visible transform oscillation.

The operator bound limits how much such oscillation can occur. A counting argument converts this into a packing estimate for the bad geometric scales. The David–Semmes geometric criterion then turns that packing control into the required big pieces of Lipschitz images.

The proof strategy therefore separates an analytic task, limiting the total amount of bad behavior, from a geometric task, converting rare bad scales into substantial parametrized pieces.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

AD regularity is essential to the stated theorem. Both upper and lower ball-mass bounds are assumed. Removing either bound leads to a different problem and is not a consequence of the claimed result.

The dimension nnn is an integer. The theorem is not a rectifiability statement for arbitrary fractional-dimensional measures. Its higher-codimension range is explicit, while the other integer cases are supplied by prior work.

Uniform rectifiability allows complicated global topology and does not provide one Lipschitz graph covering the whole support. The map furnished in each ball may vary with the ball and need not be injective.

Finally, bounded truncations, variation bounds and principal values are different analytical statements. The manuscript starts from the first and derives further consequences through geometry; the stronger properties should not be silently inserted into its hypotheses.

8. Sources and further reading

The main comparisons are Nazarov–Tolsa–Volberg’s codimension-one theorem, Mas–Tolsa’s variation characterization, and Tolsa’s work on uniform measures. David and Semmes’s Analysis of and on uniformly rectifiable sets (1993) develops the geometric framework.

Optional introductions to rectifiable sets and Riesz transforms explain the surrounding terminology; the measure-dependent kernel and quantitative hypothesis used here are stated above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Riesz transforms and uniform rectifiability in higher codimension (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Controlling the triangular Hilbert transform across all scales
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 082 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Singular integrals balance positive and negative contributions near a singularity. The ordinary Hilbert transform performs this cancellation along one variable. What happens when two functions move in different coordinate directions, so their interactions become entangled?

The triangular Hilbert transform is a basic example. One input is shifted horizontally, the other vertically, but both use the same shift parameter and the same singular kernel. Pairing the output with a third function produces a cycle of three overlapping pairs of variables.

Family 082 contains three manuscripts. One claims a maximal estimate over both truncation endpoints, a later paper strengthens this to annular variation for every exponent above two, and another treats a dyadic model with unrestricted real inputs. The continuous results allow complex inputs; the dyadic theorem has its own precise real-input formulation.

2. Background and essential definitions

A finite annular truncation

For functions F,GF,GF,G on R2\mathbb R^2R2, define

Bε,R(F,G)(x,y)=∫ε<∣t∣<RF(x+t,y)G(x,y+t) dtt,0<ε<R<∞.B_{\varepsilon,R}(F,G)(x,y)=\int_{\varepsilon<|t|<R}F(x+t,y)G(x,y+t)\,\frac{dt}{t},\qquad0<\varepsilon<R<\infty.Bε,R​(F,G)(x,y)=∫ε<∣t∣<R​F(x+t,y)G(x,y+t)tdt​,0<ε<R<∞.

The lower cutoff avoids the singularity at zero; the upper cutoff avoids an uncontrolled infinite tail. The odd factor 1/t1/t1/t makes cancellation between positive and negative shifts essential.

The operator is bilinear because it depends linearly on each input separately. Hölder’s inequality suggests the exponents L3×L3→L3/2L^3\times L^3\to L^{3/2}L3×L3→L3/2, since 1/3+1/3=2/31/3+1/3=2/31/3+1/3=2/3. Pairing the output with another L3L^3L3 function gives a scalar trilinear form.

A change of variables writes that form as

Λε,R(G0,G1,G2)=∭ε<∣a+b+c∣<RG0(a,b)G1(b,c)G2(c,a)a+b+c da db dc.\Lambda_{\varepsilon,R}(G_0,G_1,G_2)=\iiint_{\varepsilon<|a+b+c|<R}\frac{G_0(a,b)G_1(b,c)G_2(c,a)}{a+b+c}\,da\,db\,dc.Λε,R​(G0​,G1​,G2​)=∭ε<∣a+b+c∣<R​a+b+cG0​(a,b)G1​(b,c)G2​(c,a)​dadbdc.

Each factor sees two of the three variables, and the shared pairs form a triangle. The symmetric point means all three input exponents equal three. It does not mean the input functions themselves are symmetric.

Maximal size and variation

The maximal transform is

B∗(F,G)(x,y)=sup⁡0<ε<R<∞∣Bε,R(F,G)(x,y)∣.B_*(F,G)(x,y)=\sup_{0<\varepsilon<R<\infty}|B_{\varepsilon,R}(F,G)(x,y)|.B∗​(F,G)(x,y)=0<ε<R<∞sup​∣Bε,R​(F,G)(x,y)∣.

The endpoints may be chosen separately at each output point. This is stronger than bounding each fixed truncation by a common norm constant.

For r>2r>2r>2, the annular variation is

Vr(F,G)=sup⁡0<t0<⋯<tJ(∑j=1J∣Btj−1,tj(F,G)∣r)1/r,V_r(F,G)=\sup_{0<t_0<\cdots<t_J}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{J}|B_{t_{j-1},t_j}(F,G)|^r\right)^{1/r},Vr​(F,G)=0<t0​<⋯<tJ​sup​(j=1∑J​∣Btj−1​,tj​​(F,G)∣r)1/r,

where the supremum includes all finite partitions. It measures accumulated changes across disjoint annuli, not merely the largest single value. Taking J=1J=1J=1 shows that variation controls the maximal transform. Rational endpoints give the same supremum while making measurability immediate.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The flat operator appears in Demeter and Thiele’s work on the two-dimensional bilinear Hilbert transform. Its cyclic dependence makes it a model problem for entangled singular integrals. Thiele’s contribution to Some problems in harmonic analysis records the symmetric triangular estimate as a central question.

Kovač, Thiele and Zorin-Kranich obtained bounds for a Walsh or dyadic model when one input has a specified structural form. Their work already captures important related operators, but does not allow all three inputs to vary freely in the claimed new dyadic range.

Another line of progress measured how slowly truncated norms grow with the number of scales. Tao established sublogarithmic cancellation for multilinear Hilbert transforms, and Zorin-Kranich extended this kind of cancellation to simplex transforms. Durcik, Kovač and Thiele obtained power-type cancellation. At the symmetric triangular tuple, the bound retained a square-root dependence on the logarithmic scale range.

Results with curved shifts, such as (t,t2)(t,t^2)(t,t2), or with an average over direction parameters gain additional cancellation. They do not directly settle the flat shifts (t,t)(t,t)(t,t) underlying this family.

The manuscripts develop a matrix-energy approach from earlier telescoping and Bellman-function methods. The historical difficulty is that a triangle is a cyclic, non-bipartite interaction, so methods adapted to simpler patterns of shared variables do not transfer automatically.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Continuous maximal and variation estimates

For arbitrary complex F,G∈L3(R2)F,G\in L^3(\mathbb R^2)F,G∈L3(R2), the maximal manuscript states

∥B∗(F,G)∥3/2≤C∥F∥3∥G∥3.\|B_*(F,G)\|_{3/2}\le C\|F\|_3\|G\|_3.∥B∗​(F,G)∥3/2​≤C∥F∥3​∥G∥3​.

The later annular manuscript states the stronger family of bounds

∥Vr(F,G)∥3/2≤Cr∥F∥3∥G∥3(r>2).\|V_r(F,G)\|_{3/2}\le C_r\|F\|_3\|G\|_3\qquad(r>2).∥Vr​(F,G)∥3/2​≤Cr​∥F∥3​∥G∥3​(r>2).

Partitions can depend on the output point, and there is no bound on how many endpoints fall within one dyadic interval of radii.

The papers obtain a joint principal value as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow0ε↓0 and R↑∞R\uparrow\inftyR↑∞, both almost everywhere and in L3/2L^{3/2}L3/2. The variation paper also states norm convergence of the supremum of the remaining errors over sufficiently small lower and sufficiently large upper cutoffs. Pairing with a third input gives the symmetric scalar triangular estimate.

The dyadic absolute-sum theorem

The dyadic model uses intervals [2kn,2k(n+1))[2^kn,2^k(n+1))[2kn,2k(n+1)) on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞). A triple at one scale is admissible when its three integer indices have bitwise XOR equal to zero. XOR is binary addition without carries. Each interval has a Haar sign function, equal to one on its left half and minus one on its right half.

For the corresponding local trilinear contributions LIL_ILI​, the dyadic manuscript claims

∑k∈S∑I admissible at k∣LI(F0,F1,F2)∣≤40∏v=02∥Fv∥L3(R+2)\sum_{k\in S}\sum_{I\text{ admissible at }k}|L_I(F_0,F_1,F_2)|\le40\prod_{v=0}^2\|F_v\|_{L^3(\mathbb R_+^2)}k∈S∑​I admissible at k∑​∣LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​)∣≤40v=0∏2​∥Fv​∥L3(R+2​)​

for every finite scale set SSS and arbitrary real L3L^3L3 inputs. Each LIL_ILI​ is the integral of the cyclic product over the interval triple, multiplied by the three Haar signs and by 2−k2^{-k}2−k.

Because the absolute values are taken separately, coefficients of modulus at most one may vary independently among admissible triples. This is a theorem for a distinct operator; it is not an automatic replacement for the continuous principal-value statement.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, the continuous estimates settle the symmetric triangular Hilbert-transform problem and give strong control of its truncation behavior. The dyadic theorem removes structural restrictions on the inputs and controls even the sum of absolute local contributions.

Uniformity in the number of scales is decisive. A bound growing like the square root of the scale count demonstrates cancellation, but still diverges as more and more scales are included. The new claims remove that dependence in the appropriate norm.

Variation is stronger still: it limits repeated oscillation as the cutoffs change. This provides a natural route to convergence of singular integrals rather than only boundedness of isolated truncations. The family would therefore advance both the boundedness and convergence aspects of an important entangled operator.

6. The main idea

Encode the cycle with matrices

Sample the three pair-dependent inputs on a finite grid. Each input becomes a matrix between the coordinate spaces of the two variables it uses. Their cyclic product is then represented by a matrix trace, which naturally retains the triangular arrangement.

At each vertex of the triangle, place the two incident matrices side by side in a row operator RRR. The energy is

tr⁡((R∗R)3/2).\operatorname{tr}\bigl((R^*R)^{3/2}\bigr).tr((R∗R)3/2).

Here R∗R^*R∗ is the conjugate transpose, and the positive matrix power is defined using eigenvalues. The exponent gives the energy the same cubic scaling as a product of three inputs.

The manuscripts state matrix inequalities whose constants do not grow with the grid size. This dimension independence is necessary before passing from sampled functions to continuous ones.

Pay for truncations through changes in energy

In the continuous argument, Gaussian weights smooth the sampled inputs. As the Gaussian variance changes, a heat-flow identity makes the decrease of the nonnegative energy control the required cyclic products.

A pointwise choice of truncation means that different entries of the matrix representing the dual output test switch on and off at different scales. The energy can jump at these switches. The maximal paper’s extra estimate bounds the total cost of those jumps using the input norms, without charging separately for every scale.

The variation paper must handle many disjoint annuli. It first proves a count estimate: the sum of the absolute contributions from at most mmm disjoint annuli has norm bounded by

Cmlog⁡(2+m)∥F∥3∥G∥3.C\sqrt m\log(2+m)\|F\|_3\|G\|_3.Cm​log(2+m)∥F∥3​∥G∥3​.

Sorting the increments by size and grouping their ranks into dyadic blocks gives a convergent series when r>2r>2r>2. The square-root growth is precisely why that variation range appears.

Hard annular endpoints create additional errors beyond smooth Gaussian cutoffs. The paper groups endpoints by scale and uses a frequency-block estimate to control many jumps together, rather than paying a linear cost in their number.

A discrete telescoping counterpart

For the dyadic theorem, Gaussian flow is replaced by passage from an interval triple to its four XOR-admissible child triples. The local contribution is bounded by an increase in average child energy.

Summing these increases over the tree makes intermediate energies cancel. Only controlled boundary terms remain. This telescoping is what allows an estimate independent of the finite scale set, even with absolute local contributions.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The continuous claims are at the symmetric L3×L3→L3/2L^3\times L^3\to L^{3/2}L3×L3→L3/2 point. The family does not state the full expected range of unequal exponents or all higher simplex transforms.

The variation theorem requires r>2r>2r>2. It makes no endpoint assertion at r=2r=2r=2, and the constant may depend on rrr. Its pointwise partition supremum is stronger than a variation quantity formed after taking output norms; these two formulations should not be confused.

The dyadic estimate uses the specified XOR model and real inputs. Its absolute sum is a sum of absolute local integrals, not the integral of the absolute value of the singular kernel times the inputs. Cancellation still occurs inside each local contribution.

The principal value is joint in the two cutoffs. This is stronger than proving convergence only along one predetermined sequence of annuli, and it remains distinct from absolute integrability of the untruncated kernel.

8. Sources and further reading

Thiele’s problem formulation, the structured-input dyadic theorem, and the power-type cancellation theorem provide the main historical comparisons. The three source manuscripts below state the continuous variation, dyadic absolute-sum and continuous maximal results separately.

Optional introductions to the Hilbert transform and Haar wavelets explain the continuous kernel and the discrete signs used in the models.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Annular variation of the triangular Hilbert transform at the symmetric point (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An L³ bound for the dyadic triangular Hilbert form (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The maximal triangular Hilbert transform at the symmetric point (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Hilbert transforms along a changing direction field
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 083 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Imagine a photograph in which every pixel comes with an arrow. At each pixel, compare the image values on opposite sides along the indicated line, giving nearby differences more weight than distant ones. When all arrows agree, this is a familiar one-dimensional singular integral applied independently along parallel lines. When the arrows turn from place to place, the measurements interact in a much less orderly way.

The question is whether a controlled rate of turning is enough to control the total size of the output. This is a version of a problem associated with Elias Stein: can the Hilbert transform along a Lipschitz direction field satisfy a uniform square-integrability estimate?

The family’s single manuscript claims such an estimate for a sufficiently short segment, with a length determined by the field’s Lipschitz constant. The distinction between short and arbitrarily long segments matters. The direction is also frozen at the point where the answer is evaluated: the integration does not follow a curved trajectory of the field.

2. Background and essential definitions

A unit direction field is a map v:R2→S1v:\mathbb R^2\to S^1v:R2→S1, where S1S^1S1 is the unit circle. It is Lipschitz with constant LLL if

∣v(x)−v(y)∣≤L∣x−y∣|v(x)-v(y)|\leq L|x-y|∣v(x)−v(y)∣≤L∣x−y∣

for all points x,yx,yx,y. Thus nearby arrows cannot differ too much. The natural length associated with this condition is 1/L1/L1/L: over much smaller distances, the permitted change of direction is small.

For an inner cutoff ε\varepsilonε and outer cutoff aaa, define

Hv,aεf(x)=∫ε<∣t∣<af(x−tv(x)) dtt.H^{\varepsilon}_{v,a}f(x)=\int_{\varepsilon<|t|<a}f(x-tv(x))\,\frac{dt}{t}.Hv,aε​f(x)=∫ε<∣t∣<a​f(x−tv(x))tdt​.

The vector v(x)v(x)v(x) stays fixed throughout this integral. Positive and negative values of ttt give opposite signs because of 1/t1/t1/t. That cancellation is the central feature of a Hilbert transform; taking absolute values inside the integral would lose it.

The cutoff removes the singularity at t=0t=0t=0. For a smooth function, the contributions on the two sides combine into a difference, which vanishes to first order as ttt tends to zero. This makes the symmetric principal value meaningful.

The L2L^2L2 norm is

∥f∥2=(∫R2∣f(x)∣2 dx)1/2.\|f\|_2=\left(\int_{\mathbb R^2}|f(x)|^2\,dx\right)^{1/2}.∥f∥2​=(∫R2​∣f(x)∣2dx)1/2.

A uniform L2L^2L2 estimate says that the output’s squared size, integrated over the plane, is at most a fixed multiple of the input’s. Uniformity in the inner cutoff is essential: a bound deteriorating as ε→0\varepsilon\to0ε→0 would not settle the intended singular-integral question.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Constant directions reduce to the classical Hilbert transform. The difficulty begins when the selected line depends on both coordinates of the evaluation point. Stein’s question is related to Zygmund’s differentiation problem for averages over shrinking segments, although a positive averaging operator and a signed singular integral have different cancellation mechanisms.

Earlier results exploited additional regularity or structure. Analytic fields allowed methods unavailable for a general Lipschitz field. Another approach restricted Fourier frequencies to a single annulus, a band between two comparable distances from the origin. Lacey and Li obtained weak L2L^2L2 and strong LpL^pLp, p>2p>2p>2, estimates in an annular setting. Such estimates do not by themselves combine into a strong L2L^2L2 estimate across all frequency scales.

A geometric advance was Lacey and Li’s Lipschitz Kakeya maximal theorem. It controls averages over short rectangles for which the field points approximately along the rectangle on a prescribed fraction of its area. The cost worsens as this fraction decreases. Their later memoir, On a conjecture of E. M. Stein on Hilbert transforms on vector fields (2010), related this geometry to the transform, with additional hypotheses in its conditional full-transform results.

A separate line treated fields depending on only one coordinate. Bateman and Thiele’s work gave full-line principal-value bounds for measurable fields of that type in a substantial exponent range, including L2L^2L2. That restriction is significant: a direction depending freely on both coordinates cannot be reduced to the same argument. Related work considered suitable Lipschitz foliations or specially separated, lacunary sets of directions.

Di Plinio, Guo, Thiele and Zorin-Kranich’s Square functions for bi-Lipschitz maps and directional operators (2018) supplied a principle for reassembling frequency bands. The new manuscript credits that earlier principle. Its claimed advance is the strong, sufficiently summable band estimate for an unrestricted planar Lipschitz field, together with the uniform treatment of the displayed hard cutoffs.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that absolute constants a∗∈(0,1/2)a_*\in(0,1/2)a∗​∈(0,1/2) and C∗<∞C_*<\inftyC∗​<∞ exist such that every unit field with Lipschitz constant at most one satisfies

sup⁡0<ε<a∗∥Hv,a∗εf∥2≤C∗∥f∥2.\sup_{0<\varepsilon<a_*}\|H^{\varepsilon}_{v,a_*}f\|_2\leq C_*\|f\|_2.0<ε<a∗​sup​∥Hv,a∗​ε​f∥2​≤C∗​∥f∥2​.

The constants do not depend on the particular field or the inner cutoff. Rescaling gives the corresponding short length a∗/La_*/La∗​/L for a field with Lipschitz constant L>0L>0L>0. A constant field, for which L=0L=0L=0, is handled separately by one-dimensional theory and permits any finite outer length.

For smooth rapidly decreasing inputs, the principal value exists pointwise, and the estimate gives a bounded operator. Density then produces its bounded extension to all of L2L^2L2.

There is a crucial placement of the supremum here: it lies outside the norm. The statement controls every truncated operator with the same constant. It does not state the stronger bound obtained by taking the supremum of the absolute outputs at each point and then taking its L2L^2L2 norm.

The manuscript presents this as a strong L2L^2L2 resolution of the short-transform question, and hence stronger than the corresponding weak-type estimate. Here these are the source’s claims, with the stated truncation and regularity conventions retained.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. A general Lipschitz direction field is a central threshold case in the study of directional singular integrals. It allows considerable geometric variation while retaining a first-order constraint on how quickly the directions change. An estimate at precisely this regularity would substantially advance a longstanding interaction between Fourier analysis and Kakeya geometry.

The result’s strength is its uniformity. A theorem for one especially regular field, with a constant depending on many of its derivatives, does not address a sequence of increasingly intricate fields with the same Lipschitz bound. The claimed constant handles that whole class at its natural short length.

It also combines two kinds of control that are individually insufficient. Geometry limits how often many thin directional packets can crowd together. Oscillation allows packets with different frequencies to cancel. Obtaining a full L2L^2L2 estimate requires both, without paying anew for every frequency band or angular scale.

This rating concerns the potential mathematical significance of the claim. It does not turn the principal-value extension into an assertion about pointwise convergence for every rough input, nor does it treat the manuscript as independently verified.

6. The main idea

Reduce to a frequency band, then make its estimate summable

After localization and rotation, the field is represented by a bounded slope. The argument isolates a vertical frequency band. Within that band, it tests an input supported on a set FFF against a function supported on another set EEE.

The desired estimate has the usual square-root size (∣E∣∣F∣)1/2(|E||F|)^{1/2}(∣E∣∣F∣)1/2, multiplied by an additional factor that decreases as a power of the logarithm of the ratio of the two measures. This extra decrease makes it possible to sum over the different sizes of a general function. A commutator argument then reassembles vertical bands without losing control of the two truncation endpoints.

Use geometry to limit significant directions

A wave packet is localized in both position and frequency. Its spatial footprint is a thin rectangle, while its oscillation carries a direction label. Ordinary size estimates remove packets that contribute little. The others are grouped under larger rectangles where their direction is sufficiently popular on the test set.

Lacey–Li’s theorem controls those larger rectangles. The manuscript then combines concentration estimates along reference lines with the Lipschitz condition to bound the number of directions that can remain significant at a given resolution. This is geometric preparation; it does not yet supply the final cancellation.

Extract a small gain repeatedly without accumulating a large constant

The oscillatory step studies a finite sum of exponentials with separated frequencies. M1 claims a strict improvement in its coefficient exponent with operator constant exactly one. Even a harmless-looking constant larger than one could become disastrous if multiplied once at every level of a long hierarchy of directions.

Directions are therefore organized in nested angular intervals, each carrying both positive mass and an oscillatory amplitude. The finite-frequency gain is applied to normalized energies. Errors are tied to the fraction of mass lost along a branch, so their total can be controlled by a telescoping quantity rather than by the number of levels.

Packets that stop between selected levels create additional residual terms. Square-sum and variation estimates handle these terms. The final interpolation and averaging steps convert the repeated small phase gain into the logarithmic improvement needed for the original band estimate.

The recurring objective is concrete: no estimate may grow simply because the analysis used more scales, narrower frequency bins, or a deeper directional hierarchy.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The field is unit length and Lipschitz on the plane, and the segment is short relative to its Lipschitz constant. The theorem does not state a full-line bound for every varying field. The more permissive full-line results for one-coordinate fields use a different structural hypothesis.

The path is a straight segment in the direction at the output point. Replacing it with an integral curve of the vector field changes the operator. Likewise, replacing hard time cutoffs with smooth frequency truncations produces a related but distinct formulation.

Uniform boundedness of individual truncations is not the same as boundedness of their pointwise maximum. The claimed bounded extension on L2L^2L2 is also not, by itself, a declaration that principal values converge almost everywhere for every L2L^2L2 function.

Further exponent ranges, maximal or variation inequalities, and longer segments are natural directions beyond the displayed theorem. The digest does not infer these from the short strong L2L^2L2 estimate.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s opening section states the theorem and carefully separates earlier annular, one-coordinate, analytic and lacunary results. Its subsections on the geometric reduction and phase iteration are the basis for section 6 above.

For historical context, Lacey–Li’s linked Kakeya paper and their 2010 memoir explain why short rectangles and directional popularity arise. Bateman–Thiele’s Lᵖ estimates for the Hilbert transforms along a one-variable vector field (2013), and the 2018 square-function paper named above, give primary accounts of two different partial solutions. Full bibliographic details are in M1.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A uniform Hilbert transform estimate for Lipschitz directions (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A nearly full interval can avoid every scaled geometric sequence
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 084 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Take a measurable subset of the real line with positive length. Must it contain a translated and rescaled copy of any pattern you choose? For a finite pattern, the answer is yes. A sufficiently small version can fit inside even a rather irregular set of positive measure.

An infinite pattern is different. Erdős conjectured that every infinite set can be defeated: some positive-measure set contains none of its translated and nontrivially rescaled copies. One particularly resistant example was the geometric sequence

12,14,18,….\frac12,\frac14,\frac18,\ldots.21​,41​,81​,….

Its points crowd together exponentially near zero. Removing a small amount of material while hitting every possible translated and rescaled copy is consequently difficult.

The two manuscripts in this family claim first the dyadic case, with ratio 1/21/21/2, and then every fixed geometric ratio. Their avoiding sets are compact and can occupy almost all of the unit interval. The later claim covers each ratio separately; it does not say that a single set simultaneously avoids every geometric progression.

2. Background and essential definitions

Lebesgue measure, written m(E)m(E)m(E), is the usual notion of length for measurable subsets of the line. An affine copy of a set A⊂RA\subset\mathbb RA⊂R has the form

x+sA={x+sa:a∈A},s≠0.x+sA=\{x+sa:a\in A\},\qquad s\ne0.x+sA={x+sa:a∈A},s=0.

The number xxx translates the pattern. A positive sss changes its size, while a negative sss also reflects it. Excluding s=0s=0s=0 prevents collapsing the whole pattern to one point.

A set is measure universal if every measurable set of positive measure contains such a copy. Erdős’s conjecture says that no infinite set is measure universal.

For a fixed q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1)q∈(0,1), write

Gq={qn:n=1,2,3,…}.G_q=\{q^n:n=1,2,3,\ldots\}.Gq​={qn:n=1,2,3,…}.

This sequence approaches zero, but zero itself is not included. The distinction becomes useful in the construction: a neighborhood of a copy’s limiting point will still contain sufficiently late members of the copy.

Why are finite patterns universal? If FFF is finite and AAA has finite positive measure, sufficiently small translations change AAA only a little in measure. Consequently the intersection of the finitely many sets A−saA-saA−sa, for a∈Fa\in Fa∈F, still has positive measure when sss is small enough. A point xxx in that intersection satisfies x+sF⊂Ax+sF\subset Ax+sF⊂A. There is no comparable automatic conclusion for infinitely many intersections.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Erdős formulated the similarity problem in 1974. Falconer’s On a problem of Erdős on sequences and measurable sets (1984), followed by Eigen’s work in 1985, treated positive decreasing sequences whose successive ratio tends to one. Those sequences approach zero much more slowly, in relative terms, than a fixed geometric sequence.

Humke and Laczkovich developed further criteria through finite covering problems. Kolountzakis’s Infinite patterns that can be avoided by measure (1997) introduced a probabilistic criterion involving large finite subsets with sufficiently well-spaced points. The account by Chlebík presents a translation-invariant form: roughly, the smallest gap, after normalizing the diameter, must not shrink exponentially fast in the number of selected points. Geometric progressions fail that test precisely because their gaps shrink exponentially.

Additive structure gave another route. Bourgain proved in 1987 that the sum of three infinite sets is nonuniversal. Later results treated certain two-fold sums, including a sum of two dyadic sequences. A 2026 manuscript on geometric summands extended this direction. Avoiding a sumset, however, does not imply avoiding each smaller pattern contained inside it: the latter is the harder requirement.

Other notions of size and allowed transformations lead to different answers. Cruz, Lai and Pramanik constructed large-dimensional avoiding sets, with the relevant dimension-one subsets having zero Lebesgue measure. Feng, Lai and Xiong’s bi-Lipschitz embedding result allows geometric sequences to embed in every positive-measure set when the map may distort individual distances within fixed factors. Affine maps are much more rigid.

Against this background, M2, dated September 25, claims the dyadic affine case. M1, dated October 5, extends the construction to every fixed q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1)q∈(0,1). The order of those dates explains the relationship between the two papers: the dyadic construction is a special case of the later, broader statement.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that for every fixed q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1)q∈(0,1) and every η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1)η∈(0,1), there is a compact set Eq,η⊂[0,1]E_{q,\eta}\subset[0,1]Eq,η​⊂[0,1] such that

m(Eq,η)>1−ηm(E_{q,\eta})>1-\etam(Eq,η​)>1−η

and, for every x∈Rx\in\mathbb Rx∈R and s≠0s\ne0s=0, at least one positive integer nnn satisfies

x+sqn∉Eq,η.x+sq^n\notin E_{q,\eta}.x+sqn∈/Eq,η​.

Thus the set misses at least one point from every affine copy of the entire infinite sequence. Both signs of the dilation are included. No restriction is placed on the location of the limiting point xxx.

M2 gives the same conclusion with q=1/2q=1/2q=1/2. The general paper retains nested dyadic grids in its construction, but adapts their resolutions to the chosen geometric ratio. Its parameters, and the resulting avoiding set, may depend on qqq.

The statement concerns avoidance of a complete infinite copy. It does not say that the set avoids long finite geometric patterns. In fact, because its measure is positive, it must contain affine copies of every fixed finite truncation. The translation and scale needed for those finite copies may change as the truncation grows.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The geometric case is a central and longstanding obstruction in the Erdős similarity problem. A method that handles exponentially shrinking gaps would go beyond the earlier spacing criteria and resolve one of the most prominent test cases of the conjecture.

The near-full-measure conclusion makes the phenomenon especially striking. For any prescribed small percentage, the construction claims that one can remove less than that percentage of the unit interval and destroy every affine copy of a chosen infinite geometric sequence. Positive measure guarantees every finite pattern, yet even measure arbitrarily close to one need not guarantee this particular infinite pattern.

The distinction is about exact configurations, not numerical approximation. A set may contain points extremely close to an entire progression without containing the progression itself. Small holes arranged at many scales can exploit that difference.

The probabilistic mechanism also has independent conceptual interest: it controls an uncountable range of translations and dilations using finite random choices and a carefully organized hierarchy. The score reflects this significance if the manuscript claims hold; the full conjecture for arbitrary infinite sets remains outside their stated conclusion.

6. The main idea

Build the holes first

Instead of directly describing a large avoiding set, construct a small open set that intersects every forbidden copy. Its complement inside [0,1][0,1][0,1] is then compact and has large measure.

The first target is normalized: build a one-periodic open set HHH of very small density that meets every x+tGqx+tG_qx+tGq​ with t∈[1,2]t\in[1,2]t∈[1,2]. Periodicity allows translation to be studied on one unit interval. Scaled and reflected copies of such sets, with summable measure budgets, then cover all positive and negative dilation sizes.

Route each point through a finite tree

A naive random selection of tiny intervals gives many opportunities to hit a fixed copy. Its weakness is the number of possible scales: inspecting every possible change on the finest grid may cost more than the random estimates can afford.

The manuscripts instead use a finite ordered tree. Independent binary tables on grid cells route a point to a leaf. At each branch the first successful child is chosen; if all tested children fail, the final child is used by default. A separate random table at the leaf selects membership in the hole set with a small probability ppp. This keeps the expected total density small.

Different edges receive separated windows of sequence indices. The gaps between windows make earlier routing decisions stable under the later, smaller translations, except near a small set of grid boundaries. At the first default on a point’s route, the unused children provide many fresh opportunities for translated sequence points to hit the selected set.

Make the scale count local

The decisive organization concerns which grids a particular group of tests needs. Its index window is chosen long enough relative to its following gap and descendant subtree. The number of possible dilation patterns for that group can then be counted using its own portion of the construction, rather than the finest grid anywhere in the tree.

Independent tests give a rapidly decreasing probability of missing every opportunity. The local scale count is arranged to grow slowly enough for that probability to dominate it. For general qqq, dyadic grid resolutions are chosen comparable to the geometric separation at the relevant indices; the branching number is allowed to depend on the ratio.

Finally, some centers may remain exceptional. Their set has small measure and can be covered by a small open neighborhood. If a copy converges to a center inside this neighborhood, sufficiently late points also lie in it. Adding these neighborhoods repairs the remaining copies without exhausting the measure budget.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The ratio qqq is fixed before the avoiding set is constructed. The paper expressly makes no simultaneous assertion for all ratios. Constants and choices can depend on qqq, especially when its geometric spacing changes substantially.

The full Erdős similarity conjecture concerns every infinite subset of the line, not just a geometric null sequence. That larger problem is not resolved by the theorem stated here.

Affine avoidance also differs from avoidance under more flexible maps. A bi-Lipschitz image may fit even where no affine image does. Likewise, Hausdorff dimension one is weaker than positive Lebesgue measure for this question; earlier dimension results do not supply the present measure conclusion.

The construction is an existence argument using finite random choices and an infinite assembly of scale budgets. It does not provide a simple interval-removal recipe with practical numerical parameters. Any resulting set has no nonempty interval in its interior, since an interval contains small affine copies of the sequence. Its large measure therefore coexists with persistent small-scale gaps.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 supplies the all-ratios theorem, the historical distinctions and the local scale-count mechanism. M2 presents the earlier dyadic construction. Their introductions and normalized hitting-set propositions are the main sources for this explanation.

Chlebík’s linked paper provides a useful primary account of the older spacing criteria. The linked papers on sumsets, large-dimensional avoidance and bi-Lipschitz embeddings explain why several superficially similar partial results leave the fixed geometric affine problem untouched.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The geometric case of the Erdős similarity conjecture (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The dyadic case of the Erdős similarity conjecture (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Schrödinger evolution returns to rough data at the exact threshold
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 080 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

A solution of an evolution equation should approach its initial data as time goes to zero. For smooth data this expectation is usually straightforward. For rough data, convergence in an average norm can hold even when the values at individual points behave badly.

Carleson’s Schrödinger convergence problem asks how much Sobolev regularity guarantees almost-everywhere return to the initial state. Earlier theorems identified the critical regularity in dimensions at least two up to a strict inequality. The question left at the boundary was whether the exact critical exponent also works.

The two manuscripts in family 080 claim that it does: one handles the plane, and the other all higher dimensions. They also specify a common pointwise representative of the evolution, constructed by removing Gaussian regularization uniformly in time on one full-measure spatial set.

2. Background and essential definitions

The free evolution

The free Schrödinger equation is

i∂tu+Δu=0,u(x,0)=f(x),i\partial_tu+\Delta u=0,\qquad u(x,0)=f(x),i∂t​u+Δu=0,u(x,0)=f(x),

where Δ=∑j=1n∂xj2\Delta=\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_{x_j}^2Δ=∑j=1n​∂xj​2​. With the Fourier convention f^(ξ)=∫e−ix⋅ξf(x) dx\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dxf​(ξ)=∫e−ix⋅ξf(x)dx, its formal solution is

u(x,t)=1(2π)n∫Rneix⋅ξ−it∣ξ∣2f^(ξ) dξ.u(x,t)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{ix\cdot\xi-it|\xi|^2}\widehat f(\xi)\,d\xi.u(x,t)=(2π)n1​∫Rn​eix⋅ξ−it∣ξ∣2f​(ξ)dξ.

For general square-integrable fff, the Fourier transform is defined by completion in L2L^2L2. The integral need not be absolutely convergent at each point. This is why the choice of a pointwise representative matters.

The evolution always converges to fff in L2L^2L2 as t→0t\to0t→0. That fact alone does not force convergence at almost every point along all times. Norm convergence can conceal large values moving through smaller spatial sets.

Sobolev regularity as a frequency penalty

The inhomogeneous Sobolev space Hs(Rn)H^s(\mathbb R^n)Hs(Rn) consists of functions satisfying

∥f∥Hs2=1(2π)n∫Rn(1+∣ξ∣2)s∣f^(ξ)∣2 dξ<∞.\|f\|_{H^s}^2=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}(1+|\xi|^2)^s|\widehat f(\xi)|^2\,d\xi<\infty.∥f∥Hs2​=(2π)n1​∫Rn​(1+∣ξ∣2)s∣f​(ξ)∣2dξ<∞.

The exponent sss measures a fractional number of square-integrable derivatives. Larger sss penalizes high frequencies more strongly. For data near frequency NNN, the Sobolev norm contributes roughly the factor NsN^sNs.

The critical exponent in dimensions n≥2n\ge2n≥2 is

sn=n2(n+1).s_n=\frac{n}{2(n+1)}.sn​=2(n+1)n​.

Thus s2=1/3s_2=1/3s2​=1/3, s3=3/8s_3=3/8s3​=3/8, and s4=2/5s_4=2/5s4​=2/5. An estimate that works only for s>sns>s_ns>sn​ does not establish membership at equality, however close sss is allowed to be.

Gaussian regularization and Lebesgue values

For a>0a>0a>0, define

Uaf(x,t)=1(2π)n∫Rneix⋅ξ−it∣ξ∣2−a∣ξ∣2f^(ξ) dξ.U_af(x,t)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{ix\cdot\xi-it|\xi|^2-a|\xi|^2}\widehat f(\xi)\,d\xi.Ua​f(x,t)=(2π)n1​∫Rn​eix⋅ξ−it∣ξ∣2−a∣ξ∣2f​(ξ)dξ.

The Gaussian factor damps high frequencies, making the integral absolutely convergent for L2L^2L2 data. The manuscripts define the desired evolution by taking a↓0a\downarrow0a↓0 first.

At almost every point, a locally integrable function has a Lebesgue value

f∗(x)=lim⁡r↓01∣B(x,r)∣∫B(x,r)f(y) dy.f^*(x)=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac1{|B(x,r)|}\int_{B(x,r)}f(y)\,dy.f∗(x)=r↓0lim​∣B(x,r)∣1​∫B(x,r)​f(y)dy.

Using this representative avoids dependence on arbitrary changes to fff on a null set.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Carleson proved the one-dimensional positive result at s=1/4s=1/4s=1/4, and Dahlberg and Kenig showed that lower regularity cannot work in general. The one-dimensional problem therefore already included its endpoint.

In higher dimensions, Sjölin and Vega obtained convergence for s>1/2s>1/2s>1/2. Restriction and bilinear methods gradually lowered the planar threshold. Among the milestones recalled by the manuscripts are s>2/5s>2/5s>2/5 from Tao’s bilinear restriction theorem and s>3/8s>3/8s>3/8 from Lee’s work.

Bourgain’s counterexample forces the necessary condition s≥n/(2(n+1))s\ge n/(2(n+1))s≥n/(2(n+1)) in dimensions at least two. Crucially, it does not show failure at equality.

Du, Guth and Li proved planar convergence for s>1/3s>1/3s>1/3 in 2017, combining polynomial partitioning and decoupling. Du and Zhang reached s>n/(2(n+1))s>n/(2(n+1))s>n/(2(n+1)) in higher dimensions. Their fractal restriction estimates also influenced related geometric problems.

These theorems and Bourgain’s obstruction determined the threshold except for the equality case. The new papers address that remaining case. They also build on the older question of selecting a representative continuous in time outside one spatial exceptional set, studied by Sjögren and Sjölin at higher regularity.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The endpoint in every dimension at least two

The planar paper treats f∈H1/3(R2)f\in H^{1/3}(\mathbb R^2)f∈H1/3(R2). The higher-dimensional paper treats every fixed n≥3n\ge3n≥3 and f∈Hsn(Rn)f\in H^{s_n}(\mathbb R^n)f∈Hsn​(Rn).

In either case, the manuscript states that there is a full-measure set EfE_fEf​ of spatial points and a representative v(x,t)v(x,t)v(x,t) such that, for each x∈Efx\in E_fx∈Ef​, the function of time is continuous on [0,1)[0,1)[0,1), satisfies v(x,0)=f∗(x)v(x,0)=f^*(x)v(x,0)=f∗(x), and obeys

lim⁡a↓0sup⁡0<t<1∣Uaf(x,t)−v(x,t)∣=0.\lim_{a\downarrow0}\sup_{0<t<1}|U_af(x,t)-v(x,t)|=0.a↓0lim​0<t<1sup​∣Ua​f(x,t)−v(x,t)∣=0.

Consequently the Gaussian limit exists for every real 0<t<10<t<10<t<1 on the same set EfE_fEf​, and

lim⁡t↓0v(x,t)=f∗(x).\lim_{t\downarrow0}v(x,t)=f^*(x).t↓0lim​v(x,t)=f∗(x).

No radial symmetry, compact Fourier support or additional logarithmic strengthening of HsnH^{s_n}Hsn​ is assumed.

The maximal estimate behind the representative

For bounded-frequency data, the papers establish a local maximal estimate of the form

∫B(x0,1)sup⁡0≤t<1∣eitΔf(x)∣ dx≤Cn∥f∥Hsn,\int_{B(x_0,1)}\sup_{0\le t<1}|e^{it\Delta}f(x)|\,dx\le C_n\|f\|_{H^{s_n}},∫B(x0​,1)​0≤t<1sup​∣eitΔf(x)∣dx≤Cn​∥f∥Hsn​​,

uniformly in the center and the frequency cutoff. The output is local L1L^1L1. In particular, the planar paper does not assert the stronger endpoint local L3L^3L3 maximal estimate.

The higher-dimensional manuscript uses specific information-calculus and time-tree ingredients from the planar companion. It supplies further packet estimates in the required dimensions rather than treating the planar conclusion itself as a higher-dimensional theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. If correct, this family completes the Sobolev threshold for almost-everywhere Schrödinger convergence in all dimensions at least two. It reaches equality at the exponent already singled out by the preceding positive results and counterexamples.

Endpoint questions are structurally different from merely improving a decimal exponent. Away from the endpoint, a small positive regularity margin can absorb losses when frequency pieces are summed. At equality that reserve disappears, forcing a method to preserve the precise square-summation structure of the Sobolev norm.

The common representative is also substantive. A separate almost-everywhere statement for each fixed time does not automatically give one spatial set valid for uncountably many times. The claimed uniform Gaussian limit supplies that missing coherence and makes the limiting evolution precise.

6. The main idea

Geometry of high-frequency packets

Schrödinger wave packets travel along tubes in spacetime. Their directions come from the paraboloid (ξ,∣ξ∣2)(\xi,|\xi|^2)(ξ,∣ξ∣2), which records the relation between spatial frequency and temporal oscillation.

To study a time supremum, select a time at each spatial point where the evolution is large. The resulting graph in spacetime carries a measure that reflects ordinary spatial volume. Estimating waves against this measure connects the maximal problem to fractal restriction estimates.

The manuscripts separate transverse interactions, where several packet directions are genuinely independent, from narrow configurations, where directions or positions concentrate near lower-dimensional structures. In transverse regions they claim a definite power saving. Narrow regions require more careful geometry to avoid losing that gain during rescaling.

The planar paper develops a bilinear estimate for smooth packet arrays that remains uniform over the number of scales. The higher-dimensional paper analyzes concentration near polynomial walls, then uses additional curvature tests to organize the relevant portions into approximately affine plates. Estimates in one fewer dimension become applicable after that flattening.

Sum frequencies on one time tree

A high-frequency estimate with an extra factor NεN^\varepsilonNε would prove only Hsn+εH^{s_n+\varepsilon}Hsn​+ε convergence. Reaching HsnH^{s_n}Hsn​ requires removal of that growing loss before the final frequency sum.

The papers use one common selected-time graph for all frequency pieces. A binary tree organizes the time choices, distinguishing a heavier child from a lighter sibling at each split. Spatial localization supplies decay as one moves down the tree, while a weak estimate with output exponent above two supplies a summable advantage for the lighter branches.

The claimed outcome retains a sum of squared frequency contributions, matching the definition of the HsnH^{s_n}Hsn​ norm. A crude sum of their absolute norms would generally impose an extra requirement on the initial data.

Remove regularization simultaneously in time

Once the uniform maximal control is available, smooth approximations can be made close outside suitably small spatial exceptional sets. The paper organizes countably many error envelopes so that the Gaussian approximate identity converges uniformly over the time interval on the remaining full-measure set.

This avoids taking an uncountable intersection of time-dependent full-measure sets. Such an intersection need not have full measure. The order of limits and the common exceptional set are therefore part of the theorem’s construction, not just conventions added afterward.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result concerns the free Euclidean Schrödinger equation. Potentials, nonlinear terms, boundaries and curved spatial manifolds are different settings, with potentially different thresholds and representatives.

The Gaussian parameter tends to zero before the time limit is taken. The statement does not authorize interchanging these limits arbitrarily or identifying the result with every possible pointwise summation prescription without further argument.

The claimed maximal control is local in space and has L1L^1L1 output. Stronger endpoint maximal estimates remain separate questions. Almost-everywhere convergence also permits an exceptional spatial null set and provides no pointwise rate of convergence.

Bourgain’s obstruction below sns_nsn​ explains the sharp regularity threshold for a theorem covering every datum in the Sobolev class. It does not say that every individual function below that threshold must diverge.

8. Sources and further reading

The essential primary comparisons are Bourgain’s necessary condition, Du–Guth–Li’s planar theorem, and Du–Zhang’s higher-dimensional theorem. The two source manuscripts below give the endpoint claims and the exact Gaussian-first representative.

Optional background on Sobolev spaces and Lebesgue points explains the regularity and representative conventions used here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Endpoint convergence for the planar Schrodinger equation (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Endpoint pointwise convergence for the Schrodinger equation in higher dimensions (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Taking the largest disk average without creating too much variation
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 085 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Averaging usually smooths a function. But suppose that at every point we try all possible disk sizes and keep the largest average. Different points may choose completely different radii, so the resulting function is no longer an ordinary convolution. Can that selection create substantially more variation than the original function possessed?

This is a regularity question for the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator, one of the basic tools of analysis. Bounds away from the integrability endpoint have been known for decades. At the endpoint, the usual short argument breaks down, and the geometry of the averaging sets becomes decisive.

Family 085 contains one manuscript. It claims that, for disks centered at the evaluation point in the plane, the integral of the output’s gradient is bounded by an absolute constant times the integral of the input’s gradient. The output itself need not be integrable over the whole plane. Keeping those two conclusions separate is essential to understanding the result.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a locally integrable function f:R2→Rf:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb Rf:R2→R, its centered disk maximal function is

Mf(x)=sup⁡r>01πr2∫B(x,r)∣f(y)∣ dy.Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{\pi r^2}\int_{B(x,r)}|f(y)|\,dy.Mf(x)=r>0sup​πr21​∫B(x,r)​∣f(y)∣dy.

Here B(x,r)B(x,r)B(x,r) is the open disk of radius rrr centered at xxx. Every positive radius is allowed, and the absolute value is taken before averaging. The word centered means that the disk’s center must be the output point; allowing arbitrary disks containing that point defines a different operator.

The Sobolev space W1,1(R2)W^{1,1}(\mathbb R^2)W1,1(R2) consists of globally integrable functions whose first weak derivatives are also globally integrable. A weak derivative is defined by integration by parts against smooth test functions. It allows a notion of gradient for functions that need not be differentiable everywhere in the classical sense.

The quantity

∫R2∣∇f(x)∣ dx\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\nabla f(x)|\,dx∫R2​∣∇f(x)∣dx

measures total first-order variation, with Euclidean length used for the gradient vector. Membership in Wloc1,1W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}Wloc1,1​ requires these integrability properties only on bounded regions.

There is also a larger space, BVBVBV, of functions of bounded variation. Their distributional derivatives may be measures with singular parts, such as mass concentrated on a jump curve. A bound on a derivative measure alone is therefore weaker than proving that the derivative is represented by an integrable function. The manuscript addresses both the size estimate and this regularity distinction.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kinnunen’s 1997 Sobolev theorem established boundedness of the maximal operator on W1,pW^{1,p}W1,p for p>1p>1p>1. A central pointwise comparison bounds the gradient of the maximal function by a maximal function of the input gradient. The strong LpL^pLp maximal inequality then completes the argument.

At p=1p=1p=1, that last step fails: the maximal operator is not strongly bounded on L1L^1L1. Hajłasz and Onninen’s 2004 paper asked whether the gradient estimate could nevertheless survive. Failure of the standard proof did not settle the endpoint question.

One dimension supplied important partial solutions. Tanaka treated the uncentered operator, and Aldaz and Pérez Lázaro obtained the sharp variation constant one with additional regularity conclusions. Kurka’s centered one-dimensional theorem controlled variation by an absolute constant. Intervals have a linear ordering that helps organize their extrema; disks in the plane lack that ordering.

Higher-dimensional results imposed structure on the input or changed the averaging geometry. Radial inputs, which depend only on distance from the origin, and block-decreasing inputs admitted results unavailable for arbitrary functions. Weigt proved variation estimates for dyadic maximal operators and for the uncentered cube operator. Axis-parallel cubes, dyadic cubes and centered disks have different overlap patterns.

Fractional maximal operators introduce a positive power of radius. Endpoint gradient estimates for these operators also advanced, but the positive order supplies a geometric advantage that disappears at order zero. Lahti and Weigt’s conditional regularity theorem explained how a suitable variation bound could yield Sobolev regularity for the centered operator. M1 claims the missing planar centered-disk bound and gives its own argument removing singular derivative mass.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every real-valued f∈W1,1(R2)f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb R^2)f∈W1,1(R2), M1 states that MfMfMf belongs to Wloc1,1(R2)W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2)Wloc1,1​(R2), has a globally integrable weak gradient, and satisfies

∫R2∣∇Mf(x)∣ dx≤C∫R2∣∇f(x)∣ dx,\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\nabla Mf(x)|\,dx\leq C\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\nabla f(x)|\,dx,∫R2​∣∇Mf(x)∣dx≤C∫R2​∣∇f(x)∣dx,

where CCC is an absolute finite constant. No radiality, monotonicity or compact-support hypothesis is imposed. The manuscript does not determine the best constant.

It also states an intermediate signed estimate. For a smooth compactly supported real function ggg, let

Atg(x)=1πt2∫B(x,t)g(y) dy,Sa,bg(x)=sup⁡a≤t≤bAtg(x).A_tg(x)=\frac{1}{\pi t^2}\int_{B(x,t)}g(y)\,dy,\qquad S_{a,b}g(x)=\sup_{a\leq t\leq b}A_tg(x).At​g(x)=πt21​∫B(x,t)​g(y)dy,Sa,b​g(x)=a≤t≤bsup​At​g(x).

These averages retain the sign of ggg. When b/ab/ab/a is a power of two, the claimed gradient bound for Sa,bS_{a,b}Sa,b​ has a constant independent of the number of radius scales between aaa and bbb. A single radius is included.

That uniformity is the bridge to all radii. The signed formulation is also useful when a local mean is subtracted from the input: subtracting a constant changes average values but not their gradients. An estimate available only after replacing the localized function by its absolute value would not preserve the same cancellation.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. This would resolve a major planar case of a longstanding endpoint regularity problem for a foundational operator. It concerns arbitrary Sobolev inputs and the usual centered disks, rather than a symmetry class or an auxiliary averaging geometry.

The statement reveals a difference between controlling a function and controlling its variation. For a nonzero nonnegative compactly supported function, large disks centered far away can still collect its total mass. In the plane this gives a tail comparable from below to a constant times ∣x∣−2|x|^{-2}∣x∣−2, whose integral diverges logarithmically. Thus one cannot expect MfMfMf itself to lie in global L1L^1L1, even for very pleasant inputs.

The gradient can nevertheless be globally integrable. The theorem claims precisely that more selective regularity property. It would show that choosing the best disk at each point does not create unlimited first-order variation.

The score also reflects the remaining scope. This is the plane with centered disks. It does not, as stated, resolve all dimensions, all convex averaging bodies, the optimal constant, or continuity of the map taking an input to the gradient of its maximal function.

6. The main idea

Work with finitely many scales while keeping constants uniform

The proof first considers radii in a finite dyadic band. For each fixed radius, differentiating the average is manageable. The difficulty is that the maximizing radius changes with the center, and summing a separate estimate for every radius scale would accumulate an unacceptable factor.

At an interior maximizing radius, the derivative with respect to radius vanishes. Rotational symmetry supplies another moment identity for a disk. Together, these identities allow cancellation in thin boundary shells, especially when much of the relevant mass is concentrated near one shell point.

The manuscript packages this into a directional estimate: if most gradient mass points into a given cone, then components of the output gradient pointing against that cone can be bounded. Localized error pieces with zero total vector mass become cheaper when observed at a much larger scale.

Give cancellation and changing directions separate budgets

The input gradient is distributed over nested spatial grids using nonnegative tent functions. Scalar positive and negative pieces are paired from fine scales upward. Each cancellation is charged at its scale of origin, with a discount when it is used at coarser scales. The resulting cell costs have a total bounded by the original gradient’s integral.

A second construction tracks vector mass along refinement paths. Its purpose is different: it controls the price of changing the direction used in the local estimate. A direction change creates an endpoint between radius bands; variation of the direction choice across space creates extra terms when integrating by parts.

The manuscript uses a finite-state distribution of directional choices to budget both costs. This avoids pretending that there is one globally suitable direction for a general input, or that selecting a new direction at every scale is free.

Preserve cancellation until the final assembly

Consecutive scales with the same chosen direction form a run. Local estimates are applied to each run and averaged over the possible histories of directional choices. Baseline averages pay for run endpoints.

When the spatially varying history weights are differentiated, their normalization gives a cancellation: derivatives of probabilities in a row sum to zero. The argument subtracts a preceding baseline before taking absolute values. That order matters, because an early absolute value would discard the identity that makes the remaining costs summable.

Finally, approximation and expanding radius bands give a bounded derivative measure for the maximal function. Signed localization, subtraction of local means and Poincaré’s inequality show that this measure has no singular part. It is therefore a genuine integrable weak gradient, not merely a finite measure.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The input is real-valued and belongs to the inhomogeneous space W1,1W^{1,1}W1,1: both it and its weak derivatives are globally integrable. The conclusion gives local Sobolev regularity plus a global gradient bound, not global membership of MfMfMf in W1,1W^{1,1}W1,1.

All averaging sets are Euclidean disks centered at the output point in R2\mathbb R^2R2. Uncentered disks, higher-dimensional balls and other shapes should not be substituted silently. Earlier theorems for cubes or radial inputs remain distinct results.

The estimate asserts boundedness. Continuity of the gradient map under convergence of inputs is an additional question, as illustrated by separate one-dimensional continuity results. Nor does the manuscript claim the sharp numerical value of CCC.

The exposition follows M1’s stated theorem and its multiscale mechanism. It does not assess the proof’s correctness. The main mathematical boundary to retain is the passage from a finite variation measure to an absolutely continuous derivative: both are needed for the claimed endpoint Sobolev conclusion.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s introduction gives the theorem, the signed finite-band estimate and an unusually detailed account of the two separate multiscale constructions. Those are the sources for sections 4 and 6.

The linked papers by Kinnunen and Hajłasz–Onninen establish the original regularity setting and endpoint question. Kurka’s interval theorem, Weigt’s cube theorem and Lahti–Weigt’s conditional result explain three different partial advances without identifying them with the planar centered-disk claim.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An Endpoint Gradient Bound for the Centered Disk Maximal Operator (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Three interacting signals and the trilinear Hilbert transform
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 086 · Real and complex analysis
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

The Hilbert transform compares a function on opposite sides of a point, with a singular weight that emphasizes small distances. Its boundedness is a cornerstone of harmonic analysis. What happens when three different signals are sampled at three different speeds and multiplied before that comparison is made?

For the speeds 1,2,31,2,31,2,3, the resulting operator is

T(f1,f2,f3)(x)=p.v.⁡∫Rf1(x−t)f2(x−2t)f3(x−3t) dtt.T(f_1,f_2,f_3)(x)=\operatorname{p.v.}\int_{\mathbb R} f_1(x-t)f_2(x-2t)f_3(x-3t)\,\frac{dt}{t}.T(f1​,f2​,f3​)(x)=p.v.∫R​f1​(x−t)f2​(x−2t)f3​(x−3t)tdt​.

The family’s single manuscript claims that this trilinear Hilbert transform maps three L3L^3L3 inputs into L1L^1L1. In plain terms, cubic integrability of each input should control the total absolute size of their singular interaction.

The corresponding bilinear theory has been established for decades. Adding a third input is not a routine extension. It allows quadratic oscillations in the inputs to align so that their apparent complexity disappears in the product. The central challenge is to control those alignments simultaneously over arbitrarily many scales.

2. Background and essential definitions

The norm ∥f∥p=(∫∣f∣p)1/p\|f\|_p=(\int |f|^p)^{1/p}∥f∥p​=(∫∣f∣p)1/p measures a function’s size in LpL^pLp. Hölder’s inequality suggests the exponent relation

13+13+13=1.\frac13+\frac13+\frac13=1.31​+31​+31​=1.

Indeed, a pointwise product of three L3L^3L3 functions belongs to L1L^1L1. But the transform averages shifted products over a singular measure dt/tdt/tdt/t, and ordinary Hölder alone does not control this additional integration.

The notation p.v.⁡\operatorname{p.v.}p.v. means symmetric principal value: remove the interval (−ε,ε)(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)(−ε,ε), integrate, and let ε\varepsilonε decrease to zero. The starting inputs are Schwartz functions, meaning smooth functions that, together with all derivatives, decay faster than any power. For these inputs the symmetric cancellation handles the singularity, and rapid decay handles the tails.

A phase is a complex oscillation of absolute value one, such as e2πiQ(x)e^{2\pi iQ(x)}e2πiQ(x). Linear phases correspond to individual Fourier frequencies. Quadratic phases have Q(x)=ax2+bx+cQ(x)=ax^2+bx+cQ(x)=ax2+bx+c, so their local frequency changes with position.

A useful way to study the output norm is to pair the transform with a bounded test function f0f_0f0​. The resulting integral contains four factors sampled along an arithmetic progression: after reversing the sign of the integration variable, their arguments are x,x+t,x+2t,x+3tx,x+t,x+2t,x+3tx,x+t,x+2t,x+3t. This four-term structure explains why quadratic behavior enters.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The classical linear Hilbert transform exploits the cancellation of its odd kernel. The bilinear transform introduced interactions between two shifted functions and required much more elaborate time-frequency analysis. Lacey and Thiele’s papers Lᵖ estimates on the bilinear Hilbert transform for 2 < p < ∞ (1997) and On Calderón’s conjecture (1999) established the landmark bilinear results.

In a time-frequency argument, a function is decomposed into pieces localized in both space and frequency. For the trilinear operator, however, linear frequency localization does not fully capture the persistent quadratic patterns. The progression identity underlying these patterns is discussed in the next section.

Tao’s Cancellation for the multilinear Hilbert transform made progress on finite truncations. The elementary estimate grows logarithmically with the ratio of the largest and smallest scales. Tao obtained a sublogarithmic improvement, demonstrating nontrivial cancellation and linking the problem to higher-order uniformity. A bound that still grows with the scale range does not give the uniform estimate claimed here.

Another approach changes the geometry of the sampling paths. Hu and Lie’s work on the curved trilinear Hilbert transform uses curvature as a source of oscillation. Straight arithmetic-progression paths retain degeneracies absent from those curved problems. The new manuscript treats the fixed straight-line operator displayed above.

Its principal structural input is the degree-two case of Leng, Sah and Sawhney’s quantitative inverse theorem for Gowers norms. Such inverse theorems turn an unexpectedly large multilinear average into evidence of correlation with structured oscillations. M1 credits that result while emphasizing that detecting structure at one scale does not itself control the sum over scales.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that an absolute finite constant CCC satisfies

∥T(f1,f2,f3)∥L1(R)≤C∏j=13∥fj∥L3(R)\|T(f_1,f_2,f_3)\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}\leq C\prod_{j=1}^{3}\|f_j\|_{L^3(\mathbb R)}∥T(f1​,f2​,f3​)∥L1(R)​≤Cj=1∏3​∥fj​∥L3(R)​

for all complex Schwartz inputs. It follows that the operator has a unique bounded trilinear extension from L3×L3×L3L^3\times L^3\times L^3L3×L3×L3 to L1L^1L1.

The displayed slopes are fixed at 1,2,31,2,31,2,3. The manuscript calls this a resolution of that case of the standard trilinear Hilbert transform conjecture. It does not state the entire conjectured range of input and output exponents, or a theorem uniform over arbitrary slope configurations.

Why is quadratic structure relevant? Let

(c0,c1,c2,c3)=(−1,3,−3,1).(c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3)=(-1,3,-3,1).(c0​,c1​,c2​,c3​)=(−1,3,−3,1).

For each a=0,1,2a=0,1,2a=0,1,2, one has

∑j=03cj(x+jt)a=0.\sum_{j=0}^{3}c_j(x+jt)^a=0.j=0∑3​cj​(x+jt)a=0.

This is the vanishing of a third finite difference on a polynomial of degree at most two. Consequently, four appropriately matched quadratic phases can multiply to one along the progression. Highly oscillatory individual factors may thus create a nonoscillatory product. A successful estimate must organize this possibility rather than assume that oscillation automatically produces cancellation.

The bounded extension is a norm statement. The digest does not replace it with a stronger unquoted assertion about almost-everywhere convergence of every hard truncation for arbitrary rough inputs.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Boundedness of the straight trilinear Hilbert transform is a central problem in multilinear harmonic analysis. The symmetric L3L^3L3 input case is a natural scale-balanced target, and a uniform estimate there would overcome a barrier not addressed by the bilinear theory or by curved analogues.

The result would also strengthen the connection between additive combinatorics and singular integrals. Higher-order uniformity was developed to recognize structured patterns in arithmetic progressions. Here the same kind of structure must be tracked through a continuous integral, with infinitely many spatial and frequency scales.

There is a substantial difference between finding a structured explanation for one large local average and preventing many such explanations from accumulating without bound.
