The manuscript’s proposed contribution lies largely in this second step: it combines quantitative structure detection with projection, localization and counting arguments whose cost does not grow with the total depth of the decomposition.

The importance rating concerns that potential advance if the stated theorem is correct. It also leaves room for the broader conjecture: a single exponent triple for one slope configuration is a major result without being the complete multilinear theory.

6. The main idea

Replace the singular integral by local progression forms

The proof decomposes the integral into pieces associated with dyadic intervals, whose lengths differ by powers of two. Each local piece sees four progression coordinates inside a common interval and has cancellation in each anchored coordinate.

For a finite collection spanning NNN scales, let CNC_NCN​ stand for the best constant in an appropriate local estimate. An elementary bound makes CNC_NCN​ finite but allows it to grow with NNN. The aim is to establish an inequality of the form

CN≤A+θCN,0<θ<1,C_N\leq A+\theta C_N,\qquad 0<\theta<1,CN​≤A+θCN​,0<θ<1,

with AAA and θ\thetaθ independent of NNN. Rearranging then gives a uniform bound. This is called absorption: an error controlled by a sufficiently small fraction of the quantity being estimated can be moved to the other side.

Detect quadratic structure without losing track of it

The inverse theorem identifies quadratic structure when a local progression average is too large. M1 develops continuous local versions of that input and decomposes bounded functions into structured approximations and remainders.

Those approximations change as one passes to smaller intervals. Repeatedly projecting onto new structured spaces could introduce a loss at every generation. The manuscript therefore assigns additional orthogonal coordinates that retain information about each selected component, and claims a compression bound for products of inherited projections. Its cost depends on controlled budgets rather than the full depth of the spatial tree.

The construction also uses two different approximation accuracies. Delaying some of the more accurate fits preserves compatibility with earlier, coarser choices. This is a way to prevent newly detected structure from forcing a complete restart at every scale.

Separate coherent contributions from errors

The quadratic curvature of the four arguments is localized jointly. Matched components receive fixed mode expansions, and graphs of frequency relationships separate persistent coherent pieces from errors that can be summed by square-energy estimates.

The remaining coherent pieces are tested along progression scales. A counting estimate gives an additional positive-power gain when the relevant tests have small density. The argument retains cancellation at all four anchors; discarding one of these conditions would change the estimate being used.

Finally, parameter choices balance the gains against localization and approximation losses. The small-density gains and compressed projection costs supply the small coefficient in the absorption inequality. The proof’s organizing principle is not that every local contribution is tiny, but that repeated significant contributions must obey a common structural budget.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The operator is one-dimensional in its input variable, with three scalar complex-valued inputs, fixed shifts x−t,x−2t,x−3tx-t,x-2t,x-3tx−t,x−2t,x−3t, and output in L1L^1L1. It should not be confused with the two-dimensional triangular Hilbert transform in family 082, despite the related names and multilinear cancellation problems.

The full trilinear conjecture asks for a wider exponent range. The theorem presented here gives the 3,3,33,3,33,3,3 case. Further maximal, variation, weighted or slope-uniform estimates require their own statements and are not inferred from bounded extension by density.

Curved transforms are also separate operators. Curvature can create useful oscillation; the straight-line setting here instead permits exact quadratic phase cancellation. That distinction is part of the difficulty, not a cosmetic change in notation.

The manuscript relies on a quantitative inverse theorem as an external structural input and supplies the claimed continuous organization across scales. This digest reports that dependency and strategy without auditing the proof or treating the inverse theorem alone as a proof of the transform estimate.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s first section states the operator, norm bound and limitations. Its local-form reduction explains the uniform-in-depth absorption target, while the introduction outlines the projection compression, joint curvature localization and scale-counting steps.

The linked papers by Tao and by Leng–Sah–Sawhney provide the primary higher-order-uniformity background. Hu–Lie’s curved-transform paper states a broader conjectural context and explains why curved and straight configurations should be distinguished. The two Lacey–Thiele papers named above are the historical bilinear starting point.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An L3 bound for the trilinear Hilbert transform (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How small can a convex body and its polar be together
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 087 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

A long thin convex body has small extent in some directions and large extent in others. Its polar reverses that relationship: directions in which the original body is narrow become directions in which the polar can extend far. Their volume product therefore measures shape in a way that ordinary volume does not.

Mahler’s problem asks how small this product can be. There are two versions. Among centrally symmetric bodies, cubes and their relatives are the proposed minimizers. Among arbitrary convex bodies, the proposed minimizers are simplices, the higher-dimensional analogues of triangles and tetrahedra.

This family contains three manuscripts. Two claim the sharp inequalities and complete equality classifications in every dimension. The third claims a stronger geometric embedding statement for the product of a symmetric body with its polar, viewed as a region in position–momentum space. Functional inequalities connect the same questions to convex functions and probability densities.

2. Background and essential definitions

A convex body K⊂RnK\subset\mathbb R^nK⊂Rn is compact, has nonempty interior, and contains the segment between any two of its points. Write ∣K∣|K|∣K∣ for its nnn-dimensional volume. If zero lies in its interior, its polar is

K∘={y:⟨x,y⟩≤1 for every x∈K}.K^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\text{ for every }x\in K\}.K∘={y:⟨x,y⟩≤1 for every x∈K}.

For an origin-symmetric body, K=−KK=-KK=−K, the product ∣K∣∣K∘∣|K||K^\circ|∣K∣∣K∘∣ is unchanged by an invertible linear map: the two volumes acquire reciprocal determinant factors.

For a body without a prescribed center, polarity depends on where the origin is placed. The Santaló point s(K)s(K)s(K) is the unique interior point minimizing the polar volume. The affine-invariant product is

P(K)=∣K∣ ∣(K−s(K))∘∣.P(K)=|K|\,|(K-s(K))^\circ|.P(K)=∣K∣∣(K−s(K))∘∣.

A simplex is the convex hull of n+1n+1n+1 affinely independent points. The symmetric candidate class is larger. Hanner polytopes start with centered intervals and are built recursively by taking Cartesian products or convex hulls of two bodies placed in complementary coordinate subspaces. Cubes and cross-polytopes are examples, but mixed constructions also occur.

For a concrete normalization, the cube [−1,1]n[-1,1]^n[−1,1]n has volume 2n2^n2n. Its polar is the cross-polytope {y:∑i∣yi∣≤1}\{y:\sum_i|y_i|\leq1\}{y:∑i​∣yi​∣≤1}, of volume 2n/n!2^n/n!2n/n!. Their product is 4n/n!4^n/n!4n/n!, the symmetric conjecture’s exact target.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Mahler’s work in the 1930s established the planar setting and connected volume products to the geometry of numbers. In the general planar problem, Meyer later completed the equality classification for arbitrary convex bodies: triangles are the minimizers.

Higher-dimensional sharp results were known under additional structure. Saint-Raymond proved the symmetric inequality for unconditional bodies, those unchanged by independently reversing coordinate signs. Meyer and Reisner identified the Hanner equality cases in that class. Zonoids, obtained as limits of sums of segments, also admitted the sharp symmetric inequality, with parallelotopes as their equality cases.

Iriyeh and Shibata proved the three-dimensional symmetric theorem. A 2026 preprint by Chen, Li, Xi and Xu treats the general three-dimensional problem as well. In other dimensions, shadow-system methods gave sharp results for polytopes with few vertices, and local theorems showed that simplices or Hanner bodies could not be improved by nearby perturbations. Local minimality is not a global classification.

A different line obtained the right exponential order without the exact constant. Bourgain and Milman’s reverse Santaló theorem was fundamental here. Kuperberg’s Gauss-linking approach, and complex-analytic work by Nazarov and others, developed additional methods. These estimates did not provide the sharp constants claimed in M1 and M2.

Symplectic geometry supplied another connection. Artstein-Avidan, Karasev and Ostrover computed a different capacity of symmetric polar products and related a proposed volume–capacity inequality to Mahler’s conjecture. Particular polar products were known to contain large symplectic balls. M3 claims the unrestricted symmetric-body version. It also explicitly notes that the unrestricted Viterbo volume–capacity conjecture was disproved by Haim-Kislev and Ostrover; the special polar-product theorem is not a revival of that general conjecture.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The symmetric and general volume products

M1 states that every origin-symmetric convex body in every dimension n≥1n\geq1n≥1 satisfies

∣K∣∣K∘∣≥4nn!,|K||K^\circ|\geq\frac{4^n}{n!},∣K∣∣K∘∣≥n!4n​,

with equality exactly for invertible linear images of Hanner polytopes.

M2 states that every convex body satisfies

P(K)≥(n+1)n+1(n!)2,P(K)\geq\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2},P(K)≥(n!)2(n+1)n+1​,

with equality exactly for simplices. No smoothness or symmetry is assumed. Because the Santaló point minimizes the polar volume, the same lower bound holds when polarity is taken about any interior point.

These are separate sharp statements. The general lower constant is smaller than the symmetric one in dimensions at least two, so the general theorem alone does not prove the sharp symmetric theorem.

Functional consequences

For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function φ\varphiφ, define its convex conjugate by

φ∗(y)=sup⁡x{⟨x,y⟩−φ(x)}.\varphi^*(y)=\sup_x\{\langle x,y\rangle-\varphi(x)\}.φ∗(y)=xsup​{⟨x,y⟩−φ(x)}.

“Proper” excludes an identically infinite function and values of negative infinity; positive infinity is allowed to restrict the support. The function e−φe^{-\varphi}e−φ is log-concave. Assuming its integral is finite and positive, the manuscripts claim

(∫e−φ)(∫e−φ∗)≥{4n,φ is even,en,φ is arbitrary.\left(\int e^{-\varphi}\right)\left(\int e^{-\varphi^*}\right)\geq\begin{cases}4^n,&\varphi\text{ is even},\\e^n,&\varphi\text{ is arbitrary}.\end{cases}(∫e−φ)(∫e−φ∗)≥{4n,en,​φ is even,φ is arbitrary.​

The second integral may be infinite. These consequences use earlier implications of Fradelizi and Meyer together with the geometric inequalities in all dimensions, not merely the dimension of the function.

Symplectic balls in polar products

M3 places KKK in position coordinates qqq and K∘K^\circK∘ in momentum coordinates ppp, with symplectic form ω0=∑jdqj∧dpj\omega_0=\sum_jdq_j\wedge dp_jω0​=∑j​dqj​∧dpj​. A symplectic embedding preserves this form, and hence volume, but is more constrained than an arbitrary volume-preserving map.

The standard ball of capacity ccc is

B2n(c)={(q,p):π(∣q∣2+∣p∣2)<c}.B^{2n}(c)=\{(q,p):\pi(|q|^2+|p|^2)<c\}.B2n(c)={(q,p):π(∣q∣2+∣p∣2)<c}.

The Gromov width is the supremum of capacities of balls that admit such embeddings into a domain. M3 claims, for every symmetric KKK and n≥2n\geq2n≥2,

cG(int⁡K×int⁡K∘)=4.c_G(\operatorname{int}K\times\operatorname{int}K^\circ)=4.cG​(intK×intK∘)=4.

It constructs embeddings for every c<4c<4c<4; it does not require an embedding at the supremum. Since the ball’s volume is cn/n!c^n/n!cn/n!, volume preservation and passage to the limit yield the symmetric Mahler inequality. M3 does not classify volume-product equality cases; that is M1’s separate contribution.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Sharp Mahler inequalities are central extremal problems in convex geometry. The claimed results would determine both the optimal constants and all minimizing shapes in arbitrary dimension, replacing broad asymptotic bounds and special-class theorems with exact global answers.

The equality classifications carry mathematical content beyond the numerical bounds. The general minimizer is a simplex, but the symmetric minimizers form a recursive family with different combinatorial shapes. Identifying all of them requires more than checking that a cube has the right product.

The symplectic statement adds a different kind of information. Having enough volume is ordinarily insufficient to fit a symplectic ball, because nonsqueezing imposes additional restrictions. A matching width theorem says that every symmetric polar product has a particular embedding capacity, regardless of corners, smoothness or strict convexity.

The functional consequences extend the significance from bodies to log-concave functions. Additional entropy–transport consequences in M1 and M2 concern distributions of gradients of convex potentials. Their hypotheses include essential continuity of the relevant log-concave densities; they are not unrestricted statements about every probability measure. The rating reflects the breadth of these claims, not an independent assessment of their proofs.

6. The main idea

Symmetry, a conformal lens, and missing volume

M1 first approximates a symmetric body by an intersection of finitely many symmetric strips. A special conformal map from a disk to a planar lens has a carefully chosen boundary distribution: a boundary coordinate becomes uniform.

This analytic construction assigns feasible simplices inside the polar body to points of the original body. A holomorphic zero-counting mass estimate gives a lower bound for an integral of their volumes. Since the simplices lie inside the polar, their total contribution cannot exceed the body–polar volume product. The normalization yields the sharp constant.

For equality, the integrated missing volume must disappear. The manuscript turns that vanishing deficit into a metric property of the associated normed space: triples admit points that simultaneously split pairwise distances additively. A classical classification of the corresponding ball-intersection structure then identifies the Hanner bodies.

General bodies, dual cones, and Gaussian projections

M2 lifts a convex body to a cone in one higher dimension. The volume-product inequality becomes a lower bound for a product of Laplace integrals over dual cones.

Nearest-point projections of biased Gaussian vectors supply paired maps into these cones. Their Jacobians, together with change of variables and entropy inequalities, reduce the desired estimate to a matrix problem. The projection derivatives at different layers need not commute, so estimating each layer independently would lose the information needed for the sharp bound.

The argument compares the whole family to a linear Gaussian matrix field, separates higher-order Gaussian components, and uses scalar inequalities on pairs of eigenvalues to control the remaining errors. In the claimed equality analysis, the matrices must commute and the cone splits into one-dimensional rays. A bounded section of that cone is a simplex.

Convert holomorphic vanishing into actual ball embeddings

M3 also uses the conformal lens, but pursues an embedding rather than a volume integral. High powers of a holomorphic coordinate create a zero of large order. A smoothing and deformation argument turns that order into a symplectic ball of a controlled capacity.

A separate uniform estimate places the constructed domain inside a product of the body and a scaled polar. The two scales have a ratio tending to four. Rescaling therefore fits every ball of capacity strictly below four into the original polar product. Approximation treats nonsmooth bodies, while a supporting-cylinder argument and nonsqueezing give the matching upper bound.

The three routes are related, but M3 does not assume the symmetric volume theorem or its equality classification. Its embedding claim is presented as an independent route to the numerical symmetric bound.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All bodies are full-dimensional compact convex sets. The symmetric statements require symmetry about the origin used for polarity. The general statement uses the Santaló point; replacing it with a centroid without explanation would change the normalization of the problem.

The equality descriptions belong to the geometric inequalities. They should not be transferred automatically to convex potentials in the functional statements, whose extremizers have a different formulation.

The Gromov width is a supremum. Embeddings below capacity four suffice, and no boundary regularity is imposed on KKK. The theorem concerns a specific position–momentum product, not every convex region in symplectic space, and does not assert that all symplectic capacities agree there.

Quantitative stability asks how close a nearly minimizing body must be to an extremizer. Efficient ways to construct the symplectic embeddings are another distinct issue. Neither follows simply from the sharp constants and qualitative equality statements summarized here.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 covers the symmetric inequality, Hanner equality cases and even functional consequences. M2 treats the general inequality, simplex equality and general functional consequences. M3 supplies the polar-product width theorem and its volume deduction.

The linked low-dimensional papers and Kuperberg’s work give primary historical landmarks. Fradelizi and Meyer’s Some functional inverse Santaló inequalities supplies the earlier geometric-to-functional implications explicitly used by the manuscripts. Klartag’s Isotropic constants and Mahler volumes develops the cone–Laplace viewpoint used in M2.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The symmetric Mahler conjecture and its equality cases (September 22, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Mahler Conjecture for General Convex Bodies (September 22, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Symplectic Balls in Symmetric Polar Products (September 22, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Representing planar and bounded-treewidth distances by cuts
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 089 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

A road network gives a distance between locations: the length of the shortest route connecting them. Can those distances be represented approximately as sums of simple yes-or-no separations? Each separation divides the vertices into two groups and charges a pair only when its endpoints fall on opposite sides.

Such a representation is an embedding into L1L^1L1, or a space with a taxicab-type distance. It is useful because cuts are easier to organize than arbitrary shortest paths, and because the same geometry measures the gap between routing many simultaneous demands and the bottlenecks detected by cuts.

The family contains two manuscripts. M1 claims one universal distortion bound for every finite planar graph with positive edge lengths. M2 claims a bound for every fixed treewidth, independent of graph size and edge-length ratios. Together they address two major cases of the Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture, usually abbreviated GNRS.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a finite connected undirected graph GGG with positive edge lengths, let dG(u,v)d_G(u,v)dG​(u,v) be the shortest-path distance. An embedding FFF into L1L^1L1 has distortion at most CCC if, after a common rescaling,

dG(u,v)≤∥F(u)−F(v)∥1≤C dG(u,v)d_G(u,v)\leq\|F(u)-F(v)\|_1\leq C\,d_G(u,v)dG​(u,v)≤∥F(u)−F(v)∥1​≤CdG​(u,v)

for every pair. No distance shrinks, and none stretches by more than CCC. An L1L^1L1 distance is the integral of an absolute difference; in finite-dimensional ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​, it is the sum of absolute coordinate differences.

A cut is a subset SSS of the vertices, with associated distance

δS(u,v)=∣1S(u)−1S(v)∣.\delta_S(u,v)=|\mathbf1_S(u)-\mathbf1_S(v)|.δS​(u,v)=∣1S​(u)−1S​(v)∣.

This is one when the cut separates the pair and zero otherwise. Every finite L1L^1L1 metric is a nonnegative combination of these cut distances:

D(u,v)=∑S⊆VwSδS(u,v),wS≥0.D(u,v)=\sum_{S\subseteq V}w_S\delta_S(u,v),\qquad w_S\geq0.D(u,v)=S⊆V∑​wS​δS​(u,v),wS​≥0.

A planar graph can be drawn without crossing edges. Bounded treewidth is a different condition. A tree decomposition arranges small vertex sets, called bags, on a tree: every edge lies in a bag, and the bags containing any fixed vertex form a connected subtree. If bags have at most kkk vertices, the decomposition has width at most k−1k-1k−1. This measures how well the graph can be organized through small separators.

The two classes are not interchangeable. Large planar grids have unbounded treewidth, while bounded-treewidth graphs need not be planar.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Linial, London and Rabinovich’s 1995 paper, and independent work by Aumann and Rabani, connected metric embeddings to approximate multicommodity flow–cut theorems. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair’s Cuts, trees and ℓ₁-embeddings of graphs formulated the broader minor-closed picture and established important special cases.

For planar metrics, Rao obtained distortion of order log⁡n\sqrt{\log n}logn​ for nnn vertices by passing through Euclidean space. That intermediate target has a limitation: even some series-parallel metrics require distortion growing like log⁡n\sqrt{\log n}logn​ into Euclidean space. A constant L1L^1L1 result therefore needs a route that uses the greater flexibility of cut geometry.

Constant distortion was already known for series-parallel graphs, with optimal constant two, and for planar graphs of fixed outerplanarity. Other results preserved only selected terminal distances, such as pairs on one face, or assumed a nonpositive-curvature realization. Those are substantial partial solutions but do not preserve every pair in every planar graph.

For treewidth, the width-two case was known. Bounded pathwidth, where bags lie on a path rather than a branching tree, also admitted uniform bounds. Random embeddings into dominating trees helped in that setting, but cannot give a uniform bound for all bounded-treewidth graphs: some series-parallel metrics already force logarithmic expected distortion into trees.

Chlamtáč, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra’s local-consistency framework supplied compatible local cut distributions and a transport theorem used in M2. Earlier approximation algorithms based on stronger relaxations contain additional consistency information; their performance does not automatically imply a constant distortion bound for the ordinary metric embedding problem.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that a finite universal constant CCC works for every finite connected planar graph and every assignment of strictly positive real edge lengths. The embedding preserves all vertex-pair distances within that factor. The bound is independent of vertex count, diameter and the ratio of largest to smallest positive distances.

M2 states that for each integer k≥2k\geq2k≥2, a finite constant CkC_kCk​ works for every graph admitting bags of cardinality at most kkk. It is independent of the number of bags, their tree’s depth and all edge-length ratios. The target can be finite-dimensional real ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​. The manuscript establishes existence of CkC_kCk​, without an explicit estimate for its dependence on kkk.

A flow consequence explains the relevance of these constants. Give edges capacities and vertex pairs nonnegative demands. Let λ∗\lambda_*λ∗​ be the largest common factor by which all demands can be routed simultaneously, allowing flows to split. Let ϕ∗\phi_*ϕ∗​ be the smallest ratio of crossing capacity to separated demand over eligible cuts. Necessarily λ∗≤ϕ∗\lambda_*\leq\phi_*λ∗​≤ϕ∗​. The claimed embeddings, through the established flow–cut equivalence, give

λ∗≤ϕ∗≤Cλ∗\lambda_*\leq\phi_*\leq C\lambda_*λ∗​≤ϕ∗​≤Cλ∗​

for planar graphs, and the same statement with CkC_kCk​ for bounded bag size, whenever λ∗>0\lambda_*>0λ∗​>0.

Using the excluded-planar-minor theorem, M2 also yields a uniform bound for graphs excluding any fixed planar graph as a minor. Combining both manuscripts with a reduction of Lee and Sidiropoulos gives bounds for their fixed-parameter almost-embeddable families. These roughly consist of a bounded-genus part with bounded-width attachments and boundedly many extra vertices. General gluing along larger cliques remains outside the conclusion.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Constant distortion for all planar graph metrics is a central metric-embedding problem with direct consequences for network routing and cut relaxations. Removing every dependence on graph size and the number of distance scales would be a qualitative improvement over a slowly growing logarithmic bound.

The bounded-treewidth result matters for a different reason: it permits arbitrary branching in the decomposition. A graph can be locally organized by small bags while still having a long, complicated global structure. The claimed constant depends only on bag size, not on how many such pieces must be coordinated.

These results also clarify the right geometric target. A network need not be well represented by one tree, or even by a distribution of dominating trees, to admit a good combination of cuts. Cut metrics allow overlapping separations that do not have to arise from one hierarchical tree geometry.

The score reflects the two major cases and their consequences, while preserving the remaining gap to full GNRS. The manuscripts do not state that every proper minor-closed family has now been handled, nor do they determine the optimal universal planar constant.

6. The main idea

Planar graphs: change cuts without losing the upper bound

M1 realizes a planar graph as vertical columns with switches at selected heights. Height represents distance from a chosen root, and the planar drawing supplies a circular order in which links do not cross. This representation preserves the graph metric.

For each cut label, active points on a column form an upper interval. The measure of labels changing along a vertical segment is controlled by its length, and switches preserve membership. Consequently every path controls the resulting cut distance. This invariant supplies the upper distortion bound even after many updates.

Obtaining lower bounds requires two systems of cuts. The first tries local changes that separate a pair at its natural distance scale. Connected-component refinement can itself certify separation. Pairs that survive both mechanisms have a restricted geometric arrangement near short paths, providing a packing bound specifically for the remaining update sites; the ambient planar metric need not have a uniform packing bound.

The second system uses the circular order to distinguish the two arcs between column indices. A transverse coordinate separates cases where an ordinary distance-like field has equal values on opposite arcs. Local formulas are interpolated so that they agree at their interfaces.

Updates are scheduled at widely separated scales. The probability that coarse changes disrupt a useful chart has a summable bound, and the total movement at later fine scales is too small to erase all separation already gained. Averaging finitely many interleaved schedules covers every pair distance.

Bounded treewidth: preserve local laws and transport separation

M2 assigns a distribution of binary cut labels to each bag. Neighboring distributions agree on their intersection, so they can be glued along the decomposition tree into a global cut law. This consistency gives exact local marginals but does not alone ensure that distant vertices are separated.

The construction uses real-valued functions whose threshold cuts generate these laws. Pairs of functions are updated in opposite directions while preserving their combined cut distribution on the current bag. A quadratic invariant controls their Lipschitz constants after arbitrarily many updates, preventing a cost proportional to tree depth.

Some pairs of functions are temporarily reserved, remaining unchanged along a path of bags. Their common cut measure transports uncertainty from a launch bag to a remote vertex through a bounded-state Markov argument. The number of states depends on bag size, not path length.

One schedule handles pairs sharing a bag; another retains selected anchors across significant distance changes. A compactness argument shows that a pair with arbitrarily poor separation would force a younger protected anchor beyond the youngest one already surviving toward an endpoint, a contradiction. This establishes a positive uniform lower factor, though without an explicit numerical formula for it.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The graphs are finite, connected and undirected, with strictly positive real edge lengths. The routing consequence concerns fractional concurrent flow with arbitrary nonnegative pair demands. It does not assert exact integral routing or equality of every flow and cut optimum.

The constants are uniform within the stated classes. In M2 they may depend on kkk, where kkk is bag cardinality and the treewidth bound is k−1k-1k−1. This indexing distinction avoids shifting the claim by one.

A finite-dimensional target exists, but the statements are not low-dimensional embedding theorems. A cut representation can use many coordinates. For rational edge lengths, M2 combines its existence theorem with earlier algorithms to obtain fixed-parameter approximation consequences; the new existence proof itself does not supply a sharp practical distortion constant.

The full GNRS conjecture additionally requires control under more general clique sums. Gluing pieces at a single vertex is not the same as gluing along larger complete subgraphs. That remaining issue is explicitly retained in the manuscripts.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives the planar column construction, its two cut systems and the fixed almost-embeddable consequence. M2 gives consistent bag laws, reserved threshold functions, the compactness argument and the bounded-treewidth statement.

The linked foundational papers explain the flow–cut equivalence and local-consistency framework. Lee and Sidiropoulos’s On the geometry of graphs with a forbidden minor is the primary source for the structural reduction used to combine the two claims.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Planar Graph Metrics Embed into L1 with Constant Distortion (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, L1 Embeddings of Graphs of Bounded Treewidth (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The smallest and unexpectedly large bodies made from shadows
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 088 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Look at a solid object from every direction and measure the area of each shadow. Those directional measurements can themselves describe a new convex body, called the projection body. How large or small can this new body be compared with the original?

The normalization is chosen so that stretching or shearing the original object does not change the answer. Consequently the problem is about affine shape, rather than size or orientation. Ellipsoids are the candidates for the smallest normalized projection volume. Simplices were proposed as the largest.

The two manuscripts in family 088 address these opposite ends. M1 claims that ellipsoids are exactly the minimizers in every dimension at least four, completing the dimensions beyond a separately established three-dimensional theorem. M2 gives a simple product construction exceeding the simplex benchmark in dimension twenty. The latter is an additional explicit counterexample: earlier work had already disproved the unrestricted simplex-maximum conjecture.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a compact convex set LLL, its support function is

hL(u)=max⁡x∈L⟨u,x⟩.h_L(u)=\max_{x\in L}\langle u,x\rangle.hL​(u)=x∈Lmax​⟨u,x⟩.

For a unit vector uuu, this records how far the set extends in the direction uuu. A convex body is compact and convex with nonempty interior.

The projection body ΠK\Pi KΠK of a convex body K⊂RnK\subset\mathbb R^nK⊂Rn is defined by

hΠK(u)=vol⁡n−1(proj⁡u⊥K).h_{\Pi K}(u)=\operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(\operatorname{proj}_{u^\perp}K).hΠK​(u)=voln−1​(proju⊥​K).

The right side is the volume of the orthogonal shadow on the hyperplane perpendicular to uuu. Opposite directions give the same shadow, so ΠK\Pi KΠK is symmetric about the origin even when KKK is not.

The quantity of interest is

Rn(K)=∣ΠK∣∣K∣n−1.R_n(K)=\frac{|\Pi K|}{|K|^{n-1}}.Rn​(K)=∣K∣n−1∣ΠK∣​.

If KKK is dilated by a factor aaa, each shadow scales by an−1a^{n-1}an−1, and the numerator scales by an(n−1)a^{n(n-1)}an(n−1). The denominator scales by the same factor. More generally, the identity

Π(TK)=∣det⁡T∣ T−TΠK\Pi(TK)=|\det T|\,T^{-\mathsf T}\Pi KΠ(TK)=∣detT∣T−TΠK

makes RnR_nRn​ invariant under every invertible linear map. Translation also leaves it unchanged.

Write κj\kappa_jκj​ for the volume of the Euclidean unit ball in dimension jjj. The projection body of the unit ball in Rn\mathbb R^nRn is a ball of radius κn−1\kappa_{n-1}κn−1​, giving

Rn(B2n)=κn−1,nκn,2−n.R_n(B_2^n)=\kappa_{n-1}^{,n}\kappa_n^{,2-n}.Rn​(B2n​)=κn−1,n​κn,2−n​.

Every ellipsoid has the same value by affine invariance.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Petty developed the projection-body framework and proposed the minimum problem. A related classical theorem also bears his name, but involves the polar of the projection body. Taking a polar changes the functional, so that established inequality does not settle the unpolarized minimum discussed here.

One approach studies repeated projection bodies. A class-reduction inequality shows that applying Π\PiΠ does not increase the normalized functional. This directs attention to bodies related by homothety to their second projection body. Saroglou and Zvavitch proved a local minimum theorem under a closeness condition on surface-area densities. Ivaki’s local uniqueness theorem established rigidity near the ball for an associated second-projection equation. Such local results do not rule out a distant global minimizer.

More recently, Chen, Feng, Li, Xi and Xu proved the unrestricted three-dimensional minimum, including ellipsoid equality. Mielke-Sulz’s 2026 manuscript treats bodies of revolution in every dimension at least three. M1 claims arbitrary bodies in the remaining dimensions n≥4n\geq4n≥4, without using the three-dimensional theorem in that proof.

At the upper end, Brannen’s Volumes of projection bodies (1996) proposed that simplices maximize RnR_nRn​. The three-dimensional paper also gives the simplex upper value there. However, Feng, Hu, Liu and Xu’s On the reverse projection inequality (2026, MathSciDoc:2608.23002) gives counterexamples in every dimension at least nine.

M2 explicitly credits that prior negative answer. Its contribution is a direct Cartesian-product witness with an exact computable value, together with an exponential excess over the simplex benchmark in sufficiently large dimensions. It should not be read as the first disproof of Brannen’s conjecture.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that every convex body in Rn\mathbb R^nRn, for every integer n≥4n\geq4n≥4, satisfies

Rn(K)≥κn−1,nκn,2−n,R_n(K)\geq\kappa_{n-1}^{,n}\kappa_n^{,2-n},Rn​(K)≥κn−1,n​κn,2−n​,

with equality if and only if KKK is an ellipsoid, including arbitrary translations and invertible linear images of the ball. No symmetry, smoothness or proximity-to-a-ball assumption is imposed.

Combined with the external three-dimensional theorem, this gives the claimed sharp minimum for all n≥3n\geq3n≥3. M1 also records consequences for lower-degree projection quantities, affine inequalities involving gradients, and isoperimetry in normed spaces. Those consequences use earlier implications and, when stated in dimension three, the separately proved three-dimensional input.

For the upper problem, let

Td=conv⁡(0,e1,…,ed),cd=Rd(Td)=(d+1)ddd!.T_d=\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d),\qquad c_d=R_d(T_d)=\frac{(d+1)d^d}{d!}.Td​=conv(0,e1​,…,ed​),cd​=Rd​(Td​)=d!(d+1)dd​.

M2 states that the twenty-dimensional body K=T10×T10K=T_{10}\times T_{10}K=T10​×T10​ satisfies

R20(K)c20=22 355 47622 020 096>1.\frac{R_{20}(K)}{c_{20}}=\frac{22\,355\,476}{22\,020\,096}>1.c20​R20​(K)​=2202009622355476​>1.

Thus two ten-dimensional simplices, placed in independent coordinate blocks, have larger normalized projection volume than a single twenty-dimensional simplex.

The underlying identity is multiplicativity for full-dimensional polytopes A⊂RrA\subset\mathbb R^rA⊂Rr, B⊂RsB\subset\mathbb R^sB⊂Rs, with r,s≥2r,s\geq2r,s≥2:

Rr+s(A×B)=Rr(A)Rs(B).R_{r+s}(A\times B)=R_r(A)R_s(B).Rr+s​(A×B)=Rr​(A)Rs​(B).

Iterating it, M2 claims that some λ>1\lambda>1λ>1 and dimension threshold NNN exist such that every n≥Nn\geq Nn≥N admits a product of simplices KnK_nKn​ with Rn(Kn)≥λncnR_n(K_n)\geq\lambda^n c_nRn​(Kn​)≥λncn​. The excess can therefore grow exponentially, rather than remaining a small fixed discrepancy.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The principal reason is the claimed unrestricted minimum theorem. Petty’s projection-volume conjecture is a central affine extremal problem, and its global equality classification would complete a picture previously known through local arguments, special shapes and dimension three.

The two papers also illustrate why an attractive extremal analogy can be only half right. Ellipsoids would indeed minimize this shadow-based functional, but simplices need not maximize it. The upper problem has more room for products and combinatorial structure than the simple candidate suggests.

M2’s exact witness makes that distinction accessible. One does not need to imagine a delicate perturbation of a complicated polytope: a product of two standard simplices already exceeds the proposed value. Its multiplicative mechanism explains why the failure becomes substantial in high dimension.

The family’s score does not assign equal novelty to both components. M2 acknowledges the earlier counterexamples, while M1 makes the broader claimed advance. Neither result determines the true best upper constant or all maximizing bodies.

6. The main idea

Turn shadow geometry into an inequality for measures

M1 associates a positive measure to a normalized convex body through first variation of volume. The measure satisfies a lower bound when integrated against support functions, and its first absolute directional moments represent the projection body.

The desired geometric inequality is then reduced to a lower bound for a two-measure pairing of the form

∬∣⟨x,y⟩∣ dη(x) dζ(y).\iint|\langle x,y\rangle|\,d\eta(x)\,d\zeta(y).∬∣⟨x,y⟩∣dη(x)dζ(y).

The measures retain information from the original bodies; they are not arbitrary probability distributions without constraints. This reformulation separates the projection-body application from a more general analytic inequality.

Remove affine directions and control the remaining harmonics

Functions on the sphere can be decomposed into spherical harmonics, the spherical analogues of Fourier modes. Degree-two components reflect changes related to linear coordinates. Higher-degree components record more complicated deviations from a Euclidean shape.

The manuscript claims a strict estimate for powers of arbitrary norms that controls those higher modes, with equality only in the Euclidean case. The degree-two contribution must be handled by choosing coordinates; it does not vanish automatically.

A variational construction selects a norm associated with the measure. To obtain a global affine position, the argument follows these choices even toward singular matrices, where norms become seminorms. A boundary calculation and fixed-point theorem then produce an invertible coordinate change in which the unwanted degree-two component disappears. The strict harmonic estimate and first-variation equality conditions return the ellipsoid classification.

Test products against the proposed maximum

M2 uses a more elementary route. For a polytope, the projection body can be expressed using its facet areas and normals. Facets of a Cartesian product come from one factor at a time. Their contributions split into complementary coordinate blocks, yielding the multiplicative identity for RnR_nRn​.

The projection body of a standard simplex can be represented as a cube plus one segment, allowing its volume to be computed exactly. Comparing the product of two ten-dimensional simplex values with the twenty-dimensional simplex value produces the stated rational number greater than one.

Repeating the ten-dimensional block gives a fixed growth rate per dimension. That rate exceeds the asymptotic exponential rate of the simplex benchmark; an additional simplex factor accommodates dimensions not divisible by ten. This is the mechanism behind the exponential separation.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Both manuscripts concern the volume of ΠK\Pi KΠK itself. Replacing it by its polar would invoke a different family of inequalities and different extremizers.

M1’s new theorem starts at dimension four. The combined all-dimensions-at-least-three conclusion credits the independent three-dimensional result. It includes nonsymmetric and nonsmooth bodies, and its equality statement is global.

M2’s explicit example is in dimension twenty. Earlier work gives counterexamples in smaller dimensions, and the product construction is not claimed to locate the first failing dimension. Its asymptotic conclusion holds above some threshold and does not specify the sharp maximum.

Finding that maximum, identifying its extremizers, and determining quantitative stability near the minimum remain separate questions. The digest reports the manuscripts’ statements and explanatory mechanisms without checking their proofs or independently adjudicating novelty.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 contains the measure reduction, strict norm estimate, affine normalization and equality analysis. M2 gives the facet formula, product identity, exact simplex computation and repeated-product consequence.

The linked three-dimensional paper and local uniqueness paper are primary sources for earlier minimum results. Saroglou’s On the shape of a convex body with respect to its second projection body explains the class-reduction viewpoint. M2’s references identify Brannen’s original upper conjecture and Feng–Hu–Liu–Xu’s earlier counterexamples.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Petty’s projection-volume conjecture in dimensions at least four (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A product counterexample to the simplex maximum for projection-body volume (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why the triangular lattice minimizes so many planar energies
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 090 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Place repelling particles in the plane at a fixed average density. Their preferred arrangement depends on how the repulsion changes with distance. Could the same arrangement minimize energy for an entire class of interactions, even when its competitors are not periodic?

The triangular lattice is the natural candidate. Each point has six equally distant nearest neighbors, and the associated Voronoi cells are regular hexagons. Its circle-packing optimality is classical. Universal energy optimality is a stronger and different question: it compares interactions at every distance, rather than merely requiring a minimum separation.

The four manuscripts in this family connect three settings. M1 and M2 claim a universal energy minimum. M3 constructs a sharp Fourier certificate for the already-known optimal packing density. M2 and M4 address neutralized long-range energies, and M4 deduces an exact next-order coefficient for logarithmic energy on the sphere.

2. Background and essential definitions

Normalize the triangular lattice AAA to have one point per unit area. A locally finite configuration CCC has centered disk density one if

NRπR2⟶1,NR=#(C∩BR),\frac{N_R}{\pi R^2}\longrightarrow1,\qquad N_R=\#(C\cap B_R),πR2NR​​⟶1,NR​=#(C∩BR​),

where BRB_RBR​ is the disk of radius RRR centered at the origin. Local finiteness means every bounded region contains finitely many points. This density assumption does not give uniform control over counts in every translated small disk.

For a nonnegative interaction ggg of squared distance, define the lower energy per particle by

Eg(C)=lim inf⁡R→∞1NR∑x,y∈C∩BRx≠yg(∣x−y∣2).E_g(C)=\liminf_{R\to\infty}\frac1{N_R}\sum_{\substack{x,y\in C\cap B_R\\x\ne y}}g(|x-y|^2).Eg​(C)=R→∞liminf​NR​1​x,y∈C∩BR​x=y​∑​g(∣x−y∣2).

The sum counts ordered pairs. A completely monotone function satisfies (−1)jg(j)(t)≥0(-1)^j g^{(j)}(t)\geq0(−1)jg(j)(t)≥0 for every nonnegative integer jjj. Examples include Gaussians g(t)=e−παtg(t)=e^{-\pi\alpha t}g(t)=e−παt, α>0\alpha>0α>0, and inverse powers g(t)=t−pg(t)=t^{-p}g(t)=t−p, p>0p>0p>0. Such functions admit positive-mixture representations by exponential kernels.

Long-range interactions need another definition. In two dimensions, ∣x∣−s|x|^{-s}∣x∣−s with 0<s<20<s<20<s<2 has a divergent raw lattice sum, and the Coulomb interaction is −log⁡∣x∣-\log|x|−log∣x∣. A jellium energy includes an oppositely charged uniform background. A renormalized energy also subtracts the singular self-energy near each point. These operations are part of the energy’s definition, not a consequence of comparing two infinite raw sums.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Classical work by Rankin, Cassels, Ennola and Diananda established the triangular minimum for convergent inverse-power sums among lattices. Montgomery’s Minimal theta functions (1988) proved the Gaussian minimum among planar lattices of a fixed density. These results compare lattices with lattices; they do not control an arbitrary nonperiodic arrangement.

Cohn and Kumar developed the universal-optimality program and singled out the triangular, E8E_8E8​ and Leech lattices. Cohn, Kumar, Miller, Radchenko and Viazovska later established the eight- and twenty-four-dimensional cases through sharp Fourier auxiliary functions and interpolation. Planar partial results treated restricted periodic competitors or sufficiently small bounded displacements of the triangular lattice.

The Fourier packing method began with Cohn and Elkies. Viazovska’s dimension-eight construction and its dimension-twenty-four counterpart attained the sharp packing bounds there. The plane already had Thue’s geometric density theorem; the unresolved analytic question was whether the two-point Fourier bound itself could attain that value. M3 addresses this sharp-certificate question, rather than claiming the first planar packing theorem.

For Coulomb energy, Sandier and Serfaty’s vortex-lattice work established the infinite-system framework, existence of a minimum, periodic approximation and triangular optimality among lattices. Their conjecture asked for the unrestricted minimum. Petrache and Serfaty’s 2020 paper connected universal optimality to Coulomb and Riesz crystallization.

Bétermin and Sandier’s spherical-energy analysis had already shown that the unknown planar minimum determines the linear term of optimal spherical logarithmic energy. M4 uses that established bridge after claiming the planar minimum directly.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Universal energy comparison

M1 and M2 both state that every locally finite density-one configuration satisfies

Eg(C)≥∑a∈A∖{0}g(∣a∣2)=Eg(A)E_g(C)\geq\sum_{a\in A\setminus\{0\}}g(|a|^2)=E_g(A)Eg​(C)≥a∈A∖{0}∑​g(∣a∣2)=Eg​(A)

for every smooth nonnegative completely monotone ggg. The comparison includes infinite values. No minimum separation, periodicity or bound on local occupancy is required.

Both papers construct sharp auxiliary functions for each Gaussian, then mix the energy inequalities. They do not claim that this mixing constructs a sharp auxiliary function for every mixed potential in the stronger per-potential formulation of the Cohn–Kumar conjecture. Nor do they classify all configurations attaining the energy minimum.

A sharp certificate for packing

With Fourier transform f^(ξ)=∫f(x)e−2πix⋅ξ dx\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dxf​(ξ)=∫f(x)e−2πix⋅ξdx, M3 claims a smooth rapidly decreasing radial function satisfying

f^(0)=1,f(0)=23,f^≥0,f(x)≤0 when ∣x∣≥1.\widehat f(0)=1,\quad f(0)=\frac2{\sqrt3},\quad\widehat f\geq0,\quad f(x)\leq0\ \text{when }|x|\geq1.f​(0)=1,f(0)=3​2​,f​≥0,f(x)≤0 when ∣x∣≥1.

The Cohn–Elkies bound then gives the optimal density π/(23)\pi/(2\sqrt3)π/(23​) for disks of radius 1/21/21/2, including nonperiodic packings. The certificate also recovers triangular uniqueness among periodic equality cases. Its extra zeros mean that it does not satisfy a separate, stronger conjectured requirement prescribing exactly the lattice-shell zero set.

Long-range energies and the sphere

M2 claims triangular minimality for its planar logarithmic and Riesz renormalized energies, with 0<s<20<s<20<s<2 in the Riesz case, and the corresponding thermodynamic jellium minima. Its exact periodic minimizers are the n2n^2n2 triangular lattice classes on compatible tori R2/(nA)\mathbb R^2/(nA)R2/(nA). This is not an assertion of equality on arbitrary square tori.

M4 gives an independent direct logarithmic result. Its admissible fields satisfy

div⁡E=2π(∑p∈Λδp−1),curl⁡E=0,\operatorname{div}E=2\pi\left(\sum_{p\in\Lambda}\delta_p-1\right),\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,divE=2π​p∈Λ∑​δp​−1​,curlE=0,

where Λ\LambdaΛ is simple and locally finite, and its centered disk counts divided by area are uniformly bounded for radii greater than one. Here δp\delta_pδp​ is a unit point mass and the constant one is the background density.

M4 first removes small disks of radius η\etaη around charges from the half-Dirichlet energy 12∫χR∣E∣2\frac12\int\chi_R|E|^221​∫χR​∣E∣2, adds the self-energy correction πlog⁡η∑pχR(p)\pi\log\eta\sum_p\chi_R(p)πlogη∑p​χR​(p), and takes η↓0\eta\downarrow0η↓0. It then divides by the area of [−R,R]2[-R,R]^2[−R,R]2 and takes a large-square limsup, using cutoffs with fixed-width boundary layers. The claimed minimum is the triangular field’s value. On a square torus of area nnn, every configuration of nnn distinct points has total renormalized energy at least nnn times that value; equality on such a torus is not asserted.

For nnn points on the unit sphere, using ordered pairs and Euclidean chord distance, M4 consequently states

min⁡∑i≠j−log⁡∣yi−yj∣=(12−log⁡2)n2−n2log⁡n+CBHSn+o(n),\min\sum_{i\ne j}-\log|y_i-y_j|=\left(\frac12-\log2\right)n^2-\frac n2\log n+C_{\mathrm{BHS}}n+o(n),mini=j∑​−log∣yi​−yj​∣=(21​−log2)n2−2n​logn+CBHS​n+o(n),

where

CBHS=2log⁡2+12log⁡23+3log⁡πΓ(1/3).C_{\mathrm{BHS}}=2\log2+\frac12\log\frac23+3\log\frac{\sqrt\pi}{\Gamma(1/3)}.CBHS​=2log2+21​log32​+3logΓ(1/3)π​​.

The gamma function extends factorials and is defined for positive ttt by Γ(t)=∫0∞xt−1e−x dx\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty x^{t-1}e^{-x}\,dxΓ(t)=∫0∞​xt−1e−xdx. The remainder o(n)o(n)o(n), divided by nnn, tends to zero.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. Universal optimality of the triangular lattice is a central crystallization problem. The claimed comparison would allow fully nonperiodic competitors, including strongly uneven local arrangements, rather than only other lattices or small perturbations of one.

The long-range claims add content that raw universal energy cannot provide when all relevant sums diverge. Neutralization and self-energy subtraction create a finite comparison capable of distinguishing configurations for Coulomb and slowly decaying Riesz interactions.

The sphere consequence is also more than the leading uniform-distribution term. Its linear coefficient records microscopic organization after the bulk and logarithmic terms are removed. Identifying that coefficient would settle the stated two-dimensional logarithmic-energy prediction of Brauchart, Hardin and Saff.

At the same time, an energy minimum is not a complete crystallization classification. Local defects or compact modifications can leave an infinite-volume energy per unit area unchanged. The manuscripts do not infer that every minimizer must literally be a perfect lattice everywhere.

6. The main idea

A lower bound that becomes exact on a lattice

For a Gaussian interaction, seek a function fff lying below it with nonnegative Fourier transform. Fourier inversion turns a finite pair sum into an integral involving

f^(ξ)∣∑x∈C∩BRe2πix⋅ξ∣2.\widehat f(\xi)\left|\sum_{x\in C\cap B_R}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\right|^2.f​(ξ)​x∈C∩BR​∑​e2πix⋅ξ​2.

Positivity permits a lower bound from frequencies near zero. After removing diagonal terms, the bound involves f^(0)−f(0)\widehat f(0)-f(0)f​(0)−f(0). Contact with the Gaussian at nonzero triangular lattice points, together with zeros on the dual lattice, makes Poisson summation identify this bound with the triangular energy.

The technical construction must control a function and its Fourier transform simultaneously, at infinitely many radii. Trigonometric factors encode a periodic superset of the triangular shell radii. Value-and-derivative interpolation imposes exact contacts; Gaussian damping supplies rapid decay.

M1 uses two finite interpolation blocks of size twenty and an infinite summable correction. M2 uses a different, larger finite construction. In both, solving the interpolation equations is separate from establishing signs between nodes and on the unbounded tail. The manuscripts describe interval arithmetic, polynomial bounds and analytic tail estimates for those tasks. These are parts of their claimed arguments, not calculations performed by this digest.

Positive-mixture representations then pass from Gaussians to completely monotone interactions at the level of nonnegative energy sums. Lower-limit arguments retain singular potentials and infinite energies without requiring a well-behaved mixed auxiliary function.

Neutralization and a direct cell comparison

M2 uses heat-kernel comparisons to connect Gaussian inequalities to neutralized periodic and field energies. Periodic approximation then transfers the minimum to the infinite system, with the source’s order of cutoffs and limits retained.

M4 follows a separate geometric route for the logarithmic case. It reduces the full-plane minimum to square-periodic fields and first studies a minimizing configuration on each torus. Separation is obtained for those finite minimizers, not imposed on every competitor.

Voronoi cells divide the torus into regions closest to individual charges. The manuscript constructs a single trial potential whose formulas match across cell boundaries and whose logarithmic singularities match the true potential. An exact energy identity leaves a sum of sector contributions plus a nonnegative square measuring the difference of gradients.

A sharp sector bound is calibrated on the regular hexagon. Areas and angles sum exactly, while Euler’s relation limits the average number of sectors to six per point. These facts give the triangular lower bound. Earlier periodic approximation and the Bétermin–Sandier asymptotic formula then deliver the full-plane and spherical consequences.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The raw energy uses centered disks, ordered pairs and a liminf. M4’s field energy removes the puncture cutoff first and then takes a square limsup. M2 uses its own field normalization and order of limits. Their constants should not be exchanged without the conversion specified in the sources.

The Riesz range is strictly 0<s<20<s<20<s<2; no endpoint theorem at s=2s=2s=2 or quantum crystallization statement is asserted. Infinite raw energies remain legitimate in the universal comparison but do not replace the renormalized theorem.

The packing certificate settles a sharpness question for an analytic bound whose numerical optimum was already known geometrically. It does not satisfy every stronger zero-set conjecture. M3 also notes a related 2026 thesis announcement whose precise relationship it does not determine from the available abstract; the digest makes no priority judgment beyond the cited accounts.

Neither the infinite-volume minimum nor the spherical asymptotic supplies an algorithm producing optimal point sets. In particular, the spherical formula is not presented as an algorithmic solution of Smale’s seventh problem.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 and M2 give distinct Gaussian interpolation constructions with the same universal-energy endpoint. M3 treats packing signs and exact normalization. M4 treats Coulomb energy directly and fixes the spherical ordered-pair convention.

The linked Sandier–Serfaty, Petrache–Serfaty and Bétermin–Sandier papers explain the long-range framework and its established implications. Brauchart, Hardin and Saff’s next-order conjectures give the spherical context. The manuscripts’ historical sections distinguish earlier lattice-only comparisons from unrestricted configuration claims.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An atomic certificate for triangular-lattice universal optimality (September 26, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Universal optimality of the triangular lattice (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, A sharp Fourier certificate for planar circle packing (September 23, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Triangular minimality for planar Coulomb renormalized energy (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A geometric-mean law for symmetric convex bodies
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 091 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

The Brunn–Minkowski inequality says that combining two shapes by adding their points produces a body with a substantial volume. It is one of the main bridges between convex geometry and inequalities in analysis.

A stronger proposal applies to shapes symmetric about the origin. Instead of taking arithmetic means of their directional support bounds, take geometric means. This generally produces a smaller body. Must its volume still be at least the geometric mean of the original volumes?

That is the logarithmic Brunn–Minkowski conjecture. The manuscript in this family claims it for arbitrary origin-symmetric convex bodies in every dimension. It also derives intermediate power-mean inequalities and, through an earlier transfer theorem, a logarithmic concavity statement for the measure of exponentially dilated symmetric bodies.

The exact definition of the interpolated body matters. A geometric mean of support functions need not itself be a support function; the construction uses an intersection of half-spaces to obtain a genuine convex body.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a convex body K⊂RnK\subset\mathbb R^nK⊂Rn, the support function is

hK(u)=max⁡x∈K⟨x,u⟩,∣u∣=1.h_K(u)=\max_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle,\qquad |u|=1.hK​(u)=x∈Kmax​⟨x,u⟩,∣u∣=1.

It records the supporting hyperplane in direction uuu. If K=−KK=-KK=−K, the origin lies in its interior and hKh_KhK​ is positive and even.

Given any positive continuous function fff on the unit sphere, its Wulff body is

W[f]=⋂∣u∣=1{x:⟨x,u⟩≤f(u)}.W[f]=\bigcap_{|u|=1}\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq f(u)\}.W[f]=∣u∣=1⋂​{x:⟨x,u⟩≤f(u)}.

The function supplies directional upper bounds; some may be redundant. The actual support function of the intersection can therefore be smaller than fff.

For 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq10≤λ≤1, the logarithmic combination of KKK and LLL is

Dλ=W[hK1−λhLλ].D_\lambda=W[h_K^{1-\lambda}h_L^\lambda].Dλ​=W[hK1−λ​hLλ​].

The ordinary Minkowski combination (1−λ)K+λL(1-\lambda)K+\lambda L(1−λ)K+λL has arithmetic-mean support function. Arithmetic–geometric mean comparison gives Dλ⊆(1−λ)K+λLD_\lambda\subseteq(1-\lambda)K+\lambda LDλ​⊆(1−λ)K+λL, explaining why a volume bound for DλD_\lambdaDλ​ is stronger.

A nonnegative function FFF is log-concave when

F((1−λ)s+λt)≥F(s)1−λF(t)λ.F((1-\lambda)s+\lambda t)\geq F(s)^{1-\lambda}F(t)^\lambda.F((1−λ)s+λt)≥F(s)1−λF(t)λ.

For a positive function, this means log⁡F\log FlogF is concave. A density e−V(x)e^{-V(x)}e−V(x) is log-concave when VVV is convex, and even when V(−x)=V(x)V(-x)=V(x)V(−x)=V(x). Gaussian densities and uniform densities on symmetric convex bodies are familiar examples.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Firey introduced power means of convex bodies, and Lutwak developed the broader LpL^pLp Brunn–Minkowski theory. The logarithmic combination appears as the limit of the power mean when ppp decreases to zero.

Böröczky, Lutwak, Yang and Zhang formulated the symmetric logarithmic conjecture and proved its planar case in The log-Brunn–Minkowski inequality (2012). Their work also related the volume formulation to a logarithmic mixed-volume inequality. The logarithmic Minkowski problem, concerning which measures arise from boundary cone volumes, is related but is not the same theorem.

Saroglou proved the inequality for bodies that are unconditional in a common coordinate basis: each body is unchanged by independently reversing coordinate signs. His 2015 paper connects this geometry to coordinatewise products and to a special diagonal-dilation property. Later results treated common reflection symmetries and unit balls of complex norms.

A second line studied infinitesimal changes of volume. Kolesnikov and Milman formulated local inequalities as spectral estimates for a geometric differential operator and obtained results for ppp close to one. Putterman established equivalence between local and global formulations in the relevant range. Van Handel proved a local logarithmic result for zonoids, which are limits of sums of segments. Additional work treated bodies of revolution and other symmetry classes.

The manuscript also acknowledges Stancu’s 2018 announcement of an all-dimensional logarithmic Minkowski inequality and its equivalent Brunn–Minkowski conclusion, with flow-asymptotic details deferred there. This digest preserves that attribution rather than presenting the new manuscript as the only prior claim of the general result.

The transfer from volume to even log-concave measures is due to Saroglou’s More on logarithmic sums of convex bodies. The new volume theorem is the input used to activate that earlier implication in every dimension.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that for all origin-symmetric convex bodies K,L⊂RnK,L\subset\mathbb R^nK,L⊂Rn, every n≥1n\geq1n≥1, and every λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]λ∈[0,1],

∣W[hK1−λhLλ]∣≥∣K∣1−λ∣L∣λ.|W[h_K^{1-\lambda}h_L^\lambda]|\geq |K|^{1-\lambda}|L|^\lambda.∣W[hK1−λ​hLλ​]∣≥∣K∣1−λ∣L∣λ.

No smoothness, common reflection basis or proximity assumption is imposed.

For every 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, it deduces the symmetric power-mean inequality

∣W[((1−λ)hKp+λhLp)1/p]∣p/n≥(1−λ)∣K∣p/n+λ∣L∣p/n.\left|W\left[((1-\lambda)h_K^p+\lambda h_L^p)^{1/p}\right]\right|^{p/n}\geq(1-\lambda)|K|^{p/n}+\lambda|L|^{p/n}.​W[((1−λ)hKp​+λhLp​)1/p]​p/n≥(1−λ)∣K∣p/n+λ∣L∣p/n.

This additive volume-power form uses normalization and a reweighting of the interpolation parameter, beyond the elementary comparison of power means.

The measure consequence applies to every even log-concave Radon measure μ\muμ. A Radon measure is finite on compact sets, though its total mass may be infinite. Log-concavity here means the corresponding multiplicative inequality under Minkowski combinations of compact sets. The claim is

μ(Dλ)≥μ(K)1−λμ(L)λ.\mu(D_\lambda)\geq\mu(K)^{1-\lambda}\mu(L)^\lambda.μ(Dλ​)≥μ(K)1−λμ(L)λ.

The manuscript includes measures supported on a proper linear subspace, not only full-dimensional densities. No probability normalization is required.

Taking KKK and LLL to be scalar dilates of the same body gives the scalar (B)-conjecture:

t⟼μ(etK)is log-concave on R.t\longmapsto\mu(e^tK)\quad\text{is log-concave on }\mathbb R.t⟼μ(etK)is log-concave on R.

The exponential parameter is important. The statement concerns multiplying every coordinate by the same factor ete^tet, not arbitrary independent coordinate dilations for every measure.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The logarithmic endpoint is a central strengthening of classical convex-volume theory. A theorem for all symmetric bodies would unify numerous special-symmetry and local results, and yield an entire interval of LpL^pLp inequalities.

The measure consequence makes the result relevant beyond Euclidean volume. It controls how Gaussian mass, uniform convex-body mass and more general even log-concave mass enter a symmetrically expanding region. Concavity of the logarithm imposes a consistent multiplicative interpolation law between different scales.

The symmetry assumption is analytically meaningful. In local spectral formulations, translations correspond to odd modes. Restricting to even data removes these modes and changes the relevant variance or eigenvalue problem. Symmetry is therefore part of the mechanism, not merely a convenient normalization.

The score concerns the claimed general inequality and its consequences. It does not assert a complete equality classification, quantitative stability theorem, or an unrestricted nonsymmetric analogue. Those are distinct mathematical questions.

6. The main idea

Approximate a body by smooth slab penalties

A symmetric polytope can be written as the intersection of finitely many slabs ∣⟨pi,x⟩∣≤hi|\langle p_i,x\rangle|\leq h_i∣⟨pi​,x⟩∣≤hi​. The proof replaces its indicator by a smooth density proportional to

exp⁡(−ε2∣x∣2−∑i(⟨pi,x⟩hi)q),\exp\left(-\frac\varepsilon2|x|^2-\sum_i\left(\frac{\langle p_i,x\rangle}{h_i}\right)^q\right),exp(−2ε​∣x∣2−i∑​(hi​⟨pi​,x⟩​)q),

where qqq is even and ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0. Large qqq penalizes points outside the slabs sharply. Letting qqq tend to infinity and then removing the Gaussian factor recovers the polytope’s volume.

Geometrically varying the slab widths becomes ordinary linear variation of their logarithms. Differentiating the logarithm of the integral twice produces a variance term minus an expected second derivative. The desired concavity is therefore reduced to a particular variance inequality for sums of even powers of linear forms.

Choose coordinates adapted to moments

Ordinary variance bounds for log-concave measures are not automatically strong enough for this endpoint. M1 instead represents the target measure as the image of a measure with density e−φe^{-\varphi}e−φ under the gradient map x=∇φx=\nabla\varphix=∇φ. These are moment coordinates, arising from earlier moment-measure theory.

The Hessian of φ\varphiφ, the matrix of second derivatives, supplies a geometry adapted to that map. The manuscript constructs it with a global upper bound and strict positivity locally. It does not assume a uniform positive lower bound everywhere.

A differential operator in these coordinates generates a dense collection of centered even test functions. The possible obstructions are affine functions: subtracting the mean removes constants, while evenness removes linear functions. This is the point where the symmetry enters the functional argument explicitly.

Turn the remainder into squares

For those test functions, a tensor calculation expresses the relevant remainder as a sum of squares. Nonnegativity of these squares yields control of each homogeneous summand separately. Two Cauchy–Schwarz steps then produce the required variance estimate.

The analytic inequality gives concavity for the smooth slab integrals. Approximation passes to polytopes and then arbitrary symmetric bodies. The measure statement follows through Saroglou’s transfer theorem, with a separate reduction to the subspace supporting a lower-dimensional measure.

This chain keeps the genuinely new claimed analytic estimate separate from the established geometric-to-measure implication.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Both bodies must be symmetric about the same origin, and the support bounds must be assembled by the Wulff intersection. Treating their geometric mean as an already-valid support function would omit a necessary part of the definition.

The stated power range is 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, with the logarithmic case interpreted separately as the endpoint. The scalar (B)-conclusion uses even log-concave measures and symmetric convex bodies; it is not a claim for arbitrary densities or sets.

The paper discusses a diagonal-dilation property for uniform measures on cubes in an equivalence used for context. That specialized property should not be confused with a general diagonal (B)-theorem for every even log-concave measure. The published consequence summarized here is scalar dilation.

Equality and stability require additional analysis beyond the displayed inequality. The digest reports the proof strategy and dependencies as stated, without verifying the tensor estimate or resolving the relationship between different announced approaches.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s first section states the volume and power-mean claims; its final section gives the measure theorem and supporting-subspace reduction. The intermediate sections develop moment coordinates, density of even tests and the tensor variance estimate.

Saroglou’s two linked papers distinguish unconditional-body results from the later transfer theorem. Van Handel’s local zonoid paper illustrates an important partial solution. The 2012 paper of Böröczky–Lutwak–Yang–Zhang supplies the conjectural and planar starting point, with full bibliographic details in M1.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The logarithmic Brunn–Minkowski conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The optimal order of overlap needed to cover high-dimensional space
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 092 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Cover the plane with translated copies of a fixed shape. A square can tile with no wasted overlap. Disks must overlap if no gaps are to remain. In higher dimensions, how much overlap can an arbitrary convex body force?

There are two versions of this question. In a lattice covering, the centers form one regular lattice. In a translative covering, they may be arranged freely, with no periodicity requirement. Allowing more freedom can only make covering easier.

The two manuscripts in this family claim matching answers at the level of worst-case dimensional order. M1 gives every convex body a single-lattice covering of density at most a constant times nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn. M2 constructs bodies for which even unrestricted translates require at least that order of density. Together, the claims locate the hardest covering problems to within absolute constant factors.

2. Background and essential definitions

A convex body K⊂RnK\subset\mathbb R^nK⊂Rn is compact, convex and full-dimensional. A set of centers XXX covers space by translates of KKK if

K+X=⋃x∈X(K+x)=Rn.K+X=\bigcup_{x\in X}(K+x)=\mathbb R^n.K+X=x∈X⋃​(K+x)=Rn.

Centers are locally finite: every bounded region contains only finitely many. Rotations of individual copies are not allowed; all copies are translations of the same body.

For a full-rank lattice Λ\LambdaΛ, its determinant is the volume of a fundamental cell. The lattice covering density is

θL(K)=inf⁡K+Λ=Rn∣K∣det⁡Λ.\theta_L(K)=\inf_{K+\Lambda=\mathbb R^n}\frac{|K|}{\det\Lambda}.θL​(K)=K+Λ=Rninf​detΛ∣K∣​.

The ratio is the average number of copies covering a point. It is not the fraction of space covered, which is already one. Density one corresponds to a covering with no overlap except on negligible boundaries.

For arbitrary centers, put QR=[−R,R]nQ_R=[-R,R]^nQR​=[−R,R]n and define

θT(K)=inf⁡K+X=Rn∣K∣lim sup⁡R→∞#(X∩QR)(2R)n.\theta_T(K)=\inf_{K+X=\mathbb R^n}|K|\limsup_{R\to\infty}\frac{\#(X\cap Q_R)}{(2R)^n}.θT​(K)=K+X=Rninf​∣K∣R→∞limsup​(2R)n#(X∩QR​)​.

A periodic covering can use finitely many cosets of one lattice, X=Λ+TX=\Lambda+TX=Λ+T. Its density is ∣T∣∣K∣/det⁡Λ|T||K|/\det\Lambda∣T∣∣K∣/detΛ, where representatives in TTT are distinct modulo the lattice. Taking the infimum over all such finite unions gives the same optimum as unrestricted translative covering, by periodization. This equality of infima does not mean that every individual covering is periodic or has a density limit.

Necessarily θT(K)≤θL(K)\theta_T(K)\leq\theta_L(K)θT​(K)≤θL​(K). An upper bound for the more restrictive lattice problem is especially strong; a lower bound for the less restrictive translative problem is especially strong.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Rogers’s 1957 covering theorem gave every convex body a translative covering of density at most

nlog⁡n+nlog⁡log⁡n+5nn\log n+n\log\log n+5nnlogn+nloglogn+5n

in dimensions at least three. Such a covering can use multiple lattice cosets. Fejes Tóth later obtained the same leading order using only logarithmically many cosets. Neither statement forces all centers to lie in one lattice.

For that stricter problem, Rogers had a larger general bound. Ordentlich, Regev and Weiss’s lattice-covering theorem improved the universal estimate to order n2n^2n2. Li and Liu’s 2026 work approached nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn with an extra iterated-logarithmic factor; their binary-correction companion reduced that remaining loss further.

Li and Liu also constructed centrally symmetric bodies whose lattice covering density is at least a constant times nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn. That lower bound rules out efficient lattices, but it does not rule out a clever irregular arrangement of centers. M2 addresses this stronger exclusion.

For Euclidean balls, classical lower bounds are linear in dimension, while known upper bounds are of order nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn. The family does not close that ball-specific gap. Its lower construction chooses a body designed to be difficult, rather than proving that balls themselves require the worst-case order.

This distinction also separates a random-center failure from a genuine covering lower bound. Showing that typical random centers miss a point leaves open exceptional efficient arrangements. M2 instead samples the body and claims that one realization defeats every low-density arrangement.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that an absolute constant CCC exists such that every convex body K⊂RnK\subset\mathbb R^nK⊂Rn, n≥2n\geq2n≥2, admits one full-rank lattice with

K+Λ=Rn,∣K∣det⁡Λ≤Cnlog⁡n.K+\Lambda=\mathbb R^n,\qquad \frac{|K|}{\det\Lambda}\leq Cn\log n.K+Λ=Rn,detΛ∣K∣​≤Cnlogn.

No central symmetry or boundary regularity is required. The constant is uniform over the shape and dimension.

M2 states that absolute constants c>0c>0c>0 and n0n_0n0​ exist such that, for every n≥n0n\geq n_0n≥n0​, some centrally symmetric convex body KnK_nKn​ satisfies

θT(Kn)>cnlog⁡n.\theta_T(K_n)>cn\log n.θT​(Kn​)>cnlogn.

The bodies can also be chosen as centrally symmetric polytopes with rational vertices. The lower bound excludes all locally finite center arrangements, via the periodic-covering reduction; it does not restrict the number of cosets in an intermediate periodic arrangement.

Combining the two claims gives

sup⁡K⊂RnθT(K)≍nlog⁡n,sup⁡K⊂RnθL(K)≍nlog⁡n.\sup_{K\subset\mathbb R^n}\theta_T(K)\asymp n\log n,\qquad\sup_{K\subset\mathbb R^n}\theta_L(K)\asymp n\log n.K⊂Rnsup​θT​(K)≍nlogn,K⊂Rnsup​θL​(K)≍nlogn.

The notation ≍\asymp≍ means bounded above and below by positive absolute constant multiples for sufficiently large nnn. The same worst-case order holds when the bodies in the suprema are restricted to centrally symmetric ones.

This is not a formula for every KKK. Cubes still tile at density one. Nor is it a sharp leading constant: the upper and lower absolute constants are not claimed to coincide.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The pair would determine the optimal order of two longstanding extremal covering problems. The upper result removes the remaining loss in a single-lattice construction; the lower result shows that unrestricted freedom of placement cannot remove the logarithmic factor in the worst case.

The lower theorem would also answer negatively the proposed universal linear bound θT(K)≤Cn\theta_T(K)\leq CnθT​(K)≤Cn. The obstruction persists even under central symmetry and can be realized by rational polytopes, so it is not tied to an exotic nonmeasurable shape or a pathological boundary.

There is a useful conceptual balance. Regular placement is powerful enough to achieve the optimal worst-case order, yet irregular placement can still help particular bodies. The two theorems do not say lattice and translative covering densities are equal for each shape.

The rating reflects the dimensional-order resolution and the breadth of the quantifiers. It does not imply that the constructions give small practical constants, efficient algorithms, or the answer for specific familiar bodies such as balls.

6. The main idea

The upper bound: many useful sections, one lattice

M1 splits coordinates into a large horizontal part and a much smaller vertical part. After an affine normalization, a Gaussian-marginal theorem controls the volumes of horizontal sections at relevant heights. A finite list of such sections approximates the geometric data needed for the covering.

A classical mean-hole estimate then supplies one horizontal lattice leaving an exponentially small uncovered fraction for every section on the list. The remaining issue is how to arrange their contributions at all heights without introducing many independent lattices.

The manuscript develops a hierarchy of binary corrections in the vertical coordinates. At each stage, adjacent integer choices form weighted branches. Two controls are retained simultaneously: the total Gaussian weight stays substantial, while each individual branch weight becomes small. The first ensures enough aggregate covering contribution; the second keeps individual sections in the range where the mean-hole estimate applies.
