A common linear shear distributes these contributions while preserving one full-rank lattice. The losses across successively smaller correction blocks are summable. A final dilation by 1+1/n1+1/n1+1/n fills the tiny remaining holes at a bounded multiplicative volume cost, since (1+1/n)n≤e(1+1/n)^n\leq e(1+1/n)n≤e.

The lower bound: choose a body that defeats every arrangement

M2 intersects a slightly enlarged ball with symmetric slabs whose normals are chosen by a Poisson process. The resulting random body retains substantial volume with positive probability, while the random cuts create many opportunities for holes in a proposed covering.

The key quantifier is “every arrangement.” A net of lattice bases cannot represent arbitrary finite unions of cosets. The paper instead localizes any hypothetical efficient periodic covering to a fixed window, keeps its center list with multiplicities, and rounds that list to a finite grid. Periodic averaging bounds the list size even for skew lattices or very short periods. Crucially, the finite class is fixed before the random body is sampled.

For a target point and a possible covering center, certain caps of slab normals would cut that target out of the corresponding translate. A hole certificate requires suitable Poisson normals to hit all the necessary cap conditions. Nearly coincident caps are dependent, so the argument groups them and controls overlaps between certificates rather than treating every event as independent.

Many targets are chosen with two levels of angular separation. A lower-tail estimate gives a probability of successful covering small enough to sum over every rounded pattern. A second-moment estimate alone would not supply that strength. One body realization therefore retains adequate volume while defeating the entire candidate class.

Periodization finally transfers the exclusion from all periodic arrangements to arbitrary translative coverings. The rational-polytope conclusion follows by approximation with the strict inequality preserved.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The estimates concern translations of a fixed convex body. Allowing each copy to rotate changes the problem. Bodies are full-dimensional, and covering density counts overlap with multiplicity.

M1 gives all dimensions n≥2n\geq2n≥2 after absorbing finitely many low dimensions into an absolute constant. M2 gives its hard examples only in sufficiently large dimensions. Neither optimizes the numerical constants or identifies a unique worst-case body.

The equality between periodic and unrestricted optimal densities is an infimum statement. It does not assert that every nonperiodic arrangement has matching upper and lower densities, or that an optimal covering must be attained.

The covering density of Euclidean balls remains a separate asymptotic question. Likewise, finding explicit small descriptions of extremal examples or efficiently constructing a near-optimal single lattice goes beyond the existence claims summarized here.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 develops the hierarchical correction and common-shear construction for the lattice upper bound. M2 develops the random-slab body, finite-pattern reduction and simultaneous exclusion for the translative lower bound.

The linked Rogers, Ordentlich–Regev–Weiss and Li–Liu papers provide the main earlier covering bounds. Eldan and Klartag’s pointwise Gaussian-marginal theorem is an explicit input to M1. M2’s appendix states the precise periodization principle needed to pass from finite unions of lattice cosets to unrestricted coverings.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A single-lattice covering bound of order n log n (September 23, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Translative covering densities of order n log n (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: When Gaussian tails in every direction control nonlinear fluctuations
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 093 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Suppose a high-dimensional random vector looks Gaussian in one limited sense: every linear projection has a Gaussian-type tail. Does that force good concentration for nonlinear observations as well, such as distance from a fixed set?

For arbitrary distributions, linear information can miss complicated internal structure. The question here adds log-concavity, a convexity condition on the density that rules out separated peaks. The manuscript claims that this combination is enough for a dimension-free logarithmic Sobolev inequality.

Such an inequality is substantially stronger than a tail estimate for one coordinate. It controls an entropy functional for every smooth test function and implies Gaussian concentration for Lipschitz functions. “Dimension-free” means that the constant depends on the common one-dimensional tail scale, but does not deteriorate merely because the vector has more coordinates.

2. Background and essential definitions

A probability density ρ\rhoρ on Rn\mathbb R^nRn is log-concave if its positive set is convex and log⁡ρ\log\rhologρ is concave there. Equivalently, one can write ρ=e−V\rho=e^{-V}ρ=e−V with a convex potential VVV, allowing V=+∞V=+\inftyV=+∞ outside the support. Uniform measures on convex bodies fit this definition, despite their discontinuous boundary densities.

Let XXX have law μ\muμ, and assume it is centered: EX=0\mathbb EX=0EX=0. The source calls it linearly aaa-subgaussian when

sup⁡∣θ∣=1Eexp⁡(⟨X,θ⟩2a2)≤2.\sup_{|\theta|=1}\mathbb E\exp\left(\frac{\langle X,\theta\rangle^2}{a^2}\right)\leq2.∣θ∣=1sup​Eexp(a2⟨X,θ⟩2​)≤2.

Every unit direction has the same exponential-square bound. Markov’s inequality then gives a tail bound of the form P(∣⟨X,θ⟩∣≥t)≤2e−t2/a2\mathbb P(|\langle X,\theta\rangle|\geq t)\leq2e^{-t^2/a^2}P(∣⟨X,θ⟩∣≥t)≤2e−t2/a2. This controls more than variance: it restricts rare large deviations in every direction.

For a nonnegative integrable function ggg, define

Ent⁡μ(g)=∫glog⁡g dμ−(∫g dμ)log⁡(∫g dμ),\operatorname{Ent}_\mu(g)=\int g\log g\,d\mu-\left(\int g\,d\mu\right)\log\left(\int g\,d\mu\right),Entμ​(g)=∫gloggdμ−(∫gdμ)log(∫gdμ),

with 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0. This is the entropy functional of the test function relative to μ\muμ, not simply the differential entropy of the random vector.

A logarithmic Sobolev inequality compares Ent⁡μ(f2)\operatorname{Ent}_\mu(f^2)Entμ​(f2) with the Dirichlet energy ∫∣∇f∣2dμ\int|\nabla f|^2d\mu∫∣∇f∣2dμ. The gradient measures local variation. The inequality therefore says that a function cannot concentrate its squared mass too sharply without paying a gradient cost.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Gross’s Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities (1975) established the Gaussian framework and its connection to hypercontractivity. One of its characteristic features is a constant independent of the number of Gaussian coordinates.

The Bakry–Émery diffusion method gives such inequalities when a smooth potential has a uniformly positive Hessian: D2V≥κID^2V\geq\kappa ID2V≥κI, κ>0\kappa>0κ>0. This is a local curvature condition. Ordinary log-concavity only requires nonnegative curvature and allows flat regions, including the interior of a uniform convex-body distribution.

Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities imply Gaussian concentration for all Lipschitz functions through Herbst’s argument. Under log-concavity, results of Milman connect strong concentration back to isoperimetry and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. The unresolved step addressed here is whether it is enough to know concentration only for linear functions.

Bizeul formulated that sufficiency conjecture in work first posted in 2023, On the log-Sobolev constant of log-concave vectors. Earlier norm-based criteria gave an entropy coefficient of order na2na^2na2, because controlling all coordinates gives a subgaussian scale of order n a\sqrt n\,an​a for the full Euclidean norm. Bizeul improved the coefficient to order n a2\sqrt n\,a^2n​a2, and established a dimension-free conclusion under rotational invariance.

These coefficients must be compared in the same convention. Some authors define a log-Sobolev parameter through its square; a bound of order n1/4an^{1/4}an1/4a for that parameter corresponds to a coefficient of order n a2\sqrt n\,a^2n​a2 in the displayed entropy inequality.

The manuscript claims removal of the remaining dimension factor without rotational symmetry. Its information-theoretic tools also build on Guo, Shamai and Verdú’s Gaussian-channel identities, which relate information gained from noisy observations to mean-square prediction error.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that a universal constant C<∞C<\inftyC<∞ exists such that, in every dimension, every centered log-concave probability measure with a Lebesgue density and linear subgaussian parameter aaa satisfies

Ent⁡μ(f2)≤Ca2∫∣∇f∣2 dμ(f∈Cc∞(Rn)).\operatorname{Ent}_\mu(f^2)\leq Ca^2\int|\nabla f|^2\,d\mu\qquad(f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)).Entμ​(f2)≤Ca2∫∣∇f∣2dμ(f∈Cc∞​(Rn)).

Here Cc∞C_c^\inftyCc∞​ denotes smooth compactly supported real test functions. The density need not be smooth, strictly positive everywhere, or uniformly curved. Uniform measures on convex bodies are included whenever the stated marginal condition holds.

The manuscript also gives a quadratic transport–entropy consequence. For probability measures with finite second moments, the Wasserstein distance is

W2(ν,μ)2=inf⁡π∫∣x−y∣2 dπ(x,y),W_2(\nu,\mu)^2=\inf_{\pi}\int|x-y|^2\,d\pi(x,y),W2​(ν,μ)2=πinf​∫∣x−y∣2dπ(x,y),

where π\piπ ranges over joint distributions with marginals ν\nuν and μ\muμ. It is the least mean-square cost of moving one distribution to the other.

If ν=fμ\nu=f\muν=fμ, its relative entropy is H(ν∣μ)=∫flog⁡f dμH(\nu\mid\mu)=\int f\log f\,d\muH(ν∣μ)=∫flogfdμ; it is infinite when absolute continuity fails. By the established Otto–Villani implication and an approximation argument, M1 states

W2(ν,μ)2≤Ca2H(ν∣μ).W_2(\nu,\mu)^2\leq Ca^2H(\nu\mid\mu).W2​(ν,μ)2≤Ca2H(ν∣μ).

The same universal coefficient convention is used in the two displayed statements. This consequence compares entire probability distributions, rather than only individual linear projections.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claimed theorem would give a sharp qualitative bridge from one-dimensional marginal tails to a strong global functional inequality throughout the log-concave class. It removes a dimension-dependent gap in a natural conjecture linking convexity, concentration and entropy.

The hypothesis is often easier to interpret than a logarithmic Sobolev inequality. It asks about scalar measurements ⟨X,θ⟩\langle X,\theta\rangle⟨X,θ⟩. The conclusion controls arbitrary smooth nonlinear tests and, through standard consequences, Lipschitz fluctuations and transport costs.

Dimension-free concentration concerns fluctuations around a typical value, not the size of that value. The Euclidean norm of a high-dimensional Gaussian vector is typically of order n\sqrt nn​, even though its deviations have a dimension-independent scale. There is no contradiction between the theorem and growth of the typical radius with dimension.

The result should also be distinguished from conjectures assuming only normalized covariance. A covariance bound controls second moments; the exponential-square condition controls much further into the tails. The manuscript does not assert a universal log-Sobolev constant for every isotropic log-concave measure without this stronger hypothesis.

6. The main idea

Normalize a hypothetical failure

The proof proceeds by contradiction. If no universal ratio between the log-Sobolev coefficient and a2a^2a2 existed, suitable truncation, smoothing and rescaling would produce measures whose log-Sobolev constants stay normalized while their linear subgaussian parameters tend to zero.

The argument then seeks incompatible descriptions of the fluctuations that could sustain such an extremal inequality. It treats separately the case where the entropy constant exceeds the Poincaré constant and the case where they coincide. A Poincaré inequality controls variance rather than entropy; its first nonconstant eigenfunction supplies the relevant object in the second case.

Observe an extremal field through Gaussian noise

From an extremizing function, the manuscript constructs a related probability law and a vector field resembling the gradient of a log-density ratio. Variational equations make that field behave approximately like a first diffusion eigenfunction.

The additional information comes from prediction. Observe a vector after adding independent Gaussian noise, and ask how much of the field can still be recovered by conditional expectation. Matching entropy contraction with a separate entropy-loss comparison forces a specific limiting prediction curve.

Repeated observations of independent copies control the cost of discarding conditional-mean directions. This information step is more restrictive than knowing a spectral estimate alone: it prescribes how predictability must deteriorate across a whole interval of noise levels.

Turn near-equality into too much information

Gaussian polynomial orthogonality converts the prediction curve into a hierarchy of nearly extremal derivative tensors. A tensor is simply a multi-index array, here recording repeated derivatives and their symmetries. Averaging matrix quantities built from these tensors produces a positive matrix field with normalized trace mass.

The symmetries force approximate commutation properties. The manuscript derives a scalar lognormal fluctuation law under a weighted trace, without assuming that all matrices in varying dimensions can be simultaneously diagonalized.

Finally, it considers Gaussian observations whose covariance depends on this matrix field. The log-Sobolev inequality bounds the information such observations can reveal. The derived fluctuation law forces a conflicting lower bound when diffusion time and a covariance cap are enlarged in the prescribed order.

Integrating over observation scales ensures that the contradiction retains matrix mass even when it is spread among many small eigenvalues. The contradiction rules out the normalized sequence of failures and yields existence of a universal constant. It is not a computation of the best constant.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The measure is centered, log-concave and has a density with respect to full-dimensional Lebesgue measure. The theorem as stated is not a direct assertion about arbitrary singular measures or nonconvex mixtures.

The subgaussian bound must hold uniformly over every unit direction. Testing only the coordinate axes is weaker, and controlling covariance alone is weaker still. The parameter aaa may depend on the distribution; dimension-free means no extra dependence on nnn beyond that parameter.

No positive curvature lower bound or density smoothness is required in the final statement. The regularizations used in the proof are part of its argument, not hidden hypotheses imposed on the original measure.

Optimal constants, efficient sampling consequences for a particular access model, and related statements under weaker marginal assumptions are separate questions. The digest reports the manuscript’s theorem and contradiction strategy without verifying its information or tensor estimates.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 states the log-Sobolev and transport inequalities and carefully specifies its entropy conventions. Its introduction outlines the extremal-law construction, prediction identity, tensor hierarchy and information contradiction.

Bizeul’s linked paper is the primary source for the conjecture and earlier dimension-dependent bound. Guo–Shamai–Verdú supplies the Gaussian-channel background. Otto and Villani’s Generalization of an inequality by Talagrand and links with the logarithmic Sobolev inequality (2000), cited in M1, is the source of the transport implication.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A dimension-free logarithmic Sobolev inequality for subgaussian log-concave measures (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Compressing finite Lp data into subpolynomially many coordinates
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 094 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

A collection of data points may live in a space with thousands of coordinates, even when only their pairwise distances matter. Dimension reduction asks whether the points can be repositioned in fewer coordinates while approximately preserving every distance.

For Euclidean distance, the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma gives a remarkable answer: a fixed distortion above one requires only a constant times log⁡n\log nlogn coordinates for nnn points. What remains true when distance is measured by a different LpL^pLp norm?

The manuscript in family 094 claims that, for every fixed 1<p<∞1<p<\infty1<p<∞, a finite nnn-point subset of real LpL^pLp can be embedded into the same type of coordinate space using no(1)n^{o(1)}no(1) dimensions. The distortion may be any fixed number greater than one. The map need not be linear, and that freedom is essential.

2. Background and essential definitions

In ℓpd=Rd\ell_p^d=\mathbb R^dℓpd​=Rd, the norm is

∥x∥p=(∑j=1d∣xj∣p)1/p.\|x\|_p=\left(\sum_{j=1}^d|x_j|^p\right)^{1/p}.∥x∥p​=(j=1∑d​∣xj​∣p)1/p.

An LpL^pLp space replaces the sum by an integral. Its elements may be functions rather than finite coordinate vectors. The target in this theorem is specifically a finite coordinate space with the same exponent ppp.

An embedding of points x1,…,xnx_1,\ldots,x_nx1​,…,xn​ has distortion at most DDD if there are target points yiy_iyi​ and a common scale s>0s>0s>0 such that

s∥xi−xj∥p≤∥yi−yj∥p≤Ds∥xi−xj∥ps\|x_i-x_j\|_p\leq\|y_i-y_j\|_p\leq Ds\|x_i-x_j\|_ps∥xi​−xj​∥p​≤∥yi​−yj​∥p​≤Ds∥xi​−xj​∥p​

for every pair. The common rescaling does not affect distortion. At D=1D=1D=1, all distances are preserved exactly up to that scale.

Let dp(n,D)d_p(n,D)dp​(n,D) be the smallest dimension that works for every such nnn-point set. It is a worst-case quantity: some individual sets, such as points on a line, need far fewer coordinates.

The notation no(1)n^{o(1)}no(1) means growth slower than every fixed positive power of nnn. Equivalently, log⁡d/log⁡n→0\log d/\log n\to0logd/logn→0. It does not mean a bounded dimension or necessarily a logarithmic one. For example, exp⁡(Clog⁡n)\exp(C\sqrt{\log n})exp(Clogn​) is subpolynomial, but eventually exceeds every fixed power of log⁡n\log nlogn.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Johnson and Lindenstrauss’s 1984 paper established the Hilbert-space result and asked about other Banach spaces. Hilbert space corresponds to p=2p=2p=2, where inner products and random linear projections give unusually strong tools.

For exact embeddings, Ball’s Isometric embedding in lᵖ-spaces (1990) gave a coordinate upper bound of (n2)\binom n2(2n​), with quadratic-order sharpness in the range 1≤p<21\leq p<21≤p<2. This bound reflects the number of pairwise distance constraints. Allowing a small distortion can change the problem dramatically.

Below two, Schechtman developed approximate finite-set bounds, eventually reaching a dimension proportional to nnn for fixed parameters. Other classical results discretize an entire finite-dimensional linear subspace of LpL^pLp. Those must preserve every vector in the subspace, whereas the present problem only asks to preserve distances between the selected points.

Linearity creates another restriction. For p≠2p\ne2p=2, fixed-distortion linear maps on some finite configurations require dimension proportional to the number of points. A nonlinear repositioning is not covered by those lower bounds.

At p=1p=1p=1, Brinkman and Charikar’s impossibility theorem obstructs strong dimension reduction even for nonlinear maps. The new theorem excludes that endpoint. For p>2p>2p>2, a 2026 lower bound of Naor and Ren rules out a universal logarithmic coordinate bound at fixed distortion. A subpolynomial upper bound is compatible with that obstruction.

The manuscript’s method uses electrical-flow localization from Gurel-Gurevich, Nachmias and Sachdeva’s 2026 paper, together with empirical sampling ideas going back to Maurey. Its contribution is a relative-error construction uniform over all pairs in an arbitrary finite configuration.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Fix 1<p<∞1<p<\infty1<p<∞, p≠2p\ne2p=2, and define

γ(p)={2−p,1<p<2,1−2/p,2<p<∞.\gamma(p)=\begin{cases}2-p,&1<p<2,\\1-2/p,&2<p<\infty.\end{cases}γ(p)={2−p,1−2/p,​1<p<2,2<p<∞.​

M1 states that for every fixed D>1D>1D>1, a finite constant Cp,DC_{p,D}Cp,D​ exists such that

log⁡nlog⁡(1+2D)≤dp(n,D)≤exp⁡(Cp,D(log⁡n)γ(p)).\frac{\log n}{\log(1+2D)}\leq d_p(n,D)\leq\exp\left(C_{p,D}(\log n)^{\gamma(p)}\right).log(1+2D)logn​≤dp​(n,D)≤exp(Cp,D​(logn)γ(p)).

Because 0<γ(p)<10<\gamma(p)<10<γ(p)<1, the upper bound is subpolynomial. For example, both p=3/2p=3/2p=3/2 and p=4p=4p=4 give the form exp⁡(Cp,Dlog⁡n)\exp(C_{p,D}\sqrt{\log n})exp(Cp,D​logn​). The constants depend on the fixed exponent and distortion.

For exact embeddings with D=1D=1D=1 and p≠2p\ne2p=2, M1 gives quadratic-order lower and upper bounds:

dp(n,1)≍n2.d_p(n,1)\asymp n^2.dp​(n,1)≍n2.

Its lower construction also includes even integers p>2p>2p>2. Thus the logarithmic growth exponent of the necessary dimension changes from two at exact distortion to zero at every fixed distortion strictly above one.

The case p=2p=2p=2 remains governed by the stronger classical bound d2(n,D)=OD(log⁡n)d_2(n,D)=O_D(\log n)d2​(n,D)=OD​(logn) for D>1D>1D>1. The manuscript is an existence theorem and does not claim an efficient algorithm for finding its nonlinear embeddings.

No uniformity is asserted as D↓1D\downarrow1D↓1, p↓1p\downarrow1p↓1, or p→∞p\to\inftyp→∞. One cannot choose these parameters to vary with nnn and retain the same asymptotic conclusion without additional estimates.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claim would establish substantial finite-set dimension reduction throughout the open range 1<p<∞1<p<\infty1<p<∞, while preserving the original exponent of the target norm. It addresses a longstanding extension of the Euclidean phenomenon beyond Hilbert geometry.

The contrast with exact embeddings is particularly sharp. A fixed tolerance, however small, would permit a worst-case coordinate count smaller than every positive power of the data size, whereas exact preservation can require quadratic dimension. The theorem does not say the constants are mild for a tiny tolerance, but it identifies a qualitative asymptotic transition.

The nonlinear nature of the embedding is also informative. A failure of random linear projection does not imply that the finite metric itself needs many coordinates. The points may admit a compact representation after a more flexible rearrangement.

This is a geometric existence result, rather than an immediate data-compression procedure. The upper bound is not claimed optimal, and for p>2p>2p>2 the known lower bounds already show that the Euclidean logarithmic answer cannot simply carry over unchanged.

6. The main idea

Build scalar coordinates through their pairwise increments

A single target coordinate assigns one real label ziz_izi​ to each point. Its normalized increment on a pair is

zi−zj∥xi−xj∥p.\frac{z_i-z_j}{\|x_i-x_j\|_p}.∥xi​−xj​∥p​zi​−zj​​.

Randomly choosing such labels gives random increments. If their ppp-th absolute moments are nearly equal for every pair, then repeated independent samples can serve as coordinates of a distance-preserving embedding.

The increments cannot be chosen independently on all pairs: they must come from one consistent list of vertex labels. Around a cycle, unnormalized differences must telescope to zero. Preserving this consistency is a central geometric constraint.

Replace simultaneous constraints by weighted tests

The manuscript first considers an arbitrary positive weighting of all pairs. It constructs bounded random consistent increments whose weighted average moment error is small. The crucial quantities—the common target moment and the bound on increment size—are uniform over the choice of weights.

A convex-separation argument then turns these weighted tests into one distribution whose moments work for every pair simultaneously. Independent sampling and a concentration estimate supply finitely many coordinates. This is the empirical-method step; the main challenge is constructing the bounded distribution with sufficiently favorable parameters.

Use electrical flows to repair consistency

A projection onto the space of consistent increments is built using a suitable reweighting of the complete graph on the data points. It is contractive in a weighted square norm and has a logarithmic bound in the maximum norm. Electrical-flow localization provides the input for this second estimate, and a fixed-point argument chooses compatible weights.

Below p=2p=2p=2, the random construction starts with symmetric ppp-stable variables, whose distributions interact naturally with LpL^pLp distances. Their heavy tails are clipped to obtain bounded increments. Projection repairs the consistency lost during clipping, while the two norm estimates control the error.

Above p=2p=2p=2, the manuscript uses overlapping magnitude truncations and signed Poisson sampling. The overlap increases useful moment mass relative to projection error. A refined independent-sum moment estimate retains a leading coefficient arbitrarily close to one, which is necessary to allow distortions arbitrarily close to one.

Substituting the resulting moment and magnitude bounds into the sampling estimate produces the stated subpolynomial exponent. The exact-embedding lower bound follows a separate route, using configurations whose equality relations force many disjoint coordinate contributions.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The input is a finite subset of a real LpL^pLp space, and the target is real ℓpd\ell_p^dℓpd​. The map may depend on the entire finite set and need not extend linearly, or even be defined, on the surrounding space.

The number of points nnn is different from the dimension of their linear span. A theorem about all vectors in a subspace cannot be substituted for this finite-distance statement. Conversely, preserving the finite set does not preserve its span.

The endpoint p=1p=1p=1 is excluded, as is p=∞p=\inftyp=∞. For fixed interior ppp, the bound remains subpolynomial but may approach polynomial-looking behavior over finite ranges when ppp is near an endpoint. The theorem gives no practical complexity guarantee.

An infinite doubling subset of Hilbert space may fail to embed into any fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space, as addressed separately in family 098. There is no contradiction: the finite-set dimension bound is allowed to grow with cardinality.

Determining the optimal dimension dependence and constructing efficient embeddings remain further questions. The digest takes the manuscript’s estimates as stated without verifying its probabilistic or electrical-flow arguments.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 states the approximate and exact dimension bounds, develops the weighted-moment criterion, and treats the two exponent ranges separately. Its appendices record the electrical-flow and refined moment estimates used in the construction.

The linked Johnson–Lindenstrauss and Brinkman–Charikar papers mark the classical positive Hilbert result and the negative L1L^1L1 endpoint. Naor’s survey of metric dimension reduction explains the distinctions between finite coordinate targets, arbitrary subspaces and linear embeddings.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Subpolynomial dimension reduction in Lp (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Where hyperbolic optimization goes beyond semidefinite representations
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 095 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Semidefinite programming describes convex constraints by requiring a symmetric matrix, whose entries depend linearly on the variables, to be positive semidefinite. Hyperbolic programming offers another broad source of convex constraints, defined by polynomials with a special real-root property.

Are these two settings ultimately the same after introducing enough extra variables? This family claims that they are not, but its three manuscripts must be distinguished carefully.

M2 constructs a specific cone in twenty-three variables with no direct semidefinite representation. M3 then gives that very cone an exact representation using auxiliary variables. M1 makes a stronger claim about a different, higher-dimensional construction: some hyperbolicity cones have no finite semidefinite lift whatsoever. The positive lift in M3 and the negative theorem in M1 concern different cones and answer different questions.

2. Background and essential definitions

A real symmetric matrix AAA is positive semidefinite, written A⪰0A\succeq0A⪰0, when zTAz≥0z^{\mathsf T}Az\geq0zTAz≥0 for every vector zzz. A spectrahedron is a set described by one finite linear matrix inequality,

A0+x1A1+⋯+xdAd⪰0.A_0+x_1A_1+\cdots+x_dA_d\succeq0.A0​+x1​A1​+⋯+xd​Ad​⪰0.

The matrices are fixed; the coordinates xix_ixi​ are the unknowns. Several inequalities can be combined into one block-diagonal matrix.

A spectrahedral shadow, or set with a finite semidefinite lift, allows auxiliary variables:

S={x:∃u∈Ra,A0+∑ixiAi+∑jujBj⪰0}.S=\left\{x:\exists u\in\mathbb R^a,A_0+\sum_i x_iA_i+\sum_j u_jB_j\succeq0\right\}.S={x:∃u∈Ra,A0​+i∑​xi​Ai​+j∑​uj​Bj​⪰0}.

Geometrically, this projects a higher-dimensional spectrahedron onto the original coordinates. Equality with the projected set is exact; taking its closure is an additional operation not included in the definition.

A homogeneous polynomial ppp is hyperbolic in direction eee if p(e)>0p(e)>0p(e)>0 and, for every xxx, the one-variable polynomial t↦p(te−x)t\mapsto p(te-x)t↦p(te−x) has only real roots. Its closed hyperbolicity cone consists of those xxx for which all these roots are nonnegative.

The determinant on symmetric matrices is the basic example: p(tI−X)=det⁡(tI−X)p(tI-X)=\det(tI-X)p(tI−X)=det(tI−X) has the eigenvalues of XXX as roots, and the cone is exactly the positive semidefinite cone. Gårding’s theory shows that hyperbolicity cones are convex in general, even without a known matrix representation.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The original Lax conjecture concerned homogeneous hyperbolic polynomials in three variables. Helton and Vinnikov’s determinantal theorem, together with the equivalence explained by Lewis, Parrilo and Ramana, gave a positive solution. This success motivated higher-dimensional representation questions.

Two formulations then diverged. A particular polynomial may fail to have a determinantal representation, while its cone could still be described by a different determinant. Brändén gave a real-zero polynomial for which no positive integral power has a definite determinantal representation. Kummer later showed that a related specialized Vámos polynomial nevertheless has a spectrahedral cone. A polynomial obstruction alone therefore does not settle the geometric question.

The generalized Lax conjecture proposes that every hyperbolicity cone is spectrahedral. The weaker Projected Lax Conjecture asks only for a finite semidefinite lift. Netzer and Sanyal’s Smooth hyperbolicity cones are spectrahedral shadows (2015) established liftability under a smoothness condition at every nonzero boundary point of the defining polynomial.

Other positive results cover elementary symmetric cones, particular low-degree cases, and stricter regularity hypotheses. Scheiderer’s smooth-cone result gives second-order-cone lifts under a Nash-smooth boundary condition. Such results leave singular cones outside their assumptions.

For general convex semialgebraic sets, Scheiderer had already developed obstructions to semidefinite lifts using local positivity and sums of squares. M1 adapts that broad strategy to hyperbolicity cones. M2 uses the classical Choi–Lam nonnegative biquadratic form for a direct-representation obstruction, while M3 shows concretely how a lift can bypass that obstruction.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A cone with no finite lift

M1 states that there exists a real homogeneous hyperbolic polynomial whose closed hyperbolicity cone is not a spectrahedral shadow. It excludes every finite matrix size, every finite number of auxiliary variables and arbitrary real coefficients in an affine pencil.

This is a nonexistence theorem for exact finite representations, not merely a lower bound saying that a representation must be large. If correct, it disproves the Projected Lax Conjecture and consequently the stronger generalized Lax conjecture.

The construction is high-dimensional. It is distinct from the explicit twenty-three-variable example in the other two manuscripts.

A smaller explicit obstruction to direct representation

M2 defines symmetric 4×44\times44×4 matrix variables X,ZX,ZX,Z and a vector y∈R3y\in\mathbb R^3y∈R3, for a total of twenty-three real coordinates. A quadratic matrix map derived from the Choi–Lam form enters a determinant formula producing a degree-twenty hyperbolic polynomial.

The manuscript claims that its cone has no finite homogeneous symmetric linear matrix representation in those original coordinates. It then removes a determinant factor, obtaining a degree-sixteen homogeneous polynomial with the same hyperbolicity cone. Neither the variable count nor the degree is claimed minimal.

For a cone containing zero, a direct affine representation can be homogenized by scaling along rays, so the obstruction also rules out direct affine pencils. It does not, by itself, rule out auxiliary variables.

An exact lift of that same explicit cone

M3 states that the cone from M2 has a homogeneous real symmetric lift with a matrix of size 100100100 and 307307307 auxiliary variables:

x∈K⟺∃v∈R307,∑ν=123xνAν+∑j=1307vjBj⪰0.x\in K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists v\in\mathbb R^{307},\sum_{\nu=1}^{23}x_\nu A_\nu+\sum_{j=1}^{307}v_jB_j\succeq0.x∈K⟺∃v∈R307,ν=1∑23​xν​Aν​+j=1∑307​vj​Bj​⪰0.

The equivalence holds on the entire closed cone, including points where XXX is singular. The stated sizes are upper bounds, not optimality claims. M3 uses M2’s nonrepresentation theorem to highlight the distinction, but presents the lift construction itself as self-contained.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The strongest claim would place a fundamental limit on representing hyperbolic optimization exactly by finite semidefinite programs. Auxiliary variables can greatly expand the expressive power of matrix inequalities, so excluding every finite lift is a substantial structural statement.

The explicit pair M2–M3 is also instructive. It shows why one must ask whether an obstruction concerns a particular polynomial, a direct representation of its cone, or every possible lifted representation. These are successively stronger demands, and failure at one level need not imply failure at the next.

The result does not say hyperbolic optimization is computationally hopeless. Hyperbolicity cones have their own barrier theory and optimization methods. Nor does absence of an exact finite lift prevent semidefinite approximations, converging hierarchies or useful representations of particular slices.

The score reflects the broad conjectural separation and the concrete illustration of representation power. It does not claim a minimal-dimensional counterexample or an algorithmic lower bound for every optimization task over the constructed cones.

6. The main idea

Start with positivity that resists a square decomposition

M2 begins with a nonnegative biquadratic form b(z,y)=zTQ(y)zb(z,y)=z^{\mathsf T}Q(y)zb(z,y)=zTQ(y)z. It is quadratic in each group of variables. The selected Choi–Lam form has a rigid property: if the square of a bilinear form is everywhere bounded above by bbb, that bilinear form must vanish.

A determinant construction turns Q(y)⪰0Q(y)\succeq0Q(y)⪰0 into a hyperbolic polynomial. For each fixed yyy, a Gram factorization gives a symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues describe the roots along the hyperbolicity direction. The factorization is chosen separately at each yyy; it is not already a linear pencil in all variables jointly.

Assuming an arbitrary direct pencil existed, rescaling and rank-one limits would produce an operator-norm identity for its kernel projections. Differentiating that identity yields bilinear squares dominated by bbb. The special positivity property forces those terms to vanish, contradicting the identity. The argument targets any hypothetical pencil rather than comparing one determinant with the defining polynomial.

A lift can recover the explicit cone through angular slices

M3 slices the yyy-space by planes parameterized by an angle. On each plane, the quadratic matrix has a factorization linear in the two plane coordinates and trigonometric in the angle. This gives a size-twenty pencil for each slice.

The continuously varying angle is replaced by a finite linear functional on trigonometric polynomials. Requiring nonnegativity on a bounded-degree family of quadratic tests becomes one finite matrix inequality. Evaluation at a single angle immediately supplies feasible lift data for points of the cone.

The converse is harder: a positive functional need not come from evaluation at an angle or from an actual measure. A degree-two matching identity provides enough tests to recover the slice inequalities for every feasible functional. At singular XXX, the same tests enforce the necessary range conditions, which is why the result represents the closed boundary exactly rather than only the interior or a closure of a projection.

Exclude all lifts with a different local obstruction

M1 builds a different positive quadratic matrix map using finite-dimensional spaces of polynomials and Hankel moment matrices. Such a matrix records a linear functional applied to products of lower-degree polynomials. Positivity on squares need not mean that the functional is integration against a measure.

The construction produces an affine section and projection of a hyperbolicity cone with a carefully designed positivity obstruction. A finite positive moment functional applied to a small polynomial patch creates a violation of order four in a scale parameter.

A hypothetical finite lift would supply local analytic lift coordinates and Gram factors. Applying the same functional to their Taylor expansions nearly preserves feasibility. The manuscript then repairs the much smaller residual error on the common matrix support, without assuming strict feasibility. The repaired feasible point would remain too close to the violating patch to eliminate the order-four discrepancy.

This contradiction is the claimed obstruction to every finite lift. The finite-field and moment calculations described in the source are components of its construction; they have not been rerun as proof checks for this digest.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The three conclusions should be read together: the explicit twenty-three-variable cone has no direct pencil but does have a lift; the no-lift theorem concerns another construction. M3 therefore refines the understanding of M2 rather than overturning its direct-representation claim.

All representations are finite and exact over the reals. Arbitrarily many but finitely many auxiliary variables are allowed in M1’s negative theorem. Approximation by semidefinite sets and infinite limiting constructions are outside that conclusion.

Smooth or strictly hyperbolic positive results have hypotheses that the counterexamples need not satisfy. Singular boundary behavior is central to the obstruction mechanisms. The sources do not claim the smallest possible degree, dimension or lift size.

M2 discusses a conflicting general positive claim in an appendix. The digest does not adjudicate that argument; it reports the present manuscripts’ stated results and keeps the logical distinction between direct and projected representations explicit.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 is the source for the no-finite-lift theorem. M2 gives the explicit polynomial, degree reduction and direct-pencil obstruction. M3 gives the size-100 lift and its exact treatment of singular boundary points.

Helton–Vinnikov’s Linear matrix inequality representation of sets (2007) and Lewis–Parrilo–Ramana’s The Lax conjecture is true (2005) provide the three-variable background. Choi–Lam’s Extremal positive semidefinite forms (1977), Netzer–Sanyal’s smooth-cone theorem and Scheiderer’s work supply the main positivity and representation precedents cited by the family.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Hyperbolicity Cones Without Semidefinite Lifts (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A nonspectrahedral hyperbolicity cone (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, An Exact Semidefinite Lift of a Nonspectrahedral Hyperbolicity Cone (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A compact metric set that still needs infinitely many dimensions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 098 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

A set may sit in an infinite-dimensional space while having very modest local complexity. Suppose every ball in the set can be covered by a fixed number of balls of half the radius. Does that mean the set can be represented faithfully in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space?

For subsets of Hilbert space, this is the Lang–Plaut problem. The hypothesis already provides Euclidean-style distances, just with infinitely many possible coordinates. The issue is whether a uniform covering bound makes infinitely many coordinates unnecessary.

The manuscript in family 098 claims a negative answer. It first constructs one doubling subset of Hilbert space that has no finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embedding at any finite distortion. It then turns finite pieces of that obstruction into a compact example inside every infinite-dimensional real Banach space.

Compactness does not remove the difficulty: the claimed obstruction can be bounded and contain all its limit points, with increasingly intricate configurations appearing at smaller and smaller scales.

2. Background and essential definitions

A metric space (X,d)(X,d)(X,d) is doubling with constant λ\lambdaλ if every ball of radius rrr can be covered by at most λ\lambdaλ balls of radius r/2r/2r/2, centered in XXX. The same number works at every location and scale.

Repeatedly applying this condition gives a polynomial bound on covering numbers as the radius shrinks. It is a notion of finite metric complexity, but does not prescribe a coordinate system or a differentiable structure.

A map f:X→Rkf:X\to\mathbb R^kf:X→Rk is bi-Lipschitz with distortion at most DDD if some a>0a>0a>0 satisfies

a d(x,y)≤∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤Da d(x,y)a\,d(x,y)\leq|f(x)-f(y)|\leq Da\,d(x,y)ad(x,y)≤∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤Dad(x,y)

for all pairs. The lower bound prevents collapsing distinct points; the upper bound prevents excessive stretching. Both kkk and DDD must be finite, but they need not be prescribed in advance.

A Hilbert space has a norm coming from an inner product. The sequence space ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​, with ∑jxj2<∞\sum_jx_j^2<\infty∑j​xj2​<∞, is the standard infinite-dimensional example. A Banach space is a complete normed vector space and need not have an inner product.

A set is compact if every sequence in it has a convergent subsequence with limit in the set. For an infinite-dimensional ambient space, boundedness and closedness alone do not guarantee compactness; the final construction explicitly arranges shrinking finite clusters to obtain it.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Lang and Plaut asked the Hilbert-subset question in Bilipschitz embeddings of metric spaces into space forms (2001). Gupta, Krauthgamer and Lee independently raised it in an algorithmic dimension-reduction context.

Assouad’s embedding theorem gives a positive result after changing the metric. If 0<α<10<\alpha<10<α<1, the snowflake distance d(x,y)αd(x,y)^\alphad(x,y)α on a doubling space admits a finite-dimensional Euclidean bi-Lipschitz embedding. This power expands small distances relative to large ones. It does not preserve the original metric up to a uniform factor across arbitrarily small scales.

Naor and Neiman’s dimension-independent snowflaking theorem bounds the target dimension in terms of the doubling constant alone when α\alphaα is near one. Its distortion still depends on α\alphaα. One cannot simply let α→1\alpha\to1α→1 and conclude a bounded-distortion embedding of the original distance.

For ambient LpL^pLp spaces with p>2p>2p>2, Lafforgue and Naor constructed doubling sets that resist finite-dimensional Euclidean embeddings. Bartal, Gottlieb and Neiman obtained related obstructions through thin Laakso configurations, and later work gave an elementary fixed-set version. Those results leave the Hilbert exponent p=2p=2p=2 untreated.

The source also records a 2017 announcement by Schioppa, subsequently withdrawn after a possible problem in its duality argument. It is historical context, not an established solution used by M1.

The new manuscript uses ordinary differentiation on planar sheets and a packing contradiction. Its compact Banach-space extension then invokes the classical Dvoretzky theorem, which supplies almost Euclidean finite-dimensional subspaces inside every infinite-dimensional Banach space.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 first states that there is a fixed subset SSS of real ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​, with its inherited Hilbert distance, whose doubling constant is at most 76 80076\,80076800, such that no embedding

S⟶RkS\longrightarrow\mathbb R^kS⟶Rk

is bi-Lipschitz for any positive integer kkk and any finite distortion. The set is chosen once; it is not reconstructed after the target dimension or distortion is announced.

A later corollary strengthens the setting in another direction. There is a universal finite constant Λ\LambdaΛ such that every infinite-dimensional real Banach space BBB contains a compact subset KBK_BKB​ that is Λ\LambdaΛ-doubling and has no finite-distortion bi-Lipschitz embedding into any finite-dimensional real normed space.

The compact set may depend on BBB, but its covering constant has a bound independent of BBB. The explicit 76 80076\,80076800 bound belongs to the initial Hilbert construction; the compact assembly uses a larger universal bound. No optimality of these constants is claimed.

M1 also observes that the original Hilbert metric can be realized isometrically in real Lp([0,1])L^p([0,1])Lp([0,1]) for each 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty1≤p<∞, using normalized Gaussian series. A linear combination of independent standard Gaussians has its ppp-th moment proportional to the corresponding Euclidean norm to the power ppp, which supplies this isometry.

The no-embedding conclusion allows arbitrary nonlinear maps. It is not merely an obstruction to linear projection or to one proposed coordinate-selection algorithm.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claim would answer a longstanding basic question about the relationship between metric covering complexity and Euclidean dimension. Doubling is a strong uniform local restriction, yet it would not suffice to compress a Hilbert subset into any finite-dimensional target while preserving the original metric up to a fixed factor.

The compact extension makes the separation particularly clear. The obstruction does not require points escaping to infinity. Instead, finite difficulties accumulate near one limit point, each at a smaller scale. A target that succeeds at every scale simultaneously would have to overcome all of them with one dimension and one distortion.

This fits consistently with finite-set dimension reduction. For any finite collection, a dimension bound may grow with its cardinality. The theorem here asks for one finite target for the entire infinite set. No single bound is forced by applying finite-set theorems to larger and larger pieces.

The Banach-space conclusion also shows that the phenomenon is not peculiar to one carefully selected ambient norm. Dvoretzky’s theorem lets the finite Hilbert obstructions be placed, with controlled distortion, in every infinite-dimensional real Banach space.

6. The main idea

Add many possible directions at widely separated scales

The first construction starts with a base plane. At level jjj, use a small scale rj=1000−jr_j=1000^{-j}rj​=1000−j and a collection of new mutually orthogonal directions. Horizontal and vertical strips are periodically colored. A base point is allowed to acquire a displacement in a color’s direction when it belongs to a strip of that color.

Points carry only finitely many such displacements. The color counts and strip aspect ratios are fixed in advance so that every pair of positive integer choices recurs infinitely often.

Despite unboundedly many colors across the construction, the set remains doubling. At a given observation radius, coarse displacement coordinates are fixed, fine coordinates have very small total diameter, and at most one intermediate level contributes a nontrivial choice of labels. Only a bounded number of its strips meet the local base region. This gives a uniform covering count.

A finite target would force too many separated offsets

Suppose a bi-Lipschitz embedding into Rk\mathbb R^kRk existed with distortion DDD. Fixing displacement coordinates and varying the base point produces a planar sheet. Its image is a Lipschitz map on an open subset of R2\mathbb R^2R2, so ordinary almost-everywhere differentiation applies.

The proof examines the two derivative columns across all sheets. It first maximizes the squared size of the horizontal column and then maximizes the vertical one among limiting horizontal maximizers. Near this ordered extremum, a nearly maximal mean derivative has little mean-square variation.

Choose a color count larger than the number of well-separated points that can fit into a radius-DDD ball in Rk\mathbb R^kRk. Recurring levels with increasingly wide strips let the argument find one horizontal and one vertical line of each color on which relative sheet offsets are nearly constant.

At crossings of differently colored lines, orthogonal source displacements remain separated. Transporting the nearly constant offsets to selected intersections produces too many separated vectors in the bounded target ball. Finite-dimensional volume packing contradicts that possibility.

The source carefully uses different error estimates in the two coordinate directions, because the horizontal lines grow longer as the strip aspect ratio increases. The fixed construction contains all required recurring scales before the hypothetical embedding is chosen.

Assemble finite obstructions into a compact set

If every finite subset of SSS embedded into one fixed Rk\mathbb R^kRk with one fixed distortion, a compactness argument would produce an embedding of all of SSS. Therefore finite witnesses already exist against each prescribed dimension and distortion.

For each integer jjj, select a finite witness against dimension jjj and distortion jjj. Dvoretzky’s theorem places its finite Hilbert span inside BBB with distortion below two. Scale these copies into tiny clusters near points at distances 2−j2^{-j}2−j along a fixed ray, then add the origin.

The clusters shrink to the origin, making the union compact. A ball meets only boundedly many clusters of comparable size; all much smaller clusters fit into one small ball near zero. This preserves a universal doubling bound. Any finite-dimensional embedding of the union would restrict to an embedding of a sufficiently demanding witness, contradicting its choice.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem preserves the original induced metric up to a multiplicative factor. Snowflaking changes that metric, so Assouad-type positive results remain compatible with the claimed obstruction.

The initial explicit Hilbert set and the final compact Banach-space set are different constructions. The latter has a universal but larger doubling bound and may depend on the ambient Banach space. Neither depends on a subsequently proposed target dimension or distortion.

Finite-dimensional normed targets are covered because any two norms on a fixed finite-dimensional space are equivalent with a finite factor. Infinite-dimensional targets, of course, remain possible: the sets already live in them.

The result does not rule out positive dimension reduction under additional geometric assumptions beyond doubling, or for finite data with dimension growing with sample size. Determining which extra conditions restore a finite-dimensional embedding remains a natural direction.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 supplies the sparse-scale Hilbert construction, derivative obstruction, Gaussian realization and compact Banach-space assembly. Its last section separates the finite-witness argument from the use of Dvoretzky’s theorem.

The linked Lang–Plaut paper states the original geometric context. Naor–Neiman explains what snowflaking can recover. The finite-set comparison in family 094 concerns a different quantifier: its target dimension may grow with the number of points.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A doubling Hilbert subset with no finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embedding (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Keeping every partial sum of a vector sequence under control
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 097 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Imagine following a sequence of short steps in Rd\mathbb R^dRd. You may reverse the direction of each step, but must keep their prescribed order. Can you choose the reversals so that the entire walk stays near the origin, however long the sequence is?

A related problem starts with steps whose total is zero. This time the directions are fixed, but you may reorder the steps. Can every intermediate position remain close to the origin?

Family 097 contains one manuscript claiming a bound of order d\sqrt dd​ for both problems when every step has Euclidean length at most one. The same signs or permutation must control all prefixes simultaneously. The total number of steps does not appear in the bound.

The rearrangement statement resolves the Euclidean Steinitz–Bergström growth question as formulated in the source. A regular simplex shows that the square-root dependence on dimension cannot be improved in order.

2. Background and essential definitions

For vectors v1,…,vNv_1,\ldots,v_Nv1​,…,vN​, a prefix sum uses the first kkk terms for some 0≤k≤N0\leq k\leq N0≤k≤N. The empty prefix is zero.

In the signed problem, choose εi∈{−1,1}\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}εi​∈{−1,1} and control

max⁡0≤k≤N∣∑i=1kεivi∣2.\max_{0\leq k\leq N}\left|\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_iv_i\right|_2.0≤k≤Nmax​​i=1∑k​εi​vi​​2​.

There is no zero-total assumption here. Each vector is either kept or reversed, and the order stays fixed.

In the rearrangement problem, assume ∑ivi=0\sum_i v_i=0∑i​vi​=0, choose a permutation π\piπ, and control

max⁡0≤k≤N∣∑i=1kvπ(i)∣2.\max_{0\leq k\leq N}\left|\sum_{i=1}^kv_{\pi(i)}\right|_2.0≤k≤Nmax​​i=1∑k​vπ(i)​​2​.

The Euclidean Steinitz constant S2(d)S_2(d)S2​(d) is the worst, over all finite zero-sum families in the unit ball, of the smallest possible maximum prefix norm. Indexed families are used so that repetitions count as distinct entries to be permuted.

A terminal balancing theorem controls only the final signed sum. It is weaker in its quantifiers: choosing a good signing separately for every prefix may give incompatible choices. The present question asks for one signing that works for every stopping time along the prescribed list.

The theorem is also offline. The signs may be chosen using the complete sequence. An online rule would have to choose a sign before seeing later vectors and is a different requirement.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Steinitz’s rearrangement theory grew from questions about conditionally convergent vector series. For general norms in dimension ddd, Grinberg and Sevast’yanov proved a bound of ddd times the unit ball. Euclidean geometry suggests a smaller square-root scale, discussed in classical work including Behrend’s 1954 account and recorded in modern form by Ambrus and Heck.

Prescribed-order signing has its own history. Banaszczyk’s work on signed vector series gave a bound with a dimension term and an additional dependence on sequence length. Bansal, Jiang, Meka, Singla and Sinha’s prefix-discrepancy paper explicitly formulates the square-root-dimensional conjecture.

A 2026 preprint by Dutta, Jha and Jiang gives an efficient bound of the form

O(d+d1/4log⁡7/4N)O\left(\sqrt d+d^{1/4}\log^{7/4}N\right)O(d​+d1/4log7/4N)

for signing, with a corresponding ordering result. M1 claims to remove the length term entirely, while making no efficient-algorithm assertion.

Chobanyan’s transference principle links signing and rearrangement. The finite form used here places positively signed vectors in their original order and negatively signed vectors in reverse order. This established principle turns a signed-prefix theorem into the zero-sum ordering theorem.

The analytic construction draws on Gaussian vector balancing and more recent directional-density and symmetrization methods. The manuscript credits Guo, Fang and Lu’s directional total-variation approach, related Dirichlet-energy formulations, and Gaussian correlation. These methods concern finding a compatible set of signs, not merely applying a final-sum theorem separately at each prefix.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that an absolute constant CCC exists such that, for every d,N≥1d,N\geq1d,N≥1 and every sequence with ∣vi∣2≤1|v_i|_2\leq1∣vi​∣2​≤1, there are signs satisfying

max⁡0≤k≤N∣∑i=1kεivi∣2≤Cd.\max_{0\leq k\leq N}\left|\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i v_i\right|_2\leq C\sqrt d.0≤k≤Nmax​​i=1∑k​εi​vi​​2​≤Cd​.

The same constant gives, for every zero-sum family, a permutation with

max⁡0≤k≤N∣∑i=1kvπ(i)∣2≤Cd.\max_{0\leq k\leq N}\left|\sum_{i=1}^kv_{\pi(i)}\right|_2\leq C\sqrt d.0≤k≤Nmax​​i=1∑k​vπ(i)​​2​≤Cd​.

Consequently the source states

12d≤S2(d)≤Cd.\frac12\sqrt d\leq S_2(d)\leq C\sqrt d.21​d​≤S2​(d)≤Cd​.

The lower example uses the d+1d+1d+1 unit vertices of a regular simplex centered at the origin. Distinct vertices have inner product −1/d-1/d−1/d, so any sum of kkk of them has squared norm k(d+1−k)/dk(d+1-k)/dk(d+1−k)/d, independently of their order. A prefix containing about half the vertices must therefore have square-root-dimensional size.

Norm comparison gives a further consequence for ℓpd\ell_p^dℓpd​, 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty1≤p≤∞: unit-ball inputs admit signed prefixes, and zero-sum inputs admit reordered prefixes, bounded by

Cdmax⁡{1/p, 1−1/p}.C d^{\max\{1/p,\,1-1/p\}}.Cdmax{1/p,1−1/p}.

The source claims sharp dimensional order for 1≤p≤21\leq p\leq21≤p≤2, not throughout the entire range above two.

There is also a colorful array version. If unit vectors are arranged in equally long rows and their global total is zero, each row can be permuted so that the aggregate of the first mmm entries of every row has norm at most 2Cd2C\sqrt d2Cd​, simultaneously for all mmm. Individual rows need not sum to zero, and the bound concerns their combined synchronous prefixes.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The result would settle the optimal dimensional order of a classical Euclidean rearrangement problem and the stronger prescribed-order signing question. The improvement is uniform in sequence length, including sequences much longer than any fixed function of dimension.

Uniform control of all prefixes is useful whenever a cumulative process may be stopped at an arbitrary stage. A small final total does not prevent a large excursion in the middle. The claimed theorem prevents those excursions through one globally coordinated choice.

The transference also clarifies the relationship between two kinds of freedom. Reversing steps in a fixed order and reordering zero-sum steps are different operations, yet the signed estimate is strong enough to control the ordering problem with the same constant.

The score reflects a substantial classical resolution and its balancing consequences. It does not imply an optimal numerical constant, an online strategy, or a polynomial-time implementation. The constructive length-dependent predecessors retain algorithmic advantages not asserted by this existence theorem.

6. The main idea

Encode all prefixes in one convex body

The proof introduces a coefficient space with one coordinate for each incoming vector, together with initial-state coordinates. Linear maps turn these coefficients into a sequence of states in Rd\mathbb R^dRd.

Each update contracts the old state and injects a multiple of the next vector. Requiring every state to remain in a prescribed ball defines a symmetric convex body in the larger coefficient space. One point of that body will encode a signing controlling the whole walk.

The contractions initially change the desired partial sums. A carefully chosen scalar shift in each incoming coefficient compensates for the lost part of the previous state. When the coefficients are finally selected in the allowed shifted-sign form, the resulting states become the actual signed prefix sums.

Turn low energy into compatible signed steps

The first analytic ingredient concerns Dirichlet energy, an integral of squared derivatives. If the coefficient body has sufficiently small energy in every positively weighted coordinate direction, the manuscript constructs one square root of a probability density whose coordinate derivatives are all controlled.

A lifted Steiner symmetrization preserves those estimates. It then permits a coordinate choice of the form q+εq+\varepsilonq+ε, where ∣q∣≤1/4|q|\leq1/4∣q∣≤1/4 and ε∈{−1,1}\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}ε∈{−1,1}. The shift may depend on earlier choices and is designed to cancel the state contraction.

This produces one compatible sequence of choices. It is stronger than showing that each individual coordinate can be selected successfully in isolation.

Bound energy without paying for the number of states

The second ingredient estimates survival of a stationary Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process in coefficient space. This is a Gaussian diffusion with a restoring drift, so its stationary distribution is Gaussian. Survival probabilities in a region are related to its Dirichlet-energy scale.

The states are organized by dyadic spectral scales of their covariance matrices. A matrix-variation estimate controls changes by an additive trace budget, even when the contractions do not commute. At each scale, groups with bounded accumulated energy retain a uniform positive probability of satisfying all their constraints over a matched time interval.

Gaussian correlation combines the groups and scales. The resulting exponential survival rate gives an energy bound independent of how many filters or prefixes occur. That independence is what removes the sequence-length term.

For the final transfer to rearrangement, start from an ordering with optimal maximum β\betaβ. If AjA_jAj​ and BjB_jBj​ are its ordinary and signed prefix sums, the positive and negative selections have sums (Aj+Bj)/2(A_j+B_j)/2(Aj​+Bj​)/2 and (Aj−Bj)/2(A_j-B_j)/2(Aj​−Bj​)/2. Positive-forward, negative-reverse ordering therefore gives maximum at most (β+Cd)/2(\beta+C\sqrt d)/2(β+Cd​)/2. Minimality of β\betaβ yields β≤Cd\beta\leq C\sqrt dβ≤Cd​.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The signing theorem allows arbitrary finite sequences of Euclidean unit-ball vectors, with no zero-total assumption. The permutation theorem requires total zero and changes no vector signs. Repetitions and zero vectors are allowed in both.

The existence choices can depend on the full input. A proof that selects signs successively after global preparation does not automatically yield an online rule. The source also makes no efficient-algorithm claim.

The Euclidean square-root bound is not a constant ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ bound for all prefixes. The stated norm-comparison consequence gives order ddd at p=∞p=\inftyp=∞. Similarly, the colorful statement controls the aggregate across rows, not each row individually.

The sharp numerical constant and the strongest algorithmic or other-norm variants remain separate questions. The digest follows the source’s Gaussian-energy strategy and dependencies without checking the analytic estimates.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 states the signing and ordering theorems, gives the simplex lower example, and proves the transference immediately in its introduction. Its final section records the ℓp\ell_pℓp​ and colorful consequences with their precise quantifiers.

The linked prefix-discrepancy and 2026 constructive papers explain earlier sequence-length dependence. Chobanyan’s rearrangement principle and Bárány’s A matrix version of the Steinitz lemma (2024), cited in M1, supply the earlier transference mechanisms used for the ordering and array consequences.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Euclidean Steinitz–Bergström theorem (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The unavoidable distortion when edit distance is represented in L1
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 099 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Edit distance measures how many insertions, deletions and substitutions turn one string into another. It captures sequence alignment rather than coordinatewise disagreement: deleting one symbol moves every later position at once.

Can a single assignment of numerical coordinates to strings reproduce all these distances approximately using an ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ distance, the sum of absolute coordinate differences? Such an embedding would turn a complicated alignment metric into a familiar geometric one.

The three manuscripts in family 099 claim that a substantial amount of distortion is unavoidable. Their lower bounds reach the exponential scale of the classical Ostrovsky–Rabani upper bound. They also supply binary coding constructions and uniform treatments of all strings below a length cap, including the empty string.

The result concerns one embedding that works for every pair in a whole domain. It is not a lower bound on the time needed to compute or approximate edit distance for one supplied pair.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let Σ\SigmaΣ be a finite alphabet with at least two symbols. Ordinary edit distance ED⁡(x,y)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)ED(x,y) gives cost one to each single-symbol insertion, deletion or substitution. Write Σ≤d\Sigma^{\leq d}Σ≤d for all words of length at most ddd, including the empty word. The length cap restricts the endpoint words, not intermediate strings in an edit script.

An injective map fff into real ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ has distortion at most DDD if a common rescaling places every image distance between ED⁡(x,y)/D\operatorname{ED}(x,y)/DED(x,y)/D and ED⁡(x,y)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)ED(x,y). Equivalently, its expansion factor multiplied by its inverse-contraction factor is at most DDD.

Let EΣ(d)E_\Sigma(d)EΣ​(d) be the smallest possible distortion on Σ≤d\Sigma^{\leq d}Σ≤d. There is no restriction on target dimension or the cost of computing the map. A lower bound therefore applies even to an enormous, computationally impractical coordinate representation.

A useful related metric permits only insertions and deletions. If LCS⁡(x,y)\operatorname{LCS}(x,y)LCS(x,y) is the length of a longest common subsequence, then

Δ(x,y)=∣x∣+∣y∣−2LCS⁡(x,y),ED⁡(x,y)≤Δ(x,y)≤2ED⁡(x,y).\Delta(x,y)=|x|+|y|-2\operatorname{LCS}(x,y),\qquad \operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq\Delta(x,y)\leq2\operatorname{ED}(x,y).Δ(x,y)=∣x∣+∣y∣−2LCS(x,y),ED(x,y)≤Δ(x,y)≤2ED(x,y).

A common subsequence is an increasing matching of equal symbols, with no requirement that they occupy corresponding positions. This matching viewpoint is crucial: a proposed lower bound must survive every possible alignment, including alignments that cross the construction’s intended block boundaries.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Levenshtein’s coding work introduced the classical insertion–deletion setting. Wagner and Fischer’s string-correction paper described edit scripts through increasing traces, connecting distance to alignment structure.

Ostrovsky and Rabani’s low-distortion embedding theorem gave an upper bound of the form

exp⁡(O(log⁡d log⁡log⁡d))\exp\left(O\left(\sqrt{\log d\,\log\log d}\right)\right)exp(O(logdloglogd​))

for fixed-length binary strings, using recursive comparisons of overlapping substrings. They also noted larger-alphabet and varying-length extensions. The new family credits this upper scale rather than presenting it as newly discovered.

The earlier lower bounds were much smaller. Andoni, Deza, Gupta, Indyk and Raskhodnikova produced binary subsets with distortion approaching 3/23/23/2. Khot and Naor’s Fourier nonembedding methods gave a growing lower bound through noisy shifts and cuts. Krauthgamer and Rabani’s 2009 theorem improved it to order log⁡d\log dlogd.

Alphabet reduction developed alongside insertion–deletion codes and synchronization strings. Replacing each symbol by a binary block must prevent a clever alignment from matching unrelated portions of neighboring blocks. Bhattacharya, Dey, Goldenberg and Koucký’s Many flavors of edit distance supplies a relevant normalized-distance conversion. The present manuscripts give additional direct coding arguments with carefully different length guarantees.

The main claimed advance is the stronger lower scale, together with complete uniform statements over finite alphabets and endpoint lengths. Several independent lower constructions reach the same order after taking logarithms.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

There are absolute constants c,C>0c,C>0c,C>0 and a threshold d0d_0d0​ such that, for every d≥d0d\geq d_0d≥d0​ and every finite alphabet ∣Σ∣≥2|\Sigma|\geq2∣Σ∣≥2,

exp⁡(clog⁡d log⁡log⁡d)≤EΣ(d)≤exp⁡(Clog⁡d log⁡log⁡d).\exp\left(c\sqrt{\log d\,\log\log d}\right)\leq E_\Sigma(d)\leq\exp\left(C\sqrt{\log d\,\log\log d}\right).exp(clogdloglogd​)≤EΣ​(d)≤exp(Clogdloglogd​).

The constants are independent of alphabet size, even when the alphabet grows with ddd. This determines

log⁡EΣ(d)=Θ(log⁡d log⁡log⁡d).\log E_\Sigma(d)=\Theta\left(\sqrt{\log d\,\log\log d}\right).logEΣ​(d)=Θ(logdloglogd​).

It does not give a constant-factor estimate for EΣ(d)E_\Sigma(d)EΣ​(d) itself. Different constants inside an exponential can leave a large multiplicative gap.

M1 gives a marked-row lower construction using finite groups with distinct prime periods. Its upper proof invokes the classical fixed-length theorem and adds uniform alphabet reduction, padding and averaging.

M2 gives two finite-circle lower constructions and two direct binary substitutions of width O(log⁡(2A))O(\log(2A))O(log(2A)) for an alphabet of size AAA. Their distortion is bounded by an absolute constant on equal-length words, simultaneously over all common lengths. It also develops a deterministic finite-dimensional histogram embedding for the uniform upper bound. “Deterministic finite-dimensional” does not by itself assert an efficient algorithm or a small target dimension.

M3 gives two independent tree-based lower constructions. Each yields binary words of one common length at most ddd, for every sufficiently large cap, not merely a sparse sequence of caps. Its two-sided conclusion uses M2’s upper theorem. An appendix separately gives a constant-distortion binary conversion for one prescribed input length MMM, over at most MMM symbols, with block width M2M^2M2; that stronger fixed-length conversion is not needed for its headline lower bounds.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claimed lower bound would close a major scale gap in a central metric-embedding problem. It grows faster than every fixed power of log⁡d\log dlogd, while remaining subpolynomial in ddd, and matches the logarithm of the established upper scale.

The restriction to binary strings of one common length makes the obstruction robust. Neither a large alphabet nor variable lengths are necessary to force the distortion. Larger domains inherit the same difficulty because they contain these binary witnesses.

The upper quantifiers are equally useful. One bound works over every finite alphabet, includes the empty word, and controls every pair in the length-capped domain. These details matter when translating a theorem between coding conventions or applications.

The result limits the quality of universal ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ representations. It does not preclude accurate pairwise distance algorithms, specialized embeddings for restricted datasets, or representations in other target geometries. The importance score reflects the geometric resolution rather than an unclaimed computational lower bound.

6. The main idea

Make some large rearrangements cheap and another displacement expensive

At each level, the lower constructions assemble a word from rows of shorter words. Different slots carry different alphabet tags, preventing matches between unrelated slots. State changes can shift the row list by one, costing only the deletion and insertion of a boundary row.

Other state changes are designed to remain expensive. Distinct prime periods ensure that a row shift cannot align too many components simultaneously. M1 emphasizes one component by repeating it in separately tagged slots. M2 uses phase points on a finite circle and a simultaneous half-turn. M3 organizes analogous obstructions through nested-period or circle-phase trees.

Charge every alignment that crosses rows

It is not enough to compare intended row pairs. An optimal subsequence matching may split one source row across several target rows.

The constructions control this explicitly. If a source row stays within one target row, it inherits lower-level separation. If it splits, the ordered tags or a long marker force a substantial unmatched target interval between consecutive matches. The charged intervals from different source rows are disjoint.

This accounting transfers local separation to the whole word without assuming that an alignment respects any row boundary. It is the geometric core shared by the different recursive designs.

Use the structure of L1 to constrain image distances

Every finite ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ metric is a nonnegative sum of cut metrics, where a cut charges one to pairs on opposite sides and zero otherwise. On the finite state group, each cut can be expanded in Fourier characters.

Characters depending on only a few components are detected by cheap simultaneous shifts: distinct prime denominators prevent their phases from cancelling accidentally. Characters that evade those tests must involve many components or carry large total leaf frequency. Averaging individual component or leaf shifts then controls that remaining Fourier mass.

Thus an ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ image cannot keep a distinguished displacement as large as the edit geometry requires while also respecting all the cheap shifts. At depth kkk, the constructions claim logarithmic distortion of order klog⁡kk\log kklogk, while logarithmic word length is of order k2log⁡kk^2\log kk2logk. Balancing these quantities gives the square-root logarithmic expression in the theorem.

Binary delimiter codes preserve enough of the separation to retain that scale. Some lower proofs tolerate a block-width-dependent loss because it is small compared with the main exponential gain; this is distinct from the separate constant-distortion coding theorems.

Build the upper map from overlapping substring histograms

For the upper bound, shorter substrings are embedded recursively. Overlapping windows are grouped using cuts in the shorter-word image, and histogram coordinates record their distributions. Overlap softens the effect of a small shift, while comparisons across multiple scales retain enough information to control the original edit distance.

M2 develops this recursion into a finite map and treats actual window lengths, including shorter words. M1 instead packages the classical fixed-length theorem with hashing and padding reductions. Their upper arguments establish the same asymptotic scale through different presentations and dependencies.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All edits are single-symbol operations of unit cost. Block moves, reversals or weighted substitutions define different metrics. Intermediate strings are not required to stay within the endpoint length cap.

The lower witness has one common binary length at most ddd; it need not have length exactly ddd. The theorem holds for every sufficiently large cap, with absolute constants. The upper and lower constants in the exponent remain unspecified and need not match.

No target-dimension restriction is imposed in defining the least distortion. The lower theorem therefore remains meaningful even though M2’s upper construction may use many coordinates. Neither statement is a direct bound on pairwise edit-distance computation time.

The coding results have different quantifiers: logarithmic-width substitutions uniform over equal lengths in M2, and a separate prescribed-length polynomial-width construction in M3. Their guarantees should not be combined into a stronger unquoted theorem.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives the prime-product displacement argument and uniform reduction to the classical upper theorem. M2 supplies the finite-circle alternatives, binary codes and histogram upper construction. M3 gives independent tree lower proofs and explicitly imports M2 only for its upper conclusion.

The linked Ostrovsky–Rabani, Khot–Naor and Krauthgamer–Rabani papers provide the earlier upper and lower bounds. Wagner–Fischer supplies the alignment framework, and Many flavors of edit distance explains related alphabet-conversion guarantees and their normalization.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Edit Distance in l1: Matching Bounds up to Constants in the Exponent (September 27, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Finite-Circle Obstructions, Binary Codes, and Histogram Embeddings for Edit Distance (September 27, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Tree Constructions for the l1 Distortion of Binary Edit Distance (September 27, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why simplices might be the most spread-out convex bodies
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 101 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Choose a point uniformly at random inside a convex body. Its covariance matrix records how far the point typically lies from the center in every direction.
