Some bodies spread their volume far from the center; others concentrate it more tightly. Which shape produces the greatest spread once changes of scale and linear coordinates have been factored out?

The relevant quantity is the isotropic constant. A long-standing sharp conjecture proposes that a simplex maximizes it in every dimension. A triangle is the two-dimensional simplex, a tetrahedron the three-dimensional one, and the general simplex is the convex hull of n+1n+1n+1 affinely independent points in Rn\mathbb R^nRn.

Family 101 claims this exact inequality and its equality classification. Its route goes through a broader probabilistic statement: among log-concave distributions with fixed covariance, products of one-sided exponential distributions have the smallest differential entropy, after allowing invertible affine changes of coordinates.

The bridge between the two problems is particularly revealing. A convex body becomes the base of a cone in one higher dimension; an exponential density on that cone converts geometric spread into an entropy comparison.

2. Background and essential definitions

Measuring spread without choosing coordinates

Let K⊂RnK\subset\mathbb R^nK⊂Rn be compact and convex with nonempty interior, and let ∣K∣|K|∣K∣ denote its volume. Its centroid and covariance matrix are

bK=1∣K∣∫Kx dx,ΣK=1∣K∣∫K(x−bK)(x−bK)T dx.b_K=\frac1{|K|}\int_Kx\,dx,\qquad\Sigma_K=\frac1{|K|}\int_K(x-b_K)(x-b_K)^T\,dx.bK​=∣K∣1​∫K​xdx,ΣK​=∣K∣1​∫K​(x−bK​)(x−bK​)Tdx.

Here a vector is a column, and the superscript TTT means transpose. For any vector vvv, the number vTΣKvv^T\Sigma_KvvTΣK​v is the variance of the coordinate vTXv^TXvTX of a uniform random point XXX in KKK. The determinant combines the variances along the covariance matrix’s orthogonal principal directions.

Define

LK=(det⁡ΣK∣K∣2)1/(2n).L_K=\left(\frac{\det\Sigma_K}{|K|^2}\right)^{1/(2n)}.LK​=(∣K∣2detΣK​​)1/(2n).

An invertible linear transformation AAA multiplies the covariance determinant by (det⁡A)2(\det A)^2(detA)2 and the squared volume by the same factor. Translation changes neither. Thus LKL_KLK​ depends on shape up to invertible affine transformation. All nondegenerate simplices in a fixed dimension have the same value.

In coordinates where ∣K∣=1|K|=1∣K∣=1, the centroid is zero, and ΣK=LK2I\Sigma_K=L_K^2IΣK​=LK2​I, the body is in isotropic position. The identity matrix III indicates equal directional variances. This terminology is a normalization, not an assumption that the body has rotational symmetry.

Entropy and convexity of a density

A probability density fff on Rm\mathbb R^mRm is log-concave if it can be written f=e−Vf=e^{-V}f=e−V for a convex function VVV, allowing V=+∞V=+\inftyV=+∞ outside its support. Uniform densities on convex bodies and one-sided exponential densities are examples. Convexity excludes separate peaks with a deep valley between them.

Its differential entropy is

h(f)=−∫Rmf(x)log⁡f(x) dx,h(f)=-\int_{\mathbb R^m}f(x)\log f(x)\,dx,h(f)=−∫Rm​f(x)logf(x)dx,

using natural logarithms and 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0. Unlike discrete entropy, this quantity can be negative and changes with the units of measurement. The affine-invariant combination relevant here is

h(f)−12log⁡det⁡Cov⁡(f).h(f)-\frac12\log\det\operatorname{Cov}(f).h(f)−21​logdetCov(f).

Both terms change by log⁡∣det⁡A∣\log|\det A|log∣detA∣ under x↦Ax+bx\mapsto Ax+bx↦Ax+b, so their difference does not change. The densities in the claimed theorem are with respect to full-dimensional Lebesgue measure; their covariance matrices are positive definite.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Bourgain’s slicing problem asks whether LKL_KLK​ has a universal upper bound independent of dimension. Its geometric formulation concerns large hyperplane sections of volume-one convex bodies. Controlling covariance and controlling sections turn out to be closely related.

Klartag obtained an O(n1/4)O(n^{1/4})O(n1/4) upper bound. Eldan’s stochastic localization method later opened a route to subpolynomial and polylogarithmic bounds through work including Chen and Klartag–Lehec. The manuscript’s historical baseline includes Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 dimension-independent result using Guan’s covariance estimate.

Consequently, this family’s claimed advance must be distinguished from establishing that some universal constant exists. It proposes the exact best constant in each dimension and identifies every extremal body.

In dimension two, Campi, Colesanti, and Gronchi proved the simplex bound, while Saroglou established the uniqueness of the maximizing shape. In higher dimensions, Rademacher showed that a simplicial polytope maximizing the isotropic constant among all convex bodies must be a simplex. A simplicial polytope has simplex-shaped facets; the restriction did not cover arbitrary convex bodies or show that every maximizer has that structure.

The entropic side also has its own history. Bobkov and Madiman developed the relation between entropy bounds for log-concave laws and slicing. Fradelizi and Marín Sola formulated the sharp entropy inequality used here and proved its equivalence, across dimensions, with the simplex inequality. Melbourne, Nayar, and Roberto established the sharp one-dimensional entropy bound, with a one-sided exponential law as extremizer.

The new manuscript therefore builds on both geometric partial results and an established equivalence. Its claimed new work is the all-dimensional sharp entropy inequality, including the equality analysis needed to recover unique simplex extremizers.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The exact simplex bound

The family has one manuscript. Its first theorem states that every convex body in every dimension n≥1n\geq1n≥1 satisfies

LK≤(n!)1/n(n+1)(n+1)/(2n)n+2,L_K\leq\frac{(n!)^{1/n}}{(n+1)^{(n+1)/(2n)}\sqrt{n+2}},LK​≤(n+1)(n+1)/(2n)n+2​(n!)1/n​,

with equality if and only if KKK is a simplex. Here n!=1⋅2⋯nn!=1\cdot2\cdots nn!=1⋅2⋯n. No symmetry, smooth boundary, or polytope assumption appears.

In dimension one, every convex body is an interval, hence a simplex, and the formula gives 1/121/\sqrt{12}1/12​. In higher dimensions the classification says all affine shapes other than simplices give a strict inequality. The right side tends to 1/e1/e1/e as the dimension grows; the statement is much more precise than a dimension-independent upper estimate.

A sharp entropy inequality and all equality cases

The second theorem claims, for every log-concave probability density on Rm\mathbb R^mRm,

h(f)≥m+12log⁡det⁡Cov⁡(f).h(f)\geq m+\frac12\log\det\operatorname{Cov}(f).h(f)≥m+21​logdetCov(f).

Equality holds precisely for distributions of

M(E1,…,Em)T+b,M(E_1,\ldots,E_m)^T+b,M(E1​,…,Em​)T+b,

where MMM is invertible, bbb is a vector, and the EiE_iEi​ are independent variables with density e−ue^{-u}e−u for u≥0u\geq0u≥0, and zero otherwise. Each has mean, variance, and entropy equal to one, so their product attains the bound.

With covariance III, the inequality reads h(f)≥mh(f)\geq mh(f)≥m. It is a lower bound restricted to log-concave densities. The familiar Gaussian maximum-entropy theorem is an upper bound at fixed covariance and has a different extremizer.

A consequence for volume products

Through an earlier implication of Klartag, the claimed sharp simplex bound also yields the nonsymmetric Mahler inequality

∣K∣ ∣K∘∣≥(n+1)n+1(n!)2|K|\,|K^\circ|\geq\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2}∣K∣∣K∘∣≥(n!)2(n+1)n+1​

when the origin lies in the interior of KKK. The polar is K∘={y:⟨x,y⟩≤1 for all x∈K}K^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\text{ for all }x\in K\}K∘={y:⟨x,y⟩≤1 for all x∈K}. This is a further route to a claim discussed in family 087. The consequence stated here is the inequality; the manuscript’s principal equality classifications concern entropy and isotropic constants.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The claim settles a sharp central problem in asymptotic convex geometry, identifies its extremizers, and establishes a corresponding distributional inequality with a broader domain than uniform measures on bodies.

An exact extremal theorem explains which geometry makes a general bound tight. Here the simplex would be the most demanding shape for isotropic spread, while independent one-sided exponentials would be the most entropy-efficient log-concave building blocks at fixed covariance.

The implication for Mahler volume also connects two major affine-invariant quantities: covariance divided by volume, and a body’s volume multiplied by its polar’s volume. The importance rating reflects that mathematical reach if the claims are correct, not an assessment of their verification status.

6. The main idea

First solve a distributional problem

The manuscript begins with a smooth density whose negative logarithm has Hessian bounded above and below by positive constants. It transports a standard Gaussian distribution to the target density by the gradient of a convex function. The derivative of this map is a positive definite symmetric matrix at each point.

The one-dimensional model is explicit. If Φ\PhiΦ is the standard Gaussian distribution function, then

t(a)=−log⁡Φ(−a)t(a)=-\log\Phi(-a)t(a)=−logΦ(−a)

takes a standard Gaussian variable to a mean-one exponential variable. Let q=t′q=t'q=t′. Rather than compare the transport derivative directly with a constant matrix, the manuscript reparametrizes it using the inverse of qqq, applied to its eigenvalues.

A carefully chosen affine normalization makes this new matrix field have Gaussian mean zero. This is a nonlinear condition and is not supplied merely by setting the target covariance equal to the identity.

The field is then separated into its part linear in the Gaussian coordinates and its higher-degree part. Gaussian energy inequalities have equality in the linear directions, so those directions require separate handling. Higher-degree terms carry an energy surplus that can control the entropy deficit.

A major technical issue is that matrix derivatives need not commute. The argument retains terms measuring differences between eigenvalues and uses them to absorb off-diagonal errors. Scalar estimates and this matrix energy accounting together are claimed to make the entropy deficit nonpositive.

Equality must survive approximation

The expected extremizers vanish outside a cone and have affine potentials on their support. They do not belong to the initial smooth, uniformly convex class. The manuscript therefore approximates general log-concave densities while preserving entropy and covariance.

A quantitative remainder forces the reparametrized derivative of a nearly extremizing transport toward a linear matrix field. Compatibility with being a derivative then forces the constant coefficient matrices to commute. Simultaneous diagonalization reduces the limiting transport to independent one-dimensional exponential transports. This is how the equality classification emerges, rather than being guessed from the sharp constant alone.

Put a convex body under an exponential roof

To return to geometry, translate KKK so its centroid is zero and form the cone

CK={(tx,t):x∈K, t≥0}⊂Rn+1.C_K=\{(tx,t):x\in K,\ t\geq0\}\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}.CK​={(tx,t):x∈K, t≥0}⊂Rn+1.

Its section at height ttt is a copy of KKK scaled by ttt. On this cone, use the density

fK(y,t)=e−tn!∣K∣ 1CK(y,t),f_K(y,t)=\frac{e^{-t}}{n!|K|}\,\mathbf1_{C_K}(y,t),fK​(y,t)=n!∣K∣e−t​1CK​​(y,t),

where the indicator is one on the cone and zero elsewhere. The normalization follows from ∫0∞tne−tdt=n!\int_0^\infty t^ne^{-t}dt=n!∫0∞​tne−tdt=n!.

The manuscript gives

h(fK)=n+1+log⁡(n!∣K∣),det⁡Cov⁡(fK)=(n+1)n+1(n+2)ndet⁡ΣK.\begin{aligned}h(f_K)&=n+1+\log(n!|K|),\\\det\operatorname{Cov}(f_K)&=(n+1)^{n+1}(n+2)^n\det\Sigma_K.\end{aligned}h(fK​)detCov(fK​)​=n+1+log(n!∣K∣),=(n+1)n+1(n+2)ndetΣK​.​

Substitution into the entropy inequality in dimension n+1n+1n+1 gives exactly the claimed simplex constant. If equality holds, the cone’s density must be an affine image of a product of exponentials. Its support is consequently a cone with n+1n+1n+1 independent generating rays. Intersecting those rays with the height-one plane makes KKK a simplex.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The entropy theorem concerns log-concave densities on full-dimensional Euclidean space. It does not give the same lower bound for arbitrary densities with a prescribed covariance, or for discrete distributions with Shannon entropy. Changing the logarithm convention would also change the numerical constants.

Smoothness and uniform curvature belong to an intermediate stage, not the final hypothesis. Uniform distributions on arbitrary convex bodies are included, and the claimed equality distributions have a boundary to their support.

The equality classification is exact. A separate geometric stability question asks how close a body must be to a simplex when its isotropic constant nearly attains the bound, with an explicit distance and dimension dependence. The manuscript’s analytic remainder and equality argument should not be read as already providing every such quantitative stability theorem.

The result also does not classify maximizers under extra symmetry constraints. A centrally symmetric body in dimension greater than one cannot itself be a simplex, so sharp bounds in restricted classes are distinct questions.

8. Sources and further reading

For the preceding dimension-independent result, see Klartag and Lehec, Affirmative resolution of Bourgain’s slicing problem using Guan’s bound, and Guan, A note on Bourgain’s slicing problem. Rademacher’s simplicial-polytope theorem records an earlier restricted extremal result.

For the entropic development, see Bobkov and Madiman, The entropy per coordinate of a random vector is highly constrained under convexity conditions; Fradelizi and Marín Sola, Entropy, slicing problem and functional Mahler’s conjecture, Indiana University Mathematics Journal 75 (2026), 825–843; and Melbourne, Nayar, and Roberto, Minimum entropy of a log-concave variable with fixed variance. Klartag’s Isotropic constants and Mahler volumes supplies the earlier implication for polar volume products.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A sharp entropy bound and the simplex inequality for isotropic constants (October 5, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Covering a tetrahedron with less cylinder area than expected
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 100 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Imagine covering a solid tetrahedron with infinitely long tubes. Each tube may point in its own direction, and its cross-section need not be circular. How small can the sum of the cross-sectional areas be?

The answer cannot be compared directly with the tetrahedron’s volume: area and volume have different units. A natural reference is its smallest shadow under orthogonal projection onto a plane. A familiar cover of a regular tetrahedron uses two tubes parallel to opposite edges, with total cross-sectional area exactly half that smallest shadow.

Was one half a universal lower bound? Family 100 reports that it is not. By allowing many slightly different directions, the manuscripts claim finite covers of a regular tetrahedron with cost strictly below the proposed threshold. The improvement is small, but its sign settles the proposed inequality. Two companion approximation theorems explain how continuously varying directions can be replaced by finitely many genuine cylinders without losing the saving.

2. Background and essential definitions

A convex body in R3\mathbb R^3R3 is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. A cylinder here means

C=B+Ru,C=B+\mathbb R u,C=B+Ru,

where uuu is a unit vector and BBB is a measurable planar set in the perpendicular plane u⊥u^\perpu⊥. Its cost is the area ∣B∣|B|∣B∣. The whole infinite cylinder is used; no height enters its cost. In particular, a triangular or parallelogram base is allowed.

Write πu⊥K\pi_{u^\perp}Kπu⊥​K for the orthogonal shadow of KKK in that plane, and define

Amin⁡(K)=min⁡∣u∣=1∣πu⊥K∣.A_{\min}(K)=\min_{|u|=1}|\pi_{u^\perp}K|.Amin​(K)=∣u∣=1min​∣πu⊥​K∣.

For a finite cover K⊆⋃i(Bi+Rui)K\subseteq\bigcup_i(B_i+\mathbb R u_i)K⊆⋃i​(Bi​+Rui​), the half-area question proposed

∑i∣Bi∣≥12Amin⁡(K).\sum_i|B_i|\geq\frac12 A_{\min}(K).i∑​∣Bi​∣≥21​Amin​(K).

Overlap is counted repeatedly in the sum. This is a covering problem, so overlap is allowed and gaps are forbidden.

A second formulation measures each tube against the shadow in its own direction:

R(C;K)=∑i∣Bi∣∣πui⊥K∣.R(\mathcal C;K)=\sum_i\frac{|B_i|}{|\pi_{u_i^\perp}K|}.R(C;K)=i∑​∣πui⊥​​K∣∣Bi​∣​.

The proposed bound R≥1/2R\geq1/2R≥1/2 is stronger, since

R(C;K)≤∑i∣Bi∣Amin⁡(K).R(\mathcal C;K)\leq\frac{\sum_i|B_i|}{A_{\min}(K)}.R(C;K)≤Amin​(K)∑i​∣Bi​∣​.

Thus a cover below the absolute half-area threshold violates both statements. The directionwise ratio is invariant under invertible affine transformations: a linear change of coordinates multiplies a base and the body’s matching shadow by the same planar area factor. The minimum-shadow normalization does not have this general affine invariance.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The ancestor is Tarski’s plank problem. A plank is the region between two parallel planes, and its cost is their separation. Bang’s plank theorem says that the total width of planks covering a convex body is at least its minimum width. Ball later established a stronger direction-dependent plank inequality for centrally symmetric bodies.

Cylinders ask for the analogous comparison one dimension further down: a planar base replaces a one-dimensional width. The geometry changes because different axes can cooperate in ways unavailable to parallel-sided planks.

Bezdek’s Tarski’s plank problem revisited, Problem 3.1, attributes both the half-area question and the two-cylinder tetrahedral example to Bang. Bezdek and Litvak subsequently proved a directionwise lower bound of 1/31/31/3 for arbitrary three-dimensional convex bodies, and the stronger bound 111 for ellipsoids. These results show that the total relative cost cannot approach zero, while leaving a gap between the general theorem and the conjectured 1/21/21/2.

Bezdek and Khan formulated the directionwise version within their codimensional cylinder covering conjectures. The regular tetrahedron seemed especially informative: its elementary two-cylinder cover attained the proposed constant. But exhibiting equality in a simple construction does not show that the construction is optimal when the number and directions of cylinders are unrestricted.

The new manuscripts focus precisely on that remaining freedom. Their proposed counterexamples keep the tetrahedron and change the cover, exploiting a small area gain from tilting while carefully preserving overlap.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Finite counterexamples with ordinary polygonal bases

M1 gives explicit finite covers with compact triangular bases. In one convenient normalization, the tetrahedron is

K={(x,y,2 t):0≤t≤1, ∣x∣≤1−t, ∣y∣≤t}.K=\{(x,y,\sqrt2\,t):0\leq t\leq1,\ |x|\leq1-t,\ |y|\leq t\}.K={(x,y,2​t):0≤t≤1, ∣x∣≤1−t, ∣y∣≤t}.

Its four vertices form a regular tetrahedron of edge length 222, and Amin⁡(K)=2A_{\min}(K)=\sqrt2Amin​(K)=2​. For 0<ε≤1/20000<\varepsilon\leq1/20000<ε≤1/2000, M1 states a construction with 2⌈2/ε2⌉2\lceil2/\varepsilon^2\rceil2⌈2/ε2⌉ cylinders and normalized cost

∑i∣Bi∣2=12−136000ε2+E(ε),∣E(ε)∣≤2ε4.\frac{\sum_i|B_i|}{\sqrt2}=\frac12-\frac{13}{6000}\varepsilon^2+E(\varepsilon),\qquad |E(\varepsilon)|\leq2\varepsilon^4.2​∑i​∣Bi​∣​=21​−600013​ε2+E(ε),∣E(ε)∣≤2ε4.

The negative quadratic term wins over the bounded fourth-order error in the stated range. The claim concerns a finite cover for each chosen parameter, not merely a limiting continuum of tubes.

M3 supplies alternative constructions using slope fields. It states that every regular tetrahedron admits finite covers below both half thresholds with compact parallelogram bases, or alternatively bounded open measurable bases. Affine invariance then gives R<1/2R<1/2R<1/2 for every nondegenerate tetrahedron. This extension is specifically directionwise; it does not assert the absolute minimum-shadow inequality for every affine image.

Turning a slope field into finitely many cylinders

M2 studies a compact label set D⊂R2D\subset\mathbb R^2D⊂R2, a continuously differentiable field VVV near DDD, and the swept set

E(D,V,L)={(s,p+sV(p)):p∈D, ∣s∣≤L},L>0.E(D,V,L)=\{(s,p+sV(p)):p\in D,\ |s|\leq L\},\qquad L>0.E(D,V,L)={(s,p+sV(p)):p∈D, ∣s∣≤L},L>0.

The derivative matrix DVDVDV describes how neighboring slopes vary. Under the pointwise conditions

tr⁡DV=0,−L−2<det⁡DV≤0,\operatorname{tr}DV=0,\qquad -L^{-2}<\det DV\leq0,trDV=0,−L−2<detDV≤0,

M2 claims finite cylinder covers with total perpendicular area arbitrarily close from above to

∫Ddp1+∣V(p)∣2.\int_D\frac{dp}{\sqrt{1+|V(p)|^2}}.∫D​1+∣V(p)∣2​dp​.

The intercept tiles are nondegenerate squares; their perpendicular projections are parallelograms. The theorem allows arbitrary compact DDD, including positive-area boundaries, and does not require the derivative’s operator norm to be small. In particular, a large shear with (DV)2=0(DV)^2=0(DV)2=0 can satisfy its conditions. This is an approximation theorem; producing a counterexample also requires choosing fields whose sweeps cover the tetrahedron at a low enough integral cost.

A radial alternative with triangular bases

M4 gives a separate approximation theorem for rays in an intercept plane. Choose independent planar vectors a,ba,ba,b, a unit normal eee, a continuous radial cap R(t)≥0R(t)\geq0R(t)≥0, and a continuously differentiable planar direction correction w(t)w(t)w(t). The sweep consists of

p0+ρ(a+tb)+s(e+w(t)),t∈[α,β],0≤ρ≤R(t),∣s∣≤L.p_0+\rho(a+tb)+s(e+w(t)),\quad t\in[\alpha,\beta],\quad 0\leq\rho\leq R(t),\quad |s|\leq L.p0​+ρ(a+tb)+s(e+w(t)),t∈[α,β],0≤ρ≤R(t),∣s∣≤L.

Its key alignment condition is w′(t)=λ(t)(a+tb)w'(t)=\lambda(t)(a+tb)w′(t)=λ(t)(a+tb), with continuous real λ\lambdaλ. For every partition of the parameter interval, and any chosen tag in each subinterval, M4 claims one triangular-base cylinder per subinterval, with the tagged direction. As the largest subinterval length tends to zero, their total cost tends to

∣det⁡(a,b)∣∫αβR(t)221+∣w(t)∣2 dt.|\det(a,b)|\int_\alpha^\beta\frac{R(t)^2}{2\sqrt{1+|w(t)|^2}}\,dt.∣det(a,b)∣∫αβ​21+∣w(t)∣2​R(t)2​dt.

Convergence is uniform over the partitions and tags. The radial cap may vanish. Applied to two suitably overlapping sweeps, this gives another all-triangular finite cover below the half-area threshold. Its prescribed directions and cylinder count are stronger structural features than merely cutting parallelogram bases into triangles.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The family claims a counterexample to a long-standing covering conjecture and introduces finite approximation methods with uses beyond the particular tetrahedron. Its scope is more specialized than an entire theory of optimal convex-body coverings, but the conceptual change is substantial.

The regular tetrahedron’s most obvious equality construction would no longer identify the correct constant. A successful sharp inequality must account for coordinated variation of cylinder directions, rather than extrapolate from a few symmetric tubes.

There is also a useful lesson about continuous optimization. An integral may suggest a cheaper cover without actually describing a legal finite arrangement. M2 and M4 address that gap explicitly, retaining coverage while controlling the added area. The finite realization is part of the mathematical claim, not a cosmetic reformulation.

6. The main idea

Tilt saves area, but can open gaps

Start with the two-cylinder cover and split its intercept regions into small patches. Assign slightly different slopes to neighboring patches. A patch tilted relative to its cylinder’s perpendicular plane has smaller projected area: the factor is (1+∣V∣2)−1/2(1+|V|^2)^{-1/2}(1+∣V∣2)−1/2. For small slopes, the saving is quadratic.

The danger is that these tilted tubes no longer fit together. Extra padding restores coverage, but padding consumes the same area that the tilt was meant to save. The constructions arrange the geometry so that the saving exceeds this repair cost.

M1 works with narrow angular sectors. The two complementary families move their separating boundaries in opposite directions at first order. After that cancellation, a controlled second-order comparison leaves a strict gain. Fine enough sectors make discretization errors smaller still.

Fields designed around the boundary

M3 constructs a smooth rational field from a stream function that is constant on wedge walls. A stream function encodes a planar field with zero divergence; its constant boundary values also make the field tangent to those walls. These properties control both the derivative and the coverage geometry.

The complementary families’ inverse labels shift oppositely at first order. Slight enlargements then leave a second-order overlap surplus, while costing less than the projected-area saving. Further constructions use singular power fields and an angular limiting field; their behavior near the apex requires separate treatment.

These are straight segments with a direction frozen at each label, not trajectories following a differential equation. That distinction matters because a flow would generally trace curves rather than cylinder axes.

Why radial alignment helps discretization

In M4, changing the parameter changes the direction initially along the existing intercept ray. This displacement can be absorbed by moving along that ray. What remains transverse to it is only quadratic in the subinterval length.

A slightly enlarged triangle therefore contains all intercepts belonging to one subinterval. Each enlargement costs a small amount, and their total tends to zero as the partition becomes finer. M2 achieves a broader finite approximation through local affine models and coverings by square intercept tiles. The two tools have different hypotheses and geometric guarantees; neither should be read as permitting arbitrary direction fields at no cost.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The main counterexample concerns infinite cylinders in three dimensions with freely chosen directions and measurable bases. It is not a statement about circular cylinders, bounded tube lengths, disjoint packings, or a prescribed small number of cylinders.

The manuscripts do not identify the optimal relative covering constant. Combining their stated tetrahedral counterexample with the earlier general theorem places the infimum for any nondegenerate tetrahedron in [1/3,1/2)[1/3,1/2)[1/3,1/2). Its exact value remains a separate question.

The approximation results also retain real restrictions: M2 has derivative conditions and a strict segment-length bound; M4 requires radial alignment. Their success does not justify replacing an arbitrary continuous family by finite tubes with the same integral cost.

Finally, the displayed improvement is a strict perturbative saving. It does not claim a large numerical reduction or the most economical practical cover. The importance lies in crossing the conjectured boundary and in the mechanisms that make that crossing possible.

8. Sources and further reading

For the historical formulation, see Károly Bezdek, Tarski’s plank problem revisited, especially Problem 3.1. Bezdek and Alexander Litvak, Covering convex bodies by cylinders and lattice points by flats, Journal of Geometric Analysis 19 (2009), 233–243, gives the earlier cylinder inequalities. Bezdek and Muhammad Khan, The geometry of homothetic covering and illumination, records the directionwise conjecture. These distinguish the original area question from its affine-invariant strengthening.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Finite angular cylinder covers below the half-area bound (September 27, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Finite cylinder approximation of ruled sets (September 27, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Slope-field perturbations of the two-cylinder covering (September 27, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Finite triangular approximation of radial sweeps (September 27, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Why three Gaussian sectors can beat arbitrarily many cells
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 096 · Convex and metric geometry
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-14

1. The question

Divide Gaussian space into finitely many measurable cells. For each cell, add up its position vectors, weighted by Gaussian probability, and square the length of the resulting vector. How large can the sum of those squared lengths be?

One might expect that more dimensions or more cells would permit increasingly elaborate partitions with larger values. The propeller conjecture predicts a strikingly simple answer: once two dimensions and three labels are available, three equal planar sectors are already optimal. Extra dimensions are ignored, and extra cells can be left empty.

The manuscript in family 096 claims this bound for every dimension and every finite number of cells. It uses the established three-dimensional propeller theorem and supplies an argument excluding improvements by extremizers with five or more active cells. A separate application evaluates a threshold in kernel clustering, with an additional dependency for the hardness conclusion.

2. Background and essential definitions

The standard Gaussian probability measure on Rd\mathbb R^dRd has density

(2π)−d/2e−∣x∣2/2.(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/2}.(2π)−d/2e−∣x∣2/2.

For a measurable cell AAA, define its first moment

z(A)=∫Ax dγd(x).z(A)=\int_A x\,d\gamma_d(x).z(A)=∫A​xdγd​(x).

This is not divided by γd(A)\gamma_d(A)γd​(A). When the cell has positive probability, it equals that probability times the conditional mean of a Gaussian vector in the cell. The source calls it an unnormalized centroid.

For a partition A1,…,AkA_1,\ldots,A_kA1​,…,Ak​, the objective is

F(A1,…,Ak)=∑i=1k∣z(Ai)∣2.F(A_1,\ldots,A_k)=\sum_{i=1}^k|z(A_i)|^2.F(A1​,…,Ak​)=i=1∑k​∣z(Ai​)∣2.

The cells may have unequal probabilities, and empty cells are allowed. Partitions are considered up to Gaussian null sets, which do not affect the integrals. Since the whole Gaussian distribution has mean zero, the cell moment vectors sum to zero.

A propeller partition consists of three sectors of angle 2π/32\pi/32π/3 in a plane. In higher dimensions, take each sector times the orthogonal complement of the plane. The additional coordinates contribute zero to each first moment by symmetry.

For a planar sector of opening 2α2\alpha2α, symmetric about a unit direction uuu, polar integration gives

z(A)=sin⁡α2πu.z(A)=\frac{\sin\alpha}{\sqrt{2\pi}}u.z(A)=2π​sinα​u.

Putting α=π/3\alpha=\pi/3α=π/3 and summing over three sectors gives 3sin⁡2(π/3)/(2π)=9/(8π)3\sin^2(\pi/3)/(2\pi)=9/(8\pi)3sin2(π/3)/(2π)=9/(8π). The conjecture is that no other finite partition can exceed this value.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Khot and Naor introduced the propeller problem in their Approximate kernel clustering. Gaussian first moments enter both their rounding analysis and their hardness framework for a discrete clustering objective.

Their geometric reduction showed that an optimizer can be sought among conical partitions determined by linear scores. It also reduced the effective ambient dimension to the span of the cell moments. They determined the three-cell value, where the propeller already supplies the optimum.

Heilman, Jagannath and Naor proved the propeller conjecture in three dimensions in 2013. Their computer-assisted argument treated the remaining four-cell conical configurations through spherical geometry and finite estimates. The present manuscript explicitly uses that theorem as an established input.

Higher-dimensional partitions can have more active cells, so the three-dimensional result does not automatically settle the full conjecture. The new argument focuses on this remaining regime. Its other geometric input is Ehrhard’s Gaussian convex-set inequality, which controls Gaussian measures of Minkowski combinations and, in the form used here, translations of convex cells.

A related literature studies noise stability: the probability that two correlated Gaussian vectors fall in the same cell, often with equal cell probabilities prescribed. Heilman’s later work gives a conditional route to propeller bounds in restricted cell counts under additional stability assumptions. That objective and those mass constraints differ from the unrestricted first-moment problem here.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that for all positive integers d,kd,kd,k, every measurable partition of Rd\mathbb R^dRd into kkk cells satisfies

∑i=1k∣∫Aix dγd(x)∣2≤98π.\sum_{i=1}^k\left|\int_{A_i}x\,d\gamma_d(x)\right|^2\leq\frac9{8\pi}.i=1∑k​​∫Ai​​xdγd​(x)​2≤8π9​.

The constant is attained whenever d≥2d\geq2d≥2 and k≥3k\geq3k≥3, using the propeller and leaving additional cells empty. The theorem does not assert that the same constant is attained when there is only one dimension or fewer than three labels. It identifies the maximum value and an attaining construction in the stated range, without giving a full classification of all equality cases.

The separate clustering application takes a rational symmetric positive semidefinite matrix A=(apq)A=(a_{pq})A=(apq​) satisfying A1=0A\mathbf1=0A1=0. It seeks a labeling σ\sigmaσ of the NNN indices by kkk labels that maximizes

∑p,q=1Napq 1{σ(p)=σ(q)}.\sum_{p,q=1}^N a_{pq}\,\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(p)=\sigma(q)\}}.p,q=1∑N​apq​1{σ(p)=σ(q)}​.

For fixed k≥3k\geq3k≥3, define

αk=8π9(1−1k).\alpha_k=\frac{8\pi}{9}\left(1-\frac1k\right).αk​=98π​(1−k1​).

A loss factor α\alphaα means achieving at least 1/α1/\alpha1/α of the optimum. M1 quotes Khot–Naor’s expected rounding guarantee at αk\alpha_kαk​ in an ideal Gaussian-sampling and exact-relaxation formulation.

Using the newly evaluated Gaussian constant, their low-influence theorem, and the separate Unique Games Theorem in family 102, M1 claims NP-hardness of deterministic approximation with every fixed loss factor strictly below αk\alpha_kαk​. The Unique Games dependency belongs to this hardness application, not to the Gaussian geometric inequality.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The result would settle a prominent Gaussian partition problem whose low-dimensional case required substantial work. It reveals that permitting many cells and dimensions does not improve this particular objective beyond a planar three-part structure.

The geometry is tied to a concrete optimization threshold. Evaluating a continuous Gaussian extremum determines a constant in the analysis of discrete clustering algorithms and, with additional complexity inputs, their limitations. This is a recurring theme in approximation theory: a geometric inequality can encode an algorithmic barrier.

The number of active cells is part of the phenomenon. A formulation requiring every cell to have equal positive mass would prevent unused labels and would ask a different question. Here the option to concentrate the partition into three active sectors is essential to the proposed answer.

The rating reflects a major result with a precise cross-disciplinary consequence, while remaining narrower than a general classification of Gaussian partition optimizers or noise-stability extremizers. It does not treat the dependent hardness theorem as a consequence of geometry alone.

6. The main idea

Replace measurable sets by competing linear scores

Optimizing directly over all measurable partitions looks infinite-dimensional. Norm duality converts the square root of the largest objective into the largest expected maximum of finitely many Gaussian linear scores, with the score vectors’ total squared norm normalized to one.

For a fixed list of vectors, assigning a point to its largest score gives a conical partition. Compactness supplies an optimizer. Among optimizers, the argument chooses one with the fewest active cells. If two nonzero centroids had a nonnegative inner product, merging their cells would not decrease the objective, conflicting with that minimal choice unless the configuration could be simplified further.

The resulting centroids have strictly negative pairwise inner products and span a space of dimension one less than the number of active cells. Thus four or fewer active cells reduce to the established three-dimensional theorem. Any counterexample must have at least five.

Compare the cost of deleting one score

Normalize the centroid lengths to numbers rir_iri​ with ∑iri2=1\sum_i r_i^2=1∑i​ri2​=1, and write PiP_iPi​ for cell probabilities, with ∑iPi=1\sum_iP_i=1∑i​Pi​=1.

Deleting one score reduces the expected maximum. Optimality gives a lower bound on that loss after recentering the remaining score vectors. Ehrhard’s inequality, applied to translations of the deleted score’s winning cone, supplies an upper bound. Comparing them constrains how small a cell probability can be relative to its centroid length.

Halfspace rearrangement provides another one-cell estimate. In the five-cell case, an additional spherical comparison in the four-dimensional centroid span strengthens the constraint. These are restrictions on each cell separately, but they do not yet rule out the whole configuration.

Make two competitors constrain each other

The argument selects the cell with smallest centroid length and projects other scores orthogonally to its centroid direction. Gaussian orthogonality makes the residual scores independent of the component in that direction.

Their first-moment identities over the selected cell vanish. For a pair of residual scores, those identities yield a bound involving the determinant of their covariance matrix. The peak density of a two-dimensional Gaussian is inversely proportional to the square root of that determinant, linking geometric competition to a quantitative probability estimate.

The pairwise inequalities constrain the largest centroid lengths relative to the smallest one. Combined with the one-cell lower bounds and the fixed total probability mass, they become incompatible with an objective above 9/(8π)9/(8\pi)9/(8π). The manuscript supplies finite rational enclosures for the final scalar comparisons, in addition to the geometric reductions.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The objective uses unnormalized first moments. Dividing each vector by the cell probability would change the optimization problem completely. The measure is the standard Gaussian, and the partition has finitely many measurable cells with no prescribed masses.

The theorem gives the universal bound and propeller attainment for d≥2,k≥3d\geq2,k\geq3d≥2,k≥3. It does not claim that every equality partition is a propeller, or that the propeller optimizes other Gaussian objectives such as equal-mass noise stability.

The clustering threshold separates an expected randomized rounding guarantee from deterministic hardness of a strict improvement. The manuscript does not supply an exact finite-bit implementation at the endpoint. Deterministic NP-hardness alone also does not exclude randomized algorithms under the sole assumption P≠NPP\ne NPP=NP.

The geometric proof depends on the established three-dimensional theorem and Ehrhard’s inequality. The hardness application adds the companion Unique Games claim and a discrete low-influence theorem. These dependencies are reported as stated; no proof or computational certificate is checked in this digest.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s introduction defines the objective, computes the propeller value and separates the geometry from clustering. Its middle sections develop score deletion and two-competitor estimates; its final application specifies the rational-input hardness statement.

The linked Khot–Naor paper is the primary source for the conjecture and rounding framework. Heilman–Jagannath–Naor supplies the three-dimensional theorem used as input, while Ehrhard’s paper gives the Gaussian convexity inequality behind the deletion estimate.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Gaussian propeller bound in every dimension (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 14 October 2026 at repository revision 1581d4c. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Adding the complexity of a base and its fibers
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 033 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Suppose a geometric space is organized as a family of smaller spaces. A surface might be made of curves, one above each point of another curve. Can the complexity of the whole be estimated from the complexity of the base and a typical fiber?

Dimension itself adds: a family of one-dimensional curves over a one-dimensional base is two-dimensional. Kodaira dimension measures a subtler kind of complexity, using global differential forms. Iitaka’s conjecture asks whether this complexity is at least the sum of the contributions from base and fiber.

Family 033 contains five manuscripts. They claim ordinary, logarithmic, and orbifold lower bounds; a stronger bound that measures how much the fibers change; an equality under smoothness conditions; and a semiampleness theorem for the moduli part of a Kähler fibration. These are related questions, but the equality needs assumptions that the lower bounds do not.

2. Background and essential definitions

Counting differential forms

For a smooth complex variety XXX of dimension nnn, the canonical line bundle KXK_XKX​ has local sections of the form f dz1∧⋯∧dznf\,dz_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dz_nfdz1​∧⋯∧dzn​. A section of mKXmK_XmKX​ is an mmm-fold tensor power of such a top-degree form. Here additive notation for line bundles means tensor product.

The space H0(X,mKX)H^0(X,mK_X)H0(X,mKX​) consists of global holomorphic sections. Ratios of sections define a rational map to projective space. The largest image dimension among these maps is the Kodaira dimension κ(X)\kappa(X)κ(X). If every positive-degree space is zero, its value is −∞-\infty−∞. Otherwise it lies between zero and dim⁡X\dim XdimX. A variety is of general type when these two dimensions agree.

For smooth projective curves, genus zero gives −∞-\infty−∞, genus one gives zero, and genus at least two gives one. These examples show that Kodaira dimension measures more than ordinary dimension: all three kinds are curves, but their canonical forms behave differently.

More generally, κ(X,L)\kappa(X,L)κ(X,L) denotes the same construction for a line bundle or rational divisor LLL. A rational divisor has rational coefficients; sufficiently divisible multiples have integer coefficients. We use κ(point)=0\kappa(\mathrm{point})=0κ(point)=0 and −∞+a=−∞-\infty+a=-\infty−∞+a=−∞.

Fibrations and boundaries

A fibration here is a proper surjective map f:X→Yf:X\to Yf:X→Y with connected fibers. A general fiber FFF avoids the exceptional parameters where behavior changes. The geometric generic fiber is the corresponding object over an algebraic closure of the function field of YYY.

A boundary Δ=∑iδiDi\Delta=\sum_i\delta_iD_iΔ=∑i​δi​Di​ records specified hypersurfaces with weights 0≤δi≤10\leq\delta_i\leq10≤δi​≤1. Simple normal crossings, abbreviated SNC, means they look locally like distinct coordinate hyperplanes. A reduced boundary has all nonzero coefficients equal to one.

If U=X∖DU=X\setminus DU=X∖D, with XXX smooth projective and DDD reduced SNC, define

κ‾(U)=κ(X,KX+D).\overline\kappa(U)=\kappa(X,K_X+D).κ(U)=κ(X,KX​+D).

This is logarithmic Kodaira dimension. It permits controlled poles along the missing boundary and is independent of the chosen smooth compactification. For example, C∗\mathbb C^*C∗ has logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero, although its compactification P1\mathbb P^1P1 has ordinary Kodaira dimension −∞-\infty−∞.

A compact Kähler manifold has a positive closed real differential form of type (1,1)(1,1)(1,1), giving a metric compatible with its complex structure. Projective manifolds are Kähler, but the converse fails. Fujiki class C\mathcal CC consists of spaces bimeromorphic to compact Kähler spaces. Bimeromorphic maps are analytic analogues of birational maps: they become isomorphisms on dense open subsets.

Variation and positivity

The variation Var⁡(f)\operatorname{Var}(f)Var(f) measures how many parameters are needed to define the whole generic fiber up to birational equivalence. Zero variation means that, after an appropriate field extension, its birational type is constant. This invariant must retain the entire function field of the fiber, not merely a canonical model or one associated period map.

A line bundle is semiample if one positive tensor power is generated by global sections everywhere. Such sections define a morphism. Nefness is a weaker positivity condition: in the projective setting it says that every curve has nonnegative degree. Nefness by itself does not guarantee global sections.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Iitaka’s theory of dimensions of divisors put the addition question into a birational framework. The target inequality for a smooth projective fibration is

κ(X)≥κ(F)+κ(Y).\kappa(X)\geq\kappa(F)+\kappa(Y).κ(X)≥κ(F)+κ(Y).

The key difficulty is global: forms available separately on fibers do not automatically fit together into enough forms on the total space.

Kawamata established major cases involving curve bases and fibers with good minimal models. Viehweg developed weak positivity of direct images of pluricanonical bundles, and Kollár treated general-type fibers. These results draw positivity from different places. A good minimal model is a birational model whose canonical divisor is semiample, while a general-type base provides enough canonical positivity to absorb auxiliary twists. M1 §1 and M4 §1 give the original references and distinguish these hypotheses.

Birkar proved the ordinary conjecture through total dimension six. Other work treats special bases, including abelian varieties and varieties of maximal Albanese dimension, which map generically finitely to their Albanese tori. Logarithmic results of Kovács–Patakfalvi and Hashizume allow boundaries under specified positivity or abundance conditions on the fibers.

Popa’s conjectural framework separates variation lower bounds from stronger additivity questions for smooth families. Earlier results on the reverse inequality required hypotheses such as good models for fibers of the base’s own Iitaka fibration. Those are not the same as assumptions on the original fibers of fff.

The moduli-part question has its own history. Ambro developed its birational formulation; Fujino–Gongyo proved important positivity properties. M5 credits the algebraic b-semiampleness theorem of Bakker–Filipazzi–Mauri–Tsimerman and addresses a compact Kähler extension allowing nonprojective morphisms. It should not be presented as the first projective b-semiampleness theorem.

The introductions also acknowledge earlier broad preprint claims of Tsuji and Maehara. They are not used as inputs in these manuscripts. The exposition here follows the current statements rather than making an independent priority assessment.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 and M4: lower bounds

M4 asserts ordinary subadditivity for every surjective projective morphism with connected fibers between smooth connected projective varieties over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. There is no dimension bound or good-minimal-model assumption on the generic fiber.

M1 gives the broader rational-SNC orbifold statement in Fujiki class C\mathcal CC:

κ(X,KX+Δ)≥κ(F,KF+Δ∣F)+κ(f∣Δ).\kappa(X,K_X+\Delta)\geq\kappa(F,K_F+\Delta|_F)+\kappa(f\mid\Delta).κ(X,KX​+Δ)≥κ(F,KF​+Δ∣F​)+κ(f∣Δ).

The last term is Campana’s birationally defined orbifold-base Kodaira dimension. Multiple fibers and source boundary coefficients contribute to it. For a base divisor DDD, its multiplicity is computed from

m(f,Δ;D)=min⁡E→Dord⁡E(f∗D)1−ΔE,m(f,\Delta;D)=\min_{E\to D}\frac{\operatorname{ord}_E(f^*D)}{1-\Delta_E},m(f,Δ;D)=E→Dmin​1−ΔE​ordE​(f∗D)​,

where EEE runs over divisors dominating DDD, and division by zero means infinity. The base coefficient is 1−1/m(f,Δ;D)1-1/m(f,\Delta;D)1−1/m(f,Δ;D). Taking the specified birational invariant is part of the theorem; one arbitrary base model is not the whole definition.

Coefficient-one boundaries are allowed. Ordinary and logarithmic subadditivity follow as stated consequences, including the characteristic-zero projective formulations.

M2: changing fibers contribute

For a projective surjection f:U→Vf:U\to Vf:U→V with connected fibers between smooth complex quasi-projective varieties, M2 assumes κ‾(V)≥0\overline\kappa(V)\geq0κ(V)≥0 and claims

κ‾(U)≥κ(F)+max⁡{κ‾(V),Var⁡(f)}.\overline\kappa(U)\geq\kappa(F)+\max\{\overline\kappa(V),\operatorname{Var}(f)\}.κ(U)≥κ(F)+max{κ(V),Var(f)}.

Singular fibers are permitted. There is no abundance or semiampleness assumption on FFF. The variation is that of the whole geometric generic fiber. When variation exceeds the logarithmic complexity of the base, this improves the ordinary lower bound.

M3: equality under stratum smoothness

Let f:(X,E)→(Y,D)f:(X,E)\to(Y,D)f:(X,E)→(Y,D) be a connected-fiber surjection of smooth projective complex reduced-SNC pairs, with Supp⁡(f∗D)⊆Supp⁡(E)\operatorname{Supp}(f^*D)\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(E)Supp(f∗D)⊆Supp(E). Assume the total space and every boundary stratum are smooth over Y∖DY\setminus DY∖D. A stratum is an irreducible component of an intersection of boundary components.

M3 claims the reverse inequality. Combining it with M1 gives

κ(X,KX+E)=κ(Y,KY+D)+κ(F,KF+E∣F).\kappa(X,K_X+E)=\kappa(Y,K_Y+D)+\kappa(F,K_F+E|_F).κ(X,KX​+E)=κ(Y,KY​+D)+κ(F,KF​+E∣F​).

Horizontal boundary components are allowed. Both −∞-\infty−∞ cases are included: if either contribution on the right is −∞-\infty−∞, all positive log-pluricanonical section spaces upstairs vanish. This is a substantive assertion, whereas a lower bound by −∞-\infty−∞ would be automatic.

M5: a moduli line defines a map

Suppose f:Y→Xf:Y\to Xf:Y→X is a connected-fiber surjection between smooth compact connected Kähler manifolds, with effective rational SNC boundary Δ\DeltaΔ of coefficients in [0,1][0,1][0,1], and

KY+Δ∼Qf∗L.K_Y+\Delta\sim_{\mathbb Q}f^*L.KY​+Δ∼Q​f∗L.

Rational linear equivalence here means equality of the corresponding actual holomorphic line bundles after a common positive multiple. The canonical bundle formula separates LLL into a canonical part, a discriminant measuring singularities, and a moduli line.

M5 claims that on some smooth compact Kähler modification S→XS\to XS→X, the moduli line MSM_SMS​ is semiample, and on every higher smooth modification ν:S1→S\nu:S_1\to Sν:S1​→S one has MS1=ν∗MSM_{S_1}=\nu^*M_SMS1​​=ν∗MS​ as rational holomorphic lines. This is b-semiampleness. It allows coefficient-one horizontal boundary and does not assume projectivity or orbifold Iitaka subadditivity.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. Iitaka subadditivity is a central structural question about the birational classification of varieties. The claimed inequalities cover arbitrary dimension and connect canonical forms, family variation, and analytic positivity.

The equality statement adds information that lower bounds cannot provide, especially when the base has no logarithmic pluricanonical forms. The Kähler moduli theorem would make a numerical-looking contribution into an actual map, allowing geometric constructions that require sections rather than just positivity.

These results also serve as inputs elsewhere in the collection. Keeping their assumptions visible is essential when applying them to abundance or minimal-model claims.

6. The main idea

Replace the fiber by the part seen by its forms

A relative Iitaka map separates a fibration into a part carrying the fiber’s pluricanonical image and a remaining part of Kodaira dimension zero. The latter has essentially one pluricanonical generator in suitable degrees. Taking a cyclic root of that generator produces a differential form on a cover.

As the base varies, this form spans a Hodge line, a line inside a family of cohomology spaces. Its positivity measures some of the variation. The canonical bundle formula packages singular-fiber effects and this moduli contribution while comparing actual section spaces.

M1 and M4 develop the needed positivity on a projective period image and control boundary and ramification terms. Their addition arguments combine sections with auxiliary positive and negative twists so that the twists cancel. This exact comparison is what returns the lower bound to the original canonical divisor.

Keep all parameters of the fiber

M2 needs more than a period map which detects only part of the geometry. It first identifies a parameter field from logarithmic forms. A flat highest Hodge line is used to obtain birational constancy of the Kodaira-zero part. A separate descent argument retains the coordinates of the relative Iitaka base and finite normalization data.

Together these steps claim that the entire fiber is defined over the controlled parameter field. Bounding its transcendence degree then bounds Var⁡(f)\operatorname{Var}(f)Var(f). Forgetting the second step would control a simpler associated object instead of the variation appearing in the theorem.

Use a section’s zero to control the upper bound

For M3, the crucial case is a base of logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero. The paper constructs a base pluriform from a total-space pluriform, retaining a zero on a specified smooth fiber. A suitably chosen general base point avoids the zero sets of all nonzero base pluriforms. Restriction to that fiber must therefore be injective on total-space sections, giving the upper growth bound.

For M5, residue constructions handle coefficient-one boundaries. An exact order calculation identifies the extended Hodge line with the threshold-defined moduli line. Product decompositions, period compactifications, and descent supply global generation. Tracking the actual line prevents an undetected flat twist from changing its section spaces.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The lower inequalities and the equality are not interchangeable. M2 requires nonnegative logarithmic Kodaira dimension of the base. M3 requires smoothness of every boundary stratum over the open base. Removing these assumptions is not part of their statements.

The discriminant used for M5’s moduli line is defined by log canonical thresholds, which measure how much a fiber divisor can be added before singularities cross the allowed limit. It is distinct from M1’s inf-multiplicity orbifold divisor.

The ordinary algebraic theorem is in characteristic zero. The analytic results concern compact Kähler or class-C\mathcal CC spaces under the stated conditions, not arbitrary compact complex manifolds. M5 supplies some globally generating multiple, without a uniform numerical bound for that multiple across all fibrations.

Natural further questions concern effective bounds, positive-characteristic analogues, and extensions beyond the specified singularity and compactness settings. The manuscripts’ claims and dependencies are reported here without an independent mathematical verification.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 §1 specifies the orbifold invariant and the lower inequality. M2 §1 defines whole-fiber variation and identifies its two constancy steps. M3 §1 states the stratum-smooth upper bound and explains the negative-infinity cases. M4 §§1 and 6–7 give the projective Hodge-line route. M5 §§1 and 4 distinguish the threshold moduli line from numerical positivity.

The linked work of Birkar and Popa supplies accessible entry points into the earlier partial results and conjectural landscape. For terminology, see the optional overview of Kodaira dimension.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Orbifold and logarithmic Iitaka subadditivity (September 26, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Logarithmic Kodaira dimension and whole-fiber variation (September 26, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The reverse logarithmic Kodaira inequality and additivity (September 26, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Projective Hodge lines and ordinary Iitaka subadditivity (September 27, 2026).
  • M5. OpenAI, B-semiampleness for compact log-smooth Kähler fibrations (September 10, 2026).

Sources consulted on 12 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Hodge classes, complex multiplication, and the search for algebraic cycles
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 032 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

Polynomial equations describe geometric objects, but topology sees them through different information: loops, surfaces, and their higher-dimensional analogues. Cohomology organizes this information into vector spaces. Which cohomology classes actually come from algebraic subvarieties?

The Hodge conjecture predicts an answer for smooth projective complex varieties. A necessary compatibility with complex coordinates should also be sufficient, once rational linear combinations of subvarieties are allowed. Family 032 claims this for every abelian variety with complex multiplication, a highly symmetric class that includes special elliptic curves and their products.

The family contains five manuscripts, labeled M1–M5 below. M1 supplies the CM theorem and arithmetic consequences. The others address powers of abelian varieties, covers of curves, certain complete intersections, and K3 surfaces. Their boundaries differ considerably. In particular, the current family does not assert an unconditional Hodge theorem for all powers of all projective K3 surfaces.

2. Background and essential definitions

From subvarieties to cohomology

A projective variety is a solution set of homogeneous polynomial equations inside complex projective space. Smoothness excludes singular points. If its complex dimension is ggg, a subvariety of codimension ppp has dimension g−pg-pg−p. An algebraic cycle is a finite formal linear combination of such subvarieties.

The vector space H2p(X,Q)H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)H2p(X,Q) is rational cohomology in degree 2p2p2p. After allowing complex coefficients it decomposes by the numbers of holomorphic and antiholomorphic directions in differential forms. The summand Hp,p(X)H^{p,p}(X)Hp,p(X) has equal numbers of the two. An algebraic cycle of codimension ppp determines a class in

Hdg⁡p(X)=H2p(X,Q)∩Hp,p(X).\operatorname{Hdg}^{p}(X)=H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)\cap H^{p,p}(X).Hdgp(X)=H2p(X,Q)∩Hp,p(X).

Such a class is a rational Hodge class. The conjecture says that every member of this space is obtained from algebraic cycles. Equivalently, the cycle-class map

cl⁡:CH⁡p(X)Q⟶Hdg⁡p(X)\operatorname{cl}:\operatorname{CH}^{p}(X)_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hdg}^{p}(X)cl:CHp(X)Q​⟶Hdgp(X)

is onto. The source identifies cycles under rational equivalence, a relation generated by algebraic families of divisors of rational functions. For understanding the conjecture, the key point is the existence of a cycle with the prescribed cohomology class, rather than the finer equivalence relation.

A divisor is a codimension-one cycle. Intersections of divisors provide many higher-codimension classes, but generally do not provide all of them. Thus solving the divisor case does not settle the conjecture.

Abelian varieties, CM, and powers

An abelian variety is a smooth projective variety with a commutative algebraic group law. Analytically it has the form Cg/Λ\mathbb C^g/\LambdaCg/Λ, with a lattice Λ\LambdaΛ of rank 2g2g2g, satisfying a projectivity condition. An elliptic curve is the one-dimensional example.

Let End⁡0(A)=End⁡(A)⊗ZQ\operatorname{End}^{0}(A)=\operatorname{End}(A)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb QEnd0(A)=End(A)⊗Z​Q. The variety has complex multiplication, abbreviated CM, if this algebra contains a commutative semisimple rational algebra of dimension 2g2g2g. These extra symmetries split cohomology into particularly manageable pieces. CM does not mean merely that the variety is defined over the complex numbers.

The power AmA^mAm is a product of mmm copies of AAA. Its classes can connect different copies, so a theorem for AAA alone need not settle all powers. The Hodge group records the symmetries preserving the Hodge tensors; additional endomorphisms can make it smaller and create additional classes.

A polarization is an ample line bundle, or the corresponding positive form on cohomology. An imaginary quadratic field is Q(−d)\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-d})Q(−d​) with d>0d>0d>0. Its action on an abelian variety gives two conjugate eigenspaces. Balanced dimensions can produce determinant-type Hodge classes called Weil classes, which may lie beyond divisor products.

Two stronger or related questions

The generalized Hodge conjecture concerns entire Hodge substructures, not only individual classes of type (p,p)(p,p)(p,p). It predicts that certain cohomology can be supported on algebraic subsets of an appropriate codimension: the classes disappear when those subsets are removed.

Over finite fields, the Tate conjecture replaces Hodge type with invariance under the arithmetic Frobenius symmetry in étale cohomology. The Hodge standard conjecture concerns positivity of an intersection pairing on algebraic classes. These are distinct statements, connected here through previously established implications.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Lefschetz (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) theorem settles the divisor case. Hodge’s broader question asks whether its relationship between complex structure and algebraic geometry continues in higher codimension. Abelian varieties offer a useful testing ground because their cohomology is the exterior algebra of degree-one cohomology, yet this linear-algebra description does not construct the missing subvarieties.

Deligne’s theorem on absolute Hodge classes showed that Hodge classes on abelian varieties retain their Hodge character under the relevant changes of complex realization. This is a strong compatibility property, but algebraicity is a further step. Pohlmann’s balance criterion and work of André and Hazama reduce CM questions to special tensors and Weil-type classes; M1 §1 describes their precise roles and cites the original papers.

There is substantial prior geometry behind the companion results. Markman’s secant-sheaf construction proves algebraicity of the Weil plane on the split sixfolds relevant to M3. M3 explicitly credits that construction and distinguishes it from its further all-powers conclusion. It also discusses earlier all-powers results of Moonen–Zarhin, Floccari, and Floccari–Fu. A new all-powers claim should therefore not be described as the first algebraicity result for those individual varieties.

Kuga and Satake associated abelian varieties with polarized K3 Hodge structures in 1967. The construction supplies a cohomological map; producing a cycle inducing the specified map is a separate conjectural assertion. Special K3 families already admit algebraic constructions. M2 discusses Paranjape’s curve-product method and more recent results before describing its larger quadratic locus.

Finally, Milne’s work on Lefschetz motives supplies the implication from the CM Hodge conjecture to the Tate conjecture for abelian varieties over finite fields. His work on polarizations supplies the standard-conjecture implication. These consequences do not require each individual Tate class to lift to a Hodge class on a single CM lifting.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: all CM abelian varieties

M1’s Theorem 1.1 asserts that the displayed cycle-class map is onto for every complex CM abelian variety and every codimension. Finite products and powers remain CM, so they are included. The paper then states the generalized Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties, the Tate conjecture for all abelian varieties over finite fields, and the Hodge standard conjecture for abelian varieties in arbitrary characteristic, using the indicated earlier implications.

The arithmetic conclusion is broader than “CM reductions only.” Conversely, it is not a Hodge theorem for every complex abelian variety. The distinction between characteristic-zero geometry and finite-field geometry matters.

M2 and M5: the precise K3 scope

A K3 surface is a smooth simply connected compact complex surface with trivial canonical bundle; here it is projective. Write TST_STS​ for the orthogonal complement of divisor classes in H2(S,Q)H^2(S,\mathbb Q)H2(S,Q), using the cup-product form qqq. This is its transcendental quadratic space.

M2 assumes a rational isometric embedding

(TS,q)↪UQ⊕2⊥⟨−1⟩4.(T_S,q)\hookrightarrow U_{\mathbb Q}^{\oplus2}\perp\langle-1\rangle^{4}.(TS​,q)↪UQ⊕2​⊥⟨−1⟩4.

Here UUU is the two-dimensional hyperbolic plane with matrix (0110)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)(01​10​); the target has dimension eight and signature (2,6)(2,6)(2,6). An embedding must preserve the actual rational quadratic form, not just its dimension or real signature.

On this locus, M2 claims algebraic cycles realizing every prescribed standard even-Clifford Kuga–Satake tensor, and ordinary and generalized Hodge conjectures for all self-powers of SSS. It includes all ample PPP-polarized surfaces for P=U⊕D8(−1)⊕D4(−1)P=U\oplus D_8(-1)\oplus D_4(-1)P=U⊕D8​(−1)⊕D4​(−1), including points where extra divisor classes appear. Here the Dj(−1)D_j(-1)Dj​(−1) are negative root lattices, and a PPP-polarization embeds this lattice into the divisor lattice with an ample class in its image.

For an arbitrary projective K3, M2 also gives an implication from algebraicity of one exact standard Kuga–Satake tensor. M5 provides a different conditional reduction: at a full-orthogonal-Hodge-group point, one algebraic nonzero map from primitive degree-two cohomology into an abelian variety’s degree-two cohomology recovers the prescribed full correspondence. If that input exists very generally throughout a polarized component, the conclusion extends across that component. The existence of this initial map remains a hypothesis.

M3 and M4: extensions beyond CM

M3 claims the rational Hodge conjecture on every self-power of a six-dimensional abelian variety with an imaginary-quadratic action and a compatible polarization whose rational Hermitian form is hyperbolic of signature (3,3)(3,3)(3,3). Hyperbolic means that it has a three-dimensional totally isotropic subspace over the quadratic field. The actual rational form is required; the signature alone is insufficient.

M3 also treats every abelian variety of dimension at most five admitting an imaginary-quadratic action, again on all powers. Both statements include nonsimple varieties and special points with extra endomorphisms. They use M1’s CM theorem.

M4 treats Jacobians, the abelian varieties associated with curves, arising from connected abelian covers of curves. At every tensor Hodge-generic point of the full marked variation, it claims the Hodge conjecture on all powers, also after taking a product with any CM abelian variety. This means that rational tensors which are Hodge at the chosen point are already Hodge throughout that variation. The base genus and compatible branching pattern are unrestricted.

M4 also claims all-power results for a very general smooth diagonal complete intersection cut out by at most two equations of one common degree at least two. “Very general” excludes a countable union of proper algebraic subsets of the full labeled parameter space. It is not a statement about every member of an arbitrarily constrained subfamily.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. The CM Hodge conjecture is a central algebraic-cycle problem with consequences reaching into arithmetic geometry. Its claimed resolution, together with the Tate and positivity implications, would affect a substantial part of the theory of abelian varieties.

The companion results emphasize a second point: understanding cohomology on all powers controls correspondences between factors, not merely subvarieties of one object. Exact correspondences can transfer questions between K3 surfaces, curves, and abelian varieties. This is why an apparently technical distinction between an arbitrary injection and the prescribed Kuga–Satake map has mathematical consequences.

The score measures the significance of these claims if correct. It does not treat the different manuscripts as five independent solutions of the unrestricted Hodge conjecture.

6. The main idea

Balanced tensors become a geometric construction

M1 uses the CM symmetries to divide degree-one cohomology into lines indexed by field embeddings. The Hodge condition becomes a balance condition: holomorphic and antiholomorphic contributions must match at every conjugate embedding. The paper reduces general balances to elementary four-factor relations, schematically

v1+v2=v3+v4,v_1+v_2=v_3+v_4,v1​+v2​=v3​+v4​,

where the viv_ivi​ encode the signs describing CM types. Auxiliary factors and polarization pairings allow these elementary pieces to be assembled and contracted back to the desired tensor.

To realize one piece algebraically, M1 constructs a projective surface carrying four degree-one classes whose product has nonzero integral. A map from that surface to a product of abelian varieties then gives an actual cycle. Algebraic divisor correspondences isolate the required component. Theta one-forms on arithmetic complex-ball quotients produce the nonzero period, while arithmetic operators identify the prescribed rational CM sources of those forms. Both the nonzero period and the rational-source identification are needed.

Supply the missing determinant classes

M3 and M4 use invariant theory: tensors fixed by the relevant symmetry groups are built from pairings and determinant lines. Pairings correspond to divisors. The harder pieces are supplied by algebraic correspondences from CM varieties, where M1 makes rational Hodge lifts algebraic.

M3 combines this with the split-sixfold Weil-plane construction and analyzes the actual Hodge group, including its changes at special points. M4 constructs determinant sources through finite quotients of curve powers and Fermat-type geometry. A Gale correspondence, relating complementary linear configurations, transfers the curve construction to the stated diagonal complete intersections.

Recover and transport an exact K3 tensor

M2 constructs a curve source for a K3-type cohomology space through auxiliary surfaces and pencils. Representation theory then recovers the full even-Clifford tensor from that source. Parameter spaces of algebraic cycles transport the specified action to other periods, with special care when the divisor lattice grows.

M5 isolates this recovery-and-specialization mechanism as a conditional theorem. It explains what a sufficient geometric input would look like without asserting that such an input exists for every K3 surface.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

Rational coefficients are essential throughout. These statements do not supply integral representatives with prescribed denominators, nor do they identify all relations among algebraic cycles modulo rational equivalence.

The CM hypothesis, M2’s rational quadratic embedding, M3’s action and polarization requirements, and M4’s genericity conditions must remain attached to their conclusions. All-powers assertions in one of these settings cannot be transferred automatically to arbitrary abelian varieties or arbitrary K3 surfaces.

The repository’s withdrawal notice withdraws three other manuscripts concerning split eightfold Weil classes, general K3 Kuga–Satake algebraicity, and products of K3 surfaces, citing a sign error and dependent constructions. Those withdrawn manuscripts are not among the five current sources listed here. Their unrestricted conclusions are not adopted in this digest.

The current sources are reported as stated. In particular, the remaining existence hypothesis in M5 is a mathematical boundary of that reduction. Finding the initial correspondence beyond the established loci, and understanding integral refinements of the cycle statements, remain natural further questions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 §§1–3 and 7–8 give the CM statement, the elementary-tensor reduction, and the consequences. M2 §§1–2 specify the K3 locus and exact-tensor criterion. M3 §§1–3 explain the all-powers extension and its debt to earlier Weil-class constructions. M4 §1 separates marked genericity from algebraic very-generality. M5 §1 states the conditional input explicitly.

For background, Deligne’s account and Milne’s papers linked above explain why compatibility, algebraicity, and arithmetic consequences are separate questions. Optional introductions to Hodge theory and complex multiplication can help with terminology; the definitions needed for the claims are given here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The rational Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties (October 6, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Algebraic Kuga–Satake correspondences and Hodge conjectures on a K3 quadratic locus (September 30, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Weil classes and Hodge classes on abelian powers (October 6, 2026).

entry.title: From nef canonical bundles to maps: abundance and uniform degrees
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 034 · Algebraic and complex geometry
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-12

1. The question

A line bundle can look nonnegative when measured on every curve yet have too few global sections to describe a map. The abundance conjecture predicts that canonical line bundles, which encode top-degree differential forms, are special: their numerical nonnegativity should produce an actual geometric fibration.

Family 034 combines fourteen manuscripts addressing this prediction and its quantitative refinements. There are three successive questions. Does a positive power have even one nonzero section? Does some power have sections generating the line at every point? Can one choose a degree depending only on dimension and specified boundary coefficients?

The answers claimed here range from projective varieties to compact Kähler spaces, which need not be projective. The leading Kähler theorem explicitly assumes logarithmic Iitaka subadditivity. A fourfold minimal-model paper is also expressly conditional. These dependencies are part of the mathematical statements, even though related manuscripts in the collection claim the needed inputs.

2. Background and essential definitions

Divisors, singularities, and adjoints

The canonical bundle KXK_XKX​ of a smooth complex nnn-fold consists of holomorphic top-degree forms. A divisor is a formal sum of hypersurfaces; a rational divisor permits rational coefficients. A pair (X,Δ)(X,\Delta)(X,Δ) adds an effective boundary Δ\DeltaΔ, and its adjoint is D=KX+ΔD=K_X+\DeltaD=KX​+Δ.

On a singular space, a divisor need not itself define a line bundle. It is Cartier when it does so locally by one equation, and Q\mathbb QQ-Cartier when some positive integer multiple is Cartier. The manuscripts concern actual multiples and their section spaces, not only their intersection classes.

The singularity conditions can be expressed on a resolution π:Y→X\pi:Y\to Xπ:Y→X: write

KY+BY=π∗(KX+Δ).K_Y+B_Y=\pi^*(K_X+\Delta).KY​+BY​=π∗(KX​+Δ).

The pair is log canonical, or lc, when all coefficients encountered in these crepant boundaries are at most one; it is Kawamata log terminal, or klt, when they are strictly less than one. The latter is more restrictive. Divisorial log terminal, or dlt, is an intermediate controlled setting in which the coefficient-one boundary supports inductive arguments. Semi-log-canonical, or slc, also permits components joined along double loci, with lc behavior after normalization and inclusion of the joining divisor.

Three levels of positivity

For a projective variety, DDD is nef if D⋅C≥0D\cdot C\geq0D⋅C≥0 for every curve CCC. It is pseudoeffective if its numerical class is a limit of effective divisor classes. On a compact Kähler space these notions use curvature classes and positive currents, generalized differential forms which can concentrate along subvarieties.

Nonvanishing means H0(X,mD)≠0H^0(X,mD)\ne0H0(X,mD)=0 for some positive Cartier multiple. Semiampleness means that some such multiple is generated by global sections everywhere. One section can vanish along a large divisor; global generation requires, at each point, a section which does not vanish there.

Kodaira or Iitaka dimension κ(X,D)\kappa(X,D)κ(X,D) is the largest dimension of a rational image defined by ratios of sections of multiples of DDD, with value −∞-\infty−∞ when there are no sections. For a nef divisor, numerical dimension ν(D)\nu(D)ν(D) instead measures nonzero intersection powers. These two dimensions need not agree merely by definition. Abundance is precisely a bridge from numerical positivity to section geometry.

A minimal model is a birational model with nef adjoint and the required singularity comparison. A good minimal model has semiample adjoint. Birational means that dense open subsets are isomorphic. The minimal model program simplifies a variety through contractions and flips; finding a nef endpoint and proving it good are separate tasks.

Uniformity and the full Iitaka field

If D∼Q0D\sim_{\mathbb Q}0D∼Q​0, some multiple defines the trivial line bundle. Its least positive trivializing degree is the index. Uniform index bounds must work across all pairs in a stated class.

For a rational divisor, define

Vm(D)=H0(X,OX(⌊mD⌋)),K(D)=k(s/t: s,t∈Vm(D)∖{0}, m>0).V_m(D)=H^0\bigl(X,\mathcal O_X(\lfloor mD\rfloor)\bigr),\qquadK(D)=k\bigl(s/t:\ s,t\in V_m(D)\setminus\{0\},\ m>0\bigr).Vm​(D)=H0(X,OX​(⌊mD⌋)),K(D)=k(s/t: s,t∈Vm​(D)∖{0}, m>0).

The floor rounds each coefficient down; on a normal variety the indicated divisorial sheaf is interpreted reflexively when it is not a line bundle. The field K(D)K(D)K(D) is the Iitaka field inside the function field k(X)k(X)k(X). Recovering it in one degree is stronger than obtaining an image of the correct dimension: a proper finite subfield has the same transcendence degree.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The threefold story already separated the main difficulties. Miyaoka treated numerical dimension one, Kawamata completed canonical abundance for minimal threefolds, and Keel–Matsuki–McKernan established the logarithmic result. Fujino’s slc work addressed the additional problem of gluing sections across components. M4 §1 gives these original references and explains how their boundary methods enter its induction.

Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan established fundamental minimal-model and finite-generation results. These do not make every nef lc adjoint semiample automatically. In particular, finite generation alone does not supply a nonzero section when all positive section spaces vanish.

The Kähler theory required analytic replacements for projective tools. Höring–Peternell constructed threefold minimal models, Campana–Höring–Peternell treated canonical abundance, and Das–Ou proved log abundance for compact Kähler lc threefolds. M1 and M14 carefully distinguish these lower-dimensional inputs from the new higher-dimensional claims.

Uniform effectivity developed along another route.
