The all-time bounded-region estimate gives local finiteness, not finite total measure of the unbounded trace. No convergence theorem for lattice step counts is asserted here. Such questions require a normalization and a separate discrete-to-continuum argument.

The remaining relationships among these measures, their exact proportionality constants where applicable, and extensions to other SLE variants are distinct questions beyond the source claims.

8. Sources and further reading

Schramm’s problem collection, Beffara’s dimension theorem, and Rezaei’s zero-measure theorem frame the question. Lawler–Rezaei and Holden–Yuan explain the related but different notions of natural length.

M1 below supplies the moment-based existence construction; M2 supplies the explicit gauge and its comparison with the exponent-one candidate. Both mathematical claims are reported as stated.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An exact Hausdorff gauge for SLE: A moment-integral and finite-batch construction (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, An explicit exact Hausdorff gauge for SLE: A regular formula from quantitative tails and dense visits (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Building the free uniform spanning forest from independent randomness
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 231 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A uniform spanning tree is a global random object: every vertex is included, cycles are forbidden, and distant edge choices can affect one another. On an infinite graph, its free-boundary limit may be a forest with several components.

Can that forest nevertheless be generated from independent random labels placed at the vertices, using a rule that respects every graph symmetry and chooses no special root?

This is the factor-of-IID question. It asks whether the apparent global coordination can be encoded measurably in independent local randomness. The rule may inspect infinitely far, so it is a structural question about random processes rather than automatically an efficient distributed algorithm.

Family 231 contains a manuscript claiming one such rule for every infinite connected locally finite simple unweighted graph. It also gives a broader factor theorem for translation-invariant strongly Rayleigh processes on countable groups, including a class of determinantal processes.

2. Background and essential definitions

Free and wired spanning forests

A spanning tree of a finite connected graph includes every vertex, is connected, and contains no cycle. The uniform spanning-tree measure gives each such tree equal probability.

For an infinite graph GGG, choose an increasing sequence of finite connected subgraphs exhausting all edges. Sample a uniform spanning tree in each and examine probabilities involving any fixed finite set of edges. The free uniform spanning forest, or FUSF, is the limiting law when no boundary vertices are identified. This limit exists and does not depend on the chosen exhaustion.

The wired construction instead identifies the outer boundary before taking the limit. Free and wired forests can differ, so a sampling result for one is not automatically a result for the other.

A graph is locally finite if each vertex has finite degree. Degrees need not have one common upper bound. Simplicity excludes loops and multiple edges; unweighted means all graph edges have the same original weight.

Factors of independent labels

Give every vertex vvv an independent uniform random variable Uv∈[0,1]U_v\in[0,1]Uv​∈[0,1]. A factor rule decides whether an edge eee is present through a measurable function

Φ(G,U,e)∈{0,1}.\Phi(G,U,e)\in\{0,1\}.Φ(G,U,e)∈{0,1}.

Equivariance means that relabeling the graph by an isomorphism and transporting its random labels transports the output in exactly the same way. Root independence means that the construction uses no distinguished vertex. Borel measurability is the standard regularity requirement ensuring that this deterministic map defines a random process.

The output coordinates need not be independent. Their dependencies are created by applying the rule to overlapping portions of the input. For example, an edge rule can depend on random labels shared with nearby edge rules.

A finitary factor has an additional property: each output can be determined from an almost surely finite random neighborhood. An ordinary Borel factor need not have this property. A uniform real label also contains an unlimited sequence of random bits, unlike a fixed finite-alphabet label.

Negative dependence and determinant laws

For a finite binary process X=(Xi)i∈FX=(X_i)_{i\in F}X=(Xi​)i∈F​, its generating polynomial is

g(z)=E∏i∈FziXi.g(z)=\mathbb E\prod_{i\in F}z_i^{X_i}.g(z)=Ei∈F∏​ziXi​​.

The law is strongly Rayleigh if this polynomial is nonzero whenever every ziz_izi​ has positive imaginary part. On a countable set, this is required for every finite-coordinate marginal. The algebraic condition implies robust forms of negative dependence: selecting one coordinate tends to discourage selecting others, and the relevant properties survive certain changes of weights.

A determinantal random subset with kernel KKK is specified by

P(A⊆X)=det⁡(Kg,h)g,h∈A\mathbb P(A\subseteq X)=\det(K_{g,h})_{g,h\in A}P(A⊆X)=det(Kg,h​)g,h∈A​

for every finite set AAA. If KKK is a Hermitian positive contraction, meaning 0≤K≤I0\leq K\leq I0≤K≤I as an operator on square-summable functions, such a law exists and is strongly Rayleigh. The determinant controls joint inclusion probabilities.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Pemantle constructed infinite-volume spanning-tree limits on the integer lattice. Benjamini, Lyons, Peres, and Schramm developed the general theory of uniform spanning forests, including the distinction between free and wired limits.

For wired forests on transient graphs, cycle popping and Wilson’s algorithm rooted at infinity already provide an IID construction. Transience means a random walk can escape rather than returning indefinitely. That construction did not settle the free-forest problem on arbitrary graphs.

Determinantal structure supplied another route in group settings. Lyons and Thom proved a stronger Bernoulli-isomorphism conclusion for the relevant invariant determinantal measures on amenable groups. Amenability permits averaging through finite sets whose boundary is small relative to their size. The unrestricted factor problem also includes nonamenable settings where that method of approximation is unavailable.

Timár established free-forest factor results for recurrent unimodular random graphs and, more generally, invariantly amenable unimodular random graphs, with stronger finitary conclusions in the stated amenable setting. The cited December 2025 version still lists the general FUSF factor question as open.

The new construction also has an information-theoretic ancestry. Eldan introduced stochastic localization; El Alaoui and Montanari described its Gaussian observation and innovation formulation. Nam, Sly, and Zhang used Brownian-driven posterior equations for factor constructions of free Ising measures on regular trees. The current manuscript adapts that observation mechanism to a countable collection of negatively dependent binary variables.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

One rule for every graph in the class

The main theorem claims a single Borel, root-independent, equivariant rule Φ\PhiΦ such that, for every infinite connected locally finite simple undirected unweighted graph,

{e∈E(G):Φ(G,U,e)=1}has law FUSF⁡G.\{e\in E(G):\Phi(G,U,e)=1\}\quad\text{has law }\operatorname{FUSF}_G.{e∈E(G):Φ(G,U,e)=1}has law FUSFG​.

The quantifier is graphwise: one rule works across the whole class. It does not first choose a random-graph distribution and tailor the construction to that law.

No amenability, transience, uniform degree bound, or degree-moment assumption is imposed. The output has the joint forest law, rather than merely the correct probability for each individual edge.

As a consequence, the FUSF is a graph factor of IID under every unimodular random-graph law supported on this class. Unimodularity is the mass-transport balance saying that expected total mass sent from a randomly rooted vertex equals expected total mass received, for every invariant nonnegative transport rule. The source does not need this balance for its stronger graphwise construction.

The conclusion is an ordinary Borel factor. It does not state a finite coding radius or a finite input alphabet.

Strongly Rayleigh laws under group translations

Let Γ\GammaΓ be a countable group, and index a binary process by its elements. Left translation acts by

(τgx)h=xg−1h.(\tau_gx)_h=x_{g^{-1}h}.(τg​x)h​=xg−1h​.

For every strongly Rayleigh law ν\nuν invariant under these translations, the manuscript claims a Borel map from independent uniform labels to ν\nuν, commuting with every translation on every label input.

The group need not be amenable or finitely generated, and finite groups are allowed. In this theorem the map may depend on Γ\GammaΓ and ν\nuν, unlike the single graphwise rule in the forest theorem.

The determinantal corollary applies whenever a Hermitian positive-contraction kernel on ℓ2(Γ)\ell^2(\Gamma)ℓ2(Γ) defines a translation-invariant law. A sufficient condition is that KKK commute with left translations. Projection kernels and complex Hermitian kernels are included; no trace-class assumption is imposed on the full operator.

This statement concerns the regular action on the group itself. It is not asserted for every action of a group on every other index set, and a factor map need not be an invertible Bernoulli isomorphism.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The free uniform spanning forest is a canonical infinite random structure. A universal graphwise IID representation would answer a substantial factor question while removing the geometric restrictions present in previous constructions.

The group theorem broadens the significance beyond spanning forests. It would connect a robust algebraic negative-dependence condition with equivariant generation from independent randomness, without relying on amenability.

The result also separates two notions often conflated in informal discussion. A process can be generated measurably from independent labels without admitting a bounded-time or finite-neighborhood sampling algorithm. The structural conclusion is strong even when no such computational guarantee is supplied.

The rating reflects broad consequences within probability on graphs and invariant random processes, while retaining the theorem’s precise distinction between graph isomorphisms and regular group translations.

6. The main idea

Reveal a target sample through Brownian noise

Temporarily suppose a sample Xe∈{0,1}X_e\in\{0,1\}Xe​∈{0,1} from the desired forest law already exists. Observe each coordinate through

Ye(t)=tXe+Be(t),Y_e(t)=tX_e+B_e(t),Ye​(t)=tXe​+Be​(t),

with independent Brownian motions BeB_eBe​. As time grows, the signal dominates the noise: the long-time slope reveals XeX_eXe​.

Given the observations, the conditional mean be(t,Y)b_e(t,Y)be​(t,Y) is a drift. Subtracting its accumulated contribution produces innovations,

W^e(t)=Ye(t)−∫0tbe(s,Y(s)) ds,\widehat W_e(t)=Y_e(t)-\int_0^t b_e(s,Y(s))\,ds,We​(t)=Ye​(t)−∫0t​be​(s,Y(s))ds,

which form independent Brownian inputs under the observation law. If the relation can be inverted deterministically, these independent inputs can generate the original correlated sample.

Negative dependence controls the inverse

For a finite weighted spanning tree, let pep_epe​ be the inclusion probability of edge eee, and let hfh_fhf​ be the logarithm of edge fff‘s weight. Differentiating gives

∂pe∂hf=Cov⁡(Xe,Xf),∑f∣∂pe∂hf∣=2pe(1−pe)≤12.\frac{\partial p_e}{\partial h_f}=\operatorname{Cov}(X_e,X_f),\qquad\sum_f\left|\frac{\partial p_e}{\partial h_f}\right|=2p_e(1-p_e)\leq\frac12.∂hf​∂pe​​=Cov(Xe​,Xf​),f∑​​∂hf​∂pe​​​=2pe​(1−pe​)≤21​.

Different edges have nonpositive covariance, while every spanning tree has the same number of edges. Together these facts bound the entire response of one inclusion probability, uniformly in graph size and weights.

The manuscript passes this response bound to a countable-coordinate drift and solves

Ze(t)=we(t)+∫0tbe(s,Z(s)) dsZ_e(t)=w_e(t)+\int_0^t b_e(s,Z(s))\,dsZe​(t)=we​(t)+∫0t​be​(s,Z(s))ds

by deterministic successive approximation. Only differences between successive approximations need a uniform bound. This matters because infinitely many independent Brownian paths are not uniformly bounded over all coordinates.

Feeding independent Brownian paths into the inverse recovers the observation process, and integer-time slopes recover the forest. Intrinsic edge-centered neighborhoods preserve graph symmetry; independent vertex labels provide independent edge paths by allocating disjoint random coordinates.

For strongly Rayleigh laws, the same covariance-row estimate holds as an inequality after suitable finite extensions. Translates of finite subsets of the group supply compatible coordinate exhaustions. They need not have small boundary, which is why the stated regular-action result requires no amenability.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The graph theorem is stated for simple unweighted locally finite graphs. Weighted finite trees appear inside the proof, but that does not automatically extend the final graphwise claim to arbitrary infinite conductance networks or multiple edges.

The construction has no stated finitary radius, runtime, or finite-bit budget. Measurability and exact equivariance are the conclusions; practical sampling complexity is a separate question. Stronger finitary results already known in special amenable settings remain stronger in that particular respect.

The group theorem allows its factor to depend on the target law and treats only the regular left action. The existence of compatible finite exhaustions is used in that form. General actions and broader negatively dependent processes require additional analysis.

The companion free-Ising factor threshold discussed in family 236 uses a related observation viewpoint with a different recovery mechanism. It is a separate theorem, not an automatic consequence of the forest result. All claims here are reported as stated by the source.

8. Sources and further reading

The uniform-spanning-forest paper and Timár’s work give the main graph-theoretic background. Lyons–Thom explains the earlier amenable-group determinantal result. For the algebraic condition used in the extension, see Borcea, Brändén, and Liggett, Negative dependence and the geometry of polynomials.

The source manuscript below states the graphwise and group-action theorems separately and develops the Brownian observation inverse that connects them.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The free uniform spanning forest is a factor of IID (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The joint scaling limit of critical Ashkin–Teller currents
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 233 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A statistical-mechanics model can have several descriptions. One records spins, another draws connected clusters, and a third builds a random height surface. Understanding each separately does not explain how they fit together. Two random objects can have familiar individual distributions while their dependence contains substantial additional information.

The Ashkin–Teller model provides a particularly rich example. Its critical parameters form a line rather than an isolated point. Along that line, a height representation is expected to approach a Gaussian free field, while two coupled collections of current clusters should become geometric structures determined by that same field.

Family 233 contains one manuscript claiming this joint continuum description throughout the stated critical line, including its four-state Potts endpoint. It retains the complete compact supports of the clusters, their nesting at every depth, and the special cluster touching the wired boundary. The proposed limit explains how a random surface encodes two interacting geometries.

2. Background and essential definitions

From spins to currents

The usual Ashkin–Teller model couples two Ising spin systems. Each vertex carries two signs, and the interaction rewards agreements within each system and an additional product of the two agreements. The dimensionless interaction strengths are denoted by JJJ and UUU.

The manuscript fixes

J>0,U≤J,sinh⁡(2J)=e−2U.J>0,\qquad U\leq J,\qquad \sinh(2J)=e^{-2U}.J>0,U≤J,sinh(2J)=e−2U.

These equations specify the critical line under consideration. Two useful parameters are

c=1+e4U,g=8πarcsin⁡ ⁣(c2),1<c≤2,43<g≤4.c=\sqrt{1+e^{4U}},\qquad g=\frac{8}{\pi}\arcsin\!\left(\frac c2\right),\qquad 1<c\leq2,\quad \frac43<g\leq4.c=1+e4U​,g=π8​arcsin(2c​),1<c≤2,34​<g≤4.

Here ggg is a continuum coupling parameter, not a lattice spacing. The lattice spacing will be δ\deltaδ.

A current is an edge configuration obtained from an expansion of the spin model. For the theorem, it is enough to describe the equivalent joint construction. Put signs τ\tauτ on square-lattice vertices and signs τ†\tau^\daggerτ† on the centers of bounded faces. The latter form the dual lattice. Fix the primal boundary signs to +1+1+1, and leave the dual boundary free.

Across a pair of crossing primal and dual edges, the two spin systems are forbidden from disagreeing simultaneously. Give an allowed spin configuration weight proportional to ttt raised to its total number of disagreements, where t=1/ct=1/ct=1/c. If the dual signs disagree, open the primal edge and close the dual edge; do the reverse if the primal signs disagree. If neither disagrees, open only the primal edge, only the dual edge, or neither, with probabilities 1−t,1−t,2t−11-t,1-t,2t-11−t,1−t,2t−1, respectively. The primal boundary edges are open.

Thus the two open-edge sets never cross. They are not complements: both edges can be closed. Their connected components are the current clusters. The primal collection has a wired boundary cluster; the dual collection has free boundary conditions.

Heights and Gaussian fields

Define a height HδH_\deltaHδ​, zero on the primal boundary, by the corner increment

Hδ(f)−Hδ(v)=12τ(v)τ†(f),H_\delta(f)-H_\delta(v)=\frac12\tau(v)\tau^\dagger(f),Hδ​(f)−Hδ​(v)=21​τ(v)τ†(f),

where vvv is incident to face fff. The spin constraint makes the increments consistent around closed paths. Heights are integers at vertices and half-integers at face centers.

A two-dimensional Gaussian free field, or GFF, is a random generalized function. Its averages against smooth test functions are jointly Gaussian; individual point values are not ordinary finite random variables. This article uses the manuscript’s field hhh with zero boundary conditions and covariance operator

GD=2π(−ΔD)−1.G_D=2\pi(-\Delta_D)^{-1}.GD​=2π(−ΔD​)−1.

Here −ΔD-\Delta_D−ΔD​ is the positive Laplacian with zero boundary values on the domain DDD. Near coincident points its Green kernel behaves as −log⁡∣z−w∣-\log|z-w|−log∣z−w∣. This factor 2π2\pi2π matters when comparing formulas with other GFF conventions.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ashkin and Teller introduced their four-component lattice model in 1943. Its coupled spins later became an important setting for critical behavior that varies continuously with a parameter. The geometric representations used here developed through work relating spin systems, percolation and height functions; Lis gave the precise spin–edge–height framework and current weights on which this manuscript builds. Original model, Lis’s representation.

An essential solved case occurs at U=0U=0U=0, where g=2g=2g=2. The relevant currents are then double random currents. Duminil-Copin and Lis identified their signed nesting field with a dimer height. Duminil-Copin, Lis and Qian subsequently obtained conformally invariant limits of the height and recursive cluster-boundary families. This supplied both a concrete continuum picture and an exploration strategy. Nesting field, double-current limits.

In 2026, Alcalde López, Heeney and Lis described the joint height and complete current-cluster collections at the Ising point, and formulated the extension along the critical line addressed here. Their broader work couples Ising magnetisation fields to a GFF. A separate paper by Alcalde López and Sepúlveda studies a stronger Ising-point excursion decomposition involving additional fields and measures. Those extra conclusions should not be attributed to the present theorem. Critical-line conjecture and Ising coupling, excursion decomposition.

The height is also related to a six-vertex model with weights (1,1,c)(1,1,c)(1,1,c). Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Lammers and Manolescu proved a GFF limit for 3≤c≤2\sqrt3\leq c\leq23​≤c≤2, and developed estimates on a larger interval. The new manuscript uses those estimates while claiming the missing covariance and Gaussianity arguments needed for its full range. The full-plane companion described in family 225 is related, but does not supply the random-domain cluster theorem by itself. Earlier six-vertex work.

The historical gap is therefore specific: extend a known joint picture beyond the Ising point, with the appropriate varying coupling, and identify entire cluster supports even near rough boundaries.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A limit for every admissible approximation

Let DDD be a bounded Jordan domain: its boundary is a simple closed curve, without a smoothness assumption. Approximate it by simple square-lattice polygons whose boundaries converge under parametrization and whose interiors eventually contain every compact subset of DDD.

For every fixed allowed (J,U)(J,U)(J,U), Theorem 2.3 claims the joint limit

(Hδ,Cδw,Cδf,C∂,δ) ⟹ (hπg,Cw,Cf,A−a,a(h)),a=π2g.\bigl(H_\delta,\mathcal C_\delta^{\mathrm w},\mathcal C_\delta^{\mathrm f},C_{\partial,\delta}\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\\left(\frac{h}{\pi\sqrt g},\mathcal C^{\mathrm w},\mathcal C^{\mathrm f},A_{-a,a}(h)\right),\qquad a=\frac\pi2\sqrt g.(Hδ​,Cδw​,Cδf​,C∂,δ​) ⟹ (πg​h​,Cw,Cf,A−a,a​(h)),a=2π​g​.

The superscripts distinguish wired and free collections. The final component singles out the wired boundary cluster. The convergence is along the full mesh limit, with no specially chosen subsequence.

Height convergence is in local Sobolev spaces Hlocs(D)H^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)Hlocs​(D) for every s<−1s<-1s<−1. These spaces permit distributions rather than pointwise functions. Equivalently for the basic interpretation, integrate the lattice height against smooth functions and obtain the corresponding Gaussian averages with the stated normalization.

For clusters, every set above a fixed positive diameter must have a nearby counterpart in Hausdorff distance, in both directions. Hausdorff distance measures whether every point of either compact set lies near the other set. The matching is not required to be one-to-one, and the topology ignores multiplicities and singleton clusters. The distinguished boundary cluster is tracked separately. The continuum collections contain only finitely many clusters larger than any fixed positive size.

How the common field determines the clusters

A two-valued local set A−α,β(h)A_{-\alpha,\beta}(h)A−α,β​(h) is a random closed set determined by the GFF. Once it is exposed, the field in each remaining component is a constant, either −α-\alpha−α or β\betaβ, plus an independent zero-boundary GFF. The parameters satisfy α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0α,β>0 and α+β≥2λ\alpha+\beta\geq2\lambdaα+β≥2λ, where λ=π/2\lambda=\pi/2λ=π/2.

This is a precise conditional description, not a contour drawn through pointwise GFF values. The set with labels ±2λ\pm2\lambda±2λ produces holes whose boundary loops have the law called CLE₄, the conformally invariant loop ensemble with parameter four.

The wired construction starts by retaining A−a,a(h)A_{-a,a}(h)A−a,a​(h). In each remaining component, subtract its constant label and apply the free construction below to the residual GFF.

For the free construction, first expose the CLE₄ holes of a zero-boundary field. A hole has label ξ2λ\xi2\lambdaξ2λ, with ξ=±1\xi=\pm1ξ=±1. Inside it, expose a further two-valued set: use relative labels −2λ,2a−2λ-2\lambda,2a-2\lambda−2λ,2a−2λ if ξ=1\xi=1ξ=1, or −(2a−2λ),2λ-(2a-2\lambda),2\lambda−(2a−2λ),2λ if ξ=−1\xi=-1ξ=−1. Retain this inner set, including its outer boundary, as one cluster. Then repeat in all its remaining components.

Measured relative to the incoming height, the retained split has labels 000 and ξ2a\xi2aξ2a. The initial CLE₄ set is an exploration device, not itself a retained current cluster. Both recursive constructions use the same realization of hhh, which specifies their joint dependence at every nesting depth.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the claim gives a broad geometric description of an interacting critical line, extending a detailed special-case theory to continuously varying parameters and the four-state Potts endpoint.

The gain over a height theorem is substantial. Knowing that a surface becomes Gaussian does not identify which microscopic edges belong to the same macroscopic object. Here, entire cluster supports and the wired boundary component are tied to canonical structures of that Gaussian field.

The result also makes parameter dependence concrete. At the Ising point, g=2g=2g=2; at the four-state Potts endpoint, g=4g=4g=4. The splitting height aaa changes accordingly, so one common family of continuum constructions describes distinct lattice interactions. The score reflects this geometric unification, while recognizing the major foundations already established in the Ising and six-vertex settings.

6. The main idea

The manuscript separates two tasks: identify the random field, then recover the complete geometry coupled to it.

First, it develops exact conditional laws for cutting along suitable explored boundaries. A current and an auxiliary complementary spin percolation are used together. This auxiliary complement must not be confused with the other current in the theorem. An appropriate explored perimeter leaves a region with constant boundary height, making its conditional field accessible.

Second, reflection positivity and estimates from the six-vertex representation constrain the plane covariance. Screening arguments control how local insertions respond to distant boundary information. Moment identities then identify Gaussian limits in the flat regions. The normalization is extracted from the free-energy response only after the necessary Gaussian convergence has been obtained.

Third, stop cluster explorations before their geometry becomes uncontrolled. The conditional limiting field in the remaining regions has the harmonic constants and independent GFF remainders characteristic of two-valued local sets. This connects discrete stopping rules to the recursive continuum constructions.

There remains a geometric problem: some pieces of a current cluster might escape detection by the height jumps around its visible holes. The manuscript uses local passage tests, collar bounds and a no-crossing argument to rule out such missing macroscopic pieces. It then matches the complete collections, including the boundary cluster and all nesting depths.

The guiding principle is that field convergence supplies information about fluctuations, while additional exploration estimates determine which fluctuations belong to the same geometric cluster. Neither step automatically replaces the other.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The parameters are fixed before taking the mesh to zero. There is no stated uniformity as c↓1c\downarrow1c↓1, equivalently g↓4/3g\downarrow4/3g↓4/3. That excluded limiting value cannot simply be added by continuity.

The result uses the specified wired/free coupling on admissible square-lattice approximations of bounded Jordan domains. It does not assert every boundary condition, lattice or off-critical perturbation has the same limit.

Cluster convergence concerns compact supports in the stated noninjective matching topology. It does not assign a limiting area measure, preserve cluster multiplicities, supply natural parametrizations, or identify all spin-domain-wall curves. Nor does it give an exact metric exponent for travelling within a cluster.

The theorem includes the four-state Potts endpoint at a fixed parameter value. This should be distinguished from taking a second limit along the critical line toward that endpoint. Its normalization also belongs to the height convention used here; replacing HHH by the unit-corner-increment height 2H2H2H changes the multiplier.

Natural further problems concern geometric measures, additional spin observables and boundary conditions beyond this coupling. Some richer statements are already known at the Ising point; extending them through the full critical line would require additional conclusions beyond this manuscript.

8. Sources and further reading

The principal source is M1, especially Sections 2.1–2.7 for the model, recursive sets, topology and joint theorem. Its introduction explains the relation to prior double-current and six-vertex results.

For the continuum objects, Aru, Sepúlveda and Werner develop bounded-type thin local sets, while Aru and Sepúlveda study two-valued sets and their geometry. These give the conditional-GFF meaning behind the recursive description. Family 232 offers a related introduction to height limits and the distinction between a field theorem and an interface theorem.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The joint scaling limit of critical Ashkin–Teller currents (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: All-temperature pressure for orthogonally invariant Ising spin glasses
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 234 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Knowing a symmetric matrix’s eigenvalues solves a quadratic optimization problem on the Euclidean sphere. It does not solve the same problem when every coordinate must be +1+1+1 or −1-1−1. A rotation preserves the sphere but moves the corners of the cube, so eigenvectors matter to an Ising spin system.

Suppose those eigenvectors are uniformly random. Can the limiting eigenvalue distribution then determine the system’s thermodynamics? Family 234 claims an affirmative answer at every fixed temperature, for compact limiting spectra without asymptotic outliers. It also treats deterministic external magnetic fields and derives zero-temperature optimization limits.

The resulting answer is a variational formula: a precisely defined optimization over possible hierarchies of spin overlaps. It need not reduce to an elementary expression, but it turns an exponentially large random sum into a deterministic mathematical problem.

2. Background and essential definitions

Random interactions and pressure

There are NNN spins, assembled into a vector σ∈{−1,1}N\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^Nσ∈{−1,1}N. Write the interaction matrix as

JN=UNTΛNUN,ΛN=diag⁡(λ1,N,…,λN,N).J_N=U_N^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_NU_N,\qquad \Lambda_N=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1,N},\ldots,\lambda_{N,N}).JN​=UNT​ΛN​UN​,ΛN​=diag(λ1,N​,…,λN,N​).

The diagonal matrix is initially deterministic. The orthogonal matrix UNU_NUN​ has Haar distribution, the uniform distribution invariant under multiplying by any fixed orthogonal matrix. Thus the spectrum is prescribed while its directions are randomized.

The manuscript uses normalized pressure

PN=1Nlog⁡[2−N∑σ∈{−1,1}Nexp⁡ ⁣(12σTJNσ)].P_N=\frac1N\log\left[2^{-N}\sum_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^N}\exp\!\left(\frac12\sigma^{\mathsf T}J_N\sigma\right)\right].PN​=N1​log​2−Nσ∈{−1,1}N∑​exp(21​σTJN​σ)​.

Larger quadratic values receive greater weight. Inverse temperature and coupling strength are absorbed into ΛN\Lambda_NΛN​. The factor 2−N2^{-N}2−N makes the spin prior a probability measure: pressure is zero when all interactions vanish. Using an unnormalized counting sum adds log⁡2\log2log2.

The empirical spectral measure

μN=1N∑i=1Nδλi,N\mu_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{\lambda_{i,N}}μN​=N1​i=1∑N​δλi,N​​

records the fraction of eigenvalues in each region; δx\delta_xδx​ denotes a point mass. Its limit is μ\muμ, a probability law supported in a compact interval. The smallest and largest eigenvalues must approach the corresponding endpoints of the support. Weak convergence of μN\mu_NμN​ alone is insufficient, because it can overlook a small number of extreme eigenvalues.

Overlaps and hierarchies

Two independent equilibrium samples at the same interaction matrix are called replicas. Their overlap is

Q(σ,τ)=1N∑i=1Nσiτi.Q(\sigma,\tau)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\sigma_i\tau_i.Q(σ,τ)=N1​i=1∑N​σi​τi​.

It is 111 for identical configurations, −1-1−1 for opposites, and near zero for largely unrelated signs. In a spin glass, several levels of similarity can survive as NNN grows.

The formula uses a nondecreasing function p:(0,1)→[0,1]p:(0,1)\to[0,1]p:(0,1)→[0,1], interpreted as a quantile description of a trial overlap hierarchy. The nonnegative convention comes from small auxiliary perturbations used in the analysis; it does not mean unperturbed finite systems have no negative overlaps.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model introduced a mean-field spin glass with Gaussian pair interactions. Parisi proposed that its low-temperature behavior requires a hierarchy of overlaps rather than one scalar similarity. Guerra proved the variational upper bound, and Talagrand established the matching pressure formula. Aizenman, Sims and Starr developed a complementary cavity formulation based on adding spins. SK model, Guerra’s bound, Talagrand’s formula, cavity principle.

Orthogonally invariant models ask how much of that picture survives with more general spectra. Statistical-mechanics calculations for the random orthogonal model and related interactions developed spectral and replica-symmetry-breaking predictions. These provided important motivation, but are different from an all-temperature theorem under explicit matrix assumptions. Marinari, Parisi and Ritort, Cherrier, Dean and Lefèvre.

Rigorous results had reached substantial high-temperature regimes. Bhattacharya and Sen treated zero-field pressure. Fan and Wu obtained a replica-symmetric formula with external fields at sufficiently high temperature. The manuscript also credits 2026 work by Fan, Misiakiewicz, Wang and Wen giving an explicit high-temperature criterion for a constant field through dynamical mean-field analysis. Zero-field result, external-field result, 2026 development.

A further ingredient comes from random-matrix theory: Guionnet and Maïda analyzed spherical integrals using the spectral R-transform, including behavior at a spectral edge. A spherical integral averages over continuously varying directions. The quenched Ising pressure averages the logarithm of a sum over cube vertices, so this earlier theorem does not by itself answer the present question. Spherical-integral theorem.

The claimed advance is to remove the high-temperature restriction while retaining the full overlap hierarchy and a general limiting spectrum.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The spectral contribution

Let λ+\lambda_+λ+​ be the top edge of the support of μ\muμ. For x>0x>0x>0, solve

∫μ(dλ)b(x)−λ=x,b(x)>λ+.\int\frac{\mu(d\lambda)}{b(x)-\lambda}=x,\qquad b(x)>\lambda_+.∫b(x)−λμ(dλ)​=x,b(x)>λ+​.

If there is no such solution, set b(x)=λ+b(x)=\lambda_+b(x)=λ+​. Define

R(x)=b(x)−1x,R(0)=∫λ μ(dλ).R(x)=b(x)-\frac1x,\qquad R(0)=\int\lambda\,\mu(d\lambda).R(x)=b(x)−x1​,R(0)=∫λμ(dλ).

This is the manuscript’s edge-extended R-transform. The edge rule is part of the definition, not an assumed analytic continuation.

For a trial overlap function ppp, put

Dp(r)=1−r−∫01(p(s)−r)+ ds,(u)+=max⁡{u,0},D_p(r)=1-r-\int_0^1(p(s)-r)_+\,ds,\qquad (u)_+=\max\{u,0\},Dp​(r)=1−r−∫01​(p(s)−r)+​ds,(u)+​=max{u,0},

and define its spectral cost by

Gμ(p)=12∫01R(Dp(r)) dr.G_\mu(p)=\frac12\int_0^1 R(D_p(r))\,dr.Gμ​(p)=21​∫01​R(Dp​(r))dr.

The function DpD_pDp​ translates the overlap hierarchy into the argument seen by the spectral transform.

The single-spin contribution

A second functional S(p)S(p)S(p) depends on the Ising spin space, but not on μ\muμ. It is built from Gaussian averaging of the single-spin expression log⁡cosh⁡z\log\cosh zlogcoshz.

Here is its finite-step definition. Choose a nonnegative nondecreasing step function hhh, with successive values h0,…,hk−1h_0,\ldots,h_{k-1}h0​,…,hk−1​ and interval lengths w0,…,wk−1w_0,\ldots,w_{k-1}w0​,…,wk−1​ summing to one. Set h−1=0h_{-1}=0h−1​=0 and ζi=∑l<iwl\zeta_i=\sum_{l<i}w_lζi​=∑l<i​wl​. For a standard normal variable ZZZ, define

(Ta,vf)(z)={a−1log⁡Eexp⁡{af(z+vZ)},a>0,Ef(z+vZ),a=0.(T_{a,v}f)(z)=\begin{cases}a^{-1}\log\mathbb E\exp\{a f(z+\sqrt v Z)\},&a>0,\\\mathbb E f(z+\sqrt v Z),&a=0.\end{cases}(Ta,v​f)(z)={a−1logEexp{af(z+v​Z)},Ef(z+v​Z),​a>0,a=0.​

Starting with Fk−1(z)=log⁡cosh⁡zF_{k-1}(z)=\log\cosh zFk−1​(z)=logcoshz, apply these operators backwards:

Fi−1=Tζi,hi−hi−1Fi,ℓ(h)=F−1(0)−hk−12.F_{i-1}=T_{\zeta_i,h_i-h_{i-1}}F_i,\qquad\ell(h)=F_{-1}(0)-\frac{h_{k-1}}2.Fi−1​=Tζi​,hi​−hi−1​​Fi​,ℓ(h)=F−1​(0)−2hk−1​​.

Each step adds a Gaussian field increment and averages it at a specified level of the hierarchy. Finally,

S(p)=sup⁡h{ℓ(h)+12∫01p(s)h(s) ds},S(p)=\sup_h\left\{\ell(h)+\frac12\int_0^1p(s)h(s)\,ds\right\},S(p)=hsup​{ℓ(h)+21​∫01​p(s)h(s)ds},

where the supremum runs over these finite step functions. This definition gives a concrete meaning to the otherwise abstract single-spin term.

The pressure and its extensions

Theorem 1.1 claims

PN⟶F(μ),EPN⟶F(μ),F(μ)=inf⁡p{S(p)+Gμ(p)}.P_N\longrightarrow F(\mu),\qquad\mathbb E P_N\longrightarrow F(\mu),\qquadF(\mu)=\inf_p\{S(p)+G_\mu(p)\}.PN​⟶F(μ),EPN​⟶F(μ),F(μ)=pinf​{S(p)+Gμ​(p)}.

The first convergence is almost sure. The Haar matrices need not be independent across dimensions. Atomic spectral laws, disconnected supports and a point-mass law are allowed; no spectral density or positive variance is required. The infimum over ppp remains outside the supremum defining SSS: the manuscript does not interchange them.

The external-field extension adds ∑ici,Nσi\sum_i c_{i,N}\sigma_i∑i​ci,N​σi​ to the exponent. The empirical law of the deterministic fields must converge in W1W_1W1​, the minimum expected absolute difference over couplings of two probability laws. This controls both distribution and first absolute moments. For finitely many field values, the formula first prescribes a mean spin in each field group, uses the corresponding constrained single-spin functional, and then optimizes those magnetizations. General field laws follow by W1W_1W1​ approximation. It is a separate extension, not merely a substitution into the zero-field expression above.

For zero-field optimization, let μβ\mu_\betaμβ​ be the law of βλ\beta\lambdaβλ when λ\lambdaλ has law μ\muμ. The claimed maximum-energy limit is

12Nmax⁡σσTJNσ⟶lim⁡β→∞F(μβ)β.\frac1{2N}\max_\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}J_N\sigma\longrightarrow \lim_{\beta\to\infty}\frac{F(\mu_\beta)}\beta.2N1​σmax​σTJN​σ⟶β→∞lim​βF(μβ​)​.

This convention maximizes the quadratic reward; physical ground-state energy has the opposite sign when the Hamiltonian is minus that reward.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, an all-temperature formula for this broad matrix class substantially extends the thermodynamic theory beyond high-temperature regimes. It links spin-glass organization to spectral data while preserving the possibility of complicated overlap hierarchies.

The result also reaches Gaussian-pattern Hopfield interactions. If GNG_NGN​ is an ⌊αN⌋\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor⌊αN⌋-by-NNN matrix of independent standard Gaussian entries, then

JN=cNGNTGNJ_N=\frac cN G_N^{\mathsf T}G_NJN​=Nc​GNT​GN​

is covered for every fixed real ccc. Positive and negative signs, followed by zero-temperature limits, determine respectively the largest and smallest lengths of signed sums of the Gaussian columns, with the manuscript’s normalizations. Thus the same thermodynamic formula has consequences for discrete quadratic optimization and Gaussian operator norms.

The score reflects the breadth of this extension, rather than suggesting the variational problem is automatically easy to compute or that an efficient optimization algorithm follows.

6. The main idea

The argument begins with a spectrum taking finitely many distinct values. Rotate equilibrium configurations into spectral coordinates and measure their overlaps separately inside each eigenspace. Their sum is the ordinary spin overlap.

Small perturbations enforce identities relating several replicas. Established ultrametricity and synchronization theory then reduce these many overlap arrays to compatible nondecreasing functions. Rotation identities connect the eigenspace functions to a single total-overlap function. This is the step that makes the eigenvalue law enter through the spectral transform.

For one pressure bound, add hierarchical Gaussian fields to a trial system and vary the interaction strength. The comparison is arranged to keep the supremum over fields inside the infimum over trial overlap functions. Preserving this optimization order is central to the stated formula.

For the other bound, couple systems with slightly different numbers of spins. Random directions within eigenspaces generate approximately Gaussian fields for the added spins. Evaluating this cavity increment produces the same single-spin and spectral terms. A concavity argument identifies the required field supremum.

Finally, approximate general compact spectra by finite alphabets and use concentration on the orthogonal group to turn mean convergence into almost-sure convergence. External fields require an additional constrained-magnetization argument. The common theme is to separate the randomness of directions, the spectral information and the hierarchy of spin similarities without discarding their interactions.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The absence of asymptotic spectral outliers is an assumption. A vanishing fraction of eigenvalues can be invisible to the empirical law yet strongly affect the cube’s energy. The manuscript also gives an example showing that weak convergence to an unbounded-support law is not enough for the conclusion.

For random spectra, the conditional eigenvector law must be Haar. Spectral convergence in probability gives pressure convergence in probability; almost-sure spectral hypotheses give almost-sure pressure convergence. Convergence of expectations additionally requires uniform integrability. A random external field dependent on the matrix requires the corresponding Haar condition after conditioning on both spectrum and field data.

The pressure includes diagonal self-interactions. Removing them subtracts half the limiting mean eigenvalue. Physical free energy at inverse temperature β>0\beta>0β>0 is minus the chosen pressure divided by β\betaβ, with the counting-prior correction included if appropriate.

An exact variational characterization need not identify its optimizer explicitly. Determining phase boundaries, fluctuation laws, computational complexity and concrete minimizing hierarchies are further questions. The thermodynamic limit is taken before the zero-temperature limit in the ground-state consequence; the manuscript does not require a uniform all-temperature finite-size estimate to obtain it.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 contains the pressure theorem and definitions in Section 1, random-spectrum and optimization consequences in Section 7, and the magnetic extension in Section 8. These conventions are essential when comparing formulas.

For overlap hierarchies, Panchenko’s ultrametricity theorem provides a central structural result. Family 222 discusses related random-perceptron variational formulas; the present manuscript compares certain Gaussian quadratic cases while treating the formulas as distinct constructions.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, All-temperature pressure for orthogonally invariant Ising spin glasses (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Random SAT thresholds, fluctuations, and computability
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 235 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Begin with an empty Boolean formula and add random clauses one by one. Initially every assignment works. Eventually no assignment satisfies all the clauses. Three questions arise: does the transition approach a definite clause density, how much does its location fluctuate between samples, and can that limiting density be computed to arbitrary accuracy?

These questions sound similar, but they require different answers. A narrow transition may have a center that drifts with system size. A limiting constant may exist without an algorithm to approximate it. An algorithm that computes the constant may still be too slow to produce useful numerical values.

Family 235 contains four manuscripts addressing these distinctions. Their current versions credit Gaia Carenini with priority for resolving the satisfiability conjecture. The family’s contributions are presented as an alternative existence argument, sharper fluctuation bounds, and computability of the threshold for three-literal clauses.

2. Background and essential definitions

The random formula

A Boolean variable takes values zero or one. A literal is a variable or its negation, and a clause is an “or” of literals. A formula in conjunctive normal form is an “and” of clauses. For example, (x1∨¬x2∨x3)(x_1\lor\neg x_2\lor x_3)(x1​∨¬x2​∨x3​) is a three-literal clause.

Fix a clause size k≥3k\geq3k≥3 and n≥kn\geq kn≥k variables. A proper random clause chooses kkk distinct variables uniformly and gives each an independent fair sign. Whole clauses are sampled independently with replacement: two clauses can be identical, but a variable does not repeat within one clause.

Let

Fn,m=C1∧⋯∧Cm,pn(m)=P(Fn,m is satisfiable).F_{n,m}=C_1\land\cdots\land C_m,\qquad p_n(m)=\mathbb P(F_{n,m}\text{ is satisfiable}).Fn,m​=C1​∧⋯∧Cm​,pn​(m)=P(Fn,m​ is satisfiable).

The density is m/nm/nm/n. Adding clauses cannot restore satisfiability, so pn(m)p_n(m)pn​(m) is nonincreasing.

The first unsatisfiable index is

Hn=min⁡{m≥1:Fn,m is unsatisfiable}.H_n=\min\{m\geq1:F_{n,m}\text{ is unsatisfiable}\}.Hn​=min{m≥1:Fn,m​ is unsatisfiable}.

Consequently, pn(m)=P(Hn>m)p_n(m)=\mathbb P(H_n>m)pn​(m)=P(Hn​>m). The last satisfiable index is Hn−1H_n-1Hn​−1; this one-clause difference matters when stating exact finite-size identities.

Location, width and computation

A limiting threshold αk\alpha_kαk​ means satisfiability tends to probability one at every fixed density below αk\alpha_kαk​, and to zero at every fixed density above it. A central transition window measures how many additional clauses are required to move between two fixed probabilities, such as 0.90.90.9 and 0.10.10.1.

The variance Var⁡(Hn)\operatorname{Var}(H_n)Var(Hn​) measures fluctuations of the entire hitting-time distribution, including its tails. The notation Θk(n)\Theta_k(n)Θk​(n) means upper and lower positive constant multiples of nnn, with constants allowed to depend on fixed kkk.

A real number is computable if one fixed finite algorithm can return a rational approximation with any requested error. This says nothing about whether the algorithm runs quickly.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The two-clause problem was settled through implication-graph methods in work of Chvátal and Reed, Goerdt, and Fernandez de la Vega. For larger fixed clause sizes, Friedgut’s sharp-threshold theorem established a narrow transition around a size-dependent density. It did not prove that these densities converge. Friedgut’s theorem.

Weighted second-moment methods of Achlioptas and Peres located the threshold to leading order as kkk grows. Statistical-physics work by Mézard, Parisi, Zecchina and collaborators developed predictions based on the organization of satisfying assignments into clusters. Ding, Sly and Sun established the predicted limiting threshold for all sufficiently large fixed kkk. This left the small fixed clause sizes outside that theorem. Large-clause threshold theorem.

For transition width, Wilson proved that a fixed central probability drop needs at least order n\sqrt nn​ clauses. Carenini first obtained an upper window bound of order n/log⁡nn/\log nn/logn, then improved it to Ok,η(n1/2+1/k)O_{k,\eta}(n^{1/2+1/k})Ok,η​(n1/2+1/k) between probabilities η\etaη and 1−η1-\eta1−η. Combined with the Abbe–Montanari criterion, her paper made public on 5 October 2026 establishes limiting thresholds for every fixed k≥3k\geq3k≥3. The present manuscripts explicitly acknowledge her priority. Carenini’s resolution, earlier window paper.

The three-clause threshold has a separate numerical history. The computability manuscript recalls established lower and upper bounds of 3.523.523.52 and 4.48984.48984.4898, and the statistical-physics prediction near 4.2674.2674.267. It does not evaluate the threshold or prove equality with that prediction.

Finally, existence and computability are genuinely different mathematical properties: a computable sequence of rational numbers can converge to a noncomputable real. Therefore finite formula enumeration plus an unspecified limiting theorem does not automatically give an algorithm with a certified stopping rule. That is the gap addressed by the fourth manuscript.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: an alternative limiting-threshold argument

For every fixed integer k≥3k\geq3k≥3, M1 claims a finite positive constant αk\alpha_kαk​ such that

lim⁡n→∞pn(⌊cn⌋)={1,0≤c<αk,0,c>αk.\lim_{n\to\infty}p_n(\lfloor cn\rfloor)=\begin{cases}1,&0\leq c<\alpha_k,\\0,&c>\alpha_k.\end{cases}n→∞lim​pn​(⌊cn⌋)={1,0,​0≤c<αk​,c>αk​.​

There is no assertion at c=αkc=\alpha_kc=αk​. The manuscript describes its proof as an alternative to Carenini’s resolution, and does not identify αk\alpha_kαk​ numerically or through the physics prediction for every small kkk.

Its finite-size center is the normalized expectation of the last satisfiable index capped at 2k+1n2^{k+1}n2k+1n. Concentration of this index is combined with comparisons between different system sizes to establish convergence of the center.

M3 and M2: fluctuations of order square root of size

M3 claims

Var⁡(Hn)=Θk(n)(k≥4),\operatorname{Var}(H_n)=\Theta_k(n)\quad(k\geq4),Var(Hn​)=Θk​(n)(k≥4),

and, by its own argument, lower bound cnc ncn and upper bound Cnlog⁡nC n\log nCnlogn for k=3k=3k=3. M2 supplies the additional three-clause estimate that removes the logarithm:

Var⁡(Hn)=Θ(n)(k=3).\operatorname{Var}(H_n)=\Theta(n)\quad(k=3).Var(Hn​)=Θ(n)(k=3).

Together, they give linear variance for every fixed k≥3k\geq3k≥3. The lower bounds come from Wilson’s transition-width theorem; the new claims concern the matching upper bounds.

For a fixed 0<η<1/20<\eta<1/20<η<1/2, define

rn(p)=min⁡{m≥0:pn(m)≤p}.r_n(p)=\min\{m\geq0:p_n(m)\leq p\}.rn​(p)=min{m≥0:pn​(m)≤p}.

The combined results imply

rn(η)−rn(1−η)=Θk,η(n).r_n(\eta)-r_n(1-\eta)=\Theta_{k,\eta}(\sqrt n).rn​(η)−rn​(1−η)=Θk,η​(n​).

Thus the central width is order n\sqrt nn​ clauses, or order n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 in density. These are fluctuations around finite-size locations. They do not establish a Gaussian limiting distribution or show that EHn−αkn\mathbb E H_n-\alpha_k nEHn​−αk​n is of order n\sqrt nn​.

M3 also gives upper variance bounds for hitting times capped at any fixed positive multiple of nnn. Its matching capped lower bound requires a sufficiently late cap; a cap before the transition can remove the randomness being measured.

M4: the three-clause threshold is computable

M4 claims that one deterministic Turing machine, given the unary precision input 1r1^r1r, halts with a rational qrq_rqr​ satisfying

∣qr−α3∣≤2−r.|q_r-\alpha_3|\leq2^{-r}.∣qr​−α3​∣≤2−r.

The machine uses no oracle, advice or noncomputable real constant. It computes the limiting density, not a satisfying assignment for a supplied formula. There is no efficiency bound, no numerical evaluation of α3\alpha_3α3​, and no corresponding computability theorem here for every clause size.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the matching variance bounds settle the fluctuation order of a central random constraint problem, while the computability theorem supplies a distinct conceptual advance beyond existence.

The score accounts for the current priority statements. Threshold existence for all fixed clause sizes is credited to Carenini; this family’s existence paper is an alternative argument. Its sharper width and variance claims remain substantial: they match the earlier square-root lower bound and control the tails that a central-window statement alone need not control.

Computability is also meaningful without practical speed. It asserts that the threshold can be approached with certified error by one finite procedure. This separates a well-defined physical constant from a constant whose value might resist all such effective approximation. It does not turn random SAT into an efficiently solved problem.

6. The main idea

Delete a clause and measure the delay

A clause is pivotal at a prefix if restoring it turns a satisfiable formula into an unsatisfiable one. Delete one clause without renumbering subsequent arrivals, and measure the resulting delay in first failure. A version of the Efron–Stein variance inequality bounds the hitting-time variance by a sum of expected squared delays.

The deleted clause singles out kkk root variables. If it is pivotal, every remaining solution gives these roots the unique assignment that falsifies it. Flipping each root creates a necessary test on the other variables, involving shorter clauses. Away from collisions where another clause meets several roots, these tests can be exposed independently.

A comparison relates how easily shorter clauses destroy a set of assignments to how long it can survive ordinary clauses. Averaging the actual root-incidence counts, instead of imposing a coarse cutoff, yields the linear bound for k≥4k\geq4k≥4. At k=3k=3k=3, the same occupation estimate is borderline and produces a logarithm.

M2 introduces a bounded monotone potential built from probabilities that several two-clauses eliminate an assignment set. Its expected increase controls the time spent in the troublesome regime. This is the claimed extra ingredient removing the three-clause logarithm.

For existence in M1, concentration is followed by an interpolation comparing one large formula to formulas on smaller blocks. Errors that are summable along geometrically increasing sizes prevent the normalized centers from drifting indefinitely.

Search from both sides of the constant

M4 constructs finite certificates for lower and upper bounds on α3\alpha_3α3​. Lower certificates come from explicit deletion estimates and finite enumeration in an auxiliary Poisson clause process. This auxiliary model permits repeated variables within a clause; separate comparisons transfer its threshold conclusions to the proper model.

For upper certificates, soften satisfiability by penalizing each violated clause. If Vn(σ)V_n(\sigma)Vn​(σ) is the number of violations, define

Zn(a,β)=∑σe−βVn(σ),P(a,β)=lim⁡n→∞1nElog⁡Zn(a,β).Z_n(a,\beta)=\sum_\sigma e^{-\beta V_n(\sigma)},\qquad P(a,\beta)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E\log Z_n(a,\beta).Zn​(a,β)=σ∑​e−βVn​(σ),P(a,β)=n→∞lim​n1​ElogZn​(a,β).

The parameter aaa is density and β>0\beta>0β>0 is the penalty. Below the threshold this pressure is nonnegative. The manuscript claims that above the threshold a positive density of unavoidable violations makes it negative for some finite penalty.

Finite rational descriptions of hierarchical trials provide computable upper bounds on this pressure and approximate its infimum. A certified negative trial therefore certifies an upper bound on α3\alpha_3α3​, and such a trial exists at every rational density strictly above it.

The algorithm fairly interleaves all lower-certificate calculations and all candidate upper-certificate searches. It stops when the certified interval is short enough. It does not need a computable rate at which finite-size expectations converge, because the interval itself supplies the stopping test.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All fluctuation constants concern a fixed clause size. The statements do not claim uniform estimates when kkk grows with nnn, arbitrary clause distributions, biased signs, or other random constraint languages.

The proper-clause model samples whole clauses with replacement but uses distinct variables inside each clause. Poissonization and repeated-variable clauses occur in intermediate arguments; their equivalence for a particular conclusion requires the transfers stated in the papers.

Linear variance and square-root central windows do not identify a limiting distribution, its variance constant, or the finite-size bias relative to αkn\alpha_k nαk​n. Those finer questions remain outside the claims. Strict-side threshold theorems also leave the probability at the exact critical density unspecified.

The computability result does not confirm the numerical prediction near 4.2674.2674.267, provide a useful runtime, or settle worst-case SAT complexity. Its soft-pressure construction for three clauses is a substantive additional argument; it should not be inferred from an even-clause interpolation theorem such as the one discussed in family 221.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 gives the alternative existence argument. M3 develops the general clause-deletion variance framework, and M2 closes its three-clause logarithmic gap. M4 supplies the two-sided certificate search and the soft-pressure completeness statement needed for computability.

For the historical division between sharpness and convergence, read Friedgut’s theorem alongside Carenini’s October 2026 paper. Ding, Sly and Sun’s large-clause theorem explains the earlier regime where the threshold was already identified with the statistical-physics prediction. Wilson’s On the critical exponents of random k-SAT (2002) supplies the lower window bound credited throughout this family.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Limiting Satisfiability Threshold for Every Fixed Clause Size (September 25, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Linear Variance of the Random 3-SAT Hitting Time (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Variance of the Random k-SAT Hitting Time (September 27, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Computing the Random 3-SAT Threshold (September 27, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The factor-of-IID threshold for the free Ising model on regular trees
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 236 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Imagine giving every vertex of an infinite tree its own independent random number. Can the vertices use one common symmetry-respecting rule to produce correlated spins with exactly the free Ising distribution?

There is an easy way to sample that distribution if one is allowed to choose a root: toss a fair coin there, then transmit its sign down the branches with independent errors. But the infinite regular tree has no distinguished vertex. A root used by the sampling rule breaks a symmetry that the final distribution itself possesses.

Family 236 claims the exact answer to this root-free generation problem. For every degree d≥3d\geq3d≥3, the free ferromagnetic Ising state is a factor of independent randomness precisely up to the reconstruction threshold, including equality. The strict impossibility beyond that threshold was already known; the claimed advance is the construction throughout the remaining range.

2. Background and essential definitions

The free Ising state

Let TdT_dTd​ be the infinite tree in which every vertex has ddd neighbors. A tree is connected and has no cycles, so two vertices have a unique connecting path. Write

b=d−1,θ=tanh⁡β,b=d-1,\qquad \theta=\tanh\beta,b=d−1,θ=tanhβ,

where β≥0\beta\geq0β≥0 is inverse temperature. The parameter bbb counts the forward branches after a first edge has been traversed.

The free zero-field Ising law can be described by broadcasting. Choose a fair spin σo∈{−1,1}\sigma_o\in\{-1,1\}σo​∈{−1,1} at a temporary root ooo. Along each outward edge, independently, let a child copy its parent with probability (1+θ)/2(1+\theta)/2(1+θ)/2, and take the opposite sign otherwise.

Despite this rooted description, the resulting law does not depend on the choice of root. On any finite connected subtree DDD, its probability is

P(σ∣D=η)=12∏{u,v}∈E(D)1+θηuηv2.\mathbb P(\sigma|_D=\eta)=\frac12\prod_{\{u,v\}\in E(D)}\frac{1+\theta\eta_u\eta_v}{2}.P(σ∣D​=η)=21​{u,v}∈E(D)∏​21+θηu​ηv​​.

Here E(D)E(D)E(D) is the edge set and η\etaη is a specified spin assignment. The formula is unchanged by relabeling the tree. Spins at distance rrr have correlation θr\theta^rθr.

“Free” identifies a particular infinite-volume Gibbs state, corresponding to no imposed boundary spins in finite-tree approximations. It should not be confused with the plus or minus states obtained by fixing the outer boundary to one sign.

A factor of IID

Give each vertex an independent uniform label Uv∈[0,1]U_v\in[0,1]Uv​∈[0,1]. A factor of IID is a measurable rule Φ\PhiΦ producing a spin configuration from the whole label collection, with the same rule used everywhere and with no distinguished root or end.

Precisely, an automorphism ggg is a bijection of the vertices preserving adjacency. Equivariance means

Φ(gU)=gΦ(U).\Phi(gU)=g\Phi(U).Φ(gU)=gΦ(U).

Relabeling the input tree and then applying the rule must agree with applying the rule first and relabeling the output. The rule can inspect infinitely many labels. A factor is therefore not necessarily a finite-radius algorithm or even a finitary coding, where each output is determined by some almost-surely finite random neighborhood.

Three thresholds worth distinguishing

The uniqueness regime ends at θ=1/b\theta=1/bθ=1/b. Above it, different Gibbs states can coexist. Reconstruction asks a different question: do spins on very distant levels retain information about the spin at a fixed vertex? For the free Ising state on a regular tree, reconstruction is possible exactly when bθ2>1b\theta^2>1bθ2>1.

The factor question asks whether independent local inputs can generate the entire law equivariantly. Nonreconstruction concerns information inside a sampled configuration; it does not itself provide such a generation rule.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The reconstruction transition for the free state was established in work of Bleher, Ruiz and Zagrebnov and of Ioffe, including the critical equality on regular trees. Subsequent work by Evans, Kenyon, Peres and Schulman developed the relation between broadcasting and Ising models on trees. Pemantle and Peres later gave a nonlinear electrical-capacity criterion that handles more general critical tree geometries. Regular-tree extremality, Ioffe’s result, broadcasting framework, capacity criterion.

For factors of IID, a finite-cluster construction already handled the uniqueness range θ≤1/b\theta\leq1/bθ≤1/b, including its boundary. At the other end, Sly’s obstruction, recorded and proved in Lyons’s account, ruled out a factor when θ>1/b\theta>1/\sqrt bθ>1/b​. Correlation bounds of Backhausz, Szegedy and Virág provide a quantitative way to see this obstruction. Lyons’s account, correlation bounds.

Nam, Sly and Zhang made the key advance beyond uniqueness. They constructed factors through infinite systems of stochastic differential equations driven by independent Brownian motions. Their theorem covered sufficiently large degree and θ≤c/b\theta\leq c/\sqrt bθ≤c/b​, for absolute constants in the stated regime, and proposed reaching the full reconstruction boundary. Their construction and conjecture.

The remaining task was not merely to take a parameter limit. Weak limits of factor laws need not themselves be factors. One must preserve measurable dependence on the independent input, especially at the endpoint where ordinary geometric-decay estimates stop working.

The present manuscript follows the observation framework of Nam, Sly and Zhang, claiming the construction for every d≥3d\geq3d≥3 all the way through equality.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Theorem 1.1 states that, for every integer d≥3d\geq3d≥3 and every β≥0\beta\geq0β≥0,

μd,β is a factor of IID⟺tanh⁡β≤1d−1.\mu_{d,\beta}\text{ is a factor of IID}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\tanh\beta\leq\frac1{\sqrt{d-1}}.μd,β​ is a factor of IID⟺tanhβ≤d−1​1​.

Here μd,β\mu_{d,\beta}μd,β​ is exactly the free, zero-field, ferromagnetic Ising law just defined.

In the permitted range, the factor can be chosen Borel measurable and equivariant under every tree automorphism on every label input. This is stronger as a choice of version than saying that equivariance holds almost surely for each fixed automorphism. The manuscript supplies a passage from the latter convention to the former for the spin factor.

For example, on the degree-three tree the uniqueness boundary is θ=1/2\theta=1/2θ=1/2, while the claimed factor construction reaches θ=1/2\theta=1/\sqrt2θ=1/2​. Throughout the interval between them, the model can have multiple Gibbs states even though its free state still admits the claimed generation from independent labels.

The negative direction is not presented as new. A centered variance-one vertex factor satisfies a correlation bound of the form

∣E[ZoZv]∣≤(1+d−2dr)b−r/2,dist⁡(o,v)=r.|\mathbb E[Z_oZ_v]|\leq\left(1+\frac{d-2}{d}r\right)b^{-r/2},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(o,v)=r.∣E[Zo​Zv​]∣≤(1+dd−2​r)b−r/2,dist(o,v)=r.

Ising correlations are θr\theta^rθr. If θb>1\theta\sqrt b>1θb​>1, their decay is too slow to obey the bound for large rrr. This explains why the proposed positive range is the largest possible one.

No finitary coding, coding-radius tail, runtime estimate or parameter-uniform construction is claimed. At β=0\beta=0β=0, the law is already independent fair signs; the substantial issue is the correlated regime.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. If correct, the theorem resolves a sharp generation question for one of the most fundamental dependent processes on a nonamenable graph. It identifies the factor threshold with the reconstruction threshold throughout the regular-tree family, including the critical point.

The result clarifies the relationship between several notions of disorder. Failure of Gibbs-state uniqueness does not prevent a particular free state from being generated from IID input. Conversely, sufficiently persistent long-range information creates an obstruction. The full interval between these two phenomena becomes explicit.

Its method also matters. It turns a representation involving an already-sampled dependent configuration into an actual measurable function of independent innovations. That distinction is useful well beyond this example: a process described using independent noise need not be recoverable from that noise alone.

6. The main idea

Hide spins in noisy observations

Temporarily sample the desired Ising configuration σ\sigmaσ, together with independent standard Brownian motions BvB_vBv​, and form

Xv(t)=tσv+Bv(t).X_v(t)=t\sigma_v+B_v(t).Xv​(t)=tσv​+Bv​(t).

Brownian motion is continuous Gaussian noise whose variance at time ttt is ttt. The signal grows linearly, so Xv(t)/tX_v(t)/tXv​(t)/t eventually reveals σv\sigma_vσv​.

Let mv(t)m_v(t)mv​(t) be the conditional mean of σv\sigma_vσv​ given all observations up to time ttt. Subtract the accumulated predicted drift:

Wv(t)=Xv(t)−∫0tmv(s) ds.W_v(t)=X_v(t)-\int_0^t m_v(s)\,ds.Wv​(t)=Xv​(t)−∫0t​mv​(s)ds.

These processes are independent Brownian innovations. They represent the new noise left after accounting for information already observed.

This is not yet a factor construction, because XXX was originally built using σ\sigmaσ. The central question is whether the entire observation process XXX, and hence the spins, can be recovered from WWW.

Compare two possible observations with the same noise

The manuscript takes two observations X,X′X,X'X,X′ independently conditional on the full innovation array WWW. It first establishes a compatibility statement ensuring that the common noise remains Brownian when both observation histories are considered together.

It then aims to show that the two observations agree. Conditional independence gives

E[(Xv(t)−Xv′(t))2∣W]=2Var⁡(Xv(t)∣W).\mathbb E[(X_v(t)-X'_v(t))^2\mid W]=2\operatorname{Var}(X_v(t)\mid W).E[(Xv​(t)−Xv′​(t))2∣W]=2Var(Xv​(t)∣W).

If the difference vanishes, the conditional variance is zero, so XXX is a measurable function of WWW. Recovering σv\sigma_vσv​ from Xv(n)/nX_v(n)/nXv​(n)/n then gives the desired spins. A uniform label can encode a Brownian path, so one independent label per vertex supplies the required input.

Why equality needs extra work

Below the reconstruction boundary, squared influences along paths contain the factor θ2r\theta^{2r}θ2r, while the number of vertices at distance rrr grows like brb^rbr. Their product is summable when bθ2<1b\theta^2<1bθ2<1, allowing a standard differential inequality to force the copies to agree.

At equality, these factors exactly cancel. The manuscript replaces the missing geometric decay with attenuation from side branches, spatial cancellation in differences between the two copies, and concentration of path averages. A further small-field estimate handles the singular behavior near observation time zero.

The final comparison uses an integrable uniqueness inequality to conclude that the discrepancy remains zero. This endpoint argument is the main additional difficulty; it cannot be replaced by simply setting bθ2=1b\theta^2=1bθ2=1 in a strictly subcritical geometric-series estimate.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns regular trees, degree at least three, the free zero-field state and nonnegative inverse temperature. It does not assert the same criterion for arbitrary trees, external fields, other spin systems or every Gibbs state on the same tree.

A measurable factor may use information arbitrarily far away. The result therefore does not automatically give a distributed algorithm with a bounded number of communication rounds, an exact sampler inspecting finitely many labels per output, or a practical numerical procedure. Coding radii and computational efficiency are separate questions.

The construction is made for each fixed degree and temperature. No uniform control as parameters vary is stated. Its pointwise equivariance concerns symmetry of the selected map, not a bound on the amount of information that map uses.

The claimed coincidence between nonreconstruction and the factor property belongs to this particular model. It is not a general theorem that every nonreconstructible process on a tree is a factor of IID. Extending the construction to irregular trees or obtaining stronger coding properties would require additional ideas and hypotheses.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 states the threshold and prior converse in Section 1. Its observation framework and critical comparison explain why reconstructing the observations from their innovations is the central task.

Nam, Sly and Zhang’s earlier paper is the direct predecessor. Lyons’s Factors of IID on Trees gives the broader context and cautions about limits of factor processes.

Family 231 uses a related innovation idea for uniform spanning forests, with a different recovery argument. Family 229 discusses reconstruction thresholds for larger spin alphabets, where the relation between branching and information has additional features.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The sharp factor-of-IID threshold for the free Ising model on regular trees (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Optimal-order mixing of the Thorp shuffle
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 238 · Probability and statistical mechanics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Split a deck into equal halves. Pair cards in corresponding positions, independently toss a fair coin to decide the order of each pair, and interleave the pairs. This is one complete Thorp shuffle.

For a deck of n=2dn=2^dn=2d cards, a single card is uniformly distributed after ddd shuffles. Does this mean the whole deck is random? No: different cards share switches, so their positions can retain joint information even when every individual position looks uniform.

Family 238 contains twelve manuscripts claiming that a constant multiple of ddd complete shuffles suffices to randomize the full permutation. Since a simple counting obstruction already requires order ddd, this gives the optimal order Θ(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n)Θ(logn) for decks whose sizes are powers of two.

The family develops several arguments and additional conditional statements. Its constants are bounds, not an identification of the precise number of shuffles needed in the leading asymptotic term.

2. Background and essential definitions

Measuring the full deck

A deck ordering is a permutation in the symmetric group SnS_nSn​, the set of all n!n!n! bijections from card labels to positions. Let UnU_nUn​ be the uniform distribution on this group, and qdq_dqd​ the permutation law of one physical shuffle.

Independent successive shuffles compose permutations. Their ttt-step law is denoted by qd∗tq_d^{*t}qd∗t​, where the asterisk means convolution. For two probability laws,

∥μ−ν∥TV=12∑π∈Sn∣μ(π)−ν(π)∣\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{\pi\in S_n}|\mu(\pi)-\nu(\pi)|∥μ−ν∥TV​=21​π∈Sn​∑​∣μ(π)−ν(π)∣

is their total-variation distance. Equivalently, it is the largest difference in probability they assign to the same event. Small full-deck distance therefore controls every statistic of the deck, including joint positions of any selected cards.

The mixing time here is the first integer ttt for which this distance is at most 1/41/41/4. Starting from a different deterministic deck translates the permutation law and leaves its distance from uniform unchanged.

Binary coordinates and sweeps

Label positions by binary strings (x1,…,xd)(x_1,\ldots,x_d)(x1​,…,xd​). A physical Thorp shuffle can be written

(x1,u)⟼(u,x1+ξu),(x_1,u)\longmapsto(u,x_1+\xi_u),(x1​,u)⟼(u,x1​+ξu​),

where addition is modulo two, uuu contains the other bits, and the ξu\xi_uξu​ are independent fair bits.

Removing the deterministic cyclic rotation turns successive shuffles into switch layers along successive coordinate directions of the binary cube. One coordinate sweep visits all ddd directions once. It costs ddd physical shuffles, not one.

A card has each coordinate refreshed once during a sweep, explaining its uniform marginal. The other cards still constrain which collective routes are possible.

Partial observations miss global information

Even observing nearly every card can miss something. A uniformly random even permutation has exactly uniform joint images for any chosen list of at most n−2n-2n−2 labels, yet its full law has total-variation distance 1/21/21/2 from uniform on SnS_nSn​. Its parity is fixed.

This example explains why a proof based on partial decks must separately control the information omitted by those observations. Parity is one obstruction; representation theory organizes all such modes of dependence.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Thorp introduced the shuffle in his 1973 study of nonrandom shuffling and Faro. Its simple mechanism became a difficult mixing-time problem because local randomness spreads through a highly structured switching network. Original paper.

Morris obtained the first upper bound polynomial in ddd, of order d44d^{44}d44, using evolving sets and a chameleon process describing conditional card probabilities. Montenegro and Tetali improved the exponent to 292929 through spectral-profile and evolving-set methods. Morris’s first bound, Montenegro–Tetali analysis.

Entropy methods brought further progress. Morris proved an O((log⁡n)4)O((\log n)^4)O((logn)4) bound for arbitrary even deck sizes, then an O(d3)O(d^3)O(d3) bound for n=2dn=2^dn=2d. The optimal logarithmic order remained beyond those estimates. General even decks, dyadic cubic-logarithmic bound.

Partial decks have their own history. Morris, Rogaway and Stegers studied ordered lists of cards in connection with enciphering on small domains. Czumaj and Vöcking showed that order (log⁡n)2(\log n)^2(logn)2 shuffles mix any fixed fraction of the deck strictly below one. Such marginal statements are useful, but they leave a separate passage to the full permutation law. Enciphering application, partial-deck result.

The new family builds on these conditional-flow ideas and on finite-group Fourier analysis, classically used by Diaconis and Shahshahani for shuffling problems. Its claimed improvement is to control the remaining collective information after only a constant number of coordinate sweeps. Fourier method for shuffles.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The headline mixing law

M1 claims the explicit asymptotic bound

∥qd∗(1600d)−Un∥TV⟶0(d→∞).\|q_d^{*(1600d)}-U_n\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow0\qquad(d\to\infty).∥qd∗(1600d)​−Un​∥TV​⟶0(d→∞).

Its proof is given independently of the companion transfer theorems. M2 gives a separate 32800d32800d32800d construction and, combining its stronger fixed-list estimate with M3’s Fourier transfer, states convergence after 512d512d512d physical shuffles. These different constants describe different arguments for the same logarithmic order.

Every physical shuffle uses n/2n/2n/2 independent fair bits. After ttt shuffles there are at most 2tn/22^{tn/2}2tn/2 possible outcomes, so

∥qd∗t−Un∥TV≥1−2tn/2n!.\|q_d^{*t}-U_n\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\geq1-\frac{2^{tn/2}}{n!}.∥qd∗t​−Un​∥TV​≥1−n!2tn/2​.

Hence

tmix(d)≥⌈2nlog⁡2 ⁣(3n!4)⌉=2d−O(1).t_{\mathrm{mix}}(d)\geq\left\lceil\frac2n\log_2\!\left(\frac{3n!}{4}\right)\right\rceil=2d-O(1).tmix​(d)≥⌈n2​log2​(43n!​)⌉=2d−O(1).

Together, the claimed upper bounds and this support obstruction give tmix(d)=Θ(d)t_{\mathrm{mix}}(d)=\Theta(d)tmix​(d)=Θ(d). They do not show that 2d2d2d is the correct leading mixing time.

Partial and conditional laws

M2 and M4 claim that after 256d256d256d shuffles, the joint images of every specified ordered list of at most 7n/87n/87n/8 cards approach the uniform law on distinct positions, uniformly over the list. M1 instead uses an averaged estimate for a uniformly sampled list after 200d200d200d shuffles. These are different inputs.

M3 proves an abstract transfer: if the images of a uniformly chosen 7n/87n/87n/8 labels approach uniform in average total variation, and the mean permutation sign tends to zero, then the product of two independent permutations with that law approaches uniform on SnS_nSn​.
