entry.title: Fractional covers, discrete convexity, and random-graph thresholds
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 175 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

When a random object first acquires a property, can its threshold be predicted from simple necessary patterns? A random graph containing a prescribed target must contain many smaller patterns, for example. Counting those patterns can show that the target is unlikely at low density.

A general version of this idea covers every successful object by elementary containment events. A fractional cover permits several partial contributions to replace a single selected event. Does this relaxation substantially improve the threshold estimate?

This family contains three related claims. M2 says integral and fractional expectation thresholds differ by only a universal factor. M3 proves a discrete-convexity statement about unions of likely sets at the original sampling density. M1 uses that theorem to split any target graph into a bounded number of pieces, each appearing near the target’s integral expectation threshold. The pieces are fixed in advance, but their embeddings need not fit together.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let XXX be a finite ground set. Its random subset XpX_pXp​ includes each element independently with probability ppp. Write μp(A)\mu_p(\mathcal A)μp​(A) for the probability that XpX_pXp​ belongs to a family A\mathcal AA of subsets.

A family F\mathcal FF is increasing if adding elements cannot destroy membership. The family of edge sets containing a triangle is an example. Assume F\mathcal FF is nonempty and is not the whole power set. Its ordinary threshold pc(F)p_c(\mathcal F)pc​(F) is the parameter where membership has probability one half.

A cover G\mathcal GG of F\mathcal FF is a collection of subsets such that every member of F\mathcal FF contains at least one S∈GS\in\mathcal GS∈G. A generator SSS need not itself guarantee the property; the cover gives necessary alternatives. Its cost is

cp(G)=∑S∈Gp∣S∣.c_p(\mathcal G)=\sum_{S\in\mathcal G}p^{|S|}.cp​(G)=S∈G∑​p∣S∣.

Since p∣S∣p^{|S|}p∣S∣ is the probability that S⊆XpS\subseteq X_pS⊆Xp​, a union bound gives μp(F)≤cp(G)\mu_p(\mathcal F)\leq c_p(\mathcal G)μp​(F)≤cp​(G). Call the family ppp-small when it has a cover of cost at most one half. Its integral expectation threshold is

q(F)=max⁡{p:F is p-small}.q(\mathcal F)=\max\{p:\mathcal F\text{ is }p\text{-small}\}.q(F)=max{p:F is p-small}.

A fractional cover assigns coefficients g(S)∈[0,1]g(S)\in[0,1]g(S)∈[0,1], requiring

∑S⊆Hg(S)≥1(H∈F).\sum_{S\subseteq H}g(S)\geq1\qquad(H\in\mathcal F).S⊆H∑​g(S)≥1(H∈F).

Its cost is ∑Sg(S)p∣S∣\sum_S g(S)p^{|S|}∑S​g(S)p∣S∣. Allowing these weighted covers defines qf(F)q_f(\mathcal F)qf​(F), again with budget one half. An integral cover is the special case of coefficients zero or one, so

q(F)≤qf(F)≤pc(F).q(\mathcal F)\leq q_f(\mathcal F)\leq p_c(\mathcal F).q(F)≤qf​(F)≤pc​(F).

For a simple example, the family of sets of size at least kkk has the fractional cover g({x})=1/kg(\{x\})=1/kg({x})=1/k on singletons. Each successful set accumulates total weight at least one. This illustrates how fractional contributions can be spread over small generators.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Kahn and Kalai proposed that ordinary thresholds are at most a logarithmic factor above expectation thresholds. This connects elementary counting obstructions with the probability of actually obtaining a complete structure.

Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan and Park proved the comparison using fractional expectation thresholds. Park and Pham proved the integral version. If ℓ\ellℓ is the larger of two and the maximum size of a minimal member of F\mathcal FF, their theorem gives

pc(F)≤Cq(F)log⁡ℓp_c(\mathcal F)\leq Cq(\mathcal F)\log\ellpc​(F)≤Cq(F)logℓ

for a universal constant. A minimal member loses the property whenever any element is removed.

Talagrand’s separate conjecture asked whether qfq_fqf​ and qqq themselves differ by only a constant. Earlier rounding results handled special supports, such as singletons, pairs and clique-based generators. More general selector methods introduced losses depending on the sizes of the weighted sets. Subsequent results reduced these to iterated logarithms. Park’s September 2026 manuscript gave a dimension-independent comparison still involving log⁡log⁡(1/q)\log\log(1/q)loglog(1/q). M2 claims to remove this remaining dependence.

Talagrand also proposed discrete convexity: sufficiently likely sets should cover most other sets using only a bounded number of unions, with the exceptional family having an inexpensive containment cover. Recent work supplied fractional versions and integral versions at a reduced density. Li’s work on spread measures is an important fractional input.

Finally, Ascoli, He, Park and Talagrand related discrete convexity to graph thresholds and proposed the decomposition resolved in M1. They proved several restricted graph classes, leaving the general interaction between high- and low-degree vertices as a principal obstacle.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: constant-factor rounding

There is a universal constant CCC such that

qf(F)≤Cq(F)q_f(\mathcal F)\leq Cq(\mathcal F)qf​(F)≤Cq(F)

for every nonempty proper increasing family on a finite nonempty ground set. Both definitions keep the same covering budget, one half.

More concretely, a fractional cover costing at most one half at density rrr can be replaced by an integral cover costing at most one half at density r/Cr/Cr/C. The constant is independent of the ground-set size, generator sizes, and number of generators. The paper supplies an explicit, unoptimized constant.

M3: discrete convexity at the same density

For any family D\mathcal DD, let Ek(D)E_k(\mathcal D)Ek​(D) consist of sets that are not contained in the union of any kkk members of D\mathcal DD. Repetitions in that union are allowed.

M3 claims a universal integer kkk such that

μp(D)≥1−1k⟹Ek(D) is p-small.\mu_p(\mathcal D)\geq1-\frac1k\quad\Longrightarrow\quadE_k(\mathcal D)\text{ is }p\text{-small}.μp​(D)≥1−k1​⟹Ek​(D) is p-small.

The family D\mathcal DD need not be increasing. The covering cost uses exactly the same ppp as the probability hypothesis.

There is also a different tradeoff: if μp(D)>1/2\mu_p(\mathcal D)>1/2μp​(D)>1/2, two unions suffice when the covering density is reduced to p/C′p/C'p/C′ for a universal constant C′C'C′. This combines Li’s fractional theorem with M2. Fewer unions and a weaker probability assumption are obtained at the price of a constant density loss; they are not the same statement as the main same-density theorem.

M1: fixed graph pieces near the expectation threshold

For a graph HHH on at most nnn vertices, let q(H;n)q(H;n)q(H;n) be the integral expectation threshold for containing HHH in G(n,p)G(n,p)G(n,p), where every possible edge appears independently with probability ppp. Let pc(H;n)p_c(H;n)pc​(H;n) be its probability-one-half containment threshold.

M1 claims universal constants k0k_0k0​ and LLL such that the edges of every HHH can be partitioned into pieces H1,…,Hk0H_1,\ldots,H_{k_0}H1​,…,Hk0​​ with

pc(Hi;n)≤Lq(H;n)(1≤i≤k0).p_c(H_i;n)\leq Lq(H;n)\qquad(1\leq i\leq k_0).pc​(Hi​;n)≤Lq(H;n)(1≤i≤k0​).

Pieces may share vertices or be empty. The partition is chosen before sampling the host graph. Each piece is tested for ordinary, non-induced containment separately. Their successful embeddings need not agree on shared vertices, so the theorem does not directly embed the whole target at density Lq(H;n)Lq(H;n)Lq(H;n).

For edgeless targets the paper sets both thresholds to zero. M1 uses M3’s same-density covering theorem as an essential companion input.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. This family addresses central structural questions about random thresholds and the difference between fractional and discrete certificates. The first comparison removes every dimension or generator-size loss, while the discrete-convexity result retains the original density.

The graph decomposition explains one way to remove the logarithmic gap in the general threshold theorem: relax the demand that all edges be embedded in one compatible copy, and a bounded number of predetermined pieces suffice. The number of pieces does not grow with the target.

These statements should be appreciated together without merging them. Constant-factor rounding concerns certificates. Discrete convexity concerns unions of likely sets. Graph decomposition concerns separately embeddable pieces. Their connections give the family broad reach, and their different quantifiers explain why none is merely a restatement of the already established Kahn–Kalai threshold bound.

6. The main idea

Capture one object at many scales

M2 assigns a probability mass to the vertices of each successful set. It then independently gives ground-set elements random integer colors, interpreted as stages of exposure. A selector estimate finds one successful set whose mass is substantially captured at every stage simultaneously.

This simultaneity is crucial. Separate estimates could choose a different successful set at each stage and would provide no common object with controlled total loss. Here the uncaptured masses decrease geometrically, so their sum is bounded. The chosen set consequently has a bounded average stage.

Fractional weights are distributed over their generators’ vertices. A bounded average stage forces a substantial amount of generator weight to occur early. Independence then gives an upper bound on a weighted product sum that conflicts with this forced contribution. The contradiction yields an integral cover at a constant reduction in density.

Turn failure of unions into cover generators

M3 uses an expansion of functions on random subsets into orthogonal components, together with a signed product identity. A set that cannot be covered by the required unions must carry substantial weight in these components.

Large individual weights can be selected directly as inexpensive generators. When weight is distributed across many smaller components, a covering lemma combines high-degree selections with random unions. This produces an integral cover initially at a reduced density.

The final step couples several random rows. Each row separately has the original Bernoulli law, but the rows are dependent so that their union has an exactly prescribed larger density. This recovers the original covering parameter. Independence within each row and careful dependence between rows serve different purposes.

Transfer typical behavior to a graph partition

M1 defines a high-probability class of random graphs with strong embedding properties. Discrete convexity places a labeled copy of the target inside the union of a bounded number of deterministic graphs from that class. Assigning each target edge to one of them begins the partition.

Further splitting separates high-degree vertices, lower-degree regions and edges crossing between them. For crossing pieces, the problem is finding distinct host vertices with prescribed neighborhoods. Hall’s matching condition must hold for every collection of requirements. A compression lemma reduces the tests needed to control all those collections, allowing typical random behavior to transfer to each fixed piece.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The comparison qf≤Cqq_f\leq Cqqf​≤Cq does not imply pc≤Cqp_c\leq Cqpc​≤Cq for every increasing property. The logarithmic gap between certificate thresholds and actual occurrence can be necessary. The new theorem removes the gap between two kinds of certificate, not every threshold gap.

Discrete convexity supplies an inexpensive cover of the exceptional family, which is stronger information than a probability bound alone. Its main theorem requires a very high starting probability and allows a large universal number of unions. The two-union corollary changes both parameters.

The decomposition pieces are fixed before the host is sampled, but their embeddings are separate. Requiring compatible embeddings would recover the whole target and is a substantially stronger request. Likewise, the theorem compares piece thresholds with the original target’s integral threshold, not with a simpler expected-copy parameter for one selected subgraph.

The universal constants are not optimized, and the headline results do not promise efficient algorithms for arbitrary families described implicitly. Their principal contribution is structural existence at the claimed scales.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 is the October 5 graph-decomposition manuscript. M2 gives the constant-factor integral–fractional comparison; M3 gives same-density discrete convexity and explains the two-union tradeoff.

Primary background includes Kahn–Kalai, the fractional threshold theorem, Park–Pham’s integral theorem, Talagrand’s original questions, and Ascoli–He–Park–Talagrand’s decomposition conjecture. The recent Li and Park manuscripts explain the immediate fractional and rounding predecessors.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Graph Decompositions at the Integral Expectation Threshold (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Integral and fractional expectation thresholds are equivalent (September 23, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Talagrand’s discrete-convexity conjecture (September 23, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Predicting graph appearance from the expected counts of all subgraphs
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 176 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A random graph cannot usually contain a complicated target if even one of the target’s smaller subgraphs has almost no expected copies. This gives a basic necessary test: increase the edge density until every subgraph has a reasonable expected count.

How far above that elementary counting scale must one go before the entire target is likely to appear? The second Kahn–Kalai conjecture predicts that only a logarithmic factor is necessary, uniformly over all target graphs, including targets that grow with the host.

The manuscript claims this statement. Its bound uses the number of target edges inside the logarithm. The main challenge is coordinating many stages of an embedding without paying a separate logarithmic penalty at each stage. The paper organizes all possible extension histories in a tree and reuses the same random sample across its levels.

2. Background and essential definitions

The random graph G(n,p)G(n,p)G(n,p) has vertices 1,…,n1,\ldots,n1,…,n. Each possible edge is present independently with probability ppp. The target HHH is a finite simple graph with at most nnn vertices and at least one edge.

For graphs GGG and FFF, let N(G,F)N(G,F)N(G,F) count ordinary subgraphs of GGG isomorphic to FFF. These copies are not required to be induced: additional host edges among the selected vertices are allowed.

The ordinary containment threshold is

pc(n,H)=inf⁡{p:Pr⁡(N(G(n,p),H)>0)≥1/2}.p_c(n,H)=\inf\{p:\Pr(N(G(n,p),H)>0)\geq1/2\}.pc​(n,H)=inf{p:Pr(N(G(n,p),H)>0)≥1/2}.

The graph expectation threshold is

pE(n,H)=inf⁡{p:EN(G(n,p),F)≥1/2 for every F⊆H}.p_E(n,H)=\inf\{p:\mathbb E N(G(n,p),F)\geq1/2\text{ for every }F\subseteq H\}.pE​(n,H)=inf{p:EN(G(n,p),F)≥1/2 for every F⊆H}.

The second definition tests every subgraph, not just HHH itself. A dense small part of a target can be a stronger obstruction than the expected count of the whole target.

For a fixed graph FFF with vvv vertices and aaa edges,

EN(G(n,p),F)=(n)v∣Aut⁡(F)∣pa.\mathbb E N(G(n,p),F)=\frac{(n)_v}{|\operatorname{Aut}(F)|}p^a.EN(G(n,p),F)=∣Aut(F)∣(n)v​​pa.

Here (n)v=n(n−1)⋯(n−v+1)(n)_v=n(n-1)\cdots(n-v+1)(n)v​=n(n−1)⋯(n−v+1), and Aut⁡(F)\operatorname{Aut}(F)Aut(F) is the group of vertex permutations preserving adjacency. Dividing by its size prevents counting equivalent labelings as different copies.

If HHH appears, then each F⊆HF\subseteq HF⊆H appears. A nonnegative integer count has expectation at least its probability of being positive. Consequently,

pE(n,H)≤pc(n,H).p_E(n,H)\leq p_c(n,H).pE​(n,H)≤pc​(n,H).

The theorem asks how large the reverse comparison must be. The thresholds use probability and expected-count level one half; changing the expected-count level to one changes the relevant scale by at most a factor two.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Thresholds for fixed subgraphs are part of classical random-graph theory, beginning with Erdős and Rényi and developed systematically by Bollobás. The present problem is more uniform: the graph HHH may change with nnn, and it may use every host vertex.

Spanning examples show why a logarithm is necessary. For a perfect matching on an even number nnn of vertices, the graph expectation threshold has order 1/n1/n1/n, while the actual containment threshold has order log⁡n/n\log n/nlogn/n. At the smaller scale, isolated host vertices obstruct a matching covering every vertex. Hamilton cycles exhibit the same kind of gap. The classical Erdős–Rényi matching paper is an early landmark.

Kahn and Kalai proposed both an abstract expectation-threshold conjecture and this graph-specific one. The abstract problem allows a cover by many possible containment patterns, rather than the copies of one chosen subgraph. Park and Pham resolved that abstract conjecture after the fractional theorem of Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan and Park.

The distinction is important. If q(FH)q(\mathcal F_H)q(FH​) denotes the integral cover threshold for containing HHH, then

pE(n,H)≤q(FH).p_E(n,H)\leq q(\mathcal F_H).pE​(n,H)≤q(FH​).

An upper bound in terms of the potentially larger quantity qqq does not automatically give one in terms of pEp_EpE​. Thus the first conjecture’s solution did not settle the second.

Mossel, Niles-Weed, Sun and Zadik obtained a logarithmic bound using a modified graph expectation parameter that also records how many copies of each test graph occur inside HHH. Dubroff, Kahn and Park obtained a three-logarithm general comparison and settled a low-density regime. Their later work treated additional test-graph classes.

Tran’s September 2026 manuscript reduced the general containment loss to two logarithms and settled several target classes. Its conditional extension distributions are a direct input to the strategy developed here. The present manuscript claims the single logarithm uniformly.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Let h=e(H)≥1h=e(H)\geq1h=e(H)≥1 be the number of target edges. The manuscript states

pc(n,H)≤min⁡{1,2048e50pE(n,H)(1+log⁡2h)}.p_c(n,H)\leq\min\left\{1,2048e^{50}p_E(n,H)(1+\log_2 h)\right\}.pc​(n,H)≤min{1,2048e50pE​(n,H)(1+log2​h)}.

The symbol eee in the constant is the base of the natural logarithm, and log⁡2\log_2log2​ has base two. The constant is explicit and universal; it does not depend on nnn or on the target.

Since a simple graph on at most nnn vertices has at most (n2)\binom n2(2n​) edges, the result implies

pc(n,H)≤6144e50pE(n,H)log⁡2n.p_c(n,H)\leq6144e^{50}p_E(n,H)\log_2 n.pc​(n,H)≤6144e50pE​(n,H)log2​n.

The minimum with one in the first formula handles cases where the other expression exceeds the largest possible edge probability. The constants are deliberately very large; the significance is the uniform single-logarithm dependence.

The underlying containment argument actually reaches probability at least two thirds at the stated density. This is more than needed for the one-half definition of pcp_cpc​, but the headline remains a threshold comparison, not a claim that the same fixed multiple gives probability tending to one in every asymptotic setting.

No bounded-degree, bounded-degeneracy or fixed-target hypothesis is imposed. Isolated vertices are permitted, subject to the total vertex bound. The target must have at least one edge so that the expectation parameter and logarithmic formulation are nontrivial.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claim resolves the graph-specific Kahn–Kalai conjecture at the correct general logarithmic scale. It says that elementary expected-copy obstructions almost determine when any graph can appear, despite the global compatibility needed to place all its edges together.

The perfect-matching example explains the strength and the limit of the statement. Counting can miss the last isolated vertices, creating a genuine logarithmic delay. The theorem claims there is no worse general obstruction, up to an absolute constant.

This is also a uniform result across targets that need very different embedding methods in individual cases. The same comparison applies to dense graphs, sparse graphs and spanning graphs. The proof’s reuse of randomness across a hierarchy is therefore valuable beyond improving a numerical exponent: it offers a way to coordinate many dependent extension choices without repeatedly paying for them.

6. The main idea

Find a core with controlled extensions

Begin with a nonempty edge subset of HHH. Select a smaller core by maximizing a suitably normalized probability that a fixed copy of that core lies inside a uniformly chosen copy of the larger graph.

The expected-count assumptions prevent the core from being almost as large as the original. Maximality also controls the distribution of the edges needed to extend it. Informally, no specified set JJJ of added edges is too likely:

Pr⁡(J⊆A)≤a∣J∣\Pr(J\subseteq A)\leq a^{|J|}Pr(J⊆A)≤a∣J∣

for a parameter aaa that is a universal multiple of pE(n,H)p_E(n,H)pE​(n,H). A distribution satisfying such inequalities is called spread. It behaves, for containment tests, as though its edges were dispersed rather than concentrated on a few compulsory choices.

Repeating the construction yields nested cores. All possible labeled copies and their possible extensions form a branching tree. Each branch describes a complete embedding history. The edge sets added along one branch are disjoint, and their sizes vary geometrically.

Replace a difficult set by a small remainder

The paper uses a Bayesian resampling idea. Take a source extension AAA, add an independent random edge set WWW, and then sample another compatible extension from the conditional distribution given the union.

The portion of the new extension outside WWW is a remainder. It is also contained in the source extension. Spread estimates make large remainders unlikely, so one sample can reduce the unresolved part substantially while retaining control of its distribution.

For one extension this is a local step. For an entire embedding tree, conditioning can distort later choices. The manuscript therefore estimates the change in probability on coordinates outside the chosen extension. Along a branch, later added edges avoid earlier ones, making that estimate applicable to the remaining continuation.

Pay for the hierarchy once

A recursively defined potential measures the chance that too many continuations fail. The local resampling bounds are applied simultaneously at every node using the same WWW, rather than an independent new sample for each level.

The result is a reduction of every level’s unresolved capacity by about one half at a controlled cost. Repeating this only logarithmically many times in hhh completes some branch, whose accumulated labels form a copy of HHH.

This is the source of the final logarithm. The graph hierarchy supplies many possible ways to extend, and the random samples reduce uncertainty across those ways together. A separate logarithmic payment at every nested scale would lose the claimed bound.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns ordinary copies in independent-edge random graphs. Induced copies impose additional nonedge requirements and are not covered by this statement. Hypergraph analogues also require their own arguments.

The graph expectation threshold checks all subgraphs. Replacing it with the expected count of HHH alone can miss a denser obstruction inside the target. The all-subgraph hypothesis is part of the theorem’s content.

The single logarithm is necessary for some targets, but often excessive for a particular graph class. Determining when it can be removed, and finding sharp constants or narrow transition windows, remain more detailed questions. The enormous universal constant here is not a practical estimate for a specific finite graph.

The proof does not depend on the companion integral–fractional equivalence in family 175; the manuscript cites that result as context. Its route instead builds the graph-specific extension hierarchy and proves the required simultaneous covering statement directly. This distinguishes the dependency structure from the nearby threshold results.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript states the graph expectation normalization explicitly and explains the distinction between the two Kahn–Kalai conjectures before introducing its extension tree.

Primary references include Kahn–Kalai’s original paper, Mossel–Niles-Weed–Sun–Zadik, Dubroff–Kahn–Park, and Tran’s conditional-extension approach. The related abstract cover notions are explained separately in family 175, while the definitions needed for the present graph theorem are included above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The second Kahn–Kalai conjecture (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Sparse higher-dimensional spaces with no hidden parity obstructions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 177 · Combinatorics
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

An expander graph is sparse but difficult to separate: a substantial set of vertices has many edges leading out. Can an analogous phenomenon hold for spaces made of edges, triangles, tetrahedra and higher-dimensional pieces, while every vertex still meets only a bounded number of pieces?

In higher dimensions, there is an additional difficulty. Local parity tests may all pass even when the tested data do not arise from the expected global construction. Such hidden obstructions are measured by cohomology. A full coboundary expander must both exclude these obstructions and quantitatively detect distance from the valid global data.

The manuscript claims arbitrarily large examples in every fixed dimension at least three, with uniformly bounded vertex incidence and expansion in every lower degree. Combined with known graph and two-dimensional results, this supplies bounded-degree coboundary expanders over the two-element field in every positive dimension.

2. Background and essential definitions

A simplicial complex is a collection of finite vertex sets closed under taking subsets. Its vertices are one-element faces, edges are two-element faces, triangles are three-element faces, and so on. An iii-face has i+1i+1i+1 vertices. A pure ddd-dimensional complex is one in which every face belongs to some ddd-face.

The field F2={0,1}\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}F2​={0,1} uses addition modulo two. An iii-cochain fff assigns a bit to each iii-face. Equivalently, it selects the faces assigned one.

Its coboundary δif\delta_i fδi​f assigns a bit to each (i+1)(i+1)(i+1)-face by adding the bits on its iii-dimensional subfaces:

(δif)(τ)=∑σ⊂τ∣σ∣=i+1f(σ)in F2.(\delta_i f)(\tau)=\sum_{\substack{\sigma\subset\tau\\|\sigma|=i+1}}f(\sigma)\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_2.(δi​f)(τ)=σ⊂τ∣σ∣=i+1​∑​f(σ)in F2​.

For i=0i=0i=0, a selected vertex set has coboundary exactly the edges crossing to its complement. For i=1i=1i=1, an edge labeling fails the triangle test when a triangle contains an odd number of labeled edges.

Applying two successive coboundaries gives zero: every smaller face is counted twice. Therefore the space of coboundaries

Bi=im⁡δi−1B^i=\operatorname{im}\delta_{i-1}Bi=imδi−1​

lies inside the space of cocycles Zi=ker⁡δiZ^i=\ker\delta_iZi=kerδi​. A cocycle passes every local parity test. A coboundary comes from data one dimension lower. Their quotient Hi=Zi/BiH^i=Z^i/B^iHi=Zi/Bi is cohomology; it records the possible gap between those notions. In degree zero, the paper takes B0B^0B0 to be the constant functions.

The norm ∥f∥\|f\|∥f∥ is a weighted fraction of faces labeled one. Sample a top-dimensional face uniformly and then one of its iii-faces uniformly; the norm is the probability of seeing a one. The distance dist⁡(f,Bi)\operatorname{dist}(f,B^i)dist(f,Bi) is the smallest such fraction of changes needed to turn fff into a coboundary.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The higher-dimensional expansion viewpoint grew through work on random complexes by Linial and Meshulam, then Meshulam and Wallach. These models keep all lower-dimensional faces and add top-dimensional faces randomly, studying when cohomological obstructions disappear.

Gromov connected filling inequalities with topological overlap and asked for large complexes combining bounded local incidence with uniform expansion properties. The resulting theory has several related notions, and their differences matter for this family.

Lubotzky and Meshulam constructed two-dimensional expanders from random Latin squares. Lubotzky, Luria and Rosenthal used random Steiner systems in every dimension. These constructions bound how many top faces meet a codimension-one face. That is weaker than bounding incidence at vertices: their lower-dimensional skeletons are complete, so a vertex meets increasingly many edges as the complex grows.

For bounded vertex degree, Kaufman, Kazhdan and Lubotzky obtained cosystolic and topological expansion from Ramanujan complexes. Evra and Kaufman established bounded-degree cosystolic expanders in every dimension. Among other properties, cosystolic expansion controls distance to the space ZiZ^iZi of cocycles. It can coexist with nonzero cohomology.

Chapman and Lubotzky proved bounded-degree two-dimensional coboundary expansion over F2\mathbb F_2F2​. Other recent work obtained degree-one coboundary expansion with suitable non-Abelian coefficients. These results did not supply all lower cochain degrees simultaneously in every higher dimension.

The new manuscript uses an established algebraic construction program and a cosystolic expansion theorem of Oppenheim and Valentiner-Branth. Its additional task is to arrange cohomology vanishing in the same sequence of bounded-degree complexes, converting the available distance-to-cocycles inequality into full coboundary expansion.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every fixed integer d≥3d\geq3d≥3, the manuscript states that there are constants D<∞D<\inftyD<∞ and ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, and finite connected pure ddd-dimensional complexes XmX_mXm​, such that their number of vertices tends to infinity and every vertex belongs to at most DDD top-dimensional faces.

For every degree 0≤i<d0\leq i<d0≤i<d and every iii-cochain fff, the claimed inequality is

∥δif∥Xm,i+1≥εdist⁡Xm,i(f,Bi(Xm)).\|\delta_i f\|_{X_m,i+1}\geq\varepsilon\operatorname{dist}_{X_m,i}(f,B^i(X_m)).∥δi​f∥Xm​,i+1​≥εdistXm​,i​(f,Bi(Xm​)).

The constants may depend on ddd, but not on the size parameter mmm, the degree iii within that range, or the cochain fff.

The statement has two inseparable parts. First, if δif=0\delta_i f=0δi​f=0, the inequality forces f∈Bif\in B^if∈Bi. Thus every cocycle is a coboundary in the stated degrees: there are no nonzero cohomology classes there. Second, a cochain far from BiB^iBi must fail a proportionate number of local tests.

In degree zero, distance to the constant functions measures the smaller weighted side of a vertex cut. The inequality becomes an ordinary expansion statement. In degree one, it says that an edge labeling far from every labeling induced by vertex bits must violate many triangle parity tests.

The degree bound is genuinely at vertices. Since the complex is pure and ddd is fixed, bounding the number of incident top faces also bounds the number of incident lower faces. This avoids the growing complete skeletons of earlier bounded-codimension-one-degree constructions.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5. The claim resolves a central existence problem in higher-dimensional expansion by combining three requirements: arbitrarily large size, bounded incidence at vertices, and full coboundary expansion in all degrees below the dimension.

The distinction from expansion toward cocycles is structural. If a nontrivial cocycle exists, it passes every local test while remaining a positive distance from the coboundaries. No quantitative improvement in the local test constant can remove that obstruction. It must be eliminated by topology or algebra.

The result also sharpens the analogy with graph expanders. Sparse graphs can globally connect a large vertex set using bounded local degree. Here a similarly sparse collection of higher-dimensional faces is claimed to control global consistency of face labelings at every lower level. Such complexes are relevant to topological combinatorics and local testing, although a particular coding or algorithmic application requires additional specifications beyond this theorem.

6. The main idea

Build large complexes with fixed local pieces

The construction starts with matrix groups over a polynomial ring Fq[t]\mathbb F_q[t]Fq​[t], where qqq is a sufficiently large fixed odd prime depending on the desired dimension. A suitable group is reduced modulo successive powers tmt^mtm, producing larger finite groups.

A coset complex is built from a group and chosen subgroups. Its vertices are tagged cosets, and a collection of vertices forms a face when the corresponding cosets have a common group element. Keeping the local subgroups fixed bounds the number of faces meeting a vertex, while the growing quotient groups increase the total size.

The manuscript first constructs complexes in a higher ambient dimension, then keeps only faces of dimension at most ddd. This retained subcomplex is called the ddd-skeleton.

Remove the global obstructions

An infinite version of the coset complex is placed inside a geometric object called an affine building. Buildings organize many simplex-shaped pieces according to matrix-group symmetries. The paper uses this geometry to prove homological vanishing in an appropriate range.

Passing that conclusion to each finite quotient is the delicate algebraic stage. Existing stability results initially control an inverse system of congruence subgroups, rather than immediately giving vanishing at every individual level. The manuscript combines them with transfer maps associated with finite quotients of odd order.

Working over F2\mathbb F_2F2​ is important here: odd integers act invertibly on these coefficients. The resulting averaging and surjectivity statements turn the system-level information into the required finite-level vanishing. This is how the paper eliminates the hidden cocycles in each constructed complex.

Combine vanishing with quantitative expansion

The existing Kac–Moody–Steinberg expansion theorem supplies a uniform estimate of the form

∥δif∥≥ηdist⁡(f,Zi)\|\delta_i f\|\geq\eta\operatorname{dist}(f,Z^i)∥δi​f∥≥ηdist(f,Zi)

on the relevant complexes. Once the new argument establishes Zi=BiZ^i=B^iZi=Bi, the target subspace becomes the space of coboundaries.

One further step is needed because the final theorem uses the ddd-skeleton and its own face-sampling weights. The manuscript compares how many top faces contain each retained face. Uniform bounds control the change in norms, and a common normalization factor cancels between successive dimensions. Thus both the expansion constant and the vertex-incidence bound remain independent of the growing quotient size.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result is over F2\mathbb F_2F2​. It does not assert the same construction and constants for every coefficient field or for arbitrary non-Abelian coefficients. The use of odd-order group quotients is specifically coordinated with characteristic two.

The dimension is fixed before choosing the constants. There is no uniform bound on DDD or ε\varepsilonε as ddd itself tends to infinity. The theorem also controls cochain degrees below ddd, not the top degree, where there are no higher faces available for the same coboundary test.

The sequence has unbounded size; it is not a promise of a complex on every prescribed number of vertices. Nor does the headline optimize the local degree or the expansion constant.

Vanishing of lower cohomology should not be confused with contractibility of the finite complexes. Contractibility is a stronger topological condition. The claimed conclusion is exactly the vanishing and quantitative inequality needed for coboundary expansion in the specified range.

8. Sources and further reading

The manuscript introduces its face weights and distinguishes cocycles from coboundaries before stating the construction. Its final section explains how the existing expansion theorem and the new vanishing result combine.

Primary background includes Gromov’s topological expansion framework, random Steiner-system expanders, Evra–Kaufman’s bounded-degree cosystolic expanders, Chapman–Lubotzky’s two-dimensional result, and Oppenheim–Valentiner-Branth’s KMS expansion theorem. These distinguish the earlier local expansion inputs from the all-degree coboundary conclusion claimed here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Bounded-degree coboundary expanders in every dimension (September 24, 2026).
