8. Sources and further reading

  • Alon, Ben-Eliezer, and Fischer, Testing hereditary properties of ordered graphs and matrices, for qualitative ordered removal.
  • Alon and Ben-Eliezer, Efficient removal lemmas for matrices, for polynomial positive cases and the earlier question.
  • Gishboliner and Shapira, Polynomial property testing, version 1, for the singleton conjecture cited by M1.

M1 gives the complete binary anchor, the ordered tree matrices, and the stated repair and copy-count estimates.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Polynomial removal fails for ordered binary matrices (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A Boolean function can beat the square-root degree bound by any factor
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 192 · Combinatorics
Importance 3/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

A Boolean function takes a string of binary inputs and returns one binary answer. Use signs −1-1−1 and +1+1+1 for the two values. Some functions closely follow individual inputs; others depend on complicated interactions among many inputs.

There are two different ways to measure this behavior. The function’s linear Fourier coefficients record its correlations with individual inputs. Its polynomial degree measures the largest interaction needed to express it exactly as a polynomial.

A conjecture of Gopalan and Servedio proposed a square-root relationship: the sum of the linear correlations should be at most the square root of the degree. Such a statement would replace the total number of input bits by a much more intrinsic measure of the function’s complexity.

The manuscript in this family claims that the proposed bound fails by arbitrarily large factors. For every chosen constant C>0C>0C>0, it constructs a finite Boolean function whose summed linear correlations exceed Cdeg⁡(f)C\sqrt{\deg(f)}Cdeg(f)​. A linear bound in the degree survives, so the question becomes how large the gap between these two scales can be.

2. Background and essential definitions

Fourier analysis on binary inputs

Let X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)X=(X1​,…,Xn​) be independent uniform random signs. For a subset S⊆{1,…,n}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}S⊆{1,…,n}, define

f^(S)=E[f(X)∏i∈SXi].\widehat f(S)=\mathbb E\left[f(X)\prod_{i\in S}X_i\right].f​(S)=E[f(X)i∈S∏​Xi​].

The empty product is one, so f^(∅)=E[f(X)]\widehat f(\varnothing)=\mathbb E[f(X)]f​(∅)=E[f(X)]. These coefficients express every function on the sign cube uniquely as

f(x)=∑S⊆{1,…,n}f^(S)∏i∈Sxi.f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}\widehat f(S)\prod_{i\in S}x_i.f(x)=S⊆{1,…,n}∑​f​(S)i∈S∏​xi​.

Each variable appears with exponent at most one; this is the multilinear representation. Its degree is

deg⁡(f)=max⁡{∣S∣:f^(S)≠0}.\deg(f)=\max\{|S|:\widehat f(S)\ne0\}.deg(f)=max{∣S∣:f​(S)=0}.

The degree is over the real numbers and represents the function exactly. It is not degree modulo two, approximate polynomial degree, or the number of input queries used by an algorithm.

For a singleton set {i}\{i\}{i}, the coefficient f^({i})=E[f(X)Xi]\widehat f(\{i\})=\mathbb E[f(X)X_i]f​({i})=E[f(X)Xi​] measures agreement with input iii: it is the probability of agreement minus the probability of disagreement.

Their signed sum satisfies

L(f):=∑i=1nf^({i})=E[f(X)∑i=1nXi].L(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat f(\{i\})=\mathbb E\left[f(X)\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right].L(f):=i=1∑n​f​({i})=E[f(X)i=1∑n​Xi​].

Thus L(f)L(f)L(f) measures correlation with the total input sum. Since a Boolean function has f(X)2=1f(X)^2=1f(X)2=1, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives L(f)≤nL(f)\le\sqrt nL(f)≤n​. The conjecture asks whether deg⁡(f)\sqrt{\deg(f)}deg(f)​ can replace n\sqrt nn​.

A surviving general bound

The influence of coordinate iii is the probability that flipping only that input changes the output. Write it as Inf⁡i(f)\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)Infi​(f), and let I(f)I(f)I(f) be the sum over coordinates.

The standard Fourier identities imply

∑i∣f^({i})∣≤I(f)=∑S∣S∣f^(S)2≤deg⁡(f).\sum_i|\widehat f(\{i\})|\le I(f)=\sum_S|S|\widehat f(S)^2\le\deg(f).i∑​∣f​({i})∣≤I(f)=S∑​∣S∣f​(S)2≤deg(f).

The last step uses ∑Sf^(S)2=1\sum_S\widehat f(S)^2=1∑S​f​(S)2=1, the analogue of Parseval’s identity for a Boolean function. So there is already a dimension-independent linear degree bound. The disputed claim is the much smaller square-root scale.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Nisan and Szegedy’s 1994 work developed the study of Boolean functions through their exact real polynomial degree. This connects a discrete input-output rule with algebraic constraints on which interactions can occur. The influence identities above belong to that established framework.

O’Donnell’s problem list attributes the square-root conjecture to Gopalan and Servedio around 2009. It also records a stronger proposal based on majority. If ddd independent signs are available, define

Bd=E∣X1+⋯+Xd∣≤d.B_d=\mathbb E|X_1+\cdots+X_d|\le\sqrt d.Bd​=E∣X1​+⋯+Xd​∣≤d​.

Majority on those signs, with a fixed output chosen at ties, has summed linear correlation BdB_dBd​. The stronger proposal would bound a degree-ddd function’s sum by this majority benchmark. The problem list records the two related questions.

Jha and Wang gave reformulations of the majority proposal and settled some special degree ranges. Kudin and Pašalić established additional low-degree cases and disproved the majority bound at degree four. That was a counterexample to the stronger inequality; it did not by itself contradict the weaker square-root bound. M1 carefully separates these statements despite varying terminology in the literature.

Another source of positive evidence came from decision trees. These compute a function by revealing information about the inputs. O’Donnell and Servedio related correlation to the expected amount of information revealed in ordinary decision trees; Blais, Tan, and Wan obtained a square-root bound involving parity decision-tree depth, where a query reveals a product of input signs.

M1’s construction uses a different kind of observation. It controls the polynomial degree of each possible output event rather than requiring the observation to be a sequence of simple queries. Algebraic cancellation then permits behavior that the earlier decision-tree bounds do not rule out.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript, M1. Its main statement is that for every real C>0C>0C>0, there are a positive integer nnn and a nonconstant Boolean function f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1} such that

∑i=1nf^({i})>Cdeg⁡(f).\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat f(\{i\})>C\sqrt{\deg(f)}.i=1∑n​f​({i})>Cdeg(f)​.

This excludes every constant-factor version of the square-root conjecture. It is stronger than finding a single function that barely exceeds the proposed constant one.

The conclusion also applies to the sum of absolute values:

sup⁡n≥1, f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}deg⁡(f)>0∑i∣f^({i})∣deg⁡(f)=∞.\sup_{\substack{n\ge1,\ f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\\\deg(f)>0}}\frac{\sum_i|\widehat f(\{i\})|}{\sqrt{\deg(f)}}=\infty.n≥1, f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}deg(f)>0​sup​deg(f)​∑i​∣f​({i})∣​=∞.

Indeed, reversing any input sign changes the sign of its linear coefficient while preserving polynomial degree. A universal bound for signed sums would therefore also bound absolute sums after suitable input reversals. M1’s examples already produce a large positive signed sum directly.

Every example in the theorem has finitely many inputs. Limits enter the construction to establish that sufficiently large finite choices exist. The source explicitly does not give useful bounds on how the dimension or replication counts grow with the requested violation factor.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 3/5. The claimed result resolves a concrete conjecture in the analysis of Boolean functions and rules out its entire constant-factor relaxation. It clarifies that exact polynomial degree can underestimate this kind of accumulated linear correlation by more than a fixed square-root factor.

Linear Fourier information is a natural way to detect which inputs align with an output. Polynomial degree is a different structural measure, central to connections between algebra and computation. Understanding their limitations helps separate forms of complexity that initially appear closely related.

The claim is also conceptually stronger than the earlier failure of the majority benchmark. A modest violation of an exact extremal candidate might still leave a universal square-root law intact. An unbounded ratio rules out that broader law too.

At the same time, the surviving linear degree bound remains valid, and the manuscript does not determine the optimal replacement. The advance changes the range of possible answers without completing the full extremal picture.

6. The main idea

First retain information, then output a sign

Instead of immediately designing the Boolean function, M1 constructs a finite-valued observation FFF of a block of input signs. It can have more than two possible outputs. Let

HN=X1+⋯+XN,TF=E[HN∣F].H_N=X_1+\cdots+X_N,\qquad T_F=\mathbb E[H_N\mid F].HN​=X1​+⋯+XN​,TF​=E[HN​∣F].

Conditional expectation means the best mean-square prediction of the input sum when the observation is known. The random variable TFT_FTF​ records that prediction. Since the input sum has mean zero, so does TFT_FTF​.

Define the retained variance by

v(F)=E[TF2].v(F)=\mathbb E[T_F^2].v(F)=E[TF2​].

A large retained variance means that observing FFF reveals substantial information about the sum. Meanwhile, impose a degree bound DDD on every event indicator 1{F=a}\mathbf1_{\{F=a\}}1{F=a}​, which is one when the output is aaa and zero otherwise.

Every function of FFF is a linear combination of those indicators, so it also has degree at most DDD. In particular, reading out the sign of TFT_FTF​ gives a Boolean function with controlled degree and correlation E∣TF∣\mathbb E|T_F|E∣TF​∣.

The construction seeks observations with v(F)/Dv(F)/Dv(F)/D arbitrarily large.

Independent averaging turns variance into correlation

Take MMM independent copies of the same observation on disjoint input blocks, with scores T1,…,TMT_1,\ldots,T_MT1​,…,TM​. Their sum has variance Mv(F)Mv(F)Mv(F). The central limit theorem says that, after normalization, this sum approaches a standard Gaussian variable as MMM grows.

Choose the final output to be the sign of that score sum, assigning either fixed sign at zero. Its degree is at most MDMDMD, while its linear correlation behaves asymptotically like

2πMv(F).\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\sqrt{Mv(F)}.π2​​Mv(F)​.

Thus the correlation divided by the square root of the degree bound is governed by v(F)/D\sqrt{v(F)/D}v(F)/D​. An arbitrarily large retained-variance ratio would give the desired Boolean counterexamples using a sufficiently large but finite number of copies.

Cancellation improves the information-to-degree ratio

The central construction starts with m+1m+1m+1 independent standardized scores, each having mean zero and variance one. Simply revealing mmm of them retains mmm units of variance.

M1 designs a more selective reporting rule. Usually it reports all but one score. On a specially chosen exceptional event it reports a single tag, and that tag predicts the total sum with mean-square error smaller than the one unit normally lost by hiding one score.

The source claims that this retains strictly more than mmm units of variance. Yet each output indicator can be expressed as a linear combination of functions depending on at most mmm of the input observations. When the observations themselves have degree bound DDD, this gives degree at most mDmDmD.

The crucial feature is cancellation in that indicator expansion. An output can depend on all m+1m+1m+1 scores without requiring their full combined degree. The saving does not come from permanently ignoring one fixed input.

A Gaussian model supplies intervals and reporting rules with a definite gain. Independent averaging transfers those rules to finite sign inputs. Repeating the gain a finite number of times makes the retained-variance ratio exceed any prescribed level, after which the sign readout completes the stated construction.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns the sum of linear coefficients, not their squared sum. Parseval’s identity still bounds the total squared Fourier mass by one. A large sum of many small linear correlations is compatible with that restriction.

The degree is exact real multilinear degree. The statement does not transfer automatically to approximate degree, arithmetic over a finite field, decision-tree depth, or circuit size. Each of those measures carries different constraints.

The construction establishes arbitrarily large violations but does not supply useful dimension bounds in terms of the desired factor. It also does not claim a simple small formula giving an optimal example at every degree.

The surviving estimate ∑i∣f^({i})∣≤deg⁡(f)\sum_i|\widehat f(\{i\})|\le\deg(f)∑i​∣f​({i})∣≤deg(f) leaves substantial room above the square-root scale. Determining the true extremal growth, finding simpler examples, and identifying important subclasses where square-root behavior survives are natural further questions.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Nisan and Szegedy, On the degree of Boolean functions as real polynomials, for the exact-degree framework and influence identities.
  • O’Donnell, Open Problems in Analysis of Boolean Functions, for the square-root and majority proposals.
  • Kudin and Pašalić, Proving the conjecture of O’Donnell in certain cases and disproving its general validity, for the earlier majority-bound counterexample.
  • Blais, Tan, and Wan, An inequality for the Fourier spectrum of parity decision trees, for the distinct decision-tree setting.

M1 develops the finite-observation construction, Gaussian comparison, and repeated amplification used in its claimed counterexamples.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Unbounded Violations of the Square-Root Degree Bound (September 26, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Keeping every triangle larger than the predicted scale
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 191 · Combinatorics
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-11

1. The question

Place nnn points in a square of side one. You would like every triangle formed by three of them to have reasonably large area. How well can you do?

This is Heilbronn’s triangle problem. It asks about the smallest triangle in a configuration, so one unfortunate triple can spoil an otherwise well-spread arrangement. Keeping points far apart is not sufficient: three widely separated points can lie almost on a line and form a very thin triangle.

The original conjecture predicted that every configuration would contain a triangle of area at most a constant times n−2n^{-2}n−2. That prediction was disproved decades ago by constructions improving the scale by a logarithmic factor. A weaker expectation allowed every arbitrarily small loss in the exponent: perhaps a triangle of area at most n−2+εn^{-2+\varepsilon}n−2+ε, up to a constant depending on ε\varepsilonε, would always exist.

The manuscript in this family claims a fixed power improvement in the opposite direction. For one absolute η>0\eta>0η>0, it constructs arbitrarily large configurations in which every triangle has area at least a constant times n−2+ηn^{-2+\eta}n−2+η. The exponent gain is extremely small, but fixed. That is enough to contradict the weaker expectation as well.

2. Background and essential definitions

The quantity being optimized

For a set PPP of points in the unit square [0,1]2[0,1]^2[0,1]2, define

Δ(P)=min⁡{p,q,r}⊂PArea⁡(pqr),\Delta(P)=\min_{\{p,q,r\}\subset P}\operatorname{Area}(pqr),Δ(P)={p,q,r}⊂Pmin​Area(pqr),

where the minimum runs over triples of distinct points. Then define

Δ(n)=max⁡P⊂[0,1]2∣P∣=nΔ(P).\Delta(n)=\max_{\substack{P\subset[0,1]^2\\|P|=n}}\Delta(P).Δ(n)=P⊂[0,1]2∣P∣=n​max​Δ(P).

Thus Δ(n)\Delta(n)Δ(n) is the largest minimum triangle area achievable with nnn points. A lower bound requires constructing a good configuration. An upper bound must apply to every configuration. The directions can be easy to confuse because the definition combines a maximum and a minimum.

A collinear triple has area zero. A positive lower bound therefore guarantees, among other things, that no three selected points lie on a line.

Area as a determinant

For plane points p,q,rp,q,rp,q,r, elementary linear algebra gives

Area⁡(pqr)=12∣det⁡(q−p,r−p)∣.\operatorname{Area}(pqr)=\frac12\left|\det(q-p,r-p)\right|.Area(pqr)=21​∣det(q−p,r−p)∣.

The determinant measures the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the two displacement vectors. Taking its absolute value and dividing by two gives the triangle area.

The construction uses another form of the same identity. An integer column u=(u1,u2,u3)Tu=(u_1,u_2,u_3)^{\mathsf T}u=(u1​,u2​,u3​)T, with positive third coordinate, represents the point

π(u)=(u1u3,u2u3).\pi(u)=\left(\frac{u_1}{u_3},\frac{u_2}{u_3}\right).π(u)=(u3​u1​​,u3​u2​​).

If three columns form a matrix AAA, then their projected triangle has area

∣det⁡A∣2A31A32A33.\frac{|\det A|}{2A_{31}A_{32}A_{33}}.2A31​A32​A33​∣detA∣​.

The entries A3jA_{3j}A3j​ are the third coordinates. Keeping them in a controlled range turns a lower bound on integer determinants into a geometric area bound.

Logarithmic and power improvements

A factor of log⁡n\log nlogn grows without bound, but more slowly than nηn^\etanη for every fixed η>0\eta>0η>0. Consequently, replacing n−2n^{-2}n−2 by (log⁡n)n−2(\log n)n^{-2}(logn)n−2 contradicts a constant-factor bound but does not contradict all bounds of the form n−2+εn^{-2+\varepsilon}n−2+ε. A fixed positive exponent gain crosses that second barrier.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Roth’s 1951 paper records Heilbronn’s original question and an elementary construction associated with Erdős. The construction uses a parabola over a finite field, producing grid points with nonzero triangle determinants before scaling. It reaches a minimum area comparable to n−2n^{-2}n−2. Random sampling followed by deleting points in small triangles also reaches that basic scale.

Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi obtained the stronger lower bound

Δ(n)≥clog⁡nn2\Delta(n)\ge c\frac{\log n}{n^2}Δ(n)≥cn2logn​

for a positive constant ccc. Their 1982 paper therefore disproved the original constant-factor conjecture. Their method treats small-area triples as forbidden triples in a hypergraph, then selects a large subset containing none. A hypergraph generalizes a graph by allowing an edge to contain more than two vertices. The original paper develops this lower-bound approach.

Upper bounds followed a separate trajectory. Roth obtained the first improvement over the elementary inverse-linear scale. Later work by Schmidt, Roth, and Komlós–Pintz–Szemerédi sharpened the estimates, the last reaching exponents arbitrarily close to −8/7-8/7−8/7.

Cohen, Pohoata, and Zakharov introduced further incidence-geometric methods. Their 2023 work passed the −8/7-8/7−8/7 exponent by a fixed amount, and their subsequent Lower bounds for incidences gives

Δ(n)≤Cεn−7/6+ε\Delta(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{-7/6+\varepsilon}Δ(n)≤Cε​n−7/6+ε

for every fixed positive ε\varepsilonε. An incidence records a point lying on, or suitably near, a geometric object such as a line; controlling many such relationships can force a small triangle. Their paper develops the incidence estimates and the triangle consequence.

These upper and lower bounds remain widely separated. M1 addresses the lower-bound side and claims to disprove the almost-n−2n^{-2}n−2 formulation. It does not close the overall exponent gap or determine the correct asymptotic order of Δ(n)\Delta(n)Δ(n).

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The family contains one manuscript, M1. It states that there are absolute constants η,c1>0\eta,c_1>0η,c1​>0 and an integer n0n_0n0​ such that

Δ(n)≥c1n−2+ηfor every integer n≥n0.\Delta(n)\ge c_1n^{-2+\eta}\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0.Δ(n)≥c1​n−2+ηfor every integer n≥n0​.

The constants are independent of the number of points. In particular, the improvement is available for every sufficiently large cardinality, not merely for a special sequence.

The weaker conjectural upper bound would say that for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 there is a constant CεC_\varepsilonCε​ with

Δ(n)≤Cεn−2+ε\Delta(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{-2+\varepsilon}Δ(n)≤Cε​n−2+ε

for all sufficiently large nnn. Taking ε=η/2\varepsilon=\eta/2ε=η/2 makes the ratio of M1’s lower bound to the proposed upper bound grow like a positive constant times nη/2n^{\eta/2}nη/2. Thus the two statements cannot both hold for large nnn.

The manuscript gives an explicit admissible expression for η\etaη in terms of its fixed construction parameters, while emphasizing that it is extremely small and unoptimized. The claim is a qualitative change in the exponent, not a practically large numerical improvement for ordinary-sized point sets.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5. The claimed result would overturn a persistent exponent-level expectation in a classical problem of discrete geometry. It also introduces a combination of arithmetic restrictions and random selection that goes beyond the earlier logarithmic improvement.

A tiny fixed exponent matters asymptotically because it eventually exceeds every logarithmic factor. The result would therefore change the plausible long-term scale of the extremal quantity, even if its explicit constants make the construction unsuitable for small examples.

The method connects geometric area to integer determinants, finite-field algebra, and congruences. This suggests a useful way of looking at the problem: instead of distributing points uniformly and then searching for bad triples, build arithmetic restrictions that make most bad triples impossible before sampling.

The rating reflects the conjectural barrier being crossed. It does not treat the claim as a complete solution of Heilbronn’s problem, since the optimal exponent remains undetermined.

6. The main idea

Build rational points through integer columns

The paper starts with integer columns satisfying

0≤u1,u2<N,N≤u3<2N.0\le u_1,u_2<N,\qquad N\le u_3<2N.0≤u1​,u2​<N,N≤u3​<2N.

Their projected points lie in the unit square. If every retained triple has determinant larger than a threshold τ\tauτ in absolute value, the area identity gives

Area⁡(pqr)>τ16N3.\operatorname{Area}(pqr)>\frac{\tau}{16N^3}.Area(pqr)>16N3τ​.

The task is therefore to sample many columns while making small determinants rare. Zero determinants need particular care because they represent collinear projected triples.

Use finite-field labels to obstruct small nonzero determinants

A finite field is a finite number system in which addition, multiplication, and division by nonzero elements obey the usual field rules. For distinct field elements x,y,zx,y,zx,y,z, the three columns

(1,x,x2)T,(1,y,y2)T,(1,z,z2)T(1,x,x^2)^{\mathsf T},\quad(1,y,y^2)^{\mathsf T},\quad(1,z,z^2)^{\mathsf T}(1,x,x2)T,(1,y,y2)T,(1,z,z2)T

have nonzero determinant. This is the algebraic reason that a finite-field parabola avoids collinear triples.

M1 assigns random labels in a fixed-degree field extension. A field norm, a multiplicative map from the extension to its smaller base field, packages the nonvanishing determinant information into a polynomial over the base field.

The construction then encodes this polynomial in a selected digit of a much larger integer determinant. A sufficiently large base controls carries between digits. Distinct labels thereby obstruct a small determinant modulo a prescribed modulus. Repeated labels are exceptional events whose probabilities can be made small.

A shared random invertible change of coordinates mixes the residue columns while preserving their determinant. The manuscript combines this with lattice counts to estimate how many integer lifts can have a given small nonzero determinant. A lattice is a discrete set of integer linear combinations of basis vectors; here it organizes the possible lifts satisfying the congruences.

Treat collinearity separately

The nonzero-determinant estimates do not automatically control determinant zero. The latter allows many columns to lie in a common plane before projection, so it requires a separate restriction.

At another prime modulus, M1 uses residues from a small part of a quadratic surface with no three points on a line. Random transformations provide enough flexibility for counting, while the chosen portion excludes certain short integer relations. The Chinese remainder theorem combines the restrictions at the two coprime moduli into compatible integer coordinates.

This second layer supplies the missing control of collinear triples, including degenerate residue patterns. Avoiding those triples is essential because even one would make the minimum area zero.

Delete the few exceptional choices

The final step is an alteration argument: sample more columns than ultimately needed, count repeated projected points and small-determinant triples, and delete one point from each offending pair or triple.

The manuscript’s estimates make the expected number of deletions smaller than the available surplus. Hence a retained set has no bad triples and still contains many points. Relating that count to the determinant threshold gives the fixed exponent gain.

The construction first produces certain cardinalities associated with growing primes. Bounds on the spacing of those sizes then permit passage to every sufficiently large nnn: retain any nnn points from a suitably sized configuration. Deleting points cannot introduce a smaller triangle.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns ordinary Euclidean triangle area in the unit square. Changing the region by a fixed scaling changes areas by a constant factor, but higher-dimensional simplex questions are not covered by its statement.

All triples must satisfy the bound, including nearly collinear ones. The result is stronger than a statement about average area or about most triples. At the same time, it says nothing about maximizing pairwise distances or controlling the shape of each triangle.

The exponent is fixed but extremely small, and the constants and size threshold are not optimized. The paper’s random construction establishes existence; the stated theorem is not an efficient numerical recipe for optimal configurations at a requested modest size.

The principal remaining problem is the correct decay rate of Δ(n)\Delta(n)Δ(n). The claimed lower bound still lies far below the cited upper bounds. Improving either side, or simplifying the arithmetic mechanism enough to obtain a meaningful exponent, would provide further progress.

8. Sources and further reading

  • Roth, On a problem of Heilbronn, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 26 (1951), 198–204, for the early formulation and finite-field construction.
  • Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi, A lower bound for Heilbronn’s problem, for the logarithmic improvement that disproved the original conjecture.
  • Cohen, Pohoata, and Zakharov, A new upper bound for the Heilbronn triangle problem and Lower bounds for incidences, for the recent upper-bound developments.

M1 gives the determinant construction, the separate treatment of zero determinants, and the stated fixed power improvement.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A power improvement in the Heilbronn triangle lower bound (September 25, 2026).

Sources consulted on 11 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Milne’s rationality conjecture and geometry after reduction
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 001 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

A geometric object defined by polynomial equations can be studied over the complex numbers or reduced modulo a prime. These two settings have different tools. Complex geometry uses topology and differential forms; geometry in characteristic ppp uses arithmetic substitutes that retain information invisible to ordinary point counting.

Suppose both descriptions produce an intersection number. Must they produce the same rational number? For actual algebraic subvarieties, the geometry supplies a common answer. The difficulty is that topology predicts classes which are not already known to come from algebraic subvarieties, while reduction can create additional divisors that did not exist upstairs.

Family 001 concerns this gap for abelian varieties. Its manuscript, M1, claims Milne’s rationality conjecture: a rational Hodge class, after good reduction, has the same rational pairing with every complementary product of divisors in all the specified cohomology theories. A stronger consequence supplies an actual algebraic cycle on the reduction, using a separate theorem about complex multiplication. Keeping these two assertions distinct is essential to understanding the result.

2. Background and essential definitions

Abelian varieties and reduction

An abelian variety is a smooth projective algebraic variety with a commutative algebraic group law. An elliptic curve is the one-dimensional example. Over the complex numbers, an abelian variety of dimension ddd looks analytically like Cd/Λ\mathbb C^d/\LambdaCd/Λ, where Λ\LambdaΛ is a lattice of rank 2d2d2d, with an additional condition ensuring projectivity.

The coefficients of the variety here belong to Q‾\overline{\mathbb Q}Q​, the field of algebraic numbers. They can be placed in a number field. Choosing a prime above a rational prime ppp then permits reduction of an integral model. Good reduction means that the resulting special fiber is again a smooth abelian variety. Write the original variety as AAA and its reduction, over an algebraic closure of the field with ppp elements, as A0A_0A0​.

Good reduction preserves much structure, but it need not preserve the collection of available algebraic subvarieties. In particular, A0A_0A0​ may have divisors that do not lift to AAA. The question is therefore not settled simply by reducing intersections already performed in characteristic zero.

Cycles, Hodge classes, and realizations

An algebraic cycle of codimension rrr is a finite formal combination of subvarieties of dimension d−rd-rd−r. Rational coefficients are allowed throughout this digest. A divisor has codimension one. Intersecting a codimension-rrr cycle with d−rd-rd−r divisors gives a zero-dimensional cycle, whose degree is a rational number.

Cohomology assigns a linear-algebraic class to a cycle. Over C\mathbb CC, the relevant group is H2r(A(C),Q)H^{2r}(A(\mathbb C),\mathbb Q)H2r(A(C),Q). Complex differential forms split cohomology into types (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), according to the numbers of holomorphic and antiholomorphic directions. A rational Hodge class in degree 2r2r2r is a rational cohomology class of type (r,r)(r,r)(r,r). Algebraic cycles give such classes. The rational Hodge conjecture asks for the converse.

A realization is one of the compatible cohomological descriptions used in different arithmetic settings. For each prime ℓ≠p\ell\ne pℓ=p, étale cohomology uses the field Qℓ\mathbb Q_\ellQℓ​ of ℓ\ellℓ-adic numbers. At ppp, crystalline cohomology plays the corresponding role. A ppp-adic completion of Q‾\overline{\mathbb Q}Q​, denoted Cw\mathbb C_wCw​, is used for the comparison in M1.

The notation Q(r)\mathbb Q(r)Q(r), and its arithmetic analogues, denotes a Tate twist. Here its role is normalization: it makes cycle classes and the trace on top-degree cohomology agree with geometric degree. Understanding the claim does not require constructing the twist explicitly.

For a divisor DDD, write c1(D)c_1(D)c1​(D) for its cohomology class. Multiplication of classes is the cup product, the cohomological counterpart of intersection. The trace Tr⁡\operatorname{Tr}Tr turns a top-degree class into its numerical intersection value. A Lefschetz class is a rational linear combination of products of divisor classes.

3. Development history and previous partial results

The broad background is the relationship between Hodge classes in characteristic zero and Tate classes in positive characteristic. A Tate class is, roughly, an appropriately normalized arithmetic cohomology class fixed by a power of Frobenius, the symmetry induced by raising coordinates to the field characteristic. These classes are candidates for algebraic cycle classes, just as Hodge classes are over the complex numbers.

Deligne’s theorem that Hodge classes on abelian varieties are absolute Hodge supplies strong compatibility between their realizations. Blasius’s work establishes the needed ppp-adic comparison. These results make it possible to transport the classes between theories, but compatibility alone does not say that pairing with a newly appearing divisor is rational. M1 reviews this distinction in its introduction; the original comparison result is Blasius’s A p-adic property of Hodge classes on abelian varieties.

Milne developed rationality formulations while studying reductions of Shimura varieties and the Langlands–Rapoport conjecture. His Rational Tate classes explains why one would like a common rational algebra inside the different Tate-class spaces. Such an algebra would support rational cohomological correspondences even before algebraic representatives were available.

One earlier positive case involves a CM abelian variety with simple ordinary reduction, together with its powers. In that setting the divisor classes on the reduction lift, removing the central obstruction. The general case must handle divisors that exist only after reduction.

A CM abelian variety has especially many commuting algebraic symmetries: for dimension ddd, its rational endomorphism algebra contains a commutative semisimple algebra of dimension 2d2d2d. “CM” abbreviates complex multiplication. Earlier work of André reduces Hodge-class questions to special determinant-type classes associated with such symmetries. Milne’s 2025 account develops the lifting strategy and explains conditional criteria along this route.

M1 claims to complete the rationality argument through carefully controlled auxiliary lifts and a common rational normalization. The stronger algebraicity consequence uses the separately stated CM Hodge theorem. Neither the historical comparison theorems nor rationality by itself should be conflated with that additional input.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

One rational number in every realization

Fix a prime ppp and a place www above it. Let A/Q‾A/\overline{\mathbb Q}A/Q​ have dimension ddd and good reduction A0A_0A0​, and let

γ∈H2r(A(C),Q(r)),0≤r≤d,\gamma\in H^{2r}(A(\mathbb C),\mathbb Q(r)),\qquad 0\leq r\leq d,γ∈H2r(A(C),Q(r)),0≤r≤d,

be a rational Hodge class. Write γ0,ℓ\gamma_{0,\ell}γ0,ℓ​ and γ0,p\gamma_{0,p}γ0,p​ for its specialized realizations. Given any Cartier divisors D1,…,Dd−rD_1,\ldots,D_{d-r}D1​,…,Dd−r​ on A0A_0A0​, M1’s Theorem 1.1 states that one number q∈Qq\in\mathbb Qq∈Q satisfies

Tr⁡ℓ ⁣(γ0,ℓ∏j=1d−rc1,ℓ(Dj))=q(ℓ≠p),\operatorname{Tr}_{\ell}\!\left(\gamma_{0,\ell}\prod_{j=1}^{d-r}c_{1,\ell}(D_j)\right)=q\qquad(\ell\ne p),Trℓ​(γ0,ℓ​j=1∏d−r​c1,ℓ​(Dj​))=q(ℓ=p),

and

Tr⁡p ⁣(γ0,p∏j=1d−rc1,cris(Dj))=q.\operatorname{Tr}_{p}\!\left(\gamma_{0,p}\prod_{j=1}^{d-r}c_{1,\mathrm{cris}}(D_j)\right)=q.Trp​(γ0,p​j=1∏d−r​c1,cris​(Dj​))=q.

The first equalities take place in Qℓ\mathbb Q_\ellQℓ​; the crystalline equality is interpreted after extending coefficients to Cw\mathbb C_wCw​. They identify the images of the same rational number in these different fields. When r=dr=dr=d, the empty divisor product means one.

The theorem includes p=2p=2p=2, arbitrary dimension, and divisors acquired only on reduction. It compares realizations at the fixed reduction place. It does not say that reductions at different places produce the same number.

A common class, then an algebraic representative

Using Milne’s equivalence between CM rationality and a good theory of rational Tate classes, M1’s Corollary 6.3 places every specialized Hodge class in one fixed such rational theory. The cohomological class is unique within that theory and has all the required realizations.

Corollary 6.4 adds the CM Hodge theorem from family 032. With this input, it claims one rational algebraic cycle zγz_\gammazγ​ on A0A_0A0​ whose cycle class equals γ0,ℓ\gamma_{0,\ell}γ0,ℓ​ for every ℓ≠p\ell\ne pℓ=p, and equals γ0,p\gamma_{0,p}γ0,p​ in the crystalline comparison. Pairing with any complementary algebraic cycle then gives its rational intersection number.

The paper explicitly separates this consequence from Theorem 1.1: its rationality proof does not use the CM Hodge theorem.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. The result addresses a structural obstacle in moving between complex geometry and arithmetic geometry. It would supply a common rational meaning to pairings computed in coefficient fields that otherwise look unrelated, while accommodating geometric classes that appear only after reduction.

For a simple analogy, several measurement systems may each report a compatible value without demonstrating that the value comes from a single rational geometric quantity. Rationality identifies that shared quantity. The algebraicity consequence goes further by supplying a geometric representative whose intersection degree explains it.

The distinction has consequences for motives, which organize cohomological information and correspondences in a common framework. Rational Tate classes provide cohomological correspondences; actual algebraic cycles provide stronger geometric information. The rating reflects the breadth of this connection and the arbitrary-dimensional scope, while recognizing that the strongest cycle statement uses a separate major theorem.

6. The main idea

Transport to a more symmetric setting

The first step moves the specialized class to an auxiliary CM abelian variety. An isogeny is a surjective group homomorphism with finite kernel; a quasi-isogeny allows rational inverses to such maps. Working up to isogeny permits the paper to use rational homomorphisms between special fibers and powers of varieties.

The transport must carry the original rational class in every realization. A collection of locally proportional classes would not suffice, since the proportionality factors might differ between coefficient fields. M1 normalizes these factors by ratios of rational divisor intersections, claiming one common rational scalar.

The maps at this stage concern reductions. The construction does not require an isogeny between the original characteristic-zero variety and its CM auxiliary.

Reduce to determinant-type classes

The CM symmetries decompose the relevant linear spaces into eigenspaces. Special Weil classes are built from their top alternating forms, analogous to determinant forms. A balanced signature means that conjugate eigenspaces occur with matching Hodge multiplicities. M1 reduces the general class to rational combinations of pullbacks of these balanced classes.

For such a class, the key claim is a dichotomy. Either all its complementary pairings with divisor products vanish, or the specialized class itself is one rational polynomial in divisor classes across all realizations. The first case supplies the rational answer zero. The second reduces the desired numerical comparison to ordinary intersections of divisors.

Lift the extra divisor with the right structure

In the second case, a suitable endomorphism produces a divisor with a nondegenerate pairing on the relevant eigenspaces. The construction chooses a filtration, a nested sequence of linear subspaces recording Hodge-type information, compatible with the divisor, the symmetry action, and the polarization.

Arithmetic deformation results are then used to realize this prescribed filtration on a second auxiliary abelian variety over a local field. This second auxiliary need not have complex multiplication and serves a different purpose from the first. Keeping its divisor and selected algebraic maps liftable is the point of the construction.

After passing to a complex realization of this lift, coefficient extraction in polynomial identities expresses the determinant-type class as a rational combination of divisor products. That rational identity specializes in every cohomology theory, and pullback returns it to the original reduction.

For the additional algebraicity statement, the CM Hodge theorem supplies an algebraic representative upstairs on the CM auxiliary. Specialization and rational pullback then give one representative on A0A_0A0​. This explains precisely where the extra theorem enters.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem concerns abelian varieties over algebraic numbers with good reduction at a fixed place. It does not cover arbitrary varieties or bad reduction. Rational coefficients are essential; an integral cycle statement with controlled denominators is stronger than what is asserted here.

The rationality conclusion tests complementary products of divisors. Pairing with arbitrary complementary algebraic cycles is part of the stronger algebraicity consequence and uses its additional CM input.

The resulting cycle lies on the special fiber. M1 does not claim that it lifts to a cycle on the original variety, or that it proves the Hodge conjecture for arbitrary abelian varieties in characteristic zero. Nor is the representing algebraic cycle asserted to be unique modulo rational equivalence: uniqueness of its class in a fixed rational cohomological theory is a different assertion.

These boundaries leave natural further questions about integral refinements, behavior under bad reduction, and lifting algebraic representatives back to characteristic zero. They also indicate why a common intersection value, a common cohomology class, and a common algebraic cycle are three distinct levels of information.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 gives the rationality statement; Corollaries 6.3 and 6.4 distinguish rational Tate classes from algebraic specialization. Its introduction describes the history and the two different auxiliary lifts.

Milne’s Rational Tate classes and Abelian motives and Shimura varieties in nonzero characteristic supply the motivating framework. His notes on abelian varieties offer background on the geometric objects, divisors, and isogenies used here.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Milne’s rationality conjecture for abelian varieties (October 7, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The full BSD formula from a small Selmer group
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 002 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

An elliptic curve can have infinitely many rational points even though its equation is very simple. The curve y2=x3+ax+by^2=x^3+ax+by2=x3+ax+b, when nonsingular and completed by its point at infinity, carries a group law. A basic arithmetic question asks how many independent rational points are needed to generate all the others, apart from a finite torsion subgroup.

The Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, usually abbreviated BSD, predicts that this arithmetic information is encoded in an analytic function built from counting points modulo primes. It predicts both an order of vanishing and an exact leading coefficient. Knowing how many times a function vanishes does not determine the first nonzero coefficient, just as knowing that a polynomial has a double root does not determine its quadratic term.

Family 002 contains three manuscripts claiming the full formula when a prime-power Selmer group has corank zero or one. M2 supplies the unrestricted converse from this arithmetic condition to analytic rank and finiteness. M3 treats the exact power of two in the coefficient formula. M1 adds the odd-prime comparisons and assembles the exact equality.

The condition is on a Selmer group, not simply the number of independent rational points already found on the curve.

2. Background and essential definitions

Three measures of rank

For an elliptic curve E/QE/\mathbb QE/Q, the Mordell–Weil theorem gives

E(Q)≅Zr⊕T,E(\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus T,E(Q)≅Zr⊕T,

where TTT is finite. The integer rrr is the Mordell–Weil rank. Rank zero means only finitely many rational points; positive rank means infinitely many.

At a prime ℓ\ellℓ of good reduction, let NℓN_\ellNℓ​ count the points of the reduced curve, including its point at infinity, and set aℓ=ℓ+1−Nℓa_\ell=\ell+1-N_\ellaℓ​=ℓ+1−Nℓ​. These counts contribute factors

(1−aℓℓ−s+ℓ1−2s)−1\left(1-a_\ell\ell^{-s}+\ell^{1-2s}\right)^{-1}(1−aℓ​ℓ−s+ℓ1−2s)−1

to the Hasse–Weil function L(E,s)L(E,s)L(E,s). There are specified factors at bad primes as well. Modularity gives analytic continuation and a functional equation with center s=1s=1s=1. The analytic rank is the order of vanishing there, written ord⁡s=1L(E,s)\operatorname{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)ords=1​L(E,s).

A Selmer group packages arithmetic compatibility conditions over Q\mathbb QQ, the real numbers, and all prime-adic completions. For a prime ppp, the full ppp-power Selmer group uses all powers pnp^npn, with the usual local conditions everywhere. It is larger than the information supplied by rational points alone.

The discrepancy is measured by the Tate–Shafarevich group, written Sha⁡(E/Q)\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)Sha(E/Q). Its elements describe principal homogeneous spaces for EEE: curves with an EEE-action which look like EEE after choosing a point. The classes in Sha have points over every completion but may have no rational point. Thus they record a failure of passing from local solvability to global solvability.

The standard exact sequence is

0⟶E(Q)⊗(Qp/Zp)⟶Sel⁡p∞(E/Q)⟶Sha⁡(E/Q)[p∞]⟶0.0\longrightarrow E(\mathbb Q)\otimes(\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_p)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sel}_{p^\infty}(E/\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)[p^\infty]\longrightarrow0.0⟶E(Q)⊗(Qp​/Zp​)⟶Selp∞​(E/Q)⟶Sha(E/Q)[p∞]⟶0.

Here [p∞][p^\infty][p∞] selects elements killed by some power of ppp. The corank sp(E)s_p(E)sp​(E) counts the copies of the divisible group Qp/Zp\mathbb Q_p/\mathbb Z_pQp​/Zp​ in the Selmer group, ignoring finite parts. It counts the rational-point rank and potentially an additional divisible contribution from Sha. If Sha is finite, then sp(E)=rs_p(E)=rsp​(E)=r. Assuming r≤1r\leq1r≤1 alone does not establish the Selmer condition.

The factors in the leading coefficient

Write ΩE\Omega_EΩE​ for the integral of the absolute value of a minimal Néron differential over all real components of E(R)E(\mathbb R)E(R). A Néron differential is the invariant differential normalized by a minimal integral model. The finite Tamagawa number cℓc_\ellcℓ​ is the index of the subgroup reducing to the identity component inside E(Qℓ)E(\mathbb Q_\ell)E(Qℓ​); it is one at good primes.

The regulator Reg⁡E\operatorname{Reg}_ERegE​ measures the volume of the full free rational-point lattice using the canonical height pairing. To fix the convention used in these manuscripts, let hx(P)=log⁡max⁡(∣u∣,∣v∣)h_x(P)=\log\max(|u|,|v|)hx​(P)=logmax(∣u∣,∣v∣) when x(P)=u/vx(P)=u/vx(P)=u/v in lowest terms, and put

H(P)=lim⁡n→∞4−nhx([2n]P),B(P,Q)=H(P+Q)−H(P)−H(Q)2.H(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}4^{-n}h_x([2^n]P),\qquadB(P,Q)=\frac{H(P+Q)-H(P)-H(Q)}2.H(P)=n→∞lim​4−nhx​([2n]P),B(P,Q)=2H(P+Q)−H(P)−H(Q)​.

The regulator is the determinant of BBB on a basis of E(Q)/TE(\mathbb Q)/TE(Q)/T, and equals one in rank zero. A subgroup of index mmm has regulator m2Reg⁡Em^2\operatorname{Reg}_Em2RegE​. This distinction matters when a construction produces some independent points without proving that they form a full basis.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer formulated their conjectures in the 1960s from computations relating rational points to point counts over finite fields. Their Notes on elliptic curves II is a primary source for this development. Tate placed the proposed rank and leading-term identities in a wider arithmetic framework, while Cassels explained how the combined expression behaves under isogeny.

The modularity work of Wiles, Taylor–Wiles, and Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor established the analytic setting for all elliptic curves over Q\mathbb QQ. The Gross–Zagier height formula relates derivatives of suitable L-functions to heights of Heegner points. Kolyvagin’s Euler systems then yield equality of analytic and arithmetic ranks, and finiteness of Sha, when analytic rank is zero or one.

Those results run from analytic information to arithmetic conclusions. A Selmer converse reverses the direction: small arithmetic Selmer corank must force a nonzero central value or derivative. That reversal is a separate problem, particularly when the curve has difficult reduction or a reducible representation on its torsion points.

Iwasawa theory, which studies arithmetic across towers of number fields, supplied increasingly strong converse and coefficient results. Kato’s zeta elements provide one direction of comparison; Skinner–Urban, Wei Zhang, and Jetchev–Skinner–Wan obtained major low-rank results under their respective local and residual hypotheses. Later work treated additional ordinary, supersingular, Eisenstein, and multiplicative cases. These labels distinguish how the curve and its torsion behave at the chosen prime; the manuscript’s historical sections explain the precise earlier restrictions.

Complex multiplication, meaning extra endomorphisms of the elliptic curve, provides another substantial theory. Burungale–Flach establish full rank-zero BSD for their class of CM curves, with consequences over Q\mathbb QQ. Exact two-primary formulas were also known in special CM and quadratic-twist settings. The family claims to remove the remaining curve and prime restrictions under the stated low-Selmer-corank hypothesis, while retaining every numerical factor in BSD.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

The complete formula

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states that, for every elliptic curve E/QE/\mathbb QE/Q, if some prime qqq satisfies sq(E)∈{0,1}s_q(E)\in\{0,1\}sq​(E)∈{0,1}, then

r=rank⁡E(Q)=ord⁡s=1L(E,s)=sq(E),#Sha⁡(E/Q)<∞,r=\operatorname{rank}E(\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)=s_q(E),\qquad \#\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)<\infty,r=rankE(Q)=ords=1​L(E,s)=sq​(E),#Sha(E/Q)<∞,

and

L(r)(E,1)r!=ΩEReg⁡E #Sha⁡(E/Q)∏ℓ finitecℓ(#T)2.\frac{L^{(r)}(E,1)}{r!}=\frac{\Omega_E\operatorname{Reg}_E\,\#\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)\prod_{\ell\text{ finite}}c_\ell}{(\#T)^2}.r!L(r)(E,1)​=(#T)2ΩE​RegE​#Sha(E/Q)∏ℓ finite​cℓ​​.

Here L(r)L^{(r)}L(r) is the rrr-th derivative, so the left side is the first nonzero Taylor coefficient. The uncompleted L-function includes all finite Euler factors. The total real period already includes every real component; no extra real-component factor is inserted.

No additional assumption is imposed on reduction, rational torsion, rational isogenies, complex multiplication, or residual Galois representations. The prime qqq supplying the input condition need not equal a prime whose valuation is being checked in the output formula.

The roles of the three manuscripts

ManuscriptPrincipal contribution within the family
M1The exact full leading-term formula, completing the odd-prime comparisons and assembling all primes.
M2The low-corank Selmer converse at every prime, with finiteness of the entire Sha group.
M3The exact two-primary leading-term formula, with no restriction at two.

To state M3 precisely, define the normalized positive quantity

QE=L(r)(E,1)(#T)2r! ΩEReg⁡E∏ℓcℓ.Q_E=\frac{L^{(r)}(E,1)(\#T)^2}{r!\,\Omega_E\operatorname{Reg}_E\prod_\ell c_\ell}.QE​=r!ΩE​RegE​∏ℓ​cℓ​L(r)(E,1)(#T)2​.

It claims that s2(E)≤1s_2(E)\leq1s2​(E)≤1 gives the rank and finiteness conclusions, QE∈Q>0Q_E\in\mathbb Q_{>0}QE​∈Q>0​, and

v2(QE)=v2 ⁣(#Sha⁡(E/Q)).v_2(Q_E)=v_2\!\left(\#\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)\right).v2​(QE​)=v2​(#Sha(E/Q)).

The valuation vpv_pvp​ counts the exponent of ppp in a nonzero rational number. Matching the valuation at two is one part of the full equality, not the whole equality.

M2 also derives the positive prime cube-sum cases ℓ≡4,7,8(mod9)\ell\equiv4,7,8\pmod9ℓ≡4,7,8(mod9): such primes are sums of two rational cubes, and the corresponding cubic has rank one and finite Sha. The paper acknowledges earlier direct treatments of these cases; this application illustrates its unrestricted converse at three.

Combining the family with the twist-density results discussed in family 006 gives the formula for a density-one set of signed squarefree twists of each fixed curve. That additional conclusion uses the distribution input.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 5/5, provisional. BSD connects rational solutions, complex analysis, local arithmetic, and the failure of the local-to-global principle. An exact leading-term formula under an unrestricted low-Selmer-corank criterion would be a major advance on a central arithmetic problem.

The word “exact” has substantial content. Equality up to an unknown power of two, or up to factors at bad primes, leaves part of the conjecture unresolved. Likewise, proving that Sha is finite does not compute its order. The family claims to retain precisely the finite information that distinguishes these assertions.

Its reach is large but qualified: the initial Selmer condition remains essential. The density-one twist consequence means that exceptions have asymptotic proportion zero in the specified family; it does not eliminate every exceptional twist or prove BSD for arbitrary rank.

6. The main idea

Force analytic nonvanishing from arithmetic smallness

For the converse, M2 reduces an odd-prime problem to showing that a certain Heegner point is not torsion. Heegner points arise from elliptic curves with complex multiplication mapped into the curve under study. The appropriate height formula then connects this point to an L-value or derivative.

Assuming the point is torsion, the paper obtains two incompatible measurements of the same auxiliary extension space. The low Selmer corank bounds how many Galois extensions satisfying specified local conditions can exist. A theta-series construction, transferred through congruences of automorphic forms, produces more such extensions than that bound permits.

A theta series is a structured generating function built from arithmetic data. Here the construction retains a truncated deformation parameter, so it records successive layers of extension information rather than only isolated character values. The stated contradiction forces the Heegner point to be non-torsion. The argument uses the separate two-converse and twist-density inputs identified in the manuscript.

Measure the error prime by prime

Once rank and finiteness are available, define

Xp(E)=vp(QE)−vp ⁣(#Sha⁡(E/Q)).X_p(E)=v_p(Q_E)-v_p\!\left(\#\operatorname{Sha}(E/\mathbb Q)\right).Xp​(E)=vp​(QE​)−vp​(#Sha(E/Q)).

For odd ppp, M1 proves a nonnegative discrepancy for non-CM curves of analytic rank at most one. A second comparison pairs EEE with a suitable quadratic twist EDE^DED of complementary analytic rank and gives

Xp(E)+Xp(ED)=0.X_p(E)+X_p(E^D)=0.Xp​(E)+Xp​(ED)=0.

Two nonnegative numbers with sum zero must both vanish. CM curves are handled using the appropriate CM rank-zero input and a paired comparison. The same numerical idea appears in M3’s treatment at two, with additional machinery suited to that prime.

The difficult step is obtaining exact comparisons. The papers encode arithmetic in integral lattices and determinant lines, which track finite indices as well as vector-space dimensions. Their quotients must be units, elements with no unwanted divisibility, rather than merely integral elements. Theta comparisons and auxiliary deformation directions exclude possible extra factors. M3 treats the distinct torsion-representation cases and the real place explicitly.

Finally, M3 supplies positivity, rationality, and the correct valuation at two; M1 supplies every odd valuation. The positive rational number QE/#Sha⁡Q_E/\#\operatorname{Sha}QE​/#Sha then has exponent zero at every prime. Its prime factorization is empty, so it equals one. That last elementary observation turns the local comparisons into the full real-valued BSD formula.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

These statements concern elliptic curves over Q\mathbb QQ. They do not assert unrestricted BSD over all number fields or in higher rank. In particular, a known Mordell–Weil rank of zero or one is not substituted for the full Selmer-corank assumption.

The precise normalizations of the period, height pairing, regulator, Euler factors, and local conditions are part of the result. Changing a height by a factor of two or using a sublattice of rational points changes the numerical formula unless the corresponding correction is made.

The family does not supply an efficient general algorithm to find a basis of rational points or compute Sha. Nor does its twist-density consequence imply a bound on every exceptional curve. Higher-corank cases and broader base fields remain outside the stated coverage.

8. Sources and further reading

The three Theorems 1.1 contain the principal assertions. M1’s introductory discrepancy calculation explains the final assembly; M2’s introduction describes the extension-length contradiction; M3’s first section distinguishes integrality from the stronger unit comparison needed at two.

The historical sources linked above explain the development from point-counting experiments to Heegner points and Iwasawa theory. Family 006 treats the complementary distribution question: how often the relevant small coranks occur among quadratic twists.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Exact Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer Formula from Low Selmer Corank (October 7, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Selmer converse for elliptic curves at every prime (October 7, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The two-primary Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer formula in Selmer corank at most one (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: A fixed zero-free region for zeta and Dirichlet L-functions
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 003 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Prime numbers become less frequent as numbers grow, but their local distribution is irregular. One way to study that irregularity is to replace the primes by a complex function whose zeros encode fluctuations in prime counts. The Riemann hypothesis predicts an extraordinarily precise location for those zeros. A weaker question has also resisted solution: can they at least be kept a fixed positive distance away from the vertical line with real part one?

Family 003 claims an affirmative answer. Its strongest manuscript, M1, states that the Riemann zeta function and every Dirichlet L-function have no zeros in

Re⁡s>78.\operatorname{Re}s>\frac78.Res>87​.

The same assertion covers finite-order Hecke L-functions over one particular quadratic number field. M2 supplies a separate presentation of a weaker fixed boundary, 11/1211/1211/12, and several arithmetic consequences. M3 addresses the exceptional real zeros called Landau–Siegel zeros through a different, algebraic argument.

The distinction between these claims and the Riemann hypothesis is substantial. Moving the forbidden boundary from one to seven-eighths would be a major advance, but the conjectured boundary is one-half. This digest reports the manuscripts’ claims; it does not establish their correctness.

2. Background and essential definitions

For a complex number s=σ+its=\sigma+its=σ+it, the number σ\sigmaσ is its real part and ttt its height. Initially, for σ>1\sigma>1σ>1, the zeta function is defined by

ζ(s)=∑n=1∞1ns=∏p prime(1−p−s)−1.\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^s} =\prod_{p\text{ prime}}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}.ζ(s)=n=1∑∞​ns1​=p prime∏​(1−p−s)−1.

The product explains why this analytic function knows about primes. Analytic continuation extends it beyond the region where this series converges, with a pole at s=1s=1s=1. A pole is a singularity, not a zero. Its nontrivial zeros lie in the critical strip 0<σ<10<\sigma<10<σ<1; the Riemann hypothesis places them on σ=1/2\sigma=1/2σ=1/2.

A Dirichlet character χ\chiχ modulo a positive integer qqq is a periodic, multiplicative function of integers. It is zero on integers sharing a factor with qqq, and takes root-of-unity values on the others. Characters separate residue classes in sums, allowing one to count primes such as those congruent to one or three modulo four. Their functions are

L(s,χ)=∑n=1∞χ(n)ns=∏p(1−χ(p)p−s)−1(σ>1).L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\chi(n)}{n^s} =\prod_p(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1} \qquad(\sigma>1).L(s,χ)=n=1∑∞​nsχ(n)​=p∏​(1−χ(p)p−s)−1(σ>1).

The conductor is the smallest modulus from which the character is induced. A character is primitive if its displayed modulus is that conductor. Real nonprincipal characters take values 0,1,−10,1,-10,1,−1; a real zero very close to one is the potential exceptional phenomenon in classical zero-free theorems.

Hecke characters generalize this language from integers to ideals of a number field. Here the field is

K=Q(−3),OK=Z[ω],ω=e2πi/3.K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3}),\qquad\mathcal O_K=\mathbb Z[\omega],\qquad\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}.K=Q(−3​),OK​=Z[ω],ω=e2πi/3.

An ideal is an additive subgroup of this ring closed under multiplication by every ring element. Its norm NaN\mathfrak aNa is the number of elements in the finite quotient OK/a\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak aOK​/a. A finite-order Hecke character η\etaη assigns roots of unity to ideals, subject to multiplicativity and congruence conditions, and is extended by zero at ideals not coprime to its conductor. Its L-series replaces nnn by NaN\mathfrak aNa.

“Fixed zero-free half-plane” means a single boundary works for every height and every character under consideration. Constants in intermediate estimates may depend on a character without changing that common boundary.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Riemann’s 1859 memoir connected prime counting with the zeros of ζ\zetaζ. In 1896, Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin proved that no zero lies on σ=1\sigma=1σ=1, leading to the prime number theorem: the number of primes up to xxx is asymptotic to x/log⁡xx/\log xx/logx. Hadamard’s original paper makes that connection explicit.

Later work pushed the zero-free region slightly left of one. A classical Dirichlet L-function theorem has a boundary of the approximate shape

σ>1−clog⁡(q(∣t∣+3)),\sigma>1-\frac{c}{\log(q(|t|+3))},σ>1−log(q(∣t∣+3))c​,

with an absolute positive constant ccc, apart from a possible simple real zero for a real character. The permitted width shrinks as conductor or height grows. Vinogradov–Korobov estimates improve the height dependence for zeta; Ford’s account and explicit estimates develop that direction. Their boundary still approaches one at large height. A fixed strip is a qualitatively different conclusion.

The possible real exception has its own history. Siegel’s 1935 theorem gives a strong lower bound for L(1,χ)L(1,\chi)L(1,χ), but its constant is ineffective: the argument does not provide a computable value. Page’s theorem severely limits how many exceptional characters can occur in a conductor range. Deuring–Heilbronn repulsion says that an exceptional zero pushes other zeros away. These results constrain the obstruction without uniformly eliminating it. M3 situates its claim in this development.

The analytic manuscripts draw on another line: Kubota’s automorphic functions, Patterson’s cubic theta series, and large-sieve inequalities controlling averages of character sums. Dunn and Radziwiłł’s work on cubic Gauss sums supplies unconditional theta-expansion formulas used in this framework. Their conditional prime asymptotic is not an input to M1. The separate unconditional Patterson claim in family 023 is also not an input to M1.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Three different statements

M1, Theorem 1.1, asserts that every finite-order Hecke L-function over K=Q(−3)K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})K=Q(−3​), and every Dirichlet L-function, is zero-free for σ>7/8\sigma>7/8σ>7/8. Principal characters may have a pole at one. The boundary line itself is excluded from the assertion.

M2, Theorem 1.1, states the same families are zero-free for σ>11/12\sigma>11/12σ>11/12. Since 7/8<11/127/8<11/127/8<11/12, M1 gives the stronger exclusion. M2 isolates a shorter argument and spells out consequences; these are companion treatments within one family, not three equivalent formulations of RH.

M3 states that there is an absolute c>0c>0c>0 such that every real zero β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1)β∈(0,1) of a primitive nonprincipal real Dirichlet character of conductor q≥3q\ge3q≥3 satisfies

(1−β)log⁡q≥c.(1-\beta)\log q\ge c.(1−β)logq≥c.

This is a uniform logarithmic gap for real zeros. It addresses the exceptional-zero problem but does not itself supply a fixed half-plane for all complex zeros. The stronger conclusions of M1 and M2 overlap its real-zero consequence.

Consequences stated in M2

Let π(x;q,a)\pi(x;q,a)π(x;q,a) count primes at most xxx congruent to aaa modulo qqq, and let φ(q)\varphi(q)φ(q) count the residue classes coprime to qqq. M2 gives

sup⁡1≤q≤x(a,q)=1∣π(x;q,a)−1φ(q)∫2xdtlog⁡t∣≪x11/12log⁡x.\sup_{\substack{1\le q\le x\\(a,q)=1}}\left|\pi(x;q,a)-\frac1{\varphi(q)}\int_2^x\frac{dt}{\log t}\right|\ll x^{11/12}\log x.1≤q≤x(a,q)=1​sup​​π(x;q,a)−φ(q)1​∫2x​logtdt​​≪x11/12logx.

Here ≪\ll≪ means bounded by an absolute constant times the expression on the right; M2 states that constant is effective. For very large qqq, the error can exceed the main term. Uniformity alone does not make this a useful relative approximation in every progression.

M2 also claims a fixed-power-of-log⁡p\log plogp bound for the least quadratic nonresidue modulo an odd prime ppp: the smallest positive integer that is not a nonzero square modulo ppp. Through the Tonelli–Shanks procedure, this gives deterministic square-root extraction in time polynomial in the number of digits of ppp. Its consequence for Miller’s primality test supplies another deterministic implementation; polynomial-time primality testing itself was already known through AKS.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. A uniform fixed zero-free region would change the available unconditional tools across analytic number theory. It addresses a central longstanding obstruction and yields consequences for prime distributions, quadratic fields, and algorithms.

The gain is stronger than a better numerical constant in the classical shrinking region. For example, knowing that no zero lies farther right than seven-eighths controls contributions from zeros by a fixed power of the scale. Classical regions often give savings that diminish with height. That difference propagates into applications.

M3 is important for a complementary reason: it claims to eliminate an obstruction whose possible existence has forced many results to carry an exception or an ineffective constant. The score reflects these mathematical consequences if the claims hold, not an assessment of proof reliability.

6. The main idea

Turn a zero question into a cancellation question

The integer Möbius function μ(n)\mu(n)μ(n) is zero if a square of a prime divides nnn, and otherwise equals (−1)k(-1)^k(−1)k when nnn has kkk distinct prime factors. In the absolutely convergent region,

1ζ(s)=∑n=1∞μ(n)ns.\frac1{\zeta(s)}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu(n)}{n^s}.ζ(s)1​=n=1∑∞​nsμ(n)​.

Strong cancellation in sums of these signs can continue the reciprocal farther left. A zero of zeta would be a pole of that reciprocal, so analytic continuation with suitable bounds excludes zeros. The same principle works for character twists and the ideal Möbius function.

M2 studies smoothed sums

A1(D)=∑aμ(a)η(a)W(Na/D),A_1(D)=\sum_{\mathfrak a}\mu(\mathfrak a)\eta(\mathfrak a)W(N\mathfrak a/D),A1​(D)=a∑​μ(a)η(a)W(Na/D),

with the manuscript’s coprimality restrictions. The smooth function WWW selects ideals whose norms are comparable to DDD. A trivial estimate is roughly DDD; the target is D11/12+εD^{11/12+\varepsilon}D11/12+ε for every positive ε\varepsilonε.

Instead of estimating this one sum directly, M2 inserts sixth-power residue characters and studies a family Au(D)A_u(D)Au​(D). A mean-square bound says that these sums are small on average. Many indices uuu that are sixth powers reproduce the original sum up to controlled omissions. Consequently, an oversized original sum would force too many large members of the family.

Poisson summation, a form of Fourier duality, transforms the average. Finite Fourier transforms of residue characters produce Gauss sums. Arithmetic identities combine these with Möbius signs to produce cubic theta coefficients. Transformation laws of the theta function and recursive mean-square estimates then provide the asserted cancellation. Retaining full cube-divisor contributions is part of that argument, not a removable cosmetic detail.

How the stronger boundary is approached

M1 also compares two descriptions of completed cubic-theta sums: a reflected expression controlled by mean-square estimates, and a Poisson expression containing a reciprocal L-function. The first stage reaches 11/1211/1211/12. A second stage changes the weighting at selected primes and uses unequal averaging scales.

A hypothetical zero produces two large finite sums with the same character and height: one has Möbius coefficients, the other does not. Separate moment estimates bound how often both can be large. The manuscript combines these bounds, while treating principal terms and residues separately, to move the common boundary to 7/87/87/8. The simultaneous treatment of Hecke characters matters even for zeta, because transformations introduce additional twists.

The algebraic route in M3

M3 translates a hypothetical exceptional zero into an imbalance between primes on which a real character takes signs +1+1+1 and −1-1−1. It then constructs a nonzero interpolation determinant from algebraic numbers in a biquadratic field, a degree-four extension obtained by adjoining two square roots.

At primes of the plentiful sign, taking a ppp-th power modulo ppp acts like a particular field conjugation. Row operations therefore force high powers of many primes to divide the determinant’s norm, which is a nonzero integer. A carefully weighted selection of polynomial rows keeps its ordinary size small. The claimed contradiction is between excessive arithmetic divisibility and this size bound. This mechanism differs from the theta-function comparisons in M1 and M2.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The Riemann hypothesis and generalized Riemann hypotheses remain open in these manuscripts: neither boundary reaches one-half. No conclusion is asserted on the line σ=7/8\sigma=7/8σ=7/8 itself. The Hecke theorem is stated for finite-order characters of the specified imaginary quadratic field, not arbitrary automorphic L-functions over all number fields.

The three source statements should retain their different strengths. M3’s logarithmic real-zero exclusion is not a substitute for M1’s full fixed half-plane. M2’s algorithmic applications also do not make every algorithm previously conditional on GRH unconditional; each reduction has its own hypotheses.

Further questions include whether the analytic estimates can reach a smaller fixed boundary, whether related methods extend to other fields and higher-degree L-functions, and which applications can make efficient use of the explicit savings. These are directions suggested by the statements, not additional conclusions of this digest.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s introduction and proof overview explain the two-stage 11/1211/1211/12-to-7/87/87/8 strategy. M2’s Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2, and Section 2 provide the shorter claim, applications, and Möbius-sum outline. M3’s introduction describes the real-zero theorem and determinant mechanism.

The historical links in Section 3 lead to primary papers. For a systematic background reference, Iwaniec and Kowalski’s Analytic Number Theory develops characters, explicit formulas, and large sieves. The Möbius function is a useful optional entry point to the cancellation viewpoint.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis: A Zero-Free Half-Plane Re(s)>7/8 (30 September 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Uniform exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeros (October 1, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals: a claimed limit of algorithms
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 004 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Suppose a computer receives a polynomial with integer coefficients, such as

f(X,Y)=X2+Y2−3.f(X,Y)=X^2+Y^2-3.f(X,Y)=X2+Y2−3.

Can one algorithm always decide whether the equation f=0f=0f=0 has a solution whose coordinates are rational numbers? The algorithm may take a long time, but it must eventually return the correct yes or no for every input. Both the polynomial and its number of variables are allowed to vary.

This is Hilbert’s tenth problem over Q\mathbb QQ. Family 004’s main manuscript, M1, claims that no such algorithm exists. It further places the problem at the same level of Turing unsolvability as the halting problem and retains that conclusion for polynomials of degree at most four.

A companion, M2, supplies an elliptic-curve theorem used in the construction. The connection is unexpected: information about rational points and L-functions becomes part of an argument about the limits of computation. The route does not produce a single polynomial definition of the integers inside the rationals, a distinction essential to understanding the claim.

2. Background and essential definitions

A polynomial is a finite sum of monomials with specified coefficients. A rational zero of f∈Z[X1,…,Xn]f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_n]f∈Z[X1​,…,Xn​] is a tuple (a1,…,an)∈Qn(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathbb Q^n(a1​,…,an​)∈Qn for which f(a1,…,an)=0f(a_1,\ldots,a_n)=0f(a1​,…,an​)=0. Rational and integer solvability differ: 2X−1=02X-1=02X−1=0 has a rational solution but no integer solution. Allowing fractions does not preserve an integer-solvability problem unchanged.

A decision algorithm must halt on both yes and no instances. Rational solvability is already computably enumerable: enumerate all rational tuples and test them exactly. If a solution exists, this search eventually finds it. If none exists, enumeration continues forever. The missing ingredient is a procedure that also settles every negative instance.

The halting problem asks whether a given program eventually stops on a given input. A Turing reduction to another problem is an algorithm allowed to ask an oracle for answers to that other problem, possibly several times and adaptively. Two problems have the same Turing degree if each can be solved with an oracle for the other. The degree of the halting problem is denoted 0′0'0′.

An existential polynomial condition asks whether additional rational witnesses exist satisfying specified polynomial equations. Saying that Z\mathbb ZZ is Diophantine in Q\mathbb QQ would mean that there is one fixed polynomial PPP such that

x∈Z⟺∃y1,…,ym∈Q:P(x,y1,…,ym)=0.x\in\mathbb Z\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y_1,\ldots,y_m\in\mathbb Q:P(x,y_1,\ldots,y_m)=0.x∈Z⟺∃y1​,…,ym​∈Q:P(x,y1​,…,ym​)=0.

That would provide a direct translation of integer problems. A Turing reduction need not have this form.

The arithmetic ingredients include elliptic curves: smooth cubic curves with a distinguished identity point and an addition law on their rational points. If an infinite-order point PPP generates a rank-one subgroup, its multiples nPnPnP can encode integers nnn. The challenge is to recover multiplication of those indices using rational polynomial conditions; the curve’s addition law directly provides only addition.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Hilbert’s original 1900 problem concerned integer solutions. Davis, Putnam, and Robinson connected equations to computably enumerable sets, and Matiyasevich’s 1970 work completed the polynomial representation theorem. Every computably enumerable relation on positive integers can be encoded by polynomial solvability. As a consequence, integer solvability cannot be decided by an algorithm. The 1961 Davis–Putnam–Robinson paper is a principal milestone in that development.

Transferring this conclusion to rational solutions has been much harder. Julia Robinson’s 1949 work defined integers within rational arithmetic using both existential and universal quantifiers. Later refinements culminated in Koenigsmann’s universal definition. Universal quantifiers mean “for every rational number”; polynomial solvability permits only existential witnesses. The quantifier difference prevents the immediate transfer one might expect.

Another approach enlarges the integers by allowing denominators from a chosen set of primes SSS. The resulting ring is Z[S−1]\mathbb Z[S^{-1}]Z[S−1]. Poonen’s 2003 construction proves undecidability for certain such rings even when the permitted primes have density one. These remain proper subrings of Q\mathbb QQ: a sparse excluded set can still carry crucial information.

More recently, Koymans and Pagano proved undecidability for every infinite ring finitely generated over Z\mathbb ZZ. Their work uses elliptic curves and additive combinatorics. The rational field is not finitely generated as a Z\mathbb ZZ-algebra: finitely many generators cannot introduce denominators involving every prime. Thus this major result does not itself settle the rational problem.

Geometry also cautions against identifying undecidability with an existential definition of the integers. Mazur’s conjecture about closures of rational points would obstruct such a definition and even certain Diophantine models of integer arithmetic. M1 pursues a finite-test oracle reduction instead. Its conclusion is designed to address the decision problem without asserting one of these stronger definability statements.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

Rational solvability and its degree

M1, Theorem 1.1, states that no algorithm decides, for an arbitrary integer-coefficient polynomial in an arbitrary finite number of variables, whether it has a rational zero.

Corollary 7.1 strengthens the computational description: the set of solvable inputs has Turing degree 0′0'0′. The same degree is asserted for each of these restricted input forms:

  • a polynomial of total degree at most four;
  • a supplied finite nonempty list of polynomials q1,…,qsq_1,\ldots,q_sq1​,…,qs​, each of degree at most two, asking whether ∑i=1sqi2\sum_{i=1}^s q_i^2∑i=1s​qi2​ has a rational zero.

There is no bound on the number of variables, the number of summands, or the sizes of the integer coefficients. The list is part of the second problem’s input; one need not recognize whether an arbitrary polynomial admits such a presentation.
