Those degree-ppp subfields are still larger than projective lines in general. An intersection calculation recovers lines after a power correction. Uniqueness propagates the correction to one global scalar. A projective lifting theorem then provides a semilinear map, meaning an additive map linear up to a field automorphism of the scalars. The multiplicative structure turns its normalized lift into a field isomorphism.

Finally,

⋂m≥1Kpm=k\bigcap_{m\ge1}K^{p^m}=km≥1⋂​Kpm=k

recovers the original algebraically closed constants. This explains why their identification need not be supplied separately.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The dimension-at-least-two and algebraically closed constant-field hypotheses are part of all three statements. The manuscripts do not claim these results unchanged for arbitrary fields, curve function fields, or finite constant fields.

The full bilinear Milnor product or the full specified commutator datum is required. Two abstract vector spaces without that relationship would not be the input described here. The pro-ℓ\ellℓ theorem also includes continuity and its ℓ\ellℓ-adic scalar ambiguity.

Perfect-closure recovery in M1 and M3 is deliberately weaker than recovering a particular inseparable presentation of a field in positive characteristic. M2 avoids that ambiguity because its coefficient prime equals the characteristic, using different information and a different method.

These are structural reconstruction theorems, not practical complexity bounds for an algorithm operating on a finite encoding of the invariants. Extensions to other base fields, lower dimension, or still smaller input data remain separate questions.

8. Sources and further reading

Each manuscript’s Theorem 1.1 states its own isomorphism theorem and ambiguity. M1’s introduction explains the finite-coefficient pencil and incidence arguments; M2’s Sections 2–5 develop derivations, projective-line recovery, and field lifting; M3 identifies the geometric data it reconstructs before applying Pop’s theorem.

The primary works linked in Section 3 trace the Galois and Milnor K-theoretic approaches. Optional background entries on function fields, valuations, and perfect fields may help with terminology; the differing reconstruction conventions are stated above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Reconstruction of Function Fields from Mod-ℓ Milnor K-Theory (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Reconstruction from Milnor K-theory modulo the characteristic (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, The Bogomolov-Pop reconstruction theorem (September 23, 2026).

entry.title: Modularity at two: geometric representations and completed Hecke families
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 010 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Algebraic numbers have symmetries: an automorphism can permute roots of polynomial equations while preserving addition and multiplication. Modular forms, by contrast, are highly symmetric analytic functions. A major theme of modern number theory is that these two worlds encode the same information in different languages.

The Fontaine–Mazur conjecture predicts that suitably constrained representations of arithmetic symmetries come from geometry. In the odd, regular, two-dimensional setting over Q\mathbb QQ, this predicts a more specific source: classical modular forms. Family 010 claims the remaining unrestricted result at the prime two, including representations whose reduction modulo two is reducible or scalar.

The family also contains a broader occurrence theorem without the geometric local hypothesis, and a theorem describing the dimension of the completed Hecke algebra in which those representations occur. Occurrence in that large algebra is called pro-modularity. It does not by itself mean that a representation comes from one classical form. Understanding this distinction is the organizing theme of the three manuscripts.

2. Background and essential definitions

Arithmetic symmetries as matrices

The absolute Galois group

GQ=Gal⁡(Q‾/Q)G_{\mathbb Q}=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb Q}/\mathbb Q)GQ​=Gal(Q​/Q)

consists of automorphisms of the algebraic numbers that fix the rationals. A two-dimensional 2-adic representation is a continuous homomorphism

r:GQ⟶GL⁡2(E),r:G_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_2(E),r:GQ​⟶GL2​(E),

where EEE is a finite extension of the 2-adic number field Q2\mathbb Q_2Q2​. The 2-adic metric regards numbers as close when their difference is divisible by a high power of two. Continuity makes the matrix action compatible with this arithmetic topology.

The representation is absolutely irreducible if it has no invariant line even after extending its coefficient field. It is odd if complex conjugation ccc satisfies

det⁡r(c)=−1.\det r(c)=-1.detr(c)=−1.

Being unramified outside finitely many primes means that away from a finite exceptional set, inertia, the local subgroup measuring ramification, acts trivially. At those good primes ℓ\ellℓ, the action of a Frobenius element has a well-defined characteristic polynomial.

A stable integral lattice allows reduction of the matrices modulo the maximal ideal of the coefficient ring. This gives the residual representation. An irreducible characteristic-zero representation can have a reducible residual representation; a scalar residual representation has every matrix proportional to the identity. At residue characteristic two, several distinctions visible in characteristic zero collapse, making deformation arguments delicate.

Geometric local conditions and modular forms

The de Rham condition is a local condition at two from 2-adic Hodge theory. It requires a full period comparison with a filtered vector space, of the kind supplied by algebraic geometry. The integers recording the filtration are the Hodge–Tate weights. In dimension two, regular means these two weights are distinct. These hypotheses are stronger than continuity or finite ramification.

A modular form is a holomorphic function on the upper half-plane satisfying a prescribed transformation law under integer matrices and suitable conditions at the boundary. Its weight specifies a power in the transformation law, and its level specifies the congruence subgroup. A cusp form vanishes at the cusps. An eigenform is a simultaneous eigenvector for commuting arithmetic operators called Hecke operators.

Classical eigenforms have associated Galois representations whose Frobenius traces and determinants match Hecke eigenvalues. A Tate twist tensors a representation with an integer power of the cyclotomic character, which records the action on roots of unity; it shifts both Hodge–Tate weights together.

The completed Hecke algebra collects compatible congruences among forms of all weights. A point of this algebra is a compatible eigenvalue system, potentially a 2-adic limit rather than one classical form of fixed weight. Its spectrum is an algebraic parameter space. Krull dimension measures the maximum length of chains of irreducible algebraic subsets, not the vector-space dimension of a space of forms.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Wiles and Taylor–Wiles developed modularity lifting by comparing rings parametrizing Galois deformations with Hecke algebras parametrizing modular eigenvalues. A deformation is a representation lifting a fixed residual representation. This framework made the passage from a modular residual system to a specified characteristic-zero lift a central problem.

The proof of Serre’s conjecture supplied modularity for odd irreducible residual representations, including characteristic two. It did not automatically prove modularity of every lift. Reducible residual representations also require different sources of modular points. Skinner–Wiles developed ordinary-family methods in this setting, while Kisin and Emerton brought local deformation geometry and the 2-adic and more general p-adic Langlands framework into the picture.

Pan’s work treated residually reducible representations and, with earlier results, established the regular two-dimensional conjecture for primes at least five. Zhang’s work at three removed the remaining odd-prime configuration. M3 places its claim at the remaining prime two.

There had already been important dyadic results. Tung’s modularity lifting theorem removed a local restriction while retaining a globally nonsolvable residual-image hypothesis. Covering a scalar restriction at the local prime two is different from covering a globally scalar residual representation. M3 claims all global residual cases.

A second history concerns families. Hida’s ordinary families, the Coleman–Mazur eigencurve, and Gouvêa–Mazur’s infinite fern revealed how modular forms vary and how families meet. Emerton formulated a dimension conjecture for the full varying-weight Hecke algebra and established the lower bound four. Newton and Thorne’s adjoint Selmer vanishing theorem supplies a key ingredient for the upper bound in M2. These precedents explain why the dimension result and modularity claims interact.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M3: classical Fontaine–Mazur modularity

M3, Theorem 1.1, assumes that a continuous irreducible two-dimensional representation over Q‾2\overline{\mathbb Q}_2Q​2​ is odd, unramified outside finitely many primes, and de Rham at two with distinct Hodge–Tate weights. It claims that the representation is a Tate twist of one associated with a classical cuspidal eigenform.

There is no hypothesis excluding scalar or reducible semisimple residual representations. This is the odd, regular, two-dimensional Fontaine–Mazur statement over Q\mathbb QQ at two, not the conjecture in arbitrary dimension or over arbitrary number fields.

M1: occurrence without a de Rham condition

M1, Theorem 1.1, starts with a continuous, absolutely irreducible

r:GQ⟶GL⁡2(E)r:G_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_2(E)r:GQ​⟶GL2​(E)

for finite E/Q2E/\mathbb Q_2E/Q2​, assuming oddness and finite ramification. It imposes no de Rham condition at two.

Its conclusion is a continuous homomorphism

λ:T2(N)⟶OE\lambda:\mathbb T_2(N)\longrightarrow\mathcal O_Eλ:T2​(N)⟶OE​

for some odd positive integer NNN, such that at every prime ℓ∤2N\ell\nmid2Nℓ∤2N,

λ(Tℓ)=tr⁡r(Frob⁡ℓ),λ(ℓSℓ)=det⁡r(Frob⁡ℓ).\lambda(T_\ell)=\operatorname{tr}r(\operatorname{Frob}_\ell),\qquad\lambda(\ell S_\ell)=\det r(\operatorname{Frob}_\ell).λ(Tℓ​)=trr(Frobℓ​),λ(ℓSℓ​)=detr(Frobℓ​).

Here OE\mathcal O_EOE​ is the integral coefficient ring and Tℓ,ℓSℓT_\ell,\ell S_\ellTℓ​,ℓSℓ​ are the Hecke operators normalized to give the characteristic polynomial

Z2−TℓZ+ℓSℓ.Z^2-T_\ell Z+\ell S_\ell.Z2−Tℓ​Z+ℓSℓ​.

The odd level NNN contains every odd ramified prime but may include auxiliary primes. The theorem does not promise occurrence at the smallest possible level or at a prescribed set of tame primes. All residual representations are allowed.

M2: dimension of the full algebra

For fixed odd NNN, let the finite-stage Hecke algebra act on all holomorphic modular forms of weights one through kkk and level Γ1(N)\Gamma_1(N)Γ1​(N), including Eisenstein forms. Using the operators away from 2N2N2N, complete at two and pass to the inverse limit over kkk. This is T2(N)\mathbb T_2(N)T2​(N).

M2, Theorem 1.1, claims that every irreducible component of its spectrum has Krull dimension four. This is the integral algebra over Z2\mathbb Z_2Z2​, with all weights and all residual systems retained. It is not a claim that each eigencurve or fixed-weight space has dimension four.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. The regular two-dimensional Fontaine–Mazur conjecture is a central bridge between abstract arithmetic representations and classical modular forms. Removing all residual restrictions at the smallest prime would complete that setting over Q\mathbb QQ, alongside the stated odd-prime results.

The companion occurrence theorem reaches representations beyond the geometric local class, placing them in a coherent modular parameter space. The dimension theorem describes the size of that full space and supports the mechanism by which modularity propagates through families.

The classical result also has downstream arithmetic uses. The height argument for Hilbert’s tenth problem in family 004 invokes its weight-two modularity consequence without a residual-image hypothesis. That application needs additional arithmetic and logic; it is not an immediate restatement of Fontaine–Mazur. The score concerns the combined significance of the claims if correct.

6. The main idea

Establish classicality through an auxiliary field

M3 first places the target in completed spaces of automorphic forms over a solvable totally real extension F/QF/\mathbb QF/Q, chosen to split completely at two. Totally real means every embedding of FFF into C\mathbb CC lands in R\mathbb RR; solvability allows descent through a sequence of manageable field extensions.

The construction works with whole deformation families. A trace records less information than an actual matrix representation, especially when the residual representation is scalar or reducible. M3 temporarily records invariant lines at selected dyadic places. Their positions impose additional constraints that make globally reducible loci small enough for a connectedness argument to pass modular occurrence from a known seed to the target family.

Occurrence is then upgraded to a classical vector. If the local representation at two is irreducible, local Langlands theory supplies locally algebraic vectors. In the reducible local case, M3 constructs a family carrying both trace and a chosen character. A dense set of specially selected weights becomes classical through Thorne’s ordinary modularity theorem. The manuscript transfers the character information to the target and uses a polynomial-orbit argument to produce a genuine locally algebraic vector there.

Only after obtaining a classical automorphic representation over FFF does the argument descend to Q\mathbb QQ. Finite-character discrepancies are corrected by twists along the solvable tower. This order matters: the manuscript does not assume a descent theorem for arbitrary pro-modular loci.

Determine the dimension at classical points

M2 combines a global lower bound with a local upper bound. It first treats the completed algebra as a finite product of complete Noetherian local rings, so its algebraic geometry is controlled by finitely generated local ideals. At two it uses determinant laws retaining both trace and determinant, avoiding formulas that would divide by two.

Classical points are dense, and the closure of Eisenstein points has dimension at most two. Since every component has dimension at least four by Emerton’s theorem, each component contains a classical cuspidal point of weight at least three.

At such a point, first-order Galois deformations are measured by adjoint cohomology. The adjoint representation describes the action on endomorphisms of the two-dimensional representation. Newton–Thorne’s vanishing theorem eliminates the global finite Selmer contribution, leaving at most three local tangent directions. A dimension comparison adds the one-dimensional arithmetic coefficient direction, giving the upper bound four and matching the lower bound. The argument allows a reducible residual system because the chosen classical point is in characteristic zero.

Spread Hecke occurrence to a nongeometric target

M1 places its unrestricted target in a sufficiently large fixed-determinant family and obtains potential Hecke occurrence after base change. It then constructs an auxiliary regular de Rham point on that family. M3 makes this auxiliary point classical; the original target need not become de Rham.

At that classical point, M2 and the adjoint Selmer bound force the local Hecke and deformation dimensions to agree. The manuscript uses this to show that the kernel cutting out Hecke occurrence vanishes on the relevant family. Specializing back gives the desired eigenvalue system for the original target.

Thus M1 uses M3 and M2. Its broader hypothesis is balanced by its weaker conclusion: a point in the completed algebra, with auxiliary tame primes permitted, rather than a classical eigenform.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M3 requires oddness, dimension two, finite ramification, and regular de Rham behavior at two. Equal Hodge–Tate weights, even representations, higher dimensions, and other base fields are outside its theorem.

M1 drops the de Rham hypothesis but concludes only pro-modularity. The level may grow by auxiliary odd primes. It does not settle the sharper formulation prescribing exactly which tame primes are allowed.

M2 concerns the particular full all-weight algebra, including Eisenstein systems, at odd level. Its dimension statement should not be transferred to a fixed determinant, fixed weight, ordinary locus, or local deformation ring without a separate argument.

The manuscripts distinguish residual restrictions from conditions on the characteristic-zero target throughout. A local theorem that allows scalar reduction is not by itself a global unrestricted modularity theorem. These distinctions also delimit future extensions of the claimed results.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states pro-modularity and its level convention; M2’s Theorem 1.1 gives the integral dimension; M3’s Theorem 1.1 gives classical regular modularity. Their introductory strategy sections explain how the family, local representation theory, and dimension arguments fit together.

The primary works linked in Sections 3 and 6 trace the odd-prime, dyadic, and adjoint-Selmer inputs. For optional introductory terminology, see Galois representations, modular forms, and p-adic numbers.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Unrestricted pro-modularity at the prime two (October 6, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Dimension of the Two-Adic Hecke Algebra at Odd Level (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Fontaine–Mazur modularity at the prime 2 (October 6, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Factoring one less than a prime: a Poisson–Dirichlet law
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 011 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Choose a large prime ppp, subtract one, and factor the result. How large should its largest prime factor be? How should the second-largest compare with it? Does requiring ppp to be prime change the large-factor pattern expected for an ordinary integer?

Ford, Konyagin, and Luca conjectured that the normalized large factors of p−1p-1p−1 follow the same Poisson–Dirichlet law that appears for random integers. Family 011 claims that law in all finite joint distributions. Its companion manuscripts address two related questions: whether Euler’s totient function can take one value almost as many times as its size allows, and whether infinitely many prime predecessors are squarefree with an even number of prime factors.

These questions share analytic machinery, but one conclusion does not automatically imply the others. Large-factor size distributions do not detect the parity of the total number of factors. Likewise, producing many smooth predecessors is weaker than determining their limiting proportion among all primes.

2. Background and essential definitions

For an integer n>1n>1n>1, let P+(n)P^+(n)P+(n) be its largest prime factor. The integer is yyy-smooth if P+(n)≤yP^+(n)\le yP+(n)≤y. Smoothness says every prime factor is small; it does not say there are few factors.

List the prime factors of p−1p-1p−1 in decreasing order, with multiplicity:

q1(p)≥q2(p)≥⋯ .q_1(p)\ge q_2(p)\ge\cdots.q1​(p)≥q2​(p)≥⋯.

After the list ends, put qj(p)=1q_j(p)=1qj​(p)=1. Define

Vj(p)=log⁡qj(p)log⁡(p−1).V_j(p)=\frac{\log q_j(p)}{\log(p-1)}.Vj​(p)=log(p−1)logqj​(p)​.

The entries are nonnegative and sum to one because the product of the prime factors is p−1p-1p−1. For p=13p=13p=13, the factors of twelve are 3,2,23,2,23,2,2; the two occurrences of two are both counted. The normalized logarithms describe how the total multiplicative size is divided among the factors.

The Poisson–Dirichlet distribution with parameter one, written PD(1)\mathrm{PD}(1)PD(1), can be constructed by randomly breaking a unit stick. Choose independent uniform random variables U1,U2,…U_1,U_2,\ldotsU1​,U2​,… on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), and set

B1=1−U1,Bj=(∏i<jUi)(1−Uj).B_1=1-U_1,\qquadB_j=\left(\prod_{i<j}U_i\right)(1-U_j).B1​=1−U1​,Bj​=(i<j∏​Ui​)(1−Uj​).

At each step, remove a uniform fraction of the remaining stick. Sort the fragments into decreasing order L1≥L2≥⋯L_1\ge L_2\ge\cdotsL1​≥L2​≥⋯. Their distribution is PD(1)\mathrm{PD}(1)PD(1). The pieces are dependent, since their total is one; this is not a model of independent factor sizes.

Euler’s totient φ(m)\varphi(m)φ(m) counts the integers from one to mmm that are coprime to mmm. Its formula is

φ(m)=m∏q∣m(1−1q).\varphi(m)=m\prod_{q\mid m}\left(1-\frac1q\right).φ(m)=mq∣m∏​(1−q1​).

The fiber size g(n)=#{m≥1:φ(m)=n}g(n)=\#\{m\ge1:\varphi(m)=n\}g(n)=#{m≥1:φ(m)=n} counts how often a particular value occurs. For example, φ(5)=φ(8)=φ(10)=φ(12)=4\varphi(5)=\varphi(8)=\varphi(10)=\varphi(12)=4φ(5)=φ(8)=φ(10)=φ(12)=4, so distinct inputs can share a totient.

Finally, Ω(n)\Omega(n)Ω(n) counts prime factors with multiplicity, while ω(n)\omega(n)ω(n) counts distinct prime factors. They agree for squarefree integers, which have no repeated prime factor. The Möbius function is zero on nonsquarefree integers and equals (−1)Ω(n)(-1)^{\Omega(n)}(−1)Ω(n) on squarefree ones.

3. Development history and previous partial results

For uniformly sampled ordinary integers, Dickman’s work and de Bruijn’s smooth-number estimates describe the largest prime factor. Billingsley obtained the joint limiting law of the ordered large factors. Donnelly and Grimmett developed a size-biased interpretation leading to the stick-breaking description. These establish the random-integer model motivating the prime-predecessor conjecture.

The restriction to p−1p-1p−1 introduces a primality constraint. Requiring a product ddd of selected factors to divide p−1p-1p−1 is equivalent to requiring p≡1(modd)p\equiv1\pmod dp≡1(modd). Thus factor statistics depend on how primes are distributed among arithmetic progressions, sometimes with very large moduli.

Ford, Konyagin, and Luca’s work on prime chains and Pratt trees formulated the full distribution conjecture. A prime chain links primes by divisibility of successive predecessors. The factorization law would describe the first generation of a recursive prime-factor tree, though independence assumptions for later generations are additional questions.

For smooth shifted primes, Baker and Harman obtained the fixed exponent 0.29610.29610.2961, together with a totient multiplicity exponent 0.70390.70390.7039. Lichtman’s work improved the smoothness threshold to every fixed exponent above approximately 0.2843110.2843110.284311, and obtained multiplicity exponent 0.71560.71560.7156. Such results produce many predecessors with all factors below a specified power, but do not reach every positive exponent or a full limiting law.

Bharadwaj and Rodgers established Poisson–Dirichlet laws for sufficiently well-distributed sequences. Applied to shifted primes, their full conclusion follows under the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture; unconditional distribution estimates yield factor statistics only in a restricted region. M2 claims to obtain the complete law unconditionally.

The totient question goes back to Erdős, with Pomerance developing the connection to smooth predecessors. The parity question faces a different classical obstacle: sieve information about divisibility can fail to distinguish even from odd numbers of prime factors. Bilinear cancellation, central to the asymptotic-sieve method of Friedlander and Iwaniec, provides a way beyond divisibility counts alone. The manuscripts develop graph estimates for that purpose.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M2: the full factor-size law

For every fixed positive integer kkk and bounded continuous function F:[0,1]k→RF:[0,1]^k\to\mathbb RF:[0,1]k→R, M2, Theorem 1.1, claims

lim⁡x→∞1π(x)−1∑3≤p≤xp primeF(V1(p),…,Vk(p))=EF(L1,…,Lk).\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac1{\pi(x)-1}\sum_{\substack{3\le p\le x\\p\text{ prime}}}F(V_1(p),\ldots,V_k(p))=\mathbb E F(L_1,\ldots,L_k).x→∞lim​π(x)−11​3≤p≤xp prime​∑​F(V1​(p),…,Vk​(p))=EF(L1​,…,Lk​).

Here π(x)\pi(x)π(x) counts primes at most xxx, so π(x)−1\pi(x)-1π(x)−1 excludes the prime two. Primes receive ordinary equal weight, and the limit holds through all real cutoffs. This describes every fixed finite collection of largest normalized factors.

In particular, for every fixed u≥1u\ge1u≥1, the manuscript deduces

#{p≤x:P+(p−1)≤x1/u}∼π(x)ρ(u),\#\{p\le x:P^+(p-1)\le x^{1/u}\}\sim\pi(x)\rho(u),#{p≤x:P+(p−1)≤x1/u}∼π(x)ρ(u),

with P+(1)=1P^+(1)=1P+(1)=1. The notation ∼\sim∼ means the ratio tends to one. The Dickman function ρ\rhoρ is determined by

ρ(u)=1(0≤u≤1),uρ′(u)+ρ(u−1)=0(u>1).\rho(u)=1\quad(0\le u\le1),\qquadu\rho'(u)+\rho(u-1)=0\quad(u>1).ρ(u)=1(0≤u≤1),uρ′(u)+ρ(u−1)=0(u>1).

The parameter uuu is fixed before xxx grows.

M1: smooth predecessors and large totient fibers

M1, Theorem 1.2, asserts that for every fixed 0<δ<1/40<\delta<1/40<δ<1/4,

#{p:2x<p≤5x, P+(p−1)≤xδ}≥x1−o(1).\#\{p:2x<p\le5x,\ P^+(p-1)\le x^\delta\}\ge x^{1-o(1)}.#{p:2x<p≤5x, P+(p−1)≤xδ}≥x1−o(1).

The vanishing quantity o(1)o(1)o(1) may depend on δ\deltaδ. The conclusion extends to every fixed positive δ\deltaδ by using a smaller exponent. It gives the full power exponent for the count, but alone does not imply a positive limiting proportion among primes.

M1, Theorem 1.1, also claims that for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, infinitely many integers nnn satisfy

g(n)>n1−ε.g(n)>n^{1-\varepsilon}.g(n)>n1−ε.

The source recalls an elementary upper bound g(n)≪ηn1+ηg(n)\ll_\eta n^{1+\eta}g(n)≪η​n1+η for every η>0\eta>0η>0. Thus its result is optimal at the level of the power exponent, not a precise asymptotic for the largest fiber.

M3: a parity conclusion

M3, Theorem 1.1, claims infinitely many primes ppp such that p−1p-1p−1 is squarefree and Ω(p−1)\Omega(p-1)Ω(p−1) is even. Equivalently,

μ(p−1)=1.\mu(p-1)=1.μ(p−1)=1.

Squarefreeness makes the distinct-factor and multiplicity conventions coincide. The theorem is an infinitude statement, not a claim that half of all prime predecessors have this property.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The full predecessor law would establish a detailed probabilistic prediction for an arithmetically constrained sequence. It goes beyond the largest-factor statistic to describe how several large factors share the logarithmic size.

The smoothness and totient statements answer longstanding extremal questions, while the parity result confronts a limitation of ordinary sieve information. Their common methods would therefore connect distributional, extremal, and parity-sensitive problems.

The connection to totients is especially concrete. If mmm is a product of distinct primes from a set SSS, then

φ(m)=∏p∈S(p−1).\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\in S}(p-1).φ(m)=p∈S∏​(p−1).

When all these predecessors use a small supply of prime factors, many different choices of SSS can produce the same product. Enough smooth predecessors allow this collision principle to create very large fibers. The score reflects the reach of the stated results if correct, without treating the different conclusions as automatic equivalents.

6. The main idea

Detect primes within a controlled factorization pattern

M1 constructs nonnegative weights on integers uuu whose factors occupy carefully chosen size bands, then seeks prime values of 2u+12u+12u+1. Some small prime factors are marked so their divisibility can be tracked. A longer factor is allowed to range over rough integers, which have no prime factors below a chosen cutoff.

Congruence estimates provide an initial sieve, but stronger cancellation is needed to remove composite candidates. The manuscript organizes multiplicative comparisons in dilation graphs. A vertex records an integer and lists of marked prime divisors; edges connect states through shifts involving products of shared and independent primes.

An ideal comparison operator uses independently sampled labels with probabilities proportional to reciprocals of primes. M1 claims that a small norm for this ideal operator transfers to cancellation in the arithmetic graph. Closed-walk expansions track repeated prime labels: a repeated divisibility condition should be charged only once, so the construction retains the relevant congruence information between appearances.

The resulting correlation estimates yield a Type II estimate, a cancellation bound for sums with two varying factor variables. Such bilinear information distinguishes prime candidates from composite factorizations more effectively than initial congruence counts. A weighted sieve then extracts enough primes with smooth predecessors. A product-and-pigeonhole argument converts that supply into the totient-fiber bound.

Obtain the entire partition, not just smooth examples

M2 uses M1’s general dilation-graph estimates but needs a separate extraction argument. Its new determinant graph controls a situation where only the predecessor side carries divisor marks. After applying Cauchy–Schwarz, pairs of factorizations become relations between primitive lattice vectors, vectors whose coordinates have no common factor.

Modulo a prime, these vectors determine projective lines. The manuscript averages their local distributions and retains repeated-line information in a signed memory expansion. A second estimate handles marks on both endpoints. Together these comparisons replace composite factor slots by suitable rough-number proxies and recover joint statistics of selected prime factors.

The first statistics are obtained inside the region where the sum of the selected logarithmic factor sizes is strictly less than one. That interior information is not yet the complete limiting law: probability could accumulate near the boundary or among omitted pieces.

M2 uses sequential size-biased sampling, choosing the next factor with probability proportional to its logarithmic size. The resulting densities are claimed to have full mass and to match the stick-breaking process. Control of the remaining unsampled mass then permits sorting and yields the ranked Poisson–Dirichlet law. The boundary argument is a necessary probabilistic step after the analytic estimates.

Preserve a parity-sensitive sign

M3 again uses M1’s graph machinery, but changes the weight. Writing p=2u+1p=2u+1p=2u+1, it chooses odd uuu with an odd number of prime factors; adjoining the factor two then makes p−1p-1p−1 have even parity.

Two extensions are needed. A long factor slot must contain a prime, rather than an arbitrary rough integer. A Liouville sign, λ(u)=(−1)Ω(u)\lambda(u)=(-1)^{\Omega(u)}λ(u)=(−1)Ω(u), must also survive the graph transformations. When the same dilation factor appears at both endpoints, its sign occurs twice and cancels because λ(d)2=1\lambda(d)^2=1λ(d)2=1.

The manuscript supplies the corresponding prime-polynomial and signed-correlation estimates, then applies a parity-selecting nonnegative weight in the sieve. It bounds the nonsquarefree contribution separately so that enough detected prime mass remains with squarefree predecessor. Smoothness by itself would not provide either this sign control or squarefreeness.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

All distribution and smoothness parameters are fixed before the prime cutoff tends to infinity. No uniform theorem for u→∞u\to\inftyu→∞ or δ→0\delta\to0δ→0 with xxx is asserted. The full law concerns every fixed finite collection of ranked factors, with the stated multiplicity and logarithmic normalization.

The predecessor law does not establish recursive independence throughout a Pratt tree. Nor does it determine the parity of the total number of prime factors, which may depend on many small factors invisible to a fixed-dimensional large-factor statistic. M3 supplies a separate infinitude result for that reason.

The totient theorem concerns infinitely many exceptionally popular values, not the behavior of every value or a typical fiber. Its power exponent is sharp in the stated sense, while finer maximal-order asymptotics are not given here. The manuscripts also do not assert effective thresholds for all their existence conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 state the fiber and smooth-predecessor results; its introduction explains the dilation graph, Type II, and sieve stages. M2’s Theorem 1.1 gives the full distribution, and Section 8 handles the passage from interior statistics to ranked factors. M3’s Theorem 1.1 and introductory outline isolate the parity extensions.

The primary papers in Section 3 place the claims beside earlier smoothness bounds and conditional distribution laws. Optional introductions to the Dickman function, Poisson–Dirichlet distributions, and Euler’s totient function provide additional background.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Weighted dilation graphs, smooth shifted primes and totient fibers (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The Poisson-Dirichlet law for prime predecessors (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Prime Predecessors with an Even Number of Prime Factors (September 17, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Largest prime factors of consecutive integers: a joint Dickman law
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 012 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

The integers nnn and n+1n+1n+1 share no prime factors. Does this local restriction leave a lasting connection between the sizes of their largest prime factors?

For example, sixteen has largest prime factor two, while seventeen is itself prime. Other neighboring pairs have the opposite ordering. A longstanding prediction says that each ordering should occur half the time. A stronger conjecture predicts a complete joint distribution: after taking logarithms and scaling by the logarithm of the integer, the two largest factors should behave like independent samples from the classical Dickman distribution.

Family 012 claims this stronger result in ordinary natural density. Every integer up to the cutoff is weighted equally, and the limit is asserted through every growing cutoff. The familiar half-and-half ordering is then a consequence of the joint law, rather than a separate analytic argument.

The challenge is dependence. Knowing the distribution of the largest factor of one integer does not determine the distribution of a neighboring pair, just as knowing two marginal probability distributions does not establish independence.

2. Background and essential definitions

Write P+(n)P^+(n)P+(n) for the largest prime factor of n>1n>1n>1, and put P+(1)=1P^+(1)=1P+(1)=1. An integer is yyy-smooth when all its prime factors are at most yyy. Thus the condition

P+(n)≤naP^+(n)\le n^aP+(n)≤na

asks whether every prime factor is below a fixed power of the integer, with 0<a<10<a<10<a<1.

The natural normalization is

Un=log⁡P+(n)log⁡n,Vn=log⁡P+(n+1)log⁡n.U_n=\frac{\log P^+(n)}{\log n},\qquadV_n=\frac{\log P^+(n+1)}{\log n}.Un​=lognlogP+(n)​,Vn​=lognlogP+(n+1)​.

Both use the denominator log⁡n\log nlogn, as in the manuscript. Replacing the second denominator by log⁡(n+1)\log(n+1)log(n+1) would have the same limit, but keeping one convention makes the ordering comparison exact.

For a set AAA of positive integers, natural density is the limit

lim⁡X→∞#(A∩[1,X])X,\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{\#(A\cap[1,X])}{X},X→∞lim​X#(A∩[1,X])​,

when it exists. A positive lower density only says that the lower limit is positive; it need not imply convergence. Logarithmic density instead uses weights 1/n1/n1/n and normalization log⁡X\log XlogX. It averages information across multiplicative scales and is weaker for this purpose than a conclusion at every ordinary cutoff.

The Dickman–de Bruijn function ρ\rhoρ is defined by

ρ(u)=1(0≤u≤1),uρ′(u)=−ρ(u−1)(u>1).\rho(u)=1\quad(0\le u\le1),\qquadu\rho'(u)=-\rho(u-1)\quad(u>1).ρ(u)=1(0≤u≤1),uρ′(u)=−ρ(u−1)(u>1).

The equation determines successive intervals from earlier ones. For example, on 1≤u≤21\le u\le21≤u≤2, it gives ρ(u)=1−log⁡u\rho(u)=1-\log uρ(u)=1−logu. Classical smooth-number theory says that the limiting distribution function of UnU_nUn​ is

H(a)=ρ(1/a),0<a≤1.H(a)=\rho(1/a),\qquad 0<a\le1.H(a)=ρ(1/a),0<a≤1.

It extends continuously to [0,1][0,1][0,1]. The proposed independence statement says that the probability of two threshold conditions tends to the product H(a)H(b)H(a)H(b)H(a)H(b).

This does not mean that all divisibility events at consecutive integers are independent. A prime cannot divide both nnn and n+1n+1n+1. The claim concerns a particular large-scale statistic after normalization, not the full factorization data.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Dickman’s 1930 work and later results of Ramaswami and de Bruijn established the one-variable smoothness law. That marginal distribution is an input and historical starting point here, not the manuscript’s new conclusion.

Erdős and Pomerance’s 1978 paper formulated the joint problem and proved that each ordering has positive lower natural density, with an explicit bound of 0.00990.00990.0099. They also showed that the ratio of the two largest factors rarely stays too close on suitable power scales. These results revealed substantial variation without identifying a limiting distribution.

Subsequent work raised the ordering lower bounds. Results of de la Bretèche–Pomerance–Tenenbaum, Fouvry, Wang, and Lü–Wang led to the value 0.20170.20170.2017. Yang’s 2026 preprint gives 0.2800.2800.280 for both orderings. In this progression, a lower bound should not be confused with existence of a natural density or the exact value one-half.

Teräväinen’s binary-correlation theorem proved the predicted joint law in logarithmic density, and hence logarithmic density one-half for the ordering. It also gave positive lower natural density for every nondegenerate interior rectangle of normalized values. This was much more than knowing that both orderings occur often, but still involved a different averaging conclusion.

Tao and Teräväinen obtained the ordinary joint law outside an exceptional set of scales of logarithmic density zero. Their later quantitative work provides logarithmic savings and parameter uniformity while retaining exceptional scales. Other work proved conditional ordinary laws under distribution assumptions for smooth numbers, or averaged the problem over shifts.

M1 claims an unconditional ordinary limit at the fixed shift one with no exceptional scales. It does not claim to retain the quantitative error term or growing-parameter uniformity of those other results.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, Theorem 1.1, states that for every fixed a,b∈(0,1)a,b\in(0,1)a,b∈(0,1),

lim⁡X→∞1X#{2≤n≤X:P+(n)≤na,P+(n+1)≤nb}=ρ(1/a)ρ(1/b).\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1X\#\left\{2\le n\le X:\begin{array}{l}P^+(n)\le n^a,\\P^+(n+1)\le n^b\end{array}\right\}=\rho(1/a)\rho(1/b).X→∞lim​X1​#{2≤n≤X:P+(n)≤na,P+(n+1)≤nb​}=ρ(1/a)ρ(1/b).

The limit is through all real XXX, with ordinary unweighted counting. The manuscript first obtains the corresponding theorem with fixed thresholds Xa,XbX^a,X^bXa,Xb, then passes to the displayed moving thresholds.

For a concrete consequence, taking a=b=1/2a=b=1/2a=b=1/2 gives the limiting proportion

ρ(2)2=(1−log⁡2)2,\rho(2)^2=(1-\log2)^2,ρ(2)2=(1−log2)2,

approximately 9.4%9.4\%9.4%. This is what the claimed theorem predicts for pairs in which both largest factors are at most n\sqrt nn​; it is not a reported numerical experiment.

Combining the joint threshold law with the marginals also gives independence for upper-tail events, recovering the Erdős–Pomerance formulation. More generally, the limiting joint distribution of (Un,Vn)(U_n,V_n)(Un​,Vn​) is the product of two identical continuous Dickman distributions.

Corollary 1.2 asserts

lim⁡X→∞1X#{2≤n≤X:P+(n)<P+(n+1)}=12.\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1X\#\{2\le n\le X:P^+(n)<P^+(n+1)\}=\frac12.X→∞lim​X1​#{2≤n≤X:P+(n)<P+(n+1)}=21​.

The reverse ordering has the same density. The deduction uses the symmetry and continuity of the limiting product distribution: it assigns equal mass to the two sides of the diagonal and zero mass to the diagonal itself. No symmetry of the finite list of consecutive pairs is assumed.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The claim would resolve a longstanding independence problem for consecutive integers in the original ordinary-density form. It identifies an entire joint law, of which the ordering question is one particularly accessible consequence.

The result would also demonstrate how a strong local dependence can disappear from a normalized large-factor statistic. Consecutive integers remain coprime, but their limiting largest-factor sizes would nevertheless be independent. Such statements are precise versions of probabilistic intuition in number theory.

Removing exceptional scales is mathematically meaningful. A theorem valid at almost all scales may still leave arbitrarily large cutoffs with different behavior. M1 claims to exclude every such bad sequence for fixed smoothness parameters. The rating reflects this advance and the proposed methods if correct, without reading a quantitative convergence speed into a qualitative limit.

6. The main idea

Encode the largest factor with finitely many labels

At a large scale xxx, divide primes above x1/Jx^{1/J}x1/J into finitely many logarithmic bins,

(xk/J,x(k+1)/J],1≤k<J,\bigl(x^{k/J},x^{(k+1)/J}\bigr],\qquad 1\le k<J,(xk/J,x(k+1)/J],1≤k<J,

with JJJ fixed. Counting prime factors in these bins gives a finite description of the large-factor pattern. The counts are bounded on the relevant integer range because too many large factors would make their product exceed that range.

Assign a unit complex number ζk\zeta_kζk​ to each bin and encode its count by a power of ζk\zeta_kζk​. Multiplying these powers produces a multiplicative bin function. Finite Fourier inversion recovers the probabilities of count patterns from averages of such functions, so independence reduces to decorrelation for arbitrary pairs of phase choices.

Subtract the mean from one bin function to obtain a centered function FxF_xFx​, and call the other gxg_xgx​. The required statement has the shape

1x∑n<xgx(n)Fx(n+1)⟶0.\frac1x\sum_{n<x}g_x(n)F_x(n+1)\longrightarrow0.x1​n<x∑​gx​(n)Fx​(n+1)⟶0.

The centered function is no longer multiplicative. This prevents a direct substitution into a general theorem about multiplicative functions. The manuscript instead exploits that multiplication by any fixed integer changes none of the large-prime bins once xxx is sufficiently large.

Amplify a hypothetical correlation

Assume a nonzero correlation persists along some sequence of scales. M1 introduces nonnegative divisor weights built at an auxiliary scale BBB. These weights amplify the putative bias while having controlled first and second moments.

Writing the integer through the chosen divisors permits the fixed-multiplier invariance to simplify one endpoint. Cauchy–Schwarz removes the bounded function gxg_xgx​ and yields a quadratic energy involving two copies of FxF_xFx​. After discarding a negligible diagonal, an exact change of variables converts the remaining terms into shifted products

Fx(n′) Fx(n′+j)‾.F_x(n')\,\overline{F_x(n'+j)}.Fx​(n′)Fx​(n′+j)​.

The result is a weighted graph of ordinary additive shifts. A persistent original correlation forces a positive amount of energy in this graph.

Approximate the graph by separate endpoint features

The edge weights depend on auxiliary-prime divisibility at both endpoints and on residue information. M1 compares these data with independent random prime sets, where each auxiliary prime is included with probability 1/p1/p1/p.

The goal is not to declare the actual integers independent. It is to approximate the specific graph kernel well enough for every bounded pairing that appears in the argument. The relevant cut norm measures the largest normalized matrix pairing with bounded test vectors, allowing those vectors to depend on the realized matrix.

Randomly splitting each endpoint’s prime set smooths its logarithmic and residue information. The manuscript uses this to approximate the kernel by a fixed finite sum of products of one-endpoint features. A sampling argument upgrades an integrated comparison to the needed cut-norm comparison; second-moment bounds control the potentially large kernel entries.

The features can then be approximated by expressions of the form

GB,v(n)=∏p∈PBp∣n1+p−v/B2,v≥0,G_{B,v}(n)=\prod_{\substack{p\in\mathcal P_B\\p\mid n}}\frac{1+p^{-v/B}}2,\qquad v\ge0,GB,v​(n)=p∈PB​p∣n​∏​21+p−v/B​,v≥0,

where PB\mathcal P_BPB​ is the chosen auxiliary prime set. This explicit form links the graph estimate back to short averages of arithmetic functions.

Apply short-interval cancellation

The manuscript establishes cancellation for short averages of FxGB,vF_xG_{B,v}Fx​GB,v​, including fixed residue restrictions, using the short-interval theorems of Matomäki–Radziwiłł and Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao. Because the bin counts lie in a finite range, interpolation by nonnegative multiplicative functions handles the fact that FxF_xFx​ itself is centered rather than multiplicative.

After the graph kernel is separated into endpoint features, its energy reduces to products of those short averages. Their vanishing contradicts the positive energy forced by the hypothetical bias.

The order of limits is part of the mechanism: the original scale xxx goes to infinity first, with auxiliary data fixed, and then BBB grows. The contradiction is applied to a subsequence of any proposed bad sequence of cutoffs, producing the claimed full ordinary limit. Refining the finite bins then recovers the largest-factor distribution.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem fixes aaa and bbb in (0,1)(0,1)(0,1). It gives no stated error rate and no uniformity when the thresholds vary with XXX. The comparison with earlier quantitative work should preserve that tradeoff: removing exceptional scales does not automatically retain stronger rates.

The displayed result concerns nnn and n+1n+1n+1. It does not state an arbitrary-length independence theorem for consecutive blocks or the entire joint factorization process. It also differs from family 011, which samples primes and studies the ranked factors of their predecessors.

The largest-factor statistic cannot encode all small-prime correlations, parity information, or coprimality constraints. Those features remain present even if this normalized joint law holds. Extensions to more shifts, sharper error bounds, and varying smoothness parameters are further questions beyond the stated conclusion.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 give the joint law and ordering density. Its introduction describes the bin encoding, divisor amplification, graph comparison, and limit order. Section 11 connects the resulting correlations to the moving-threshold law and the ordering consequence.

The primary sources in Section 3 distinguish marginal smoothness, logarithmic density, lower natural density, and almost-all-scale results. For optional definitions, see smooth numbers, natural density, and the Dickman function.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The joint Dickman law for consecutive integers (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Inverse Goldbach: why the primes cannot split into a sumset
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 013 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

The familiar Goldbach problem asks whether even integers can be expressed as sums of two primes. Ostmann’s inverse Goldbach problem reverses the structural question: can the primes themselves be obtained by adding elements from two simpler sets?

For sets A,BA,BA,B of nonnegative integers, their sumset is

A+B={a+b:a∈A, b∈B}.A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}.A+B={a+b:a∈A, b∈B}.

The requirement is demanding. Every sufficiently large prime must occur, and every sufficiently large sum must be prime. It is not enough to represent many primes while also producing many composites.

Family 013 claims that such a decomposition is impossible when both summands contain at least two elements, even if one changes finitely many members of the prime set. This is Ostmann’s conjecture on the additive indecomposability of the primes.

The apparent simplicity hides a tension between local and global information. Avoiding composites forces restrictions modulo every prime. Covering all large primes forces the summands to be sufficiently large and sufficiently well coordinated. The manuscript aims to show that these demands cannot coexist.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let P\mathcal PP be the positive primes and N0={0,1,2,…}\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}N0​={0,1,2,…}. The symmetric difference

S△T=(S∖T)∪(T∖S)S\mathbin{\triangle}T=(S\setminus T)\cup(T\setminus S)S△T=(S∖T)∪(T∖S)

consists of elements belonging to exactly one of the sets. Saying that (A+B)△P(A+B)\triangle\mathcal P(A+B)△P is finite means that the two sets agree beyond some threshold. This is eventual equality, not equality of densities or an approximation in proportion.

The condition on summand size removes trivial decompositions. For example, {0}+P=P\{0\}+\mathcal P=\mathcal P{0}+P=P, but one summand has only one element. Both finite and infinite sets are initially allowed as long as each has at least two elements.

Define the counting functions

A(x)=#(A∩[0,x]),B(x)=#(B∩[0,x]).A(x)=\#(A\cap[0,x]),\qquad B(x)=\#(B\cap[0,x]).A(x)=#(A∩[0,x]),B(x)=#(B∩[0,x]).

If every large prime at most xxx must be a sum, then there must be enough pairs, so roughly

A(x)B(x)≳xlog⁡x.A(x)B(x)\gtrsim\frac{x}{\log x}.A(x)B(x)≳logxx​.

Several pairs can represent the same prime, so this is only a necessary lower bound. An upper bound of order xxx would still leave room between the two estimates.

For a prime qqq, the residue set A mod qA\bmod qAmodq records which remainders occur. If sufficiently large a∈Aa\in Aa∈A and b∈Bb\in Bb∈B satisfy a≡−b(modq)a\equiv-b\pmod qa≡−b(modq), then a+ba+ba+b is divisible by qqq. Once the sum exceeds qqq, it is composite. Therefore the tails of AAA and −B-B−B must occupy disjoint residue sets modulo every qqq.

A sieve combines such local restrictions across many primes to bound the size of an integer set. An inverse sieve asks what structure a set must have if it nearly attains those bounds. Squares provide a model example: modulo an odd prime, they occupy about half the residue classes, yet there are about x\sqrt xx​ squares below xxx.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Ostmann formulated the conjecture in his 1956 treatise on additive number theory. Laffer and Mann later showed that a hypothetical nontrivial eventual decomposition must have two infinite summands. This already rules out representing the primes as finitely many fixed translates of another set.

Work of Hornfeck, Pomerance–Sárközy–Stewart, Hofmann–Wolke, and Elsholtz progressively restricted possible decompositions. Elsholtz combined large and larger sieves to force both summands to have approximately square-root size, up to logarithmic factors, and ruled out three nontrivial summands. A ternary impossibility is not the binary result: adding a third set creates additional constraints.

Elsholtz and Harper sharpened the binary size restrictions. In their positive-integer formulation, a hypothetical decomposition forces each counting function between quantities of the approximate forms

xlog⁡xlog⁡log⁡xandxlog⁡log⁡x,\frac{\sqrt x}{\log x\log\log x}\quad\text{and}\quad\sqrt x\log\log x,logxloglogxx​​andx​loglogx,

up to constants. Such bounds sharply narrow the possibilities without contradicting prime coverage.

Green and Harper’s inverse-sieve work proposed a structural route. Sets near the square-root bound and occupying about half the classes modulo primes should resemble quadratic images. A sufficiently strong classification would imply Ostmann’s conjecture. Their work established important partial results, not the required full inverse theorem.

Hanson proved that suitable sets have additive correlation and a substantial intersection with a quadratic image. More recent quadratic inverse-sieve work strengthened the intersection conclusions, as described in M1’s introduction. Large intersections still fall short of near-containment in one quadratic structure, especially when the quadratic may vary with the scale.

The manuscript claims a different final route: use the simultaneous residue restrictions together with coverage of every sufficiently large prime, without proving the general inverse-sieve classification. Its stated advance is a contradiction for the prime sumset problem itself.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1, Theorem 1.1, states that for every pair A,B⊆N0A,B\subseteq\mathbb N_0A,B⊆N0​ with ∣A∣,∣B∣≥2|A|,|B|\ge2∣A∣,∣B∣≥2,

(A+B)△Pis infinite.(A+B)\mathbin{\triangle}\mathcal P\quad\text{is infinite}.(A+B)△Pis infinite.

Equivalently, no finite modification of the set of primes can be written as a sumset of two nontrivial sets of nonnegative integers.

The conclusion contains two possible ways a candidate decomposition can fail: it can omit infinitely many primes, or contain infinitely many nonprimes, or both. In particular, if it contains every sufficiently large prime, then it must contain infinitely many composite numbers. The only nonprime nonnegative integers that are not composite are zero and one, so finite initial irregularities cannot account for that infinite failure.

No density or regularity assumptions on the summands are imposed. They need not be arithmetic progressions, polynomial images, computable sets, or sets with a known asymptotic counting formula.

The theorem does not say that two nontrivial sets cannot produce some primes, or even infinitely many primes. It says their full sumset cannot agree eventually with the full prime set. The exact coverage and exclusion conditions are both used in the manuscript.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Ostmann’s conjecture is a longstanding structural question about how an arithmetically defined set can arise from addition. Resolving it would show that the entire prime set has a rigidity invisible from its density alone.

The challenge is stronger than a simple parity obstruction. Choosing one summand even and the other odd can ensure odd sums, but oddness leaves many composites. One must simultaneously avoid divisibility by every prime while still reaching every large prime. Existing size bounds demonstrated the narrowness of that possibility; the claimed theorem rules it out completely.

The method would also connect local residue information, multiplicative character estimates, and global additive coverage. Its significance includes overcoming the need for a general structural classification that earlier conditional approaches sought. The score measures that mathematical importance if the claim is correct.

6. The main idea

Reduce to two infinite summands

Assume eventual equality. If AAA were finite, two distinct elements of AAA would require two fixed translates of the tail of BBB to consist of primes. A standard upper-bound sieve limits such a set to order x/(log⁡x)2x/(\log x)^2x/(logx)2. Finitely many translates of it cannot cover the order x/log⁡xx/\log xx/logx primes below xxx. M1 includes this short reduction before tackling infinite summands.

For the remaining case, set D=−BD=-BD=−B. At each prime qqq, sufficiently long tails of AAA and DDD occupy disjoint subsets of Fq\mathbb F_qFq​, the field of residues modulo qqq. Complete those subsets to a partition Sq,SqcS_q,S_q^cSq​,Sqc​. Collision estimates, which count how often two elements share a residue, show that on suitable averages these parts must be approximately balanced and the summands approximately uniform within them.

This creates many local partitions. The problem is to exploit their compatibility across primes without assuming they all have a simple algebraic form.

Eliminate persistent character patterns

A multiplicative character on Fq\mathbb F_qFq​ assigns roots of unity to nonzero residues and is multiplicative, with value zero at zero. The quadratic character distinguishes nonzero squares from nonsquares. Translating its argument produces a test centered at a chosen residue.

M1 first studies persistent correlations with translated quadratic characters. Moment estimates and Poisson summation are used to force independently chosen local centers into a common rational pattern. A quadratic large-sieve argument would then confine positive portions of the summands to a small family of quadratic structures, contradicting the required collision behavior.

Higher-order characters require further repeated Cauchy–Schwarz steps. Auxiliary anchor variables separate copied terms and control diagonal coincidences. The output is a mixed-character decorrelation estimate. This is a statement about the specific residue patterns forced by a hypothetical decomposition, not a general classification of all large sets with restricted residues.

Use prime coverage as an additional input

Avoiding composite sums supplied the residue partitions. Coverage of all large primes now supplies something different: their additive Fourier transforms cannot be too small on too much of the relevant prime average.

For a function fff on Fq\mathbb F_qFq​, its additive Fourier transform is

f^(a)=1q∑x∈Fqf(x)e−2πiax/q.\widehat f(a)=\frac1q\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_q} f(x)e^{-2\pi i ax/q}.f​(a)=q1​x∈Fq​∑​f(x)e−2πiax/q.

It measures correlation with additive oscillations. M1 compares a nonnegative sumset statistic with an average over primes, deriving a lower bound that retains more coverage information than the preliminary estimate for A(x)B(x)A(x)B(x)A(x)B(x).

This lower bound is central. A contradiction based only on sets avoiding certain residue classes would face the legitimate square-like examples that motivate the inverse-sieve problem. The full decomposition assumption contributes an extra positive statistic.

Force incompatible upper and lower bounds

Repeated transfers arrange terms in binary-tree patterns. A finite-field comparison uses the mixed-character decorrelation to control their correlations. Its hypotheses allow nonuniform pointwise values, which is necessary for the actual Fourier transforms of the residue indicators.

The arithmetic comparison then keeps track of repeated prime labels, coprimality restrictions, and the possible exceptional real character in prime-distribution estimates. In the final step, M1 averages over permutations of many bulk variables. Most pairs of arrangements overlap in too few components to maintain a large correlation. The remaining exceptional pairs and diagonal terms are bounded separately.

The resulting upper bound is claimed to contradict the positive lower bound inherited from prime coverage. The transfer depth is chosen large but fixed before the main scale grows. This is how the argument seeks to exclude every hypothetical eventual decomposition rather than merely improve its counting bounds.

M1 cites the zero-free theorem from family 003 only for an optional refinement in Remark 5.4. It explicitly states that the relevant proof uses its classical prime-distribution estimate and exceptional-character treatment instead. The indecomposability theorem is therefore not presented as depending on that new zero-free claim.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The summands lie in the nonnegative integers, and each must contain at least two elements. The theorem concerns eventual equality after finitely many changes. It does not give a quantitative lower bound on how many composite sums a covering pair must produce.

A sumset can contain an interesting thin set of primes without being an eventual decomposition of all primes. Results and questions about such thin sumsets remain distinct. The theorem also does not resolve the ordinary binary Goldbach conjecture, whose target is the even integers and whose summands are primes.

The argument does not establish Green–Harper’s general inverse-sieve conjecture. A broad classification of sets near sieve bounds remains a separate structural problem. Other multiplicatively defined sets, restricted summand classes, and quantitative measures of failure require their own conclusions.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 states the eventual indecomposability result. Section 2 handles finite summands and residue restrictions; Sections 3–5 develop character decorrelation and the separate use of prime coverage; Sections 6–9 complete the tree comparison and contradiction.

The Elsholtz–Harper and Green–Harper papers linked in Section 3 explain the square-root barrier and the inverse-sieve approach. Optional background on sumsets and sieve theory may help place the problem within additive and analytic number theory.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The additive indecomposability of the primes (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Zilber–Pink: when too many special intersections force structure
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 016 · Number theory
Importance 5/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

Two surfaces in three-dimensional space usually meet along a curve. Two curves in that space usually miss each other. Algebraic geometry packages this expectation in the formula

expected dimension=dim⁡X+dim⁡T−dim⁡S,\text{expected dimension}=\dim X+\dim T-\dim S,expected dimension=dimX+dimT−dimS,

where X,TX,TX,T lie in an ambient space SSS. An intersection larger than this prediction suggests a structural reason.

The Zilber–Pink principle asks what happens when TTT ranges over infinitely many arithmetically special subvarieties. A fixed pair might be easy to study, but infinitely many moving special targets could conceivably produce infinitely many exceptional intersections. The conjecture predicts strong finiteness once the special structure already forced by XXX is taken into account.

Family 016 contains four manuscripts. M1 claims the general abelian version over algebraic numbers. M2–M4 treat three types of special points on curves in the moduli space of principally polarized abelian surfaces, culminating in the curve case there. The two settings share a philosophy but have different meanings of “special.”

2. Background and essential definitions

The fixed abelian variety

An abelian variety is a connected projective algebraic group. An elliptic curve is the one-dimensional example; a product of elliptic curves gives examples in higher dimensions. A torsion point τ\tauτ satisfies mτ=0m\tau=0mτ=0 for some positive integer mmm.

Inside an abelian variety AAA, a special subvariety is a torsion coset

T=B+τ,T=B+\tau,T=B+τ,

where BBB is a connected abelian subgroup. This combines a subgroup direction with a finite-order translation. For an irreducible subvariety XXX, let S=⟨X⟩spS=\langle X\rangle_{\mathrm{sp}}S=⟨X⟩sp​ be the smallest torsion coset containing it.

An irreducible component YYY of X∩TX\cap TX∩T, with T⊆ST\subseteq ST⊆S special, is atypical if

dim⁡Y>dim⁡X+dim⁡T−dim⁡S.\dim Y>\dim X+\dim T-\dim S.dimY>dimX+dimT−dimS.

The ambient dimension is that of SSS, not automatically that of AAA. Otherwise a subvariety already lying in a smaller torsion coset would create misleading exceptional intersections.

For example, a curve in a three-dimensional abelian variety and a special curve have expected intersection dimension −1-1−1. Any intersection point is therefore atypical. A special surface has expected intersection dimension zero with the same curve, so an isolated intersection point is not atypical by this test.

“Maximal atypical” means maximal by inclusion among atypical subvarieties of XXX. Finiteness of maximal ones allows an infinite collection of exceptional points to lie inside one positive-dimensional exceptional subvariety.

The varying abelian surface

The moduli space A2\mathcal A_2A2​ parametrizes principally polarized abelian surfaces. A polarization supplies the algebraic analogue of a positive form; principal means its associated map to the dual abelian variety is an isomorphism. The space A2\mathcal A_2A2​ has dimension three, so it is often called the Siegel threefold.

Its special subvarieties are Shimura-special loci, including their Hecke translates. They encode extra endomorphisms or related Hodge-theoretic structure. A Hecke translate changes the abelian variety by a suitably compatible finite isogeny. An isogeny is a surjective homomorphism with finite kernel. A curve is Hodge generic if it lies in no proper special subvariety.

For an elliptic curve, complex multiplication, or CM, means that its geometric rational endomorphism algebra is an imaginary quadratic field instead of Q\mathbb QQ. For an abelian surface AsA_sAs​, write

End⁡0(As)=End⁡Q‾(As)⊗ZQ.\operatorname{End}^0(A_s)=\operatorname{End}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}(A_s)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q.End0(As​)=EndQ​​(As​)⊗Z​Q.

The full algebra matters. The matrix algebra M2(Q)M_2(\mathbb Q)M2​(Q) corresponds to a surface isogenous to the square of a non-CM elliptic curve. An indefinite quaternion division algebra is instead a four-dimensional noncommutative algebra over Q\mathbb QQ, with every nonzero element invertible, which becomes M2(R)M_2(\mathbb R)M2​(R) over R\mathbb RR. It is not the split algebra M2(Q)M_2(\mathbb Q)M2​(Q).

3. Development history and previous partial results

Raynaud’s Manin–Mumford theorem established the torsion-point case: an irreducible subvariety with Zariski-dense torsion points must itself be a torsion coset. Zilber’s unlikely-intersection formulation and Pink’s semiabelian and Shimura formulations extend the problem to moving special subvarieties of positive dimension.

In abelian varieties, Viada and Rémond–Viada obtained early curve results in powers of CM elliptic curves. Habegger and Pila proved the curve theorem for arbitrary abelian varieties over number fields. Their 2016 paper also gives higher-dimensional results under additional quotient-dimension or height restrictions. Barroero, Kühne and Schmidt later treated curves in general semiabelian varieties. M1’s introduction distinguishes these curve theorems from unrestricted higher-dimensional maximal-atypical finiteness.

Higher-dimensional partial results included non-density when every quotient has the expected image dimension, non-density at a fixed height bound, and finiteness of certain codimension-one or codimension-two exceptional subvarieties. These are meaningful advances, but a fixed height cutoff cannot cover points of arbitrarily large height without another argument.

For A2\mathcal A_2A2​, André–Oort supplies finiteness of special points on a Hodge-generic curve. Pila and Tsimerman established this case, and Tsimerman’s later general theorem covers the broader Siegel setting. Positive-dimensional special targets require more.

Daw and Orr developed reductions from large Galois orbits to finiteness and proved important cases under degeneration assumptions. Their work on large Galois orbits under multiplicative degeneration obtains the full curve conclusion when the closure meets the zero-dimensional boundary stratum. Papas obtained further interior-period results with hypotheses involving reduction and the number of supersingular places of proximity. M2–M4 aim to remove such restrictions for the three relevant loci.

The common counting strategy comes from Pila and Zannier: arithmetic supplies many conjugates, while tame geometric counting allows few unless an unexpected algebraic structure appears. The new manuscripts place their height and period estimates within that existing framework.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1: finitely many maximal atypical subvarieties

Let AAA be any abelian variety over a number field and X⊆AQ‾X\subseteq A_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}X⊆AQ​​ irreducible. M1 claims that XXX has only finitely many maximal atypical subvarieties, measured inside ⟨X⟩sp\langle X\rangle_{\mathrm{sp}}⟨X⟩sp​.

No restriction on dimension, simplicity, complex multiplication, point height or point degree is imposed. A key intermediate statement is universal non-density. If XXX lies in no proper torsion coset and d=dim⁡Xd=\dim Xd=dimX, then

X∩A[d+1]is not Zariski dense in X,X\cap A^{[d+1]}\quad\text{is not Zariski dense in }X,X∩A[d+1]is not Zariski dense in X,

where A[r]A^{[r]}A[r] is the union of all torsion cosets of codimension at least rrr. Zariski non-density means containment in a proper algebraic closed subset. For an irreducible curve, a proper closed subset is finite; in higher dimensions, non-density alone is weaker than finiteness.

M1 applies a universal reduction through optimal subvarieties to pass from this non-density theorem for all ambient varieties to the maximal-atypical conclusion. It also claims a finite-rank translated version: if Γ⊂A(Q‾)\Gamma\subset A(\overline{\mathbb Q})Γ⊂A(Q​) satisfies

dim⁡Q(Γ⊗ZQ)<∞,\dim_{\mathbb Q}(\Gamma\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q)<\infty,dimQ​(Γ⊗Z​Q)<∞,

and XXX lies in no translate of a proper algebraic subgroup, then

X(Q‾)∩(A[d+1](Q‾)+Γ)X(\overline{\mathbb Q})\cap\bigl(A^{[d+1]}(\overline{\mathbb Q})+\Gamma\bigr)X(Q​)∩(A[d+1](Q​)+Γ)

is not Zariski dense. This stronger geometric hypothesis excludes arbitrary proper translates, not just torsion translates. The group Γ\GammaΓ need not be finitely generated: division hulls and torsion groups are included.

M2–M4: three special-curve branches

Let C⊂A2C\subset\mathcal A_2C⊂A2​ be a reduced irreducible closed Hodge-generic curve over Q‾\overline{\mathbb Q}Q​. The manuscripts claim finiteness for the following sets of algebraic points:

ManuscriptCondition on the represented abelian surface
M2Isogenous to E1×E2E_1\times E_2E1​×E2​, with at least one elliptic factor having CM.
M3Full geometric rational endomorphism algebra equal to an indefinite quaternion division algebra over Q\mathbb QQ.
M4Isogenous to E2E^2E2 for a non-CM elliptic curve EEE, equivalently full endomorphism algebra M2(Q)M_2(\mathbb Q)M2​(Q).

The isogenies in the product descriptions need not preserve the given principal polarization. All degrees, CM fields, endomorphism orders, relevant quaternion algebras and polarizations are allowed. None of these statements requires the curve to meet a boundary, and complete curves are included.

M4 combines the three branches with the classification of special curves and André–Oort for special points. Its resulting theorem is

C(Q‾)∩⋃Z⊂A2 specialdim⁡Z≤1Z(Q‾)is finite.C(\overline{\mathbb Q})\cap\bigcup_{\substack{Z\subset\mathcal A_2\ \mathrm{special}\\\dim Z\le1}}Z(\overline{\mathbb Q})\quad\text{is finite}.C(Q​)∩Z⊂A2​ specialdimZ≤1​⋃​Z(Q​)is finite.

For a curve not Hodge generic in A2\mathcal A_2A2​, M4 also records the corresponding formulation inside its smallest special closure SCS_CSC​, using special targets with dim⁡Z<dim⁡SC−1\dim Z<\dim S_C-1dimZ<dimSC​−1.

A quantitative ingredient, not an effective list

For a mixed product point in M2, let N(s)N(s)N(s) be the least product-isogeny degree and DDD the absolute discriminant of the CM factor’s endomorphism order. Set c(s)=max⁡{N(s),D}c(s)=\max\{N(s),D\}c(s)=max{N(s),D}. M2 claims

#(Gal⁡(Q‾/K)⋅s)≥c c(s)1/42,\#\bigl(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb Q}/K)\cdot s\bigr)\ge c\,c(s)^{1/42},#(Gal(Q​/K)⋅s)≥cc(s)1/42,

with c>0c>0c>0 depending on the fixed curve and its field of definition KKK. The exponent is a usable positive power, not an optimized constant. The statement does not claim effectivity; its inputs include a potentially ineffective class-number estimate.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 5/5. Taken as stated, M1 settles a central arbitrary-dimensional form of the abelian Zilber–Pink conjecture. M2–M4 complete another substantial case, curves in A2\mathcal A_2A2​, by treating all three special-curve branches without boundary restrictions.

The broad idea is that unexpectedly large intersections cannot occur in infinitely many unrelated ways. In the abelian setting they must be contained in finitely many maximal exceptional subvarieties. In the Hodge-generic curve setting the exceptional set itself is finite.

These conclusions strengthen the structural meaning of a dimension count. They also connect diverse methods: canonical heights, period estimates, reduction at primes, Galois orbits and geometry of definable sets. The scope merits the highest relative rating without implying that all mixed-Shimura or semiabelian versions are covered.

6. The main idea

Separate the height scales

M1 starts from a hypothetical Zariski-generic sequence of unlikely-intersection points. The canonical, or Néron–Tate, height behaves quadratically under multiplication and acts like a squared norm modulo torsion. Different projections of the points may have bounded heights or heights growing at very different rates.

The manuscript separates these scales by taking suitable quotients and normalizing each level independently. The subgroup relations then approach a limiting linear projector. Geometric positivity, built from Ax-type results and finitely many exceptional directions, constrains how this projector can annihilate the normalized points.

When every level diverges, a generalized Vojta–Rémond height inequality gives the contradiction. A bounded level needs a different argument: compare two limiting measures on a fixed low-height factor, one associated with a product map and another with consecutive differences. Their incompatible densities yield arithmetic positivity. Small sections then vanish to high order at the marked points, and a product theorem cuts out a smaller auxiliary variety, contradicting minimality.

The uniformity concerns the auxiliary varieties and their fields of definition; it does not assume that the marked intersection points have bounded degree.

Turn special structure into many controlled conjugates

M2 uses the gluing description of a mixed product surface. A product isogeny has degree n2n^2n2, while its rank-one degeneration length carries a reciprocal factor 1/n1/n1/n. This produces a height estimate growing roughly linearly in nnn, up to the CM discriminant contribution. A balanced period construction on a related abelian threefold yields a stronger n4/3n^{4/3}n4/3 contribution. Comparing them forces the required Galois-orbit growth.

M3 and M4 instead study a rank-five quadratic system arising from trace-zero endomorphisms self-adjoint for the polarization. Extra endomorphisms supply positive two-dimensional planes. Period transport compares a fixed interior exceptional point with a varying target.

At suitable finite places, traces of endomorphism products give local equations. Comparing Frobenius-conjugate equations eliminates coefficients that depend on the prime. Grouping by conjugate data controls the number of equation types even when many primes contribute.

An interpolation and product-formula argument then gives a polynomial height bound in the field degree:

h(t)≤C [K(t):K]κ.h(t)\le C\,[K(t):K]^\kappa.h(t)≤C[K(t):K]κ.

Here hhh is a fixed logarithmic height and C,κC,\kappaC,κ depend on the curve. Auxiliary level markings ensure that the equations are genuinely nonidentical; M4 uses a second marking to handle bad reduction at the chosen center.

Finally, endomorphism bounds convert height control into polynomially controlled arithmetic coordinates or large Galois orbits. Pila–Wilkie-type counting forces an algebraic family if there are too many such points. Monodromy or the established Daw–Orr implication then contradicts Hodge genericity. The elliptic-square argument is proved separately before being combined with the other branches.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

M1 concerns torsion cosets in abelian varieties over algebraic numbers. It does not by itself prove Zilber–Pink for every semiabelian variety, every transcendental base field or every mixed Shimura variety. Its finite-rank consequence retains the stronger no-proper-translate assumption.

The A2\mathcal A_2A2​ conclusion is a theorem about curves. It does not cover arbitrary higher-dimensional subvarieties of every Ag\mathcal A_gAg​. M3 requires equality of the full endomorphism algebra with a quaternion division algebra; merely embedding such an algebra into something larger is not its stated condition.

No uniform or effective bound on the number of exceptional subvarieties is claimed. Finiteness alone does not provide a terminating procedure listing every exceptional point. Effective counts, explicit enumeration and extensions to broader moduli spaces remain additional problems.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 and Corollary 1.3 state the abelian and finite-rank conclusions. M2’s Theorems 1.1–1.2 give the mixed-product finiteness and Galois-orbit bound. M3’s Theorem 1.1 specifies the full quaternionic endomorphism condition. M4’s Theorems 1.1–1.3 separate the elliptic-square branch from the combined curve theorem.

The Habegger–Pila and Daw–Orr papers linked in section 3 give primary accounts of the earlier partial results and counting framework. The introductions of all four manuscripts carefully identify the height, period and monodromy inputs. Optional background on abelian varieties and complex multiplication can supplement the definitions above.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, The abelian Zilber-Pink conjecture (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The E×CM component of Zilber-Pink for curves in A2 (September 24, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Quaternionic division points on curves in the Siegel threefold (September 24, 2026).
  • M4. OpenAI, Elliptic squares and Zilber-Pink for curves in A2 (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 10 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: How well can fractions approximate pi?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 017 · Number theory
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-10

1. The question

The fractions 22/722/722/7 and 355/113355/113355/113 approximate π\piπ surprisingly well for their small denominators. But isolated successes do not tell us how good rational approximations can remain as the denominator grows. The real question is whether there are infinitely many exceptionally accurate fractions.

Family 017 claims the sharp answer: the irrationality exponent of π\piπ is exactly two. Roughly, errors of order the inverse square of the denominator occur infinitely often, but improving the exponent by any fixed positive amount eventually becomes impossible.

This also answers a question that initially looks unrelated. Does the positive series

∑n=1∞1n3sin⁡2n\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^3\sin^2 n}n=1∑∞​n3sin2n1​
