This forces additional global resources onto one side of the gadget. The selected side records the vertex-cover choice. Tests corresponding to graph edges are placed near the relevant intervals so that incompatible local choices cannot all be accommodated with the available resources.

The trees and intervals are analytical components of a numerical construction. The final instance is ordinary one-dimensional bin packing, with rational scalar item sizes.

Use five item roles near one fifth

An intended bin combines five roles: a row item, an anchor, two kinds of auxiliary resource, and a flag. Small perturbations of sizes near one fifth encode labels, ordering constraints, and interval endpoints.

Because all sizes exceed one sixth, no bin can contain six items. Carefully separated numerical coordinates ensure that a five-item bin fits only when the encoded conditions cooperate.

For example, an anchor can act like a deadline while auxiliary lengths determine a completion coordinate. Feasibility of that bin becomes an inequality comparing completion with deadline. Prefix counts of such inequalities translate into interval-coverage requirements.

Control unintended packings

An arbitrary packing is free to mix roles and labels. The paper assigns integer scores to items and uses conservation of total scores to show that a packing with only a fixed number of extra bins has only a bounded number of serious deviations from the intended patterns.

A second ordering argument controls mismatched labels. The error at a vertex is bounded independently of the number of internal positions in its gadget, allowing the coverage tests to retain their force.

For the structural LP gap, the paper uses a small graph and fractional mixtures of the two local states. Each local state uses its labeled items consistently, while averaging balances global inventories. A distribution over physical copies yields the fractional solution of value BBB, and the five-item bound supplies a matching lower bound on that value.

The fractional mixture can combine locally valid choices that no equally economical integral packing can realize simultaneously. This is the source of the gap.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The unbounded-gap theorem does not establish a matching logarithmic lower bound in terms of item count or optimum. The constructed instances can grow very rapidly as the prescribed gap increases.

A fixed maximum number of items per bin is different from a fixed number of distinct sizes. The construction may use many numerical sizes. Goemans and Rothvoss give polynomial-time solvability when the number of item types is fixed, a different parameter regime.

The hardness result concerns worst-case inputs and fixed additive allowances. It does not rule out useful heuristics, exact algorithms for small instances, or stronger guarantees under additional structure.

The next quantitative question is how the largest possible full-LP gap grows with instance size, beyond merely being unbounded.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Definitions 1.1 and Theorems 1.2–1.3 distinguish the two LP formulations, the unconditional structural gap, and the hardness reduction. The historical cutting-stock and approximation papers linked above explain why none of these statements is equivalent to the existence of a good multiplicative approximation scheme.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Additive hardness and unbounded configuration gaps in bin packing (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: The Courtade–Kumar and Hellinger conjectures
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 119 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

If you compress a collection of independent fair bits into one bit, which summary remains most informative after the original bits are independently corrupted? Family 119 claims sharp inequalities saying that a single coordinate is optimal. Its two manuscripts also distinguish a general randomized-summary theorem from a stronger-looking square-root comparison involving Hellinger affinity.

1. The question

Let X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)X=(X1​,…,Xn​) be independent uniform signs, each equal to plus or minus one. Before noise is applied, choose a Boolean summary f(X)f(X)f(X), also taking values plus or minus one.

Each coordinate then passes through an independent bit-flip channel, producing a noisy vector YYY. A receiver sees all of YYY, rather than only one further Boolean summary. How much information about f(X)f(X)f(X) remains?

A natural candidate is a coordinate, f(X)=Xif(X)=X_if(X)=Xi​. Majority combines many inputs, while parity uses all inputs symmetrically, but combining more bits need not preserve more information about a one-bit summary.

The Courtade–Kumar conjecture says no Boolean summary beats a coordinate. The family claims this conclusion, a sharp extension to randomized binary summaries, and a separate Hellinger inequality that also implies the Boolean information bound.

2. Background and essential definitions

The noise parameter

Write Yi=XiZiY_i=X_iZ_iYi​=Xi​Zi​, where the independent noise signs satisfy EZi=ρ\mathbb E Z_i=\rhoEZi​=ρ. For ordinary flip probability ε∈[0,1/2]\varepsilon\in[0,1/2]ε∈[0,1/2],

ρ=1−2ε.\rho=1-2\varepsilon.ρ=1−2ε.

Thus ρ=1\rho=1ρ=1 means no noise and ρ=0\rho=0ρ=0 means the output is independent of the input. The manuscripts also allow negative correlation; symmetry makes absolute correlation the relevant quantity in the information bound.

Entropy and mutual information

The binary entropy in bits is

h2(p)=−plog⁡2p−(1−p)log⁡2(1−p),h_2(p)=-p\log_2p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p),h2​(p)=−plog2​p−(1−p)log2​(1−p),

with 0log⁡20=00\log_2 0=00log2​0=0. It is one for a fair bit and zero for a deterministic bit.

Mutual information I(U;Y)=H(U)−H(U∣Y)I(U;Y)=H(U)-H(U\mid Y)I(U;Y)=H(U)−H(U∣Y) measures how much observing YYY reduces uncertainty about UUU. It is not the same as the probability of predicting UUU correctly.

For a coordinate summary, the other noisy coordinates carry no extra information, and

I(Xi;Y)=1−h2(ε).I(X_i;Y)=1-h_2(\varepsilon).I(Xi​;Y)=1−h2​(ε).

The main Boolean comparison says this is an upper bound for every fff.

Randomized summaries and output bias

A randomized binary summary UUU can be described by its conditional mean

u(x)=E[U∣X=x]∈[−1,1].u(x)=\mathbb E[U\mid X=x]\in[-1,1].u(x)=E[U∣X=x]∈[−1,1].

The value u(x)u(x)u(x) determines the conditional probabilities of its two outputs. Ordinary Boolean functions are the special case u(x)∈{−1,1}u(x)\in\{-1,1\}u(x)∈{−1,1}.

The mean m=Ef(X)m=\mathbb E f(X)m=Ef(X) measures output bias. A fair input vector need not produce a fair summary: an AND-like rule may output one only rarely.

The noise operator is the conditional averaging map Tρu(y)=E[u(X)∣Y=y]T_\rho u(y)=\mathbb E[u(X)\mid Y=y]Tρ​u(y)=E[u(X)∣Y=y]. It describes the receiver’s posterior mean of the summary. A single coordinate satisfies Tρxi=ρyiT_\rho x_i=\rho y_iTρ​xi​=ρyi​.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Courtade and Kumar formulated the information question in work presented in 2013 and published in 2014. Its simple appearance hides a dimension-independent comparison over every Boolean function.

Partial results established the conjecture in high-noise regimes. Samorodnitsky proved it for all Boolean functions in a dimension-independent high-noise range. Yu’s work on stability and later local optimality enlarged ranges for balanced functions.

Other results addressed neighboring formulations. Pichler, Piantanida, and Matz proved coordinate optimality when the noisy observation is itself reduced to one Boolean output. That is not the same as letting the receiver observe the full vector.

The 2017 Hellinger conjecture of Anantharam and collaborators replaced the entropy comparison by a square-root affinity inequality and showed that it implies the Courtade–Kumar conclusion. Chen and Nair developed mean-dependent bounds and dimension-induction methods in this direction.

Chen, Gohari, and Nair proposed a differential approach: control instantaneous information loss under gradually increasing noise, then integrate the inequality. Both manuscripts in this family develop that viewpoint.

The source history also includes several September 2026 preprints announcing full Courtade–Kumar proofs, including Chen and collaborators, Ky and Tran, and Mahdavifar and Beirami. M1 explicitly acknowledges overlap: an estimate in the first of these also yields its soft-channel contraction when integrated while retaining initial information. Its additional claims concern its proof route and mean-dependent production bound. M2’s Hellinger statement is a distinct functional inequality.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

In bit units, the Boolean consequence is

I(f(X);Y)≤1−h2(ε)I(f(X);Y)\le1-h_2(\varepsilon)I(f(X);Y)≤1−h2​(ε)

for every dimension and every Boolean fff. Signed coordinates attain equality.

To state M1’s more general comparison, define

ψ(a)=1−h2 ⁣(1+a2),0≤a≤1.\psi(a)=1-h_2\!\left(\frac{1+a}{2}\right),\qquad 0\le a\le1.ψ(a)=1−h2​(21+a​),0≤a≤1.

This is increasing, so it has an inverse on [0,1][0,1][0,1]. M1 claims that every randomized binary summary satisfies

I(U;Y)≤ψ ⁣(∣ρ∣ ψ−1(I(U;X))).I(U;Y)\le\psi\!\left(|\rho|\,\psi^{-1}(I(U;X))\right).I(U;Y)≤ψ(∣ρ∣ψ−1(I(U;X))).

The papers use natural logarithms; this display is the same normalized statement in bits. A soft coordinate with u(x)=axiu(x)=a x_iu(x)=axi​ attains the bound at the corresponding initial information level.

For a deterministic summary, I(f(X);X)=H(f(X))I(f(X);X)=H(f(X))I(f(X);X)=H(f(X)). Substituting its actual output entropy gives a stricter upper curve when the output is biased. This does not assert that every fixed output bias attains that refined curve.

For M2, put K(t)=1−t2K(t)=\sqrt{1-t^2}K(t)=1−t2​. Its claim is

K(m)−EK(Tρf)≤1−K(ρ),m=Ef.K(m)-\mathbb E K(T_\rho f)\le1-K(\rho),\qquad m=\mathbb E f.K(m)−EK(Tρ​f)≤1−K(ρ),m=Ef.

It applies to every Boolean output bias and every ρ∈[−1,1]\rho\in[-1,1]ρ∈[−1,1]. Signed coordinates attain equality. M2 also reproduces the established implication from this inequality to the Boolean information bound.

M1 additionally states a mean-dependent lower bound on instantaneous entropy production, stronger than the information-only rate in specified regimes. It should be distinguished from simply restating the finite-noise Boolean conclusion.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. The problem asks for an exact extremal principle at the intersection of information theory and Boolean-function analysis. A dimension-independent sharp comparison explains how much information a single-bit compression can retain through product noise.

The randomized-summary result is especially interpretable: match two summaries by the information they initially contain, then compare how much survives. The coordinate-based summary supplies the claimed optimal curve at every initial-information level.

The Hellinger inequality connects this information question with another measure of statistical distinguishability. Its inclusion of biased outputs matters because restricting to balanced functions would omit much of the Boolean class.

The rating reflects the scope of the functional statements and methods. It does not imply exclusive priority for the ordinary Courtade–Kumar conclusion, which the manuscripts themselves compare with contemporaneous claims.

6. The main idea

Increase the noise continuously

Set ρ=e−t\rho=e^{-t}ρ=e−t, so increasing time ttt adds more noise. The operators Te−tT_{e^{-t}}Te−t​ compose like a continuous evolution.

Information decreases along this evolution. Its derivative can be expressed through local costs on edges of the discrete cube, where neighboring inputs differ in one bit. If one bounds the rate of information loss by the rate for a coordinate carrying the same information, integration yields the desired finite-noise comparison.

A linear rate estimate is not sharp enough. The coordinate curve is nonlinear, and the proof must preserve the extra information in that curvature.

Join two smaller cubes carefully

Splitting along one input coordinate produces two lower-dimensional functions. Their information-loss rates contribute, but joining them adds another cost.

M1 optimizes that joining cost while tracking both mean and conditional entropy. Its local optimizer consists of one interior pair and possibly the two corners corresponding to common deterministic outputs. The construction uses two entropy capacities and comparisons describing how adding common outputs changes the required cost.

Keeping the mean is essential: an information-only local inequality does not close the induction for every coupled pair. The manuscript combines profiles so the dimension induction survives all bias regimes.

Interpret the square-root expression

For a nonconstant Boolean summary, let P+P_+P+​ and P−P_-P−​ be the laws of the noisy vector conditional on the two summary outputs. Their Hellinger affinity is

A(P+,P−)=∑yP+(y)P−(y).A(P_+,P_-)=\sum_y\sqrt{P_+(y)P_-(y)}.A(P+​,P−​)=y∑​P+​(y)P−​(y)​.

Large affinity means the two conditional laws overlap substantially. The left side of M2’s inequality equals K(m)(1−A(P+,P−))K(m)(1-A(P_+,P_-))K(m)(1−A(P+​,P−​)), a bias-weighted distinguishability measure.

M2 combines an asymmetric dimension induction in one noise range with an energy-continuation argument in the remaining range. At a hypothetical first failure, the rate comparison would contradict the required crossing behavior. It treats different bias regimes separately and attributes fixed scalar inequalities to exact finite arithmetic certificates included with the manuscript.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The input bits are independent and uniform. Arbitrary output bias means the summary may be unbalanced; it does not mean the theorem permits arbitrary nonuniform input distributions.

The summary is binary. Multi-bit compression, correlated input noise, and other channels require separate statements. Nor is the bound a universal claim that a coordinate optimizes every conceivable accuracy or stability criterion.

M1’s sharpness is at fixed initial information over randomized binary channels. Determining all optimizers under additional fixed-bias constraints is a different question, and the manuscript does not claim every biased Boolean source reaches its refined upper curve.

8. Sources and further reading

M1 states the soft-channel theorem, Boolean refinement, and entropy-production comparison. M2 defines the Hellinger affinity interpretation and its implication to Courtade–Kumar. The original conjecture papers and the differential-method sources linked above provide the main historical path without requiring their technical details to follow the claims.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Sharp binary-information contraction on the discrete cube (September 24, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, Hellinger contraction with arbitrary Boolean output bias (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Trace reconstruction: how many incomplete copies reveal a string?
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 122 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Suppose a message is copied repeatedly, but each copying operation independently loses some characters. The characters that survive remain in order; their original positions disappear. Can enough damaged copies recover the original message exactly?

For example, the binary string 10110 might produce 110, 011, or 1010. An observed zero does not reveal which original position it occupied. This uncertainty about alignment is what makes deletion errors fundamentally different from ordinary bit flips.

The trace-reconstruction problem asks for a method that works for every original string, including highly repetitive strings chosen to be difficult. Its two resources are the number of damaged copies, called traces, and the computation needed to interpret them. These resources need not coincide: a small collection of observations could contain enough information while extracting that information remains expensive.

This family contains three complementary manuscripts. One claims a reconstruction algorithm with quasipolynomial sample and time bounds. Another develops a related sample bound through a different analytic construction. The third claims that polynomially many samples cannot suffice at any fixed nontrivial deletion probability, even with unlimited computation. Together they describe a much narrower, though still unresolved, range for worst-case reconstruction.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^nx∈{0,1}n be the unknown string. Each position is deleted independently with known probability qqq, and retained with probability p=1−qp=1-qp=1−q. A trace is the resulting shorter string, including its length. Different traces are independent. Neither deleted symbols nor original position labels are supplied.

A worst-case guarantee means that the reconstruction succeeds with probability at least 2/32/32/3 for each fixed xxx. The probability comes from the deletion process and any internal randomness. It is not an average over randomly chosen original strings.

A polynomial sample bound has the form nCn^CnC, with a fixed constant CCC. A quasipolynomial bound is larger, typically

exp⁡((log⁡n)C).\exp\bigl((\log n)^C\bigr).exp((logn)C).

For C>1C>1C>1, this exceeds every fixed power of nnn, but remains much smaller than exp⁡(na)\exp(n^a)exp(na) for every fixed a>0a>0a>0. Constants may depend on a channel parameter when that parameter is held fixed; a uniform theorem must explain the dependence when the parameter is part of the input.

For two possible originals x,yx,yx,y, write Dq(x)D_q(x)Dq​(x) and Dq(y)D_q(y)Dq​(y) for their trace distributions. Their total variation distance is

TV⁡(P,Q)=12∑w∣P(w)−Q(w)∣.\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\frac12\sum_w |P(w)-Q(w)|.TV(P,Q)=21​w∑​∣P(w)−Q(w)∣.

The sum ranges over possible observed strings. Small distance means that one trace gives little power to distinguish the candidates. A sample lower bound constructs originals whose entire trace distributions are close, rather than merely making one selected statistic uninformative.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Levenshtein developed general sequence-reconstruction questions, and Batu, Kannan, Khanna, and McGregor studied the independent-deletion model in connection with sequence alignment. Early worst-case algorithms required sample counts exponential in a fractional power of the original length.

A major step came from generating-function methods. De, O’Donnell, and Servedio, and independently Nazarov and Peres, obtained bounds of order exp⁡(O(n1/3))\exp(O(n^{1/3}))exp(O(n1/3)) at a fixed channel. Chase subsequently obtained exp⁡(O(n1/5log⁡5n))\exp(O(n^{1/5}\log^5 n))exp(O(n1/5log5n)). These results used increasingly informative features of the traces. Restrictions on algorithms using only coordinate means or short local statistics also explained why some natural approaches could not reach much further. See the mean-based analysis and Chase’s upper-bound paper.

The immediate precursor is especially important: Burudgunte, Valiant, and Wang already claimed a quasipolynomial sample bound in their 2026 preprint. That work used statistics involving a small number of positions that could be far apart. It did not provide a quasipolynomial-time reconstruction algorithm. The new algorithmic manuscript therefore addresses efficient decoding as well as quantitative sample dependence; it is not the first quasipolynomial sample claim.

Lower bounds followed a different path. Holden and Lyons, and then Chase, hid a small defect in repetitive backgrounds. Their complete-trace lower bounds were polynomial, with Chase reaching order n3/2/log⁡7nn^{3/2}/\log^7 nn3/2/log7n. The gap left open whether some sufficiently large fixed power of nnn might always suffice. The third manuscript claims a negative answer to that question. Its historical starting points include Holden–Lyons and Chase’s lower bound.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

An algorithm with controlled sample and computation costs

M1 assumes that nnn and a rational retention probability p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1]p∈(0,1] are known. Let LLL be the binary encoding length of ppp. For q>0q>0q>0, define

X=1+log⁡n1+log⁡(1/q),B=p−1(log⁡n)X2(1+log⁡X)6.X=1+\frac{\log n}{1+\log(1/q)},\qquadB=p^{-1}(\log n)X^2(1+\log X)^6.X=1+1+log(1/q)logn​,B=p−1(logn)X2(1+logX)6.

For q=0q=0q=0, set X=1X=1X=1; reconstruction then simply reads an undeleted trace. M1 states that absolute constants C,cC,cC,c give a sample bound M=⌈exp⁡(CB)⌉M=\lceil\exp(CB)\rceilM=⌈exp(CB)⌉ and a computation bound (n+L+M)c(n+L+M)^c(n+L+M)c on a single uniform multitape Turing machine.

The time bound holds on every well-formed trace stream and every internal random-bit sequence. Success is at least 2/32/32/3 for every original binary string. In particular, for fixed positive ppp, both resources are quasipolynomial, with logarithm of order at most

Op ⁣((log⁡n)3(1+log⁡log⁡n)6).O_p\!\left((\log n)^3(1+\log\log n)^6\right).Op​((logn)3(1+loglogn)6).

For deletion probabilities q≤n−κq\le n^{-\kappa}q≤n−κ, with fixed κ>0\kappa>0κ>0, the stated bounds become polynomial in n+Ln+Ln+L.

A related sample theorem

M2 gives the corresponding quantitative sample scale through a latest-anchor induction with frequency-restricted masks. It also treats strings of general symbols when retained symbols are observed exactly. Its claim concerns sample complexity; it does not supply the efficient decoding guarantee of M1. Its comparisons with the earlier quasipolynomial result concern specified parameter choices, not every conceivable refinement of that earlier method.

A superpolynomial obstruction

M3 states that, at each fixed q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1)q∈(0,1), exact worst-case binary reconstruction requires

nΩ(log⁡log⁡n)n^{\Omega(\log\log n)}nΩ(loglogn)

traces, even with unrestricted computation and any fixed positive success probability. More quantitatively, when q3log⁡n→∞q^3\log n\to\inftyq3logn→∞, the lower bound is eventually nclog⁡(q3log⁡n)n^{c\log(q^3\log n)}nclog(q3logn) for every fixed 0<c<1/(4log⁡2)0<c<1/(4\log2)0<c<1/(4log2).

Thus polynomial reconstruction in the low-deletion regime and superpolynomial lower bounds at fixed deletion probability concern different parameter ranges. They do not conflict.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. Trace reconstruction is a central model for inference with missing positional information. The family combines a substantial algorithmic improvement with an information-theoretic barrier, and separates the cost of acquiring observations from the cost of interpreting them.

The lower bound would rule out an entire hoped-for complexity class of reconstruction procedures at fixed noise. The algorithm would show that recovering the information need not require searching through all 2n2^n2n candidate originals, even though the permitted sample count is still superpolynomial.

The implications are clearest for the mathematical model. DNA-related reconstruction and communication through synchronization errors help motivate it, but actual data can have substitutions, insertions, correlated errors, or nonidentical copying conditions. The stated theorems do not automatically handle these features. Their significance is a clearer boundary for a fundamental idealized problem, not an immediate prescription for a laboratory pipeline.

6. The main idea

Decode a prefix through feasible statistical descriptions

A naive decoder evaluates every candidate string. M1 instead extends a candidate prefix one bit at a time. For each possible next bit, it asks whether a collection of estimated trace statistics can be consistent with that prefix.

The consistency test uses moment matrices. If PPP is any polynomial in random variables, then E[P2]≥0\mathbb E[P^2]\ge0E[P2]≥0. Arranging moments in a matrix turns such conditions into positive semidefiniteness: every quadratic form built from the matrix must be nonnegative. These constraints summarize many potential completions without explicitly listing them.

The claimed separation theorem says that the wrong next bit cannot satisfy the required constraints when the trace statistics are accurate enough. The correct prefix has quantitative slack, allowing finite rational computations with a controlled stopping rule. This last point matters: an abstract feasibility formulation alone would not establish the advertised time bound.

The statistics involve a few trace positions at a time, but those positions can be widely separated. Analytic estimates pass information between scales and connect weighted position statistics to the deletion channel. M2 uses related multiscale information, organizing the comparison around a latest anchor and masks whose Fourier frequencies occupy a controlled range. In both treatments, retaining some long-distance information avoids the limitations of exclusively local measurements.

Hide alignment uncertainty repeatedly

M3 reverses the goal. It constructs pairs of originals whose differences become exceptionally difficult to locate. If two side segments can produce the same observations with substantial probability, an observer remains uncertain about the position of a central discrepancy.

The construction repeats this mechanism at several scales. Signed patterns in the central segment make contributions cancel after averaging over the hidden displacement. The Prouhet–Thue–Morse pattern supplies a familiar example of signs with strong cancellation properties, but the manuscript must control whole trace distributions, including correlations between nested pieces.

At each scale, either averaging suppresses a difference or the remaining term must contain many already-small differences from the previous scale. Iterating this alternative produces the stated superpolynomial indistinguishability. The intuition is repeated loss of location information, rather than an assumption that the decoder happens to inspect the wrong statistic.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

There is still a substantial gap. At a fixed channel, the lower-bound exponent is of order (log⁡n)(log⁡log⁡n)(\log n)(\log\log n)(logn)(loglogn), while the upper-bound exponent is of order (log⁡n)3(\log n)^3(logn)3, with additional iterated-logarithm factors. Determining the correct asymptotic scale remains open in these manuscripts.

The guarantees are worst-case and exact: every original must be recovered, not approximately reconstructed or recovered on average. Special classes of strings, random originals, and very small deletion probabilities can behave differently. A restricted-statistics lower bound also has a different meaning from M3’s unrestricted sample lower bound.

M1 includes finite-precision computation and uniform parameter handling, but offers no small practical constants. M2’s broader symbol setting should not be silently attached to every computational guarantee of M1. Likewise, the lower bound does not imply that ordinary real-world instances require the worst-case number of samples.

The claims here are reported from the manuscripts. The central remaining questions concern tight sample bounds, simpler efficient decoders, and the extent to which the methods survive changes to the noise model.

8. Sources and further reading

The primary historical links above distinguish sample bounds, efficient decoding, and restricted-statistics barriers. For a complementary regime, Chen and coauthors’ low-deletion reconstruction algorithm illustrates why the channel parameter belongs in the theorem statement. The three source manuscripts below respectively provide the algorithm, the anchor-based sample analysis, and the unrestricted lower bound.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Uniform quasipolynomial-time trace reconstruction (October 5, 2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, A latest-anchor induction with spectrally compact masks for worst-case trace reconstruction (October 5, 2026).
  • M3. OpenAI, Quantitative lower bounds for trace reconstruction (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Almost-linear expected-time approximation of edit distance
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 121 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

Edit distance measures how many insertions, deletions, and substitutions turn one string into another. Its familiar dynamic program examines a quadratic grid of possibilities. Family 121 claims that, for any fixed requested multiplicative accuracy, a randomized algorithm can estimate the distance in almost-linear expected time. The claim carefully distinguishes a numerical estimate from constructing an edit script and fixed accuracy from accuracy that changes with input length.

1. The question

The strings cat and cut differ by one substitution. Changing cat to cart requires one insertion. More complicated pairs may align only after several shifts, so comparing characters position by position can be misleading.

For long inputs, quadratic time can be expensive. Can we obtain an estimate as close to the true distance as desired while spending almost only the time needed to read the strings?

A constant-factor estimate might say the distance is between one hundred and a thousand. A (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon)(1+ε)-approximation with ε=0.01\varepsilon=0.01ε=0.01 narrows the allowed excess to one percent. Maintaining this precision while skipping most of the dynamic-programming grid is the main challenge.

The manuscript claims such an approximation for every fixed rational ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1)ε∈(0,1), on arbitrary explicitly stored input strings with unit edit costs.

2. Background and essential definitions

Edit operations and alignment paths

The unit-cost edit distance ED⁡(x,y)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)ED(x,y) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform xxx into yyy. Each operation costs one; matching equal symbols costs zero.

Let D(i,j)D(i,j)D(i,j) be the distance between the first iii symbols of xxx and first jjj symbols of yyy. The standard recurrence is

D(i,j)=min⁡ ⁣{D(i−1,j)+1, D(i,j−1)+1, D(i−1,j−1)+1xi≠yj}.D(i,j)=\min\!\left\{D(i-1,j)+1,\ D(i,j-1)+1,\ D(i-1,j-1)+\mathbf1_{x_i\ne y_j}\right\}.D(i,j)=min{D(i−1,j)+1, D(i,j−1)+1, D(i−1,j−1)+1xi​=yj​​}.

The indicator 1xi≠yj\mathbf1_{x_i\ne y_j}1xi​=yj​​ is one when the symbols differ and zero otherwise. Boundary values are D(i,0)=iD(i,0)=iD(i,0)=i and D(0,j)=jD(0,j)=jD(0,j)=j.

This can be viewed as a shortest path through a grid. Horizontal and vertical steps insert or delete a symbol; diagonal steps match or substitute. An alignment specifies such a path. The difference between its two coordinates is its current shift.

Approximation and zero distance

The claimed output is a nonnegative integer D^\widehat DD satisfying, with the stated probability,

ED⁡(x,y)≤D^≤(1+ε)ED⁡(x,y).\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\le\widehat D\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y).ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y).

This is a one-sided multiplicative estimate on successful runs. If the strings are equal, their distance is zero, and a multiplicative approximation must return zero too. The algorithm explicitly does so deterministically.

A distance estimate does not identify the individual edits achieving that distance. Producing such a script is a separate output requirement absent from the theorem.

Fixed accuracy and expected complexity

Write N=∣x∣+∣y∣N=|x|+|y|N=∣x∣+∣y∣. The time bound is N1+o(1)N^{1+o(1)}N1+o(1) as NNN grows, for each fixed rational ε\varepsilonε. The hidden constants and threshold may depend on ε\varepsilonε.

This does not promise polynomial dependence on 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε. In particular, one cannot substitute an accuracy such as ε=1/N\varepsilon=1/Nε=1/N and infer an almost-linear exact algorithm.

“Worst-case expected time” means the expectation is bounded for every input pair, with randomness only inside the algorithm. Individual random executions may take longer than the expectation bound.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Levenshtein’s work on errors in transmitted strings helped establish edit distance as a basic measure of sequence difference. Wagner and Fischer gave the standard quadratic dynamic program.

Masek and Paterson achieved a logarithmic speedup under their alphabet and cost assumptions. Distance-sensitive algorithms offered another route: Ukkonen and Landau and Vishkin exploited cases where the number of edits is small.

For unrestricted exact computation, Backurs and Indyk showed that a strongly subquadratic deterministic algorithm would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, a conjecture about satisfiability algorithms. This conditional barrier concerns exact answers and does not prohibit fixed-accuracy approximation.

Early fast approximations allowed factors growing with string length. Ostrovsky and Rabani developed low-distortion embeddings, while later hierarchical methods and precision sampling improved the tradeoff between runtime and approximation factor.

Chakraborty and collaborators reached constant-factor approximation in truly subquadratic time. Subsequent algorithms brought near-linear exponents first for sufficiently far input pairs and then, in Andoni and Nosatzki’s work cited by M1, for general pairs with a constant depending on the chosen runtime exponent.

For factors arbitrarily close to one, Mao and Rubinstein obtained a randomized approximation scheme with a substantial improvement over quadratic time. The present manuscript claims to combine that fixed near-one accuracy with an almost-linear expected exponent.

These earlier milestones solve different points on a two-parameter tradeoff. A fast algorithm with an unspecified large constant factor is not already an approximation scheme, and a near-one factor does not alone imply near-linear work.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

M1 states that one uniform randomized algorithm, given x,yx,yx,y and rational ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1)ε∈(0,1), returns an integer D^\widehat DD such that

Pr⁡[ED⁡(x,y)≤D^≤(1+ε)ED⁡(x,y)]≥23.\Pr[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\le\widehat D\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)]\ge\frac23.Pr[ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y)]≥32​.

For every fixed rational accuracy, its worst-case expected running time is N1+o(1)N^{1+o(1)}N1+o(1) on a logarithmic-word RAM.

The alphabet consists of integer labels of polynomially bounded magnitude in N+2N+2N+2, so each symbol fits in O(log⁡(N+2))O(\log(N+2))O(log(N+2)) bits. The number of distinct symbols need not be constant.

The bound includes reading the input, preprocessing, numerical work, random sampling, and data-structure operations. Equal strings return zero deterministically. The algorithm uses exact computation below an accuracy-dependent size threshold, which the paper describes as very large.

There is no claimed joint bound when accuracy varies with NNN, no polynomial dependence on inverse accuracy, and no requirement to reconstruct an edit script. These are material parts of the theorem’s scope.

5. Why the advance matters

Importance: 4/5, provisional. Edit distance is a central string problem with uses in sequence comparison, text processing, and algorithms for noisy data. A near-one approximation in almost-linear expected time would substantially improve the theoretical accuracy–time frontier.

The result would also sharpen our understanding of the gap between exact and approximate computation. Conditional barriers for exact edit distance could coexist with highly accurate fixed-factor estimates much closer to input-reading time.

The claim is not an immediate application benchmark. Its thresholds and dependence on accuracy may be prohibitive, and real sequence-analysis systems often use weighted substitutions or domain-specific alignment penalties outside the unit-cost model.

The score reflects the broad importance of the problem and the asymptotic tradeoff, while retaining those computational and modeling qualifications.

6. The main idea

Replace the full grid with a hierarchy of intervals

The first string is recursively split into intervals. A state pairs one source interval with a target interval in the second string. Its true cost is the edit distance between those substrings.

An action assigns target intervals to the source interval’s children. Their boundaries need not line up perfectly; explicit penalties account for gaps and overlaps. This flexibility lets the algorithm compare nearby candidate alignments without enumerating every exact grid path.

The starting estimates are coarse upper bounds. They are computed only when requested, although the successful accuracy event covers the entire possible state domain. That is needed because later requests depend on earlier random answers.

Predict narrow bands of plausible shifts

An optimal alignment’s shift changes as insertions and deletions accumulate. Preliminary cost estimates predict how that shift should evolve across an interval. The algorithm restricts attention to a narrow band around the predicted target positions.

The analysis compares these bands with an optimal alignment that is fixed for mathematical accounting, not computed by the algorithm. A cost-weighted measure of deviation telescopes across the interval hierarchy.

This shows that places where the prediction fails cannot consume too much total alignment cost. Elsewhere, the computed band contains a suitable comparison action or the difference in substring lengths already explains most of the cost.

Refine estimates using sampled comparisons

Within a band, a prediction rule balances candidate actions using an entropy regularization term. This is a method of avoiding excessive commitment to one option while learning from evaluated child costs.

Shared samples let nearby candidates reuse information. Bounds on cumulative excess relative to the comparison alignment control the error of each refinement pass. Repetitions and medians then turn these bounds into improved simultaneous upper estimates.

The manuscript handles possible intermediate underestimates explicitly, so an error in one subtree cannot cancel an unrelated overestimate and make the total analysis look artificially good.

Count the recursive work as carefully as the error

A numerically accurate recursion could still be quadratic if it evaluates too many child states. The algorithm therefore distinguishes operations that reuse stored values from those that request new values at the current refinement level.

Along a dependency path, a request either descends the interval tree or moves to an earlier refinement stage. Counting these possibilities bounds the expected number of actual evaluations. The same accounting includes finite optimization, exact random sampling, and rational arithmetic.

This joint control of alignment error and recursive query count is the route to the claimed almost-linear exponent.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The theorem estimates one supplied pair. It does not construct one common low-distortion embedding for all strings, so lower bounds for such embeddings address a different task.

Insertions, deletions, and substitutions all cost one. Arbitrary weighted or metric edit costs are outside this statement.

The guarantee is expected time with success probability at least two thirds, at fixed accuracy. Stronger bounds on every run, efficient dependence on changing accuracy, practical constants, and edit-script reconstruction are separate questions.

An asymptotic approximation scheme should therefore be read as an answer about what growth rates are possible, rather than a claim that a standard quadratic implementation can immediately be replaced for ordinary input sizes.

8. Sources and further reading

M1’s Theorem 1.1 and the following paragraph specify the fixed-accuracy and output conventions. Its introduction traces the approximation frontier, and its proof overview separates alignment prediction from the accounting needed to keep recursive work small.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, An Almost-Linear Approximation Scheme for Edit Distance (September 24, 2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Three-machine scheduling: exact optimization with precedence constraints
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 124 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Three identical machines must complete a collection of jobs. Every job takes one unit of time, but some jobs must finish before others can start. What is the shortest possible completion time?

The simplicity of the ingredients is deceptive. If there are no dependencies, divide the jobs into groups of three. If every job depends on the preceding one, execute them in a single chain. General dependency patterns sit between these extremes: a locally sensible choice can leave machines idle later, while postponing an available job can help another part of the schedule finish sooner.

The question is about exact optimization for arbitrary precedence constraints. It asks for the mathematically best schedule, not merely one whose duration is close to optimal. With two machines, classical polynomial algorithms are known. With an unrestricted number of machines supplied as input, the general problem is NP-complete. The fixed case of three machines has long occupied the gap between these two facts.

This manuscript claims a uniform deterministic polynomial-time solution for three machines. Its explicit polynomial has an enormous exponent, so the proposed resolution concerns computational complexity rather than practical scheduling speed.

2. Background and essential definitions

Represent the jobs by the vertices of a directed acyclic graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E). An edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) means that job uuu must finish before job vvv starts. Acyclicity excludes contradictory requirements such as a job indirectly preceding itself. Write n=∣V∣n=|V|n=∣V∣.

For a deadline TTT, a schedule assigns each job a slot:

τ:V⟶{1,…,T}.\tau:V\longrightarrow\{1,\ldots,T\}.τ:V⟶{1,…,T}.

It is feasible when no slot contains more than three jobs and

τ(u)<τ(v)for every (u,v)∈E.\tau(u)<\tau(v)\qquad\text{for every }(u,v)\in E.τ(u)<τ(v)for every (u,v)∈E.

Slot ttt corresponds to the interval [t−1,t)[t-1,t)[t−1,t). The makespan is the latest completion time. Jobs are nonpreemptive: once started, each occupies one machine for its entire unit of processing.

Two elementary lower bounds are the longest chain of dependent jobs and ⌈n/3⌉\lceil n/3\rceil⌈n/3⌉, the capacity bound. Neither alone describes the interactions among different branches of the precedence graph. The optimization problem must account for those interactions throughout the schedule.

An antichain is a set of mutually incomparable jobs: no job in the set precedes another through any directed path. Each slot is an antichain of size at most three. A linear extension is a total ordering of the jobs that respects every precedence relation. It supplies a consistent priority order, but simply placing jobs in that order need not produce an optimal schedule.

The manuscript assumes an explicitly listed finite graph. Input length includes the binary encoding of its vertices, edges, and any deadline. Polynomial time is measured in this full input length.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Fujii, Kasami, and Ninomiya studied optimal scheduling on two processors in the late 1960s. Coffman and Graham subsequently gave their influential optimal two-processor algorithm. These results established that unrestricted precedence constraints do not by themselves force intractability when the number of machines is two.

Ullman’s 1975 complexity results showed NP-completeness when the machine count is part of the input. This does not settle a fixed value such as three: a reduction may use an increasing number of machines. The fixed-three question consequently appeared among the open problems in Garey and Johnson’s classic book on NP-completeness.

Several restricted cases became tractable. Garey, Johnson, Tarjan, and Yannakakis obtained efficient algorithms for special precedence structures called opposing forests. Dolev and Warmuth gave a bound depending on the height of the precedence graph and the number of machines. When both are fixed, their bound is polynomial; arbitrary graphs can have height growing with the number of jobs. Their bounded-height work also developed structural normalization of schedules.

More recently, Nederlof, Swennenhuis, and Węgrzycki obtained a subexponential exact algorithm. For three machines, its time is of the form 2O(nlog⁡n)2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}2O(n​logn). This improves substantially on unrestricted exponential search, but remains above every fixed polynomial.

Approximation developed alongside exact algorithms. Levey and Rothvoß used linear-programming hierarchies, followed by quasipolynomial approximation schemes and simpler combinatorial approaches. A representative account is Das and Wiese’s scheduling scheme. These methods can approach the optimal makespan arbitrarily closely under fixed parameters. They do not automatically decide whether a particular integer deadline is achievable.

The new manuscript builds on the structural decomposition viewpoint: identify small boundaries in a schedule, then describe and combine the portions between them. Its claimed additional step is to keep every relevant subproblem describable with bounded information, regardless of recursion depth.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph of n≥1n\ge1n≥1 unit jobs, the manuscript states that a single deterministic algorithm constructs a minimum-makespan schedule on three identical machines. Given a deadline 1≤T≤n1\le T\le n1≤T≤n, it also decides feasibility exactly and returns a schedule when one exists.

If LLL denotes total binary input length, the stated multitape Turing-machine bound is

O ⁣((L+2)150020).O\!\left((L+2)^{150020}\right).O((L+2)150020).

The large exponent is part of the claim’s interpretation. It establishes a fixed polynomial independent of the input; it does not describe an algorithm suitable for current industrial instances. Both deciding feasibility and writing an optimal schedule are included.

No release dates, communication delays, machine eligibility rules, or additional resources are present. All processing times equal one. The machines are identical, and a job may run on any of them. The graph may otherwise contain arbitrary precedence constraints.

The use of integer slots is also justified within this model. Starting from any feasible real-time schedule, fix each machine’s job order. Add those order constraints to the precedence graph, then start each job as early as its predecessors permit. Because durations are integral, the resulting starts are integral and completion times do not increase. Thus restricting attention to slots does not lose a better schedule hidden at fractional starting times.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The claim resolves a longstanding exact-complexity question for a basic scheduling model. Three machines are the first fixed machine count beyond the classical two-machine theory, making this boundary especially informative.

The conceptual importance extends beyond whether one particular exponent is useful. A polynomial algorithm says that the enormous set of potential schedules has enough structure to admit a finite description of manageable asymptotic size. It identifies information that can be discarded while preserving the possibility of an optimal completion.

The contribution also illustrates the distinction between a classification theorem and an efficient implementation. A degree of 150020 is prohibitive, but replacing a superpolynomial search with a polynomial one can reveal a structural principle that later algorithms improve. Such improvements are prospects, not consequences already supplied by the manuscript.

The score reflects the central scheduling question and the proposed decomposition method. It does not imply that arbitrary scheduling problems become easy, or that the same method already handles four or more fixed machines.

6. The main idea

Fill empty capacity with harmless jobs

For a deadline TTT, first reject if n>3Tn>3Tn>3T. Otherwise add 3T−n3T-n3T−n isolated dummy jobs. They have no precedence constraints, so they can occupy unused capacity without obstructing real jobs.

A feasible schedule then consists of exactly TTT antichain triples. Deleting the dummy jobs recovers a schedule for the original instance. This conversion makes the combinatorial object more regular: every time slot has the same size.

Describe an interval by its relation to a few boundaries

Suppose selected slots divide a feasible schedule into intervals. If the set of jobs belonging to one interval is known, any feasible reordering of that set preserves its temporal relationship to all jobs outside the interval. This suggests dynamic programming: solve smaller intervals and concatenate compatible solutions.

The obstacle is identifying the interval’s job set. Naming the triples at its endpoints is not enough. Many jobs can be unrelated to those boundary jobs, and repeated subdivisions can accumulate an ever-longer record of earlier choices. Without additional structure, there could be exponentially many distinguishable subproblems.

The manuscript claims that a suitably normalized feasible schedule admits global descriptions of bounded size. The descriptions use simple tests: whether a job precedes or follows a member of a selected triple, whether it belongs to the triple, and whether it lies before a cutoff in a fixed linear extension. Boolean combinations of these tests specify a subset of all jobs.

“Global” matters here. A formula must identify the intended jobs throughout the original instance, not merely behave correctly inside an interval whose membership is already assumed known. Otherwise hidden information about the ancestors of the interval would remain necessary.

Prevent descriptions from growing with recursion

The structural argument moves separators through a schedule while adjusting a priority cutoff. It also treats the two sides of a central slot by reversing time and precedence. Short lists of upward-closed sets carry the information needed at a boundary: if a job belongs to such a set, its successors in the current direction belong as well.

According to the manuscript, exchange conditions and boundary conditions allow obsolete information to be removed. When the direction changes, a paired representation prevents the previous history from expanding the description indefinitely. The final description has a fixed upper bound on its number of logical tests.

The algorithm enumerates all descriptions within a fixed allowance, evaluates the corresponding job sets, and solves them in increasing size. Compatible accepted pieces provide a larger schedule; predecessor records recover an explicit solution. The allowance is extremely generous, producing the huge polynomial exponent, but remains independent of nnn.

One subtlety is that normalized schedules are used as existence witnesses. The algorithm does not first compute an optimal schedule in order to normalize it. It searches the finite family of descriptions, while the structural theorem claims that some successful decomposition must occur in that family whenever the deadline is feasible.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The result is exact and deterministic in the stated encoding, but its running time is theoretical. Reducing the description family, the exponent, or the overhead of searching it would be necessary before practical relevance could be assessed.

The assumptions are substantial. Different job lengths change which exchanges preserve feasibility. Release dates and communication delays can couple an interval to its surroundings. Machine-dependent processing or eligibility rules destroy the symmetry among the three slots available at a time. None of those variants follows from this theorem.

The claim also does not establish a polynomial algorithm for every fixed machine count. The structural bounds exploit triples and the way three-machine boundaries limit inherited information. Extending them would require additional arguments.

Finally, approximation and exact optimization answer different questions. Earlier approximation schemes remain meaningful even if their assumptions overlap, particularly when their computational costs are more reasonable. This manuscript’s stated advance is a complexity classification and an explicit exact construction, reported here without independent proof verification.

8. Sources and further reading

The historical papers linked above trace the progression from two-processor algorithms through restricted precedence classes, approximation schemes, and subexponential exact search. The source manuscript below provides the precise input model, bounded-description theorem, and explicit polynomial-time accounting. Its introduction distinguishes these earlier advances from the claimed fixed-three resolution.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Three-Machine Unit-Job Scheduling (2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Metric k-median: approaching the sharp approximation threshold
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 125 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

A city wants to open at most kkk service centers. Residents use their nearest open center, and the objective is to minimize the total travel distance. Candidate sites are fixed in advance. How close can an efficient algorithm come to the best possible placement?

This is metric kkk-median, a basic clustering and facility-location problem. The word “metric” means that distances satisfy the triangle inequality; the locations need not lie in a Euclidean plane. The model includes networks and many other finite distance spaces.

Exact optimization is computationally difficult, so the central question asks for an approximation guarantee. If the optimum cost is OPT\mathrm{OPT}OPT, an α\alphaα-approximation always returns cost at most αOPT\alpha\mathrm{OPT}αOPT. A smaller factor is better.

Opening a few extra facilities can greatly simplify the problem. The real challenge is obtaining a good cost while respecting the budget of kkk on every output. This family contains two approaches to that challenge. Its strongest claim reaches every fixed factor above 1+2/e1+2/e1+2/e, approximately 1.736, matching the known hardness boundary in the specified candidate-facility model.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let JJJ be the finite client set, FFF the finite set of allowed facilities, and ddd the metric on their locations. The two sets are specified separately; the problem does not require F=JF=JF=J. For a nonempty chosen set S⊆FS\subseteq FS⊆F, define

d(j,S)=min⁡i∈Sd(j,i),cost⁡(S)=∑j∈Jd(j,S).d(j,S)=\min_{i\in S}d(j,i),\qquad\operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{j\in J}d(j,S).d(j,S)=i∈Smin​d(j,i),cost(S)=j∈J∑​d(j,S).

The optimum is the minimum of this cost over 1≤∣S∣≤k1\le |S|\le k1≤∣S∣≤k. Distances are rational numbers encoded in binary, so their precision contributes to input size. Empty client sets can be handled immediately with cost zero.

A fractional relaxation allows a facility to be partly open. Let yi∈[0,1]y_i\in[0,1]yi​∈[0,1] describe its opening amount, and let xijx_{ij}xij​ be the fraction of client jjj‘s assignment sent there. Standard constraints are

∑ixij=1,xij≤yi,∑iyi≤k.\sum_i x_{ij}=1,\qquad x_{ij}\le y_i,\qquad \sum_i y_i\le k.i∑​xij​=1,xij​≤yi​,i∑​yi​≤k.

The objective is ∑i,jd(j,i)xij\sum_{i,j}d(j,i)x_{ij}∑i,j​d(j,i)xij​. Every actual solution gives a feasible fractional solution, so the fractional optimum is a lower bound on the true optimum. Rounding means converting fractional openings into actual facilities while controlling the cost increase.

Assignment fractions do not impose service capacities: one open facility can serve many clients. This distinction matters when several clients share the same fractional supplier.

A pseudo-approximation permits a constant additive number of extra facilities, returning at most k+ck+ck+c. It is an intermediate tool, not a feasible answer to the original budget-constrained problem. The manuscripts must eventually remove those extra facilities.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Metric kkk-median helped shape several central techniques in approximation algorithms. Charikar, Guha, Tardos, and Shmoys obtained a constant-factor guarantee through linear-programming rounding. Jain and Vazirani connected the problem with facility location through opening prices and primal-dual methods. Bounded-swap local search supplied a different route, with the classical 3+ε3+\varepsilon3+ε guarantee of Arya and coauthors.

An opening price penalizes each facility, but a price constraint is not the same as an exact cardinality constraint. Li and Svensson’s pseudo-approximation reduction made this gap more manageable: a constant additive surplus can be removed at an arbitrarily small extra approximation loss, with an accuracy-dependent computational overhead.

Subsequent rounding improvements brought the factor through values above two. Cohen-Addad and coauthors reached 2+ε2+\varepsilon2+ε, announced in 2025, through a construction combining a logarithmic surplus of facilities with recovery arguments. Their full manuscript is a direct predecessor of M1. A later iterative graph-rounding framework is the main structural predecessor of M2.

On the hardness side, maximum-coverage gaps yield the threshold 1+2/e1+2/e1+2/e for the general candidate-facility model. The distinction between separately specified facilities and the restriction F=JF=JF=J is discussed by Anand and Lee. M2 uses that existing hardness result to interpret its algorithmic claim as a threshold theorem; it does not present a new hardness reduction as the principal advance.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

A deterministic algorithm near the hardness boundary

M2 states that, for every fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a set S⊆FS\subseteq FS⊆F satisfying

∣S∣≤k,cost⁡(S)≤(1+2e+ε)OPT.|S|\le k,\qquad\operatorname{cost}(S)\le\left(1+\frac2e+\varepsilon\right)\mathrm{OPT}.∣S∣≤k,cost(S)≤(1+e2​+ε)OPT.

Polynomial time refers to the full binary encoding length of the finite rational metric. The polynomial may depend on ε\varepsilonε. This is not a claim of a single running-time bound polynomial jointly in input size and 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε.

Combined with the known hardness under P≠NP\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}P=NP, the claim makes 1+2/e1+2/e1+2/e the infimum of deterministic polynomial-time approximation factors in this model. An infimum need not be attained: algorithms for every factor strictly above the boundary do not automatically give an algorithm at the boundary itself.

Recovery from a nearly adequate anchor

M1 develops a different tool. An anchor is an already supplied facility set of the required size. Imagine an unknown comparison solution whose client clusters mostly have accurate, distinct representatives in that anchor. A small exceptional set of clusters lacks such representatives.

Under a precise total proxy-error promise, positive integral distances of polynomially bounded diameter, and at most L0log⁡NL_0\log NL0​logN exceptional clusters, M1 claims recovery with factor 1+2/e+ε1+2/e+\varepsilon1+2/e+ε in polynomial time. Here N=∣J∣+∣F∣N=|J|+|F|N=∣J∣+∣F∣, and the accuracy parameters and L0L_0L0​ are fixed. The algorithm is given the anchor, but not the comparison solution, the good/bad partition, or its proxy map.

The dependence on the number of exceptional clusters is single-exponential, which makes logarithmically many exceptions affordable. The promise does not require the anchor itself to be locally optimal.

M1 also combines recovery with payment accounting to claim an independent randomized (2−σ)(2-\sigma)(2−σ)-approximation for an absolute σ>0\sigma>0σ>0 on arbitrary finite rational metrics. It respects kkk on every output and gives both high-probability and expected-cost guarantees. This general-metric consequence has a weaker factor than M2, but arises from a different argument.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The strongest claim closes a major approximation gap for a foundational clustering problem. Matching an algorithmic upper bound to a conditional hardness boundary identifies how much loss efficient computation must tolerate, up to the endpoint issue.

The exact facility budget makes the result more substantial than a cost guarantee obtained by opening extra centers. In applications, a cardinality constraint can represent a genuine limit on facilities, equipment, or representatives. The mathematical theorem treats that constraint directly in its final output.

The companion recovery result also isolates a potentially useful principle: an anchor may be enough when only a few comparison clusters are poorly represented. Its running-time dependence distinguishes a truly single-exponential parameter cost from bounds such as kO(k)k^{O(k)}kO(k), which need not become polynomial when kkk grows logarithmically.

The rating concerns theoretical significance. Neither manuscript establishes small constants or competitive performance on practical clustering datasets, and the threshold should not be transferred without qualification to Euclidean metrics or other restricted models.

6. The main idea

Round while retaining useful assignments

M2 begins with the fractional solution and places opening amounts on a fixed grid. The grid spacing depends on accuracy but not on the number of clients or the metric’s bit length. Nearby representative clients define bundles of opening mass; deficits are rounded together with the facilities that supply them.

An iterative directed graph then coordinates openings and erasures of fractional copies. Opening one facility can remove several competing copies, gradually turning fractional mass into actual choices. The analysis balances these actions so that the final number of openings exceeds kkk by only an accuracy-dependent constant.

The cost argument tracks more than the first facility that becomes available to a client. Some cheaper surviving assignments remain useful even after an opening. A potential function records both their remaining cost and a bound on the client’s eventual connection distance. Keeping this information creates a compensating decrease that pays for harmful erasures elsewhere.

This is the claimed source of the improvement below two within the graph framework. A directed comparison inequality controls the average change of the potential. Cases in which one opening erases many copies require separate treatment before averaging, because the decision to force an opening depends on the realized graph.

The analysis initially uses randomness. M2 then replaces local choice distributions by polynomial-size rational distributions preserving the moments actually used in the estimates. Since the number of rounds depends only on accuracy, it can enumerate the relevant histories and choose the best eligible outcome. Finally, the Li–Svensson reduction removes the constant additive surplus. Both derandomization and budget repair are necessary parts of the final theorem.

Repair an anchor without losing the budget

M1 samples clients in proportion to how poorly the current reference facilities serve them. It alternates guesses about missing cluster locations with removals of existing facilities. Temporary leaf copies organize possible replacements without pretending those copies are legitimate final sites.

A favorable sequence of sampling decisions identifies enough of the exceptional structure. The manuscript charges difficult radius guesses to disjoint client groups, limiting the total probability loss to an exponential in the exceptional count. A subset dynamic program handles some replacement choices; a submodular savings problem handles the others. Submodularity means that the marginal benefit of an extra choice decreases as more choices have already been made.

The completion step removes as many original facilities as it adds replacements. Separately, payment inequalities retain enough budget to pay for every opening while improving connection costs. The manuscript attributes bounded-price strictness to earlier work; its contribution here is a self-contained argument compatible with the particular execution and its recovery procedure.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The threshold is for arbitrary finite rational metrics with a separately specified candidate set. Restricting candidate centers to the clients changes the hardness question. Specialized geometric metrics may allow stronger guarantees and require separate analysis.

M1’s refined recovery theorem has a normalized integral-distance promise. The paper does not assert that an arbitrary promised anchor keeps that promise after capping and rounding distances. Its general-metric application constructs and analyzes anchors after normalization, then transfers the final result back.

M2’s approximation factors approach 1+2/e1+2/e1+2/e but do not claim the exact endpoint. The constants, grid sizes, and number of rounds can depend heavily on accuracy. Practical implementation and a favorable dependence on ε\varepsilonε remain separate issues.

Finally, the intermediate comparison with the fractional objective includes extra facilities. It should not be read as a direct exact-budget rounding theorem with the same bound for the original relaxation. The surplus-removal reduction is part of the stated route to the final guarantee.

8. Sources and further reading

The linked historical papers explain fractional rounding, local search, pseudo-approximations, and the model-dependent hardness boundary. M1 below supplies the anchor recovery and payment approach; M2 supplies the deterministic threshold claim. They belong to one family but provide distinct algorithms and should not be merged into an unstated common guarantee.

Source manuscripts

  • M1. OpenAI, Single-exponential recovery and bounded-price strictness for metric k-median (2026).
  • M2. OpenAI, The approximation threshold for metric k-median (2026).

Sources consulted on 9 October 2026 at repository revision fd4aeeb. Download the manuscript citations.

entry.title: Perfect matching: why exact semidefinite descriptions must be large
entry.content:
← All digests

Family 126 · Theoretical computer science
Importance 4/5 · Provisional editorial rating
Sources consulted 2026-10-09

1. The question

Some optimization problems are easy to solve but difficult to describe compactly in a particular mathematical language. Perfect matching is a striking example. A perfect matching pairs every vertex of a graph with exactly one other vertex, using permitted edges. Efficient algorithms can optimize edge weights over such pairings.

One might therefore hope to express all perfect matchings through a small system of convex constraints, then use a general optimization solver. Linear descriptions are already known to require exponential size, even when auxiliary variables are allowed. Semidefinite constraints are more expressive: they require a symmetric matrix to have no negative eigenvalues and can compress some structures that linear inequalities describe poorly.

Does that extra expressive power make a compact exact description of perfect matching possible? This manuscript claims an exponential lower bound even for unrestricted real semidefinite formulations. It strengthens the statement by treating a family of positively shifted matching matrices, where the entries that were originally zero become positive.

The distinction between solving and representing is central. The claim does not make matching computationally intractable. It limits one general-purpose way of encoding its entire feasible region.

2. Background and essential definitions

Let KnK_nKn​ be the complete graph on an even number nnn of vertices. A perfect matching MMM contains n/2n/2n/2 disjoint edges. Its incidence vector 1M\mathbf1_M1M​ has one coordinate per edge, equal to one when that edge belongs to MMM, and zero otherwise.

The perfect matching polytope is

Pn=conv⁡{1M:M is a perfect matching of Kn}.P_n=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }K_n\}.Pn​=conv{1M​:M is a perfect matching of Kn​}.

Here conv⁡\operatorname{conv}conv means all convex combinations. Points in the polytope can be interpreted as averages of perfect matchings, and optimizing a linear edge-weight objective over it gives the same optimum as optimizing over individual matchings.

For a vertex set UUU, let δ(U)\delta(U)δ(U) be the edges with exactly one endpoint in UUU. If ∣U∣|U|∣U∣ is odd, any perfect matching crosses this cut an odd positive number of times. Thus

∣M∩δ(U)∣≥1.|M\cap\delta(U)|\ge1.∣M∩δ(U)∣≥1.

The difference ∣M∩δ(U)∣−1|M\cap\delta(U)|-1∣M∩δ(U)∣−1 is the slack of this inequality at MMM: the amount by which the inequality exceeds equality.

A real symmetric matrix AAA is positive semidefinite, abbreviated PSD, if vTAv≥0v^{\mathsf T}Av\ge0vTAv≥0 for every real vector vvv. A semidefinite lift represents a polytope as an affine image of an affine slice of the cone of PSD matrices. Auxiliary coordinates are allowed; the lift’s size is the matrix dimension.

For a nonnegative matrix SSS, its PSD rank is the least rrr for which PSD matrices Fu,GvF_u,G_vFu​,Gv​ of size rrr satisfy

Su,v=tr⁡(FuGv)S_{u,v}=\operatorname{tr}(F_uG_v)Su,v​=tr(Fu​Gv​)

for every row and column. The trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A general factorization theorem connects PSD rank of slack matrices to the smallest semidefinite lift.

3. Development history and previous partial results

Edmonds’s 1965 description established the role of degree equations, nonnegative edge coordinates, and odd-cut inequalities in the matching polytope. There are exponentially many odd vertex sets, but that alone does not prove that every possible formulation must be large: extra variables can sometimes replace many inequalities by a much smaller system.

Yannakakis developed the factorization approach to this question and proved strong lower bounds for symmetric linear formulations. Symmetry restrictions require the representation to respect relabeling of the original problem in a specified way. Rothvoß later removed that restriction and proved exponential linear extension complexity for matching.

Semidefinite lifts remained a separate issue. Gouveia, Parrilo, and Thomas established the cone-factorization framework, while Lee, Raghavendra, and Steurer developed general lower-bound methods connecting semidefinite formulations to sums of squares and low-degree obstructions.

For matching specifically, Braun and collaborators proved that there is no small coordinate-symmetric semidefinite formulation. That is not the same as excluding arbitrary formulations: a small representation might encode vertices in an asymmetric way. Braun and Pokutta also proved exponential nonnegative rank for the positively shifted matching matrices considered here, a result about scalar nonnegative factorizations rather than PSD factors.

A further boundary comes from approximation. Kaniewski, Lee, and de Wolf constructed matrices of subexponential PSD rank that approximate unshifted matching slacks with extremely small entrywise error. Their query-complexity paper therefore makes exactness especially important. An exact lower bound cannot simply be described as an equally strong barrier to every numerical approximation.

4. What the new manuscripts claim

For every fixed real ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1)ρ∈(0,1), form the matrix indexed by odd vertex sets UUU and perfect matchings MMM:

An(ρ)U,M=∣M∩δ(U)∣−1+ρ.A_n(\rho)_{U,M}=|M\cap\delta(U)|-1+\rho.An​(ρ)U,M​=∣M∩δ(U)∣−1+ρ.

The manuscript states that there is an absolute c>0c>0c>0 such that, for all sufficiently large even nnn,

rank⁡psdAn(ρ)≥2cn.\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{psd}}A_n(\rho)\ge2^{cn}.rankpsd​An​(ρ)≥2cn.

The threshold for “sufficiently large” may depend on ρ\rhoρ, but the exponential rate ccc does not. The factors are arbitrary real PSD matrices: there is no imposed symmetry, sparsity, coordinate action, or bound on numerical precision. They must reproduce every entry exactly.

The statement implies an exponential lower bound for the unshifted matrix An(0)A_n(0)An​(0). Indeed, adding one scalar block to an unshifted factorization can supply the constant ρ\rhoρ, increasing its size by at most one. If the shifted matrix requires exponential size, the original does too.

Adding the nonnegativity rows gives a slack matrix for the full matching polytope. The manuscript consequently claims that every exact real semidefinite lift of PnP_nPn​ has exponential size.

The endpoint ρ=1\rho=1ρ=1 is deliberately excluded. At that value, the entries are simply ∣M∩δ(U)∣|M\cap\delta(U)|∣M∩δ(U)∣, which have a diagonal PSD factorization indexed by the (n2)\binom n2(2n​) edges. Thus the transition at the endpoint is substantial: every fixed shift below one is claimed to require exponential size, while one itself permits polynomial size.

5. Why the advance matters

Provisional importance: 4/5. The claim would establish a strong limitation on unrestricted semidefinite representations of a central combinatorial polytope. It extends the separation between efficient optimization and concise convex formulation from linear programming to a more expressive framework.

The absence of symmetry assumptions is important. A representation lower bound is stronger when it allows all possible ways of choosing auxiliary coordinates, including ones with no visible relationship to the graph’s labels. The positive-shift theorem also shows that the proposed obstruction is not merely a count of exact zeros in the ordinary slack matrix.

The result would inform the limits of generic optimization formulations, rather than invalidate specialized matching algorithms. It also adds to the broader study of when positivity can be certified with low-complexity algebraic expressions. The methods may be useful elsewhere, but such extensions require separate arguments.

The score reflects the generality of the representation barrier. It does not imply a matching lower bound for every approximate relaxation or every algorithm that happens to use semidefinite programming as one component.

6. The main idea

Start with a globally inconsistent parity pattern

The proof strategy begins on an auxiliary expanding graph. Each incidence between a vertex and an edge receives a bit. At each vertex, the bits must have a prescribed parity, meaning a specified sum modulo two. Choose these parity requirements so that their total is odd.

If the two incidence bits on every edge agreed, summing the vertex constraints would count each edge bit twice, producing an even total. Therefore at least one edge must disagree. Subtracting 1−ρ1-\rho1−ρ from the number of disagreements gives a function that is positive on every legitimate assignment.

Local information can nevertheless fail to detect this global contradiction. The manuscript constructs a linear functional that behaves nonnegatively on squares of sufficiently low-complexity functions, yet assigns a negative value to this particular positive function. Such a functional is a certificate that the function cannot have the required low-degree sum-of-squares representation.

Encode the obstruction inside matching

Each auxiliary vertex is replaced by a cell containing a fixed number of matching vertices. Designated terminals represent incidences; the remaining vertices are paired internally. Restrictions on cuts make the internal pairs contribute no crossing edges. The crossing count then records precisely the disagreements in the parity construction.

This places the algebraic obstruction inside the shifted matching matrix. The remaining challenge is to show that a small PSD factorization would yield a low-complexity sum-of-squares representation of the obstructed function.

Average without discarding matrix information

PSD matrices admit square-root factorizations, suggesting a connection with sums of squares. But averaging squares is not the same as squaring averages. Replacing one by the other would lose essential information.

The manuscript instead builds an exact decomposition into several matrix-valued branches. Fourier characters on the incidence bits organize each branch by the vertex blocks it involves. Local averaging within cells makes high-complexity contributions small, with bounds that do not grow with the PSD matrix dimension.

A product-averaging theorem then concentrates each branch near a suitable Fourier character. Multiplying by that character shifts its retained terms to low degree while preserving their squares. After controlling the discarded contribution, the purported small factorization would contradict the separating functional.

The conceptual chain is therefore: a small exact PSD representation would force a low-complexity positivity certificate; a parity obstruction rules out that certificate; and a matching construction transfers the obstruction to the desired matrix. This is a description of the manuscript’s route, not an independent verification of its estimates.

7. Scope, limitations, and open questions

The lower bound concerns exact factorizations over the reals and exact semidefinite lifts. It does not impose a finite-precision restriction, which strengthens that exact statement. At the same time, it does not automatically prohibit approximate matrices with small entrywise error or relaxations whose optimization values are only approximately correct.

The shift ρ\rhoρ is fixed before nnn tends to infinity. The allowed threshold depends on it, so the theorem should not be used without further analysis for a sequence ρn\rho_nρn​ approaching one rapidly. The explicit polynomial-size factorization at one explains why this quantifier matters.

The underlying graph for the stated family is the complete graph of even order. Restricted graph classes can have much simpler matching polytopes. The theorem does not say that every individual matching instance requires an exponential formulation.

Natural further questions concern which approximations evade the obstruction, how the transition near ρ=1\rho=1ρ=1 behaves quantitatively, and whether the averaging tools yield lower bounds for other polytopes. Specialized polynomial-time matching remains entirely compatible with the claim.

8. Sources and further reading

Edmonds provides the polyhedral starting point; Rothvoß gives the unrestricted linear lower bound; Gouveia–Parrilo–Thomas explain the factorization correspondence. The linked symmetric-SDP and approximate-slack papers clarify the two principal distinctions in the new claim.
